title: Meet the First Dinosaurs
text: This rocky "Valley of the Moon" holds some of the most primitive dinosaurs ever found, like Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus. Back then dinosaurs were rare newcomers: only about 6 percent of the fossil land animals here are dinosaurs. Beaked reptiles called rhynchosaurs and cynodonts, relatives of mammals, were far more common.

source.name: University of California Museum of Paleontology

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory

title: The Plateosaurus Mud Trap
text: Around 80 skeletons of Plateosaurus, long-necked plant-eaters 5 to 8 meters long, have been dug up here. Some seem to have died of exhaustion struggling against sticky mud. It is a unique mass grave of early giant plant-eaters. Back then this spot was a clay mud plain in a mostly hot, dry climate.

source.name: State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart

title: A Pile of Speedy Dinosaurs
text: A huge "graveyard" of Coelophysis, a skinny meat-eater up to almost 3 meters long, was discovered here in 1947. Researchers think a flash flood buried the animals together. One skull even flew to space aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1998!

source.name: New Mexico Secretary of State: State Fossil

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: Our Tiny Furry Cousins
text: Morganucodon was a tiny, furry, shrew-like animal, less than 10 cm long, and one of the earliest relatives of mammals. Thousands of its little teeth and jaws come from a single rock-fissure site in South Wales. It was an insect-eater that fed mainly on beetles.

source.name: University of Bristol, Palaeobiology (Bristol Dinosaur Project)

source2.name: Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales, 'Meet Morgie'

title: The Lava That Split a Supercontinent
text: As Pangaea began to rip apart, enormous floods of lava poured out along the crack that would become the Atlantic Ocean. The tall cliffs across the river from New York City are cooled magma from this time. The eruptions helped cause a mass extinction that cleared the way for dinosaurs to take over.

source.name: Columbia Climate School / Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory

title: China's Famous Long-Neck
text: Lufengosaurus was a plant-eater about 6 meters long, named in 1941 by Chinese fossil pioneer Yang Zhongjian. In 2017, scientists reported traces of collagen protein inside one of its 195-million-year-old ribs. That is over 100 million years older than any protein found in a fossil before!

source.name: Nature Communications (Lee et al. 2017), via PubMed Central

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: The Oldest Dinosaur Nests
text: Scientists found clutches of Massospondylus eggs here, some with tiny embryos still curled up inside. Rows of nests at different levels show mothers came back to the same spot again and again. It's one of the oldest dinosaur nesting sites known.

source.name: University of Toronto News (Reisz et al., PNAS 2012)

title: A Crested Dinosaur in Antarctica
text: Cryolophosaurus, the "frozen crested lizard", was a big meat-eater about 8 meters long with a bony crest on its head; its discoverer compared the crest to Elvis Presley's hair. Its bones were found in 1990-91 on Mount Kirkpatrick in the Transantarctic Mountains. Back then Antarctica was a lush land with trees, giant amphibians and dinosaurs.

source.name: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County

source2.name: US Antarctic Program

title: Footprints by an Ice Age Lake
text: Human footprints were found here on the shore of an Ice Age lake, alongside tracks of giant ground sloths and dire wolves. Seeds above and below them date the prints to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, much older than many scientists expected for people in the Americas. Most were made by children and teenagers.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, White Sands National Park: Fossilized Footprints

title: The World's Oldest Pottery
text: Broken bits of clay pots found in this cave are about 20,000 years old, the oldest pottery known anywhere. That's around 10,000 years before people here started farming! Hunter-gatherers may have used the pots to cook food during the coldest part of the Ice Age.

source.name: Science (Wu et al. 2012), abstract via Europe PMC

source2.name: Science News

title: A Bone That Might Count
text: This small bone, nearly 20,000 years old, has groups of notches carved along it, like tally marks. Notches like these are often read as count marks, and some researchers think they were used to add or multiply. Nobody is sure, but people living by Lake Edward seem to have been keeping track of something.

source.name: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

source2.name: Smithsonian Human Origins Program

title: The Land Bridge Between Continents
text: So much water was locked up in ice sheets that the sea dropped by up to 300 feet (about 90 meters). Asia and North America were joined by a broad, treeless plain called Beringia, stretching more than 1,000 miles (1,600 km) from north to south. Mammoths, horses, and eventually people crossed it.

source.name: US National Park Service (Beringia)

source2.name: US National Park Service (Bering Land Bridge National Preserve)

title: The Lost Land Under the North Sea
text: Britain wasn't an island: it was joined to mainland Europe by a low land now called Doggerland, which reached towards today's Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. Fishermen still find ancient bones and tools on the seabed. Rising seas slowly swallowed it, and a giant tsunami about 8,150 years ago hit what was left.

source.name: National Geographic Education

source2.name: PNAS (Allaby et al. 2026), via PubMed Central

title: The Painted Cave
text: Ice Age artists painted and engraved hundreds of animals on these cave walls, mostly horses, along with stags and huge bulls, using mineral pigments. The cave was found again on 12 September 1940 by four teenagers aged 15 to 17 near the village of Montignac. Today the fragile original is closed, and visitors tour exact copies instead.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture, Lascaux

source2.name: Bradshaw Foundation

title: Japan's First Potters
text: Broken pots found at this site are the earliest known pottery in Northeast Asia, and among the oldest in the world. These first pots were plain, without the rope patterns of later Jōmon ware. Burnt food stuck to the shards shows they were used for cooking. The Jōmon period lasted more than 10,000 years.

source.name: Jomon Japan (official site, Jomon Prehistoric Sites World Heritage)

source2.name: Government of Japan, Kizuna

title: Houses Made of Mammoth Bones
text: On the cold steppe of Ice Age Ukraine, hunters built four round dwellings out of mammoth bones, each several meters across. One of them used the bones of at least 37 mammoths, mostly gathered from animals that had already died. New dating shows people lived here about 18,000 years ago.

source.name: Open Research Europe (Chu et al. 2025), via PubMed Central

source2.name: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies)

title: Campers at the End of the World
text: People built a long tent-like shelter here, cooked over fires, and even gathered seaweed from distant beaches for food and medicine. A layer of peat sealed the camp and kept wood, plants, and even human footprints from rotting. It showed humans reached the far south of the Americas surprisingly early.

source.name: Science (Dillehay et al. 2008), abstract via Europe PMC

source2.name: PLOS ONE (Dillehay et al. 2015), via PubMed Central

title: When Australia Was Bigger
text: Australia, New Guinea, and Tasmania were one big continent that scientists call Sahul. People could walk to Tasmania across land that's now a stormy sea. Aboriginal Australians had already lived here for tens of thousands of years, and some of their stories may remember the seas rising.

source.name: The Conversation (Bird, Cooper, Turney, Curnoe, Russell and Ulm; ARC Centre of Excellence CABAH)

source2.name: The Conversation (Reid and Nunn, Univ. of New England / Univ. of the Sunshine Coast)

dateLabel: About 9500 BCE, as the Ice Age ended
title: A Temple Older Than Farming
text: Hunter-gatherers carved huge T-shaped stone pillars here, some over 5 meters tall, decorated with foxes, snakes, and vultures. It was built more than 6,000 years before Stonehenge. Nobody knows exactly how they organized such a big project without farms or cities.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine

title: The Envoy Who Opened the Way West
text: In 138 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent an officer named Zhang Qian west to make allies of the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. He was captured and held for about ten years, escaped, and finally came home 13 years later with amazing reports about Central Asia. His journey opened the way for envoys between Han China and Central Asia, and brought grapes and alfalfa to China.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington: Selections from the Han Narrative Histories (Shiji ch. 123, Hirth translation)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zhang Qian' (read in browser)

title: Han Armies Reach Korea
text: In 108 BCE Emperor Wu's Han armies overthrew Gojoseon, Korea's first known kingdom, and replaced it with four Chinese colonies called commanderies. The most successful, Lelang, ruled from Pyongyang, became the centre of Chinese culture in Korea. The other three were abandoned within about 30 years, and in 313 CE the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo conquered Lelang too.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nangnang' (Lelang)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Korea' (The use of metals and the emergence of tribal states)

title: The Ancient Computer
text: Sponge divers exploring a shipwreck in 1901 pulled up a shoebox-sized lump of bronze gears. It turned out to be a hand-cranked machine that predicted eclipses and tracked the Sun, Moon, and planets. Nothing this complicated shows up again for over 1,000 years.

source.name: Scientific Reports via PubMed Central, Freeth et al. 2021, 'A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism'

source2.name: Scientific American

title: Beware the Ides of March
text: Julius Caesar was stabbed by a group of senators who feared he wanted to rule like a king. It happened in a meeting hall next to the Theatre of Pompey, whose ruins are now home to a shelter for stray cats. Instead of saving the Republic, his death led to Rome's first emperor, Augustus.

source.name: National Geographic History, 'Inside the conspiracy to kill Julius Caesar'

source2.name: Discover Magazine, Sean Mowbray, 'Cats Today Find Safety Where Julius Caesar Was Stabbed'

title: Cleopatra's Alexandria
text: Cleopatra VII, the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, spoke many languages and was the first in her Greek-speaking family to learn Egyptian. Her city had a giant lighthouse and a famous library. Fun fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid!

source.name: National Geographic, 'Key facts about Cleopatra's life and legacy'

source2.name: American Research Center in Egypt (ARCE), 'Cleopatra VII: Scholar, Patron, Queen'

title: Land of the Pyramid Queens
text: The Kingdom of Kush built about 200 steep pyramids around its capital, Meroë, and Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt. Powerful queens called kandakes sometimes ruled on their own. Kush was also an iron-making center, and heaps of leftover iron slag still lie near the city.

source.name: National Geographic History, 'The Nubian kingdom of Kush, rival to Egypt'

source2.name: The Conversation (university researcher), 'the forgotten queens of ancient Nubia'

title: The Rose-Red City
text: The Nabataeans carved tombs and temples right into pink sandstone cliffs and grew rich from the incense trade. They were water geniuses, building dams and channels to survive in the desert. The famous "Treasury" building was carved a little later, around the 1st century CE.

source.name: National Geographic History, 'Ancient Petra, Jordan's Lost Oasis'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / ICOMOS, Petra

title: Stone Stories at Sanchi
text: Four stone gateways covered in carvings of the Buddha's life were added to the Great Stupa, first built by Emperor Ashoka. Curiously, the Buddha himself is never shown as a person, only as symbols like a wheel, an empty throne or a pair of footprints. Inscriptions name the donors of the carvings; one records a gift from the ivory workers of nearby Vidisha.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Great Stupa at Sanchi'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi

title: Drums of Bronze
text: The Đông Sơn people of northern Vietnam cast big bronze drums with a shining star or sun in the middle of the top, ringed by birds and boats full of people in feather headdresses. The oldest drums were used in funeral rituals, and many were traded far away, as far as Indonesia. Today the drum is a symbol of Vietnam, displayed in many public places.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Mahōra Thuk bronze drum (66.38), catalogue text by J. Kenneth Moore

source2.name: W.G. Solheim II, 'A Brief History of the Dongson Concept', Asian Perspectives (Univ. of Hawai'i ScholarSpace)

title: A Giant Maya Pyramid in the Jungle
text: Long before the famous Maya cities, El Mirador was a huge capital linked by raised stone roads. Its La Danta temple is one of the largest pyramids in the world by volume. Today you can only get there by hiking for days or flying in by helicopter.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: Ancient Mesoamerica (Cambridge University Press), Hansen et al., LiDAR analyses in the Mirador-Calakmul Karst Basin

title: Giant Drawings in the Desert
text: The Nazca people moved dark stones aside to draw a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider, and long straight lines across the desert. Some are so big they're best seen from the air or nearby hills. The dry, calm weather has kept them safe for about 2,000 years.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Nazca Lines, Peru'

title: The First Fleet Arrives
text: Eleven British ships arrived carrying over a thousand people, many of them convicts, to set up a prison colony. The Gadigal people of the Eora Nation had lived around this harbor for thousands of years. The date is still debated today: some call it Australia Day, others call it Invasion Day.

source.name: Dictionary of Sydney: First Fleet

source2.name: ABC News: Invasion Day protests draw thousands calling for date change (26 Jan 2019)

title: The Emperor Says "No, Thanks"
text: Britain sent Lord Macartney with elaborate clocks, globes and other gifts to the Qianlong Emperor, hoping to open more trade. The emperor met him at his summer palace here and politely refused, writing that China had no need for Britain's goods. China's refusal is often seen as background to later clashes such as the Opium Wars.

source.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Two Edicts from the Qianlong Emperor (1793)

source2.name: Henrietta Harrison, 'A Faithful Interpreter? Li Zibiao and the 1793 Macartney Embassy', Oxford Research Archive

title: The Stone That Cracked a Code
text: French soldiers rebuilding a fort found a stone with the same message written three ways: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script, and in Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, it became the key to the long-lost hieroglyphs. Jean-François Champollion finally cracked them in 1822.

source.name: Fondation Napoléon (napoleon.org): The Rosetta Stone, a journey from Alexandria to London

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Rosetta Stone

title: Tipu's Tiger
text: Tipu Sultan, the "Tiger of Mysore", fought the British East India Company for years. When his fortress fell in 1799, the British took a life-size wooden tiger attacking a European soldier, with a little organ inside that made growls and screams. You can still see it in a museum in London.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Tippoo's Tiger (museum no. 2545(IS))

title: Fishing for Electric Eels
text: Near Calabozo, explorer Alexander von Humboldt watched local fishermen drive horses into a pond so electric eels would zap them and wear themselves out. Then the eels could be caught safely. Humboldt got a painful shock too, and he used the captured eels for his own experiments on their electricity.

source.name: Catania K.C., 'Leaping eels electrify threats, supporting Humboldt's account of a battle with horses', PNAS 2016, PubMed Central

source2.name: Catania K.C., 'The Astonishing Behavior of Electric Eels', Front Integr Neurosci 2019, PubMed Central

title: The Million-Person City
text: Edo was one of the biggest cities on Earth, with roughly a million people. Under the Tokugawa shoguns it had busy theaters, street stalls selling soba noodles and tempura, and publishers selling colorful woodblock prints. The artist Hokusai, who later made "The Great Wave", was working here.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tokyo-Yokohama metropolitan area, History

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hokusai (Richard Lane)

title: Haiti Declares Freedom
text: After more than 12 years of revolution, formerly enslaved people defeated Napoleon's army and declared Haiti independent. It became the only nation born from a successful uprising of enslaved people. Haitians still celebrate New Year's Day, their Independence Day, with soup joumou, a pumpkin soup once reserved for slave owners.

source.name: Library of Congress Research Guide, Women in the Haitian Revolution

source2.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Joumou soup

title: A Scholar Builds a Caliphate
text: The scholar Usman dan Fodio led a movement that united many Hausa states into the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest empires in Africa in the 1800s. His daughter Nana Asma'u became a famous poet and teacher who trained a network of women educators. Some people in northern Nigeria can still recite her poems today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Usman dan Fodio (Thomas Hodgkin)

source2.name: University of Kansas News, book on Nana Asma'u and Yan Taru (2023)

title: An Emperor Crowns Himself
text: Napoleon Bonaparte became Emperor of the French in a huge ceremony with the Pope watching. At the big moment, he placed the crown on his own head. The painter Jacques-Louis David captured the scene in a painting almost 10 meters wide.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, The Coronation of Napoleon (Alicja Zelazko)

source2.name: Musée du Louvre collections, David study 'L'Empereur Napoléon Ier se couronnant lui-même'

title: "Ocean in View!"
text: After crossing the Rocky Mountains, the Lewis and Clark expedition reached the Pacific coast. They got help from Native peoples all along the way, including Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman who traveled with her baby. They spent a very rainy winter in a small fort they built here: it rained on all but 12 of their 106 days.

source.name: US National Park Service, Lewis and Clark National Historical Park, History & Culture

source2.name: US National Park Service, Lewis and Clark National Historical Park: Frequently Asked Questions

title: One Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
text: Kamehameha I united the Hawaiian Islands into one kingdom by 1810. Years earlier he made the "Law of the Splintered Paddle", protecting ordinary people, such as the elderly, women and children, from attack by powerful chiefs and warriors. That law is written into Hawaiʻi's state constitution today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kamehameha I

source2.name: Hawaii State Legislature, Constitution of the State of Hawaii, Article IX, Section 10

title: Saying Sorry
text: Prime Minister Kevin Rudd formally apologized in Parliament to the Stolen Generations: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children taken from their families under past government policies. Thousands gathered in Canberra to witness it, and crowds watched it on television at sites around the nation. Many felt that a vital first step toward healing had begun.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments - National Apology

source2.name: State Library Victoria, 'Apology to the Aborigines'

title: The Doomsday Seed Vault
text: Deep inside an Arctic mountain, this vault stores backup copies of seeds from almost every country, more than a million samples. If crops are lost to war or disaster, the seeds can be sent back. In 2015, scientists made the first withdrawal to replace seeds lost in the war in Syria.

source.name: Crop Trust: Svalbard Global Seed Vault

title: The Miracle on the Hudson
text: A flock of geese knocked out both engines of a passenger jet just after takeoff. Captain "Sully" Sullenberger glided the plane down onto the Hudson River, and all 155 people on board survived. Ferry boats rushed over to pick people off the wings.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution: Scientists Identify Geese in Hudson River Plane Crash

source2.name: FAA Lessons Learned: US Airways Flight 1549

title: The Tallest Building on Earth
text: The Burj Khalifa stands 828 meters tall, more than twice the height of the Empire State Building. Its top floors see so far along Earth's curve that the Sun sets about four minutes later up there than at the bottom! Its shape was partly inspired by a desert flower called the spider lily.

source.name: Burj Khalifa official website: Architecture & Design

source2.name: CTBUH Skyscraper Center: Burj Khalifa / Empire State Building

title: Catching the Higgs Boson
text: Scientists using the Large Hadron Collider, a 27-km ring of magnets buried underground, announced they had found the Higgs boson. This tiny particle helps explain why things have mass. Physicists had been hunting for it for almost 50 years.

source.name: CERN: The Higgs boson

source2.name: CERN: The Large Hadron Collider

title: A Brand-New Human Relative
text: Cavers squeezed through gaps only about 20 cm wide to reach a hidden chamber full of bones. They belonged to a new human relative, Homo naledi, with a small brain but hands and wrists a lot like ours. They lived roughly 236,000 to 335,000 years ago, around the same time as the earliest members of our own species.

source.name: Dirks et al. 2015, eLife (PMC4559842): Geological and taphonomic context for Homo naledi

source2.name: Dirks et al. 2017, eLife (PMC5423772): The age of Homo naledi

title: A Bridge That Dives Under the Sea
text: The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge is a 55-km chain of bridges, islands, and tunnels across the sea. In the middle it dives into a 6.7-km undersea tunnel so ships in one of the world's busiest deep-water channels can sail over it. It turned a trip of several hours into well under one.

source.name: Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge Authority / HKSAR Government: HZMB (Hong Kong Section)

source2.name: HKSAR Government, Greater Bay Area: Key Infrastructure

title: The First Photo of a Black Hole
text: Telescopes around the world, including ALMA high in the Atacama Desert, teamed up to act like one Earth-sized telescope. Together they took the first picture of a black hole: a glowing orange ring around a dark shadow in the galaxy M87. That black hole is about 6.5 billion times heavier than our Sun.

source.name: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration: Press release, April 10, 2019

title: Landing Near the Moon's South Pole
text: Chandrayaan-3 launched from this island space center and made India the first country to land near the Moon's south pole. Its little rover, Pragyan, rolled around testing the lunar soil. India became only the fourth country ever to land gently on the Moon.

source.name: Press Information Bureau, Govt of India: Year End Review of Department of Space (2023)

source2.name: ISRO: Chandrayaan-3 details

title: Lystrosaurus, the Great Survivor
text: After the worst mass extinction ever wiped out most life on Earth, a stubby, pig-sized plant-eater with two tusks thrived. In some Karoo rock layers, most of the fossils, about three-quarters by recent counts, are Lystrosaurus. It is also found in India and Antarctica, lands that were then joined in the supercontinent Pangaea.

source.name: University of Washington News

source2.name: Frontiers in Earth Science (Botha 2020)

title: A 22-Metre Giant from China
text: Mamenchisaurus was a giant long-necked plant-eater about 22 metres long. It lived in China in the Late Jurassic, between about 155 and 145 million years ago. It was named in 1954 by the Chinese fossil pioneer Yang Zhongjian, also known as C. C. Young.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: Half Bird, Half Dinosaur
text: Archaeopteryx had feathered wings like a bird but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a dinosaur. Its skeleton was found in fine limestone in 1861, just two years after Darwin published his theory of evolution. It became famous as a perfect in-between creature.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

source2.name: University of California Museum of Paleontology

title: A Wall Made of Dinosaur Bones
text: Giant long-necked dinosaurs like Apatosaurus and Diplodocus lived here about 150 million years ago. In 1909 fossil hunter Earl Douglass found eight Apatosaurus tailbones in a sandstone hill, the start of a hugely productive quarry. Today visitors can stand inside a building and see a rock wall studded with around 1,500 real dinosaur bones.

source.name: US National Park Service: Quarry Exhibit Hall

source2.name: US National Park Service: Earl Douglass

title: The First Fuzzy Dinosaur
text: Described in 1996, Sinosauropteryx was the first dinosaur outside the bird family found with feathers: a coat of simple fuzz. Scientists later spotted traces of its colour pattern, including a striped, banded tail. It was only about a metre long, and it changed how everyone pictures dinosaurs.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: A Giant Found on a Sheep Ranch
text: Patagotitan was a titanosaur, one of the long-necked giants, about 37 metres long and weighing around 57 tonnes, though estimates vary. A ranch worker spotted a bone on a Patagonian ranch in 2010, and scientists dug up the remains of at least six individuals. Its species name honours the ranch's owners, the Mayo family.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory: Patagotitan)

source2.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (Carballido et al. 2017)

title: Australia's Dinosaur by the Inland Sea
text: When Muttaburrasaurus lived, much of inland Australia was covered by a shallow sea. This plant-eater had a strange bump on its snout. A cattle grazier named Doug Langdon found its skeleton beside the Thomson River in 1963, and it is now Queensland's official state fossil.

source.name: Queensland Government (State fossil emblem: Muttaburrasaurus langdoni)

source2.name: Australian Museum

title: The River Monster with a Sail
text: Spinosaurus was a huge predator with a tall sail on its back, adapted to life in and around the rivers of North Africa. The bones of the first skeleton, described by Ernst Stromer and kept in Munich, were destroyed in the war in 1944. A newer partial skeleton from Morocco's Kem Kem beds has brought it back to life.

source.name: ZooKeys (Ibrahim et al. 2020, "Geology and paleontology of the Upper Cretaceous Kem Kem Group of eastern Morocco")

source2.name: Science (Ibrahim et al. 2014, "Semiaquatic adaptations in a giant predatory dinosaur"), abstract

title: Two Dinosaurs Frozen Mid-Fight
text: In 1971 a Polish-Mongolian team found a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops locked together: the raptor's claw in its rival's neck, its arm caught in the other's beak. Both were buried mid-battle, maybe by a collapsing sand dune. Real Velociraptors were only about the size of a turkey, and covered in feathers.

source.name: American Museum of Natural History, OLogy card 038 'Fighting Dinosaurs'

source2.name: Natural History Museum (London), Dino Directory: Velociraptor

title: The Dragon of Mukawa
text: In 2003 Yoshiyuki Horita found dinosaur bones along a creek in Mukawa, Hokkaido. They turned out to belong to a nearly complete duck-billed dinosaur about 8 metres long, buried in rocks from the sea floor, so its body probably floated out to sea. Named in 2019, Kamuysaurus takes its name from kamuy, the Ainu word for a deity.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Kobayashi et al. 2019, "A New Hadrosaurine ... from the Marine Deposits of the Late Cretaceous Hakobuchi Formation, Yezo Group, Japan")

title: Sue, the Most Famous T. rex
text: In 1990 fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson spotted bones sticking out of a cliff, and they became one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. After a long legal fight, it sold at auction in 1997 for more than 8 million dollars. Sue now lives at the Field Museum in Chicago.

source.name: Field Museum, Chicago

title: The Day the Asteroid Hit
text: About 66 million years ago a large asteroid slammed into what is now Chicxulub, on the coast of Mexico's Yucatán. Debris from the impact has been found in rocks of this age all around the world. Scientists reviewing the evidence concluded that the darkness and cooling that followed triggered one of the biggest mass extinctions in Earth's history.

source.name: Science (Schulte et al. 2010, "The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary"), abstract

title: India's Great Floods of Lava
text: Around the time the dinosaurs died out, about 66 million years ago, enormous floods of lava poured across India. More than 90 percent of the lava in the Deccan Traps erupted in less than a million years, and most of that came just after the extinction. Scientists still debate how much its gases added to the chaos of the asteroid strike.

source.name: Science (Sprain et al. 2019, "The eruptive tempo of Deccan volcanism in relation to the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary"), abstract

title: The Whale That Walked
text: Pakicetus was a wolf-sized land animal that lived in the early Eocene, yet it is one of the earliest known whales. Skeletons described in 2001 showed that these first whales lived on land rather than in the sea. They also showed that whales are close relatives of the even-toed hoofed mammals, not of the extinct meat-eaters once thought to be their kin.

source.name: Nature (Thewissen et al. 2001, "Skeletons of terrestrial cetaceans and the relationship of whales to artiodactyls"), abstract

title: The Lake That Kept Its Secrets
text: Animals buried here about 47 million years ago were preserved in amazing detail: whole skeletons, with feathers, skin, hair and even stomach contents. The fossils were discovered through mining for oil shale. In 1971 the old pit was proposed as a rubbish dump, but public concern saved it, and it became a World Heritage Site in 1995.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Messel Pit Fossil Site)

title: Whales with Tiny Feet
text: Today this is Egypt's Western Desert, but in the Eocene it was a sea full of early whales, and many complete skeletons still lie here. Fossils of Basilosaurus from Egypt have small hind limbs with feet. These whales were in the last stages of losing their back legs, a leftover from their land-living ancestors.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Wadi Al-Hitan, Whale Valley)

source2.name: Science (Gingerich, Smith & Simons 1990, "Hind limbs of Eocene Basilosaurus: evidence of feet in whales"), abstract

title: Antarctica Freezes Over
text: About 34 million years ago carbon dioxide levels fell and Antarctica iced over fast. Models suggest the glaciers began on high ground like the Gamburtsev Mountains. Discovered in 1958, these mountains have jagged, Alps-like peaks and valleys, yet they are completely hidden beneath the ice sheet and have only been mapped using radar.

source.name: Nature (Bo et al. 2009, "The Gamburtsev mountains and the origin and early evolution of the Antarctic Ice Sheet"), abstract

source2.name: Nature (Ferraccioli et al. 2011, "East Antarctic rifting triggers uplift of the Gamburtsev Mountains"), abstract

title: When Kangaroos Had Fangs
text: Riversleigh's fossils come from Australian rainforests that are now gone. They include marsupial lions, a small 'Fangaroo' with huge canine teeth, and a giant rat-kangaroo that ate meat, along with crocodiles and dozens of kinds of bats. UNESCO counts Riversleigh among the world's greatest fossil sites, covering roughly 10 to 30 million years ago.

source.name: Australian Museum (Riversleigh fossil site)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Mediterranean Dries Up
text: When the link to the Atlantic was cut off, the Mediterranean Sea largely evaporated, leaving thick layers of salt on its floor. Rivers carved deep canyons to reach the sunken basin. About 5.3 million years ago the Atlantic broke back through at Gibraltar, and some scientists think the sea refilled astonishingly quickly.

source.name: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature 462:778-781

source2.name: University of Southampton

title: Footprints in Volcanic Ash
text: Early human relatives walked across wet volcanic ash, and later ash falls buried and preserved their trail. Mary Leakey's team found animal tracks here in 1976, and in 1978 Paul Abell spotted the human-like trail: about 70 footprints stretching 27 metres. They show upright walking with a heel-first, human-like stride and a big toe in line with the others.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - Human Origins

title: Lucy, Named After a Beatles Song
text: In 1974 Donald Johanson and Maurice Taieb found the partial skeleton of an Australopithecus afarensis, an early human relative, about 3.2 million years old. She got her nickname that night, while the team celebrated to the Beatles' song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds. In Ethiopia she is also called Dinknesh, Amharic for 'you are marvellous'.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - Human Origins

title: A Land Bridge Joins the Americas
text: When the Isthmus of Panama finally rose from the sea about 2.8 million years ago, North and South America were linked. Animals crossed both ways: the ancestors of today's opossums, armadillos and porcupines went north, while the ancestors of bears, cats, dogs, horses and llamas went south.

source.name: O'Dea et al. 2016, Science Advances (abstract via PubMed)

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory

title: A Giant Ape Found in a Drugstore
text: Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived, perhaps 3 metres tall and weighing 200 to 300 kilograms. It first came to light when a scientist found one of its huge teeth being sold as a 'dragon tooth' in a Hong Kong medicine shop, reported in 1935. We still know it only from four jaws and nearly 2,000 teeth.

source.name: Zhang et al. 2024, Nature 625:535-539

title: First Humans Outside Africa
text: Fossils from Dmanisi in Georgia, about 1.77 million years old, belong to some of the earliest humans known outside Africa. One skull belonged to an elderly man who had lost all but one of his teeth years before dying. Surviving that long may mean others in his group took care of him.

source.name: Lordkipanidze et al. 2005, Nature 434:717-718

source2.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - Human Origins

title: Older Than Any Pottery Bowl
text: Ice Age people here shaped small figurines out of local clay and fired them in hearths. Made about 31,000 to 27,000 years ago, the Venus of Dolní Věstonice and its neighbours belong to the oldest known ceramic tradition, with no link to the cooking pots invented much later. The Venus still preserves the finger impressions of its maker.

source.name: Farbstein et al. 2012, PLOS ONE

source2.name: Vandiver et al. 1989, Science, 'The origins of ceramic technology at Dolní Věstonice' (abstract)

title: Africa's Oldest Painted Stones
text: Seven small stone slabs with traces of animal figures, painted in charcoal, ochre and white, were found in Apollo 11 Cave in the Huns Mountains of Namibia. Dated to about 25,500-23,500 BC, they were long the oldest known artwork of any kind from Africa, and remain among its oldest pictures of animals.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

title: A Siberian Boy's Surprising DNA
text: A young boy was buried at Mal'ta, near Lake Baikal, about 24,000 years ago. When scientists published his DNA in 2013, they found he was related both to western Eurasians and to Native Americans, but not closely to East Asians. Between 14 and 38 percent of Native American ancestry may come from his ancient population.

source.name: Raghavan et al. 2014, Nature (PubMed Central)

title: The Oldest Grass Bed
place: Ohalo II, Sea of Galilee, Israel
text: Hunter-gatherers built brush huts by the lake, slept on beds of soft grass and ground wild barley and wheat on stone slabs. They gathered well over a hundred kinds of plants. The camp lay hidden underwater until a drought in 1989 lowered the lake and revealed it.

source.name: Snir et al. 2015, PLOS ONE

source2.name: Nadel et al. 2004, PNAS (PubMed Central)

title: When You Could Walk to Borneo
text: With so much water locked in ice sheets, sea levels were about 120 metres lower. Sumatra, Java and Borneo were joined to mainland Asia in a huge lowland called Sundaland, crossed by rivers and covered partly by forest and partly by open savannah. People and animals like tigers and rhinos could simply walk between what are now islands.

source.name: PNAS (Raes et al. 2014), via PubMed Central

title: Footprints on an Ancient Lakeshore
text: Adults and children walked across soft clay by a lake in outback Australia, and their tracks hardened. Hundreds of these footprints were found in 2003 by Mary Pappin Jr, a young Mutthi Mutthi woman. They are one of the largest sets of Ice Age human footprints known in the world, and some show people running.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: Australian Museum

title: The Ceiling a Girl Discovered
text: In 1879 a young girl named María was the first to notice the painted animals on the ceiling of this cave. Her father published the find, but experts doubted it for more than 20 years, until 1902, because they could not believe Ice Age people made such art. The red and black bison seem to bulge, painted over natural bumps in the rock.

source.name: Museo Nacional y Centro de Investigación de Altamira (Spanish Ministry of Culture)

source2.name: Bradshaw Foundation

title: Ice Age Sweet Tooth
text: The Cave of Pigeons holds one of the oldest cemeteries in North Africa. The people buried here ate lots of acorns and pine nuts, and their teeth show it: nearly all the adults had cavities, a level of tooth decay usually linked with farming thousands of years later.

source.name: PNAS (Humphrey et al. 2014), via PubMed Central

title: The World's Oldest Bread Crumbs
text: In a stone hearth in the Black Desert, archaeologists found charred crumbs of flatbread baked by Natufian hunter-gatherers. It was made from wild cereals and the roots of a marsh plant. That means people were baking bread around 4,000 years before farming began.

source.name: PNAS (Arranz-Otaegui et al. 2018), via PubMed Central

title: History Written in Poop
text: Some of the oldest evidence of people in North America is dried human poop. Scientists pulled human DNA from these fossilized droppings, called coprolites, in caves in Oregon's desert. They show people were living here more than a thousand years before the famous Clovis hunters.

source.name: Science (Gilbert et al. 2008), abstract via Europe PMC

title: A Puppy Cared For by People
text: About 14,000 years ago, a young dog was buried alongside people at Oberkassel in Germany. Its teeth show it had been seriously ill, probably with canine distemper, for at least six weeks before it died. It could not have survived that long without people caring for it closely, a sign of real affection.

source.name: Frontiers in Veterinary Science (Serpell 2021), via PubMed Central

title: Spear Points Among Mammoth Bones
text: In the 1930s, beautifully flaked stone spear points were found with mammoth bones near Clovis, New Mexico. Each point has a groove at its base so it could be fixed tightly to a spear. Clovis points have since turned up across much of North America.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (L. A. Tedesco, 'Blackwater Draw')

source2.name: Science Advances (PMC), zooarchaeology of early Paleoindians: Clovis ~13,400/13,050-12,800 cal BP

title: The Big Freeze Comes Back
text: Just as the Ice Age was ending, the Northern Hemisphere suddenly plunged back into near-glacial cold. Ice cores drilled in Greenland record the swing, which ended about 11,500 years ago with a jump of 10°C in a decade. The period is named after Dryas, a little cold-loving flower that became common in Europe at the time.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

title: Naia, the Girl in the Black Hole
text: A teenage girl fell into a deep pit in a then-dry cave, alongside animals like a saber-toothed cat. Rising seas later flooded the cave, and divers found her skeleton in 2007. Her DNA links the earliest Americans to Native Americans living today.

source.name: Science News

title: The Sahara Turns Green
text: As the Ice Age faded, monsoon rains pushed north and much of the Sahara became grassland dotted with lakes. Lake Chad swelled to many times its present size. Hippos, crocodiles and fishing communities lived in places that are sand dunes today.

source.name: PNAS via PubMed Central (Armitage et al. 2015, Lake Mega-Chad)

source2.name: PNAS via PubMed Central (Drake et al. 2011, Green Sahara)

title: Luzia, Rescued from the Ashes
text: Luzia, a young woman who died at about 20, is one of the oldest people found in the Americas. Her skeleton was dug up in a Brazilian rock shelter in 1974–75 and later named Luzia by Walter Neves, in honour of the famous fossil Lucy. After a 2018 fire destroyed Brazil's National Museum, staff found her broken skull in a metal box and identified about 80 percent of it.

source.name: Revista Pesquisa FAPESP (São Paulo Research Foundation), 'A América de Luzia' and interview 'Walter Neves: O pai de Luzia'

source2.name: National Geographic Brasil, 'Fragmentos do crânio de Luzia são encontrados em escombros do Museu Nacional' (19 Oct 2018)

title: Early Rice Along the Yangzi
text: At Shangshan, people settled into some of the first villages of the lower Yangzi, made pottery and used more and more grinding stones. They mixed rice husks into the clay of their pots, and tiny plant remains suggest rice domestication may have begun here around the start of the Holocene. Today rice sustains more than half the people on Earth.

source.name: PNAS via PubMed Central (Zuo et al. 2017)

title: Jericho Builds a Tower
text: Beside a never-failing spring, people settled at Jericho perhaps as early as 9000 BCE, making it one of the oldest continuously lived-in places in the world. By the 9th to 8th millennium BCE it was a sizeable permanent settlement, and its people built a massive stone wall with a ditch and a great stone tower. No one knows for sure what the tower was for.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Horse People of Botai
text: Around 3500 BCE, villagers at Botai on the Kazakh steppe kept horses: archaeologists have found evidence of bridling, milking and corralling. That makes Botai the earliest known horse-herding community. DNA later delivered a twist: today's domestic horses do not descend from the Botai horses at all, but from a later lineage on the western steppes.

source.name: Nature (Librado et al. 2021)

title: China's 5,000-Year-Old Dams
text: The Liangzhu people built a walled city in the marshlands of China's Yangtze Delta, plus a network of dams and levees begun about 5,100 years ago, one of the world's oldest large water-management systems. Builders stacked bundles of clay wrapped in grass, a bit like sandbags. Finely carved jades were buried in the graves of the elite.

source.name: PNAS (Liu et al. 2017, 'Earliest hydraulic enterprise in China, 5,100 years ago')

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Iceman's Last Hike
text: In 1991, hikers in the Alps found a man who had lain frozen in the ice for over 5,000 years. Nicknamed Ötzi, he carried a copper axe, wore shoes padded with dry grass, and had 61 tattoos. His last meals included ibex and red deer, and a flint arrowhead in his left shoulder shows his final day was not a peaceful one.

source.name: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Writing Starts With Bookkeeping
text: By about 3200 BCE Uruk was the largest settlement in southern Mesopotamia, if not the world. Its scribes drew simple pictographs on clay tablets, not poems but records of goods, barley and workers' rations. Pressed into soft clay with a stylus, the signs grew into wedge-shaped cuneiform, a script used for some three thousand years.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Great Jōmon Village
text: From about 3900 to 2200 BCE, a large Jōmon settlement thrived here in northern Japan, with pit houses, storage pits, roads and big pillar-supported buildings. Chestnuts, walnuts and fish bones show what people ate, and more than 2,000 clay figurines have been dug up. Jōmon pottery is named for its cord-pattern decoration.

source.name: Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, official World Heritage website

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Kenya's Lakeside Pillar Cemetery
text: As rains faded and Lake Turkana shrank, East Africa's earliest herders built a huge shared cemetery on its shore, marked with tall stone pillars. Hundreds of people were buried there over about 700 years, many wearing beads and ornaments. It shows that mobile herders, not only kings with cities, could build big monuments.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History

source2.name: PNAS (Hildebrand et al. 2018)

title: Caral: Pyramids in Peru
text: While Egyptians were building pyramids, people in Peru's Supe Valley were building their own, with plazas, homes, and sunken circular courts. About 5,000 years old, Caral is called the oldest centre of civilization in the Americas. In its amphitheater, archaeologists found 32 flutes made from pelican and condor bones.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine

title: Merer's Pyramid Diary
text: In 2013, in caves near the Red Sea, archaeologists found rolls of papyrus including the journal of an official named Merer. He led a crew of about 200 men and logged boat trips hauling limestone from the Tura quarries up the Nile to Giza, late in the reign of King Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid. They are the oldest known inscribed papyri in the world.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine

title: Stonehenge's Long-Distance Stones
text: Stonehenge's giant sarsen stones went up around 2500 BCE, lined up with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Smaller bluestones were hauled about 240 kilometers from Wales, and a 2024 study traced the central Altar Stone all the way to northern Scotland. Exactly how people moved them is still debated.

source.name: English Heritage

source2.name: Nature (Clarke et al. 2024, Altar Stone)

title: Mohenjo-daro's Amazing Drains
text: This Indus Valley city was carefully planned, with streets crossing at right angles, brick houses with small bathrooms, and an elaborate drainage system. On its high mound stood the 'Great Bath', a large tank surrounded by a veranda. UNESCO calls it the best-preserved city of the Indus civilization, dating back to the 3rd millennium BCE.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The First Author We Know By Name
text: Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, served as high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur around the 23rd century BCE. She is credited with hymns and poems, most famously a collection dedicated to the goddess Inanna. She is the earliest author in history whose name we know.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Hammurabi's Laws in Stone
text: King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws carved onto a tall black stone, covering everything from stolen oxen to doctors' fees and tavern prices. Punishments often depended on whether you were noble, commoner, or enslaved. The stone was later carried off as war loot and was rediscovered in Iran in 1901.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Yale Law School, Avalon Project: The Code of Hammurabi (L. W. King translation)

title: Kerma, Kingdom of Cattle
text: Kerma, on the Nile in today's Sudan, was the first capital of a powerful Nubian kingdom, long mistaken for an Egyptian outpost. It grew rich on gold, cattle herding and river trade, and around 1630 BCE its rulers even raided Egypt. Kerma's kings were buried under large mounds, lying on beds, surrounded by hundreds of sacrificed courtiers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine: 'Why Sudan's Remarkable Ancient Civilization Has Been Overlooked by History'

title: The Island That Blew Its Top
text: One of the largest volcanic eruptions known tore apart the island of Thera, today's Santorini, and buried the town of Akrotiri under ash and pumice. Its multi-story houses still stand, with some of the finest Minoan wall paintings found anywhere. Experts still argue over the date: about 1500 BCE, or as early as the 1620s BCE.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Stone Towns on the Sahara's Edge
text: Along the cliffs of Dhar Tichitt, people built large dry-stone villages; the biggest had almost 600 walled compounds and narrow passageways. They raised livestock, especially cattle, and grew pearl millet, a hardy grain that is still a staple in many parts of West Africa. The land was wetter then, with lakes in the valleys, and the villages flourished during the region's last major humid phase.

source.name: African Archaeological Review (2022), 'Spatial Organization and Socio-Economic Differentiation at the Dhar Tichitt Center of Dakhlet el Atrouss I (Southeastern Mauritania)' (Springer, read in browser)

source2.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2021), Champion et al., 'Agricultural diversification in West Africa: an archaeobotanical study of the site of Sadia (Dogon Country, Mali)' (PMC full text)

title: Hatshepsut's Shopping Trip to Punt
text: Hatshepsut, who ruled Egypt as a female king, sent ships to the faraway land of Punt, on the African coast beyond the southern end of the Red Sea. Carvings at her temple show the expedition bringing home gold, ebony, animal skins, baboons and living myrrh trees. The trees were planted in the gardens of her temple at Deir el-Bahari.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: An Alphabet Written in Wedges
text: Scribes in the port city of Ugarit used an alphabet of 30 signs, pressed into clay tablets with a wedge-shaped stylus like cuneiform, but written from left to right. Rediscovered in 1929, the tablets revealed forgotten Canaanite myths. Ugarit was so cosmopolitan that its scribes worked in four languages and seven different scripts.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Bronze Age Cargo Ship
text: In 1982, a Turkish sponge diver near Kaş described strange 'metal biscuits with ears' on the seabed. They were copper ingots from a ship wrecked around 1320 BCE, carrying copper and tin in the ten-to-one mix needed for bronze, plus glass ingots, ebony, ivory, and ostrich eggshells. A gold scarab naming Queen Nefertiti was on board too.

source.name: Institute of Nautical Archaeology

title: Poverty Point's Giant Earthworks
text: Hunter-fisher-gatherers in what is now Louisiana moved nearly two million cubic yards of soil, basketful by basketful, to build six curved ridges, five mounds and a central plaza. The biggest mound stands 72 feet tall. They brought in stone from up to 800 miles away, part of a huge trading network.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Poverty Point World Heritage Site (State of Louisiana)

title: Fu Hao, Queen and General
text: Fu Hao is believed to have been a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, and she was also a noted military leader. Her tomb near Anyang, excavated in 1976, was the first major Shang royal tomb to be found intact. It held more than 440 bronze vessels and 590 jade objects.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Chinese bronzes, The Shang dynasty

title: Sanxingdui's Bug-Eyed Bronzes
text: In 1986, workers digging near Guanghan uncovered pits packed with astonishing bronzes: masks with eyes bulging out like telescopes, a 2.6-meter standing figure, and a bronze tree almost four meters tall. They look nothing like Shang bronzes from the same time, revealing a mysterious culture that left no writing.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

title: The Giant Stone Heads of the Olmec
text: The Olmec of Mexico's Gulf Coast carved 17 enormous basalt heads, from about 1.5 to 3.4 meters tall. Each wears a helmet-like cap, and they are generally thought to be portraits of rulers. The Olmec were also rubber makers, mixing tree latex with vine juice; their Aztec name means 'rubber people'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Lapita Sailors Head Into the Pacific
text: The Lapita people sailed east into the open Pacific and were the first settlers of islands such as Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. They carried domesticated plants and animals with them and left pottery stamped with fine toothed patterns. Their settlements laid the foundations of the societies that later grew up across Polynesia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: PLOS ONE / PubMed Central (Kinaston et al. 2014, Teouma)

title: Korea, Land of Dolmens
text: Korea is the land of dolmens, stone tombs made of a huge capstone resting on upright slabs. According to UNESCO, its Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa sites hold the highest density and greatest variety of dolmens of any country. Gochang alone has more than 440, built in the first millennium BCE as burial chambers for important people.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Student Who Tripped on History
text: In 1966, an American student tripped over a tree root in a Thai village and landed face-first beside ancient pottery. Digging revealed a community that grew wet rice, kept farm animals and cast bronze tools and ornaments. The site's dates have been revised several times; UNESCO now places its occupation from about 1500 to 900 BCE.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: TIME (19 Nov 1984, 'Hidden Treasures at a Dead End')

title: The Deer Stones of Mongolia
text: Bronze Age herders on the Mongolian steppe raised standing stones up to four meters tall, covered with carvings of stylized stags. These 'deer stones' date from about 1200 to 600 BCE, were used for ceremonies and funerals, and usually stand beside large burial mounds called khirgisüürs. About 1,500 are known across the Eurasian steppe, more than 80 percent of them in Mongolia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Queen Dido's Oxhide Trick
text: Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Carthage on the coast of North Africa; tradition dates it to 814 BCE. In Virgil's telling, Queen Dido's people bought as much land as a bull's hide could encircle, and the citadel hill was named the Byrsa. Carthage grew into a trading power that controlled much of the trade in purple dye from murex shells.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University (Virgil, Aeneid 1.335-370, trans. Williams)

title: The First Olympics Had One Race
text: According to Greek tradition, the first Olympic Games had just one event: a sprint of about 190 meters called the stadion. The winner listed for that year is Koroibos, said to be a cook from nearby Elis. Winners got a wreath of olive leaves, and the games went on for over a thousand years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: International Olympic Committee

title: Piye, the Kushite Conqueror of Egypt
text: King Piye of Kush, in today's Sudan, invaded Egypt from the south and ended the rule of its rival petty kings. After the last holdouts submitted, he sailed home to his capital near Mount Barkal with the spoils. A great stela found there recounts his deeds, and his conquest laid the foundations of Egypt's 25th dynasty.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Cyrus Builds the Persian Empire
text: Cyrus the Great started out ruling a small Persian kingdom and built one of the largest empires the world had yet seen. After taking Babylon in 539 BCE, he let peoples who had been forcibly settled there, including the Jews, return home, and the Jews could rebuild their temple in Jerusalem. His simple stone tomb still stands at Pasargadae, his capital.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art

source2.name: National Geographic

title: Confucius, the Wandering Teacher
text: Confucius taught that good government starts with good people: rulers should care for others, children should respect their parents, and everyone should be eager to learn. He spent years traveling between rival states in search of a ruler who would use his ideas, mostly without luck. Tradition says his students collected his sayings in the Analects, and his family tree is the longest on record.

source.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

source2.name: Focus Taiwan (Central News Agency)

title: Payday Tablets of Persepolis
text: Over 30,000 clay tablets from Persepolis record food handed out to workers under Darius I, including barley, flour, wine, and beer. Women worked alongside men, and teams were often led by a woman who got the highest ration of all. New mothers got bonus rations, though twice as much for a boy as for a girl.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'WOMEN i. In Pre-Islamic Persia' (M. Brosius)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'PERSEPOLIS ELAMITE TABLETS'

title: Awakening Under the Bodhi Tree
text: Here, tradition says, a wandering prince named Siddhartha Gautama sat beneath a fig tree and reached enlightenment, becoming the Buddha, 'the awakened one.' His teachings spread across Asia. A branch of the tree was carried to Sri Lanka and planted at Anuradhapura in 288 BCE, where it still grows. The tree at Bodh Gaya today is said to descend from the original.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya (statement read via UNESCO open-data API)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Mahabodhi Temple Complex (statement read via UNESCO open-data API)

title: Voting With Broken Pots
text: In democratic Athens, citizens could vote to send a powerful man away for 10 years by scratching his name on a broken bit of pottery called an ostrakon. Even Themistocles, hero of the naval victory at Salamis, was exiled this way. Archaeologists found 190 shards with his name written by just a handful of people, perhaps prepared in advance.

source.name: The Open University (OpenLearn)

source2.name: Robin Osborne, 'The Politics of Expulsion: Ostracism at Athens', Omnibus 33

title: The Face From the Bog
text: In 1950, peat cutters in Denmark found a man so well preserved they thought he was a recent crime victim. He had lived about 2,400 years ago and still wore a pointed sheepskin cap and a belt. His last meal was a porridge of barley, flax, and wild seeds, with some fish. He was probably a sacrifice.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: Ancient Europe 8000 B.C.-A.D. 1000: Encyclopedia of the Barbarian World (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com

title: The World's Oldest Carpet
text: In the Altai Mountains, nomadic horse riders buried their leaders in log tombs that filled with ice, freezing everything inside. One tomb held the oldest known knotted-pile carpet, bordered with rows of deer and horsemen. Bodies from these tombs even kept their tattoos of real and fantastic animals.

source.name: Scientific Reports via PubMed Central (X-ray microscopy of Pazyryk textiles)

source2.name: PBS NOVA, 'Ice Mummies: Siberian Ice Maiden' (transcript)

title: Alexander Meets King Porus
text: Alexander the Great crossed the Hydaspes River in a storm and defeated King Porus, whose army included war elephants. Impressed by Porus, Alexander let him keep ruling. Soon after, his exhausted soldiers refused to march farther east, and Alexander turned back. He named a new city here after his beloved horse, Bucephalus.

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 60-61 (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius, University of Chicago)

source2.name: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 62 (same edition)

title: Ashoka's Messages in Stone
text: After his bloody conquest of Kalinga, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka was filled with regret and turned toward Buddhist ideas of nonviolence. He had messages carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, promising wells, shade trees, and medical care for both people and animals. Their script stayed unreadable until James Prinsep cracked it in 1837.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (University Grants Commission, India), 'The Mauryan Empire'

title: Jenne-Jeno, a Town Without Kings?
text: On the floodplains of the inland Niger Delta, people settled Jenne-Jeno around 250 BCE and grew African rice. Over centuries it became a busy trading town with ironworkers and clay figurines. Archaeologists have found no sign of a very wealthy ruling class, so power may have been shared among different groups.

source.name: Journal of African History (Cambridge University Press), McIntosh & McIntosh, 'The Inland Niger Delta before the Empire of Mali: Evidence from Jenne-Jeno'

source2.name: National Geographic History

title: Measuring Earth With a Shadow
text: Eratosthenes learned that at noon on midsummer in Syene, today's Aswan, the sun shone straight down a well. In Alexandria, farther north, a stick still cast a small shadow at that moment. Using that angle and the distance between the two cities, he estimated the size of the whole Earth and got remarkably close.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

title: Hannibal's Elephants Cross the Alps
text: The Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army, horses, and 37 war elephants from Spain over the snowy Alps to attack Rome from the north. Many soldiers and animals died on the way, and historians still argue over which mountain pass he used. He went on to beat the Romans in huge battles, but never captured Rome.

source.name: PubMed Central (peer-reviewed article), 'Energy costs of Hannibal's alpine crossing'

title: An Army Made of Clay
text: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an struck pieces of a clay soldier. It belonged to an army of roughly 8,000 life-size warriors, plus horses and chariots, buried to guard China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife. They were once painted in bright colors. His own burial mound has still not been opened.

source.name: National Museums Liverpool

source2.name: National Geographic

title: Lady Dai's Last Snack
text: Xin Zhui, wife of the Marquis of Dai, was buried in a tomb sealed so tightly with clay that her skin was still soft when it was opened in the early 1970s. Her tomb held more than a thousand objects, including lacquerware, embroidered silk and a gauze robe weighing only 49 grams. Doctors found 138 melon seeds inside her, so her last snack was probably melon.

source.name: PubMed Central (peer-reviewed), 'Coronary Arteriosclerotic Disease Existed in China Over 2,200 Years Ago'

source2.name: CGTN, 'Mawangdui Han Tomb's oriental sleeping beauty'

title: Scrolls in the Desert Caves
text: In 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd searching for a stray animal found a cave near the Dead Sea with clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Eventually, pieces of more than 900 manuscripts turned up, written mostly between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE. They include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, about a thousand years older than those known before.

source.name: Israel Antiquities Authority, Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library

source2.name: Israel Antiquities Authority, Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library: Introduction

title: Hopewell's Continent-Wide Trade
text: People of the Hopewell tradition in Ohio built giant earthworks shaped like circles, squares, and an octagon lined up with the rising and setting moon. Their trade reached across North America, bringing obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from Lake Superior, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, and even shark teeth.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks'

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, Hopewell Culture NHP: History & Culture

title: Pompeii Frozen in Ash
text: When Mount Vesuvius erupted, ash buried the Roman town of Pompeii and froze daily life in place. Archaeologists found loaves of bread still in a bakery oven and walls covered in graffiti, from election slogans to jokes. A young eyewitness across the bay, Pliny the Younger, later described the eruption in letters.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pompeii' (W. F. Jashemski)

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Pompeii's Graffiti Captures Every Joke, Boast and Argument...'

title: A Birthday Party on the Frontier
text: At a Roman fort in northern England, letters written in ink on thin wooden slips survived in soggy soil. One is a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman. Another mentions socks and underpants sent to a soldier, a reminder that the frontier was chilly.

source.name: Roman Inscriptions of Britain online, Tab. Vindol. 291

source2.name: Roman Inscriptions of Britain online, Tab. Vindol. 346

title: Cai Lun's Better Paper
text: Cai Lun, an official at the Han court, presented the emperor with a way to make paper from tree bark, hemp, old rags, and fishing nets. Paper existed before him, but his recipe made it cheaper and better. It slowly spread across Asia and, roughly a thousand years later, reached Europe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cai Lun'

source2.name: Smithsonian Folklife Festival 2002, 'Paper' (The Silk Road)

title: A Roman Coin in the Mekong Delta
text: Óc Eo, linked to the sea by canals, is thought to have been the main port of Funan, an early kingdom in the Mekong Delta. Diggers found Indian beads, Chinese bronzes, and a gold coin of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius dated 152 CE. Goods traveled thousands of kilometers to get here, showing how connected the ancient world already was.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of Southeast Asia: Rise of indigenous states'

source2.name: The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Archaeology (Oxford Reference), 'Oc Eo, Vietnam'

title: The City of the Gods
text: Teotihuacan grew into the largest city of the ancient Americas, home at its height to an estimated 125,000 to 200,000 people. Most lived in some 2,000 apartment compounds, including a neighborhood of migrants from Oaxaca. Its Pyramid of the Sun is among the biggest in the Americas. The Aztecs named it centuries later; its people's own language is still unknown.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Teotihuacan'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan'

title: Queen Himiko Writes to China
text: Chinese records describe Himiko, a queen of Wa (early Japan) who ruled through spiritual power and was rarely seen after becoming ruler. In 238 or 239 CE she sent envoys to the Wei court, which sent back a gold seal and 100 bronze mirrors. Where her land of Yamatai lay is still debated: northern Kyushu or the Nara region.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Japan: The Yayoi period' (Chinese chronicles)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Himiko'

title: Zenobia Challenges Rome
text: Zenobia ruled the desert trading city of Palmyra for her young son, then seized Egypt and much of Rome's eastern lands. She even issued coins showing herself as empress. The emperor Aurelian defeated and captured her in 272 CE. Some ancient writers say she was paraded through Rome, others that she died on the way, but she lived on in legend as the queen who challenged an empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zenobia'

source2.name: Talanta (Proceedings of the Dutch Archaeological and Historical Society) 40-41, A. Senden, 'Zenobia in nummis'

title: Aksum's King Picks a New Faith
text: King Ezana of Aksum, a trading kingdom in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, became one of the first rulers anywhere to adopt Christianity. His coins swapped the old crescent-and-disc symbol for the cross. Aksum was one of only a few powers of its time to strike coins in gold, silver and copper, and some of its giant stone pillars still stand.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Foundations of Aksumite Civilization and Its Christian Legacy'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Aksum'

title: The Stele of a Korean Conqueror
text: King Jangsu of Goguryeo, a Korean kingdom, raised a stone about 6.4 meters tall to honor his late father, King Gwanggaeto the Great. Its roughly 1,800 carved characters celebrate his conquests across Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula. The stele still stands on the Chinese side of the Yalu River, and scholars still argue over parts of its text.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Goguryeo'

title: The Tattooed Lady of Cao
text: In the mid-2000s, archaeologists in northern Peru unwrapped the mummy of a young Moche woman covered in tattoos of snakes, spiders, and other creatures. She was buried with gold jewelry, war clubs, and spear-throwers, objects Moche experts see as classic male warrior gear. It suggests women could hold great power in Moche society.

source.name: El Brujo Archaeological Complex (Fundacion Wiese), 'Lady of Cao: History, Funerary Bundle, and Moche Power'

source2.name: Harvard University, Dept. of History of Art and Architecture, event 'Elegant in Life, Ambiguous in Death' (Dumbarton Oaks)

title: Ajanta's Painted Caves
text: Buddhist monks carved prayer halls and monasteries into a horseshoe-shaped cliff at Ajanta and covered the walls with brilliant paintings of the Buddha's past lives, princesses, and elephants. Long hidden by jungle, the caves were rediscovered in 1819 by a British army officer of the Madras Regiment who was out on a hunting trip.

source.name: Archaeological Survey of India, 'World Heritage: Ajanta Caves'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, '11 Caves That Made History'

title: Aryabhata Sets the Earth Spinning
text: Aryabhata wrote that he was 23 years old in 499 CE, around when he produced a book in verse packed with astronomy and math. He worked out pi as about 3.1416, explained eclipses as shadows rather than demons swallowing the sun, and suggested that Earth spins on its axis. India named its first satellite after him in 1975.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive, University of St Andrews, 'Aryabhata I'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Aryabhata' (satellite)

title: The Lydenburg Heads
text: A young boy noticed pieces of fired clay eroding out of a gully near Lydenburg in South Africa; they turned out to be seven heads, made around 500 CE by early farming communities. The two largest may have been worn as masks or helmets. They are among the oldest known Iron Age artworks from Africa south of the equator.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Lydenburg Heads (ca. 500 A.D.)'

source2.name: University of Cape Town, Centre for Curating the Archive, 'Lydenburg heads'

title: Hagia Sophia's Floating Dome
text: Emperor Justinian's giant church in Constantinople was finished in less than six years. Its huge dome sits on a ring of windows, so it seems to float on light. It stayed the world's largest cathedral for about a thousand years, and visitors can still spot Viking runes scratched into the parapets of its upper galleries.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hagia Sophia'

source2.name: National Museum of Denmark, 'Viking graffiti'

title: A King Sails Into the Afterlife
text: An Anglo-Saxon king, probably Rædwald of East Anglia, was buried inside a ship about 27 metres long that had been hauled up onto a hill. The wood rotted away long ago, leaving a ghostly outline of iron rivets in the sand. His treasures included a stunning iron helmet and silver bowls made in faraway Byzantium.

source.name: National Trust (Sutton Hoo)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sutton Hoo)

title: A Monk's Long Walk to Nalanda
text: The Chinese monk Xuanzang slipped out of the Tang empire in defiance of a travel ban, crossed deserts and mountains, and reached Nalanda, a giant Buddhist university in India. He studied there among more than ten thousand monks. He later carried more than 650 texts home to Chang'an and spent the rest of his life translating them.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Xuanzang)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Nalanda Mahavihara)

title: King Pakal's Hidden Tomb
text: K'inich Janaab Pakal took the throne of the Maya city of Palenque at the age of twelve and ruled for about 68 years, until he died in 683 at around eighty. He was buried deep inside the Temple of the Inscriptions. Archaeologists only reached his tomb in 1952, after following a hidden staircase, and found Pakal wearing a mask of jade.

source.name: National Geographic History

source2.name: INAH, revista Lakamha' (H. Orea Magana, 'La conservacion de la tumba de K'inich Janaab' Pakal')

title: The Golden Dome of Jerusalem
text: Caliph Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock over a stone linked both to Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac and to the Prophet Muhammad's ascent to heaven. It is the oldest Islamic monument still standing, its walls glittering with mosaics and Arabic writing. The bright gold dome you see today is much newer: it is covered with gold leaf donated by Jordan's late King Hussein.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: The Art of the Umayyad Period (661-750)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Dome of the Rock)

title: Chang'an, City of a Million
text: Tang dynasty Chang'an was probably the most populous city on Earth, home to around a million people. Walls divided it into more than a hundred quarters whose gates were locked at night, while drum towers called out the time. Its two great markets sold horses, silks and tea, along with exotic goods brought from as far as Persia and India.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington (Chang'an essay)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Tang Dynasty (618-907)

title: The First Book All About Tea
text: Lu Yu, an orphan raised by the abbot of a Buddhist monastery, wrote the Classic of Tea, the first known book devoted to the drink. It explains how to harvest, process and brew tea, and which tools to use. He judged water from mountain streams to be ideal, river water good enough and well water inferior.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art

source2.name: Nutrients (MDPI, peer-reviewed) 2019, 'The Influence of Water Composition on Flavor and Nutrient Extraction in Green and Black Tea' (PMC6356489)

title: Borobudur, a Mountain of Stories
text: Java's Shailendra kings built Borobudur, one of the greatest Buddhist monuments in the world. Pilgrims walk round and round its terraces, more than 5 kilometers in all, climbing upward past carved reliefs that tell Buddhist stories. Later it lay buried under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries, until it was uncovered again in 1814.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Borobudur Temple Compounds)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Borobudur)

title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom
text: Under the Abbasid caliphs, Baghdad's scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and pushed their ideas further. Here the mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations whose title gave us the word 'algebra'. His own name, turned into Latin, became the word 'algorithm'.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews (al-Khwarizmi)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Bayt al-Hikmah)

title: The Lace-Fine Bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu
text: In what is now southeastern Nigeria, artists cast bronzes covered in string and lace-like designs, among the most technically accomplished bronzes ever made. Isaiah Anozie found the first pieces in 1938 while digging a water cistern at his compound. Tens of thousands of glass beads, much of the glass made in Mesopotamia and Iran, show the town was linked to long-distance trade networks.

source.name: McIntosh et al., 'Igbo-Ukwu at 50', African Archaeological Review 2022 (PMC)

source2.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Igbo-Ukwu (ca. 9th Century)'

title: The Serpent Shadow of Chichen Itza
text: Chichen Itza was one of the greatest Maya cities of the Yucatán. Its step pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps if you count all four stairways plus the top platform, one for each day of the year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, late-afternoon shadows form a wavy serpent sliding down the stairs toward a stone snake head.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chichen Itza'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Pre-Hispanic City of Chichen-Itza (via data.unesco.org)

title: Murasaki Writes The Tale of Genji
text: A lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, known to us only by the nickname Murasaki Shikibu, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel. It follows a dashing prince's loves and heartbreaks across 54 chapters. Court women wrote stories in Japanese using kana, a script developed in this era, while Chinese was the learned language of men.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'The Tale of Genji'

source2.name: Library of Congress blog, 'The Tale of Genji: 1,000 Years of Romance' (2025)

title: The Chola Temple Tower
text: King Rajaraja I of the Chola dynasty completed the Brihadisvara Temple, among the largest Hindu temples in India, with a granite tower about 60 metres tall. Its top is a single carved rock said to weigh about 80 tonnes, and legend says it was hauled up a ramp some 6 kilometres long. The temple is believed to have employed up to 400 dancers.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples (via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Brihadishvara Temple' (Sanat Pai Raikar; read in browser)

title: Vikings Reach North America
text: Norse sailors from Greenland built a small camp of turf houses at the northern tip of Newfoundland, nearly 500 years before Columbus. Scientists dated it exactly thanks to a solar storm in 993, which left a radiation marker in tree rings. Counting rings from that marker showed Norse metal tools cut wood here in 1021.

source.name: Kuitems et al., 'Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021', Nature 601 (2022) (PMC)
