source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site (via data.unesco.org)

title: The First Gunpowder Recipe
text: Song dynasty officials finished the Wujing Zongyao, a military handbook with the oldest known written formulas for gunpowder. Mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal, Song armies packed the powder into bombs launched by catapults. Funnily enough, gunpowder had been stumbled upon earlier by Taoist alchemists who were searching for medicines to help people live longer.

source.name: Peter A. Lorge, The Asian Military Revolution, ch. 1 'China through the Yuan' (Cambridge University Press)

source2.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'The First Fireworks: Origins of the Rocket'

title: Cahokia, City of Mounds
text: Near today's St. Louis, Cahokia was the largest city north of Mexico, home to perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people. They built over 100 earthen mounds, and the biggest, Monks Mound, has a base about as large as Egypt's Great Pyramid. Corn farming fed the city, and people played chunkey, throwing spears to mark where a rolling stone disc would stop.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: National Geographic

title: Angkor Wat Rises in the Jungle
text: King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat as a Hindu temple to the god Vishnu; it later became Buddhist. It is the largest religious monument in the world. One of its famous bas-reliefs shows gods and demons working together to churn an ocean of milk, with Vishnu at the centre.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Churches Carved Down Into Rock
text: Ethiopia's King Lalibela is credited with eleven churches cut straight down into solid volcanic rock. Instead of stacking stones, workers dug a deep trench around a block, then hollowed it out, carving windows and pillars as they went. The cross-shaped Church of Saint George stands apart from the others, and pilgrims still worship at Lalibela today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'The Rock-hewn Churches of Lalibela' (Kristen Windmuller-Luna)

title: Temüjin Becomes Genghis Khan
text: At a great gathering near the Onon River, the Mongol tribes proclaimed Temüjin their supreme ruler, Genghis Khan. He had grown up poor and hunted after his father was poisoned. His empire soon stretched across Asia; according to Marco Polo, its relay riders changed horses at stations about 40 km apart and could carry messages hundreds of kilometres in a day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pony Express: Conceiving the idea' (Joseph J. Di Certo; read in browser)

title: Polynesian Voyagers Reach Aotearoa
text: Steering double-hulled canoes by stars, waves and birds, Polynesian voyagers became the first people to settle New Zealand, one of the last big lands on Earth reached by humans. Wairau Bar is among the earliest sites. Settlers met moa, flightless birds up to about 3 metres tall, which were hunted to extinction within one or two centuries.

source.name: Bunbury et al. 2022, PNAS (via Europe PMC)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (moa)

title: The Stone Walls of Great Zimbabwe
text: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a rich trading kingdom in southern Africa. Its Great Enclosure has walls up to 11 metres high, built of granite blocks fitted together without any mortar. Finds there include Chinese porcelain and Persian pottery traded via the coast, and the modern country of Zimbabwe is named after it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Great Zimbabwe'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument (read via data.unesco.org)

title: Mansa Musa's Golden Pilgrimage
text: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan and camels loaded with gold. He handed out so much gold that its value in Cairo dropped for years. A famous 1375 atlas by a mapmaker from Majorca shows him on a throne holding a round gold object, perhaps a nugget.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Musa I of Mali' (J. C. de Graft-Johnson)

source2.name: British Library blog, 'African kings on medieval and renaissance maps'

title: Tenochtitlan Rises From a Lake
text: According to legend, the Mexica (Aztecs) settled where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco. They farmed chinampas, garden plots built up from lake mud and reeds. Tenochtitlan grew into one of the largest cities in the world, and that eagle-on-a-cactus scene sits on Mexico's flag today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tenochtitlan'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Flag of Mexico' (Whitney Smith)

title: Ibn Battuta Visits Kilwa
text: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta sailed down the Swahili coast and praised Kilwa as one of the most beautiful, well-built towns he had seen. Kilwa grew rich by controlling gold traded from inland Africa across the Indian Ocean. Its sultans minted their own copper coins for centuries, and some have turned up as far inland as Great Zimbabwe.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara (read via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe (read via data.unesco.org)

title: The Black Death Arrives by Ship
text: In early October 1347, twelve Genoese galleys docked at Messina in Sicily, carrying plague from the Black Sea. Spread by fleas on rats and from person to person, the Black Death killed perhaps a quarter to a third of Europe's people within a few years. One lasting legacy: 'quarantine' comes from the Italian for forty, the days arriving ships were held.

source.name: Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC), Tognotti 2013, 'Lessons from the history of quarantine' (PMC)

source2.name: Michele da Piazza (Michael Platiensis), chronicle of 1347, trans. C. H. Clarke, hosted at University of Szeged

title: A Giraffe Arrives at the Ming Court
text: During the era of Admiral Zheng He's treasure-fleet voyages, envoys from Bengal brought a giraffe from East Africa to the Yongle Emperor. Court officials declared it a qilin, a lucky mythical beast, and a court painter recorded it. Zheng He's fleets sailed as far as the Swahili coast, decades before Portuguese ships reached the Indian Ocean.

source.name: The Met, 'Giraffe with Two Keepers' (47.18.21) catalogue text

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng He'

title: Ulugh Beg's Star Observatory
text: Ulugh Beg, a Timurid prince who loved astronomy more than war, built a great observatory in Samarkand. Its giant curved instrument, sunk into a trench in the hillside, tracked the Sun and stars precisely. His team catalogued about 1,000 stars and measured the length of the year to within about a minute of today's value.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ulugh Beg'

source2.name: Stanford University (F. P. Jazra), 'The Significance of Ulugh Beg's Zij-i Sultani'

title: King Sejong Invents an Alphabet
text: King Sejong the Great created Hangul so ordinary Koreans, not just scholars who had mastered Chinese characters, could read and write. Some consonant letters are drawn to show the shape of the mouth and tongue making that sound. Its official guide, published in 1446, explained the principles behind the letters and praised the new script's excellence.

source.name: Korean Cultural Center New York (Korean government), 'The spirit and principles behind Hangeul's creation'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Joseon dynasty'

title: Machu Picchu in the Clouds
text: High in the Andes, the Inca built Machu Picchu, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti. Its finest stone blocks were fitted without mortar so tightly that a credit card can't slip between them, a method that helped the walls ride out earthquakes. Spanish conquerors never found it, and it became world-famous after Hiram Bingham's visit in 1911.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Machu Picchu'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu (read via data.unesco.org)

title: Gutenberg Prints a Bible
text: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg finished printing about 180 Bibles using movable metal type and oil-based ink. Movable type had been invented earlier in China and Korea, but his press helped books spread quickly across Europe. Around 49 copies survive today, and many had their colourful decorations painted in by hand after printing.

source.name: Library of Congress, 'The Gutenberg Bible' (Bible Collection exhibit)

source2.name: Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin, 'The Gutenberg Bible'

title: Columbus Lands in the Bahamas
text: After about five weeks at sea from the Canary Islands, Christopher Columbus's three ships reached an island in the Bahamas, home to the Lucayans, a Taíno people. Columbus insisted he had reached Asia. His voyages tied the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia, but for the Lucayans they were a catastrophe: within a generation they had been carried off to forced labour and wiped out.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Christopher Columbus: The first voyage)

source2.name: Florida Museum of Natural History (University of Florida), Caribbean Archaeology: Peoples of the Turks & Caicos / Lucayans

title: Vasco da Gama Reaches Calicut
text: Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and, guided by a pilot hired in Malindi, crossed the Indian Ocean to Calicut. The local ruler, the Zamorin, was unimpressed by his cheap gifts of cloth, hats and honey. Still, the voyage opened the first sea route from western Europe to India, and more Portuguese fleets soon followed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Vasco da Gama)

source2.name: Project Gutenberg: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499, tr. E. G. Ravenstein (Hakluyt Society, 1898)

title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
text: After a long siege, Hernán Cortés's Spanish troops and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, especially Tlaxcalans, captured the Aztec capital. A smallpox epidemic had already killed huge numbers of its people, including the emperor Cuitláhuac. The last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, was captured, and Mexico City was later built on top of the ruins.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Hernan Cortes)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Cuitlahuac; Cuauhtemoc)

title: First Voyage Around the World
text: The battered ship Victoria limped home with just 18 of the roughly 270 men who had set out three years earlier. Ferdinand Magellan had been killed in the Philippines, so Juan Sebastián Elcano led the final stretch. The survivors were puzzled to find their logbook a day behind: sailing west around the globe, they had 'lost' a day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ferdinand Magellan: Discovery of the Strait / Circumnavigation)

source2.name: Blair & Robertson, The Philippine Islands vol. 34 (Pigafetta's account), Project Gutenberg

title: A Kongo King Protests the Slave Trade
text: Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, wrote to the king of Portugal complaining that Portuguese traders were seizing his free people, even nobles' sons and his own relatives, and selling them as slaves. He asked for priests, teachers, doctors and pharmacists, and begged that no more traders be sent, since Kongo did not wish to export slaves.

source.name: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History (Nzinga Mbemba to King Joao III, 1526; trans. from Thornton 2023)

source2.name: Cambridge University Press, 'Cross-Cultural Experiments: The Materiality of Medicine in West-Central Africa' (doi 10.1017/9781108868020.003)

title: Potosí's Mountain of Silver
text: Silver was found in Cerro Rico, a mountain in the Andes, and Potosí boomed into one of the biggest cities in the Americas, about 4,000 metres above sea level. Its silver flowed to Spain and all the way to China. The wealth came at a terrible cost: Indigenous men were forced into dangerous mines under a labour draft called the mita.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Potosi)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (City of Potosi)

title: Sinan's Masterpiece in Istanbul
text: The architect Mimar Sinan finished the Süleymaniye Mosque for Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, when the Ottoman Empire was at its height. Sinan started out as a military engineer and went on to design hundreds of buildings. Clever air currents carried the soot from the mosque's hundreds of oil lamps into a special 'soot room' above the entrance.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Historic Areas of Istanbul)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sinan, the Ottoman Empire's Master Architect)

title: The Manila Galleons Set Sail
text: After Spain made Manila its colonial capital, great galleons crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco in Mexico, usually about once a year. They carried Mexican silver west and Chinese silk and porcelain east, linking Asia and the Americas for about 250 years. The eastbound crossing took around six months.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Manila galleon)

source2.name: Guampedia (Jillette Leon-Guerrero, 'Navigation and Cargo of the Manila Galleons')

title: Admiral Yi's Turtle Ships
text: When Japanese armies invaded Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin fought back at sea, partly with turtle ships, warships with a covered roof bristling with iron spikes to stop enemies from boarding. In 1592 he lured a Japanese fleet into Hansan Bay and wrapped around it in a 'crane wing' formation. Yi won every sea battle he fought against the Japanese.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Yi Sun-shin)

source2.name: EBSCO Research Starters (Jason Ridler, 'Battle of the Yellow Sea', 2019)

title: Sweet Potatoes Reach China
text: A Chinese merchant, Chen Zhenlong, brought sweet potato vines home to Fujian from Spanish-ruled Luzon in the Philippines, reportedly hidden in a rope. When famine struck, the governor urged farmers to plant them. This American crop thrived on poor hillsides, and along with maize and peanuts it helped China's population grow over the next two centuries.

source.name: Fuzhou Municipal People's Government (article from the city gazetteer office), 'China's father of the sweet potato' Chen Zhenlong

source2.name: Asia for Educators, Columbia University, 'China in 1750: demographic change'

title: Shah Abbas Rebuilds Isfahan
text: Shah Abbas I made Isfahan the capital of Safavid Iran and built Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the 'Image of the World', one of the largest city squares in the world at 560 metres long. Lined with mosques, a palace and a bazaar, its vast sandy esplanade hosted polo matches, celebrations and parades of troops.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (ISFAHAN vii. Safavid Period)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Meidan Emam, Esfahan), text via UNESCO open data API

title: Galileo Spots Jupiter's Moons
text: Galileo Galilei pointed his home-made telescope at Jupiter and saw four little 'stars' that moved around it night after night. They were moons, proof that not everything in the sky circles the Earth. He named them after the powerful Medici family to win their favour, but today we call them Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

source.name: Museo Galileo, Florence (In depth: Jupiter's moons)

source2.name: NASA Science (Night Sky Notes: From Galileo to Clipper, Exploring Jupiter's Moons)

title: Nzinga Bargains with Portugal
text: Nzinga, sister of the king of Ndongo, came to Luanda to negotiate with the Portuguese governor. A famous story says he offered her no chair, so she sat on a kneeling attendant's back to meet him at eye level. She later ruled Ndongo and Matamba, outwitting the Portuguese for decades with war, diplomacy and alliances with the Dutch.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Nzinga)

source2.name: South African History Online, 'Njinga Ana de Sousa'

title: Shah Jahan Begins the Taj Mahal
text: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth after bearing him 14 children. More than 20,000 workers built the complex over about 22 years. Work began around 1632, and its gleaming white marble is inlaid with semi-precious stones.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Taj Mahal)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Taj Mahal), text via UNESCO open data API

title: Tulip Mania Goes Bust
text: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared, especially striped ones, whose stripes were actually caused by a virus. The most expensive bulbs cost around 5,000 guilders, while a master craftsman earned about 300 guilders a year. Then in early February 1637 the bottom fell out of the market: most buyers would not pay, and sellers were left holding the bulbs.

source.name: Britannica Money (Tulip Mania, by Doug Ashburn)

source2.name: The Conversation, Anne Goldgar (King's College London), 'Tulip mania: the classic story of a Dutch financial bubble is mostly wrong'

title: Japan's Tiny Window: Dejima
text: Japan's Tokugawa shoguns sharply limited contact with Europeans and moved Dutch traders onto Dejima, a small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbour. For about two centuries it was the only place Europeans could trade in Japan. Through it came books on Western medicine and science, which Japanese scholars studied as 'Dutch learning'.

source.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary database (MLIT): Dejima Dutch Trading Post

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (sakoku)

title: Coffee Sails from Mocha
text: Yemen was the world's main source of coffee, and its port of Mocha shipped beans across the Middle East and the Ottoman world and, more and more, to Europe. Sufi mystics in Yemen drank coffee to stay awake through night-time prayers. The port's name stuck around, and today a café mocha is a mix of coffee and chocolate.

source.name: The Conversation (Ibrahim Al-Marashi, CSU San Marcos), 'The Mocha monopoly', republished by Down To Earth

source2.name: JSTOR Daily, Matthew Wills, 'Why Coffee is Sometimes Called Mocha'

title: The Pueblo Revolt
text: Led by a Tewa religious leader named Popé, Pueblo peoples rose up against Spanish colonists who had banned their religion and forced them to work. Runners carried knotted cords between villages; each day one knot was untied, counting down to the uprising. The Spanish were driven out of Santa Fe and stayed away for 12 years.

source.name: Architect of the Capitol: Po'pay statue

source2.name: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis: '1680: The Pueblo Revolt'

title: Newton Explains Gravity
text: Cambridge professor Isaac Newton published the Principia, showing how one force, gravity, makes apples fall and also keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits. His three laws of motion revolutionized science and still explain how aircraft and rockets fly. The astronomer Edmond Halley urged him to write it and even paid for the printing out of his own pocket.

source.name: The Newton Project (University of Oxford), Brewster's Life of Newton, ch. XII

source2.name: Cambridge University Library, Newton Papers: Principia

title: The Kangxi Dictionary
text: The Qing emperor Kangxi ordered scholars to compile a giant dictionary of Chinese characters, completed in 1716. It lists more than 40,000 characters, sorted under 'radicals', shared building-block shapes. Most standard dictionaries still arrange characters by radical and stroke count today, and Kangxi himself ruled for six decades, from 1661 to 1722.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kangxi' and 'Chinese languages' (Kangxi zidian entries)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of China: The Ming dynasty'

title: Dahomey's Women Soldiers
text: The West African kingdom of Dahomey had an all-female military regiment, the Agojie, whom Europeans called 'Amazons'. They trained fiercely, guarded the king's palace and fought in many wars. Dahomey also grew rich by selling war captives into the Atlantic slave trade, a painful part of its story. The 2022 film The Woman King was inspired by them.

source.name: The Conversation, Dominique Somda (University of Cape Town), 'The Woman King is more than an action movie'

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, Meilan Solly, 'The Real Warriors Behind The Woman King' (Sept 15, 2022)

title: Watching Venus from Tahiti
text: James Cook sailed to Tahiti so astronomers could time Venus crossing the face of the Sun, to help work out the distance from Earth to the Sun. The Tahitian navigator and priest Tupaia then joined the voyage and drew a remarkable chart of Pacific islands from his own knowledge. He also helped the British talk with Māori in New Zealand.

source.name: National Library of Australia, Digital Classroom: Transit of Venus

source2.name: University of Potsdam, Institute of English and American Studies: Tupaia's Map

title: America Declares Independence
text: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in a document drafted mostly by Thomas Jefferson, which proclaimed that all men are created equal. Yet many signers, Jefferson included, enslaved people, a contradiction critics pointed out even at the time. Surprisingly, most delegates didn't sign the famous handwritten copy until August 2.

source.name: U.S. National Archives: The Declaration of Independence: A History

source2.name: Thomas Jefferson Foundation (Monticello): Thomas Jefferson, Liberty & Slavery

title: Gorée and the Door of No Return
text: Gorée, a small island off Dakar, was a European trading post during the Atlantic slave trade, when millions of Africans were forced across the ocean to the Americas. Its House of Slaves, built in the late 1700s, is now a museum and memorial. Historians debate how many captives actually passed through Gorée, but its 'Door of No Return' has become a powerful symbol.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Island of Gorée

source2.name: Associated Press (Rukmini Callimachi), 'Obama visits slave site of disputed importance', 27 June 2013

title: Túpac Amaru II's Rebellion
text: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a descendant of the last Inca ruler, took the name Túpac Amaru II and led a huge uprising against Spanish colonial abuses in the Andes. His wife, Micaela Bastidas, issued orders, organised supplies and coordinated attacks. The Spanish crushed the revolt and executed them both in Cusco in 1781, but both are honoured as heroes in Peru today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tupac Amaru II

source2.name: Biblioteca Nacional del Perú: Sara Beatriz Guardia, 'Micaela Bastidas' (digital edition)

title: Laki's Poison Fog
text: The Laki volcano in Iceland erupted from a crack about 25 kilometres long for eight months, pouring out lava and poisonous gas. Most of Iceland's sheep died, and in the famine that followed about a fifth of Iceland's people perished. A strange haze drifted over Europe, and that summer the English naturalist Gilbert White saw the sun turn blood-coloured at sunrise and sunset.

source.name: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory: Volcano Watch, Laki and Eldgjá

source2.name: Mortality induced by PM2.5 exposure following the 1783 Laki eruption, PubMed Central

title: Storming the Bastille
text: Angry Parisians, worried about soaring bread prices and royal troops, stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress-prison, looking for gunpowder. Inside they found just seven prisoners. The attack became the symbol of the French Revolution, July 14 is now France's national holiday, and Lafayette later sent one of the Bastille's keys to George Washington.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bastille

source2.name: George Washington's Mount Vernon: Bastille Key

title: The Haitian Revolution Begins
text: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, then the most profitable colony in the Americas thanks to its sugar and coffee, organised and planned a huge revolt. Led later by Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man, they fought off French, Spanish and British armies. In 1804 Haiti became the first nation founded by people who had freed themselves from slavery.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Haitian Revolution

source2.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: The United States and the Haitian Revolution, 1791-1804

title: Mary Anning's Sea Dragon
text: On the crumbly cliffs of England's south coast, Mary Anning's brother Joseph found the skull of an ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped reptile from the age of dinosaurs, in 1811, when Mary was 12. About a year later Mary dug out the rest of the skeleton. She sold fossils to help pay her poor family's debts. Scientists often overlooked her, but today she is celebrated as a pioneering palaeontologist.

source.name: Natural History Museum (London), Mary Anning: the unsung hero

source2.name: Natural History Museum (London), Mary Anning: the unsung hero

title: Tambora and the Year Without Summer
text: Mount Tambora blew apart in the biggest eruption in recorded history, killing tens of thousands of people on the island. Its ash veiled the sky so well that 1816 became the Year Without a Summer, with snow in June in New England. Stuck indoors during that gloomy summer, Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mount Tambora

source2.name: UC Berkeley News, 200th anniversary of Tambora eruption (2015)

title: The First Steam Railway for Everyone
text: George Stephenson's engine, Locomotion No. 1, pulled wagons of coal and cheering passengers along the world's first public railway to use steam engines. A man on horseback rode ahead of the train carrying a flag to warn people off the track. Within a few decades, railways would knit whole continents together.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Stockton & Darlington Railway

source2.name: Science Museum Group Collection, Steam locomotive No. 1 'Locomotion', Stockton & Darlington Railway

title: A Newspaper in Cherokee
text: The Cherokee Phoenix, the first newspaper published by a Native American nation, printed its first issue in English and Cherokee. Its Cherokee columns used a writing system invented by Sequoyah, who spoke no language other than Cherokee. His syllabary was rapidly adopted by a large number of Cherokees.

source.name: New Georgia Encyclopedia (Georgia Humanities / UGA Press), Cherokee Phoenix

source2.name: New Georgia Encyclopedia, Sequoyah

title: Hokusai's Great Wave
text: Hokusai, an artist born in 1760, designed a woodblock print of a giant wave curling over tiny boats, with Mount Fuji small in the distance. Prints like this could be made in great quantity for Edo's townspeople. Its deep blues mixed traditional indigo with Prussian blue, an exotic pigment newly available to printers, and the image has become a global icon of Japanese art.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (JP1847)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Great Wave: Anatomy of an Icon' (Marco Leona, 2020)

title: Darwin Meets the Galápagos
text: The young naturalist Charles Darwin spent about five weeks in these volcanic islands aboard HMS Beagle. The islands' vice-governor, Nicholas Lawson, told him he could tell which island a giant tortoise came from just by its shell, and Darwin noticed mockingbirds differed from island to island too. Those small differences helped spark his theory of evolution by natural selection.

source.name: Darwin Online (University of Cambridge), R. Keynes, Darwin's field notes on the Galapagos

title: Lin Zexu Destroys the Opium
text: Commissioner Lin Zexu seized more than a thousand tonnes of British opium and destroyed it by mixing it with lime and salt in trenches, then flushing it out to sea. He even wrote a letter to Queen Victoria asking her to stop the trade. Britain answered with the First Opium War, which forced China to hand over Hong Kong.

source.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, The First Opium War (essay)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Nanjing

title: The Treaty of Waitangi
text: Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed a treaty in a marquee on the lawn at Waitangi, and copies later travelled the country for more chiefs to sign. The English and Māori versions did not say quite the same thing about who would rule. New Zealanders still debate that gap today, and February 6 is now the national day.

source.name: Waitangi Tribunal (NZ Ministry of Justice), About the Treaty

source2.name: Waitangi National Trust (Waitangi Treaty Grounds), Waitangi Day

title: Women Demand the Vote at Seneca Falls
text: Around 300 people packed a small chapel for the first women's rights convention in the United States. Elizabeth Cady Stanton wrote a Declaration of Sentiments modelled on the Declaration of Independence, adding that all men and women are created equal. One hundred people signed it, including the famous abolitionist Frederick Douglass.

source.name: US National Park Service, Women's Rights NHP, The First Women's Rights Convention

source2.name: US National Park Service, Declaration of Sentiments (text and signers)

title: Gold Fever in Ballarat
text: Gold was found in Victoria, and diggers rushed in from across Australia and around the world; by 1855 about 20,000 Chinese were on the Victorian diggings. Victoria's population jumped from 76,000 in 1851 to 540,000 in 1860. In 1869 two miners at Moliagul, north of Ballarat, dug up the Welcome Stranger, a nugget weighing about 72 kilograms.

source.name: National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: Eureka Stockade

source2.name: State Library Victoria (Ergo), 'Richest discoveries'

title: The Taiping Heavenly Capital
text: Hong Xiuquan, a failed exam candidate who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, led his Taiping rebels into Nanjing and renamed it the Heavenly Capital. His movement banned opium and foot-binding and promised shared land. The civil war that followed lasted until 1864 and was one of the deadliest in human history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Taiping Rebellion'

title: The Smoke That Thunders
text: Guided by men from the Makololo chief Sekeletu, the Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached a waterfall whose spray rose like smoke above the Zambezi River. Locals already called it Mosi-oa-Tunya, the Smoke That Thunders. Livingstone renamed it for Queen Victoria, but the falls, more than a kilometre and a half wide, are known by both names today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'David Livingstone'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Mosi-oa-Tunya / Victoria Falls'

title: The Great Uprising of 1857
text: Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army rose up at Meerut, angered partly by rumours that their new rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat. The revolt spread across northern India, with leaders like Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi leading troops in battle. Afterwards, Britain abolished the Company and ruled India directly.

source.name: National Army Museum, 'Why did the Indian Rebellion happen?'

source2.name: National Army Museum, 'Decisive events of the Indian Rebellion'

title: The Meiji Restoration
text: After more than 250 years of shogun rule, a coup in Kyoto proclaimed the young Emperor Meiji ruler of Japan. The court moved to Edo and renamed it Tokyo, the Eastern Capital. By 1871 the old feudal class privileges, including those of the samurai, were abolished, and Japan built railways, industry and schools so fast that by 1919 it counted among the world's five great powers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Meiji Restoration'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Meiji Restoration'

title: Mendeleev's Table With Gaps
text: Chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by weight and found their properties repeated in a pattern. His boldest move was leaving empty spaces for elements nobody had found yet, and predicting what they would be like. When gallium was discovered in 1875, it matched his forecast closely, and his periodic table hangs in classrooms everywhere.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Dmitri Mendeleev'

title: The Suez Canal Opens
text: A new canal about 164 kilometres long joined the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, so ships no longer had to sail all the way around Africa. A sea voyage from Rotterdam to Mumbai became about 41 percent shorter. Much of the digging was done by Egyptian peasants forced into labour, and many thousands died building it.

source.name: Suez Canal Authority, Canal History

source2.name: The Conversation (Jonathan Parry, University of Cambridge)

title: The Zulu Victory at Isandlwana
text: When Britain invaded the Zulu kingdom, King Cetshwayo's army of about 20,000 warriors overran a British camp beneath the distinctive hill of Isandlwana. It was one of the worst disasters the British Army suffered in the late 1800s. A partial solar eclipse occurred during the battle, and one Zulu warrior recalled the sun turning black; Britain still conquered the kingdom months later.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battles of Isandlwana and Rorke's Drift'

source2.name: National Army Museum, 'The Battle of Isandlwana, 22 January 1879'

title: The Loudest Sound in History
text: The volcanic island of Krakatoa exploded with a bang heard on Rodrigues Island, nearly 4,800 kilometres away across the Indian Ocean. Its tsunamis killed tens of thousands of people along the coasts of Java and Sumatra. Ash in the upper air turned sunsets around the world a glowing red for months.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory, Anak Krakatau

source2.name: NOAA NCEI, On This Day: Historic Krakatau Eruption of 1883

title: Brazil Ends Slavery
text: Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law, a two-article decree that freed everyone still enslaved in Brazil. Brazil had taken in nearly half of all enslaved Africans landed alive in the Americas, and it was the last independent country in the Americas to end slavery. Rio de Janeiro exploded in celebration as an excited crowd filled the city centre.

source.name: Arquivo Nacional (Brazil), Você sabia que a Lei Áurea faz parte do acervo do Arquivo Nacional?

source2.name: Câmara dos Deputados (Brazil), Rádio Câmara: Em 1888, a princesa Isabel assinou a Lei Áurea

title: The First Country Where Women Vote
text: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let all women vote in national elections, Māori women included. Campaigners led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures, and Sheppard pasted the petition sheets end to end into a roll about 270 metres long. Less than two months after it reached Parliament, 109,461 women had enrolled to vote.

source.name: New Zealand Parliament, Suffrage Day, 19 September: celebrating women's right to vote

source2.name: New Zealand Parliament, 'A monster' petition! 125th anniversary of the suffrage petition

title: The First Movie Night
text: In the Salon Indien of the Grand Café in Paris, the Lumière brothers charged admission to watch moving pictures on a screen. The programme was ten films, each under a minute, including workers walking out of their own factory. Only about thirty people came the first night, but within weeks up to 2,500 spectators a day were flocking in.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Lumière brothers

source2.name: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Passerelles: Invention du cinéma

title: Ethiopia Wins at Adwa
text: Emperor Menelik II's huge Ethiopian army, with Empress Taytu leading troops of her own, defeated an invading Italian force near Adwa. It was the first crushing defeat of a European power by African forces in the colonial era and checked Italy's empire-building. The victory became an emblem for Pan-African movements, and Ethiopians still gather to celebrate it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Adwa

source2.name: Anadolu Agency, 'Ethiopians celebrate 125th anniversary of Adwa Victory'

title: Korea Becomes an Empire
text: King Gojong declared himself emperor at a new altar in Seoul, announcing that Korea answered to no other country. His Korean Empire raced to modernise, and electric streetcars began rattling through Seoul in 1899, just five years after Kyoto's. Japan annexed Korea in 1910, ending the empire after just thirteen years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gojong

source2.name: Seoul Metropolitan Government, Hwangudan Altar

title: The Hidden Library of Dunhuang
text: Around 1900 a Daoist monk named Wang Yuanlu found a sealed cave packed with tens of thousands of old scrolls on the Silk Road. Among them was a copy of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, the oldest dated printed book in the world. In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein bought many manuscripts, including the Diamond Sutra, and carried them off to Britain.

source.name: International Dunhuang Programme (British Library): Buddhist caves: Dunhuang

source2.name: International Dunhuang Programme (British Library): Buddhist texts: The Diamond Sutra

title: Yaa Asantewaa and the Golden Stool
text: When a British governor demanded the Golden Stool so that he could sit on it, the Asante were outraged: the sacred stool was believed to hold the spirit of the whole nation. Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, rallied fighters and besieged the British fort at Kumasi. She was captured and exiled, but the British never got the Golden Stool.

source.name: The Open University (OpenLearn Create, TESSA Ghana): The Yaa Asantewaa War of 1900

source2.name: Wasserman, B. (1961) 'The Ashanti War of 1900: A Study in Cultural Conflict', Africa 31(2) (Cambridge)

title: Twelve Seconds in the Air
place: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, USA
text: Bicycle makers Orville and Wilbur Wright flew the first powered, controlled aeroplane over windy sand dunes. Orville's first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet (37 metres); later that day Wilbur flew 852 feet in 59 seconds. The brothers had tossed a coin to decide who would try first, Wilbur won, but his try three days earlier stalled.

source.name: National Park Service, Wright Brothers National Memorial: The First Flight

source2.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: 1903 Wright Flyer

title: A Railway for Pilgrims
text: The Ottoman Hejaz Railway reached Medina, linking it to Damascus across about 1,300 kilometres of desert. Paid for partly by donations from Muslims around the world, it cut a pilgrim's journey from weeks on a camel caravan to a few days. During the First World War, raiders blew up its tracks, and much of it was never rebuilt.

source.name: AramcoWorld: Ottoman-Era Hijaz Railway's Legacy Endures, Chugging Toward Revival (2026)

source2.name: The Spectator Archive, 29 August 1908, p.1 (Times correspondent en route to Medina ceremonies)

title: The Tunguska Blast
text: Something from space, probably a small asteroid or comet, exploded in the air above the Siberian forest. It flattened around 80 million trees over an area bigger than London, yet left no crater. For a few nights afterwards, the sky over Europe glowed so brightly that people said they could read outdoors at midnight.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: The Tunguska event explained

source2.name: NASA History: 115 Years Ago, the Tunguska Asteroid Impact Event

title: Zapata's Land and Liberty
text: During the Mexican Revolution, the peasant leader and horse trainer Emiliano Zapata issued the Plan of Ayala in November 1911. It demanded that land seized by big haciendas be given back to the villages that held titles to it, and declared President Madero unfit to carry out the revolution. Zapata adopted the slogan "Tierra y Libertad" (Land and Liberty).

source.name: Orden Jurídico Nacional (Mexican Government): Plan de Ayala, full text

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Emiliano Zapata

title: Tagore Wins the Nobel Prize
text: The Bengali poet Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, for his song-poems Gitanjali. He ran an open-air school at Santiniketan where classes were often held under trees. He also wrote songs that later became the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Rabindranath Tagore (by W. Andrew Robinson)

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: Rabindranath Tagore, Facts

title: The Christmas Truce
text: In the first winter of the First World War, soldiers along parts of the front stopped fighting on their own for Christmas. British and German troops climbed out of their trenches, sang carols, swapped cigarettes and chocolate, and in some places kicked a football around. Generals made sure it never happened on that scale again.

source.name: Imperial War Museums: The Real Story of the Christmas Truce

source2.name: National Army Museum: Christmas in the First World War

title: Two Samoas, Two Fates
text: The 1918 flu pandemic reached Western Samoa from Auckland, New Zealand, and more than a fifth of the population died. Just across the water, the U.S. Navy imposed a strict quarantine on American Samoa. Thanks to that quarantine, American Samoa recorded no flu deaths at all, a lesson that public health experts still cite.

source.name: Epidemiology and Infection (PMC): Pacific islands which escaped the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic and their subsequent mortality experiences

title: Tutankhamun's Tomb Found
text: Howard Carter's team uncovered a step cut into the rock, leading down to the almost untouched tomb of a boy pharaoh. Inside were more than 5,000 objects, from a solid gold coffin to furniture, chariots and weapons. Tutankhamun had little claim to fame in his own time, but his tomb made him perhaps the best-known pharaoh of all.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Discovering Tutankhamun: The Photographs of Harry Burton

source2.name: Griffith Institute, University of Oxford: Tutankhamun, 1st Season (1922-1923)

title: A Lost City on the Indus
text: Archaeologists announced that ruins dug up near the Indus River belonged to a forgotten civilization about 4,500 years old. Mohenjo-daro had grid-like streets, an elaborate drainage system and a huge public bath, and some houses even had their own bathing rooms. Its people wrote in a script that nobody has managed to read to this day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mohenjo-daro

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Indus civilization

title: The Mould That Saved Millions
text: Returning from a holiday, scientist Alexander Fleming noticed that a fuzzy mould had landed on one of his dishes of bacteria and killed the germs around it. He named the mystery substance penicillin. It took other scientists more than a decade to turn it into a medicine, but antibiotics have since saved countless lives.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Alexander Fleming

source2.name: American Chemical Society: Alexander Fleming Discovery and Development of Penicillin (National Historic Chemical Landmark)

title: Peking Man's Skull
text: In a limestone cave near Beijing, the young Chinese archaeologist Pei Wenzhong dug up an ancient skullcap of Homo erectus, an early human relative who lived there hundreds of thousands of years ago. More fossils followed. In 1941, while being shipped to safety during the war, the bones vanished, and nobody knows where they are.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Peking Man Site at Zhoukoudian (via UNESCO open-data API)

source2.name: Discourses of Race and Rising China (2019), PMC

title: Gandhi's Salt March
text: Mahatma Gandhi walked about 385 kilometres over 24 days to the sea to protest a British tax on salt, something every family needed. He set out with 78 followers, and crowds grew at every village. At Dandi beach he picked up a lump of salt, breaking the law and inspiring protests across India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Salt March

source2.name: National Gandhi Museum, 'Dandi March and Salt Satyagraha' (via mkgandhi.org, Gandhi Research Foundation)

title: The Bombing of Hiroshima
text: An American plane dropped the first atomic bomb used in war on Hiroshima, killing tens of thousands of people in an instant and many more later. Three days later Nagasaki was bombed, and Japan soon surrendered. A domed building near the blast survived as a ruin, and today it stands in a peace park as a reminder.

source.name: U.S. Department of Energy OSTI, Manhattan Project: The Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome) (via UNESCO open-data API)

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
text: Bedouin shepherds exploring a cave above the Dead Sea found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade, searchers recovered pieces of hundreds more from nearby caves. Some are over 2,000 years old, including the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, preserved by the bone-dry desert air.

source.name: Israel Antiquities Authority, Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library: Discovery and Publication

source2.name: Israel Antiquities Authority, Leon Levy DSS Digital Library: Introduction

title: Independence at Midnight
text: At the stroke of midnight, India became independent after about two centuries of British rule, and Pakistan had been born a day earlier. Jawaharlal Nehru marked the moment with his famous Tryst with Destiny speech. But the hurried partition uprooted more than ten million people and brought terrible violence on both sides of the new border.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Partition of India

source2.name: Free Press Journal, FPJ Archives: Nehru's Tryst with Destiny

title: The People's Republic Is Proclaimed
text: After decades of war, Mao Zedong stood atop Tiananmen, the old gate to the imperial palace, and proclaimed the People's Republic of China. The defeated Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan. Mao's portrait still hangs on that same gate, looking out over one of the largest public squares in the world.

source.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Chinese Revolution of 1949

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tiananmen Square

title: Top of the World
text: Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa climber, and Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, became the first people confirmed to stand on the summit of Everest. They stayed only about fifteen minutes. The news reached London just as Queen Elizabeth II was crowned, and Tenzing became a hero across Nepal and India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Edmund Hillary'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tenzing Norgay'

title: Ghana Breaks Free
text: The British colony called the Gold Coast became independent Ghana, one of the first countries in sub-Saharan Africa to win freedom from colonial rule. As midnight struck in Accra, leader Kwame Nkrumah told cheering crowds that Ghana was free forever. Its new flag carried a black star, a symbol of African emancipation and unity in the struggle against colonialism.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kwame Nkrumah'

source2.name: UPI Archives, 'Ghana, first Negro native colony, born' (6 March 1957)

title: Sputnik Beeps From Orbit
text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, from the steppes of Kazakhstan. It was a shiny metal ball about the size of a beach ball, circling Earth every 96 minutes. Radio fans around the world could tune in to its simple beep-beep signal, and the Space Race had begun.

source.name: NASA History Office, Roger D. Launius, 'Sputnik and the Origins of the Space Age'

source2.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'Music Box, Sputnik Model'

title: The Strongest Earthquake Ever Recorded
text: Southern Chile was struck by the most powerful earthquake ever measured, about magnitude 9.5. The ground shook hard for several minutes, and the tsunami it caused raced across the whole Pacific. Waves hit Hawaii about fifteen hours later and reached Japan, on the far side of the ocean, almost a day after the quake.

source.name: NOAA Science On a Sphere, 'Tsunami Historical Series: Chile - 1960'

source2.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, 'On This Day: 1960 Chilean Earthquake and Tsunami'

title: The First Bullet Train
text: Just days before Tokyo hosted the Olympics, the Shinkansen began zipping between Tokyo and Osaka at up to 210 kilometres per hour. It was the world's first high-speed railway line. Its trains became famous for punctuality, with average delays measured in seconds, and other countries soon copied the idea.

source.name: International Union of Railways (UIC), 'High-Speed Rail History'

source2.name: JR Central, 'Tokaido Shinkansen' (average delay 12 seconds as of 2019)

title: Footprints on the Moon
text: Four days after launching from Florida, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins circled overhead. Hundreds of millions of people watched the grainy black-and-white broadcast. With no wind on the Moon, their bootprints in the grey dust are probably still there.

source.name: NASA, 'July 20, 1969: One Giant Leap For Mankind'

source2.name: NASA StarChild, 'Apollo 11' (Level 1)

title: Farmers Find the Terracotta Army
text: Farmers digging a well during a drought struck pieces of a clay head. They had found the edge of a buried army made to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor. Archaeologists estimate there are around 8,000 life-sized soldiers, each with its own face, plus horses and chariots.

source.name: National Geographic, 'About Emperor Qin's Terra Cotta Army'

source2.name: National Geographic, 'Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor'

title: The Khmer Rouge Empty a Capital
text: Khmer Rouge soldiers marched into Phnom Penh and, within days, forced its whole population out into the countryside. Their leaders wanted to restart history at Year Zero, abolishing money, schools and religion. In under four years, up to two million Cambodians died, and survivors today keep the memory alive at memorials and museums.

source.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, 'Day One: April 17, 1975'

source2.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, 'Explore Cambodia 1975-1979'

title: The Last Case of Smallpox
text: Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook, became the last person on Earth to catch smallpox naturally, a disease that had killed hundreds of millions over history. He recovered, and in 1980 the world declared smallpox wiped out, the first human disease ever eradicated. Maalin later spent years helping vaccinate children against polio.

source.name: US CDC, 'History of Smallpox'

source2.name: WHO, 'History of smallpox vaccination'

title: The Moon Goddess Under the Street
text: Electricity workers digging in downtown Mexico City hit a giant carved stone disc about three metres wide. It showed Coyolxauhqui, an Aztec moon goddess, and it marked the foot of the Templo Mayor, the great temple of Tenochtitlan. The government let 13 buildings be torn down, and the digs revealed the heart of the Aztec capital beneath the modern streets.

source.name: INAH (Mexico), bulletin on the anniversary of the Coyolxauhqui discovery

source2.name: INAH Repositorio, Coyolxauhqui monolith record

title: Uluru Returns to Its Owners
text: The Australian government handed the title to Uluru back to the Anangu, its traditional owners, who then leased it back as a national park. Anangu had long asked visitors not to climb the sacred rock. On the same date in 2019, the climb was closed for good.

source.name: Parks Australia, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park: History

source2.name: Parks Australia, Uluru climb closure

title: People Power on EDSA
text: Huge crowds filled EDSA, a major Manila highway, to protest the dictator Ferdinand Marcos after a stolen election. Nuns knelt in front of tanks, and people handed flowers and food to soldiers, many of whom switched sides. After four days, Marcos fled the country, and Corazon Aquino became president.

source.name: TIME, 'The Philippines: Anatomy of a Revolution' (1986)

source2.name: TIME, 'Has the Philippines Moved On From Ferdinand Marcos' Dictatorship?'

title: The Seoul Olympics
text: South Korea, whose economic miracle had risen from the rubble of war, hosted the Summer Olympics with a friendly tiger mascot named Hodori. After two Games hit by boycotts, the United States and the Soviet Union met at a Summer Olympics for the first time since 1976. The Games also helped push South Korea toward democracy.

source.name: International Olympic Committee, Seoul 1988

source2.name: Korea.net, 'Olympic mascots symbolize protection, harmony'

title: The Berlin Wall Opens
text: At a confused press conference, an East German official announced new travel rules and said, by mistake, that they started right away. Thousands rushed to the checkpoints, and overwhelmed guards opened the gates. Berliners climbed onto the wall that had split their city for 28 years and began chipping off pieces as souvenirs.

source.name: Berlin.de (State of Berlin), 'Opening and fall of the Berlin Wall'

source2.name: Bundesregierung, 'Chronik der Deutschen Einheit: 09. November 1989'

title: Mandela Walks Free
text: After 27 years in prison for fighting apartheid, the system of racial segregation, Nelson Mandela walked out of the gates of Victor Verster Prison with Winnie Mandela by his side, raising his fist in the ANC salute. His speech that day was broadcast live around the world. Four years later he voted for the first time in his life and became South Africa's president.

source.name: South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

source2.name: TIME, 'Prisoner' (1990 archive)

title: The First Website Goes Public
text: British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web so researchers at a physics lab could share documents, and in 1991 he opened it to the public. The very first website explained what the web was and how to use it. It ran on a single computer with a handwritten label warning people not to switch it off.

source.name: CERN, 'A short history of the Web'

title: Hong Kong Changes Hands
text: At midnight on a rainy night, the British flag came down and Hong Kong returned to China after more than 150 years as a British colony. Under a deal called one country, two systems, the city was promised its own laws and way of life for fifty years. The last British governor sailed away on the royal yacht.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Handover of Hong Kong

source2.name: Imperial War Museums: Chris Patten arrives on board HMY Britannia (CT 1626)

title: The Woman Who Planted Millions of Trees
text: Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her Green Belt Movement paid rural women a small amount for each tree seedling they grew, fighting soil erosion and giving them income at the same time. Together they planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya, despite Maathai being beaten and arrested for her activism.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Wangari Maathai - Speed read

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: Wangari Maathai - Nobel Lecture

title: The Ship That Blocked the World
text: Strong winds are thought to have pushed the Ever Given, a container ship about 400 metres long, sideways across the Suez Canal. For six days, hundreds of ships piled up at both ends while global trade waited. Photos of one small digger scooping at the giant ship's bow became a popular online joke about tackling impossible tasks.

source.name: The Conversation: Suez Canal blockage - how cargo ships like Ever Given became so huge

source2.name: Georgia Southern University Magazine: How did the Suez Canal blockage back up shipping for months?

title: A Sea Reptile Caught Giving Birth
text: Chaohusaurus was an early ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped sea reptile only about a metre long. One fossil from Chaohu, reported in 2014, shows a mother with babies inside her and one baby halfway out. The surprise: it was coming out head-first, the way land animals are born, a hint that ichthyosaurs had ancestors that lived on land.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Motani et al. 2014), via PubMed Central

source2.name: National Geographic

title: The Maybe-First Dinosaur
text: Nyasasaurus may be the oldest dinosaur ever found, or at least a very close cousin of dinosaurs. Its few bones were dug up in Tanzania in the 1930s, then sat in a London museum for decades. It was only formally described in December 2012, which could push the dinosaur story back 10 to 15 million years.

source.name: University of Washington News

title: The Reptile with a Fishing-Rod Neck
text: This mountain beside Lake Lugano was once a shallow sea, and its rocks are packed with fossil fish and marine reptiles. The star is Tanystropheus, whose stiff neck was about three times as long as its torso. It was probably an ambush hunter, and the larger species ate fish and squid. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

source.name: State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart (press release)

source2.name: Swiss Journal of Palaeontology (special issue editorial), via PubMed Central

title: When It Rained for a Million Years
text: For roughly a million years or more, Earth's dry Triassic climate turned humid and rainy, a change geologists can read in rock layers like those of the Dolomites. Many animals and plants vanished during this Carnian Pluvial Event. Afterwards, dinosaurs spread and diversified fast, so a very long rainy spell may have helped set the stage for them.

source.name: Nature Communications (Bernardi et al. 2018), via PubMed Central

title: Nevada's Giant Sea Monster
text: Today this spot is high desert, but Shonisaurus once swam here in a sea that covered much of Nevada. These ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles the size of a school bus. Bones of some 37 animals were found beside the old mining town of Berlin, and in 1977 Nevada made Shonisaurus its official state fossil.

source.name: University of California Museum of Paleontology

source2.name: University of Nevada, Reno

title: Trees That Turned into Rainbow Stone
place: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
text: Giant logs washed into Triassic rivers and were buried quickly and deeply. Over time, silica dissolved from volcanic ash soaked in and replaced the wood with quartz, while traces of iron, carbon and manganese gave it its colours. Taking any is illegal: with over half a million visitors a year, the park could be stripped within a few years.

source.name: US National Park Service: Petrified Wood

source2.name: US National Park Service: Petrified Forest FAQ

title: A Crater You Can See from Space
text: A space rock about 5 kilometres wide slammed into what is now Quebec, leaving one of the world's largest impact craters. Erosion has worn it down to about 72 kilometres across, and a ring-shaped lake now fills part of it. Easy to spot from space and a favourite of astronaut photographers, it is sometimes called the 'Eye of Quebec'.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory

title: One of the First Flying Reptiles
text: Eudimorphodon showed that pterosaurs, the flying reptiles of the dinosaur age, were already in the air in the Triassic. Found in 1973 at Cene, near Bergamo, it was about the size of a seagull, with a wingspan of roughly a metre and a long tail. Its many sharp, pointed teeth were used to catch small fish over warm, shallow lagoons.

source.name: Museo Civico di Scienze Naturali di Bergamo

title: The Real Dilophosaurus
text: Dilophosaurus was a seven-metre hunter with two thin bony crests on its head. Its bones were first found in 1940 by Jesse Williams, a Navajo man, and dug up in 1942. Movie fans may picture it spitting venom with a frilly collar, but there is no fossil evidence for either. That was pure Hollywood.

source.name: University of California Museum of Paleontology

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: Lava Over Africa and Antarctica
text: As the supercontinent Gondwana started to crack, huge floods of lava poured out over what are now southern Africa and Antarctica, then joined together. The lava covered about three million square kilometres. Its gases warmed the planet and starved parts of the ocean of oxygen, and the thick lava layers now form Lesotho's dramatic mountains.

source.name: Duncan et al. 1997, Journal of Geophysical Research 102(B8), 'The timing and duration of the Karoo igneous event, southern Gondwana' (abstract via Crossref)

source2.name: Science Advances 2022, 'Reduced plate motion controlled timing of Early Jurassic Karoo-Ferrar large igneous province volcanism'

title: Ichthyosaur Mothers in Black Shale
text: The seabed here was so low in oxygen that dead animals were not eaten or rotted away. That is why the Posidonia Shale holds ichthyosaurs with their full body outlines, even fins and tail flukes. Some mothers still carry babies inside them, proof that these sea reptiles gave birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

source.name: De La Garza, Sjövall, Hauff & Lindgren 2023, Palaeontology 66(4) e12668, 'Preservational modes of some ichthyosaur soft tissues from the Jurassic Posidonia Shale of Germany' (Lund University record)

source2.name: Miedema et al. 2023, BMC Ecology and Evolution (Staatliches Museum für Naturkunde Stuttgart), ichthyosaur fetal orientation

title: Dinosaurs by a Salty, Fiery Lake
text: In Patagonia, rocks from a salty rift-valley lake, a bit like the lakes of East Africa today, hold long-necked dinosaurs such as Patagosaurus and hunters like Eoabelisaurus. The rocks are full of charcoal, a sign that wildfires swept through often. Nearby volcanoes kept erupting, so these dinosaurs lived in a smoky, restless world.

source.name: Royal Society Open Science 2024, 'The oldest monofenestratan pterosaur from the Queso Rallado locality (Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Toarcian) of Chubut'

source2.name: Olivera et al. 2026, Journal of Micropalaeontology 45:335, palynofacies of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation

title: Giant Footprints on a Scottish Beach
text: On the rocky shores of Skye, low tide reveals footprints left by long-necked dinosaurs wading through a shallow lagoon. Some prints are over half a metre wide. Middle Jurassic dinosaur fossils are rare worldwide, so these tracks, studied closely since 2015, give a valuable glimpse of a time scientists know surprisingly little about.

source.name: Brusatte, Challands, Ross & Wilkinson 2015, Scottish Journal of Geology 51(2), 'Sauropod dinosaur trackways in a Middle Jurassic lagoon on the Isle of Skye, Scotland' (University of Edinburgh repository)

source2.name: Blakesley et al. 2025, PLOS ONE, 'A new Middle Jurassic lagoon margin assemblage of theropod and sauropod dinosaur trackways from the Isle of Skye'

title: The Spike-Bearing Lizard of Niger
text: Spinophorosaurus was a long-necked plant-eater found in Niger's desert near Aderbissinat, with a backbone about 13 metres long. Its name means 'spine-bearing lizard', because the scientists who described it in 2009 thought two spiky bones sat near the tip of its tail. The rocks are hard to date, but it probably lived in the Middle Jurassic.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Remes et al. 2009)

title: The Biggest Fish Ever
text: Leedsichthys may be the largest bony fish that has ever lived, possibly around 16 metres long. Despite its size, it was gentle: like a whale shark, it swam with its mouth open, filtering tiny animals from the water. Its remains come from the Oxford Clay near Peterborough, and it is named after collector Alfred Leeds.

source.name: Peterborough Museum, The Jurassic Gallery large print guide

source2.name: Cambridge Prisms: Extinction 2024, 'The extinct marine megafauna of the Phanerozoic'

dateLabel: Middle Jurassic, roughly 165 million years ago
title: A Giant Found on a Cattle Station
text: In 1924 a station manager named Arthur Browne told the Queensland Museum about some strange bones found near Roma. They belonged to Rhoetosaurus, a long-necked dinosaur about 15 metres long, described in 1926. Its species name, brownei, honours him, and its genus name comes from Rhoetos, a giant of Greek myth.

source.name: Australian Museum

title: The First Dinosaur Painted in True Colour
text: Anchiornis was a crow-sized feathered dinosaur with wing feathers on both its arms and its legs. Traces of pigment in its fossils let scientists work out its colours: one specimen was mostly black and grey, with a red-brown crest on its head and brown speckles on its face. It lived in China in the Late Jurassic.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: Africa's Great Dinosaur Dig
text: Tendaguru Hill holds bones of Giraffatitan, a towering long-neck, and spiky Kentrosaurus. Between 1909 and 1913, hundreds of local Tanzanian workers dug and carried over 250 tonnes of fossils to the coast for a German museum, during colonial rule. The giant Giraffatitan skeleton now stands in Berlin, one of the tallest mounted dinosaurs anywhere.

source.name: Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, 'Research and Responsibility' Tendaguru project page

source2.name: Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, 'The World of Dinosaurs' exhibition page

title: A Hidden Mega-Volcano
text: Deep under the Pacific, about 1,600 kilometres east of Japan, lies Tamu Massif, an extinct volcano roughly the size of New Mexico. It formed in just a few million years and then went quiet. In 2013 scientists suggested it might be the biggest single volcano on Earth, though they still debate whether it is one volcano or several.

source.name: University of Houston College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics news, 'Scientists Confirm Existence of Largest Single Volcano on Earth' (5 Sept 2013)

source2.name: Sager et al. 2019, Nature Geoscience 12:661-666, 'Oceanic plateau formation by seafloor spreading implied by Tamu Massif magnetic anomalies' (abstract)

title: The Fast Runner of Kirkwood
text: Nqwebasaurus was a small, speedy theropod, a relative of the meat-eating dinosaurs. Its name mixes Xhosa words for the local Kirkwood district and 'fast runner'. Oddly, it had stomach stones in its belly, the kind plant-eaters and ostriches swallow to grind up food, so it may have eaten more plants than its cousins.

source.name: The Conversation, 'Unraveling the mystery of how dinosaurs get their names' by Prof. Anusuya Chinsamy-Turan (University of Cape Town)

source2.name: PLOS ONE 2012, 'Abdominal contents from two large Early Cretaceous compsognathids' (lists Nqwebasaurus among theropods with gastroliths)

title: Lava as Africa and Brazil Split
text: As South America and Africa began to pull apart, enormous lava floods poured out over both sides of the crack. Today most of the lava lies in Brazil's Paraná Basin, while a smaller severed piece forms Namibia's Etendeka hills, an ocean apart. The same hotspot may also have built volcanic islands far out in the South Atlantic, like Tristan da Cunha.

source.name: Scientific Reports 2023, 'Ignition of the southern Atlantic seafloor spreading machine without hot-mantle booster'

source2.name: Nature Communications 2023, 'Evidence for compositionally distinct upper mantle plumelets since the early history of the Tristan-Gough hotspot'

title: One of the First Flowers Lived Underwater
text: Montsechia is one of the oldest known flowering plants, and it did not look like a pretty bloom at all. It grew underwater in lakes, a bit like the modern hornwort in fish tanks. Its fossils in Spanish limestone show that flowering plants, now most plants on Earth, were around about 130 million years ago.

source.name: Gomez et al. 2015, PNAS 112:10985, 'Montsechia, an ancient aquatic angiosperm' (abstract via Europe PMC)

source2.name: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology 2022 (Ceratophyllum gynoecium review)

title: The Dinosaur with a Spiky Neck
text: Amargasaurus was a long-neck about 12 metres long, with a double row of tall spines running along its neck and back. They may have held up a twin 'sail' of skin, though nobody knows for sure. It lived in what is now Argentina and was named in 1991.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: The Biggest Underwater Lava Plateau
text: North of the Solomon Islands, the Pacific seafloor hides the Ontong Java Plateau, the largest of the ocean's great volcanic plateaus. Its main building phase was around 120 million years ago. Some scientists think it once formed a single super-plateau with the Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus, which would make it the biggest volcanic event recorded in Earth's history.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Tejada et al. 2023, "New evidence for the Ontong Java Nui hypothesis")

title: SuperCroc of the Sahara
text: What is now desert in Niger was once a land of rivers, home to Sarcosuchus, a crocodile relative that grew to about 11 or 12 metres long and weighed around 8 tonnes. Teams led by Paul Sereno recovered several partial skeletons in 1997 and 2000, and it was nicknamed 'SuperCroc'. Its long snout ended in a bulge scientists call a bulla.

source.name: Science (Sereno et al. 2001, "The giant crocodyliform Sarcosuchus from the Cretaceous of Africa"), abstract

source2.name: University of Chicago Chronicle

title: Fossil Fish Inside Stone Eggs
text: In northeast Brazil, rounded limestone lumps called concretions formed around dead fish, sealing them like time capsules. Split one open and you might find a fish preserved in 3D, sometimes with traces of muscle, gut lining and even its last meal still inside. These fish-bearing stones are extremely common on the slopes of the Chapada do Araripe.

source.name: University of Portsmouth research portal (Martill et al., "Mass mortality of fishes in the Santana Formation (Lower Cretaceous) of Brazil"), abstract

title: Dinosaurs of the Polar Night
text: Back then, Victoria lay inside the Antarctic Circle, so dinosaurs here lived through dark polar winters. At Dinosaur Cove, diggers tunnelled into the sea cliff to reach fossils, including Leaellynasaura, a small plant-eater about a metre long with enlarged eyes. It was named after Leaellyn Rich, the daughter of the palaeontologists who described it.

source.name: Australian Museum (Leaellynasaura amicagraphica)

source2.name: PeerJ (Herne et al. 2018)

title: A Feathered Dinosaur Tail in Amber
text: In 2016 scientists described the feathered tail of a small dinosaur trapped in amber, fossil tree resin, from Kachin State in Myanmar. About 99 million years old, it probably belonged to a young coelurosaur, a kind of meat-eating dinosaur. The amber kept the feathers in 3D, along with traces of soft tissue, in far finer detail than fossils squashed in rock.

source.name: Current Biology (Xing et al. 2016, "A Feathered Dinosaur Tail with Primitive Plumage Trapped in Mid-Cretaceous Amber"), abstract

title: The Tyrannosaur with Great Ears
text: Timurlengia was a horse-sized cousin of T. rex, named after the Central Asian ruler Timur (Tamerlane). Its species name, euotica, means 'well-eared'. CT scans of its braincase, published in 2016, showed it already had the advanced brain and the inner ear tuned to low sounds of later giants. Tyrannosaurs, it seems, got smart heads first and giant bodies later.

source.name: PNAS (Brusatte et al. 2016, "New tyrannosaur from the mid-Cretaceous of Uzbekistan...")

title: When India Waved Goodbye to Madagascar
text: India and Madagascar were once joined. Around 88 million years ago, a hotspot deep in the Earth helped rip them apart, and India began its long drift north. On the little St. Mary's Islands off the Karnataka coast, lava from that time cooled into neat six-sided rock columns you can walk among today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List entry 'Geological Heritage of St' Mary's Island Cluster' (submitted by India, 2025)

title: A Schoolboy's Sea Dragon
text: In 1968 a high school student named Tadashi Suzuki found bones in a riverbank near Iwaki. They belonged to Futabasaurus, a long-necked plesiosaur over six metres long, and many bones show bite marks from sharks. It became so famous in Japan that it starred in the movie Doraemon: Nobita's Dinosaur.

source.name: Iwaki City Digital Museum (Iwaki City), 'Futabasaurus suzukii'

source2.name: Sato, Hasegawa & Manabe 2006, Palaeontology 49:467, 'A new elasmosaurid plesiosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of Fukushima, Japan' (abstract via Crossref); plus Heibonsha encyclopedias on Kotobank

title: A Giant Dinosaur Nursery
text: At Auca Mahuevo in Patagonia, scientists found a nesting ground of titanosaurs, the biggest long-necked dinosaurs. Some eggs still held tiny embryos, and a few even preserve patches of scaly skin, among the only skin from unhatched dinosaurs ever found. Together they give a rare peek at baby giants before they hatched.

source.name: Communications Biology (Pittman et al. 2022)

title: Madagascar's Cannibal Dinosaur
text: Majungasaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur from Madagascar with a single horn on top of its head. Scientists found dinosaur bones covered in its tooth marks, and some of those bones belonged to its own kind. Before this discovery, the evidence for dinosaurs eating members of their own species had been thin and patchy.

source.name: Nature (Rogers, Krause & Curry Rogers 2003, "Cannibalism in the Madagascan dinosaur Majungatholus atopus"), abstract

source2.name: Scientific Reports (Delcourt 2018)

title: The Oldest Known Bird Voice Box
text: Vegavis was a bird that lived in Antarctica while dinosaurs still roamed, about 66 to 69 million years ago. In 2016, CT scans of a fossil revealed its syrinx, the voice box birds use to make everything from songs to honks. It was the first bird voice box ever found from the age of dinosaurs.

source.name: Nature (Clarke et al. 2016, "Fossil evidence of the avian vocal organ from the Mesozoic"), abstract

title: Dinosaurs Ate Grass After All
text: In 2005, researchers looked at fossil dinosaur dung from India under the microscope and found phytoliths, tiny silica bits made by plants, from at least five kinds of grass. The dung probably came from titanosaurs, the giant long-necks. So some dinosaurs did eat grass, and grasses had already spread and diversified before the dinosaurs died out.

source.name: Science (Prasad et al. 2005, "Dinosaur coprolites and the early evolution of grasses and grazers"), abstract

title: The First Penguins
text: Just a few million years after the asteroid wiped out the big dinosaurs, penguins were already living in New Zealand. Four skeletons of Waimanu were found in the Waipara Greensand of Canterbury, in rocks about 61 to 62 million years old. They are the oldest penguin fossils known and sit at the very base of the penguin family tree.

source.name: Molecular Biology and Evolution (Slack et al. 2006, "Early penguin fossils, plus mitochondrial genomes, calibrate avian evolution"), abstract

source2.name: Nature Communications (Mayr et al. 2017)

title: The Snake as Long as a Bus
text: Titanoboa is the largest snake ever discovered, about 13 metres long and more than a tonne in weight. Its fossils turned up in the Cerrejón coal mine in Colombia, in rocks from one of the oldest known tropical rainforests. Scientists worked out that a snake this huge could only survive where the average temperature was at least 30 to 34°C.

source.name: Nature (Head et al. 2009, "Giant boid snake from the Palaeocene neotropics reveals hotter past equatorial temperatures"), abstract

source2.name: PLOS ONE (Zaher et al. 2019)

title: The Great Heatwave and the Tiny Horses
text: About 56 million years ago, a huge release of carbon warmed the planet by about 5 °C, an event called the PETM. In Wyoming's Bighorn Basin, fossil teeth show that the earliest horse, Sifrhippus, shrank by about 30 percent to the size of a small house cat, then grew again as it cooled. Scientists study it as a clue to today's warming.

source.name: Science (Secord et al. 2012, "Evolution of the earliest horses driven by climate change in the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum"), abstract

source2.name: University of Florida / UNL press release via EurekAlert (Secord et al. 2012)

title: Our Tiny Primate Great-Grandparent
text: Archicebus, described in 2013, is the oldest nearly complete primate skeleton ever found, about 55 million years old. This tree-dwelling animal from China was only the size of a pygmy mouse lemur and probably ate insects by day. It sits at the very base of the tarsier lineage, close to its split from the one leading to monkeys, apes and us.

source.name: Nature (Ni et al. 2013, "The oldest known primate skeleton and early haplorhine evolution"), abstract

title: The Fern That Cooled the World
text: Drilling near the North Pole revealed that the Arctic Ocean was once carpeted with Azolla, a tiny floating fern. For hundreds of thousands of years it bloomed, died and sank, locking away huge amounts of carbon in the seafloor. Some scientists think this helped tip Earth from a hothouse toward a cooler climate.

source.name: Nature (Brinkhuis et al. 2006, "Episodic fresh surface waters in the Eocene Arctic Ocean"), abstract

source2.name: Geobiology (Speelman et al. 2009, "The Eocene Arctic Azolla bloom: environmental conditions, productivity and carbon drawdown"), abstract

title: The Mega Penguin
text: Palaeeudyptes klekowskii was a giant penguin that lived in Antarctica in the Eocene, far bigger than any penguin alive today. Its fragmentary bones rank among the very largest penguin fossils ever found. Scientists think such giants disappeared later, when seals and whales spread through the seas and began to compete with them.

source.name: Nature Communications (Mayr et al. 2017, "A Paleocene penguin from New Zealand substantiates multiple origins of gigantism in fossil Sphenisciformes")

title: When Apes and Monkeys Went Separate Ways
text: In 2013 scientists described two fossil primates from the same Tanzanian rocks: Rukwapithecus, an early ape, and Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey. Found together, they show that the ape and monkey families had already split by about 25 million years ago. Just a couple of fossil jaw pieces told the story.

source.name: Nature (Stevens et al. 2013, "Palaeontological evidence for an Oligocene divergence between Old World monkeys and apes")

title: Mary Leakey's Ape Skull
text: In 1948 Mary Leakey spotted a fossil skull on Rusinga Island in Lake Victoria. It belonged to Proconsul, a tailless early ape that climbed through forest trees on all fours. The skull caused a sensation and was flown to Britain for study. Proconsul helps show what our ape ancestors were like before humans existed.

source.name: African Fossils virtual laboratory (Turkana Basin Institute / National Museums of Kenya / Stony Brook University), 'Proconsul' skull entry

source2.name: PeerJ 2016, 'First steps of bipedality in hominids: evidence from the atelid and proconsulid pelvis' (states proconsulids lacked tails and were above-branch quadrupeds)

title: Rhinos Buried in Volcanic Ash
text: About 12 million years ago a huge volcano erupted in what is now south-western Idaho, nearly 1,450 kilometres (900 miles) away, and its ash blanketed a Nebraska waterhole. Horses, camels and finally the big rhinos slowly suffocated as their lungs filled with the dust. Their whole skeletons were preserved, and rhino skulls often still have grass seeds stuck between the teeth.

source.name: University of Nebraska State Museum - Ashfall Fossil Beds

title: The Whale That Hunted Whales
text: Livyatan was a giant sperm whale relative with a 3-metre head and enormous teeth more than 36 centimetres long. Unlike today's squid-eating sperm whales, it probably hunted baleen whales. Its skull was found in Peru's coastal desert in November 2008. It is named after the Biblical sea monster Leviathan and Moby-Dick author Herman Melville.
