source.name: Lambert et al. 2010, Nature 466:105-108

source2.name: National Geographic

title: Toumaï, Hope of Life
text: In July 2001 a team led by Michel Brunet found a small but nearly complete skull in Chad's Djurab Desert. Named Sahelanthropus, it is about 7 million years old and may be one of the oldest members of the human family, from near the time our line split from chimpanzees. Its nickname Toumaï means 'hope of life' in the local language.

source.name: Australian Museum

source2.name: Lebatard et al. 2008, PNAS (abstract via PubMed)

title: Ardi, Older Than Lucy
text: Ardi is a partial skeleton of Ardipithecus, more than a million years older than Lucy. Found in 1994, it took scientists 15 years to study and publish. Ardi walked upright on the ground but still had a big toe that could grab branches like a thumb, a mix of tree climber and walker.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - Human Origins

title: The Oldest Stone Tools
text: In 2015 archaeologists announced stone tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya that are about 3.3 million years old, some 700,000 years older than the oldest tools known before. Some are big and heavy, weighing two kilograms or more, and were made by pounding stone against stone. Scientists had long supposed the first toolmakers belonged to our own genus, Homo; these finds point to someone earlier.

source.name: Harmand et al. 2015, Nature 521:310-315

title: Early Tools Far from Africa
text: On the Loess Plateau of central China, scientists found stone tools in 17 layers of ancient soil and dust, the oldest dated to about 2.1 million years ago. Reported in 2018, they suggest human relatives left Africa earlier than anyone thought, before the famous early humans of Dmanisi in Georgia, who lived about 1.8 million years ago.

source.name: Zhu et al. 2018, Nature 559:608-612

title: The Oldest Campfire Clues
text: About 30 metres inside Wonderwerk Cave, scientists found burnt bone and ash from plants about a million years old. Because the burning happened again and again so far inside the cave, wildfires are an unlikely cause. It is the earliest secure evidence of fire at an archaeological site, probably tended by Homo erectus.

source.name: Berna et al. 2012, PNAS 109:E1215-E1220

title: Mammoth Hunters North of the Arctic Circle
text: People were living on the Yana River in Arctic Siberia, north of the Arctic Circle, about 27,000 radiocarbon years ago, roughly twice as old as any other known Arctic site when it was reported in 2004. They made spear foreshafts from woolly rhino horn and mammoth ivory, and seem to have hunted mammoths mainly for ivory rather than meat.

source.name: Pitulko et al. 2004, Science, 'The Yana RHS site' (abstract, Europe PMC)

source2.name: Discover Magazine

title: Two Children Wrapped in Ivory Beads
text: On the edge of today's city of Vladimir, two children aged about 10 and 12 were buried head to head, covered in more than ten thousand mammoth-ivory beads between them, with 16 spears of mammoth ivory. A grown man nearby wore 25 ivory armbands and about 3,000 beads. It is the most elaborate Ice Age burial known.

source.name: Trinkaus & Buzhilova 2018, Antiquity (Cambridge University Press)

source2.name: University of Cambridge research news (Sikora et al. 2017, Science)

title: Ice Age Settlers of the Solomons
place: Kilu Cave, Buka Island, Papua New Guinea
text: People had reached Buka Island, at the northern end of the Solomon Islands chain, by about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, some 25,000 years earlier than anyone had found in that island group before. The evidence comes from Kilu, a rock shelter dug by archaeologists Stephen Wickler and Matthew Spriggs. It pushed the story of these Pacific islands deep into the Ice Age.

source.name: Wickler & Spriggs 1988, Antiquity (Cambridge University Press)

title: The Pocket-Sized Venus
text: Just 11 centimetres tall, small enough to carry in a hand, this figure of a woman was carved from a limestone not found near Willendorf, then tinted with red ochre. It dates to about 28,000-25,000 BCE and was found in 1908. Nobody knows whether it was a fertility figure, a mother goddess or a lucky charm.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Venus of Willendorf

title: Tiny Tools in a Rainforest Cave
text: In Sri Lanka's rainforest caves, people made microliths, tiny shaped stone tools. At Batadomba-lena, geometric microliths occur in every level, starting about 36,000 years ago, and nearby Kitulgala Beli-lena has them in a layer about 31,000-26,000 years old. Only Africa has clearly older ones, from about 71,000 years ago; Europe's appear from about 45,000 years ago.

source.name: Wedage et al. 2019, PLOS ONE

title: Australia's Oldest Dated Drawing
text: A rock shelter in Arnhem Land, its ceiling held up by natural stone pillars, holds Australia's oldest securely dated art: a charcoal drawing more than 28,000 years old. The name means 'hole in the rock' in the Jawoyn language. Jawoyn people visited within living memory, but outsiders only learned of it in 2006.

source.name: Delannoy, David, Geneste et al., 'Engineers of the Arnhem Land plateau', ch. 10 in The Archaeology of Rock Art in Western Arnhem Land (ANU Press, Terra Australis)

source2.name: Same volume, ch. 1 and ch. 12 (ANU Press)

title: The Painted Cave Now Under the Sea
text: About 27,000 years ago, people stencilled 65 hands on these cave walls by blowing black and red paint around their fingers. Back then the entrance was on dry land, far from the shore. Today it lies 37 metres underwater, and diver Henri Cosquer found it in 1985. Later artists even painted seals and great auks here.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture: Grotte Cosquer

source2.name: Bradshaw Foundation: The Cosquer Cave (text by Jean Clottes)

title: An Airport's Ice Age Graveyard
text: Workers building a new airport on Ishigaki Island in 2007 found a cave full of human bones. One nearly complete skeleton, a man in his thirties or forties, is about 27,000 years old, the oldest complete skeleton found in East Asia. With at least 19 people laid to rest, it is Japan's first known Stone Age burial ground.

source.name: Katagiri Chiaki (Okinawa Prefectural Archaeological Center), 'Shiraho-Saonetabaru Cave site and cliff-burial culture of the southern islands', Gakujutsu no Doko (Science Council of Japan) 2020

source2.name: Ryukyu Shimpo, 'First Paleolithic cemetery in Japan: 19 individuals at Shiraho-Saonetabaru' (20 May 2017)

title: The Ice Sheets at Their Biggest
text: Between about 29,000 and 19,000 years ago, the ice sheets of the last ice age reached their greatest extent, covering about 8 percent of Earth's surface. The Scandinavian Ice Sheet grew up to 3 kilometres thick, and so much water was locked up that seas stood about 125 metres lower than today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Last glacial maximum

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Scandinavian Ice Sheet

title: The Spotted Horses of Pech Merle
text: On a cave wall in southern France, artists painted two horses covered in black dots about 25,000 years ago. Many assumed the spots were symbolic, until a 2011 DNA study showed leopard-spotted horses really existed in the Ice Age. Scientists still argue about it, but the painters may simply have drawn what they saw.

source.name: Pruvost et al. 2011, PNAS (PubMed Central)

title: The Lapedo Child
text: In 1998, archaeologists in a Portuguese valley found the skeleton of a child about four years old, buried around 24,500 years ago with a pierced shell and red ochre. Some researchers think the child's sturdy build shows a mix of Neanderthal and modern human ancestry, a hint that the two groups once had families together.

source.name: Duarte et al. 1999, PNAS (PubMed Central)

title: Earth's Biggest Grassland
text: At the height of the ice age, a cold, dry grassland stretched from Spain across Central Asia and Siberia all the way to Canada's Yukon. Scientists call it the mammoth steppe, and it was the largest habitat on Earth. Woolly mammoths, wild horses, bison and woolly rhinos grazed across it. Almost nothing quite like it survives today.

source.name: Biological Reviews 2019, 'Climate-driven ecological stability as a globally shared cause of Late Quaternary megafaunal extinctions: the Plaids and Stripes Hypothesis'

source2.name: PLOS ONE 2017 (University of Western Ontario / Government of Yukon), isotopic dynamics of southern Yukon soils and plants

title: Walking to Sri Lanka
place: Adam's Bridge, India and Sri Lanka
text: Adam's Bridge is a 48-kilometre chain of sandbanks and shoals between India and Sri Lanka, much of it less than a metre deep. Geologic evidence suggests it is what remains of a former land connection, exposed when Ice Age seas were lower. Tradition calls it Rama Setu, the causeway built by Rama's army in the epic Ramayana.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Adam's Bridge

title: Spear Points Thin as Leaves
text: During the coldest part of the Ice Age, Solutrean toolmakers in France and Spain shaped stone into leaf-like 'laurel leaf' points. One unfinished point found in central Spain was made of stone from south-west France, 600 to 700 km away. Researchers think such pieces were swapped as special gifts to keep far-apart groups in touch.

source.name: Science Advances (Sánchez de la Torre et al. 2026), via PubMed Central

title: The Most Southerly People on Earth
text: During the last ice age, Aboriginal people living along the wild rivers of south-west Tasmania were the most southerly humans on Earth. Kutikina Cave is one of their sites. In the early 1980s a plan to dam the rivers set off Australia's largest conservation battle, ended by a High Court ruling in 1983. The cave has since been returned to the Aboriginal community.

source.name: Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service

title: A Desert Camp with Brushwood Huts
text: In what is now dry desert in Jordan, hunter-gatherers once camped beside a wetland. Around 19,000 years ago they built brushwood huts, among the oldest homes known in the region, hunted gazelles and collected seashells carried from distant coasts. The camp was big and busy enough that it may have been a seasonal meeting place for many groups.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Maher et al. 2012), via PubMed Central

title: Nile Campers Grinding Tubers
text: In a big wadi beside the Nile north of Aswan, Ice Age people camped again and again as part of their seasonal round. Charred tubers of wild nut grass are the most common plant food found there, and grinding stones show plants were a key part of meals. Most of the animal bones are from fish, especially Nile catfish.

source.name: Antiquity Project Gallery (Banks et al.)

source2.name: PLOS ONE (Buckley et al. 2014), via PubMed Central

title: When Africa's Biggest Lake Dried Up
text: Lake Victoria, today the largest lake in Africa, dried out completely for almost 4,000 years towards the end of the last ice age. It filled up again about 16,000 years ago. Yet it now holds as many as 500 kinds of cichlid fish, and scientists think they evolved in the short time since it refilled.

source.name: University of Bern

source2.name: Science (Johnson et al. 1996), abstract via Europe PMC

title: Cousins of the First Americans
text: On the western bank of the Yenisei River, Ice Age people lived about 17,000 years ago. DNA from a man's arm bone and a female's tooth found here shows they were closely related to the much older Mal'ta boy from near Lake Baikal, whose people share ancestry with Native Americans.

source.name: Nature (Raghavan et al. 2014), via PubMed Central

source2.name: Nature (Fu et al. 2016), via PubMed Central

title: The Tabon Cave Skull
text: In 1962, a team led by Robert Fox of the National Museum of the Philippines found part of a human forehead bone and two pieces of jawbone in a cave on Palawan. The forehead bone is about 16,500 years old, though other human bones from the cave turned out to be older. Tabon birds, which dig into the cave floor, had churned up the layers.

source.name: Comptes Rendus Palevol (Détroit et al. 2004), Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle

title: The Floods That Carved the Scablands
text: Again and again, an ice dam holding back Glacial Lake Missoula burst, sending water racing across what is now Washington State. Dozens of floods scoured out giant coulees and left huge ripple marks. Geologist J Harlen Bretz began studying the scablands in 1922 and argued for great floods, but his idea was dismissed for decades before it was accepted.

source.name: US National Park Service, Ice Age Floods National Geologic Trail

source2.name: US National Park Service, Ice Age Floods: People

title: The North Warms in a Few Decades
text: About 14,500 years ago, Earth's climate began to shift from a cold glacial world towards a warmer one. An ice core drilled in Greenland shows how sudden the change was there: weather patterns switched within one to three years, and the air warmed over about 50 years. A sharp cold snap, the Younger Dryas, later interrupted the warm-up.

source.name: Science (Steffensen et al. 2008), abstract via Europe PMC

source2.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

title: Cups Made from Skulls
text: About 14,700 years ago, people in Cheddar Gorge carefully cleaned and shaped human skulls into cups or bowls. Cut marks show it was skilled, deliberate work, probably part of a ritual. The same cave later gave up Cheddar Man, who lived around 10,000 years ago, the oldest almost complete skeleton of our species found in Britain.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London (Cheddar Man)

title: Spear Points with a Mastodon
text: Near Venezuela's Caribbean coast, a 1976 dig by a team including José Cruxent found El Jobo stone tools lying with the butchered bones of a young mastodon. At least 13,000 years old, the kill is older than North America's Clovis culture. The researchers concluded the El Jobo style grew up on its own in northern South America.

source.name: Science (Bryan, Casamiquela, Cruxent, Gruhn and Ochsenius 1978), abstract via Europe PMC

title: A Bone Spear Tip in a Mastodon Rib
place: Manis Mastodon Site, Sequim, Washington, USA
text: At the Manis site in Washington State, a mastodon rib has the tip of a spear point stuck in it, and the point itself was carved from mastodon bone. Dated to about 13,800 years ago, it shows people were hunting these giants in the Pacific Northwest long before the Clovis culture.

source.name: Science (Waters et al. 2011), abstract via Europe PMC

title: One of the Oldest Signs of War
text: Beside the Nile, more than 60 men, women and children were buried in the oldest known cemetery in the Nile Valley, at least 13,400 years old. Many skeletons carry wounds and bits of stone weapons, some wounds healed, pointing to repeated raids rather than a single battle. A 2021 study suggests big climate swings drove the fighting.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Crevecoeur et al. 2021), via PubMed Central

title: Graves Lined with Flowers
text: In a cave on Mount Carmel, Natufian people lined graves with green and flowering plants such as Judean sage, between about 13,700 and 11,700 years ago. It is the earliest clear evidence of flowers used in burials. Stone mortars were cut into the cave floor beside the graves, and food remains hint at funeral feasts.

source.name: PNAS (Nadel et al. 2013), via PubMed Central

title: Island People Who Came by Boat
text: In 1959, Phil Orr found part of a human thigh bone on Santa Rosa Island. About 13,000 years old, it is arguably the earliest dated human bone in North or South America. Because it was found on an island, it shows that people were already using boats along the California coast at that early date.

source.name: US National Park Service, Channel Islands National Park

title: A Puzzling Skull from Nigeria
text: In 1965, Thurstan Shaw's team dug up a skeleton in this rock shelter in south-western Nigeria. The skull, roughly 13,000 years old, has a long, low shape that mixes old and modern features, a hint that ancient human lineages lingered in West Africa surprisingly late.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Harvati et al. 2011), via PubMed Central

title: Big-Game Hunters at the Tip of the World
text: At Fell's Cave in far southern Patagonia, most of the animal bones left by early hunters come from Ice Age giants that are now extinct. Across the region, people using 'fishtail' spear points hunted native horses and giant ground sloths. By about 11,600 years ago, these big animals had all but vanished.

source.name: Science Advances (Prates, Medina and Perez 2025), via PubMed Central

title: Reindeer Hunters with Bows
text: During the cold snap called the Younger Dryas, the Ahrensburgian people, the last reindeer hunters of northern Europe, roamed the plains of what is now northern Germany. At Stellmoor, near Ahrensburg, wooden arrows survived in the wet ground. Dated to about 12,000 to 11,000 years ago, they are the oldest direct evidence of the bow and arrow.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), 2023

source2.name: PLOS ONE via PubMed Central (Ahrensburgian reindeer hunters)

title: Paintings Dated by Wasp Nests
text: In the Kimberley, finely painted human figures in ceremonial dress with long headdresses cover rock shelter walls. Dating paint is hard, so in 2020 scientists dated old mud-wasp nests lying over and under the paintings, suggesting most figures were painted about 12,000 years ago. The work was done with Traditional Owners, who use names such as Gwion Gwion for the figures.

source.name: Science Advances via PubMed Central (Finch et al. 2020)

source2.name: ANSTO (Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation)

title: A Goddess Stone in the Son Valley
text: At a late Stone Age tool site in the Son Valley, archaeologists found a natural triangular piece of sandstone, its layers forming triangles, set in a ring of stones about 11,000 years ago. The excavators suggested it was a shrine to Shakti, the female principle, because villagers nearby still keep and worship very similar stones today. It may be one of the oldest shrines in India.

source.name: Antiquity 57 (1983), Kenoyer, Clark, Pal & Sharma, 'An upper palaeolithic shrine in India?' (Cambridge Core abstract and editorial note)

source2.name: J. Desmond Clark oral history, Regional Oral History Office, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley (2002), full text via Internet Archive

title: A Village That Started with Pigs
text: In southeastern Turkey, people settled into the oldest known permanent village in Anatolia, living in half-sunken huts on stone foundations. While sheep and goats are often thought to have come first, Hallan Çemi's earliest attempts at taming animals seem to have involved pigs. Villagers ate wild lentils, almonds and pistachios, and traded for obsidian and green copper ore from far away.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (B. L. Peasnall, 'Intricacies of Hallan Çemi', 2002)

title: Africa's First Pots
text: In ravines at Ounjougou in Mali, archaeologists found pottery made before 9400 BCE, the earliest known in Africa. Very early pots are also known from East Asia. The first African pots appeared in a warm, wet period when the Sahara region was rich in wild grasses, and people probably used them to boil the seeds.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge University Press), Huysecom et al. 2009

title: Headdresses Made from Deer Skulls
text: Beside an ancient lake in Yorkshire, hunters about 11,000 years ago turned red deer skulls, antlers still attached, into headdresses. Twenty-four have been found, more than nine in ten of all those known from prehistoric Europe. They may have been ritual headgear or hunting disguises. Waterlogged ground preserved antler and other materials that normally rot away.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Little et al. 2016)

title: Perak Man, Buried with Care
text: In a cave called Gua Gunung Runtuh in Malaysia's Lenggong Valley, archaeologists found Perak Man, Southeast Asia's oldest most complete human skeleton. He is radiocarbon dated to about 10,000 years ago. Other caves in the same limestone hill also hold prehistoric burials, part of a valley record of early people that stretches back nearly two million years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Early Millet in Northern China
text: About 35 kilometres west of Lake Baiyangdian lies one of the most important early Neolithic sites on the North China Plain, about 11,500 to 11,000 years old. Its people made pottery, kept dogs and ground plants on stone slabs. Starch grains on those grinding stones show they were already using millet, which may have been slowly turning into a farmed crop.

source.name: PNAS via PubMed Central (Yang et al. 2012)

source2.name: Evolutionary Human Sciences 2024 via PMC

title: A Clash by Lake Turkana
text: By a lagoon west of Lake Turkana, the remains of 27 people were found, including six children. Ten of the twelve most complete skeletons show signs of a violent death, and two men had stone tips lodged in their bones. Researchers in 2016 called it the earliest dated evidence of conflict between groups of hunter-gatherers.

source.name: University of Cambridge

source2.name: Nature (Mirazón Lahr et al. 2016)

title: The First Goat Herders
text: In the Zagros Mountains of western Iran, villagers at Ganj Dareh were managing goats by about 8200 BCE, some of the earliest evidence of goat herding anywhere. Scientists spotted it from the bones: most males were eaten young while females were kept alive for breeding. DNA shows these goats were close relatives of the ancestors of later domestic goats.

source.name: PNAS via PubMed Central (Daly et al. 2021)

title: A Chief Buried Under Golden Bulls
text: In a great burial mound in the northwest Caucasus, an important person was laid to rest with eight long gold and silver tubes and little bull figures. Long thought to be canopy poles or sceptres, they may really be straws for sharing beer. Dug up in 1897, the Maikop kurgan is described as the richest burial mound of the Early Bronze Age.

source.name: St Petersburg University news, on Trifonov, Savelieva et al., Antiquity 2022, 'Party like a Sumerian: reinterpreting the sceptres from the Maikop kurgan'

title: The Goddess Temple of Niuheliang
text: In the hills of northeast China, the Hongshan people built stone burial mounds, altars and a 'Goddess Temple' between about 5,500 and 5,000 years ago. Inside the temple were parts of six clay figures with female features, including a life-size head. Graves nearby held only jade, carved into dragons, birds, tortoises and people.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List: Sites of Hongshan Culture)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Oldest Picture of a Wagon
text: A clay pot from a farming village in southern Poland is decorated with simple drawings that look like a four-wheeled wagon. It is one of the oldest images of a wheeled vehicle anywhere. Wheels seem to have spread across Europe and the Middle East surprisingly fast, almost as soon as they were invented.

source.name: Archaeological Museum in Kraków, 'Vase from Bronocice'

source2.name: Antiquity 73 (1999), Bakker, Kruk, Lanting & Milisauskas, 'The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles in Europe and the Near East' (abstract via Crossref)

title: The World's First Swords
text: In a palace complex on a 30-metre-high mound on the Malatya plain, archaeologists found exceptional metal weapons made of copper mixed with arsenic, among them the earliest swords so far known in the world. The rulers seem to have shown them off as signs of their new power. The palace also reveals a sophisticated system of administration that existed before writing.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: PNAS 2015, Frangipane, via PMC

title: Egypt's First Written Labels
text: Tombs at Abydos that are older than Egypt's First Dynasty held small ivory labels carved with signs, along with pottery and the names of early kings. The inscribed labels show that Egyptian writing had reached an advanced stage earlier than anyone had realised, long before the first pharaohs ruled a united Egypt.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Newgrange Catches the Winter Sun
text: Stone Age farmers in Ireland built a huge round mound of stones, about 85 metres across, with a long stone passage inside. Above the entrance is a small 'roof-box'. On mornings around the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year, the rising sun shines through it, along the passage and into the chamber deep inside for a few minutes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Heritage Ireland (Office of Public Works)

title: Stone Age Homes With Furniture
text: On the windy Orkney Islands, villagers built snug houses linked by covered passages, with beds, shelves and dressers all made of stone. Because trees were scarce, stone furniture was the clever solution. The village lay hidden under sand until a fierce storm in 1850 blew the dunes away.

source.name: Historic Environment Scotland

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The King Who Wore Two Crowns
text: A carved slate slab from Hierakonpolis shows King Narmer wearing the crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Two fabulous animals on it may symbolize the joining of the two lands, so it is often read as a picture of Egypt's unification. It stands about 64 centimeters tall and is kept in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Script Nobody Can Read Yet
text: Accountants in Susa and across the Iranian plateau pressed signs into clay tablets in their own writing system, now called Proto-Elamite. About 1,700 tablets survive, mostly records counting farm goods, people and institutions. Yet it is one of the oldest scripts still largely undeciphered, so we can read the numbers but not most of the words.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (Cambridge Elements), 'Proto-Elamite' (2025, book abstract via Crossref)

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (C. L. Hamlin, 'A Proto-Elamite Account Tablet from Susa', 1968)

title: Merneith, Egypt's First Woman Ruler?
text: Merneith was buried at Abydos in a vast tomb complex in the royal cemetery of Egypt's earliest kings. An ancient list of rulers from the time of King Den names her as "king's mother." Historians think she may have ruled as regent while Den was a child, which would make her one of the earliest women known to have governed Egypt.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine

title: Wagon Herders Remix Europe's DNA
text: The Yamnaya were herders on the grasslands north of the Black Sea who lived with cattle, wagons and horses. Ancient DNA shows their descendants spread deep into Europe, and a big share of many Europeans' ancestry traces back to them. Many scholars think they also spread early Indo-European languages.

source.name: Nature (Haak et al. 2015)

source2.name: Science News

title: The Woman With a Golden Eye
text: In the 'Burnt City' of eastern Iran, archaeologists found a woman in her late twenties, buried between 2900 and 2800 BCE with what they believe is an artificial eyeball. It was made of bitumen paste and gold and once held in place with fine thread. A mark in her eye socket suggests she wore it for a long time, though some experts think it was an eyepatch.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

title: Gilgamesh, the Real King of Uruk
text: Gilgamesh is the hero of a famous Mesopotamian epic, but he was probably a real king who ruled Uruk sometime in the first half of the 3rd millennium BCE; the Sumerian king list names him. Later poets made him part god, a great builder and warrior who fights the forest guardian Humbaba and loses a precious plant to a serpent.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Imhotep Stacks the First Pyramid
text: For King Djoser, the architect Imhotep translated earlier Egyptian building into stone, stacking six tiers into a giant staircase about 60 meters tall. It is the oldest known monument of cut stone in the world. Imhotep became so famous that later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Father's Advice in Clay
text: In the Instructions of Shuruppak, an ancient Sumerian text, a wise father gives advice to his son. Some tips are timeless, like don't speak arrogantly to your mother. Others are delightfully practical, like don't buy a donkey that brays, and don't put your field right next to a road.

source.name: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford

title: Peseshet, Overseer of Healer Women
text: A false door in a tomb at Giza, uncovered in 1929–30, names a woman called Peseshet with the title 'Overseer of Healer Women'. She lived during Egypt's Old Kingdom and is a genuine ancient Egyptian woman healer. Fun twist: the 'first woman doctor' Merit Ptah, often quoted online, seems to be a 1930s mix-up based on Peseshet.

source.name: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (on Kwiecinski, J. Hist. Med. 2019)

title: A Lost Culture Found by Looters
text: Beginning in 2001, ancient cemeteries south of Jiroft in southeastern Iran were plundered, and carved chlorite stone vessels poured onto the antiquities market before archaeologists could dig. Police confiscated many pieces. Scholars link them to a thriving Bronze Age culture of the later third millennium BCE, whose style of carved stonework also turns up in Mesopotamia and around the Persian Gulf.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Jiroft iii. General Survey of Excavations'

title: From Tavern Keeper to King
text: The Sumerian King List, a long list of rulers, names exactly one woman: Kubaba (written Kug-Bau) of Kish, a tavern keeper who 'made firm the foundations of Kish' and became king. The list claims she ruled for 100 years, which is surely exaggerated, so her story has to be read with caution.

source.name: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford (Sumerian King List)

title: Ebla's Lost Palace Archive
text: In 1975, archaeologists digging at Ebla found the city's archives: more than 17,000 clay tablets and fragments, lying almost in the order they had been stored on their now-collapsed shelves. A fire had destroyed the city. The tablets include vocabularies and student exercises, showing that Ebla was a major centre of learning in the 3rd millennium BCE.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Sargon Builds the First Empire
text: Sargon started out as a cupbearer, the king's drink-server, in the city of Kish. He went on to conquer the cities of Sumer and beyond, often called the world's first empire. A later legend says he was set adrift as a baby in a basket on the river. His capital Akkad has never been found.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Boy King's Excited Letter
text: Harkhuf, a governor from Elephantine and overseer of caravans, journeyed deep into Nubia to trade. On one trip, under King Pepi II, he brought back a Pygmy from inner Africa. The young king was so delighted that he sent Harkhuf a letter, and Harkhuf proudly had it copied onto the walls of his tomb.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Desert Capital of the Oxus
text: Gonur Depe was a great walled city of the Oxus Civilization, a Bronze Age culture of Central Asia that few people have heard of. At its heart stood a fortified palace, supplied by clay water pipes, and skilled potters worked in the city. Some rich graves even held whole four-wheeled wagons whose wooden wheels had metal rims.

source.name: Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, exhibition wall texts 'Margiana. A Bronze Age Kingdom in Turkmenistan' (2018)

title: The Mega-Drought That Shook Empires
text: Around 2200 BCE, the climate of northern Mesopotamia turned sharply drier and windier. In northern Syria, the city of Tell Leilan was abandoned after four centuries of urban life, and its soil layers record the change. The archaeologists who dug it link this abrupt dry spell to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, and neighbouring regions collapsed at the same time.

source.name: Science (Weiss et al. 1993, 'The genesis and collapse of third millennium north Mesopotamian civilization')

title: An Indus Port and Its Bead Shops
text: Lothal was an Indus port town near the coast of Gujarat. Its huge walled basin, 217 meters long, has been identified as a tidal dockyard where boats sailed in at high tide. Lothal also had a bead-making factory, and finds linked to the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia show how far its trade reached.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal

title: The Oldest Law Code We Have
text: Long before the famous Code of Hammurabi, King Ur-Nammu of Ur, or perhaps his son Shulgi, issued a set of laws. It is the oldest law code yet discovered. Dating from the middle of the 21st century BCE, it dealt with matters such as bodily injuries, runaway slaves and witchcraft.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Stone Age Sunrise Calendar
text: At Taosi, a large walled town of the late Neolithic, archaeologists found a half-circle of rammed earth whose curved wall is cut by twelve gaps. Seen from a central point, two of the gaps lined up with sunrise on the summer and winter solstices around 2100 BCE. Many see it as one of China's earliest observatories, used to track the seasons.

source.name: Science in China Series G 52 (2009), Wu, Chen & Liu, 'Astronomical function and date of the Taosi observatory' (abstract, Springer)

source2.name: Springer Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy (2015), X. Sun, 'Taosi Observatory' (abstract)

title: The First Spoked-Wheel Chariots
text: On the steppe east of the Ural Mountains, people of the Sintashta culture placed light, two-wheeled vehicles with spoked wheels in their graves around 2000 BCE. Pulled by teams of horses and built to carry people rather than goods, they are the earliest evidence of such chariots in the region. Before this, heavy wagons with solid disc wheels were pulled by cattle.

source.name: Antiquity (Lindner 2020, 'Chariots in the Eurasian Steppe')

title: The World's Oldest Noodles
text: At Lajia in northwestern China, archaeologists found a sealed earthenware bowl with long, thin noodles still inside, about 4,000 years old. They were made from millet, not wheat. People still argue over whether the Chinese, Italians or Arabs invented noodles first, but these show the craft was already known here 4,000 years ago.

source.name: Nature (Lu et al. 2005, 'Millet noodles in Late Neolithic China')

title: Dilmun, Island of Merchants
text: Dilmun, on today's Bahrain, was a trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, shipping copper, pearls and dates. Between about 2200 and 1750 BCE its people built some 11,700 burial mounds, the grandest of them two-storey royal towers at A'ali. A Sumerian myth even called Dilmun a pure, pristine land without sickness.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Minoans Build Knossos
text: On Crete, the Minoans built their first palace at Knossos, a group of buildings around a rectangular courtyard. The later palace had long storerooms for grain and oil, and colorful wall paintings of dolphins and bull-leaping. Ancient writers placed the mythical Labyrinth near Knossos, and some think the palace itself was meant.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Temple of the Crossed Hands
text: High in the Andes near today's Huánuco, people built small temples at Kotosh around 2000–1800 BCE, at the very end of the time before pottery. One temple wall carries mud reliefs of crossed hands, giving it its nickname. Later temples were built right on top of the older ones.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Letters From Assyrian Traders
text: From about the 20th to the 18th century BCE, merchants from Assyria lived in a trading quarter at Kanesh in Anatolia, the end station for caravans from home. They traded Assyrian textiles for Anatolian copper and silver. Thousands of their clay tablets survive, the earliest historical documents found in Anatolia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: West Africa's Early Village Farmers
text: In the second millennium BCE, perhaps pushed south as the Sahara and Sahel dried, the Kintampo people settled across today's Ghana. They built wattle-and-daub structures, kept sheep or goats, and grew cowpea, pearl millet and oil palm while still foraging. They also left stone arm bands, beads and, at some sites, clay figurines.

source.name: Nyame Akuma (Society of Africanist Archaeologists), no. 48, 1997: Casey et al., 'Report of Investigations at the Birimi Site in Northern Ghana'

source2.name: Antiquity (Cambridge University Press): D'Andrea et al., 'Early domesticated cowpea from central Ghana'

title: A Medical Papyrus for Women
text: Found by Flinders Petrie in 1889 in the town of Lahun, beside the pyramid of King Senusret II, the Kahun Papyrus is one of the oldest Egyptian healing texts. It deals with women's health, listing a woman's symptoms, the healer's diagnosis and the treatment. It dates to the late Twelfth or early Thirteenth Dynasty, almost 4,000 years ago.

source.name: UCL Petrie Museum, Digital Egypt for Universities: Kahun Medical Papyrus (UC 32057)

source2.name: UCL Digital Egypt for Universities: Lahun Papyri

title: Pythagoras, a Thousand Years Early
text: A small clay tablet from Babylonia, now called Plimpton 322 and kept at Columbia University, holds a table of numbers in four columns and 15 rows. In 1945 Neugebauer and Sachs showed that it lists Pythagorean triples, whole numbers that fit the sides of right triangles. Babylonian scribes knew this over a thousand years before Pythagoras.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

title: A Dragon Made of Turquoise
text: Erlitou, in central China, had palaces and a bronze foundry, and many scholars link it to the legendary Xia dynasty. In a noble's grave in the palace area, a 70-centimeter dragon made of more than 2,000 tiny turquoise pieces lay on the body, between shoulder and hip. It is one of the earliest dragon images in China.

source.name: Journal of Gems & Gemmology 26(5) 2024, Li Cunxin, 'Study on Archaeological Cleaning and Restoration of Turquoise-Inlaid Dragon-Shaped Artifact from Erlitou Site' (abstract; China University of Geosciences)

source2.name: China.org.cn (China Internet Information Center), 'Archaeologists Find Oldest Chinese Dragon Totem', quoting CASS Institute of Archaeology researchers Du Jinpeng and Xu Hong

title: The Mystery Disc of Phaistos
text: In 1908, the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found a clay disc in the palace of Phaistos on Crete, covered on both sides in a spiral of 241 signs showing people, birds, plants and ships. The signs were pressed into the wet clay with tiny seals, a bit like early printing. Despite many attempts, nobody has convincingly read this one-of-a-kind object.

source.name: Heraklion Archaeological Museum

title: The Oldest Known Mesoamerican Ballcourt
text: Near the Pacific coast of Chiapas, villagers built an earthen court about 80 meters long for the Mesoamerican ballgame, the oldest known by some 500 years. The game was played with a rubber ball. Mesoamericans were making rubber by 1600 BCE, mixing latex with juice from a morning glory vine to make it tough and workable.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America), 'Oldest Ballcourt', 1998

source2.name: MIT News: 'Rubber processed in ancient Mesoamerica, MIT researchers find'

title: Shang Walls of Pounded Earth
text: Around 1600 BCE, early Shang rulers built a city at Zhengzhou ringed by a massive wall enclosing about 3.2 square kilometers. It was made of rammed earth and measured 36 meters wide at its base. By one estimate, it would have taken 10,000 people more than 12 years to build.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Gold Mask of Mycenae
text: In 1876, Heinrich Schliemann dug up royal graves at Mycenae and found a gold face mask, which he hoped belonged to Agamemnon of Trojan War fame. The mask is actually around 300 years too old for that. It still shows how rich Greece's first warrior kings had become.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Rice Fields in Bronze Age Korea
text: Between about 3,500 and 3,000 years ago Korea entered the Bronze Age Mumun period, and intensive farming finally took hold. Villagers grew more rice, along with wheat, soybeans, red beans and hemp, and laid out ridged dry fields and paddy fields in the south. Within about 500 years, paddy farming and bronze reached Japan.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Origins of agriculture (Korea)

title: Linear B: Greek's Oldest Records
text: After Mycenaeans took over Knossos, scribes there wrote clay tablets in a script called Linear B. In 1952, Michael Ventris, an architect who had loved codes since boyhood, showed it was the oldest known form of Greek. The thrilling secret texts? Detailed administrative records, used only for running the palace economy.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Rigveda: Hymns Kept by Memory
text: In the Punjab region of today's India and Pakistan, poets composed the Rigveda, about a thousand hymns to gods such as Agni, the sacred fire, and the warlike Indra. For well over a thousand years it was passed on by memory, not writing, guarded by families of priests. It is the oldest of Hinduism's sacred books.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Egtved Girl's Summer Burial
text: A girl of 16 to 18 was buried in an oak coffin one summer's day in 1370 BCE, wearing a short tunic, a knee-length corded skirt and a bronze belt plate decorated with spirals. Her hair, teeth, nails and clothes survived. At her feet stood a small bark bucket that had once held a kind of beer.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark

title: Akhenaten's City of the Sun
text: Pharaoh Akhenaten broke with tradition, devoting himself to the sun disc, the Aten, and building a brand-new capital on an empty site beside the Nile. Art changed too: house shrines showed the king in the affectionate embrace of his family. About four years after his death the city was abandoned, leaving behind portrait busts of Queen Nefertiti.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Tutankhamun's Dagger From Space
text: Wrapped in the linen around young King Tutankhamun's mummy was a dagger with a golden hilt, a rock crystal pommel and an iron blade. In 2016, scientists found that the blade holds lots of nickel and cobalt, so its iron came from a meteorite. Egypt did not yet smelt its own iron, so 'iron from the sky' was a treasure fit for a pharaoh.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Eos (American Geophysical Union), E. Deatrick, 'Pharaoh's Iron Dagger Made from a Meteorite, Study Confirms' (1 June 2016)

title: Elam's Great Ziggurat
text: King Untash-Napirisha of Elam founded a holy city with a giant stepped temple tower, a ziggurat. Many of its baked bricks carry cuneiform writing naming Elam's gods. It is the best-preserved ziggurat anywhere and the largest outside Mesopotamia, even though the city around it was never finished.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Ramesses Carves a Mountain in Nubia
text: Ramesses II had two temples cut into a cliff in Nubia, with four giant seated statues of himself out front. Twice a year, the sunrise shines deep inside to light up statues in the back room. In the 1960s, the whole temple was cut into blocks and moved uphill to escape a dam's rising lake.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Bronze Age Battlefield
text: Chance finds of weapons, horse bones and human skeletons along the banks of the River Tollense led archaeologists to the remains of a Bronze Age battle. The fighters used arrows and wooden clubs, and some came with horses. Wounds on the bones show vicious face-to-face combat, a fight missing from any written record.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge University Press): Jantzen et al. 2011, 'A Bronze Age battlefield? Weapons and trauma in the Tollense Valley, north-eastern Germany'

title: The Fall of Ugarit
text: The trading city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, with its palaces, temples and libraries, flourished from about 1450 BCE. Then, around 1200 BCE, it fell. Its end coincided with invasions by raiders known as the Sea Peoples, and with earthquakes and famines, part of a wave of troubles across the eastern Mediterranean.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The First Recorded Strike
text: The skilled craftsmen who carved royal tombs lived in their own village and were paid in grain. Under Ramesses III, their rations came late again and again. So they put down their tools and sat in protest outside temples, until officials delivered. It is the first workers' strike in recorded history.

source.name: Museo Egizio, Turin (Papyrus Collection)

title: Questions Burned Into Turtle Shells
text: Shang kings asked about harvests, wars and even toothaches by heating turtle shells and cattle bones until they cracked. The question was written on the bone, and the shape of the crack gave the answer. Found at Anyang, the last Shang capital, these oracle bones carry the earliest known writing in China, and they name the kings who ruled there.

source.name: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco, Education, 'An Introduction to the Shang Dynasty (approx. 1500–1050 BCE)'

title: Grey Pots of the Vedic Heartland
text: Across the upper Ganges plains, people made a grey pottery now called Painted Grey Ware. Archaeologists recognised it as a culture after digs at Hastinapura in 1950-51, and date it from about 1100 BCE, in the Iron Age. Later Vedic texts place the powerful Kuru clan in this same region, where iron technology helped farming villages settle along the rivers.

source.name: INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (UGC, Government of India): Iron Age - Antiquity of Iron in India

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Alphabet Goes Viral
text: Phoenician scribes used just 22 letters, all consonants, instead of hundreds of signs. Phoenician sailors carried the alphabet across the Mediterranean, and the Greeks borrowed it and added vowels. Our letter A began as a sign for 'ox', and if you flip it upside down, you can still see the horns.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Zhou Win the Mandate of Heaven
text: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at the Battle of Muye, around 1046 BCE. The Zhou taught that Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule, and would take it away if he became tyrannical. This idea, the Mandate of Heaven, was later used by Chinese historians to explain why each dynasty fell and another took its place.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tianming' (Mandate of Heaven), revised by Matt Stefon

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Giant Maya Platform Seen by Laser
text: Early Maya people built a flat artificial plateau about 1,400 meters long, the oldest and largest Maya monument found so far. It is so long and low that from the ground you cannot tell it is there. Its discovery was announced in 2020, after lidar, laser scans taken from aircraft, revealed its shape.

source.name: Nature (Inomata et al. 2020)

source2.name: University of Arizona News

title: The Goggle-Eyed Figures of Jōmon
text: Late Jōmon people in northern Japan shaped clay figures called dogū. The most famous one, found at Tsugaru in Aomori and now in the Tokyo National Museum, has huge eyes that look like goggles, a contorted body and patterns all over. The museum dates it to between 1000 and 400 BCE and lists it as an Important Cultural Property.

source.name: Tokyo National Museum (object J-38392)

dateLabel: Under way by 1000 BCE (began about 4000-2000 BCE)
title: Bantu Farmers on the Move
text: From the borderlands of today's Cameroon and Nigeria, Bantu-speaking peoples began spreading across Africa between 4,000 and 6,000 years ago, the most dramatic population movement in the continent's recent past. Over many centuries it reshaped Africa's languages and cultures. That's why some 500 related languages, from Zulu to Swahili, are spoken today.

source.name: Nature (Fortes-Lima et al. 2024)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Chavín's Temple of Sound
text: High in the Andes, the temple of Chavín was a pilgrimage center with a maze of stone galleries inside, complete with vents and drains. Among its carvings is a great stone called the Lanzón. Researchers studying the site's acoustics work with its conch-shell trumpets, called pututus, which may once have filled the galleries with sound.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Stanford University CCRMA, Chavín de Huántar Archaeological Acoustics Project

title: A Party for 69,574 Guests
text: To open his new capital at Kalhu (Nimrud), Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II threw a ten-day feast for 69,574 people, according to a stone stela he set up outside his throne room. The inscription says the guests were wined and dined, then sent home 'in peace and joy'. Easily one of history's biggest parties.

source.name: Oracc 'Nimrud: Materialities of Assyrian Knowledge Production' (University of Pennsylvania Museum / UK AHRC project)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Polynesia's First Beach Village
text: Lapita sailors, famous for their decorated pottery, reached Tonga and settled Nukuleka about 2,800 years ago. Archaeologists identify it as a founder colony for the first settlement of Polynesia, dated very precisely from coral tools left at the site. The village has been lived in continuously ever since, beside a lagoon that is good for fishing.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Burley, Weisler & Zhao 2012)

title: A Steppe Chief and His Many Horses
text: In the Tuva mountains of Siberia, early Scythian-style nomads built a huge burial mound with wooden log chambers arranged like spokes of a wheel. Around a chief and his companions they buried well over a hundred horses. It is one of the oldest known tombs of the horse-riding nomads of the steppe.

source.name: Antiquity (2024), Caspari et al., 'A spectral cavalcade: Early Iron Age horse sacrifice at a royal tomb in southern Siberia' (Cambridge Core, open access)

source2.name: Sensors 19 (2019), Caspari et al., early nomadic funerary architecture in the 'Siberian Valley of the Kings' (PMC)

title: La Venta's Buried Mosaics
text: Between about 800 and 400 BCE La Venta was the leading Olmec center, with a 30-meter clay mound on what was then an island in the Tonalá River. The Olmec laid three huge mosaic pavements here, each showing a jaguar mask, and deliberately buried them soon after they were finished. Their gift was not meant for human eyes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Yerevan's Ancient Fortress
text: Armenia's capital, Yerevan, traces its history back to the fortress of Erebuni, founded in the 780s BCE. Archaeology shows that people had already lived on the spot for thousands of years. The city grew into an important center of trade and has survived a long history of sieges and conquerors, from Romans and Arabs to Mongols and Persians.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Great Dam of Sheba
text: At Maʾrib, capital of the kingdom of Saba, which is often linked with the Queen of Sheba, engineers built a great dam about 580 meters long, with sluice gates to control the water. Its canals turned dry land into a huge oasis that fed the region for centuries. Its final collapse, long after, is even remembered in the Quran.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

dateLabel: Second half of the 8th century BCE
title: A Cheeky Poem on a Drinking Cup
text: Greek settlers on the island of Ischia scratched a short verse onto a clay drinking cup, one of the earliest surviving examples of written Greek. It says, roughly, 'I am Nestor's cup, good to drink from', and promises that whoever drains it will at once be seized by desire for Aphrodite, goddess of love.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Gigante et al. 2021)

title: Guan Zhong Makes Salt Pay
text: When Duke Huan became ruler of Qi in 685 BCE, he made Guan Zhong his chief adviser, even though Guan had backed his rival for the throne. Together they brought in a uniform tax system, a central army, and state monopolies on salt and iron. Qi became the leading power of the Spring and Autumn period, heading a league of states from 651 BCE.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Qi' (ancient state, China)

source2.name: ChinaKnowledge (Ulrich Theobald), 'Guanzi' (section 'The politician')

title: A King Who Collected Books
text: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, who could read Sumerian and obscure Akkadian scripts, gathered a great library of clay tablets at Nineveh: omens, prayers, science and stories. More than 20,000 tablets and fragments survive in the British Museum, even though enemies sacked the city in 612 BCE. Thanks to the library, we can still read the Epic of Gilgamesh.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The First Coins Have a Lion
text: The kingdom of Lydia began stamping small lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver panned from its rivers, with designs such as a lion's head. Ancient Greek writers credited the Lydians with inventing coinage, and the coins themselves back them up. Later the Lydian king Croesus introduced the first coins of pure gold.

source.name: Archaeological Exploration of Sardis (Harvard Art Museums / Cornell): J. H. Kroll, 'The Coins of Sardis'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Sappho Sings of Love
text: On the island of Lesbos, Sappho wrote lyric poems admired in every age for their beauty. In antiquity she was counted among the greatest poets, and Plato is said to have hailed her as 'the tenth Muse'. Her work once filled nine books, but only one poem survives complete; the rest are fragments, many recovered from ancient papyrus since 1898.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Poetry Foundation

title: An Eclipse Stops a War
text: The Lydians and Medes had been at war for five years when, in the middle of a battle, day suddenly turned to night. Herodotus says both sides stopped fighting and were eager to make peace. He also claims Thales of Miletus had foretold it, though modern scholars doubt he could have. Astronomers match it to the total eclipse of May 28, 585 BCE.

source.name: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center: Solar Eclipses of History

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Babylon's Brilliant Blue Gate
text: King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon with a dazzling entrance, the Ishtar Gate, covered in shiny blue glazed bricks. Rows of lions, bulls and dragons march along its walls. Archaeologists shipped its pieces to Berlin, where a reconstruction stands in a museum today.

source.name: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, New York University

title: Laws Cast on a Bronze Cauldron
text: Zichan, chief minister of the small state of Zheng, had the state's penal laws cast in bronze for all to see. It is often described as the earliest recorded publication of written laws in China. A critic, Shuxiang, warned that once people knew the rules they would appeal to the written word, and lawsuits and bribery would multiply.

source.name: University of Hong Kong, Department of Philosophy (Chad Hansen)

source2.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

title: Nok Sculptors and Iron Smelters
text: In central Nigeria, the Nok people made striking clay sculptures of people with fancy hairstyles and large triangular eyes with pierced pupils. Around this time they were also smelting iron, among the earliest in West Africa. The first Nok sculpture turned up in a tin mine near the village of Nok in 1928.

source.name: National Geographic

title: Ethiopia's Ancient Stone Temple
text: In the highlands of Tigray, builders in the kingdom of D'mt raised a tall temple of perfectly fitted stone blocks, laid without mortar. Its style closely copies temples of Saba across the Red Sea in Yemen. Still standing, roofless, after about 2,700 years, it is the oldest standing building in Ethiopia.

source.name: ISPRS Archives XXXVIII-5/W16 (2011), Lindstaedt, Mechelke, Schnelle & Kersten (German Archaeological Institute / HafenCity University), 'Virtual reconstruction of the Almaqah Temple of Yeha in Ethiopia'

source2.name: Jordan Journal for History and Archaeology 15(2), 'The Yeha Temple (Ethiopia) at the beginning of the first millennium BC: southern Arabian influence' (abstract via Crossref)

title: A City on a Flattened Mountain
text: The Zapotec people levelled the top of a mountain ridge in Oaxaca to build Monte Albán, their leading city for about a thousand years. Its plaza is lined with temples and a ball court. Hundreds of carved stones, nicknamed the Danzantes or 'dancers', show twisted human figures, probably defeated enemies rather than party guests.

source.name: INAH (Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Mexico)

source2.name: FAMSI research report (Heather S. Orr, Danzantes of Building L)

title: The First Stretch of the Grand Canal
text: King Fuchai of Wu ordered a canal dug to link the Yangtze and Huai rivers so his army could sail north to fight. This Han Gou canal was later absorbed into the Grand Canal, which grew to about 1,800 kilometers. Barges still use parts of it, making it the longest artificial river on Earth.

source.name: Hangzhou Municipal Government (Culture, Radio, TV and Tourism Bureau)

source2.name: University of Massachusetts Boston, Building the World

title: Hanno Sails Down Africa
text: The Carthaginian navigator Hanno is said to have led a large fleet down Africa's west coast in the 400s BCE, founding towns and a trading post. His report, said to have been set up in a temple in Carthage, survives only in a Greek version that scholars doubt. It describes a tribe of hairy women called 'Gorillai', and in 1847 Thomas Savage borrowed the word for a great ape: gorilla.

source.name: American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language (word history of 'gorilla')

source2.name: History in Africa (Cambridge University Press), 'The Periplus of Hanno in the History and Historiography of Black Africa'

title: The Swirly Art of the Celts
text: Across much of Europe, Celtic metalworkers began decorating swords, neck rings and shields with flowing spirals and curling plant shapes. The style is named after La Tène, a spot on Lake Neuchâtel where thousands of objects were pulled from the water in the 1850s. Many seem to have been thrown in on purpose as offerings.

source.name: Stanford University Archaeolog (Patrick Hunt)

title: Building the Parthenon
text: Work began on a marble temple for Athena on the Acropolis, paid for partly with tribute money from Athens' allies. The builders added subtle refinements: the steps curve upward slightly and the columns bulge a little in the middle. Scholars debate whether this was to correct optical illusions or to make the building seem alive. It held a huge gold-and-ivory statue of the goddess.

source.name: Reed College, 'Reading Greek Temples: The Parthenon'

source2.name: PBS NOVA, interview with Jeffrey Hurwit (University of Oregon)

title: Anuradhapura, City of Giant Tanks
text: Sri Lanka's chronicles say King Pandukabhaya made Anuradhapura his capital, and it flourished as the island's political and religious capital for 1,300 years. He is credited with building one of its first reservoirs, called tanks, to store water for farming. Many of these ancient artificial lakes were later restored and are still in use today, more than two thousand years on.

source.name: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 'Reservoirs of Sri Lanka and their fisheries'

source2.name: University of Peradeniya research repository

title: The Marquis and His 65 Bells
text: A small-state ruler, Marquis Yi of Zeng, was buried about 2,400 years ago with a whole orchestra, including a set of 65 bronze bells, one a gift from the king of Chu. Soldiers came across the tomb in 1977, and each bell sounds two notes, one when struck at the centre and another at the side. It is the largest and best-preserved set of bronze bells in the world.

source.name: UNESCO Memory of the World Register

source2.name: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination form (Hubei Provincial Museum), hosted by National Archives Administration of China

title: Mozi, the Anti-War Engineer
text: The thinker Mozi taught 'impartial care': be as concerned for strangers as for your own family. He condemned wars of conquest, and some of his followers became experts at defending cities under attack. Later members of his school studied geometry, mechanics and optics, and their writings already discuss the images light makes when it passes through a tiny hole.

source.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Mohism'

source2.name: Fundamental Research (2025) review via PubMed Central

title: Iron Furnaces by Lake Victoria
text: In the Great Lakes region of East Africa, farmers of the Urewe culture were smelting iron in brick-built furnaces, making this one of the oldest well-dated ironworking centres in Africa. They also made pottery with a dimple in the base that archaeologists use to trace them. These communities are linked to the spread of Bantu-speaking peoples, whose languages now have over 300 million speakers.

source.name: African Studies Centre Leiden, AfricaBib (abstract of Clist 1987, Muntu 6: 35-62)

source2.name: PLOS ONE

title: Pāṇini's Grammar Machine
text: The scholar Pāṇini described the whole Sanskrit language in about 4,000 short rules, packed so tightly they work almost like computer code. His grammar, the Ashtadhyayi, is still studied in India. Modern linguists and even computer scientists admire how he built complex words step by step from tiny pieces.

source.name: University of Cambridge

title: Shang Yang Remakes Qin
text: Minister Shang Yang began harsh reforms in the state of Qin: rank was earned mainly by fighting or producing extra grain, and neighbours and relatives had to report each other's crimes. He also set standard measures, and a bronze measuring vessel made under his direction survives in the Shanghai Museum. His system turned Qin into a formidable military power that later conquered all its rivals.

source.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Legalism in Chinese Philosophy'

source2.name: China Daily (quoting Shanghai Museum deputy director Li Zhongmou)

title: The Tomb That Named All Mausoleums
text: Mausolus, ruler of Caria, began a gigantic tomb for himself, and after he died in 353 BCE his sister and queen Artemisia II carried on the work with top Greek sculptors. Topped by a stepped pyramid and a chariot statue, it became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Medieval earthquakes damaged it and its stones were reused in Bodrum's castle, but its name lives on in every 'mausoleum' today.

source.name: National Geographic History

title: Chandragupta Founds the Maurya Empire
text: With his clever adviser Chanakya, the young Chandragupta overthrew the Nanda kings and made Pataliputra the capital of a new empire that spread across much of South Asia. A Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, lived there and described the city, ringed by a wooden wall with holes for shooting arrows. Jain tradition says Chandragupta later gave up his throne to live as a monk.

source.name: INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (University Grants Commission, India), 'The Mauryan Empire'

source2.name: Strabo, Geography 15.1.36 (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius, University of Chicago)

title: Rice Paddies Reach Japan
text: Wet-rice farming, brought by migrants from the Korean Peninsula, had spread across western Japan by this time, along with bronze and iron. This is the Yayoi period, named after the Tokyo neighborhood where its pottery was first found in 1884. Newer dating suggests the first paddies in Kyushu go back to about 900 BCE. Moated settlements appeared, and fighting between groups went on for centuries.

source.name: Evolutionary Human Sciences via PubMed Central (Hudson/Barnes, 'Japan considered from the hypothesis of farmer/language spread')

source2.name: Yoshinogari Historical Park (official site), 'History of Yoshinogari'

title: The Embroidered Mummies of Paracas
text: On Peru's desert south coast, the Paracas people wrapped their honored dead in layers of stunning woven and embroidered cloth, making 'mummy bundles'; 429 were found in one cemetery. One mantle shows 32 different figures of animals, people, plants and tools. The Paracas also carried out the earliest known skull surgery in Peru, cutting large openings, and about 40 percent of patients survived.

source.name: Bard Graduate Center

source2.name: National Geographic (interview with John Verano, Tulane University)

title: Dujiangyan Tames a River
text: The Qin governor Li Bing split the flood-prone Min River with an island shaped like a fish's mouth, sending water into irrigation channels without building a dam. Workers cut through a mountain by heating rock and then cooling it with water. The system still waters the Chengdu Plain today, over 2,200 years later.

source.name: China Daily (feature on the UNESCO site Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Parthians Ride In
text: Arsaces, leader of a nomadic tribe, took over the Persian region of Parthia and founded an empire that lasted almost 500 years. Parthian horsemen were famous for turning in the saddle to shoot arrows while retreating. That trick may be the origin of the English phrase 'a parting shot'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ARSACIDS ii. The Arsacid dynasty'

source2.name: Merriam-Webster, 'Parthian' (Did you know? note on 'Parthian shot' / 'parting shot')

title: A Canal Over the Watershed
text: After unifying China, the First Emperor of Qin ordered Shi Lu to dig the Lingqu canal to carry grain, finished in 214 BCE, helping Qin conquer the far south. Linking the Xiang and Li rivers, it joined the Yangtze and Pearl River basins. For over 2,000 years it was the main water route between central China and the south, and it still serves irrigation and flood control.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Lingqu Canal (Ref. 5814)

title: A Decree in Three Scripts
text: Egyptian priests issued a decree praising the boy king Ptolemy V and had it carved in hieroglyphs, everyday Demotic script and Greek. One broken copy was dug up in 1799 by French soldiers building fortifications at Rosetta. Because scholars could read the Greek, the Rosetta Stone became the key that let Champollion publish his decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1821-22.

source.name: American Research Center in Egypt (ARCE)

source2.name: British Museum blog, 'Everything you ever wanted to know about the Rosetta Stone'

title: Hipparchus Notices the Sky Drifting
text: Using his own careful observations and older records, including Babylonian data, the astronomer Hipparchus worked out that the equinoxes slowly drift against the background of stars. He had discovered the 'precession of the equinoxes', caused by a slow change in the direction of Earth's axis. He also invented a scale of star brightness that astronomers still use today, in updated form.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

source2.name: Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer), entry 'Hipparchus of Nicaea', hosted by St Andrews

title: War for the Heavenly Horses
text: Emperor Wu wanted the powerful horses of Dayuan in Central Asia, said to sweat blood. When Dayuan refused to hand them over, he sent armies to a land Sima Qian placed about 10,000 li west of China. The first attempt failed, but the second besieged the capital for more than forty days and came home with a few dozen prized horses and about 3,000 ordinary ones.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington: Selections from the Han Narrative Histories (Shiji ch. 123)

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington: Shiji ch. 123 (Hirth translation)

title: Sima Qian Finishes His History
text: Court historian Sima Qian completed the Shiji, a history covering well over 2,000 years in 130 chapters, from the legendary Yellow Emperor to his own day. After angering the emperor, he chose a humiliating punishment over death so he could finish it. With lively biographies of assassins, merchants and jesters, it became the model for later Chinese dynastic histories.

source.name: Asia for Educators, Columbia University: Sima Qian's Letter to Ren An

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sima Qian'

title: The Silver Cauldron in the Bog
text: Peat cutters in Denmark found a silver cauldron decorated with gods, elephants and a seated figure wearing antlers. It had been taken apart and laid in a bog, likely as an offering. Its style suggests it was made far away in southeastern Europe, showing how far precious objects traveled in Iron Age Europe.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark, 'The dating and origin of the silver cauldron'

source2.name: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Gundestrup Cauldron'

title: Tea Appears on a Chore List
text: The writer Wang Bao drew up a contract for a servant, listing all his duties. Among them: going to the town of Wuyang to buy tea. Dated to 59 BCE, it is the first clear written record of tea as a drink, and it suggests a tea market had already formed.

source.name: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Chinese Academy of Social Sciences), 'Tea culture brewed in the Yangtze River basin'

source2.name: Scientific Reports (via PubMed Central), Lu et al., 'Earliest tea as evidence for one branch of the Silk Road across the Tibetan Plateau'

title: Silla's King Hatched From an Egg
text: Korean tradition says the kingdom of Silla was founded when village elders crowned Bak Hyeokgeose, a boy who hatched from a glowing egg. Silla grew from a small state into the power that united most of Korea. Counting from its legendary start, it lasted about 1,000 years, one of the longest-running dynasties anywhere.

source.name: Korea.net (official website of the Republic of Korea)

source2.name: The Korea Times, Mark Peterson (Brigham Young University), 'Longest dynasties' (2020)

title: The Oldest Long Count Date
text: A stone monument in southern Mexico carries a date in the Long Count, a calendar that counted days from a starting point in 3114 BCE. Its date works out to 36 BCE, the oldest known. The Maya later used this system on hundreds of monuments, writing numbers with dots, bars and a shell for zero.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine, 'Time, Kingship, and the Maya Universe: Maya Calendars'

source2.name: PubMed Central (peer-reviewed), 'Non-power positional number representation systems, bijective numeration, and the Mesoamerican discovery of zero'

title: Wang Zhaojun Goes North
text: A palace lady named Wang Zhaojun, who is said to have volunteered, was sent to marry the leader of the Xiongnu, the nomad power on China's northern border, sealing a peace deal. She lived the rest of her life on the steppe. Remembered as one of China's Four Great Beauties, she is often painted on horseback holding a pipa lute.

source.name: China Daily (Inner Mongolia)

source2.name: University of Hawai'i OER textbook (P. Patterson and B. Parkinson), 'Steppe Peoples of Central Asia'

title: The Kandake Who Stood Up to Rome
text: Kush's queen Amanirenas sent armies against Roman Egypt and carried off statues of Augustus. One bronze head was buried beneath temple steps at Meroë, where visitors would walk over the emperor; archaeologists dug it up in 1910. After years of fighting, Kush won a peace deal that canceled Rome's demands for tribute.

source.name: University of Liverpool News, 'Mary Beard discusses the revolutionary politics of the Meroe Head of Augustus'

source2.name: The Conversation (university researcher), 'the forgotten queens of ancient Nubia'

title: Rome Meets the Desert Farmers
text: The Roman general Balbus marched deep into the Sahara, captured Garamantian towns and celebrated a triumph in Rome. The Garamantes ran a desert kingdom by digging networks of underground tunnels, called foggaras, to bring ancient groundwater to their fields. They grew wheat, grapes and dates in the middle of the sand.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America), 'Kingdom of the Sands'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Garamantes' (Fezzan excerpt)

title: Counting Nearly 60 Million People
text: Han officials recorded a census of the whole empire. The count preserved for 2 CE lists about 12.2 million households and 59.6 million people, and remarkably it has survived for 2,000 years. Since modern estimates put the world's population then at roughly 170 to 400 million, perhaps one in every four or five humans lived under Han rule.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'China: The practice of government' (Han dynasty)

source2.name: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Estimates of World Population

title: Ambush in the Teutoburg Forest
text: Arminius, a Germanic chief who had served in the Roman army, led three Roman legions into a trap in muddy forest country and destroyed them. Rome gave up on conquering land east of the Rhine. The battlefield was rediscovered in 1987 by a British officer with a metal detector who found Roman coins and sling stones.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battle of the Teutoburg Forest'

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America), review 'Lost Legions'

title: Polynesia's Long Pause
text: Seafarers had settled Tonga and Samoa about 800 BCE, and then stayed put for over a thousand years. During this long pause, a distinct Polynesian language and culture took shape. Later, voyagers in double-hulled canoes sailed east, steering by the stars and ocean swells, to reach islands as remote as Hawai'i and Rapa Nui.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2018), 'Early cessation of ceramic production for ancestral Polynesian society in Tonga'

source2.name: PLOS ONE (2023), 'Estimated energetic demands of thermoregulation during ancient canoe passages from Tahiti to Hawaii and New Zealand'

title: A Preacher From Galilee
text: Jesus, a Jewish teacher from Galilee who spoke Aramaic, drew crowds with his teaching and was crucified in Jerusalem on the orders of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. His small group of followers spread the message that he had risen. Within three centuries, Christianity had become a major religion of the Roman world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jesus'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pontius Pilate'

title: The Trưng Sisters Rise Up
text: Two sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in northern Vietnam, and tradition says women generals fought at their side. They ruled as queens for about three years before a Han army defeated them. Vietnam still honors them with temples, street names and a yearly festival.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Trung Sisters'

source2.name: Vietnam News Agency (VietnamPlus), 'Uprising by national heroines commemorated'

title: Pepper Ships to Muziris
text: Greek-speaking merchants from Roman Egypt rode the monsoon winds to Muziris on India's southwest coast to buy pepper, pearls and silk cloth. A sailors' guidebook, the Periplus, describes the port. The Roman writer Pliny grumbled that India drained about 50 million sesterces from the empire every year.

source.name: Journal of Global History (Cambridge University Press, 2023), article on Indo-Roman trade

source2.name: Fordham University Internet History Sourcebooks, The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (Schoff trans.), sec. 56

title: The Gold Seal Found by a Farmer
text: Chinese records say Emperor Guangwu gave a seal to envoys from Na, a small state in Japan. In 1784 a farmer on Shikanoshima island dug up a gold seal with a snake-shaped handle, reading 'King of Na of Wa, vassal of Han'. It is only about 2.3 centimeters across and is now a national treasure.

source.name: Fukuoka City Museum via Google Arts & Culture, 'The Gold Seal Kan no Wa no Na no Kokuou'

source2.name: Japan Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (Kyushu Regional Bureau), 'Interaction with the continent (6)'

title: Boudica Burns Roman Towns
text: After Roman officials seized her kingdom and abused her family, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a huge British uprising. Her forces burned Colchester, London and St Albans before Roman troops defeated them. Beneath London, archaeologists still find a layer of burnt debris from that fire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Boudicca'

source2.name: Current Archaeology, 'AD 50 - The story of Roman London'

title: The Buddha Gets a Face
text: For centuries, artists showed the Buddha only through symbols like footprints or an empty throne. Around this time sculptors in Gandhara and Mathura began carving him in human form. Gandharan statues mix Indian ideas with Greek-style wavy hair and draped robes, a legacy of Alexander's conquests.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Kushan Empire'

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Gandhara'

title: Ban Zhao Finishes the Book of Han
text: When her brother Ban Gu died before completing his history of the Han dynasty, scholar Ban Zhao finished it, continuing its eight tables. She also taught the empress and palace ladies, including astronomy and mathematics, and wrote 'Lessons for Women'. She is called China's first woman historian.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ban Zhao'

source2.name: World History Connected (Univ. of Illinois Press), Yuen Ting Lee, 'Ban Zhao: Scholar of Han Dynasty China'

title: The Envoy Who Almost Reached Rome
text: General Ban Chao sent Gan Ying west to find Daqin, the Chinese name for the Roman Empire. Gan Ying reached a great sea, possibly the Persian Gulf, but Parthian sailors warned him the voyage could take up to two years. He turned back. The Parthians may have wanted to keep their role as silk middlemen.

source.name: University of Washington Silk Road Seattle, Hou Hanshu 'Western Regions' (trans. John E. Hill)

title: The Dome With a Hole in the Top
text: Under Emperor Hadrian, Romans finished the Pantheon, a temple with a concrete dome 43 meters wide. A round opening at the top, about 8 meters across, is the only window, and rain still falls onto the floor below. Nearly 1,900 years later, it remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pantheon'

source2.name: MIT News, 'Riddle solved: Why was Roman concrete so durable?' (2023)

title: Kanishka's Gods on Coins
text: Kanishka became ruler of the Kushan Empire, which stretched from Central Asia into northern India along the Silk Road. His coins show a crowd of gods: Greek, Persian, Hindu and the Buddha.
