He switched official inscriptions from Greek to the local Bactrian language, and Buddhist tradition remembers him as a great patron.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kanishka'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kushan Dynasty ii. Inscriptions of the Kushans'

title: The Dragon Jar That Felt Earthquakes
text: Astronomer Zhang Heng built a metal jar with eight dragons around it, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed frog. When the ground shook, a ball dropped, showing the quake's direction. Once a ball fell when no one felt anything, and days later reports arrived of an earthquake more than a thousand kilometres away.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zhang Heng'

source2.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews), 'Zhang Heng'

title: The Grand Anicut Still Works
text: The Chola king Karikala, who probably ruled in the late 2nd century CE, is credited with building the Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, a barrier across the Kaveri River where it divides, sending water into farm canals. It is still in use today and is considered one of the oldest water-control structures in the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kaveri River'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Karikalan' (India: Southern Indian kingdoms excerpt)

title: The Yellow Turbans Rebel
text: Zhang Jue, a faith healer who led a Daoist movement awaiting an age of Great Peace, promised a new age would begin in 184. Hundreds of thousands of followers rose up wearing yellow headscarves. The Han crushed the revolt, but the warlords who did it grew so strong that the dynasty fell apart.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yellow Turbans'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cao Cao'

title: Champa Breaks Away
text: A local official broke away from Han China and founded a kingdom in central Vietnam that Chinese records called Linyi. The Cham kingdoms of Champa grew up in the same region, though historians debate exactly how they link to Linyi. Champa traded by sea for over a thousand years, and its brick temple towers for Hindu gods still stand.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Champa'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'My Son Sanctuary'

title: Defeat at Red Cliffs
text: In 208 the warlord Cao Cao pushed south toward the Yangtze, but his tired army was struck by sickness. At Red Cliffs, near today's Wuhan, Huang Gai of Sun Quan's forces sent burning ships, driven by the wind, into Cao Cao's fleet and camp. Cao Cao never crossed the Yangtze, and China split into three kingdoms, a story retold in the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

source.name: Rafe de Crespigny, 'Man from the Margin: Cao Cao and the Three Kingdoms' (51st Morrison Lecture), ANU Open Research

source2.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Su Shi, 'The Red Cliff' (introduction)

title: Taupō Blows Its Top
text: One of the most violent eruptions of the last 5,000 years tore through New Zealand's North Island around 232 CE, sending scorching ash flows across about 20,000 square kilometers. No people saw it, because humans had not yet reached New Zealand. Its caldera is now filled by Lake Taupō, the country's largest lake.

source.name: GeoNet (GNS Science / New Zealand government), 'Taupō volcano'

source2.name: Nature Communications (2019), Hogg et al., 'Wiggle-match radiocarbon dating of the Taupo eruption'

title: Mani Starts a World Religion
text: The prophet Mani began preaching a faith that saw the universe as a struggle between light and darkness. He was also a painter and illustrated his own holy books. Manichaeism spread from North Africa to China, and the young Augustine, later a famous Christian thinker, followed it for about a decade.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Manicheism i. General Survey'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mani'

title: Chinese Envoys Visit Funan
text: The kingdom of Wu sent two envoys, Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, to Funan, a trading power on the Mekong. They reported walled towns, people paying taxes in gold, silver and pearls, and books and archives written in a script like India's. Their accounts are some of the earliest descriptions of a Southeast Asian kingdom.

source.name: Kenneth R. Hall, Maritime Trade and State Development in Early Southeast Asia (University of Hawai'i Press, 1985), ch. 3 (open access on UH Press Manifold)

source2.name: ChinaKnowledge (Ulrich Theobald), 'Funan'

title: The Lord of Sipán's Golden Peanuts
text: A Moche warrior-priest was buried with gold and silver headdresses, ear spools and a necklace of giant metal peanuts, half gold and half silver. His tomb, found in 1987, was one of the first rich Moche burials discovered untouched by looters. Archaeologists compare it to Tutankhamun's tomb for the Americas.

source.name: Current World Archaeology, 'Tombs of the Lords of Sipán'

title: Aksum Mints Its Own Gold
text: Around 290 CE, King Endubis became the first ruler of Aksum to issue coins, striking them in gold, silver and copper with Greek writing. Only three other powers of the time, including Rome and Persia, made coins in all three metals. Aksumite gold coins have turned up as far away as India and southern Arabia, where a hoard of over 800 was found near Aden.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Foundations of Aksumite Civilization and Its Christian Legacy'

source2.name: Anglo-Ethiopian Society, lecture 'An Introduction to Axumite Coinage' (Vincent West, 27 March 2007)

title: Anthony Moves to the Desert
text: An Egyptian named Anthony gave his family's land to his neighbours and his money to the poor, then moved into the desert to live alone in prayer. Others followed him, and Christian monasticism grew from Egypt's hermits. The Monastery of Saint Anthony still stands near the mountain by the Red Sea where he later settled.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'St. Anthony of Egypt'

source2.name: Athanasius, Life of St. Anthony, ch. 2-3 (NPNF translation, New Advent)

title: Diocletian Sets the Price of Eggs
text: Fighting runaway inflation, Emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for well over a thousand items, from eggs and beer to barbers' fees and even a lion. Stone copies give a rare peek at Roman shopping. The edict flopped: it was impossible to enforce across the vast empire and was scarcely applied.

source.name: Aphrodisias Excavations (New York University / University of Oxford), 'Diocletian's Price Edict'

source2.name: The Conversation (university historians), 'Skyrocketing prices are an age-old problem. Here's how Roman emperors battled runaway inflation'

title: Miwnay's Angry Letter
text: A bag of letters by Sogdian merchants from Central Asia was lost near Dunhuang and found in 1907 in a ruined watchtower. One is from a woman named Miwnay, stranded with her daughter after her husband left. She writes that she would rather have married a dog or a pig. The letters reveal Silk Road life.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Asian Art, 'The Sogdians: Ancient Letters' (Nicholas Sims-Williams)

title: The Boat Sunk as a Gift
text: People in southern Denmark sank a 23-meter oak boat in Nydam bog along with masses of weapons, at a site archaeologists see as an offering of war booty after battle. Found in 1863 and tree-ring dated to about 310-320 CE, it is the oldest known boat built in the 'clinker' style, with overlapping planks fastened by metal pins.

source.name: Museum fuer Archaeologie Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums), 'Iron Age / The famous Nydam Boat'

source2.name: Radiocarbon 61(5), 2019 (Hüls, Meadows & Rau), 'Interpreting 14C measurements on 3rd-4th century AD iron artifacts from Nydam'

title: Constantine's New Rome
text: Emperor Constantine dedicated a new capital on the old Greek town of Byzantium, where Europe meets Asia. He filled it with statues hauled from across the empire. Constantinople would be the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for over 1,100 years and is today's Istanbul.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Istanbul: Constantinople'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Constantine I'

title: Wine Cups at the Orchid Pavilion
text: At a spring festival in 353, the calligrapher Wang Xizhi and his friends floated wine cups down a stream; when a cup reached a guest, he had to write a poem or drink three cups as a penalty. Wang wrote a preface for their poems that became the most famous calligraphy in China. A Tang emperor reportedly had the original buried with him.

source.name: National Palace Museum, Taipei, exhibition 'A Penchant for the Orchid Pavilion'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lanting Xu'

title: Buddhism Arrives in Korea
text: In 372 a Chinese Buddhist monk named Sundo arrived at the court of Goguryeo, the northernmost of Korea's Three Kingdoms, as Buddhism came in from the Chinese state of Former Qin. King Sosurim supported the new faith and that same year founded a Confucian academy. From Korea, Buddhism would later travel on to Japan.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Goguryeo'

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Korea, 1-500 A.D.'

title: Strangers From Teotihuacan Arrive
text: A warlord named Siyaj K'ak' arrived at Tikal with ties to the giant city of Teotihuacan, about 1,000 kilometers away. On that same day, Tikal's king died. Soon a new king took the throne, the son of a mysterious ruler nicknamed 'Spearthrower Owl', and Mexican-style art spread through Maya cities.

source.name: David Stuart (Peabody Museum, Harvard), 'The Arrival of Strangers', Pre-Columbian Art Research Institute / Mesoweb

source2.name: National Geographic, 'Archaeologists have discovered a 1,600-year-old Maya altar...'

title: The Pillar That Won't Rust
text: Gupta-era smiths forged an iron pillar over 7 meters tall and weighing about 6 tonnes, inscribed for a king named Chandra. After roughly 1,600 years outdoors, it has barely rusted. Scientists found the iron contains phosphorus that helps form a thin protective layer on the surface.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Iron Pillar of Delhi'

title: Faxian Walks to India
text: The Chinese monk Faxian crossed deserts and mountains to India to find Buddhist rule books. He described Gupta India as peaceful, with free hospitals for the poor in Pataliputra, and said criminals were usually just fined rather than executed or beaten. He sailed home by way of Sri Lanka, surviving storms, after about 14 years away.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Faxian'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chandragupta II'

title: Hypatia of Alexandria
text: Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher who led a school of Platonist philosophy in Alexandria, drawing students from far and wide, and often met with the city's Roman governor. She wrote commentaries on math texts. In 415 she was murdered by a Christian mob during a bitter political feud, and she later became a symbol of learning and women in science.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hypatia' (Michael Deakin)

source2.name: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History VII.15 (NPNF translation, New Advent)

title: Nalanda Opens Its Doors
text: Under the Gupta kings, a Buddhist monastery at Nalanda grew into a huge centre of learning with lecture halls and dormitories. At its peak it drew thousands of students from as far away as China, Korea and Southeast Asia. Entrance was famously hard: the gatekeeper quizzed newcomers with tough questions, and most failed.

source.name: Nalanda University (Government of India), 'History and Revival'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nalanda'

title: Ilopango Buries Maya Farmland
text: The Ilopango volcano exploded in a gigantic eruption that ranks among the 20 biggest blasts of sulfur into the stratosphere in the last 2,000 years. Ash blanketed farms and villages of the southeastern Maya region, and people had to leave for generations. The volcano's collapsed crater is now a lake right next to San Salvador.

source.name: PNAS (via PubMed Central), Smith et al. 2020, 'The magnitude and impact of the 431 CE Tierra Blanca Joven eruption of Ilopango, El Salvador'

source2.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, 'Ilopango'

title: A Keyhole Tomb Twice a Pyramid's Length
text: During the Kofun period, Japan's rulers were buried under huge keyhole-shaped mounds. The biggest, Daisen Kofun, is about 486 meters long, twice the length of the Great Pyramid's base, and is surrounded by three moats. Thousands of clay figures called haniwa once lined the tomb, which is linked to Emperor Nintoku.

source.name: Sakai City (official), 'Nintoku-tenno-ryo Kofun'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mausoleum of Nintoku'

title: Giant Buddhas at Yungang
text: The monk Tanyao persuaded the Northern Wei court to carve five colossal Buddhas into a sandstone cliff near the capital, possibly honoring past emperors. Work went on for decades. Today the Yungang Grottoes hold about 51,000 statues in 252 caves and niches, with the biggest Buddhas reaching up to 17 meters tall.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yungang caves'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Yungang Grottoes'

title: The Last Western Emperor Steps Down
text: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and returned the leftover imperial regalia to the emperor Zeno in Constantinople. The year 476 is traditionally considered the end of the Western Roman Empire. The boy was spared because of his youth, given a pension and sent to live with relatives in southern Italy.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Romulus Augustulus' (with 'Odoacer')

source2.name: Michael Maas, 'Reversals of Fortune: An Overview of the Age of Attila', The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Attila (Cambridge University Press)

title: A Palace on the Lion Rock
text: King Kashyapa built a fortress palace on top of a granite rock rising about 180 meters from the jungle, entered through the paws of a giant brick lion. Painted women still decorate a sheltered rock face. Later visitors scratched hundreds of poems and comments onto the rock's walls, early graffiti now treasured by scholars.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sigiriya'

source2.name: National Geographic History, 'Sigiriya, the Lion Fortress of Sri Lanka'

title: Mazdak Preaches Sharing
text: In Sasanian Persia, a preacher named Mazdak led an egalitarian movement that attacked the privileges of the elite and demanded that wealth be shared among the poor. King Kavad I supported it for a time, alarming nobles and priests. Kavad later withdrew his support and his son Khosrow I crushed the movement, but its discontent kept simmering for generations.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mazdakism'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'IRAN ii. Iranian History (1) Pre-Islamic Times'

title: Clovis Picks Paris as His Capital
text: Clovis, king of the Franks, took the small river town of Paris and later made it the center of his kingdom; he was buried there in 511. He converted to Catholic Christianity and worked closely with the bishops of Gaul. His people gave their name to a whole country: 'France' comes from the Franks.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Paris'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Clovis I'

title: Aksum Sails Across the Red Sea
text: King Kaleb of Aksum sent armies across the Red Sea against Himyar in Yemen, and in 525 the Aksumites crushed it. For a time, an African kingdom ruled part of Arabia. Aksum, a great trading power that commanded the ivory trade, even minted its own coins, which have turned up as far away as India and Sri Lanka.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Himyar'

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Foundations of Aksumite Civilization and Its Christian Legacy'

title: Benedict's Rule for Monks
text: A monk named Benedict founded a monastery on a hilltop south of Rome. His short rulebook set out a balanced day of prayer, work and reading, much later summed up in the motto 'pray and work'. By about 800 it guided most monasteries in western Europe, which became the chief keepers of learning, copying and saving many ancient books.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Monte Cassino Abbey'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'St. Benedict'

title: The First Great Plague
text: A deadly plague broke out at the Egyptian port of Pelusium and spread along trade routes to Constantinople. DNA from old skeletons shows it was caused by the same germ as the later Black Death. It returned again and again for about two hundred years, emptying cities around the Mediterranean.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Plague of Justinian'

title: A Gift of Buddha Statues to Japan
text: A king of Baekje in Korea sent a golden Buddha statue and holy texts to the Japanese court. Some nobles loved the new faith while others feared it would anger Japan's own gods. After years of quarrels the Soga clan's side won, and Buddhism grew into one of Japan's great traditions.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Japan: Yamato decline and the introduction of Buddhism)

source2.name: Asia for Educators, Columbia University

title: Tikal Loses a Great War
text: The mighty Maya city of Tikal was defeated by its rival Calakmul and allies such as Caracol. Afterwards Tikal raised no new carved monuments for over a century, a quiet stretch archaeologists call the 'hiatus'. Later Tikal bounced back and built some of its tallest temples.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (R. Sharer, 'Time of Kings and Queens')

source2.name: A. F. Chase & D. Z. Chase, 'The Materialization of Classic Period Maya Warfare' (Caracol Archaeological Project)

title: The Sui Reunite China
text: After nearly three hundred years of split kingdoms, the Sui dynasty conquered the south and joined China back together. The Sui lasted less than forty years, yet they built a huge new capital and set up exams for officials. Their work laid the ground for the golden age of the Tang.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sui dynasty)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Tang Dynasty (618-907)

title: A Village Frozen by Ash
text: A nearby volcano buried this Maya farming village under several meters of ash. The people seem to have escaped, but they left everything behind: sleeping mats, pots with beans, and a garden of manioc plants. It is often called the 'Pompeii of the Americas' because it shows everyday life, not kings.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: University of Colorado Boulder

title: Digging the Grand Canal
text: Emperor Yang of Sui forced huge numbers of laborers to link China's great rivers with canals. The Grand Canal let rice and goods float from the rich south to the north. Its terrible cost, together with his failed wars in Korea, helped topple his dynasty, but parts of the world's longest canal are still used by boats today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Grand Canal)

title: A Voice in the Cave of Hira
text: A merchant named Muhammad often went to a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca to think, and Muslims believe that there he received the first words of the Quran from the angel Gabriel. His wife Khadija, a successful businesswoman, is often considered the first person to believe his message. Within a century, Islam had spread from Spain to Central Asia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Muhammad)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: The Birth of Islam

title: Brahmagupta's Rules for Zero
text: The astronomer Brahmagupta wrote a book that treated zero as a real number you can add, subtract and multiply. He also gave rules for negative numbers, calling them 'debts' and positive numbers 'fortunes'. These Indian ideas passed to mathematicians in the Islamic world and later to Europe, shaping the math we use every day.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

source2.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, 'A history of Zero'

title: Princess Wencheng Goes to Tibet
text: A Tang princess named Wencheng traveled the long road to Lhasa to marry the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. Tradition says she brought a famous Buddha statue still kept in the Jokhang Temple. Tibetan Buddhists later revered her as an incarnation of White Tara, and her marriage linked two powerful empires.

source.name: The Treasury of Lives (biographical encyclopedia of Tibet)

source2.name: Rubin Museum of Art, Project Himalayan Art (C. D. Warner)

title: Damascus Becomes an Empire's Capital
text: Muawiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate and ruled from Damascus. Within decades the empire stretched from Spain to India, one of the largest the world had seen. The Umayyads made Arabic the language of government and minted new coins decorated only with writing, replacing the figures that earlier Islamic coins had shown.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: The Art of the Umayyad Period (661-750)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Umayyad dynasty)

title: Silla Unites Korea
text: The kingdom of Silla teamed up with Tang China to defeat its rivals Baekje and Goguryeo. Then Silla turned around and pushed the Tang armies out too. Much of the Korean peninsula was ruled as one kingdom for the first time, and its capital Gyeongju grew rich, building famous Buddhist sites like Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Korea: Unified Silla)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa Temple)

title: Srivijaya's Stone Announcement
text: A stone inscription found near Palembang, dated 683, tells how a ruler set out with a large body of troops after seeking blessings for success. Like most of Srivijaya's earliest inscriptions, it is written in Old Malay. Srivijaya became a sea power that controlled the Strait of Malacca and a stopping place for Buddhist pilgrims from China.

source.name: SPAFA Digest (J. G. de Casparis, 'Some Notes on the Epigraphic Heritage of Srivijaya')

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Srivijaya empire)

title: China's Only Female Emperor
text: Wu Zetian declared her own dynasty and became the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right. She expanded the exams for officials so talent mattered more than family. She even created a new written character for her own name, Zhao, meaning 'the sun, moon and sky'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Wuhou)

source2.name: Origins: Current Events in Historical Perspective (Ohio State University / Miami University), 'Wu Zetian: The Only Woman Emperor in Chinese History'

title: The Temple by the Waves
text: Pallava kings built this granite temple right at the edge of the Bay of Bengal. It is one of the oldest structural stone temples in South India, built from cut blocks rather than carved out of a cliff. When the waves of the 2004 tsunami receded, they scoured away sand near the temple and exposed carved stone animals long hidden from view.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram)

source2.name: Associated Press via CBS News, 'Hidden City Uncovered By Tsunami' (2005)

title: Japan's Oldest Book
text: The Kojiki, or 'Record of Ancient Matters', was presented to Empress Genmei in 712. It mixes myths, poems, songs and family trees, telling how the gods created the Japanese islands. A court retainer named Hieda no Are, famed for his memory, had learned the old tales by heart, and a scholar wrote them down using Chinese characters.

source.name: Kokugakuin University

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Kojiki)

title: The Battle of Talas
text: Armies of the Abbasid Caliphate and Tang China clashed near the Talas River in Central Asia. The Abbasids won, and Tang power in the region began to fade. A popular story says captured Chinese papermakers taught the craft in Samarkand, though historians think paper had already started spreading west.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica ('Paper ii. Paper and Papermaking')

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Chinese Turkestan iii. From the Advent of Islam to the Mongols' (I. Togan)

title: The Great Buddha Opens Its Eyes
text: At Tōdai-ji temple a giant bronze Buddha, cast with about 500 tons of copper, was dedicated. An Indian monk named Bodhisena painted in its eyes in a grand ceremony with thousands of monks. Objects used at the event, including the brush, are still kept in the temple's wooden storehouse, the Shōsōin.

source.name: Tokyo National Museum

source2.name: Nippon.com (Nippon Communications Foundation)

title: Baghdad, the Round City
text: Caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris River, laid out as a perfect circle with the palace in the center. Within decades Baghdad was a great center of learning, where scholars met in well-stocked bookshops around the main mosque. A paper factory opened there in the 790s, and books soon multiplied across the Islamic world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Baghdad: History)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: The Art of the Abbasid Period (750-1258)

title: A Temple Carved From One Rock
text: Under Rashtrakuta kings, workers carved the Kailasa temple downward from a single cliff of basalt. Instead of stacking blocks, they cut away 150,000 to 200,000 tons of solid rock. The result is a full temple four stories high, with halls, towers and life-size stone elephants, all from one piece of stone.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Ellora Caves)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ellora Caves)

title: Tibet's First Monastery
text: King Trisong Detsen founded Samye, the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet. Its layout is a model of the universe, with a central temple standing for a sacred mountain. Tibetan tradition says a great debate was held there between Indian and Chinese Buddhist teachers, and the Indian school won.

source.name: The Treasury of Lives (biographical encyclopedia of Tibet)

title: Vikings Raid Lindisfarne
text: Raiders from Scandinavia attacked the island monastery of Lindisfarne, taking treasure and leading some monks away in chains. The shock spread across Europe, and it is remembered as the Vikings' first major attack in western Europe. The monks had earlier made the beautiful Lindisfarne Gospels, which survived and are now in the British Library.

source.name: English Heritage (Lindisfarne Priory: the Viking raid)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Viking)

title: Charlemagne's Elephant
text: Caliph Harun al-Rashid of Baghdad sent Charlemagne a gift: an elephant named Abul-Abbas, brought west by envoys and delivered in 802. Tame elephants came only from India, so few people in northern Europe had ever seen one. The Royal Frankish Annals recorded the gift, and an Irish monk later wrote of the excitement it caused.

source.name: University of Cambridge repository (Apollo), 'Abbasid-Carolingian Diplomacy in Early Medieval Arabic Apocalypse'

title: The Birth of the Khmer Empire
text: On the sacred Kulen mountain, Jayavarman II had himself declared a 'universal king'. This ceremony is seen as the start of the Khmer Empire, which later built Angkor. Laser scans from airplanes have since revealed a hidden city of roads and canals under the forest on the mountain.

source.name: PNAS (Evans et al. 2013, 'Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar')

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Jayavarman II)

title: Two Women in a Viking Ship
text: Two women were buried inside a beautiful carved longship, along with sleighs, a cart, beds, fifteen horses and even a bucket of apples. Wood from the burial chamber dates the grave to 834. Nobody knows exactly who they were, but the rich grave shows women could hold high status in Viking society.

source.name: Museum of the Viking Age, University of Oslo

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Oseberg ship' (R. Ostberg)

title: Pueblo Bonito's Many Rooms
text: Ancestral Puebloan people began building Pueblo Bonito, a great house that grew to around 800 rooms. A long wall running almost exactly north to south splits the building in two, and on nearby Fajada Butte a carved spiral seems to have marked the solstices with a dagger of sunlight. Cacao traces in jars show they traded with Mesoamerica, far to the south.

source.name: Crown & Hurst, 'Evidence of cacao use in the Prehispanic American Southwest', PNAS 106(7) 2009 (PMC)

source2.name: National Park Service, Chaco Culture NHP: Pueblo Bonito

title: Fatima Founds a School in Fez
text: Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy immigrant from Kairouan, is said to have spent her inheritance founding the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez. It became a famous center of learning and is often called one of the oldest universities still running. Its library still holds manuscripts up to about 1,200 years old.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Qarawiyyin' (rev. Adam Zeidan)

source2.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT), 'Jami' al-Qarawiyyin' (search excerpt only)

title: An Alphabet for the Slavs
text: Two brothers from Byzantium, Cyril and Methodius, came to Great Moravia to preach in the local Slavic language. Cyril created a new alphabet, Glagolitic, to write it down. His students later developed Cyrillic, which is used today for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian and other languages.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saints Cyril and Methodius'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cyrillic alphabet'

title: The Oldest Dated Printed Book
text: A man named Wang Jie paid for a copy of the Diamond Sutra to be printed from carved wooden blocks, 'for his parents'. It is the oldest printed book with a clear date. It lay sealed in a cave library at Dunhuang for about 900 years until it was found in 1900.

source.name: Linda Hall Library of Science, Engineering & Technology, 'The Diamond Sutra' (Scientist of the Day)

title: Kyiv Becomes the Heart of Rus
text: According to the old chronicles, Prince Oleg seized Kyiv in 882 and made it his capital, a city later hailed as the 'mother of Rus cities'. Kyivan Rus grew rich on the Dnieper River trade route to Constantinople. Each spring, boat convoys carried the furs and captives collected as tribute over the winter down the river to the Byzantine capital.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kyivan Rus'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Oleg'

title: Goryeo Gives Korea Its Name
text: General Wang Geon founded the Goryeo dynasty, which soon reunited the Korean peninsula. The English name 'Korea' comes from Goryeo. The kingdom became famous for jade-green celadon pottery and for carving the whole Buddhist canon on over 80,000 wooden printing blocks.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Goryeo dynasty'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon (via data.unesco.org)

title: Ibn Fadlan Meets the Rus
text: An envoy from Baghdad named Ibn Fadlan traveled north to the Volga Bulgars. He wrote a vivid report of the Rus traders he met there, tall people covered in tattoos. His account also includes a rare eyewitness description of a Viking ship funeral, recording each step of the ceremony.

source.name: University of Utah, Ethics of Suicide Digital Archive: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Risala (922)

source2.name: University of California Press sample chapter, 'The Rus' (translation of Ibn Fadlan's Risala)

title: A Palace City Near Córdoba
text: Caliph Abd al-Rahman III began building Madinat al-Zahra, a dazzling palace city outside Córdoba, with halls decorated in marble. Later writers even told of a glittering pool of quicksilver, though historians treat such stories as fanciful. Córdoba itself was then the largest city in Europe, home to some 100,000 people by the year 1000.

source.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT), 'Madina al-Zahra'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Caliphate City of Medina Azahara (via data.unesco.org)

title: Spikes in the Bạch Đằng River
text: Ngô Quyền hid iron-headed poles in the riverbed and lured a Southern Han fleet upriver at high tide. When the tide fell, the enemy ships were swept onto the spikes. His victory ended a long era of Chinese domination and laid the foundation for an independent Vietnamese kingdom.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ngo Quyen'

source2.name: Cambridge University Press, The Making of the Modern Chinese Navy, ch. 1 'Battle of Bach Dang River (938)' (summary)

title: The Stone Warriors of Tula
text: The Toltec city of Tula rose to power in central Mexico. Its temple roof was held up by giant stone warriors, each over four meters tall. The Toltecs were famed builders and craftsmen, and later Aztec rulers claimed Toltec royal blood to strengthen their own right to rule.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tula' (ancient city)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Toltec'

title: The Song Dynasty Begins
text: General Zhao Kuangyin took power and founded the Song dynasty. The Song used civil service exams to bring educated scholars into government and check the power of military men. Under them China saw booming cities, paper money, printed books and a fast-ripening rice from Champa that let some farmers harvest two crops a year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Song dynasty'

source2.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Song Dynasty module (Champa rice; scholar-officials)

title: The Fatimids Found Cairo
text: After conquering Egypt, the Fatimid general Jawhar founded a new capital just north of the old city of Fustat and named it al-Qahira, 'the Triumphant'. Soon after, the Fatimids built al-Azhar mosque, which grew into one of the oldest universities still running. Egypt grew rich as the go-between in trade linking the Mediterranean with India.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Cairo (via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Al-Azhar University'

title: Kyiv Chooses a Religion
text: Prince Volodymyr of Kyiv became a Christian and had his people baptized in the Dnieper River. A chronicle says his envoys were amazed by the services in Constantinople and could not tell 'whether we were in heaven or on earth.' The choice tied Rus to Byzantine art, writing and faith.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vladimir I'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kyivan Rus'

title: The Rising Dragon Capital
text: In 1010 King Lý Thái Tổ moved Đại Việt's capital to a spot on the Red River and named it Thăng Long, 'Rising Dragon'. It remained Vietnam's main capital until 1802, when the Nguyễn dynasty moved the court to Huế. The city is Hanoi today, and in 2010 it celebrated its thousandth birthday.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hanoi'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Imperial Citadel of Thang Long - Hanoi (via data.unesco.org)

title: How Our Eyes Really See
text: The scholar Ibn al-Haytham wrote his Book of Optics in Fatimid Egypt between about 1011 and 1021, while he was under house arrest. He argued that we see because light enters our eyes, not because our eyes send out rays. He tested ideas with careful experiments, including a dark room with a tiny hole, an early camera obscura.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibn al-Haytham'

source2.name: Annals of Saudi Medicine 2007, 'Ibn Al-Haytham: father of modern optics' (PMC)

title: The First Government Paper Money
text: Merchants in Sichuan, where people used iron coins, swapped paper notes called jiaozi so they did not have to haul heavy strings of coins. In the 1020s the Song government took over and issued official paper money. It was the world's first government-issued paper money, centuries before Europe used banknotes.

source.name: Hoover Institution (Stanford University), 'The Rise and Demise of Paper Money in Imperial China'

source2.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Song Dynasty module, 'Money'

title: King Anawrahta Brings Scriptures to Pagan
text: Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan Empire, conquered the Mon city of Thaton and carried its royal family, scholars and craftsmen back to his capital. Theravada Buddhism spread across Burma. Over the next two centuries Pagan's rulers and people filled the plain by the Irrawaddy River with temples and stupas, and more than 3,500 monuments survive today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Anawrahta'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Bagan (via data.unesco.org)

title: The Golden Kingdom of Ghana
text: The writer al-Bakri described the West African empire of Ghana, rich from trading gold for salt across the Sahara. He wrote that the king kept all large gold nuggets for himself and let people keep only the gold dust. Its capital had separate towns for traders and the royal court.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ghana' (historical West African empire)

source2.name: Al-Bakri, trans. J.F.P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (CUP 1981), excerpt at John Jay College, CUNY

title: Omar Khayyam's Super Calendar
text: The Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah asked a team of astronomers, including the poet Omar Khayyam, to fix the calendar. Their Jalali calendar, adopted in 1079, started each year at the spring equinox, so it kept in step with the seasons very precisely. Solar calendars based on it are still official in Iran and Afghanistan today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Omar Khayyam'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Calendars ii. In the Islamic period' (and iii. Afghan calendars)

title: The First University in Europe
text: Law students who came to Bologna made contracts with teachers and banded together by homeland, and their groups grew into the University of Bologna. It is considered the oldest university in the Western world, and its law school drew students from all over Europe. In 1158 Emperor Frederick I granted its scholars special protections for their travels.

source.name: University of Bologna (official site), 'Our history: from the 12th to the 20th century'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'University of Bologna'

title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays
text: In his garden retreat, the scholar Shen Kuo wrote a book of notes on everything from fossils to printing. It contains the first known reference to the magnetic compass and the first description of movable-type printing. He also described a buried forest of stone bamboo where no bamboo grew, and guessed the climate had once been different.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shen Kuo'

source2.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Song Dynasty module, 'Experiment' (Shen Gua's petrified bamboo passage)

title: Crusaders Take Jerusalem
text: After a three-year march from Europe, knights of the First Crusade captured Jerusalem. They killed many of the city's Muslim and Jewish residents. The crusader states lasted almost two hundred years, until 1291, and Italian cities used them to expand trade with the Muslim world, while returning crusaders brought home a taste for spices.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'First Crusade'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Crusades: The results of the Crusades' (read in browser)

title: Li Qingzhao, Poet on the Run
text: Li Qingzhao, China's most celebrated woman poet, fled south after Jurchen armies captured the Song capital. She and her husband had collected rare books, rubbings and bronzes, and most were lost in the chaos. Her husband died in 1129, and she later wrote the story of their collection. She remains an iconic figure, and her lines are still quoted today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Renditions, Chinese University of Hong Kong

title: The Great Aleppo Earthquake
text: A huge earthquake shook northern Syria in October 1138, shattering the walls of Aleppo's citadel and wrecking towns nearby. A 15th-century writer claimed 230,000 deaths, but that figure really belongs to a different quake in Georgia. The Crusader castle of Harim and the Muslim-held citadel of Atharib were both ruined, and both Christian and Muslim chroniclers wrote about it.

source.name: N.N. Ambraseys 2004, 'The 12th century seismic paroxysm in the Middle East: a historical perspective', Annals of Geophysics 47(2/3)

source2.name: Sbeinati, Darawcheh & Mouty 2005, 'The historical earthquakes of Syria', Annals of Geophysics 48(3) (earth-prints.org)

title: Hildegard's Visions
text: The abbess Hildegard of Bingen finished Scivias, a book describing her religious visions. She also composed music, wrote about plants and medicine, and invented her own secret language. Popes, kings and an emperor were among her correspondents, and people wrote to her asking for advice and prophecies. Her songs are still performed today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Epistolae: Medieval Women's Letters (Columbia University Libraries / CTL), 'Hildegard of Bingen'

title: Saladin Ends the Fatimid Caliphate
text: Saladin, a Kurdish general, took control of Egypt and ended two centuries of Fatimid rule. In 1176 he ordered a fortress built on the Muqattam Hills, the start of Cairo's great Citadel. He later united Egypt and Syria and won back Jerusalem, and even his crusader enemies praised him for his fairness.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Paul E. Walker)

source2.name: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, 'Cairo Citadel'

title: Nan Madol, City on the Reef
text: On more than a hundred artificial islets off Pohnpei, builders stacked huge basalt columns into walls, palaces and tombs. It became the ceremonial centre of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled the island. The basalt was brought from quarries elsewhere on Pohnpei, and nobody knows exactly how they moved stones weighing several tonnes.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, Christopher Pala, 'Nan Madol: The City Built on Coral Reefs' (read in browser)

title: The Sea Battle of Dan-no-ura
text: The Minamoto clan crushed their rivals, the Taira, in a sea battle in a narrow strait. The child emperor Antoku and his attendants leapt into the sea and drowned. Seven years later, Minamoto no Yoritomo took the title of shogun and set up Japan's first shogunate, putting samurai in charge for centuries.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Antoku; Gempei War)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'shogun' (read in browser)

title: The Smiling Faces of the Bayon
text: King Jayavarman VII built a new walled city at Angkor with the Bayon temple at its center. Its towers are carved with about 200 huge calm, smiling faces. He also built a network of hospitals and rest houses along the roads of his empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Magna Carta at Runnymede
text: Rebel barons forced King John of England to agree to the Magna Carta, or 'Great Charter'. It said even the king had to follow the law. The deal broke down within months, but later kings reissued it, and its ideas later helped inspire the United States Constitution and Bill of Rights.

source.name: The Magna Carta Project, University of East Anglia

source2.name: The National Archives (UK) blog

title: The Golden Rhino of Mapungubwe
text: On a flat-topped hill above the Limpopo River, rulers lived apart from ordinary people, an early sign of royal power in southern Africa. In a royal grave archaeologists found a small wooden rhinoceros covered in thin sheets of gold. Mapungubwe traded ivory and gold with the Indian Ocean coast and is seen as a forerunner of Great Zimbabwe.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: University of Pretoria Museums (Mapungubwe Collection)

title: Sundiata, the Lion King of Mali
text: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina and founded the Mali Empire. As a child he was said to be unable to walk. His story is still sung by griots, West Africa's storytellers, in the Epic of Sundiata.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Oxford University Press, Patterns of World History (von Sivers et al.) Learning Link: Document - The Epic of Sundiata

title: Razia, Sultan of Delhi
text: Razia became the only woman ever crowned in the Delhi Sultanate. She threw off women's dress and veil, wore a coat and cap, and rode openly among the people on an elephant. Her father had chosen her over her brothers, but nobles resented a woman ruler, and she reigned for less than four years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Minhaj-us-Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, as translated in A. V. Williams Jackson (ed.), History of India vol. 5 (1906), ch. 5 'Raziya' (ibiblio)

title: Onfim's Homework Doodles
text: A boy named Onfim, about six or seven years old, practiced his letters on strips of birch bark. Between lessons he drew himself as a brave warrior on horseback stabbing an enemy. His scraps survived in Novgorod's wet soil and are among the many birch-bark letters dug up there.

source.name: Live Science (Kristina Killgrove, PhD archaeologist)

title: The Mystery Eruption Solved
text: The Samalas volcano exploded in one of the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years. Scientists saw its sulfur in ice cores for decades before tracking it to Lombok. The Babad Lombok, a history written on palm leaves, describes how the blast destroyed the capital city of Pamatan.

source.name: Lavigne et al. 2013, PNAS (via PubMed Central)

source2.name: Nature Communications 2025 (via Europe PMC)

title: Mogadishu's Trading Mosque
text: The Fakhr al-Din Mosque was built in Mogadishu, a port at the northern end of the Swahili coast, by the city's first sultan. A glazed tile in it is inscribed with the year 1269, and its prayer niche used marble from India. Like other Swahili coast ports, Mogadishu traded with Arabs, Persians and Indians, and it even minted its own coins.

source.name: Archnet (MIT / Aga Khan Trust for Culture)

source2.name: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Coins Are Minted on the Swahili Coast' (Blaine Horrocks, 2022)

title: Kublai Khan Founds the Yuan
text: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, declared the Yuan dynasty and built a capital called Khanbaliq where Beijing is today. The Mongols soon ruled all of China. Merchants and travelers like Marco Polo came from far away, and paper money was made the empire's only legal currency.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: CEPR VoxEU column: Hanhui Guan, Nuno Palma and Meng Wu, 'The rise and fall of paper money in Yuan China, 1260-1368' (23 Mar 2024)

title: The Rise of Majapahit
text: Prince Raden Wijaya used an invading Mongol army to defeat his rival, then turned on the Mongols and drove them away. He founded the Majapahit kingdom on Java. It grew into a great island empire, and its capital Trowulan had temples, markets and a network of water canals and reservoirs.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre Tentative List: Trowulan - Former Capital City of Majapahit Kingdom

title: The City of Victory
text: Two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded the Vijayanagara Empire in South India. Its capital at Hampi grew to metropolitan size, with temple towns, bazaar streets and royal palaces. Foreign visitors praised it as one of the most beautiful cities of its time, and its royal Elephant Stables still stand among the boulders.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vijayanagara'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Hampi (read via data.unesco.org)

title: The Bronze Heads of Ife
text: Artists in the Yoruba city of Ife cast lifelike heads in copper alloy and shaped others in clay. They probably show kings and important people. When a set of the metal heads was dug up by builders in 1938, their skill challenged Western people who had looked down on African art.

source.name: Afriques/African archaeology journal (OpenEdition), 'A Copper Alloy Head Count: Contextualising and Accounting for the Wunmonije Compound Discoveries of Ile-Ife'

source2.name: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Ife (from ca. 6th Century)'

title: A Farm Boy Founds the Ming
text: Zhu Yuanzhang grew up poor, lost his family to famine and became a monk. He then led rebels who drove out the Mongols and founded the Ming dynasty. The Ming went on to rebuild the Great Wall and make blue-and-white porcelain loved around the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hongwu'

source2.name: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Ming Dynasty (1368-1644)'; UNESCO Great Wall (id 438) for Ming wall-building

title: Timur Makes Samarkand Shine
text: Timur, also called Tamerlane, made Samarkand his capital in 1370 and began wars of conquest from Turkey to India. He brought craftsmen from conquered lands to Samarkand. They raised grand mosques and tombs with huge bulbous domes and colourful tilework, starting one of the most brilliant periods in Islamic art.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Timur'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Samarkand - Crossroad of Cultures (read via data.unesco.org)

title: Rapa Nui's Giant Moai
text: Polynesian islanders carved nearly a thousand giant moai figures from volcanic rock. Many stood on stone platforms along the coast, close to the villages of the communities that built them. Experiments suggest teams may have 'walked' the statues upright, rocking them from side to side with ropes.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rapa Nui National Park (read via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: PLOS One (2025), 'Megalithic statue (moai) production on Rapa Nui (Easter Island, Chile)' (PMC)

title: The Joseon Dynasty Begins
text: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo and founded the Joseon dynasty. It lasted over 500 years, making it Korea's longest-lived dynasty. Joseon soon moved its capital to Hanyang, now Seoul, and built its life around Confucian ideas of learning and duty.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Joseon dynasty'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Joseon dynasty'

title: The Golden Pavilion
text: The retired shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built a villa covered in gold leaf beside a quiet pond. After his death it became the Zen temple Kinkaku-ji. A monk burned it down in 1950, and the version standing today is a careful rebuild.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kinkaku-ji'

source2.name: Shokoku-ji (official temple site), Kinkaku-ji history

title: Zheng He's Treasure Fleet
text: Admiral Zheng He set sail with hundreds of ships, some of the largest wooden ships of their age. Over seven voyages his fleets reached India, Arabia and East Africa. Zheng He was a Muslim from Yunnan who had been taken to the Ming court as a boy.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng He'

source2.name: The Met, 'Giraffe with Two Keepers' (47.18.21) catalogue text

title: The Aztec Triple Alliance
text: Three city-states, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, joined forces against their overlords. This Triple Alliance grew into the Aztec Empire, which collected tribute from hundreds of towns across Mexico. Texcoco's ruler Nezahualcoyotl was famous as a poet and engineer who built aqueducts and dikes in the lake.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Itzcoatl' (curated excerpts from full Britannica articles)

source2.name: Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale), 'Montezuma I', via Encyclopedia.com

title: Pachacuti Remakes the Inca World
text: When the Chanca attacked the Inca around 1438, a prince who stayed to defend Cusco won two great victories, then took power and the title Pachacuti. He turned a small kingdom into a fast-growing empire. He also rebuilt Cusco and is linked to the building of Machu Picchu.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Machu Picchu'

title: Oba Ewuare Builds Benin
text: Oba Ewuare the Great expanded the Kingdom of Benin and rebuilt its capital with walls and moats. Across the kingdom ran a network of earthen walls and ditches some 16,000 kilometres long. He organized the palace chiefs, whose ranks included royal craft guilds, and later brass casters made thousands of plaques showing the court's battles and rituals.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Benin (historical kingdom, West Africa)'

source2.name: Art Institute of Chicago, 'Benin—Kings and Rituals: Court Arts from Nigeria' (exhibition themes 'Oba Ewuare and the Portuguese', 'The Hierarchy at Court', 'The Oba's Palace')

title: Sufis Brew the First Coffee
text: Sufi mystics in Yemen began roasting coffee beans and brewing a drink to stay awake during night prayers. It is the earliest clear evidence of coffee drinking. Coffee houses soon spread to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul, and the port of Mocha gave its name to a coffee style.

source.name: UC Santa Cruz, Center for World History, 'Coffee, 1400-1800'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'coffee'

title: The Fall of Constantinople
text: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II, only 21, captured Constantinople after a siege of 55 days. His giant cannons battered the old walls, and his ships were dragged overland to get past a chain across the harbor. It ended the Byzantine Empire, more than 1,100 years after Emperor Constantine founded the city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fall of Constantinople'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mehmed II' and 'Fall of Constantinople'

title: Sonni Ali Builds the Songhai Empire
text: Sonni Ali, ruler of Gao, began a string of conquests along the Niger River. His cavalry and fleet of war canoes took Timbuktu and Djenné. In almost thirty years of fighting he turned a small kingdom into the Songhai Empire, which grew into the largest state in West Africa's history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sonni Ali'

source2.name: OpenStax, World History Volume 2, 3.2 The Songhai Empire (Rice University)

title: The Inca Conquer Chan Chan
text: Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom, was the largest earthen city of the pre-Columbian Americas, its mud-brick palaces decorated with reliefs of sea birds and other figures. Around 1470 the Inca conquered it. They took Chan Chan's famed silversmiths to Cusco, so Chimú craft lived on inside the Inca Empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chimu'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Chan Chan Archaeological Zone (read via data.unesco.org)

title: Askia Muhammad Takes Songhai
text: A general named Muhammad Ture seized the throne of the Songhai Empire, the biggest state West Africa had ever seen. As Askia Muhammad he backed Islamic scholars in Timbuktu and made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca. His tomb in Gao, a mud-brick pyramid bristling with wooden beams, still stands today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Muhammad I Askia)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tomb of Askia)

title: A Teenage Shah Crowned in Tabriz
text: Ismail, only about 14 years old, was crowned shah in Tabriz and founded the Safavid dynasty. He declared Twelver Shia Islam the official faith of his realm, a choice that still shapes Iran's identity today. He was also a poet, writing verses in Azerbaijani Turkish under the pen name Khatai.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Esmail I Safawi: i. Biography; ii. His Poetry)

title: Portugal Storms Rich Kilwa
text: Kilwa was a wealthy Swahili trading city that minted its own copper coins and built a grand coral-stone mosque. In 1505 a Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida seized the city and built a fort there, as Portugal tried to control the rich Indian Ocean trade routes. The island's ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Francisco de Almeida; Kilwa)

title: The Poet King of Vijayanagara
text: Krishnadevaraya took the throne of the Vijayanagara Empire. A Portuguese visitor thought its capital at Hampi looked as large as Rome and called it the best-provided city in the world. The king was also a writer: he composed a long Telugu poem, and tradition says his court was graced by eight master poets, nicknamed the 'elephants of the eight directions'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (India: The Vijayanagar empire)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Group of Monuments at Hampi)

title: Michelangelo Finishes the Ceiling
text: After four years of work, Michelangelo unveiled his paintings across the Sistine Chapel ceiling, including the famous Creation of Adam. Despite the legend, he painted standing on a scaffold he designed, not lying on his back. He even wrote a grumpy poem to a friend about the aches it caused.

source.name: Vatican Museums (Sistine Chapel: The Ceiling)

source2.name: Casa Buonarroti (via Google Arts & Culture), sonnet and self-portrait sheet, AB XIII 111

title: An Admiral's Map on Gazelle Skin
text: The Ottoman admiral Piri Reis drew a world map on gazelle-skin parchment, combining around twenty older sources, including one he said came from Columbus. It shows the coasts of Africa and South America. Only a piece survives, and it lay forgotten until it was found in Istanbul's Topkapı Palace in 1929.

source.name: Ohio State University, 'Wind Rose' map history site (1513 / World Map / Piri Reis)

title: Luther's 95 Theses
text: A monk and professor named Martin Luther wrote 95 arguments against the Church selling 'indulgences', payments said to shorten punishment after death. Thanks to the new printing presses, copies spread across Germany within weeks. His protest grew into the Protestant Reformation, splitting Western Christianity for good.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ninety-five Theses)

title: Lapulapu Defeats Magellan
text: Ferdinand Magellan demanded that Lapulapu, a chief on Mactan Island, obey the king of Spain. Lapulapu refused, and when Magellan's men waded ashore through the shallows, his warriors overwhelmed them and killed Magellan. Today the Philippines honors Lapulapu: a city on Mactan and a state award, the Order of Lapu-Lapu, bear his name.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ferdinand Magellan: Discovery of the Strait)

source2.name: VERA Files (fact check on Lapulapu, citing NHCP)

title: Babur Founds the Mughal Empire
text: Babur, a prince from Central Asia, beat the much larger army of the Delhi Sultan at Panipat, helped by cannons and matchlock guns. The victory began the Mughal Empire. Babur wrote a frank memoir, the Baburnama, where he grumbled that India lacked the good melons and grapes of his homeland.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Babur)

source2.name: Project Gutenberg: The Babur-nama in English, tr. A. S. Beveridge (1922)

title: Atahualpa's Room of Ransom
text: Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushed and captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca. To win his freedom, Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold, and his people brought gold and silver from all over the empire. The Spanish executed him anyway in 1533, opening the way to conquering the Inca Empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Atahuallpa)

title: The Americas' First Printing Press
text: Giovanni Paoli, an Italian printer known in Spanish as Juan Pablos, sailed from Seville and set up the first printing press in the Americas in Mexico City. The first known book from it was a short Christian guide written in both Spanish and Nahuatl, the Aztec language. Sadly, no copy of that book has survived.

source.name: Library of Congress blog (Hispanic Heritage Month: Early Titles by the Americas' First Printing Press)

title: Sher Shah's Silver Rupiya
text: Sher Shah Suri drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India and ruled North India for five busy years. He issued a standard silver coin called the rupiya, the ancestor of today's rupee. He also improved the great road across North India, with rest houses for travelers along the way.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sher Shah of Sur)

source2.name: Reserve Bank of India, Currency Museum: Mughal coinage

title: Guns Wash Up in Japan
text: In 1543 a ship carrying Portuguese traders sought shelter from a storm on the small island of Tanegashima. The local lord bought two of their matchlock guns and had a local swordsmith copy them. Soon Japanese workshops were making guns by the thousands, the weapon was simply called a 'tanegashima', and samurai warfare changed forever.

source.name: EBSCO Research Starters (M. McCaskey, 'Europeans Begin Trade with Japan', 2022)

source2.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary database (MLIT), 'Guns in Early Modern Japan'

title: Tomatoes Enter a European Book
text: Italian doctor Pietro Andrea Mattioli published a book of plants with the earliest known European mention of the tomato, a newcomer from the Americas. He called it a new kind of eggplant that turned red or gold and was cooked like one. Ten years later he named it pomi d'oro, 'golden apples'.

source.name: PeerJ (van Andel et al., 'Sixteenth-century tomatoes in Europe', 2022), PubMed Central

title: Spain Debates Conquest Itself
text: In 1550 Spain's king halted new conquests in the Americas and called a formal debate on how Indigenous Americans should be treated. Friar Bartolomé de las Casas argued against their conquest; scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued it was justified. The judges were slow to rule and conquest went on, but the debate was a watershed in thinking about human rights.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Bartolome de Las Casas)

source2.name: History Today (Mathew Lyons, 'The Valladolid Debate on the Rights of Indigenous People', vol. 73 no. 8, 2023)

title: The Deadliest Earthquake Ever
text: On January 23, 1556, a huge earthquake struck Shaanxi province in central China. About 830,000 people are thought to have died, the highest toll of any recorded earthquake. Many lived in yaodong, cozy cave homes carved into soft loess hills, which collapsed when the ground shook.

source.name: USGS (Cool Earthquake Facts)

source2.name: USGS (Today in Earthquake History, January 23)

title: St. Augustine Is Founded
text: Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on land of the Timucua people. It is the oldest continuously inhabited city founded by Europeans in the mainland United States, older than Jamestown by 42 years. Its stone fort, the Castillo de San Marcos, was built from shell-filled coquina rock.

source.name: National Park Service (St. Augustine Town Plan Historic District)

source2.name: National Park Service (The First Thanksgiving; Castillo de San Marcos)

title: Ming China Reopens the Sea
text: The Ming dynasty had long banned private sea trade. In 1567 the new Longqing emperor opened the port of Yuegang in Fujian, licensing Chinese merchants to trade abroad, though Japanese merchants were still shut out. Nearby kilns boomed, and porcelain from Yuegang's trade flowed to Spanish merchants in Manila, who shipped it across the Pacific on the galleons.

source.name: J. K. Kung & C. Ma, 'Autarky and the Rise and Fall of Piracy in Ming China' (working paper, later J. Economic History)

source2.name: Guanyu Wang (Art Museum, CUHK), 'Chinese Porcelain in the Manila Galleon Trade', in Archaeology of Manila Galleon Seaports (Springer, 2019)

title: Akbar's Red Sandstone City
text: Mughal emperor Akbar began building a brand-new capital of red sandstone at Fatehpur Sikri. In its House of Worship he hosted debates where Muslim scholars were joined by Hindu pandits, Parsi priests, Jain monks and Jesuits. The court left after about 15 years, possibly over water shortages, and the city survives in good condition.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Fatehpur Sikri; Akbar)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fatehpur Sikri)

title: Li Shizhen's Giant Medicine Book
text: Doctor Li Shizhen finished the Compendium of Materia Medica after decades of travel, reading and research. It describes nearly 1,900 medicines from plants, animals and minerals, with some 11,000 prescriptions. He tried remedies on patients and even on himself to test what earlier doctors and scholars had claimed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Li Shizhen)

source2.name: Harvard Magazine (Carla Nappi, 'Li Shizhen', Jan.-Feb. 2010)

title: Betrayal at Honnō-ji Temple
text: Oda Nobunaga was close to uniting war-torn Japan when his own general, Akechi Mitsuhide, attacked him at Honnō-ji temple in Kyoto. Nobunaga died as the temple burned. Yasuke, an African man who served Nobunaga as a retainer, was in Kyoto that night and fought in the clash.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Yasuke, by Thomas Lockley)

title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke
text: About 118 English men, women and children sailed to Roanoke Island in 1587, and a baby named Virginia Dare became the first English child born in the Americas. When John White finally returned with supplies in 1590, the settlers had vanished. The only clue was the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post, the name of a nearby Native people and their island.

source.name: National Park Service, Fort Raleigh NHS (1587: The Lost Colony)

source2.name: National Park Service (North Carolina: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site)

title: Morocco's Guns Topple Songhai
text: Morocco's sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent an army of mercenaries under Pasha Judar, many armed with muskets, against the Songhai Empire of West Africa. At Tondibi in March 1591 they routed a far larger Songhai army of archers and cavalry, reportedly some 27,000 strong. The once-mighty Songhai Empire never recovered.

source.name: Journal of African History (L. Kaba, 'Archers, Musketeers, and Mosquitoes: The Moroccan Invasion of the Sudan and the Songhay Resistance 1591-1612'), Cambridge

title: Fort Jesus Guards Mombasa
text: The Portuguese began building Fort Jesus to control Mombasa's harbor on the Swahili coast. Its Italian architect, Giovanni Battista Cairati, based its layout on the Renaissance ideal of the human body's proportions. It changed hands many times, and Omani Arabs captured it in 1698 after a siege of nearly three years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fort Jesus, Mombasa), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: National Museums of Kenya (Fort Jesus)

title: The Battle That Made the Shoguns
text: Tens of thousands of samurai clashed in a foggy mountain valley at Sekigahara. Tokugawa Ieyasu won after several enemy commanders switched sides mid-battle. Three years later he became shogun, and his family ruled a mostly peaceful Japan for more than 250 years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Battle of Sekigahara, by Myles Hudson)

title: Matteo Ricci's Map of the World
text: Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci, who learned Chinese and wore local dress, made a giant world map with his collaborator Li Zhizao. It was the first map in Chinese to show the Americas. Unlike European maps, which put the Atlantic in the middle, it placed China and the Pacific Ocean near the center, in keeping with Chinese mapmaking traditions.

source.name: University of Minnesota Libraries, James Ford Bell Library (1602 World Map of Matteo Ricci)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Matteo Ricci, by Joseph Hsing-san Shih)

title: First Europeans Land in Australia
text: Dutch captain Willem Janszoon sailed the little ship Duyfken to Cape York Peninsula, making the first recorded European landing in Australia. He thought it was part of New Guinea. Meetings with Aboriginal people went badly, and the land had been their home for at least 50,000 years already.

source.name: Western Australian Museum (Dirk Hartog: Pre-1616)

source2.name: Australian National Maritime Museum (1606: Contact at Cape Keerweer)

title: Heo Jun's Mirror of Medicine
text: Royal doctor Heo Jun finished the Dongui Bogam, a 25-volume encyclopedia of East Asian medicine. He worked on it for years, even while in exile, and stressed preventing illness through healthy living. It is still used in Korean medicine and is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World.

source.name: J Community Hosp Intern Med Perspect (2021), 'Heo Jun: physician of the people' (PMC7850328)

source2.name: Korea.net (official website of the Republic of Korea), 'What is the Dongui Bogam?'

title: Nurhaci Founds the Later Jin
text: Jurchen chief Nurhaci declared himself khan of a new state, the Later Jin. He organized his people into the 'Eight Banners', military-social units marked by colored flags, and had a writing system made for his language. His heirs renamed the people Manchus and went on to conquer all of China as the Qing dynasty.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Nurhachi, by Franz H. Michael)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Banner system)

title: Manhattan Changes Hands
text: Dutch director Peter Minuit traded goods valued at 60 guilders with the Lenape for Manhattan Island, where the town of New Amsterdam was growing. The Lenape probably saw it as sharing the land, not selling it forever. The busy fur-trading town later became New York City.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Peter Minuit)

title: The Last Aurochs Dies
text: Aurochs were giant wild cattle, ancestors of today's cows, that once roamed across Eurasia and North Africa. The last ones survived in Poland, where kings kept the sole right to hunt them and protected them in the royal forests of Jaktorów. The very last one, a cow, died a natural death in 1627, as a royal inspection reported in 1630.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (aurochs)

source2.name: Animal Genetic Resources (Cambridge), 'History of the aurochs in Poland'

title: A Samurai in Siam's Court
text: Yamada Nagamasa, a Japanese adventurer, led the Japanese quarter of Ayutthaya, home to perhaps 500 to 1,000 people. He helped revive trade with Japan, commanded the Japanese guard at the Siamese king's palace and was ennobled. Caught up in a royal power struggle, he was sent south as governor of Ligor (Nakhon Si Thammarat) and poisoned there in 1630.

source.name: The Historical Journal (Cambridge): 'Narrating Japan's Early Modern Southern Expansion'

source2.name: Journal of the Siam Society 95 (2007), Iwamoto, 'Yamada Nagamasa and His Relations with Siam'

title: Ethiopia's City of Castles
text: Emperor Fasilides made Gondar his permanent capital after Ethiopian rulers had moved their royal camps around for centuries. He built a stone castle with huge towers and battlements, plus a bathing pavilion in a pool, and later emperors added more palaces and churches. The royal enclosure, Fasil Ghebbi, mixes Ethiopian traditions with Indian, Arab and European influences.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Gonder)

title: A Handbook of How Things Are Made
text: Scholar Song Yingxing, who had failed the imperial exams six times, published the Tiangong Kaiwu in 1637, a guide to Chinese technology with 123 illustrations. It explains how everyday things were made, from silk, paper and ink to wine, boats, carts and even firearms. Early in the 20th century, scholars rediscovered the book in Japan.

source.name: University of Chicago Press (Dagmar Schäfer, The Crafting of the 10,000 Things: Knowledge and Technology in Seventeenth-Century China)

source2.name: Jesus College, Cambridge: China Centre lecture by Prof. Dagmar Schäfer (Max Planck Institute for the History of Science)

title: Aceh's Century of Queens
text: Taj ul-Alam became sultana of Aceh, a powerful trading kingdom on Sumatra, after her husband died. She ruled for 34 years and was the first of four women who led Aceh one after another until 1699. Islamic literature and scholarship flourished under their rule.

source.name: Mehmet Ozay, 'Women as Rulers Phenomenon in Southeast Asian Islamic Society: The Queens of Aceh', World Journal of Islamic History and Civilization 1(3) 2011 (Universiti Teknologi Malaysia)

title: Tasman Meets Māori in Golden Bay
text: Dutch explorer Abel Tasman became the first known European to reach New Zealand. In Golden Bay, Māori in canoes attacked a small Dutch boat and four sailors were killed. Local descendants call it a cultural misunderstanding, while one archaeologist thinks the iwi was guarding its kūmara gardens. Tasman quickly sailed on north.

source.name: Princeton University Library, Pacific Islands maps exhibit: Abel Tasman

source2.name: RNZ (Radio New Zealand)

title: The Last Ming Emperor Falls
text: As rebel leader Li Zicheng's army broke into Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor took his own life on a hill behind the Forbidden City. Weeks later a Ming general opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to the Manchus. They took Beijing, and the Qing dynasty ruled China until 1912.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chongzhen'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Wu Sangui'

title: Sailing Past Asia's Tip
text: Russian Cossack Semyon Dezhnev and his crew sailed single-deck boats called kochi around the far eastern tip of Asia, through the strait between Asia and America. They did it about 80 years before Vitus Bering, whose name the strait now carries. Dezhnev's reports lay unheeded in the archives of Yakutsk for almost a century.

source.name: Encyclopedia Arctica (Stefansson), Dartmouth College Library: 'Semen Dezhnev'

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, Beringia: Origin

title: A Vegetable Garden Becomes Cape Town
text: Jan van Riebeeck landed for the Dutch East India Company to set up a supply station where ships could get fresh water, meat and vegetables on the long trip to Asia. The Company's Garden he started still exists. The settlement grew into Cape Town, and pushed the Khoekhoe people off their grazing lands.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jan van Riebeeck'

source2.name: City of Cape Town, The Company's Garden

title: The Great Fire of Edo
text: Fanned by strong winds, a fire raged through Edo, Japan's crowded wooden capital, for three days. It burned about 60 percent of the city and killed somewhere between 30,000 and 100,000 people; the main tower of Edo Castle burned and was never rebuilt. Afterward the city added wide roads and embankments as firebreaks.

source.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Library, Edo-Tokyo digital museum: 'Reconstruction of the city after Great Fire of Meireki'

source2.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Library, Edo-Tokyo digital museum: Edo Castle keep

title: Koxinga Takes Taiwan
text: Koxinga, a Ming loyalist commander, besieged the Dutch Fort Zeelandia for about nine months. The Dutch surrendered and left Taiwan in early 1662. Koxinga, whose mother was Japanese, died months later, but his family ruled Taiwan until the Qing took it in 1683.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng Chenggong' (Ralph C. Croizier)

title: London Burns from a Bakery
text: A fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane and spread through London's wooden houses for four days. It destroyed over 13,000 homes and old St Paul's Cathedral. Diarist Samuel Pepys famously buried his wine and Parmesan cheese in his garden to save them.

source.name: London Museum: The Great Fire of London

source2.name: Diary of Samuel Pepys, 4 Sept 1666 (Project Gutenberg text of the primary source)

title: Shivaji Crowned at Raigad
text: Shivaji, a Maratha leader famed for lightning raids and hill forts, was crowned Chhatrapati, or emperor, at his clifftop fortress of Raigad. He had challenged the mighty Mughals and built a navy to guard the coast. The Maratha state he founded became a major power in India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shivaji'

source2.name: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism, Government of India), Shivrajyabhishek Sohala

title: Tiny Animals in a Drop of Water
text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Delft cloth merchant with no university education who learned to grind lenses and built tiny but powerful microscopes. Looking at water, he saw swarms of living 'animalcules', what we now call microbes, and wrote to London's Royal Society about them. Its scientists were doubtful at first, but they confirmed what he saw.

source.name: Lane N. 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil Trans R Soc B 2015 (PMC)

source2.name: UC Museum of Paleontology, Berkeley: Antony van Leeuwenhoek

title: The Great Cavalry Charge at Vienna
text: An Ottoman army had besieged Vienna for two months when a relief force arrived. Polish King Jan III Sobieski led a massive charge of some 20,000 horsemen, spearheaded by his famous hussars, which lasted about half an hour. The siege broke, and the Ottomans slowly began losing territory in Europe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Siege of Vienna (1683)'

source2.name: Polish History Museum (polishhistory.pl), 'The Battle of Vienna (1683): The Clash that Saved Europe'

title: China and Russia Draw a Border
text: After clashes along the Amur River, Kangxi's Qing China and Russia signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk. It was China's first treaty with a European state. The two sides had no shared language, so two Jesuit priests helped negotiate in Latin, and the final treaty was written out in Latin, Mongolian, Manchu, Chinese and Russian.

source.name: The China Project, James Carter (Saint Joseph's University), 'The near miracle that was China's first modern treaty with a European state'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Treaty of Nerchinsk'

title: Sor Juana Defends Women's Learning
text: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, a nun and the foremost poet of colonial Mexico, was told by the bishop of Puebla, writing as 'Sister Filotea', to focus on religious rather than secular studies. In 1691 she replied with a brilliant letter defending women's right to knowledge. Largely self-taught, she mastered Latin and cut her hair to punish herself for mistakes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz'

source2.name: National Museum of Women in the Arts, 'The Tenth Muse'

title: The Fall of Free Palmares
text: For most of a century, people who escaped slavery built Palmares, a free settlement of thousands in the hills of northeast Brazil. In 1694 a colonial army destroyed its capital after a long siege. Its leader Zumbi was killed on November 20, 1695, a date Brazil now marks as Black Consciousness Day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Palmares'

source2.name: Agência Brasil (EBC), 'Zumbi dos Palmares: a 17th century Negro leader's death is celebrated' (2003)

title: A Tsar Works in a Shipyard
text: Young Tsar Peter of Russia toured Western Europe with a huge delegation, the Grand Embassy. In Dutch shipyards he worked with his own hands as a ship's carpenter, travelling under a fake name. He brought home shipbuilders and ideas to modernize Russia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Peter I: The Grand Embassy (1697-98)' (L. A. Nikiforov)

title: The Golden Stool of the Asante
text: According to Asante tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye called a golden stool down from the sky onto the lap of King Osei Tutu. It is believed to house the soul of the Asante nation. The stool must never touch the ground, and even the king does not sit on it: it rests on its own chair.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Gold in Asante Courtly Arts'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Golden Stool' (topic page)

title: A Capital Built on a Swamp
