text: Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg on marshy land at the mouth of the Neva River, wanting a 'window to Europe'. Tens of thousands of forced laborers drained the swamps, and many died. In 1712 it became Russia's capital, with canals and palaces designed in a European style.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'St. Petersburg: History'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg (text via data.unesco.org API)

title: Mount Fuji's Last Eruption
text: Just weeks after a huge earthquake, Mount Fuji erupted from a new crater on its side. Ash fell on Edo, some 60 miles away, and the sky grew so dark that people lit candles in the daytime. Homes and fields in villages near the mountain were buried, and Fuji has not erupted since.

source.name: Koyama et al., 'Reconstruction of the 1707 Hoei eruption of Fuji Volcano', JpGU 2002 abstract (Shizuoka Univ.)

source2.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Fujisan

title: New Orleans Is Founded
text: French colonist Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded a town on a sharp bend of the Mississippi River and named it after the Duke of Orléans. Built on swampy ground prone to floods, it grew into a city blending many heritages, where citizens of African descent helped make New Orleans the birthplace of jazz.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of New Orleans' (Joy Juanita Jackson)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'New Orleans'

title: Japan Opens to Dutch Learning
text: Shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune relaxed the ban on foreign books, as long as they weren't about Christianity. Japanese scholars began studying Dutch books on medicine, astronomy and geography, a movement called Rangaku, 'Dutch learning'. Later a group of doctors watched a dissection, were amazed by how accurate a Dutch anatomy book was, and translated it.

source.name: National Diet Library (Japan), 'Japan-Netherlands Exchange: Boom in Dutch Studies'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'rangaku'

title: Easter Day at Rapa Nui
text: Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen reached a remote Pacific island on Easter Sunday, so he named it Easter Island. Its people, the Rapa Nui, had carved hundreds of giant stone statues called moai. The one-day visit turned violent when the Dutch crew killed several islanders in a misunderstanding.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Easter Island' (incl. History section)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rapa Nui National Park (text via data.unesco.org API)

title: The Ottoman Printing Press
text: İbrahim Müteferrika, a Hungarian-born convert to Islam, became the first Muslim to run a printing press in the Ottoman Empire. Its first book, in 1729, was a big two-volume Arabic dictionary. He went on to print maps, histories and science books, but his permission covered only non-religious works, so religious texts stayed handwritten.

source.name: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis: 'Ibrahim Muteferrika, First Muslim Printer of the Ottoman Empire' (2023)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibrahim Muteferrika'

title: Linnaeus Names Nature
text: Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in Leiden, a plan to sort every plant, animal and mineral into groups. The first edition was only 11 large pages, but he kept expanding it, and by the 10th edition of 1758 it was a substantial two-volume set. His two-part naming system, like Homo sapiens, is still how scientists name species.

source.name: Linnean Society of London, 'Naming Nature'

source2.name: Library of Congress catalog: Systema naturae, 1735, facsimile of the 1st ed.

title: Nader Shah Takes the Peacock Throne
text: Persian ruler Nader Shah crushed the Mughal army at Karnal and marched into Delhi. After a deadly massacre, he carried away enormous treasure, including the jeweled Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. His empire soon stretched from the Indus River to the Caucasus Mountains.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Nāder Shah' (Ernest Tucker)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nādir Shāh'

title: A Pact in the Desert Oasis
text: In the mud-brick oasis town of Diriyah, local ruler Muhammad ibn Saud made an alliance with preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. The ruler would back the preacher's strict reform movement, and the preacher would support the ruler. Their pact founded the first Saudi state, ancestor of today's Saudi Arabia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab

title: An Encyclopedia of Everything
text: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert published the first volume of the Encyclopédie, aiming to gather all human knowledge. It covered crafts and machines as well as philosophy, with detailed illustrated plates. Its questioning ideas angered authorities, who banned it, but it kept being printed and became a symbol of the Enlightenment.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Encyclopédie

title: Lisbon's Triple Disaster
text: On All Saints' Day morning, a massive earthquake shook Lisbon while churches were full. A tsunami followed, then fires burned for days, killing tens of thousands. The city was rebuilt with buildings designed to withstand another earthquake, and philosophers such as Voltaire and Rousseau argued over why such disasters happen.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lisbon earthquake of 1755

source2.name: Cambridge University Library, Languages across Borders blog, Sonia Morcillo, 'The Lisbon earthquake of 1755'

title: A King Orders Potatoes Planted
text: Many Europeans distrusted the potato, a newcomer from the Andes. In 1756 Frederick the Great of Prussia issued an order commanding that it be grown as food, though at first his people ignored his decrees. It became a staple, and today visitors still leave potatoes on his grave at his palace of Sanssouci.

source.name: Associated Press (via WDIV ClickOnDetroit): Generations of Germans believe Frederick the Great brought potatoes to Germany. It's a myth

source2.name: Deutsches Historisches Museum, LeMO: 'Der König überall', 1886

title: A Betrayal at Plassey
text: Robert Clive's East India Company troops faced the far larger army of Bengal's ruler, Siraj ud-Daulah. Clive had secretly promised the throne to Siraj's commander Mir Jafar, whose troops held back. A rainstorm also soaked Siraj's gunpowder. The win gave a trading company control of rich Bengal and began British rule in India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Plassey

title: Dream of the Red Chamber
text: Cao Xueqin, a writer from a once-rich family that had fallen on hard times, wrote a huge novel about the rise and fall of a grand household. Copies circulated by hand before being printed in 1791. With hundreds of characters, it is one of China's greatest novels, and its fans even have a name for its study: 'Redology'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dream of the Red Chamber / Cao Zhan

source2.name: The Conversation, Josh Stenberg (University of Sydney), 'Why you should read China's vast, 18th century novel, Dream of the Red Chamber'

title: The Fall of Ayutthaya
text: After a siege of more than a year, a Burmese army captured and burned Ayutthaya, the glittering Siamese capital for over 400 years. Within months a general named Taksin rallied the Siamese, drove out the Burmese and founded a new capital at Thonburi, on the riverbank that is now part of Bangkok.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic City of Ayutthaya

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taksin

title: The Great Bengal Famine
text: After a drought in 1769 and floods in 1770 ruined crops, a terrible famine swept Bengal, now under East India Company control. Millions of people died, possibly a third of the population. The Company kept pressing for high land taxes during the crisis, and its revenue collections in 1771 were even higher.

source.name: Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh): Famine

title: Tea in Boston Harbor
text: Angry about a British tax on tea, colonists, some disguised as Mohawk people, boarded three ships and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor. Britain responded with harsh punishments, pushing the thirteen colonies closer to revolution.

source.name: Massachusetts Historical Society: Coming of the American Revolution, Boston Tea Party

source2.name: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis (Law Library blog), 'The 250th Anniversary of the Boston Tea Party' (Dec 2023)

title: The 'Friendly Islands' of Tonga
text: James Cook visited Tonga, a Polynesian kingdom with powerful chiefs, in 1773, 1774 and 1777. He nicknamed it the Friendly Islands for the courtesy shown to strangers, and chiefs staged night dances with music for his crews. Yet William Mariner, an Englishman who later lived there, heard that some chiefs had plotted to kill Cook but couldn't agree on a plan.

source.name: Captain Cook Society: A Cook's Tour of Tonga

source2.name: Royal Museums Greenwich collections: 'A Night Dance by Men, in Hapaee' (after John Webber)

title: A New Planet from a Back Garden
text: William Herschel, a musician who built his own telescopes, spotted a fuzzy object from his home in Bath. It turned out to be Uranus, the first planet discovered since ancient times. His sister Caroline, who helped him, became a famous astronomer too, finding several comets.

source.name: Herschel Museum of Astronomy (Bath Preservation Trust): FAQs

source2.name: European Space Agency: Caroline and William Herschel, Revealing the invisible

title: The First Hot-Air Balloon Show
text: Paper-maker brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier filled a big cloth-and-paper balloon with hot air from a fire and launched it before a crowd in their hometown. A few months later, a sheep, a duck and a rooster rode one at Versailles. By November, two men flew over Paris.

source.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Montgolfier Brothers

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Balloon flight, Historical development (Don Piccard)

title: Madagascar's Rice-Field King
text: Ambohimanga, a hilltop royal town, was the cradle of the Merina dynasty. Its king Andrianampoinimerina, who reigned from 1787, reunited the Merina kingdom, which had been split among four warring rulers, and gave it uniform laws. He reportedly told his son that the sea should be the edge of his rice fields, meaning the kingdom should cover the whole island.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Madagascar, Political evolution from 1650 to 1810 (Aidan Southall)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Royal Hill of Ambohimanga

title: A Lunar New Year Victory
text: Nguyễn Huệ, a leader of the Tây Sơn rebels, crowned himself Emperor Quang Trung and rushed his army north. During the Tết New Year holiday, his troops surprised and routed a large Qing army occupying Thăng Long, today's Hanoi. The victory is still celebrated at the Đống Đa festival each year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tay Son Brothers / history of Vietnam

source2.name: Viet Nam News: Festival celebrates the 236th anniversary of the Ngọc Hồi-Đống Đa victory

title: Kamehameha Wins Oʻahu
text: Kamehameha invaded Oʻahu with about 10,000 soldiers and drove its defenders up Nuʻuanu Valley. Hundreds of them, and some of their families, jumped or were forced to their deaths from the steep cliffs at the valley's head rather than accept defeat. The victory made Kamehameha ruler of most of the Hawaiian Islands, and Kauaʻi joined his kingdom peacefully in 1810.

source.name: Library of Congress Subject Headings: Nuʻuanu, Battle of, Oahu, Hawaii, 1795

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kamehameha I

title: King Jeongjo's Fortress of Filial Love
text: King Jeongjo built Hwaseong Fortress near the tomb of his father, who had died tragically. Scholar Jeong Yak-yong designed cranes and pulleys that sped up construction. The builders kept such detailed records that the walls could be faithfully restored after damage in the Korean War.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hwaseong Fortress

source2.name: Korea.net (Korean government): Visit world heritage sites

title: A Milkmaid's Secret Beats Smallpox
text: Country doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught mild cowpox seemed safe from deadly smallpox. He took material from a milkmaid's cowpox sore and scratched it into the arm of a boy, James Phipps, who then resisted smallpox. The word 'vaccine' comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

source.name: Riedel S., 'Edward Jenner and the history of smallpox and vaccination', Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent) 2005, PubMed Central

title: The One-Eyed Lion of Punjab
text: In 1801 the Sikh leader Ranjit Singh, only about twenty, was proclaimed Maharaja of Punjab in Lahore. Childhood smallpox had left him blind in one eye, yet he modernized his army, hiring European officers to train it. His kingdom stretched from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej River, but it collapsed within about six years of his death.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ranjit Singh (Khushwant Singh)

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Maharaja Ranjit Singh (painting, O114210)

title: Gia Long Stitches Vietnam Together
text: After decades of civil war, Nguyễn Ánh won decisive victories at Huế and Hanoi in 1802 and became Emperor Gia Long, ruling a reunited Vietnam from Huế. His court first asked Qing China to recognise the name Nam Việt. China refused, and after long negotiations the country officially took the name Việt Nam in 1804.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gia Long

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: history of Vietnam (William S. Turley)

title: A European Court Moves to Rio
text: Fleeing Napoleon's invading army, Portugal's royal family and a horde of nobles and officials sailed across the Atlantic and landed in Brazil in 1808. Rio de Janeiro suddenly became the capital of a whole empire, the only time a colony served as the seat of government for its mother country. Rio soon gained a royal library, a botanical garden and a royal printing office.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brazil: Independence

source2.name: Brown University Library, Five Centuries of Change in Brazil: Pedro I and Pedro II

title: Hidalgo Rings the Bell
text: Before dawn on September 16, 1810, the village priest Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell in Dolores and called his parishioners to rise against Spanish rule. Thousands of farmers and workers joined him, starting Mexico's war of independence. Every year on the night of September 15, Mexico's president still rings that same bell and repeats the cry.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla

source2.name: UCLA Library, Frontera Collection blog: From Columbus to Hidalgo

title: Napoleon's Frozen Retreat
text: In 1812 Napoleon marched into Russia with the largest army Europe had ever seen. He reached Moscow in September, only to find it emptied and soon burning, with no one willing to surrender. Forced to retreat as winter closed in, he saw only about 112,000 of some 612,000 men return, and his army could never replace the trained men and horses it lost.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, French invasion of Russia

title: Shaka Takes the Zulu Throne
text: Around 1816 Shaka became chief of the Zulu, then a small chiefdom. He reorganized fighters into disciplined age-based regiments and armed them with short stabbing spears for close combat, instead of long spears thrown from a distance. By 1824 Shaka had no major rival in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, though his wars also brought huge upheaval to neighbors.

source.name: South African History Online, The Mfecane: Understanding a Period of Transformation in Southern Africa

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Shaka (Donald R. Morris)

title: San Martín Crosses the Andes
text: In early 1817 General José de San Martín led an army of thousands, plus mules and horses, from Argentina over icy Andes passes more than 3,000 meters high. It took about three weeks. Arriving in Chile by surprise, his army won the Battle of Chacabuco and freed Santiago from Spanish rule, a key step toward independence across South America.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Chacabuco

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, José de San Martín

title: A Trading Post Called Singapore
text: In 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company signed a deal with local Malay rulers to set up a trading post at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. He made it a free port open to all nations. The island then had about 1,000 people, mostly orang laut sea peoples, but by 1833 Chinese, Malays, Bugis, Indians and Arabs all lived and traded there.

source.name: National Library Board Singapore, Infopedia: 1819 Singapore Treaty

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sir Stamford Raffles

title: Bolívar Wins at Boyacá Bridge
text: In 1819 Simón Bolívar did the unexpected: he marched his army across flooded plains and freezing Andes passes in the rainy season. On August 7 he caught Spanish royalist forces near a bridge over the Boyacá River, and the bulk of the royalist army surrendered. Three days later he entered Bogotá, and the victory led to the new republic of Gran Colombia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Boyacá

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Simón Bolívar

title: A Prince Declares Brazil Free
text: On September 7, 1822, Prince Pedro, son of Portugal's king, proclaimed Brazil's independence on the plain of Ipiranga near São Paulo, and is remembered for crying "Independence or death!" On December 1 he was crowned Pedro I, Emperor of Brazil. Unusually, Brazil broke away from Portugal with a member of Portugal's own royal family as its new ruler.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brazil: Independence

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pedro I

title: Prince Diponegoro's Java War
text: In 1825 the Javanese prince Diponegoro rose against Dutch colonial rule after officials marked out a public road through his estate. Seen by many as a holy leader, he fought a guerrilla war for five years. In 1830 the Dutch invited him to peace talks, then arrested him and exiled him for life to Sulawesi.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diponegoro

source2.name: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination, Babad Diponegoro (Indonesia/Netherlands)

title: Madagascar's Iron Queen
text: In 1828 Ranavalona I took the throne of the Merina kingdom after her husband's death and ruled Madagascar for 33 years. She pushed back hard against European influence, expelling missionaries and resisting British and French pressure. Her rule was harsh on Christians and opponents, so she is remembered both as a defender of independence and as a feared ruler.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Madagascar: Formation of the kingdom (1810-61), excerpted on its Ranavalona I page

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Africana (African Union project; Dictionary of African Biography), Queen Ranavalona I

title: Ram Mohan Roy's Long Campaign
text: For years the Bengali scholar Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against sati, the custom of a widow dying on her husband's funeral fire. In December 1829 the British governor banned it in Bengal. Roy, who read Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English, also founded a reform movement and argued for women's property rights and modern schools.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ram Mohan Roy

source2.name: Women in World History (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media, George Mason University), Sati: Official Documents, Regulation XVII of 1829

title: Emir Abdelkader Takes Command
text: In 1832, two years after France invaded Algeria, tribes near Mascara chose the young scholar Abdelkader to lead their resistance. He fought the French for some fifteen years before surrendering. Later, living in Damascus in 1860, he sheltered thousands of Christians during deadly riots, earning praise worldwide. A town in Iowa, Elkader, is named after him.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdelkader (Marcel Emerit)

source2.name: Grinnell College news, A Muslim Saint in Iowa

title: Slavery Ends in Jamaica, Slowly
text: On August 1, 1834, Britain's law abolishing slavery took effect in Jamaica and its other colonies. But freed people were forced into unpaid "apprenticeship" until full freedom came on August 1, 1838. Enslavers were paid £20 million in compensation while the formerly enslaved received nothing, a loan that, by one way of counting, British taxpayers were still paying off until 2015.

source.name: The National Archives (UK), The 1833 Abolition of Slavery Act and compensation claims

source2.name: UK Parliament, The West Indian colonies and emancipation

title: Ox Wagons on the Great Trek
text: From 1836, thousands of Dutch-speaking settlers called Voortrekkers loaded families into ox wagons and left Britain's Cape Colony, angry at British rule and the end of slavery. They pushed north and east into lands already home to the Ndebele, Zulu, Sotho and others. The journey led to new Boer republics and to years of conflict with African kingdoms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Great Trek

source2.name: South African History Online, Great Trek 1835-1846

title: A Scholar Rebels for the Hungry
text: During the Tenpō famine, Ōshio Heihachirō, a former Osaka official and follower of Wang Yangming's Neo-Confucian philosophy, sold his library to help starving people. In 1837 he led an armed revolt against city officials and wealthy merchants. It was crushed in a single day, but the shogun's government was shocked that a former faithful official had rebelled.

source.name: Nippon.com, 'The Warnings of Famines Past' (Abe Haruki)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Japan: The maturity of Edo culture (excerpt on Ōshio Heihachirō page)

title: The Edict of the Rose Chamber
text: On November 3, 1839, the Ottoman government proclaimed a royal decree known as the Edict of Gülhane, or "Rose Chamber." It promised subjects of every religion security of life, property and honour, plus a standardized tax system. This began the Tanzimat, meaning "reorganization," decades of reforms meant to modernize the empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tanzimat

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mustafa Reşid Paşa

title: Hong Kong Becomes British
text: The First Opium War ended in 1842 with a treaty signed aboard a British warship near Nanjing. Qing China had to hand Hong Kong Island to Britain, open five ports to foreign trade and pay a huge sum in silver. Chinese writers later called it the first of the "unequal treaties," and Hong Kong stayed British until 1997.

source.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, The First Unequal Treaty

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Nanjing

title: Ada Lovelace Writes a Program
text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace, daughter of the poet Lord Byron, translated an article about Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine and added her own notes, three times longer. One note set out step-by-step instructions for the machine to calculate special numbers, often called the first computer program. The machine was never built, but a programming language, Ada, is named after her.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ada Lovelace

source2.name: Computer History Museum, The Babbage Engine: A Brief History

title: The Potato Blight Strikes Ireland
text: In 1845 a water mold began rotting potato crops across Ireland, where the poorest third of the people depended almost entirely on potatoes. Over the next several years about one million people died and more than a million emigrated, mostly to North America. Even today, the island of Ireland has fewer people than its pre-famine population of about 8.5 million.

source.name: University College Cork, Atlas of the Great Irish Famine 1845-1852

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Great Famine

title: Liberia Declares Independence
text: On July 26, 1847, Liberia declared itself an independent republic, the first in Africa to do so. It had been founded by an American society as a home for freed Black Americans, and its first president, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, was born in Virginia. Its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.

source.name: Library of Congress, Teaching with the Library blog: Liberia, Africa's Oldest Independent and Democratic Republic

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Joseph Jenkins Roberts

title: A School for Girls in Pune
text: In 1848 Savitribai Phule and her husband Jyotirao opened a school for girls in Pune, at a time when most Indian girls never learned to read. Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers. People threw mud and dung at her on the way to class, so she carried a spare sari and kept going.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Savitribai Phule

title: The Black Ships Arrive
text: In July 1853, four American warships led by Commodore Matthew Perry appeared off Uraga, at the entrance to Edo Bay. Two were coal-burning steamships, and they entered under a cloud of black smoke; Japanese artists rushed to draw the "black ships." Perry demanded that Japan open to trade after about two centuries of tightly limited contact, and a treaty followed the next year.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

source2.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, Black Ships & Samurai (J. Dower)

title: India's First Passenger Train
text: On April 16, 1853, about 400 passengers in 14 carriages left Bori Bunder in Bombay for Thane, roughly 34 kilometres away, to a 21-gun salute, and the day was declared a public holiday. In the years that followed, railways spread rapidly across India, connecting people, goods and ideas faster than ever before.

source.name: Press Information Bureau, Government of India, 'From Steam to Speed' backgrounder (15 Apr 2026)

title: The Prophecy of Nongqawuse
text: In 1856 a Xhosa teenager named Nongqawuse said ancestors had told her that if people killed their cattle and threw away their grain, the dead would return and a whirlwind would sweep all white people into the sea. Many believed her, at a time of colonial pressure and a deadly cattle disease. Huge numbers of cattle were killed, and tens of thousands died in the famine that followed.

source.name: J. B. Peires, ''Soft' Believers and 'Hard' Unbelievers in the Xhosa Cattle-Killing', Journal of African History 27(3), 1986 (Cambridge)

source2.name: Journal of Natal and Zulu History 26 (2008), K. Breckenridge, 'Power without Knowledge'

title: Darwin Publishes His Big Idea
text: On November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, written at his country home, Down House. The first printing sold out to booksellers right away. It explained how living things change over time through natural selection, and fun fact: the word "evolution" does not appear in the first edition at all, though the very last word of the book is "evolved."

source.name: Darwin Online (John van Wyhe, ed.), R. B. Freeman introduction to On the Origin of Species

title: The Burning of the Garden of Gardens
text: In October 1860, near the end of the Second Opium War, British and French troops looted and then burned the Yuanmingyuan, the Qing emperors' vast garden palace outside Beijing. The fires took days to destroy its halls and gardens. Among the stolen treasures were twelve bronze zodiac animal heads, some of which have since come home to China.

source.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, 'The Summer Palace of the Qing Emperors & its Destruction'

source2.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, 'The Controversy Surrounding the 12 Zodiac Animal Heads'

title: Russia Frees Its Serfs
text: In 1861 Tsar Alexander II signed a decree freeing some 20 million serfs, peasants who had been tied to landowners' estates. It came two years before Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation in the US. The catch: freed peasants had to pay for their land through "redemption payments" planned to last 49 years, so many stayed poor.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Emancipation Manifesto'

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Before Lincoln Issued the Emancipation Proclamation, This Russian Czar Freed 20 Million Serfs'

title: Two Minutes at Gettysburg
text: In November 1863, during the US Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln spoke at a new cemetery for soldiers killed at Gettysburg. The featured speaker before him talked for about two hours; Lincoln's speech was about 270 words and lasted roughly two minutes. It called for "a new birth of freedom" in a nation dedicated to the idea that all men are created equal, and became world-famous.

source.name: Library of Congress, Teaching with the LOC blog

source2.name: Library of Congress, Gettysburg Address exhibition

title: A Monk Counts His Peas
text: In the garden of his monastery in Brno, the monk Gregor Mendel grew and crossed thousands of pea plants, tracking traits like flower color and seed shape. In 1865 he presented the rules he found for how traits pass from parents to offspring. Almost nobody noticed until 1900, long after his death, when scientists rediscovered his work and founded genetics.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gregor Mendel' (Robert Olby)

source2.name: Nature Education Scitable, 'Gregor Mendel and the Principles of Inheritance'

title: China Builds Its Own Arsenal
text: In 1865, as part of the Self-Strengthening Movement, Qing officials Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang developed the Jiangnan Arsenal in Shanghai to make modern arms, and in 1868 it built China's first modern steamship. Its translation bureau, led by the Englishman John Fryer, turned more than 160 foreign works into Chinese. The idea was to adopt Western technology without changing China's institutions or ideas.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jiangnan Arsenal' (rev. Zhihou Xia)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Self-Strengthening Movement'

title: Canada Is Born
text: On July 1, 1867, the British colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined to form the Dominion of Canada, with four provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Its capital was Ottawa, a former lumber town picked by Queen Victoria partly as a compromise between rival cities. July 1 is still celebrated as Canada Day, though Indigenous peoples had no seat at the table.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Confederation' (P.B. Waite et al.)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Ottawa'

title: Russia Takes Samarkand
text: In May 1868 Russian troops captured Samarkand, the old Silk Road city that Timur had made the greatest cultural centre of Central Asia. The defeated Emirate of Bukhara lost territory, paid an indemnity and was left at Russia's mercy. Samarkand soon gained a new section built after the Russian conquest, beside its medieval old city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Central Asia vii. In the 18th-19th Centuries'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Samarkand'

title: The Golden Spike
text: On May 10, 1869, workers drove a ceremonial golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining two railroads into the first line across the United States. Most of the workers who blasted the western section through the Sierra Nevada were Chinese immigrants. A trip from coast to coast shrank from months to days.

source.name: National Park Service, Golden Spike NHP, 'Chinese Labor and the Iron Road'

source2.name: Stanford Report, 'Giving voice to Chinese railroad workers' (2019)

title: An Empire Proclaimed in Versailles
text: On January 18, 1871, while Paris was under siege, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, in the palace of defeated France. Dozens of German states became one empire, which Germans saw as revenge for past French humiliations. In 1919 France's leader Clemenceau savoured his own revenge as Germany signed the treaty ending World War I in that same hall.

source.name: Palace of Versailles, 'Proclamation of the German Empire, 1871'

source2.name: Palace of Versailles, 'Hall of Mirrors'

title: A King Says Stand Up
text: In 1873, soon after his coronation, King Chulalongkorn of Siam issued a famous edict abolishing the custom of prostration, letting people bow instead. Over his long reign he also abolished slavery, reformed the courts and finances, and reorganized the government. By balancing the colonial powers against one another, he avoided colonial rule and left behind an independent kingdom.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chulalongkorn'

source2.name: Cambridge University Press, P. Jory, A History of Manners and Civility in Thailand, ch. 2 abstract

title: Zanzibar's Slave Market Closes
text: In June 1873, under a treaty with Britain, Sultan Barghash agreed to close all public slave markets in his lands, including Zanzibar's, the last permanent slave market in East Africa. A British missionary society bought the site, and an Anglican cathedral was later built on the very spot, with its high altar placed over the old whipping post.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Urban Heritage Atlas: Stone Town of Zanzibar

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tanzania: Zanzibar'

title: The Impressionists Are Named
text: In April 1874 a group of artists often snubbed by the official Paris Salon held their own show in a photographer's old studio. A critic mocked Claude Monet's hazy harbor painting, Impression, Sunrise, as a mere sketch or "impression," and the whole movement got its name. Some of the painters, a group including Berthe Morisot, later adopted the name themselves.

source.name: National Gallery of Art, '1874: The Birth of Impressionism'

source2.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Impressionism: Art and Modernity'

title: Tonga Writes a Constitution
text: In 1875 King George Tupou I gave Tonga a written constitution. Revised over the years, it is still in use today, one of the oldest written national constitutions in the world. During his long reign Tonga became a unified, independent kingdom with a legal code and modern government, though it later became a British protectorate from 1900 until 1970.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tonga: History'

source2.name: Matangi Tonga, 'Tonga's Constitution among the oldest in the world' (2014)

title: Mr. Watson, Come Here
text: On March 10, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell spoke into his new device in Boston and his assistant Thomas Watson heard him from another room: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Bell had filed his patent on February 14, just hours before a rival inventor, Elisha Gray, filed papers on a similar idea. Within years telephone wires crisscrossed cities.

source.name: Library of Congress Information Bulletin, 'Watson, Come Here' (April 2004)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alexander Graham Bell'

title: Korea's Doors Forced Open
text: In 1876 Japan, after sending gunboats to Korean waters, pressed Joseon into signing a treaty on Ganghwa Island. It opened Korean ports to Japanese trade and let Japanese citizens be tried by their own officials. Only about twenty years after American ships had forced Japan open, Japan was now doing the same to its neighbor.

source.name: Modern Asian Studies (Cambridge), 'Informal diplomacy in Choson Korea ... 1873-1876'

source2.name: Review of Korean Studies (Lee Keun-Gwan), 'Trope of a Sovereign State: Treaty-Making by Korea 1876-1899'

title: Egypt for the Egyptians
text: Colonel Ahmed Urabi led a movement against foreign control of Egypt under the slogan "Egypt for Egyptians." In July 1882 British warships bombarded Alexandria, and that September British troops defeated Urabi's army. Keen to safeguard the Suez Canal, Britain occupied Egypt and kept a strong grip on the country until after World War II.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ʿUrābī Pasha

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Egypt: Renewed European intervention, 1879–82

title: Dividing Africa Around a Table
text: From November 1884 to February 1885, representatives of 14 countries, a dozen European states plus the United States and the Ottoman Empire, met in Berlin to settle rival claims in Africa. No Africans were invited. The conference sped up the "Scramble for Africa," and the Congo was recognized as the personal property of Belgium's King Leopold II.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Berlin West Africa Conference

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Leopold II

title: The Mahdi Takes Khartoum
text: In January 1885 the forces of Muhammad Ahmad, a religious leader called the Mahdi, captured Khartoum after a siege of more than ten months. British general Charles Gordon died in the fighting. A British relief force arrived just two days too late, and the Mahdist state went on to rule Sudan until 1898.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Siege of Khartoum

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Omdurman

title: Congress Meets in Bombay
text: In December 1885, 72 delegates from across British India met at a college in Bombay to found the Indian National Congress. One of its organizers was A. O. Hume, a retired British official. At first it asked politely for a bigger Indian voice in government; decades later, under leaders like Gandhi, it led the fight for independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Indian National Congress

source2.name: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Mumbai Legacy Project (D Ward): Badruddin Tyabji

title: The New Flower City
text: In the late 1880s Taytu, wife of the future Emperor Menelik II, persuaded him to move from cold Entoto, where firewood was scarce, to hot springs at the foot of the plateau. She named the new town Addis Ababa, meaning "new flower." As firewood ran short again, eucalyptus trees were imported from Australia in 1905 and spread to give the city forest cover.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Addis Ababa

title: The Yellow River Breaks Free
text: In September 1887 the Yellow River burst its levees near Kaifeng in Henan province and began flowing south into the Huai River. The flood covered thousands of square miles and buried many villages under silt. Estimates of the dead range from about 900,000 to two million, making it one of the deadliest floods in history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Yellow River: Hydrology

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Huang He floods

title: Japan Gets a Constitution
text: On February 11, 1889, Emperor Meiji presented Japan's first constitution, modeled partly on Prussia's after officials toured Europe to study. It created an elected parliament called the Diet, which first met in 1890. Only a tiny share of men could vote at first, and the emperor kept enormous power.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Itō Hirobumi

source2.name: National Diet Library (Japan), Birth of the Constitution of Japan: text of the Meiji Constitution

title: Tragedy at Wounded Knee
text: On December 29, 1890, US soldiers surrounded a band of Lakota people at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota. Fighting broke out while troops were disarming them, and around 250 or more Lakota, many of them women and children, were killed. The massacre is often seen as the end of the long wars against Native nations on the Plains.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Wounded Knee Massacre

title: The Queen of Hawaiʻi Is Overthrown
text: On January 17, 1893, a group of mostly American businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani of Hawaiʻi. She gave up power under protest to avoid bloodshed. Hawaiʻi was annexed by the US in 1898, and in 1993 the US Congress formally apologized. The queen was also a gifted songwriter who wrote "Aloha ʻOe."

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sanford B. Dole

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Liliuokalani

title: Gandhi Thrown Off a Train
text: In June 1893 a young Indian lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi, holding a first-class ticket, was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg after a passenger objected to a "coloured" man in his compartment. He spent a freezing night in the station waiting room. He later called it a turning point that set him on the path of nonviolent protest.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mahatma Gandhi: Sojourn in England and return to India

source2.name: High Commission of India, Pretoria, Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa

title: The Donghak Peasants Rise
text: In 1894 Korean farmers, many following the Donghak or "Eastern Learning" religion, rose up against corruption and foreign encroachment and soon seized the provincial office at Jeonju. The Joseon court asked Qing China for troops, and Japan sent its own soldiers too. The rival armies clashed, setting off the First Sino-Japanese War.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Donghak Uprising

source2.name: Review of Korean Studies, Park Maeng-soo, 'Japan's "Distorted" Memory of the Donghak Peasant Uprising and the Sino-Japanese War'

title: Peace Talks at Shimonoseki
text: In April 1895 Qing China signed a treaty at Shimonoseki ending its war with Japan. China gave up Taiwan, recognized Korea's independence and paid a huge indemnity. During the talks, China's elderly envoy Li Hongzhang was shot in the face by a Japanese extremist; he survived, and the embarrassed Japanese side softened some terms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Shimonoseki

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Li Hongzhang

title: The First Modern Olympics
text: In April 1896 the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, with track events in an ancient stadium restored in white marble. About 240 athletes from 14 nations took part, all men. The crowd went wild when Spyridon Louis, a Greek often described as a water carrier, won the brand-new marathon, which followed the legendary route of a messenger from Marathon to Athens.

source.name: International Olympic Committee (olympics.com), Athens 1896

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Athens 1896 Olympic Games

title: José Rizal's Last Poem
text: José Rizal, a doctor, novelist and speaker of many languages, wrote novels exposing abuses under Spanish rule in the Philippines. Accused of inspiring revolution, he was executed by firing squad in Manila on December 30, 1896. The night before, he wrote a farewell poem and hid it inside a small alcohol stove, which he left to his sister Trinidad.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, José Rizal

source2.name: Philippine Daily Inquirer: Haggling over the 'Ultimo Adios', by historian Ambeth Ocampo

title: The Curies Find Radium
text: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie announced two new elements found in the ore pitchblende: polonium, named after Marie's homeland Poland, and radium. Their July 1898 paper was the first to use the word "radioactivity." Their papers are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes, and readers must wear protective clothing and sign a waiver to consult them.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Marie and Pierre Curie and the discovery of polonium and radium

source2.name: Christian Science Monitor: Marie Curie: Why her papers are still radioactive (2011)

title: The Hundred Days' Reform
text: In June 1898 the young Guangxu Emperor, advised by Kang Youwei, began issuing decrees to modernize schools, the army and government. After about 100 days, Empress Dowager Cixi seized power in a coup, imprisoned the emperor in his palace and had six reformers executed. A few moderate measures survived, such as new modern schools, including the university that became Peking University.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hundred Days of Reform

source2.name: Peking University News: Imperial University of Peking founded during the Hundred Days' Reform

title: Samori Touré's Last Stand
text: From 1883 Samori Touré, founder of a powerful Muslim kingdom in West Africa, fought French colonial armies, buying modern repeating rifles from traders in Freetown and setting up his own firearms industry. When pushed back, he tried to rebuild his state further east. He was finally captured in September 1898 and exiled to Gabon, where he died in 1900.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Samory

source2.name: Legassick, M. (1966) 'Firearms, Horses and Samorian Army Organization 1870-1898', Journal of African History (Cambridge)

title: Independence From a Balcony
text: On June 12, 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo's government proclaimed Philippine independence from Spain at his house in Kawit, as the new national flag was unfurled and a band played the national march. But months later Spain sold the islands to the US for $20 million. Filipinos then fought a bitter war against American rule.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Spanish-American War, 1898

source2.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Philippine-American War, 1899-1902

title: The Boxers Rise in Shandong
text: After Yellow River floods devastated northern China in 1898, groups calling themselves the Righteous and Harmonious Fists spread through Shandong in 1899. Foreigners nicknamed them "Boxers" for their martial-arts rituals, which many believed made them immune to bullets. Angry at missionaries and foreign power, they marched on Beijing in 1900, where an eight-nation foreign army crushed them.

source.name: Origins (Ohio State University and Miami University): The Boxer Rebellion, by Harry Hughen

source2.name: Origins (Ohio State University): The Boxer Rebellion

title: Mount Pelée Buries a City
text: On the morning of May 8, 1902, Mount Pelée on the Caribbean island of Martinique sent a glowing avalanche of hot gas and ash racing down onto the town of Saint-Pierre. It struck in less than a minute, and nearly all of the town's roughly 28,000 people died. One of only two known survivors, Louis-Auguste Cyparis, was shut in a prison dungeon and later toured with a circus.

source.name: San Diego State University, How Volcanoes Work: The eruption of Mt. Pelee, Martinique

source2.name: EARTH Magazine (American Geosciences Institute): Benchmarks: May 8, 1902, by Julia Rosen

title: The Herero and Nama Genocide
text: In 1904 the Herero people of German South West Africa rose against colonists who had seized their land and cattle. After a battle at Waterberg, German troops drove survivors into the Omaheke desert and later held many in deadly camps; the Nama people suffered too. Tens of thousands died, and Germany has since acknowledged it as genocide, sealed in a 2021 agreement with Namibia.

source.name: NPR: Germany Officially Recognizes It Committed Genocide In Present-Day Namibia (May 28, 2021)

source2.name: South African History Online: Herero revolt 1904-1907

title: Exposing the Congo's Rubber Terror
place: Boma, Democratic Republic of the Congo
text: King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo Free State as his personal project, forcing villagers to collect wild rubber under brutal punishments. In 1904 British consul Roger Casement published a report based on his own trip upriver. Along with campaigns by missionaries and journalists, it helped build the pressure that led Belgium to take the colony away from Leopold in 1908.

source.name: breac: A Digital Journal of Irish Studies (University of Notre Dame): Plasman and Thewissen, The Three Lives of the Casement Report

title: China Ends the Imperial Exams
text: In 1905 the Qing government abolished the imperial examinations, which had chosen officials for about 1,300 years. Candidates wrote essays on Confucian classics in tiny cells that doubled as their bedrooms; Nanjing's Jiangnan Examination Hall alone had over 20,000 cells. The same year the court ordered new elementary schools and urged more students to study in Europe and America.

source.name: Princeton University, Department of History: Benjamin A. Elman, Civil Examinations and Meritocracy in Late Imperial China

source2.name: US Office of the Historian, FRUS 1905, doc. 211 (imperial edicts of 1-2 Sept 1905)

title: San Francisco Shakes and Burns
text: At 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, a huge earthquake struck San Francisco, and fires burned for days, destroying more than 80 percent of the city's buildings. Around 3,000 people died. Because city records burned, many Chinese immigrants could claim they were born in San Francisco and bring over relatives, the so-called "paper sons."

source.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program: The Great 1906 San Francisco Earthquake

source2.name: US National Archives: San Francisco Earthquake, 1906

title: Persia Gets a Parliament
text: In the summer of 1906, thousands of merchants, clerics and workers in Tehran camped in the garden of the British legation, refusing to leave until the shah agreed to reform. In August Mozaffar ad-Din Shah gave in and allowed a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis. The first Majlis met that October.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Constitutional Revolution ii. Events

source2.name: EBSCO Research Starters: Persia Adopts a Constitution, by Gregory C. Kozlowski

title: The Taste Called Umami
text: Chemist Kikunae Ikeda wondered why dashi, a broth made from kombu seaweed and one of his favorite dishes, tasted so good. He found the secret was glutamate and named its savory flavor umami, from the Japanese word for delicious. In 1908 he patented a way to make it as a seasoning, MSG, and soon a company called Ajinomoto was selling it.

source.name: Japan Patent Office: Ten Japanese Great Inventors, Kikunae Ikeda (Sodium Glutamate)

source2.name: BioMed Research International (PMC): Umami the Fifth Basic Taste

title: The Bomb That Toppled an Empire
text: In October 1911 revolutionaries in Hankou accidentally set off a bomb they were building, and police found their membership lists. With nothing left to lose, soldiers in nearby Wuchang rose up on October 10. Province after province joined, and in February 1912 the boy emperor Puyi abdicated, ending China's 2,000-year-old imperial system.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Chinese Revolution (1911-12)

source2.name: The China Project: Double 10: The Wuchang Uprising and the end of the Qing, by James Carter (2023)

title: First to the South Pole
text: On December 14, 1911, Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and four companions became the first people to reach the South Pole. Their secret weapons were skis, sled dogs and reindeer-skin clothing sewn to a pattern from the Netsilik Inuit of the Arctic. They beat Robert Falcon Scott's British team by about five weeks, and Scott's party died on their return journey.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Roald Amundsen

source2.name: Roald Amundsen's Uranienborg (MiA - Museene i Akershus): 1910-1912 Fram expedition. Clothing

title: A Shortcut Between Two Oceans
text: The cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official trip through the Panama Canal, cutting thousands of kilometres off the voyage around South America. Giant water-filled locks lift ships about 26 metres up to an artificial lake and back down again. Tens of thousands of workers, many from the Caribbean, built it, and thousands died of disease and accidents along the way.

source.name: Panama Canal Authority: 107-year timeline

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Panama Canal

title: The Landing at Gallipoli
text: Allied troops, including Australians and New Zealanders, landed on Ottoman beaches hoping to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the First World War. The campaign failed after eight months, with heavy losses on both sides. An Ottoman officer there, Mustafa Kemal, later founded modern Turkey, and April 25 is still remembered as Anzac Day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gallipoli Campaign

source2.name: Australian War Memorial: Gallipoli

title: The Storming of the Winter Palace
text: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd, arresting the ministers of the government in the tsars' old Winter Palace. Russia still used the old Julian calendar, so locals called it the October Revolution even though it was November elsewhere. A civil war followed, and in 1922 the Soviet Union was born.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Russian Revolution (The February Revolution and the Bolshevik Revolution)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Soviet Union

title: Students Fill Tiananmen Square
text: About 3,000 Beijing students marched in fury after the peace talks ending the First World War handed German-held land in Shandong to Japan instead of back to China. The May Fourth Movement grew into a wider push for science, democracy and writing in everyday spoken Chinese instead of the old classical style. Many future leaders, including founders of the Communist Party, came out of it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: May Fourth Movement

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tiananmen Square

title: Korea Declares Independence
text: Under Japanese rule, Korean leaders signed a Declaration of Independence, and a student read it aloud in Seoul's Tapgol Park, sparking peaceful protests across the country. About two million people joined, and the colonial police cracked down hard. A teenage schoolgirl, Yu Gwan-sun, died in prison after torture, and March 1st is now a public holiday.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: March First Movement

source2.name: Korea JoongAng Daily: The quiet city park where independence was declared

title: Insulin Saves a Dying Boy
text: At the University of Toronto, Frederick Banting, Charles Best and their colleagues purified insulin, the hormone that people with diabetes lack. In January 1922 a 14-year-old boy, Leonard Thompson, became the first person treated, and he recovered. The discoverers sold the patent to the university for a symbolic one dollar each so the medicine could reach as many people as possible.

source.name: PMC: The discovery of insulin revisited: lessons for the modern era

title: The Great Kantō Earthquake
text: A huge earthquake struck just before noon, when families were cooking lunch over open flames, so fires swept through wooden Tokyo and Yokohama. More than 100,000 people died, and in the chaos false rumours led mobs to kill thousands of Korean residents. Japan now marks September 1 as Disaster Prevention Day with drills in schools and offices.

source.name: The Japan Times (Deep Dive podcast transcript, 2023)

source2.name: The Japan Times (2016, Disaster Prevention Day)

title: A Republic Rises in Ankara
text: After the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Mustafa Kemal declared the Republic of Turkey and made Ankara, his wartime headquarters, its capital instead of Istanbul. His reforms moved fast: in 1928 Turkish switched from Arabic script to Latin letters, and he toured the country with a chalkboard teaching it himself. In 1934 parliament gave him the surname Atatürk, meaning "Father of the Turks."

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kemal Atatürk (Norman Itzkowitz)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kemal Atatürk: nationalist movement

title: Television's First Public Show
text: In an attic room in Soho, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed scientists a flickering moving picture of a human face. His mechanical television used spinning discs to scan the image line by line. Early tests used a ventriloquist's dummy nicknamed Stooky Bill, whose painted face gave a sharp, high-contrast picture under the hot, bright lamps.

source.name: English Heritage, Blue Plaques: John Logie Baird

source2.name: University of Strathclyde news (2026 centenary)

title: Black Tuesday
text: After years of wild buying, panic swept the New York Stock Exchange and share prices collapsed, wiping out fortunes in days. The crash helped trigger the Great Depression, when banks failed and millions around the world lost their jobs. At its worst, more than one in five American workers was unemployed, and hungry people lined up at bread lines and soup kitchens.

source.name: Federal Reserve History, Stock Market Crash of 1929

source2.name: Federal Reserve History, The Great Depression

title: The First Football World Cup
text: Uruguay, the reigning Olympic champion, hosted the first World Cup and built the Estadio Centenario to mark 100 years of its constitution. Only 13 teams came, since the trip from Europe took weeks by ship. In the final Uruguay beat neighbour Argentina 4–2, and the day after the win was declared a national holiday.

source.name: FIFA, 1930 tournament review

source2.name: FIFA, Estadio Centenario turns 90

title: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
text: After three decades of campaigns starting from Riyadh, Abdulaziz Ibn Saud united the regions of Najd and Hejaz into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. At first it was a poor desert country living largely on pilgrims visiting Mecca. That changed in 1938, when an American-run well near Dammam finally struck oil after years of failed drilling.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ibn Saud (John Bagot Glubb)

source2.name: Aramco World, Well Done, Well Seven (1988)

title: The Long March Begins
text: Surrounded by Nationalist armies, about 86,000 Communist troops and staff broke out of their base in Jiangxi in October 1934 on a year-long retreat. Fighting all the way, they crossed 18 mountain ranges and 24 rivers on a trek of about 10,000 kilometres. Only about 8,000 reached Shaanxi with Mao, but the march made Mao Zedong the party's undisputed leader.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Long March

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Long March

title: Black Sunday Dust Storm
text: A towering wall of dust rolled across the southern Great Plains, turning a sunny afternoon pitch dark. Years of drought and ploughing up prairie grass had let the soil simply blow away, and a reporter's story about the storm gave the region its name, the Dust Bowl. Many people left the Plains in the 1930s, but research shows only a minority went to California.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Norman, The Black Sunday Dust Storm of 14 April 1935

source2.name: National Bureau of Economic Research Digest, Tracking the Dust Bowl Migrants of the 1930s

title: Shots at the Marco Polo Bridge
text: A night-time clash between Chinese and Japanese troops near this old stone bridge, famous for its hundreds of carved lions, grew into full-scale war. The Second Sino-Japanese War lasted until 1945 and cost millions of Chinese lives, including the Nanjing Massacre that December. Today a museum of the war stands beside the bridge.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Marco Polo Bridge Incident

source2.name: Beijing Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau (visitbeijing.com.cn), The Red Blood Journey of Lugou Bridge

title: Mexico Takes Back Its Oil
text: President Lázaro Cárdenas took over the foreign oil companies operating in Mexico after they ignored a court ruling on workers' pay. To help pay the companies compensation, ordinary Mexicans lined up to donate money, jewellery and even chickens. The new state company, Pemex, became a symbol of national pride, and March 18 is still celebrated.

source.name: Senado de la República (Mexico), Efeméride: aniversario de la Expropiación Petrolera (2025)

source2.name: Archivo General de la Nación (Mexico), #AGNRecuerda la expropiación petrolera

title: The War Begins at Westerplatte
text: In the early hours, a German battleship opened fire on a small Polish army depot on the Westerplatte peninsula, among the first shots of the Second World War in Europe. About 200 Polish soldiers held out for seven days instead of the few hours expected. The war that followed would kill tens of millions of people worldwide.

source.name: Polish History Museum (polishhistory.pl), The defence of Westerplatte

source2.name: Museum of Gdańsk, Guardhouse No. 1 at Westerplatte

title: Teenagers Find Lascaux Cave
text: Four teenagers exploring near Montignac in 1940 found walls covered in Ice Age paintings of horses, bulls and deer, dated to somewhere between about 17,000 and 23,000 years ago. After the cave opened to visitors in 1948, crowds and artificial lighting faded the colours and spread algae, bacteria and crystals. It was closed in 1963, and visitors now tour replicas.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture, Lascaux: The discovery

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Vézère Valley (via UNESCO open-data API)

title: D-Day on the Normandy Beaches
text: About 156,000 Allied soldiers crossed the English Channel by sea and air to land on five Normandy beaches in one day, the largest seaborne invasion in history. Planners fooled Germany with a fake army of inflatable tanks pointed at a different stretch of coast. Thousands died that day, and within a year Nazi Germany had surrendered.

source.name: Imperial War Museums, Operation Fortitude: D-Day's Deception Strategy

source2.name: Eisenhower Presidential Library, World War II: D-Day, The Invasion of Normandy

title: The United Nations Charter
text: Delegates from 50 countries met in San Francisco and signed the Charter creating the United Nations, hoping to prevent another world war. The charter came into force on October 24, now celebrated as United Nations Day. Poland missed the conference but signed soon after, becoming the 51st founding member.

source.name: United Nations, The San Francisco Conference

title: Indonesia Proclaims Independence
text: Two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno, together with Mohammad Hatta, proclaimed Indonesia's independence, reading a short, typed text at his house in Jakarta. The Dutch, who had ruled the islands for centuries, fought to return. After four years of war and diplomacy, the Netherlands recognised Indonesia's independence in 1949.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sukarno

source2.name: SBS (Australian public broadcaster), Independence of the Republic of Indonesia, August 17, 1945

title: A New State and a Lasting Divide
text: David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in a Tel Aviv museum as British rule in Palestine ended. War with neighbouring Arab states followed, and around 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes. Palestinians remember this as the Nakba, meaning "catastrophe," and some families still keep the keys to houses they left.

source.name: United Nations, Question of Palestine: About the Nakba

source2.name: UNRWA, Palestine refugees

title: Apartheid Becomes Law
text: The National Party won South Africa's whites-only election and began building apartheid, an Afrikaans word meaning "apartness." New laws sorted every person by race and decided where they could live, work, study and even whom they could marry. Black South Africans, the large majority, could not vote in national elections until 1994.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, apartheid

source2.name: South African History Online, A history of Apartheid in South Africa

title: The Silence of the Maracanã
text: A record crowd, officially 173,850 and widely believed to be over 200,000, packed Rio's new Maracanã stadium expecting Brazil, who needed only a draw, to win the World Cup. Instead little Uruguay came from a goal behind to win 2–1 and silenced the stadium. Brazilians still remember the shock as the Maracanazo.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'FIFA World Cup' (Brazil 1950)

source2.name: FIFA, Maracanazo (Uruguay 2-1 Brazil, 1950)

title: Photo 51 and the Shape of DNA
text: At King's College London, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling took an X-ray picture of DNA showing a blurry X shape. Shown to James Watson without her knowledge, it helped him and Francis Crick work out the double helix in 1953. Franklin died young in 1958, and her key role was only widely recognised much later.

source.name: King's College London, 'The story behind Photograph 51'

source2.name: King's College London, 'Rosalind Franklin'

title: The Korean War Stops but Never Ends
text: Korea was split at the 38th parallel in 1945, and in 1950 the North invaded the South, starting a war that drew in the United States, China and many others. After three years and millions of deaths, an armistice was signed at Panmunjom. No peace treaty followed, so a heavily guarded strip about 4 kilometres wide still divides the peninsula.

source.name: US National Archives, Milestone Documents: Armistice Agreement for the Restoration of the South Korean State (1953)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Korean War

title: Victory at Dien Bien Phu
text: French forces built a fortress in a remote valley, confident they could hold it. With unheard-of physical effort, Viet Minh fighters brought some 200 artillery pieces through the jungle, while bicycles pushed by hand carried supplies. The French surrendered after 56 days of battle, ending their rule in Indochina and leaving Vietnam split in two.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battle of Dien Bien Phu'

source2.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Dien Bien Phu & the Fall of French Indochina'

title: Asia and Africa Meet at Bandung
text: Leaders from 29 newly independent or soon-to-be-free countries in Asia and Africa gathered in Bandung, Indonesia. Sukarno, Nehru, Zhou Enlai and Nasser called for an end to colonialism and for staying out of the Cold War rivalry. The meeting planted the seeds of the Non-Aligned Movement, a bloc of countries that refused to pick a superpower.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Bandung Conference (Asian-African Conference), 1955'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bandung Conference'

title: Nasser Takes the Suez Canal
text: Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser announced in a speech that Egypt was taking over the Suez Canal from its British and French owners. Britain, France and Israel invaded that autumn, but pressure from both the United States and the Soviet Union forced them to withdraw. The crisis showed that Europe's old empires could no longer act alone.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Suez Crisis'

source2.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Suez Crisis, 1956'

title: Things Fall Apart Is Published
text: Chinua Achebe, a young broadcaster in Lagos, published a novel about Okonkwo, a famous Igbo wrestler and prosperous farmer whose world is upended by British missionaries and colonial rule. Told from inside Igbo society, it challenged the way European writers had portrayed Africans. It has since been translated into more than 50 languages.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chinua Achebe'

source2.name: Guardian News and Media via Mail & Guardian, 'Achebe: Founding father of African fiction dies' (22 March 2013)

title: Seventeen-Year-Old Pelé Wins It All
text: Brazil beat host Sweden 5–2 in the World Cup final, and a 17-year-old named Pelé scored twice, then wept on the pitch. It was Brazil's first world title, eight years after the heartbreak of 1950. He went on to win three World Cups, still the record for any player.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pelé'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'FIFA World Cup' (Sweden 1958)

title: The Cuban Revolution Wins
text: Dictator Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba on New Year's Day, and a week later Fidel Castro rolled into Havana to cheering crowds. His rebellion had begun in 1956 when Castro and 81 men landed from the yacht Granma, and only about a dozen escaped the first fighting. Castro's Cuba soon drew close to the Soviet Union, just 150 kilometres from the United States.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cuban Revolution'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cuba'

title: Lumumba's Independence Day Speech
text: In 1960, the "Year of Africa," 17 African countries became independent. At the Congo's ceremony, with Belgium's king listening, Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba gave an unscheduled speech about the suffering of colonial rule. Within months he was overthrown, and in January 1961 he was executed by Katangan separatists alongside Belgian officers, becoming a symbol of African freedom.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Patrice Lumumba'

source2.name: Library of Congress, Worlds Revealed blog, 'Mapping the Year of Africa' (2023)

title: The First Human in Space
text: Yuri Gagarin, the son of a carpenter on a collective farm, blasted off in Vostok 1 and circled Earth once in about 108 minutes. Near the end he ejected and parachuted down in the Saratov region, near the town of Engels, where a startled farm woman and her young relative watched him land. The flight brought him immediate worldwide fame.

source.name: European Space Agency, 'The flight of Vostok 1'

source2.name: NASA, 'April 1961 - First Human Entered Space'

title: Algeria Wins Its Freedom
text: After eight years of war against France, Algeria became independent, ending French rule that had begun in 1830. The war was brutal for civilians and divided France itself, bringing its government down in 1958. Most European settlers left in a mass exodus, and July 5 is now celebrated as Algeria's Independence Day.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Algeria' (country page)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Algerian War' and 'Algeria'

title: Samoa Leads the Pacific to Freedom
text: Western Samoa, run by New Zealand since the First World War, became the first Pacific Islands nation to regain its independence in the 20th century. Its elected parliament is made up of matai, the chiefs who lead Samoa's extended families. Today Samoans hold their big Independence Day celebrations every June.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of Samoa' (Sophie Foster)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Samoa: Government and society' / 'Cultural life'

title: The March on Washington
text: About 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to demand civil rights and jobs for Black Americans. Martin Luther King Jr. was nearing the end of his prepared speech when gospel singer Mahalia Jackson urged him to tell the crowd about his dream, and he began to improvise. The Civil Rights Act passed the following year.

source.name: King Institute, Stanford, 'March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom'

source2.name: King Institute, Stanford, 'I Have a Dream'

title: Uhuru for Kenya
text: At midnight the British flag came down in Nairobi and Kenya's flag went up, a moment Kenyans call Uhuru, Swahili for "freedom." Jomo Kenyatta, who had been jailed by the British for years during the Mau Mau uprising, became its first leader. December 12 is now celebrated every year as Jamhuri Day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jomo Kenyatta' (John A. Rowe)

source2.name: National Museums of Kenya via Google Arts & Culture, 'Discover Kenya's Birthplace'

title: Singapore Becomes a Nation
text: After just two years as part of Malaysia, tiny Singapore was pushed out and became independent with no natural resources and little fresh water. Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew broke down in tears on television when announcing the split. Today the island is one of the world's busiest ports and a prosperous trading hub.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Singapore'

title: India's Green Revolution
text: After droughts and chronic food shortages, scientists like M. S. Swaminathan brought in short, sturdy wheat varieties first bred in Mexico by Norman Borlaug. With irrigation and fertiliser, Punjab's farmers grew far bigger harvests, and by 1971 India was self-sufficient in food. The boom also had costs, such as depleted groundwater and heavy chemical use.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, 'Norman Borlaug - Biographical' (Nobel Peace Prize 1970)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Green revolution'

title: The Nigerian Civil War
text: After violence against Igbo people in northern Nigeria, the southeast declared itself the independent Republic of Biafra. During the three-year war that followed, a blockade caused terrible famine, and perhaps a million or more people died, many of them children. French doctors who worked there went on to help found Médecins Sans Frontières, the medical aid charity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Biafra'

source2.name: Médecins Sans Frontières UK, 'History'

title: The Internet's First Message
text: A student at UCLA tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over ARPANET, a new network funded by the US military. He typed L, then O, and the system crashed before he could finish the word. So the first message ever sent on the internet's ancestor was simply "LO."

source.name: Leonard Kleinrock, UCLA Computer Science, 'The Day the Infant Internet Uttered its First Words'

source2.name: DARPA, 'ARPANET'

title: The Birth of Bangladesh
text: East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by some 1,800 kilometres of India, had long protested being treated unequally, starting with a fight in 1952 to have Bengali recognised as a national language. In 1971 a brutal crackdown led to a war of independence, and about ten million refugees fled to India. Bangladesh won its freedom that December.

source.name: Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh), 'War of Liberation, The'

source2.name: UNHCR, 'UNHCR honoured by Bangladesh for helping millions in 1971 conflict'

title: Nixon Goes to China
text: US President Richard Nixon flew to Beijing and met Premier Zhou Enlai and Chairman Mao, after more than twenty years without diplomatic relations. The visit followed "ping-pong diplomacy," when China invited the American table tennis team in 1971. Soon after, China gave the Washington zoo two giant pandas, Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing, which drew huge crowds.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

source2.name: US National Archives, 'Pandaversary'

title: The Coup in Chile
text: Chile's armed forces overthrew elected socialist president Salvador Allende, bombing the presidential palace, La Moneda; Allende died inside. General Augusto Pinochet then ruled for 17 years, and thousands of people were killed or disappeared. His rule finally ended after Chileans voted "No" to him in a 1988 referendum, with a cheerful rainbow ad campaign.

source.name: NPR, 'The U.S. set the stage for a coup in Chile' (2023)

source2.name: NPR, 'The Story Of No Is The Story Of Modern Chile' (2013)

title: The Sydney Opera House Opens
text: Danish architect Jørn Utzon won a design contest in 1957 with sail-like shells that engineers struggled for years to figure out how to build. He quit in 1966 after disputes and never returned to see it finished. Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973, ten years late and far over budget, and it is now a World Heritage Site.

source.name: Australian Government DCCEEW, National Heritage List: Sydney Opera House

source2.name: Dictionary of Sydney, 'Utzon's Opera House'

title: Meet Lucy
text: Paleoanthropologists in Ethiopia's Afar region found about 40 percent of the skeleton of a human relative who lived about 3.2 million years ago. That night the team played the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds," and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh, meaning "you are marvellous" in Amharic.

source.name: Arizona State University, Institute of Human Origins, 'About the Fossil Lucy'

source2.name: ASU News, 'Lucy at 50'

title: The Fall of Saigon
text: As North Vietnamese forces closed in, American helicopters lifted thousands of people from rooftops in the largest helicopter evacuation ever. On April 30 a tank crashed through the gates of the presidential palace, ending the Vietnam War. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City, and in the following years hundreds of thousands of "boat people" fled by sea.

source.name: US Naval History and Heritage Command, H-Gram 090

source2.name: US Naval History and Heritage Command, Marolda, 'By Sea, Air, and Land', ch. 5

title: The Soweto Uprising
text: Thousands of Black schoolchildren marched against a rule forcing them to be taught half their subjects in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and a photo of 12-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried by another student shocked the world. Protests spread across the country, and June 16 is now Youth Day in South Africa.

source.name: South African History Online, '16 June 1976 - Soweto Uprising'

source2.name: South African History Online, 'Hector Pieterson'

title: Eighteen Thumbprints in Xiaogang
text: Facing hunger, 18 farmers in a poor village secretly agreed to split the collective fields into family plots, sealing the deal with red thumbprints. It was risky, but their harvest soared. Under Deng Xiaoping's new Reform and Opening policy, the idea spread nationwide, and the original contract is now held by the National Museum of China.

source.name: NPR Planet Money, 'The Secret Document That Transformed China'

source2.name: Xinhua, 'Xiaogang Village: name fixed in China's memory as start of reform'

title: Khomeini Returns to Iran
text: After months of mass protests drove the Shah out, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini flew home from exile in France. Millions of people gathered in Tehran to welcome him. Within weeks the monarchy collapsed, and a referendum that spring turned Iran into an Islamic Republic, reshaping the politics of the whole region.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iran ii. Iranian History (2) Islamic period'

source2.name: The Conversation, 'World politics explainer: the Iranian Revolution'

title: Music on the Move
text: Sony released the Walkman, a pocket cassette player with light headphones, and suddenly people could carry their own soundtrack. Early models had two headphone sockets so friends or couples could listen together. Sony expected to sell about 5,000 a month but sold 50,000 by the end of that summer, and went on to sell hundreds of millions of Walkmans worldwide.

source.name: Smithsonian Music / National Museum of American History, Sony TPS-L2 'Walkman'

source2.name: IEEE Spectrum, 'Consumer Electronics Hall of Fame: Sony Walkman'

title: The Gwangju Uprising
text: When students in Gwangju protested against military rule, soldiers responded with brutal force, and citizens armed themselves and took control of the city. The army crushed the uprising on May 27, and estimates of the dead range from about 200 to 2,000. It played a pivotal role in Korea's democratization, and novelist Han Kang, born in Gwangju, wrote about it in Human Acts.

source.name: The Conversation, 'Three novels by Nobel winner Han Kang...'

source2.name: NobelPrize.org, Han Kang Facts

title: Finding the Virus Behind AIDS
text: At the Pasteur Institute, Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier identified the virus later named HIV, which causes AIDS. Knowing the cause made blood tests possible and, eventually, medicines that let people with HIV live long lives. The two were awarded the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Physiology or Medicine 2008 press release

source2.name: Europe PMC record: Barré-Sinoussi et al., Science 1983, 'Isolation of a T-lymphotropic retrovirus from a patient at risk for AIDS'

title: The Chernobyl Disaster
text: A safety test went wrong at the Chernobyl nuclear plant, and a reactor exploded, spreading radioactive material across Europe. The nearby town of Pripyat, home to about 49,000 people, was evacuated and still stands empty. With humans gone, the exclusion zone has become an accidental wildlife refuge for wolves, elk and rare Przewalski's horses.

source.name: National Geographic, 'Chernobyl disaster facts and information'

source2.name: The Conversation, 'Chernobyl has become a refuge for wildlife 33 years after the nuclear accident'

title: Saving the Ozone Layer
text: Two years after scientists reported a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica, countries signed the Montreal Protocol to phase out the chemicals causing it, such as those in old spray cans and fridges.
