Together with the Vienna Convention, it became the first environmental treaty ratified by every country in the world. The ozone layer is now slowly healing.

source.name: UNEP Ozone Secretariat, Ozone Timeline

source2.name: British Antarctic Survey, 'The ozone hole discovery'

title: The Soviet Flag Comes Down
text: Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on Christmas Day, and that evening the red Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time. The Soviet Union split into 15 independent countries, from Estonia to Kazakhstan. The Cold War rivalry that had shaped the world since 1945 was over.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'The Collapse of the Soviet Union'

title: Nollywood Is Born
text: Nigerian businessman Kenneth Nnebue teamed up with co-writer Okechukwu Ogunjiofor to make a thriller called Living in Bondage, shot on video and sold straight to VHS. It became a smash hit and launched Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry. Today Nollywood is one of the largest film industries in the world by number of films made, turning out more than 2,000 films a year.

source.name: The Conversation, 'From Nollywood to New Nollywood'

source2.name: UN News, 'Nigeria surpasses Hollywood as world's second largest film producer' (2009)

title: The Genocide Against the Tutsi
text: In about 100 days, extremists killed more than a million people, overwhelmingly Tutsi, along with Hutu who opposed the killing, while the world largely failed to act. Neighbours were turned against neighbours by radio propaganda. Each April Rwandans hold Kwibuka, meaning "remember," and the Kigali Genocide Memorial is the resting place of about 250,000 victims.

source.name: United Nations, Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda

source2.name: Kigali Genocide Memorial, About

title: The Kobe Earthquake
text: At 5:46 in the morning a powerful earthquake shook Kobe, toppling buildings and an elevated highway, and more than 6,000 people died. Over a million volunteers poured in from across Japan to help. The response was so big that 1995 is often called the "first year of volunteerism" in Japan.

source.name: Nippon.com, '25 Years after Disaster: Looking Back on the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake'

source2.name: Kobe University News, 'Passing down experiences from the earthquake'

title: Hello, Dolly
text: At the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, a lamb was born that was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Because that cell came from a mammary gland, scientists jokingly named her after country singer Dolly Parton. Dolly went on to have six lambs of her own, and she is now on display at the National Museum of Scotland.

source.name: National Museums Scotland, 'Dolly the sheep'

title: The Good Friday Agreement
text: After about 30 years of violence known as the Troubles, in which some 3,500 people died, Northern Ireland's main parties reached a peace deal on Good Friday. Voters on both sides of the Irish border approved it in referendums. It created a power-sharing government in which unionists and nationalists would rule together.

source.name: CAIN Archive, Ulster University: The Agreement (text)

source2.name: CAIN Archive, Ulster University: 1998 Referendum results

title: September 11 Attacks
text: Terrorists hijacked four airliners, crashing two into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon, while passengers fought back on the fourth. Nearly 3,000 people died. Today two huge memorial pools sit in the towers' footprints, with the victims' names carved around their edges.

source.name: National Park Service, Flight 93 National Memorial: September 11, 2001 Timeline

source2.name: National September 11 Memorial & Museum

title: The African Union Is Launched
text: African leaders met in Durban to launch the African Union, replacing the Organisation of African Unity founded in 1963. The new group aimed for deeper cooperation, with peacekeeping, a continental parliament and dreams of a single market. Its headquarters is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and today it has 55 member states covering the whole continent.

source.name: African Union: Overview

title: SARS Sweeps Out of Guangdong
text: A new coronavirus first appeared in Guangdong province in late 2002 and spread to dozens of countries in 2003. Italian WHO doctor Carlo Urbani spotted the outbreak in Vietnam and raised the alarm, then caught the disease and died. Around 8,000 people fell ill, and the lessons learned shaped how the world prepared for future pandemics.

source.name: CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases: Progress in Global Surveillance and Response Capacity 10 Years after SARS (2013)

source2.name: World Health Organization: WHO remembers Dr Carlo Urbani

title: The Indian Ocean Tsunami
text: One of the strongest earthquakes ever recorded struck off Sumatra, sending waves across the Indian Ocean that killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries. Aceh was hit hardest. On nearby Simeulue island, an old oral tradition called smong taught people to run uphill when the sea drew back, and almost everyone survived.

source.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program: Today in Earthquake History (Dec 26)

source2.name: Rahman et al. 2020, IJERPH (PMC7660313): Grandmothers' tsunami stories on Simeulue

title: The Beijing Olympics
text: The Beijing Games opened at 8 p.m. on 8/8/08, since eight is a lucky number in Chinese culture. The ceremony, featuring 2,008 drummers, was held in the "Bird's Nest" stadium, nicknamed for its twig-like lattice of huge steel beams. In 2022 Beijing became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

source.name: Olympics.com (IOC): Opening Ceremony - Beijing 2008

source2.name: Olympics.com (IOC): Beijing 2022

title: A Fruit Seller Sparks the Arab Spring
text: Mohamed Bouazizi, a young street vendor, set himself on fire after market inspectors confiscated his wares, and his desperate act set off nationwide protests. Within a month Tunisia's longtime president fled. Uprisings spread across the Arab world in what became known as the Arab Spring, and in 2015 a group of Tunisian organisations won the Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Peace Prize 2015 presentation speech

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Peace Prize 2015 press release

title: The Tōhoku Tsunami and Fukushima
text: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Japan's northeast coast sent a tsunami crashing ashore, leaving about 18,500 people dead or missing. The waves knocked out cooling at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, and three reactors overheated and melted their cores. Old stone markers along the coast, like one at Aneyoshi set up after a 1933 tsunami, had warned residents not to build homes below them.

source.name: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission: Backgrounder on NRC Response to Lessons Learned from Fukushima

source2.name: USC Dornsife: As collective memory fades... (Aneyoshi tsunami stone)

title: Gangnam Style Breaks the Internet
text: South Korean rapper Psy released a song poking fun at the flashy lifestyle of Seoul's wealthy Gangnam district, with a goofy invisible-horse-riding dance. In December 2012 it became the first video on YouTube to reach one billion views. It helped carry K-pop, Korea's pop music, to audiences around the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: PSY

source2.name: Guinness World Records: Gangnam Style first video viewed 1 billion times (20 Dec 2012)

title: The West African Ebola Epidemic
text: An Ebola outbreak that began in a village in southern Guinea spread into Liberia and Sierra Leone, becoming the largest ever recorded. More than 28,000 people were infected and over 11,000 died, including hundreds of health workers. Safe burials helped slow the spread, and a vaccine tested in Guinea during the epidemic gave substantial protection.

source.name: CDC: History of Ebola Disease Outbreaks

source2.name: CDC MMWR Suppl. 65(3): CDC's Response to the 2014-2016 Ebola Epidemic

title: The Paris Climate Agreement
text: Almost every country on Earth agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C. Small Pacific and Caribbean island nations, threatened by rising seas, pushed hard for the tougher goal with the slogan "1.5 to stay alive." Each country sets its own plan and is meant to raise its ambition every five years.

source.name: United Nations: The Paris Agreement

source2.name: Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School: Forging a Global Agreement on Climate Change

title: A Pandemic Shuts the World
text: A new coronavirus first identified in Wuhan in late 2019 spread across the globe, and the World Health Organization declared a pandemic in March 2020. Cities emptied, schools moved online and by April more than 3.9 billion people, half of humanity, were being asked to stay home. Scientists developed effective vaccines in under a year, far faster than ever before.

source.name: World Health Organization: WHO Timeline - COVID-19

source2.name: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance: How did scientists manage to develop safe COVID-19 vaccines in just ten months?

title: The Hunga Tonga Eruption
text: An undersea volcano in Tonga erupted with the largest atmospheric explosion ever recorded by modern instruments, blasting an ash column about 57 kilometres high, into the mesosphere. Its pressure wave circled the planet several times, and the boom was heard as far away as Alaska. The eruption cut Tonga's undersea internet cable, leaving the country almost cut off from the world.

source.name: University of Reading: Hunga Tonga volcano created biggest ever explosion

source2.name: NASA Aura mission: Evolution of an Underwater Volcano

title: Messi's World Cup Final
text: The first World Cup held in the Middle East, played in November and December to avoid the hot Qatari summer, ended with one of the greatest finals ever. Argentina and France drew 3–3, with Kylian Mbappé scoring a hat-trick. Argentina won on penalties, finally giving Lionel Messi the one trophy he had never won.

source.name: Olympics.com: Lionel Messi scores twice, Argentina beat France in 2022 World Cup final

source2.name: FIFA media release, 'One year to go, Qatar 2022: first FIFA World Cup in Middle East and Arab World'

title: Siberia's Lava Floods and the Great Dying
text: For roughly a million years, gigantic eruptions poured lava across Siberia, building the rocks now called the Siberian Traps. They are the main suspect for the end-Permian extinction about 252 million years ago, when more than 96 percent of sea species and 70 percent of land species vanished. The layered basalt still forms the canyon-cut Putorana Plateau.

source.name: MIT News (Burgess & Bowring, Science Advances 2015)

source2.name: IUCN World Heritage Outlook: Putorana Plateau

title: A Fuzzy Dinosaur From Siberia
text: Kulindadromeus, the 'Kulinda runner', lived in Siberia between 168 and 166 million years ago. Volcanic ash preserved it so well that scientists could see both scales and feather-like fuzz on its body. That was a big surprise, because it sits far from the bird branch of the dinosaur family tree, hinting that simple 'protofeathers' may have been common to many dinosaurs.

source.name: Cincotta et al. 2019, PeerJ 7:e6239 (Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences), 'The rise of feathered dinosaurs: Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus, the oldest dinosaur with feather-like structures'

title: Lake Baikal Begins to Open
text: Lake Baikal in south-east Siberia is the oldest lake in the world, about 25 million years old, and also the deepest, at about 1,700 metres. It holds around 20 percent of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth. Its great age and isolation have produced one of the richest and most unusual collections of freshwater animals anywhere.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Lake Baikal)

title: Toolmakers of Frozen Yakutia
text: In 1967 archaeologist Yuri Mochanov began digging a cave above Siberia's Dyuktai River and found stone tools, bone artifacts and stone beads left by Ice Age hunters. Their leaf-shaped stone points, carefully flaked on both sides, look strikingly like early tools in North America, so the Dyuktai finds are used as clues to how people moved between Asia and the Americas.

source.name: Gómez Coutouly 2016, Antiquity 90, 'Migrations and interactions in prehistoric Beringia: the evolution of Yakutian lithic technology'

source2.name: Science Advances 2018, 'Current evidence allows multiple models for the peopling of the Americas'

title: Sarazm, Where the Land Begins
text: Sarazm, whose name means 'where the land begins', is one of the oldest settlements in Central Asia, lived in from the 4th millennium BCE to the end of the 3rd. It grew up between mountain pastures and a wide valley suited to farming and irrigation. Its people traded across a huge area, from the Central Asian steppes to the Iranian Plateau and the Indus valley.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Steppe Migrants Reach the Altai
text: Around 3000 BCE, herders of the Afanasievo culture lived in the Altai Mountains and the Upper Yenisei region of southern Siberia. Their DNA links them to the Yamnaya people of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, far to the west, and their graves turn up as far as central Mongolia. They seem to have brought dairy herding to the eastern steppe.

source.name: Cell via PubMed Central (Jeong et al. 2020)

title: The Last Mammoths of Wrangel Island
text: Mammoths vanished from mainland Eurasia and North America around 10,000 years ago, but a small herd held on far out in the Arctic Ocean on Wrangel Island. Radiocarbon-dated bones show they survived until about 2000 BCE, several centuries after the Great Pyramid of Giza was built. Living cut off in small numbers, they built up genetic defects.

source.name: PLOS Genetics (Rogers & Slatkin 2017)

source2.name: Cell (Dehasque et al. 2024)

title: The Stone Faces of the Yenisei
text: Early Bronze Age people of the Okunev culture lived in the Minusinsk Basin of southern Siberia. On tall stone stelae, some found at their burial grounds, they carved mysterious masked faces, perhaps of a sun god, some with three eyes. New Okunev art is still being found, such as a mask-like face painted in red ochre on a rock in Khakassia.

source.name: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation, ARTEFACT museum guide: 'Stela depicting a schematic mask', Khakassia National Museum of Local History

source2.name: TASS, 'Unique 4,000-year-old rock art discovered in Siberia' (Okunev panel at Sorsk Pillars, Khakassia)

title: The Andronovo Herders
text: Across western Siberia and Kazakhstan, Bronze Age communities shared a way of life archaeologists call the Andronovo culture. They lived in earth huts, grew crops and raised cattle, sheep and horses, and decorated their flat-bottomed pots with geometric patterns. Scholars link them to the Indo-Iranian branch of peoples.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Queen Tomyris Defeats Cyrus the Great
text: Tomyris was queen of the Massagetae, nomads of the Central Asian steppe, and her story comes from the Greek historian Herodotus. He says she refused a marriage offer from Persia's Cyrus the Great, who then invaded, and that her army defeated and killed him, about 530 BCE. Other ancient writers told different versions of his death. Later painters such as Rubens loved to show her with Cyrus's head.

source.name: Fordham University Internet Ancient History Sourcebook (Herodotus, Histories I.201-214)

source2.name: Royal Collection Trust

title: The Ice Maiden's Deer Tattoos
text: In the 5th century BCE, a young woman of the Pazyryk culture was buried in a log chamber high on Siberia's Ukok Plateau, with six horses laid beside it. Ice formed inside the tomb and preserved her for about 2,400 years. When archaeologists opened it in 1993, her skin still showed animal-style tattoos of deer-like creatures on her shoulder, arm and thumb.

source.name: PBS NOVA, 'Ice Mummies: Siberian Ice Maiden' (transcript)

title: Roxana Marries Alexander
text: Roxana, a daughter of the Bactrian noble Oxyartes, was captured when Alexander the Great took a mountain fortress in Sogdiana, and in spring 327 BCE she married him in a full Macedonian ceremony. Plutarch says Alexander fell in love when he saw her dancing at a banquet, but adds that the match also suited his plans, winning goodwill among the peoples he had conquered.

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 47 (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius, University of Chicago)

source2.name: Arrian, Anabasis 4.19 (de Sélincourt trans.), via Livius.org

title: The Golden Man of Issyk
text: In a Saka burial mound about 50 km east of Almaty, a young person was laid to rest in a wooden chamber with an iron sword and dagger and more than 4,000 gold ornaments. Found in 1969, the dazzling outfit earned the nickname 'Golden Man'. Radiocarbon dating places the burial at about 400 to 300 BCE, and ancient DNA now suggests he was probably male, settling a long debate.

source.name: The British Academy (Hermann Parzinger, Albert Reckitt Archaeological Lecture 2016)

source2.name: The Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge ('Gold of the Great Steppe' exhibition labels)

title: A Greek City on the Oxus
text: Where the Amu Darya (the ancient Oxus) meets the Kokcha River, the Seleucid king Antiochus I founded a Greek city in the early 3rd century BCE. It reached its final form under the Greco-Bactrian king Eucratides, with a huge palace, a colossal gymnasium, and a mud-brick theatre as large as Babylon's. Locals call the ruins Ai-Khanoum, 'Lady Moon'.

source.name: American Journal of Archaeology 118.2 (2014), L. Martinez-Sève, 'The Spatial Organization of Ai Khanoum' (abstract)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ĀY ḴĀNOM' (P. Bernard)

title: The Xiongnu Tombs of Noin-Ula
text: In hills north of today's Ulaanbaatar lie the burial mounds of Xiongnu nobles; one held a Chinese lacquer cup dated 13 CE. A worker for a gold-mining company stumbled on them by chance in 1912. Inside were Chinese silks and lacquerware, felt carpets, and woollen textiles made as far away as Parthia, carried along the Silk Road.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Central Asian arts: Visual arts' (Mongolian Huns)

source2.name: Science First Hand (SB RAS), 'The Kurgan for the Moon-faced'

title: Kanishka's Stone, in Greek Letters
text: In 1993, a stone carved for the Kushan emperor Kanishka was found by chance at Rabatak in northern Afghanistan, written in the Bactrian language using Greek letters. Scholars in London, Nicholas Sims-Williams and Joe Cribb of the British Museum, realised it named four Kushan kings. The text may even boast that Kanishka swapped Greek for the local 'Aryan' language.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kushan Dynasty ii. Inscriptions of the Kushans'

source2.name: N. Sims-Williams (SOAS), 'New Light on Ancient Afghanistan: The Decipherment of Bactrian' (lecture, hosted by Univ. of Tokyo)

title: The Metalworkers Who Built an Empire
text: The Türks lived inside the empire of the Rouran, their overlords, and seem to have specialized in metalworking. In 552 their leader Bumin rebelled and, allied with the Wei dynasty of northern China, destroyed the Rouran. His Türk empire soon stretched from China's borders to Byzantium's, and the Türks were the first people known to have spoken a Turkic language.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (History of Central Asia: The Middle Ages)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Juan-juan'

title: The Painting of the Ambassadors
text: In the mid-600s, a grand Sogdian house in Samarkand had a room painted with scenes of the wider world: a Chinese lady in a boat, perhaps a princess or an empress, what many scholars read as a Nowruz procession, and Turkic soldiers guiding ambassadors from lands including China and Korea. The murals were found in 1965, when local officials pushed a road through the old city mound.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (M. Compareti, 'Afrasiab ii. Wall Paintings')

title: Turkic Words Carved in Stone
text: Two tall stone memorials in Mongolia's Orkhon Valley honour the Turkic brothers Bilge Qaghan and Kul Tigin. Raised in 732 and 735, they tell the Turks' history in the Old Turkic alphabet, the oldest surviving Turkic writing, with a separate text in Chinese on one side. Found in 1889, the mysterious script was cracked in 1893 by the Danish scholar Vilhelm Thomsen.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Orhon inscriptions)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape)

title: Bukhara's Brick-Lace Tomb
text: Built in the 10th century for the Samanid dynasty, this small tomb is one of the earliest known secular mausoleums in the Islamic world. Its baked bricks do two jobs at once, holding up the dome and forming woven-looking patterns, the first time Central Asian builders used brick so fully. It still stands, though the Mongols destroyed Bukhara in 1220.

source.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT), 'Ismoil Somoniy Maqbarasi'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Centre of Bukhara (via data.unesco.org)

title: The Teenage Court Doctor of Bukhara
text: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, grew up in Bukhara, the Samanid capital, and had memorised the entire Quran by age 10. At about 17 he entered the service of the Samanid ruler Nuh II as a physician. His later Canon of Medicine became a standard textbook at European universities, and some, like Padua and Salamanca, still required it in the 1700s.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Avicenna'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Avicenna ii. Biography' and 'xiii. Influence on medical studies in the West'

title: The Caravan That Unleashed the Mongols
text: In 1218 a Mongol trade caravan of around 450 men reached Otrar, a Silk Road oasis town near the Syr Darya. Its governor, Inalchuq, called them spies and had the whole caravan killed. When the Khwarazmian sultan then put to death an envoy Genghis Khan sent to complain, the Mongols invaded, besieging Otrar for nearly five months and destroying its citadel.

source.name: E-history.kz (official History of Kazakhstan portal)

title: The Silver Drinks Tree of Karakorum
text: The Mongol capital had a show-stopping centrepiece: a silver tree, designed by an enslaved Parisian goldsmith, that poured drinks for the khan's guests. The Flemish friar William of Rubruck saw it in 1254 and described a city with mosques, a church and a dozen temples. He sniffed that a French abbey was ten times grander than the palace.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington (William of Rubruck's account, trans. Rockhill)

title: The Last Wedding in Norse Greenland
text: In September 1408, Thorstein Olafsson and Sigrid Björnsdóttir married in the stone church at Hvalsey, Greenland. Letters about their wedding are the last written record of the Norse Greenlanders; after that, the colony fades from history. The couple settled in Iceland, and the roofless church still stands as the best-preserved Norse ruin in Greenland.

source.name: University of Houston, Engines of Our Ingenuity, Episode 2091 'Hvalsey Church'

source2.name: ABC News, 'Archaeologists Find Clues to Viking Mystery'

title: An 11-Year-Old King in Ferghana
text: Babur's father, ruler of the Ferghana Valley, died at the fort of Akhsi when his dovecote, pigeons and all, toppled into a ravine. In 1494 his 11-year-old son took the throne and at once faced invading armies led by his own uncles. Babur won and lost Samarkand, wandered for years, and later founded the Mughal Empire in India, telling it all in his Turkic memoir, the Baburnama.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Babur)

source2.name: Project Gutenberg: The Babur-nama in English, tr. A. S. Beveridge (1922)

title: Yermak Storms the Khanate of Sibir
text: Hired by the wealthy Stroganov merchant family, the Cossack leader Yermak set out in 1581 with about 840 men against the Tatar Khanate of Sibir. In 1582 his gun-armed men beat Khan Kuchum's larger army and took its capital, Qashliq, beginning Russia's conquest of Siberia, where fur traders and trappers soon followed. He later drowned, reportedly dragged down by chain mail sent by the tsar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Yermak Timofeyevich)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Siberia, History)

title: A Winter in 'The Saved House'
text: Hunting for a sea route to Asia across the Arctic, Willem Barentsz's ship got stuck in the ice off Novaya Zemlya in 1596. The 17-man crew built a lodge of driftwood and ship's timbers they called the Saved House, and lived through the winter on salted beef and fox meat. Barentsz died on the way home, but in 1871 a Norwegian seal hunter found the house.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Willem Barents)

source2.name: Arctic 48(3), 1995 (L. Hacquebord, 'In Search of Het Behouden Huys'), University of Calgary

title: Tigers on a Samarkand School
text: Between 1619 and 1636, the military commander Yalangtush Bahadur built the Sherdar Madrasa, an Islamic school, on Samarkand's Registan square opposite the older madrasa of Ulugh Beg. Its name refers to the bold tiger-lion mosaics on its façade, shown with a blazing sun. Covered in colourful tiles and painted plants, it is one of Samarkand's most famous sights.

source.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT): Shir Dar Madrasa

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Samarkand / Rigestan Square)

title: Siberia Mapped Upside Down
text: Working in Tobolsk around 1700, the architect Semyon Remezov drew three manuscript atlases of Siberia, one commissioned by Tsar Peter I in 1696. In the Muscovite mapping tradition, he built his maps around river systems with no coordinate grid, so south is often at the top. One historian estimates he drew some 80 percent of that century's surviving Siberian maps.

source.name: Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies, Harvard University: 'Siberia Through 17th-Century Eyes'

source2.name: Houghton Library, Harvard University: 'Early Maps of Siberia Digitized'

title: The Sea Cow Gone in 27 Years
text: Shipwrecked on Bering Island with Vitus Bering's expedition in 1741, naturalist Georg Steller described a giant cousin of the dugong, up to 10 metres long, that munched kelp and breathed with loud snorts. Unafraid of boats, it was hunted for its meat and fat, and within 27 years of its European discovery it was extinct.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: Steller's sea cow

source2.name: National Geographic, 'The 30-foot sea cow quickly hunted to extinction because of its tasty meat'

title: First Ship Across the Antarctic Circle
text: Just before noon on 17 January 1773, James Cook's Resolution became the first ship to sail south of the Antarctic Circle. Cook was hunting for Terra Australis, a rumoured giant southern continent. He later pushed to 71° South and swept across the Pacific, proving no such land lay in temperate waters, though he predicted land beyond the ice.

source.name: Captain Cook Society: The Second Voyage

source2.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: History of Antarctic explorers

title: A Mammoth With Its Skin Still On
text: In 1799 Ossip Shumachov, a Tungus chief, found a frozen woolly mammoth in Siberia's Lena River delta. In 1806 the botanist Mikhail Adams recovered its skeleton, much of its skin and more than one pood (about 40 pounds) of hair, writing that no scientist had yet examined a mammoth with its flesh and hair. In St Petersburg its substitute tusks were mounted on the wrong sides.

source.name: Linda Hall Library: Scientist of the Day, Mikhail Adams

source2.name: M. Adams, 'Some account of a journey to the Frozen Sea, and of the discovery of the remains of a mammoth', Philosophical Magazine 29 (1807), via Zenodo

title: Franklin's Ships Vanish in the Ice
text: In 1845 Sir John Franklin sailed from England with two ships and 129 men to chart the last gaps in the Northwest Passage. Both ships became trapped in ice near King William Island, and no one came home. Inuit accounts helped searchers piece together the tragedy, and the wrecks of Erebus and Terror were finally found in 2014 and 2016.

source.name: Parks Canada, Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror NHS, Franklin's 1845 expedition

source2.name: Parks Canada, Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror NHS, History

title: Russia Takes the Desert Khanate of Khiva
text: Khiva, an oasis city on the edge of the Qaraqum desert, had beaten Russia twice: in 1717 a Russian army was wiped out, and in 1839 a bitter winter killed most of the invaders' camels. In 1873, after expeditions had crossed the deserts to scout the way, Russian columns finally conquered the khanate, and its khan declared himself an "obedient servant" of the tsar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Central Asia vii. In the 18th-19th Centuries'

source2.name: Cambridge University Press, Morrison, The Russian Conquest of Central Asia, ch. 2 abstract

title: HMS Challenger Finds the Deepest Trench
text: On a four-year voyage that laid the foundations of oceanography, HMS Challenger's crew measured depth by lowering a weighted hemp line and timing each 25 fathoms as it ran out. On 23 March 1875, sailing north towards Japan, they discovered the Mariana Trench; its deepest spot is still called Challenger Deep. The expedition catalogued over 4,000 species new to science.

source.name: Cornell University Library, Challenging the Deep exhibit

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London

title: The Last Wild Horse Gets a Name
text: Explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky brought back specimens of a wild horse from Central Asia, and in 1881 zoologist Ivan Poliakov formally described it as a wild species. Called takhi in Mongolia, it has 66 chromosomes, two more than domestic horses. After the last wild one was seen in the Dzungarian Gobi in 1969, zoo-bred horses returned to Mongolia in 1992.

source.name: PMC: An Update on Status and Conservation of the Przewalski's Horse (Animals, 2022)

source2.name: Smithsonian's National Zoo, Przewalski's horse

title: Abai, Poet of the Kazakh Steppe
text: Before Abai Qunanbaiuly, most Kazakh poetry was spoken aloud rather than written down, and he is honoured as the founder of Kazakh written literature. Nicknamed 'Abai', meaning 'attentive' or 'cautious', by his grandmother, he translated Pushkin, Lermontov, Goethe and Byron into Kazakh. In his Book of Words he urged Kazakhs to educate their children.

source.name: Adebiportal.kz (Kazakh national literature portal, QazContent JSC), Kunanbaev Abay

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kazakh literature

title: Chekhov Visits the Prison Island
text: In 1890 the writer Anton Chekhov made a long, hard journey across Siberia by horse carriage and riverboat to reach Sakhalin, a prison colony north of Japan. Within three months he filled over ten thousand census cards, interviewing almost everyone there. He watched a convict receive ninety lashes, and his book Sakhalin Island, exposing brutal officials, added to pressure to reform Russia's prisons.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Anton Chekhov

source2.name: Hektoen International, Michael Bloor (Cardiff University), 'Anton Chekhov and the Sakhalin Penal Colony' (2017)

title: Starting the World's Longest Railway
text: On 19 May 1891, the future Tsar Nicholas II laid the cornerstone of the Trans-Siberian Railway in Vladivostok, on the Pacific coast. Tens of thousands of workers built its sections at the same time. Since 1916 it has run wholly through Russia from Moscow to Vladivostok: about 9,288 kilometres across eight time zones, still the longest railway line in the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Trans-Siberian Railroad

source2.name: Scientific Russia, To Connect Russia: History of the Trans-Siberian Railway

title: Nansen Lets the Ice Carry His Ship
text: Wreckage from a ship that sank off Siberia washed up years later near Greenland, giving Fridtjof Nansen a bold idea. In September 1893 he let his ship Fram freeze into the pack ice north of the New Siberian Islands and drift with the current. He then set off with dogs and sledges, reached a record 86°14′N, and later met a British explorer by chance.

source.name: Fram Museum (Oslo), The first Fram expedition 1893–1896

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Fridtjof Nansen

title: Endurance Sinks, and Is Found Again
text: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was trapped in Antarctic pack ice and finally sank in the Weddell Sea on 21 November 1915. Amazingly, the whole crew survived: they reached Elephant Island in lifeboats while Shackleton and five others sailed off for help. In March 2022 searchers found the wreck 3,008 metres down, in 'a brilliant state of preservation'.

source.name: Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust / Endurance22: Endurance is Found (press release, 9 March 2022)

source2.name: Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust: History of Shackleton's Endurance

title: The Asharshylyq, Kazakhstan's Great Famine
text: When Soviet leaders forced collectivization on Kazakhstan, herds were seized and nomadic families were pushed onto collective farms that did not suit the steppe. The result was the Asharshylyq, a man-made famine from 1930 to 1933 in which more than 1.5 million people died. Roughly a third of all Kazakhs perished, and over a million refugees fled the republic.

source.name: Harvard Davis Center, Remembering the Kazakh Famine (Sarah Cameron)

source2.name: Cornell University Press, The Hungry Steppe (Sarah Cameron)

title: The Soviet Bomb on the Kazakh Steppe
text: Early on the morning of 29 August 1949, the Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb, RDS-1, at the Semipalatinsk Test Site in Kazakhstan, with a yield of about 20 kilotons. A US B-29 weather plane caught its radioactive debris on 3 September, and President Truman announced the news. The shock pushed the United States toward the hydrogen bomb, speeding up the nuclear arms race.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nuclear weapon: The Soviet Union' (Thomas B. Cochran)

source2.name: OSTI (US DOE): Machta, 'Finding the site of the first Soviet nuclear test in 1949', Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc. 1992

title: Marie Tharp Finds a Crack in the Ocean
text: Barred from research ships because she was a woman, geologist Marie Tharp drew maps from depth soundings others collected. In 1952, lining up profiles across the North Atlantic, she spotted a V-shaped valley running down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Her colleague Bruce Heezen first dismissed it as 'girl talk', but her rift valley helped prove plate tectonics.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 'Soundings, Sea-Bottom, and Geophysics' (history quotes)

source2.name: Library of Congress blog, 'Marie Tharp: Mapping the Ocean Floor'

title: Down to the Bottom of Challenger Deep
text: On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the floor of Challenger Deep, the deepest point in Earth's seabed. Past 9,000 metres a loud crack shook the vessel: a viewing window had split. They spent twenty minutes on the bottom before a cloud of stirred-up sediment blocked their view.

source.name: Naval History and Heritage Command (US Navy), H-Gram 041-6: 'Trieste and the First Dive to Deepest Part of the Oceans, January 1960'

source2.name: Naval History and Heritage Command, H-Gram 041-6

title: The Vanishing Sea
text: The Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest body of inland water, takes its name from a Kyrgyz phrase meaning 'Sea of Islands': it held more than 1,000 islands. From the 1960s, Soviet irrigation projects diverted the rivers that fed it, and it began to shrink fast. In 2014 the eastern lobe of its southern part disappeared completely.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory, 'World of Change: Shrinking Aral Sea'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Aral Sea'

title: Surtsey, a Brand-New Island
text: On 14 November 1963, an undersea eruption broke the surface off southern Iceland and kept going until 1967, building an island named after Surtur, a fire giant of Norse myth. Declared a nature reserve while still erupting, Surtsey is a living laboratory, open only to scientists, who watch plants and animals arrive.

source.name: Surtsey Research Society (Surtseyjarfélagið)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Surtsey (read via data.unesco.org open-data API)

title: The Hole in the Sky Over Antarctica
text: At Halley station on Antarctica's Brunt Ice Shelf, British scientists had measured ozone since 1956. When springtime readings dropped sharply, Joe Farman at first suspected a faulty instrument, but a replacement gave the same results. After checking and rechecking, Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jon Shanklin published in May 1985, revealing that ozone over Antarctica was disappearing each spring because of man-made chemicals.

source.name: British Antarctic Survey, 'Marking 40 years since the discovery of the ozone hole'

source2.name: British Antarctic Survey, 'The ozone hole discovery'

title: The Ice That Remembers 420,000 Years
text: Vostok Station sits at Earth's 'Pole of Cold', where the world's coldest recorded temperature, −89.2°C, was measured in 1983. Russian and French scientists drilled deep into the ice sheet here, reaching a record 3,623 metres in 1998 but stopping short of Lake Vostok hidden beneath, for fear their drilling fluid could pollute it. Their ice core holds a climate record stretching back 420,000 years, through four earlier ice ages.

source.name: Nature, Stauffer, 'Cornucopia of ice core results' (1999)

source2.name: Nature, Petit et al., 'Climate and atmospheric history of the past 420,000 years from the Vostok ice core' (1999)

title: A Finger Bone Reveals Lost Humans
text: In 2008, archaeologists in Siberia's Denisova Cave dug up a finger bone from a young girl. In 2010 its DNA revealed a previously unknown group of ancient humans, now called Denisovans. They mixed with our own ancestors, and many Melanesians and Aboriginal Australians still carry their DNA. Another bone came from a child with a Denisovan father and Neanderthal mother.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: Denisovans

source2.name: American Journal of Human Genetics, Reich et al. 2011, 'Denisova admixture and the first modern human dispersals into Southeast Asia and Oceania'

title: Thailand's Puzzling Early Giant
text: Found in red sandstone in 1998, Isanosaurus was first hailed as one of the oldest sauropods, the long-necked plant-eaters. Newer dating makes it Early Jurassic and its family tree is still argued over. Its single thighbone is 76 cm long, and the animal was probably not even fully grown when it died.

source.name: Licht et al. 2026, Communications Earth & Environment (Nature Portfolio), 'A revised early Jurassic to Albian chronology for dinosaur evolution in tropical Asia'

source2.name: Buffetaut et al. 2000, Nature 407:72-74, 'The earliest known sauropod dinosaur' (abstract)

title: A Dinosaur Named for a Princess
text: Phuwiangosaurus was a long-necked sauropod that roamed northeastern Thailand in the Early Cretaceous. Its bones turned up in Phu Wiang in 1982, and its species name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, a royal fan of geology and fossils. One half-grown skeleton is about 60 percent complete, partial skull included.

source.name: Heliyon 2022, 'Geoeducational assessments in Khon Kaen National Geopark, Thailand' (Khon Kaen University authors)

source2.name: Licht et al. 2026, Communications Earth & Environment, revised Khorat Plateau dinosaur chronology

title: The Fish Hunter of Laos
text: Ichthyovenator was a spinosaurid, one of the sail-backed dinosaurs with long snouts built for catching fish. Described from Laos in 2012, it was the first definite spinosaurid found in Asia. Its fossils show something unusual: a wavy sail that dipped down over the hips, so it looked as if it had two sails instead of one.

source.name: Naturwissenschaften (Allain et al. 2012, "The first definitive Asian spinosaurid from the Early Cretaceous of Laos"), abstract

title: The Hòa Bình Pebble Toolmakers
text: As the Ice Age ended, hunter-gatherers across Southeast Asia made strikingly similar tools, often large river cobbles flaked on one side only. About a century ago, French archaeologist Madeleine Colani dug many rock shelters in the limestone hills of Hòa Bình. Ever since, this toolmaking tradition has been called the Hoabinhian, after the Vietnamese province where she worked.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Current World Archaeology / The Past (C. Higham)

title: Spirit Cave's Ice Age Foragers
place: Pang Mapha, Mae Hong Son, Thailand
text: High on a cliff in northwest Thailand, Spirit Cave was used by Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago. When Chester Gorman dug it in 1966, he argued its plant remains were the earliest evidence of possible cultivation in mainland Southeast Asia. A recent re-study of its animal bones, from bats to freshwater crabs, suggests people stayed there only now and then.

source.name: Asian Perspectives 55(1) 2016, Conrad, Higham, Eda & Marwick, reinvestigation of the Spirit Cave fauna (University of Hawai'i ScholarSpace, full text)

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine, 'Chester Gorman' (obituary)

title: A Sea Road of Green Jade
text: Farmers from Taiwan settled northern Luzon about 4,000 years ago, and green Taiwanese jade soon followed them across the sea. Over the centuries it reached Vietnam, Borneo, Thailand and beyond, one of the most extensive sea trade networks for a single stone in the prehistoric world. Workshops carved it into three-pointed lingling-o earrings and double-headed animal pendants.

source.name: PNAS (Hung et al. 2007, 'Ancient jades map 3,000 years of prehistoric exchange in Southeast Asia')

title: The Fishers and Pig-Keepers of Mán Bạc
text: At Mán Bạc, among limestone hills on the edge of the Red River Delta, archaeologists have excavated about a hundred burials from the time of Vietnam's Phùng Nguyên culture. The villagers fished, hunted and were just beginning to domesticate pigs, though no firm evidence of rice farming has been found. Today the site lies about 25 km from the coast.

source.name: ANU Press, Terra Australis 33: Matsumura & Oxenham, 'Introduction: Man Bac Biological Research Objectives'

source2.name: ANU Press: Man Bac: The Excavation of a Neolithic Site in Northern Vietnam

dateLabel: Perhaps as early as 1000 BCE (UNESCO: 500 BCE-500 CE)
title: The Plain of Giant Stone Jars
text: More than 2,100 stone jars, some up to 3 meters tall, are scattered across a plateau in Laos. Excavations, starting with Madeleine Colani, found human remains and beads, so the jars are tied to funerals. UNESCO dates the sites to 500 BCE-500 CE, though one study suggests some jars were set up centuries earlier. Unexploded bombs long kept archaeologists away.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: PLOS ONE (Shewan et al. 2021)

title: Sa Huỳnh's Two-Headed Earrings
text: Along Vietnam's central coast, Sa Huỳnh people buried their dead in large jars, often with rich offerings of beads and tools. They used both iron and bronze implements and wore jade ear pendants shaped like two-headed animals. Similar ornaments and pottery turn up in the Philippines and across Southeast Asia, showing that their trade networks reached far over the sea.

source.name: Nguyen Kim Dung, 'The Sa Huynh Culture in Ancient Regional Trade Networks', in New Perspectives in Southeast Asian and Pacific Prehistory (ANU Press, Terra Australis 45, 2017)

title: The Rings of Cổ Loa
text: Cổ Loa is ringed by three earthen ramparts; the outer one runs about 8 km, and the middle wall stands up to 10 meters high. Vietnamese chronicles say King An Dương Vương founded the Âu Lạc kingdom around 258 BCE and built Cổ Loa as his capital. Excavations suggest most of the middle rampart went up in the 3rd century BCE, on ground cleared in the 4th century BCE.

source.name: Kim, Lai Van Toi & Trinh Hoang Hiep 2010, 'Co Loa: an investigation of Vietnam's ancient capital', Antiquity 84 (full text, author copy)

source2.name: Antiquity / Cambridge Core abstract

title: Beikthano, Myanmar's Oldest City
text: Beikthano, whose name means 'City of Vishnu', is the earliest known Pyu city in Myanmar, and its brick buildings give the earliest dates for brick construction in all of Southeast Asia. Its outer walls enclosed about 900 hectares. The Pyu city-states flourished from about 200 BCE, linked by trade networks to Southeast Asia, China, and India.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Pyu Ancient Cities' (1444)

source2.name: J. Stargardt, 'From the Iron Age to early cities at Sri Ksetra and Beikthano, Myanmar', Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 47(3), 2016 (full text)

title: Iron Smelters of the Bujang Valley
text: At Sungai Batu, beneath Mount Jerai, archaeologists found jetties, iron-smelting sites and a clay-brick monument whose round base they date to about 110 CE. Its excavators call the site part of the oldest civilisation in Southeast Asia. The wider Bujang Valley holds over 50 ancient temples, making it Malaysia's richest archaeological area.

source.name: BenarNews (Radio Free Asia affiliate), 'Malaysia's Sungai Batu Among Oldest Southeast Asian Civilizations: Archaeologists' (2016)

source2.name: Malay Mail, 'Centuries-old temple ruins in Bujang Valley furtively destroyed' (2013)

title: A Valley Given to Shiva
text: King Bhadravarman of Champa set up a stone giving land in the Mỹ Sơn valley, between mountains and a great river, to Bhadreśvara, a form of Shiva. For about nine centuries Cham kings built temples there, and a French scholar later recorded nearly seventy monuments. Sadly, heavy US bombing in August 1969 caused great destruction.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'My Son Sanctuary'

source2.name: DHARMA project (ERC), Arlo Griffiths, edition of Mỹ Sơn stela C. 72

title: Borneo's Oldest Inscriptions
text: In eastern Borneo, King Mulavarman of Kutai left seven inscriptions on yūpa, stone sacrificial posts, written in Sanskrit in an early Pallava script. The short texts were set up to commemorate sacrifices the king held. Dated to the late 300s, these posts carry the oldest known inscriptions in the Indonesian archipelago.

source.name: ANU Press (Australian National University), 'The Earliest Indic State: Kutai'

title: Lý Bí Founds Vạn Xuân
text: Lý Bí led a revolt against the Chinese governor of Giao-chao, a province then ruled by China's Liang dynasty, and captured its capital at Long Biên in 542. In 544 he declared himself emperor of a new state, Vạn Xuân, in what is now northern Vietnam. Chinese forces defeated him in 547, but his brief kingdom became a proud memory of independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ly Nam De' (Ly Bon)

source2.name: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge), 'The Annan Protectorate in northern Vietnam during the Tang period (679-907)'

title: The Butuan Boats
text: Wooden plank boats found buried at Butuan since the 1970s are the oldest watercraft known in Philippine archaeology. At least nine have been reported, and they are often called balangay. Their builders joined planks edge to edge with wooden dowels and tied the ribs to carved lugs, a method shared across island Southeast Asia.

source.name: L. S. P. Lacsina, 'Traditional island Southeast Asian watercraft in Philippine archaeological sites' (Museum of Underwater Archaeology proceedings)

title: Prambanan, House of Shiva
text: An inscription of 856 marks what may be the founding of a great Shiva temple in Java, and says a river was diverted to fill a pool of purifying water for pilgrims. Prambanan's tall central tower stands among what were once 240 temples. Local people call it Lara Jonggrang, or 'Slender Maiden', after a statue of the goddess Durga inside.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Prambanan Temple Compounds (via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Prambanan' (rev. Virginia Gorlinski)

title: A Debt Cancelled on Copper
text: One of the oldest documents ever found in the Philippines is a receipt: a copper plate clearing the descendants of a man named Namwran of a debt in gold. Dated to the Saka year 822, or 900 CE, it is written mainly in Old Malay and names a place called Tundun. It was found in the Lumbang River in Laguna.

source.name: National Museum of the Philippines, '9th to 10th century archaeological evidence of maritime relations...' (2022)

source2.name: B. Villareal III, 'The Laguna Copper-Plate Inscription: A Local Language-game Validation', URSP Research Journal 8(1), 2022 (quotes Postma's translation)

title: Ananda, Bagan's Perfect Temple
text: King Kyansittha founded the Ananda Temple in Bagan around 1090, one of the largest and most imposing of the early Bagan temples. Legend says eight monks inspired it by describing their cave temple, Nandamula, which some place in the Himalayas. Glazed plaques showing the Buddha's past lives, some with Mon writing, taught religion to people in pictures.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Pagan article, via Ananda Temple page)

source2.name: Sahapedia (Ayan Ghosh)

title: The Stone That Speaks Thai
text: The Ram Khamhaeng Inscription has long been seen as the earliest example of Thai script, usually dated to 1292. Future king Mongkut found it in the 1830s while still a monk. In 1987 a historian compared it to the Piltdown hoax and asked if it was fake; later microscope tests suggest it really is old.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: SPAFA Journal (SEAMEO SPAFA): Chiraporn Aranyanak, 'The Scientific Investigation of the Inscription of King Ram Khamhaeng'

title: A Chinese Visitor's Angkor Diary
text: Yuan diplomat Zhou Daguan reached Angkor in 1296 and stayed about a year. His report, The Customs of Cambodia, is a key eyewitness account of daily Khmer life. He noted that all trading was done by women, and that hundreds of palace women carried candles in royal parades, even in daylight.

source.name: National Library of Australia, Digital Classroom: 'The way of life in the Khmer Empire'

source2.name: Yale University eHRAF World Cultures: Publication information, The Customs of Cambodia (Siam Society, 1987)

title: Gajah Mada's Palapa Oath
text: Gajah Mada, born a commoner, became chief minister of Majapahit after crushing a rebellion in 1331. Tradition says he swore the Palapa Oath: he would not enjoy palapa until he had conquered the whole archipelago for Majapahit. Under him Majapahit reached its peak, and today he is an Indonesian national hero.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gajah Mada' (Leo Suryadinata)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gajah Mada' (Leo Suryadinata)

title: A Kingdom Named for Ayodhya
text: The date 4 March 1351 is traditionally given as the founding of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, when Ramathibodi I became king of a state based on Ayutthaya, Lop Buri and Suphan Buri. Its full name, Dvaravati Sri Ayudhya, recalls the legendary city of Ayodhya. Sixteenth-century Portuguese and Spanish writers ranked Siam among the three greatest kingdoms of eastern Asia, with China and Vijayanagara.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ramathibodi I'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic City of Ayutthaya (read via data.unesco.org)

title: Land of a Million Elephants
text: In 1353 Fa Ngum, raised in exile at the Khmer court of Angkor, proclaimed himself king of Lan Xang, "a million elephants". His conquests covered nearly all of present-day Laos and much of northern and eastern Thailand, and the kingdom lasted until it split apart in the early 1700s. Lan Xang was the first unified state of the Lao people.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fa Ngum'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lan Xang'

title: A Mouse Deer Picks a Capital
text: Legend says Parameswara, a prince who had lost Singapura, was standing under a tree when a tiny mouse deer kicked one of his hunting dogs. Inspired, he founded his kingdom on the spot and named it after the tree, the melaka. Malacca grew into a great trading port, and Admiral Zheng He's Chinese fleet called there on its first voyage of 1405–07.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Melaka'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng He'

title: Lê Lợi and the Returned Sword
text: After ten years of guerrilla war, Lê Lợi drove Ming armies out of Vietnam and took the throne in 1428. Legend says his magic sword belonged to the Dragon King, and that after victory he gave it back through a giant turtle in a Hanoi lake. That lake is still called Hoàn Kiếm, the Lake of the Restored Sword.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Le Loi'

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Beloved Giant Turtle Dies, Leaving Only Three Alive on Earth' (2016)

title: Portugal Seizes Malacca
text: In 1511, Afonso de Albuquerque's Portuguese fleet captured Malacca, the port through which spices from the Spice Islands were distributed. Malay rule there ended, and the fugitive sultan and his son founded a new sultanate in Johor. Under the Portuguese, Malacca became the most important trading port in Southeast Asia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Afonso de Albuquerque)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Melaka)

title: Bayinnaung's Mega-Empire
text: Crowned king of Burma in 1551, Bayinnaung made Pegu (today's Bago) his capital and reigned for three decades. He conquered the Shan States, took Chiang Mai in Lan Na, briefly occupied the capitals of Lan Xang and twice captured Ayutthaya in Siam, making his realm the most powerful kingdom in mainland Southeast Asia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Bayinnaung)

source2.name: EBSCO Research Starters (Carl L. Bankston, 'Burmese-Laotian Wars', 2022)

title: Ternate Sends the Portuguese Packing
text: In 1570 the Portuguese assassinated Sultan Hairun of Ternate, a clove-rich island in Maluku, setting off an anticolonial revolt. His son, Sultan Babullah, kept up the fight until the people of Ternate took the Portuguese fort and drove the Portuguese off the island in 1575. Under Babullah, who ruled until 1583, Ternate's power spread across the archipelago.

source.name: Journal of Global History (Cambridge University Press): Stephanie Mawson, 'Malay magic on the colonial frontier', 2026 (citing L. Andaya, The World of Maluku)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ternate Island'

title: Spain Versus the Sultan of Brunei
text: In 1578 Spanish forces from newly conquered Manila attacked Brunei, a rich Muslim trading sultanate whose great sultan Bolkiah had once ruled practically all of Borneo and the Sulu islands. The Spanish briefly occupied Brunei and destroyed its famous mosque, but disease ravaged their troops and they were soon forced to abandon the conquest.

source.name: ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute Working Paper No. 3 (Barbara Watson Andaya, 'Islam and Christianity in Southeast Asia 1600-1700')

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (History of Brunei)

title: The Dutch Build Batavia
text: In 1619 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) built Batavia on the ruins of the town of Jayakarta, on Java's north coast. The canal-crossed port became the hub of the company's trading network across Asia. It stayed a European colonial city for about 320 years and is today's Jakarta.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Jakarta: History)

title: The Price of Nutmeg
text: Nutmeg and mace grew only on the tiny Banda Islands, and the Dutch wanted all of it. In 1621 Jan Pieterszoon Coen's forces conquered the islands. Of perhaps 13,000 to 15,000 Bandanese, only about 1,000 survived to be enslaved; many died of hunger after fleeing to the mountains, and the Dutch brought in enslaved workers from elsewhere to replace them.

source.name: Atlas of Mutual Heritage (Dutch National Archives / Cultural Heritage Agency): Great Banda

source2.name: JSTOR Daily (H.M.A. Leow, 'The Violent History Behind Nutmeg')

title: Vietnamese in the Latin Alphabet
text: Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes worked as a missionary in Tonkin, northern Vietnam, from 1627 to 1630. In 1651 he printed in Rome a Vietnamese-Portuguese-Latin dictionary, building on the work of earlier missionaries. It helped spread chữ Quốc ngữ, writing Vietnamese in Latin letters with tone marks, the script Vietnam uses today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alexandre de Rhodes'

source2.name: Bibliothèque nationale de France, France-Vietnam heritage: Romanisation

title: A Village Headman Founds Yangon
text: Alaungpaya was a village headman of humble origins when the Mon kingdom of Pegu captured Burma's capital in 1752. He organized resistance, founded the Konbaung dynasty and went on the offensive. In 1755, after a lightning campaign into Mon country, he founded a new port called Yangon at the site of the Mon fishing village of Dagon.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Alaungpaya

title: An Englishman Becomes Rajah
text: In 1841 the Sultan of Brunei granted land around Kuching to the English adventurer James Brooke, who took the title Rajah of Sarawak. His family, the "White Rajahs", ruled Sarawak as their own state for 105 years, steadily taking more land from Brunei. Their rule ended in 1946.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sarawak

title: The Novel That Shamed Coffee Profits
text: Max Havelaar, an 1860 novel by Multatuli (pen name of Eduard Douwes Dekker), shows an honest official battling corruption in Lebak, Java. It exposed how Dutch rules forced Javanese farmers to grow export crops like coffee. Its famous first line is spoken by a smug Amsterdam coffee broker.

source.name: DBNL, Lexicon van literaire werken (Eep Francken), 'Max Havelaar'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Max Havelaar'

title: Mouhot Didn't Discover Angkor
text: French naturalist Henri Mouhot reached Angkor in January 1860, and his travel journals made it famous in Europe. He is often said to have "discovered" it, but Buddhist monks had long cared for Angkor Wat as a pilgrimage site, and Spanish missionaries had described it by 1601. Mouhot died near Luang Prabang, Laos, the next year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Henri Mouhot'

source2.name: National Geographic History, 'Seeking the Hidden Temples of Cambodia'

title: Burma's Last King
text: Thibaw, who studied in a Buddhist monastery as a young prince, became the last king of Burma. In November 1885, in the Third Anglo-Burmese War, British forces invaded Upper Burma and captured his capital, Mandalay; Thibaw was deposed and sent into exile in India. The annexation of Upper Burma was announced on 1 January 1886.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Thibaw

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Anglo-Burmese Wars

title: Dubois Finds Java Man
text: Searching for human ancestors, Eugène Dubois found the top of an early human skull at Trinil, by the Solo River, in 1891; his team also dug up molars and a thighbone, finds he called "the missing link". Java Man is roughly 700,000 to 1 million years old. Trinil yielded the type specimen of the species now called Homo erectus.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins: Trinil 2

source2.name: PMC: The oldest gibbon fossil from insular Southeast Asia: evidence from Trinil (PLoS One, 2014)

title: French Gunboats at Paknam
text: On 13 July 1893, French warships forced their way past Siamese forts at Paknam, at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River. France won the clash and blockaded Siam's ports, and the peace deal handed France the lands east of the Mekong that now form most of Laos. Siam lost territory but kept its independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Thailand: Chulalongkorn and the foundations of modern Thailand

source2.name: US Office of the Historian, Foreign Relations of the United States 1893, doc. 537 (Boyd dispatch)

title: Kartini's School for Girls
text: Javanese noblewoman Kartini was kept in seclusion at home as a teenager, so she reached out to the world through letters to Dutch friends. In 1903 she and her sister Roekmini opened a school for upper-class girls with ten pupils, and after marrying the Regent of Rembang she kept teaching. Her letters were published in 1911, and her birthday is a national holiday in Indonesia.

source.name: Leiden University Libraries (KITLV): Kartini Letters

source2.name: Women in World History (Gale) via Encyclopedia.com: Kartini (1879-1904)

title: Siam's Bloodless Revolution
text: On 24 June 1932, a small group called the Khana Ratsadon, the People's Party, staged a coup in Bangkok. Without bloodshed it ended absolute monarchy in Siam. King Prajadhipok, the last absolute king, kept his throne but was forced to accept a constitution, making Siam a constitutional monarchy.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pridi Phanomyong

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Prajadhipok

title: Ho Chi Minh Declares Independence
text: On 2 September 1945, Ho Chi Minh read a declaration of independence to a crowd at Ba Đình Square, founding the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Emperor Bảo Đại had abdicated a week before. Surprisingly, the text quoted the American Declaration of Independence and France's Rights of Man, partly to win Allied support.

source.name: Fordham University Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Vietnamese Declaration of Independence (1945)

source2.name: Library of Congress Federal Research Division, Vietnam: A Country Study (countrystudies.us mirror)

title: Burma Becomes Independent
text: On 4 January 1948, Burma became independent under a treaty in which Britain recognised it as a fully independent sovereign state, ending British rule over the whole country that began with the annexation of Upper Burma in 1886. Thakin Nu, later known as U Nu, signed the treaty as Burma's prime minister. The date is still Myanmar's Independence Day.

source.name: United Nations Treaty Series vol. 70, No. 904: Treaty between the UK and Burma (1947)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Anglo-Burmese Wars

title: The Deep Skull of Niah Cave
text: In a trial trench nicknamed "Hell" in the West Mouth of Niah's Great Cave, Tom and Barbara Harrisson's team uncovered a human skull in 1958. Later studies dated it to about 37,000 years ago. Researchers now think it belonged to an older woman, not a teenage boy as first proposed, and that she was most like today's Indigenous peoples of Borneo.

source.name: Curnoe et al. 2016, 'Deep Skull from Niah Cave and the Pleistocene Peopling of Southeast Asia', Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

source2.name: Curnoe et al. 2018, PLoS One (PMC5991356)

title: Five Neighbors Form ASEAN
text: On 8 August 1967, ministers from Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed the Bangkok Declaration, creating ASEAN. It came right after the tense Konfrontasi conflict between neighbors. Its informal style of making decisions by consensus still guides the group, and 8 August is celebrated as ASEAN Day.

source.name: ASEAN Secretariat, 'The Founding of ASEAN'

source2.name: Royal Thai Embassy, Washington D.C., 'Thailand and ASEAN'

title: The Petronas Twin Towers
text: From 1998 to 2004, Kuala Lumpur's 88-story Petronas Towers were the tallest buildings in the world, at 451.9 meters. Architect César Pelli drew the floor plan from the Rub el Hizb, an eight-pointed Islamic star. They remain the tallest twin skyscrapers on Earth.

source.name: CTBUH Skyscraper Center: Petronas Twin Tower 1

source2.name: PETRONAS Twin Towers official website: Design + Structure

title: Timor-Leste Is Born
text: During Indonesia's invasion and occupation, a UN-backed truth commission estimated that between 106,000 and 180,000 Timorese died from massacre, starvation and disease from 1975 to 1983. After 24 years of occupation, East Timorese voted in 1999, with more than 78 percent choosing independence. Militia violence followed, so UN-backed peacekeepers stepped in and the UN oversaw the transition. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste became independent.

source.name: National Security Archive, George Washington University: U.S. sought to preserve close ties to Indonesian military... (2019)

source2.name: United Nations Peacekeeping: East Timor - UNTAET

title: The Hobbit of Flores
text: In 2003, in Liang Bua cave, scientists found the skeleton of a grown human relative standing only about 1.1 meters tall. Nicknamed the "Hobbit", Homo floresiensis lived on Flores until about 50,000 years ago. Its small size is thought to come from island dwarfism, where animals shrink over generations on islands.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program

title: The Wild Boars Cave Rescue
place: Tham Luang Cave, Chiang Rai, Thailand
text: Twelve boys from the Wild Boars junior football team and their 25-year-old assistant coach went exploring a cave in northern Thailand when monsoon floods trapped them. Found alive after nine days, all 13 were brought out by divers between 8 and 10 July 2018. Saman Kunan, a former Thai military diver who volunteered to help, died during the rescue.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Thai cave rescue ends after last four boys and coach are saved (11 July 2018)

title: A Supercontinent Named for Indian Forests
text: Long ago, India was joined to Africa, Antarctica, Australia and South America in one giant southern landmass, where Glossopteris plants grew widely. In 1885 the geologist Eduard Suess named it Gondwana-Land. He borrowed a name that Henry Medlicott had given in 1872 to rocks of a region in central India; in Sanskrit it means 'forested land of the Gonds'.

source.name: Geological Magazine (Cambridge University Press)

source2.name: Freie Universität Berlin, Geosciences

title: The Big-Legged Lizard
text: Barapasaurus was an early long-necked dinosaur, about 14 meters long, that lived in India in the Early Jurassic. Its name means 'big leg lizard'. It was named in 1975 by the Indian scientists Jain, Kutty, Roy-Chowdhury and Chatterjee.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory)

title: The Snake in the Dinosaur Nest
text: In Gujarat, scientists found a fossil snake about 3.5 meters long, coiled around a dinosaur egg beside a crushed sauropod hatchling only 50 centimeters long. They named it Sanajeh, Sanskrit for 'ancient gape'. The scene suggests this snake raided dinosaur nesting grounds for baby giants, a dinner frozen in stone.

source.name: PLoS Biology (Wilson et al. 2010, "Predation upon hatchling dinosaurs by a new snake from the Late Cretaceous of India")

title: India Crashes Into Asia
text: After racing north at 18 to 20 centimeters a year, unusually fast for a tectonic plate, India collided with Asia roughly 50 million years ago and slowed to about 5 centimeters a year. The slow-motion crash closed the old Tethys Sea and pushed up the Himalayas. According to the USGS, the range is still rising by more than a centimeter a year.

source.name: Nature (Kumar et al. 2007, "The rapid drift of the Indian tectonic plate"), abstract

source2.name: U.S. Geological Survey (This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas)

title: An Ancient Ape by the Tinau River
text: In 1983 scientists reported a fossil ape found at Tinau Khola, the Tinau River, in the Siwalik foothills of south-western Nepal. It is about 9 to 9.5 million years old. It resembles small apes of the same age from Pakistan and India, and it helped fill a gap on the map between ape fossils from north-western India and southern China.

source.name: Munthe et al. 1983, Nature 303:331-333

source2.name: Nature abstract, Munthe et al. 1983 (read in browser)

title: Foundations in a Rainforest Cave
text: Inside Belilena Cave in Sri Lanka's rainforest, archaeologists found the rubble base of a wall about 15,000 years old, one of only two structures known from prehistoric Sri Lanka. People here ate giant squirrels, tree snails and wild breadfruit. A tiny lagoon snail in layers about 21,000 years old suggests salt was traded from the coast over 80 kilometers away.

source.name: S. U. Deraniyagala, 'The Prehistory and Protohistory of Sri Lanka' (Central Cultural Fund, 2007; digitized by archaeology.lk)

title: Paintings Under Bhimbetka's Rocks
text: In the forested foothills of central India's Vindhya Range, about 700 natural rock shelters hold one of India's largest collections of prehistoric art. The oldest paintings, large outlines of rhinoceroses and bears, date to the late Old Stone Age. Later artists added smaller scenes of animals and people, and painting carried on right into historical times.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The World's Oldest Ploughed Field
text: Outside the town wall of early Kalibangan, archaeologists uncovered a ploughed field, often called the earliest known in the world. Its furrows cross in a grid, closely spaced one way and widely spaced the other. Farmers nearby still plough like this to grow two crops in one field, a pulse in one direction and mustard in the other.

source.name: Harappa.com, quoting excavator B.K. Thapar (South Asian Archaeology, 1973)

source2.name: Journal of World Prehistory (2017), C. A. Petrie & J. Bates, ''Multi-cropping', Intercropping and Adaptation to Variable Environments in Indus South Asia' (PMC full text)

title: Dholavira's Giant Signboard
text: Near the north gate of the Indus city of Dholavira lay ten big symbols made of gypsum pieces, each about 37 centimeters tall. They were once set on a wooden board some 3 meters long that fell face-down; the wood rotted but the letters stayed in place. It is one of the longest Indus inscriptions known, and nobody can read it.

source.name: Harappa.com (J. M. Kenoyer & R. H. Meadow's Indus research site), 'Dholavira and Its Mysterious Sign Board' (citing Bisht 1998-99 and Frontline 2010)

title: Sixteen Great Realms and a Republic
text: Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen 'great realms', the Mahajanapadas, including Gandhara in the northwest and Anga in the east. Some, such as Magadha and Kosala, were ruled by kings, but others had no monarch. The best known was the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, a league of eight or nine clans with its headquarters at Vaishali, which flourished in the time of the Buddha and Mahavira.

source.name: INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (University Grants Commission, India)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vaishali'

title: Ashoka Marks the Buddha's Birthplace
text: Twenty years after he was crowned, Emperor Ashoka came to Lumbini and set up a stone pillar saying the Buddha was born here. He even cut the village's taxes to one-eighth of its harvest. Later forgotten, the pillar was rediscovered in 1896, and its inscription helped pin down the birthplace.

source.name: National Geographic History

source2.name: Lumbini Development Trust (Government of Nepal)

title: A Monk Meets a King on the Mountain
text: Sri Lankan chronicles say Mahinda, a monk and son of Emperor Ashoka, arrived on a June full moon and met King Devanampiya Tissa on the hill of Mihintale. His preaching brought Buddhism to the island. Every year on Poson, the June full moon, crowds of pilgrims still climb Mihintale's long stone stairways to remember the meeting.

source.name: H.R. Perera, 'Buddhism in Sri Lanka: A Short History' (Buddhist Publication Society, Kandy), hosted by Access to Insight

source2.name: The Sunday Times (Sri Lanka)

title: Taxila, a City of Teachers
text: Old Buddhist stories, the Jatakas, describe Taxila as a great centre of learning, where students studied the Vedas and many arts, from archery to medicine and surgery. It was not a university with lecture halls, but a city where teachers housed their own pupils. The royal adviser Chanakya studied there, and the city was later ruled by the Mauryas and then the Indo-Greeks.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Taxila' (Baij Nath Puri / Editors)

source2.name: G.P. Malalasekera, Dictionary of Pali Proper Names, 'Takkasilā' (hosted at palikanon.com)

title: A King's Life Carved in the Elephant Cave
text: In a cave called Hathigumpha, 'elephant cave', near Bhubaneswar, King Kharavela of Kalinga had seventeen lines carved telling his life story. They describe his military campaigns and public works, including extending a canal dug long before by a Nanda king. Though Kharavela followed Jainism, he called himself a worshipper of every religious sect.

source.name: B.M. Barua, Old Brahmi Inscriptions (University of Calcutta, 1929), 'Inscription of Kharavela in the Hathigumpha' (hosted at wisdomlib.org)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'India' (Kalinga section, via 'Khāravela' entry)

title: Sushruta's Book of Surgery
text: The Sushruta Samhita, a Sanskrit medical book built up by many authors over centuries, describes surgery in amazing detail. It explains how to rebuild a cut-off nose using a flap of skin from the cheek. It also lists over a thousand illnesses and tells students to practice cutting on gourds and dead animals.

source.name: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open (2024), 'Sushruta: The Father of Indian Surgical History'

source2.name: The Wire, Kiran Kumbhar (historian, Univ. of Pennsylvania), 'The History of Sushruta and the Famous Indian Nose Job'

title: Tamil Poems of Love and War
text: The Sangam poems are the oldest Tamil literature, traditionally said to come from literary academies in Madurai. Gathered into eight anthologies and a set of ten longer idylls, they sing of akam, love and inner feelings, and puram, heroism and the praise of kings. Their fresh, vivid style keeps them treasured classics.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sangam literature'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sangam literature'

title: Kalidasa Sends a Message by Cloud
text: Kalidasa is often called ancient India's greatest poet and playwright, probably writing in the Gupta era. His play Shakuntala is still performed today. In his poem Meghaduta, a lonely spirit asks a passing rain cloud to carry a message to his beloved, and even tells it not to skip the city of Ujjain.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kalidasa'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Meghaduta'

title: Chaturanga, Grandparent of Chess
text: The first certain mention of chaturanga comes from India in the 500s. Its name means 'having four members', for the four divisions of an army: elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers. Played on an 8-by-8 board, it spread west through Persia and became chess, which is why the bishop's Persian and Arabic name, pil or fil, means 'elephant'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chess: History'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Chess'

title: The Temples of Khajuraho
text: Kings of the Chandela dynasty built Khajuraho's temples between about 950 and 1050 CE. There were once about 85, but only around two dozen survive. Their soaring Nagara-style towers and richly carved walls are crowded with sculptures, a few of them famously erotic. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Khajuraho'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Khajuraho Group of Monuments (via data.unesco.org)

title: The Chola Navy Sails to Srivijaya
text: In 1025 the navy of the Chola emperor Rajendra I crossed the Bay of Bengal to raid Srivijaya, the sea power controlling the Strait of Malacca. The Cholas seized its capital, Palembang, captured its king and carried off his treasure; a Chola inscription at Thanjavur boasts of the city's 'golden gates'. Srivijaya never regained its old prosperity.

source.name: Kenneth R. Hall, Maritime Trade and State Development in Early Southeast Asia (University of Hawai'i Press, 1985), chs. 4 and 8 (open access on UH Press Manifold)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Srivijaya empire'

title: The Sea of King Parakramabahu
text: Under King Parakramabahu I, an older reservoir from the 300s was enlarged with new sections into a giant artificial lake called Parakrama Samudra, the 'Sea of Parakrama'. It covers about 22 square kilometers, and its water still irrigates rice fields today. It is linked to a famous motto: let not one drop of rain reach the sea without being useful to people.

source.name: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

source2.name: International Lake Environment Committee Foundation (ILEC), World Lake Database: Parakrama Samudra

title: A Stone Chariot for the Sun
text: King Narasimha Deva I built the Konark Sun Temple around 1250 as a giant stone chariot for the sun god Surya. It has 24 carved wheels, each about 3 meters across, once pulled by seven stone horses, with carvings that refer to the seasons and months. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda and used it as a landmark along a coast known for shipwrecks.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: Ibn Battuta, Judge of the Maldives
text: After a shipwreck off India wrecked his mission to China, the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta went to the Maldive Islands. Their rulers wanted a chief judge who knew Arabic and Islamic law, so they sent him gifts and made it hard to leave. He served as qadi, married into the ruling family and grew so involved in politics that he left for Sri Lanka.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibn Battuta'

source2.name: ORIAS, UC Berkeley, 'The Travels of Ibn Battuta: Escape from Delhi to the Maldive Islands and Sri Lanka: 1341-1344'

title: Madhava Adds Up Forever
text: In Kerala, the astronomer Madhava of Sangamagrama found ways to write pi and sine as infinite series, sums that go on forever but home in on an exact value. That was centuries before similar results appeared in Europe. His work inspired a Kerala school of followers, such as Nilakantha and Jyesthadeva, who carried his ideas forward for generations.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, 'Madhava of Sangamagramma'

source2.name: MacTutor, University of St Andrews, 'An overview of Indian mathematics'

title: Kabir, the Weaver Poet
text: Legend says baby Kabir was abandoned and then found and raised by a Muslim weaver in Varanasi. He grew up to compose sharp, simple couplets called dohe that attacked the empty rituals of Hindu and Muslim authorities alike. His songs entered the Sikh scripture, and many of his couplets are still commonly quoted by speakers of North Indian languages.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kabir'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Adi Granth'

title: Guru Nanak at Kartarpur
text: After vanishing while bathing in a river and reappearing days later, young Nanak returned saying, 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.' Years of travel later, he settled in the village of Kartarpur, where the first Sikh community grew around him, singing his hymns together. Sikhs still keep langar, a free communal kitchen where anyone may eat regardless of religion, caste or gender.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Guru Nanak)

title: Mirabai, the Princess Who Sang
text: Born into a Rajput royal family, Mirabai married the crown prince of Mewar in 1516, but her heart belonged to the god Krishna. Legends say her in-laws tried to poison her for her devotion and she survived. A huge number of hymns are credited to her, though scholars have traced only six to manuscripts from before 1700.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Mira Bai)

source2.name: N. Melnikova, 'Mīrābāī—a Saint or a Rebel?', Cracow Indological Studies 20(2), 2018

title: The Holy Book Comes to Amritsar
text: Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, finished compiling the first Sikh scripture, the Adi Granth, and placed it in the temple at Amritsar in 1604.
