The temple has four entrances, a sign that people from all backgrounds are welcome. Today its free kitchen serves vegetarian meals to every visitor, whoever they are.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Golden Temple)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Adi Granth)

title: A Fortress Where Two Rivers Meet
text: Ngawang Namgyal, the first leader to unite Bhutan, began Punakha Dzong in 1637, and the fortress-monastery was completed in 1639. It stands where the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers flow together and became the capital of his new state. Every king of Bhutan is crowned there, receiving sacred scarves from the stupa holding Ngawang Namgyal's remains.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre Tentative List (Dzongs: the centre of temporal and religious authorities)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Punakha)

title: The Dome That Echoes Back
text: Sultan Mohammad Adil Shah of Bijapur built himself a huge tomb whose dome, 44 meters across, was the largest unsupported dome in India. Work began late in his reign, and after his death in 1656 it was never completed as first intended. In its whispering gallery the faintest whisper carries across the dome, and a single sound can echo about 10 to 11 times.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Islamic Art of the Deccan'

source2.name: Archnet, Gol Gumbaz

title: Cloth Too Popular for England
text: Calico, a cotton cloth named after the port of Calicut, today's Kozhikode, became wildly fashionable in England once cheap Indian cottons arrived in bulk. To protect English manufacturers, Parliament passed the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721, the second forbidding calico for clothing and home use. Repeal came in 1774, just as new machines let British cotton makers compete.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Western colonialism: The English'

source2.name: Abigail L. Swingen, 'Calico Madams and South Sea Cheats', Journal of British Studies 63:1 (2024), Cambridge University Press

title: Giant Stone Instruments in Delhi
text: Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur loved astronomy, so he built five observatories across India. The one in Delhi was completed around 1724. Its instruments are giant masonry structures, like the Samrat Yantra, a sundial about 70 feet tall. He built them because he found existing instruments too small to take correct measurements of the sky.

source.name: Delhi Tourism (Government of NCT of Delhi): Jantar Mantar

source2.name: NASA Sun-Earth Day 2005: Jantar Mantar

title: Gorkha Takes the Kathmandu Valley
text: King Prithvi Narayan Shah of little Gorkha spent decades conquering neighboring hill principalities. The Malla kings of Nepal Valley, now called the Kathmandu Valley, were weakened by family quarrels and no match for him. He conquered the valley in 1769, then moved his capital to Kathmandu, laying the foundation for the modern state of Nepal.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Prithvi Narayan Shah

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nepal: History'

title: Measuring India, One Triangle at a Time
text: On April 10, 1802, William Lambton laid out a baseline near Madras, starting the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. Teams hauled huge theodolites across the land, mapping it in chains of triangles for decades. By 1852 the survey had shown that Peak XV, later called Everest, was the highest mountain on Earth, using calculations by Radhanath Sikdar, a Calcutta-born mathematician whose job title was 'computer'.

source.name: Royal Society blog, 'Mapping India' (2023)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mount Everest

title: A Railway Built on Harappa
text: By 1873, when Alexander Cunningham dug at Harappa, railway contractors had already carted away bricks from its ancient mounds as ballast for the Lahore and Multan Railway. He estimated the ruins supplied enough for about 100 miles of track. Nobody yet knew these bricks were around 4,500 years old, made by a forgotten Indus civilization.

source.name: Harappa.com (J.M. Kenoyer, R. Meadow), Cunningham's 1853-1873 report

source2.name: Harappa.com (Kenoyer & Meadow), Cunningham's 1872-73 ASI report

title: The Rani of Jhansi's Last Stand
text: When her husband died, the British refused to accept the boy he had adopted as heir and took over Jhansi. During the 1857 uprising, Rani Lakshmibai became one of the rebellion's leaders. After British troops stormed Jhansi, she escaped (legend says by leaping from the fort on horseback), fought on, and died in battle near Gwalior in June 1858.

source.name: National Army Museum, 'Decisive events of the Indian Rebellion'

source2.name: National Army Museum, 'Why did the Indian Rebellion happen?'

title: Sri Lanka's First Tea Garden
text: Scottish planter James Taylor planted tea on just 19 acres of the Loolecondera estate near Kandy in 1867, copying the way Assam planters in India processed the leaves. Two years later, a fungus called coffee rust began ruining the island's coffee farms, and planters rushed to tea instead. By 1899 nearly 400,000 acres of Ceylon were under tea.

source.name: Sri Lanka Tea Board, 'Story of Ceylon Tea'

source2.name: Molecular Plant Pathology (2017), Talhinhas et al., 'The coffee leaf rust pathogen Hemileia vastatrix', PMC6638270

title: 'Sisters and Brothers of America'
text: A young Indian monk named Swami Vivekananda traveled to Chicago for the Parliament of the World's Religions. He opened his speech to a crowd of nearly seven thousand with 'Sisters and brothers of America!' and later wrote that two minutes of deafening applause followed. His talks helped introduce Hindu philosophy and yoga to many Westerners.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, September 11, 1893

source2.name: CBS Chicago, Exhibit of Sept. 11, 1893, speech on tolerance returns to Art Institute of Chicago

title: India's First Feature Film
text: Dadasaheb Phalke decided to make movies after watching a silent film about the life of Christ. His silent film Raja Harishchandra, generally regarded as India's first full-length feature, opened to the public in May 1913, with intertitles in English and Hindi. Women shunned film acting then, so a young male actor played the queen.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dadasaheb Phalke

source2.name: Screening the Past (La Trobe University journal): P.K. Nair, 'In the Age of Silence - Beginnings of Cinema in India'

title: A Clerk's Letter Full of Formulas
text: Srinivasa Ramanujan, a clerk at the Madras Port Trust, wrote to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy on 16 January 1913, enclosing a long list of unproved theorems. At first some at Cambridge wondered whether it was a hoax, but Hardy decided the formulas could only come from 'a mathematician of the highest class'. Ramanujan also left notebooks filled with theorems.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Srinivasa Ramanujan

source2.name: Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai: E. H. Neville, 'From obscurity to fame' (Ramanujan memoir)

title: Light Changes Color: The Raman Effect
text: Wondering why the Mediterranean looked so blue on a sea voyage, C. V. Raman began studying how light scatters. In Calcutta on February 28, 1928, he and his colleagues confirmed that a little scattered light changes its wavelength. The discovery won Raman the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and India now celebrates February 28 as National Science Day.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, C. V. Raman Biographical

source2.name: NobelPrize.org, Raman Nobel Lecture (1930)

title: Dying for the Bengali Language
text: Pakistan's government wanted Urdu as the only national language, though most people in East Bengal spoke Bengali. On February 21, 1952, students at Dhaka University defied a ban and marched, and police shot dead several protesters. Bengali won official status in 1956, and UNESCO now marks February 21 as International Mother Language Day.

source.name: Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh), 'Language Movement'

title: The World's First Woman Prime Minister
text: After her husband, Ceylon's prime minister, was assassinated in 1959, Sirimavo Bandaranaike was persuaded to lead his party. Some newspapers called her the 'Weeping Widow' because she wept at rallies, but she won the July 1960 election and became the first woman in the world democratically elected prime minister. She went on to serve three terms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sirimavo Bandaranaike'

source2.name: Daily Mirror (Sri Lanka), D.B.S. Jeyaraj, 'The Weeping Widow who Became the World's First Woman Prime Minister' (2025)

title: India's First Satellite
text: Built by ISRO, India's space agency, the satellite Aryabhata was launched on April 19, 1975, aboard a Soviet rocket. It was named after the great ancient astronomer. A power failure ended its experiments after just four days, but India had joined the space age, and the satellite appeared on two-rupee notes for over twenty years.

source.name: U R Rao Satellite Centre (ISRO), 'Aryabhata'

source2.name: NASA HEASARC, 'The Aryabhata satellite'

title: The Bhopal Gas Disaster
text: Overnight on December 2–3, 1984, toxic methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant run by Union Carbide India in Bhopal. Nearly half a million people were exposed as the cloud drifted over sleeping neighborhoods. Thousands died, and it is often called the world's worst industrial disaster. Its harm to survivors’ health lasted for decades.

source.name: NPR Goats and Soda, 'The world's worst industrial disaster harmed people even before they were born' (2023)

source2.name: PMC, 'Mental health of survivors of 1984 Bhopal disaster' (Indian J Psychiatry)

title: Sri Lanka Wins the World Cup in Lahore
text: In the 1996 Cricket World Cup final, played under floodlights at Lahore's Gaddafi Stadium, Sri Lanka faced mighty Australia. Chasing 242, Aravinda de Silva smashed 107 not out, and Sri Lanka won by seven wickets with 22 balls to spare. It was a giant moment for a small island nation and for cricket across South Asia.

source.name: ESPNcricinfo, full scorecard, Wills World Cup Final 1996

title: The Gorkha Earthquake
text: Just before noon on April 25, 2015, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck northwest of Kathmandu, killing about 9,000 people. It wrecked buildings across the Kathmandu Valley, including parts of the famous Taleju Temple, and brought down the entire nine-story Dharahara tower. It also set off an avalanche that killed around 20 people at Everest Base Camp, the deadliest day ever on the mountain.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nepal earthquake of 2015

source2.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program: Today in Earthquake History (Apr 25)

title: The Biggest Crowd on Earth
text: The Kumbh Mela is a Hindu pilgrimage held in a roughly 12-year cycle linked to the orbit of Jupiter. At Prayagraj in 2025, officials reported about 660 million visits, making it the largest gathering ever recorded. Pilgrims take a ritual dip where rivers meet to cleanse their sins, though a deadly crowd crush in January was a tragic reminder of the risks.

source.name: Press Information Bureau, Govt of India: Mahakumbh 2025 - A Spectacle of Faith, Unity, and Tradition

source2.name: PBS NewsHour: At least 30 people killed in a stampede at massive Maha Kumbh festival

title: The Urn Burials of Adichanallur
text: In southern Tamil Nadu, archaeologists in 2004 unearthed 169 clay urns holding human skeletons. Carbon dating later placed samples from the site between about 905 and 696 BCE. The burial ground lies about 25 kilometers from Korkai, an ancient seaport mentioned in early Tamil Sangam poetry.

source.name: The News Minute, 'Adichanallur: A brief history on one of the oldest archaeological sites in India' (interviews ASI excavation director T. Sathyamurthy)

title: Gargi Questions the Sage
text: According to the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, King Janaka of Videha offered 1,000 cows, each decorated with gold, to the wisest scholar at his gathering. The philosopher Gargi Vachaknavi stood up and challenged the famous sage Yajnavalkya with puzzling questions about atman, the soul. She is remembered as one of the most brilliant women of the Upanishads.

source.name: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad with Shankara's commentary, tr. Swami Madhavananda (Advaita Ashrama), sections 3.1.1 and 3.6.1 (full text via Internet Archive)

dateLabel: Pleistocene Ice Age (roughly 1.8 million years ago onward)
title: The Largest Marsupial Ever
place: Wellington Caves, New South Wales, Australia
text: Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived: nearly 4 metres long and up to about 2,800 kilograms, though still smaller than a hippo or rhino. Its bones are known from Wellington Caves and many other sites, and in 1838 it became the first fossil mammal named from Australia. It lived alongside the first Aboriginal people for thousands of years.

source.name: Australian Museum

title: The Ancestors of Kow Swamp
text: Beside an old lake shore at Kow Swamp lay perhaps the largest group of human burials known from the late Ice Age, about 15,000 to 9,000 years old. Archaeologists dug them up in the late 1960s without the Traditional Owners' approval. Around 1990 the remains were returned to the Yorta Yorta community, who reburied them.

source.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Stone and Cupper 2003), abstract via Europe PMC

source2.name: National Museum of Australia, Repatriation handbook ch. 2

title: Australia's Oldest Known Boomerangs
text: In 1973, archaeologist Roger Luebbers dug wooden boomerangs out of a peat bog at Wyrie Swamp in South Australia. At about 10,000 years old, they are the oldest known boomerangs in Australia. Wet peat kept the wood from rotting away, and one is now kept by the South Australian Museum.

source.name: South Australian Museum, "Alive with Wonder: Highlights of the South Australian Museum"

title: The Wandjina of the Kimberley
text: Wandjina are powerful creator beings painted in rock shelters, found only in the Kimberley region of northwest Australia. The ghostlike figures have large white faces and no mouths, and the paintings are traditionally renewed by repainting. They are far from ancient history: the Mowanjum community, home to Worrorra, Ngarinyin and Wunambal people, are custodians of Wandjina law and imagery today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: ANU Press, Humanities Research XV.2 (2009), 'Antiquity of the Wandjina'

title: Seafarers Reach the Marianas
text: About 3,500 years ago, Austronesian-speaking seafarers crossed some 1,300 miles of open ocean to settle the Mariana Islands, becoming the ancestors of the Chamorro people. Most evidence points to a start in the northern or central Philippines, though a route from Indonesia has also been proposed. Their descendants made pottery, wove coconut leaves and later built latte structures.

source.name: Guampedia (Guam's online encyclopedia): 'Origin of Guam's Indigenous People'

source2.name: Guampedia: Ancient Guam

title: The Mysterious Ambum Stone
text: This finely pecked stone carving from Enga Province in the New Guinea highlands is now in the National Gallery of Australia. Similar Enga stone figures have been carbon dated to about 3,500 years ago. It may show an echidna or a mythical creature. It was made as a pestle, and was later used as a fertility object.

source.name: Bowers Museum: 'Sailing Stones: Prehistoric Art of Melanesia'

title: The Dingo Lands in Australia
text: The oldest directly dated dingo bones in Australia, from Madura Cave on the Nullarbor Plain, are between 3,348 and 3,081 years old. Dingoes probably arrived by boat with people from Southeast Asia. They may have helped drive the thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, off the mainland, though this is debated. Dingoes never reached Tasmania, where thylacines hung on.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Nature): Balme, O'Connor & Fallon 2018, 'New dates on dingo bones from Madura Cave'

title: Ancient Pots Under a Ferry Wharf
text: In the early 1970s, blasting and dredging to make a berth for Samoa's inter-island ferries hit something unexpected: a Lapita village now under the sea. The dredging brought up thousands of pieces of locally made pottery, about 3,000 years old. It remains the only place in Samoa with decorated, dentate-stamped Lapita pottery, made by the famous Lapita voyagers.

source.name: Pacific Science 29 (1975), R. C. Green & H. G. Richards, 'Lapita Pottery and a Lower Sea Level in Western Samoa' (University of Hawai'i ScholarSpace, full text)

source2.name: Radiocarbon 43 (2001), F. Petchey, 'Radiocarbon Determinations from the Mulifanua Lapita Site, Upolu, Western Samoa' (abstract via Crossref)

title: Secrets in Fiji's Sand Dunes
place: Sigatoka Sand Dunes, Viti Levu, Fiji
text: Fiji's tall coastal dunes hold layers of human settlement going back about 2,600 years and have produced the largest collection of complete Lapita pots in the Pacific. A burial ground dug in 1987-88 held 55 people buried around the middle of the first millennium CE. Shifting sands keep uncovering pottery and stone tools, and in 1989 the dunes became Fiji's first national park.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2024), 'Life histories in Fiji as reconstructed from first millennium CE Sigatoka Sand Dune burials using isotopes' (PMC11081393)

source2.name: National Trust of Fiji, 'Sigatoka Sand Dunes'

title: A Sea Culture Between Two Lands
text: Archaeologists still debate when people first lived on the Torres Strait Islands, between Australia and New Guinea; some sites hint at much earlier visits. By about 3,000 to 2,500 years ago, seafaring people with ties to New Guinea were settling many of the islands, living mainly by hunting and gathering from the sea. On some islands, gardening later became important too.

source.name: Australian National University Open Research (David et al. 2004, Archaeology in Oceania)

source2.name: Memoirs of the Queensland Museum, Cultural Heritage Series (Barham et al. 2004)

title: First Homes in Chuuk Lagoon
text: Chuuk Lagoon is a wide Micronesian lagoon whose name means 'high mountains' in the Chuukese language. People were living here about 2,000 years ago: pottery from a site now underwater off Fefen island dates from about 2,350 to 1,650 years ago. Much later the lagoon became a Japanese fleet anchorage, heavily bombed by American forces in February 1944.

source.name: Jeffery, McKinnon & Van Tilburg 2021, 'Underwater Cultural Heritage in the Pacific', International Journal of Asia Pacific Studies 17(2)

source2.name: Naval History and Heritage Command, H-Gram 026-3 'Operation Hailstone - Carrier Raid on Truk Island, 17-18 February 1944'

title: The Rise of the Tuʻi Tonga
text: From at least the 10th century, Tonga was ruled by a line of sacred kings, the Tuʻi Tonga. Their chiefdom became a maritime power whose influence spread widely across the central Pacific. From the 1300s-1400s their capital at Lapaha, on the lagoon at Mua, grew into a ceremonial centre of huge stone-faced royal tombs, with a wharf for mooring large double-hulled canoes.

source.name: Clark, Burley & Murray 2008, 'Monumentality and the development of the Tongan maritime chiefdom', Antiquity 82 (ANU Open Research full text)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tonga: History' (Sione Latukefu)

title: Stone Mushrooms of the Marianas
place: House of Taga, Tinian, Northern Mariana Islands
text: About 1,000 years ago, the Chamorro people began raising houses on latte stones: stone pillars topped with rounded caps, set curved side down and flat side up. The caps may have helped keep crabs and vermin out. The largest standing latte, at the House of Taga on Tinian, are about 15 feet long overall, and on Rota even bigger latte were left unfinished in their quarry.

source.name: Guampedia (Guam's online encyclopedia), Lawrence J. Cunningham, 'Latte Structures'

source2.name: Guampedia, 'Latte's Significance' and 'Latte Structures' (Lawrence J. Cunningham)

title: Taputapuātea, Heart of the Voyagers
text: On Raiatea stands Taputapuātea, a marae complex whose central marae, an open-air temple, is dedicated to the god ʻOro. Its importance grew with the power of the Tamatoa line of chiefs, and it became the centre of an alliance reaching across much of Polynesia, held together by canoe voyaging. UNESCO lists it as a testimony to 1,000 years of Maʻohi civilisation.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taputapuatea (via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taputapuātea (read in browser)

title: Voyagers Find Hawaiʻi
text: Polynesian voyagers reached the Hawaiian Islands sometime between about 1000 and 1290; scholars still debate the exact date, and one major radiocarbon study puts it in the 1200s. Small settlements grew into chiefdoms ruling whole islands, and chiefs used genealogy chants to prove their right to rule. For a while canoes sailed between Hawaiʻi and Tahiti, but those voyages ended by about 1400.

source.name: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS (via PubMed Central)

source2.name: Matsumoto & Berger, He Huakaʻi Honua: Journeys in World History I (Honolulu Community College / UH Pressbooks), ch. 8

title: The 'Stonehenge of the Pacific'
text: King Tuʻitātui built Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, 'the Burden of Maui', in the 13th century: two upright coral limestone slabs topped by a third. Each upright weighs roughly 30 to 40 tons above ground. Some say it honoured his two sons; others think it may also mark sunrise at the solstices and equinoxes.

source.name: World History Commons (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media / World History Association)

title: Leluh, the Walled Island City
text: On little Lelu Island off Kosrae stood Leluh, the island's ancient capital, built with walls of basalt and coral. At its peak about 1,500 people lived there, from kings and chiefs to commoners. In the 14th century its rulers built pyramid-shaped coral tombs, where royal bodies were laid before the bones were reburied on the reef.

source.name: Science Advances, Richards et al. 2015, 'New precise dates for the ancient and sacred coral pyramidal tombs of Leluh (Kosrae, Micronesia)' (PMC)

source2.name: Archaeology magazine (AIA), 'Leluh Island's Temporary Royal Tombs Are 700 Years Old' (2015)

title: Goodbye to the Biggest Eagle Ever
text: Haast's eagle, weighing up to about 15 kilograms, was the largest eagle known to have existed. It hunted moa, giant flightless birds that could weigh around 200 kilograms. After Māori arrived, people overhunted the moa and burned forests where its prey lived, and the eagle died out about 500 to 600 years ago, around the same time as the moa.

source.name: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa, 'Haast's eagle'

source2.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2021), 'New Zealand's extinct giant raptor (Hieraaetus moorei) killed like an eagle, ate like a condor' (PMC)

title: Magellan Meets the Flying Proas
text: After crossing the Pacific, Magellan's three hungry ships reached Guam. Chamorro outrigger canoes called proas raced out so fast they seemed to fly, and Magellan named the place the Islands of Lateen Sails. Chamorros then helped themselves to things on deck, following their own ideas about sharing property, and the Spanish branded the islands the 'Islands of Thieves'.

source.name: Guampedia (Ferdinand Magellan)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ferdinand Magellan: Discovery of the Strait)

title: Chief Roi Mata's Grave Found by Legend
text: Roi Mata was a chiefly title in central Vanuatu, and its most famous holder lived around 1600. In 1967 French archaeologist José Garanger, guided by local people who knew the traditions, found his grave on Eretoka island. More than 50 people were buried with him. His home, death place and grave became World Heritage Sites in 2008.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Chief Roi Mata's Domain), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Vanuatu history, Roy Mata)

title: A Dinner Plate Left on a Beach
place: Cape Inscription, Dirk Hartog Island, Australia
text: Dutch skipper Dirk Hartog's ship Eendracht came unexpectedly upon islands off Western Australia on its way to the East Indies. Before sailing off, Hartog nailed a pewter plate to a post, scratched with the date, the ship's name and the names of its senior crew. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where it is kept today, calls it the earliest surviving Western object from Australia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Dirck Hartog)

source2.name: Rijksmuseum, object NG-NM-825 (Dirck Hartogh dish)

title: Money Too Heavy to Carry
text: Yapese voyagers quarried their famous rai, stone discs with a hole in the middle, mainly on faraway Palau; quarrying there intensified after European contact, and iron tools came to be used to bore the holes. Big stones rarely moved: everyone simply remembered who owned them. Island tradition tells of a rai lost to the seabed in a storm that still counted as money.

source.name: University of Oregon news: 'UO team puts an ancient spin on a new digital currency' (Scott Fitzpatrick)

source2.name: Houston Museum of Natural Science, Dirk Van Tuerenhout (curator of anthropology), 'Hard currency: Stone money of the Yap Islands'

title: Tupaia Maps the Pacific
text: Tupaia, a priest and navigator from a Raiatean family of master navigators, joined Captain Cook's ship Endeavour in 1769. He once described nearly 130 islands to the British, and from August 1769 helped draw a chart that grew to show 74 islands across a vast stretch of ocean. In New Zealand he became an interpreter, adviser and bringer of news from islands Māori had left long ago.

source.name: University of Potsdam, Institute of English and American Studies: Tupaia's Map

source2.name: New Zealand Geographic, 'Tupaia'

title: Captain Cook's Last Voyage Ends
text: Cook's ships first reached Kealakekua Bay during Makahiki, a festival for the god Lono, and were warmly received. Returning for repairs after the season ended, tensions grew over thefts and reprisals. When Cook tried to take the ruling chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage over a stolen boat, a fight broke out on the beach, killing Cook, four marines and a number of Hawaiians.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Cook Landing Site

source2.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: The Death of Captain James Cook, 14 February 1779

title: Sea Cucumbers for China
text: For generations, fleets of fishermen from Makassar in Sulawesi sailed to the coast they called Marege, now Arnhem Land, to gather trepang, or sea cucumber, a delicacy in Chinese markets. Yolngu people traded and worked with them and learned to make dugout canoes and work metal. Stands of tamarind trees still mark their old camps; the last fleet sailed in 1907.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Trade with the Makasar

source2.name: Museums Victoria Collections: Aboriginal People & Trade

title: The Bounty Mutineers' Hideaway
text: HMS Bounty had come to Tahiti to collect breadfruit plants when Fletcher Christian led a mutiny in 1789. He and eight mutineers, with Tahitian companions, hid on remote Pitcairn Island and burned the ship. When outsiders found them in 1808, only one mutineer, John Adams, was still alive. Their descendants still live there.

source.name: Internet Archaeology 11: Settlement at Pitcairn Island

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Pitcairn Island

title: A Few Rabbits Run Wild
text: Settler Thomas Austin had wild rabbits sent from England and released 13 on his Barwon Park estate on Christmas Day 1859, so they could be hunted for sport. By 1866, hunters had bagged 14,000 there. Within 50 years rabbits covered almost the whole continent, overgrazing native plants and causing soil erosion, despite a rabbit-proof fence built across Western Australia between 1901 and 1907.

source.name: National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: Rabbits introduced

title: A Script No One Can Read
text: In 1864 the missionary Eugène Eyraud became the first outsider to report rongorongo, rows of glyphs carved on wooden tablets. Soon after, Peruvian slave raids and epidemics devastated Rapa Nui, and no new tablets were made after the late 1860s. No one has deciphered rongorongo, and none of the 27 surviving inscribed objects remain on the island.

source.name: Scientific Reports (2024), Ferrara et al., 'The invention of writing on Rapa Nui', PMC10837134

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Did the People of Easter Island Invent a Writing System From Scratch?'

title: Father Damien Goes to Molokaʻi
text: Belgian priest Damien De Veuster arrived at the isolated leprosy settlement on Molokaʻi in 1873. He bandaged sores, built houses and a water system, enlarged the church, buried the dead and shared poi with residents. In 1884 it was announced that he had caught leprosy himself, but he kept working until his death in 1889. He was declared a saint in 2009.

source.name: National Park Service, Kalaupapa National Historical Park

source2.name: Vatican, biography of St Damien De Veuster (canonization 2009)

title: The Measles Epidemic That Struck Fiji
text: Just after Fiji became a British colony, the high chief Cakobau and two of his sons visited Sydney and came home early in 1875 carrying measles. No quarantine procedure existed yet, and Fijians had no immunity. The disease swept the islands, killing more than 40,000 people, roughly a quarter of the population, and officials reported whole families carried off and starvation rampant.

source.name: ANU Press, 'Ma'afu, prince of Tonga, chief of Fiji', ch. 12

source2.name: ANU Press, 'The General's Goose', ch. 1

title: Parihaka's Peaceful Resistance
text: Led by Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kākahi, the Māori village of Parihaka resisted land confiscation without violence, ploughing disputed land and fencing across roads. On 5 November 1881 about 1,600 troops and volunteers marched in to find singing children on the road, girls skipping and 500 loaves baked to feed the men. Te Whiti and Tohu were held 16 months without trial.

source.name: The Conversation (Alexander Gillespie, University of Waikato), How NZ's colonial government misused laws to crush non-violent dissent at Parihaka

source2.name: Papers Past (National Library of New Zealand), Star (Christchurch), 7 November 1881, 'The March on Parihaka'

title: Proof That Platypuses Lay Eggs
text: European scientists doubted that a furry mammal could lay eggs, until Cambridge zoologist William Caldwell spent months searching along Queensland's Burnett River, helped by about 150 Aboriginal Wakkawakka people. In 1884 they finally found eggs. His four-word telegram to a scientific meeting in Montreal read simply: 'Monotremes oviparous, ovum meroblastic.'

source.name: History Today, Placing the Platypus

source2.name: University of Cambridge Museum of Zoology, William Caldwell (1859–1941)

title: Tarawera Buries the Pink and White Terraces
text: In the small hours of 10 June 1886, Mount Tarawera split open along a rift about 17 kilometres long. The rumbling was heard as far south as Blenheim in the South Island, and between about 108 and 120 people died. The eruption destroyed the Pink and White Terraces, celebrated at the time as one of the great natural wonders of the world.

source.name: GeoNet (GNS Science / EQC), About Okataina volcano

source2.name: Auckland War Memorial Museum, The eruption of Mt Tarawera

title: Six Colonies Become One Australia
text: On 1 January 1901, six British colonies became the states of the Commonwealth of Australia. New Zealand and Fiji had also been part of the federation talks but stayed out. As a compromise, the new capital had to be in New South Wales but at least 100 miles from Sydney. On 9 May 1901 the first federal parliament was opened in Melbourne's grand Exhibition Building.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Federation

source2.name: Parliament of Australia, Parliamentary Library FlagPost: First Sitting of the Commonwealth Parliament

title: Duke Kahanamoku Surfs Sydney
text: Hawaiian Olympic swimming champion Duke Kahanamoku gave a surfing show at Freshwater Beach on Christmas Eve 1914, now seen as a turning point for Australian surfing. He carved his board from a piece of sugar pine he bought locally. The board is still kept by the Freshwater Surf Life Saving Club.

source.name: NSW Government Environment and Heritage, Blue Plaques: Duke Kahanamoku

source2.name: Northern Beaches Council, Manly Art Gallery & Museum: Duke Kahanamoku and the early development of surfing in Australia

title: The Last Tasmanian Tiger
text: The thylacine, a striped, dog-like marsupial nicknamed the Tasmanian tiger, was hunted for decades under government bounty schemes as a supposed threat to livestock. The last known one died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936. Australia now marks that date as National Threatened Species Day, and scientists have even mapped its genome.

source.name: National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: Extinction of thylacine

source2.name: Genome Research (2023), Historical RNA expression profiles from the extinct Tasmanian tiger, PMC

title: The Battle for the Kokoda Track
text: In 1942, Japanese forces tried to reach Port Moresby by marching over the steep, jungle-covered Owen Stanley Range along the Kokoda Track. Australian and Papuan troops fought them in isolated mountain jungle, where carrying supplies was a constant struggle. From Ioribaiwa the Japanese could see the lights of Port Moresby at night before withdrawing, and were pushed back to the north coast by November.

source.name: Australian War Memorial, Kokoda Trail Campaign

source2.name: Libraries ACT (ACT Government), Kokoda Campaign: Ioribaiwa and Imita

title: Bikini Atoll's Nuclear Tests
text: In 1946, the United States moved Bikini's 167 residents away, promising they could return, and began testing atomic bombs on the atoll. Between 1946 and 1958 it set off more than 20 nuclear weapons there; one 1954 blast was about 1,000 times stronger than the Hiroshima bomb. Contamination left the atoll unsafe to live on for a long time.

source.name: UN Human Rights Council report A/HRC/57/77 (2024)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site (via UNESCO open-data API)

title: The Wave Hill Walk-Off
text: Led by Vincent Lingiari, about 200 Gurindji stockmen, domestic workers and their families walked off the Wave Hill cattle station. Their white union supporters saw it as a strike over wages, but the Gurindji really wanted their land back. The dispute lasted nine years, until Prime Minister Gough Whitlam handed back part of it in 1975, inspiring the song 'From Little Things Big Things Grow'.

source.name: National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: 'Wave Hill Walk-Off'

source2.name: National Film and Sound Archive, australianscreen, 'From Little Things Big Things Grow' curator's notes

title: Hōkūleʻa Sails to Tahiti
text: In 1976, the double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Maui to Tahiti without instruments. No living Hawaiian then knew the old deep-sea wayfinding, so master navigator Mau Piailug from Satawal in Micronesia guided it. The trip backed the idea that Polynesians explored the Pacific on purpose, and became a symbol of Hawaiian cultural revival.

source.name: Polynesian Voyaging Society (Hokulea.com), 50th anniversary of the 1976 voyage

source2.name: Polynesian Voyaging Society, History

title: Mabo: The Land Was Never Empty
text: Torres Strait Islander Eddie Mabo and others took Queensland to court over land on Mer. In 1992 the High Court rejected the idea that Australia had belonged to no one when the British arrived, and recognised native title for the first time. The ruling even pops up in the 1997 comedy film The Castle: 'It's Mabo... it's the vibe.'

source.name: National Museum of Australia, 'Mabo decision'

source2.name: ABC News, 'Straight to the pool room: Why The Castle is still a classic 25 years on'

title: A Climate Treaty for Tuvalu
text: The small island nation of Tuvalu and Australia signed the Falepili Union, a treaty covering climate change, security and migration. Australia created a special visa pathway, initially up to 280 places a year, for Tuvaluans to live, work and study there, and pledged to expand a project reclaiming land in Funafuti against rising seas. Falepili is a Tuvaluan idea of good neighbourliness, care and mutual respect.

source.name: Australian Government DFAT: Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union treaty

source2.name: DFAT: Treaty text - Falepili Union

title: Alberta's Dinosaur Graveyard
text: The badlands of Dinosaur Provincial Park in southern Alberta hold some of the most important dinosaur fossils ever found, dating back 75 to 77 million years. More than 44 dinosaur species have turned up here. Over 350 articulated specimens, including more than 150 complete skeletons, now sit in more than 30 major museums.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Dinosaur Provincial Park)

dateLabel: Late Cretaceous, over 70 million years ago
title: The Good Mother Lizard
text: Maiasaura was a duck-billed dinosaur named in 1979 from fossils found near the town of Choteau, Montana. Remains of its babies have been found both inside and outside the nests. Studies suggest the hatchlings stayed in the nest for about 40 to 75 days and needed their parents to look after them, just as its famous name suggests.

source.name: PeerJ (Prieto-Marquez & Guenther 2018, "Perinatal specimens of Maiasaura from the Upper Cretaceous of Montana")

source2.name: Scientific Reports (2025, "Neonatal state and degree of necessity for parental care in Maiasaura")

title: The Triceratops Mistaken for a Bison
text: Triceratops, with its huge bony frill and three horns, roamed western North America at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, reaching about 8 to 9 metres long. When a pair of its brow horns turned up near Denver in 1887, paleontologist Othniel Marsh first named them as a giant extinct bison, Bison alticornis. More skulls soon revealed the truth.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine, Riley Black, 'When Triceratops Was a Giant Bison' (2011, summarising Carpenter 2007)

source2.name: Natural History Museum (London), Dino Directory: Triceratops

title: Yellowstone's Biggest Blast
text: About 2.1 million years ago, the Yellowstone hotspot unleashed the largest of its three giant eruptions. It blasted out about 2,450 cubic kilometres of rock and ash, which hardened into the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff. So much magma poured out that the ground above collapsed, leaving a huge crater, or caldera, made of three overlapping collapse areas.

source.name: U.S. Geological Survey - Yellowstone Volcano Observatory

title: The Sticky Trap of La Brea
place: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles, USA
text: In the middle of today's Los Angeles, natural asphalt has oozed from the ground for tens of thousands of years. During the Ice Age, animals got stuck in it, and predators that came to eat them got stuck too. That's why the pits hold so many dire wolves and saber-toothed cats, plus mammoths, giant ground sloths and American lions.

source.name: La Brea Tar Pits and Museum (Natural History Museums of Los Angeles County)

source2.name: La Brea Tar Pits and Museum, mammal collections

title: Clues in a Groundhog Burrow
text: In 1955, farmer Albert Miller found what looked like a prehistoric tool in a groundhog hole under a rock overhang on his family's farm in Avella, Pennsylvania. He kept it quiet until archaeologist James Adovasio began digging in 1973. The excavation turned up nearly two million artifacts and remains, and the museum says people camped here about 19,000 years ago.

source.name: Senator John Heinz History Center (Meadowcroft Rockshelter)

title: Mastodon Butchers Under a River
place: Page–Ladson site, Aucilla River, Florida, USA
text: Page–Ladson is a sinkhole now lying under Florida's Aucilla River, so archaeologists dig it in scuba gear. About 14,550 years ago it held a pond, and people there butchered or scavenged a mastodon, leaving stone tools behind. Cut marks on a tusk, mastodon tracks and dung in the same layers help tell the story.

source.name: Science Advances (Halligan et al. 2016), via PubMed Central

title: A Cowboy's Hunch at Folsom
text: After a flash flood in 1908, George McJunkin, a formerly enslaved cowboy and ranch foreman, noticed bison bones in an arroyo that were far bigger than any he had seen. He died in 1922, before experts came. In 1927, diggers found a spear point lying between the ribs of an extinct Ice Age bison, proof that people hunted in North America far earlier than experts believed.

source.name: SAPIENS (Wenner-Gren Foundation), by S. Nash, Denver Museum of Nature & Science

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service

title: The Cliff of the Buffalo Jump
text: For nearly 6,000 years, Plains peoples drove bison over this 10-metre cliff in the Alberta foothills. Using their deep knowledge of the land and of buffalo behaviour, hunters funnelled herds into drive lanes marked with stones that ended at the edge. The butchered bones and tools at the foot of the cliff lie more than 11 metres deep.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia

title: Watson Brake, Older Than the Pyramids
text: Around 3500 BCE, hunter-gatherers in northern Louisiana began piling up earth that became eleven mounds joined by ridges, forming an oval about 260 metres across. They kept building, in bursts, until some time after 3000 BCE. Watson Brake is considered the oldest surviving mound complex in North America, older than Egypt's pyramids, and shows that people without farming could plan enormous projects.

source.name: American Antiquity 70 (2005), Saunders et al., 'Watson Brake, a Middle Archaic Mound Complex in Northeast Louisiana' (abstract via Crossref/Cambridge)

source2.name: University of Washington News, 'Oldest existing New World mound complex identified' (1997, on Saunders et al., Science)

title: Explorers of the World's Longest Cave
text: Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system on Earth, and Native Americans were exploring it and mining its minerals thousands of years ago. One ancient miner, later nicknamed "Lost John," was found in 1935 beneath a large boulder that he had apparently dislodged while digging out gypsum. His remains were later returned to a secret place inside the cave.

source.name: US National Park Service, Mammoth Cave timeline

source2.name: US National Park Service, 'Prehistoric Cave Discoveries'

title: Copper Tools of the Great Lakes
text: Archaic peoples around the Great Lakes worked copper for thousands of years, with some artifacts dated as early as about 6500 BCE. They collected very pure native copper near Lake Superior, then heated and hammered it into points, knives and fishhooks. At Oconto, Wisconsin, a burial ground used around 4000 to 3000 BCE held at least 45 people, some buried with copper tools and a bracelet.

source.name: Wisconsin Historical Society, National Register record for the Oconto Site

source2.name: Radiocarbon (Pompeani et al. 2021)

title: Greenland's 4,000-Year-Old Genome
text: The Saqqaq were the first known culture to settle in Greenland. Tufts of one man's hair, frozen in permafrost for about 4,000 years, let scientists sequence his genome in 2010. He probably had brown eyes, thick dark hair and shovel-shaped front teeth, and his closest living relatives are peoples of northeastern Siberia.

source.name: Nature (Rasmussen et al. 2010, 'Ancient human genome sequence of an extinct Palaeo-Eskimo')

title: North America's Own First Crops
text: Farming wasn't invented in just a few famous places. Eastern North America was one of ten or more independent centres of plant domestication. By about 1800 BCE, people at the Riverton site in Illinois were growing domesticated goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder and bottle gourd, and perhaps squash. Their sunflower seed was already as big as a farmed one, a telltale sign of domestication.

source.name: PNAS: Smith & Yarnell 2009, 'Initial formation of an indigenous crop complex in eastern North America at 3800 B.P.'

title: The Dorset, Hunters at the Ice Holes
text: From about 500 BCE, the Dorset people lived across the Canadian Arctic, hunting seals at their breathing holes in the sea ice and burning oil in soapstone lamps. Surprisingly, there is almost no sign that they used bows and arrows. They carved tiny figures of people and animals in ivory and antler, and many Inuit identify them with the Tuniit, giants remembered as earlier inhabitants of the land.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia

source2.name: Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge

title: The Giant Earthen Serpent
text: Winding 411 metres along a ridge in Ohio, the Great Serpent Mound is a giant snake built of earth. Who built it is still debated: radiocarbon dates presented in 2014 point to the Adena culture around 300 BCE, while charcoal from a 1991 dig suggests about 1100 CE. Its head and oval roughly line up with the summer solstice sunset, and it sits inside an ancient impact crater.

source.name: University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Department of Physics & Astronomy (archaeoastronomy pages)

source2.name: Ohio History Connection, Serpent Mound

title: Ancient Duck Decoys of Lovelock Cave
text: Guano miners first reported ancient finds in Lovelock Cave, Nevada, and in 1924 archaeologists Mark Harrington and Llewellyn Loud dug there again. The cave held 11 duck decoys made of bundled tule, a tall reed-like plant, covered in feathers, with heads painted to look real. Radiocarbon tests reported in 1986 gave two of them radiocarbon ages of about 2,080 and 2,250 years, making them the oldest known duck decoys.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Infinity of Nations: 'Duck decoys' (13/4512, 13/4513)

source2.name: Online Nevada Encyclopedia (Nevada Humanities), Pat Barker, 'L.L. Loud and the Beginning of Nevada Archaeology'

title: Ivory Treasures of Point Hope
place: Ipiutak Site, Point Hope, Alaska, USA
text: On a narrow spit poking into the Chukchi Sea, more than 500 ancient house ruins line the beach ridges at Ipiutak, many ringed by whale and walrus bones. The people who lived here over 1,800 years ago made elaborate decorative carvings in ivory, wood, bone and stone. Their communities seem to have peaked between about 650 and 870 CE.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, 'Ipiutak Site' (National Historic Landmark)

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, 'Ipiutak Site'

title: A Sun Temple on the Tropic of Cancer
text: At Altavista in Zacatecas, an outpost on Mesoamerica's northwestern frontier near the Tropic of Cancer, priests linked to Teotihuacan founded a ceremonial centre between about 400 and 450 CE. From markers pecked into a nearby hilltop, the summer solstice sun rises over a distant peak. Hundreds of ancient mines dot the region, and scholars think turquoise from the far north later passed through centres like this.

source.name: INAH (Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia), 'Alta Vista (Chalchihuites)'

source2.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge University Press), Aveni, Hartung & Kelley 1982, 'Alta Vista (Chalchihuites), Astronomical Implications of a Mesoamerican Ceremonial Outpost at the Tropic of Cancer' (abstract)

title: The Canal Builders of Phoenix
text: Long before Phoenix was a city, the Hohokam people dug canals from the Salt and Gila Rivers to water fields in the desert. Using stone hoes, they built the largest and most complex irrigation systems in the Americas north of Peru, hundreds of miles of canals, before leaving around 1400. Some of today's Phoenix canals still follow their original routes.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service (Hohokam Culture)

source2.name: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (Salt River Project)

title: Erik the Red Names Greenland
text: Outlawed from Iceland, Erik the Red explored a little-known land to the west around 982. Back home, he gave it an appealing name, Greenland, saying people would be attracted to a place with a favourable name. In 985 he returned with colonists: of 25 ships that set out, only 14 arrived. Erik built his farm, Brattahlíð, in what became the Eastern Settlement.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Erik the Red' (Birgitta Wallace)

title: The Thule Head East
text: Around 800 years ago, the Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit, began moving east from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic, all the way to Greenland. They depended on hunting whales, and some archaeologists think a search for new sources of metal helped drive the move. With dog sleds, kayaks and big skin boats called umiaks, they spread fast and replaced the Dorset culture in most regions.

source.name: Scientific Reports 2023, 'Bidirectional dispersals during the peopling of the North American Arctic' (via Europe PMC)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Early Inuit (Thule Culture)' (read in browser)

title: Cliff Palace, a Town in a Canyon Wall
text: Under a sandstone overhang at Mesa Verde, Ancestral Puebloans built Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, and lived there in the 1200s. It has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas, round sunken rooms for ceremonies, and walls once plastered in colors like yellow, white and red. Richard Wetherill and Charles Mason came upon it in December 1888 while looking for stray cattle.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service (Mesa Verde)

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service (Mesa Verde history timeline)

title: Moundville's Plaza of Mounds
text: On a bluff above Alabama's Black Warrior River, Mississippian people built a planned town of 29 earthen mounds around a huge, leveled plaza. Founded around 1120, it was guarded on three sides by a wooden palisade with bastions, and in size and complexity it was second only to Cahokia. Its mounds slowly fell out of use between 1300 and 1450.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama (John H. Blitz, University of Alabama)

source2.name: University of Alabama Museums, Moundville Archaeological Park: The Ancient Site

title: Paquimé's Macaw Pens
text: In the desert of northern Mexico, Paquimé grew into a city of multi-storey adobe apartments with more than 1,000 rooms. Its people built a complex water system and ballcourts, and kept rows of pens for scarlet macaws, birds native to tropical lands at least 500 kilometres farther south, and bred them for their feathers. The city flourished until about 1450.

source.name: Antiquity (2024), 'High levels of consanguinity in a child from Paquimé, Chihuahua, Mexico' (PMC)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Zone of Paquimé, Casas Grandes (read via data.unesco.org)

title: The Great Law of Peace
text: Haudenosaunee oral history tells how the Peacemaker, Hiawatha and Jikonhsaseh, the first to accept the peace, persuaded five warring nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, to unite under the Great Law of Peace. Its date is much debated. The Onondaga became the Firekeepers, and the Hiawatha wampum belt recorded the pledge.

source.name: Onondaga Nation (official site), 'History'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Haudenosaunee Confederacy'

title: John Cabot Finds a New Found Land
text: Sailing from Bristol in a small ship called the Matthew, Italian navigator Giovanni Caboto, known in English as John Cabot, made landfall in North America on June 24, 1497. Nobody knows exactly where; for the 500th anniversary in 1997, a replica Matthew landed at Bonavista, Newfoundland, welcomed by Queen Elizabeth II. King Henry VII rewarded him with £10.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography (Cabot, John)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (John Cabot)

title: The Tree That Saved Cartier's Crew
text: In 1535 Jacques Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence to the Iroquoian town of Stadacona, where his ships froze in for winter. Scurvy killed 25 of his 110 men before Domagaya, an Iroquoian man, shared a cure brewed from a tree called annedda, which saved the rest. Cartier repaid his hosts by kidnapping Chief Donnacona. He also used the word "Canada," from kanata, meaning village.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography (Donnacona)

source2.name: Government of Canada, Canadian Heritage (Origin of the name Canada)

title: Eight Years Lost Across the Continent
text: In November 1528, survivors of a doomed Spanish expedition wrecked their homemade boats near Galveston Island, Texas. Only four, including Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and Estevanico, an enslaved Moroccan, lived through the next eight years among Native peoples, at times enslaved, later working as traders and healers. In 1536 they finally met fellow Spaniards near Culiacán.

source.name: Texas State Historical Association (Texas Day by Day: The Remarkable Journey of Cabeza de Vaca)

source2.name: Handbook of Texas (TSHA), 'Estevanico' by Donald E. Chipman

title: Pocahontas, Beyond the Legend
text: Born Amonute and also called Matoaka, Pocahontas was a Powhatan girl who visited the English fort at Jamestown and played games with the boys there. In 1613 colonists captured her and held her for ransom. Baptized Rebecca, she married tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614 and died in England in 1617. Many of John Smith's famous tales about her are disputed.

source.name: National Park Service, Historic Jamestowne (Pocahontas: Her Life and Legend)

title: Squanto's Lessons at Plymouth
text: Tisquantum, or Squanto, was a Patuxet man kidnapped by an English captain in 1614 and sold in Málaga, Spain. When he finally got home in 1619, an epidemic had wiped out his people, and the Pilgrims later settled on his village's site. In 1621 he became their interpreter and guide, telling them to plant corn with fish and catching eels by treading them out with his feet.

source.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums (Tisquantum)

source2.name: Pilgrim Hall Museum (Tisquantum / Squanto)

title: The Orphan Tsunami
text: Around 9 p.m. on January 26, 1700, a megathrust earthquake of magnitude about 8.7 to 9.2 ripped along the Pacific Northwest coast. Its tsunami crossed the ocean to Japan, where puzzled villagers recorded destructive waves with no earthquake. Scientists linked those records to "ghost forests" of drowned red cedars and to Indigenous oral traditions of a great shaking and flood.

source.name: Pacific Northwest Seismic Network (University of Washington / University of Oregon): 1700 Cascadia Subduction Zone Earthquake

source2.name: USGS image caption: 'Dead red cedar forest' (Copalis River, Washington)

title: Seeking Lost Vikings, Founding Nuuk
text: Norwegian priest Hans Egede sailed to Greenland in 1721 hoping to find descendants of the old Norse settlers, cut off for centuries. He found none, only the Kalaallit, whose language he set out to learn while preaching Christianity. In 1728, after King Frederick IV took over the colony, it moved to the mainland as Godthåb, 'Good Hope', today Nuuk, Greenland's capital.

source.name: University of Copenhagen, Selected Names: 'Haabetz Colonie'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hans Egede' (curated excerpts from Arctic, Greenland, Eskimo-Aleut languages articles)

title: The Cherokee Trail of Tears
text: After the Indian Removal Act of 1830, the US government forced southeastern nations to move west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee had even won a Supreme Court case in 1832, but it brought them no relief. In 1838 they were held in camps, then marched west in groups of about 1,000 through heavy autumn rain and, later, ice-bound rivers. Perhaps 4,000 Cherokee died.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Trail of Tears

source2.name: US National Park Service, Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, History & Culture

title: Harriet Tubman Escapes, Then Goes Back
text: Born Araminta Ross into slavery in Maryland, Harriet Tubman escaped in the fall of 1849, travelling by night and using the North Star to reach Philadelphia. Then she went back, again and again. Over about 13 missions she guided around 70 enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad. Called "Moses," she later said she "never lost a passenger." In the Civil War she became a Union scout and spy.

source.name: US National Park Service, Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad

source2.name: US National Park Service, Harriet Tubman (people)

title: Chinese Railroad Workers Go on Strike
place: Sierra Nevada near Truckee, California, USA
text: Chinese workers eventually made up about 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce, blasting tunnels through Sierra Nevada granite for the transcontinental railroad, for less pay than white workers. On June 24 or 25, 1867, about 3,000 stopped work, asking for $40 a month and ten-hour days. The company cut off their food and supplies, and the strike ended after about a week, though pay rose over time.

source.name: Library of Congress Research Guides, '1867 Sierra Strike'

source2.name: Stanford Report, 'Giving voice to Chinese railroad workers' (2019)

title: Canada's Bent Last Spike
text: On November 7, 1885, financier Donald Smith drove the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Canada's first transcontinental railway. A ceremonial silver spike had been made, but Smith hammered in a plain iron one, and his first poor swing bent it so badly it had to be replaced. Chinese labourers did much of the building, yet none appears in the famous photo.

source.name: Library and Archives Canada, Treasures Revealed podcast episode 16: Last spike

source2.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography, Smith, Donald Alexander

title: Lady Liberty's Hidden Chain
text: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France, designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel. Built in France, it crossed the Atlantic in crates and was dedicated on October 28, 1886. Look closely at her feet: she strides over a broken chain and shackle, honouring the end of slavery in the United States.

source.name: US National Park Service, Statue of Liberty Facts

source2.name: US National Park Service, Abolition (Statue of Liberty NM)

title: Gold on Bonanza Creek
text: On August 16, 1896, George Carmack and two Tagish men, Skookum Jim (Keish) and Tagish Charlie, struck gold on a Klondike creek. It's unclear who actually found it, but Carmack was named the discoverer because they feared officials wouldn't accept an Indigenous claimant. About 100,000 people set out for the goldfields, each required to bring a year's worth of supplies; only about 30,000 completed the trip.

source.name: Parks Canada, Discovery Claim National Historic Site

source2.name: US National Park Service, Gold Discoverers (Klondike Gold Rush NHP)

title: Ford's Moving Assembly Line
text: Ford's moving assembly line started in October 1913 at its Highland Park plant. Similar moving production lines were already used in bakeries, mills, breweries and meatpacking plants. Building the Model T this way slashed costs: its price fell from $850 in 1908 to $260 by 1924. Fun fact: early Model Ts came in colours like red and gray, and all-black paint came only after 1913.

source.name: Library of Congress Research Guides: Ford Implements the Moving Assembly Line (This Month in Business History)

source2.name: Detroit Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Detroit: Model T

title: The Harlem Renaissance
text: In the 1920s, Harlem became the heart of a flowering of African-American music, art, theatre and writing, fed by the Great Migration out of the South. Alain Locke's 1925 anthology The New Negro showcased writers such as Zora Neale Hurston and Langston Hughes, while Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong lit up the music scene. Its influence reached Black writers as far away as Paris.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Harlem Renaissance (George Hutchinson)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Alain Locke

title: The Golden Gate Bridge Opens
place: Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco, USA
text: When the Golden Gate Bridge opened on May 27, 1937, its 4,200-foot main span made it the longest suspension bridge in the world. Before cars were allowed, an estimated 200,000 people crossed on foot or on roller skates. The US Navy had suggested painting it with black and yellow stripes, but architect Irving Morrow chose the now-famous International Orange.

source.name: Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District (FAQs and Painting the Bridge)

source2.name: PBS American Experience, Irving Morrow

title: The Navajo Code Talkers
text: On May 4, 1942, twenty-nine Navajo men were sworn into the US Marines at Fort Wingate, New Mexico, to build a secret code from their then-unwritten language. Later it emerged that some code talker recruits had been as young as 15. At Iwo Jima, six code talkers sent and received over 800 messages without error, and their code was never broken, yet it stayed classified until 1968.

source.name: Naval History and Heritage Command, Navajo Code Talkers: World War II Fact Sheet

source2.name: U.S. National Archives (Riverside), first 29 Navajo recruits sworn in at Fort Wingate

title: Behind the Wire at Manzanar
text: After Executive Order 9066 in 1942, some 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forced from their homes. Manzanar, in California's Owens Valley, held 11,070 people between March 1942 and November 1945, about two-thirds of them US citizens by birth. They tended orchards, made camouflage netting and played baseball and softball, while photographers Ansel Adams and Dorothea Lange documented their lives.

source.name: National Park Service, Manzanar NHS: Japanese Americans at Manzanar

source2.name: National Park Service, Manzanar Orchards

title: Rosa Parks Keeps Her Seat
text: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat for a white passenger on a segregated Montgomery bus. She was no random tired seamstress: she had served as secretary of the local NAACP since 1943. "The only tired I was, was tired of giving in," she said. The bus boycott that followed lasted 381 days.

source.name: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University, 'Parks, Rosa'

source2.name: King Institute, Stanford, 'Montgomery Bus Boycott'

title: Canada Raises the Maple Leaf
text: Until 1965, Canada used the Red Ensign, which carried Britain's Union Jack in its corner. After the Great Flag Debate, Prime Minister Lester Pearson's government chose historian George Stanley's single-leaf design, and the Maple Leaf was raised on Parliament Hill on February 15, 1965. Its eleven points were chosen after a model flag was tested in a wind tunnel; the first 13-point leaf lost detail at a distance.

source.name: Government of Canada, Canadian Heritage, 'History of the National Flag of Canada'

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Flag of Canada: Alternate Designs'

title: Apple Starts in a Family Home
text: On April 1, 1976, Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne founded Apple Computer Company at Jobs' parents' home in Los Altos, California. Their first product, Wozniak's hand-built Apple I, sold for $666.66 as a single bare circuit board without even a case; buyers added their own keyboard, display and power supply. Wayne withdrew about twelve days later and was paid $800.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, 'Apple I Microcomputer'

source2.name: Computer History Museum, 'Celebrating Apple at 50'

title: Mount St. Helens Blows Its Side
text: For weeks, a bulge on Mount St. Helens' north slope grew by about 6.5 feet a day. At 8:32 a.m. on May 18, 1980, an earthquake set off the largest landslide in recorded history, and the volcano exploded sideways. Within 15 minutes an ash column rose more than 15 miles high. Fifty-seven people were killed or never found, including innkeeper Harry R. Truman.

source.name: University of Washington Libraries, Mount St. Helens Eruption Timeline (Easterbrook collection)

source2.name: USGS, 'Eruption column from May 18, 1980 Mount St. Helens eruption'

title: Nunavut, "Our Land"
text: On April 1, 1999, Canada's map changed: Nunavut, meaning "our land" in Inuktitut, became a territory of its own, following a 1993 land claims agreement with Inuit. It is Canada's largest and northernmost territory, covering over 2 million square kilometres, yet home to only about 37,000 people, most of them Inuit. Its capital, Iqaluit, is Canada's most northerly capital.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Nunavut (Peter Kikkert)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Iqaluit

title: Canada Hears the Survivors
text: For more than a century, at least 150,000 Indigenous children were sent to Canada's residential schools, and about 3,200 are known to have died there. From 2008 to 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission gathered nearly 7,000 statements. In 2015 it issued 94 Calls to Action and concluded the system amounted to cultural genocide. The testimony is kept at a national centre in Winnipeg.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Ry Moran)

source2.name: Parks Canada: The Residential School System National Historic Event

title: Argentina's Slow-Walking Giant
text: Argentinosaurus was a plant-eating titanosaur about 35 metres long and around 70 tonnes, one of the largest land animals known. Its fossils are incomplete, so its exact size is uncertain. When scientists built a computer model of its skeleton and muscles, the 83-tonne virtual giant managed only a slow walking pace, well within the range of a walking human.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (Dino Directory: Argentinosaurus)

source2.name: PLOS ONE (Sellers et al. 2013, "March of the Titans")

title: The Horned Hunter With Scaly Skin
text: Carnotaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur from Argentina with a pair of thick, cone-shaped horns sticking out above its eyes. Its skeleton was found with rare impressions of its skin still pressed into the rock. A study of its tail bones suggests it had huge leg-pulling muscles there, which may have made it a fast runner.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Persons & Currie 2011, "Dinosaur Speed Demon: The Caudal Musculature of Carnotaurus sastrei...")

title: The Terror Bird With the Biggest Bird Skull
text: Kelenken was a "terror bird", a giant hunting bird that lived in Patagonia about 15 million years ago. Its skull, about 71.6 centimetres long with a very long beak, is the largest known of any bird. The species, Kelenken guillermoi, is named after Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala, who discovered the fossil at Comallo in Argentina and helped clean it.

source.name: Bertelli, Chiappe & Tambussi 2007, Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (Universidad Nacional de La Plata repository)

title: Hunters Who Took Down a Giant Sloth
place: Campo Laborde, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: Megatherium was a giant ground sloth that roamed the grassy Pampas. At Campo Laborde, at the edge of an old swamp, people killed and butchered one about 12,600 years ago. It is the only confirmed giant ground-sloth kill site in the Americas, a clue that human hunting may have helped wipe these giants out.

source.name: Science Advances (Politis et al. 2019), via PubMed Central

title: Painted Cliffs and a Fierce Debate
text: Many rock shelters in Serra da Capivara are covered in paintings; the oldest site with surviving, dated rock art is about 10,500 radiocarbon years old. The real argument lies underneath Pedra Furada: hearths and chipped stones claimed to be as old as 48,000 years. Archaeologist Niède Guidon's team said people arrived far earlier than anyone thought; many experts think nature made them.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: South America's Oldest Textiles
text: High in Peru's Andes, dry Guitarrero Cave preserved things that usually rot away, including wooden artifacts and cords. Scraps of twined plant-fiber fabric and cord, perhaps from bags, mats or bedding, are about 11,000 to 12,100 years old, the oldest textiles found in South America. Most remains come from short stays in the cave around 8000–7000 BCE.

source.name: University of New Mexico Newsroom, 'Carbon Dating Identifies South America's Oldest Textiles' (2011, on Jolie et al., Current Anthropology)

source2.name: Science 229 (1985), Lynch et al., 'Chronology of Guitarrero Cave, Peru' (abstract, Europe PMC)

title: The First Farmers Grew Squash
text: Foragers who used this small cave in Oaxaca left behind pieces of squash. Some are directly dated to about 10,000 years ago, making them the earliest known domesticated squash, thousands of years older than the cave's earliest maize, from about 6,300 years ago. Squash, maize and beans later became the "Three Sisters," planted side by side.

source.name: PLOS ONE 2023, Kennett et al., Trans-Holocene Bayesian chronology from El Gigante rockshelter (PMC)

source2.name: Scientific Reports 2024, cucurbit use in the Mesoamerican Neotropics (PMC)

title: Cacao's First Farmers
text: Cacao was long thought to have been first domesticated in Mesoamerica. But at Santa Ana-La Florida, in the upper Amazon of southeast Ecuador, starch grains, chemical traces and ancient DNA show people were using cacao about 5,300 years ago. It is the earliest evidence of cacao use in the Americas and the oldest known centre of cacao domestication.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (Zarrillo et al. 2018)

title: The Little Clay Ladies of Valdivia
text: Around 4000–3500 BCE, people on the coast of Ecuador carved tiny stone figures, the earliest representational images known in the Americas. About 500 years later they began shaping them in clay. Most of these Valdivia figurines seem to show women, with elaborately styled hair added as a separate cap of clay, and many were found near hearths.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

title: The World's First Mummy Makers
text: On the desert coast of northern Chile, the Chinchorro, sea-going hunter-gatherers who lived there from about 5450 to 890 BCE, made the oldest known artificial mummies in the world. They did it for men, women and children of every rank, taking bodies apart and carefully putting them back together.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Oldest Rubber Balls Ever Found
text: At the foot of El Manatí hill in swampy southern Veracruz, early Olmec people left offerings: 33 wooden busts, stone axes and 14 rubber balls. The balls, estimated at 3,200 to 3,600 years old, are the oldest known, and tell us about the early Mesoamerican ballgame. Human remains found with them show it was a ritual place.

source.name: INAH (Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia), Boletín 456, 15 Sept 2025

source2.name: MIT News: 'Rubber processed in ancient Mesoamerica, MIT researchers find'

title: A Stone Slab of Mystery Signs
text: In the 1990s, road builders in Veracruz found a carved stone slab in the rubble of a gravel quarry near the Olmec center of San Lorenzo. On it are 62 unknown signs, including ones that look like maize and an insect. Dated to about 900 BCE, it may be the earliest writing in the Americas, but nobody can read it yet.

source.name: Science News (Society for Science), B. Bower, 'Scripted Stone: Ancient block may bear Americas' oldest writing' (2006)

source2.name: Science 313 (2006), Rodríguez Martínez et al., 'Oldest writing in the New World' (abstract, Europe PMC); also Archaeology magazine (AIA) 'What We Learn: The Cascajal Block' (2007)

title: Canoe Farmers Settle the Caribbean
text: From the Orinoco River in South America, pottery-making farmers took to the sea, reaching Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands and parts of the Lesser Antilles from about 500 BCE. Archaeologists call them Saladoid, after the site of Saladero in Venezuela. They grew manioc and made polished pots with white-on-red and multicoloured painted designs, and they are thought to have spoken an Arawakan language.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service

source2.name: Florida Museum of Natural History, University of Florida

title: The Biggest Pyramid on Earth
text: Building began by about the 2nd century BCE, and over roughly a thousand years this temple grew into the largest pyramid by volume anywhere, bigger even than Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza. By the time the Spanish arrived it was so overgrown it looked like a hill, and in the late 1500s they built a church on top. Archaeologists have dug about 8 km of tunnels inside.

source.name: INAH (Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia, Mexico), Lugares INAH: Cholula

source2.name: University of Calgary, G. McCafferty, 'The Great Pyramid' (Cholula)

title: The World's First Platinum Smiths
text: On the mangrove coast where Ecuador meets Colombia, the Tumaco-La Tolita people built earth mounds and became master metalworkers. Flourishing between roughly 400 BCE and 500 CE, they crafted gold and a metal hardly anyone else could handle: platinum. Experts call them the only culture in the ancient world known to have isolated and worked it.

source.name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino, 'La Tolita'

source2.name: Latin American Antiquity (Cambridge), 'La Tolita-Tumaco Culture: Master Metalsmiths in Gold and Platinum' (abstract)

title: Colombia's Valley of Stone Guardians
text: In the hills where the Magdalena River begins, chiefdom societies raised burial mounds guarded by stone statues of gods and mythical animals. About 600 statues are known, most carved between roughly 1 and 900 CE, some over 4 metres tall. The first written account came from a friar, Juan de Santa Gertrudis. UNESCO calls it South America's largest group of megalithic sculptures.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'San Agustín Archaeological Park'

source2.name: Instituto Colombiano de Antropología e Historia (ICANH), 'Parque Arqueológico San Agustín'

title: A City Swallowed by Lava
text: Cuicuilco was one of the first true urban centres in the Basin of Mexico, with a pyramid begun a few centuries BCE, and it rivalled Teotihuacan. Radiocarbon dates suggest that sometime between about 245 and 315 CE the nearby volcano Xitle erupted and lava covered the city, and its people resettled elsewhere in the valley. Today the ruins sit among the streets of southern Mexico City.

source.name: Aberystwyth University Research Portal: abstract of 'Timing of the prehistoric eruption of Xitle Volcano and the abandonment of Cuicuilco pyramid, southern Basin of Mexico'

source2.name: Oregon State University, Volcano World: 'Xitle: The Volcano that Engulfed a City'

title: Painted Pots at the Amazon's Mouth
text: On Marajó Island, where the Amazon meets the Atlantic, people made large painted pottery decorated with animals, including funeral urns nearly a meter tall, from about 300 to 1350 CE. They built big earth mounds as platforms for whole villages of longhouses, lifting them above seasonal floods. These finds point to a complex society in the Amazon.

source.name: University of California, Berkeley, ORIAS, 'Ancient Marajo'

source2.name: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Marajoara' (Anna C. Roosevelt), via encyclopedia.com

title: Tiwanaku, the Stone in the Center
text: Near Lake Titicaca, Tiwanaku grew from a small settlement into a planned city that reached its peak between about 500 and 900 CE. Its Gate of the Sun shows a front-facing figure holding a staff in each hand. An old Aymara name for the site means "stone in the center", from a belief that it lay at the center of the world.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Tiwanaku: Spiritual and Political Centre of the Tiwanaku Culture'

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine, 'Reed Boats and Experimental Archaeology on Lake Titicaca'

title: The Wari Empire Terraces the Andes
text: From their capital Huari, near today's Ayacucho in Peru's highlands, the Wari ruled an empire across the highlands and coast between about 600 and 1000 CE, irrigating terraced fields with canals. In 2013 archaeologists announced the first unlooted Wari royal tomb, at El Castillo de Huarmey. It held noblewomen and more than a thousand fine objects, from gold ear ornaments to silver bowls.

source.name: National Geographic, 'First Unlooted Royal Tomb of Its Kind Unearthed in Peru' (2013)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Huari)

title: Sixteen Kings on One Stone
text: In 776, King Yax Pasaj of Copán had a square altar carved with all sixteen rulers of his dynasty, four on each side, each sitting on his own name glyph. The line starts with the founder Yax K'uk' Mo', who began ruling in 426, shown handing the royal scepter to Yax Pasaj himself, linking the new king directly to the founder.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (R. Sharer, 'Copan Altar Q')

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Maya Site of Copan)

title: The Murals That Tell a Battle
text: Around 790, artists covered three rooms of a small temple at Bonampak, an ally of the larger city of Yaxchilan, with murals of a new heir, a raid and the fate of its captives. Though somewhat faded, the paintings are remarkably well preserved. Outsiders only saw them in 1946, when local Lacandon Maya led the photographer Giles Healey there.

source.name: Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, Harvard University

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Bonampak)

title: Eight Deer, the Jaguar-Claw King
text: Lord Eight Deer of Tilantongo was born in 1063 and died in 1115, the son of Lord Five Crocodile, high priest at Tilantongo. Painted Mixtec books, including the Codex Zouche-Nuttall, tell of his conquests, his visits to oracles and his war with the rival queen Lady Six Monkey. Lord Four Jaguar gave him a tecuhtli nose ornament, a symbol of the highest authority.

source.name: FAMSI, John Pohl, 'Mesoamerica Ancient Books: Mixtec Group Codices' (pages 3 and 7)

source2.name: FAMSI, John Pohl, 'Codex Bodley'

title: The Maya Book of Venus
text: This Maya folding book of bark paper, painted in glyphs, holds remarkably accurate tables tracking the planet Venus and the moon, with intervals that match eclipses. Bought from a private owner in Vienna in 1739, it entered the royal library in Dresden, Germany, in 1744 and survived heavy water damage in World War II.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: National Geographic

title: Taíno Ballcourts in the Mountains
text: By the 1200s, Taíno people were using a ceremonial center above Puerto Rico's Tanamá River, with about 13 plazas and ballcourts, or bateyes, edged with lines of stones. It is the largest ballcourt site in the West Indies, and some of its stones carry carved petroglyphs. The best known, the "Caguana woman," is a fertility symbol that many Taíno today see as Atabey.

source.name: Latin American Antiquity (Cambridge University Press): Rivera-Collazo, Rodríguez-Delgado & Rodríguez-Miranda 2022, 'Lidar Inspection for Indigenous Architecture at Caguana Ceremonial Complex, Borikén'

source2.name: American Indian magazine (Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian), 'Abuelas, Ancestors and Atabey', Fall 2018

title: The Golden Raft of El Dorado
text: The Muisca of Colombia's highlands cast this small gold raft with figures aboard using the lost-wax method, probably between 1200 and 1500. Many link it to the ceremony behind the El Dorado legend: a new chief sailed a raft on Lake Guatavita while gold and emerald offerings were thrown into the water. Found in a cave at Pasca in 1969, it is now a national emblem.

source.name: Banco de la República, Enciclopedia Banrepcultural, 'Balsa muisca'

source2.name: Banco de la República, Enciclopedia Banrepcultural, 'Balsa muisca'
