title: The Inca Road and Its Grass Bridges
text: The Inca ran an empire of about 12 million people without wheels, tied together by more than 30,000 km of roads. Relay runners called chasquis carried messages and quipus, while llama caravans hauled goods. Rope bridges spanned the gorges, and at Queshuachaca villagers still weave a new grass bridge over the Apurímac River every June.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Qhapaq Ñan, Andean Road System (read via data.unesco.org)

source2.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Knowledge, skills and rituals related to the annual renewal of the Q'eswachaka bridge'

title: Anacaona, Poet Queen of the Taíno
text: Anacaona was a Taíno poet, composer and ruler of Jaragua on Hispaniola. For years she cooperated with the Spanish, even as they enslaved her people. In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Jaragua with about 270 men, trapped dozens of Taíno leaders and burned them alive; Anacaona was later hanged. Caribbean poems and songs still honor her.

source.name: BBC News Mundo (republished by Acento, 12 Oct 2022)

title: The Order to Burn the Knotted Cords
text: Quipus were bundles of knotted cords the Inca used to keep records, with knots marking numbers in a base-ten system. In 1583 the Third Council of Lima, a Church meeting, declared quipus idolatrous and ordered them destroyed. Many were lost, though more than 600 survive, and simple knotted cords stayed in use in remote Andean villages.

source.name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino (Quipu: Counting with knots in the Inka Empire)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (quipu)

title: The Eruption That Froze Russia
text: On February 19, 1600, Huaynaputina in southern Peru exploded in the largest eruption in South America's recorded history, killing some 1,500 people and hurting the region's economy for decades. Its sulfur haze cooled the Northern Hemisphere, bringing bitter winters, and it is linked to Russia's famine of 1601 to 1603, the worst in Russian history.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program (Huaynaputina)

source2.name: The Columbia Encyclopedia, 6th ed. (via Encyclopedia.com), 'Huaynaputina'

title: Barbados Bets Everything on Sugar
text: In the 1640s, with help from Dutch traders and exiles from northern Brazil, who brought sugar know-how and windmills, the small island of Barbados turned to sugar cane. Planters first relied on white indentured servants but soon forced more and more enslaved Africans to do the brutal work. The island was stripped of its forests, a grim sign of how sugar was reshaping the Caribbean.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (History of Barbados)

source2.name: College of Charleston Libraries, Lowcountry Digital History Initiative, 'Barbados Influence'

title: The Pirate Port That Sank
text: Port Royal was nicknamed the "wickedest city in the world," a rich harbor full of privateers and pirates. On June 7, 1692, an earthquake and tsunami sank most of the city below sea level. About 2,000 people died at once and 3,000 more in the following days. A pocket watch found in the harbor in 1959 had stopped at about 11:43 a.m.

source.name: USGS Historic Earthquakes: Jamaica 1692 June 07 (archived; quotes Texas A&M Institute of Nautical Archaeology Port Royal Project)

source2.name: National Geographic, 'How the wickedest city on Earth was sunk by an earthquake'

title: The Guaraní Fight for Their Missions
place: São Miguel das Missões, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
text: Seven Jesuit mission towns east of the Uruguay River were home to some 30,000 Guaraní people. In 1750 Spain and Portugal redrew the border and ordered the towns moved. Led by Sepé Tiaraju, the Guaraní refused. Sepé was killed on February 7, 1756, and three days later a Spanish-Portuguese army of about 3,200 attacked at Caiboaté, where about 1,500 Guaraní died and only four Europeans.

source.name: Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF), Impressões Rebeldes: Resistência indígena nos campos de Caiboaté

source2.name: Tau Golin (Universidade de Passo Fundo), 'Cartografia da Guerra Guaranítica', Anais do I Simpósio Brasileiro de Cartografia Histórica (2011)

title: Túpac Katari Besieges La Paz
text: Julián Apasa, an Aymara leader, took the name Túpac Katari and claimed to rule as viceroy for the Inca Túpac Amaru. In March 1781 tens of thousands of Aymara community troops laid siege to Spanish-ruled La Paz for more than six months. His wife Bartolina Sisa rode into El Alto as the 'female viceroy'. The rebellion was crushed, and both were executed.

source.name: Sinclair Thomson, 'Moments of Redemption', e-misférica 12.1, Hemispheric Institute (NYU)

title: Peru's Fortune in Bird Droppings
text: Seabird droppings piled up on Peru's Chincha Islands made a prized fertilizer called guano. In 1841 the first full cargo reached Britain, and the islands became so valuable that Spain's seizure of them led to war from 1864 to 1866. The digging was done largely by Chinese contract workers in horrific conditions; a report from the time said very few, if any, survived more than a few months.

source.name: Clark & Foster, 'Ecological Imperialism and the Global Metabolic Rift', International Journal of Comparative Sociology 50 (2009), author copy

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Chincha Islands

title: The War That Emptied Paraguay
text: From 1864 to 1870, Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay at once. The war ended when President Francisco Solano López was killed at Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870. Battle, hunger and disease killed perhaps 60 to 69 percent of Paraguayans, and an 1870 census found young women outnumbering men four or five to one. Argentina and Brazil annexed about 140,000 square kilometres of Paraguayan territory.

source.name: Latin American Research Review 34:1 (1999), Whigham & Potthast, 'The Paraguayan Rosetta Stone' (Cambridge)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'War of the Triple Alliance'

title: Tango Is Born by the River
text: In the 1880s, a new partner dance took shape along the Río de la Plata, the river between Argentina and Uruguay. Many scholars trace the word to Ki-Kongo and say "tango" once covered the dances, drums and meeting places of Black communities there. In the early 1900s tango swept Paris, though by late 1913 its teachers were banished for being too racy.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, tango

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, The First Tango in Paris Made a Stir Worth Remembering

title: The Doctor Who Blamed the Mosquito
text: In 1881 Havana doctor Carlos Finlay, who had trained in eye medicine in Paris, proposed that a mosquito spreads yellow fever from sick people to healthy ones. When he presented the idea to Havana's Royal Academy, the audience met it with ridicule. About twenty years later Walter Reed's US Army board proved him right, and Reed acknowledged Finlay's invaluable contribution.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Carlos J. Finlay

source2.name: Hektoen International, Enrique Chaves-Carballo, 'Carlos J. Finlay: The mosquito man' (2020)

title: An Opera House in the Rainforest
text: Rubber made Manaus, deep in the Amazon, fabulously rich, and the city built an opera house that opened on December 31, 1896. Its dome wears 36,000 glazed tiles from Alsace in the colors of Brazil's flag, with iron columns from Glasgow and Carrara marble from Italy inside. Manaus declined in the 1920s, when the world price of natural rubber collapsed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Manaus

source2.name: National Geographic, famous theatres around the world worth visiting

title: Machu Picchu Reaches the World
text: On July 24, 1911, local resident Melchor Arteaga led Yale scholar Hiram Bingham up to Machu Picchu. The Inca site was never truly lost: local people already knew of it. Bingham made it world-famous, but thousands of objects from his excavations went to Yale, which only began returning them to Peru in 2011, after a long dispute.

source.name: Yale News: Peru-Yale partnership for the future of Machu Picchu artifacts (4 June 2015)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Machu Picchu

title: The Dapper Skull of the Day of the Dead
text: Printmaker José Guadalupe Posada drew an elegant skeleton lady to poke fun at Mexicans who aped European high-society fashions. He called her La Calavera Garbancera, and her earliest known printing dates to around 1913. In 1947 Diego Rivera painted her into a giant mural, naming her La Calavera Catrina, and she became a beloved symbol of the Day of the Dead.

source.name: University of Wisconsin-Madison, Community Altar project: José Guadalupe Posada and the Famous Catrina (E. Belén Chávez-Galván)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: José Guadalupe Posada

title: The First Samba School
text: In 1928, musicians in Rio's Estácio neighborhood founded Deixa Falar ("Let Them Talk"), considered the first samba school. It stood near a teachers' school, and its founders came to be known as "professors". In 1929 it paraded at Carnival as a bloco calling itself a samba school, and its formula gained wide attention at the 1930 and 1931 carnivals.

source.name: Dicionário Cravo Albin da Música Popular Brasileira, Ismael Silva

source2.name: Scripta Nova (Univ. of Barcelona) XVI-418(47): N. da Nóbrega Fernandes (UFF), 'Escolas de samba, identidade nacional e o direito à cidade'

title: Frida Kahlo Paints Two Fridas
text: In 1939, the year she divorced painter Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo painted an unusually large canvas: two versions of herself sitting side by side. One wears a white European-style dress, the other a traditional Tehuana dress, and a single blood vessel links their exposed hearts, perhaps reflecting her German father and Mexican mother. The couple remarried a year later.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Frida Kahlo

title: Evita and the Women's Vote
text: Eva Perón moved to Buenos Aires at 15 to become an actress, and later became Argentina's First Lady. She was largely responsible for winning women the vote: on September 9, 1947, Congress gave final approval to Law 13,010, granting women equal political rights. She died of cancer at just 33.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eva Perón

source2.name: Gobierno de Argentina, 23 de septiembre de 1947: Día del voto femenino

title: The Town That Became Macondo
text: Gabriel García Márquez spent his childhood in his grandparents' house in Aracataca, a small Colombian town that became the model for Macondo, the setting of One Hundred Years of Solitude. Published in 1967, the novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family. It has sold more than 50 million copies in more than 25 languages, and in 1982 he won the Nobel Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, 'Gabriel García Márquez - Biographical' (Nobel Prize in Literature 1982)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' (Drew Milne)

title: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
place: Plaza de Mayo, Buenos Aires, Argentina
text: Under Argentina's military dictatorship, thousands of young people were "disappeared": seized by security forces and never seen again. On April 30, 1977, their mothers began gathering in the square in front of the presidential palace, defying a ban on assemblies. Their white headscarves, first made from babies' diapers, bear their children's names. They still gather on Thursdays.

source.name: Government of Argentina, 'Las Madres de Plaza de Mayo cumplieron 45 años de lucha'

source2.name: El Economista (Argentina), 'Taty Almeida cuenta la historia del panuelo blanco'

title: Itaipu Dam Switches On
text: Brazil and Paraguay built a giant dam together on the Paraná River, and its first generator started running on May 5, 1984. It became one of the world's biggest producers of hydroelectric power. The cost was high: about 65,000 people were displaced, and the reservoir drowned Guaíra Falls, which probably had the greatest volume of falling water in the world.

source.name: Itaipu Binacional, 'Nossa história'

source2.name: Global Infrastructure Hub (G20), 'Itaipu Hydroelectric Dam'

title: The Mudflow That Buried Armero
text: Virtually dormant since 1916, Nevado del Ruiz erupted on November 13, 1985, melting snow and ice into huge mudflows called lahars. They swept over Armero, killing more than 20,000 of its 29,000 residents, even though scientists had explained the danger to Colombia's parliament that September. A photo of Omayra Sánchez, a girl trapped in the debris, became the World Press Photo of the Year.

source.name: Oregon State University, Volcano World: Nevado del Ruiz

source2.name: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: Armero, Colombia

title: Lonesome George, Last of His Kind
text: In 1971 a scientist spotted a lone giant tortoise on Pinta Island, where introduced goats had devastated the tortoises' food supply. He was the last known Pinta Island tortoise, and was moved to the Charles Darwin Research Station. Lonesome George became a worldwide symbol of conservation long before he died on June 24, 2012.

source.name: Charles Darwin Foundation: Remembering the Story of Lonesome George

source2.name: Galapagos Conservancy: The Lonesome George Story (Linda Cayot)

title: The Condor House and Its Golden Crowns
text: Kuntur Wasi was a hilltop temple in Peru's northern Andes, one of the most important ceremonial centers of its time. From 1988, Japanese-led excavations found tombs holding gold crowns, including one with fourteen human faces. The treasures stayed home: touring exhibitions in Japan raised funds, and in 1994 a museum opened in the village, run by an association of local men and women.

source.name: Agencia Andina (Peru's state news agency), 'Cajamarca: renovado museo Kuntur Wasi reabre sus puertas' (quoting the Ministry of Culture's DDC Cajamarca)

source2.name: MINCETUR (Peru Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism), national tourism inventory sheet 'Museo de Sitio Kuntur Wasi'

title: Bugs Frozen in Lebanese Amber
text: Around 130 million years ago, sticky tree resin on the northern coast of the supercontinent Gondwana trapped tiny insects, fungi and even bacteria. Hardened into amber, it is the oldest amber with lots of creatures inside. Many lived just before flowering plants spread, so these drops show a world of bugs that had never visited a flower.

source.name: BMC Ecology and Evolution 2025, 'The oldest continuous association between astigmatid mites and termites preserved in Cretaceous amber'

source2.name: Vršanský et al. 2025, National Science Review, 'Jurassic Park approached: a coccid from Kimmeridgian cheirolepidiacean Aintourine Lebanese amber' (Slovak Academy of Sciences)

dateLabel: Early Pleistocene, about 1.5 million years ago
title: A Bulldozer Finds Early Humans
text: At 'Ubeidiya, south of the Sea of Galilee in the Jordan Valley, bulldozers turned up human bone fragments before excavations began in 1960. Early humans lived here in the early Ice Age alongside hippos, rhinos, elephants and big cats, and made Acheulean stone tools. In 2022 scientists identified a backbone from a child aged about 6 to 12 among the old finds.

source.name: Barash et al. 2022, Scientific Reports 12:1721

title: The Caucasus Hunter's DNA
text: A piece of skull bone from a cave in western Georgia, about 13,300 years old, gave up its owner's genome. He belonged to the Caucasus hunter-gatherers, a group that had split from western Europe's hunters about 45,000 years ago. His people later passed on a large share of the DNA of the Yamnaya herders who spread into Europe around 3000 BC.

source.name: Nature Communications (Jones et al. 2015), via PubMed Central

title: Cyprus and the Pygmy Hippos
text: In a collapsed rock shelter on Cyprus's south coast lies a dense layer of bones from pygmy hippos, a tiny species found only on this island. Stone tools and burnt bones show people were here about 12,500 years ago, the earliest undisputed sign of humans on Cyprus. Did the newcomers hunt the hippos? Experts still fiercely debate it; some think the bones piled up naturally.

source.name: PLOS ONE via PubMed Central (Zazzo et al. 2015)

title: Buried With Her Puppy
text: The Natufians were hunter-gatherers known for stone-built houses and settled villages, long before farming. At ʿAin Mallaha, about 12,000 years ago, a woman was buried with her hand resting on a puppy. This tender grave is one of the earliest signs that people and dogs, or tamed wolves, had become companions.

source.name: Nature (Davis & Valla 1978)

source2.name: PLOS ONE via PubMed Central (Maher et al. 2011)

title: The Royal Mailbag of Mari
text: King Zimri-Lim ruled Mari on the Euphrates for almost 30 prosperous years from a palace of nearly 300 rooms. Its scribes' rooms held thousands of clay tablets: diplomatic letters, reports from across the kingdom, and legal and economic records. Then Hammurabi of Babylon captured and destroyed the city, and the ruined palace kept the archive for archaeologists.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Oldest Surviving Peace Treaty
text: After a long conflict, the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II made peace, backed by a defense pact and a royal marriage. It is the oldest known peace treaty. A clay tablet copy, found in 1906 at the Hittite capital Hattusa, is kept in Istanbul. A copper replica hangs at United Nations headquarters, near the Security Council Chamber.

source.name: United Nations Gifts: Replica of Peace Treaty between Hattusilis and Ramses II

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: Was Troy Real?
text: Troy was destroyed and rebuilt so often that its mound holds nine cities stacked like a layer cake. In the Late Bronze Age, Hittite records call it Wilusa, a vassal of their empire, and the layer named Troy VIIa ended about 1180 BCE. Was this Homer's Troy? Archaeologists still debate how much truth hides inside the legend.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

title: Purple From Smelly Sea Snails
text: Tyrian purple, named after the Phoenician city of Tyre, was a dye made from murex sea snails and highly prized in the ancient world. In 1909 a chemist processed 12,000 snails and got just 1.4 grams of pigment. The snail's fluid starts almost colourless, and the purple develops in air and sunlight.

source.name: Molecules (MDPI, peer-reviewed): Cooksey 2001, 'Tyrian Purple: 6,6'-Dibromoindigo and Related Compounds'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: The Great Mound at Midas's Capital
text: Forget the golden touch: Midas was a real king of Phrygia, called Mita of the Mushki in Assyrian records. At his capital, Gordion, stands a burial mound still 53 metres high. Tree-ring dating puts its wooden tomb chamber at about 740 BCE, too early for Midas himself, so the man in his sixties buried inside may have been his father, Gordios.

source.name: Penn Museum, Digital Gordion: Iron Age Gordion

title: A Tunnel to Save Jerusalem's Water
text: Jerusalem's Gihon spring lay outside the city wall, a big problem in a siege. As Assyria threatened, King Hezekiah of Judah strengthened his capital and dug the famous Siloam tunnel, which carried the spring's water to a reservoir inside the walls. The Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BCE, but Jerusalem itself was not captured.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

title: A Royal Boast 100 Metres Up a Cliff
text: King Darius the Great had his story carved about 100 metres up a cliff beside an ancient trade route: how, he boasted, he fought nineteen battles in a single year to crush rebel kings. The text appears in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In 1835, Henry Rawlinson began copying it with a local Kurdish boy's help, a key step in cracking cuneiform.

source.name: The Conversation (Louise Pryke, Macquarie University)

source2.name: University of Texas at Arlington (translation of the Behistun inscription)

title: "The Sea! The Sea!"
text: Ten thousand Greek soldiers hired to help a Persian prince seize the throne were stranded when he died in battle. Led partly by the writer Xenophon, they marched north through deserts and snowy mountains. On reaching a mountaintop above the Black Sea, they shouted "Thalatta! Thalatta!", meaning "The sea! The sea!" Xenophon's book Anabasis tells the whole adventure.

source.name: Fordham University Internet Ancient History Sourcebook (Xenophon, Anabasis)

title: Burning a Wonder for Fame
text: In 356 BCE the great Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders, burned down. Tradition blames a man named Herostratus who wanted to be famous at any cost, so the city banned anyone from saying his name. Legend adds that Alexander the Great was born the same day, and the goddess was too busy to save her temple.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Romana (James Grout), hosted by the University of Chicago

title: The Library That Named Parchment
text: The Attalid kings of Pergamon, above all Eumenes II, built up a library said to hold about 200,000 scrolls, the great rival of Alexandria's. Ancient writers said parchment, prepared animal skin for writing, was invented here, and the word comes from the city's name. Plutarch reports a claim that Mark Antony gave the whole collection to Cleopatra, though no one knows if that happened.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Romana (J. Grout), hosted by the University of Chicago

title: Rome's Richest Man Meets Parthia
text: Crassus, the wealthiest man in Rome, marched seven legions into the desert hoping for glory. Near Carrhae, the Parthian general Surena surrounded them with armoured cavalry and horse archers, kept supplied with arrows by a train of camels. Most Romans were killed or captured, and Crassus died during truce talks, ending Rome's First Triumvirate.

source.name: National Geographic History, 'Crassus was the richest man in Rome'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'CARRHAE'

title: The Painted Synagogue Saved by an Earth Wall
text: In 244 or 245 CE, the Jewish community of Dura-Europos, a frontier town on the Euphrates, finished enlarging their synagogue and covered its walls with painted scenes from the Bible. About a decade later, Roman soldiers buried it inside a great earth bank built to strengthen the city wall against the Persian siege of 256. The buried west wall survived almost complete until archaeologists dug it out in 1932.

source.name: Yale University Art Gallery, Dura-Europos: 'Synagogue'

source2.name: Sasanika: Late Antique Near East Project (University of California, Irvine), 'Dura-Europos'

title: Nino and the Grapevine Cross
text: A woman named Nino arrived in the Kingdom of Iberia, in today's Georgia, preaching Christianity. Church tradition says she healed Queen Nana and then won over King Mirian III, who made Christianity the official religion, traditionally around 326. She is said to have carried a cross of grapevine branches tied with her own hair, and her grave is honoured at Bodbe in eastern Georgia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Georgian Orthodox church'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Historical Monuments of Mtskheta' (Mirian III established Christianity as official religion; read via UNESCO open data)

title: An Alphabet Built for Armenian
text: Around 405, the scholar Mesrop Mashtots created a brand-new alphabet of 36 letters so Armenians could write their own language. According to his pupil Koryun, the first words written in it were the opening line of the Book of Proverbs. Back in the royal city of Vagharshapat, he set about translating and teaching, and with just two added letters, Armenians still use his alphabet today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint Mesrop Mashtots'

source2.name: Koryun, The Life of Mashtots, tr. Bedros Norehad (armenianhouse.org)

title: The Spiral Minaret of Samarra
text: Caliph al-Mutawakkil built the Great Mosque of Samarra in the mid-800s, and when it was finished it was the largest mosque in the world, the mosque building alone measuring 239 by 156 metres. Its minaret, the Malwiya, rises about 55 metres, wrapped by a ramp that spirals five times to the top, so you walk up the outside like a helter-skelter.

source.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT), 'Jami' al-Mutawakkil (Samarra)'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Samarra Archaeological City (via data.unesco.org)

title: Ferdowsi Finishes the Book of Kings
text: The poet Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, or Book of Kings, around 977 and finished it on 8 March 1010. It retells Iran's legends and history in some 50,000 to 60,000 rhyming couplets. Much of it was based on an older Middle Persian Book of Kings that ran down to the end of Sasanian times.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ferdowsi'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ferdowsi, Abu'l-Qasem i. Life'

title: An Emperor Captured at Manzikert
text: Near Manzikert, the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army and captured the wounded Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes himself. The sultan released him only after the emperor agreed to give up important territories. The defeat weakened Byzantine control of Anatolia and opened the way for Turkish raiding and settlement there.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Battle of Manzikert' (Tony Bunting)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Alp Arslan'

title: Tamar, the King of Georgia
text: In 1184 Tamar became sole ruler of Georgia, an exception to succession rules that recognized only male heirs. Many nobles were suspicious of a woman on the throne, but church inscriptions hailed her as 'King of Kings'. Her reign was the peak of Georgia's Golden Age, and the poet Shota Rustaveli, an adoring subject, later wrote the national epic, The Knight in the Panther's Skin.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Shota Rustaveli, by Donald Rayfield)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Tamara, queen of Georgia)

title: Al-Jazari's Book of Robots
text: At the Artuqid court of Amid, today's Diyarbakır, the engineer al-Jazari finished a book in 1206 describing fifty mechanical devices, with instructions to build them. They included clocks, moving peacocks, drinking vessels, fountains and hand-washing machines. His elephant clock marked each half hour: a bird turned, a falcon dropped a ball into a dragon's mouth, and the driver struck the elephant.

source.name: Science Museum Group Collection

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Elephant Clock', folio from al-Jazari's Book of the Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (catalogue entry by Francesca Leoni)

title: Rumi Meets a Wandering Dervish
text: Rumi was a respected teacher in Konya until he met a mysterious wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, in 1244. The friendship turned him into a mystic poet. When Shams vanished, Rumi poured his grief into verse, later writing the Masnavi. After his death, his whirling meditation became the dance of the whirling dervishes, and today he is a best-selling poet in America.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: BBC Culture, Jane Ciabattari, 'Why is Rumi the best-selling poet in the US?' (21 Oct 2014)

title: The Mongols Take Baghdad
text: Hulegu, a Mongol prince, attacked Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid caliphs, early in 1258. Despite brave resistance by the caliph's troops and townspeople, the city was taken on 13 February and suffered a week of looting and massacre. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim, was executed along with most of his family.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Hulagu Khan' (Reuven Amitai)

title: Mecca Bans Coffee
text: Coffee, grown in Yemen from the 1400s, spread quickly among Arabs and gave rise to a new kind of meeting place, the coffeehouse. In 1511 the ruler of Mecca issued a decree banning the drink. The ban did not succeed: coffee kept spreading, and later attempts to outlaw it, such as England's in 1675, failed too.

source.name: Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings (A. B. Weisse, 'Coffee: grounds for concern?', 2015), PubMed Central

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'coffee'

title: The Ardabil Carpet
text: Weavers under Shah Tahmasp spent about four years making a pair of silk-and-wool carpets for the shrine at Ardabil; nobody knows for certain where they were woven. The London one is over 10 metres long, with about 5,300 knots in every 10-centimetre square, and its woven date of 1539–40 is the earliest on any Persian carpet.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum (collections record: The Ardabil Carpet)

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum (The Ardabil Carpet)

title: Sinan's Dome Rivals Hagia Sophia
text: The architect Mimar Sinan called the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne his masterpiece. Built for Sultan Selim II, it is crowned by a single great dome about 31.5 metres across, roughly as wide as the dome of Hagia Sophia. Four soaring, slender minarets, the loftiest in Turkey, frame it and dominate the city skyline.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Selimiye Mosque and its Social Complex)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sinan, the Ottoman Empire's Master Architect; Sinan)

title: Persia and England Take Hormuz
text: For over a century, a Portuguese fortress on Hormuz Island controlled shipping in and out of the Persian Gulf. In 1622 Shah Abbas's army teamed up with English East India Company ships and captured it, ending Portuguese rule. Earlier in the same campaign, the famous Arctic explorer William Baffin was killed in the Anglo-Persian attack on nearby Qeshm island.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Hormuz)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (William Baffin)

title: Evliya Çelebi Hits the Road
text: Evliya Çelebi first described his home city of Istanbul, and in 1640 began travelling beyond it. He avoided court jobs that might tie him down and kept wandering for about 40 years. His ten-book Book of Travels, the longest travel account in Islamic literature, is still a favourite window into Ottoman life, even recording details of the many languages he heard.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Evliya Celebi)

source2.name: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination, Evliya Çelebi's 'Book of Travels'

title: Lady Mary Learns Smallpox Engrafting
text: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of Britain's ambassador, arrived in Edirne in March 1717. Smallpox had killed her brother and scarred her face, so she watched closely as locals practised engrafting: putting a little smallpox matter into a scratch to cause a mild case and protection. Back in England, she campaigned to spread the idea.

source.name: Royal Society blog, 'Lady Mary's letters' (2024)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lady Mary Wortley Montagu'

title: A Shepherd Clan's Son Crowned Shah
text: Nader was born in 1688 into a humble pastoral family of the Afshar Turkmen. He rose to command Iran's armies, and in February 1736 he gathered the realm's leaders at a vast camp on the Moghan steppe and asked them to choose either him or a Safavid prince to rule. On 8 March 1736 he was crowned Nader Shah.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Nāder Shah' (Ernest Tucker)

title: Mount Ararat Shakes and Slides
text: On July 2, 1840, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Mount Ararat, near where three tectonic plates meet. It set off huge avalanches and mud and debris flows, possibly with a small eruption, that buried the village of Akori and its old Armenian monastery. More than 1,000 people died, and the governor's palace at Doğubayazıt was badly damaged.

source.name: Geoheritage (Springer Nature), 'The Geoheritage of Mount Ararat and its Vicinity' (2026)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mount Ararat

title: Layard Digs Up Assyria
text: In 1845, the young adventurer Austen Henry Layard began digging the mounds of Nimrud on the Tigris. Over two years he uncovered huge stone palace carvings of the Assyrian kings. His book Nineveh and Its Remains became a bestseller, and he later found the famous library of Ashurbanipal too.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Austen Henry Layard

source2.name: NYU Institute for the Study of the Ancient World Library, Austen Henry Layard and the early exploration of Nimrud

title: A College Opens With 16 Students
text: The Syrian Protestant College opened in Beirut with just 16 students, led by its president Daniel Bliss. At first classes were taught in Arabic, until a crisis in 1882 led to a switch to English. Renamed the American University of Beirut in 1920, it began admitting women to its schools of medicine, pharmacy and dentistry, and to its arts and sciences faculty, in 1921.

source.name: American University of Beirut, History

source2.name: American University of Beirut, Faculty of Medicine history

title: A Whole Country Quits Smoking
text: In 1890 the shah sold an Englishman a 50-year monopoly over all Iranian tobacco. Merchants and clerics revolted; Isfahan boycotted tobacco even before a top cleric issued a ruling against using it in December 1891. The ban worked so well that, it was said, even the shah's harem quit. In January 1892 he cancelled the deal.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Isfahan viii. Qajar period

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Qajar dynasty viii. 'Big Merchants' in the late Qajar period

title: Oil Strikes Just Before Giving Up
text: After seven years and close to half a million pounds, the company searching for oil in Persia cabled its engineer, Reynolds, to stop operations altogether. Reynolds held off replying, and on 26 May 1908 his well at Masjed Soleyman struck oil, the first oil field in the Middle East. The company behind the find grew into today's BP.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: D'Arcy, William Knox

source2.name: AAPG Explorer: The First Oil Field in the Middle East, by Rasoul Sorkhabi (2018)

title: Camels Take Aqaba From the Desert
text: During the Arab Revolt, Sherif Nasir, the Howeitat leader Auda abu Tayi and T. E. Lawrence set out in May 1917 with a small band of about 50 Arab fighters. They gathered allies on a long desert march and attacked the Red Sea port of Aqaba from the land side. On 6 July its Ottoman garrison surrendered, the Arab forces' first major victory.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: T.E. Lawrence

source2.name: Clio Visualizing History: The Taking of Akaba - 1917 (Lowell Thomas and Lawrence of Arabia exhibit)

title: Turkey Switches Alphabets in Months
text: In 1928 Turkey replaced the Arabic-based Ottoman script with a new Latin-based alphabet. Atatürk announced the change in a speech at Sarayburnu in Istanbul on 9 August, cut an expert commission's long-term plan down to three months, and toured the country teaching the letters himself. From 1 December 1928, newspapers were banned from printing in Arabic letters.

source.name: OPUS Journal of Society Research (Tosun Durmuş 2026, Marmara Univ.), via DergiPark

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kemal Atatürk

title: The Seventh Well Strikes It Rich
text: American geologist Max Steineke and Saudi Bedouin guide Khamis bin Rimthan kept searching after six wells near Dammam came up short. On 4 March 1938, Dammam No. 7 struck oil in commercial quantities about 1,440 metres down, the first in Saudi Arabia. Later nicknamed the Prosperity Well, it pumped over 32 million barrels before closing in 1982.

source.name: Aramco, Elements magazine: The desert pioneer behind our first oil discovery (2025)

source2.name: Aramco World, Well Done, Well Seven (1988)

title: Mosaddegh Nationalizes Iran's Oil
text: In 1951 Iran's new prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddegh, nationalized the British-run Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, whose refinery at Abadan had grown to be the world's largest. Britain answered with gunboats, a boycott and an appeal to the UN Security Council, and Time named Mosaddegh its Person of the Year. In 1953 a British and American-backed coup overthrew him, which the US admitted in 2013.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mohammad Mosaddegh'

source2.name: National Security Archive (George Washington University), 'CIA Confirms Role in 1953 Iran Coup' (19 Aug 2013)

title: A Revolution Armed With Roses
text: After disputed elections, Georgians protested for twenty days in November 2003. At the climax, demonstrators led by Mikheil Saakashvili burst into parliament holding red roses, and President Eduard Shevardnadze resigned. The peaceful change of power, called the Rose Revolution, became one of the first of the so-called colour revolutions across the former Soviet world.

source.name: Global Nonviolent Action Database, Swarthmore College: Georgians overthrow a dictator (Rose Revolution), 2003

source2.name: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty: The 10th Anniversary of Georgia's Rose Revolution

title: Saudi Women Take the Wheel
text: Until 2018, Saudi Arabia was the only country where women were banned from driving. In 1990, around 40 women drove through Riyadh in protest, and in 2011 activists like Manal al-Sharif posted videos of themselves at the wheel. The ban was finally lifted on 24 June 2018, though many of the campaigners were still under arrest.

source.name: Amnesty International: Saudi Arabia - Women now allowed to drive, but more reforms must follow (21 June 2018)

source2.name: Al Jazeera: Saudi women hit the road as driving ban is lifted (24 June 2018)

title: Twin Earthquakes Shake Turkey and Syria
text: Before dawn on 6 February 2023, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck south-central Turkey near the Syrian border, followed about nine hours later by a magnitude 7.5 shock. By the end of March more than 57,000 people had died. The aftershocks stretched for about 400 kilometres, from the Mediterranean coast inland to Malatya.

source.name: USGS: Frequently Asked Questions about 2023 Earthquakes in Turkiye

source2.name: University of Potsdam / GFZ, DFG Research Training Group NatRiskChange, 'Task Force on the 2023 Türkiye Earthquake Sequence'

title: The Dinosaur Known Only by Its Arms
text: In 1965 a Polish-Mongolian expedition in the Gobi dug up a pair of giant arms 2.4 metres long, and little else. For almost fifty years Deinocheirus stayed a mystery. Two fuller skeletons, described in 2014, revealed a heavily built giant with a long snout, a deep jaw and tall spines on its back that ate both plants and fish.

source.name: Nature (Lee et al. 2014, "Resolving the long-standing enigmas of a giant ornithomimosaur Deinocheirus mirificus"), abstract

title: Two Teeth From Yuanmou
text: Two human front teeth dug from the Yuanmou Basin in Yunnan are thought to belong to Homo erectus. Magnetic dating of the rock layers puts them at about 1.7 million years old, the earliest known sign of humans in mainland East Asia. Stone tools were found too, and fossils and pollen show these people lived in open country with patches of forest, near a lake or swamp.

source.name: Zhu et al. 2008, Journal of Human Evolution (abstract via PubMed)

source2.name: Zhu et al. 2018, Nature 559:608-612

title: The World's Oldest Fishhooks
text: In a cave on Okinawa Island, archaeologists found fishhooks ground from the shells of Trochus sea snails. Dated to about 23,000 years ago, they were reported as the world's oldest fishhooks, as old as or older than ones from Timor and New Ireland in Papua New Guinea. Ice Age islanders here were clearly skilled at living off the sea.

source.name: Fujita et al. 2016, PNAS (PubMed Central)

title: Taiwan's First Footprints
text: Stone tools in the Baxian Caves on Taiwan's east coast are the island's earliest evidence of people, about 30,000 years old. The caves were carved by waves at sea level, but the land has risen so much that they now sit high on a cliff. The caves are the main site of the Changbin culture, which lasted until about 5,000 years ago.

source.name: National Tsing Hua University Library exhibition 'Taiwan coastal sites' (Baxian Caves; NTHU Institute of Anthropology)

source2.name: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Encyclopedia of Taiwan Indigenous Peoples (NCCU), 'Baxian Cave archaeological site'

title: Korea's Oldest Pots
text: At Gosan-ri on Jeju Island, people made a unique kind of pottery with plant fibers mixed into the clay. It is found only at early sites on Jeju and is the oldest known pottery in Korea. A 2020 radiocarbon study of charcoal found with the pots dated them to about 7670–7550 BCE, younger than some earlier estimates.

source.name: Radiocarbon (Cambridge University Press), Kim et al. 2020

title: Farmers on the Roof of the World
text: High on the Tibetan Plateau, Neolithic villagers at Karuo built a settlement with houses, paved roads and stone walls. Excavated in 1978–79, it was the first settlement site ever dug on the plateau, yielding stone tools, pottery and bone objects. Seeds suggest millet was probably grown there from about 2700 BCE, alongside hunting, fishing and foraging.

source.name: ChinaCulture.org (P.R. China Ministry of Culture)

source2.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2021), Karuo archaeobotany

title: The City That Rewrote China's Story
text: At Shimao, on the loess highland of northern China, archaeologists have uncovered a great Bronze Age centre that was thriving by about 2000 BCE. It challenges the old idea that Chinese civilisation began later in the Central Plains: important symbols once thought to be Central Plains inventions were created much earlier here.

source.name: Antiquity (Jaang, Sun, Shao & Li 2018, 'When peripheries were centres')

title: Japan's Great Stone Rings
text: Late Jōmon people in northern Japan built two great rings of river stones around 2000–1500 BCE. The larger, the Manza circle, is 52 metres across; its neighbour, Nonakado, is 44. Around them stood pillar-supported buildings, storage pits and graves, and a line through the two centres points to the summer-solstice sunset. It is part of a World Heritage Site.

source.name: Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, official World Heritage website

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

title: The Boat Coffins of Xiaohe
place: Xiaohe Cemetery, Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China
text: In a seven-metre mound of sand in the desert near the dried-up lake Lop Nur, Bronze Age people buried their dead in boat-shaped coffins. The dry desert turned the bodies into some of the famous Tarim mummies; Xiaohe's oldest burials date to about 1900–1700 BCE. DNA showed a surprise: they were a long-isolated local people, not newcomers from the west.

source.name: Nature: Zhang et al. 2021, 'The genomic origins of the Bronze Age Tarim Basin mummies'

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: 'The Mummies of East Central Asia'

title: The First Bronze to Say 'China'
text: Inside this early Zhou bronze wine vessel, a 122-character inscription tells of King Cheng and his new capital near today's Luoyang. It includes the words 'zhong guo', the first recorded use of the name later used for China. The vessel was unearthed near Baoji, Shaanxi, in 1963 and is now kept in the Baoji Bronze Ware Museum.

source.name: CGTN (China Global Television Network)

source2.name: China Daily (government portal edition)

title: A Bronze Age Rice Village
text: Songguk-ri was the largest Bronze Age village in southwestern Korea, with over 110 small round pit-houses and a palisade wall around parts of it. A prominent stone cist grave held a rare lute-shaped bronze dagger, a bronze chisel and jade beads, probably for a local leader. Plant remains suggest rice, grown in wet paddy fields, was commonly eaten by ordinary villagers.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Research (2024), 'Community Formation in the Chulmun (Neolithic) and Mumun (Bronze Age) Periods of Korea'

source2.name: Korea.net (official website of the Republic of Korea), 'Heritage & Relics of Korea, part 1'

title: The Oldest Copy of the Tao Te Ching
text: In late 1993 archaeologists excavated a tomb near the old Chu capital, dated to around 300 BCE, and found about 800 bamboo slips, 730 of them with writing. Among the texts were the oldest known manuscripts of the Laozi, the Tao Te Ching, alongside Confucian writings. Robbers had entered the tomb earlier, so nobody knows how much was lost.

source.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Laozi'

source2.name: Early China (Cambridge University Press), P. Goldin, 'Xunzi in the Light of the Guodian Manuscripts' (abstract)

title: Modu Builds a Steppe Empire
text: The historian Sima Qian tells how Modu trained his riders to shoot wherever his whistling arrow flew, then used that loyalty to kill his father and seize power around 209 BCE. He united the steppe nomads into the Xiongnu Empire. Around 200 BCE his horsemen surrounded the Han emperor himself at Pingcheng, and Han China agreed to send yearly gifts of silk, wine and rice.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington, 'Xiongnu'

source2.name: Sima Qian, Shiji (Chinese text), Project Gutenberg ebook 24226, ch. 110 (Xiongnu) and ch. 8 (Gaozu)

title: The King of Dian's Golden Seal
text: The Dian kingdom of Yunnan was famous for bronzes showing animals in combat and lively scenes of daily life. In 109 BCE its king accepted Han overlordship and received a gold seal from Emperor Wu. When archaeologists opened a rich royal tomb at Shizhaishan in December 1956, that very seal, inscribed 'Seal of the King of Dian', proved the kingdom in the old histories was real.

source.name: Bulletin of SOAS 87(2), 2024, 'The Southwest Silk Road: artistic exchange and transmission in early China' (open access)

source2.name: China Daily, Deng Zhangyu, 'Discoveries give the ancient past a future'

title: The 27-Day Emperor's Treasure Tomb
text: Liu He was made emperor of Han China and then thrown out after just 27 days. Later demoted to Marquis of Haihun, he died in 59 BCE. His tomb held more than 10,000 objects, including 478 gold ingots and plates weighing about 115 kilograms, a long-lost version of the Analects and the earliest surviving portrait of Confucius.

source.name: Fairbank Center for Chinese Studies, Harvard University, 'Excavating the Marquis of Haihun's Tomb'

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

title: Yoshinogari's Moats and Watchtowers
text: Yayoi villagers on Kyushu dug a deep V-shaped moat about 2.5 kilometres long around their settlement, topped with fences and watchtowers. Inside stood raised storehouses, shrines and bronze-casting workshops. Excavated from 1986, it closely matches Chinese descriptions of Queen Himiko's land of Yamatai, though no proof links the two.

source.name: Yoshinogari Historical Park (national government park), 'The History of Yoshinogari'

source2.name: Yoshinogari Historical Park, FAQ (Japanese) and Reconstructed Buildings pages

title: Letters Buried in the Taklamakan
text: Niya, the little kingdom of Jingjue, was a busy oasis on the southern Silk Road at the edge of the Taklamakan Desert. Explorer Aurel Stein dug up hundreds of wooden tablets there, some sealed with clay, holding official documents written in Kharoshthi, an Indian script. The Han histories counted 3,360 people here, and by the 3rd century it was a dependency of Shanshan, formerly called Loulan.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Stein Collection' (object O90079, Niya)

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington), John E. Hill, Weilue translation and notes, section 5.4 (quoting Stein on the Han shu)

title: A Goguryeo Tomb Full of Paintings
text: Anak Tomb No. 3 is the earliest dated painted tomb of Goguryeo, with portraits of the dead man and his wife and a great procession of some 250 figures. Its ink epitaph of 357 names Dong Shou, but after 70 years scholars still argue whether he was an exile from the northern state of Former Yan or the tomb is really a Goguryeo king's.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Korean art: Three Kingdoms period'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Complex of Koguryo Tombs'

title: A Sword From Baekje to Japan
text: This strange iron blade, 75 centimetres long, has three branches sprouting from each side, so it was made for ritual, not fighting. Its gold-inlaid inscription, dated 369, says it was made for the ruler of Wa (Yamato) and mentions the king of the Korean kingdom of Baekje and a prince. It has long been kept at Isonokami Shrine as a sacred object.

source.name: Kokugakuin University, Encyclopedia of Shinto, 'Shichishito'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Japan: Rise and expansion of Yamato'

title: The Sword's Hidden Gold Letters
text: An iron sword dug from a burial mound in 1968 looked ordinary, until rust removal during conservation in 1978 revealed 115 Chinese characters inlaid in gold. They name a warrior, Wowake, who served Great King Wakatakeru, usually identified as Emperor Yūryaku. Most date it to 471, making it a precious early example of Japanese names written in Chinese characters.

source.name: Saitama Prefectural Museum of the Sakitama Ancient Burial Mounds, 'Kinsakumei tekken' (gold-inlaid iron sword)

source2.name: Gyoda City (official), 'Musashi Sakitama Inariyama Kofun excavated objects'

title: The World's Oldest Wooden Buildings
text: Prince Shōtoku founded Hōryū-ji in 607, just decades after Buddhism reached Japan. Fire destroyed it in 670, but rebuilding began soon after, and its main hall and pagoda are among the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world. The pagoda's 32.5-metre central pillar comes from a Japanese cypress tree felled in 594.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Horyu Temple)

title: Queen Seondeok's Star Tower
text: Built in the reign of Queen Seondeok of Silla (632–647), Cheomseongdae is the oldest surviving observatory in Asia and maybe the world. The bottle-shaped tower stands 9 metres tall, and its curved body is said to use 365 cut stones, one for each day of the year. Stargazers probably climbed in through a window halfway up.

source.name: UNESCO-IAU Portal to the Heritage of Astronomy

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Gyeongju Historic Areas)

title: The Rebellion That Broke the Tang
text: An Lushan, a general who had won the trust of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, marched his army out of Fanyang in December 755. The rebels captured the capital Chang'an, and the emperor fled to Sichuan. The war dragged on until 763 as rebel leaders were killed by their own sons, leaving the Tang dynasty badly weakened.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (An Lushan)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Xuanzong)

title: Chang Pogo, King of the Yellow Sea
text: A commoner from the coast, Chang Pogo became an officer in a Tang army, then came home angry at pirates who seized Koreans and sold them as slaves. In 828 the Silla king let him set up the Cheonghae garrison on Wando with 10,000 men. From there his fleet dominated trade between Silla, Tang China and Japan, and Wando villagers still honour him as a guardian god.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Korea: Unified Silla)

source2.name: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies), '장보고' (Jang Bogo)

title: The Town Named After an Emperor
text: Potters in this Jiangxi town were already making fine ware when Emperor Zhenzong's reign, called Jingde, gave the place its new name in 1004. By the late 1100s it was exporting porcelain in great quantities, and later it made blue-and-white wares for the Ming court and ran the Qing imperial kilns. It still makes porcelain today and is nicknamed China's Porcelain Capital.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jingdezhen'

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Jar with dragon (Xuande), 37.191.1

title: Goryeo's Jade-Green Celadon
text: Korean potters learned celadon from China, but by the mid-1100s Goryeo had its own style. Their special trick, sanggam, was a way of inlaying designs such as flying cranes with black and white slip, a technique rare in China. A Song envoy who visited in 1123 compared Goryeo wares with China's famous celadons, and many pieces came from kilns at Gangjin.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline (Soyoung Lee)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Goryeo Celadon (re-read)

title: Eighty Thousand Blocks Against the Mongols
text: When Mongol invaders burned Korea's first set of Buddhist printing blocks, King Gojong ordered a new one, hoping to win the Buddha's help. Carving began in 1237 and took about twelve years. The result, 81,352 wooden blocks with over 52 million characters, survives in pristine condition at Haeinsa temple after more than 750 years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

source2.name: Korea.net (Korean Culture and Information Service, Government of the Republic of Korea)

title: The Divine Wind
text: Kublai Khan sent fleets of Mongol, Chinese and Korean troops against Japan twice, in 1274 and 1281. After the first attack, the samurai built a stone wall about 20 kilometres long along Hakata Bay. Typhoons wrecked the invasion fleets, and the Japanese called them kamikaze, 'divine wind', a word reused centuries later for suicide pilots.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica

source2.name: City of Fukuoka official site (gofukuoka.jp): Genko Borui articles

title: Huang Daopo Brings Home Cotton Know-How
text: According to a well-known legend, Huang Daopo was a child bride so badly treated by her in-laws that she fled to Hainan, where the local Li people taught her about cotton. In the mid-1290s she returned to Songjiang, near Shanghai, and taught local people, spreading tools such as a treadle wheel that spun three threads at once. A textile industry then prospered around her village.

source.name: Shanghai Municipal People's Government Information Office

source2.name: Harriet T. Zurndorfer (Leiden University), 'The Resistant Fibre: The Pre-modern History of Cotton in China', LSE Global Economic History Network paper

title: The Oldest Book Printed With Metal Type
text: Monks at Heungdeok Temple printed a collection of Zen Buddhist teachings using movable metal type in 1377, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible. Only the second volume of that printing survives. A French diplomat acquired it while serving in Korea in the late 1800s, and it now sits in the National Library of France, its ownership a long-running controversy.

source.name: University of Utah, 'From Jikji to Gutenberg' research project

source2.name: Seoul National University, SNU NOW, '[Alumni Story] A History of Ownership' (2009)

title: The Forbidden City Is Finished
text: Built from 1406 to 1420 for the Yongle Emperor, Beijing's walled palace covers 72 hectares, with nearly 10,000 rooms and great halls raised on a triple marble terrace. 24 Ming and Qing emperors lived there, and the last emperor, Puyi, stayed until 1924. Since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum, now visited by millions.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Forbidden City'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (read via data.unesco.org)

title: The Philosopher Who Won a War
text: Wang Yangming taught that knowing and doing are one thing. In 1519 he got to prove it: when the Prince of Ning rebelled, Wang surrounded the prince's base at Nanchang and, four days later, beat him in battle and captured him. His ideas spread across China and later inspired Japanese reformers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Wang Yangming)

source2.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Wang Yangming)

title: Sen no Rikyū and the Way of Tea
text: Born into a merchant family in the busy port of Sakai, Sen no Rikyū became tea master to Toyotomi Hideyoshi and shaped the tea ceremony around rustic simplicity, called wabi. His tiny two-mat Tai-an tea room still stands at a temple in Kyoto Prefecture. In 1591 Hideyoshi ordered him to take his own life, for reasons that remain unclear.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sen Rikyu)

source2.name: Sakai City (official site): Sen no Rikyu

title: Okuni Invents Kabuki
text: Said to have served at the Grand Shrine of Izumo, Okuni led a troupe of female dancers who in 1603 performed on a makeshift stage in the dry bed of Kyoto's Kamo River, sometimes dressed as a young man. The style became known as Okuni Kabuki. Ironically, the shogun banned women from kabuki in 1629, and men still play every role today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Okuni)

source2.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (Kabuki theatre)

title: The White Heron Castle
text: Ikeda Terumasa, made lord of Himeji after the Battle of Sekigahara, rebuilt Himeji Castle from 1601 to 1609 into a huge complex of 83 buildings. Its gleaming white walls earned it the name White Heron Castle. In 1945 bombing destroyed most of the city around it, and local stories tell of a firebomb that landed in the castle without exploding.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Himeji-jo), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (White Heron Castle)

title: King Injo's Mountain Fortress
text: When the Qing invaded Korea in 1636, King Injo fled into Namhansanseong, a mountain fortress built and defended by Buddhist monk-soldiers. He held out for 47 days against a huge Qing army while food ran low. After Ganghwa Island fell, Injo and the crown prince surrendered at Samjeondo, bowing in submission before the Qing emperor Hong Taiji.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Namhansanseong), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: Gyeonggi Provincial Government (Namhansanseong Fortress)

title: The Fifth Dalai Lama's Palace
text: In 1645 the Fifth Dalai Lama began building the Potala on a hill in Lhasa, on the site of an older palace linked to Songtsen Gampo. Enclosed by massive walls of rammed earth and stone, it rises 13 floors and holds over 1,000 rooms and some 200,000 statues. For centuries it served as the Dalai Lamas' winter palace.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Potala Palace' (Kathleen Sheetz)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace (text via data.unesco.org API)

title: A Dutch Sailor Stuck in Joseon
text: In 1653 the Dutch ship carrying bookkeeper Hendrick Hamel wrecked off Jeju Island on its way to Japan. Joseon would not let foreigners leave, so the crew stayed thirteen years, helped by another shipwrecked Dutchman, Jan Weltevree. In 1666 Hamel escaped by boat to Japan, and his journal became the first Western eyewitness account of Korea.

source.name: Atlas of Mutual Heritage (Dutch Cultural Heritage Agency / Nationaal Archief): Sperwer wreck

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Korea: The introduction of Roman Catholicism'

title: Bashō Walks the Narrow Road North
text: In spring 1689 the poet Matsuo Bashō and his friend Sora set out on foot from Edo to the deep north, visiting places old poets had praised, such as Matsushima and Hiraizumi. His travel diary mixing prose and haiku, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, appeared in 1702. Sora's own diary shows Bashō polished the facts for art.

source.name: Nippon.com (Nippon Communications Foundation), Fukasawa Shinji, 'The Narrow Road Through the Hinterlands: Walking with Bashō on a Journey of Invention'

source2.name: Nippon.com, Richard Medhurst, 'Fish Tears and Farewells: The Start of a Poetic Journey'

title: Kim Jeong-ho's Folding Map of Korea
text: In 1861 the mapmaker Kim Jeong-ho printed Daedongyeojido, a map of Korea at a scale of about 1:160,000. It came as 22 folding booklets printed from woodblocks carved on both sides. Joined together, they form a map about 6.7 metres tall and 3.8 metres wide, marking mountain ridges, rivers, towns, roads and military posts, and woodblock printing let it circulate widely.

source.name: Korea Heritage Service, Heritage Search: Daedong yeojido (Treasure)

source2.name: National Museum of Korea, Daedong yeojido woodblocks

title: Tomioka's French-Built Silk Mill
text: Meiji Japan opened this model silk mill in 1872 with 300 reeling machines from France, worked mostly by young women. At first no one would come: French staff were seen drinking red wine, and rumours spread that they drank fresh blood. The manager's daughter, Yū, volunteered as the first worker to reassure families. The mill ran until 1987.

source.name: Nippon.com (Nippon Communications Foundation), 'The World Heritage Tomioka Silk Mill'

title: The End of the Ryukyu Kingdom
text: For centuries the Ryukyu Kingdom kept up tributary ties with both China and Japan. In March 1879 Meiji official Matsuda Michiyuki landed with police and army units and told the royal court that the kingdom was abolished and Okinawa Prefecture created. King Shō Tai was ordered to live in Tokyo, ending some 500 years of Ryukyu Kingdom rule.

source.name: Nippon.com (Nippon Communications Foundation), Shuri Castle: At the Heart of the Former Ryukyu Kingdom

source2.name: Okinawa Prefectural Educational Center, Okinawa's History: Dissolution of the Domains and Establishment of the Prefectures

title: British Troops March to Lhasa
text: Fearing Russian influence, Lord Curzon, Britain's viceroy of India, sent Francis Younghusband into Tibet with a military escort, and the force set out from Sikkim in December 1903. Tibetan soldiers with old weapons faced machine guns, and many were killed. The British stormed the fortress at Gyantse, entered Lhasa in August 1904 and forced a trade treaty on Tibet.

source.name: National Army Museum: 40th Pathans at Lhala House, Lhasa, August 1904 (NAM. 1987-11-97-15)

source2.name: National Army Museum: Tibetan casualty, 31 March 1904 (NAM. 1960-02-111-121)

title: Qiu Jin, the Woman Knight-Errant
text: Qiu Jin learned to ride and use a sword, left her marriage to study in Japan, and called herself the Female Knight-Errant of Jian Lake. Back in Shaoxing she ran a school that trained revolutionaries. After a failed uprising against the Qing she was executed in 1907, aged 31, and is now honoured as a hero of feminism and the republic.

source.name: Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale), 'Qiu Jin (c. 1875-1907)', via Encyclopedia.com

title: China's Own Railway Through the Mountains
text: The Beijing–Zhangjiakou line, opened in 1909, was the first railway in China designed and built entirely by Chinese engineers. To climb the steep mountains near Badaling, chief engineer Zhan Tianyou laid a zigzag track shaped like the character 人 (person). That cut the length of tunnel needed at Badaling, and trains could descend the slopes more gradually.

source.name: China Daily: Nation makes tracks for progress (2 Aug 2019)

source2.name: China Daily: Qinglongqiao zigzag section 'which Zhan designed' (1 Oct 2022)

title: An Jung-geun at Harbin Station
text: Korean independence activist An Jung-geun shot Itō Hirobumi, Japan's former Resident-General of Korea, at Harbin in 1909, and was executed in 1910. Koreans honour him as a martyr, while Japan's government has called him a terrorist. In prison he wrote admired calligraphy, signed with a handprint missing a fingertip, cut off as a pledge.

source.name: Seo-gu District Office, Busan Metropolitan City (Korean local government): An Jung-geun calligraphy (Treasure No. 569-6)

source2.name: The Korea Herald: An's prison handwriting repatriated from Japan

title: Mongolia Breaks Away From the Qing
text: As the Qing dynasty crumbled, Mongol leaders in Urga declared independence on December 1, 1911. Four weeks later, on December 29, they enthroned the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, the highest Buddhist lama in Mongolia, as Bogd Khan ("Holy King"), uniting religious and political power. His state lasted until 1924.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mongolia, Independence and revolution

source2.name: The Journal of Northeast Asian History 19(1), 'Khaisan and the 1911 Independence of Mongolia' (Hankuk University of Foreign Studies)

title: Taiwan's 228 Incident
text: On February 27, 1947, Monopoly Bureau agents in Taipei struck a widow selling cigarettes, and one of them, fleeing an angry crowd, fatally shot a bystander. Protests spread across Taiwan, and the Nationalist government crushed them, killing thousands of civilians; for decades the event was taboo. Today February 28 is Peace Memorial Day, marked with ceremonies where a bell of peace rings for the victims.

source.name: Memorial Foundation of 228, The 228 Incident

source2.name: Taipei Times, Taiwan in Time: 228, after the apology

title: The Poisoned Bay of Minamata
text: In 1956 doctors in Minamata identified a terrible nerve disease. A Chisso chemical factory, making acetaldehyde since 1932, had been releasing mercury waste into the bay, poisoning fish and the families who ate them. Local cats staggered and spun in circles, a 'dancing disease', and thousands of people were eventually recognised as victims, making Minamata a landmark in fighting pollution.

source.name: Ministry of the Environment, Japan, 'Minamata Disease: The History and Measures' (ch. 2)

source2.name: EBSCO Research Starters, Minamata Bay Mercury Poisoning Begins to Claim Victims (Arlene R. Courtney)

title: Ramen in Three Minutes
text: In a small workshop in Ikeda, Momofuku Ando of Nissin invented instant noodles, launched in 1958 as Chikin Ramen; frying the cooked noodles dried them for long storage. Cup Noodles followed in 1971. By 2017 the world ate more than 100 billion servings a year, and South Koreans ate the most per person.

source.name: Nissin Foods Holdings, corporate history

source2.name: CUPNOODLES MUSEUM Osaka Ikeda (Momofuku Ando Instant Ramen Museum)

title: The Cultural Revolution Begins
text: In August 1966 Mao Zedong put up a poster titled 'Bombard the Headquarters', attacking party leaders, and Red Guards rose up across China. For ten years schools closed, teachers and scientists were persecuted, millions of city youths were sent to the countryside, and many people died. In 1981 the party itself called it its most severe setback since the People's Republic was founded.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cultural Revolution'

source2.name: Wilson Center Digital Archive (UMD), 'Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party' (27 June 1981)

title: Tu Youyou's Hunt for a Malaria Cure
text: In 1969 chemist Tu Youyou was put in charge of a secret malaria project, and her team gathered over 2,000 old Chinese recipes. An ancient text by Ge Hong told her to soak sweet wormwood in water rather than boil it, so she extracted it at low heat. In 1972 her team isolated artemisinin and tested it on patients in Hainan, and she won the 2015 Nobel Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, 'Tu Youyou - Biographical' (Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2015)

title: Kim Hak-sun Breaks the Silence
text: On August 14, 1991, Kim Hak-sun became the first woman in Korea to testify publicly that the Japanese army had forced her into sexual slavery as a so-called comfort woman. That December she sued the Japanese government. Hundreds of other survivors, in South Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines, Indonesia and beyond, also came forward, turning a hidden wartime crime into a global human rights issue.

source.name: Korea.net, 'Remaining tasks on 30th anniversary of first testimony by comfort woman victim'

source2.name: Asian Women's Fund, 'How did the Comfort Women Issue come to light?'

title: Spirited Away Enchants the World
text: Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli released Spirited Away, the tale of ten-year-old Chihiro trapped in a bathhouse for spirits, in 2001. It became Japan's top-grossing film, a record it held until 2020. It shared the Golden Bear in Berlin, and in 2003 it won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, the first anime film ever to win an Oscar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Spirited Away

source2.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences: Governors Awards 2014 - Hayao Miyazaki

title: The Three Gorges Dam
text: Sun Yat-sen first proposed damming the Yangtze in 1919, as part of a plan to industrialize China. The Three Gorges Dam's wall, 185 metres high and over 2.3 kilometres long, was finished in 2006, and by 2012 all 32 main turbines were running, making it the world's most productive hydroelectric dam. The reservoir forced at least 1.3 million people to leave their homes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Three Gorges Dam

source2.name: Education About Asia (Association for Asian Studies), Berkman (1998)

title: Parasite Makes Film History
text: Bong Joon Ho's Parasite follows a poor family from a Seoul semi-basement flat who sneak into a rich family's life. In May 2019 it became the first Korean film to win the Palme d'Or at Cannes, and in 2020 the first non-English-language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture, a high point of the Korean wave.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Parasite / Bong Joon-Ho

source2.name: The Conversation: Parasite - at last the Oscars jumps the one-inch subtitles barrier

title: The First Austronesians in Taiwan
place: Dapenkeng, Bali District, New Taipei, Taiwan
text: Between about 3500 and 3000 BCE, the Tapenkeng (Dapenkeng) culture, Taiwan's earliest Neolithic, appeared and spread around the island and to the Penghu Islands. Many scholars think its people came across the strait from coastal China as early Austronesians, the first step in a migration that later reached far into the Pacific. They made cord-marked pottery and stone beaters for making bark cloth.

source.name: Antiquity 88 (2014), Hung & Carson, 'Foragers, fishers and farmers: origins of the Taiwanese Neolithic' (abstract via Crossref/Cambridge)

source2.name: Springer, 'Tapa Beaters from 5000 to 4200 BP in Taiwan' (chapter abstract, read in browser); also Asian Perspectives review of Tsang, Archaeology of the P'eng-hu Islands (UH ScholarSpace) for Penghu and cord-marked ware

title: The Secret History of the Mongols
text: After Genghis Khan died in 1227, an unknown author wrote the story of his family and his life. The colophon says it was finished at a great assembly by the Kherlen River, at Ködöe Aral, in a Year of the Mouse; many scholars say 1228, while others argue for 1252. The full text survives only in an early Ming version that wrote its Mongolian sounds in Chinese characters.

source.name: C.P. Atwood, 'The Date of the Secret History of the Mongols Reconsidered', Journal of Song-Yuan Studies 37 (2007), Indiana University ScholarWorks

title: Mongolia's Peaceful Democratic Revolution
text: From December 1989, demonstrators gathered in Ulaanbaatar's main square to demand democracy, and in March 1990 some went on hunger strike there. On March 9, 1990, the whole ruling politburo resigned. Political parties were legalized, Mongolia held multi-party elections that July, and a new democratic constitution took effect in 1992. It was part of the wave of revolutions of 1989.

source.name: Swarthmore College, Global Nonviolent Action Database, 'Mongolians win multi-party democracy, 1989-1990'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mongolia: Government and society'

title: The Daka Skull
text: Found in December 1997 in Ethiopia's Middle Awash, the Daka skull cap belonged to a Homo erectus who lived about a million years ago. The same layer held thighbones and a shinbone from other individuals, many animal fossils, and Acheulean hand axes and cleavers. The skull looks so much like its Asian cousins that its finders argue Homo erectus was one widespread species.

source.name: University of California, Berkeley - press release (Asfaw et al., Nature 2002)

source2.name: Asfaw et al. 2002, Nature 416:317-320

title: Footprints on a Norfolk Beach
text: In May 2013, stormy seas scoured the sand off an ancient mud layer on an English beach and revealed footprints left by about five people, adults and children together. They are the oldest known human footprints outside Africa. Scientists raced to photograph them in 3D, because within about two weeks the tide had washed them away forever.

source.name: Ashton et al. 2014, PLOS ONE 9(2): e88329

title: The Pioneers of Gran Dolina
text: At Gran Dolina in Spain's Atapuerca hills, diggers from 1994 found bones of Homo antecessor, a name meaning "pioneer", among Western Europe's first known people. A youngster's face looks surprisingly modern. Many bones carry cut marks just like those on butchered animals, a sign of cannibalism, though scientists still debate exactly what happened and why.

source.name: Australian Museum

source2.name: Fernández-Jalvo et al. 1999, Journal of Human Evolution (abstract via PubMed)

title: Campfires by the Jordan River
text: At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, beside the upper Jordan River, burned seeds, wood and flint suggest that humans controlled fire nearly 790,000 years ago. Clusters of burnt flint show where hearths probably were. Fish teeth found around them had been gently heated, perhaps the oldest known evidence of cooking, so dinner was probably cooked fish.

source.name: Goren-Inbar et al. 2004, Science (abstract via PubMed)

source2.name: Zohar et al. 2022, Nature Ecology & Evolution

title: The Jaw That Named a Species
text: On October 21, 1907, a huge human jawbone turned up 24 metres down in a sand pit at Mauer, near Heidelberg. The next year Otto Schoetensack named a new species from it, Homo heidelbergensis. In 2010 the sands were dated to about 609,000 years old, making the jaw the oldest human fossil then known from central and northern Europe.

source.name: Wagner et al. 2010, PNAS 107:19726-19730

title: The First Stone-Tipped Spears?
place: Kathu Pan, Northern Cape, South Africa
text: At Kathu Pan in South Africa, archaeologists studied stone points about 500,000 years old. Impact breaks at their tips and shaping near their bases suggest they were fixed to wooden shafts as spear tips. If so, early humans were building multi-part tools about 200,000 years earlier than anyone had thought.

source.name: Wilkins et al. 2012, Science (abstract via PubMed)

title: Butchers on an Ancient Beach
text: At Boxgrove in southern England, early humans about 500,000 years ago skilfully butchered large animals, leaving behind many horse, deer and rhinoceros bones and finely made hand axes. The site also gave Britain its oldest human fossils, a shin bone and two teeth, from a tall, muscular human assigned to Homo heidelbergensis.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London

source2.name: Roberts, Stringer & Parfitt 1994, Nature (abstract via PubMed)

title: The Oldest Wooden Building Work
text: Beside Kalambo Falls in Zambia, scientists in 2023 announced two logs at least 476,000 years old, joined crosswise by a deliberately cut notch, perhaps part of a raised platform or walkway on wet ground. That is older than our own species. Wood almost never survives this long, so the find shows early humans could shape tree trunks into large structures.

source.name: Barham et al. 2023, Nature 622:107-111

title: The People of Arago Cave
text: The Caune de l'Arago is a cave perched above the Verdouble valley in southern France. Diggers have found 152 human remains there, including the famous Arago 21 skull, discovered on 22 July 1971 and about 450,000 years old. A child's tooth unearthed in 2018 is about 560,000 years old, the oldest human remain yet found in France.

source.name: Musée de Préhistoire de Tautavel (Centre Européen de Préhistoire)

title: The Pit of Bones
place: Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain
text: Deep in a Spanish cave lies the Sima de los Huesos, "pit of bones", holding the remains of at least 28 people from about 430,000 years ago. DNA recovered from the bones shows they were early relatives of the Neanderthals. Their skulls already have Neanderthal-like faces and jaws.

source.name: Meyer et al. 2016, Nature 531:504-507

source2.name: Arsuaga et al. 2014, Science (abstract via PubMed)

title: The Flood That Made Britain an Island
place: Strait of Dover, between England and France
text: Britain was once joined to France by a chalk ridge. About 450,000 years ago, ice sheets dammed a huge lake in the southern North Sea, and it spilled over the ridge in giant waterfalls. Deep holes in the Channel floor look like the plunge pools they carved. A later catastrophic flood finished the breach, setting Britain up to become an island.

source.name: Gupta et al. 2017, Nature Communications 8:15101

title: Smart Stone Tools Under Lava
text: At Nor Geghi 1 in Armenia, archaeologists found old-style two-faced tools together with Levallois tools, made by shaping a stone core first so a ready-made flake comes off in one blow. It is the earliest known case of both methods in use side by side outside Africa. The mix suggests local people worked out the Levallois trick themselves, rather than learning it from newcomers.

source.name: Adler et al. 2014, Science (abstract via PubMed)

title: Carrying Stone from Far Away
text: In Kenya's Olorgesailie basin, sites about 320,000 years old hold stone points and tools made of rock, such as obsidian, carried in from 25 to 50 kilometres away or more. The same people dug out iron-rich rocks to make red pigment. These are some of the earliest signs of the wide-ranging, colour-using habits we think of as modern human behaviour.

source.name: Brooks et al. 2018, Science (abstract via PubMed)

source2.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - Human Origins

title: The Oldest Homo Sapiens
text: Human fossils have been known from Jebel Irhoud since the 1960s, but their age was long uncertain. New digs and dating published in 2017 put them at about 315,000 years old and showed they were early Homo sapiens, our own species. That makes them the oldest securely dated members, and suggests our species emerged across the whole of Africa, not only in the east.

source.name: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546:289-292

source2.name: Max Planck Society

title: The World's Oldest Complete Spears
text: In an open-cast coal mine at Schöningen, excavators found nine wooden spears and a lance lying among the butchered remains of more than 50 horses on an old lakeshore. They are the oldest complete wooden hunting weapons known. Their age is debated: first put at 400,000 years, then about 300,000, while a 2025 study argued for about 200,000, made by Neanderthals.

source.name: Hutson et al. 2025, Science Advances 11: eadv0752

title: Broken Hill Man's Toothache
text: In 1921, miners at a lead and zinc mine in Zambia unearthed one of the best-preserved ancient human skulls, the first early human fossil ever found in Africa. Dated to about 299,000 years, it has large brow ridges and terrible teeth: ten of its upper teeth have cavities. Zambia has long asked Britain to send it home, and talks were agreed.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London

source2.name: Smithsonian Human Origins Program

title: Small Brains in a Pitch-Dark Cave
place: Rising Star Cave, Gauteng, South Africa
text: Homo naledi had a brain less than half the size of ours, yet lived until roughly 335,000 to 236,000 years ago, alongside early Homo sapiens. Its bones lie deep in an unlit cave chamber. Some researchers argue the dead were deliberately buried and that naledi carved marks on the walls, but many scientists strongly dispute both claims.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London

source2.name: Scientific American

title: A Skull from a Spring
text: At the Florisbad spring in South Africa, Professor T. F. Dreyer found a partial human skull in 1932, lying at the bottom of an old spring vent. A tooth found with it was dated to about 259,000 years, though a 2026 study suggests it may be younger, perhaps 212,000 to 154,000 years. Experts have called it Homo heidelbergensis or an early Homo sapiens.

source.name: Smithsonian Human Origins Program

source2.name: Communications Earth & Environment (2026)
