title: The Jaw from Azykh Cave
text: Azykh (Azokh) Cave in the Caucasus was dug for about twenty years from the 1960s. In a layer about 300,000 years old, the diggers found a piece of human jawbone, later classified as Homo heidelbergensis. Cave bears hibernated here too, and researchers think people sometimes came in afterwards to take meat and skins from bears that had died.

source.name: IPHES (Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution)

source2.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Fernández-Jalvo et al. 2010), abstract

title: Early Humans of the Omo River
text: In 1967, a team directed by Richard Leakey found human remains by the Omo River in southwestern Ethiopia: Omo I, a partial skull and skeleton, and Omo II, a nearly complete skullcap. Both are Homo sapiens, though Omo I looks more modern than Omo II. Volcanic ash above them shows the fossils are at least 233,000 years old, among the oldest of our species.

source.name: Nature (Vidal et al. 2022)

source2.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Fleagle et al. 2008), abstract

title: A Sapiens in Greece? Maybe!
text: Two broken skulls were found in the late 1970s in a cliffside cave on Greece's southern coast. In 2019, one over 170,000 years old was found to be Neanderthal-like, while the other, over 210,000 years old, was identified as an early Homo sapiens. If right, it is the oldest trace of our species outside Africa, but some experts doubt it because the skull is so incomplete.

source.name: Nature (Harvati et al. 2019)

source2.name: Science News

title: An Early Traveller's Jaw
text: In Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, diggers found an adult upper jawbone with several teeth. In 2018 it was dated to about 177,000 to 194,000 years ago, at least 50,000 years older than any modern human fossil then known outside Africa. Only the Apidima skull from Greece, announced a year later, is claimed to be older.

source.name: Science (Hershkovitz et al. 2018), abstract

source2.name: The Leakey Foundation

title: Neanderthal Rings Deep Underground
text: Some 336 metres inside a French cave, early Neanderthals broke off stalagmites and arranged them into ring-shaped structures, the larger more than five metres across, with traces of fire on them. Dated in a 2016 study to about 176,500 years ago, they are among the oldest known well-dated constructions made by humans. Nobody knows what they were for.

source.name: Nature (Jaubert et al. 2016)

title: Seafood in an Ice Age Cave
place: Pinnacle Point, Mossel Bay, South Africa
text: During a long ice age that made much of Africa cooler and drier, people lived in sea caves at Pinnacle Point on South Africa's south coast. By about 164,000 years ago they were eating shellfish, the earliest evidence then known of humans using seafood. They also ground red ochre, perhaps for body paint, and heated stone to make it easier to shape into tools.

source.name: Nature (Marean et al. 2007), abstract

source2.name: Science (Brown et al. 2009), abstract

title: Hippo Hunters of Herto
text: By a shallow lake in Ethiopia's Afar region, early Homo sapiens butchered hippos and buffalo with stone tools. Their fossils, found in 1997, are about 160,000 years old. Three skulls, two adults and a child of six or seven, carry cut marks that point to rituals for the dead, perhaps removing the flesh before keeping and handling the bones.

source.name: UC Berkeley News

title: Neanderthal Eagle-Claw Jewellery
text: At Krapina in Croatia, one of the largest known Neanderthal sites with about 900 human fossils, diggers more than a century ago found eight white-tailed eagle talons about 130,000 years old. Cut marks, polished patches and notches suggest they were strung together and worn, perhaps as a necklace or bracelet. That is long before modern humans arrived in Europe.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Radovčić et al. 2015)

source2.name: Museums of Hrvatsko Zagorje - Krapina Neanderthal Museum

title: Stone Tools on an Island
text: A survey in southern Crete in 2008 and 2009 turned up very old stone tools, some of them dated by their geological setting to at least 130,000 years ago. That was a shock, because Crete has been an island for millions of years. It pushes the history of Mediterranean seafaring back by more than 100,000 years: somehow, early humans crossed open water.

source.name: Hesperia, American School of Classical Studies at Athens (Strasser et al. 2010)

source2.name: Journal of Quaternary Science (Strasser et al. 2011), abstract

title: Early Footsteps in Arabia
place: Jebel Faya, Sharjah, United Arab Emirates
text: Stone tools buried at Jebel Faya, in what is now the United Arab Emirates, are up to about 125,000 years old. They resemble tools made in east Africa at the time, suggesting people crossed from Africa by a southern route. Low sea levels made the crossing easier, and more rain then turned Arabia greener.

source.name: Science (Armitage et al. 2011), abstract

source2.name: ScienceDaily (AAAS press release)

title: When Hippos Swam in England
text: During the Last Interglacial, a warm spell about 129,000 to 115,000 years ago, hippos lived in Europe. In Britain their bones are the classic sign of that period: they have been dug up under Trafalgar Square in London and from Victoria Cave in Yorkshire. Genes show they were the same species as today's African hippos.

source.name: Quaternary Science Reviews (Penkman et al. 2013)

source2.name: Current Biology (2025), abstract

title: A Child Buried with Antlers
text: At Qafzeh Cave in Lower Galilee, early Homo sapiens buried their dead about 100,000 to 90,000 years ago. One child of 12 or 13, who had survived a serious head injury, was laid with red deer antlers on the chest. Lumps of red ochre and seashells carried 35 kilometres from the coast, some stained with ochre, were found in the cave too.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Coqueugniot et al. 2014)

source2.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Bar-Yosef Mayer et al. 2009), abstract

title: Harpoons for Giant Catfish
text: At Katanda on the Semliki River, archaeologists Alison Brooks and John Yellen found barbed harpoon points carved from bone in 1988, about 90,000 years old. The site is full of fish bones, mostly catfish, so these were specialised fishers. Some of the giant catfish they speared weighed up to 68 kilograms, enough to feed a crowd.

source.name: Science (Yellen et al. 1995), abstract

source2.name: Smithsonian Human Origins Program

title: Shell Beads Far from the Sea
text: In the Grotte des Pigeons at Taforalt in Morocco, layers about 82,000 years old hold small sea-snail shells with holes, some worn from hanging on a string and covered in red ochre. The cave lies about 40 kilometres from the sea, so the shells were carried inland. Similar beads at other North African sites hint at networks linking early communities.

source.name: PNAS (Bouzouggar et al. 2007)

title: A Child Laid to Rest
text: In a cave near Kenya's coast, archaeologists found the grave of a child about two and a half to three years old, buried about 78,000 years ago. It is the oldest known human burial in Africa. A small pit had been dug on purpose, and the child was laid in it curled up and then covered with earth.

source.name: Nature (Martinón-Torres et al. 2021), abstract

title: The Oldest Drawing
text: On a small flake of rock from a seaside cave, someone drew a crosshatch of red lines with an ochre crayon about 73,000 years ago. It is the oldest known drawing, by at least 30,000 years. The same cave held engraved ochre, shell beads, and an even older paint workshop, 100,000 years old, that used abalone shells as pots.

source.name: Nature (Henshilwood et al. 2018)

source2.name: Science (Henshilwood et al. 2011), abstract

title: A Newborn Neanderthal
text: In Mezmaiskaya Cave in the North Caucasus, researchers found the skeleton of a Neanderthal baby who died only one or two weeks after birth, still lying in position in the cave's oldest Neanderthal layer. Its brain was already as big as a modern newborn's. Its DNA showed that this Neanderthal mitochondrial line did not pass into living humans.

source.name: PNAS (Ponce de León et al. 2008)

source2.name: PNAS (Pinhasi et al. 2011)

title: Did Neanderthals Paint Caves?
place: Cave of La Pasiega, Cantabria, Spain
text: In 2018, scientists dated mineral crusts lying over a red painted sign in a Spanish cave and reported it was older than 64,800 years. That would mean Neanderthals painted it, at least 20,000 years before modern humans reached Europe. Other researchers dispute the dating and argue for about 47,000 years, so the question is still hotly argued.

source.name: Science (Hoffmann et al. 2018), abstract

source2.name: Science (Slimak et al. 2018, Comment), abstract

title: Decorated Water Bottles
place: Diepkloof Rock Shelter, Western Cape, South Africa
text: About 60,000 years ago, people in a South African rock shelter carried water in ostrich eggshells and engraved them with patterns of lines and hatching. Some 270 decorated fragments from about 25 containers have been found. The repeated designs may be early symbols, like a group's own logo on its water bottles.

source.name: PNAS (Texier et al. 2010)

title: A Modern Human Among Neanderthals
text: In Manot Cave in northern Israel, researchers found the top of a modern human skull about 54,700 years old. It shows our species lived in the region at the same time as Neanderthals, close to when the two are thought to have interbred. Its shape suggests these people were related to the first modern humans who later settled Europe.

source.name: Nature (Hershkovitz et al. 2015)

title: Neighbours in the Rhône Valley
text: A rock shelter above the Rhône was used by Neanderthals and Homo sapiens, sometimes only years apart. A 2022 study dated a modern human visit to about 54,000 years ago, among the earliest in Europe. A Neanderthal found there, nicknamed Thorin, came from a group that stayed genetically isolated for about 50,000 years.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London (press release on Slimak et al. 2022, Science Advances)

source2.name: Slimak et al. 2024, Cell Genomics (abstract hosted by CARTA, UC San Diego)

title: The Neanderthal Who Was Cared For
text: In a cave in the Zagros Mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, Ralph Solecki's team found Neanderthal skeletons in the 1950s. One older man, Shanidar 1, was probably blind in one eye, hard of hearing and had a withered arm, yet his injuries healed, so his group probably cared for him. Pollen from another skeleton's famous "flower burial" may instead have been left by bees.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins: Shanidar 1

source2.name: Liverpool John Moores University news (Hunt et al. 2023, Journal of Archaeological Science)

title: Early Sapiens in the Balkans
text: Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria holds some of the oldest Homo sapiens remains in Europe, about 46,000 to 43,000 years old. Their DNA shows Neanderthal ancestors only about five to seven generations back. Surprisingly, these people were more closely related to present-day East Asians and Native Americans than to present-day Europeans.

source.name: Max Planck Society (press release on Hajdinjak et al. 2021, Nature)

title: Europe's Biggest Blast
text: Just west of today's Naples, the Campi Flegrei volcano produced the largest explosive eruption in Europe in 200,000 years. Its ash fell over a vast area of the Mediterranean region. It may have caused a volcanic winter in an already cold climate, and scientists debate whether it hurt the last Neanderthals.

source.name: Fitzsimmons et al. 2013, PLOS ONE (PubMed Central)

title: The Lion-Man
text: Carved from mammoth ivory with stone tools about 40,000 years ago, the Lion-man has a human body and a cave lion's head. Its fragments were found in a German cave on 25 August 1939, the last day of digging before World War II, and lay unrecognised for about 30 years. After later digs found more pieces, it was rebuilt in 2012-13 from more than 300 fragments.

source.name: Museum Ulm, official Lion Man site (loewenmensch.de)

source2.name: British Museum blog: The Lion Man, an Ice Age masterpiece

title: A Neanderthal Hashtag
text: Deep inside a seaside cave in Gibraltar, crossed lines like a hashtag were cut into the rock floor and later buried under a layer more than 39,000 years old containing only Neanderthal stone tools. Its discoverers see it as Neanderthal abstract art. Some researchers think Gorham's Cave was one of the last Neanderthal homes, though that is debated.

source.name: Rodriguez-Vidal et al. 2014, PNAS (PubMed Central)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gorham's Cave Complex

title: The Lions of Chauvet
text: Cavers found it in December 1994: a French cave covered in lions, horses, rhinos and bears, painted mostly about 37,000 to 33,500 years ago. A rockfall later sealed the entrance, keeping everything untouched. The floor still holds cave bear paw prints and their sleeping hollows, plus torch smudges left by the painters.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture: Chauvet-Pont d'Arc Cave

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Chauvet-Pont d'Arc (by Jean Clottes)

title: East Asia's Oldest Hand Axes
text: In the Bose Basin of southern China, archaeologists found big cutting tools, including hand axes, much like those being made in Africa and western Eurasia at the same time. They lie with tektites, glassy droplets that rained from the sky, dated to about 803,000 years ago. When reported in 2000 they were the oldest known large cutting tools in East Asia.

source.name: Hou et al. 2000, Science (abstract via PubMed)

title: Someone Butchered a Rhino in Luzon
text: In 2018, archaeologists reported 57 stone tools lying with the nearly complete skeleton of an extinct Philippine rhinoceros that showed clear signs of butchery. It pushed the first known human relatives in the Philippines back to about 709,000 years ago. Nobody knows which kind of human it was, but they must have crossed the sea to get there.

source.name: Ingicco et al. 2018, Nature 557:233-237

title: The Hobbits' Great-Grandparents
text: At Mata Menge, in the So'a Basin on the island of Flores, diggers in 2014 found a piece of jaw and six teeth about 700,000 years old, the oldest human fossils on the island. They lay among simple stone tools and the bones of island animals. The jaw and teeth are tiny, and scientists think these people were ancestors of the famous 'hobbits' who lived on Flores much later.

source.name: van den Bergh et al. 2016, Nature 534:245-248

source2.name: Brumm et al. 2016, Nature (abstract via PubMed)

title: Life in Peking Man's Cave
text: Homo erectus, nicknamed Peking Man, lived at the Zhoukoudian caves near Beijing; the lower tool-bearing layers are about 770,000 years old. Burned bones there were long hailed as the oldest proof that humans tamed fire. But a 1998 study found burned bones beside stone tools and no ash or charcoal at all, so whether Peking Man really kept fires here is debated.

source.name: Shen et al. 2009, Nature (abstract via PubMed)

source2.name: Weiner et al. 1998, Science (abstract via PubMed)

dateLabel: Middle Pleistocene (often given as about 580,000 years ago)
title: The Nanjing Skull
text: A broken skull known as Nanjing 1 was recovered at Tangshan, in the hills near Nanjing. It belonged to a Homo erectus who lived in the Middle Pleistocene, hundreds of thousands of years ago. It shares typical features with Homo erectus fossils from Africa and Europe, yet differs from Peking Man, hinting at regional variety among China's early humans.

source.name: Liu et al. 2005, American Journal of Physical Anthropology (abstract via PubMed)

title: A Zigzag Doodle on a Shell
text: A freshwater mussel shell from Trinil, the site where Java Man was found, carries a neat zigzag pattern scratched into it. Researchers think Homo erectus made it between about 540,000 and 430,000 years ago. That is far older than any other known geometric engraving, though nobody can say whether it meant anything.

source.name: Joordens et al. 2015, Nature 518:228-231

title: Hexian Man of Longtan Cave
place: Longtan Cave, He County, Anhui, China
text: During 1980 and 1981, Chinese scientists dug into Longtan Cave in Hexian, just north of the Yangtze River, and found a nearly complete early human skullcap, part of a lower jaw and loose teeth. The fossils are dated to about 412,000 years ago. Oddly, the teeth look more primitive than those of Peking Man.

source.name: Xing et al. 2014, PLOS ONE 9(12): e114265

title: A Smarter Way to Make Stone Tools
text: At Attirampakkam in southern India, around 385,000 years ago, give or take 64,000, toolmakers moved away from big hand axes to smaller tools made with the Levallois technique: shaping a stone core first, then striking off a ready-made flake or point. That is much earlier than experts expected for South Asia, and the new style lasted there until about 172,000 years ago.

source.name: Akhilesh et al. 2018, Nature 554:97-101

title: Digging Sticks 300,000 Years Old
text: Wood almost never survives this long, but at Gantangqing in south-west China archaeologists found 35 wooden tools between about 361,000 and 250,000 years old. They came with stone tools, antler hammers and cut-marked bones. Many are digging sticks and small pointed hand tools, showing how much these early people relied on wood.

source.name: Liu et al. 2025, Science (abstract via PubMed)

title: The Cave People of Hualongdong
text: Hualong Cave, in the hills of Anhui, was discovered in 2005, and a first dig in 2006 found a piece of human skull and a tooth. Digs from 2014 to 2019 added more than 30 human fossils about 300,000 years old, including a nearly complete skull, plus stone tools. Animal bones show these people shared their world with giant pandas and Stegodon, an extinct elephant relative.

source.name: Acta Anthropologica Sinica (IVPP, Chinese Academy of Sciences)

source2.name: PNAS (Wu et al. 2019)

title: The Big Woman of Golden Ox Hill
text: In 1984 a Peking University team found human bones in a collapsed cave at Jinniushan, 'Golden Ox Mountain'. First thought to be a man, the skeleton turned out to be a woman who lived about 260,000 years ago. At an estimated 78.6 kg, she is the largest female human fossil ever found.

source.name: PNAS (Rosenberg, Lü & Ruff 2006)

title: Dali Man's Puzzle Face
text: Found in 1978 in loess deposits in Shaanxi, the Dali skull is a nearly complete human cranium from China's Middle Pleistocene. It mixes old Homo erectus traits, like a low skull, with a bigger brain and a more modern-looking face. A 2017 study found it closest to the earliest Homo sapiens, though scientists have not agreed which species it belongs to.

source.name: American Journal of Physical Anthropology (Wu & Athreya 2013), abstract

source2.name: American Journal of Physical Anthropology (Athreya & Wu 2017), abstract via CARTA/UC San Diego

title: Goodbye, Giant Ape
text: Gigantopithecus, the largest ape that ever lived and a relative of orangutans, lived in southern China from about two million years ago. Then, sometime between about 295,000 and 215,000 years ago, it vanished. A study of 22 caves suggests more seasonal weather changed the forests, and the giant ape could not adapt its diet the way orangutans did.

source.name: Nature (Zhang et al. 2024)

title: Hunters of the Northern Steppe
text: By the Liyi River, a tributary of the Sanggan, Xujiayao has yielded archaic human fossils, tens of thousands of stone tools and about 5,000 animal fossils. The people here were skilled horse hunters, and woolly rhino teeth and ostrich eggshells point to a cold, open landscape. The fossils date to roughly 199,000 to 138,000 years ago, and proteins now link them to Denisovans.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Tu et al. 2015)

source2.name: Nature (2026), abstract

title: A Denisovan on the Roof of the World
place: Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe, Gansu, China
text: In 1980 a local monk found a strange jawbone in Baishiya Karst Cave, high on the Tibetan Plateau. Decades later, ancient proteins showed it belonged to a Denisovan who lived at least 160,000 years ago. Fittingly, people of the Himalayas today carry a gene for coping with thin air that was passed on to them by Denisovans.

source.name: Max Planck Society

title: Dragon Man of Harbin
text: This skull was reportedly found in 1933 by workers building a bridge over the Songhua River in Harbin, and its history afterwards is long and confused. It is massive, larger than any other archaic human skull known, with a brain as big as ours. Named 'Dragon Man' in 2021, it was shown by protein tests in 2025 to be Denisovan.

source.name: The Innovation (Shao et al. 2021)

source2.name: Science (Fu et al. 2025), abstract

title: The Little People of Luzon
text: In 2007 a small human foot bone turned up in Callao Cave on Luzon, dated to at least 67,000 years ago. Twelve more teeth and bones from at least three people followed, and in 2019 they were named a new species, Homo luzonensis. To reach Luzon at all, their ancestors must somehow have crossed open sea.

source.name: Nature (Détroit et al. 2019), abstract

source2.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Mijares et al. 2010), abstract

title: The Mosaic Skulls of Xuchang
text: At Lingjing, near Xuchang in central China, archaeologists pieced together two skulls about 105,000 to 125,000 years old. They are a puzzle: big-brained like other humans of their time, low and broad like earlier East Asian people, and with ear bones and a skull back like Neanderthals. They may record groups mixing across Eurasia.

source.name: Science (Li et al. 2017), abstract

title: The Last of Homo Erectus
text: Beside Java's Solo River, digs between 1931 and 1933 found twelve skullcaps and two shin bones of Solo Man, the youngest and most advanced kind of Homo erectus. They date to about 117,000 to 108,000 years ago, the last known appearance of a species that had reached Java more than 1.5 million years earlier.

source.name: Nature (Rizal et al. 2020), abstract

title: Early Moderns in Zhiren Cave
text: In 2007, in Zhiren Cave, scientists found two human teeth and the front of a jaw sealed under layers of flowstone. The chin looks modern, but the jaw is sturdy like older humans. The flowstone shows they are more than 100,000 years old. Their animal neighbours included Asian elephants, and a quarter of the large mammals found with them are now extinct.

source.name: PNAS (Liu et al. 2010)

title: The Narmada Skull
place: Hathnora, Narmada Valley, Madhya Pradesh, India
text: In 1982 a fossil human skullcap was found in the central Narmada valley of Madhya Pradesh. First named a kind of Homo erectus, 'Narmada Man' was later judged an early Homo sapiens with some features all its own. A very short, sturdy collarbone later turned up in the same deposit at Hathnora. The fossils' exact age remains uncertain.

source.name: American Journal of Physical Anthropology (Kennedy et al. 1991), abstract

source2.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Sankhyan 1997), abstract

title: Forty-Seven Teeth in Fuyan Cave
text: Fuyan Cave held 47 fully modern human teeth, first dated to more than 80,000 and at most 120,000 years old. That would make them some of the earliest Homo sapiens outside Africa. The date is strongly debated: a 2021 study using ancient DNA and radiocarbon argued that the teeth are far younger, from within the last 12,000 years.

source.name: Nature (Liu et al. 2015), abstract

source2.name: PNAS (Sun et al. 2021)

title: Denny, Daughter of Two Peoples
text: Among more than 2,000 unidentified bone scraps from Denisova Cave, one sliver belonged to a girl at least 13 years old. Her DNA revealed something astonishing: her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan. She is the first known child of parents from two different human groups, proof that they met and had families.

source.name: Nature (Slon et al. 2018)

source2.name: Nature (Douka et al. 2019)

title: Hobbits, Giant Storks and Mini Elephants
text: The small people of Flores, Homo floresiensis, lived around Liang Bua cave about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago. Their island was full of oddities: giant storks almost two metres tall, Komodo dragons and small Stegodon elephants, which the hobbits may have eaten. Their stone tools continue until about 50,000 years ago.

source.name: Nature (Sutikna et al. 2016), abstract

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London

title: The Toba Super-Eruption
text: About 74,000 years ago, the Toba volcano in Sumatra exploded in one of the largest volcanic eruptions known on Earth. Ash fell across India, and tiny shards of its volcanic glass have even been found in South Africa. Scientists still debate how badly it affected the climate and the people alive at the time.

source.name: Nature (Smith et al. 2018), abstract

source2.name: Science (Petraglia et al. 2007), abstract

title: Tools Above and Below the Ash
text: At Jwalapuram, in the Jurreru River valley of southern India, stone tools lie both under and over a layer of ash from the Toba eruption, which drifted all the way from Sumatra. The tools above and below look much the same, so people seem to have kept living in the region after the blast.

source.name: Science (Petraglia et al. 2007), abstract

title: The Neanderthal Child of Teshik-Tash
text: In 1938, A. P. Okladnikov found the skull of a child aged about 8 to 11 in the Teshik-Tash cave in Uzbekistan, about 70,000 years old. Some thought it looked like an early modern human, but skull shape and DNA show the child was a Neanderthal, one of the easternmost then known.

source.name: Smithsonian Human Origins Program

source2.name: American Journal of Physical Anthropology (Gunz & Bulygina 2012), abstract

title: Australia's Oldest Campsite
text: In a rock shelter on Mirarr country in northern Australia, digs found ground ochre, grinding stones and ground-edge axe heads. A 2017 study concluded people were here about 65,000 years ago, which would make it Australia's oldest known site. Not everyone agrees: other researchers argue that an age of more than 50,000 years is unlikely to be right.

source.name: Nature (Clarkson et al. 2017)

source2.name: PNAS (O'Connell et al. 2018)

title: Moderns in the Cave of the Monkeys
text: At the top of Pa Hang Mountain in northern Laos, Tam Pa Ling, the 'Cave of the Monkeys', has yielded a modern human skull, two jaws and other bones. The first finds were at least 46,000 years old, but deeper fossils show our species was here by about 70,000 years ago, and perhaps 77,000.

source.name: Nature Communications (Freidline et al. 2023)

source2.name: PNAS (Demeter et al. 2012)

title: A Bone Needle in Siberia
text: Excavators at Denisova Cave in Siberia unearthed a bone needle about 50,000 years old, announced in 2016. Made from a large bird bone, about 7 cm long with an eye for thread, it was described by its finders as the oldest needle known. The cave was used at different times by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Denisova Cave

title: The Last Giant Lizard
place: Capricorn Caves, near Rockhampton, Queensland, Australia
text: Megalania was the largest land lizard known, a monitor up to about 5 metres long. A tiny bony skin plate from the Capricorn Caves in Queensland, about 50,000 years old, is the youngest trace of a giant lizard in Australia, though it could be from Megalania or a Komodo dragon. Giant lizards and the first Australians overlapped in time.

source.name: University of Queensland news release (as carried by Phys.org) on Price et al. 2015, Quaternary Science Reviews

source2.name: Australian Museum: Megalania prisca

title: Found While Looking for a Toilet
text: Adnyamathanha elder Clifford Coulthard and archaeologist Giles Hamm found this rock shelter in the Flinders Ranges after a toilet stop led them down a gorge. Digging showed people used it from about 49,000 years ago, some 10,000 years earlier than expected for Australia's dry interior. It held Australia's oldest known bone tool, ochre, and bones of the giant wombat-like Diprotodon.

source.name: SBS / NITV News (Australia)

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America)

title: Bows and Arrows in the Rainforest
place: Fa Hien Cave, Kalutara, Sri Lanka
text: Fa-Hien Lena, one of the largest caves in Sri Lanka, lies in the island's wet-zone rainforest. A 2020 study found bone arrow points there about 48,000 years old, the earliest clear evidence of bows and arrows outside Africa. The same people made beads from mineral ochre and shell beads brought from the coast, dated to about 45,000 years ago.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History (press release on Langley et al. 2020, Science Advances)

source2.name: PLOS ONE 2019 (Wedage et al.) via PMC

title: The Philippines' Oldest Shin Bone
text: A re-investigation of Tabon Cave on Palawan around 2000 turned up a piece of human shin bone dated to roughly 47,000 years ago, though with a margin of about 10,000 years either way. The cave's remains are the oldest modern human fossils known in the Philippines. Hearths show people were using the cave by about 40,000 years ago.

source.name: Frontiers in Earth Science (2023 peer-reviewed review citing Detroit et al. 2004)

title: Newcomers in the Altai
text: At Kara-Bom in southern Siberia, stone tools including long, pointed Levallois points date to about 46,600 years ago. They are among the earliest probable signs of modern humans in Siberia. Researchers link them to a wave of newcomers spreading from Southwest Asia, a wave that reached Siberia but apparently never took hold for good.

source.name: Zwyns 2021, Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology 4:19, 'The Initial Upper Paleolithic in Central and East Asia: blade technology, cultural transmission, and implications for human dispersals' (abstract via Crossref)

source2.name: Scientific Reports 2023, personal ornaments from Tolbor-21 (Mongolia), Table listing Kara-Bom UP2 at 46-45.5 ka

title: Up Into New Guinea's Highlands
text: In the Ice Age, New Guinea, Australia and Tasmania were one landmass called Sahul, reached only by sea. Its first settlers didn't stay on the coast. Excavations led by Glenn Summerhayes in the Ivane Valley, high in Papua New Guinea's mountains, showed people living there between about 49,000 and 44,000 years ago.

source.name: University of Queensland News (on Summerhayes et al. 2010, Science)

title: A Thighbone Sticking Out of a Riverbank
text: In 2008 an ivory carver named Nikolai Peristov noticed a bone poking out of the bank of Siberia's Irtysh River. It was the thighbone of a man who lived about 45,000 years ago. His DNA, one of the oldest modern human genomes ever read, held Neanderthal DNA too, showing the two groups had already met.

source.name: National Geographic

source2.name: Max Planck Society: Earliest modern human sequenced (Fu et al. 2014, Nature)

title: Denisovan Genes in the Pacific
text: A 2010 genome study found that Denisovans contributed about 4 to 6 percent of the DNA of present-day Melanesians; later work found similar traces in Aboriginal Australians and some Philippine groups. Because mainland Asians carry so little, some scientists argue the mixing happened in island Southeast Asia, and that Denisovans had crossed the Wallace Line, the deep-water divide between Asian and Australian wildlife.

source.name: Reich et al. 2010, Nature (PubMed Central)

source2.name: University of Adelaide repository: Cooper & Stringer 2013, Science, 'Did the Denisovans cross Wallace's Line?'

title: Tuna for Dinner
text: At Jerimalai shelter on the eastern tip of Timor-Leste, people were catching tuna and other open-ocean fish about 42,000 years ago, the oldest evidence of deep-sea fishing. Archaeologists counted more than 38,000 fish bones there. The site also produced a shell fish hook made between 23,000 and 16,000 years ago, among the earliest known.

source.name: Australian National University research portal (O'Connor, Ono & Clarkson 2011, Science, abstract)

source2.name: ANU news release (as carried by Phys.org)

title: Tianyuan Man Loved Fish
text: Tree-farm workers found Tianyuan Cave near Beijing in 2001, and digs in 2003 and 2004 recovered 34 bones from one person. Radiocarbon dating put them at 42,000 to 39,000 years old, among the oldest directly dated modern humans in eastern Eurasia. Chemical tests suggest he regularly ate freshwater fish, and his DNA links him to ancestors of present-day Asians and Native Americans.

source.name: Shang et al. 2007, PNAS (PubMed Central)

source2.name: Max Planck Society (Fu et al. 2013, PNAS, DNA study)

title: Mungo Man's Ochre Burial
place: Lake Mungo, New South Wales, Australia
text: By a lake that is now dry, a man was laid on his back with his hands in his lap and sprinkled with red ochre that must have been carried from far away. Geologist Jim Bowler found Mungo Man in 1974; he is about 42,000 years old. In 2022 he and Mungo Lady were reburied at Lake Mungo.

source.name: ABC News (Australia)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lake Mungo

title: Elephant Hunters at Lake Nojiri
text: In 1948 a lakeside innkeeper found the molar of a Naumann's elephant, an extinct Japanese elephant, at Lake Nojiri. Digs since 1962 have found stone and bone tools beside elephant and giant deer fossils, linked to about 40,000 years ago. It may have been a place where people killed and butchered elephants, though no direct proof of hunting has been found.

source.name: The Quaternary Research (Japan Association for Quaternary Research), J-STAGE

source2.name: Shinano Town (Nagano) official site: Naumann Elephant and Lake Nojiri

title: The Farthest-East Neanderthals
text: In the foothills of the Altai Mountains, Okladnikov Cave held Neanderthal-style Mousterian stone tools dated to about 44,000 to 33,000 years ago, plus broken human bones. Along with a few nearby caves, it marks the easternmost place Neanderthals are confirmed to have lived, thousands of kilometres from their European heartland.

source.name: Vassar College, Central Asia Sites: Okladnikov Cave

source2.name: Krause et al. 2007, Nature, 'Neanderthals in central Asia and Siberia' (University of Copenhagen research portal)

title: The First Tasmanians
place: Warreen Cave, Maxwell River, Tasmania, Australia
text: Warreen Cave, in the Maxwell River valley of south-west Tasmania, is the earliest known place people lived on the island: digs show Aboriginal people were there at least 35,000 years ago. Back then the sea was lower and Tasmania was joined to the mainland. Rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain about 12,000 years ago, cutting Tasmania off.

source.name: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Tasmanian Year Book: Aboriginal occupation

title: Ostrich Eggshell Beads
text: In 1923 the French scientists Émile Licent and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin discovered the Stone Age site of Shuidonggou in Ningxia, starting a century of research. Later excavations found people living here from about 41,000 years ago. Among the finds are dozens of tiny beads made from ostrich eggshell, about 31,000 to 30,000 years old.

source.name: Wei et al. 2016, PLOS ONE (PubMed Central)

title: An Army Camp Becomes a Capital
text: In 1821 an Egyptian army pitched camp just south of the spot where the Blue Nile and White Nile meet. The camp, Khartoum, grew into a garrisoned army town. Mahdist forces destroyed it in 1885, Lord Kitchener rebuilt it after 1898, and in 1956 it became the capital of independent Sudan. Today it is a hub for trade, textiles and printing.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Khartoum

title: A King Chooses an Alphabet
text: In 1820 the people of Antananarivo who could read and write could have been counted on one hand. King Radama I chose Latin letters rather than Arabic script for writing Malagasy, and in 1823 he set spelling rules, dropping letters that had double uses. He inspected schools in person, and by 1828 there were 37 schools with 2,309 students.

source.name: Dictionary of African Christian Biography (J. T. Hardyman, L. Molet): Jones, David

title: The Governor's Skull Cup
text: On 21 January 1824 a British column of 500 men under Governor Sir Charles McCarthy met a 10,000-strong Asante army at Nsamankow. When the troops needed resupply, a storekeeper mistakenly sent kegs of pasta instead of ammunition, and the men deserted. The Asante carried McCarthy's head to their capital, Kumasi, where it became a gold-rimmed drinking cup for their king.

source.name: National Army Museum (London): Ashanti war horn

title: An Egyptian Scholar in Paris
text: In 1826 a young Egyptian scholar, Rifa'a al-Tahtawi, went to Paris as religious teacher to a group of Egyptian students. He stayed five years. He was one of the first Egyptians to wrestle with how to adjust to the West, and back home he became head of Cairo's new School of Languages and later ran a translation bureau for books on history and geography.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Rifāʿah Rāfiʿ al-Ṭahṭāwī

title: The Athens of West Africa
text: Fourah Bay College opened in Freetown in 1827, the first institution of higher learning in modern sub-Saharan Africa since the one at Timbuktu. Its first registered student, Samuel Ajayi Crowther, became the first Black Anglican bishop. Until the Second World War it was British West Africans' only alternative to Europe or America for a degree, earning Sierra Leone the nickname Athens of West Africa.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre Tentative Lists: Old Fourah Bay College Building

title: A Pilgrim Scholar Comes Home
text: Born in Fouta-Toro, in today's Senegal, Umar Tal set out for Mecca at 23. On the way, Muhammad Bello, emir of Sokoto, offered him his daughter Maryam in marriage, and in Mecca he was named caliph for black Africa of the Tijani brotherhood. In 1833 he returned to the African interior, spending years with Bello before later founding the Tukulor empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Jean Claude Froelich): ʿUmar Tal

title: Tunisia Abolishes Slavery
text: In 1846 Ahmad Bey, ruler of Ottoman Tunisia, signed a decree that let enslaved Black people ask for certificates of freedom. It made the Regency of Tunis the first in the modern Islamic world to formally abolish slavery, and anti-slavery societies around the globe sent their praise. Today Tunisians remember the abolition every year on January 23.

source.name: Law and History Review (Cambridge Core): Ahmad Bey's 1846 Istiftāʾ, Its Dual Legislative Framework and Religio-Political Context

source2.name: MERIP (M'hamed Oualdi): The Politics of Commemorating the Abolition of Slavery in Post-Revolutionary Tunisia

title: Across Africa to Luanda
text: In November 1853 David Livingstone left Linyanti, near the Zambezi, with little equipment and a small party of Africans, hoping to find a trade route to the Atlantic that could undercut the slave trade. After an arduous journey they reached Luanda on 31 May 1854. That September he set off back inland to take his Makololo companions home.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: David Livingstone

title: Where the Nile Leaves the Lake
text: On 28 July 1862 the British explorer John Hanning Speke found the spot where the Nile flows out of Lake Victoria and named it Ripon Falls. He had first reached the great lake in 1858 and called it a source of the Nile, but many in England disputed him. He died in 1864 on the day he was due to debate the question.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: John Hanning Speke

title: The College That Taught Mandela
text: In 1916 the South African Native College opened beside an old British fort called Fort Hare. Its first students came from every province of South Africa and from Basutoland. Renamed the University of Fort Hare, it educated Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo and Robert Sobukwe, the poet Dennis Brutus, the painter Ernest Mancoba and students from as far north as Kenya and Uganda.

source.name: University of Fort Hare: History

source2.name: South African History Online: University of Fort Hare, Alice – Eastern Cape

title: The Prophet of Nkamba
text: In April 1921 Simon Kimbangu, raised at a British Baptist mission, suddenly became famous among the Bakongo people of Lower Congo. People said he could heal the sick and raise the dead, and thousands came to hear him preach. Belgian colonial officials arrested him that September and he died in prison, but his followers later founded the Kimbanguist church.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Simon Kimbangu

title: The Emperor Comes Home
text: When Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, Emperor Haile Selassie led the resistance but was forced into exile in 1936. During World War II he helped form an army of Ethiopian exiles in Sudan. In January 1941 British and Ethiopian forces invaded, and several months later they recaptured Addis Ababa. The emperor was reinstated, though he had to rebuild his authority.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Haile Selassie I

title: The Scarecrow's Ancient Head
text: In 1943 a visitor brought the archaeologist Bernard Fagg a terracotta head that had been perched on a scarecrow in a yam field near Jos. Similar heads had turned up in tin-mining gravel. Fagg soon gathered nearly 200 such sculptures, with almond-shaped eyes and grand hairstyles, and named the unknown civilization that made them Nok. Radiocarbon dates ranged from 440 BCE to 200 CE.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Roger Atwood): The Nok of Nigeria

title: A Shrinking Lake Seen From Space
text: In October 1968 an astronaut on NASA's Apollo 7 mission photographed Lake Chad, which then covered at least 22,000 square kilometres. Hard years followed: between 1968 and 1972, hundreds of thousands of people in the Sahel died of starvation. Through the 1970s water disappeared from the lake's northern basin, a lake that more than 30 million people rely on.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Scientists Try to Understand the Fluctuations of Lake Chad

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory: A Tale of Fire and Water

title: Taming the Nile Flood
text: Completed in 1970, the Aswan High Dam put the Nile's yearly flood under human control for the first time in history. Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, reaches far into Sudan. Ninety thousand Egyptian farmers and Sudanese Nubians had to move, and the temples of Abu Simbel were relocated. The dam also traps the rich silt that once fertilized riverside fields.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Aswan High Dam

title: Eritrea Votes for Freedom
text: After a 30-year war with Ethiopia, Eritreans voted on independence over three days in April 1993, and 99.8 percent said yes. UN monitors called the vote free and fair. In Asmara, dancers of all ages packed the avenues night after night, children paraded waving green leaves for peace, and war veterans in fighter jackets wheeled through the streets.

source.name: The Christian Science Monitor (Robert M. Press): Eritreans Celebrate Their Independence

title: A Baby Born in a Tree
text: In February 2000 floods swept Mozambique, leaving nearly 700 people dead and millions homeless. Thousands climbed trees or rooftops and waited, sometimes for days, to be rescued. One mother gave birth on top of a tree, and a South African helicopter crew rescued her and baby Rositha shortly afterwards. Television footage of the rescue was broadcast worldwide.

source.name: BBC News: Miracle baby flies to US (17 July 2000)

title: Liberia's Iron Lady
text: In November 2005 Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, 67, became Africa's first elected female head of state after winning Liberia's presidential run-off against former football star George Weah. Supporters called her the Iron Lady. She had been imprisoned in the 1980s for criticising a military regime and had twice gone into exile, and she promised to fight corruption.

source.name: BBC News: Profile: Liberia's 'Iron Lady' (23 November 2005)

title: Money on a Mobile Phone
text: On 6 March 2007, Kenya's Safaricom officially launched M-PESA, a service for sending money by mobile phone. It grew out of a 2005 pilot in which airtime dealers' shops were given phones with an M-PESA menu. A month after launch it had 19,671 active users, and by that November it had more than a million.

source.name: Safaricom Newsroom: The M-PESA wonder: How it all begun

title: A Telescope Spots 1,300 Galaxies
text: On 16 July 2016, South Africa's science minister Naledi Pandor released the first image from MeerKAT, a radio telescope in the Northern Cape. Using just 16 of its planned 64 dishes, it showed more than 1,300 galaxies in the distant universe, in a patch of sky where only 70 had been known. MeerKAT is a forerunner of the Square Kilometre Array.

source.name: Observatoire de Paris – PSL: MeerKAT First Light image

title: An Art Museum in a Grain Silo
place: V&A Waterfront, Cape Town, South Africa
text: On 22 September 2017, Zeitz MOCAA opened at Cape Town's V&A Waterfront as the world's largest museum dedicated to contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. It sits inside a 57-metre grain silo built in 1921. London's Heatherwick Studio, working with South African architects, carved the galleries and atrium out of the silo's dense concrete tubes.

source.name: Zeitz MOCAA: Zeitz MOCAA officially opens

source2.name: Zeitz MOCAA: Zeitz MOCAA opens, designed by Heatherwick Studio

title: Africa's First Olympic Games
text: In 2026 Senegal hosted the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event ever held in Africa. About 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 came to compete in Dakar, Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly. Beach wrestling made its debut as a nod to Senegalese wrestling, the national sport, and the mascot Ayo was a young lion in a Fulani hat.

source.name: AP News (Mark Banchereau): Africa hosts Youth Olympic Games in Senegal

title: Cabral Lands in Brazil
text: A Portuguese fleet of 13 ships bound for India swung far west into the Atlantic, and on April 22, 1500, its commander Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted land. He named it the Island of the True Cross and claimed it for Portugal after a stay of only 10 days. The country later took its name, Brazil, from a dyewood called pau-brasil.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Pedro Álvares Cabral

title: A Stockade Named Asunción
text: Spanish settlers finished a stockade beside the Paraguay River on the Feast of the Assumption, August 15, 1537, and named the place Asunción. When Buenos Aires was abandoned in 1541, its people fled here, and for nearly half a century Asunción was the centre of Spanish activity in eastern South America. Intermarriage between Indigenous people and Spaniards shaped the largely mestizo character of Paraguay.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Asunción

title: Drifting Down the Amazon
place: Confluence of the Napo and Amazon rivers, Loreto, Peru
text: In April 1541, Francisco de Orellana left a Spanish expedition east of Quito with a brigantine and 50 soldiers to look for food. His men persuaded him they could not go back, so they drifted with the current until they reached the river's mouth in August 1542. Back in Spain, his tales of tribes led by women like the Amazons of Greek myth probably gave the river its name.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Francisco de Orellana

title: Saint Paul's Day Settlement
place: Pátio do Colégio, São Paulo, Brazil
text: Jesuit missionaries founded a small settlement on a plateau above Brazil's Atlantic coast on January 25, 1554. That day was the anniversary of the conversion of St. Paul, which gave the city its name, São Paulo. The founding site, the Pátio do Colégio, is now a cultural centre in what has grown into the foremost industrial centre in Latin America.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: São Paulo

title: A 1,189-Page Letter to a King
text: Around 1615, the Andean nobleman Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala finished a chronicle for King Philip III of Spain: 1,189 pages with 398 drawings. Writing in Spanish, Quechua, Aymara and Latin, he praised Andean civilization and showed Peru's society turned upside down by Spanish rule. His original manuscript is now kept in the Royal Library in Copenhagen.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala

source2.name: Royal Library, Copenhagen: Guaman Poma, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1615/1616)

title: The First Saint of the Americas
text: On April 12, 1671, Rosa of Lima became the first person born in the Western Hemisphere to be canonized by the Catholic Church. She had lived in a hut in her family's garden, caring for the sick and hungry and selling her lace, embroidery and flowers to help the poor. She is the patron saint of Peru, South America, gardeners and embroiderers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: St. Rose of Lima

title: Gold Rush in the General Mines
text: In the 1690s, bands of adventurers from the São Paulo settlements found gold in the hills of Minas Gerais, which means General Mines, setting off a mad rush. Diamonds turned up in 1729. The wealth made Ouro Prêto a city of great splendour with beautifully decorated churches, but by 1800 the richest gold sources had been used up.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Minas Gerais

title: Earthquake and Wave Strike Lima
text: On October 28, 1746, a massive earthquake ravaged Lima, a city of 50,000. Half an hour later, a tsunami destroyed the nearby port of Callao, which was rebuilt about three-quarters of a mile from its old site. The viceroy's plans to rebuild Lima met opposition from the Church, the Spanish Crown and the city's multiracial population.

source.name: Duke University Press: Shaky Colonialism, The 1746 Earthquake-Tsunami in Lima, Peru

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Callao

title: Cuffy's Uprising in Berbice
text: On February 23, 1763, enslaved people rose up at the Magdalenenburg plantation in the colony of Berbice, and the revolt spread to other plantations. One leader, Cuffy, was a freeborn Akan man from West Africa. Five to six thousand enslaved people lived there with only 350 white colonists. The uprising was crushed in 1764, but February 23 is a national holiday in Guyana.

source.name: The Black Archives (Amsterdam): Berbice Rebellion

title: The Battle That Freed Venezuela
text: On June 24, 1821, Simón Bolívar led about 6,500 troops, including volunteers from the British Isles, against Spanish royalists on the plains west of Caracas. José Antonio Páez and his llaneros, or plainsmen, helped rout the Spanish right wing while patriot cavalry crushed the centre. The victory at Carabobo virtually freed Venezuela from Spanish control.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Carabobo

title: A Giant Skull for Eighteen Pence
place: Sarandí stream near the Río Negro, Uruguay
text: On November 26, 1833, Charles Darwin heard of giant bones at a farmhouse by a stream feeding Uruguay's Río Negro. He rode over and bought, for eighteen pence, a skull as big as a hippo's. Richard Owen named the animal Toxodon, from the curve of its teeth. It probably weighed more than a tonne and looked a bit like a cross between a hippo and a rhino.

source.name: Darwin Online: Charles Darwin, Journal and Remarks 1832–1836 (1839)

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London: What was Toxodon?

title: The Baroneza Gets Up Steam
place: Porto de Estrela, Guanabara Bay, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
text: On April 30, 1854, Emperor Pedro II opened a 14.5-kilometre railway from a port at the far end of Guanabara Bay to Raiz da Serra, near Petrópolis. Irineu Evangelista de Souza, later Baron of Mauá, had won the concession in 1852. Its locomotive, the Baroneza, made in Manchester in 1852, was the first steam locomotive to run in Brazil and is still preserved in Rio de Janeiro.

source.name: DNIT (Brazilian National Department of Transport Infrastructure): Histórico das ferrovias

title: A Wave That Crossed the Pacific
text: A great earthquake struck Iquique in 1877 and sent a tsunami 24 meters high crashing along the coasts of Peru and Chile. The wave kept going across the whole Pacific, from Samoa to California. In Hawaii it destroyed dozens of homes in Hilo and killed 5 people, and hundreds of people were killed in Japan.

source.name: USGS: Today in Earthquake History, May 10

source2.name: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory: Volcano Watch, Commemorating and then monitoring tsunami

title: The Fingerprint That Solved a Crime
text: After a terrible double murder in Necochea in 1892, investigators found a bloody fingerprint at the scene. They asked Juan Vucetich, who was developing a fingerprint identification system, to study it. The print matched the victims' mother, Francisca Rojas, who then confessed. It was the first successful use of fingerprint identification in a murder investigation.

source.name: US National Library of Medicine, Visible Proofs: Juan Vucetich and the origins of forensic fingerprinting

title: Sailors Rise Against the Lash
text: On the night of November 22, 1910, sailors led by 30-year-old João Cândido took over four Brazilian navy ships, including the battleships Minas Gerais and São Paulo. They warned that if the inhumane punishments were not banned, the capital would be blown sky-high. Congress unanimously approved an amnesty and corporal punishment was abolished, but in the following days hundreds of sailors were arrested without trial.

source.name: Agência Senado (Brazilian Senate): Em 1910, marujos denunciaram chibata na Marinha e racismo no Brasil pós-abolição

title: A Chilean Tug to the Rescue
text: Shackleton's men had been stranded on Elephant Island for 137 days when the Chilean steel tug Yelcho, commanded by Luis Pardo, sailed from Punta Arenas on August 25, 1916. On August 30 she reached the island, took all 22 men aboard and left before the ice could trap her. The Yelcho's bow is preserved in Punta Arenas as a historic monument.

source.name: Scott Polar Research Institute, University of Cambridge: Endurance exhibition essay

source2.name: Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales de Chile: Proa del escampavía Yelcho

title: Opera from the Rooftop
text: On August 27, 1920, four friends, Enrique Susini, César Guerrico, Luis Romero Carranza and Miguel Mujica, climbed onto the roof of the Teatro Coliseo in Buenos Aires. From there they broadcast Wagner's opera Parsifal live by radio. People nicknamed them the locos de la azotea, the rooftop madmen, and their broadcast marked the beginning of radio broadcasting in Argentina.

source.name: Buenos Aires City Government: La radio cumple 100 años

title: Women Vote in Cerro Chato
text: On July 3, 1927, women cast ballots in Cerro Chato, a small Uruguayan town whose administration is shared by three departments: Durazno, Florida and Treinta y Tres. Uruguay's government celebrates it as the first time women voted in Latin America. The house where they voted became departmental heritage in 2013 and is now the Museum of the First South American Women Citizens.

source.name: Uruguay Ministry of Tourism: Cerro Chato celebró el 97º aniversario del primer voto femenino en Latinoamérica

source2.name: Presidency of Uruguay: Argimón encabezó en Cerro Chato celebración del 97º aniversario del primer voto femenino

title: The Avalanche That Buried Yungay
text: On May 31, 1970, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck near the coast of northern Peru, one of the most destructive earthquakes in the world. About 50,000 people were killed and 20,000 went missing in the Ancash and La Libertad regions. The shaking set off a catastrophic avalanche of rock, ice and mud that buried the town of Yungay, home to about 20,000 people.

source.name: USGS: Today in Earthquake History, May 31

title: Cochabamba's Water War
text: When Cochabamba's water system was handed to a private consortium in 1999, some households saw their bills double or even triple. Farmers who had built their own irrigation canals for generations started the protests, then joined factory workers, students and neighbourhood groups. After months of strikes and road blockades, in which a 17-year-old boy was shot dead, the government cancelled the contract in 2000.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Katie Angell): Cochabamba water war

title: The Teddy Bear of the Cloud Forest
text: In August 2013, Smithsonian scientists announced the olinguito, the first carnivore species discovered in the American continents in 35 years. The 2-pound animal looks like a cross between a house cat and a teddy bear and lives in the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador. It had hidden in plain sight, overlooked in museum collections and even shown in zoos, until a team led by Kristofer Helgen tracked it down.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution: Smithsonian scientists discover new carnivore, the olinguito

title: Peace Signed at the Teatro Colón
text: On November 24, 2016, a Final Peace Agreement between Colombia's government and the FARC guerrillas was signed at the Teatro Colón in Bogotá. Six years of tough negotiations, held in Havana, Cuba, had ended a 52-year internal armed conflict. President Juan Manuel Santos, who had surprised Colombians who knew him as a security hawk, won the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Juan Manuel Santos, Biographical

title: The Town a Volcano Buried
text: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded León on the shore of Lake Managua in 1524, facing the Momotombo volcano. An eruption in 1578 partly destroyed it, and an earthquake in 1610 finished the job, so the town was moved. Slowly buried, the ruins stayed untouched for over 350 years until their discovery in 1967.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ruins of León Viejo

title: The Pipil Push Back
text: When Pedro de Alvarado's Spanish troops arrived in 1524, the Pipil, a Nahua people west of the Lempa River, met them with determined opposition. In 1525 a second expedition founded a town called San Salvador near the Pipil capital of Cuscatlán. Pipil warriors forced the settlers to withdraw, and the town was resettled several times before it was permanently established in 1528.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of El Salvador (Markus Schultze-Kraft)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: San Salvador

title: The Mudflow That Erased a Capital
text: Guatemala's Spanish capital, Santiago, was rebuilt in 1527 near the Almolonga Valley. In 1541 a lahar, a volcanic mudflow, swept down the slopes of Volcán de Agua and buried the city. Survivors moved again to the Valley of Panchoy, where the new capital, today's Antigua Guatemala, served for 230 years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Antigua Guatemala

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Antigua Guatemala

title: Padre Tembleque's Giant Aqueduct
place: Tepeyahualco, Hidalgo and State of Mexico, Mexico
text: Between 1555 and 1572, the friar Francisco de Tembleque and local Indigenous communities built a water system running about 48 kilometres. Its arcade over the Tepeyahualco Ravine reaches 39.65 metres, with 68 round arches. Builders used adobe instead of wooden scaffolding, mixing Roman engineering with Mesoamerican skills, and one branch still works today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aqueduct of Padre Tembleque Hydraulic System

title: An Encyclopedia of the Aztec World
text: In 1577, at the Colegio de la Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, the friar Bernardino de Sahagún and a group of Nahua elders, authors and artists completed a twelve-book encyclopedia. Written in side-by-side Nahuatl and Spanish and painted with nearly 2,500 images, it ended up in the Medici library in Florence and is now called the Florentine Codex.

source.name: Getty Research Institute: Digital Florentine Codex

title: The Buccaneer Who Burned Panama
text: Old Panama City was a rich hub where silver from the Andes was carried across the isthmus. In 1671 the Welsh buccaneer Henry Morgan crossed the isthmus with nearly 2,000 men, beat a large Spanish force on January 18, and entered the city, which burned to the ground. A new Panama was built about 8 kilometres southwest in 1674.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sir Henry Morgan

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Panama City

title: A Volcano Born in a Valley
text: On September 29, 1759, the small volcano of Jorullo suddenly rose from the floor of a valley in Michoacán. It soon covered the surrounding farmland in a thick layer of ash. Lava flows, mudflows and explosions followed, people had to leave, and the eruption went on until 1774.

source.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program: Michoacán-Guanajuato

source2.name: Yale Peabody Museum Postilla: Paynter, Avifauna of the Jorullo region, Michoacán, Mexico

title: Humboldt Lands at Acapulco
text: In the spring of 1803 the scientist Alexander von Humboldt and botanist Aimé Bonpland sailed from Guayaquil to Acapulco and spent their expedition's last year studying Mexico. Humboldt's Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain described its geography, people and mines. It protested against slavery, and its accounts of Mexican silver mines drew a wave of English investment.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Alexander von Humboldt

title: An Orphan Who Became President
text: Benito Juárez was born in the mountain village of Guelatao to Indigenous parents, who both died when he was three. At 12 he left his uncle to join his sister in the city of Oaxaca and start school. He went on to study law and served as Mexico's president from 1861 to 1872, becoming a national hero.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Benito Juárez (Walter V. Scholes)

title: Three Guarantees for a New Mexico
text: At Iguala, the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide joined forces with the rebel Vicente Guerrero. His Plan of Iguala promised three guarantees: independence from Spain, equality for Spaniards and Creoles, and the Catholic faith. The Army of the Three Guarantees swept the country, and in August 1821 Spain's representative signed a treaty recognizing Mexico's independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Agustín de Iturbide

title: Five Lands, One Republic
text: In July 1823 delegates met in Guatemala City and declared the United Provinces of Central America: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Their constitution abolished slavery and gave each state its own president. Civil war soon followed, and by April 1839 only El Salvador stayed loyal; about 25 later attempts to restore the union failed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: United Provinces of Central America

title: A Railway for Gold Seekers
text: After gold was found in California in 1849, fortune seekers crowded the isthmus of Panama looking for the quickest route. Work on a railroad began in 1850, and the final spike was driven at Culebra just after midnight on January 27, 1855. The single track ran about 76 kilometres, and by 1869 it had carried tens of thousands of forty-niners.

source.name: University of Florida Libraries, Panama Canal Museum Collection: Panama Canal Railroad Construction

source2.name: Smithsonian Libraries: Make the Dirt Fly! Why build a canal?

title: Mexico Sings Its Anthem
text: Mexico's national anthem was sung for the first time on September 15, 1854, at the Teatro Santa Anna, on land where the Palacio de Bellas Artes stands today. The words were by Francisco González Bocanegra of San Luis Potosí and the music by Catalan bandmaster Jaime Nunó. An Italian opera company performed it, with tenor Lorenzo Salvi.

source.name: Secretaría de Educación Pública (gob.mx): ¿Sabías que un día como hoy se cantó por primera vez el Himno Nacional Mexicano?

title: The Real Story of Cinco de Mayo
text: On May 5, 1862, a poorly equipped mestizo and Zapotec force under General Ignacio Zaragoza defeated invading French troops at Puebla. The French were not driven out for another five years, but the victory became a symbol of Mexican resistance. Cinco de Mayo is not Mexico's Independence Day, which falls on September 16.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Cinco de Mayo

title: Madero Calls Mexico to Rise
text: Dictator Porfirio Díaz said he would retire in 1910, then ran again. His rival Francisco Madero, a short, vegetarian landowner's son, was arrested before the vote, escaped to Texas and called for an armed uprising on November 20. In Chihuahua, Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa kept the rebellion alive, and Díaz resigned in 1911.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Francisco Madero

title: The Volcano in a Cornfield
text: On a February afternoon, farmer Dionisio Pulido was burning branches in his field when he watched a volcanic vent open. Parícutin grew more than 150 metres in its first week and erupted for nine years, displacing five communities. Scientists rushed in: it was the first time in modern history they could study the birth of a volcano.

source.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program: Michoacán-Guanajuato (Parícutin)

source2.name: USGS: Ruined San Juan, Parícutin Volcano in background

title: Arenal Wakes Up
text: Arenal had been quiet for centuries when it exploded at 8 a.m. on July 29, 1968. Ash, rock and lava rained down and dammed rivers, and 4,000 people were evacuated from towns including Pueblo Nuevo and Tabacón. The eruption killed 65 people. It started an eruptive period of explosions and slow lava flows that lasted until December 2010.

source.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program: Arenal

title: The Last Mainland Colony Goes Free
text: Belize, called British Honduras until 1973, was Britain's last colony on the American mainland. Neighbouring Guatemala claimed its land, so Belizeans took their case to the United Nations in the 1970s. On September 21, 1981, Belize became independent with a British defence guarantee and joined the UN, even though the dispute was still unresolved.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Belize (O. Nigel Bolland), Independence

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Belize

title: The Cave of Giant Crystals
text: In 2000, two miners digging a new tunnel in the Naica mine broke into a cave 300 metres underground. Inside were translucent gypsum beams up to 11 metres long and weighing up to 55 tons, in heat around 58 °C. Bathed in mineral-rich water, they grew for many hundreds of thousands of years; today only the mine's pumps keep the cave dry.

source.name: National Geographic: Mexico's Giant Crystal Cave Comes to Light

source2.name: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory: Naica Mine, Chihuahua, Mexico

title: Berta Cáceres and the Sacred River
text: Berta Cáceres, a Lenca woman, co-founded COPINH, a council of Indigenous organizations in Honduras, in 1993. She led a campaign against the Agua Zarca dam on the Gualcarque River, sacred to the Lenca, that kept construction equipment away and halted the project. Despite death threats, she kept going until March 3, 2016, when gunmen killed her at home.

source.name: Goldman Environmental Prize: Berta Cáceres

title: An Earthquake on an Anniversary
text: At 1:14 p.m. on September 19, 2017, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck about 80 kilometres southeast of Mexico City, killing hundreds. It hit 32 years to the day after a magnitude 8.0 quake in 1985. Because of that anniversary, Mexico City had held an earthquake drill just hours earlier, and some reports credit Mexico's warning system with reducing casualties.

source.name: USGS: Volcano Watch, Summer 2017 goes out like a lion with hurricanes and earthquakes

source2.name: USGS: Magnitude 7.1 Earthquake in Mexico

title: Mexico's First Woman President
text: Claudia Sheinbaum was sworn in before Mexico's Congress as the country's first woman president, after 65 presidents who were all men. A climate scientist who studied energy engineering and worked with the UN climate panel, she had been mayor of Mexico City. "Now is the time of transformation, now is the time of women," she said.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Claudia Sheinbaum sworn in as Mexico's first female president

source2.name: RTÉ News: Sheinbaum sworn in as Mexico's first woman president

title: Cannons Beat Cavalry at Chaldiran
text: Sultan Selim I marched an army of more than 100,000 into Iran to face Shah Ismail I. The Ottomans had heavy cannon and musket-armed Janissaries; the Safavids relied on cavalry charges and had no artillery. The Safavid army was routed, Tabriz was taken, and the frontier that followed still shapes the border between Turkey and Iran.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Chaldiran

title: Süleyman Rings Jerusalem With Walls
text: The walls that still wrap around Jerusalem's Old City were put up in 1538–40 by the Ottoman sultan Süleyman the Magnificent, mostly on the foundations of older Crusader-era walls. Today people walk in through gates such as the Jaffa and Damascus gates. The Golden Gate stays sealed, because Jewish legend says the messiah will enter through it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Old City of Jerusalem

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Wall of Süleyman

title: Istanbul's First Coffeehouses
text: Around 1554–55, Hakim from Aleppo and Shams from Damascus arrived in Istanbul and each opened a large shop in the Tahtakale district serving coffee. Their coffeehouses became meeting places where groups of twenty or thirty gathered to read books or play tric-trac and chess. Shams seems to have gone home to Syria after three years, with a profit of 5,000 gold pieces.

source.name: Robert Mantran, 'Le café à Istanbul au XVIIe siècle', in Le café en Méditerranée (IREMAM, OpenEdition Books)

title: From Captive to Sultan's Wife
text: Captured as a girl by Crimean Tatar raiders and sold in a Constantinople slave market, Hürrem, known in Europe as Roxelana, entered Süleyman the Magnificent's harem. Unusually, the sultan freed and married her. The pair wrote poetry to each other, she wrote to the king of Poland, and she commissioned buildings from the architect Sinan. She died in April 1558.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Robert Lewis): Roxelana

title: The Boy Sultan Retakes Baghdad
text: Murad IV became Ottoman sultan at age 11 and at first ruled through his mother, Kösem, as regent. Once in full control, he crushed mutinous troops, banned tobacco and closed coffeehouses and wineshops. Taking personal command in the war against Iran, he reconquered Baghdad in 1638 after a siege that ended in a massacre of soldiers and citizens alike.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Murad IV

title: The Last Man of the Arabia Expedition
text: King Frederick V of Denmark sent out the first scientific expedition to Arabia, with surveyor Carsten Niebuhr among its members. The party visited the Nile, Mount Sinai and Jidda, then went overland to Mocha. In 1763 the expedition's philologist and naturalist died, and the rest visited Sanaa, Yemen's capital. Niebuhr ended up the sole survivor and wrote 'Description of Arabia' (1772).

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Carsten Niebuhr

title: The Ruler Who Refused to Be Shah
text: Karim Khan Zand re-entered his capital, Shiraz, and stayed there for the rest of his life. Defying everyone's expectations, he refused the title of shah. He kept the title wakil instead, reinterpreting it as 'deputy of the subjects' or 'people's deputy'. That same year he allowed the East India Company to set up a trading post at Bushehr.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Karim Khan Zand

title: The Siege of Al-Diriyah
text: After Wahhabi forces seized Karbala and Mecca, the Ottoman sultan asked Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali to crush them. His son Ibrahim Pasha won over Arabian tribes with diplomacy and lavish gifts, then reached the Wahhabi capital, Al-Diriyah, in April 1818. After six months of fighting, Abd Allah I surrendered and was beheaded in Constantinople. Al-Diriyah was razed to the ground.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Al-Dir'iyyah

title: The End of the Janissaries
text: For centuries the Janissaries were the Ottoman sultan's elite soldiers, and they often toppled sultans who crossed them. In June 1826 they revolted again when they learned that Sultan Mahmud II was forming new, Western-style troops. Mahmud had cannon fired on their barracks. Most Janissaries were killed, and the event became known as the Auspicious Incident.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Janissary

title: America's First Handshake in Arabia
text: At Muscat, American special agent Edmund Roberts and Seyed Syeed bin Sultan of Muscat signed a treaty of Amity and Commerce. It was the first formal act of recognition between the United States and Oman, and these dealings were some of America's earliest official contacts with the Middle East. A U.S. consulate opened in Muscat in 1880.

source.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: Oman

title: A Merchant's Son Becomes the Bab
text: In Shiraz, a merchant's son named Ali Mohammad wrote and chanted a commentary on the Quran's chapter of Joseph, then declared himself the Bab, or Gateway. He gathered 18 disciples who carried his message across Persia. Religious scholars decided he was dangerous, and he was executed in Tabriz in 1850, but his movement gave rise to the Babi religion.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: The Bab

title: The Reformer Who Fell From Favour
text: From humble beginnings, Mirza Taqi Khan rose from scribe to chief minister of Iran, taking the title Amir Kabir. He slashed spending, built Tehran's bazaar, founded the Dar al-Fonun college and banned overly ornate writing in government papers. Nobles and the queen mother turned the young shah against him, and he was exiled to Kashan and murdered there on the shah's orders.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mirza Taqi Khan

title: The Lady with the Lamp
text: During the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale and her nurses reached Constantinople and found the army hospital at nearby Scutari dirty, full of vermin and short of basic supplies. They ran food kitchens, washed linen, wrote soldiers' letters home and set up reading rooms. Walking among the beds at night with a light, she earned the nickname 'the Lady with the Lamp'.

source.name: National Army Museum: Florence Nightingale, the Lady with the Lamp

title: The Sultan's First Parliament
text: The Ottoman constitution of December 1876 was the first full constitution in any Islamic country apart from a Tunisian law of 1861. It created a two-chamber Parliament, which met in March 1877. Sultan Abdulhamid II kept most of the power, though: the Parliament was dissolved in less than a year and was not called back until 1908.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ottoman Empire, The 1875-78 crisis

title: Nomads Settle in Desert Colonies
text: Ibn Saud began organizing the Ikhwan, a religious and military brotherhood, in 1912. To break old tribal loyalties, Bedouin were settled in oasis colonies called hijrahs, which offered homes, mosques, schools, farm tools and training, and arms. Some hijrahs held 10 people, others 10,000. The colonies pushed Bedouin to abandon nomadic life, and by 1918 the Ikhwan were ready for Ibn Saud's elite army.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ikhwan

title: A King Without a Kingdom Finds One
text: Faisal, son of the sharif of Mecca, was declared king of Syria in 1918, but was forced into exile when France occupied Damascus in July 1920. In March 1921 Britain decided to sponsor him as king of Iraq instead. He was enthusiastically welcomed and crowned in August 1921, and later negotiated Iraq's full independence and League of Nations membership by 1932.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Faisal I

title: The Cedar Flag of Independence
text: When Lebanon's new government stripped French influence from the constitution, the French arrested the president and almost the whole government on November 11, 1943. An insurrection and British diplomatic intervention made France back down, and independence was proclaimed on November 22. A new flag dropped the French Tricolour but kept the green cedar, a biblical symbol of strength and wealth.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Barnett and Ochsenwald): History of Lebanon

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Whitney Smith): Flag of Lebanon

title: The Ground Splits in Khorasan
text: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Khorasan province, causing severe damage over 20,000 square kilometres. An estimated 12,000 to 14,000 people were killed. In the village of Dasht-e Bayaz all buildings were levelled, including a mosque thought to be 800 years old. A field study afterwards uncovered a major fault rupture in the ground.

source.name: Nature (M. Niazi, 1968): Fault Rupture in the Iranian (Dasht-e-bayaz) Earthquake of August 1968

title: A Super Cyclone Heads for Arabia
place: Gulf of Oman coast, near Muscat, Oman
text: Cyclones in the Arabian Sea rarely grow beyond tropical-storm strength, but Gonu became a Category 5 storm with sustained winds of 255 kilometres per hour. That made it the most powerful cyclone to threaten the Arabian Peninsula since record keeping began in 1945. It weakened as it neared Oman, its centre staying just offshore, then turned north toward Iran.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Tropical Cyclone Gonu

title: A Rain of Light in Abu Dhabi
place: Saadiyat Island, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
text: Louvre Abu Dhabi, born of a 2007 agreement between the governments of Abu Dhabi and France, opened its doors to the public. Architect Jean Nouvel designed a 'museum city' under a 180-metre dome made of almost 8,000 unique metal stars. When sunlight filters through, it creates a moving 'rain of light' beneath the dome.

source.name: Louvre press office: Louvre Abu Dhabi to welcome visitors from November

title: A Lost Town in the Khaybar Oasis
text: Archaeologists described al-Natah, a fortified Bronze Age town in the Khaybar oasis built around 2400–2000 BCE. It had about 50 houses built to a standard plan and linked by small streets, a necropolis of tower-tombs, and perhaps 500 residents. Tombs held metal weapons, including an axe and a bronze dagger, and a 14.5-kilometre rampart surrounded the oasis.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Charloux et al., 2024): A Bronze Age town in the Khaybar walled oasis

title: A Prisoner Prince Becomes Sultan
text: Qaboos bin Said, born in Salalah and trained at Sandhurst in England, was kept a virtual prisoner by his father for six years. In 1970 he took over the palace in a coup and sent his father into exile. He quickly began building roads, hospitals, schools and ports, and ruled as sultan until his death in 2020.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Qaboos bin Said

title: Wheat and Millet Meet in the Mountains
text: Long before 3000 BCE, farmers in western Asia grew wheat while farmers in China grew broomcorn millet. At Begash, a herders' camp in the highland steppe of eastern Kazakhstan, archaeologists found both grains together, in a cremation burial from the camp's earliest phase. They are among the earliest crops known to have reached the mountains of Inner Asia, carried along herders' networks.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Earliest direct evidence for broomcorn millet and wheat in the central Eurasian steppe region

source2.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC): Early agriculture and crop transmission among Bronze Age mobile pastoralists of Central Eurasia

title: A Steppe King and Queen in Gold
text: In Tuva's 'Valley of the Kings', every burial mound dug before had been robbed in ancient times, but Arzhan-2 held an untouched grave. A man and a woman lay in a larch-wood chamber, their clothes sewn with some 5,000 tiny gold cats.
