He wore a massive gold torque covered in deer, boars, camels, snow leopards and wolves, and carried weapons of iron, then a new metal.

source.name: State Hermitage Museum: The discovery of an outstanding 'royal' burial of the Scythian period in Tuva

source2.name: Radiocarbon (Cambridge Core): Chronology of key barrows of the Scythian period in Tuva (Arzhan-1 and Arzhan-2)

title: The Polymath From Beyond the Oxus
text: Al-Biruni was born in Khwarezm, beyond the Oxus River, and once wrote in a poem that he did not even know his own father. He became perhaps the most original polymath of the Islamic world, writing 146 titles, almost half on astronomy and mathematics. His great book on India recorded its science, religion and customs, but only 22 of his works survive.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: al-Biruni (George Saliba)

title: Gravestones That Named the Plague
text: In the Chüy Valley near Lake Issyk-Kul lived trading communities whose gravestones, dated 1338–1339, give 'pestilence' as the cause of death. Scientists recovered DNA of the plague bacterium from people buried there. The strain sits at the root of the family of plague strains linked to the Black Death, pointing to an origin in the Tian Shan region, where related strains still live in marmots.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia

title: Timur's Giant Dome for a Sufi Master
text: Khoja Ahmed Yasawi was a distinguished Sufi master of the 12th century. In 1389 Timur began a vast mausoleum for him, 38.7 metres tall, and is said to have joined in the building work himself. Its dome is the largest in Central Asia. When Timur died in 1405, the main entrance was left unfinished, and the ideas tested here were reused in Samarkand.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi

title: The Breakaway That Made the Kazakhs
place: Chu and Talas rivers, Zhambyl Region, Kazakhstan
text: Around 1465, two leaders, Karay and Jani Beg, led some 200,000 unhappy subjects of the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr into Mughulistan. Its khan of Mughulistan settled them between the Chu and Talas rivers. People called them the Kazakh, 'independent' or 'vagabond', Uzbeks. They became more nomadic than the Uzbeks and soon ruled almost the entire steppe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kazakhstan – History

title: The Great Disaster on the Steppe
text: In 1723 the Dzungars, western Mongols led by Tsewang Rabtan, launched a devastating invasion of the eastern Kazakh lands. Oddly, they were helped by Swedish officers, prisoners captured by Russia at the Battle of Poltava who had drifted this far east. Kazakhs still remember it as the 'Great Disaster', and it pushed some of them to seek Russian protection.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kazakhstan – History

title: Shots at the Lena Gold Mines
text: At the Lena gold mines in Siberia, a file of workers about three thousand strong marched out of the deforested hills toward a company settlement on the Bodaibo River. A company of soldiers stood waiting beyond a bridge. Troops killed some 200 workers, and the massacre revived the workers' movement, with strikes and demonstrations breaking out in many of Russia's biggest cities.

source.name: Slavic Review (Cambridge Core): The Ninth Circle: The Lena Goldfield Workers and the Massacre of 4 April 1912

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Russia – The last years of tsardom

title: The 1916 Revolt and Flight
text: In the middle of World War I, Russia decided to draft Central Asians as unarmed workers to dig trenches and build fortifications. Many Kyrgyz and Kazakhs refused and rose in open revolt. The uprising was met with brutal, prolonged repression, and after it was crushed many Kyrgyz and Kazakhs fled across the mountains to Xinjiang in China.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kyrgyzstan – History

source2.name: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty: Convoy in Kyrgyzstan commemorates 1916 anti-Russia revolt

title: Hujum: The Campaign Against the Veil
text: On International Women's Day 1927, activists in Tashkent launched the hujum, a campaign to end the paranja, the head-to-toe veil worn by urban Muslim women. Many women publicly burned their veils, but then quietly wore them again or swapped them for shawls. In the first years thousands of women were attacked and hundreds killed, often by their own male relatives.

source.name: Davis Center, Harvard University: The Thorny Road to Emancipation: Women in Soviet Central Asia

title: The Coldest Village in the North
text: On 6 February 1933 the village of Oymyakon in eastern Siberia, 800 metres up, recorded −67.8°C (−90°F), the World Meteorological Organization's record low for Asia. Verkhoyansk had logged similar cold in 1892, but with less accurate spirit thermometers. Most Russian climatologists consider Oymyakon the coldest place in the Northern Hemisphere.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: WMO Region II (Asia) – Lowest Temperature

title: The Khan Whose Skull Became a Cup
text: By 1500 the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani had made himself master of Samarkand, and he went on to take Herat in 1507. In 1510 the Iranian shah Ismail I ambushed his army near Merv, beating 28,000 Uzbeks with only 17,000 Iranians. Shaybani was killed trying to escape, and Ismail had his skull made into a jewelled drinking goblet.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ismail I

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Central Asia – Timur and the Uzbeks (Denis Sinor et al.)

title: The White Huns Beat Persia
text: The Hephthalites, or White Huns, entered Bactria early in the 5th century. A Byzantine writer said they lived in towns rather than as nomads, and buried nobles in mounds together with their companions. The Persian king Peroz fought them three times, all disastrously; in the last, in 484, he charged to his death into a hidden ditch with all his cavalry.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Hephthalites

title: The Hill of Gold
place: Tillya Tepe, near Sheberghan, Jowzjan, Afghanistan
text: At Tillya Tepe in northern Afghanistan, a nomad chieftain and five women were buried wearing crowns, swords and clothes covered in tiny gold pieces, many set with turquoise and garnets. Their jewellery blends nomadic, Greek, Indian and Chinese imagery. Hidden in a Kabul bank vault through 25 years of war, the hoard was found intact in 2003.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Afghanistan's Dazzling National Treasures, Hidden for 25 Years

title: Taharqa, Pharaoh from Kush
text: Taharqa, a king from Kush in Nubia, became the fourth ruler of Egypt's 25th dynasty in 690 BCE. In 671 the Assyrian king Esarhaddon captured Memphis, but once the Assyrians withdrew, Taharqa came back and wiped out their garrisons. Finally beaten by Ashurbanipal, he fled south to Nubia, where he was buried in a large pyramid at Nuri.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taharqa

title: Masinissa Unites Numidia
text: Masinissa grew up in Carthage and first fought for it, then switched sides to Rome. His Numidian cavalry were essential to the victory at Zama that ended Carthage's power, and after the peace of 201 BCE he ruled two rival Numidian peoples. He wanted a strong, united state, so he brought in Carthaginian farming methods and settled many seminomadic Numidians as farmers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Masinissa

title: The Bookworm King of Mauretania
text: As a small boy, Juba II was paraded through Rome after his father's defeat, yet he grew up well educated in Italy. In 25 BCE he became king of Mauretania, ruling with his influential wife Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Juba wrote prolifically in Greek on history, geography, grammar and theatre, and kept a large library at his capital, Caesarea.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Juba II

title: An Emperor Rebuilds His Hometown
text: Septimius Severus, born at Leptis Magna on the Libyan coast, became Roman emperor in 193. He freed his hometown from property and land taxes and paid for an ambitious building programme: a colonnaded street, a huge four-way arch and an improved harbour. The town's Hunting Baths still show painted hunting scenes, including a leopard hunt, and the names of honoured hunters.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Leptis Magna

title: Perpetua's Prison Diary
text: Perpetua, a young mother in Carthage, was arrested in 203 while preparing for Christian baptism, which the emperor had banned. In prison she kept a diary of her trial, her father's pleas and her dreams. Her text is one of the rare surviving documents written by a woman in the ancient world, and it was read aloud in Carthage's churches for centuries.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Perpetua (by Joyce Ellen Salisbury)

title: Augustine Becomes Bishop of Hippo
text: Augustine was born in 354 in Tagaste, a small Roman town in Numidia, and studied in Carthage before seeking a career in Rome and Milan. Back in Africa he was pressed, against his will, into serving the church at Hippo, where he became bishop in 396. More than five million words of his writings survive, including the Confessions and The City of God.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: St. Augustine (by James O'Donnell)

title: Refuge at the Negus's Court
text: Islam first reached Ethiopia peacefully. According to tradition, in 615 the Prophet Muhammad sent small groups of his followers to the court of the Negus, probably the Christian ruler of Aksum, in what is called the first hijra. Nobody knows whether any of them stayed, but by the tenth century Islam had spread further through trade, preaching and missionaries.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Insoll, The archaeology of complexity and cosmopolitanism in medieval Ethiopia

title: Nubia Holds Off an Army
text: In 641 and 652 the Nubians were one of the few peoples able to repel the Arab invasions. After a failed siege of the Makurian capital, Old Dongola, in 652, both sides agreed a pact called the baqt. Nubia sent enslaved people north, which Makurians apparently saw as payment for grain and food, and the deal lasted for some five hundred years.

source.name: University of Warsaw, Virtual Nubia: Nubian Kingdoms

source2.name: Bulletin of SOAS (Cambridge Core): Ottewill-Soulsby, The circle of the world: the global diplomacy of Caliph al-Mansur

title: Kairouan, a Forest of Columns
text: Founded in 670, Kairouan was the oldest Arab-Muslim base in the Maghreb and served as capital of Ifriqiya for five centuries. Its Great Mosque, rebuilt in the 9th century, has a prayer hall held up by a forest of marble and porphyry columns. Builders later added giant open-air reservoirs, the Basins of the Aghlabids, to bring the town water.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kairouan

title: Timbuktu's Earthen Mosques Rebuilt
text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque was first built under Sultan Kankan Moussa after his pilgrimage to Mecca. Between 1570 and 1583 the city's judge, Imam Al Aqib, rebuilt and enlarged it, and he restored the Sankore and Sidi Yahia mosques too. At its height the city had 180 Koranic schools and 25,000 students, and traded manuscripts, Saharan salt, gold, cattle and grain.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Timbuktu

title: A Sultan's Walled City
text: Meknes began as an Almoravid military stronghold in 1061. When Sultan Moulay Ismail began his reign in 1672, he made it his capital and turned it into an imperial city mixing Islamic and European styles. Ramparts up to 15 metres high, pierced by nine monumental gates, enclose 25 mosques, ten bathhouses, palaces, vast granaries and merchants' inns.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic City of Meknes

title: Kimpa Vita, Kongo's Peace Prophet
place: Kingdom of Kongo (near Mbanza Kongo), Angola
text: From 1704 a young Kongolese woman, Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita, said she was possessed by Saint Anthony. She taught that Jesus was a Kongolese and criticised Italian Capuchin missionaries for not supporting Black saints. Her followers among ordinary people hoped to end Kongo's civil wars between rival claimants to the throne, but in 1706 she was burned at the stake.

source.name: Cambridge University Press: John Thornton, The Kongolese Saint Anthony

title: A Timbuktu Scholar in Exile
text: After Morocco conquered Timbuktu, the jurist Ahmad Baba was accused of plotting rebellion and deported to Marrakesh in 1594. Even as a captive he was allowed to teach and practise law, and he compiled a biographical dictionary of famous jurists. Allowed home after the sultan died in 1603, he wrote an Arabic grammar that is still used in northern Nigeria.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ahmad Baba

title: Ahmad Gran Sweeps Into Ethiopia
text: Ahmad Gran, leader of the Muslim state of Adal, built an army of Somalis and made skilful use of firearms. In 1531 he launched a large-scale invasion of Christian Ethiopia, and at his height he held more than three-quarters of the kingdom. He was killed in battle, and the Ethiopian ruler Galawdewos won back his kingdom in 1543.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ahmad Gran

title: Kanem's King Turns to Islam
place: Kanem, northeast of Lake Chad, Chad
text: Kanem-Bornu, probably founded around the mid-9th century, was a trading empire around Lake Chad with its first capital at Njimi. Toward the end of the 11th century its king, Umme, became a Muslim, and from then on it was an Islamic state. Its location made it a meeting point for trade between North Africa, the Nile valley and lands to the south.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kanem-Bornu

title: Stone Walls Without Mortar
text: Near Lake Victoria, pastoral communities probably built the dry-stone settlement of Thimlich Ohinga in the 16th century. Its walls, 1.5 to 4.5 metres high, interlock their stones without any mortar or cement. The enclosures protected people and livestock, supported craft industries, and marked out family lineages. This walling tradition lasted until the mid-20th century.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Thimlich Ohinga Archaeological Site

title: Khami, Heir to Great Zimbabwe
text: After Great Zimbabwe was abandoned in the mid-16th century, Khami grew into the hilltop capital of the Torwa dynasty. Its granite walls carry chevron and chequered patterns, and it still has the longest decorated wall in the region. Finds of Ming porcelain from China and Rhineland stoneware from Europe show that Khami traded with distant lands.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Khami Ruins National Monument

title: Nubia's Temples Become Churches
text: In the 6th century the middle Nile was split into three Nubian kingdoms: Nobatia, Maqurrah and Alwah. In 543 a missionary named Julian began preaching in Nobatia, whose capital was Pachoras (modern Faras), and his successor Longinus later carried the faith south to Alwah. Nubians took up Christianity with considerable enthusiasm, building churches along the Nile and refurbishing ancient temples for Christian worship.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Sudan

source2.name: University of Warsaw, Virtual Nubia: Nubian Kingdoms

title: Egypt Pushes Deep Into Nubia
text: Under Pharaoh Thutmose I, whose reign began in 1493 BCE, Egypt conquered the northern Sudan as far as Kurgus. Nubia was then run by a viceroy, with Kush governed from Napata. Its gold and emerald mines supplied Egypt, yet beyond the Egyptian outposts Nubians kept their own customs and crafts, and a blended culture grew up in Kush.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Sudan

title: Ife's Own Glass Beads
place: Igbo Olokun, Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria
text: Archaeologists digging at Igbo Olokun, in the Yoruba city of Ile-Ife, recovered glass beads along with the materials used to make them. Analysis dates the main glass-working there to between the 11th and 15th centuries AD. Bead-making at Ife was largely independent of glass traditions known farther afield, and the site may be one of West Africa's earliest known glass workshops.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Babalola, McIntosh, Dussubieux and Rehren, Ile-Ife and Igbo Olokun in the history of glass in West Africa

title: Alexander's City on the Syr Darya
text: Archaeology shows a town already stood here on the Syr Darya, at the entrance to the Ferghana Valley, by the 6th to 5th century BCE. During his campaigns in the region in 329–327 BCE, Alexander the Great appears to have built a city called Alexandria near or around the site. Today it is Khujand, renamed Leninabad in 1936 and given back its old name in 1990.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Khojand (Keith Hitchins)

title: The Two-Year Siege of Bactra
text: In 208 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III invaded Bactria to win back his eastern lands. The Greek king Euthydemus lost a cavalry battle and was besieged in Bactra until 206. He talked his way out: he warned he might withdraw his guards on the Syr Darya and let Scythian invaders in, and won recognition as king after handing over his elephants.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Euthydemus (A. D. H. Bivar)

title: Nader Shah Empties Khiva's Slave Market
text: Khiva's slave market sold Persians seized in Khorasan and Russians captured along Russia's Siberian borders and the Caspian shore. When the Persian ruler Nader Shah took Khiva after a brief campaign in 1740, he ordered all its slaves set free and had a town built for them near Abivard, called Khiva-abad. One reliable source counts 7,000 freed Persians alone.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Khiva (Paolo Sartori and Yuri Bregel)

title: A Khanate Born in the Ferghana Valley
text: In 1709 Shahrukh Biy, a chief of the Uzbek Ming tribe, defeated his rivals, built a fortress near modern Kokand and was proclaimed ruler. His family later claimed descent from a legendary baby: the story said Babur, leaving Ferghana for India, placed his infant son in a golden cradle and left him behind so his line could one day lead the valley.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Kokand Khanate (T. K. Beisembiev and Scott C. Levi)

title: Kokand's Mountain Army Takes Tashkent
text: After Kokand expanded into the Pamirs, Alem Khan drafted Tajik conscripts from his new subjects into an army of up to 6,000 men called the Ghalcha, rigorously trained and armed with up-to-date weapons. After uniting the Ferghana Valley, his troops conquered Tashkent in 1809–1810 and ended the rule of its Khoja religious leaders, helping turn Kokand into a regional power.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Kokand Khanate (T. K. Beisembiev and Scott C. Levi)

title: The Vega Rounds Siberia's Northern Tip
place: Cape Chelyushkin, Taymyr Peninsula, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
text: The steam vessel Vega left Tromsø, Norway, on July 21, 1878, carrying the Swedish geologist and explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld. On August 19 it reached Cape Chelyushkin, roughly the midpoint of the voyage. Frozen in near the Bering Strait from late September until July 1879, the Vega went on to complete the first full voyage through the Northeast Passage.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Adolf Erik, Baron Nordenskiöld

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Northeast Passage

title: The Biggest Gold Coin of Antiquity
text: Eucratides I, who ruled Bactria from 170 to 145 BCE, was one of the last and most powerful Greek kings there. His mints struck coins found as far away as the Black Sea, including the largest gold coin of ancient times, a 20-stater piece now in Paris. A new design showed the twin heroes, the Dioskouroi, charging on horseback with stars on their caps.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Eucratides (Paul Bernard)

title: Bukhara's Great Silk Market
text: Built in 1577 on Bukhara's main commercial street, this covered market was once called the Great Market and became a centre of Central Asia's famed silk trade. Nineteen domes cluster around a high central dome above alcoves for merchants' stalls. It is the only survivor of the city's six covered markets, which linked up with caravanserais, bathhouses, madrasas and mosques.

source.name: Archnet (Aga Khan Documentation Center at MIT): Tim Abdullah Khan, Bukhara

title: A Very Good Enclosed Port
place: Point Loma, San Diego, California, USA
text: On June 27, 1542, Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sailed from Navidad, Mexico, leading the first known European expedition along today's US West Coast. Three months later he reached "a very good enclosed port", now San Diego Bay, where the Kumeyaay had lived for thousands of years. Cabrillo's records became the first written account of this coast by a newcomer.

source.name: National Park Service, Cabrillo National Monument: Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo

title: The Ground Tears Open in Arizona
text: Around the year 1085, the ground in northern Arizona was torn open and lava erupted into the sky. The eruption buried homes and displaced the people living nearby, and stories they told about it survive to the present day. The volcano is named for the rusty red cinders near its peak, and it was the most recent eruption in Arizona.

source.name: National Park Service, Sunset Crater Volcano: History & Culture

source2.name: National Park Service: Sunset Crater Volcano National Monument

title: A Hard First Winter at Quebec
text: Samuel de Champlain arrived off Cap Diamant on July 3, 1608, and chose "the point of Quebec" for a settlement where the fur trade with First Nations could be controlled. His men built a storehouse and two-storey living quarters, and he foiled a plot to murder him. That winter scurvy struck hard: sixteen of the 25 men died.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Samuel de Champlain

title: Fool's Gold from Baffin Island
place: Frobisher Bay, Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: Martin Frobisher came looking for the Northwest Passage in 1576 and met the Inuit of Baffin Island, but he took home a lump of ore an assayer claimed held gold. In 1577 he returned with orders to dig ore, and clashes with the Inuit followed. In the end about 1,350 tonnes of ore were shipped to England, and none of it contained precious metals.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Sir Martin Frobisher

title: Beaver Hats Build a Company
text: European demand for felt hats made from beaver fur led to the Hudson's Bay Company, chartered on 2 May 1670 with exclusive trading rights over the lands drained by rivers flowing into Hudson Bay. Indigenous peoples trapped in fall and winter, when pelts were best, then travelled to the trading posts in summer to swap furs for metal tools, guns, textiles and food.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Hudson's Bay Company

title: The Wendat Scatter but Survive
place: Christian Island, Georgian Bay, Ontario, Canada
text: Before 1600 the Wendat of today's Ontario numbered about 20,000 to 25,000, living in villages of up to 3,500 people and growing corn, beans and squash. Epidemics then cut them to about 9,000. In 1648 and 1649, Haudenosaunee warriors armed with Dutch firearms dispersed them, and about 1,000 fled to Christian Island. The Wendat nation still lives on at Wendake, Quebec.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Wendat (Huron)

title: North America's Oldest Pots
place: Stallings Island, Savannah River, Georgia, USA
text: About 3,800 years ago, Stallings Island in the Savannah River was the population center of a hunter-gatherer society. Its people made Stallings fiber-tempered pottery, the oldest pottery in North America, long before farming reached Georgia. They left a two-acre heap of freshwater shellfish remains, over ten feet thick in places. By 3,500 years ago the island had been abandoned.

source.name: New Georgia Encyclopedia (Kenneth E. Sassaman, University of Florida): Stallings Island Site

title: The Pipe Shaped Like a Man
text: An Adena sculptor carved this pipe from Ohio pipestone sometime between 800 BCE and 1 CE. It shows a muscular young man with flexed knees and an open mouth, perhaps dancing or singing. Tobacco burned in a bowl between his feet, and the smoke travelled through his body to a mouthpiece on his head. It lay near the left hand of an important man buried in the Adena Mound.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art (Susan E. Bergh): Centennial Loan: Adena Pipe

title: The First People of the Eastern Arctic
text: Roughly 5,000 years ago, the first permanent residents of the Eastern Arctic arrived, likely crossing the Bering Strait from Chukotka. Archaeologists call them Palaeo-Inuit, while Inuit oral histories call the earliest Arctic people Tuniit. The Pre-Dorset lived in skin tents held down by rings of watermelon-sized boulders, and fixed tiny pressure-flaked stone blades to handles of bone, ivory or wood.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (Patrick Jolicoeur): Pre-Dorset

dateLabel: Built up between 50 BCE and 300 CE
title: Canada's Only Earthen Serpent
place: Serpent Mounds, Rice Lake, near Keene, Ontario, Canada
text: On a bluff above Rice Lake lies Canada's only known effigy mound: a winding earthen serpent about 60 metres long, 8 metres wide and up to 1.8 metres high. It grew gradually between 50 BCE and 300 CE from six separate burial places, a sign of a sacred spot visited for ceremonies. Higher-status people were buried at its base, while commoners were scattered through the fill.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (Walter A. Kenyon): Serpent Mounds

title: Rattles Made from Skulls
place: Pinson Mounds, near Jackson, Tennessee, USA
text: Around 100 CE, people at Pinson Mounds raised the northern Twin Mound over four log- or fabric-covered tombs holding sixteen adults. Some wore fiber headdresses with copper ornaments and freshwater pearl necklaces, and an elderly man lay with two rattles cut from human skulls, filled with river pebbles. Pottery shows that people from as far as southern Georgia and Louisiana joined rituals here.

source.name: Tennessee Encyclopedia (Robert C. Mainfort Jr. and Mary L. Kwas): Pinson Mounds State Archaeological Park

title: An Ivory Woman from the Bering Sea
text: On St. Lawrence Island, an Old Bering Sea artist carved this woman from walrus ivory, 21 cm tall. Her people lived largely from the sea, hunting walrus, seal and whale, and they incised their harpoon heads with spirit images honoring the animals they hunted. Nobody is sure what such figures were for: some experts call them dolls, perhaps once dressed, others ceremonial objects.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Female Figure, Old Bering Sea (2001.760)

title: Sixteen Summers, Two Wet Ones
place: Mesa Verde region, southwest Colorado, USA
text: Tree rings show that from 1275 to 1290 the Southwest suffered severe drought, with only two wet years in sixteen. It likely helped empty Mesa Verde: some 40,000 Ancestral Pueblo farmers left southwest Colorado in the late 1200s as drought wrecked the conditions their maize crops needed. They presumably moved to the Pajarito Plateau in the northern Rio Grande, where the climate was steadier.

source.name: NOAA Climate.gov: Southwest droughts since 1200s

source2.name: Santa Fe Institute: Ancient climate change explains historical migration (Kohler, Nature Communications)

title: Spiro, a Trading Hub on the Arkansas
place: Spiro Mounds, near Spiro, Oklahoma, USA
text: Between 850 and 1450, Mississippian people at Spiro built twelve mounds, ceremonial areas and a support city. Their trade links reached from the Rocky Mountains to the Virginia coast and from Florida's Gulf Coast to the Great Lakes. Craig Mound held more than 600 burials and thousands of objects of stone, copper, shell, basketry and fabric, though looters tore into it from 1933 to 1935.

source.name: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (Dennis A. Peterson): Spiro Mounds

title: Cahokia's Outpost in Wisconsin
place: Aztalan, near Lake Mills, Wisconsin, USA
text: Between 1050 and 1100, Mississippian people, many likely from the great city of Cahokia, built a fortified town on the Crawfish River and lived alongside local Woodland people. Inside massive log and clay walls stood three platform mounds, topped by a temple with a sacred fire, a mortuary and probably the chief's house. Early settlers wrongly linked it to the Aztecs, hence the name Aztalan.

source.name: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources: Aztalan State Park History

source2.name: Mississippi Valley Archaeology Center, University of Wisconsin–La Crosse: Aztalan

title: The Rocks That Teach
place: Petroglyphs Provincial Park, near Peterborough, Ontario, Canada
text: On a sloping slab of marble in Ontario are some 900 carvings of turtles, snakes, humans and other beings, likely made by Algonquian-speaking people between 600 and 1,100 years ago. It is the largest known single concentration of Indigenous rock art in Canada, and 31 gneiss hammerstones were found nearby. The Anishinaabe call it Kinoomaagewaapkong, "the rocks that teach."

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (Nancy Rahtz, Lisa Roach): Petroglyphs Provincial Park

title: Taos, Five Storeys of Adobe
text: Taos Pueblo belongs to a series of settlements established along the Rio Grande valleys in the late 13th and early 14th centuries that survive today, and its people claim a presence in the valley since time immemorial. Its North and South Houses rise five storeys in terraced tiers of adobe. Even now, power lines and piped water are banned inside the walled village.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Taos Pueblo

title: Whale Oil from Gran Baya
text: In the 1530s, Basque mariners founded a summer whaling station they called Gran Baya on the Strait of Belle Isle. Crews hunted whales along the coast, butchered them and rendered the fat in ovens, then shipped the oil to Europe to light lamps. Archaeologists found cooperages, wharves, a cemetery and sunken ships. After some 70 years, the local whales were gone.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Red Bay Basque Whaling Station

title: Earthworks That Track the Moon
place: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, near Chillicothe, Ohio, USA
text: Between 1 and 400 CE, small, egalitarian groups in southern Ohio who foraged, fished and farmed gathered from time to time to build huge earthen squares, circles and octagons with remarkable precision. Some line up with the cycles of the Sun and the far more complex cycles of the Moon, knowledge that would have taken generations to codify. They even sculpted hilltops to enclose vast, level plazas.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks

title: Kolomoki, a Crowded Woodland Town
place: Kolomoki Mounds, near Blakely, Georgia, USA
text: From around 350 to 600 CE, Kolomoki in southwest Georgia was perhaps one of the most populous settlements north of Mexico. Its biggest mound, Mound A, stands about 56 feet tall, though digs on its flat summit have not revealed what it was for. In two burial mounds, mourners left large caches of pottery, some decorated with animal and human forms.

source.name: New Georgia Encyclopedia (Thomas J. Pluckhahn, University of South Florida): Kolomoki Mounds

title: North America's Oldest Irrigation Canals
place: Las Capas, outside Tucson, Arizona, USA
text: About 1200 BCE, farmers at Las Capas, outside today's Tucson, dug at least eight canals carrying water from the nearby Santa Cruz River to a regular grid of small fields, each about 250 square feet. Stretching over as many as 100 acres, it is the oldest documented irrigation system in North America. The labor was so great that researchers doubt its builders simply walked away from it.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), Top 10 Discoveries: Early Irrigators, Tucson, Arizona

title: Rings Made of Oyster Shells
text: Between about 4,200 and 3,000 years ago, people on the Georgia coast piled oyster shells, bone, soil and broken artifacts into great rings, the largest more than nine feet high and 300 feet across. Sapelo Island has three of them. Residents ate shellfish, sea catfish, deer and acorns from live oaks. Archaeologists still debate whether the rings were year-round villages, feasting places, or both.

source.name: New Georgia Encyclopedia (Victor Thompson, University of West Florida): Coastal Shell Rings

title: The Revolt That Ruled St. John
place: Coral Bay, St. John, U.S. Virgin Islands
text: In 1733 a small group of African labourers on Danish-ruled St. John, remembered as the "Alminas" after the plantation where it began, rose up against the planters. For a time the island was ruled by enslaved Africans, and planters were driven into the sea and onto nearby cays. The Danes put the uprising down only with the help of French troops.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Contact Period Sites in the U.S. Virgin Islands

title: Dutch Raiders Torch San Juan
text: In 1625 Dutch privateers led by Boudewijn Hendricksz attacked San Juan, hoping for a firmer hold in the Caribbean. Civilians fled, and Hendricksz even lived in La Fortaleza, but while he attacked El Morro, small local militias struck back at the Dutch. Unable to take the city, he gathered the wealth from people's homes and burned San Juan to the ground before sailing away.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: History of the Fortifications

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: San Juan Timeline

title: Fire Reveals the First Bahamians
text: Mud from the Blackwood Sinkhole on Great Abaco holds charcoal from ancient fires, showing that the Lucayan people were clearing land with slash-and-burn farming around 830 CE. Before they came, the island had pine and palm forests and a world ruled by reptiles, including giant tortoises and crocodiles. Burning let pines take over, and large land reptiles began to disappear after 1000 CE.

source.name: Texas A&M University Geosciences News: Study: Bahamas Were Settled Earlier Than Believed

title: Britain Storms the Morro
text: Early in 1762 Britain sent ships and troops under Admiral Sir George Pocock and the Earl of Albemarle against Havana, whose harbour was guarded by the high Morro Castle. The siege lasted from 6 June to 13 August. After mines breached the castle's walls, it was stormed on 30 July; its veteran defender, Luis de Velasco, was badly wounded and died two days later.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: The Capture of Havana, 1762: Storming of Morro Castle, 30 July

source2.name: Royal Collection Trust, Military Maps: Havana 1762

title: A Free Kingdom's Mountain Fortress
text: After independence, Henri Christophe was asked to build a huge fortress on the Pic Laferrière to protect Haiti. The Citadelle, standing 970 metres up and able to hold 2,000 soldiers, opened in 1813, the same year as his Sans-Souci Palace below. UNESCO calls them the first monuments built by enslaved Black people who had won their freedom.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: National History Park – Citadel, Sans Souci, Ramiers

title: Old Havana Joins World Heritage
text: In 1982 UNESCO added Old Havana and its forts to the World Heritage List. The city's bay was a required stop on ships' routes to the New World, so it gained some of the oldest and largest stone forts in the Americas. Its five big plazas are lined with baroque and neoclassical buildings and houses with arcades, balconies and inner courtyards.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Old Havana and its Fortification System

title: Fireburn and the Three Queens
place: Frederiksted, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands
text: On St. Croix, then Danish, the law fixed a day wage and let workers change jobs only once a year, on 1 October. On that day in 1878, with wages barely enough to live on, workers gathered in Frederiksted rose up. Around 50 plantations and most of the town burned. Three women remembered as Queen Mary, Queen Agnes and Queen Mathilda became symbols of resistance.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: Fireburn

title: Garvey Comes Home to Jamaica
text: Deported by the United States government in December 1927, Marcus Garvey was greeted by enthusiastic crowds when he reached his Jamaican homeland on 10 December. He spoke to large welcoming crowds in Kingston, and his People's Political Party was formed to run reform candidates. In August 1929 his Universal Negro Improvement Association held its convention at Kingston's Edelweiss Park, with a parade watched by thousands.

source.name: UCLA James S. Coleman African Studies Center, Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers Project: Volume VII Introduction

title: Maria Strikes Puerto Rico
text: At about 6:15 in the morning on 20 September 2017, Hurricane Maria came ashore at Yabucoa as a strong Category 4 storm with winds of 155 mph. Puerto Rico had not felt a hurricane that strong since San Felipe II in 1928. Maria destroyed the dome of the weather radar at Guavate, sank over 300 boats and tore the roof off a hospital in Arecibo.

source.name: U.S. National Weather Service, San Juan: Hurricane Maria 2017

title: Goodbye to the Caribbean Monk Seal
text: In June 2008 NOAA confirmed that the Caribbean monk seal was extinct, the first type of seal lost to human causes. Europeans first recorded it on Columbus's second voyage in 1494, when eight seals were killed for meat. Resting and nursing on beaches made the seals easy for hunters. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952, at Serranilla Bank between Jamaica and the Yucatán.

source.name: NOAA news release via ScienceDaily: Caribbean Monk Seal Gone Extinct From Human Causes, NOAA Confirms

title: A Colonist Changes His Mind
text: Bartolomé de Las Casas began as part of the problem: he took part in the Spanish conquest of Cuba and was granted an encomienda, which made him an owner of Indigenous workers. Remembering that Dominican friars refused to absolve Indian owners, he repented, and in 1514 gave up his encomienda and told the Cuban governor. Later, in his History of the Indies, he angrily attacked the system.

source.name: Virginia Tech, Digital History Reader: Bartolomé de Las Casas, History of the Indies (excerpt and introduction)

title: A Fortress 150 Years in the Making
place: Castillo San Cristóbal, San Juan, Puerto Rico
text: In 1634 work began on a new fort at San Juan, Castillo San Cristóbal, along with the city walls. San Cristóbal was built to protect the city from an attack by land from the east. It took over 150 years to complete and is considered the largest fortress built in the Americas.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: Castillo San Cristóbal

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: San Juan Timeline

title: A Magazine Against the Censors
text: In 1941, while Martinique was under the Vichy regime, the poet Aimé Césaire created the journal Tropiques. His first editorial declared, "We can no longer afford to live as parasites within the world." Suzanne Césaire, one of its most active writers, published seven articles in it. A naval officer censored the journal in 1943, and it came back only after Vichy fell.

source.name: Brown University Library, Liberation Journals Index: Tropiques

title: Hamilton Writes Up a Hurricane
text: On the night of 31 August 1772 a terrible hurricane struck St. Croix. Days later Alexander Hamilton described it in a letter to The Royal Danish American Gazette: roaring sea and wind, almost constant lightning, crashing houses and shrieking people. Much of the island's buildings were flattened, families wandered the streets without shelter, and he noticed the rain tasted surprisingly salty.

source.name: National Archives, Founders Online: Alexander Hamilton to The Royal Danish American Gazette, 6 September 1772

title: The Night Cuba Went Dark
text: Around 11 a.m. on 18 October 2024, Cuba's Antonio Guiteras power plant stopped working, and the national grid went offline, leaving millions of Cubans without electricity. The government halted classes and shut some state workplaces to save power. Officials blamed breakdowns at old, poorly maintained plants, fuel shortages, and rising demand from businesses and home air conditioners.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (Associated Press): Cuba's electrical grid goes offline after major power plant fails

title: England's Consolation Prize
text: In 1655 Oliver Cromwell's "Western Design" sent a fleet under Admirals Sir William Penn and Robert Venables to the Caribbean. Driven back from Hispaniola, they captured Spanish Jamaica instead. Spain fought on, and only gave the island up formally in the Treaty of Madrid in 1670. Meanwhile escaped enslaved Africans, the Maroons, built free lives in the Blue Mountains and Cockpit Country.

source.name: Lancaster University, Disputatious Societies project: Jamaica

title: A Funeral Fit for a King
text: Bob Marley died of a brain tumour on 11 May 1981, in a Miami hospital. His funeral in Jamaica a few days later drew hundreds of thousands of people, including the prime minister. Marley had carried reggae and Rastafarianism to a worldwide audience, and a Jamaican broadcaster said his success abroad proved to Jamaicans that they could be something good.

source.name: BBC News: Marley's legend undiminished (10 May 2001)

title: The Bay That Named an Island
text: Europeans first reached Puerto Rico with Columbus on his second voyage, in November 1493. In 1508 Juan Ponce de León arrived to establish one, and in August he came upon San Juan Bay, calling the area "puerto rico". San Juan was settled there, and shortly afterwards work began on fortifications for the city.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: History of the Fortifications

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan NHS: San Juan Timeline

title: Where Olmec Became Maya
place: Tak'alik Ab'aj, El Asintal, Retalhuleu, Guatemala
text: On Guatemala's Pacific slopes, Tak'alik Ab'aj grew up beside a long-distance trade route running from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec to present-day El Salvador. Its 1,700-year history, from 800 BCE to 900 CE, saw Olmec traditions give way to early Maya culture. Its mix of sculpture styles is more varied than at other Mesoamerican sites, and Indigenous groups still visit to perform rituals.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: National Archaeological Park Tak'alik Ab'aj

title: The Left-Handed Founder of Copán
text: In 426 CE K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' became the founder of Copán's royal dynasty, and the city stayed a prosperous Maya capital until 822. University of Pennsylvania archaeologists found a tomb deep inside the Acropolis they link to him. The bones show a man over 50 with old injuries, including a severe blow to his right forearm, perhaps from blocking with a shield.

source.name: Penn Museum: Early Copan Acropolis Program

source2.name: Penn Today: Penn Archaeologist Featured on PBS 'NOVA' for Un-earthing Tomb of Founder of Mayan City of Copan

title: A Date Written in Bars and Dots
text: Stela C from Tres Zapotes, on Mexico's Gulf Coast, carries a Long Count date written in bars and dots, 7.16.6.16.18, or 31 BCE, one of Mesoamerica's oldest calendar inscriptions. Matthew Stirling found its bottom half in 1939, and the top turned up thirty years later. His reading started a debate over whether writing and calendars began with the Maya or on the Gulf Coast.

source.name: FAMSI, Richard Diehl: Death Gods, Smiling Faces and Colossal Heads: Archaeology of the Mexican Gulf Lowlands

title: Lady K'abal Xook's Blood Offering
text: On October 24, 709, at Yaxchilán, Lady K'abal Xook pulled a rope, probably studded with obsidian blades, through her tongue while her husband, the ruler Itzamnaaj Bahlam, held a flaming torch above her. Her blood fell onto bark paper in a bowl. The scene was carved on a limestone lintel, now in the British Museum, considered one of the masterpieces of Maya art.

source.name: British Museum (via Google Arts & Culture): Yaxchilan Lintel 24

title: El Tajín, City of 17 Ballcourts
text: El Tajín was lived in from about 800 to 1200 CE and became the most important centre in north-east Mesoamerica after Teotihuacan fell. Some 15,000 to 20,000 people lived there. The city had 17 ballcourts, and UNESCO calls its Pyramid of the Niches a masterpiece of ancient American architecture. Carved reliefs and wall paintings at the site record scenes of ritual and daily life.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: El Tajin, Pre-Hispanic City

title: Paquimé, Desert Town of Macaws
text: In the Chihuahua Desert, Paquimé peaked in the 14th and 15th centuries, with some 2,000 adobe rooms and doors shaped like a T. It linked the Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest with Mesoamerica. Scarlet macaws were an important trade item in the region, and Paquimé is the only site with evidence of substantial macaw-breeding facilities.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Zone of Paquimé, Casas Grandes

source2.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Prehistoric Macaw Breeding in the North American Southwest

title: Two Kings Finish the Great Temple
text: In the year 8 Reed, or 1487, workers finished enlarging Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, and chroniclers say grand ceremonies followed, with prisoners sacrificed. A greenstone plaque marked the moment. It shows the rulers Tízoc and Ahuízotl offering their own blood to the Earth, with a bale of hay between them holding their bloody knives. It is now in Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology.

source.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología (via Google Arts & Culture): Lápida conmemorativa del Templo Mayor

title: Quiriguá Carves Its History in Stone
text: Under Cauac Sky, who reigned from 723, Quiriguá became the capital of a prosperous, independent Maya state. Its Great Plaza is the largest known public space in the whole Maya area. Sculptors carved its sandstone stelae without metal tools, recording eclipses, myths and political events, and Quiriguá was one of only two cities to regularly mark the end of five-year periods.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Park and Ruins of Quirigua

title: Gifts Dropped Into Lake Titicaca
place: Khoa Reef, near the Island of the Sun, Lake Titicaca, Bolivia
text: Underwater excavations at Khoa Reef, near Bolivia's Island of the Sun, found puma-shaped incense burners, sacrificed young llamas, and gold, shell and stone ornaments, radiocarbon dated to 794–964 CE. Anchors nearby suggest religious leaders dropped the offerings during rituals held from boats. Researchers think such ceremonies helped bind lakeside groups into the Tiwanaku state.

source.name: Penn State News: Rise of religion pre-dates Incas at Lake Titicaca

source2.name: EurekAlert! (AAAS): release on Delaere, Capriles and Stanish, PNAS 2019

title: The Stone Warriors of Sechín
text: Peru's National Library dates the temple of Cerro Sechín and its carved stones to about 1900 BCE, calling them the oldest of their kind on the continent. Around the great temple, a wall shows 20 carved warriors alongside the remains of defeated or sacrificed enemies. Scholars still debate whether it shows a bloody battle or human sacrifice. Julio C. Tello discovered the site in 1937.

source.name: Biblioteca Nacional del Perú: page on Sechín and its stone warriors

title: Thirteen Towers That Track the Sun
text: In Peru's Casma Valley desert, people at Chankillo built a line of 13 towers along a hilltop ridge, used between about 250 and 200 BCE. Watching the sun rise and set behind the towers from two observation points, they could mark the solstices, the equinoxes and every other date of the year to within 1 or 2 days. The site probably served a solar cult.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Chankillo Archaeoastronomical Complex

title: Painted Houses for the Dead
text: Between about 600 and 900 CE, people in Colombia's Andes carved huge tombs into volcanic rock beneath hilltops at Tierradentro. Stairs lead down to chambers up to 12 metres wide, with columns and walls painted red and black on white. The tombs copy the inside of houses of the time, linking the homes of the living above ground with those of the ancestors below.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: National Archeological Park of Tierradentro

title: A Whole Hilltop Carved Into a Temple
place: Fuerte de Samaipata, Florida Province, Santa Cruz, Bolivia
text: By about 300 CE, people of the Mojocoyas culture began shaping a huge red sandstone rock above Samaipata in Bolivia. About 220 metres long, it is carved all over with animals, geometric shapes, niches and water channels used in rituals. UNESCO calls it one of the most colossal ancient ceremonial works of the Andes and Amazon. The Inca later made the site a provincial capital.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Fuerte de Samaipata

title: Uxmal Saves Every Drop of Rain
text: Founded around 700 CE in Yucatán's Puuc hills, Uxmal grew from a farming town into a Maya capital of up to 20,000 people. Builders dug reservoirs called chultunoob to store rainwater, and sculptures of Chaac, the rain god, cover its buildings. Instead of a grid, the city was laid out to match the hills and events in the sky such as the rising and setting of Venus.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pre-Hispanic Town of Uxmal

title: Deer Caught in Painted Nets
text: The Ventarrón Temple on Peru's north coast was first built around 2300–2035 BCE, and its wall paintings are among the oldest in the Americas. Beside an altar, two murals show deer caught in nets, painted in reds, pinks, yellow, white, black and grey. Scientists found the painters mixed mineral pigments, iron oxides, clays and earths to create this wide range of colours.

source.name: Heritage Science (peer-reviewed): The origins of mural painting in Ancient Peru: archaeometric preliminary study of the Ventarrón mural paintings

title: Cacao Before Chocolate
place: Puerto Escondido, Ulúa Valley, Cortés, Honduras
text: Pottery shards from Puerto Escondido in Honduras, dated to 1100 BCE, held the earliest chemical evidence of cacao drinking that Cornell and Penn Museum scientists had found. The first cacao drinkers probably fermented the pulp around the seeds into an alcoholic brew. They poured it from bottles with long, skinny spouts, quite unlike the wide jugs later used to froth chocolate.

source.name: Cornell Chronicle: In search of wine, ancients become earliest chocoholics

dateLabel: About 100 BCE (paintings made c. 100 BCE–1300 CE)
title: The Great Murals of Baja California
place: Sierra de San Francisco, Mulegé, Baja California Sur, Mexico
text: From about 100 BCE to 1300 CE, a people who have since disappeared painted the rock shelters of Baja California's Sierra de San Francisco. Some huge panels hold hundreds or even thousands of figures of people, sea creatures and land animals in red, black, white and yellow. The dry climate and hard-to-reach ravines have kept them remarkably well preserved.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rock Paintings of the Sierra de San Francisco

title: Towns Hidden Under the Amazon Forest
text: Beginning around 500 BCE, people in the Upano Valley of Ecuador's Amazon, near a massive volcano, built 15 settlements linked by an intricate road system. Laser scanning from the air, called lidar, revealed them under the forest across a 600-square-kilometre stretch of the valley. The farmers here grew maize, beans, sweet potatoes and yucca.

source.name: Science News: An ancient, massive urban complex has been found in the Ecuadorian Amazon

title: Carvings of a Famine at Vichama
text: About 3,800 years ago, people of the Caral civilization at Vichama, on Peru's coast, carved 32 wall reliefs that archaeologists call the Dance of Death and Life. They show dead adults with ribs showing and, above them, young people between two fish. A human-like toad, linked to the coming of rain, tops the building. Archaeologist Ruth Shady ties the scenes to a famine caused by climate change.

source.name: Andina (Peru's state news agency): Vichama registra evidencias del cambio climático que afectó a la Civilización Caral

dateLabel: July 13, 139 CE (eclipse recorded on the stone)
title: A Stone That Remembers an Eclipse
text: La Mojarra Stela 1, a volcanic stone over four tonnes and 2.2 metres tall, shows a figure in profile holding a glyph, beside 21 columns of signs. Its writing system, still not understood though it resembles Maya script, is one of the oldest and most complete in the Americas. Researcher Fernando Winfield Capitaine reads one glyph as the solar eclipse of July 13, 139 CE.

source.name: Universidad Veracruzana, Gaceta No. 63: article on the Estela de La Mojarra at the Museo de Antropología de Xalapa

title: The Oldest Lowland Maya Village
text: Cuello, in northern Belize, was settled around 1200 BCE and remains the oldest known lowland Maya village. Archaeologist Norman Hammond's team dug there from 1975 to 2002, finding houses, early public buildings and almost 200 burials showing ranks and long-distance trade. They also found the earliest known Mesoamerican sweatbath, which the Maya call a pib na.

source.name: Anthropological Notebooks, Norman Hammond: The dawn and the dusk: beginning and ending a long-term research program at the Preclassic Maya site of Cuello, Belize

title: A Queen's Victory Temple
text: At Pattadakal in Karnataka, Chalukya builders of the 7th and 8th centuries blended temple styles from northern and southern India. Nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary stand together here. The masterpiece is the Temple of Virupaksha, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to celebrate her husband's victory over the kings from the South.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal

title: The Great Monastery of Paharpur
text: A clay seal names King Dharmapala, who ruled from 770 to 810, as the first builder of Somapura Mahavihara, the Great Monastery in north-west Bangladesh. Its central shrine rose about 70 feet, wrapped in bands of terracotta plaques, and in its final phase 177 cells formed its outer wall. It stayed a famous centre of learning until the 12th century and influenced Buddhist buildings as far away as Cambodia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur

title: A Brick City Swallowed by Jungle
text: In the 15th century the general Ulugh Khan Jahan built the city of Khalifatabad, now Bagerhat, in south-west Bangladesh within a few years. Its baked-brick mosques, tombs, bridges, roads and water tanks show expert planning, and it needed no walls because people could retreat into the Sundarbans mangroves. After Khan Jahan died in 1459, the jungle covered the city.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat

title: A Temple Topped With Floating Bricks
text: Work on the Rudreshwara, or Ramappa, Temple in Telangana began in 1213 and is thought to have gone on for some 40 years. Kakatiya builders gave its tower lightweight porous "floating bricks" to make the roof less heavy. Its bracket figures, carved from hard dolerite with a metal-like shine, show dancers in the regional styles of Kakatiya culture.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana

title: An Upside-Down Temple for Water
text: Rani-ki-Vav, the Queen's Stepwell at Patan in Gujarat, was first built as a memorial to a king in the 11th century. Designed as an upside-down temple honouring the sacredness of water, it steps down seven levels past more than 500 main sculptures. At its deepest level a tank lies 23 metres below ground, and the well shaft goes down 30 metres.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat

title: Sculptors Who Signed Their Work
text: In the 12th and 13th centuries, Hoysala architects in Karnataka invented a new temple style to give their kingdom its own identity. Star-shaped shrines at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are covered in lifelike carvings, including the legend of Sala killing a tiger. Unusually for the subcontinent, the artists left many signatures, a sign of the high standing they enjoyed.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas

title: Kalhana's River of Kings
text: In 1148 the Kashmiri poet Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini, a history of Kashmir in 7,826 Sanskrit verses split into eight books. He studied inscriptions about temples and land grants, coins, ruins and family records. His ideal was a poet who, like a judge, records the past free from love or hatred, though his early chapters still mix legend with history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Rajatarangini

title: A Bengali Teacher Heads for Tibet
text: Atish Dipankar was born in Vajrayogini village in Vikramapura, Bengal, and became head of the great Vikramashila monastery. Invited by a Buddhist king of Tibet, he began his journey there in 1040. In Tibet he wrote, translated and edited more than two hundred books, many from Sanskrit into Tibetan. He died near Lhasa, and in 1978 his ashes were brought to Dhaka.

source.name: Banglapedia: Dipankar Srijnan, Atish

title: A Young Newar Artist Goes East
text: The Newars are the traditional people of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley. In 1261 Pakpa invited a young Newar artist, Anige (also called Araniko), to the Yuan court of the Mongol rulers, along with 24 other Himalayan artisans. Between 1270 and 1279 Anige helped design and oversee the White Stupa in Beijing, and he rose to become director of all artisan classes.

source.name: Rubin Museum, Project Himalayan Art (Isabelle Charleux): Newar Artist's Buddhist Monument for the Mongol Rulers in Beijing

title: Underground Homes in Kashmir
place: Burzahom, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: From about 3000 BCE, the first settlers at Burzahom in Kashmir lived in pits dug into the soil with long stone axes, and their cut-marks can still be seen. Some pits were 3.95 metres deep, wide at the bottom and likely roofed with birch. People made tools of stone, bone and antler, and an engraved stone shows a hunting scene with a human and a dog.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: The Neolithic Settlement of Burzahom

title: A Town Planned From Day One
place: Rehman Dheri, near Dera Ismail Khan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
text: Around 3300 BCE people began a settlement at Rehman Dheri in north-west Pakistan, and it seems to have had a formal plan from its earliest phases. A wall enclosed a grid of streets and lanes dividing regular blocks. Walls of houses still show up in the morning dew, and kilns and slag mark small workshops. It is a rare, undisturbed picture of how towns began in South Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Archaeological Site of Rehman Dheri

title: Letters on Pots at Keeladi
text: According to Tamil Nadu's Department of Archaeology, carbon dating puts some finds at Keeladi as early as 580 BCE. Its people built brick walls and clay floors, left bones of cows, buffalo and goats that hint at farming, and played board games. They wrote on pottery in the Tamil-Brahmi script, and digs have turned up spinning and weaving tools, cloth-dyeing works, brick kilns and pottery workshops.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine (Livia Gershon): Archaeologists Unearth Ancient Dagger Linked to Enigmatic Indian Civilization

title: The Oldest Known Case of Leprosy
text: At Balathal in Rajasthan, a middle-aged man was buried inside a stone enclosure, in layers of burned cow dung ash. Changes to the bones of his nose and upper jaw point to leprosy, showing the disease was present in India by about 2000 BCE. It is the oldest documented skeletal evidence for the disease, and the authors say the unusual burial may reflect how people with leprosy were treated.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Robbins et al.): Ancient Skeletal Evidence for Leprosy in India (2000 B.C.)

title: Seventy Who Walked Out of Kalunga
text: In 1814 the East India Company went to war with Gorkha. At the hill fort of Kalunga, also called Nalapani, about 600 Goorkha soldiers under Balbhadra held off attackers, and the British commander Gillespie was killed on 31 October. On the night of 29 November the 70 survivors charged out and escaped. Two memorials were later raised, one to each side.

source.name: The Gurkha Museum: The Battle of Kalunga

source2.name: National Army Museum: Gurkhas

title: Newspapers Under Police Watch
text: On March 14, 1878, during Viceroy Lord Lytton's rule, the Vernacular Press Act became law. Papers had to hand police the proof sheets of their contents before printing, and police rather than judges decided what was seditious. Papers such as Somprakash, Amrita Bazar Patrika and Dacca Prakash were targeted. Many papers were fined and editors jailed until Lord Ripon's government withdrew the Act.

source.name: Banglapedia (Sirajul Islam): Vernacular Press Act, 1878

title: Half a Million Tombs on Makli Hill
text: Near the Indus delta in Sindh, the hill of Makli holds about half a million tombs and graves, one of the largest cemeteries in the world. Kings, queens, saints and scholars of nearby Thatta lie here. Among the finest stone tombs is that of Jam Nizamuddin II, who reigned from 1461 to 1509. The monuments fuse Gujarat-style Hindu and Mughal influences into a local style.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historical Monuments at Makli, Thatta

title: One Woman's DNA From Rakhigarhi
text: Rakhigarhi in Haryana was the largest town of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and charcoal from its main living area dates to 2800–2300 BCE. Scientists screened 61 skeletons from its graves before finding a tiny amount of DNA in one woman's remains. Her genes point to ancestors related to ancient Iranians and South-east Asian hunter-gatherers, though those ancestors almost certainly lived in South Asia for thousands of years.

source.name: Cell, via PubMed Central (Shinde et al.): An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers

source2.name: Nature India (Biplab Das): Where did the Indus Valley people come from?

title: A Capital Left to the Jungle
place: Anuradhapura, North Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: Anuradhapura grew around a cutting of the Buddha's fig tree, brought in the 3rd century BCE by Sanghamitta, founder of an order of Buddhist nuns. It flourished as Sri Lanka's political and religious capital for 1,300 years, until an invasion in 993 led to its abandonment. Polonnaruwa became the new capital, and Anuradhapura's palaces and monasteries lay hidden in dense jungle for many years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred City of Anuradhapura

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ancient City of Polonnaruwa

title: A River Becomes a Border
text: Ranjit Singh, Maharaja of the Punjab, hoped to bring together all the Sikh lands up to the vicinity of Delhi, but the English thwarted him. In 1809 they made him sign the Treaty of Amritsar, which fixed the Sutlej River as his eastern boundary. He turned his ambitions elsewhere, and by 1820 he ruled the whole Punjab between the Sutlej and Indus rivers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Khushwant Singh): Ranjit Singh

title: Bhutan Chooses a King
text: For centuries Bhutan had two supreme authorities: a dharma raja for spiritual affairs and a deb raja for worldly matters, while regional governors often fought their way into office. In 1907, after the dharma raja died and the deb raja withdrew into a life of contemplation, a council of lamas, abbots, councillors and laymen chose Ugyen Wangchuk of Tongsa as hereditary king.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Pradyumna P. Karan): Bhutan, History

title: Mehrgarh Packs Up and Moves
text: Near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, people lived at Mehrgarh for thousands of years, leaving layers over 11 metres deep from the seventh to the third millennium BCE. Small mud-brick storerooms and early cattle and barley farming grew into a Bronze Age village with its own crafts. By 2600 BCE the settlement had shifted to Naushero, some six kilometres south.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Archaeological Site of Mehrgarh

title: The Great Kathmandu Earthquake
text: A chronicle from Kathmandu records that on June 7, 1255, an earthquake brought down temples and houses, killing one third of the inhabitants, including King Abhaya Malladeva. Survivors left the country, and aftershocks were felt for four months. Geologists have since traced its surface rupture east of the city, on a similar stretch of fault to the rupture of the great 1934 earthquake.

source.name: Earth, Planets and Space (Bollinger et al.): Slip deficit in central Nepal: omen for a repeat of the 1344 AD earthquake?

title: Pots With Rims Like Flames
text: Around 3300 BCE, Jōmon potters in the middle Shinano River basin developed a striking new style: flame-shaped pottery covered in three-dimensional patterns with no gaps. Experts think these pots were generally used in rituals such as festivals, yet they were certainly used for boiling too. The style vanished by about 2800 BCE. Tokamachi's museum now displays such pots alongside National Treasures.

source.name: Tokamachi City Museum: Jomon period and the area of flame-type pottery

title: The Bear Who Became a Mother
text: Korean legend says Dangun, the first king of the Koreans, took the throne in 2333 BCE. In one telling, a bear and a tiger hoped to become human and were told to stay in a cave eating only mugwort and garlic. The tiger gave up, but the bear became a woman and Dangun's mother. An altar on Ganghwa Island is said to have been built by Dangun himself.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tangun (Dangun)

title: Goguryeo's First Cliff-Top Capital
place: Wunü Mountain City, Huanren, Liaoning, China
text: Tradition says the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo was founded in 37 BCE by Jumong (Chumo), a leader of one of the Buyeo tribes, though modern historians think the state formed earlier. UNESCO says Wunü Mountain City was built that year as its first capital, walled partly in stone and partly by sheer cliffs, with a palace, watchtower, houses and warehouses inside.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Goguryeo

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom

title: Gifts for a Sacred Sea Island
text: From the 4th century CE, people prayed for safety at sea on Okinoshima, an island 60 km off Kyushu, leaving offerings at its ritual sites. Many gifts were exquisitely made and came from overseas, showing busy contact between Japan, the Korean Peninsula and the Asian continent. The rituals lasted until the end of the 9th century, and the island is still sacred today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region

title: Baekje Retreats to Ungjin
text: In the late 5th century the northern kingdom of Goguryeo seized Baekje's lands along the Han River, so Baekje moved its capital south to Ungjin, today's Gongju. UNESCO dates Baekje's later capitals, temples and tombs from 475 to 660. In these years Baekje refined Chinese ideas in city planning, building, art and Buddhism and passed them on to Japan.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Baekje Historic Areas

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Baekje

title: A Temple for Two Sets of Parents
text: UNESCO dates Bulguksa Temple on Mount Tohamsan to 774, in Silla times. Minister Kim Dae-seong oversaw it in memory of his parents in this life, and the nearby Seokguram Grotto for his parents in a previous life. Inside the granite grotto, a great Buddha gazes out to sea under a domed ceiling built from more than 360 stone slabs.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa Temple

title: A New Capital Without Temples
text: In 794 Japan's government moved into Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, a planned city laid out between the Katsura and Kamo rivers on the model of ancient Chinese capitals. Leaders wanted to escape the heavy Buddhist influence of old Nara, so new temples were banned, except two flanking the great southern gate. Kyoto stayed the imperial capital until the middle of the 19th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kyōto, History

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto

title: Designing Xanadu on the Grassland
place: Site of Xanadu (Shangdu), Zhenglan Banner, Inner Mongolia, China
text: In 1256 Kublai Khan's Chinese adviser Liu Bingzhong designed a new city on the edge of the Mongolian plateau: Xanadu. Planned by Chinese feng shui, with mountains behind and a river in front, it also held nomadic encampments and a royal hunting ground. Kublai rose to power here, and foreign travellers' tales later made Xanadu a legend around the world.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Site of Xanadu

title: Tsongkhapa's Strict New Monastery
place: Ganden Monastery, near Lhasa, Tibet, China
text: In 1409 Ganden Monastery was founded near Lhasa for the Gelug school of Tsongkhapa, a Tibetan lama who wanted monks to live by strict rules again. He restored celibacy, banned alcohol and meat, demanded higher learning and had his followers wear yellow. Drepung and Sera soon followed, and the Gelug school's leaders, the Dalai Lamas, later came to rule Tibet.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dge-lugs-pa (Gelug)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tsong-kha-pa

title: The Bridge of Nations Bell
text: In 1458, under King Shō Taikyū of the Ryūkyū Kingdom, a bronze bell was cast with a boastful inscription in classical Chinese. It calls Ryūkyū a bridge between the nations, an island paradise filled with treasures from foreign lands. The words were not empty: this small maritime kingdom grew rich as a trading hub, reselling goods from across East and Southeast Asia.

source.name: Nippon.com (Uezato Takashi): Okinawa: The Unique Culture of the Ryūkyū Islands

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu

title: A Monastery on a Fallen Capital
text: In 1585 the Buddhist monastery of Erdene Zuu was built on the site of Karakorum, the old Mongol imperial capital that Chinese forces had destroyed in 1388. UNESCO calls it the earliest surviving Mongol Buddhist monastery and a setting for the growth of a Mongolian form of Buddhism. Today it is a museum, surrounded by grassland still grazed by nomadic herders.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Karakorum

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape

title: Mongolia's Artist-Lama
text: In 1639 Zanabazar, a son of the line of the Tüsheet Khans of Khalkha, was declared the reincarnation of the Tibetan scholar Taranatha, who had taught in Mongolia for 20 years. Enthroned in 1640 as the Javzandamba Khutagt, he was hailed as the "High Enlightened One." He was also an artist: his superb statues of the goddess Tara are now kept in Ulaanbaatar's Green Palace museum.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mongolia, The successor states of the Mongol empire

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Green Palace

title: A Royal Show for China's Envoy
text: In 1719 a performance was staged at Shuri Castle to entertain an important envoy from China, who had come to recognize a new Ryūkyū king. It was the first performance of what became kumiodori, Okinawa's traditional musical theatre, now on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. The royal government directed these arts, the local elite cultivated them, and all the dancers were men.

source.name: Nippon.com (Uezato Takashi): Okinawa: The Unique Culture of the Ryūkyū Islands

title: A Dutch Anatomy Book in Japanese
text: In 1771 the doctors Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and Nakagawa Jun'an watched the dissection of executed bodies at Kozukappara in Edo, carrying a Dutch anatomy book. Amazed at how accurate it was, they decided to translate it. After years of work, including inventing Japanese words for many body parts, they published it as Kaitai shinsho, the New Book of Anatomy, in 1774.

source.name: Nagoya University Medical Library: 1774 Sugita Genpaku, Kaitai Shinsho

source2.name: U.S. National Library of Medicine, Historical Anatomies: Johann Adam Kulmus

title: A Six-Year-Old Sent to America
text: When Japan's Iwakura Mission set off for the United States and Europe in 1871, three young girls went along, tasked by the empress with learning how to start women's education in Japan. The youngest, Tsuda Umeko, was just six. She later studied at Bryn Mawr College, and in 1900 she founded the English School for Women, which flourishes today as Tsuda University.

source.name: Government of Japan, Highlighting Japan: Daughters of Meiji: Bringing Women's Education to Japan

title: The Short-Lived Kingdom of Kashgaria
text: In 1864 Yakub Beg, an adventurer from Kokand, entered Xinjiang amid Muslim uprisings against Qing rule and built his own kingdom of Kashgaria, centred at Kashgar. Russia and Britain both signed trade treaties with him, and the Ottoman sultan named him emir. Then a Qing army under the scholar-general Zuo Zongtang marched west, and on May 16, 1877, Kashgaria came to an end.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Yakub Beg

title: A School Named for Pear Blossoms
text: On May 31, 1886, the American Methodist missionary Mary F. Scranton founded a girls' school in Seoul. Early in 1887 King Gojong of Joseon named it Ewha Haktang to celebrate the start of women's education in Korea. The name may come from pear blossoms (ewha) scattered near the school. In 1946 Ewha became the first university permitted by Korea's Ministry of Education.

source.name: Ewha Womans University: Founding Spirit & History

source2.name: Ewha Womans University: School Name

title: Masks Against the Manchurian Plague
text: In October 1910 a deadly airborne plague broke out in Manchuria, probably spread by marmots hunted for fur that could be dyed to imitate mink. It killed more than 60,000 people. The Cambridge-trained doctor Wu Lien-teh showed it was pneumonic plague, won permission to cremate the dead and urged everyone to wear face masks. By the end of April 1911 the epidemic was declared over.

source.name: Le Infezioni in Medicina (Michaleas et al., via PMC): The Manchurian pandemic of pneumonic plague (1910–1911)

title: The Dalai Lama Slips Away
text: On March 10, 1959, rumours that Chinese authorities planned to kidnap the Dalai Lama brought crowds out in Lhasa to surround his summer palace and protect him. Amid the chaos, on March 17 he escaped under cover of darkness, disguised as a Tibetan soldier. He settled in Dharamshala, India, and tens of thousands of Tibetans followed him into exile.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: 14th Dalai Lama

title: Okinawa Swaps Dollars for Yen
text: On May 15, 1972, Okinawa returned to Japanese sovereignty, and its money changed from the dollar to the yen. People in Naha lined up to swap their dollars. Before reversion, signal fires were lit on Okinawa's northern tip and on a nearby island across the water, expressing the hope that this day would come. The extensive US military bases there, however, stayed in operation.

source.name: Nippon.com: Okinawa Since 1945: A Photo Retrospective

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Okinawa

title: Live TV Reunites Lost Families
place: Korean Broadcasting System (KBS), Seoul, South Korea
text: From June 30 to November 14, 1983, South Korea's KBS television broadcast live reunions of families torn apart by war. The show ran for 453 hours and 45 minutes. Its archive of videotapes, producers' journals, applications and photographs is now on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, a record of the deep scars the Cold War left on ordinary people.

source.name: UNESCO Memory of the World: The Archives of the KBS Special Live Broadcast "Finding Dispersed Families"

title: A Wooden Town on a Lake
text: Around 738–737 BCE, people of the Lusatian culture founded a fortified settlement at Biskupin in what is now Poland. It had about 100 houses whose gable walls adjoined each other, lined up along 11 perpendicular streets joined by a ring street running inside the rampart. A breakwater outside the rampart kept lake waves from damaging the defences.

source.name: Archaeological Museum in Poznań: Bronze Age and the Dawn of Iron Age

title: The Warship That Sank in Minutes
text: On 10 August 1628 Vasa, the most powerful warship in the Baltic, sank in Stockholm harbour just minutes after setting sail for the first time. Its upper hull was too tall and heavy, and its gun ports had been left open. About 30 people died. Searchers confirmed the wreck in 1956, and on 24 April 1961 it broke the surface again.

source.name: Vasa Museum: The disaster

source2.name: Vasa Museum: The salvage

title: A New Star in Cassiopeia
text: On the early evening of 11 November 1572, after a session of alchemy experiments, the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe spotted an extra star in Cassiopeia and had his assistant confirm it. His careful observations, published in 1574, helped show the star truly belonged to the heavens, not the nearby world below the Moon. Astronomers now call it Tycho’s supernova.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Tycho Brahe

source2.name: NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory: Tycho’s Supernova Remnant

title: A Promise of Religious Peace
text: When the last Jagiellonian king died in July 1572, Poland had no rules for running the state without a king. A general convention met in Warsaw in January 1573 and agreed the Confederation of Warsaw, which set out peaceful co-existence for nobles of all religious denominations. In 2003 UNESCO added the document to its Memory of the World Register.

source.name: UNESCO Memory of the World: The Confederation of Warsaw of 28th of January 1573

title: A Parliament in a Rift Valley
text: In 930 Icelanders set up the Althing, an open-air assembly for the whole island, in a dramatic rift valley at Þingvellir. For two weeks each year it made laws and settled disputes, and it kept meeting there until 1798. Visitors can still see fragments of around 50 booths built from turf and stone, where people stayed during the assembly.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Þingvellir National Park

title: Denmark’s Birth Certificate
text: Around 965 King Harald Bluetooth raised a huge rune stone at Jelling between two burial mounds, in memory of his parents Gorm and Thyra. Its inscription boasts that Harald won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christians. One face shows the earliest picture of Christ in Scandinavia, and the stone is often called Denmark’s birth certificate.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: The Jelling Stone

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Jelling Mounds, Runic Stones and Church

title: The Last Stand of the Dacian King
text: King Decebalus united the Dacian tribes of what is now Romania and led them in wars against the Roman emperors Domitian and Trajan. In 106 the emperor Trajan seized the capital, Sarmizegetusa, for a second time, and the defeated king took his own life. Dacia became a Roman province, and Trajan’s Column in Rome still shows scenes of the war.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Decebalus

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains

title: A Poet Banished to the Black Sea
text: In 8 CE the emperor Augustus banished the famous Roman poet Ovid to Tomis, a port on the Black Sea first settled by Greeks. Ovid blamed his love-advice poem Ars amatoria and a mysterious “error”.
