From exile he wrote the Tristia and Letters from the Black Sea, pleading for pardon, but neither Augustus nor Tiberius relented. He died at Tomis in 17 CE.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ovid

title: Rome’s Great Enemy Meets His End
text: Mithradates VI, king of Pontus, contested Rome’s power in Asia Minor. After Pompey defeated him, he set himself up at Panticapaeum, today’s Kerch, and was planning to invade Italy by way of the Danube. In 63 BCE his own troops, led by his son Pharnaces, turned against him. When his attempt to poison himself failed, he ordered a Gallic mercenary to kill him.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mithradates VI Eupator

title: Painted Walls of a Thracian Tomb
text: Near Seutopolis, capital of the Thracian king Seutes III, a tomb was built around the end of the 4th century BCE. Its narrow corridor and round burial chamber are painted with murals of Thracian burial rituals and culture. Found in 1944, the frescoes are Bulgaria’s best-preserved artworks from the Hellenistic period, and visitors now see a copy in a nearby museum.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak

title: A Cathedral of Many Domes
text: Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise founded Saint Sophia Cathedral, built between 1037 and 1044 by local builders working with Byzantine masters. One large central dome rises above 12 smaller ones, and inside, an 11th-century mosaic of Christ Pantocrator gazes down from the central dome. Yaroslav founded Ukraine’s first library here, and his sarcophagus still survives inside.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Saint Sophia Cathedral

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kyiv: Saint-Sophia Cathedral and Related Monastic Buildings, Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra

title: Chasing Scythians Who Would Not Fight
place: Lower Danube into Scythia, Odesa Oblast, Ukraine
text: In about 513 BCE the Persian king Darius I marched into Europe over a pontoon bridge across the Bosporus, then crossed the Danube on a bridge of boats into Scythia. The Scythians refused battle and retreated, laying waste to the land as they went. After chasing them for a month, harassed and facing October weather, Darius turned back.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Darius iii. Darius I the Great

title: A Fireball Hits an Inhabited Island
text: Scientists once disagreed by as much as 6,000 years about when a space rock blasted the Kaali crater on the Estonian island of Saaremaa. By radiocarbon dating charcoal trapped in the debris thrown out by the impact, a 2016 study concluded it most probably formed shortly after 1530–1450 BCE. People already lived on Saaremaa when the bolide struck.

source.name: Losiak et al., Meteoritics & Planetary Science (2016): Dating a small impact crater, abstract via Estonian geoscience literature database

title: A University for Prague
text: In 1348 Charles IV, King of Bohemia and Holy Roman Emperor, founded a university in Prague. Modelled on the universities of Bologna and Paris, it was the first of its kind north of the Alps and east of Paris, with faculties of theology, liberal arts, law and medicine. The reformer Jan Hus later served as its rector.

source.name: Charles University: History

title: Mongol Explosives at the Sajó River
text: On 10 April 1241 Mongol forces under Batu Khan and his general Subutai attacked King Béla IV’s Hungarian army at the Sajó River. Using catapult-fired explosives, they forced a crossing and encircled the Hungarian camp. Béla fled to Croatia, and the Mongols burned Pest. When he returned, he began rebuilding with a strong network of fortifications.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Mohi

title: An Empress’s Private Gallery
text: In 1764 Catherine the Great founded the Hermitage as a court museum beside the Winter Palace, a private gallery for the art she collected. It opened to the public only in 1852. Today it fills five connected buildings and holds nearly three million items, from Stone Age objects to modern works, including one of the world’s richest collections of European painting.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hermitage

title: A Printer’s ABC Book in Lviv
text: Ivan Fedorovych had printed church books in Moscow before he settled in Lviv in 1572. Working at Saint Onuphrius Monastery, in 1574 he published a new edition of the Apostolos with his own life story at the end, plus an Azbuka, a primer for learning letters. His Lviv tombstone praises him for having renewed neglected printing.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Fedorovych (Fedorov), Ivan

title: Linnaeus Walks Into Lapland
text: On 12 May 1732 the 25-year-old Carl Linnaeus set out from Uppsala for Lapland. Over six months he covered more than 2,000 km, guided through wild country by the Saami people, who fascinated him. He described about a hundred plants new to science, plus birds, fish and minerals. The Linnean Society in London still keeps his travel diary and a carved walking stick.

source.name: Linnean Society of London: Linnaeus in Lapland

title: Six Weeks to Write a Constitution
text: On 10 April 1814, 112 elected representatives arrived at Eidsvoll Verk to write a constitution for Norway. After six weeks of intense work and votes in May, the Constitution was dated 17 May 1814, and the Danish prince Christian Frederik was elected King of Norway. By November that year, Norway had entered a union with Sweden under an amended Constitution.

source.name: Eidsvoll 1814 (Norwegian Parliament): The Constituent Assembly

source2.name: Eidsvoll 1814: The story of 1814 in 1-2-3

title: A Poet Sent Into Exile
text: In 1820 Aleksandr Pushkin published Ruslan and Ludmila, a romantic poem drawing on Russian folklore. That May, his political verses got him banished from St Petersburg to the remote south, first to Yekaterinoslav, now Dnipro in Ukraine. Travels in the Caucasus and Crimea during his exile gave him material for a famous cycle of romantic poems.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Aleksandr Pushkin

title: Cadets Rise Up in Warsaw
text: When Tsar Nicholas I signalled he might use the Polish Army against a revolution in Paris, a secret society of infantry cadets launched an uprising in Warsaw on 29 November 1830. They seized weapons from the arsenal and armed the city’s people. The revolt spread into Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine, but when Russian troops attacked Warsaw in September 1831, the Polish Army withdrew.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: November Insurrection

title: Riga, a Port for Hanseatic Trade
text: Riga was founded as a port town in 1201. From the 13th to the 15th century it was one of the key centres of the Hanseatic League in Eastern Europe, growing rich on trade with central and eastern Europe. Many of its earliest buildings were later lost to fire or war, but the medieval core still reflects that prosperity.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Riga

title: The Potter in 120,000 Beads
text: On the mangrove edge of the Bang Pakong River, a woman who probably died in her 30s was buried in garments stitched with more than 120,000 shell disc beads. Beside her ankle lay a potter's anvil and burnishing stones, so archaeologist Charles Higham thinks she was a specialist potter. A baby buried nearby had a miniature clay anvil of its own.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Ochre use in burial practices in Thailand, from the Neolithic to the Iron Age

source2.name: World Archaeology: Charles Higham, A prehistoric mystery

title: Rowing Souls on a Burial Jar
place: Manunggul Cave, Lipuun Point, Palawan, Philippines
text: In Manunggul Cave on Palawan, people used this earthenware jar about 2,700 years ago to protect the remains of the dead. On its lid, two small figures sit in a boat: the souls of the dead rowing their way to the afterlife. The jar shows a society that believed in the soul and life after death thousands of years before contact with organized religions.

source.name: Cultural Center of the Philippines Encyclopedia of Philippine Art: Manunggul Jar

title: A New Capital Across the River
text: In 1782 General Chao Phraya Chakkri took the throne as Rama I and moved the court of Siam from the west to the east bank of the Chao Phraya River. A wide bend in the river formed a natural moat, while to the east lay a swampy delta called the Sea of Mud. Rama I modeled his new city on the former capital, Ayutthaya.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Bangkok

title: Francis Light Lands on Penang
text: In 1786 Captain Francis Light of the British East India Company founded Fort Cornwallis on the island of Penang. The town that grew around it, George Town, flourished as a port of call on the India-China shipping run and drew Hokkien, Cantonese and Indian traders. Its shophouses and religious buildings of many faiths are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: George Town, Malaysia

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca

title: Sugar and Coffee Instead of Rice
text: In 1830 Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch introduced the Culture System in the Dutch East Indies. Javanese villagers were meant to set aside one-fifth of their rice fields for export crops such as sugar, coffee and indigo, or work 66 days for the government. In practice farmers lost more land and labor than that, and were left responsible when crops failed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Culture System

title: A Fever Dream of Evolution
text: Towards the end of February 1858, after a serious attack of malaria, naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace wrote an essay on how varieties of living things can drift away from their original type. He dated it from Ternate in the Moluccas and mailed it to Charles Darwin, who had reached the same idea independently. Their papers were read together in London on July 1, 1858.

source.name: Darwin Online: Darwin and Wallace 1858, On the tendency of species to form varieties (Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society)

source2.name: Mètode (Universitat de València), Xavier Bellés: The naturalist who got ahead of Darwin

title: The Fall of a Greek Courtier
text: Constantine Phaulkon sailed to Siam as a boy, learned Thai quickly, and rose to become King Narai's leading minister, inviting French troops and missionaries in. When Narai fell seriously ill in 1688, an anti-French faction led by the king's foster brother Phetracha overthrew him. Phaulkon was executed at Lop Buri, the French garrisons were expelled, and the new king, Phetracha, limited foreign influence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Constantine Phaulkon

title: The Last Prau to Marege
text: From at least 1700, hundreds of fishermen sailed each December from Makassar to northern Australia, a coast they called Marege, to catch, boil and dry trepang (sea cucumber) for sale to China. They brought Yolŋu people metal knives and axes, tobacco and words such as rrupia (money). After 1901 Australia banned the trepangers, and in 1907 the last prau made the voyage.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Trade with the Makasar

title: The Han Swallow Nam Viet
text: Nam Viet, or Southern Yue, was a kingdom stretching from southern China across the Red River delta as far south as Da Nang. In 111 BCE the Han emperor Wu Ti conquered it. Chinese settlement and culture followed into northern Vietnam, but the attempt to absorb Vietnam into China also made its people increasingly aware of their own identity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nam Viet

title: Roman Envoys Arrive by Vietnam
text: According to China's Book of the Later Han, in 166 CE envoys sent by Andun, king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), arrived through Rinan on the central Vietnamese coast. They offered elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn and turtle shell. The chronicler grumbled that the gifts were neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts might be exaggerated.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): The Western Regions according to the Hou Hanshu, trans. John E. Hill

title: Sultan Agung Marches on Batavia
text: Sultan Agung of Mataram brought his central Javanese kingdom to its greatest power, subduing coastal states from Tuban to Surabaya. Openly contemptuous of trade, he kept no real navy. In 1629 his forces attacked Batavia to drive out the Dutch, but superior Dutch naval forces held the city. Agung then turned east and fought the Balinese in Java.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Agung, sultan of Mataram

title: The Blind Naturalist of Ambon
text: In 1698 a blind German merchant, Georg Rumphius, sat in a whitewashed cottage on the spice island of Ambon, dictating detailed descriptions of crabs, sea snails, metals, stones and other rare things. He had lived most of his adult life there. He died alone on his island while the manuscript inched toward print, and in 1705 The Ambonese Curiosity Cabinet finally appeared in Amsterdam.

source.name: The New York Review of Books, Tim Flannery: Wonders of a Lost World

title: The King of Siam's Eclipse
text: King Mongkut of Siam worked out that a solar eclipse would cross his kingdom on August 18, 1868, and calculated that totality would last 6 minutes, 46 seconds. French astronomers found his prediction came within two seconds of their own. He watched from the jungle village of Wakor, but on the trip a mosquito gave him malaria, and he died six weeks after the expedition.

source.name: Science History Institute: The Eclipse That Killed a King (and May Have Saved a Kingdom)

title: A Garden That Grew an Industry
text: Singapore's botanic garden was created in 1859, first as a 'Pleasure Garden' in the English Landscape Style and later as an Economic Garden for plant research. Kew Gardens in Britain supplied the first rubber seedlings, but it was Singapore's garden that planted, developed and distributed them across much of Southeast Asia, helping plantation rubber expand. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Singapore Botanic Gardens

title: Tragedy Inside Batavia's Walls
text: For more than a century Chinese settlers had helped build Batavia, the Dutch East India Company's Asian headquarters. Then ecological decline, epidemics, runaway immigration and feuds among colonial officials broke that partnership. In October 1740, after a Chinese peasant uprising, the city's inhabitants massacred their Chinese neighbours inside the walls, looting house to house and sparing not even hospitals and prisons.

source.name: Leiden University: A Colonial Tragedy, The Chinese Massacre at Batavia, 1740 (Leonard Blussé)

title: A Governor Moves to Lifau
text: António Coelho Guerreiro was the first governor of Timor to actually live there, settling at Lifau, a sheltered bay favoured by merchants. A plan he ordered in 1702 shows a church of Saint Anthony and a hospital. He also had a large earth-and-stone fort built above the sea, guarding a community made up mainly of Portuguese mestizos and Chinese. Lifau stayed the centre of Portuguese power until 1769.

source.name: Heritage of Portuguese Influence (HPIP, Gulbenkian Foundation): Lifau

title: Bodawpaya Swallows Arakan
text: In 1784 King Bodawpaya of Myanmar invaded Arakan, the maritime kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, captured its king, Thamada, and deported more than 20,000 people as slaves. When Arakan became a province in 1785, Myanmar's border touched British India for the first time. Bodawpaya, who proclaimed himself a messianic Buddha, also began the Mingun pagoda, which would have stood 500 feet high if finished.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bodawpaya

title: The Price of a Throne
text: In 1794 the Siamese placed a refugee Cambodian prince, Eng, on the Cambodian throne. In exchange they took two provinces, Battambang and Siem Reap, which included the ruins of Angkor, and kept them until 1907. Squeezed between Siam and Vietnam, Cambodia went through 22 monarchs between 1603 and 1848, its kings losing territory and sovereignty by seeking foreign protection.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (David P. Chandler): Cambodia, Tai and Vietnamese hegemony

title: A Warehouseman's Secret Society
text: When Spain arrested the reformer José Rizal in 1892, shocked activists from a less privileged class quickly formed the Katipunan. Its leader, Andrés Bonifacio, was a self-educated warehouseman, and its aim was to expel the Spanish from the islands. For the first time, Filipino rebels combined nationalist goals with education. In August 1896 friars uncovered its plans, forcing an early revolt.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Gregorio C. Borlaza et al.): Philippines, The 19th century

title: One Vietnam, Two Governments
text: From about 1620 Vietnam was split in two. The Nguyen family, who had governed the south from Hue since 1558, refused to obey the Trinh princes who ran the north in the name of powerless Le emperors. For 50 years the Trinh tried to reconquer the south by force. Their last campaign failed in 1673, and a 100-year truce followed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vietnam, Two divisions of Dai Viet

title: Vientiane's Great Stupa
text: King Setthathirath I (ruled 1548–71) moved the capital of the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang from Luang Prabang to Vientiane, a river port on a plain beside the Mekong, and drove back invasions around 1565 and 1570. The city's outstanding building, the stupa That Luang, dates from about 1566. Lao civil servants under Prince Phetsarath restored it during the French colonial period.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vientiane

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Pierre-Bernard Lafont et al.): History of Laos

title: Coins With a Hole in the Middle
text: Short of money, Governor Lachlan Macquarie imported 40,000 Spanish silver 'pieces of eight' and had their centres stamped out so they could not leave the colony. The job went to William Henshall, a convicted forger, who worked in a basement workshop. The first batch of holey dollars and dumps, Australia's first minted coins, was delivered on 25 February 1814.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Holey dollar

title: The Black Line Across Lutruwita
text: During the Black War, Lieutenant-Governor George Arthur ordered settlers to form a human chain to push the Oyster Bay, Big River, North Midlands and Ben Lomond peoples onto the Tasman Peninsula. On 7 October 1830 more than 2,200 men reported for duty. Most Aboriginal people slipped back into their own lands; only two were documented as captured.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, The Black Line

title: A Nest for the Māori Language
text: Kōhanga reo means 'language nest': a place where little children are totally immersed in the Māori language, customs and values, with their whānau involved in their learning. The first one opened at Pukeatua in Wainuiomata on 13 April 1982. Since then more than 50,000 children have attended, and many are now parents of a second generation of kōhanga children.

source.name: Te Kōhanga Reo National Trust: Mō Mātau (About Us)

title: Digging Ditches at Kuk Swamp
place: Kuk, Western Highlands, Papua New Guinea
text: High in New Guinea's highlands, people at Kuk had grown bananas, taro and yam on mounds at the swamp's edge for thousands of years. From about 4,000 years ago they began draining the wetland itself, digging ditches with wooden tools. Kuk is one of the few places on Earth where farming seems to have been invented independently.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kuk Early Agricultural Site

title: The Coming of the Light
place: Erub (Darnley Island), Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: On 1 July 1871 the Reverend Samuel MacFarlane of the London Missionary Society anchored at Erub, travelling with South Sea Islander evangelists and teachers. Torres Strait Islanders remember this as the Coming of the Light. Christianity brought deep changes to every part of island life, and other islands celebrate their own Coming of the Light on the dates missionaries arrived there.

source.name: State Library of Queensland: Erub, Coming of the Light

title: Taken to the Cane Fields
text: In 1863, 67 South Sea Islanders were brought to Brisbane to work on a cotton plantation. They were the first of more than 62,000 men, women and children from about 80 islands, including Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands. Many were kidnapped, or 'blackbirded'. Activist Faith Bandler said of her father's experience: 'I maintain that it was a form of slavery.'

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Islander labourers

title: The Pearl Divers Go on Strike
place: Thursday Island, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: By the 1920s Australia supplied most of the world's mother-of-pearl shell, and Thursday Island was a hub for hundreds of luggers. In January 1936 Torres Strait Islander workers across the region refused to crew the pearling boats, demanding fairer conditions and more local control. The strike helped lay the groundwork for lasting reforms to how Islanders were represented and governed.

source.name: Australian National Maritime Museum: Pearling Elders exhibition honours Torres Strait pearling Elders

title: When Polynesia Met the Americas
text: The sweet potato comes from the Americas, yet it turns up in the ancient archaeological record of Polynesia. A 2020 genetic study of 807 people from 17 Pacific islands and 15 Native American groups found the answer in DNA: around AD 1200, Polynesians in eastern Polynesia met a Native American group most closely related to people living in present-day Colombia.

source.name: Nature: Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement (Ioannidis et al., 2020)

source2.name: Stanford Medicine News: Polynesians and Native Americans made early contact

title: Devils and Tigers Leave the Mainland
text: Tasmanian devils and thylacines (Tasmanian tigers) once roamed across Australia. By radiocarbon-dating fossil bones from across southern Australia, researchers from the University of Adelaide and Flinders University estimated that both disappeared from the mainland at the same time, about 3,200 years ago. That timing suggests a common cause, a clue to why both vanished on the mainland but survived in Tasmania.

source.name: Flinders University News: Tassie tiger and devil do the timewarp

title: Cooking Fires on Majuro Atoll
text: The Marshall Islands were first settled around the beginning of the Christian era by Micronesians who may have been influenced by Lapita culture. Charcoal from earth ovens dug up in Laura village on Majuro has been radiocarbon-dated to about 30 BCE and 50 CE. These early Marshall Islanders were skilled navigators who made long canoe voyages among the atolls.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Marshall Islands, History

title: Footprints in Rangitoto's Ash
place: Pūharakeke, Motutapu Island, Auckland, New Zealand
text: Around 1397 CE, Rangitoto volcano in Auckland's harbour erupted, burying signs of Māori occupation on neighbouring Motutapu Island under ash. At the Sunde site, footprints of people and their dogs are preserved between the ash layers. Māori clearly witnessed the eruption, yet surprisingly no traditional account of it seems to exist.

source.name: Journal of Pacific Archaeology: New Zealand's own Pompeii? The Sunde site, Motutapu Island (Brassey, 2024)

title: Australia Votes 'Yes'
text: Australia's constitution said Aboriginal people should not be counted in the population. After ten years of campaigning, led by groups such as FCAATSI with Kungarakan man Joe McGinness as a co-head, a referendum was held on 27 May 1967. Nearly 91 per cent voted 'yes', so First Nations peoples would be counted and the Commonwealth could make laws for them.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Indigenous referendum

title: A Nation of 800 Languages
text: Papua New Guinea was home to an estimated 1,000 tribes speaking more than 800 languages, and few believed they could unite. On 15 September 1975 the Australian flag, flying since 1906, was lowered for the last time at Hubert Murray Stadium. Independence came on 16 September, and Michael Somare, a former teacher and radio broadcaster from East Sepik, spoke to the new nation by midnight radio.

source.name: RNZ: Papua New Guinea's 50th anniversary of independence, how a nation of 800 languages was united

title: Two Māori Chiefs Meet King George
place: Bay of Islands, Northland, New Zealand
text: On 2 March 1820 the Ngāpuhi chiefs Hongi Hika and Waikato sailed from the Bay of Islands for England. At Cambridge they helped Professor Samuel Lee finish the first full guide to written Māori. King George IV gave Hongi two muskets, a coat of chain mail and a helmet. Back in Sydney, Hongi bought large amounts of muskets, and his later wars reached a devastating new scale.

source.name: Fletcher Trust Collection: Hongi and Waikato (John Jackson)

source2.name: Waitangi Treaty Grounds: Wives, Weaponry and War (Hongi Hika's haerenga)

title: Cave Camps in Palau's Rock Islands
text: Palau's Rock Islands are hundreds of mushroom-shaped limestone islands set in turquoise lagoons. From about 3,100 years ago people visited their caves seasonally to harvest the rich sea life, leaving rock art and burials behind. This use went on for some 2,500 years; later, permanent stone villages with defensive walls and terraces were built on a few of the islands.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rock Islands Southern Lagoon

title: Shell Fish-Hooks of the Sydney Coast
place: Port Jackson (Sydney Harbour), New South Wales, Australia
text: Archaeology traces shell fish-hooks on the New South Wales coast back almost 1,000 years. Around Sydney, men fished with spears while women used hook and line. Eora women shaped crescent hooks (burra or bara) from turban shell, fished from bark canoes with fires going, and spat chewed shellfish on the water instead of using bait.

source.name: Australian Museum: Aboriginal fishing in Port Jackson, and the introduction of shell fish-hooks to coastal New South Wales (Attenbrow)

source2.name: Dictionary of Sydney: Eora fisherwomen (Lisa Murray)

title: Australia's Oldest Pottery
place: Jiigurru (Lizard Island group), Great Barrier Reef, Queensland, Australia
text: In 2006 a few pieces of pottery turned up in Blue Lagoon on Jiigurru, 33 km off Cape York Peninsula. Excavations found 82 pieces, some decorated with pigment and incised lines. Radiocarbon dating shows they are between 2,950 and 1,815 years old, the earliest securely dated pottery in Australia, and the clays show it was likely all made right there on the island.

source.name: The Conversation: Aboriginal people made pottery and sailed to distant offshore islands thousands of years before Europeans arrived (Ulm, McNiven, McLean)

title: Samoan Voyagers Settle Niue
text: Niue is a raised coral island about 65 km around, far out in the southwestern Pacific. Archaeological evidence shows it was settled about 900 CE by people from Samoa. According to Niuean tradition, a second group, a war party from Tonga, arrived in the 16th century. Today's Niuean language is a Polynesian tongue related to both Tongan and Samoan.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Niue

title: Fiji Becomes a Crown Colony
text: Trade in sandalwood, sea cucumbers and muskets fuelled rivalries among Fiji's chiefs, and cotton planters arriving in the 1860s brought new fights over land. No chief could rule the whole group, and on 10 October 1874 Fiji became a British crown colony. Its first governor, Sir Arthur Gordon, banned sales of Fijian land and governed through the traditional chiefly structure.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Fiji, History

title: Nauru Picks Its Independence Day
text: In World War II, 1,200 Nauruans were taken to Truk (now Chuuk) as forced labourers for Japan. On 31 January 1946, 737 survivors came home. When the tiny phosphate island won independence, its people chose that same date: on 31 January 1968, the 22nd anniversary of the return from Truk, Nauru became a republic, with Hammer DeRoburt dominating its politics for two decades.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nauru, History

title: Tonga's Sacred King Shares Power
text: From at least the 10th century, Tonga was ruled by a line of sacred kings and queens, the Tuʻi Tonga. About 1470 the reigning Tuʻi Tonga handed his worldly powers to his brother, who took the title Tuʻi Haʻa Takalaua. A similar handover about 1600 created a third royal line, the Tuʻi Kanokupolu, whose holders eventually became Tonga's rulers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tonga, History

title: Utu for Te Ara: The Boyd
text: On the voyage from Sydney, the crew of the brig Boyd flogged the Ngāti Pou chief Te Ara. When the ship reached Whangaroa in 1809 to load kauri timber, his people took utu (retaliation): about seventy crew and passengers were killed, and the ship burned after gunpowder accidentally exploded. Wrongly blamed, the Bay of Islands chief Te Pahi saw his village attacked by whalers a year later.

source.name: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa: The blowing up of the Boyd (Steele and Watkins, 1889)

title: Ottar Tells a King About the North
text: About 890 CE, Ottar (Ohthere), a chieftain from what is now Troms in Norway, told King Alfred the Great about his journeys. He had sailed round the North Cape and along the coast of Lapland to the White Sea. Ottar owned 600 tame reindeer, but his main income was tax collected from the Sámi, paid in hides and whale and seal skins.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: European exploration – Exploration of the Atlantic coastlines

source2.name: Sámi Parliament (Sametinget): The Sami – an Indigenous People in Sweden (timeline)

title: The Eruption That Made a Wasteland
text: In 1362, Öræfajökull, Iceland's highest peak, blew apart in the island's largest explosive eruption since it was settled. Rich farmland at the foot of the volcano was buried under thick ash and swept by pyroclastic flows, while meltwater floods raced down the glaciers. The area was abandoned and renamed Öræfi, meaning "wasteland". Its ash has been found as far away as Greenland and western Europe.

source.name: The Open University (McGarvie, Stevenson, Nicholls): Is Iceland's tallest volcano awakening?

source2.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program: Öræfajökull

title: Islands Mortgaged for a Dowry
text: When Princess Margaret of Denmark married James III of Scotland, her father, King Christian I, couldn't afford a dowry. So he mortgaged first Orkney, then Shetland, to his new son-in-law. In May 1469 he wrote to the islanders telling them to obey the king of Scots and pay him taxes until the islands were redeemed. Christian paid them no more attention, and James annexed the islands in 1472.

source.name: Shetland Museum and Archives (Brian Smith): 550 Years Ago: how Shetland became part of Scotland

title: A Fatal Winter on the Kola Coast
text: In 1553 England sent three ships north-east under Sir Hugh Willoughby, searching for a sea passage to China. Willoughby, with two ships, wintered in a harbour on the Kola Peninsula, where he and all his men perished. His chief pilot, Richard Chancellor, separated in a gale, reached what is now Arkhangelsk and travelled overland to Moscow. A lucrative trade with Russia followed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Arctic – Study and exploration

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Richard Chancellor

title: The Trader Who Vanished
place: Arctic coast of Chukotka, Russia (exact site unknown)
text: Russian trader Nikita Shalaurov tried to sail east from the Kolyma River to the Bering Strait in 1762, but ice stopped him. Trying again in 1764, he and his party disappeared. What happened came from the people who lived there: the Chukchi later told of finding the expedition's wintering site littered with skeletons.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Arctic – Study and exploration (The Northeast Passage)

title: Cook Pushes Through the Bering Strait
text: In 1778 the English navigator James Cook sailed north through the Bering Strait and pushed west along the Arctic coast as far as Cape North, today's Cape Shmidt. His voyage provoked Catherine the Great of Russia to send her own expedition to explore the Chukchi Peninsula, led by Joseph Billings, who had been Cook's assistant astronomer.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Arctic – Study and exploration (The Northeast Passage)

title: Music and Dancing at Gilbert Sound
text: On July 29, 1585, English navigator John Davis entered a fjord near today's Nuuk and named it Gilbert Sound. On nearby islands his crew met many Greenlanders, and friendship was established. Davis took musicians on his voyages and had his sailors dance to the music. His narratives give what Vilhjalmur Stefansson called the first reasonably good description of Greenland's people in modern literature.

source.name: Dartmouth College, Encyclopedia Arctica (Eloise McCaskill Popini): John Davis

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: John Davis

title: Reindeer Hauling Silver Ore
text: In 1635 Queen Kristina's government in Sweden decided to start mining silver at Nasafjäll, a mountain in Sápmi, the Sámi homeland. The Sámi were forced to haul the ore to the coast with their reindeer. Later in the 17th century they were also made to provide transport for mines in other parts of Sápmi.

source.name: Sámi Parliament (Sametinget): The Sami – an Indigenous People in Sweden (timeline)

title: The Drums Ordered Burned
text: In 1685 the Swedish state decided to hold idolatry trials in all the Lappmarks, the Sámi districts. The drums of Sámi shamans were to be burned, and anyone who disobeyed could be flogged against the courthouse wall or made to run the gauntlet. Cult images called sieidi and sacrificial sites were destroyed, and sacred Sámi places were desecrated.

source.name: Sámi Parliament (Sametinget): The Sami – an Indigenous People in Sweden (timeline)

title: Cape Disappointment, South Georgia
text: On January 17, 1775, James Cook landed at Possession Bay on icy South Georgia and claimed it for King George III, calling it a land "doomed by nature". Sailing on to its southern tip, he realised this was not the great Southern Continent, so he named the spot Cape Disappointment. His journal notes on its seals, whales, penguins and seabirds laid the foundation for early studies in natural history.

source.name: South Georgia Museum: 250 Years of Discovery – Captain Cook's Antarctic Voyage

source2.name: South Georgia Museum: History of South Georgia

title: Greenland Votes to Leave Europe's Club
text: When Denmark joined the European Community, 70 per cent of Greenlanders had voted against membership. Fishing made up half their exports, and they wanted it under Greenland's own control. In a second referendum in February 1982, a small majority of 52 per cent chose to leave. After long talks over fishing rights, Greenland set 1 January 1985 as the date its new status would take effect.

source.name: UK Parliament, Hansard (House of Commons, 20 July 1984): Greenland (Withdrawal From EEC)

title: The Dog-Days King of Iceland
text: In 1809 a Danish adventurer, Jørgen Jørgensen, landed in Reykjavík with eight sailors, captured the Danish governor and locked him aboard ship. On June 26 he proclaimed himself "Protector of Iceland, Commander in Chief by Land and Sea", tried to restore the ancient Althing and sold cheap grain. Within two months a British warship took him away. Icelanders remember him as the Dog-Days King.

source.name: Reading Museum: Jørgen Jørgensen: the King of Iceland

title: Norway Goes, the Islands Stay
place: Tórshavn, Faroe Islands (treaty signed at Kiel)
text: On January 14, 1814, the Treaty of Kiel ended fighting between Denmark and Sweden in the Napoleonic Wars. Denmark had to hand Norway to Sweden, ending a union that began in 1380. But the old Norwegian settlements far out in the North Atlantic, Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands, stayed with Denmark. Even so, losing Norway disrupted Denmark’s political and economic life.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Treaty of Kiel

title: Kidnapped to Copenhagen
place: Itivdleq Fjord, south of Sisimiut, Greenland
text: In 1605 ships sent by King Christian IV to rediscover Greenland traded nails and old iron with Greenlanders for clothing, sealskins and narwhal tusks, then kidnapped four of them. One was shot. The survivors, today called Umik, Oqaq and Kigutikkaaq, could row their kayaks as fast as ten of the king's boatmen. Homesick, they built an umiak in Denmark and tried to escape.

source.name: ScienceNordic (Jens Winther Johannesen, Museum of Copenhagen): Did a recently found bird spear belong to a kidnapped Greenlander?

title: Following the Barking Seals
place: St. George Island, Pribilof Islands, Alaska, USA
text: An Unangan story told of Iggadaagix, a chief's son from Unimak Island, who was blown by a storm to misty islands full of fur seals. Guided by that tale, Russian navigator Gavriil Pribylov followed the sound of barking seals through Bering Sea fog in June 1786 and found St. George Island. Aleuts were then brought from the Aleutian Chain to harvest and process the seals.

source.name: NOAA Office of Response and Restoration: Pribilof Islands Historic Preservation – History, Russian period

title: Traders, Taxes and the Right to Hunt
text: The Swedish Crown gave the Birkarls, traders thought to come from what is now Tampere in Finland, the right to trade with the Sámi and collect taxes from them. An agreement concluded in 1328 said that the Sámi must not be prevented from hunting. The Birkarls divided the Sámi lands into trade districts called Lappmarks.

source.name: Sámi Parliament (Sametinget): The Sami – an Indigenous People in Sweden (timeline)

title: A Prince Without a Kingdom Takes Kabul
text: Babur spent ten years trying to win back Samarkand, his ancestor Timur's old capital, but lost both it and his home principality of Fergana to the Uzbek ruler Muhammad Shaybani Khan. In 1504 he seized Kabul with his personal followers and made it his capital, investing in public buildings and gardens. By his own account, Kabul's climate and its fruit made him fall in love with the city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Babur

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Kabul

title: Ground Rising Like an Elephant
text: On 6 July 1505 an earthquake shook the Kabul region, and an eyewitness account survives. In Paghman every house fell and 70 or 80 people died, while along the fault the ground in places rose "as high as an elephant" and elsewhere sank as deep. Thirty-three aftershocks struck that day, and Babur needed about a month of hard work to repair Kabul's fort.

source.name: USGS Open-File Report 2006-1185: Macroseismic effects (earthquake catalog for Afghanistan)

title: An Englishman in Bukhara's Markets
text: On 23 December 1558 the English traveller Anthony Jenkinson reached Bukhara, a city ringed by a high wall of earth where every craft had its own quarter and market. Indian traders brought fine white cloth that people wound around their heads, Persians brought woollen and linen cloth, and Russians brought hides and sheepskins. Wars, though, had blocked the caravans from China.

source.name: University of Washington, Silk Road Seattle: Anthony Jenkinson's explorations on the land route to China (ed. Lance Jenott)

title: Bukhara's Imposing New Madrasa
text: In 1652 the imposing Abdullaziz-Khan madrasa was added to Bukhara, one of the fine buildings of the city's 17th century. Between the 9th and 16th centuries Bukhara had been a great centre of Muslim theology, with over two hundred mosques and more than a hundred madrasas. Big madrasas rose at busy crossroads, near domed markets such as the Dome of the Moneychangers.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Bukhara

title: A Shah Crowned Near Kandahar
text: Ahmad Khan commanded a group of Abdali cavalry for Nadir Shah of Persia. When Nadir Shah was assassinated, the Afghan chiefs elected Ahmad as their shah, and in 1747 he was crowned near Kandahar, where coins were struck in his name and he set up his capital. Remembered as the founder of the state of Afghanistan, he is buried in a mausoleum in Kandahar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ahmad Shah Durrani

title: Kabul Becomes the Capital
text: Ahmad Shah's son Timur Shah received only nominal homage from Afghanistan's tribal chiefs and spent much of his reign putting down their rebellions. In 1776 he moved his capital from Kandahar to Kabul, away from the fractious tribes. Kabul then reportedly had about 10,000 people, including the walled Chindawol quarter built by the Kizilbash garrison that had served under Nadir Shah.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Kabul

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Timur Shah (excerpt from the Afghanistan article, The Durrani dynasty)

title: The Disastrous Retreat from Kabul
text: In 1839 a British army invaded Afghanistan and installed Shah Shoja as king, but Afghans would tolerate neither foreign occupation nor an imposed ruler, and revolts spread. After the British political agent was killed during talks, some 4,500 British and Indian troops and 12,000 camp followers marched out of Kabul on 6 January 1842. Afghan bands swarmed around them, and the retreat ended in a bloodbath.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Afghanistan, Dost Mohammad (1826-39; 1843-63)

title: A Disguised Dervish Reaches Khiva
text: In autumn 1861 Arminius Vámbéry, born in 1832 near Pressburg, left Constantinople disguised as a Sunni dervish under the name Rashid Effendi. Crossing Persia, he reached Khiva in June 1863, then travelled by way of Bukhara and Samarkand to Herat. Fearing suspicion, he could take notes only in secret. It was the first journey of its kind undertaken by a European.

source.name: Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Isidore Singer and Louis H. Gray: Vambéry, Arminius

title: Russia Captures Tashkent
text: Tashkent, whose name means "Stone Village" in Uzbek, had been ruled by the khanate of Kokand since 1809. When Russian forces captured it in 1865, it was a walled city of some 70,000 people and already a leading centre of trade with Russia. In 1867 it became the seat of Russia's new governorate-general of Turkistan, and a European city grew up beside the old one.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tashkent

title: 1,200 Photographs of Turkestan
text: Governor-General Konstantin von Kaufman commissioned the Turkestan Album, produced mainly in Tashkent and St. Petersburg in 1871 and 1872. Its six volumes hold about 1,200 photographs, plus plans, watercolours and maps, covering Samarkand's Islamic architecture, local peoples and daily life, trades such as textile-making, mining and baking, and Russian military campaigns. The Library of Congress bought a set in 1934.

source.name: Library of Congress Research Guides: Turkestan Album

title: The Last Stand at Gök-Tepe
text: Before 1924 the Turkmens never had even nominal political unity, and the Tekke tribe led the fight against Russia's advance. In 1869 Russian troops landed on the Caspian coast and founded the port of Krasnovodsk. Fierce resistance was finally broken by General Mikhail Skobelev at the Battle of Gök-Tepe, now Gökdepe, in 1881, the year the region became Russia's Transcaspian province.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Turkmenistan, Turkmen tribes and Russian invasion

title: A Line Drawn Through the Mountains
text: Under Emir Abd al-Rahman Khan, who fought some 20 small wars to show his peoples that Kabul's government was strong, the British and Russians drew the borders of modern Afghanistan. The Durand Line of 1893 divided zones of responsibility between British India and Afghanistan but was never meant as a formal international boundary. Afghanistan became a buffer between tsarist Russia and British India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Afghanistan, Dost Mohammad (1826-39; 1843-63) and Abd al-Rahman Khan (1880-1901)

title: An Earthquake Builds the Tallest Dam
text: In 1911 an earthquake triggered a colossal rock slide in the Pamir Mountains that blocked the Murgab River. The slide left a natural dam about 600 metres high, the highest dam, natural or man-made, in the world. Behind it grew Lake Sarez, 60 km long and up to 550 m deep. The lake has never spilled over; it seeps out as large springs.

source.name: USGS Publications Warehouse: Usoi Landslide Dam and Lake Sarez, Pamir Mountains, Tajikistan (Schuster and Alford, 2004)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tajikistan

title: A King's Decade of Reforms
text: In 1923 Amanullah Khan changed his title from emir to king and began a decade of reforms in Afghanistan: a new constitution, permission for women to remove their veils, and coeducational schools. His wife Soraya was the daughter of the nationalist publisher Mahmud Tarzi. The changes offended conservative religious and tribal leaders, civil war broke out in 1928, and Amanullah abdicated in 1929.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Afghanistan, Dost Mohammad (1826-39; 1843-63) and later rulers

title: Ashgabat's Deadly Earthquake
text: On 5 October 1948 an earthquake of magnitude Ms 7.3 struck Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan, and claimed tens of thousands of lives. For decades little was known about the fault behind it. A 2023 study involving University of Jena geologists used old seismograms and 1960s satellite images, finding that a complex fault system ruptured and that parts of it probably still store strain.

source.name: Friedrich Schiller University Jena: New paper on the 1948 Aşgabat earthquake in Turkmenistan

title: Khiva's Inner Town Is Protected
text: Khiva was the last resting place for caravans before they crossed the desert to Persia. In 1967 the Uzbek SSR made its walled inner town, Itchan Kala, a State Architectural and Historic Reserve, and since 1969 it has been a museum-reserve. Behind brick walls up to ten metres high stand 51 monuments and 250 homes, and the Djuma Mosque rests on 212 columns.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Itchan Kala

title: The Last Soviet Soldier Leaves
text: Talks held in Geneva under United Nations auspices produced peace accords in April 1988, and Soviet troops began leaving Afghanistan that May. The last Soviet soldier left in February 1989. By then the war had pushed more than five million Afghan refugees into Pakistan and Iran. Despite predictions that the Najibullah government would quickly collapse, the civil war went on.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Afghanistan, Civil war, communist phase (1978-92)

title: Peace After Tajikistan's Civil War
text: Soon after Tajikistan declared independence in 1991, it slid into civil war, as communists fought to keep power against an alliance of Islamic and democratic forces. By the mid-1990s the fighting had left tens of thousands dead and displaced more than half a million people. In June 1997 a peace agreement brokered by the United Nations, Russia and Iran essentially ended the war.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tajikistan, Independence

title: The Treasures in the Bank Vault
text: Masterpieces of the Kabul Museum were thought lost in decades of war. In fact, the museum's staff had secretly crated them and placed them in a secure bank vault, where they stayed hidden for twenty-five years. Only in 2004 were the crates opened, revealing that the works had survived intact, among them turquoise-inlaid gold from the first-century nomadic tombs of Tillya Tepe.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Afghanistan: Hidden Treasures from the National Museum, Kabul (exhibition, 2009)

title: The End of Turkmenbashi
text: Saparmurad Niyazov, who called himself Turkmenbashi, "leader of the Turkmen," built an elaborate personality cult in independent Turkmenistan. A gold statue of him on Ashgabat's Neutrality Arch rotated to face the Sun, his book Rukhnama was required reading in schools and even part of driving exams, and he renamed the months after himself and his family. He died suddenly in late 2006.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Turkmenistan, Turkmen tribes and Russian invasion (Independence)

title: A Vanishing Inland Sea
text: Fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, the Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake in the world. In the 1960s the Soviet Union began a major project diverting water to irrigate farmland in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. As the sea dried up, its fisheries and the communities that depended on them collapsed. In 2014 the eastern lobe of the South Aral Sea completely disappeared.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: World of Change, Shrinking Aral Sea

title: Rogun Dam Switches On
text: Construction of Tajikistan's Rogun Dam began in 1976, but the project languished after the Soviet Union collapsed, and a flood damaged it in 1993. Work resumed in 2016, and on 16 November 2018 President Emomali Rahmon inaugurated its first unit, which began producing electricity while building continued. Uzbekistan, downstream, had dropped its opposition, and its representatives attended the ceremony.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tajikistan, Independence

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tajikistan

title: Millet Pressed Into Pots
place: Lower Tilemsi Valley, Gao Region, Mali
text: Potters in northern Mali mixed plant chaff into their clay, and the imprints survived. Archaeologists studying these sherds found spikelets of domesticated pearl millet in pots from the third millennium BC. In the Lower Tilemsi Valley, people combined herding and millet farming with fishing, hunting and collecting from about 2500 BC, the oldest evidence of this way of life.

source.name: African Archaeological Review (via PMC): Transition From Wild to Domesticated Pearl Millet Revealed in Ceramic Temper at Three Middle Holocene Sites in Northern Mali

title: Stone Villages on the Tichitt Cliffs
text: Around 2200 BC, herders moving away from the drying Sahara settled on the sandstone cliffs of Dhar Tichitt. They grew bulrush millet and built villages of dry stone walls, more than a thousand of them across the region. The Tichitt culture lasted until an intense dry spell in the middle of the first millennium BC led people to abandon the area.

source.name: Comptes Rendus Géoscience (A. Holl): Coping with uncertainty, Neolithic life in the Dhar Tichitt-Walata, Mauritania

source2.name: African Archaeological Review: The Tichitt Culture and the Malian Lakes Region

title: A Walled Town by Lake Chad
text: Near Lake Chad, the farming town of Zilum was ringed by a ditch and probably an earthen rampart, among the oldest signs of community defence south of the Sahara. Between about 1,750 and 2,500 people lived there, growing pearl millet and cowpeas and raising cattle, sheep and goats. Archaeologists found no sign that they used metal tools at all.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (C. Magnavita): First Millennia BC/AD Fortified Settlements at Lake Chad

title: A Thousand Stone Circles
text: Along the River Gambia stand more than 1,000 stone circles, with burials dated from the 3rd century BC onward. Builders cut laterite pillars with iron tools, some weighing up to 7 tons. Sine Ngayène in Senegal is the largest site, with 52 circles and 1,102 carved stones, and the quarry where they were cut lies about a kilometre away.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Stone Circles of Senegambia

title: Zubo's Great Ditch
place: Zubo, near Lake Chad, Borno State, Nigeria
text: Between the first and third centuries AD, the town of Zubo near Lake Chad was enclosed by a ditch about 2,600 metres long, wrapped around some 46 hectares. One test trench found it 4.5 metres wide and about 2.3 metres deep. Scatters of iron slag show smiths worked here, and farmers in this period added sorghum to their millet and cowpeas.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (C. Magnavita): First Millennia BC/AD Fortified Settlements at Lake Chad

title: Camels Open the Gold Road
text: Around the fifth century, camels let Berber-speaking people begin crossing the Sahara. The Soninke kingdom of ancient Ghana grew up between the desert, the main source of salt, and the gold fields of the upper Sénégal River. Its rise seems tied to the start of the trans-Saharan gold trade, and the Soninke kept the location of their gold mines secret from Muslim traders.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th–14th Century)

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Western Sudan, 500–1000 A.D.

title: The Walled Ruins of Loropéni
text: Laterite walls up to six metres tall surround an abandoned town near Burkina Faso's borders with Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Togo. Radiocarbon dates show Loropéni goes back at least to the 11th century. Its Lohron or Koulango people controlled the mining and working of gold, and the site flourished from the 14th to the 17th century before being deserted.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ruins of Loropéni

title: Kumbi Saleh Under Siege
place: Kumbi Saleh, Hodh Ech Chargui, Mauritania
text: Kumbi Saleh, a trading and political centre of the Ghana empire, was described in the 11th century as two towns, one of them Muslim with many mosques. Around 1076 it was besieged by the Almoravids, Berber warriors whose raids aimed to seize the trans-Saharan gold trade. Their attacks drained Ghana's strength and helped bring the old empire's decline.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Western and Central Sudan, 1000–1400 A.D.

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Western Sudan, 500–1000 A.D.

title: Brass Weights for Gold Dust
text: Muslim Dyula traders from the north brought cloth and metal wares to the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana, exchanging them for kola nuts and gold dust. To measure the gold, the Akan developed brass weights, some later shaped like everyday objects or figures from proverbs. When the Portuguese arrived in 1471, they joined this trade, offering firearms for gold dust and enslaved people.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Guinea Coast, 1400–1600 A.D.

title: A Mud Pyramid for Askia
text: In 1495, back from Mecca, the Songhai emperor Askia Mohamed built a 17-metre pyramid of mud in his capital, Gao, and made Islam the empire's official religion. The tomb doubles as a minaret, with pieces of wood built in as permanent scaffolding. Its plaster must be renewed regularly after the rare but violent rains wear it away.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tomb of Askia

title: Idia, Benin's First Queen Mother
text: Oba Esigie, who ruled Benin from 1504 to 1550, won a power struggle with his brother Arhuaran for the throne, then defeated the Ata of Idah, ruler of Igala. In both fights he was helped by the political strategy and spiritual power of his mother, Idia. To thank her, he created the court title of Queen Mother, or Iyoba, giving her authority equal to senior town chiefs.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Guinea Coast, 1400–1600 A.D.

title: The Baga Head for the Coast
text: Between 1720 and 1730, an Islamic revolution led by the Fulbe in the Futa Jallon highlands of central Guinea pushed several peoples toward the sea. The best known are the Baga, who settled on the coast of present-day Guinea. They carried with them artistic ideas from the Mande world, which found new life in their carved wooden sculpture.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Guinea Coast, 1600–1800 A.D.

title: Cannons Against the Slave Trade
text: Most forts on the River Gambia were built to control trade, including the trade in enslaved people. The Six-Gun Battery of 1816, and Fort Bullen of 1826 across the river mouth, were different. Built after Britain's 1807 Abolition Act, they are the only known defences in the region built specifically to stop the slave trade.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kunta Kinteh Island and Related Sites

title: A Blacksmith Brings Home Cocoa
text: Missionaries had planted cocoa on the Gold Coast decades earlier, but it was Tetteh Quarshie who got it growing widely. A native of Osu in Accra, he had worked as a blacksmith on Fernando Po. In 1879 he returned with cocoa pods and set up a farm at Akwapim Mampong. Farmers bought pods from him, and cocoa spread across the Eastern Region.

source.name: Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD): Cocoa Story

title: A King Invents a Script
text: Around 1895 Njoya, king of the Bamum in Cameroon's grasslands, invented a writing system of 510 picture signs. He revised it six times, ending with a syllabary of 83 characters and 10 numerals. His scribes wrote a history of the Bamum and a book on medicine, and in 1912 he opened the first of 47 schools teaching his script.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bamum

title: Djenné Rebuilds Its Great Mosque
text: Djenné's first Great Mosque is said to have been dedicated by Koi Konboro, the town's first king to convert to Islam. It was rebuilt more than once, and the remarkable earthen mosque standing today went up in 1906–1907. Around it, nearly 2,000 traditional houses survive, raised on mounds to stay above the seasonal floods.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Western and Central Sudan, 1000–1400 A.D.

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Old Towns of Djenné

title: A Canal Opens Abidjan to the Sea
text: Abidjan sits on the Ébrié Lagoon, cut off from the ocean by a sandbar, so at first it relied on the small port at Port-Bouët. In 1950 the Vridi Canal opened the lagoon to the sea. The city soon became the main shipping and financial centre of French-speaking West Africa, exporting coffee, cocoa, timber, bananas and more.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Abidjan

title: The Land of Upright People
text: Thomas Sankara took power in Upper Volta in 1983, promising to fight corruption, empower women and expand schooling and health care. In his first year 10 million trees were planted against desertification. On the coup's first anniversary he renamed the country Burkina Faso, roughly "land of upright people" in Mossi and Dyula, its two most widely spoken languages.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Carina Ray): Thomas Sankara

title: Benin Votes Out Its Ruler
text: Mathieu Kérékou seized power in Benin in 1972 and later followed a Marxist-Leninist path. In 1989 he dropped that ideology, and a new constitution came in 1990. At the first multiparty elections in 1991, Kérékou was defeated by Nicéphore Soglo, a former cabinet member. Kérékou came back by beating Soglo at the ballot box in 1996.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Robin Law and others): History of Benin

title: Ennedi's Arches and Ancient Art
text: In 2016 UNESCO added Chad's Ennedi Massif to the World Heritage List. Water and wind have carved this sandstone plateau into canyons, cliffs, natural arches and rock pillars. Permanent water in its largest canyons supports plants, animals and people, and thousands of paintings and carvings on its rocks form one of the largest collections of rock art in the Sahara.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ennedi Massif, Natural and Cultural Landscape

title: Farming the Desert Rivers
place: Ancient Bactria, Amu Darya (Oxus) valley, northern Afghanistan
text: Around 2200 BCE, people in southwestern Central Asia began irrigating their fields, which let them move down from the foothills into oases along rivers flowing into the desert. Along the Oxus and Murghab rivers, new permanent settlements with large fortified buildings appeared, helped by lively trade with Iran, Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. This paved the way for the Oxus civilization, which took shape from about 2000 BCE.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Central and North Asia, 8000–2000 B.C.

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Shaft-hole axe head with bird-headed demon, boar, and dragon

title: A Tin Mine Near the Clouds
text: At Mushiston, about 3,500 metres up in Tajikistan's Hissar Mountains, radiocarbon dates show that Andronovo miners were digging underground as early as the late 3rd millennium BCE. The ore there holds copper and tin together, the two ingredients of bronze. Scientists found this natural bronze in about a third of the ancient objects they tested, from both steppe and Oxus peoples.

source.name: Frontiers in Earth Science (Berger et al. 2023): The rise of bronze in Central Asia

title: The Lady in the Fleece Robe
text: Oxus-civilization sculptors made small seated women from two stones: a body of soft green chlorite or steatite and a head of white limestone. Their robes have a pattern that may imitate sheep's fleece, and excavated examples come from Margiana in southern Turkmenistan. On local stamp seals a similar woman sits among animals or mythical creatures, so she may have been seen as divine.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Seated female, Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Central and North Asia, 2000–1000 B.C.

title: Sogdiana's First Walled City
place: Koktepa, Payariq District, Samarkand Region, Uzbekistan
text: Long before Samarkand rose to power, herders on the Bulungur River near it settled down to farm and built one of the earliest cities of Sogdiana, now called Koktepa. By the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, a huge square cult platform and a ruler's residence were both guarded by massive walls. Houses grew from half-buried huts into many-roomed mudbrick homes.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Koktepa, An Early Urbanization Centre of the Zarafshan Valley

title: Oasis Kingdoms Join Persia
text: Around 545 BCE, many of the city-states and small kingdoms of western Central Asia became satrapies, or provinces, of the Persian Achaemenid empire. They paid taxes and tribute to a distant central government, while Persian armies kept the peace. This system of rule from far away lasted even after Alexander the Great defeated the Persians, carrying on under his successors, the Seleucids.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Central and North Asia, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: A Golden Chariot from the Oxus
text: This gold chariot, just 19.5 centimetres long, is one of the finest pieces of the Oxus Treasure, the most important surviving gold and silver from Persia's Achaemenid period. Four horses or ponies pull two riders in Median dress, from Iran, the heart of the empire. On the front is Bes, an Egyptian dwarf-god who was a popular protector.

source.name: British Museum via Google Arts & Culture: Oxus chariot model

title: A Round Temple for Stargazing
text: In ancient Khorezm, builders raised an unusual circular two-storey building, 44.4 metres across, ringed by walls, nine towers and a ditch. Its ground floor was not lived in, but upstairs excavators found incense burners, altars, painted pots with myths and figurines of Khorezmian gods. Archaeologists think Koykrylgan-kala began as a fortified temple where people made astronomical observations.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Ancient towns and fortresses of the Aral Sea region

title: Central Asia's Oldest Wall Paintings
text: Akchakhan-kala may have been one of the first capitals of ancient Khorezm. Since 1995, Karakalpak archaeologists working with the University of Sydney have dug up fragments of wall paintings there, including a portrait gallery of Khorezm's rulers and images of Zoroastrian gods. Dated to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, they are the oldest known wall paintings in Central Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Ancient towns and fortresses of the Aral Sea region

title: The Tower of Silence
place: Chilpik, south of Nukus, Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan
text: On a lonely hill above the Amu Darya stands Chilpik, a ring of walls up to 15 metres high, built in the first centuries CE. It is thought to be a dakhma, where Zoroastrians laid out the dead so the soft tissue would be cleaned from the bones. Fire, water, earth and air were sacred, so ceramic troughs carried rainwater away from the bodies.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Chilpik the Tower of Silence

title: The Hall of Twenty-Three Kings
text: The tall palace of Toprak-kala, a seat of Khorezm's rulers, was full of shrines. In the Hall of Kings a fire burned before large statues of 23 Khorezmian kings, and another hall showed men and women dancing in pairs. Its archive held records on leather and lists of men on wood. Early in the 4th century CE the palace emptied and became a citadel.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Ancient towns and fortresses of the Aral Sea region

title: One Bride, Two Brothers
text: A hoard of leather documents from the kingdom of Rob, written in the Bactrian language using Greek letters, records everyday life over four centuries. The earliest dated one, from about 342 CE, is a marriage contract in which one woman agrees to marry two brothers at the same time. Scholar Nicholas Sims-Williams says this practice of polyandry was apparently typical of the region.

source.name: University of Tokyo: Nicholas Sims-Williams, New Findings in Ancient Afghanistan (Bactrian documents)

dateLabel: First half of the 5th century CE
title: Panjikent Builds Its Walls
text: In the 5th century, the people of Panjikent ringed their town with a rammed-earth wall almost four miles long, against rival Sogdian cities and raiding nomads. In the sacred quarter, one temple honoured Adhvagh, the great god, and another the town's patron goddess Nana, which also held chapels to local, Iranian and Hindu deities, a sign of Sogdian openness.

source.name: Smithsonian, The Sogdians: The City of Panjikent and Sogdian Town-Planning (Alexander Brey)

title: A Pilgrim Monk in Samarkand
text: In 630 the Chinese monk Xuanzang, on his long journey to India, reached Sogdiana and stayed in Samarkand. He found its Buddhist temples abandoned, and his disciples were attacked by local Mazdaists. The king punished the attackers and let him ordain new monks, though historians suspect Xuanzang exaggerated that welcome. His travel book is one of the few firsthand accounts of the Sogdians.

source.name: Smithsonian, The Sogdians: Influencers on the Silk Roads: Xuanzang (Matthew Z. Dischner)

title: A Queen's Gift to a Healing God
text: A Bactrian deed dated to 710, in the month called Second New Year, records a queen giving land and a slave girl to the god Kamird and his priest, apparently to thank him for healing a family member. She was married to a ruler with a Turkish name and was called the princess of the Khalas, perhaps one of the earliest mentions of the Turkish Khalach tribe.

source.name: University of Tokyo: Nicholas Sims-Williams, New Findings in Ancient Afghanistan (Bactrian documents)

title: The Last Stand on Mount Mugh
place: Mount Mugh, Zerafshan Valley, Sughd, Tajikistan
text: In 722 Arab forces captured Panjikent, and its ruler Devashtich fled to a small mountain castle, where he was defeated and later executed. His archive stayed hidden until a shepherd found a basket of documents in 1932. Written on leather, Chinese paper and willow sticks, they include a furious letter in which Devashtich scolds an ally for being a weak messenger.

source.name: Smithsonian, The Sogdians: The Castle on Mount Mugh and Its Documents (Pavel Lurje)

title: Heroes on Panjikent's Walls
text: Wealthy Sogdians in Panjikent decorated their reception halls with murals in layers. Huge gods, often the goddess Nana, filled one wall; epic legends such as the Rustam cycle, painted around 740, ran across others; and along the bottom, small panels showed fables, like a blacksmith with an ape assistant. The wealthiest owners also built rows of shops along the street to rent out.

source.name: Smithsonian, The Sogdians: The City of Panjikent and Sogdian Town-Planning (Alexander Brey)

dateLabel: Built between the early 8th and mid-9th centuries
title: The Mosque of Nine Domes
place: Noh Gunbad, Balkh, Balkh Province, Afghanistan
text: Noh Gunbad, the Nine Domes mosque near Balkh, was built sometime between the early 8th century and the first half of the 9th. It is believed to be the oldest and most important early Islamic building in Afghanistan. All nine domes have fallen, leaving three columns and two arches, but rare carved stucco survives, thought to be in early Abbasid or Samanid style.

source.name: Aga Khan Development Network: The nine domes of the Universe, Noh Gunbad Mosque, Balkh

title: Merv, Capital of Sultan Sanjar
text: Merv reached the height of its glory as the capital of the Seljuq sultan Sanjar, who reigned from 1118 to 1157. His mausoleum, with elegant brickwork, carved stucco and surviving wall paintings, is one of the finest buildings of the Seljuk period. In 1221 the Mongols destroyed the city, and although it was rebuilt in the 15th century, it never regained its old prosperity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Merv

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: State Historical and Cultural Park "Ancient Merv"

title: Bukhara's Great Brick Minaret
text: The Qarakhanid ruler Arslan Khan first built a wooden mosque and minaret here, but tradition says the minaret fell and wrecked the mosque. In 1127 a brick minaret replaced it. Standing 46 metres tall, it still dominates Bukhara's skyline, and UNESCO calls it a masterpiece of decoration in brick. The complex around it is named after it: Poi Kalon, at the foot of the Great One.

source.name: Archnet (MIT / Aga Khan Trust for Culture): Poi Kalon

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Bukhara

title: The Leaning Minaret of Urgench
text: Named after Qutlugh Timur, the Golden Horde's governor of Khorezm, this minaret was finished between 1321 and 1330, possibly on foundations from the 11th century. Now 60 metres tall, it once reached 65, and 145 steps spiral up inside. Historians think its top also served as a lighthouse and watchtower. Today it leans dangerously towards a nearby mausoleum.

source.name: Archnet (MIT / Aga Khan Trust for Culture): Manar-i Qutlugh Timur

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kunya-Urgench

title: Ninety-Five Elephants for a Mosque
text: After his campaign in India, Timur founded a vast mosque in Samarkand in May 1399. He brought back skilled workers from Hindustan and 95 elephants pulling carts of huge stones. Its courtyard, 109 by 167 metres, could hold up to ten thousand worshippers. The Spanish envoy Clavijo called it the noblest mosque in the city, yet it later fell into ruin.

source.name: Manazir Journal 5 (2023), Elena Paskaleva: Samarqand's Congregational Mosque of Bibi Khanum

title: A Fort on the Lena
text: In 1632 a fort was founded on the low right bank of the Lena River, and in 1642 it was moved 70 km upstream to the spot where Yakutsk stands today. For a long time it was a small town of wooden houses, and from the 19th century dissidents were exiled there. It is now capital of Sakha, where temperatures of −68 °C have been recorded.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Yakutsk

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Siberia

title: Bering Goes Looking for America
text: Tsar Peter the Great wanted to know whether Asia and North America were joined by land, so in 1724 he put the Danish navigator Vitus Bering in charge of finding out. On July 13, 1728, Bering sailed from Kamchatka and in August passed through the strait into the Arctic Ocean. Bad weather hid the American coast, but he concluded that Siberia and America were not joined.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vitus Bering

title: A Khan Turns to Russia
text: Abulkhair, khan of the Kazakhs' Young Juz, had asked Russia for protection. In February 1731 Empress Anna signed a charter for him, and her envoy A. I. Tevkelev reached the khan's camp on the Irgiz River on October 5. On October 10 much of the gathered Kazakh leadership backed accepting Russian rule, yet the threat of devastating Dzungar invasions did not go away.

source.name: e-history.kz (History of Kazakhstan portal): Beginning of accession of Kazakhstan to the Russian Empire

title: Abylay, Khan of All Three Zhuzes
place: Kazakh Khanate; buried at Turkestan, Kazakhstan
text: In 1771, after Khan Abilmambet died, influential figures from all three Kazakh zhuzes proclaimed Abylay their khan. He had first won fame as a batyr, or warrior, in battles with the Dzungars in 1730–1740, and he cleverly used disputes between the Russian and Chinese empires to serve the Kazakh Khanate. He was later buried in the mausoleum-mosque of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi.

source.name: e-history.kz (History of Kazakhstan portal): Abylay Khan (Abilmansur)

title: The Princess Who Followed to the Mines
place: Mines near Nerchinsk, Zabaykalsky Krai, Russia
text: After the failed Decembrist uprising of 1825, most of the rebels were banished to Siberia. Maria Volkonskaya followed her exiled husband in 1827, though her father told her to forget him. The tsar's terms were harsh: she had to leave her son behind and could own no valuables. Reaching Nerchinsk by sledge, she sneaked into the freezing mines with letters from home.

source.name: Women in World History (via Encyclopedia.com), Karin Loewen Haag: Volkonskaya, Maria (1805–1863)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Decembrist

title: A Fort Among the Apple Trees
text: In 1854 the Russians built the military fortification of Zailiyskoye where the Big and Small Almaty rivers leave the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains; it was renamed Verny in 1855. Cossacks, peasant settlers and Tatar merchants soon moved in nearby. In 1921 the city took the name Alma-Ata, from the Kazakh Almaty, "father of apples", after the many apple trees around it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Almaty

title: The Town Named Rule the East
text: Russia founded Vladivostok in 1860 as a military outpost on Golden Horn Bay, on the Sea of Japan. Its name has been read as "Rule the East" or "Lord of the East". The main Russian naval base on the Pacific moved here in 1872, and the town became a city in 1880. In Soviet times it was closed to foreign shipping from the late 1950s until 1990.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vladivostok

title: The Explorer Who Named a Horse
text: On November 1, 1888, the explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky died at Karakol on Lake Issyk-Kul, of typhus caught by drinking river water. On five major expeditions he had described a wild camel and a wild horse, now named after him, and gathered 5,010 birds and a herbarium of more than 15,000 plants. In his memory, Karakol was renamed Przhevalsk.

source.name: Encyclopedia.com (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography; Encyclopedia of World Biography): Nikolai Mikhailovich Przhevalsky

title: Trains Finally Circle Lake Baikal
place: Southern shore of Lake Baikal, Irkutsk Oblast, Russia
text: In 1891 Sergei Witte of the finance ministry persuaded Tsar Alexander III to begin a railway across Siberia to the Pacific. It was built in several stretches at once, but Lake Baikal remained a barrier: cargo and passengers had to cross by ferry until a line around the lake opened in 1905. Today the Trans-Siberian runs 9,288 km from Moscow to Vladivostok.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Trans-Siberian Railroad (Sanat Pai Raikar)

title: The Quake That Shook Verniy
place: Kemin–Chilik fault, northern Tien Shan, Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan border
text: On January 3, 1911, a great earthquake struck the northern Tien Shan. Surface ruptures stretched for about 200 km along the Kemin–Chilik fault zone, and in Verniy, today's Almaty, almost every building was damaged and about 400 people were killed. Scientists who re-read old seismograms from 23 stations put its magnitude at about 8, the strongest instrumentally recorded quake in the region.

source.name: Geophysical Journal International (Kulikova and Krüger, 2015): Source process of the 1911 M8.0 Chon-Kemin earthquake

title: Alash Orda Declares a Kazakh State
text: In 1916 an order calling up Central Asians for military service set off a revolt, and brutal Russian punitive expeditions drove many Kazakhs east. In 1917 Kazakhs formed Alash Orda, a national and socialist-minded organisation, which that same year proclaimed an independent Kazakh state. It did not last: by 1920 the whole Kazakh steppe was under Bolshevik control from Moscow.

source.name: Lex (Den Store Danske): Kasakhstans historie før 1920

title: Jamila, a Kyrgyz Love Story
text: In 1958 the Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aytmatov published Jamila, later translated into English as Jamilia. Born in the village of Sheker in 1928, he lost his father to Stalin's purges and wrote in both Kyrgyz and Russian. His stories return again and again to love and friendship, wartime courage, and young Kyrgyz people breaking free from restrictive custom and tradition.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Chingiz Aytmatov

title: Jeltoqsan: Students Defy Moscow
text: On December 16, 1986, Moscow announced that the popular Kazakh party chief Dinmukhamed Kunayev would be replaced by Gennady Kolbin, an ethnic Russian. Next morning mostly students gathered on Brezhnev Square in Alma-Ata to protest. Police and soldiers attacked them, and estimates of the dead run from 200 to 1,000. A monument and Jeltoqsan ("December") Street now remember them.

source.name: Lex (Den Store Danske), Mia Tarp, Roskilde University: Zjeltoqsan-massakren

title: A Tattooed Woman in the Ice
text: In 1993 Russian archaeologists on the Ukok Plateau found a frozen grave of a noble Pazyryk woman from the 4th century BC, untouched by robbers. Inside the frozen larch vault lay her mummy, its arms covered with tattoos, and six horses were buried with her. An MRI scan in 2010 found a dislocated right hip, a damaged right shoulder and signs of severe infection.

source.name: SCIENCE First Hand (Siberian Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences): The mummy continues to reveal secrets

title: A New Capital on the Steppe
text: In 1994 Kazakhstan resolved to move its capital from Almaty, in the southeast, to Aqmola on the Ishim River, a move completed in 1997. In 1998 the city was renamed Astana, meaning "Capital". Japanese architect Kurokawa Kishō designed its broad avenues and blue-and-gold buildings, and with winter averages of −22 °C it is one of the coldest capitals in the world.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Astana

title: The Salt Lake at Asia's Heart
text: In 2003 the Uvs Nuur Basin, shared by western Mongolia and Russia's Republic of Tuva, joined the World Heritage List. At its centre is Uvs Nuur, a large, shallow and very salty lake vital to migrating birds. Around it cold desert, steppe, forest, glacial lakes and even tundra meet, and the mountains shelter snow leopards, argali sheep and Asiatic ibex.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Uvs Nuur Basin

title: Lyuba, the Baby Mammoth
place: Yamal Peninsula, Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, Russia
text: In May 2007 Yuri Khudi, a Nenets reindeer herder, spotted a baby woolly mammoth eroding out of a riverbank on the Yamal Peninsula.
