Named Lyuba after his wife, she is the most complete mammoth carcass ever found, weighing about 110 pounds, the size of a large dog. X-rays showed she had tiny tusks, no larger than a human finger.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), Eric A. Powell: Lyuba the Baby Mammoth, Yamal Peninsula, Russia

title: The Sacred Mountain of Osh
text: Rising above the city of Osh in the Fergana Valley, Sulaiman-Too has been revered as a sacred mountain for at least a millennium and a half. Its five peaks hold caves with petroglyphs, 17 places of worship still in use and two largely reconstructed 16th-century mosques. Some sites are believed to cure headaches and back pain. UNESCO listed it as World Heritage in 2009.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sulaiman-Too Sacred Mountain

title: Magnitude 8.8 off Kamchatka
place: Pacific Ocean off Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Kamchatka, Russia
text: On July 29, 2025, a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck 35 km deep off the Kamchatka Peninsula, about 120 km from Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky. It was one of the most powerful ever recorded and set off tsunami alerts across the Pacific, yet damage in the city was relatively minor and no deaths were reported. Here the Pacific plate dives into the mantle beneath the region.

source.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program: M 8.8 - 2025 Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia Earthquake

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky

dateLabel: About 3000 BCE (comb pottery made c. 5000–1000 BCE)
title: Comb-Pattern Pots of Amsa-dong
place: Amsa-dong, Gangdong District, Seoul, South Korea
text: By about 3000 BCE, Neolithic life in Korea was well established, and its signature object was comb-pattern pottery. At Amsa-dong, a major dwelling site on the Han River east of today's Seoul, people made wide-mouthed storage and cooking pots with pointed or round bases, scratching diagonal lines into the damp clay, perhaps with a comb-like tool, before firing.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 8000–2000 B.C.

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea (history), The Stone Age

title: Bronze Comes to the Peninsula
text: Around the 10th century BCE, metalworking arrived in Korea, probably from the northern mainland, and thick-walled plain pottery replaced the older comb-pattern wares. By the 7th century BCE a Bronze Age culture flourished. Korean bronzes held more zinc than those of neighbouring cultures, and graves have yielded daggers, spearheads, small bells and geometric-patterned mirrors.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: Shiny Red Pots for the Dead
text: In about the 6th century BCE, Korean potters began making burnished red wares from fine, iron-rich clay. They painted on a pigment such as ochre, then polished the pot before firing to give it a glossy red sheen. Most turn up in stone cist and dolmen tombs, and the thin-walled vessels were probably meant mainly for rituals.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: The Eggplant-Pattern Jars
place: Gyeongsang and Jeolla provinces, South Korea
text: Around the 5th century BCE, potters in Korea's far south made round-bodied jars painted on the shoulders with long dark grey and brown patches that remind people of eggplants. Painting colour onto the clay was a bold break from the scratched and raised decoration of Neolithic pots. These jars are found only in the Gyeongsang and Jeolla provinces.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: Iron That Drew Traders From Japan
place: Lower Nakdong River valley, near Gimhae, South Korea
text: Iron technology reached Korea from China around 300 BCE, and by the 2nd century BCE iron was being produced in the south of the peninsula. Chinese accounts say iron from the Byeonhan region, in the lower Nakdong River valley, was prized across the peninsula and even attracted traders from Japan. Iron ploughs and sickles also changed farming.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea (history), The use of metals

title: Wiman Takes Over Gojoseon
place: Daedong River basin, near Pyongyang, North Korea
text: Around 194 BCE, a man named Wiman became ruler of Gojoseon, Korea's first known kingdom. Old accounts say he defected from China, but Britannica notes he was more likely a local. His new state, Wiman Joseon, had strong armies and wealth, and it brought neighbouring states to the north, east and south under its control until Han China conquered it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea (history), The use of metals and the emergence of tribal states

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: Goguryeo Ends Chinese Lelang
place: Lelang Commandery site, near Pyongyang, North Korea
text: In 313 CE the northern kingdom of Goguryeo seized the lands of Lelang, a Chinese commandery near modern Pyongyang. Lelang had been a Chinese colonial base for more than 400 years after Han armies invaded in 108 BCE. Its fall ended Chinese rule there, as the peninsula moved toward three rival kingdoms: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1–500 A.D.

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000 B.C.–1 A.D.

title: A Queen's Golden Plate at Mireuksa
place: Mireuksa Temple Site, Iksan, North Jeolla, South Korea
text: When workers took apart Mireuksa's stone pagoda in 2009, they found a gold plate about 15.5 by 10.5 cm carrying 193 Chinese characters. It says the pagoda, thought to be Korea's oldest surviving stone pagoda, was built in 639. It also names King Mu's queen as the daughter of a high Baekje official, not Princess Seonhwa of Silla.

source.name: The Korea Times: Buddhist Urn, Relics Found at Mireuk Temple in Iksan (2009)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Baekje Historic Areas

title: The Bell That Cries Emile
place: Gyeongju National Museum, Gyeongju, South Korea
text: King Gyeongdeok began a huge bell for his late father, using 72,000 kg of copper, but died first; his son King Hyegong finished it on December 14, 771. A grim legend says a child was cast into the metal, so it rang 'emile, emile' like a resentful child. Yet a 1999 analysis found no phosphorus that human remains would leave, so the story is likely untrue.

source.name: Gyeongju National Museum (Google Arts & Culture): The Bell of King Seongdeok the Great

title: Mount Paektu Blows Its Top
place: Mount Paektu, on the North Korea–China border
text: In the final months of 946, Mount Paektu erupted, perhaps throwing about 100 cubic kilometres of ash and pumice into the sky. Scientists pinned the date using a 264-year-old tree buried by the eruption and ash in Greenland ice cores. A Japanese temple chronicle records 'white ash falling like snow' on 3 November 946.

source.name: University of Cambridge: Fossilised tree and ice cores help date huge volcanic eruption 1,000 years ago to within three months

title: Korea's Oldest Surviving History Book
text: In 1145 the Confucian scholar-official Kim Busik and his team presented the Samguk sagi, or Histories of the Three Kingdoms, to the Goryeo king Injong. It is the older of Korea's two earliest surviving histories. The compilers drew on earlier documents that are now lost, which makes their book a precious window on Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1000–1400 A.D.

title: King Sejong Measures the Rain
text: In 1441 King Sejong and a group of scholars invented the cheugugi, a copper cylinder for collecting rain, described as the world's oldest rain gauge. Officials recorded how deep the rain fell and when it started and stopped. Wars and fires destroyed many early records, but measurements at the royal palace in Seoul continued until a modern gauge replaced it in 1907.

source.name: Scientific Data (Nature Portfolio): Precipitation data in Seoul, Korea during 1778–1907

title: Korea's Own Cobalt Blue
place: Official royal kilns, Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea
text: Joseon's court loved plain white porcelain, made at official kilns in Gwangju near Seoul that moved every few decades to find enough firewood. Then came blue-and-white ware, painted in cobalt under the glaze. Records show that in 1465 Korean potters first successfully used cobalt found at home, which cost less than cobalt imported from China.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Korea, 1400–1600 A.D.

title: Admiral Yi's Last Battle
place: Noryang Strait, Namhae, South Gyeongsang, South Korea
text: In 1597 Admiral Yi Sun-shin was falsely accused and demoted to common soldier, and the navy was nearly destroyed. Reinstated with the few ships left, he restored Korea's control of the sea. On December 16, 1598, off Noryang, he was killed by a stray bullet while chasing the retreating Japanese, who were withdrawing after Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Yi Sun-shin

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea (history), Foreign invasions

title: Rebuilding the Royal Ancestors' Shrine
place: Jongmyo Shrine, Jongno District, Seoul, South Korea
text: Jongmyo holds the spirit tablets of Joseon's kings and queens, where kings came to pray for the safety of the people. First built in the late 14th century, it was destroyed during the Japanese invasion and rebuilt in the early 17th century. Its ancestral rites, Jongmyo Jerye, are still performed today with their ritual music and dance.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Jongmyo Shrine

title: The Merchant Who Fed Jeju
place: Jeju City, Jeju Island, South Korea
text: Despite her low rank as a female entertainer, Kim Man-deok (1739–1812) became a merchant and medical practitioner on Jeju. When severe drought struck the island in 1794, she spent her whole fortune sharing crops with her neighbours. King Jeongjo gave her a court post and let her fulfil a lifelong wish: a trip to Geumgangsan Mountain.

source.name: Korea.net (Korean government): Meet the Joseon businesswoman who saved Jeju

title: A New Faith Called Eastern Learning
text: In May 1860 Choe Je-u, a poor scholar's son who kept failing the civil-service exams, said he had received a mandate to found a religion that would make Korea as strong as the West. He called it Donghak, 'Eastern Learning', and taught that everyone was equal before heaven. Poor rural communities flocked to it, and the government executed him in 1864.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Choe Je-u

title: The Regent Who Shut the Door
text: King Gojong was too young to rule when he took the throne in 1864, so his father, the Daewon-gun, ran the country. He closed many private Confucian academies and refused Western ships seeking trade. Koreans burned the American ship General Sherman at Pyongyang and drove off two French attacks in 1866, hardening his resolve to keep the doors shut.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea (history), Opening the door

title: Water Lights in the Palace
text: Korea's first electric lamp was switched on between January and March 1887 at Gyeongbokgung Palace, lighting grounds that included the royal residence Geoncheonggung. The palace had signed a contract with an Edison company in 1884. The water-powered plant stood near Hyangwonji pond, and people called its lights 'mulbul', meaning water light. Archaeologists located the plant's site in 2015.

source.name: The Korea Times: Site of 1st electricity generation found (2015)

title: A Baekje King's Tomb Found by Accident
place: Songsan-ri Royal Tombs, Gongju, South Chungcheong, South Korea
text: On July 5, 1971, workers digging drains at the Songsan-ri royal tombs in Gongju stumbled on a tomb. Inscriptions inside showed it belonged to the Baekje royal couple, King Muryeong and his queen. The excavation was rushed through in a single day and night, and a later report counted 2,561 artifacts of eighty-eight types.

source.name: National Museum of Korea, Journal of Korean Art and Archaeology vol. 16: Critical Review on the Metalworks in the Tomb of King Muryeong

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Baekje Historic Areas

title: Han Kang Wins the Nobel Prize
text: On October 10, 2024, South Korean author Han Kang won the Nobel Prize in Literature, born in Gwangju in 1970, 'for her intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life'. She began as a poet in 1993; her novels include The Vegetarian, Human Acts and We Do Not Part.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Han Kang – Facts – 2024

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: The Nobel Prize in Literature 2024 – Press release

title: Whales on the Rocks Win World Heritage
place: Bangucheon Stream, Ulju, Ulsan, South Korea
text: In 2025 UNESCO added the Petroglyphs along the Bangucheon Stream to the World Heritage List. Over about 6,000 years, from 5,000 BCE to the 9th century CE, local artists carved animals, hunters and writing into the cliffs. The animals are so detailed that species can be identified, and the scenes of whales and whaling are rare in rock art worldwide.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Petroglyphs along the Bangucheon Stream

title: A Mountain Sanctuary of 10,000 Stones
place: Saimaly-Tash, Fergana Range, Jalal-Abad Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: High in the Fergana mountain range lies Saimaly-Tash, one of the world's biggest collections of rock pictures, with about 10,000 carved stones. The earliest date back to the third and early second millennia BCE. Hunters, cattle breeders and early farmers kept returning to this sacred place for thousands of years, carving images linked to their worship of mountains, totems and the sun.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Saimaly-Tash Petroglyphs

dateLabel: From about 1500 BCE (second half of the 2nd millennium BCE)
title: Sun-Headed Gods of Tanbaly Gorge
text: Around a green, spring-fed gorge in the dry Chu-Ili mountains, Bronze Age herders began pecking pictures into shiny black rocks. About 5,000 carvings survive, and the oldest are the most striking: big, deeply cut figures of sun-headed deities, beings dressed in furs, disguised people and many animals. Possible altars in the central canyon suggest sacrifices were offered here.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Petroglyphs of the Archaeological Landscape of Tanbaly

title: Milk Clues in Ancient Teeth
text: Hardened plaque on the teeth of Late Bronze Age people buried in northern Mongolia still holds milk proteins from cattle, sheep and goats. It shows dairying had reached the eastern steppe by about 1300 BCE. Yet their DNA came mostly from local hunter-gatherers of the Baikal region, so these people adopted herding and milk from outsiders rather than being replaced by them.

source.name: PNAS (Jeong et al. 2018): Bronze Age population dynamics and the rise of dairy pastoralism on the eastern Eurasian steppe

title: Standing Stones Carved with Stags
text: Bronze Age nomads raised stone pillars up to four metres tall, carved with stylised stags, often beside big burial mounds and the remains of sacrificed horses. About 1,500 are known, most of them in Mongolia. Smithsonian archaeologist William Fitzhugh thinks they portray real people, with earrings, belts and tools, lined up in rows like successions of clan leaders.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Deer Stone Monuments and Related Bronze Age Sites

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine (NMNH): Meet the Smithsonian Scientist Studying the Mysterious Mongolian Deer Stones

title: Riders Carved in the High Altai
text: In glacier-cut valleys of Mongolia's far west, people kept carving rocks for 12,000 years, so the pictures work like a diary of changing lives. The earliest show hunters of big game, later ones show the rise of herding, and carvings from the early 1st millennium BCE record a new turn: a nomadic way of life that depended on the horse.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai

title: The Giant Mounds of Besshatyr
place: Besshatyr, Ili River, Almaty Region, Kazakhstan
text: Beside the Ili River, Saka nomads raised 81 burial mounds of stone, some up to 105 metres across and 18 metres high. In one small mound archaeologists found two people buried with short iron daggers, quivers of bronze-tipped arrows, carnelian beads and hollow gold beads. Openings in the big mounds may have stayed open for worship and sacrifices after burial.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads: Early Period (Prehistory)

title: Chinese Silk Before the Silk Road
text: Long before the famous Silk Roads opened, silk was already travelling west. Pieces of Chinese silk turned up in the royal Saka mounds at Esik, and even in an ordinary late Saka cemetery in north-eastern Zhetysu, radiocarbon-dated to the 4th–3rd centuries BCE. They show trade linking China and the nomads of south-eastern Kazakhstan.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads: Early Period (Prehistory)

title: Horses Wearing Golden Ibex Horns
text: In 1998–1999 a Kazakh, French and Italian team opened a frozen prince's tomb at Berel in the Kazakh Altai, dating to the early 3rd century BCE. Beside two human bodies lay thirteen horses, buried in harness. Some wore masks topped with fake ibex horns carved from wood and painted gold.

source.name: Anthropozoologica (Lepetz 2013): Horse sacrifice in a Pazyryk culture kurgan: the princely tomb of Berel'

title: The Women Who Ruled the Frontier
text: At Takhiltyn Khotgor, on the far western frontier of the Xiongnu Empire, the grandest tombs were built for women. They lay in fine coffins with golden sun and moon emblems of imperial power, flanked by commoner men in simple graves; one held six horses and part of a chariot. Researchers say women held great power along the frontier.

source.name: Max Planck Society: Multiethnic structure of Mongolia's first nomadic empire

source2.name: Science Advances (Lee et al. 2023): Genetic population structure of the Xiongnu Empire at imperial and local scales

title: The Man Behind the Red Mask
text: A man of the Tashtyk culture of southern Siberia was buried wearing a painted red death mask. Hermitage researchers could not remove it without damaging him, so they used a CT scan. It revealed a gash from his left eye to his ear, stitched shut, perhaps so he would not look disfigured in the afterlife, and a hole in his skull, likely made when his brain was removed.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): Face Off

title: The Cold Summers Locked in Larch
text: Old Siberian larch wood preserved on the ground in the Russian Altai holds a record of summer warmth. Its tree rings, read alongside trees from the Alps, show a sudden, long cooling after big volcanic eruptions in 536, 540 and 547. Scientists call the cold spell from 536 to about 660 the Late Antique Little Ice Age, and link it to movements of peoples out of the Asian steppe.

source.name: Nature Geoscience (Büntgen et al. 2016): Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD

title: Navikat, a Town of Many Faiths
text: Under the Western Turkic and Turgesh khanates of 560–760, the Chui Valley became one of Eurasia's main centres, linked by the Northern Silk Roads to Byzantium and China. At Navikat, digs uncovered a Zoroastrian fire altar, Christian votive stones in the citadel and two Buddhist temples outside the walls, a mix of Turkic, Indian, Sogdian and Chinese cultures.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads Sites in Kyrgyzstan

title: Xuanzang Passes Through Suyab
place: Ak-Beshim (Suyab), near Tokmok, Chui Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: Xuanzang wrote that he visited Suyab in 630, a Silk Road trading town in the Chui Valley that existed from the 5th to the 11th centuries. Later in the 7th century the Tang dynasty built the Suyab Garrison here as a stronghold. Russian and Kyrgyz archaeologists have studied its ruins, now called Ak-Beshim, since 1939.

source.name: International Institute for Central Asian Studies (IICAS): Ak Beshim (Suyab) 2019

title: The Island Building Dated to a Season
text: Uyghurs built a huge clay complex covering a whole island in a Tuvan mountain lake. A burst of cosmic radiation in 775 left a radiocarbon signal in tree rings, and finding it in the foundation wood showed building began in summer 777. That fits the reign of Bögü Khagan, who made Manichaeism the state religion, so it was probably a monastery, left almost unused.

source.name: PNAS (Kuitems et al. 2020): Radiocarbon-based approach capable of subannual precision resolves the origins of the site of Por-Bajin

title: The Kimak Tower of Kozy-Korpesh
place: Kozy-Korpesh–Bayan Sulu Mausoleum, Abai Region, Kazakhstan
text: Between the 8th and 11th centuries, steppe nomads built tall stone and brick towers called dyng for ancestor rituals. One of the most remarkable still stands over 11 metres high and once held statues of a man and a woman. It is tied to the epic of Kozy-Korpesh and Bayan Sulu, but was probably built for the Kimak dynasty.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Monumental Monuments and Sanctuaries of the Early Steppe Tradition of Central Eurasia

title: Balasagun, a City with Water Pipes
text: Balasagun was founded in the 10th century and became one of the capitals of the eastern Karakhanid khanate, alongside Kashgar. Archaeologists found a central fortress, craft shops, bazaars, a bathhouse and a water main with pipes from a nearby canyon. Its Muslim rulers tolerated other faiths, and Christian gravestones survive. The Mongols spared the city and renamed it Gobalik, 'good city'.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads Sites in Kyrgyzstan

title: A Stone Inn at 3,200 Metres
place: Tash-Rabat, At-Bashy Valley, Naryn Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: High in the At-Bashy valley, at 3,200 metres, caravans heading for Kashgar over the Torugart pass could shelter at Tash-Rabat. This square caravanserai of slate slabs was built in Karakhanid times, in the 11th–12th centuries, with a central corridor, a hall under a big dome and 19 smaller domes. It stayed in use until Timur's time.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads Sites in Kyrgyzstan

title: Saraychik, Resting Place of Khans
text: Batu Khan founded Saraychik on the Ural River in the mid-1200s as a stop on the Silk Road to Urgench. It became a spiritual centre of the Golden Horde, where khans such as Mengu-Timur and Zhanibek were buried. Digs in its mud-brick neighbourhoods turned up Syrian glass, Chinese porcelain, Khorezm bowls and bronze dishes from Iran.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Silk Roads: Volga-Caspian Corridor

title: Spells on a Pyramid's Walls
text: Inside the pyramid of Unas, last king of the 5th dynasty, the walls of the inner chambers were covered with prayers, hymns and spells meant to protect the dead king and keep him supplied in the afterlife. These Pyramid Texts are the oldest surviving body of Egyptian religious and funerary writing, and they were later gathered into the Book of the Dead.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Pyramid Texts

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Book of the Dead

title: A Scribe's Maths Homework
text: A scribe named Ahmose dated this papyrus to year 33 of Apophis, a Hyksos king. It is probably a mathematics textbook, with eighty-four problems on division, multiplication, fractions, areas and volumes, used by scribes learning by worked examples. At 296 centimetres long, it was found near the Ramesseum at Thebes and may once have been cut in half by robbers to raise its price.

source.name: British Museum: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (EA10057)

title: Six Hours of Arrows
text: Libyans, joined and armed by roving Sea Peoples, pushed toward Memphis and Heliopolis. At dawn one spring day the aged pharaoh Merneptah, Ramses II's 13th son, let his archers shoot for six hours while his infantry and chariots held firm, and the invaders fled. Of the four victory texts he ordered, the Israel Stela holds the earliest known mention of Israel.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Merneptah

title: A Libyan Chief Becomes Pharaoh
text: Sheshonk I came from a line of Libyan chiefs who held the title great chief of the Meshwesh and had settled at Bubastis in the Nile Delta. A general under the last king of the 21st dynasty, he probably took the throne without a struggle, founding the 22nd dynasty. Reliefs at Karnak celebrate his victories in Palestine.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sheshonk I

title: Greek Traders on the Nile
text: In the 7th century BCE, Greeks from Miletus set up Naukratis, a trading station on the western branch of the Nile Delta, and Greeks from other cities soon followed. It was the earliest Greek settlement in Egypt and stayed a meeting point of peoples for more than 1,200 years. Finds range from Egyptian faience amulets and Greek pottery to Cypriot statuettes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Naukratis

source2.name: British Museum: Naukratis, Greeks in Egypt (research project)

title: Phoenicians on the Atlantic Edge
text: Around the middle of the 7th century BCE, Phoenicians founded an outpost on Mogador, a small island off Morocco's Atlantic coast, the farthest-flung settlement of their Mediterranean world. Excavators found a possible shrine to the goddess Astarte, and slag, bellows and iron rods showing iron working. Layers on the island have also yielded bones of elephants, lions and peacocks.

source.name: German Archaeological Institute (e-Forschungsberichte): Marzoli & El Khayari, Mogador (Essaouira), Marokko

source2.name: University of Southampton, MarEA project: Essaouira's Coastal Heritage, Morocco

title: Islanders Found Cyrene
text: About 631 BCE, emigrants from the Aegean island of Thera founded Cyrene in what is now Libya. Their leader Battus became its first king, and his family, whose kings were named alternately Battus and Arcesilaus, ruled for eight generations. Cyrene grew into one of the principal cities of the Greek world, later famous for its medical school and scholars.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Cyrene, ancient Greek colony, Libya

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Cyrene

title: A Wedding Contract on Elephantine
text: On July 3, 449 BCE, on Elephantine Island in the Nile, a man named Ananiah asked Meshullam for the hand of his daughter Tamut, and a scribe, Nathan son of Ananiah, set it down in Aramaic on papyrus. Egypt was then under Persian rule. A later papyrus, dated October 30, 434 BCE, records Ananiah giving Tamut part of a house.

source.name: Brooklyn Museum: Marriage Document (47.218.89)

source2.name: Brooklyn Museum: Property Transfer Document, Ananiah Gives Tamut Part of a House (47.218.91a-b)

title: Alexander Asks the Desert Oracle
text: Crowned with the pharaohs' double crown at Memphis, Alexander the Great founded Alexandria, then marched along the coast and inland to Siwa, an oasis with about 200 springs, to consult the famous oracle of the god Amon. The priest greeted him as a pharaoh, son of Amon. Alexander asked about the success of his expedition but revealed the answer to no one.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Alexander the Great (Frank W. Walbank)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Siwa Oasis

title: The Punic Town Nobody Rebuilt
text: After the Roman general Regulus destroyed it around 255 BCE, during the First Punic War, the town of Kerkuane on Tunisia's Cap Bon was abandoned and never lived in again. That makes it the only Phoenician-Punic city known to survive without a Roman town on top. Its checkerboard streets, houses, shops, workshops, temples and port remain much as they were.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Punic Town of Kerkuane and its Necropolis

title: Ptolemy's Greatest Book
text: About 150 CE in Alexandria, the astronomer Ptolemy completed his Mathematical Collection, later known as the Almagest, from an Arabic-Greek hybrid meaning "the greatest". It explained the wandering paths of the Sun, Moon and planets as combinations of perfect circular motions around a motionless Earth. His Earth-centred picture of the universe went on to prevail in the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ptolemy

title: Walls for a Frontier City
text: At the foot of Jebel Zerhoun, Volubilis began as a Mauritanian capital in the 3rd century BCE and became a Roman outpost, a metropolis of the province of Mauritania Tingitana. In 168–169 CE a rampart was built around it. Inside lie mosaics, marble and bronze statues and hundreds of inscriptions that mix Libyco-Berber, Punic and Roman cultures.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Volubilis

title: The Vandals Seize Carthage
text: In 428 King Gaiseric ferried his Vandal people, 80,000 by his own count, from Spain to Africa. After years of fighting he made a treaty with Rome, then in a surprise move on October 19, 439, captured Carthage and threw off Roman overlordship. His fleets soon controlled much of the western Mediterranean, and in 455 the Vandals plundered Rome itself.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gaiseric

title: The Priestess of the Aurès
text: From 693 an Arab army under Hassan ibn al-Numan pushed west from Egypt, but in the eastern Aurès Mountains it met stiff resistance from Jawara Berbers led by a woman the Arabs called al-Kahina, "the Priestess". One historian argues she was a Christian Berber queen allied with the Byzantines. After her defeat in 698, Hassan occupied Carthage and began building Tunis nearby.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: North Africa, From the Arab conquest to 1830

source2.name: Journal of Early Christian History: Hendrickx, Al-Kahina, The Last Ally of the Roman-Byzantines in the Maghreb (abstract)

title: A Caravan Capital in the Hills
text: In 776 or 777, Ibadi tribes in western Algeria proclaimed Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam, a man of Persian origin raised in Tunisia, as their imam, and he at once began building a capital at Tahart, modern Tiaret. Trade caravans crisscrossing the Maghrib met there, and Tahart grew rich and cosmopolitan through local and trans-Saharan trade until the Fatimids conquered it in 909.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: North Africa, From the Arab conquest to 1830

title: A Red-Brick Giant in Cairo
place: Mosque of Ibn Tulun, Cairo, Egypt
text: In 876 Ahmad ibn Tulun, the Turkish governor of Egypt and Syria, built a huge red-brick mosque on the site of present-day Cairo. Its crenellated walls and carved stucco arches recall the Abbasid architecture of Iraq. The minaret, rebuilt in 1296–99, has three floors shaped square, spiral and octagonal. Centuries later the mosque served as a belt factory, then as shops.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mosque of Ahmad ibn Tulun

title: Desert Warriors Found Marrakesh
text: In 1070–1072 the Almoravids, a confederation of Saharan Berber tribes driven by religious reform, founded Marrakesh. Their city became a political, economic and cultural capital whose influence reached from North Africa to Andalusia, and it eventually gave its name to the Moroccan empire. The palm grove that still surrounds the city is credited to these same Almoravid founders.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Medina of Marrakesh

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Almoravids

title: A Mahdi in the Atlas Mountains
text: Around 1120 a Berber state grew up at Tinmel, in Morocco's Atlas Mountains, inspired by the preacher Ibn Tumart and his demands for puritanical moral reform and a strict idea of the unity of God. In 1121 he proclaimed himself the mahdi, a promised messianic figure, and began war on the Almoravids. His followers, the Almohads, built an empire across North Africa and Spain.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Almohads

title: A Mosque With Its Own Hospital
text: Mamluk builders liked to group buildings with different jobs into one complex. The Qalawun mosque in Cairo, built in 1284–85, joined a mausoleum, a madrasa and a hospital in a single architectural unit. Mamluk patrons also put their great monuments close together, so streets like Bayn al-Qasrayn became galleries of masterpieces, with facades and minarets competing for effect.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Islamic arts (Mamluk architecture)

title: Ibn Battuta Leaves Tangier
text: In 1325, aged 21, Ibn Battuta left his home town of Tangier on pilgrimage to Mecca, travelling overland through Tunis and Tripoli to Egypt. There a passion for travel was born, and he set himself a rule never to travel any road a second time. His book, the Rihlah, describes some 120,000 km of journeys, reaching as far as China and Sumatra.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ibn Battuta

title: Plague Comes to Tunis
text: In 1349 the Black Death struck Tunis and took both parents of young Ibn Khaldun, born in the city in 1332. He grew up to write the Muqaddimah, one of the earliest nonreligious philosophies of history, in a castle near Frenda in Algeria. In it he named the Black Death as the main cause of a great change in his age, "a world brought into existence anew."

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ibn Khaldun

title: Painted Cows of Laas Geel
text: On a granite hill in Somaliland, some twenty rock shelters are covered with many-coloured paintings. Made in the 3rd millennium BCE by the region's first cattle breeders, they show flat-backed cattle, a two-coloured cow wearing a decorated chest-piece, and clothed people with arms opened wide. Nobody expected such art here until a French team found the site in December 2002.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture, Archéologie: Laas Geel, the African Lascaux

title: Africa's First Ancient Genome
text: About 4,500 years ago, a man was buried face-down in Mota, a cave in the highlands of Ethiopia cool and dry enough to preserve his DNA for thousands of years. From his petrous bone, a thick part of the skull just behind the ear, scientists read the first ancient human genome from Africa ever sequenced. Modern people of those highlands are his direct descendants.

source.name: University of Cambridge: Ancient genome from Africa sequenced for the first time

title: Sacred Baboons from Punt
text: Egyptians traded with the land of Punt for at least 1,100 years, bringing home incense, gold, leopard skins and living baboons, which were honoured as forms of Thoth, god of the moon and wisdom. Scientists tested two baboon mummies from Egypt's New Kingdom and found they were born outside Egypt, most likely in Eritrea, Ethiopia or Somalia, which helps narrow down where Punt lay.

source.name: Dartmouth College via EurekAlert!: Mummified baboons shine new light on the lost land of Punt

source2.name: Dartmouth Anthropology: Mummified Baboons Shine New Light on the Lost Land of Punt

title: Herders' Grinding-Stone Circles
text: Around 3,000 years ago, early livestock herders settled at Luxmanda, the southernmost known site of eastern Africa's Pastoral Neolithic. Its rubbish heaps are full of pottery, stone tools and livestock bones. Excavators were surprised to find circles of large lower grinding stones, twelve in just one dug section. The discovery, unprecedented for the era, challenges old ideas about how these herders moved and ate.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Grinding-stone features from the Pastoral Neolithic at Luxmanda, Tanzania

title: A Merchant's Guide to Adulis
place: Adulis, Northern Red Sea Region, Eritrea
text: A first-century merchant's sailing guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes Adulis as a port on a Red Sea bay. Ships brought cloth, glass, copper, wine, olive oil and iron for spears used against elephants, and left with ivory, tortoiseshell and rhinoceros horn. The local ruler, Zoscales, was called miserly and always striving for more, but he knew Greek literature.

source.name: Fordham University, Internet Ancient History Sourcebook: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

title: Aksum's Skyscrapers of Stone
text: In the 3rd and 4th centuries CE, Aksum raised exquisitely carved stone stelae. The tallest still standing rises over 23 metres, carved to look like a nine-storey building. A giant some 33 metres long lies where it fell, perhaps while being erected, possibly the largest single stele people ever tried to raise. In the 4th century, King Ezana left inscriptions in Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

title: An Early Church in Aksum's Lands
place: Beta Samati, near Yeha, Tigray, Ethiopia
text: At Beta Samati, an Aksumite trade and religious town 6.5 km north-east of Yeha, archaeologists uncovered a basilica built during the fourth century CE, measuring 18.7 by 12.4 metres. Finds included a gold ring with a carnelian engraved with a bull's head, and a pendant inscribed in Ge'ez, 'venerable cross'. In Ethiopia, the basilica form seems to have first appeared together with Christianity.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Beta Samati, discovery and excavation of an Aksumite town

title: Eight Mosques Under Shanga
place: Shanga, Pate Island, Lamu County, Kenya
text: Beneath the ruined stone town of Shanga, archaeologist Mark Horton uncovered a succession of eight earthen mosques, the oldest going back to the eighth century, shortly after Islam was founded. His seven-year excavation also found clear evidence that the stone town was preceded by a distinctively indigenous African one.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): Stone Towns of the Swahili Coast

title: Farms That Trapped the Mud
text: Just east of Tanzania's Crater Highlands, farmers at Engaruka built the largest abandoned irrigated and terraced landscape in East Africa, occupied for about 400 years before it was abandoned in the 18th century. Drystone check dams caught river sediment, creating more than 1,000 hectares of fields, in places over 2 metres deep, and some fields were deliberately flooded to make paddy-like soils.

source.name: Quaternary Research (Cambridge Core): Lang and Stump, terraced landscape at Engaruka, Tanzania

source2.name: University of York Research Portal: Geoarchaeological evidence for the construction, irrigation, cultivation and resilience of the terraced landscape at Engaruka

title: The Last Dodo Seen
text: When Dutch sailors landed on Mauritius in 1598, they met the dodo, a bird about 70 cm tall that had evolved from pigeon-like ancestors. Unafraid of people, dodos were hunted by the sailors, and animals brought by newcomers killed the birds and likely ate their eggs. The last reliable sighting came in 1662, or possibly 1680. Dodos were probably leaner and more agile than legend says.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: The dodo bird, the real facts about this icon of extinction

title: First Settlers on Sainte-Anne
text: No people lived in the Seychelles until 1770, when a few families of French colonists arrived with enslaved people from the colony of Île de France and settled on little Sainte-Anne island, facing Mahé. The aim was to develop timber and spices. By 1789 the islands counted 69 French colonists, three soldiers, 32 people of mixed descent and 487 enslaved people.

source.name: Encyclopædia Universalis (Charles Cadoux): Seychelles, Histoire

title: Fourteen Steps to a New Life
text: After slavery was abolished in the British Empire in 1834, Britain chose Mauritius for a 'great experiment' using indentured instead of enslaved labour. Between 1834 and 1920, almost half a million indentured labourers arrived from India at Aapravasi Ghat in Port Louis, to work on sugar estates or be sent on to other colonies. Each newcomer climbed a flight of 14 steps into the depot.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aapravasi Ghat

title: The Rarest Stamps of Mauritius
text: On September 21, 1847, Mauritius issued two postage stamps, a One Penny orange-red and a Two Pence deep blue, engraved and printed by jeweller Joseph Osmond Barnard and marked 'Post Office Mauritius'. Only 500 of each were printed, and they quickly sold out. Just 12 survive today; two unused ones, bought by Mauritian companies in 1993, are displayed in Port Louis.

source.name: Mauritius Post: Postal Museum

title: A Palace of Grass and Reeds
text: On Kasubi hill in Kampala, a palace of the Kabakas, the kings of Buganda, was built in 1882 and turned into a royal burial ground in 1884. Its huge circular, domed tomb house, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, was raised from wooden poles, spear grass, reeds and wattle, and holds four royal tombs. It is still the most active religious place in the kingdom.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi

title: The Man-Eaters of Tsavo
text: In March 1898, the British began building a railway bridge over Kenya's Tsavo River. Over nine months, two maneless male lions developed a taste for humans. Lt. Col. John Henry Patterson shot them in late 1898 and said they had killed 135 people, but later research by Field Museum scientists cut that estimate to 35. In 1925 he sold the lions to the Chicago museum.

source.name: Field Museum: Tsavo Lions

title: Mary Leakey Finds Nutcracker Man
text: In 1959 at Olduvai Gorge, Mary Leakey found a nearly complete adult male skull about 1.8 million years old. First named Zinjanthropus boisei, and still nicknamed 'Zinj', it now belongs to the species Paranthropus boisei, or 'Nutcracker Man'. It has a big crest on top, wide cheekbones and very large cheek teeth, and is sometimes called 'hyper-robust'.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins: OH 5

title: The Boy from Nariokotome
text: In 1984 at Nariokotome in West Turkana, fossil hunter Kamoya Kimeu found the skeleton of a Homo erectus boy who lived about 1.6 million years ago. About 40% complete, it shows he was eight or nine when he died and already 1.6 metres tall. His long legs and narrow shoulders resemble those of people living in hot, dry climates today.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins: KNM-WT 15000

title: The Obelisk Comes Home
text: The 1,700-year-old Aksum Obelisk, 24 metres high and weighing 150 tons, was carted off to Rome by Italian soldiers during Mussolini's invasion in 1937. Italy decided to return it in April 2005. In 2008, UNESCO teams mounted the third and final block, and the obelisk stood once again at its original location in Aksum.

source.name: UN News: UNESCO teams successfully reinstall Ethiopian obelisk to original site

title: Villagers Settle the Rainforest
place: Congo rainforest, Democratic Republic of the Congo
text: Around 800 BCE, a long period of busy human activity began in the Congo rainforest. Archaeologists traced it by studying 1,149 radiocarbon dates linked to 115 pottery styles from 726 sites. They link these first rainforest settlers, of about 2,700 years ago, to Bantu-speaking communities, whose spread was huge, fast and adapted to many different environments.

source.name: Ghent University via EurekAlert!: Prolonged disease epidemic possibly caused population collapse in Central Africa 1600-1400 years ago

source2.name: Royal Museum for Central Africa: Disease epidemic in Central Africa 1500 years ago

title: The First Sheep or Goats
text: In a small rock shelter in Namibia's Erongo region, archaeologists found two teeth from domesticated sheep or goats. They show that herd animals were in southern Africa as early as the end of the first millennium BCE, earlier than any evidence known before. The layers also held stone tools, ostrich eggshell beads and a piece of pottery.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): 'Of Sheep and Men': Earliest Direct Evidence of Caprine Domestication in Southern Africa at Leopard Cave (Erongo, Namibia)

title: The Rainforest Goes Quiet
place: Congo rainforest, Republic of the Congo
text: Between 400 and 600 CE, the communities of the Congo rainforest went through a major population collapse. It happened as the climate turned wetter, and researchers think a long-lasting epidemic, perhaps plague, may have been the cause, though they have no firm proof. Significant resettlement of the region did not restart until around 1,000 years ago.

source.name: Royal Museum for Central Africa: Disease epidemic in Central Africa 1500 years ago

source2.name: Ghent University via EurekAlert!: Prolonged disease epidemic possibly caused population collapse in Central Africa

title: Glass Beads from Across the Sea
text: Chibuene was an Indian Ocean port on the coast of Mozambique, between the mouths of the Limpopo and Zambezi rivers. Glass beads found there form the oldest series in archaeologists' classification of trade beads in sub-Saharan Africa, dated to the 7th–8th centuries and probably made in the Middle East. Later blue, turquoise and yellow Zhizo beads also arrived through Chibuene.

source.name: Heritage (MDPI), Koleini, Colomban, Pikirayi and Prinsloo, University of Pretoria repository: Glass Beads, Markers of Ancient Trade in Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Copper Treasures by the Lakes
place: Sanga, Upemba Depression, Haut-Lomami, DR Congo
text: Beside the lakes of the Upemba Depression, Kisalian communities buried their dead at sites such as Sanga with pottery, iron tools and copper ornaments. Some of the richest graves belonged to children and women, suggesting women played a significant role in society. Fish hooks, harpoons and braziers used for cooking in boats show how much life depended on the water.

source.name: Royal Museum for Central Africa (Nicolas Nikis, Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa): Upemba Depression

title: The Maravi Confederacy Rises
text: Bantu-speaking peoples who migrated into the Malawi region from the north between the 13th and 15th centuries brought centralized government with them. About 1480 they established the Maravi Confederacy. In the 16th century it covered most of today's central and southern Malawi, and at its height in the 17th century its system of government reached into present-day Zambia and Mozambique.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Owen Jato Kalinga et al.): Malawi – History

title: A Stone Cross Comes Home
text: In 1486 the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão erected a limestone cross, 3.5 metres tall, on the coast of present-day Namibia, inscribed in Latin and Portuguese with King John II's claim to the land. In 1893 it was taken to Germany. In 2019 Berlin's German Historical Museum agreed to return it; Namibia's ambassador said it was important for reconstructing Namibians' own history.

source.name: Deutsches Historisches Museum: The Stone Cross from Cape Cross (press release, 2019)

title: A Kongo King Is Baptized
text: On 3 May 1491, Nzinga a Nkuwu, king of Kongo, was baptized and took the name João I, after the king of Portugal; his son Mvemba a Nzinga was baptized too. Portuguese explorers had first reached Kongo in 1483. The son, as King Afonso I, made Catholicism the state religion, and Kongo artists later made brass crucifixes blending Christian imagery with older Kongo cosmology.

source.name: Yale News: Art historian Cécile Fromont uncovers Kongo's Christian visual culture

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kongo (historical kingdom)

title: A Fortress on a Coral Island
text: The Fortress of St Sebastian, built between 1558 and 1620, is the oldest surviving fort on the Island of Mozambique, a coral island linked to Indian Ocean trade since the 10th century. The island was the seat of Portuguese colonial government until 1898. Its stone-and-lime town stands beside a macuti town of palm-leaf roofs built in traditional African style.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Island of Mozambique

title: Shyaam the Great Unites the Kuba
place: Kuba kingdom, between the Sankuru and Kasai rivers, Kasai, DR Congo
text: Around 1625, an outsider named Shyaam aMbul aNgoong unified the chiefdoms between the Sankuru, Lulua and Kasai rivers into the Kuba kingdom. Oral histories say he had travelled west to the Pende and Kongo kingdoms. Under him came better iron-making and American crops such as maize, tobacco, cassava and beans. His royal portrait figure shows him with a board for lele, a strategy game.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (Alexander Ives Bortolot): Kingdoms of the Savanna: The Kuba Kingdom

title: The Rozwi Drive Out the Portuguese
place: Zimbabwe plateau and Zambezi valley, Zimbabwe
text: From 1693 to 1695, the armies of the Changamire, rulers of the Rozwi state between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, drove the Portuguese from all their stations in the interior. Their ruler Changamire Dombo I also conquered some of the most fertile and mineral-rich land. The Changamire remained the leading power of the region until their state was destroyed about 1830.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Changamire Dynasty

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Changamire Dombo I

title: An Exiled Scholar Reaches the Cape
place: Macassar, near Faure, Western Cape, South Africa
text: On 16 April 1694, Shaykh Yusuf of Makassar, an Islamic scholar and sworn enemy of the Dutch East India Company, reached the Cape from Ceylon as an exile, with an entourage of 49 people. The Dutch soon moved the group to the outskirts of Cape Town. He died there in 1699, and the shrine, or kramat, over his grave remains a place of pilgrimage.

source.name: Al-Jāmi'ah: Journal of Islamic Studies (Najma Moosa, University of the Western Cape): Debunking prevailing scholarly views pertaining to the apostasy of alleged descendants of Shaykh Yusuf of Makassar

title: Moshoeshoe Saves His Kingdom
text: From his mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, Moshoeshoe united small groups into the Sotho nation. After a long land war with the Boers of the Orange Free State, he faced complete defeat in 1867. That was prevented in 1868, when the British high commissioner annexed his reduced territory as Basutoland. The Sotho still honour Moshoeshoe as the father of their country.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Moshoeshoe

title: A Heart Under the Mpundu Tree
text: On 1 May 1873 the explorer David Livingstone died in Chitambo's village, in what is now Zambia. His companions buried his heart beneath a mpundu tree, and Jacob Wainwright carved an inscription into its bark. They then carried his body to Dar es Salaam on the coast, from where it was shipped to England. The carved bark is now held by the Royal Geographical Society.

source.name: Royal Geographical Society: Photograph of mpundu tree and Livingstone tree bark

title: A Tent Town Called Egoli
text: Johannesburg was founded as a mining camp in 1886, a few months after the Main Reef of gold was found at Langlaagte. That first camp had a few thousand people, 14 liquor stores and one hotel, but no sanitation. Prospectors and work-seekers poured in, and by 1896 the city had 100,000 people. Its Zulu name, Egoli, means 'the Place of Gold'.

source.name: City of Johannesburg: 125th Anniversary of the founding of Johannesburg (mayoral speech, 2011)

title: Three Kings Outwit Rhodes
text: In 1895 three chiefs, Khama III of the Bangwato, Sebele I of the Bakwena and Bathoen I of the Bangwaketse, travelled to Britain. They pleaded not to be handed to Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and won assurances from Queen Victoria. Rhodes wrote that he was too angry to keep dictating. A bronze monument to the three now stands in Gaborone.

source.name: Botswana Daily News (Government of Botswana): Three Dikgosi Monument attracts 6 000

source2.name: University of Edinburgh, Whites Writing Whiteness (Liz Stanley): Two Cecil Rhodes letters

title: Nehanda, Mother of the Nation
text: Charwe was recognised as a medium for Nehanda, a founding ancestor spirit. After white settlers occupied the land, she was tried for ordering the 1896 killing of Native Commissioner Henry Pollard, and was hanged in March 1898. A photograph taken at her arrest became famous, and after Zimbabwe's independence in 1980 Nehanda was revered as the 'Mother of the Nation'.

source.name: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History (Diana Jeater and Ruvimbo Rusike): Nehanda

title: 20,000 Women March on Pretoria
text: On 9 August 1956, up to 20,000 women of all races marched to the Union Buildings in Pretoria against new laws forcing women to carry passes. Led by Lilian Ngoyi, Helen Joseph, Rahima Moosa and Sophia Williams De Bruyn, they delivered petitions to Prime Minister J.G. Strijdom's office. The day is now celebrated as National Women's Day.

source.name: University of Cape Town Libraries: Women's Day, 9 August

source2.name: Rhodes University: History of Lilian Ngoyi

title: A Dam That Moved a People
text: In 1959 the Kariba Dam was completed across the Zambezi River, a concrete arch 128 metres high on the border of today's Zambia and Zimbabwe. Creating its lake required the resettlement of more than 30,000 Batonka people and the evacuation of thousands of wild animals in 'Operation Noah'. Some Africans opposed it as a symbol of the unpopular Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kariba Dam

title: A New Heart Before Dawn
place: Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, South Africa
text: Just before 6 a.m. on Sunday, 3 December 1967, surgeons at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town completed the world's first human heart transplant. Grocer Louis Washkansky, aged 53, received the heart of Denise Darvall, a 25-year-old car accident victim. Chris and Marius Barnard led the team. Washkansky died of pneumonia 18 days later.

source.name: University of Cape Town News: 50th anniversary of the first human heart transplant

title: A Nuclear Reactor Made by Nature
text: In 1972, physicist Francis Perrin and his colleagues in France noticed that uranium ore from a mine at Oklo in Gabon held 0.717% uranium-235 instead of the usual 0.720%. Further tests showed the ore was natural but had gone through fission on its own over two billion years ago, with water slowing the neutrons. It is Earth's only known natural nuclear reactor.

source.name: International Atomic Energy Agency: Meet Oklo, the Earth's Two-billion-year-old only Known Natural Nuclear Reactor

title: Lava Above Goma
place: Mount Nyiragongo, near Goma, North Kivu, DR Congo
text: On 22 May 2021, Mount Nyiragongo erupted above the city of Goma. The lava, ash and gas killed over 30 people and destroyed houses, schools and health centres. Fearing another eruption, authorities told residents of ten Goma districts to leave, an order affecting about 400,000 people, and thousands crossed the border into Rwanda.

source.name: UN News: Thousands in Goma evacuated amid fears of further volcanic eruption

title: Malta's Underground Labyrinth
text: Around 2500 BCE, people on Malta carved three levels of chambers deep into soft limestone, the lowest more than ten metres down. This underground cemetery once held the remains of about 7,000 people. Its walls carry the only prehistoric paintings found on the islands, one niche echoes when you speak into it, and a tiny clay 'Sleeping Lady' was found inside.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hal Saflieni Hypogeum

title: Stone Towers Found Only in Sardinia
text: In the Middle to Late Bronze Age, Sardinians began building nuraghi: cone-shaped defensive towers of dressed stone with vaulted rooms inside, found nowhere else in the world. At Su Nuraxi people kept living for centuries, adding walls under Carthaginian pressure. Later the towers lay buried until archaeologists began digging them out in the 1950s.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Su Nuraxi di Barumini

title: The Etruscans' Painted Tombs
text: The Etruscans cut some 6,000 graves into the rock outside Tarquinia. About 200 of them are painted, the earliest dating from the 7th century BCE. Many tombs copy the shape of Etruscan houses, and their wall paintings of daily life are among the few major artworks of pre-Roman times to survive around the Mediterranean.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Etruscan Necropolises of Cerveteri and Tarquinia

title: Greek Sailors Settle Corsica
text: Corsica's dolmens and standing stones show people lived there from at least the 3rd millennium BCE, but its recorded history starts about 560 BCE. That is when Greeks from Phocaea, in Asia Minor, founded the town of Alalia on the island's east coast. Carthaginians and then Romans followed, and the Latin the Romans brought became the root of today's Corsican dialect.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Corsica (History)

title: Archimedes Defends Syracuse
text: When Rome besieged Syracuse in 213 BCE, the mathematician Archimedes built war machines so effective that they long delayed its capture. The city fell in 212 or 211 BCE, and Archimedes was killed in the sack. He had found how a sphere relates to the cylinder around it, and was so proud of it that he asked for that shape on his tomb.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Archimedes, by Gerald J. Toomer

title: Numantia Holds Out Against Rome
text: The Celtiberian town of Numantia beat back Roman armies again and again, and in 137 BCE even captured one. In 133 BCE Scipio Aemilianus surrounded it with about ten kilometres of continuous ramparts. After an eight-month siege, hunger forced the survivors to surrender, ending serious resistance to Rome in Celtiberia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Numantia

title: A Little Rome in Spain
text: In 25 BCE, after his campaigns in northern Hispania, Augustus founded the colony of Augusta Emerita, today's Mérida. Planned as an idealised model of Rome, it became capital of Lusitania, the empire's westernmost province. Its theatre, amphitheatre, vast circus, great bridge over the Guadiana and water-supply system still survive.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida

title: Tariq's Mountain
text: In May 711 the Berber general Tariq ibn Ziyad landed on Gibraltar with about 7,000 men, mostly Berbers, Syrians and Yemenis. The rock became known as Jabal Tariq, 'Mount Tarik', the origin of its name. Within months he had defeated the Visigothic king Roderick and taken Toledo. With Musa ibn Nusayr he went on to occupy more than two-thirds of the Iberian Peninsula.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tariq ibn Ziyad

title: New Numbers Arrive in Europe
text: As a boy, Leonardo of Pisa, later called Fibonacci, studied calculation with an Arab master in North Africa, where his merchant father worked. In 1202 he published Liber abaci, the 'Book of the Abacus', which introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe. It showed how place value works and used the numbers for real problems like profit, barter and money changing.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Fibonacci, by Frances Carney Gies

title: Giotto Paints a Chapel in Padua
text: Around 1305, Giotto covered the walls of a small chapel in Padua, built on the site of a Roman arena, with scenes in three tiers. In one, the Star of Bethlehem is painted as a realistic comet. UNESCO says these frescoes marked the start of a revolution in wall painting, with new ways of showing space that heralded Renaissance perspective.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Giotto, by Peter J. Murray

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Padua's fourteenth-century fresco cycles

title: A Monastery for a Victory
text: After the Portuguese beat the Castilians at Aljubarrota in 1385, King João I kept a vow by building the Monastery of Batalha. Its church was finished in 1416, and for two centuries it was the monarchy's great workshop. João, his queen Philippa of Lancaster and their son Prince Henry the Navigator are buried there.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Monastery of Batalha

title: A City Born From a Siege
text: The Siege of Malta in 1565 captured Europe's imagination, and it moved the Knights of St John to build a brand-new capital. Founded in 1566, Valletta was planned as a single late-Renaissance design, with a regular grid of streets inside bastioned walls. Today its 320 monuments are packed into just 55 hectares.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: City of Valletta

title: Sicily Rebuilds in Baroque Style
text: A catastrophic earthquake struck Sicily in 1693. In the decades after, eight towns, including Catania, Noto, Ragusa and Modica, were rebuilt in the late Baroque style. Catania rose on its old site, while Noto moved to a new one. The work brought fresh ideas in town planning and earthquake-resistant building.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto

title: Volta Stacks Up a Battery
text: Alessandro Volta, physics professor at Pavia, tested tiny currents between metal disks by putting them on his tongue. In 1800 he announced the first electric battery: a pile of zinc and silver disks separated by cloth soaked in salt water. It gave the first continuous electric current, and within six weeks others used it to split water.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Alessandro Volta

title: A Girl Spots Bison on the Ceiling
place: Altamira Cave, Santillana del Mar, Cantabria, Spain
text: In 1879 Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola was digging in Altamira cave when his eight-year-old daughter, Maria, noticed bison painted on the ceiling of a side chamber. He published the finds in 1880, but most experts called the paintings modern forgeries. They were accepted as genuine only at the end of the century and are now dated to about 14,800 to 13,100 years ago.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Altamira

title: The First Children's House
text: In Rome's poor San Lorenzo quarter, about 50 young children lived unsupervised in renovated apartment blocks, with no toys and no teacher. Maria Montessori, then a medical officer of hygiene, agreed to help if conditions on food and sanitation were met. On January 6, 1907, the first Casa dei Bambini, or Children's House, opened there.

source.name: Association Montessori Internationale: On this Day, First Casa dei Bambini

title: A Farmer Finds Malta's Temples
text: In 1913 a farmer, Lorenzo Despott, came across the Tarxien Temples, four megalithic buildings from the late Neolithic. Sir Themistocles Zammit led excavations from 1915 to 1919. Finds included stone carvings of spirals and animals and the lower half of a colossal statue in a pleated skirt. After 2000 BC, newcomers used part of the site as a cremation cemetery.

source.name: Heritage Malta: Tarxien Temples

title: Guernica Bombed, Picasso Responds
text: On April 26, 1937, during Spain's civil war, German aircraft bombed the Basque city of Guernica for three hours, killing or wounding a third of its people. In Paris, Picasso turned the news into a huge black-and-white painting in about three weeks for the Spanish Republic's world's fair pavilion. He refused to let it go to Spain while Franco ruled; it arrived in 1981.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Guernica, by Alicja Zelazko

title: Carnations in the Rifles
text: By 1974, more than a decade of colonial wars in Africa had worn out Portugal's army, and part of it rose against the Estado Novo dictatorship that had ruled since 1933. The song 'Grândola Vila Morena' was the signal to begin on April 25. Images of the revolution show young soldiers with carnations in their rifles.

source.name: The Conversation: The 50th anniversary of Portugal's Carnation Revolution, by Fernando Camacho Padilla (Universidad Autónoma de Madrid)

title: Hikers Find the Iceman
place: Tisenjoch, Schnalstal/Val Senales, South Tyrol, Italy
text: In 1991 hikers on a glacier in South Tyrol stumbled on Ötzi, a man who died over 5,300 years ago and was preserved in the ice. He was about 46, carried a valuable copper axe and had 61 tattoos. An X-ray in 2001 revealed a flint arrowhead in his shoulder: it cut an artery, and he bled to death within minutes.

source.name: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: The Iceman

source2.name: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: The mummy

title: Wheat Comes to a Stilt Village
text: At Haimenkou in northwest Yunnan, people lived in houses raised on stilts and farmed rice and millet, crops that had spread from Central China. Then new grains arrived: wheat found there has been directly dated to 1440–1310 BCE, and barley appears too. Around the same time, bronze objects begin to show up at the site.

source.name: PMC: The origins of multi-cropping agriculture in Southwestern China: Archaeobotanical insights from third to first millennium B.C. Yunnan

title: The First Horse Dentists
text: Herders of the Deer Stone-Khirigsuur culture in Mongolia buried horses by the dozens, hundreds or even thousands. In young horses from these ritual burials, researchers found partly sawn baby teeth: attempted dental surgery from around 1150 BCE, the world's oldest known evidence of veterinary dental care. Later, as bronze bits came into use, herders also learned to remove painful wolf teeth.

source.name: EurekAlert! (PNAS release): Horse dentistry may have originated in Mongolian Steppe

source2.name: Max Planck Society: Oldest evidence of horse veterinary care discovered in Mongolia

title: Jinsha's Gold and Rainbow Jades
text: Found in 2001 on the edge of Chengdu, Jinsha was a major centre on the Chengdu Plain, with finds dated to 1000–650 BCE. Diggers recovered about 40 gold objects and more than 700 bronzes. A gold band of birds and fish pierced by arrows almost matches one from Sanxingdui, and buried bronzes stained Jinsha's jades green, blue, purple and black.

source.name: Cambridge Core (Bulletin of SOAS): The Southwest Silk Road: artistic exchange and transmission in early China

source2.name: Scientific Reports: Nondestructive analysis of alterations of Chinese jade artifacts from Jinsha, Sichuan Province, China

title: Red Drummers on the Cliffs
text: High on steep karst cliffs above the Zuojiang River, the Luoyue people painted their ceremonies at 38 sites, starting around the 5th century BCE. The scenes have been read as rituals of the bronze drum culture once common across southern China. Local people still revere the painted mountains and perform rituals there.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Zuojiang Huashan Rock Art Cultural Landscape

title: The Southern Kingdom of Nanyue
text: Under the Qin, the small city of Panyu, now Guangzhou, ruled a southern prefecture. When the Qin broke apart in 207 BCE, General Zhao Tuo set up an independent kingdom called Nanyue. It stretched across today's Guangdong and Guangxi and south to Da Nang in Vietnam, staying independent until the Han emperor Wudi conquered it in 111 BCE.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nam Viet

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Guangzhou, history

title: The Village of Slate Coffins
text: In July 1980, building a new railway station in Taitung uncovered Taiwan's largest prehistoric settlement. Archaeologists found nearly 1,600 slate coffins and over 20,000 objects of clay, stone and jade. The Peinan people built their homes facing away from the mountain, and about 1,900 years ago they left the site for reasons no one knows.

source.name: National Museum of Prehistory (Taiwan): Peinan Site Park

source2.name: National Museum of Prehistory (Taiwan): Permanent Exhibition, Peinan Site Park

title: A Giant Buddha Guards the River
text: Where three rivers meet at Leshan, boats kept wrecking. In 713 a monk named Hai Tong began carving a Buddha into the red sandstone cliff to watch over them. It took 90 years to finish. The 71-metre statue has fingers 8.3 metres long, and rock from the work filled the riverbed, which did make the water safer.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Leshan Giant Buddha

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mount Emei Scenic Area, including Leshan Giant Buddha Scenic Area

title: Nanzhao Rises by Lake Er
text: In 729 a chief named Piluoge brought six small kingdoms in western Yunnan together as Nanzhao, with its power centred near Lake Er. Its mountain capital beat back Chinese attacks in 751 and 754. Nanzhao controlled trade routes toward Myanmar and India, mined salt and gold, and its artisans taught the weaving of cotton and silk gauze.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nanzhao

title: The Khan Who Wouldn't Step Down
place: Bairin Left Banner, Inner Mongolia, China
text: Abaoji was elected great khan of the Khitan tribes for a three-year term, but when it ended he refused to resign. By 916 he had set up a Chinese-style dynasty with his son as heir, and grouped his warriors into units called ordos. The Khitans later named their dynasty Liao and honoured Abaoji as its founder.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Abaoji

title: The Jurchen Found the Golden Dynasty
text: The Jurchen tribes of Manchuria had been subjects of the Khitan Liao. From 1115 they threw off their overlords and founded the Jin dynasty, with its first capital at Huining. Though they took a Chinese dynasty name, they kept their own script and speech and banned Chinese clothing and customs from their armies.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jin dynasty (1115–1234)

title: A Manchu Palace in Shenyang
text: In 1625 Nurgaci began a palace in Shenyang for the Manchu rulers who would soon found the Qing dynasty. Its buildings were laid out according to the Manchu eight-banner system, which makes it unique among palaces. Inside the Qingning Palace are places for shamanist sacrifices, a Manchu custom kept up for centuries.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties in Beijing and Shenyang

title: The Dutch Drive Out the Spanish
text: Spanish forces had seized Keelung in 1626. In 1642 the Dutch expelled them and, with help from Indigenous peoples, took control of the whole island. The Dutch East India Company dug wells, surveyed land, brought in oxen to plough the fields, and developed a written form of language for Indigenous peoples.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taiwan, history (Dutch period)

title: One Port for the Whole World
text: Western traders came to Guangzhou for tea, rhubarb, silk and spices. In 1757 the Qing emperor ordered that it be the only port open to foreign commerce. Foreign merchants had to stay in a small riverbank area outside the city wall with their 13 warehouses, called factories, and foreign women and firearms were banned.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Canton system

title: A Heavenly Kingdom Rises in Guangxi
text: Hong Xiuquan, a failed exam candidate, believed visions showed he was Jesus Christ's younger brother. Leading the God Worshippers among poor peasants of Guangxi, he proclaimed the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace on January 1, 1851. His followers banned foot-binding and opium, organized separate men's and women's divisions, and the rebellion went on to cost an estimated 20 million lives.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taiping Rebellion

title: Catching the Plague Germ
text: On June 15, 1894, as an epidemic was devastating Hong Kong, the doctor Alexandre Yersin landed there with a microscope and an autoclave. Working in a straw hut, he used a sample from the swollen bubo of a patient who had died. With it he identified the plague bacillus, the germ later named Yersinia pestis.

source.name: Institut Pasteur: A historic fight against emerging infectious diseases

title: Asia's First Republic Lasts Ten Days
text: After losing a war with Japan, China signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, giving Taiwan to Japan. When the news reached the island, local leaders proclaimed the Republic of Taiwan, called Asia's first republic. With no recognized leader and no real army, it lasted only about ten days before Japan began its colonial rule.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taiwan, history (Dutch period to Japanese empire)

title: An Island of Many Styles
text: The tiny island of Kulangsu, facing Xiamen, became an international settlement in 1903. Local Chinese, overseas Chinese returning home, and foreigners from many countries built 931 historic buildings there. Out of this mix grew a new architectural style, Amoy Deco, blending local southern Fujian traditions with Art Deco and modernist ideas, and copied across Southeast Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kulangsu, a Historic International Settlement

title: A Railway Blast That Wasn't
text: On the night of September 18, 1931, Japanese troops claimed a Chinese attack on their railway near Mukden and seized the city. The explosion did so little damage that trains kept running. Most observers believe the army staged it without its government's approval. Within three months Japanese troops had spread throughout Manchuria.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mukden Incident

title: A Lifeline Through the Mountains
text: With Japan occupying China's coast, the Chinese began building a 1,154-kilometre highway from Kunming to Lashio in Burma, completing it in 1939. For three years war goods came by sea to Rangoon, by train to Lashio, then up the road into China. Japan closed the route in April 1942 by seizing Lashio.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Burma Road

title: A Window Into the Cambrian Seas
text: On July 1, 1984, Hou Xianguang discovered the Chengjiang fossils in the hills of Yunnan. They preserve soft bodies, guts and delicate gills of sea creatures from 530 million years ago, when almost all major animal groups appeared. Researchers have since reported more than 300 species, including the oldest known fossil chordates.

source.name: Yunnan University: YNU marks 40th anniversary of unique Chengjiang fossil find

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Chengjiang Fossil Site

title: The Great Wenchuan Earthquake
text: On May 12, 2008, a magnitude-7.9 earthquake struck the mountains of Sichuan, where the Indian-Australian plate pushes against the Eurasian plate. Ground was thrust up by about 9 metres in places. Almost 90,000 people were counted dead or missing, including more than 5,300 children, many of them students in collapsed schools.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sichuan earthquake of 2008

title: The Griffin Warrior's Grave
place: Near the Palace of Nestor, Pylos, Messenia, Greece
text: In May 2015, University of Cincinnati archaeologists Jack Davis and Sharon Stocker uncovered a grave in an olive grove near Pylos, built around 1500–1450 BCE. Its owner lay with bronze weapons, a helmet made of boar tusks, ivory combs, a mirror and more than 50 sealstones. An ivory plaque carved with a griffin gave him his modern nickname: the Griffin Warrior.

source.name: National Geographic: This 3,500-year-old tomb held the treasures of Greece's 'Griffin Warrior'

title: Greeks Settle the Danube Coast
place: Histria (Istros), near Lake Sinoe, Constanța County, Romania
text: Greeks from the city of Miletus founded Istros, later called Histria, in 657–656 BCE. It was the oldest Greek colony on the western shore of the Black Sea and grew into an important commercial and cultural centre for 14 centuries. Systematic digging began in 1914 under Vasile Pârvan, and a museum beside the ruins now holds its finds.

source.name: Museum of National History and Archaeology Constanța (MINAC): Histria Museum Complex

title: Column Bases Spun on a Lathe
text: Around 570–560 BCE, the builders Rhoecus and Theodorus began a colossal temple to the goddess Hera on the Aegean island of Samos. It measured 52.5 by 105 metres, stood on at least 100 columns, and its moulded column bases were turned on a lathe designed by Theodorus. Samos also cut a 1,036-metre tunnel through a mountain to bring water to its city.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pythagoreion and Heraion of Samos

title: Democracy by Neighbourhood
text: In 508 BCE the Athenian noble Cleisthenes sided with the popular Assembly against rival aristocrats and pushed through sweeping reforms. Political rights now depended on belonging to a deme, a local township, instead of a family clan. Ten new tribes mixed people from the city, the coast and the inland areas, and a Council of 500 took 50 members from each tribe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Cleisthenes of Athens (Russell Meiggs)

title: The Palace of Macedon's Kings
text: Around 340 BCE a monumental palace rose at Aigai, the royal capital of ancient Macedon. UNESCO calls it the biggest building of classical Greece. Beside it lies a royal cemetery of more than 500 burial mounds, where in 1977–78 archaeologists found the unlooted tombs of Philip II, father of Alexander the Great, and of his grandson Alexander IV, a worldwide sensation.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Aigai (modern name Vergina)

title: A City Named for Alexander's Sister
text: Thessaloniki was founded in 316 BCE and named for a sister of Alexander the Great. After 146 BCE it became the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Standing on the Via Egnatia, the road from the Adriatic Sea east to Byzantium, it grew into a great military and commercial station, and the Apostle Paul later wrote two letters to its people.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Thessaloníki

title: A Family in the Earthquake House
text: At around dawn on July 21, 365 CE, an earthquake wrecked the Roman city of Kourion on Cyprus. In the mid-1980s a University of Arizona team led by David Soren found a man of 25, a woman of 19 and a baby of one and a half, cradled against each other beneath fallen plaster and heavy stone blocks in what is now called the Earthquake House.

source.name: University of Arizona News: U of A expert's discovery to be displayed in Cyprus archaeological museum

title: A Horseman Carved in a Cliff
text: Early in the 8th century, as the Bulgarian state was taking shape, sculptors carved a rider triumphing over a lion into a 100-metre cliff at Madara, the main sacred place of the First Bulgarian Empire. UNESCO says the relief has no parallel in Europe. Inscriptions beside it record events from 705 to 801 in the reigns of the Khans Tervel, Kormisos and Omurtag.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Madara Rider

title: Saint Sava's Marble Monastery
text: Studenica Monastery was founded in the late 12th century by Stefan Nemanja, who established the medieval Serbian state, and its Church of the Virgin was built of white marble. There, in 1219, Nemanja's youngest son, Saint Sava, launched the independent Serbian Orthodox Church. He also wrote the first literary work in the Serbian language.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Studenica Monastery

title: The Painted Walls of Boyana
text: On the edge of Sofia stands Boyana Church, first built in the 10th century and enlarged in the early 13th century by the Sebastocrator Kaloyan with a second, two-storey church. Its frescoes were painted in 1259. UNESCO ranks them among the most important collections of medieval painting, with figures full of spiritual expressiveness and vitality, painted in harmonious proportions.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Boyana Church

title: Thirty Days Before Entering Town
text: In 1377 the Great Council of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered visitors from plague-stricken areas to stay apart for 30 days, a period called the trentino.
