It is described as the first quarantine. As the practice spread to other port cities, the wait grew to 40 days, quarantino in Italian, and that number gave English the word quarantine.

source.name: CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases: Etymologia: Quarantine

source2.name: PMC (Emerging Infectious Diseases): Lessons from the History of Quarantine, from Plague to Influenza A

title: Montenegro's First Printed Book
text: On January 4, 1494, the printing house of Đurđe Crnojević on Obod finished the Oktoih prvoglasnik, the first South Slavic book printed in Cyrillic. Crnojević had bought the press in Venice in 1492, and Hieromonk Macarius did the printing with the help of seven unnamed monks. Montenegro's National Library calls it the first state printing house in the world.

source.name: National Library of Montenegro: History

title: Three Principalities, One Prince
text: Prince Michael of Walachia, remembered as Michael the Brave, defeated the Transylvanian ruler Andreas Báthory in 1599. In May 1600 he conquered Moldavia and took the title prince of Ungro-Walachia, Transylvania and Moldavia. Within months he lost both new lands, but 19th-century Romanian nationalists hailed him as the pioneer of national unity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Michael, prince of Walachia

title: The Day the Parthenon Exploded
text: For over two thousand years the Parthenon stood almost intact, serving as a church and later a mosque. Then in 1687 Venetians fighting the Ottoman Turks bombarded the Acropolis, and a powder magazine inside the temple blew up, destroying the centre of the building. Trying to carry off sculptures as loot, the Venetians accidentally smashed several more.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Parthenon

title: The Venus de Milo Comes to Light
text: In 1820 a marble statue of the goddess Aphrodite was found on the island of Melos. Carved around 150–125 BCE from Parian marble and 204 cm tall, it was made of two blocks joined at the hips, and holes show it once wore a bronze diadem and bracelet. The Marquis de Rivière gave it to King Louis XVIII, and it reached the Louvre in 1821.

source.name: Musée du Louvre, Collections: Vénus de Milo (LL 299)

title: The League Founded at Prizren
text: In 1878 Albanians met in Prizren, a town in Kosovo, and founded the Albanian League. It aimed to unite Albanian lands, then split among four Ottoman provinces, into one autonomous state, and to develop Albanian language, literature, education and culture. The Ottomans suppressed the league in 1881, but by then it had become a powerful symbol of Albania's national awakening.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Albania (Peter R. Prifti)

title: An Easter Earthquake Remakes Ljubljana
text: Late on Easter Sunday, April 14, 1895, at 23:17, an earthquake of intensity 8–9 struck with its epicentre at Ljubljana. Engineers inspected 1,420 structures and ruled that 145 houses had to be pulled down, while Austrian military pioneers put up more than 60 wooden barracks for the homeless. Ivan Hribar, mayor from 1896, became a central figure in modernising the city after the disaster.

source.name: Historia Provinciae (Institute of Slavic Studies, Russian Academy of Sciences), L. A. Kirilina: The 1895 Earthquake in Ljubljana: Catastrophe and Impetus for the Modernization of the City

title: The Kishinev Pogrom Shocks the World
text: In 1897 Jews made up almost half of Kishinev's people. Before Passover 1903 the local paper Bessarabets falsely accused them of murdering a Christian child, and on April 6–7 a mob killed 49 people, maimed 586 and wrecked 1,350 Jewish houses and 588 shops. Protests followed across Europe and the United States, and Hayim Nahman Bialik's poem In the City of Slaughter recalled the horror.

source.name: YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe: Kishinev (Wolf Moskovich)

title: Albania Declares Independence at Vlorë
text: In October 1912 Albania's Balkan neighbours declared war on the Ottoman Empire, and Greek, Serbian and Montenegrin armies advanced into Albanian lands. To save the country, Albanian national delegates met at a congress in the port of Vlorë, led by Ismail Qemal, a former high Ottoman official. On November 28, 1912, they issued the Vlorë proclamation declaring Albania's independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Albania (Peter R. Prifti)

title: Skopje Rises From the Rubble
text: In the early morning of July 26, 1963, a massive earthquake struck Skopje. Over 1,000 people died, over 3,000 were seriously injured, and three-quarters of the city's people lost their homes. Within days 35 nations asked the UN General Assembly to take up relief, and in 1965 an institute for earthquake engineering and urban planning was founded in the city with UNESCO's help.

source.name: United Nations: Secretary-General's message on the fortieth anniversary of the Skopje Earthquake

title: Timișoara Sparks a Revolution
text: Romania's uprising against the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu began with small protests in Timișoara on December 16, 1989. When he ordered security forces to fire on the crowds, the army was pushed to switch sides, and demonstrations spread to Bucharest. On December 22 the army joined the protesters, and on December 25 Ceaușescu and his wife were tried by a military tribunal and executed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Romania – The revolution of 1989

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Timișoara

title: The Bridge Keepers' Bridge Returns
text: Mostar takes its name from the mostari, the keepers of its bridge over the Neretva River. Its Old Bridge, built by the Ottoman architect Hajruddin after a design by his teacher Sinan, was destroyed with most of the old town in the 1990s conflict. Rebuilt in 2004 with help from a UNESCO-founded scientific committee, it now stands as a symbol of reconciliation.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Old Bridge Area of the Old City of Mostar

title: Tombs Built by Giants?
text: Around 3400 BCE the Funnel Beaker people, the first farmers in northern Europe, were building huge stone tombs called hunebeds in Drenthe. Ice Age glaciers had carried the boulders from southern Finland, and the biggest stone of the largest tomb, D27 at Borger, weighs over 20 tons. Later locals thought giants built them. Fifty-four still stand.

source.name: Hunebedcentrum Borger: D27 - The largest hunebed

source2.name: Het Hunebed Nieuwscafe (Hunebedcentrum), N. Lemmers and A. Harvey: Dutch Hunebeds and the Funnel Beaker Culture

title: A Village Dated to the Year
text: In 3384 BCE a single house went up beside a bay of Lake Constance, and tree rings in its posts reveal the exact year. The village grew to perhaps fifty houses of white fir, home to people who ate hazelnuts, fish, frogs and red deer. In 3370 BCE the whole village burned, and it was never rebuilt.

source.name: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland (HLS): Arbon

source2.name: Ancient Europe 8000 B.C.-A.D. 1000: Encyclopedia of the Barbarian World (via Encyclopedia.com): Arbon-Bleiche 3

title: Greek Colonists Found Marseille
text: Greek colonists from Phokaia in Asia Minor founded Massalia, today's Marseille, in 600 BCE. According to the story, the deal with the locals was sealed when the Greek leader married Gyptis, daughter of the Ligurian king Nannus. The city grew rich trading rare metals, set up outposts from Spain to Corsica, and kept speaking Greek until the 5th century CE.

source.name: The Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites (Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University): Massalia

title: The Lady of Vix's Giant Vase
text: Around 470-460 BCE a powerful woman was buried near Vix, laid on a four-wheeled ceremonial wagon with a torc on her body. Beside her stood a bronze krater 1.64 metres tall and weighing 208.6 kilograms, made around 530 BCE in the Greek colony of Sybaris in southern Italy. Nobody knows how it reached Vix. Archaeologists found the tomb in January 1953.

source.name: Musee du Pays Chatillonnais - Tresor de Vix: The Vix treasure

title: Caesar Traps Vercingetorix
text: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix shut his army inside the hilltop town of Alesia. Caesar's soldiers built a double ring of fortifications about 40 kilometres long, one line to keep the Gauls in and one to keep a huge Gaulish relief army out. When the battle was lost, Vercingetorix surrendered the next day, and 70,000 people were deported, most as slaves.

source.name: Musee d'Archeologie nationale: Vercingetorix et Alesia

title: An Emperor Speaks Up for Gauls
text: In 48 CE Emperor Claudius urged the Roman Senate to let leading men from Gaul hold Roman offices and sit in the Senate. Part of his speech survives, engraved on a bronze plaque weighing 222.5 kilograms. Only 81 lines in two columns remain. The plaque was found in 1528 in a vineyard on the Croix-Rousse hill in Lyon.

source.name: Lugdunum, musee et theatres romains (collections): Table claudienne

source2.name: HiSoMA (CNRS / Maison de l'Orient): TABVLA - La Table Claudienne 500 ans apres sa decouverte

title: Three Valleys Make a Pact
text: In 1291 the communities of Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden formed a 'perpetual league' in a document known as the Federal Charter, or Bundesbrief. It set out rules on mutual aid and resisting outside threats. Switzerland's day of remembrance, 1 August, commemorates this alliance, though historians still debate the charter's nature, authenticity and real importance.

source.name: Swiss American Historical Society Review (BYU ScholarsArchive), Albert Winkler: The Federal Charter of 1291 and the Founding of the Swiss State

title: Weavers Beat the Knights
text: On July 11, 1302, outside Kortrijk, an untrained Flemish militia made up mostly of craft guild members, especially weavers, defeated a professional force of mounted knights. They stood on ground ringed by streams and moats, so the horsemen could not charge. The battle is named for the spurs supposedly taken from the losers, and it helped start an 'infantry revolution'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of the Golden Spurs

title: The Night the Dike Broke
text: In the night of 18-19 November 1421, a poorly maintained dike near Broek gave way and floodwater poured over the Grote Waard farmland in Holland. Later chroniclers claimed 10,000 to 100,000 victims, but one chronicle speaks of 2,000 drowned. Researchers say sinking land made the floods so catastrophic. The drowned area gradually became the Biesbosch wetland.

source.name: National Geographic Nederland, Esmee van Dijk: De Sint-Elisabethsvloed verdronk dorpen en vormde de Biesbosch

source2.name: Utrecht University, Weerts, Cohen and Kleinhans: The 1421 St.Elisabeth flooding 'event' and the loss of De Groote Waard

title: The Mystic Lamb Unveiled
text: On May 6, 1432, a huge altarpiece was installed in a chapel of St John's Church in Ghent, now St Bavo's Cathedral. Its inscription says Hubert van Eyck began it and his brother Jan finished it for Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut. Called 'the first major oil painting', it shows crowds gathering in paradise to worship the Lamb of God.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Emilie E.S. Gordenker: Ghent Altarpiece

source2.name: Sint-Baafskathedraal Gent: The Ghent Altarpiece

title: A New Map of the Human Body
text: In June 1543 the Basel printer Johannes Oporinus published De humani corporis fabrica, a giant anatomy book by Andreas Vesalius, a professor of anatomy at Padua. Vesalius relied heavily on the ancient doctor Galen, but he did his own dissections, confirming some of Galen's claims and refuting others. The book's woodcuts, by several artists linked to Titian's workshop, shaped anatomy pictures for centuries.

source.name: U.S. National Library of Medicine, Historical Anatomies on the Web: Andreas Vesalius

source2.name: U.S. National Library of Medicine, Historical Anatomies on the Web: Vesalius, Bibliographic Information

title: Rembrandt's Marching Militia
text: In 1642 Rembrandt signed and dated a huge group portrait, 379.5 by 453.5 centimetres, for the great hall of the headquarters of one of Amsterdam's civic guard companies. It shows Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, dressed in black, telling his lieutenant to start the company marching as the guardsmen get into formation. The famous name, The Night Watch, only came into use in the late 18th century.

source.name: Rijksmuseum: The Night Watch, Rembrandt van Rijn, 1642 (SK-C-5)

title: An Artist Sails for Butterflies
text: In 1699 Maria Sibylla Merian, an artist who ran a workshop in Amsterdam with her daughters, set off for Suriname with her youngest daughter, Dorothea Maria Graff. To help pay, she sold paintings and much of her collection. The two women raised insects and recorded how they changed, until illness, possibly malaria, sent them home in 1701. Her 1705 book had 60 hand-coloured engravings.

source.name: Rijksmuseum: 10 things to know about Maria Sibylla Merian's insects of Suriname

source2.name: Science History Institute: Maria Sibylla Merian

title: Doctor and Porter Top Mont Blanc
place: Mont Blanc, near Chamonix, Haute-Savoie, France
text: In 1786 Michel-Gabriel Paccard, a doctor from Chamonix, and his porter Jacques Balmat became the first people to reach the summit of Mont Blanc, the highest peak in Europe. It was one of the most important climbs in mountaineering history. But Marc-Theodore Bourrit, who had failed to climb it, jealously published a biased account, starting the myth that Balmat deserved all the credit.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mont Blanc

title: A Ghost Story Contest by the Lake
text: In the summer of 1816, Byron, Percy Shelley, Mary, then 18, and John Polidori gathered at a house on Lake Geneva. The eruption of Mount Tambora had brought an unusually cold, dark and wet summer, so Byron challenged each of them to devise a ghost story. At the Villa Diodati, Mary first thought of Frankenstein, and Polidori produced the world's first published vampire story.

source.name: The Conversation, Richard Gunderman (Indiana University): How a volcano in Indonesia led to the creation of Frankenstein

title: The Opera That Started a Country
place: Theatre de la Monnaie, Brussels, Belgium
text: On August 25, 1830, the Theatre de la Monnaie in Brussels staged Daniel Auber's opera La Muette de Portici. The patriotic song 'Amour sacre de la Patrie' brought the audience to its feet and into the streets, and the protest grew into a revolt against Dutch rule. Belgian independence was proclaimed on October 4, and the London Conference recognised it in January 1831.

source.name: EBSCO Research Starters, Edward P. Keleher and Bernard A. Cook: Belgian Revolution

title: A Fortress Taken Apart for Peace
text: At the London Conference of 1867, Luxembourg was declared neutral. The Prussian garrison left the city and work began on dismantling its mighty fortress, which had grown up around the castle Count Siegfried built on the Bock promontory after 963. Taking the fortress apart took 16 years, finishing in 1883, and cost more than 1.8 million gold francs.

source.name: Ville de Luxembourg: From castle to fortress

title: Einstein's Big Year in Bern
text: From March to September 1905, Albert Einstein, a technical expert at the patent office in Bern, surprised the world of physics with five papers on three topics. He explained the long-puzzling Brownian motion, wrote on the energetic properties of light and the 'electrodynamics of moving bodies', and showed that energy and mass are equivalent, as captured in E = mc2.

source.name: Einstein House Bern (Albert Einstein Society): Einstein and Bern

title: Nonsense Nights at Cabaret Voltaire
text: In February 1916 Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings, German performers who had fled the war to neutral Switzerland, turned a Zurich cafe into the Cabaret Voltaire. It lasted only five months, but its poetry readings, dances, masks and Hennings's handmade puppets laid the foundations of Dada. Friends recited 'simultaneous' poems mixing words with drawn-out syllables, gurgles and whistles.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Leonard A. Lauder Research Center: Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings

title: Behind the Opekta Building
text: On 6 July 1942 the Frank family went into hiding in the Secret Annex of the Opekta company building at Prinsengracht 263, Amsterdam. They moved ten days earlier than planned because Margot had received a call-up to work in Germany, and left a note suggesting they had fled the country. Anne, given a diary for her 13th birthday, hid there until the arrest of 4 August 1944.

source.name: Anne Frank House Research: Frank family in hiding

source2.name: Anne Frank House: 1942 Going into hiding

title: The Sea Breaks Through
text: On the night of 31 January to 1 February 1953, the sea tore 96 large and nearly 400 small breaches in the Dutch dikes. An area of 200,000 hectares flooded, and 1,836 people drowned along with 182,000 animals. Within twenty days the government set up a Delta Committee to plan better protection, leading to the Delta Act and the Delta Works.

source.name: Watersnoodmuseum: The history of the Delta Works

title: Swiss Women Finally Get the Vote
text: On February 7, 1971, Swiss women won the right to vote and stand for election nationally, after two-thirds of the country's men approved it. In 1959 voters had refused, by 66.9% to 33%. When the first women took their seats in parliament, each was welcomed with a rose. Women in Appenzell Inner Rhodes had to wait until 1990 to vote there.

source.name: The Swiss Parliament: Women's suffrage in Switzerland, 100 years of struggle

source2.name: SWI swissinfo.ch: The long road to women's suffrage in Switzerland

title: Stones Older Than Stonehenge's Circle
place: Calanais (Callanish), Isle of Lewis, Scotland, UK
text: Between 2900 and 2600 BCE, people on the Isle of Lewis raised the Calanais Standing Stones, before the main circle at Stonehenge. A 4.8m monolith stands at the heart, with lines of smaller stones radiating out and a small chambered tomb inside the circle. Peat slowly buried the site, and only peat cutting in 1857 revealed how tall the stones really are.

source.name: Historic Environment Scotland: Calanais Standing Stones, History

title: The Archer Who Came From Afar
text: Around 2300 BCE a man was buried near Amesbury with about 100 objects, including three copper knives, 16 flint arrowheads and two small gold hair tresses. Scientists found he grew up in central Europe, most probably in what is now Switzerland. Archaeologists uncovered his grave in May 2002, digging ahead of a new housing development.

source.name: Wessex Archaeology: The Amesbury Archer

title: A Cape Beaten From Gold
place: Bryn yr Ellyllon, Mold, Flintshire, Wales, UK
text: This Bronze Age cape was laboriously beaten out of a single ingot of gold, then decorated with ribs and bosses that mimic strings of beads amid folds of cloth. In 1833 workmen quarrying stone in a mound called the Goblins' Hill found it crushed around a skeleton, with amber beads. It was so flimsy it may only have been worn on special occasions.

source.name: British Museum: The Mold Gold Cape (1836,0902.1)

source2.name: Coflein (Royal Commission, Wales): Bryn yr Ellyllon, Mold

title: Dinner Left in the Bowl
place: Must Farm, Whittlesey, Cambridgeshire, England, UK
text: Around 850 BCE, families in the Fens lived in roundhouses built on stilts above a slow-moving river. Less than a year after it was built, the village was destroyed by a catastrophic fire. Archaeologists later found a bowl still holding its final meal of wheat porridge mixed with animal fats, along with the finest textiles of this period found in Europe.

source.name: University of Cambridge (via EurekAlert!/AAAS): Must Farm news release, 19 March 2024

title: A Shield Thrown to the Thames
place: River Thames, Battersea, London, England, UK
text: Pulled from the River Thames near Battersea, this Iron Age treasure is really a bronze cover for a wooden shield. Its swirling La Tène-style scrolls are studded with 27 pieces of opaque red glass. Experts find it hard to date closely, but its British-style central boss shows it was almost certainly made in Britain.

source.name: British Museum: The Battersea Shield (1857,0715.1)

title: A Temple Built to Be Burned
place: Navan Fort (Emain Macha), County Armagh, Northern Ireland, UK
text: Around 95 BCE, people at Navan Fort raised a timber-ringed structure 40 metres across. As soon as it was finished, they filled it with stones and burnt it to the ground, creating the great mound that still dominates the site. Archaeologists now think such buildings were huge temples, and Irish legend makes Navan the seat of the kings of Ulster.

source.name: Queen's University Belfast: Research unveils early Kings of Ulster and Iron Age temples at Navan Fort

title: Rome's Turf Wall in Scotland
place: Antonine Wall, between the Forth and Clyde, Scotland, UK
text: In the years after AD 142, Emperor Antoninus Pius had the Roman army build a turf wall on a stone base right across Scotland, from the Clyde to the Forth. Soldiers of three legions recorded their work on carved distance slabs showing scenes of their campaign. The new frontier did not last: it was abandoned in the 160s for Hadrian's Wall.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Antonine Wall (David J. Breeze)

title: Treasure Hidden as Rome Left
text: As Britain was passing out of Roman control, someone buried a fortune at Hoxne: about 15,000 coins, jewellery and silver tableware, probably in a wooden box. The newest coins date to 407–408. Among the treasures is a silver pepper pot shaped like an imperial lady, with a turning base for sprinkling spice that came from India.

source.name: British Museum: The Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot (1994,0408.33)

source2.name: Suffolk Heritage Explorer: HXN 019, The Hoxne Hoard

title: The Gospels Painted on Calfskin
text: Close to the year 800, monks most likely working on the island of Iona wrote the four Gospels in Latin on calfskin, colouring them with blue from indigo or woad and yellow made from arsenic. After a Viking raid in 806 killed 68 of the community, the monks fled to Kells in Ireland. The book is now in Trinity College Dublin.

source.name: Trinity College Dublin Library: The Book of Kells

title: Brian Boru's Last Battle
text: Brian Boru rose from king of a small state in Munster to high king of all Ireland. When the men of Leinster and the Northmen of Dublin rose against him, the armies met at Clontarf on 23 April 1014. Brian was too old to fight, and his son Murchad won the day, but fleeing Northmen stumbled on Brian's tent and killed him.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Brian, king of Ireland

title: Every Ox, Cow and Pig Counted
text: At Christmas 1085 William the Conqueror ordered an inquest into who held land in England and what it was worth. Jurors answered royal commissioners' questions, and Domesday Book records about 270,000 people and 13,000 settlements. One chronicler grumbled that not one ox, cow or pig was left out.

source.name: The National Archives (UK): Domesday

title: Wales Proclaims Its Own Prince
text: On 16 September 1400 Owain Glyndŵr's followers proclaimed him Prince of Wales at his court in Glyndyfrdwy, and the same day he and his kinsmen attacked the town of Ruthin. His rising, which lasted until 1409, was the last of many attempts to free Wales from English rule. In 1403 the future Henry V burned his home at Sycharth.

source.name: Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales: Owain Glyndŵr and a timber from Sycharth

source2.name: Dictionary of Welsh Biography (National Library of Wales): Owain Glyndŵr

title: The King Watched His Ship Sink
place: The Solent, off Portsmouth, Hampshire, England, UK
text: Built between 1509 and 1511, the Mary Rose was Henry VIII's favourite warship. On 19 July 1545, while the king watched, she capsized and sank very quickly in the Solent; no one is sure exactly why. Only about 30 men survived. Lifted from the seabed in 1982, she has given up as many as 19,000 artefacts.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Mary Rose

title: Armada Gold off the Causeway
place: Lacada Point, near the Giant's Causeway, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, UK
text: In October 1588 La Girona, a galleass of the Spanish Armada, sank at Lacada Point near the Giant's Causeway, and most of the 1,400 people on board died. A huge amount of gold went down with her. Divers later raised a hoard of ornate jewellery, including a gold salamander set with rubies, now on display in the Ulster Museum.

source.name: Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council: Celebrating the Girona gold 50 years on

title: The Great Storm of 1703
place: Goodwin Sands, off Deal, Kent, England, UK
text: In November 1703 a storm wreaked havoc across southern Britain, and it remains one of the worst in British recorded history. Off the Goodwin Sands a sailor watched navy ships including the Northumberland and Restoration go down. Daniel Defoe, who had seen his barometer drop unnaturally low, asked people to send in their memories and published them as The Storm in 1704.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich, Library & Archive blog: The Great Storm of 1703

source2.name: University of York, Borthwick Institute for Archives: The Great Storm of 1703

title: Hallelujah, First Heard in Dublin
text: Handel's Messiah, source of the famous Hallelujah Chorus, was first performed not in London but at the New Musick Hall in Fishamble Street, Dublin, on 13 April 1742. It premiered at Easter rather than Christmas and was a triumphant success. Dublin soon made annual charity performances of Messiah a tradition, while London was slower to warm to it.

source.name: Trinity College Dublin Library: Music in 18th-century Dublin

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Messiah (Betsy Schwarm)

title: Six Million Visit the Crystal Palace
text: The Great Exhibition opened on 1 May 1851, and in five months over 6 million people came to see it, paying between 1 and 5 shillings a day. Visitors could gaze at the Koh-i-Noor diamond, a penknife with 80 blades, beehives shaped like little town houses and a locomotive. Outside, Prince Albert's model houses showed how workers' homes could be improved.

source.name: Royal Collection Trust: Great Exhibition of 1851, The Exhibition

title: The Bridge of Giant Spans
text: When the Forth Bridge opened across the Forth estuary in 1890, it had the world's longest spans, at 541 metres. It was the earliest great multispan cantilever bridge, built from about 54,000 tons of mild steel, then a fairly new material, resting on three towers. Its form is largely unaltered, and passenger and freight trains still cross it today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: The Forth Bridge

title: Three Dots Across the Atlantic
text: Many people assumed the curve of the Earth made it impossible to send radio signals across the Atlantic. Guglielmo Marconi built a transmitter of unprecedented power at Poldhu in Cornwall, and in Newfoundland his team raised an aerial on a kite. On 12 December 1901 they heard three faint dots, the letter S in Morse, though the weak signal left some unconvinced.

source.name: History of Science Museum, University of Oxford: Marconi, Atlantic Crossing

title: A Republic Proclaimed at the GPO
place: General Post Office, O'Connell Street, Dublin, Ireland
text: On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, Irish Volunteers and the Irish Citizen Army seized Dublin's General Post Office, and Patrick Pearse read a proclamation announcing an Irish republic. After nearly a week of street fighting, they surrendered on 29 April. The execution of Pearse and 14 other leaders turned many Irish people against British rule.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Easter Rising

title: A Festival to Reunite People
text: After the devastation of the Second World War, the Edinburgh International Festival was founded in 1947 to reunite people through great art. The idea began on a walk along Princes Street, when soprano Audrey Mildmay told Rudolf Bing the city would be a wonderful setting. Eight theatre groups turned up uninvited to that first festival, and so the Festival Fringe was born.

source.name: Edinburgh International Festival: Our history

title: Windrush Docks at Tilbury
text: On 22 June 1948 the ship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury near the Thames Estuary. Its log recorded 1,027 passengers, over 800 of them from Caribbean islands such as Jamaica, Barbados and Trinidad. Britain needed workers to rebuild after the Second World War, and ministers especially wanted such workers to staff the newly created National Health Service.

source.name: Royal Mint Museum: Windrush

title: Deep Houses by the Pacific
text: On a coastal terrace facing the Pacific, in what is now Hakodate, Jōmon people built a hub settlement with more than 100 pit dwellings and large earthen mounds. Some houses were dug over two metres deep. A burned whale vertebra found in one dwelling hints at animal rituals, and food remains include sea mammals, fish, shellfish, nuts and wild grapes.

source.name: World Heritage Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan (official site): Ofune Site

title: Giant Rings for the Dead
text: Near rivers where salmon and trout swim upstream, Jōmon people in central Hokkaido dug huge circular pits and piled the earth into rings to make shared cemeteries. Kiusu has nine of these earthwork burial circles, and the largest is 83 metres across. Many graves inside held powdered red pigment, and some had standing stones that may have served as tombstones.

source.name: World Heritage Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan (official site): Kiusu Earthwork Burial Circles

title: Red Lacquer From a Bog
text: At Korekawa, in today's Hachinohe, the wet ground of a boggy lowland preserved things that usually rot away. Archaeologists have dug up bows, combs, bracelets and containers painted with red lacquer, along with clay figurines. The Jōmon people here also built a watering place to leach the bitterness out of horse chestnuts so they could eat them.

source.name: World Heritage Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan (official site): Korekawa Site

title: A Bronze Bell Full of Pictures
text: This bronze bell, or dōtaku, reportedly found in Kagawa Prefecture, was the first dōtaku named a national treasure. Its pictures show men hunting deer and wild boar, women pounding with a mortar and pestle, and herons eating fish, glimpses of a life built around wet rice farming. Men are drawn with circle heads and women with triangle heads. When new, the bell shone a brilliant gold.

source.name: ColBase (National Institutes for Cultural Heritage), Tokyo National Museum: Bell ("Dōtaku") J-37433

title: Envoys From Wa to the Han Court
text: Chinese official records say that in 57 and 107 CE envoys from Wa, the Chinese name for Japan, travelled to the court of the Han dynasty. They presented woven cloth, jade, pearls, cinnabar, bows and arrows, and even slaves. In return they received brocade, silk, gold, swords, bronze mirrors, and jade and red beads.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Japan, 1–500 A.D.

title: A Clay Boat for the Soul
place: Saitobaru Tumulus No. 170, Saito, Miyazaki, Japan
text: Found at Saitobaru Tumulus No. 170 in Miyazaki, this 5th-century clay haniwa shows a large boat built with plank walls rather than hollowed from a block of wood. It has no mast, just twelve rowlocks, six on each side, for rowers who rowed facing backward. It hints at sea exchange at the time, and may have symbolized the soul of the tomb’s occupant setting off on a new journey.

source.name: ColBase (National Institutes for Cultural Heritage), Tokyo National Museum: Tomb Sculpture ("Haniwa"): Boat J-21498

title: A Million Tiny Pagodas
text: After the Emi Rebellion of 764 was crushed, Empress Shōtoku commissioned one million miniature wooden pagodas to thank the Buddhist deities, and shared them among Japan's ten major temples. Each white-painted pagoda held a printed Buddhist invocation called a darani. These are among the oldest printed texts known in the world, probably printed from bronze plates, though some scholars say woodblocks.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: One of the "One Million Pagodas" (Hyakumanto)

title: A Hall for the End of the World
text: Many Japanese believed that 1052 was the first year of Mappō, the age when the world began its decline. That year the regent Fujiwara no Yorimichi turned a villa from his father, Michinaga, into a Buddhist temple at Uji. In 1053 its Phoenix Hall was completed, housing a 2.4-metre Amida Buddha by Jōchō, said to be the finest Buddhist sculptor of the Heian period.

source.name: Byodoin Temple (official site): Byodoin Temple, Past & Present

title: The Fall of Golden Hiraizumi
text: In the 11th and 12th centuries Hiraizumi, in northern Japan, rivalled Kyoto politically and commercially. Its rulers, the Ōshū Fujiwara family, built temples and Pure Land gardens as visions of Buddhist paradise on earth, and the heavily gilded temple of Chūson-ji shows how rich they were. In 1189 the city lost its political status and much of it was destroyed, a rise and fall that inspired many poets.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hiraizumi – Temples, Gardens and Archaeological Sites Representing the Buddhist Pure Land

title: The Buddha Who Lost His Roof
text: According to the chronicle Azumakagami, work on Kamakura’s Great Buddha began in 1252. The colossal copper Amida Buddha stands some 11.3 metres tall and weighs around 121 tons, and the priest Jōkō is believed to have gathered donations from the people to build it. Typhoons in 1334 and 1369 destroyed the hall around it, and since then the statue has sat out in the open.

source.name: Kotoku-in (official site): The Great Buddha and the Teachings of Kotoku-in

title: Xavier and Anjirō Reach Kagoshima
text: On 15 August 1549 a Portuguese ship entered the port of Kagoshima carrying the Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier and Anjirō, a Japanese man he had met in Malacca who had just been baptized. Xavier called the Japanese “the best people yet discovered” and learned to adapt his methods. When he left in late 1551, he entrusted about 2,000 Christians in five communities to his companions.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: St. Francis Xavier

title: The Last Stand at Hara Castle
text: In 1637, driven by famine and the tyranny of their local lord, nearly the entire population of the Shimabara Peninsula rose up, led by the charismatic 16-year-old Amakusa Shirō. Almost 37,000 rebels, including women and children, held out in Hara Castle against more than 120,000 shogunate troops. A final assault in April 1638 destroyed the castle, and the shogunate then increased its repression of Christianity.

source.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual database: Hara Castle Ruins

source2.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual database: The Edict Banning Christianity and the Shimabara Rebellion

title: Prints Burst Into Colour
text: Woodblock prints let anyone with a bit of extra cash own pictures of glamorous courtesans, exciting kabuki actors and famous romantic views, the art of the “floating world.” In 1765, new technology made it possible to print single sheets in a whole range of colours. The last quarter of the 18th century then became the golden age of Japanese printmaking.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Art of the Pleasure Quarters and the Ukiyo-e Style

title: Asama Buries Its Villages
text: Asama’s 1783 eruption, one of its largest in history, began with moderate explosions on 9 May and reached its climax on 3–5 August. On 4 and 5 August the Agatsuma and Kambara pyroclastic flows swept down the north flank, and the Kambara flow destroyed several villages. Together with mudflows called lahars, they killed 1,377 people. The Onioshidashi lava flow ended the eruption.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program: Asamayama

title: Secret Christians Step Forward
text: When Ōura Church was built in Nagasaki in 1864 for French residents, Christianity was still banned in Japan. Then, in 1865, a group of peasants who had secretly kept their faith visited the French priest Bernardo Petitjean and told him they were Christians. They had survived 250 years of persecution, and the church became a memorial to their revival. The ban was lifted in 1873.

source.name: Web Japan (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan), Japan Atlas: Oura Catholic Church

title: Japan’s First Woman Doctor
text: In 1885 Ogino Ginko passed the medical practitioner’s exam and opened Ogino Hospital as the first registered woman doctor in Japan. Born in Saitama in 1851, she had married at 16, fallen ill and divorced, then studied at Tokyo Women’s Normal School and the private medical school Kōju-in. In 1894 she went to Hokkaido, where she ran a medical practice.

source.name: National Diet Library, Japan: Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures – OGINO Ginko

title: The Day a Mountain Fell
text: On 15 July 1888 Bandaisan, above Lake Inawashiro, blew apart in a violent explosive eruption. Its Kobandaisan peak collapsed, sending a huge debris avalanche 11 kilometres that buried several villages and formed several large lakes, including Lake Hibara. Seen from the south the volcano still looks like a cone, but much of its north side is missing.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program: Bandaisan

title: Predicting the Meson
text: In 1935 Hideki Yukawa, a young lecturer at Osaka University, published a paper proposing a new field theory of nuclear forces and predicting a new particle, the meson. When American physicists found one type of meson in cosmic rays, he was encouraged to keep developing his idea. In 1949 he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Hideki Yukawa – Biographical

title: 358 Bronze Swords in a Hillside
text: In 1984, on a forested hillside in Izumo, archaeologists uncovered 358 bronze swords that had been laid out in neat rows and buried, with 16 spearheads and 6 bells found nearby. Made by Yayoi-period people some 2,000 years ago, the blades are all very similar in design. Experts still disagree about why the weapons were left there.

source.name: Public Relations Office, Government of Japan (Highlighting Japan): Shimane Museum of Ancient Izumo

source2.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual database: The World of Bronze Implements and Great Swords

title: The Kyoto Climate Deal
text: On 11 December 1997, at the third UN climate conference, delegates adopted the Kyoto Protocol. It committed industrialized countries to limit and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with binding targets for 37 of them and the European Union adding up to an average 5 per cent cut from 1990 levels over 2008–2012. A complex ratification process delayed its start until 2005.

source.name: UNFCCC: The Kyoto Protocol

title: Fire at Shuri Castle
text: Around 2.30 in the morning of 31 October 2019, a security alarm went off at Shuri Castle, on a hilltop overlooking Naha. Fire ripped through the wooden castle and destroyed its main building. Built about 500 years ago in the Ryukyu Dynasty and almost destroyed in World War Two, the reconstructed castle was the largest wooden building in Okinawa.

source.name: BBC, republished by RNZ: Blaze engulfs Japanese World Heritage site

title: A National Museum for the Ainu
text: The Ainu are an indigenous people of northern Japan, especially Hokkaido, with their own language, oral literature such as Yukar, and distinctive patterns on clothes and crafts. In 2008 both houses of Japan’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution seeking to recognize them as an indigenous people. On 12 July 2020, Upopoy, the National Ainu Museum and Park, opened in Shiraoi.

source.name: Foundation for Ainu Culture: Overview of the Foundation for Ainu Culture 2025 (PDF)

title: Pictures Pecked Into Granite
text: Bronze Age artists in western Sweden pecked and ground pictures into smooth granite using stone hammers and points. Their panels show people, animals, weapons and boats, with lively scenes of travel, power, warfare and worship. Northern Bohuslän has at least 1,500 known rock carving sites, often placed in commanding spots in the landscape, where they probably served as centres of worship.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rock Carvings in Tanum

title: The Sky on a Bronze Disc
place: Mittelberg hill near Nebra, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany
text: About 3,600 years ago, people on the Mittelberg hill near Nebra ritually buried a bronze disc with two precious swords, two axes, two spiral arm-rings and a chisel. The disc shows the sun, the moon and a boat sailing between the horizons at night. Detectorists dug it up illegally in 1999. It is the oldest known concrete picture of astronomical phenomena.

source.name: State Museum of Prehistory Halle: The Nebra Sky Disc

source2.name: UNESCO Memory of the World: Nebra Sky Disc

title: A Horse That Pulls the Sun
text: In September 1902, the first ploughing of the former Trundholm bog in north-western Zealand turned up a bronze horse pulling a sun disc on wheels. Made around 1400 BCE, the Sun Chariot illustrates the belief that a divine horse drew the sun on its eternal journey. The elegant spirals on its golden sun disc reveal that it was made in the Nordic region.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: The Sun Chariot

title: Salt Miners of Hallstatt
text: Underground salt mining at Hallstatt started up again in the 8th century BCE, when the valley was home to a flourishing, highly organised Iron Age society with trade links across Europe. Archaeologists now call it the Hallstatt Culture. The town's name means "salt settlement", and salt kept the region prosperous right up to the middle of the 20th century.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hallstatt-Dachstein / Salzkammergut Cultural Landscape

title: Raiders Sunk in a Bog
text: Around 350 BCE, an army of 80 to 100 warriors sailed in four or five boats to attack the Danish island of Als, and lost. The victors sank the enemy's weapons, shields, tools and one of their boats in Hjortspring bog as thanks for their victory. Nobody knows where the raiders came from, but their boat can be seen at the National Museum.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: The army from Hjortspring Bog

title: A Roman Victory Carved in Rock
text: In 179 CE, a Roman special unit of 855 soldiers spent the winter in enemy territory at Laugaricio, today's Trenčín. To celebrate a victory over the Germanic Quadi, they carved an inscription into the castle rock honouring the emperors and the troops. It names their commander, Marcus Valerius Maximianus of the Second Legion, and is still visible in the town centre.

source.name: Trenčín Self-Governing Region: Roman inscription

source2.name: Hungarian Cultural Institute of Upper Hungary, Értéktár: The Latin inscription on Trenčín castle rock

title: A Roman Organ for the Guild
text: In 228 CE, a local dignitary named Gaius Julius Viatorinus gave a portable organ to the textile dealers' guild of Aquincum, now part of Budapest. It had 52 pipes in four rows of 13. When fire swept the town in the mid-3rd century, the organ fell into a basement and lay buried until archaeologist Lajos Nagy found nearly 400 of its pieces in 1931.

source.name: Aquincum Museum: The Aquincum organ

title: Queen Margaret Unites the North
text: Queen Margaret already ruled Denmark, Norway and Sweden when, in 1397, she called the three nations to a meeting in Kalmar. After about a month of talks, they agreed to form a joint Scandinavian union, and her grandnephew Eric of Pomerania was crowned joint king. Each kingdom was meant to keep its own laws and customs, though union rulers did not always respect that.

source.name: Swedish History Museum: Queen Margaret and the Union of Kalmar

title: Viking Carvings on a Stave Church
text: Built around 1130 on a promontory above the Sognefjord, Urnes is one of the oldest stave churches in Norway. Its famous north-wall portal was reused from an older church on the same site and dates from about 1070, carved in the Urnes style, the last of the Viking Age styles. Inside, carved capitals show mythic animals such as centaurs and griffins.

source.name: Fortidsminneforeningen (Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments): Urnes Stave Church

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Urnes Stave Church

title: Copernicus Finally Publishes
text: Nicolaus Copernicus's great book, De revolutionibus, did not appear in print until 1543, the year he died at Frauenburg, now Frombork. In it he argued that Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun once a year and turns daily on its own axis. He wrote that he had held the work back not for nine years, as the Roman poet Horace advised, but for 36.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nicolaus Copernicus

title: Europe Cracks the Porcelain Secret
text: Europeans prized Chinese and Japanese porcelain but did not know how to make true hard-paste porcelain until 1709, when the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger discovered the materials needed. Augustus the Strong, elector of Saxony, had pushed his experiments, and in 1710 he set up a factory at Meissen, just outside Dresden. It became the first European manufactory of hard-paste porcelain.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: German and Austrian Porcelain in the Eighteenth Century

title: The Magic Flute Opens in Vienna
place: Theater auf der Wieden, Vienna, Austria
text: On September 30, 1791, Mozart's last opera, The Magic Flute, premiered at the rustic Theater auf der Wieden near Vienna, not long before his death that December. Its librettist, Emanuel Schikaneder, played the birdcatcher Papageno himself. The Queen of the Night, written for Mozart's sister-in-law Josepha Hofer, is famed as perhaps the highest and most difficult role ever composed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: The Magic Flute (Linda Cantoni, Betsy Schwarm)

title: Pest's Day of Revolution
text: On March 15, 1848, young radicals who had met at Pest's Pilvax café led a demonstration through the city. Their 12 Points, listing the nation's demands, were printed at the Landerer and Heckenast press, and thousands heard the National Song recited at University Square. A crowd of ten thousand gathered at the National Museum, where Petőfi spoke. Censorship was abolished that day.

source.name: Hungarian Government, March 15 site: The 12 Points (A 12 pont)

title: Berta Benz Takes the Car
text: Engineer Carl Benz applied for a patent on his motor vehicle in 1886, and his wife Berta shared in its success. In 1888 she set off with her sons on a first long-distance drive, from Mannheim to Pforzheim, without telling her husband. It was no pleasure trip: the three struggled to get petrol and keep the car running, but they covered the route of almost 100 kilometres.

source.name: Deutsches Museum: Eine Ikone der Automobilgeschichte wird 140

title: Norwegian Women Win the Vote
text: On June 11, 1913, Norway's parliament, the Storting, voted unanimously for universal suffrage, giving the vote to Norwegian citizens, men and women, over the age of 25. Women had won limited voting rights in 1907 and the vote in local elections in 1910. In March 1911, Anna Rogstad, called in as a substitute member, became the first woman to take a seat in the Storting.

source.name: Stortinget: Anna Rogstad, the first woman in the Storting

source2.name: Stortinget: Centenary of women's suffrage in Norway 1913–2013

title: The Prague Spring
text: In January 1968, Alexander Dubček became head of Czechoslovakia's Communist Party, and reforms followed: a freer press, new clubs, active churches, and Boy Scouts replacing the official youth movement. International opinion called it "socialism with a human face." On the evening of August 20, Soviet-led forces invaded. People resisted passively, even removing road signs so the troops would lose their way.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Prague Spring (Z.A.B. Zeman)

title: Hosing Down a Lava Flow
text: When Eldfell volcano erupted on Heimaey on January 23, 1973, the islanders were safely carried to mainland Iceland within a few hours. Then lava crept toward the harbour, the lifeblood of this fishing town. Firemen, a harbour boat and the pumping dredge Sandey sprayed seawater on the lava, and after 15 days of pumping almost half a million cubic metres, a solid barrier stopped the flow.

source.name: U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 97-724: Lava-Cooling Operations during the 1973 Eruption of Eldfell Volcano

title: A Crane Operator Sparks Solidarity
text: On August 7, 1980, Anna Walentynowicz, a gantry crane operator at the Gdańsk Lenin Shipyard since 1950, was summarily dismissed. A strike began on August 14, and the strike committee drew up its 21 Demands, putting them up on boards at the shipyard's Gate No. 2. The Gdańsk Agreement was signed on August 31, and Lech Wałęsa became leader of the new union movement.

source.name: European Solidarity Centre: How did Solidarność (Solidarity) come to be?

title: Radioactive Shoes at Forsmark
place: Forsmark nuclear power plant, Uppsala County, Sweden
text: On April 28, 1986, staff at Sweden's Forsmark nuclear plant were found to be contaminated as they passed the plant's radiation detectors, and one worker's shoes showed radioactivity. About 800 people were sent away, some leaving their contaminated shoes behind. But the radiation had arrived on winds from the east, and this was how the world first learned of the Chernobyl accident.

source.name: Swedish Radiation Protection Institute (SSI): Tio år efter kärnkraftolyckan i Tjernobyl (SSI information 96:01)

source2.name: Vattenfall (Forsmark operator): 30 år sedan Tjernobyl upptäcktes i Forsmark

title: Boats and Demons Carved in Rock
place: Lake Onega, Pudozhsky District, Republic of Karelia, Russia
text: Between about 4500 and 3500 BCE, Neolithic hunter-fisher-gatherers in Karelia carved more than 4,500 petroglyphs into rocks at Lake Onega and by the White Sea, 300 km apart. The Onega carvings show birds, forest animals, figures interpreted as demons, and sun and moon signs, while the White Sea panels depict boats, hunting scenes and animal and human footprints.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Petroglyphs of Lake Onega and the White Sea

title: Granite Cairns Above the Sea
text: On a rocky ridge near the Gulf of Bothnia, Bronze Age people piled granite boulders into 33 burial cairns, with no earth fill, between about 1500 and 500 BCE. One rare square cairn is nicknamed the 'Church Floor'. The cairns are linked to sun worship spreading from Scandinavia and may have marked a kin group's land, a custom thought to have come with farming.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Bronze Age Burial Site of Sammallahdenmäki

title: Greek Traders on the Boh Estuary
place: Olbia, near Parutyne, Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine
text: Greek settlers from Miletus and other Ionian cities founded Olbia on the Boh River estuary in the early 6th century BC. They traded wine, olive oil, fine dishes, cloth and glassware with Scythians and other steppe peoples in exchange for grain, cattle, wool, fish and slaves. To help trade, the city minted its own bronze, silver and occasionally gold coins.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Olbia

title: Vineyards of a Crimean Greek City
text: Dorian Greeks founded Tauric Chersonese in south-west Crimea in the 5th century BCE and laid out its streets on a grid. Its farmland was divided into some 400 equal plots, many planted with vineyards whose wine the city exported. By the 3rd century AD it was known as the most productive wine centre of the Black Sea, trading with Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and peoples to the north.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ancient City of Tauric Chersonese and its Chora

title: A Trading Town on the Don
place: Tanais, near Rostov-on-Don, Rostov Oblast, Russia
text: At the beginning of the 3rd century BC, Greeks of the Bosporan Kingdom founded Tanais near the mouth of the river of the same name, today's Don. It became a trade centre between steppe nomads and Greeks, home to a mixed population of Greeks, Sarmatians and Maeotians. Goths destroyed it in the mid-3rd century AD, and digging at the site began in 1853.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Tanais

title: Amber Gatherers Puzzled by Rome
place: Eastern Baltic shore (Sambia coast), Kaliningrad Oblast, Russia
text: In his Germania, written in 98, the Roman historian Tacitus described the Aestii on the eastern shore of the 'Suevic sea'. He called them the only people who gathered amber, which they named 'glesum', in the shallows and on the shore. Useless to them, it was brought to Rome in shapeless lumps, and the Aestii marvelled at the price they received.

source.name: Perseus Digital Library (Tufts University): Tacitus, Germania, chapter 45 (trans. Church and Brodribb)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tacitus

title: A Gothic King Facing the Huns
place: Between the Don and Dniester rivers, Ukraine
text: Ermanaric, king of the Ostrogoths, ruled a vast empire in Ukraine that apparently stretched between the Don and Dniester rivers, feared by neighbouring peoples. When the Huns invaded in the 370s, he despaired of resisting them and took his own life. His kingdom was destroyed, and his people were subject to the Huns for about 75 years. Legends about him spread into English and Norse literature.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ermanaric

title: Ladoga, Gateway of the North
text: Tree-ring dating shows the first wooden houses at Ladoga, on the Volkhov River near Lake Ladoga, were built no later than 753 CE. Throughout the Viking Age, Scandinavian traders, craftsmen and farmers reached it by sea through the Gulf of Finland and the Neva River. In the early eleventh century, Yaroslav the Wise gave the area to his wife, Ingegerd Olofsdotter, as a semi-autonomous earldom.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (The Global North, ed. Carol Symes): N. V. Grigorjeva, Archaeological Evidence for Staraya Ladoga as an Early Scandinavian Emporium

title: White Stone Cathedral of Vladimir
text: Built in 1158 inside Vladimir's kremlin, the Cathedral of the Assumption was meant to be the religious centre of all Russia. Its facade is divided into five sections by columns and covered in carved reliefs. Mongols destroyed most of its 12th-century frescoes in 1238, but in 1408 the painters Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chernii added new murals, including a famous Last Judgment.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal

title: A Princess-Nun's Jewelled Cross
text: Princess Predslava of Polotsk took monastic vows as Euphrosynia and later led a nunnery. Around 1161 she ordered master Lazar Bogsha to make a cross holding relics of saints and particles of the Holy Sepulchre, covered with gold plates, precious stones and pearls, with his autograph inscribed at the bottom. Moved to the Mogilev Museum in 1928, it later disappeared without a trace.

source.name: Saint Petersburg State University, Medieval Russian Princesses project: Predslava of Polotsk

title: Lithuania's First and Only King
text: Mindaugas, seen as the founder of the Lithuanian state, imposed himself over rival nobles, including his own brother and nephews. He accepted baptism from the Livonian Knights in 1250 or 1251, easing pressure from the west, and in 1253 received a royal crown from Pope Innocent IV. He later returned to paganism and was murdered by Samogitian rivals in 1263.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mindaugas

title: An ABC Book for Finnish Readers
text: Mikael Agricola, who had studied under Luther at Wittenberg, published his first book, the reading primer Abckiria, probably in 1543. Only pieces of two pages of that first edition survive, but in 1966 eight missing pages turned up in a library in Västerås, Sweden, completing the text. Later Bishop of Turku, Agricola is called the father of written Finnish.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland: Mikael Agricola's anniversary

title: The Radziwills' Castle at Nesvizh
text: From 1583 until 1939 the powerful Radziwill family built and kept a castle complex at Nesvizh in central Belarus. Its ten connected buildings, including a palace, family archive and arsenal, ring a six-sided courtyard inside a moat, with a dam leading to the domed Corpus Christi church. Artists from Belarus, Poland, Italy and Germany working there formed a new architectural school.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Architectural, Residential and Cultural Complex of the Radziwill Family at Nesvizh

title: A Cossack Hetman Sparks a Revolution
text: At the end of December 1647 Bohdan Khmelnytsky left for the Zaporizhia with just 300 to 500 men and was elected hetman there, starting a Cossack uprising that quickly became a national revolution. By 1648 Polish officials warned that the Cossacks wanted to rule in Ukraine. After his victories, people in Kyiv hailed him as a Moses and liberator of the Rus' people.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Khmelnytsky, Bohdan

title: Twenty-Two Wooden Domes
place: Kizhi Island, Lake Onega, Republic of Karelia, Russia
text: After lightning burned the old churches on Kizhi Island in 1693, new ones rose on the very same spot. Tree-ring dating places the Church of the Transfiguration after 1713-14. Rising 37 m and crowned with 22 bulb-shaped domes, it was used only in summer. Local legend says Master Nestor built it without nails, using nothing but an axe.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kizhi Pogost

title: Measuring the Earth From Tartu
text: The Tartu Observatory, then known as Dorpat, was the starting point of a huge chain of survey triangles observed between 1816 and 1855 under astronomer F. G. W. Struve. Running 2,820 km from near Norway's North Cape to the Black Sea, it was designed to pin down the size and shape of the Earth. Today 34 of its 265 main stations are World Heritage.

source.name: International Federation of Surveyors (FIG): First for Surveyors and a first for World Heritage

title: A Country Doctor Builds an Epic
text: While working as district medical officer in Kajaani, Elias Lönnrot made trips to hear folk singers, among them Arhippa Perttunen of Archangel Karelia in 1834. He combined different versions of poems on the same subject into one story. The first Kalevala, its preface signed on February 28, 1835, had 32 poems and 12,078 lines, and only 500 copies were printed.

source.name: Kalevala Society: Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala process

title: A Steppe Saved Forever
text: In 1898 Friedrich Falz-Fein ordered that a large plot of feather-grass steppe at Askania-Nova be conserved forever. His zoo there let animals such as zebras, ostriches and saiga antelope roam partly free, and he helped capture rare Przewalski's horses in Mongolia for a herd. It became Ukraine's oldest nature preserve, though Russian forces took control of it in March 2023.

source.name: Askania-Nova Biosphere Reserve (official site)

source2.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Askaniia-Nova Biosphere Reserve

title: Finnish Women Win the Ballot
text: After the General Strike of 1905, Finland confirmed a one-chamber parliament in 1906 and gave women the right both to vote and to stand for election, the first European country to do so. Married women were freed from having their husbands act as their guardians. In the first parliamentary elections, in 1907, nineteen women became Members of Parliament.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland: Finland - unquestionably a pioneer of democracy

title: A Symphony for a Starving City
text: Dmitri Shostakovich began his Seventh Symphony in besieged Leningrad and finished it in February 1942. The score was flown into the city over German lines, and conductor Karl Eliasberg pushed a starving orchestra through rehearsals; musicians fainted from hunger or cold, and three died. On August 9 the haggard players performed it in the city Hitler had claimed would fall that month.

source.name: NPR (via Texas Public Radio): Amid Hunger And Cold, An Unforgettable Symphony Premiere

title: Scythian Gold Under a Burial Mound
place: Tovsta Mohyla, near Pokrov, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine
text: In 1971 archaeologist Borys Mozolevsky excavated Tovsta Mohyla, a Scythian burial mound of the 4th century BC. Its untouched side vault held a noblewoman and a child, and the mound gave up more than 600 gold objects. The star was a gold pectoral made by Greek masters around 370-360 BCE, showing griffins attacking horses and a boy milking a sheep.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Tovsta Mohyla

source2.name: National Museum of the History of Ukraine (Google Arts & Culture): The Pectoral from Tovsta Mohyla

title: Holding Hands Across Three Countries
text: On August 23, 1989, people in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania formed a human chain 600 km long. The date marked 50 years since the 1939 German-Soviet non-aggression pact and its secret protocol. UNESCO calls it a unique and peaceful demonstration that united the three countries in their drive for freedom, and its documents joined the Memory of the World register in 2009.

source.name: UNESCO Memory of the World: The Baltic Way - Human Chain Linking Three States in Their Drive for Freedom

title: Chariots Clash at Kadesh
place: Kadesh, on the Orontes River near Homs, Syria
text: Beside the Orontes River, Pharaoh Ramses II marched on the Hittite-held city of Kadesh and was tricked by two fake deserters. King Muwatallis's Hittites struck with heavy three-horse chariots, and some 5,000 chariots joined one of history's largest chariot battles. Neither side truly won, yet both claimed victory, and the stalemate led to the first recorded peace treaty.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Kadesh

title: Sheba's Oasis Capital
text: Maʾrib, capital of the kingdom of Saba (Sheba) from about 950 BCE, grew rich on a trading monopoly on frankincense and myrrh. Its great dam, about 580 metres long, had sluice gates and watered more than 9,600 hectares of farmland. When the dam finally failed, the 'flood of Arim' entered the Qurʾān and Islamic legend.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Maʾrib

title: A King Carves His Side of the Story
text: King Mesha of Moab set up a black basalt stela at Dibon, about 1.1 metres high. Its 34 lines tell how Israel's King Omri had conquered Moab, blaming the anger of the god Chemosh, and then boast of Mesha's own successful revolt. Found in 1868, it is the only long written document to survive from Moab and is now in the Louvre.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Moabite

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dibon

title: A Canal Still Flowing After Urartu
text: The kingdom of Urartu, whose capital Tushpa stood at modern Van, built its first known irrigation project under King Meinua. The 'Canal of Meinua' carried fresh water about 45 kilometres from a plentiful spring to the southern edge of Van, and it still does. Urartian kings borrowed script and styles from Assyria but produced their own answers to its achievements.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Urartu

title: Darius Flees at Issus
place: Plain of Issus, Gulf of İskenderun, Hatay, Turkey
text: On a coastal plain by the Gulf of İskenderun, Alexander the Great led a charge across the Pinarus River and smashed the left wing of King Darius III's Persian army. Darius escaped, but his family was captured and his camp was sacked. The ancient writer Arrian claimed only 450 Macedonians died, and that Alexander himself was wounded.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Issus

title: Antioch, Where the Caravans Ended
text: Seleucus I Nicator, once a general of Alexander the Great, founded Antioch near the mouth of the Orontes River in 300 BCE. It soon became the western end of caravan routes carrying goods from Persia and Asia to the Mediterranean. Under Rome it grew into the empire's third largest city, and it was here that Jesus's followers were first called Christians.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Antioch

title: A Harbour Built in the Open Sea
text: Herod the Great rebuilt a Phoenician town called Straton's Tower and renamed it Caesarea after his patron, Emperor Augustus. Its artificial harbour was probably the first ever built entirely in open sea, shielded by two huge breakwaters of concrete blocks filled with rubble. An aqueduct brought spring water from almost 16 kilometres away, and the port linked Rome with Asian trade.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Caesarea

title: Nabataean Tombs in the Arabian Sands
place: Hegra (al-Hijr / Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ), AlUla, Saudi Arabia
text: South of Petra, the Nabataean city of Hegra flourished above all in the 1st century CE on a caravan route between Arabia, the Mediterranean and Asia. Its people carved 111 monumental tombs straight into sandstone, 94 with decorated facades. They also sank wells into the rock to farm the desert, and those wells are still in use.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hegra Archaeological Site (al-Hijr / Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ)

title: A Sun Temple on a Canyon Edge
text: High above the Azat River canyon, King Tiridates I restored Garni after Roman forces destroyed it and built a temple there in 77 CE. A Greek inscription found in 1945 says he raised an 'impregnable fortress' for his sister, the queen, and names the stonecutter Menneas. The temple stands on a podium ringed by 24 basalt Ionic columns.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List, submitted by Armenia): The Archaeological Complex of Garni

title: Palmyra Posts Its Tax Rates
text: In 137 CE the caravan city of Palmyra set up a stone slab in its agora listing taxes on goods brought into and out of town. Carved in both Greek and the local Palmyrene language, the rates differed for loads carried by camel, donkey or donkey cart. The stele is now in the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.

source.name: Getty Research Institute: The Legacy of Ancient Palmyra

title: One King for All of Yemen
text: Through the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, Ḥimyarite rulers based at Ẓafār fought on and off with Sabaean kings. In the last decades of the 3rd century CE their king Shammar Yuharʿish ended the independence of Saba and Hadhramaut, uniting all of Yemen. He took the title 'King of Saba and the Raydān and Hadhramaut and Yamnat' and sent envoys to the Persian court at Ctesiphon.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Arabia: Ḥimyarites

title: The Walls That Guarded Constantinople
text: In 413 the regent Anthemius built a mighty wall across the land side of Constantinople, though it carries the name of young Emperor Theodosius II. An outer wall followed in 447, with a moat in front. The inner wall stands about 9 metres high and 5 metres thick, and the 7-kilometre defences were breached only once, by Ottoman cannon.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Theodosius II

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Istanbul

title: The Journey That Started a Calendar
text: Escaping persecution in Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad accepted an invitation to Yathrib, later called Medina. There he agreed the Constitution of Medina with local clans, and the Muslim community became a political body for the first time. In 639 Caliph ʿUmar made this migration, the Hijrah, the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hijrah

title: A Fifth Wonder for Damascus
place: Great Mosque of Damascus, Damascus, Syria
text: Caliph al-Walīd I built the earliest surviving stone mosque on a site sacred for thousands of years, from an Aramaean temple to a church of St. John the Baptist. He told Damascenes their climate, water, fruits and baths already beat the world, and this mosque made five. Over an acre of mosaics once showed a dreamlike paradise landscape.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Great Mosque of Damascus

title: A Desert Bathhouse Full of Paintings
text: In the semi-arid land east of Amman, the Umayyad caliphs built a small pleasure palace with a reception hall and a bath complex. Its walls are covered in paintings of hunts, animals, birds and portraits, labelled in Greek and Arabic. On the dome of the hot room is one of the earliest surviving maps of the heavens painted on a dome.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Quseir Amra

title: An Island Church Wrapped in Carvings
text: On an island in Lake Van, the architect Manuel built the Armenian Church of the Holy Cross between 915 and 921. Its outer walls are richly carved with vines, animals, apostles, the Mother of God, Bible scenes and a portrait of its founder, King Gagik of the Artsruni family. Inside, frescoes show mostly New Testament scenes.

source.name: Den Store Danske (lex.dk): Achtamar

title: The Knights' Greatest Castle
text: In 1142 the Knights of St. John, or Hospitallers, took over a hilltop that had held an earlier Muslim stronghold and made it Krak des Chevaliers. Its two rings of towered walls, split by a wide moat, could hold a garrison of 2,000 men. They kept it until 1271, when the Mamlūk sultan Baybars I captured it.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Krak des Chevaliers

title: Thirst at the Horns of Hattin
place: Horns of Hattin, near Tiberias, Israel
text: Marching across a hot, dry plain to relieve Tiberias, about 20,000 Crusaders ran out of water while Saladin's cavalry harassed them. After a night without water they were driven back against two hills, the Horns of Hattin, and crushed. Saladin spared King Guy of Jerusalem, and the very next day began his campaign to retake Jerusalem.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Ḥaṭṭīn

title: Turan Melek's Hospital of Stone
text: At Divriği, Emir Ahmet Shah founded a great mosque, while his wife Turan Melek founded the hospital joined to it, designed by the architect Hurrem Shah. Its rooms surround a domed atrium with an open oculus over a pool. The stone portals are carved so exuberantly, each in its own style, that UNESCO calls the ensemble a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği

title: The Quake That Emptied Ani
text: Ani, on a plateau above a ravine bordering Armenia, had been capital of the Armenian Bagratid kingdom and a crossroads for Silk Road caravans. Byzantine, Seljuk and Georgian rulers kept it busy, but the Mongol invasion, a devastating earthquake in 1319 and shifting trade routes began its decline. By the 18th century the city was nearly abandoned.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Ani

title: Building the First Ottoman Capital
text: The Ottomans took Bursa in the 1320s and made it their first great capital. Sultans built complexes outside the old walls with a mosque, school, public bath and a kitchen for the poor, and neighbourhoods grew around them. The nearby village of Cumalıkızık belonged to Orhan Ghazi's complex and supplied its income.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bursa

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Bursa and Cumalıkızık

title: The Box Called the Standard of Ur
place: Royal Cemetery, Ur, Dhi Qar, Iraq
text: Found by Leonard Woolley in Ur's Royal Cemetery, this hollow wooden box is covered in mosaics of shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli set in bitumen. One side shows a Sumerian army with chariots and prisoners led before the king. The other shows peace: people bringing animals and fish, and the king feasting while a singer and a lyre player entertain.

source.name: British Museum: The Standard of Ur (1928,1010.3)

title: An Elephant for the Assyrian King
text: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, carved in black limestone and 197 centimetres tall, glorifies the king and his minister. Five rows of captioned panels show tribute pouring in: horses from north-west Iran, gifts from Jehu of Israel, and an elephant and an ape from Egypt. Austen Henry Layard dug it up at Nimrud.

source.name: British Museum: The Black Obelisk (1848,1104.1)

title: Cyrus Takes Babylon
text: After Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, a fired clay cylinder written in Babylonian cuneiform told his side of the story. It claims the god Marduk chose him, that he entered the city without a fight, and that he sent gods back to their temples and returned people to their homes. Hormuzd Rassam later excavated it at Babylon.

source.name: British Museum: The Cyrus Cylinder (1880,0617.1941)

title: The Eclipse Before Gaugamela
place: Plain east of Mosul, Nineveh Governorate, Iraq
text: Darius III flattened a whole plain so his scythed chariots and cavalry could charge, but Alexander broke through a gap in his centre and Darius fled. A lunar eclipse on 20 September was read as foretelling Persia's defeat. The exact date of the battle, long debated, was settled by Babylonian astronomical diaries.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Gaugamela (Ernst Badian)

title: Hatra Beats a Roman Emperor
text: Hatra, a fortified caravan city in the desert steppe of northern Iraq, besieged by Emperor Septimius Severus in 193 and again in 197, held out both times. His siege engines were burned and Hatrene archers struck down many of his soldiers, forcing him to withdraw. Trajan had already failed there in 117, and Hatra then reached its peak of prosperity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Hatra (Rüdiger Schmitt)

title: Ardashir Becomes King of Kings
text: On 28 April 224, Ardashir, a rebel from Persis, defeated the Parthians in the plain of Hormazjan in Media. Still on the battlefield, he took the title King of Kings, founding the Sasanian empire. He had the battle carved into a rock relief at Firuzabad, and he started his own calendar era from this victory.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ardašīr I, i. History (Josef Wiesehöfer)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ctesiphon

title: A Roman Emperor Taken Prisoner
text: In 260 the Sasanian king Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian in battle and led him, his commanders and senators away to Persis. Shapur boasted of it in an inscription and in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur. They show Valerian standing, unchained and in his regalia, while Shapur on horseback holds him by the wrist.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Šāpur I: History (A. Shapur Shahbazi)

title: A Copy of Antioch Beside the Tigris
text: After capturing Antioch in Syria in 540, the Sasanian king Khosrow I forcibly moved its people to a new city beside his capital Ctesiphon. Named Weh-Antiok-Khosrow, it was modelled on Antioch's plan, with its own hippodrome and bath, and built partly with marble taken in Syria. By the late 6th century it had about 30,000 people.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ctesiphon

title: A Dust Storm at Qadisiyya
text: At a frontier garrison town in Sasanian Iraq, Arab Muslim warriors faced a larger Persian army under Rostam. After three days of fighting, a dust storm blew sand into the Persians' eyes, Rostam was killed, and the royal standard was captured. The capital Mada'in soon fell. Scholars still argue over the exact year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Qādesiya, Battle of (D. Gershon Lewental)

title: Two Copies of World History a Year
place: Rab'-e Rashidi, Tabriz, East Azerbaijan, Iran
text: Rashid al-Din, a doctor who became vizier to the Mongol Ilkhans, wrote the Compendium of Chronicles, sometimes called the first world history, covering peoples from the Franks to the Chinese. In a deed dated 9 August 1309 for his quarter in Tabriz, he ordered two copies made every year, one Arabic and one Persian, to send to cities across the Arab world and Iran.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Jāmeʿ al-tawāriḵ (Charles Melville)

title: Hormuz, Market of the World
text: Hormuz stood on a hot island with no fresh water or plants, so all its supplies had to be shipped in. Yet in 1442 the traveller Abd-al-Razzaq Samarqandi found it a major emporium, visited by merchants from Egypt, China, Java, Bengal, Zanzibar and beyond. Its rulers had moved there from the mainland to escape raiders.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Hormuz ii. Islamic Period (Willem M. Floor)

title: Ninety-Two Weddings at Susa
text: In 324 BCE at Susa, Alexander and ninety-one of his companions married Iranian noblewomen in a single lavish ceremony meant to dazzle. Historians are careful about calling it a plan to fuse two peoples: no Macedonian women were married to Iranians. Alexander needed Iranian officials and soldiers, but his Macedonian nobles would not share power easily.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Alexander the Great (Pierre Briant)

dateLabel: About 300 BCE (start of the 3rd century BCE)
title: Greek Temples on a Kuwaiti Island
text: At the very beginning of the 3rd century BCE, a Hellenistic fortress rose on the shore of Failaka Island, at the head of the Gulf. Inside were homes and two temples. Temple A looks Greek, yet its columns mix Ionian capitals with Persian bases. Nearby, silver coins of Alexander the Great turned up in an older sanctuary.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Failaka Island: A Palimpsest of Human Civilizations

title: The Last Cuneiform Tablet
text: An astronomical almanac from Uruk, tablet W22340a, is the latest datable cuneiform text found so far. Working from the tablet's own predictions of events in the sky, the scholars H. Hunger and T. de Jong dated it to year 326 of the Parthian (Arsacid) era, or 79/80 CE. They argue that it shows cuneiform and astronomy surviving deep into the first century CE, in Uruk as well as Babylon.

source.name: University of Amsterdam (dare.uva.nl): Hunger and de Jong, Almanac W22340a from Uruk: the Latest Datable Cuneiform Tablet, Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 104 (2014)

title: Shushtar's Waterfalls of Engineering
text: Completed in the 3rd century CE, probably on foundations from the 5th century BCE, Shushtar's water system split the Karun river into canals that fed the city, turned mills and irrigated a semi-desert plain. It blended Elamite and Mesopotamian know-how with Roman influence. Persians and Arabs alike called its great weir a Wonder of the World, and it still works.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Shushtar Historical Hydraulic System

title: Samarra, the Caliphs' Second Capital
text: From 836 to 892, Samarra on the Tigris served as the Abbasid caliphs' capital, the second after Baghdad. Abandoned fairly early, it kept its original city plan, its giant mosques and unusual spiral minarets. Craftsmen there developed a new carved stucco style and lustreware pottery made to imitate gold and silver dishes. Most of the site is still unexcavated.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Samarra Archaeological City

title: Grammar Versus Logic
text: Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi, born in Siraf on the coast of Fars, served as a judge in Baghdad for fifty years and taught everything from grammar to Euclid's geometry. In 932 he won fame in a public debate, arguing that grammar beats logic as a tool for telling truth from falsehood. Despite his fame, he earned his living copying manuscripts.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Sirāfi, Abu Saʿid Ḥasan (David Pingree)

title: Al-Sufi Maps the Night Sky
text: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, an astronomer born in Ray who worked close to the Buyid rulers, wrote the Book of the Fixed Stars. It describes every constellation in both Greek and Arab tradition, with drawings and star tables set for 1 October 964.
