Read for centuries, it even reached Europe, where he was called Azophi; a Moon crater bears that name.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: ʿAbd-al-Raḥmān b. ʿOmar Ṣūfī (Paul Kunitzsch)

title: A 53-Metre Brick Tomb Tower
text: In 1006, Qabus ibn Voshmgir, a Ziyarid ruler who was also a writer, built a 53-metre tomb tower near his capital, Jorjan. Made of unglazed fired brick, its hollow shaft rises from a ten-pointed star plan to a conical roof. Its cone-roofed form became a model for tomb towers across Iran, Anatolia and Central Asia, and it is all that survives of Jorjan.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gonbad-e Qābus

title: The Turquoise Dome of Soltaniyeh
text: Between 1302 and 1312, the Ilkhanid ruler Oljaytu built his mausoleum in Soltaniyeh, then capital of the Mongol Ilkhanid dynasty in Iran. Its 50-metre dome, covered in turquoise-blue tiles, is the earliest surviving double-shelled dome in Iran and became a model for later Islamic domes. Eight slender minarets surround it, and one scholar said it anticipated the Taj Mahal.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mausoleum of Oljaytu (Soltaniyeh)

title: Hulegu's Star Observatory
text: After the Mongol conquest, Hulegu Khan gave the scholar Nasir al-Din Tusi libraries and Baghdad endowment funds to build an observatory at Maragheh, his new capital. Tusi built great brass instruments, and scholars came from many lands, Muslim and non-Muslim. The chronicler Bar Hebraeus praised spheres more wonderful than those Ptolemy set up in Alexandria. Traces of the 1259 observatory survive west of town.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ṭusi, Naṣir-al-Din i. Biography (George E. Lane)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Marāgheh

title: The Most Lavish Book of Kings
text: In the royal workshop at Tabriz, Safavid artists began what may be the most luxuriously illustrated copy of the Shahnama, Iran's epic 'Book of Kings', ever produced. Its 759 pages of elegant script hold 258 paintings by two generations of leading artists, including Sultan Muhammad. In 1568 it was sent to the Ottoman sultan Selim II as a gift, with an embassy whose thirty-four camels carried luxurious presents.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: The Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp

title: The Port That Named Mocha
text: In 1636 the Red Sea port of Mokha passed from Ottoman control to the Zaydi imam of Yemen, and it went on to prosper through the 17th and early 18th centuries. Coffee was its chief export. Indian traders swapped metal goods for Yemeni coffee and myrrh, and the English and Dutch East India companies kept trading posts there. The word 'mocha' comes from this town.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mokha

title: Oman Takes Back Muscat
text: On their way to India, the Portuguese sacked Muscat in 1507 and soon controlled the whole Omani coast. More than a century later, Oman's own Ya'rubid dynasty drove them out, recapturing Muscat in 1650. The Omanis then went on the attack, occupying Portuguese settlements in the Persian Gulf and on the East African coast. Two 16th-century Portuguese forts still overlook the town.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Oman, The early period

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Muscat

title: A Jeweller Rides Into Isfahan
text: The French Huguenot jeweller Jean Chardin reached Isfahan on 24 June 1673, after travelling from Paris by way of Istanbul, the Black Sea, Georgia and Tabriz. He brought jewels that the late Shah Abbas II had ordered, plus clocks and watches to sell. Chardin spent four and a half years in Persia and wrote the most detailed foreign account of the country in his time.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Chardin, Sir John

title: The Fall of Safavid Isfahan
text: In 1722 Ghilzai Afghans led by Mahmud, a former Safavid vassal, defeated the Persian army a few miles east of Isfahan and took the capital after a long siege. Shah Husayn was murdered in his cell at a beautiful religious school built in his mother's name. Isfahan never fully recovered: for years most of the city lay in rubble and its population dwindled.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Isfahan

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Iran, Shah Abbas I and the later Safavids

title: A Pearl Town Rises in Qatar
text: Qatar's modern history conventionally begins in 1766, when families from Kuwait, notably the Khalifah family, settled at the new town of Al Zubarah. It grew into a walled pearl-diving and trading centre with links across the Indian Ocean, Arabia and Western Asia. Mostly destroyed in 1811 and later abandoned, it lay under blown desert sand that protected its palaces, mosques, courtyard houses and fishermen's huts.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Qatar, History

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Al Zubarah Archaeological Site

title: Tabriz Reduced to Rubble
text: Tabriz lies in earthquake country and has been devastated at least six times in its recorded history. The worst blow came on 7 January 1780, when an earthquake reduced all the city's buildings to rubble. That is why Tabriz has very few historic monuments today. One that survives is the Blue Mosque, built in 1465.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Earthquakes iv. The historical record of earthquakes in Persia

title: Raiders Strike the Karbala Shrine
text: The tomb of Husayn at Karbala is one of the most important Shi'i shrines and centres of pilgrimage. In 1801 Sunni Wahhabi raiders destroyed it, the climax of a wave of incursions from Arabia that troubled Suleyman Pasha the Great, Baghdad's powerful Mamluk governor. The shrine was soon rebuilt, and large numbers of Iranians still visit it on pilgrimage.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Karbala

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Iraq, The 16th-century conquest of Iraq and later Ottoman rule

title: Flood and Plague End an Era
text: In 1831 floods devastated Baghdad, and in the same year plague decimated its population. The double disaster helped bring down Dawud Pasha, the last Mamluk governor of Iraq, who had been buying European weapons and hiring European advisers. The arrival of a new Ottoman governor that year ended the Mamluk period, and direct rule was gradually imposed across the region.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Iraq, The fall of the Mamluks and the consolidation of British interests

title: The Coalhole of the East
text: Steamships sailing to India needed a coaling station on the Red Sea route, and in 1839 the British captured Aden from its sultan. The harbour became so heavily used for loading coal that it was nicknamed the 'Coalhole of the East'. That same year the British moved their base from the old coffee port of Mokha to Aden, sealing Mokha's decline.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Aden

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mokha

title: Persia's First Modern College
text: On 29 December 1851 the Dar al-Fonun, or 'polytechnic college', was officially opened in Tehran, marking the beginning of modern education in Persia. It was the project of the reforming grand vizier Amir Kabir, who was dismissed two days before its Austrian teachers arrived. Lessons were taught in French, with translators following the instructors from class to class.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Dar al-Fonun

title: Qatar Steps Out of Bahrain's Shadow
text: In 1867 a dispute between Bahrain's Khalifah rulers and the people of Qatar escalated into a major confrontation in which Doha was virtually destroyed. Until then Britain had treated Qatar as a Bahraini dependency. In 1868 it signed a separate treaty with Mohammed ibn Thani, setting Qatar on course for independence and for rule by the Thani family, until then one of several important families.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Qatar, History

title: A Governor Remakes Baghdad
text: Arriving as governor in 1869 with a hand-picked team, Midhat Pasha transformed Baghdad. He knocked down part of the old city wall and built a tramway to suburban Kazimayn, a public park, a water supply, a hospital and paved, lighted streets. He also founded a printing press, and Iraq's first newspaper, Al-Zawra, began publication.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Iraq, The governorship of Midhat Pasa

title: Movies Above a Pastry Shop
text: The shah's photographer shot what was probably the first film by a Persian cameraman in 1900. Regular film shows came to Tehran in 1913, when Ardashir Khan, who had worked at Pathe in Paris, opened a projection room above a French bookshop and pastry counter. On busy days a piano and a violin accompanied the films, and seasonal refreshments were served.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Cinema i. History of Cinema in Persia

title: A Railway Through Two Mountain Ranges
text: Work began in 1927 on a railway linking the Caspian Sea with the Persian Gulf. Completed in 1938, the 1,394-kilometre line crosses two mountain ranges and needed 174 large bridges, 186 small bridges and 224 tunnels, including 11 spiral tunnels. Unusually, it was paid for with national taxes to avoid foreign investment and control. Iran worked with 43 construction contractors from many countries.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Trans-Iranian Railway

title: A Secret Telegram From Ur
text: On 4 January 1928 the Penn Museum received a telegram from archaeologist Leonard Woolley at Ur. Sent in Latin to keep the news discreet, it announced an intact, stone-built tomb of a queen then called Shubad, now read as Puabi. Woolley described a dress woven with gems, flowers, crowns and animal figures, and a tomb 'magnificent with jewels and golden cups'.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: A Telegram of Discovery from Ur

title: Bahrain's Pearl Divers Lose Their Trade
text: For millennia, harvesting pearls from Gulf oyster beds shaped Bahrain's economy, and the trade peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Then, in the 1930s, Japan's development of cultured pearls brought a sudden, catastrophic collapse. Merchants' houses, shops and a mosque in Muharraq, plus the fort where pearling boats set off, still recall this proud but dangerous way of life.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pearling, Testimony of an Island Economy

title: North Yemen Becomes a Republic
text: In September 1962 Imam Ahmad of Yemen died, and his son Muhammad al-Badr became imam. Within a week, army officers staged a coup and declared the Yemen Arab Republic. The young imam escaped from his battered palace into the northern highlands to rally the tribes. Egypt quickly sent troops to defend the new republic, while Saudi Arabia backed the royalists.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Yemen, The age of imperialism

title: The Emirates Join Together
text: After Britain announced in 1968 that its forces would leave the Persian Gulf by late 1971, the Trucial States, Qatar and Bahrain began planning a confederation. Qatar and Bahrain chose independence instead. In December 1971 the former Trucial States, except Ras al-Khaimah, formed the United Arab Emirates, with Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi as president. Ras al-Khaimah joined in February 1972.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: United Arab Emirates, History

title: Kuwait's Oil Wells Ablaze
text: In February 1991 Iraq's leader Saddam Hussein had Kuwait's oil wells set on fire. In April, astronauts on the Space Shuttle photographed black smoke from more than 700 burning wells blowing south. The fires were put out much faster than first predicted, so most of the damage stayed near the northwestern Persian Gulf, though smoke residue still stained the desert months later.

source.name: NASA Earth Observations: Oil Well Fires and Smoke, Kuwait, April 1991 (STS037-152-91)

source2.name: NASA Earth Observations: Southern Kuwait (STS044-75-27)

title: An Arab Probe Orbits Mars
place: Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre, Dubai, United Arab Emirates
text: On 9 February 2021 the UAE's Hope probe fired its thrusters for about 27 minutes, spending nearly half its fuel, and slipped into orbit around Mars. It was the first interplanetary mission led by an Arab nation. Engineers from the Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre and the University of Colorado built the orbiter to study the Martian atmosphere from bottom to top.

source.name: Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado Boulder: Emirates Mars Mission to Arrive at Mars on Feb. 9th

source2.name: University of Colorado Boulder Research Report: Historic Mars mission accomplished

title: The Great Gilan Earthquake
text: On 20 June 1990 a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Gilan and Zanjan provinces, southwest of the Caspian Sea. The largest 20th-century earthquake to hit an urban area in Iran, it killed over 40,000 people and left more than 500,000 homeless. It destroyed the towns of Rudbar, Manjil and Lowshan and 700 villages, and buried several thousand livestock under debris.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Earthquakes iv. The historical record of earthquakes in Persia

title: A Flower Shaped From Earth
text: In the 2004 dig season at La Blanca in Guatemala, archaeologists digging what they took for an elite home found something unique: a monument modelled from clay and earth in the shape of a quatrefoil, a four-petalled flower. Made in the early Middle Formative period, it is the earliest known example of this motif in Mesoamerican art.

source.name: FAMSI (Michael Love, California State University, Northridge): Excavations at La Blanca, Guatemala

title: Royals in Red at the Pyramid's Top
text: Around 700 BCE, two rulers at Chiapa de Corzo were laid in a tomb on top of a pyramid, coated head to toe in red pigment. The man wore a pearl-beaded loincloth, and both had jade beads shaped like howler monkeys and crocodiles. Announced in 2010, it is the oldest known pyramid tomb in Mesoamerica, mixing Olmec and early Zoque styles.

source.name: National Geographic: Pyramid Tomb Found: Sign of a Civilization's Birth?

title: A Captive Named 1 Motion
place: San José Mogote, Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico
text: After enemies burned its main temple, San José Mogote carved a stone showing a rival captive with his heart removed, and laid it flat in a corridor so people would walk over him. Between his feet is his name in glyphs, "1 Motion". It is the oldest known carved stone with Zapotec writing, made late in the Rosario phase (900–600 BCE).

source.name: University of Michigan Museum of Anthropological Archaeology: Origins of Hieroglyphic Writing

source2.name: University of Michigan Museum of Anthropological Archaeology: Origins of Social Inequality

title: The Oldest Maya Calendar Date
text: The Maya razed and rebuilt the Las Pinturas pyramid at San Bartolo seven times, burying thousands of painted plaster fragments inside. Two of them fit together like a jigsaw to show the date "7 Deer" from the 260-day sacred calendar. Painted between 300 and 200 BCE, they are the earliest known record of a Maya calendar, reported by David Stuart's team in 2022.

source.name: Science News: This hieroglyph is the oldest known record of the Maya calendar

title: A Woman in Copán's Richest Tomb
text: Deep under Copán's temples, a carved stone records a royal tomb dedicated in AD 437 by the city's second king, son of the founder. Tunnelling archaeologists found the Margarita Tomb there, the richest burial yet found at Copán. The team thought it held the founder or his son, until researcher Jane Buikstra identified the bones as those of a woman.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: Tunneling into the Heart of the Copan Acropolis

title: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís
text: From around 500 CE, chiefdoms in Costa Rica's Diquís Delta set nearly perfect stone balls in their villages, some up to 2.57 metres across. How they were made, and what they meant, is still largely a mystery. Thick layers of sediment buried them for centuries, saving them from the looting that hit most sites in Costa Rica.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís

title: Caracol's Star War on Naranjo
text: In AD 631, Caracol's king K'an II won a "star war", believed to mean all-out war, against Naranjo, 42 km away. Naranjo's own royal monuments stopped for 71 years, and Caracol placed its own texts there, perhaps using the city as a second capital. Caracol itself grew dramatically in population after its victories.

source.name: Arlen F. Chase and Diane Z. Chase (Caracol Archaeological Project): The Materialization of Classic Period Maya Warfare

dateLabel: Second half of the 7th century CE
title: Xochicalco, a Fortress on the Hills
text: As Teotihuacan lost its grip, new towns sought safe high ground. Xochicalco was founded in the second half of the 7th century on a series of hills, with ramparts, moats and huge terraces linked by stairs and ramps. Its buildings mixed styles from central Mexico, the Gulf Coast and the Maya region, in a troubled age of trade rivalry.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Monuments Zone of Xochicalco

title: Panama's River of Gold
text: Between about 700 and 900 CE, the Coclé people buried their dead beside the Río Grande de Coclé with gold plaques and pendants showing animal-human figures. The cemetery lay undisturbed until a 1927 flood scattered gold beads along the banks. In 1940 a Penn Museum team dug Burial 11, thought to be a paramount chief's, holding 23 people in three layers.

source.name: University of Pennsylvania Almanac: Beneath the Surface: Life, Death and Gold in Ancient Panama

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: The Excavations at Sitio Conte

title: Drought and Feuds Topple Mayapán
text: Mayapán was the largest Maya capital of Yucatán in the 1200s and 1300s. A 2022 study found that civil strife rose with drought between 1400 and 1450, as rival families fought. The city collapsed between 1441 and 1461; its final mass grave, at the foot of the Temple of K'uk'ulkan, held likely relatives of the ruling Cocom family.

source.name: Nature Communications (Kennett et al., 2022): Drought-induced civil conflict among the ancient Maya

title: Balboa Sees the South Sea
text: Local people told the Spaniards of a sea to the south. On September 1, 1513, Vasco Núñez de Balboa set out with 190 Spaniards and hundreds of Indigenous porters, crossing jungles, rivers and swamps. From a peak in Darién he sighted the Pacific, the first European to see its eastern shore, then claimed the "South Sea" for Castile at the Gulf of San Miguel.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Benjamin Keen): Vasco Núñez de Balboa

title: A Silver Town in a Narrow Valley
text: Zacatecas was founded in 1546 after the discovery of a rich silver lode, on the steep slopes of a narrow valley. It became one of New Spain's most important mining towns. Its cathedral, built between 1730 and 1760, shows European and Indigenous decorative ideas side by side on its richly carved Baroque façades.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Zacatecas

title: A Cathedral Built for Earthquakes
text: Work on León Cathedral began in 1747, to a design by Guatemalan architect Diego José de Porres Esquivel, and lasted into the early 19th century. Its low, thick towers were a response to earthquakes. Inside, plenty of natural light falls on a wooden Flemish altarpiece and on Stations of the Cross painted by Nicaraguan artist Antonio Sarria.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: León Cathedral

title: The Earthquakes That Moved a Capital
text: For 230 years, Santiago de Guatemala in the Panchoy Valley survived floods, eruptions and tremors. Then in 1773 the Santa Marta earthquakes destroyed much of the town. The authorities moved the capital to a safer place, which became Guatemala City. Some residents stayed behind, and their old town became known as "La Antigua Guatemala", its principal monuments still preserved as ruins.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Antigua Guatemala

title: Fifty Dollars for a Maya City
text: In 1839, US diplomat John Lloyd Stephens and English artist Frederick Catherwood pushed through civil war and dark jungle to Copán, where a magnificently carved stela stunned them. Stephens "purchased" the site for $50, and Catherwood drew its ruins. Their 1841 book and his drawings caused a storm of interest that launched the archaeology of Middle America.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: John Lloyd Stephens

title: The Maya Rise in Yucatán
text: In 1847 a Maya uprising broke out on Yucatán's southeastern frontier, where commercial sugar was spreading. Led by Jacinto Pat and Cecilio Chi, the rebels by mid-1848 were on the verge of taking Mérida and Campeche, but went home for the planting season. Some, the Cruzob, kept an independent Maya state built around a Talking Cross until 1901.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (Gilbert M. Joseph), via Encyclopedia.com: Caste War of Yucatán

title: Central America Unites Against Walker
text: Invited by one Nicaraguan faction in 1855, American adventurer William Walker soon became virtual master of the country, a key shipping link between the oceans. On July 12, 1856, he made himself president. A coalition of Central American states fought him until he surrendered on May 1, 1857. Landing in Honduras in 1860, he was executed there.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: William Walker

title: Santa María Blasts Open
text: After a long quiet spell, Guatemala's Santa María produced one of the 20th century's largest eruptions on October 24–25, 1902. Its explosions were heard in Costa Rica, ash rose 27–29 km high and fell as far as Mexico City, and much of the Pacific coastal plain went dark by day. It tore a 1.5-km-wide crater in the volcano's flank.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program: Santa María

title: Eulalia Guzmán Finds the Rain King
text: In 1934, archaeologist Eulalia Guzmán travelled to the remote hamlet of Chalcatzingo to check reports of "stones with reliefs". On the hillside she recorded four carvings. The largest, nicknamed "El Rey" by villagers, shows a person seated in a cave-like niche beneath rain clouds and falling raindrops. Later excavations placed such carvings at about 700–500 BCE.

source.name: The PARI Journal (David C. Grove, University of Florida): Chalcatzingo: A Brief Introduction

title: Costa Rica Gives Up Its Army
text: When Costa Rica's legislature annulled the 1948 presidential election, coffee farmer José Figueres led an uprising using arms he had hidden on his farm near Cartago. The civil war lasted two months. Afterwards, a junta led by Figueres wrote a new constitution that abolished the army and gave women the right to vote.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: José Figueres Ferrer

title: Rigoberta Menchú Wins the Peace Prize
text: Born in 1959 into a poor K'iche' Maya family, Rigoberta Menchú picked coffee on big plantations as a child. In 1979 the army killed her brother; her father died in 1980 when security forces stormed the Spanish Embassy, and her mother died soon after. She fled to Mexico in 1981, told her story to the world, and won the 1992 Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Rigoberta Menchú Tum, Biographical

title: A Lost City Under the Rainforest
place: La Mosquitia, Gracias a Dios, Honduras
text: In 2012, laser scans from a plane revealed earthworks and ceremonial buildings hidden under Honduras's Mosquitia rainforest. In 2015, Honduran and American archaeologists reached the site and found plazas, an earthen pyramid and a cache of over 50 carved stone objects, including a "were-jaguar" head. The culture that built the city thrived about 1,000 years ago, and still has no name.

source.name: National Geographic (Douglas Preston): Exclusive: Lost City Discovered in the Honduran Rain Forest

title: The Oldest Gold in the Americas
text: Near Lake Titicaca, an elderly person was buried wearing a necklace of nine gold beads mixed with green stones. Radiocarbon dates put the grave at 2155 to 1936 BCE, making the beads the earliest worked gold yet found anywhere in the Americas. Surprisingly, the owners were not rich kings but a small community of hunters and gatherers starting to settle down.

source.name: PNAS (via PubMed Central): Four-thousand-year-old gold artifacts from the Lake Titicaca basin, southern Peru

title: The Temple of the Fox
place: Buena Vista, Chillón Valley, Lima, Peru
text: In the Chillón Valley near Lima stands a temple from about 2200 BCE. At its entrance, archaeologist Robert Benfer found a mural of a fox carved inside a painted llama. Its offering chamber lines up with a rock on an eastern ridge, pointing to where the sun rises on December 21, the southern summer solstice.

source.name: University of Missouri release via Phys.org: Researcher unearths earliest Western sculptures and astronomical alignments in Peru

title: The Lady of Pacopampa
text: In 2009 a Japanese-Peruvian team found a woman buried at the ancient temple of Pacopampa in Peru's northern highlands. About 1.55 metres tall, she lay curled up and surrounded by gold pendants, necklaces and plates. Team leader Yuji Seki estimated she was 30 to 40 years old and lived 800 to 900 years before Christ.

source.name: AFP via Phys.org: Japanese help uncover ancient Peru remains

source2.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): 3,000-Year-Old Tomb Found in Peru

title: Pyramids of the Bolivian Savanna
place: Llanos de Mojos, near Casarabe, Beni, Bolivia
text: From about 500 CE, the Casarabe people built towns in the flooded savannas of the Bolivian Amazon. Laser scans from the air, called lidar, revealed terraces 5 metres high, conical pyramids 21 metres tall, straight causeways, checkpoints and water reservoirs. The finds challenge the old idea that western Amazonia was only thinly populated before the Spanish arrived.

source.name: University of Exeter: Newly discovered ancient Amazon settlements revealed by lidar

title: Colombia's Lost City in the Clouds
place: Teyuna (Ciudad Perdida), Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Magdalena, Colombia
text: Archaeologists believe the Tairona built Teyuna in the 9th century in the jungle-covered Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, with a staircase of around 1,200 steps. Between 2,000 and 8,000 people may have lived there. It was abandoned in the 1600s, and the nearby Kogi, Wiwa, Arhuaco and Kankuamo peoples are seen as living descendants of the Tairona.

source.name: National Geographic: Tales of ancient treasures lured looters to Colombia's 'Lost City'

title: The Tomb of the Wari Queens
text: Around 750 CE, three or possibly four royal women of the Wari Empire were laid to rest at Castillo de Huarmey, beside 40 noblewomen seated in burial positions. The tomb, found unlooted in 2013 by Polish and Peruvian archaeologists, held over 1,300 objects, including weaving tools of gold and silver. It hints at how powerful women were at the top of Wari society.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): A Wari Matriarchy?

title: The Mapuche Win at Curalaba
text: In 1598 Mapuche warriors defeated a Spanish force at Curalaba in southern Chile, and the governor, Martín García Oñez de Loyola, was beheaded. The Spanish were forced to fall back north of the Biobío River, abandoning the cities they had founded in the south. Valdivia fell in 1599, followed by La Imperial and Angol in 1600.

source.name: Memoria Chilena (Biblioteca Nacional de Chile): La Guerra de Arauco (1550-1656)

title: South America's First Woman Doctor
text: A decree of 1877 finally let Chilean girls sit university entrance exams, and Eloísa Díaz entered the University of Chile's medical school in 1881. On January 3, 1887, President Balmaceda handed her the title of surgeon. She went on to inspect Santiago's public schools and led the national school medical service from 1911 until 1940, caring for children's health and food.

source.name: Memoria Chilena (Biblioteca Nacional de Chile): Eloísa Díaz Insunza (1866-1950)

title: A Nobel Prize for Gabriela Mistral
text: On December 10, 1945, the Chilean poet Gabriela Mistral received the Nobel Prize in Literature from King Gustav. No Latin American had ever won it before, and only four women had. The Swedish Academy praised her lyricism, inspired by powerful feeling, as a symbol of Latin American idealism. Her home town, Vicuña, had already named her its favourite daughter in 1925.

source.name: Memoria Chilena (Biblioteca Nacional de Chile): Premio Nobel de Literatura (1945)

title: The Day Bogotá Burned
text: On April 9, 1948, the popular Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán was shot dead in Bogotá. His furious working- and middle-class supporters attacked government buildings, churches and a Conservative newspaper, and many shops were looted. Hundreds were killed or wounded before order returned on April 11, and the riot deepened the partisan violence tearing Colombia apart.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (Helen Delpar), via Encyclopedia.com: Bogotazo

title: The Zenú Tame a Flooded Land
place: San Marcos, La Mojana, Sucre, Colombia
text: From about 200 BCE, the Zenú turned one of the Americas' biggest flood zones, in Colombia's Caribbean lowlands, into farmland. They dug canals up to four kilometres long and raised ridges about three metres high, in fishbone, fan and chessboard patterns, to steer the water away. These ditches and raised fields covered about half a million hectares and are still visible today.

source.name: LACMA (Los Angeles County Museum of Art): Zenú ditch-and-raised-field systems

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List): Pre-Hispanic Hydraulic System of the San Jorge River

title: 143 Million Bricks for the Sun
place: Huacas de Moche, Moche Valley, La Libertad, Peru
text: Around 100 CE, the Moche began building the Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna in Peru's Moche Valley. The sun-dried adobe bricks carry makers' marks, ranging from hand- and footprints to circles and squiggles. When finished, the Huaca del Sol held an estimated 143 million bricks, painted red on the outside.

source.name: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Central and Southern Andes, 1–500 A.D.

title: The Cañari Noblewoman of Ingapirca
text: Around 1200 at Ingapirca, northeast of Cuenca in the southern Andes of Ecuador, a Cañari noblewoman aged between 20 and 30 was buried with all her finery. Ten male and female attendants were laid to rest with her. Her grave was marked with a stone pavement and a standing stone slab, called a stela, at one end.

source.name: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Northern Andes, 1000–1400 A.D.

title: The Diaguita and Their Duck Jugs
text: Around 1000 CE, the Diaguita culture clearly emerged in the Huasco, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa valleys of northern Chile. They lived from farming, herding and the sea, and painted pottery with white, black and red geometric designs, including a famous duck-shaped jug. They reached their peak around 1300 and joined the Inka Empire around 1400.

source.name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino: The art of being Diaguita – A bit of history

title: A Sailing Raft Meets a Spanish Ship
text: The Manteño people of coastal Ecuador dove for bright red Spondylus shells and sailed balsa rafts, with trade reaching as far as western Mexico. Around 1526, a giant Indigenous sailing raft met a Spanish ship. It carried silver and gold ornaments, textiles and mirrors to barter, and the Spanish sailors took the raft's crew captive.

source.name: UC Berkeley ORIAS: Manteño

title: South America's First Printing Press
text: Italian-born printer Antonio Ricardo sailed from Acapulco in 1580 with his press and settled in Lima. On July 14, 1584, he printed a decree removing ten days from the calendar, the earliest known work from a South American press. He then printed the Doctrina Christiana, a catechism with Spanish set above parallel columns of Quechua and Aymara.

source.name: John Carter Brown Library: Antonio Ricardo, a 16th century printer on both sides of the Equator

title: Measuring the Earth at the Equator
text: In 1736 French scientists including La Condamine, Bouguer and Godin reached Quito, joined by two Spanish naval officers, and laid out a 10-kilometre baseline near the equator. High altitude, suspicious locals and bitter quarrels slowed them by years. But their survey confirmed that the Earth is flattened at the poles, backing Newton over Descartes.

source.name: Physics World (Institute of Physics): review of Measure of the Earth by Larrie D. Ferreiro

title: Humboldt on Chimborazo
text: In 1802 Alexander von Humboldt climbed Chimborazo to 19,286 feet, the highest anyone had then climbed. Snow fell, his shoes were terrible, and their soles were shredded on jagged rocks until his feet bled. Stopped by a huge crevasse below the peak, he saw nature as a global force with matching climate and vegetation zones.

source.name: National Geographic: Interview with Andrea Wulf on Alexander von Humboldt

title: Victory on a Volcano's Slopes
text: On May 24, 1822, rebel forces commanded by Antonio José de Sucre defeated Spanish royalists on the lower slopes of Pichincha, an Andean volcano. The next day the rebels occupied nearby Quito. Simón Bolívar was acclaimed liberator, and Ecuador was joined to the new but short-lived Republic of Gran Colombia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Pichincha

title: Bolivia's National Revolution
text: In April 1952 the MNR party, backed by armed workers, civilians and peasants, overthrew Bolivia's military regime. That year everyone got the vote when literacy requirements were scrapped, and in October the three largest tin-mining companies were nationalized. A sweeping land reform in 1953 gave Indigenous peoples land and freed them from servile labour obligations.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bolivia – The rise of new political groups and the Bolivian National Revolution

title: Whale Hunters of Babitonga Bay
text: On Brazil's southern coast, the Sambaqui people built huge mounds of shells. Studying old museum collections from these mounds, scientists found bone harpoons and whale remains suggesting that southern right whales and humpbacks were probably hunted here 5,000 years ago. Whale bones were also placed in graves, showing how much these giant animals mattered to coastal life long before Europeans arrived.

source.name: Nature Communications: Molecular and zooarchaeological identification of 5000 year old whale-bone harpoons in coastal Brazil (2026)

title: A Plaza Village in the Wetlands
place: Los Ajos, wetlands of Rocha, Uruguay
text: Archaeologists once thought only small bands of hunter-gatherers lived in the La Plata basin. Then digs at Los Ajos, a mound complex in southeastern Uruguay's wetlands, revealed a circle of households around a central public plaza. Its farmers grew maize, squash, beans and tubers, the earliest crops known in southern South America, and later raised seven platform mounds around the plaza.

source.name: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute via EurekAlert: A complex agricultural society in Uruguay's La Plata basin, 4,800-4,200 years ago

source2.name: Nature: Evidence for cultivar adoption and emerging complexity during the mid-Holocene in the La Plata basin (Iriarte et al., 2004)

title: Cuba's Ancient Shell-Mound Cemetery
text: Canímar Abajo, near Matanzas in Cuba, is a mound built up from shells, and people buried their dead in it. Radiocarbon dating puts its older burials between 1380 and 800 BCE. Chemical clues locked in the teeth of these early islanders suggest they mostly stayed put, living off nearby coastal food rather than roaming widely, the earliest such evidence in the Antilles.

source.name: Radiocarbon (Cambridge Core): Radiocarbon and Stratigraphic Chronology of Canímar Abajo, Matanzas, Cuba (Roksandic et al., 2015)

source2.name: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam research portal: Earliest evidence of sedentism in the Antilles (PNAS, 2025)

title: The Standing Stones of Tafí
place: Los Menhires, El Mollar, Tafí del Valle, Tucumán, Argentina
text: More than 2,000 years ago, people of the Tafí valley carved tall stone monoliths, called menhirs or huancas, decorated with human, animal and phallic figures. Their story did not end in ancient times: in the 1970s a de facto government forcibly moved them to an arbitrary corner of the valley, and only around 2002 were they relocated to where they stand today.

source.name: Argentina.gob.ar (Comisión Nacional de Monumentos): Menhires de Tafí del Valle, Lugar Histórico Nacional

title: Giant Ditches Under the Rainforest
text: In Brazil's Acre state, people dug huge geometric ditches in circles and squares, some up to 11 metres wide and 4 metres deep. The forest later hid more than 450 of these geoglyphs until modern deforestation revealed them. Few objects lie inside, so they may have been ritual gathering places, built in forest that people had already been managing for thousands of years.

source.name: University of Exeter news: Hundreds of ancient earthworks built in the Amazon (2017)

source2.name: PNAS: Impact of pre-Columbian 'geoglyph' builders on Amazonian forests (Watling et al., 2017)

title: The City of Firsts
place: Colonial City, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
text: Founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1498 at the mouth of the Ozama River, Santo Domingo became home to the first cathedral, hospital, customs house and university in the Americas. In 1502 Governor Nicolás de Ovando moved it to the west bank and gave it a checkerboard street grid, a layout copied by town planners across the New World.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Colonial City of Santo Domingo

title: Seeking Freedom to Worship
text: In 1647, religious dissidents in Bermuda wanted an island where they could worship as they pleased. Led by Captain William Sayle, the Company of Eleutherian Adventurers sailed with about 70 settlers, probably landing on Eleuthera, then known as Cigatoo. Their dream of a thriving plantation colony was dashed by poor soil, quarrels among themselves and Spanish interference.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: The Bahamas, British colonization

title: A Portuguese Outpost Facing Buenos Aires
text: In 1680 the Portuguese founded Colonia del Sacramento on a short peninsula on the Río de la Plata, directly facing Spanish Buenos Aires. Fought over for a century, it was finally lost by its founders. Unlike Spanish towns with their rigid checkerboard grids, Colonia's narrow cobbled streets follow the shape of the land, mixing Portuguese and Spanish building traditions.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Quarter of the City of Colonia del Sacramento

title: The Morant Bay Rebellion
text: On October 11, 1865, a revolt by Black Jamaicans broke out at Morant Bay. Governor Edward Eyre crushed it so harshly that executions passed 400. He then had the island's legislature abolish itself, making Jamaica a crown colony. In Britain, thinkers such as John Stuart Mill demanded Eyre be tried for murder, while Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin and Alfred, Lord Tennyson took his side.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Edward John Eyre

title: The Kasato Maru Reaches Santos
place: Port of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil
text: Under a contract with São Paulo state, recruiters struggled to find Japanese families for its coffee farms, even registering fake married couples. The Kasato Maru left Kobe on April 28, 1908 and reached Santos on June 18. On six plantations the emigrants found floorless shacks, harsh foremen and a poor harvest, and within months came strikes and night-time escapes.

source.name: National Diet Library (Japan): 100 Years of Japanese Emigration to Brazil, Voyage, assigned to plantations and leaving plantations

source2.name: National Diet Library (Japan): 100 Years of Japanese Emigration to Brazil, Prehistory of emigration to Brazil

title: Montserrat's Volcano Awakens
text: In July 1995 the Soufrière Hills volcano began the first eruptions in Montserrat's recorded history, with lava domes that grew and collapsed in turn. The capital, Plymouth, was abandoned, and in June 1997 nineteen people were killed. More than two-thirds of Montserratians left the island, and the southern two-thirds of it has been off limits ever since.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Montserrat

title: The Earthquake That Shook Haiti
text: At 4:53 PM on January 12, 2010, a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck about 25 km southwest of Port-au-Prince. Léogâne, even closer to the epicentre, was essentially levelled, and the National Palace and cathedral were badly damaged. Some three million people were affected and over a million left homeless. Death toll estimates ranged widely, from 85,000 to more than 300,000.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: 2010 Haiti earthquake

title: Jade Raptors of Vieques
place: La Hueca, Sorcé, Vieques, Puerto Rico
text: In the 1980s archaeologists at La Hueca, on the island of Vieques, found a new pottery style they called Huecoid, along with tiny greenstone and jadeite carvings of birds of prey clutching human heads. The raptors shown are not native to the islands, possibly carved from imported stone, a sign of busy links between the South American mainland and the Antilles.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Bulletin: Arte del Mar, Art of the Early Caribbean (James A. Doyle, 2020)

title: Hill Towns of the Humahuaca Valley
place: Coctaca, Quebrada de Humahuaca, Jujuy, Argentina
text: The Quebrada de Humahuaca has been a trade route for 10,000 years. From about 900 until the Inca arrived around 1430 to 1480, it held flourishing pre-Hispanic towns and villages. At Coctaca, stone-walled farming terraces, thought to have begun around 1,500 years ago and still in use today, are linked to a string of fortified towns called pucaras.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Quebrada de Humahuaca

title: The Weeping Spirit of Cohoba
text: Around 1000 CE, a Taíno artist carved this zemí, a sacred figure, from hard guaiacum wood, probably on Hispaniola. Powdered cohoba, a hallucinogen, was placed on the flat top and inhaled through snuff tubes during ceremonies. The thin, squatting figure has tears streaming down its face, perhaps showing a fasting shaman feeling the drug's effects. Radiocarbon tests date it to 974–1020 CE.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Zemí cohoba stand, Taíno, ca. 1000 CE

title: Road-Linked Towns of the Xingu
place: Upper Xingu, Xingu Indigenous Park, Mato Grosso, Brazil
text: Together with Kuikuro researchers, archaeologists mapped large settlements in Brazil's Upper Xingu dating from about 1250 to 1600. Towns with circular plazas sat 3 to 5 km apart, linked by straight roads 10 to 50 m wide, and were ringed by ditches up to 5 m deep. Bridges, ponds and causeways shaped the wetlands, and some are still used today.

source.name: Science: Amazonia 1492, Pristine Forest or Cultural Parkland? (Heckenberger et al., 2003)

title: Freedom Comes to British Guiana
text: When full emancipation came in 1838, Black freedmen in British Guiana left the plantations and set up their own settlements along the coastal plain. Planters then brought in workers from several places, above all indentured labourers from India. Indentured labourers who earned their freedom settled in coastal villages near the estates, a pattern that took hold in the late 19th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Guyana, History

title: Freedom, but Not Yet
text: On July 1, 1863, the Netherlands abolished slavery in Suriname and its Caribbean islands. But many freed people were forced to keep working on plantations for ten more years under 'State Supervision' for a miserable wage, to limit owners' losses. The scheme failed totally, and for many, slavery did not really end until July 1, 1873.

source.name: Government of the Netherlands: Slavery Memorial Year

source2.name: International Institute of Social History: Colony Suriname mapped out

title: The Gusher at Lake Maracaibo
place: La Rosa field, Cabimas, Zulia, Venezuela
text: On December 14, 1922, the Los Barrosos-2 well near Cabimas blew out, spewing oil for nine days and soiling Lake Maracaibo with some 840,000 barrels. Residents carried an image of San Benito to the well and prayed; when it suddenly stopped, many credited the saint. The gusher helped turn Venezuela from a coffee and cacao exporter into a giant oil producer.

source.name: AAPG Explorer: One Hundred Years of a Lost Blowout (Orlando Méndez)

title: Europe's Christmas Rocket
place: Guiana Space Centre, Kourou, French Guiana
text: On Christmas Eve 1979, the first Ariane 1 rocket lifted off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, after an earlier December attempt was called off. It carried a small test satellite, CAT-1. Afterwards hundreds of people celebrated in the assembly hall, champagne flowed, and firefighters cheerfully soaked everyone with water. Ariane went on to give Europe its own access to space.

source.name: European Space Agency: 40 years of Ariane

source2.name: ESA Historical Archives: Christmas in Kourou

title: The Mississippi Valley Shakes
place: New Madrid region, Missouri and Arkansas, USA
text: At about 2:15 in the morning, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck northeast Arkansas, the first of three great shocks that hit the region by February 1812. People were woken by the shaking as far away as New York City and Washington, D.C. Huge waves on the Mississippi overwhelmed boats, and the ground sank to form Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee.

source.name: USGS: Summary of 1811-1812 New Madrid Earthquakes Sequence

title: Laura Secord's Long Walk
place: Queenston to Beaver Dams, Ontario, Canada
text: During the War of 1812, Laura Secord heard of a planned American surprise attack and set off herself to warn Lieutenant James FitzGibbon. Avoiding the direct road, she went through fields and woods along Twelve Mile Creek. Two days later, Indigenous warriors ambushed the Americans at Beaver Dams and FitzGibbon took their surrender, yet official reports never mentioned her.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Ingersoll, Laura (Secord)

title: A Fur Trade Village on the Columbia
text: In 1825 the Hudson's Bay Company moved its base about 100 miles up the Columbia River to the fertile plain of Vancouver. Outside the fort's walls grew a village of workers' homes, including many Hawaiians who served as mill hands, sailors, gardeners, soldiers and cooks. At its peak the village held around 535 men, 254 Indian women and 301 children.

source.name: National Park Service: Hawaiians at Fort Vancouver

title: What Hath God Wrought
text: Inside the U.S. Capitol, Samuel Morse tapped out a telegraph message along a test line to Baltimore that Congress had paid $30,000 to build. The words, "What Hath God Wrought," were suggested by Annie Ellsworth, daughter of the patent commissioner. Morse's partner Alfred Vail then returned an identical message from Baltimore.

source.name: U.S. Senate (archived page): First Telegraph Messages from the Capitol

title: Tragedy on Grosse Île
text: Fleeing famine in Ireland, more than 100,000 immigrants arrived at Quebec and the quarantine island of Grosse Île in a single season. Many were already sick with typhus, which soon became an epidemic. That year over 5,000 people died at sea, and 5,424 were buried on Grosse Île.

source.name: Parks Canada: 1847, A tragic year at Grosse Île

title: Sojourner Truth Speaks in Akron
text: Born into slavery as Isabella Baumfree, Sojourner Truth walked away to freedom "by daylight" in 1827. At the 1851 Women's Rights Convention in Akron, held in the Old Stone Church, she gave her famous speech. Oddly, the well-known "Ain't I a Woman?" version was printed twelve years later; a report published about a month after the speech lacks that phrase.

source.name: National Park Service: Sojourner Truth

title: Gold Fever on the Fraser
place: Fraser Canyon near Yale, British Columbia, Canada
text: When news of Fraser River gold reached San Francisco, miners rushed north; about 80 per cent came from California. Some 30,000 gold seekers lined the river in 1858. They disrupted the salmon fishery of the Nlaka'pamux, sparking the Fraser Canyon War, and fears of an American takeover led Britain to create the colony of British Columbia on 2 August.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Fraser River Gold Rush

title: Oil Strikes at Titusville
text: Edwin Drake struck oil only 69 feet down near Titusville, after driving iron pipe into the ground, a method he is credited with inventing. The well yielded an average of 1,000 gallons a day for three years. Engineers count this well as the start of the modern phase of the petroleum industry.

source.name: ASME (American Society of Mechanical Engineers) Landmark #40: Drake Oil Well

title: Freedom News Reaches Texas
text: Two and a half years after Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, Union general Gordon Granger, whose troops had reached Galveston the day before, issued General Order No. 3 declaring the enslaved people of Texas free. African American communities in Texas have celebrated the day since 1866. Juneteenth is the oldest known celebration of the end of slavery in the United States.

source.name: U.S. National Archives: The Original Juneteenth Document

title: The Métis Win a Province
text: Worried about losing their land and way of life, the Métis of Red River formed a provisional government led by Louis Riel. Their list of rights became the basis of the Manitoba Act, which made Manitoba Canada's fifth province, protected French and English in its legislature and courts, and set aside about 1,400,000 acres for the Métis.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Manitoba Act

title: The World's First National Park
text: Photographs by Jackson, paintings by Moran and sketches by Elliot from the Hayden Expedition caught the imagination of Congress. Just six months after that expedition, President Ulysses S. Grant signed the act setting Yellowstone aside as "a public park or pleasuring-ground" for the people. Many tribes have a traditional connection to this land and its resources.

source.name: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park (Yellowstone)

title: A School Begins in a Shanty
text: Tuskegee Institute was founded on Independence Day, with former slave Lewis Adams among its first commissioners. Its first classes met in an old, leaky building owned by Butler Chapel AME Zion Church. That September, the new principal, Booker T. Washington, bought an abandoned farm called The Old Burnt Place for $500, putting $200 down.

source.name: National Park Service: Tuskegee Institute's Founding

title: Canada Bans the Potlatch
text: Canada amended the Indian Act to outlaw the potlatch, a Northwest Coast ceremony of feasting, dancing and sharing of wealth, from 1 January 1885. Officials saw it as a barrier to assimilation. The vague law was hard to enforce, and many communities kept potlatching in secret until the ban ended in 1951.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Potlatch Ban

title: The Dam Breaks at South Fork
text: After hours of rain and telegraph warnings, the South Fork Dam broke at about 3:10 p.m., sending 20 million tons of water down the valley. The flood hit Johnstown at 4:07, its debris piling up at a stone railway bridge that then caught fire. The death toll was set at 2,209, and Clara Barton's Red Cross team arrived on June 5.

source.name: National Park Service: Johnstown Flood Timeline

source2.name: National Park Service: Johnstown Flood Frequently Asked Questions

title: Two Peach Baskets
text: Asked to invent an indoor winter game, Canadian instructor James Naismith borrowed ideas from "duck on a rock," a stone-lobbing game from his Ontario childhood. The building's superintendent had no spare boxes, only two peach baskets, so Naismith fastened them to ten-foot balconies. Two teams of nine played the first game of basketball, which was very rough.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: James Naismith

title: Ellis Island Opens Its Doors
place: Ellis Island, New York Harbor, USA
text: On New Year's Day the new immigration station on Ellis Island processed nearly 700 immigrants. The very first was Annie Moore, a teenager from Ireland. By the end of the fiscal year more than 400,000 people had passed through, and between 1892 and 1924 over 12 million immigrants were processed here.

source.name: National Park Service: This Month in History, January (Ellis Island)

source2.name: National Park Service: Ellis Island Chronology

title: The Maple Leaf Rag
text: Scott Joplin and Missouri publisher John Stark sent copies of the "Maple Leaf Rag" to the U.S. Copyright Office. The tune may be named for the Maple Leaf Club in Sedalia, a Black dance hall where Joplin often played. Selling for 50 cents, with a penny per copy for Joplin, it sold 75,000 copies in six months and became ragtime's signature piece.

source.name: Library of Congress Blog: Scott Joplin, the Magical Maple Leaf Rag

title: Anne of Green Gables Appears
text: Lucy Maud Montgomery wrote her first novel while living in Cavendish, but every publisher rejected it, so she kept it in a hat box. Finally published in June 1908, the story of orphan Anne Shirley sold more than 19,000 copies in five months. Mark Twain called Anne the dearest child "since the immortal Alice."

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Anne of Green Gables

title: Fire at the Triangle Factory
place: Greenwich Village, New York City, New York, USA
text: Near closing time on a Saturday, fire broke out on the top floors of the Asch Building, home of the Triangle Waist Company. Owners had often locked exit doors, the ninth-floor fire escape led nowhere, and fire ladders were stories too short. Of 500 workers, many of them young immigrant women, 146 died.

source.name: Cornell University ILR School, Kheel Center: The Triangle Factory Fire

title: The First Calgary Stampede
text: American trick roper Guy Weadick thought Calgary was the perfect place for a big rodeo, and four local businessmen paid for it. The first Stampede's parade featured 2,000 Indigenous people in full dress and about 14,000 spectators. Tom Three Persons thrilled the crowd riding the famous bronco Cyclone, but the show was not repeated until 1919.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Calgary Stampede

title: Fire at Mabila
place: Mabila (exact site uncertain), central Alabama, USA
text: Chief Tascaluza, an elaborately plumed leader of the Mabila, refused Hernando de Soto's demand for bearers and was held hostage. On the morning of October 18, 1540, Soto's troops reached Mabila, the palisaded capital. A quarrel between a Spanish officer and a townsman turned violent, and in the melee the Spaniards set fire to the town, burning it and many of its people.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama: European Exploration and Colonial Period

title: A French Fort Built with Timucua Help
text: On June 30, 1564, French colonists under Laudonnière began building Fort de la Caroline in today's Florida. They chose the spot partly for their ties with the Timucua-speaking Mocama people, who they hoped would provide food, since the French never seriously tried farming. The local leader Saturiwa sent 80 men to help raise the triangular fort of earth, wood and turf.

source.name: National Park Service, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve: Settlement and Conflict

title: The White Lion at Point Comfort
place: Old Point Comfort, Hampton, Virginia, USA
text: On August 25, 1619, the privateer ship White Lion reached Old Point Comfort in Virginia carrying enslaved Africans from the kingdom of Ndongo, in present-day Angola. English privateers had seized them from the Spanish slave ship São João Bautista in the Gulf of Mexico. At Point Comfort, 15 women and 17 men were traded to English colonists for food.

source.name: National Park Service: Arrival of the First Africans in 1619

title: The Colonies' First Printed Book
text: The Bay Psalm Book, printed in Cambridge in 1640, was the first book printed in British North America. Its press had belonged to Reverend Jose Glover, who died crossing the Atlantic; his widow Elizabeth set it up at Harvard College. Running it fell to their indentured servant Stephen Daye, a locksmith. Perhaps 1,700 copies were printed, and only 11 survive.

source.name: New York Public Library: New in Digital Collections: The Bay Psalm Book

title: Jeanne Mance and Ville-Marie
text: Jeanne Mance landed at Quebec in August 1641 and was part of the small group that founded Ville-Marie, the future Montreal, on 17 May 1642. That autumn she opened the Hôtel-Dieu, its hospital. In the desperate year of 1651 she offered the governor, Maisonneuve, 22,000 livres given to her hospital so he could fetch help, and her advice saved Montreal.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Mance, Jeanne

title: The Quake That Buried Trees
place: Charlevoix, between Baie-Saint-Paul and La Malbaie, Quebec, Canada
text: In 1663 an earthquake of about magnitude 7.5, the largest ever to hit eastern North America, shook what is now Quebec. Its epicentre was probably between Baie-Saint-Paul and La Malbaie, and it set off huge landslides, some more than 300 kilometres away, that buried whole trees. Geological Survey of Canada researchers radiocarbon-date those trunks to learn how often such quakes strike.

source.name: Natural Resources Canada: Why are researchers interested in an earthquake that occurred over 300 years ago?

title: Canoes onto the Mississippi
place: Mouth of the Wisconsin River, near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, USA
text: In mid-May 1673, Louis Jolliet and Father Marquette set out from Michilimackinac by canoe, following Green Bay and the Fox River, then portaging to the Wisconsin. In June, after a journey of more than 500 miles, their canoes entered the Mississippi. They went far enough south to be certain it emptied into the Gulf of Mexico, then turned back, fearing capture by the Spaniards.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Jolliet, Louis

title: Tekakwitha Becomes Catherine
place: Gandaouagué, Mohawk Valley, New York, USA
text: Tekakwitha, daughter of a Kanyen'kehà:ka (Mohawk) father and an Algonquin mother, survived the smallpox that killed her parents when she was four, though it scarred her and weakened her eyes. At Easter 1676, aged 20, she was baptized Catherine. Persecuted at home, she later travelled several hundred kilometres to the mission at Kahnawà:ke. In 2012 she became the first Indigenous woman in North America made a saint.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha

title: The Rat's Last Speech
text: Kondiaronk, a Wendat chief from Michilimackinac whom the French called Le Rat, persuaded Indigenous nations to gather at Montreal for the Great Peace of 1701. Over 700 allied people arrived in 200 canoes. Though sick with fever, he spoke for nearly two hours about his peacemaking. He died the next day and was buried in Notre-Dame church: Here lies the Rat, Huron Chief.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Kondiaronk

title: Freedom at Fort Mosé
place: Fort Mose, St. Augustine, Florida, USA
text: Enslaved Africans in the Carolina Colony learned they could escape their British masters and find freedom in Spanish Florida if they became Catholic and pledged to serve the Spanish Crown. In 1738 Governor Manuel de Montiano gave them land about two miles north of St. Augustine. Led by Francisco Menendez, Fort Mosé held thirty-eight men and their families, about one hundred people.

source.name: National Park Service, Fort Matanzas: Fort Mose

title: Calling Out Liberty at Stono
text: On September 9, 1739, enslaved men near South Carolina's Stono River took guns and powder from a warehouse and set off toward Spanish Florida, which had promised freedom. A letter from that year says they grew from twenty to above sixty, marching with colours displayed and two drums beating, calling out Liberty. The militia routed them the next day; perhaps a hundred people died.

source.name: Charleston County Public Library, Charleston Time Machine: The Stono Rebellion of 1739: Where Did It Begin?

title: A Naturalist's Hurried Day in Alaska
text: On July 20, 1741, men from Vitus Bering's ship St. Peter went ashore on Kayak Island for water. The naturalist Steller hurried down the beach and found a still smouldering fire, scraps of fish and a cellar stocked with fish, signs of Alaska Natives who stayed unseen. He described the plants until told to come aboard immediately or be left behind.

source.name: National Park Service: Bering Expedition Landing Site

title: Indigo and Enslaved Labour
text: With her father called back to Antigua, the young Eliza Lucas managed her family's plantations and the enslaved workers on them. She was determined to perfect growing indigo, a dye plant, around Charleston, and in 1744 she grew enough to begin making dye. Built on the exploitation of enslaved workers, the trade boomed: in 1747, 138,300 pounds of dye were exported to England.

source.name: National Park Service, Charles Pinckney National Historic Site: Eliza Lucas Pinckney

title: A Key on a Kite String
text: In June 1752, while waiting for Philadelphia's Christ Church steeple to be finished, Benjamin Franklin decided a kite could reach the storm clouds just as well. He attached a metal key, and his 21-year-old son William was the only witness. When the key showed signs of electrical charge, Franklin knew lightning was a form of electricity, and championed pointed lightning rods.

source.name: The Franklin Institute: Franklin's Lightning Rod

title: Acadians Forced from Grand-Pré
text: Acadian families at Grand-Pré had built dykes to drain salt marsh into rich farmland. In 1755 New England officer John Winslow took charge of deporting them, and some 2,200 Acadian men, women and children were sent away from Les Mines, about a third of the nearly 6,000 deported from Nova Scotia that year. Longfellow later set his poem Evangeline here.

source.name: Parks Canada: History of Grand-Pré National Historic Site

title: Pontiac Moves on Detroit
text: After the British commander Amherst ended the custom of giving presents and limited trade to the forts, Pontiac, war chief of the Ottawas at Detroit, called secret councils from 27 April 1763, stirred partly by the prophet Neolin. On 7 May he entered the fort with some 300 men, but Gladwin had doubled the guard. From 26 May, other forts across the region fell.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Pontiac

title: The Kumeyaay Strike Back
place: Mission San Diego de Alcalá, San Diego, California, USA
text: The Kumeyaay were angry that Spanish missionaries took land, destroyed food-gathering places and harmed Native women and children. Village headmen and doctors planned an attack, and fifteen of twenty-five nearby rancherias sent warriors. Around one o'clock on the night of November 5, 1775, more than six hundred people surrounded Mission San Diego, set it on fire and killed three people, including Father Luis Jayme.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Native Knowledge 360: The 1775 Kumeyaay Revolt and Destruction of Mission San Diego

title: Yuquot, Already Ancient
place: Yuquot (Friendly Cove), Nootka Island, British Columbia, Canada
text: When Captain James Cook reached Nootka Sound in March 1778, Yuquot was already ancient. The Mowachaht had lived there for over 4,300 years; it was the capital for 17 tribes of the region and the origin of Nuu-chah-nulth whaling. Soon its harbour became a hub of the sea otter trade, and Spain held its only garrison in present-day Canada here.

source.name: Parks Canada, Directory of Federal Heritage Designations: Yuquot National Historic Site of Canada

title: Mum Bett Sues for Freedom
text: Enslaved in Colonel Ashley's house, Mum Bett overheard men discussing a bill of rights saying all people were born free and equal. Lawyer Theodore Sedgwick took her case, and on August 22, 1781, a Great Barrington jury ruled she was not Ashley's property, awarding her and Brom 30 shillings each. She took the name Elizabeth Freeman and later bought her own house.

source.name: National Constitution Center: Elizabeth Freeman, her case for freedom and the Massachusetts Constitution

title: Awa'uq, the Refuge Rock
place: Awa'uq, off Sitkalidak Island, Kodiak archipelago, Alaska, USA
text: On August 14, 1784, Russian fur trader Grigorii Shelikhov attacked several thousand Alutiiq people sheltering on a refuge rock, a small steep-walled island off Sitkalidak Island. After a standoff, his men crossed a spit exposed at low tide and fired cannon and muskets; estimates of the dead range from 200 to 500. The place is still called Awa'uq, meaning to become numb.

source.name: Alutiiq Museum and Archaeological Repository: Alutiiq Museum Launches Refuge Rock Monument Planning Project (press release, August 12, 2026)

title: The River That Ran the Wrong Way
place: Mackenzie River delta, Northwest Territories, Canada
text: Fur trader Alexander Mackenzie left Fort Chipewyan on 3 June 1789, searching for a water passage across the continent to the Pacific. His party included a Chipewyan man known as English Chief. But the great river ran north, not west. Mackenzie pushed on to the sea anyway, spent four nights on Whale Island, and was back at the fort after 102 days.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Mackenzie, Sir Alexander

title: Chloe Cooley's Scream
text: On 14 March 1793, Adam Vrooman tied up Chloe Cooley, the Black woman he enslaved, and forced her into a boat to sell her across the Niagara River into New York. She resisted fiercely. Her scream alerted Peter Martin, a Black Loyalist, who reported it to the government. That July, Upper Canada passed the first law in a British colony restricting the slave trade.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Chloe Cooley

title: The Komagata Maru Is Turned Away
text: In May 1914 the Komagata Maru anchored in Vancouver's harbour with 376 passengers, many of them Punjabi, challenging rules designed to keep immigrants from India out of Canada. Friends on shore sent food and water as conditions on board grew desperate. On July 23, 355 passengers left for Asia; 20 were later killed in a clash with police and troops at Budge Budge near Kolkata.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Komagata Maru (Guru Nanak Jahaz)

title: The Halifax Explosion
text: After colliding with another ship, the French munitions ship Mont-Blanc burned for nearly 20 minutes, then exploded at 9:04 a.m., one of the largest human-made blasts before 1945. Railway dispatcher Vincent Coleman stayed at his telegraph key warning trains away and was killed. Nearly 2,000 people died, and Halifax still sends Boston a Christmas tree each year to thank it for its help.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Halifax Explosion

title: Winnipeg Walks Off the Job
text: Within hours of the call on May 15, 1919, almost 30,000 men and women in Winnipeg left their jobs, from police and firemen to telephone operators. They wanted collective bargaining, better wages and better working conditions. On Bloody Saturday, June 21, violence killed two people and federal troops occupied the streets. It remains the largest strike in Canadian history.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Winnipeg General Strike of 1919

title: The Group of Seven's First Show
place: Art Gallery of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada
text: Seven Toronto painters, most of whom earned their living as commercial artists, held their first exhibition at the Art Gallery of Toronto on May 7, 1920. Influenced by their peer Tom Thomson, who had died in 1917, they painted the rugged, wind-swept forests of the Canadian Shield and presented themselves as Canada's first national school of painters.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Group of Seven

title: Greenwood Burns in Tulsa
text: Greenwood was a vibrant Black neighbourhood in Tulsa, with two newspapers, churches, a library branch and many Black-owned businesses. During eighteen terrible hours on May 31 and June 1, 1921, more than one thousand homes and businesses there were destroyed, and credible estimates of the dead range from fifty to three hundred. Black Tulsans began rebuilding within days, though many families never recovered.

source.name: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture: Tulsa Race Massacre

title: A Kansas Farm Boy Finds Pluto
text: Clyde Tombaugh was a farm boy from Kansas who won a job at Lowell Observatory after sending sketches of planets seen through his homemade telescope. Comparing glass photographic plates in a blink comparator, he spotted Pluto on February 18, 1930. A girl named Venetia Burney suggested naming it after the Roman god of the underworld, and the observatory chose her name.

source.name: Lowell Observatory: Secrets of Lowell, The Pluto Discovery Dome

source2.name: NASA Science: Pluto Facts

title: Hoover Dam Tames the Colorado
text: During the Great Depression, thousands of families came to Black Canyon to build the largest dam of its time across the Colorado River. In all, 21,000 men worked on it, pouring three and one-quarter million cubic yards of concrete. To cool the concrete, ice water was pumped through more than 582 miles of steel pipe, and all features were finished by March 1, 1936.

source.name: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation: Hoover Dam Frequently Asked Questions

source2.name: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation: The Story of Hoover Dam

title: Marian Anderson Sings for 75,000
text: Constitution Hall, the only Washington venue big enough for contralto Marian Anderson's usual audience, banned Black performers. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt quit the organisation that owned it in protest, and an outdoor concert was arranged instead. On Easter Sunday 1939, Anderson opened with "My Country, 'Tis of Thee" before an integrated crowd of 75,000. The whole concert lasted 25 minutes.

source.name: National Park Service: Marian Anderson and Constitution Hall

title: Jackie Robinson Takes the Field
place: Ebbets Field, Brooklyn, New York, USA
text: In front of 26,623 fans at Ebbets Field, Jackie Robinson started at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers, the first African American in the major leagues since 1884. He went hitless but reached base on an error and scored the go-ahead run against the Boston Braves. Despite all the uproar around him, he won baseball's first ever Rookie of the Year Award.

source.name: National Baseball Hall of Fame: Robinson debuts five days after signing with Dodgers

title: Henrietta Lacks's Cells Live On
place: Johns Hopkins Hospital, Baltimore, Maryland, USA
text: In 1951 Henrietta Lacks, a young mother of five, was treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins. A sample of her cells went to Dr. George Gey's lab, where other samples quickly died but hers doubled every 20 to 24 hours. She died at 31, but her "HeLa" cells, collected under the looser rules of the 1950s, helped develop the polio and COVID-19 vaccines.

source.name: Johns Hopkins Medicine: The Legacy of Henrietta Lacks

title: The Little Rock Nine Walk In
place: Central High School, Little Rock, Arkansas, USA
text: In September 1957, Arkansas's governor used the National Guard to keep Black students out of Little Rock's Central High, and an angry mob of over 1,000 gathered outside. President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division. At 9:22 a.m. on September 25, soldiers escorted the nine students through the front doors. The next May, Ernest Green became the school's first Black graduate.

source.name: National Park Service, Little Rock Central High School NHS: Crisis Timeline

title: Saskatchewan's Medicare Showdown
text: When Saskatchewan's medical care insurance plan came into force on July 1, 1962, most doctors closed their offices in protest. The province brought in doctors from Britain, and local citizens organised clinics of their own. A British physician who had helped launch Britain's health system mediated, and on July 23 both sides signed an agreement in Saskatoon, ending the strike.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Saskatchewan Doctors' Strike

title: Alaska's Good Friday Earthquake
place: Prince William Sound and Anchorage, Alaska, USA
text: At 5:36 p.m. on March 27, 1964, a magnitude 9.2 earthquake struck Alaska's Prince William Sound region and shook for about 4.5 minutes, the most powerful ever recorded in U.S. history. Some ground rose by about 11.5 meters, and a wave reached 67 meters at Valdez Inlet. Of the 131 people killed, 122 died in tsunamis; Anchorage suffered the worst property damage.

source.name: USGS: Largest Earthquake in Alaska

source2.name: USGS: The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake

title: Expo 67 on a Brand-New Island
place: Île Notre-Dame and Île Sainte-Hélène, Montreal, Quebec, Canada
text: The highlight of Canada's centennial, Expo 67 was built partly on a new island, Île Notre-Dame, created in the St. Lawrence River. Under the theme "Man and His World", visitors saw Buckminster Fuller's geodesic dome and Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67 housing. Planners expected 26 million visits, but the fair recorded over 50 million paid admissions in 183 days.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Expo 67

title: A Bronx Party Starts Hip-Hop
place: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx, New York, USA
text: Cindy Campbell threw a back-to-school party in a community room at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue so she could buy new clothes. Her brother Clive, DJ Kool Herc, who had come from Jamaica at 12, was 18. He played the drum "breaks" of funk records back to back on two turntables, and the building is now considered the birthplace of hip-hop.

source.name: NPR: 50 years ago, a summer party in the Bronx gave birth to hip-hop

source2.name: New York State, Empire State Plaza: Birthplace of Hip-Hop

title: Sally Ride Rides Into Orbit
text: On June 18, 1983, space shuttle Challenger lifted off from Launch Pad 39A carrying NASA astronaut Sally Ride, the first American woman in space. Her STS-7 mission had the first five-person crew and made the first release and retrieval of a satellite using the Canadian robotic arm. Challenger later touched down at Edwards Air Force Base in California.

source.name: NASA: 40 Years Ago, STS-7 and the Flight of Sally Ride

title: Calgary Hosts the Winter Games
text: Calgary's 1988 Games were the first Olympic Winter Games held in Canada, the first with alpine skiing on artificial snow and the first with indoor speed skating. Skier Karen Percy became the first Canadian to win a Winter Olympic medal at home. Crowds also cheered two underdogs: the Jamaican bobsled team and British ski jumper Eddie "the Eagle" Edwards.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Canada at the 1988 Olympic Winter Games

title: The Standoff Over the Pines
text: A plan to expand a golf course and build townhouses on disputed land at Kanesatake, including a Kanyen'kehà:ka (Mohawk) burial ground, sparked a 78-day standoff in 1990 between Mohawk protesters, Quebec police, the RCMP and the Canadian Army. A police corporal was killed. The golf course expansion was cancelled, but the land was never transferred to the Mohawks of Kanesatake.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Kanesatake Resistance (Oka Crisis)

title: The Great Ice Storm
place: St. Lawrence Valley, Quebec and Ontario, Canada
text: Between January 4 and 10, 1998, parts of the St. Lawrence Valley got up to 100 mm of ice pellets and freezing rain. Nearly 1.4 million customers in Quebec lost power. Dairy farmers had to discard over 10 million litres of milk, some maple producers lost almost their entire sugar bush, and over 15,000 troops deployed in Canada's largest peacetime military operation.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Ice Storm of 1998

title: Hurricane Katrina Floods New Orleans
text: Hurricane Katrina reached Category 5 over the Gulf of Mexico, then came ashore near Grand Isle, Louisiana, and moved into Mississippi on August 29, 2005. Breaks in the levees separating New Orleans from Lake Pontchartrain left at least 80% of the city under water by August 31. Katrina caused 1,833 deaths and is the costliest hurricane ever to hit the United States.

source.name: National Weather Service, Mobile/Pensacola: Hurricane Katrina

title: Lava in Leilani Estates
place: Leilani Estates, Island of Hawaiʻi, Hawaii, USA
text: On May 3, 2018, lava broke out inside Leilani Estates, a neighbourhood on Kīlauea's lower East Rift Zone. A magnitude 6.9 earthquake followed the next day. Lava covered over 700 structures and 30 miles of road and added 875 acres of new land, while the draining magma made parts of the summit caldera floor collapse. The last active lava was seen in September.

source.name: USGS: 2018 Lower East Rift Zone Eruption and Summit Collapse

title: An Inuk Governor General
text: Born in Kangiqsualujjuaq in Nunavik, Mary Simon became Canada's 30th governor general on July 26, 2021, the first Indigenous person in that role. Earlier she was the first Inuk in Canada to hold the rank of ambassador and helped set up the Arctic Council. Responding to her appointment, she spoke in both Inuktitut and English.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Mary Simon

title: Pemulwuy Fights Back
place: Botany Bay, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: Two years after the First Fleet arrived, the Bidjigal warrior Pemulwuy began resisting the settlers moving onto his people's land around Botany Bay. In December 1790 he was involved in the fatal wounding of the governor's gamekeeper, and from 1792 he led raids on farms. Badly wounded in 1797, he escaped capture until he was shot dead in 1802.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Pemulwuy

title: Bennelong Sails to England
place: Warrane (Sydney Cove), New South Wales, Australia
text: In December 1792 the Wangal man Bennelong and his younger relative Yemmerawannie sailed with Governor Arthur Phillip to England, the first Aboriginal people known to visit. They went to theatres and had their portraits painted, but Yemmerawannie fell sick and died there. Suffering from the cold and homesickness, Bennelong finally reached home in September 1795.

source.name: Australian Dictionary of Biography (Emma Dortins): Bennelong (1764–1813)

title: Sailing Around Van Diemen's Land
place: Derwent estuary and Mount Wellington, Tasmania, Australia
text: On 7 October 1798, surgeon George Bass and Matthew Flinders set out in the Norfolk, a 25-ton sloop built on Norfolk Island, to prove Bass's hunch that a strait separated the mainland from Van Diemen's Land. They sailed through it and back around the south, exploring the Derwent estuary, where Bass climbed Mount Wellington on Christmas Day.

source.name: Australian Dictionary of Biography: George Bass (1771–1803)

title: Death or Liberty at Castle Hill
place: Castle Hill, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: On the night of 4 March 1804, a hut was set alight at the Castle Hill Government Farm as a signal. Led by Irishmen, around 300 convicts overpowered their guards, crying 'Death or Liberty', and planned to seize Parramatta and Sydney and return to Ireland. Troops crushed Australia's first uprising, and an estimated 39 convicts died in the fighting and punishments.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Castle Hill Rebellion

title: An Axe Instead of a Stone
text: On 12 August 1829, a party travelled through the bush to lay a foundation stone for Perth, capital of the new Swan River Colony on Whadjuk country.
