Finding no suitable stones, Helena Dance, the only woman in the party, marked the occasion by cutting a tree with an axe. It was Australia's first free-settler colony set up with private money.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Founding of Perth

title: Justice After Myall Creek
place: Myall Creek station, near Bingara, New South Wales, Australia
text: Just before sunset on 10 June 1838, a group of armed convicts, ex-convicts and one settler led away Wirrayaraay people who had camped at Myall Creek station seeking safety; the remains of at least 28 people were later found. Unusually, the crime was investigated. In December seven men were hanged, the first British subjects executed for massacring First Nations people.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Myall Creek massacre

title: Stonemasons Win the Eight-Hour Day
text: On 21 April 1856, Melbourne stonemasons downed tools and walked off the job because their employers refused to cut working hours. The strike brought the bosses to the table, and the masons won an agreement to work no more than eight hours a day. Workers celebrated in a popular ditty: eight hours to work, eight hours to play, eight hours to sleep.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Eight-hour day

title: Australia's First Touring Cricket Team
place: Lake Wallace station, near Edenhope, Victoria, Australia
text: In 1868 thirteen Jardwadjali, Gunditjmara and Wotjobaluk men, stockmen who had learned cricket on western Victorian stations, became the first Australian cricket team to tour England. Between May and October they played 47 matches, winning 14, losing 14 and drawing 19. The star was all-rounder Unaarrimin, also known as Johnny Mullagh, who took 245 wickets.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Aboriginal cricket team

title: A Wire Through the Red Centre
text: On 22 August 1872, workers joined the northern and southern halves of the Overland Telegraph at Frews Ponds. Its 36,000 poles linked Port Augusta with Darwin, along a route that partly followed an Aboriginal trade route used for millennia. Once it was connected to an undersea cable from Java, news that had taken months to reach England could travel in hours.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Overland telegraph

title: Paddy Hannan's Bag of Gold
text: On 10 June 1893, prospectors Paddy Hannan, Thomas Flanagan and Dan O'Shea found gold near the surface of the dry red soil east of Coolgardie. Working in secret, each won the equivalent of several years' wages in a week. On 17 June Hannan rode into Coolgardie with about 100 ounces of gold, and the next morning the rush to Kalgoorlie began.

source.name: Australian Dictionary of Biography: Patrick Hannan

title: Votes and Seats for Women
text: On 18 December 1894, South Australia's parliament gave women both the vote and the right to stand for parliament, making the colony the first electorate in the world with equal political rights for men and women. Campaigners such as Mary Lee and Mary Colton had gathered a petition with more than 11,600 signatures, around 400 feet long with its pages glued end to end.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Women's suffrage

title: A Capital Gets Its Name
place: Capital Hill, Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, Australia
text: At a ceremony on 12 March 1913, Lady Denman announced the name of Australia's new federal capital: Canberra, with the stress on the first syllable. The district was already known by that name, derived from the Ngunnawal/Kamberri people whose country it is. Over 4000 spectators watched, but real construction of the city did not get going until the 1920s.

source.name: National Archives of Australia: Lady Denman, wife of the Governor-General, names Canberra

title: A Doctor Who Flies In
text: In 1928 John Flynn's Australian Inland Mission set up its Aerial Medical Service at Cloncurry, bringing medical help by air to remote outback homes. Flynn's mission had started with one nursing sister, one padre, a nursing hostel and five camels. In 1929 Alfred Traeger's pedal radio completed Flynn's vision of a 'canopy' of safety for the inland.

source.name: Australian Dictionary of Biography: John Flynn

title: A Day of Mourning
place: Australian Hall, Elizabeth Street, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: While Sydney celebrated 150 years since the British arrival, Aboriginal people met at the Australian Hall on 26 January 1938 and declared the day a Day of Mourning for their lost land, freedom and kin. Organised by Jack Patten, William Ferguson and William Cooper, it was the first time Aboriginal activist groups from different states had fully worked together.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Day of Mourning

title: Migrants Build the Snowy Scheme
place: Adaminaby, Snowy Mountains, New South Wales, Australia
text: On 17 October 1949, Prime Minister Ben Chifley and other leaders fired the first blast at Adaminaby to begin the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Scheme. More than 100,000 people worked on it before its official opening in 1972, and migrants from more than 30 nations made up about 65 per cent of the workforce. Sadly, 121 men were killed in industrial accidents.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Snowy Mountains Hydro

title: Petitions Painted on Bark
place: Yirrkala, Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia
text: When land near Yirrkala was cut from their reserve for bauxite mining without telling them, the Yolngu petitioned Parliament in August 1963. The text, typed in English and Yolngu Matha, was pasted onto bark, and senior artists painted clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay around it to show their ownership. The Yolngu call them Näku Dhäruk: bark, and word or message.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Näku Dhäruk – Yirrkala bark petitions

title: Moonwalk Pictures via Parkes
place: Parkes Observatory (Murriyang), New South Wales, Australia
text: At 12.56 pm on 21 July 1969, Australian time, 600 million people watched Neil Armstrong step onto the Moon. NASA's Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra was the prime receiver, but CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope, Murriyang, also caught the TV signals despite wind gusts of 110 km per hour. NASA chose its images for the following two hours and 12 minutes.

source.name: CSIRO: Apollo 11 Moon landing

title: Desert Stories in Acrylic
text: In 1971 men at Papunya, a government settlement west of Alice Springs, began painting their traditional designs with acrylic paint on small boards. That August, Kaapa Tjampitjinpa became the first Aboriginal Australian to win a contemporary art award, and over the following months more than 600 paintings were sold. The Western Desert art movement had begun.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Papunya Tula

title: Cyclone Tracy Hits Darwin
text: In the small hours of Christmas Day 1974, Cyclone Tracy crossed the coast near Fannie Bay, with gusts reaching 217 km/h before the wind gauge was destroyed. It killed 66 people and devastated 80 per cent of Darwin. Red Cross leader Joan Allridge sheltered under her kitchen table with two other adults, six children, a cat, four kittens, a dog and three birds.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Cyclone Tracy

title: The Bionic Ear
text: On 1 August 1978, Professor Graeme Clark of the University of Melbourne, inspired by his father's struggle with deafness, implanted a prototype bionic ear in Rod Saunders, who was totally deaf. It became the first cochlear implant to reliably give speech understanding to severely and profoundly deaf people. Clark later recalled going next door and bursting into tears of joy.

source.name: Bionics Institute: Professor Graeme Clark AC

source2.name: National Museum of Australia: Bionic ear prototype

title: No Dams on the Franklin
place: Franklin and Gordon rivers, Tasmania, Australia
text: In December 1982 protesters blocked access to the site where Tasmania's Hydro-Electric Commission planned a dam that would flood the wild Franklin River. Bob Brown recalled some 6,000 people registering to help and nearly 1,500 being arrested. The campaign saved a key wilderness area and eventually led to the Greens forming as a federal political party.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Franklin Dam and the Greens

title: Cathy Freeman's Golden Run
place: Stadium Australia, Sydney Olympic Park, New South Wales, Australia
text: Ten days after lighting the Olympic cauldron, standing in a pool of water as it rose around her, Cathy Freeman won the women's 400 metres at the Sydney Olympics on 25 September 2000. Born in Mackay to a Kuku Yalanji mother and a Birra Gubba father, she said running at its best felt 'like there are ants in your blood'.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments, Cathy Freeman

title: Hudson Set Adrift in James Bay
text: Henry Hudson's ship Discovery spent the winter of 1610–11 at the southern end of James Bay, probably in Rupert Bay. In June 1611 the crew mutinied. Hudson, his son John and seven companions were set adrift in a small boat and never seen again. He never found a passage to Asia, but Hudson Strait and Hudson Bay still carry his name.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Henry Hudson (Douglas Hunter)

title: A Danish Winter at Churchill
text: In 1619 King Christian IV of Denmark and Norway sent Jens Munk with two ships, the Unicorn and the Lamprey, and about 60 men to find a Northwest Passage. Frozen in at the mouth of the Churchill River, the crew was struck by cold and scurvy. Only Munk and two sailors survived, sailing home in July 1620. Munk's memoirs, published in 1624, inspired later voyages.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Jens Munk North-West Passage expedition 1619–20

source2.name: Manitoba Heritage Council: Commemorative plaque, Jens Munk

title: Henry Kelsey Sees the Prairies
text: In 1690 the Hudson's Bay Company sent Henry Kelsey inland from York Fort to invite distant peoples to come and trade furs. Travelling by canoe and on foot with Cree traders, he spent two years crossing parkland and prairie, becoming the first European to see the Prairies. Fluent in Cree and Assiniboine, he was described as never happier than when travelling among Indigenous people.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Henry Kelsey (Robert Coutts)

title: Matonabbee Leads the Way North
place: Bloody Falls, Coppermine River, near Kugluktuk, Nunavut, Canada
text: Samuel Hearne is famous for walking to the Arctic Ocean, but the Dene leader Matonabbee made it possible. His party, with Hearne the only European, left in December 1770 and reached the Coppermine River in July 1771. There, Dene men caught up in a violent conflict with the Inuit killed about 20 sleeping Inuit, an event remembered as the Bloody Falls Massacre.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Samuel Hearne (James H. Marsh, Daniel Panneton)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Matonabbee (David Lee)

title: From Canada, by Land
place: Dean Channel, near Bella Coola, British Columbia, Canada
text: On 22 July 1793, fur trader Alexander Mackenzie of the North West Company reached the Pacific at Dean Channel after crossing the continent with Indigenous guides. Using grease and vermilion, he painted a message on a rock: 'Alexander Mackenzie, from Canada, by land, the twenty-second of July, one thousand seven hundred and ninety-three.' In 1789 he had travelled with Dene leader Aw-gee-nah to the Arctic Ocean instead.

source.name: Parks Canada: First Crossing of North America National Historic Site

source2.name: Parks Canada: Sir Alexander Mackenzie (c. 1762-1820)

title: The Tlingit Sapling Fort
text: After defeating the Russians in 1802, the Kiks.ádi Tlingit built Shís'gi Noow, the 'Sapling Fort', near Indian River. On 1 October 1804 Russian forces landed in front of it, backed by the sloop Neva, and their leader Baranov was shot in the chest. When the Tlingit reserve gunpowder exploded in a canoe, the clans left on what is now called the Survival March.

source.name: National Park Service, Sitka NHP: The Battle of 1804

title: Not a Piece of Pemmican
text: Treaty 6 talks at Fort Carlton opened with a sacred Cree pipe ceremony. When the Crown's Alexander Morris spoke of reserves, Pitikwahanapiwiyin (Poundmaker) objected that the land was theirs, not a piece of pemmican to be cut up and handed back. Chiefs Mistawasis and Ahtahkakoop, seeing the bison hunt ending, chose to negotiate, and the treaty was signed on 23 August 1876.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Treaty 6 (Michelle Filice)

title: Skiing Across Greenland's Ice
text: On 15 August 1888, Fridtjof Nansen and five companions, including Sámi travellers Samuel Balto and Ole Ravna, left their boats upturned at Umivik and set off across Greenland's ice. On 26 September they reached the sea at Ameralik fjord, completing the first crossing of Greenland. They missed the last ship home and wintered at Godthaab, which Nansen admitted was not very disagreeable.

source.name: Royal Scottish Geographical Society: Fridtjof Nansen, the first crossing of Greenland (Jo Woolf)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Roald Amundsen (Carolyn Harris)

title: Avalanche on the Chilkoot Trail
place: Between Sheep Camp and the Scales, Chilkoot Trail, Alaska, USA
text: Heavy snow and warm winds made the Chilkoot slopes unstable in spring 1898. Alaska Natives refused to pack goods above Sheep Camp, but some Klondike stampeders ignored the warnings. On 3 April an avalanche buried the trail, probably killing over 65 people, the deadliest event of the gold rush. Many victims lie in the Slide Cemetery near Dyea.

source.name: National Park Service: The Palm Sunday Avalanche

title: Lessons from the Inuit at Gjoa Haven
place: Gjoa Haven, King William Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: Roald Amundsen's ship Gjøa slipped out of Oslo in a storm in June 1903 to escape creditors. During two winters at what is now Gjoa Haven, he measured the North Magnetic Pole and studied Inuit dress, sled dogs and survival skills, writing that he would never meet better people. In August 1906 the Gjøa reached Nome, the first ship through the Northwest Passage.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Roald Amundsen (Carolyn Harris)

title: The Century's Biggest Eruption
place: Novarupta, Katmai National Park, Alaska, USA
text: On 6 June 1912 a brand-new volcano, Novarupta, exploded in the largest eruption of the 20th century. In Kodiak, a foot of ash smothered the town and the darkness was so complete that a lantern at arm's length could scarcely be seen. In 1916 botanist Robert Griggs found a valley full of tens of thousands of steaming vents and named it the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.

source.name: National Park Service: The Great Eruption of 1912

source2.name: National Park Service, Katmai: Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes

title: Sled Dogs Race Diphtheria
text: In 1925 diphtheria swept through icebound Nome, and without antitoxin doctors feared nearly everyone infected could die. Relays of dog teams carried serum 674 miles from Nenana through gales, whiteouts and temperatures of -85 degrees, delivering it in 127.5 hours without a single broken vial. Togo, aged 12, led his team over 261 miles, the longest and most dangerous leg; Balto ran 55.

source.name: National Park Service: Togo

source2.name: Alaska State Archives: Serum Run of 1925

title: Exiled to the High Arctic
place: Craig Harbour and Grise Fiord, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: In July 1953, seven Inuit families from Inukjuak in northern Quebec boarded the ship CD Howe, promised plentiful wildlife and a chance to return after two years. Joined by families from Pond Inlet, they were split up and left at Craig Harbour and Resolute Bay, about 2,000 km from home. Canada apologized in 2010 for the hardship and its broken promise.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Inuit High Arctic Relocations in Canada (Samia Madwar)

source2.name: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada: Apology for the Inuit High Arctic relocation

title: Printmaking Comes to Cape Dorset
place: Kinngait (Cape Dorset), Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: In 1957 printmaking was introduced at Cape Dorset, with artist James Houston as the spark. He later studied with Japanese printmaker Un'ichi Hiratsuka and brought Japanese papers and methods back north. Inuit artists drew at home and sold drawings to their co-operative, where others turned them into prints of Arctic animals, legends and spirits, first issued in editions of 30.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Inuit Printmaking (Bente Roed, Sandra Buhai Barz)

title: Oil on Prince William Sound
place: Bligh Reef, Prince William Sound, Alaska, USA
text: On 24 March 1989 the fully loaded tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef. Nearly 11 million gallons of oil spilled into the sensitive habitats of Prince William Sound, at the time the largest single oil spill in American history. In August 1990 the Oil Pollution Act strengthened the federal government's power to prevent and respond to disastrous spills.

source.name: NOAA National Ocean Service: Oil Spills, Exxon Valdez

title: Greenlanders Recognized as a People
text: On 21 June 2009 the Self-Government Act came into force, replacing the Home Rule arrangement Greenland had had since 1979. It recognizes the people of Greenland as a people with the right to self-determination under international law and makes Greenlandic the official language. If Greenlanders choose independence, negotiations with Denmark must begin, and any agreement needs a referendum.

source.name: Prime Minister's Office of Denmark: Greenland

title: Franklin's Erebus Found at Last
place: Wilmot and Crampton Bay, Nunavut, Canada
text: On 1 September 2014, Government of Nunavut archaeologists checking an Inuit tent ring on a small island spotted a rusted piece of metal shaped like a bicycle fork. It was a davit pintle matching the plans of HMS Erebus. The next day the wreck itself was found. Since 2008 the search had drawn on Inuit knowledge, past and present.

source.name: Parks Canada: Finding HMS Erebus

title: Dogs of the Green River Shell Heaps
place: Indian Knoll, Green River, Ohio County, Kentucky, USA
text: Around 5,000 years ago, families along Kentucky's Green River gathered mussels and left deep shell heaps. Archaeologists found 182 dog burials at these sites, one of the largest samples anywhere in the Southeast and Midwest. Some dogs were laid beside men, women or children. Graves also held copper from the Great Lakes and shell from the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

source.name: Kentucky Heritage Council: Green River Archaic (booklet, 2006)

title: The Wheel of Stones at Majorville
place: Majorville Cairn and Medicine Wheel, near Bassano, Alberta, Canada
text: On a prairie hilltop west of the Bow River, a 9-metre cairn is joined to a 27-metre ring of cobbles by 28 stone spokes. People have used the site continuously for about 4,500 years, adding objects layer by layer, so the oldest lie at the centre. Iniskim, the buffalo-calling stones central to Blackfoot ceremonies, were found in the cairn, and offerings are still left today.

source.name: Canada's Historic Places: Majorville Cairn and Medicine Wheel

title: First Arrivals in the Far North
text: Around 2400 BCE, the people archaeologists call Independence I reached Peary Land in northern Greenland, where muskox were the main land animal. They lived in tent rings with a solid mid-passage and a square hearth, room for four to six people. Sites often hold five or more dwellings, suggesting working groups of 20 to 30 people.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: Prehistory of Greenland, Independence I

title: Little Deer Folded from Willow
text: Between 4,000 and 2,000 years ago, hunters folded single split twigs, often willow, into deer and bighorn sheep and left them in remote Grand Canyon caves, usually under rock cairns. Some are pierced by a tiny stick like a spear. Because the caves are so hard to reach, they were not toys; their exact purpose is still a mystery.

source.name: National Park Service, Grand Canyon: Archaeological Resources

title: A Desert Cave Used as a Storeroom
place: Hidden Cave, Grimes Point, near Fallon, Nevada, USA
text: Waves of ancient Lake Lahontan carved Hidden Cave. Around 3,800 years ago, ancestors of the Toi-Ticutta, the Cattail-Eaters, now the Fallon Paiute-Shoshone Tribe, began using it. They did not live inside but dug pits and buried tools and supplies to collect later. Many artifacts were found unbroken and grouped together, which is why archaeologists call it a cache.

source.name: Churchill County Museum: About Hidden Cave

source2.name: Bureau of Land Management: Grimes Point Archaeological Area / Hidden Cave

title: Gardens for Clams
place: Northern Quadra Island, British Columbia, Canada
text: Indigenous people of the Northwest Coast built rock walls at the low-tide mark, with a flattened terrace of beach behind them, to farm clams. Dating of gardens on northern Quadra Island shows they were in use 3,500 years ago. Such beaches can be two to four times more productive than unwalled ones, and First Nations kept the walls up into the 20th century.

source.name: PLOS ONE: 3500 years of shellfish mariculture on the Northwest Coast of North America (Smith et al., 2019)

title: Following the Beverly Caribou
text: About 2,600 to 2,500 years ago, the earliest Taltheilei hunters appeared on the Barrenlands, living along the migration route of the Beverly caribou herd. They made ground stemmed lanceheads, knives and triangular scrapers. Much later, Taltheilei hunters borrowed the bow from neighbours, and archaeologists see them as ancestors of the Chipewyan.

source.name: Carleton University, Rangifer Central: Taltheilei (after B. C. Gordon, Archaeological Survey of Canada)

title: Pilgrims to Crystal River
place: Crystal River Archaeological State Park, Florida, USA
text: People settled at Crystal River on Florida's Gulf coast about 2,500 years ago, once the river and estuary could feed a large settled population. The six-mound site, with burial mounds, temple mounds, a plaza and a substantial midden, served as a ceremonial centre for 1,600 years. As many as 7,500 people may have travelled there each year to trade and bury their dead.

source.name: Florida State Parks: Crystal River Archaeological State Park

source2.name: Florida State Parks: Crystal River Archaeological State Park, History

dateLabel: About 400 BCE (start of the Marpole phase)
title: The Great Shell Heap of Marpole
place: Marpole Midden, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
text: From about 400 BCE to 450 CE, people of the Fraser Delta piled up one of the largest pre-contact middens on Canada's Pacific coast, up to 4.6 metres deep. Mostly mollusc shells, it also held bone and stone tools, utensils and ornaments. The skill with wood and the sea seen here carried on in later Northwest Coast cultures such as the Musqueam.

source.name: Parks Canada Directory of Federal Heritage Designations: Marpole Midden National Historic Site

source2.name: Canada's Historic Places: Marpole Midden National Historic Site of Canada

title: Ivory Art of the Bering Sea
text: On St. Lawrence Island, Old Bering Sea hunters lived on walrus, seal and whale. They decorated their ivory harpoon heads and socket pieces with spirit images honouring the animals they hunted. They also carved human figures from walrus ivory, most often women; one at the Met is 21 centimetres tall. Some experts call them dolls, others ceremonial objects.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Female Figure, Old Bering Sea (2001.760)

title: Bushy Corn of Turkey Pen
place: Turkey Pen Shelter, Cedar Mesa, Utah, USA
text: At Turkey Pen Shelter, a Utah cave, a farming community raised turkeys, wove baskets and shoes, and got about 80 percent of its diet from maize. Genomes from fifteen 1,900-year-old cobs show plants that were shorter and bushier than modern corn and flowered faster, an adaptation to the short growing season of the highlands.

source.name: Nature (news, Heidi Ledford, 2017): Ancient genomes show how maize adapted to life at high altitudes

title: A Sun Calendar Near the Tropic
text: Founded around 400–450 by priests linked to Teotihuacan, Alta Vista became the chief ceremonial centre of the Chalchihuites culture, peaking between 700 and 900. Lined up with three mountain peaks and the Tropic of Cancer, it served as a calendar on the eastern horizon, tracking the Sun through the year to anticipate seasons for farming and to mark ritual dates.

source.name: INAH: Chalchihuites, un centro ceremonial para observar al Sol

source2.name: INAH: Alta Vista, un centro ceremonial solar en Zacatecas

title: The Bow Comes to the Chumash Coast
text: For thousands of years, Chumash hunters on the Santa Barbara coast threw darts with the atlatl. Around AD 500 the bow and arrow replaced it. In this era fishing and sea-mammal hunting grew more important, large permanent settlements rose along the coast, and the museum dates the tomol, a plank canoe, to about 2,000 years ago.

source.name: Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History: Chumash Life, Timeline

dateLabel: Late Woodland period, from about 1,400 years ago
title: Bears and Birds Made of Earth
place: Effigy Mounds National Monument, near Harpers Ferry, Iowa, USA
text: In the Late Woodland period, people along the Upper Mississippi began shaping earthen mounds into animals: birds, bears, deer, bison, turtles, panthers and water spirits. One cluster, the Marching Bear Group, holds 10 bear-shaped mounds. Archaeologists still debate whether they marked seasons or territories, while the tribes descended from the builders describe them as sacred places.

source.name: National Park Service, Effigy Mounds National Monument: Effigy Moundbuilders

source2.name: National Park Service: The Bears of Effigy Mounds

title: Arrows Frozen in Yukon Ice
place: Alpine ice patches, southwest Yukon, Canada
text: Melting ice patches in southwest Yukon have released about 146 well-preserved hunting tools of antler, bone, wood and stone, studied by archaeologists together with First Nation researchers. They show that hunters threw darts with spear-throwers from at least 8,360 years ago until about 1,250 years ago, when the bow and arrow abruptly took over.

source.name: Arctic (University of Calgary journal): Hare et al., Ethnographic and Archaeological Investigations of Alpine Ice Patches in Southwest Yukon

title: Ash Falls on the Yukon
text: A huge Alaskan eruption in AD 846–848 buried parts of Yukon and the Northwest Territories under 5 to 50 centimetres of volcanic ash. Many local ecosystems bounced back fast, but caribou and salmon, whose routes crossed the thick ash, were hit harder. Researchers think it pushed hunter-gatherer families to live with less affected relatives for up to a century.

source.name: Arctic (University of Calgary journal): Kristensen, Beaudoin and Ives on the White River Ash eastern lobe

title: Ontario's First Village Houses
text: Around 900 to 1000 AD, the first elliptical houses appeared in southwestern Ontario, forerunners of the Iroquoian longhouse, as people began a settled village life. Corn had gradually entered the diet, and by the end of the 12th century corn, beans, squash and sunflower grew at village sites, often built on hills near a small stream.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (Michel Gagné): Woodland Culture

title: Mimbres Bowls with a Hole
place: Mimbres River Valley, Grant County, New Mexico, USA
text: Between AD 1000 and 1130, Mimbres artists painted bold bowls: about two-thirds with geometric patterns, a third with figures. People buried their dead under their homes with a bowl placed on the skull, its centre tapped out as a kill hole, perhaps to let a spirit rise. Around 1130 the bowls stopped being made.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): On the Trail of the Mimbres

title: Council Chamber Under the Earth
text: Mississippian people at Ocmulgee built a sod-covered earth lodge whose clay floor is carbon-dated to the year 1015. Seats ran around the edge of the room, with a smaller group under the figure of an eagle, so it was probably a meeting place. Crews rebuilt the walls and roof in the late 1930s, but visitors still step onto the original floor.

source.name: National Park Service: Ocmulgee Mounds Earth Lodge

source2.name: National Park Service: Georgia: Ocmulgee National Monument

title: Baker, a Planned Fremont Village
place: Baker Village, near Baker, Nevada, USA
text: Baker Village, the westernmost known Fremont site, was lived in from about 1220 to 1295. Its more than 15 buildings followed a specific plan. Fremont people farmed corn, beans and squash with irrigation, stored food in adobe structures, made grey coiled pottery, and wore moccasins cut from the hock of a deer or sheep leg.

source.name: National Park Service, Great Basin National Park: Fremont Culture

title: The Crow Creek Village Attack
place: Crow Creek Site, near Chamberlain, South Dakota, USA
text: Around 1325, raiders attacked a fortified village in south-central South Dakota. At least 486 people, perhaps 60 percent of the villagers, were later laid in the ditch that ringed the village. Their bones show scalping, skull fractures and other wounds, and the scarcity of young women suggests the attackers took captives. It is grim evidence of warfare on the Plains.

source.name: University of Tennessee dissertation abstract: Willey, Prehistoric Warfare on the Great Plains (Crow Creek)

title: Cliff Houses of Cuarenta Casas
text: In caves of the Sierra Madre Occidental, families built multi-level rooms of adobe and rammed earth, linked by wooden staircases, with small doorways for defence. Part of the trade network of Paquimé, they handled turquoise, Gulf of California shells, copper and exotic feathers. Around the 15th century the site was abandoned, perhaps through climate change, conflict or shifting trade.

source.name: INAH Lugares: Sala Introductoria a la Zona Arqueológica de las Cuarenta Casas

title: The People Who Left Kangaroo Island
place: Lashmars Lagoon, Dudley Peninsula, Kangaroo Island, South Australia, Australia
text: A seven-metre sediment core from Lashmars Lagoon on Kangaroo Island's Dudley Peninsula helped Adelaide University researchers show that the last reliable evidence of people on the island is at least about 5,000 years old, in line with Indigenous oral histories of people leaving. Afterwards fire stayed rare for another 3,000 years in a wetter climate, then increased over the past 2,000 years as it dried.

source.name: Adelaide University News (2026): Ancient sediments on Kangaroo Island show climate change drove fire activity in the absence of people

title: A 5,000-Year-Old Island Midden
place: Maizie Bay, Konomie (North Keppel Island), Queensland, Australia
text: On Konomie (North Keppel Island), off central Queensland, archaeologist Mike Rowland excavated and radiocarbon dated a midden at Maizie Bay to nearly 5,000 years old. The Woppaburra describe their ancestors as sea-faring saltwater people, island specialists who travelled between Konomie, Woppa (Great Keppel) and other islands for seasonal food. Konomie is their spiritual motherland and creation place.

source.name: Australian Museum: Woppaburra people of the Keppel Islands (Woppaburra Land Trust)

title: The Fire-Devil From the Sun
place: Henbury Meteorites Conservation Reserve, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Around 4,700 years ago a large nickel-iron meteoroid blazed across the Central Australian sky, and its fragments carved out more than a dozen craters up to 180 metres across. Luritja elders later said this was where a fire-devil ran down from the sun, set the land ablaze and killed people. Rainwater pooling in the craters was forbidden, for fear the fire-devil would fill drinkers with iron.

source.name: UNSW Newsroom (Duane Hamacher): Finding meteorite impacts in Aboriginal oral tradition

title: Stone Axes on the Move
place: Sydney region, New South Wales, Australia
text: About 4,500 years ago ground-edged stone axes appeared in south-eastern Australia. Usually made from tough igneous or metamorphic rock, they were traded across nations along routes often up to 200 km long, and one axe head in the Australian Museum travelled 1,000 km from its source. Gadigal people in Sydney called them mogo and used them to make bark canoes, cut wood, hunt and build shelters.

source.name: Australian Museum: First Nations timeline

title: The Stranded People of Flinders Island
place: Flinders Island, Furneaux Group, Tasmania, Australia
text: Rising seas flooded the land bridge to Tasmania and left a group of people on Flinders Island in Bass Strait. Radiocarbon-dated middens show people lived there until about 4,500 years ago, then disappeared. Archaeologist Robin Sim found no sign that they had watercraft, so the middens were probably left by an isolated, stranded population, whose decline he linked to a mid-Holocene climate shift.

source.name: ANU Open Research: Robin Sim, The archaeology of isolation? Prehistoric occupation in the Furneaux Group of Islands (PhD thesis, 1998)

title: When the Bullin Shrieked
text: The most recent volcanic activity at Mount Gambier and Mount Schank happened about 4,300 years ago. An Aboriginal story tells of Craitbul and his family, who buried food overnight to cook in earth ovens on Mount Muirhead until the bullin shrieked in the night. They fled to Mount Schank, then Mount Gambier, where their ovens flooded. Researcher Patrick Nunn sees an ancient memory of eruptions.

source.name: The Conversation (Patrick D. Nunn): When the bullin shrieked: Aboriginal memories of volcanic eruptions thousands of years ago

title: Return to Vanderlin Island
place: Vanderlin Island, Sir Edward Pellew Group, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Rising seas cut Vanderlin Island, in the Gulf of Carpentaria, off from the mainland about 6,700 years ago, and people seem to have moved to higher ground. Archaeologists Robin Sim and Lynley Wallis found a gap of several thousand years in its record, then signs that people steadily recolonised these new islands from about 4,200 years ago, with occupation growing after 1,300 years ago.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 67 (2008), Sim and Wallis: Northern Australian offshore island use during the Holocene: the archaeology of Vanderlin Island (ANU Research Portal)

title: Clay-Ball Ovens of the Murray
place: Calperum Station, Riverland, South Australia, Australia
text: On the Murray River floodplain at Calperum Station, Aboriginal people built earth-oven mounds from at least about 4,000 years ago and used them until European invasion. Flinders University researchers and the River Murray and Mallee Aboriginal Corporation excavated six mounds and found charcoal, mussel shell and clay balls that held heat in underground ovens, probably used to cook bulrush tubers for food and fibre.

source.name: ANSTO: Murray River earth mounds reveal Aboriginal cooking practices spanning 4000 years

source2.name: Flinders University Research: Aboriginal earth mounds of the Calperum floodplain (The Holocene, 2022)

dateLabel: Before about 1300 BCE (at least 3,300 years ago)
title: Tasselled Figures Under a Wasp Nest
place: Lawley River area, northwest Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia
text: In the northwest Kimberley, Mambi Gwion figures, also called Tassel Bradshaws, are painted in red with a darker red outline, tassels on the head, clearly drawn fingers and a paunch. A mud wasp nest over a 'cage-shape' motif painted on top of them gave a minimum age of about 3,300 years, which indirectly dates the figures underneath to earlier still.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2016), Ross, Westaway, Travers, Morwood and Hayward: Into the Past: A Step Towards a Robust Kimberley Rock Art Chronology (PMC)

title: Torres Strait's First Gardens
place: Dauar, Murray Islands, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: On Dauar, one of the Murray Islands in eastern Torres Strait, excavations in 1998 to 2000 revealed widespread land clearance and gardening from at least 2,000 years ago, the earliest horticulture yet established in the strait. Plant traces such as starch grains supported this. Sand in Dauar's pottery, dated 2,000 to 700 years ago, points to New Guinea and exchange with Papuan lowland groups.

source.name: JCU ResearchOnline: M. J. Carter, North of the Cape and south of the Fly: the archaeology of settlement and subsistence on the Murray Islands (PhD thesis, 2004)

title: Coming Back to Dabangay
place: Dabangay, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Dabangay, on the island of Mabuyag in western Torres Strait, is one of only two known mid-Holocene sites in the strait. Eleven new radiocarbon dates, combined with nine earlier ones, show people lived there for a long stretch from about 7,200 to 3,200 years ago, then barely used it. Around 1,815 years ago a second sustained settlement began, and it has lasted right up to the present.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 76 (2013), Wright: short report on the re-excavation of Dabangay, Mabuyag (Australian Archaeological Association)

title: Older Than the Linguists Thought
place: Nalkurdalayarrb, Sweers Island, South Wellesley Islands, Queensland, Australia
text: The South Wellesley Islands in the Gulf of Carpentaria are Kaiadilt country, and reaching Bentinck Island from the mainland needs a 10 km open-water crossing. Linguists had suggested people first arrived within the last 1,000 years. But a radiocarbon date from a shell midden at Nalkurdalayarrb on Sweers Island shows occupation by about 1,580 years ago, almost double that estimate.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2010), Ulm et al.: Radiocarbon and linguistic dates for occupation of the South Wellesley Islands (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Island-Made Pots on Mabuyag
place: Mui, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: In 2006 archaeologists digging a one-metre square at Mui, on Mabuyag in western Torres Strait, found two joining pottery sherds 1.35 metres down. Charcoal above and below dated them to about 1,300 to 1,600 years ago. The sand in the clay came from Mabuyag itself, so these thin-walled plain pots were made locally, perhaps after pottery technology reached the region about 1,700 years ago.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2009), Wright and Dickinson: Movement of ideas not materials: locally manufactured pottery on Mabuyag Island (ANU Open Research)

title: The Vanishing Bondi Points
place: Bondi, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: Small stone tools called backed artefacts, or microliths, appeared in Sydney's archaeological record and then disappeared about 1,500 years ago. Once nicknamed Bondi points after the suburb where they were first identified, they have one blunted side, perhaps for gripping or fixing to a spear shaft or gum handle. Microscope and residue studies suggest uses from woodworking and skin-working to spear points and scarification.

source.name: Australian Museum: First Nations timeline

title: Spirits Painted on Dauan
place: Kabadul Kula, Dauan, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Kabadul Kula, a painted boulder shelter on Dauan island just 10 km from the Papua New Guinea coast, holds 47 red ochre paintings, among them a dogai female spirit, dancing figures, a crayfish and canoes. Digging beneath one panel, archaeologists found ochre fragments, most dropped between 1,200 and 1,400 years ago, linked to an early phase of painting. They were then Torres Strait's oldest rock art dates.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 69 (2009): Kabadul Kula and the Antiquity of Torres Strait Rock Art (ANU Open Research)

title: Boulders Tended for Centuries
place: Packsaddle Valley, Pilbara, Western Australia, Australia
text: Near Packsaddle Valley in the Pilbara, people built a stone arrangement complex at least 1,360 years ago. Luminescence dating of sediment trapped beneath the boulders shows they returned to re-erect fallen stones at least twice, about 800 and 480 years ago. Care for the site seems to have ended around 380 years ago, when four boulders toppled over.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 49 (2023), Gliganic, Slack and Meyer: Tending to tradition: Dating stone arrangement maintenance in northwest Australia (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: A Busy Southeast Queensland Coast
text: Radiocarbon dates from Aboriginal sites across southeast Queensland tell a striking story. Archaeologists Sean Ulm and Jay Hall found that big increases in the number of occupied sites, and in how quickly new sites were set up, came only after about 1,200 years ago, and only along the coastal strip. They argued this was a real change in how people lived, not just a quirk of preservation.

source.name: Australian Archaeology '95 (Tempus 6, 1996), Ulm and Hall: Radiocarbon and cultural chronologies in southeast Queensland prehistory (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Where the Old People Lived
place: Wirrngaji, Bentinck Island, South Wellesley Islands, Queensland, Australia
text: Kaiadilt elder Dawn Naranatjil pointed out Wirrngaji, a large shell midden on an old beach ridge on Bentinck Island, as a promising place to dig, 'where the old people used to live'. A small test pit found a thin lower shell layer dated to about 1,048 years ago, beneath a thick upper layer about 860 years old. Glass on the surface shows people lived there into recent times.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2010), Ulm et al.: Radiocarbon and linguistic dates for occupation of the South Wellesley Islands (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Dugong Feasts at Goemu Village
place: Goemu village, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Goemu village on Mabuyag has one of the largest midden deposits recorded in Torres Strait. One of its long mounded middens formed about 950 to 1,000 years ago, from a way of life centred on hunting dugong and turtle, topped up with fishing and shellfishing on nearby reef flats and mangroves. Land snails show that shade trees once grew where grassland is now.

source.name: Memoirs of the Queensland Museum, Cultural Heritage Series (2015), McNiven et al.: Midden formation and marine specialisation at Goemu village, Mabuyag (Monash University)

title: Mountains of Shell at Weipa
place: Mandjungaar, Weipa Peninsula, Cape York, Queensland, Australia
text: More than 500 shell mounds dot the Weipa area of western Cape York Peninsula. At Mandjungaar, at the request of Ndrua'angayth custodians, archaeologists dated a dome-shaped mound and found people began building it about 800 years ago, adding to it for centuries. Most shells came from one bivalve, Tegillarca granosa, from intertidal mudflats. A neighbouring mound stands 4 metres high.

source.name: Queensland Archaeological Research 21 (2018), Morrison, Wight and Evans: Report on excavation of a shell mound site at Mandjungaar

dateLabel: Before about 1360 CE (at least 650 years ago)
title: A Star-Yam on the Shelter Wall
place: Upper Bush Spirit Creek, northwest Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia
text: At the headwaters of Bush Spirit Creek in the northwest Kimberley, a large motif painted in a 'star-yam' form covers the back wall of a big rockshelter. Mud wasps later built a nest over it, and luminescence dating of the nest gave a minimum age of about 650 years. The method reads a light-sensitive signal that builds up while grains stay covered.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2016), Ross, Westaway, Travers, Morwood and Hayward: Into the Past: A Step Towards a Robust Kimberley Rock Art Chronology (PMC)

title: A Lapita Village on Stilts
place: Talepakemalai, Eloaua Island, Mussau Islands, Papua New Guinea
text: No later than 1350 BCE, Lapita people on Eloaua Island built houses on stilts over a shallow lagoon. The waterlogged mud kept many of their wooden posts and stakes from rotting. Archaeologists have recovered more than 44,000 pieces of pottery, nearly 95,000 animal remains and 1.43 tonnes of discarded shells from this village, which was probably lived in for 400 to 500 years.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita database: Talepakemalai (ECA)

title: Fiji's First Village
place: Bourewa, Rove Peninsula, Viti Levu, Fiji
text: Fiji's earliest known settlement, Bourewa, was first lived in about 1100 BCE by Lapita voyagers. They built houses on stilt platforms along a sand barrier, with a coral reef on one side and a tidal inlet on the other. At first they lived mostly by gathering food from the sea. Gardens of taro and yam came about 300 years later.

source.name: Nunn, P. D. (2009), Geographical Research 47(3): Geographical influences on settlement-location choices by initial colonizers: a case study of the Fiji Islands

title: Lapita Reaches the Mainland
place: Caution Bay, Central Province, Papua New Guinea
text: About 2,900 years ago, Lapita seafarers settled at Caution Bay on the south coast of Papua New Guinea. The sites, reported in 2011, were the first known Lapita settlements on the New Guinea mainland. These marine specialists ate shellfish, fish and sea turtles, and left behind pottery, shell armbands, stone adzes and obsidian tools as they spread westward along the coast.

source.name: McNiven et al. (2011), Australian Archaeology 72: New direction in human colonisation of the Pacific: Lapita settlement of south coast New Guinea

title: Potters Come to Yule Island
place: Oposisi, Yule Island, Central Province, Papua New Guinea
text: About 2,000 years ago, pottery-making villagers appear to have spread along the Papuan south coast, and the village of Oposisi on Yule Island is key to understanding them. New radiocarbon dates confirm its story began around then. Diggers also found much more obsidian than expected, carried from Fergusson Island 600 km to the east, a sign of strong long-distance links.

source.name: Allen, Summerhayes, Mandui and Leavesley (2010), Journal of Pacific Archaeology 2(1): New Data from Oposisi: Implications for the Early Papuan Pottery Phase

title: The Blast That Made Rabaul Harbour
place: Rabaul Caldera, East New Britain, Papua New Guinea
text: Around 683 CE, a catastrophic eruption at Rabaul ranked 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, with pyroclastic flows and a caldera explosion. The 8 by 14 km caldera is open to the east, where the sea floods in as Blanche Bay. This sheltered harbour later became home to Rabaul, the island's largest city until a major eruption in 1994.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program: Rabaul

title: Tongan Glass Reaches Tikopia
text: Archaeologists chemically traced volcanic glass dug up on Tikopia, a Polynesian Outlier island. Its first settlers kept sailing back to a Melanesian homeland, but long voyages later dwindled. Then, about 765 years before present, glass from Tonga began to arrive. Such imports were surprisingly rare, and the researchers suggest Tongans may have targeted Tikopia for political expansion.

source.name: McCoy et al. (2020), Quaternary Research 98: Obsidian and volcanic glass artifact evidence for long-distance voyaging to the Polynesian Outlier island of Tikopia

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of the Solomon Islands

title: Kuwae: Legend of a Lost Island
place: Kuwae caldera, between Epi and Tongoa, Shefa, Vanuatu
text: Between Epi and Tongoa islands lies Kuwae, a mostly underwater caldera 6 by 12 km wide. Local legends of a great eruption, plus radiocarbon dates from pumice flows, have been linked to a peak in ice cores dated to 1452 CE. Other scientists think the deposits came from smaller eruptions, and that the ice spike came from another, unknown South Pacific volcano.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program: Kuwae

title: Naming the Islands of Solomon
text: In 1568 the Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña, who had sailed from Peru, became the first European to reach these islands. False rumours spread that he had found gold, and even the place where the biblical King Solomon got gold for his temple, so they were called the Islas de Solomón. Later Spanish voyages in 1595 and 1606 could not find them again.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of the Solomon Islands

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Álvaro de Mendaña de Neira

title: The Time of Darkness
place: Long Island, Madang Province, Papua New Guinea
text: Around 1660, Long Island exploded in a catastrophic eruption, rated 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. Ash fell across the New Guinea Highlands, inspiring legends of a 'Time of Darkness'. Part of the volcano collapsed, and today its huge caldera is filled by Lake Wisdom, with a small newer cone, Motmot Island, rising from the water.

source.name: Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program: Long Island

title: Cook Lands at Balade
text: Melanesian people had lived on this island since about 3000 BCE when, in 1774, the British navigator James Cook landed at Balade on its east coast. He named it New Caledonia after his father's native Scotland. Regular contact with Europeans only began in 1841, when sandalwood traders from Australia introduced islanders to iron.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of New Caledonia

title: The Vanishing of La Pérouse
place: Vanikoro, Santa Cruz Islands, Temotu, Solomon Islands
text: After leaving Botany Bay in March 1788, the French explorer La Pérouse and his ships La Boussole and Astrolabe simply vanished. Nothing more was known until 1826–27, when Peter Dillon found evidence that the ships had been near Vanikoro. In 1828 Dumont d'Urville saw wreckage there and heard from islanders that about 30 men from the ships had been killed on shore, while other well-armed sailors escaped.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jean-François de Galaup, comte de La Pérouse

title: The Chief of Bau Converts
text: Bau is a tiny island off Viti Levu, yet its rulers grew mighty in the 1800s, helped by trade wealth and muskets. By the 1850s Bau dominated western Fiji under Cakobau, whose great rival was the Tongan chief Maʻafu. In 1854 Cakobau became a Christian, bringing most Fijians under the influence of Methodist missionaries.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Fiji

title: The Kanak Uprising of 1878
place: West coast from Bouloupari to Poya, New Caledonia
text: In 1878 Kanak people rose up along New Caledonia's west coast, from Bouloupari to Poya, angry at land seizures and settlers' cattle feeding in their gardens. The revolt seriously threatened French rule, but the French crushed it by destroying villages and crops. Louise Michel, a deported Paris revolutionary who had befriended the Kanaks, supported the uprising.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of New Caledonia

source2.name: Encyclopedia of Modern Europe (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com: Michel, Louise (Susan K. Foley)

title: The Leonidas Reaches Levuka
text: On 14 May 1879 the ship Leonidas reached Levuka with the first indentured labourers from India, after a harrowing 72-day voyage from Calcutta. Cholera and smallpox broke out on board, and 17 of the 498 men, women and children died before arriving. About 60,000 Indians would follow. 'Girmit' comes from the 'agreement' they signed.

source.name: Lowy Institute, The Interpreter (Lisa Singh, Australia India Institute, University of Melbourne): Two dates, one wound: what Girmit Day means for Fiji's future

title: Two Empires, One Government
text: In 1906 Britain and France agreed to rule the New Hebrides, now Vanuatu, together as an Anglo-French condominium. British and French resident commissioners in Port-Vila each kept charge of their own citizens while jointly ruling the islanders. For most ni-Vanuatu, though, little changed: missionaries and planters remained the Europeans they actually dealt with.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Vanuatu

title: An Anthropologist in a Tent
place: Kiriwina, Trobriand Islands, Milne Bay, Papua New Guinea
text: In 1915 the Polish-born scholar Bronisław Malinowski began two long stays in the Trobriand Islands. He lived in a tent among the people, learned to speak their language fluently and wrote down what he saw as it happened. His Trobriand studies of exchange, farming, family life, magic and myth helped found modern social anthropology.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bronisław Malinowski (Raymond William Firth)

title: Basiana and the Kwaio Revolt
text: In 1927, Kwaio men on Malaita killed government tax collectors, led by a man named Basiana. Colonial authorities struck back with a savage punitive expedition, backed by an Australian warship, that burned and looted villages and killed many Kwaio. Basiana and some of his companions were hanged, and his young sons were forced to watch.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of the Solomon Islands

title: A Hidden Valley Full of People
place: Wahgi Valley, Western Highlands, Papua New Guinea
text: In the early 1930s, outsiders met nearly a million Highlanders previously unknown to Europeans. On 15 February 1933, gold-seeking explorers Mick and Danny Leahy looked down on the crowded Wahgi Valley from Mount Erimbari. Mick's photographs and films of these meetings, some of them violent, became the 1983 documentary First Contact.

source.name: Australian Dictionary of Biography (ANU): Leahy, Michael James (Mick)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Papua New Guinea, The colonial period

title: A Message Carved on a Coconut
place: Blackett Strait, Western Province, Solomon Islands
text: In August 1943 a Japanese destroyer rammed the US patrol boat PT-109, commanded by John F. Kennedy, in Blackett Strait. Two Solomon Islander scouts, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, found the stranded crew, and Gasa showed Kennedy how to scratch a message into a green coconut husk: '11 alive ... need small boat'. Rescue boats later met Kennedy at a prearranged spot.

source.name: Australian War Memorial: Coastwatcher Arthur Reginald Evans and the rescue of John F. Kennedy and PT-109

title: The New Hebrides Become Vanuatu
text: On 30 July 1980 the New Hebrides became the independent Republic of Vanuatu, ending Anglo-French rule. Just before, Jimmy Stevens of the Na-Griamel Party had tried and failed to make Espiritu Santo a separate country. Father Walter Lini of the Vanua'aku Pati, meaning 'Our Land Party', became the first prime minister.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Vanuatu

title: New Caledonia Votes on Its Future
text: On 4 November 2018 New Caledonians voted on independence from France, the first of up to three referendums promised by the 1998 Nouméa Accord. About 56 percent chose to stay with France. The margin was much narrower than expected, raising the hopes of independence supporters, and a second vote in 2020 was closer still, at about 53 percent.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of New Caledonia

title: Bougainville Votes to Leave
text: In late 2019, after three weeks of voting with 85 percent turnout, 97.7 percent of Bougainville's voters chose independence from Papua New Guinea. The vote was promised after peace ended a 1988–1997 conflict, centred on the Panguna gold and copper mine, in which about 20,000 people died. The result was non-binding: Papua New Guinea's parliament has the final say.

source.name: The Conversation (Anna Powles, Massey University): Bougainville has voted to become a new country, but the journey to independence is not yet over

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Papua New Guinea, Attempts at secession

title: Lost Birds of Ofu
place: Toʻaga, Ofu Island, Manuʻa, American Samoa
text: The Toʻaga site on Ofu holds a record of people living there from about 3,200 to 1,900 years ago, including an unbroken run of pottery dating back over 3,000 years. Its ancient rubbish heaps hold the bones of birds that no longer live on the island, such as megapodes, shearwaters and the Tahiti petrel, driven to extinction there by human activity.

source.name: National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa: The To'aga Site

title: Palau's Ancient Rockshelter Cemetery
place: Chelechol ra Orrak, Rock Islands, Palau
text: Under later layers of everyday living, archaeologists at the Chelechol ra Orrak rockshelter in Palau found an extensive cemetery holding at least 50 people. Radiocarbon dating and statistical modelling show burials going back about 3,000 years, making it one of the earliest cemetery sites in the Pacific Islands and one of the only cemeteries in Remote Oceania from the first stages of settlement.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Fitzpatrick and Jew, Radiocarbon dating and Bayesian modelling of one of Remote Oceania's oldest cemeteries at Chelechol ra Orrak, Palau (2018)

title: Settlers Spread to Haʻapai
text: Tonga was the first part of Polynesia to be settled, beginning on Tongatapu. Dating of charcoal and coral tools shows that Lapita colonists reached the central Haʻapai islands only 70 to 90 years later. There, the decorated Lapita pottery vanished startlingly fast, within 32 to 49 years, as people shifted toward the ancestral Polynesian way of life.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Burley et al., Bayesian Modeling and Chronological Precision for Polynesian Settlement of Tonga (2015)

title: The Green Pyramids of Palau
text: Palauan oral tradition says a huge serpent wound around the hills of Babeldaob and shaped their terraces. Researchers from Kiel University and the German Archaeological Institute found that people built them by hand over generations, perhaps starting around 500 BCE. Planting pits point to gardening on the terraces, while summits up to ten metres high may have held burials of the elite.

source.name: Kiel University press release (idw): The green pyramids of Palau (2022)

title: When Tonga Stopped Making Pots
text: After decorated Lapita pottery faded, people in Tonga kept making plain pots in many shapes, including jars, bowls and cups. Using 44 radiocarbon dates from 13 sites across Tonga, archaeologists found that this Polynesian Plainware phase ended no later than about 2,350 years ago, after only about 350 years. Why potting stopped is still a mystery; the researchers call existing explanations mostly speculation.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Burley, Connaughton and Clark, Early cessation of ceramic production for ancestral Polynesian society in Tonga (2018)

title: Samoans Sail to the Gilberts
text: The first people of the Gilbert Islands and Banaba came from Southeast Asia by way of Micronesia. Around the 14th century, the southern islands received a wave of newcomers from Samoa. Soon afterwards the islanders adopted a gerontocratic style of government, meaning one based on rule by the elders. Much later, Spanish explorers sighted some of the islands in the 16th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Kiribati

title: Toolmakers High on Mauna Kea
place: Mauna Kea, Island of Hawaiʻi, USA
text: High on Mauna Kea, mostly between 11,000 and 12,400 feet, specialist adze makers quarried basalt and shaped stone tools. Radiocarbon dates show the quarry in use by 1000 CE, and more intensively after 1400. Workers brought food and clothing and lived on site, usually from July to October, beside more than 35 shrines to the mountain's gods.

source.name: National Park Service: Mauna Kea Adz Quarry

title: The Hill of Long Life
place: Puʻuloa, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, Hawaiʻi, USA
text: Puʻuloa, whose name can be translated 'Hill of long life', holds over 23,000 petroglyphs pecked into lava dated between 1200 and 1450 CE. Most are cupules, or small holes. A 1914 account describes the lava mound as a place to leave a newborn's umbilical cord, believed to ensure the child a long life. Other carvings show people, canoe sails and feathered capes.

source.name: National Park Service, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park: Puʻuloa Petroglyphs

title: Spanish Ships Reach the Marquesas
text: In April 1595 Álvaro de Mendaña sailed from Callao, Peru. After only five weeks at sea his ships sighted islands, and he at first claimed he had reached his goal. Realising his mistake, he named them Las Marquesas de Mendoza after his Peruvian sponsor. The islanders were treated cruelly: about two hundred were killed, often shot down, Queirós reported, for sport.

source.name: Princeton University Library, Pacific Voyages: Mendaña and Queirós

title: A Safe Haven for Kapu Breakers
place: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau, Island of Hawaiʻi, USA
text: Hōnaunau became a royal centre in the early 1600s. Breaking a kapu, a sacred law, could mean death, but a lawbreaker or defeated warrior who reached the puʻuhonua was safe. A great wall of stones fitted without mortar marks its sacred space, and the Hale o Keawe temple held the bones of 23 aliʻi (chiefs), giving it immense mana.

source.name: National Park Service: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau park brochure

title: A Mission Lands at Hagåtña
text: In June 1668 the supply boat San Diego arrived off Hagåtña, Guam's main village, carrying the Jesuit Diego Luis de San Vitores. Maga'låhi Kepuha of Hagåtña became the first adult CHamoru baptised and gave land for the first Catholic church. The welcome did not last: defiant CHamorus resisted, but were eventually overpowered by the colonisers' weapons.

source.name: Guampedia: Father Diego Luis de San Vitores (Tanya M. Champaco Mendiola)

title: Mai Sails to England
text: Mai, called 'Omai' in England, came from the island of Raʻiātea. In 1773 he sailed to England aboard the Adventure, part of James Cook's second voyage. The first Polynesian visitor to Britain, he became a celebrity, mixing with royalty and the elite and posing for leading artists. In 1776 he returned to Polynesia, where he died a few years later.

source.name: Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge: Journeys with Mai

title: Prince Lee Boo Goes to London
text: In 1783 the British packet ship Antelope was wrecked near Palau. Its crew spent about three months building a schooner from the wreck, the first long contact between Europeans and the people of Ulong and Koror. Lee Boo, second son of Abba Thulle, sailed to England with Captain Henry Wilson, briefly became a celebrity, and died of smallpox there in 1784.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Portrait of Captain Henry Wilson, 1740-1810

source2.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Prince Lee Boo Second Son of Abba Thulle (print, 1788)

title: Kaʻahumanu Breaks the Kapu
place: Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, Island of Hawaiʻi, USA
text: When Kamehameha I died in 1819, his favourite queen Kaʻahumanu became kuhina nui, or premier, to his successor Liholiho. She worked to overcome the religious taboos placed on women and won a major victory by persuading the new king to eat publicly with women. That shared meal of the king and his father's wives began the collapse of the kapu system.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kaahumanu

source2.name: National Park Service: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau park brochure

title: Rapa Nui Joins Chile
place: Hanga Roa, Rapa Nui (Easter Island), Chile
text: On 9 September 1888 Captain Policarpo Toro of the Chilean corvette Angamos took possession of Rapa Nui for Chile, and King Atamu Tekena and the Council of Chiefs signed the act of cession. Chile's attempt to settle colonists went so badly that they left in 1892. From 1895 the state leased the island for almost sixty years to a company that ran it as a vast sheep ranch.

source.name: Memoria Chilena (Biblioteca Nacional de Chile): Incorporándola al territorio chileno

title: 21,269 Hawaiians Say No
text: In 1897 two Hawaiian patriotic leagues, one for men and one for women, gathered 21,269 signatures of Native Hawaiians against annexation by the United States. Four delegates carried the 556-page petition to Washington, where it was read to the Senate on 9 December. The annexation treaty was defeated, although Hawaiʻi was later taken over by a joint resolution needing only a simple majority.

source.name: U.S. National Archives: Petition Against the Annexation of Hawaii (1897)

title: The Island That Was Mined Away
text: Soon after high-grade phosphate was discovered on Banaba in 1900, the Pacific Phosphate Company began mining. By the time mining stopped in 1979, twenty-one million tons had been removed, thirteen million of them spread across Australian farms. Colonial authorities told the Banabans their homeland had become uninhabitable, and most were relocated to Rabi Island in Fiji in December 1945.

source.name: Brookings Institution: Jane McAdam, Relocation across borders: a prescient warning in the Pacific (2013)

source2.name: Te Papa Tongarewa, Collections Online: T-shirt (Banaba The Rock of Micronesia)

title: A Great Orator Sent Into Exile
text: Lauaki Namulauʻulu Mamoe was famed for his mastery of history and legend and his skill as a speaker and negotiator. He led the Mau of Pule, named after influential orator groups on Savaiʻi. In 1909 the German governor, Wilhelm Solf, had him taken into custody, and he, nine other chiefs and their families were exiled to Saipan. Lauaki died of dysentery on the voyage home.

source.name: Te Papa blog: Safua Akeli, Recalling the splendour of Sāmoan oratory: Lauaki Namulauʻulu Mamoe (2012)

title: Black Saturday in Apia
text: On 28 December 1929 a peaceful crowd paraded through Apia to welcome home members of the Mau who had been exiled in New Zealand. A New Zealand police sergeant fired a machine gun to deter the crowd, and other police fired rifles; 11 Samoans and one police officer died. The dying Mau leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III urged: 'If I die, peace must be maintained at any price.'

source.name: Te Ao Māori News: Black Saturday, remembering 95 years of Samoan resistance and loss (2024)

title: Pouvanaa's Dream of a Tahitian Republic
text: In 1957 France gave more powers to French Polynesia's Territorial Assembly. The next year Pouvanaa a Oopa, vice president of the Council of Government, announced a plan to break away from France and form an independent Tahitian republic. He was arrested and the movement collapsed, but calls for self-rule continued, and in 1984 the territory became autonomous.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of French Polynesia

title: Bombs Beneath Mururoa
place: Mururoa Atoll, Tuamotu Islands, French Polynesia
text: France began testing nuclear weapons on Mururoa in 1963, and under worldwide pressure moved its tests underground in 1975. Testing was suspended in 1992, but President Jacques Chirac ordered it resumed in 1995. Amid widespread opposition France exploded a bomb under Mururoa, and rioting followed in the territory. The last device was detonated in January 1996.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of French Polynesia

title: A Back-Up Homeland for Kiribati
text: Rising sea levels, thought to be caused by climate change, threaten to flood and eventually submerge Kiribati's low-lying islands. The government has looked at ways to keep its citizens safe, from helping skilled workers emigrate to building artificial islets. In 2014 it bought about 20 square km of land on Vanua Levu in Fiji, a possible future homeland that could meanwhile grow extra food.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Kiribati

title: Volcanic Glass on a Faraway Island
place: Low Flat, Raoul Island, Kermadec Islands, New Zealand
text: Raoul Island in the Kermadecs lies about 800 kilometres from mainland New Zealand, yet archaeologists found obsidian there from Mayor Island (Tūhua) in the Bay of Plenty. It shows that at least one voyage reached Raoul from Aotearoa. Radiocarbon dating suggests people lived briefly at the Low Flat site and only during the 14th century.

source.name: Archaeology in Oceania: The prehistoric chronology of Raoul Island, the Kermadec Group (Higham, 1997)

source2.name: Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand: Long-distance prehistoric two-way voyaging, the case for Aotearoa and Hawaiki (P. Adds, 2012)

title: Tarawera's Ash Clock
place: Mt Tarawera, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand
text: Around 1314, Mt Tarawera erupted the pale Kaharoa tephra, the most recent rhyolite eruption in Aotearoa, probably during the southern winter. Its ash spread over much of the eastern and northern North Island. Archaeologists use the layer as a time marker: only one trace of people has turned up beneath it, a seed gnawed by a Pacific rat on the Coromandel Peninsula.

source.name: New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics: Tephrochronology in Aotearoa New Zealand (Lowe and others, 2021)

title: A Voyaging Canoe With a Turtle
place: Anaweka, north-west Nelson, South Island, New Zealand
text: A storm on the remote north-western tip of the South Island uncovered a 6-metre section of an ocean-sailing canoe, carved from a single mataī timber and caulked with tōtara bark. Dated to about 1400, the Anaweka waka was built in Aotearoa as an early adaptation to a new land. A sea turtle carved on its hull links it with wider Polynesian culture and art.

source.name: PNAS (via PubMed Central): An early sophisticated East Polynesian voyaging canoe discovered on New Zealand's coast

title: The Last of the Moa
text: Using more than 600 radiocarbon dates, a team including George Perry of the University of Auckland showed that moa vanished quickly and at about the same time across New Zealand. Hunting began around 1314. The giant flightless birds were gone from the South Island lowlands by the end of the 1300s, and total extinction probably came by about 1425.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): The Arrival of People Doomed New Zealand's Moa

title: A Village Sealed in a Swamp
place: Kohika, Rangitaiki Plains, near Matatā, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand
text: Around the late 17th century, people of the Bay of Plenty lived at Kohika, a palisaded swamp pā that may have been ringed by water. A massive flood ended village life, and the waterlogged ground preserved its wood: digging sticks, paddles, bowls, combs, carved house posts and pātaka parts. Most of its obsidian came from Mayor Island (Tūhua).

source.name: Department of Conservation: Archaeology of the Bay of Plenty (Garry Law), section 10.5 Kohika

source2.name: Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga: Kohika Pā

title: Tupaia, the Voice of the Endeavour
text: When Cook's Endeavour reached Aotearoa, the only person aboard who could speak with Māori was Tupaia, a Polynesian priest and navigator. He missed the first landing at Tūranga-nui, where the chief Te Maro was shot, but later calmed many tense meetings. Oral histories show Māori thought Tupaia was the ship's captain, and when Cook returned, people wept to learn he had died.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: On tour with Tupaia

source2.name: Te Papa Collections Online: Tupaia - priest and navigator

title: A French Camp on Moturua
place: Waipao Bay, Moturua Island, Bay of Islands, New Zealand
text: From May to July 1772, French explorer Marion du Fresne camped on Moturua Island, setting up a hospital, a forge and officers' tents. Relations broke down when du Fresne and some crew were attacked while fishing in Te Kuri's cove in Manawaora Bay. The French retaliated by destroying Paeroa pā, where an estimated 250 Māori warriors died.

source.name: Department of Conservation: Moturua Island Scenic Reserve

source2.name: Department of Conservation: European discovery, heritage topics

title: Pinpointing Aotearoa in Dusky Sound
place: Astronomer's Point, Tamatea/Dusky Sound, Fiordland, New Zealand
text: In autumn 1773 Cook's Resolution spent five weeks in Tamatea/Dusky Sound. The crew cleared about an acre of forest, set up a forge and brewed beer from rimu and mānuka leaves to fight scurvy. Astronomer William Wales tested a copy of Harrison's H4 chronometer here, making New Zealand the most accurately located place on the globe at that time.

source.name: Department of Conservation: Astronomer's Point, historic sites in Fiordland National Park

title: Tuki's Chalk Map of Home
text: In May 1793 two Northland chiefs, Tuki Tahua and Ngahuruhuru, were kidnapped aboard the Daedalus and taken to Norfolk Island to teach convicts flax-working. They knew little of it, since flax work was a women's skill. Instead Tuki chalked a map of Aotearoa on a floor, showing the spirits' pathway running the length of the North Island to Te Reinga.

source.name: University of Otago Library, Hocken Collections: Reproduced map of New Zealand drawn in chalk by Tuki Tahua and Ngahuruhuru

source2.name: University of Otago Library: He Tirohanga Ki Muri, general items

title: Ruatara's Christmas at Oihi
place: Oihi Bay, Rangihoua, Bay of Islands, New Zealand
text: Ruatara, chief of Rangihoua pā, prepared for Samuel Marsden's first sermon by fencing half an acre and building a pulpit draped in black Māori cloth, with upturned canoes for seats. At 10am on Christmas Day 1814 Marsden preached while Ruatara interpreted for his people. Then three hundred warriors danced a furious haka around the preacher.

source.name: Department of Conservation: Oihi Mission Station 1814-1832, Historic Heritage Assessment (Melina Goddard, 2010)

source2.name: Department of Conservation: Rangihoua Heritage Park

title: Rangatira Declare Independence
place: Bay of Islands, Northland, New Zealand
text: On 28 October 1835, 34 northern rangatira signed He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence; by 1839, 52 had signed, including Te Wherowhero, later the first Māori King. It declared Aotearoa an independent Māori state where foreigners could not make laws. Eruera Pare Hongi, a relation of Hongi Hika, wrote out the Māori copy that was signed.

source.name: Archives New Zealand: The Declaration of the Independence of New Zealand

title: The Quake That Lifted Wellington
place: Wairarapa Fault, near Martinborough, New Zealand
text: At 9:11 pm on 23 January 1855, the Wairarapa Fault ruptured in a magnitude 8.2 earthquake that killed between 7 and 9 people. At Muka Muka on Palliser Bay the ground rose 2.7 metres, and Wellington's harbour shoreline changed considerably. The Basin Reserve sports ground sits on land lifted from a waterway, and a huge slip cut the track to Petone.

source.name: GeoNet (GNS Science): M 8.2 Wairarapa, Tue, Jan 23 1855

title: A Māori King at the River Meeting
text: In the 1850s the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement, grew to counter European demands for land. Pōtatau Te Wherowhero was chosen as king, a role he eventually agreed to accept, and in 1858 Ngāruawāhia became his capital. The site lies where the Waikato and Waipā rivers meet, in the heartland of Waikato-Tainui, and the Kīngitanga flag flew from a flagstaff there.

source.name: Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga: Pōtatau Te Wherowhero Monument and Kīngitanga Reserve

title: Four Seats for Māori
text: The Māori Representation Act 1867 created four Māori electorates: three in the North Island and one covering the South Island, Stewart Island and nearby islands. Māori men aged 21 and over could vote with no property qualification, twelve years before non-Māori men. Meant to last only five years, the seats were extended indefinitely in 1876, and the first election came in 1868.

source.name: New Zealand Parliament Library: Origins of the Māori seats

title: Frozen Lamb Sails for London
text: Carcasses from Totara Estate near Oamaru were carried by rail in the cool early morning to Port Chalmers and frozen aboard the ship Dunedin, fitted with a coal-powered Bell Coleman freezing plant. It sailed for London on 15 February 1882 with 5000 lamb carcasses and arrived on 24 May with only one carcass condemned, launching New Zealand's frozen meat industry.

source.name: RNZ: Meat industry celebrates 140 years since first frozen shipment to the UK

source2.name: Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga: Totara Estate

title: The Natives Kick Off a Marathon Tour
text: On 23 June 1888 Joe Warbrick's 'Natives' rugby team, Māori players later joined by five Pākehā, played its first match in Napier, beating Hawke's Bay 5 to nil. By the time they came home in August 1889 they had played 107 matches in New Zealand, Australia and Britain, winning 78. Their pre-match haka and black jerseys aroused curiosity overseas.

source.name: New Zealand Rugby Museum: June 23, 1888, NZ 'Natives' tour begins

source2.name: Te Papa: Before the All Blacks, the New Zealand 'Natives'

title: The Deadly Flu of 1918
text: The influenza pandemic reached New Zealand in October 1918 and killed an estimated 9,000 people. Māori suffered especially severe losses, with about 2,500 deaths out of some 50,000 people. In Auckland, temporary hospitals sprang up across the city, schools and church services shut, and victims were taken from a temporary mortuary at Victoria Park to Waikumete Cemetery.

source.name: Auckland War Memorial Museum: Influenza Pandemic 1918

source2.name: Te Papa Collections Online: 1918 influenza pandemic

title: Christmas Eve at Tangiwai
place: Tangiwai, Whangaehu River, Ruapehu District, New Zealand
text: At 10:21pm on 24 December 1953, a dam of volcanic tephra holding back Mt Ruapehu's crater lake gave way, with no eruption that day. A lahar rushed down the Whangaehu River and weakened the rail bridge at Tangiwai just minutes before the Wellington to Auckland night express arrived. The bridge buckled, killing 151 of the 285 people aboard.

source.name: GeoNet (GNS Science): 70th Anniversary of the Tangiwai Railway Disaster

title: Not One More Acre
place: Te Hāpua, Far North, New Zealand
text: On 14 September 1975, about 50 marchers set out from the far north settlement of Te Hāpua, led by 79-year-old Dame Whina Cooper and Te Rōpū Matakite o Aotearoa. Under the call 'Not One Acre More', they walked all the way to Parliament in Wellington. On 13 October an estimated 5,000 marchers handed Prime Minister Bill Rowling a petition with 60,000 signatures.

source.name: Te Papa: Māori Land March, 1975

title: Bombs in Auckland Harbour
text: On 10 July 1985, French government agents attached bombs to the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior at Marsden Wharf in Tāmaki Makaurau, Auckland, and sank it. Photographer Fernando Pereira was killed. France feared the ship would draw attention to its nuclear testing at Moruroa atoll. Agents Alain Mafart and Dominique Prieur were each sentenced to 10 years for manslaughter.

source.name: Te Papa blog: You can't sink a rainbow (Kirstie Ross, 2015)

source2.name: RNZ: Rainbow Warrior bombing 40th anniversary

title: I Am the River, the River Is Me
text: On 16 March 2017, Parliament passed a law giving the Whanganui River the status of a legal person, Te Awa Tupua. Local iwi had fought for over 160 years for this recognition. Their saying explains why: 'Ko au te awa, ko te awa ko au', meaning 'I am the river and the river is me.' Te Urewera had gained the same status in 2014.

source.name: RNZ: Whanganui River to gain legal personhood

title: Justice at Last for Moriori
place: Kōpinga Marae, Rēkohu (Chatham Islands), New Zealand
text: In 1835 a sixth of the Moriori people of Rēkohu were killed and the survivors enslaved. From 1862 Moriori wrote to Governor George Grey seeking freedom, and in 1988 they filed claims. On 14 February 2020, descendants met at Kōpinga Marae to sign a settlement with the Crown that includes an agreed account of their history, an apology and $18 million.

source.name: RNZ: Moriori Treaty settlement signed

title: The Body in the Andøya Bog
