text: In 1936 a clothed skeleton, wrapped in a blanket and covered with birch bark, turned up in a bog at Skjoldehamn. The body had been laid on a reindeer pelt resting on birch sticks, and the grave dates to the 11th century, probably its later half. Its costume and pewter ornaments point to a Sámi identity, though the burial mixes several traditions.

source.name: Viking (University of Oslo journal), Asgeir Svestad: Svøpt i myra – Synspunkter på Skjoldehamnfunnets etniske og kulturelle tilknytning

title: The World's Northernmost Fortress
text: Norway's King Håkon V probably set up a fortress at Vardø around 1307, to protect the Norwegian fishing settlement, assert the crown's rule over Finnmark and guard against Karelian raids. The first firm written evidence for it dates from 1339–1340. Today's eight-pointed star fort was built in 1734–1738, and Vardøhus is counted as the northernmost fortress in the world.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Vardøhus festning

title: A Border That Wasn't a Line
place: Finnmark and the Kola Peninsula (Norway and Russia)
text: On June 3, 1326, Novgorod and Norway made peace after decades of fighting in the far north. Instead of drawing a clear frontier, their treaty created a buffer zone, the "common districts," where both sides could tax the Indigenous Sámi and exploit the region's fish and fur. The arrangement lasted until the present Norwegian-Russian border was set in 1826.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Treaty of Novgorod

title: A Stone Church Behind Walls
text: Around 1400 a Gothic stone church went up at Trondenes. It is Norway's northernmost medieval stone church, and in the Middle Ages it was ringed by a high wall with defensive towers; part of the wall and two towers still stand. Its highlights are three altarpieces made in the Hanseatic city of Lübeck in the late 1400s and early 1500s.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Trondenes kirke

title: Gold-Boiling Mangazeya
place: Mangazeya, Taz River, Yamalo-Nenets Okrug, Russia
text: In 1601 Mangazeya was built on the river Taz, beyond the Arctic Circle; Moscow's State Historical Museum calls it the first Russian city in the Arctic. Nicknamed "gold-boiling Mangazeya," it remained a centre of the fur trade until the mid-1600s. Excavations at its hillfort have turned up a chess set, beads, cases for seals and a gingerbread mould shaped like a fish.

source.name: State Historical Museum, Moscow: Siberia in the 16th–17th centuries (hall guide)

title: Blubber Town at Almost 80° North
text: In the years before 1620, Dutch whalers built up Smeerenburg, "blubber town," as their main Arctic base, boiling whale blubber in ovens on the beach. Legends spoke of up to 20,000 inhabitants, but excavations suggest about 200 workers. The remains of 12 ovens and 101 whalers' graves are still there; the station fell into disuse in the later 1600s when the whales left.

source.name: Norwegian Polar Institute, Cruise Handbook for Svalbard: Smeerenburg

source2.name: AECO site guidelines: Smeerenburg

title: Measuring the Shape of the Earth
place: Tornio River valley, Lapland, on the Finland–Sweden border
text: In 1736 the French mathematician Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis led an expedition to Lapland to measure the length of a degree along the meridian, working in the River Tornio valley into 1737. The result backed Newton: the Earth is flattened at the poles. It was the first significant triangulation survey in Northern Europe, and Voltaire later mocked Maupertuis as the "earth flattener."

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis

source2.name: National Land Survey of Finland: Struve Geodetic Arc, information for tourists

title: One of Earth's Loneliest Islands
text: In 1739 the French navigator Jean-Baptiste-Charles Bouvet de Lozier found the island that now bears his name, one of the most isolated on Earth, about 2,400 km southwest of the Cape of Good Hope. Volcanic and almost entirely ice-covered, it is ringed by ice cliffs that make landing extremely difficult. Norway annexed it in 1930 and made it a nature reserve in 1971.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bouvet Island

title: Revolt in Kautokeino
text: On November 8, 1852, Sámi followers of the Laestadian revival, a movement that preached against alcohol, stormed the trading post in Kautokeino and set it on fire. The trader and the local lensmann (sheriff) were killed and the priest was flogged. Two leaders, Mons Somby and Aslak Hætta, were beheaded in 1854; their skulls were finally handed back to descendants in 1997.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Kautokeino-opprøret

title: By Balloon Toward the Pole
text: On July 11, 1897, Salomon August Andrée, photographer Nils Strindberg and Knut Fraenkel lifted off from Danes Island in a balloon, trying to reach the North Pole. After 65 hours it was forced down onto the pack ice, and the men spent over two months on the floes before reaching White Island (Kvitøya). Their bodies, a diary and still-developable film were found there by chance in 1930.

source.name: Scott Polar Research Institute, University of Cambridge: The Andrée Expedition

source2.name: Library of Congress blog: Lost on the ice, the 1897 balloon attempt to reach the North Pole

title: The First Buildings in Antarctica
text: On February 20, 1899, Carsten Borchgrevink's team began building huts at remote Cape Adare, the first buildings ever put up on the Antarctic continent. They moved in on March 1 and spent the first Antarctic winter in cramped isolation; Nicolai Hanson died there in October, the first person to die on the continent. The huts still stand amid a huge Adélie penguin colony.

source.name: Antarctic Heritage Trust: Cape Adare buildings Antarctic's most significant

title: Whaling Comes to South Georgia
text: In 1904 the Norwegian captain Carl Anton Larsen set up Grytviken, the first whaling station on South Georgia. In summer around 400 people lived and worked there, and in 1913 station workers built a Norwegian-style wooden church in their spare time. In all, 175,250 whales were killed in the waters around South Georgia from 1904 onward; Grytviken closed in 1964.

source.name: South Georgia Museum: History of South Georgia

source2.name: South Georgia Museum: Discover Grytviken

title: Alone in the Home of the Blizzard
text: Douglas Mawson, Ninnis and Mertz left Cape Denison on November 10, 1912, to explore the coast. On December 14 Ninnis broke through a snow bridge into a crevasse, and with him went the best dogs, most of the food and the main tent. Mertz died on January 8. Mawson struggled on alone, sighting the hut on February 8, 1913, just as his ship Aurora steamed away.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division magazine: Life and death in the Home of the Blizzard

source2.name: Australian Antarctic Division, Home of the Blizzard: Mawson's fatal journey

title: A Treaty for a No-Man's-Land
text: Svalbard had long been a no-man's-land. On February 9, 1920, a treaty signed in Paris recognised Norway's full and unrestricted sovereignty over the archipelago, with conditions: citizens of the treaty countries got equal rights there, and Norway promised never to set up or allow naval bases or fortifications. The treaty came into force on August 14, 1925.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Svalbardtraktaten

title: Finnmark Burned and Emptied
text: In autumn 1944, as Soviet forces crossed the border and freed Kirkenes, Hitler ordered on October 28 that northern Norway be emptied. About 50,000 people from Finnmark and Nord-Troms were forced to leave, and coastal towns and fishing villages were razed. Around 23,000 people in Finnmark avoided evacuation; on the island of Sørøya, many survived the winter in caves.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Tvangsevakueringen av Finnmark og Nord-Troms

title: A Parliament for the Sámi
text: On October 9, 1989, King Olav V opened Norway's first official Sámi Parliament in Karasjok, set up under the Sámi Act of 1987. Voters on the Sámi electoral register elect 39 representatives from seven constituencies every four years. The parliament speaks on matters it sees as affecting the Sámi people, and since 2000 it has met in a landmark building in Karasjok.

source.name: Sámediggi (Sámi Parliament of Norway): Om Sametinget

source2.name: Store norske leksikon: Sametinget

title: Remembering Vardø's Witch Trials
text: Between 1600 and 1692, witch trials in Finnmark sentenced 91 people to death: 77 women and 14 men, most of the men Sámi. On June 23, 2011, Queen Sonja opened the Steilneset memorial at Vardø, where the condemned were burned at the stake. Architect Peter Zumthor and artist Louise Bourgeois created it, with texts based on the old court records.

source.name: Store norske leksikon: Steilneset minnested

source2.name: Norwegian Scenic Routes (Norwegian Public Roads Administration): Steilneset

title: 38°C Above the Arctic Circle
text: On June 20, 2020, Verkhoyansk in eastern Siberia, about 115 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle, reached 38°C, a temperature the World Meteorological Organization called more befitting the Mediterranean than the Arctic. It came during a long Siberian heatwave with fires and massive sea ice loss. The WMO later recognised it as a new Arctic record, in a category created for it.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: WMO recognizes new Arctic temperature record of 38°C

title: Harsha Crowned at Sixteen
text: In 606 CE a 16-year-old prince named Harsha was crowned after his elder brother was assassinated. He later declared himself ruler of Kannauj and moved his capital there, ruling a large empire in northern India until 647. A poet himself, he wrote three Sanskrit plays and sponsored the chronicler Bana, whose "Deeds of Harsha" tells the story of his early career.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Harsha

title: A Port Mosque at the Indus Mouth
text: On a creek 65 km east of Karachi lie the ruins of Banbhore, the region's best-preserved medieval port. Its stone mosque, whose prayer hall roof rested on 33 wooden pillars, carries an inscription dated 727 AD, about 16 years after Muhammad Bin Qasim's Arab conquest of Sindh. Beside the town, workshops processed textiles and made glass, glazes and metal goods.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Port of Banbhore (Tentative List)

title: Vikramashila, City of Monks
text: Tibetan tradition says the Pala king Dharmapala founded the great monastery of Vikramashila, built from the early 9th century at Antichak in Bihar. Excavators found a vast square monastery with about 208 cells, each with its own bed platform. It was famous for Tantric Buddhism, and one Tibetan writer, Taranatha, says a thousand monks lived there permanently.

source.name: Banglapedia: Vikramashila Mahavihara

title: A Zero Carved in Stone
text: Inside a temple at Gwalior is an inscription that uses a round "0" in recording a measurement of land. In 1883 the German scholar Eugen Hultzsch copied and translated it, dating the text to 876 CE. For a long time it was counted as the oldest known zero used as a placeholder in India, until carbon dating showed the Bakhshali manuscript was older.

source.name: Scientific American: The Elusive Origin of Zero

source2.name: University of Oxford GLAM: Carbon dating finds Bakhshali manuscript contains oldest recorded origins of the symbol 'zero'

title: Prithviraja's Last Battle
text: In 1191 the Rajput king Prithviraja III beat the army of Muhammad Ghuri at Taraori, about 110 km north of Delhi. Ghuri returned in 1192 with a stronger army, using mounted archers to lure Prithviraja's men out of line before heavy cavalry struck. Prithviraja was captured and executed, and Muslim control of northern India followed within a generation.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Prithviraja III

title: Raising the Qutb Minar
text: From 1199 Delhi's new Muslim rulers raised a minaret beside the Quwwatu'l-Islam, the oldest mosque in northern India, built partly of materials reused from some 20 temples. Made of red and buff sandstone carved with bands of inscriptions, the Qutb Minar stands 72.5 metres high, the tallest masonry tower in India, with balconies for the call to prayer.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi

title: A Sultan's Tomb Goes to a Saint
text: Between 1320 and 1324 the Tughluq ruler Ghiyas-ud-din built a great octagonal tomb at Multan, probably meant for his own dynasty. Instead it was given to the family of the Sufi saint Shah Rukn-i-Alam. The 35-metre red-brick tomb is framed with shisham wood beams and decorated with blue and white tiles, and over 100,000 pilgrims still visit it.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam (Tentative List)

title: A Traveller Becomes Delhi's Judge
text: Hearing that Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi was generous to Muslim scholars, the traveller Ibn Battuta headed for India and, by his own dating, reached the Indus on September 12, 1333. The sultan made him grand qadi, or judge, of Delhi. But the ruler mixed generosity with cruelty, and Ibn Battuta feared daily for his life until he left as an envoy to China.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ibn Battuta

title: Bengal's Giant Adina Mosque
text: In 1373 Sikandar Shah, son of Iliyas Shah, built the Adina Mosque at Pandua in Bengal. Banglapedia calls it the largest mosque of medieval times in the whole subcontinent, about 155 by 87 metres on the outside. Estimates of its domes range from 260 to 370, and a raised stone platform was probably a royal gallery for the ruler at prayer.

source.name: Banglapedia: Adina Mosque

title: Nimai, the Singing Saint
text: In 1486, on the night of a lunar eclipse, a boy named Vishvambhara Mishra, nicknamed Nimai, was born in Navadvipa, Bengal. As Chaitanya, he inspired devotional singing and dancing that became nightly gatherings in a neighbour's courtyard, then spilled into the streets, once causing a clash with the local qazi. He later lived in Puri until his death in 1533.

source.name: Banglapedia: Chaitanya, Sri

source2.name: Banglapedia: Vaisnava Movement

title: Pema Lingpa's Temple of Dances
text: In 1501 Pema Lingpa, Bhutan's famous "treasure revealer", built Tamzhing monastery in Bumthang. He was also skilled in metalwork and in carving wooden blocks for printing scriptures. Tamzhing is known for its unique wall paintings and is the original home of sacred dances now performed at tshechu festivals throughout Bhutan. Pema Lingpa died there in 1521, aged seventy-two.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tamzhing Monastery (Tentative List)

title: A Mughal Princess Heads for Mecca
text: In October 1576 Emperor Akbar stood beside his aunt Gulbadan, aged 53, at Fatehpur Sikri to bid her farewell. She was leading eleven other senior women of the royal household on pilgrimage to Mecca. Their route ran first to Surat, the docking port in Gujarat, and poorer pilgrims were given free passage on the Mughal ships under state policy.

source.name: Yale University Press: The Mughal Princess Who Led a Pilgrimage to Mecca (excerpt by Ruby Lal)

title: A Turkey Amazes the Emperor
text: In 1612 a shipment of exotic birds and animals gathered at the port of Cambay caused a sensation at Emperor Jahangir's court. Among them was a North American turkey. Jahangir wrote that its head and neck kept changing colour, "like a chameleon", and ordered it painted. The court artist Mansur, honoured as "Wonder of the Age", made the portrait.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Painting of a turkey cock, Mansur, ca. 1612

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Painting of a cheer pheasant, Mansur, ca. 1620

title: Escape in a Basket of Sweets
text: Forced to make peace, the Maratha leader Shivaji came to Emperor Aurangzeb's court at Agra, where he and his son were put under house arrest under threat of execution. Shivaji pretended to be ill and, as a penance, sent out huge baskets of sweets for the poor. On August 17, 1666, he and his son had themselves carried past the guards inside them.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Shivaji

title: Dhaka's Unlucky Unfinished Fort
text: In 1678 Prince Muhammad Azam, Mughal viceroy of Bengal, began a palace fortress at Dhaka, today called Lalbagh Fort or Fort Aurangabad. Aurangzeb recalled him before it was finished. The next governor, Shaista Khan, never restarted the work: his daughter Bibi Pari, the "Lady Fairy", died there in 1684, and he came to see the site as unlucky.

source.name: Banglapedia: Lalbagh Fort

title: Five Beloved Ones at Anandpur
text: On Baisakhi Day in 1699 a large crowd of Sikhs gathered at Anandpur. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh came out of a tent with a drawn sword and asked who would give his life for the faith. Five men stepped forward, one by one. They became the panj pyare, the first initiated into the Khalsa with sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Khalsa

title: Jaipur, a City on a Grid
text: In 1727 Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur. Unlike other cities in the region, set in hilly terrain, it was laid out on a plain to a grid plan interpreted through Vedic architecture. Colonnaded shops line its main streets, which meet at large public squares called chaupars. It was designed as a commercial capital, and its craft traditions continue today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Jaipur City, Rajasthan

title: Marathas and Afghans at Panipat
text: On January 14, 1761, a Maratha army under Sadashiv Rao Bhau, weakened by disease and shortage of money, marched out of its fortified camp at Panipat against Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghans. The Marathas did well at first, but late in the afternoon about 5,000 fresh Afghan cavalry turned the battle. Estimates of the dead range from 60,000 to 70,000.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battles of Panipat

title: The Day the Coast Rose
text: On April 2, 1762, a great earthquake struck violently from Dhaka along the Meghna River to Chittagong. Parts of offshore islands rose as much as 6.71 metres, while 155.4 square kilometres near Chittagong sank for good. Rivers surged, a large river dried up, and 500 people died in Dhaka. Two volcanoes were even said to have opened in the Sitakunda hills.

source.name: Banglapedia: Earthquake

title: A Judge Finds Long-Lost Language Cousins
text: Sir William Jones, who learned 28 languages in his life, sailed for Calcutta in 1783 as a supreme court judge and in 1784 founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal. He took up Sanskrit for his work on law. In his 1786 presidential talk to the Society he proposed that Sanskrit, Latin and Greek shared a common ancestry, spurring the new field of comparative linguistics.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sir William Jones

title: The Lion of the Punjab Takes Lahore
text: In July 1799 the Sikh chief Ranjit Singh seized Lahore, capital of the Punjab. The Afghan king Zaman Shah confirmed him as governor, but in 1801 he proclaimed himself maharaja and struck coins in the name of the Sikh Gurus. Blind in one eye, he went on to push back Afghan power and became known as the Lion of the Punjab.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ranjit Singh

title: Mounds Made of Burnt Cattle Dung
text: Across the Deccan, Neolithic herders left huge heaps of ash from burnt cattle dung. At Utnur, archaeologists found cattle hoof prints, pens marked by post-holes, and layers left by repeated dung burning. Radiocarbon dates suggest the ash mound began forming around 2500 BCE, making Utnur the earliest dated ash mound. Once the burning stopped, people abandoned the site.

source.name: Fuller, Boivin and Korisettar (UCL Institute of Archaeology): Dating the Neolithic of South India

title: Wheat Reaches a Deccan Hilltop
place: Sannarachamma hill, Sanganakallu, Ballari, Karnataka, India
text: Wheat and barley were first domesticated in Southwest Asia and became staple crops of the Indus civilization. Seeds from Sannarachamma, a hilltop in Bellary District, have been directly dated to 1900–1800 BCE, showing these crops had reached south India by then. The village grew up over an earlier ash mound, and people kept living there for centuries afterwards.

source.name: Fuller, Boivin and Korisettar (UCL Institute of Archaeology): Dating the Neolithic of South India

title: African Crops in a Karnataka Village
text: Hallur, in western Karnataka, has the most varied plant remains of any Neolithic site in south India. Its main village dates to about 1600–1400 BCE, and an early layer held hyacinth beans and pearl millet, crops that came from Africa. A later layer produced east African finger millet and a cotton seed dated to about 900 BCE, the earliest direct evidence of cotton in south India.

source.name: Fuller, Boivin and Korisettar (UCL Institute of Archaeology): Dating the Neolithic of South India

title: Paintings Beside a Hill of Tombs
text: On a granite hilltop near Hire Benkal, almost 1,000 Iron Age megaliths cover about 20 hectares, most of them dolmens, including giant ones with port-holes. Nearby rock shelters hold paintings, mostly from about 700–500 BCE: rows of people, a horse rider holding a battle-axe, deer, long-horned bulls and peacocks. Some scenes may even show graves like the stone circles around them.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hire Benkal, Megalithic Site (Tentative List)

title: Early Writing on Anuradhapura Pots
place: Anuradhapura, North Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: Excavators at Anuradhapura found broken pots inscribed in Brahmi, South Asia's earliest readable script. A 1996 study by R. Coningham, F. R. Allchin and colleagues dated the sherds to the beginning of the 4th century BCE, making them the earliest dated examples of Brahmi anywhere in the subcontinent. The authors suggested Sri Lanka may have played a pivotal role in developing the script.

source.name: Cambridge Archaeological Journal: Passage to India? Anuradhapura and the Early Use of the Brahmi Script

title: Forest Monks Move Into Dambulla
text: Forest-dwelling Buddhist monks began living in the natural caves at Dambulla, in central Sri Lanka, in the 3rd century BCE. Over the centuries the caves were turned into five shrines holding 157 statues and Buddhist murals covering 2,100 square metres. Pilgrims have come here for more than two thousand years, and monks still perform the daily rituals.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rangiri Dambulla Cave Temple

dateLabel: Between the 3rd century BCE and 1st century CE
title: The Oldest Linga on a Pedestal
text: In a temple at Gudimallam stands a polished reddish-brown stone linga about 1.5 metres tall, carved with a detailed Shiva standing on the shoulders of a crouching, dwarf-like figure. Dated variously between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE, it is the oldest known linga set on a pedestal and the earliest fully representational one. It was documented in 1903.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Gudimallam Stone Lingam

title: Stone Beds for Jain Monks
text: Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions show that Sittanavasal was a Jain centre from as early as 100 BCE until around 900 CE. A natural rock shelter there, Ezhadipattam, has polished rock beds where monks practised austerities. A later cave temple on the same hill, Arivar Koil or 'temple of the Jina', holds the earliest Jain frescoes in south India.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Cave Art at Sittanavasal

title: A Fleeing King's Vow
text: Driven from Anuradhapura by invaders from South India, King Vattagamani Abhaya fled to the mountains. When a temple chief mocked him for abandoning his kingdom, he vowed to replace that temple with a Buddhist monastery. After fourteen years he retook the city, in 89 BCE by one dating, and founded Abhayagiri Vihara, later the first place in Sri Lanka to house the Buddha's Tooth Relic.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Abhayagiri Vihara, Anuradhapura

title: The Buddha's Story on Amaravati's Railings
text: The great stupa at Amaravati was begun in the 3rd century BCE, but its carved stone railings were added from the mid-1st century BCE to the early 3rd century CE. The earliest reliefs show the Buddha only through symbols, such as a pair of footprints. Later carvers gave him a human form, yet at Amaravati the old symbols never disappeared.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Sculptures at Amaravati Stupa

title: A Monastery and 62,000 Cowries
text: Long before the Maldives became Muslim, a Buddhist monastery stood on the island of Kaashidhoo. Founded in the 3rd century CE, it stayed in use until about 1500. Archaeologist Egil Mikkelsen excavated about 1,800 square metres there in 1996–1998 and found a deposit of 62,000 cowrie shells beside one building. The earliest radiocarbon dates fall between 220 and 610 CE.

source.name: Kon-Tiki Museum: The Archaeology of Buddhism in the Maldives

title: A Buddhist City Now an Island
text: Nagarjunakonda, 'Nagarjuna's Hill', was the site of Vijayapuri, capital of the Ikshvaku dynasty in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. More than thirty establishments of different Buddhist sects stood there, and monks from other parts of South Asia are recorded. Sculptures at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka resemble its standing Buddhas. Today the site is an island in the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Standing Buddhas, Nagarjunakonda

title: A Reservoir Watched by a Giant Buddha
place: Kalawewa, North Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: King Dhatusena, who reigned from 455 to 473 CE, developed Kalawewa, a reservoir complex fed by the Kala Oya river system that let farming and trade flourish. Nearby at Avukana, a colossal standing Buddha was carved from a granite rock face, looking out over the water. Scholars still debate when the statue was made, with suggestions ranging from the 5th century onward.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Avukana Buddha

title: A Ten-Armed Shiva Dances at Aihole
text: Around 550 CE, under the Early Western Chalukyas, a cave temple was cut into the rock at Aihole, then known as Aryapura or Ayyavole. Inside the Ravanaphadi cave, a ten-armed Shiva dances beside Parvati and the seven mother goddesses, while a carved lotus blooms on the ceiling. Faint traces of colour suggest the walls were once painted.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Ravanaphadi Cave, Aihole

title: The Pallava King Who Wrote Comedies
text: Mahendravarman I, the Pallava king who ruled from Kanchipuram between 580 and 630 CE, is believed to have written two Sanskrit farces, one poking fun at Buddhist monks and Kapalikas. Rock inscriptions at Kudumiyanmalai record his love of music. Inscriptions in cave temples he sponsored, such as Mandagapattu, call him by playful titles like 'the curious-minded' and 'drunken sporter'.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Mahendravarman I

source2.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Pallava Art and Architecture

title: Queens' Shrines at the Kailasanathar Temple
text: Between 700 and 728 CE, the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha, built a sandstone temple to Shiva beside the Vegavathi river. Fifty-eight small shrines line its courtyard wall, and eight near the entrance are believed to have been commissioned by his queens. Its popular name, Kailasanathar, comes from an inscription saying its tower touched Shiva's realm, Kailasa.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Kailasanathar Temple, Kanchipuram

title: A Giant Carved From One Boulder
text: Completed around 983 CE, the 17.4-metre Gomateshvara statue on Vindhyagiri hill is the tallest free-standing monolithic sculpture in the world. Commissioned by Chamundaraya, a minister and general at the Western Ganga court, it shows the Jain figure Bahubali meditating so long that vines climb his legs and arms. Every 12 years, the statue's head is ritually anointed.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Gomateshvara Statue, Shravanabelagola

title: Festival Gods Buried for Safekeeping
text: Early in the 11th century, Chola artists cast bronze images of Shiva as Vrishabhavahana, 'the bull-mounted one', and his consort Uma using the lost-wax method. They were festival images, carried in processions on poles threaded through their pedestals. Probably used at the Thiruvengadu temple until the 14th century, they were then buried for safekeeping and unearthed again in the mid-20th century.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Vrishabhavahana and Uma Chola Bronzes, Thanjavur Art Gallery

title: A Diamond Paid as Tribute
text: The diamond later named Koh-i-Noor, 'mountain of light', was probably found in the 13th century in river deposits of the Krishna–Godavari delta and held by the Kakatiya dynasty, whose capital was Warangal. Around 1310, when Alauddin Khilji's forces subjugated the Kakatiyas, it was by most accounts handed over as tribute to the Delhi Sultanate, beginning centuries of changing hands.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Koh-i-Noor Diamond

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Warangal

title: A Stone Tablet in Three Languages
text: Dated 15 February 1409, this stone tablet was inscribed in Nanjing under the Ming emperor Yongle and installed at Galle by the Chinese admiral Zheng He. Written in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, it praises the Buddha, Vishnu and Allah and records offerings to a sacred mountain shrine. Found in a culvert in Galle in 1911, it is now in the Colombo National Museum.

source.name: National Library and Documentation Services Board, Sri Lanka: Trilingual Inscription (Tribhasha Sellipiya)

title: Shining Inlay on Dark Metal
text: Bidriware, metal inlay set against a dark alloy, is named after Bidar, a capital of the Bahmani Sultanate. Persian and Syrian artisans are believed to have brought the technique to the Deccan, and production in Bidar probably began under Sultan Alauddin Ahmad II (r. 1436–58), who encouraged artisans from Bijapur to settle there. Bidar is still a leading centre of the craft.

source.name: Impart (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru): Bidriware

title: Cholera Breaks Out of Bengal
text: In 1817 a particularly virulent outbreak of cholera struck Bengal. Known as 'Asiatic cholera', it began in Jessore near Calcutta, appeared throughout India, and then spread into the Far East and as far as Muscat, Tehran and Baghdad. This first cholera pandemic finally reached the Mediterranean in 1823 and died down.

source.name: PMC (Archives of Iranian Medicine): History of Cholera Outbreaks in Iran during the 19th and 20th Centuries

source2.name: US National Library of Medicine: Cholera Online, 1817-1923

title: Jung Bahadur Seizes Nepal
text: In 1846 Jung Bahadur took control of Nepal's government after killing Gagan Singh, who had plotted with the junior queen. He later exiled the king and queen, became prime minister for life and took the hereditary title Rana. His family held the office, passed from brother to brother, until 1951, while the Shah kings were left with an honorary role.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jung Bahadur

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nepal, History

title: A College for Canal Builders
text: In 1847 the Roorkee College of Civil Engineering opened, mainly to train Indian engineers for the ongoing Ganges Canal. It was later renamed Thomason College after its founder, James Thomason. It became the University of Roorkee in 1949, and in 2001 it was declared India's seventh Indian Institute of Technology, today's IIT Roorkee.

source.name: IIT Roorkee: About Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee

title: A Boy King Loses the Mountain of Light
text: Duleep Singh, born in Lahore and declared Maharaja of the Punjab at just 5, was still only 10 when the East India Company took control after two Anglo-Sikh wars. With the annexation of the Punjab in 1849, he was forced to give up his lands and the Koh-i-noor, the 'mountain of light' diamond, which joined Queen Victoria's crown jewels.

source.name: Historic Royal Palaces: Duleep Singh, the Last Sikh Maharaja

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Koh-i-noor

title: Peasants Say No to Indigo
text: In 1859 farmers in Jessore and Nadia, the two major indigo-growing districts, joined together to free themselves from the planters who forced them to grow the crop. They used social boycotts, non-cooperation and sometimes armed revolt. Dinabandhu Mitra's 1860 play Nildarpan, 'Mirror of Indigo', won them public support, and a new law then banned forcing farmers to grow indigo.

source.name: Banglapedia: Indigo Resistance Movement

title: Dreaming of a Muslim Cambridge
text: On a visit to England in 1869-70, the scholar Sayyid Ahmad Khan drew up plans for 'a Muslim Cambridge'. In May 1875 a Muslim school opened at Aligarh, and after retiring he devoted himself to turning it into a college, whose foundation stone the viceroy laid in January 1877. Despite conservative opposition, the college made rapid progress.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan

title: A Queen Proclaimed Empress
place: About four miles north-west of Delhi, India
text: On January 1, 1877, the Viceroy Lord Lytton staged an Imperial Assemblage outside Delhi to announce Queen Victoria's new title, Empress of India. Sixty-three princes attended, and about 100,000 people camped nearby with horses, elephants and camels. The painter Valentine Prinsep later spent months travelling India for sittings, squeezing nearly 160 recognisable portraits into one enormous canvas.

source.name: Royal Collection Trust: The Imperial Assemblage held at Delhi, 1 January 1877

title: A Party Born in Dhaka
text: On December 30, 1906, an All India Muslim Education Conference held at Shahbag in Dhaka gave birth to the Muslim League. Nawab Salimullah proposed creating a political platform, and the conference chairman, Nawab Viqar-ul-Mulk, supported his motion. Salimullah backed the recent Partition of Bengal and wanted a party to counter the agitation against it.

source.name: Banglapedia: Muslim League

title: Bhagat Singh's Last Day
text: Bhagat Singh popularised the cry 'Inquilab zindabad', 'Long live the revolution'. After a British police officer, J.P. Saunders, was killed by mistake and bombs were thrown in Delhi's Central Legislative Assembly, he was tried and led a prison hunger strike. On March 23, 1931, aged 23, he was hanged in Lahore with Rajguru and Sukhdev Thapar; he spent that day reading about Lenin.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bhagat Singh

title: The Lahore Resolution
text: In March 1940 Muhammad Ali Jinnah called a general session of the All India Muslim League in Lahore. On March 23 Fazlul Huq moved a resolution that Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones should form 'independent states', and it was adopted the next day. In 1946 the word 'states' was changed to the singular 'state'.

source.name: Banglapedia: Lahore Resolution

title: India Belongs Only to Me
text: 'Europe belongs to Picasso, Matisse, Braque, and many others. India belongs only to me,' wrote the painter Amrita Sher-Gil, who blended Ajanta cave painting with Paris-trained oil technique. In 1941 she moved to Lahore and was preparing her first solo show there when she fell ill and died on December 5. Her last unfinished works moved towards abstraction.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Amrita Sher-Gil

title: The Famine of Fifty
place: Undivided Bengal (today's Bangladesh and West Bengal, India)
text: Bengalis call the 1943 famine panchaxer manvantar, 'the famine of fifty', after the Bengali year 1350. Rice imports from Burma had stopped, and a wartime 'denial' policy withdrew boats from coastal districts. Rice that sold for under 6 rupees a maund in Calcutta in early 1942 reached over 100 in some districts, and between 3.5 and 3.8 million people died.

source.name: Banglapedia: Famine, 1943

title: The First Asian Games
text: In 1951 New Delhi hosted the very first Asian Games. Athletes from 11 nations competed in six sports: football, athletics, basketball, cycling, swimming and weightlifting. From 1954 the Games were held every four years, and by the 2002 Games in Pusan, South Korea, 41 nations took part in events across 38 sports.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Asian Games

title: Sharing Six Rivers
text: In 1960, after nine years of negotiations, India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty, with the World Bank also signing. The western rivers, the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, went to Pakistan, and the eastern Ravi, Beas and Sutlej to India. US President Dwight Eisenhower called it one bright spot in a depressing world picture, and it has survived frequent tensions.

source.name: World Bank: Fact Sheet, The Indus Waters Treaty 1960 and the Role of the World Bank

title: Sugar, Salt and Water
text: In 1968 doctors at the Cholera Research Laboratory hospital in Dhaka, including David Nalin, Richard Cash, Rafiqul Islam and Majid Molla, showed that a simple oral glucose-sodium drink could keep cholera patients' body salts in balance. It cut the need for intravenous fluids by 80 per cent. The Lancet later called oral rehydration therapy the most important medical advance of the 20th century.

source.name: PMC: Development of oral rehydration salt solution, a triumph of medical science

title: The Great Cyclone of 1970
text: On November 12-13, 1970, the deadliest cyclone in Bangladesh's history struck the coast, with winds of about 222 km/h and a storm surge up to about 10.6 metres. It hit places such as Char Tazumuddin, Patuakhali and Barguna, and battered Chittagong. The official death toll was 500,000 and may have been higher, including some 46,000 inland fishermen.

source.name: Banglapedia: Cyclone

title: Chipko Saves the Ash Trees
place: Mandal, near Gopeshwar, Chamoli, Uttarakhand, India
text: On April 24, 1973, villagers of Mandal near Gopeshwar, led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Mandal, stopped contractors for a sports goods company from felling 14 ash trees. This was the birth of the Chipko movement. In December they stopped the same company's agents again in the Phata-Rampur forests.

source.name: India Environment Portal (Centre for Science and Environment): Landmarks on the Chipko trail

title: Loans Without Collateral
text: In 1976 Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at the University of Chittagong, began an experiment in Jobra village: giving collateral-free credit to landless people. The rural banking project became Grameen Bank, a specialised bank set up in October 1983 and owned mostly by its borrowers, most of them poor women. In 2006 Yunus and the bank jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: Banglapedia: Grameen Bank

title: Pasang Lhamu Reaches the Top
text: On April 22, 1993, Pasang Lhamu Sherpa reached the summit of Everest by the South Col route, after attempts in 1990, 1991 and 1992. Her expedition had been organised to put the first Nepalese woman on top of the world. She died after an unprepared bivouac at the South Summit on the way down, and was honoured with the Star of Nepal.

source.name: American Alpine Journal: Asia, Nepal, Everest, First Ascent by a Nepalese Woman and Tragedy

title: Bhutan Switches On Television
text: Bhutan got its own national television on June 2, 1999, timed to celebrate the Silver Jubilee of the Fourth King's enthronement. Queen Mother Tseyring Pem Wangchuck switched on the Bhutan Broadcasting Service at Sangaygang, and broadcasts ran for just three hours a day. It all began in 1973, when volunteers went on air with a makeshift radio studio for half an hour every Sunday.

source.name: Bhutan Broadcasting Service: BBS, a journey through time, from radio pioneers to high-definition TV

title: The Kashmir Earthquake
text: On October 8, 2005, a magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook northern Pakistan and Kashmir. At least 86,000 people were killed in Pakistan and another 1,350 in India, and an estimated 4 million were left homeless. The worst damage was around Muzaffarabad, the town of Uri lost 80 percent of its buildings, and buildings collapsed as far away as Lahore.

source.name: USGS: Today in Earthquake History, October 8

title: A Schoolgirl's Secret Diary
text: From January 3, 2009, the BBC published for ten weeks the diary of an 11-year-old in Swat, under the pen name Gul Makai, a heroine of a Pakhtun folktale. The writer was Malala Yousafzai. After the Taliban outlawed girls' education in the valley, a BBC Urdu journalist phoned her for 30 minutes every day to hear about her life.

source.name: The Express Tribune: Where it all started, 'A diary that highlighted Swat's human tragedy'

title: Khao Sam Kaeo, a Port Between Oceans
place: Khao Sam Kaeo, near Chumphon, Thailand
text: Near today's Chumphon, a busy port city was active from the 4th century BCE to the 1st century CE. Archaeologists dug 136 test pits and found earthen walls, ramparts and water-control works around at least 35 hectares. Its stone, glass and copper crafts used techniques from India, Indian artisans may have worked there, and two seals with Chinese writing hint at Han merchants.

source.name: NUS Press, Southeast Asian Site Reports: Favereau and Bellina, Cultural Dynamics in the Early Multi-ethnic Ports of the Upper Thai-Malay Peninsula

title: A King Who Meditates in Stone
text: Jayavarman VII began his reign in 1181, after a troubled period that ended in 1177 with a Cham siege of Angkor. He made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion. His sandstone portraits show a mature man in humble meditation, eyes lowered and smiling calmly, with no royal insignia at all, a very human face for a mighty king.

source.name: Musée Guimet: Portrait of King Jayavarman VII

title: Koh Ker, the Rival Capital
text: In 921 King Jayavarman IV founded a new capital about eighty kilometres northeast of Angkor. The two cities co-existed as rival capitals until 928, then Koh Ker ruled alone until 944. Its builders used huge single blocks of stone, and its sculptors created the bold, lively Koh Ker Style, which shaped Khmer art long after the court moved back to Angkor.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Koh Ker, Archaeological Site of Ancient Lingapura or Chok Gargyar

title: The Temple in the Rich Forest
place: Sambor Prei Kuk, Kampong Thom, Cambodia
text: Sambor Prei Kuk, 'the temple in the richness of the forest', was Ishanapura, capital of the Chenla kingdom in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. Its 186 brick temples include rare octagonal shrines thought to show the flying palace of the god Indra. Inscriptions in Sanskrit and Old Khmer name kings and other individuals, and its style paved the way for Angkor.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Temple Zone of Sambor Prei Kuk, Archaeological Site of Ancient Ishanapura

title: The Stone Citadel of the Hồ
text: Built in 1397 between the Ma and Bưởi rivers, the Hồ Dynasty citadel was Vietnam's capital from 1398 to 1407. Its inner walls are made of huge limestone blocks, and its site was chosen by geomantic rules between two mountains. The citadel shows how Confucian ideas of royal power were taking hold in a mainly Buddhist country.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Citadel of the Ho Dynasty

title: A Sacred Axis From Mountain to Mekong
text: On the Mekong in southern Laos, the planned city of Shrestrapura grew up from the 5th century CE beneath Phou Kao mountain, also called Lingaparvata. Between the 5th and 15th centuries temples, shrines, reservoirs and a road to Angkor were laid out along a line about 10 kilometres long, from mountaintop to riverbank, to express Hindu ideas about nature and humanity. Vat Phou temple sits at its heart.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape

title: Boundary Stones on Phu Phrabat
text: When Buddhism reached the Khorat Plateau in the 7th century, people began setting up sīma stones to mark sacred ground for monks. Phu Phrabat keeps the world's largest group of these Dvaravati-period stones still in place. The same rock shelters already held much older paintings of people, hand prints, animals and patterns, made by prehistoric visitors about two thousand years ago.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Phu Phrabat, a testimony to the Sīma stone tradition of the Dvaravati period

title: Si Thep's Dancing Statues
text: Si Thep, a moated twin town of the Dvaravati world, flourished in central Thailand from the 6th to the 10th centuries. More than 112 monastery sites have been found there, and Hindus and Buddhists of two schools lived side by side. Its sculptors made free-standing figures in the swaying Tribhanga pose, full of body movement, and nearby Khao Thamorrat is a rare Mahayana Buddhist cave monastery.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: The Ancient Town of Si Thep and its Associated Dvaravati Monuments

title: Monks Shipwrecked for a Fresh Start
text: King Dhammaceti of Pegu, called from the monastery to the throne, sent twenty-two senior monks to Sri Lanka to be re-ordained on the Kalyani River near Colombo. One ship was wrecked at Colombo and its party was shipwrecked again, and several monks died on the way home. In 1476 the king recorded the story on ten stone slabs, in Pali and Mon.

source.name: Government Printing, Burma (1892): The Kalyani Inscriptions Erected by King Dhammaceti at Pegu in 1476 A.D., Text and Translation

title: A Craftswoman Signs Her Jar
place: Chu Đậu, Nam Sách, Hải Dương, Vietnam
text: A blue-and-white jar now in the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul carries an inscription naming the craftswoman Bùi Thị Hý and dating it to 1450, the 8th year of the Đại Hòa era. Chu Đậu village, where such wares are thought to have been made, was Vietnam's largest ceramics centre, producing pots for worship, home use and export.

source.name: National Museum of Vietnamese History: The cobalt blue pattern ceramic jar with swan decoration, an object recognized as Vietnam National Treasure

title: A Calendar Born in 638
text: Four burial urns found at Sri Ksetra in 1911 carry short Pyu inscriptions naming lords and the years they died. Historian Tilman Frasch argues that the dates most likely count from the Pyu–Myanmar era of 638 CE. That same Myanmar era has since been used for dating practically everything written in Myanmar, from inscriptions and manuscripts to printed books and newspapers.

source.name: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge): Tilman Frasch, Pyu urns, Indian calendars, and Myanmar culture

title: A Woman in a Boat-Shaped Coffin
place: Ban Non Wat, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: At Ban Non Wat, the first Bronze Age graves were dug much deeper than older ones. In Burial 569 a young to mid-aged woman lay in a wooden coffin with a pointed prow like a boat. She wore 2,382 shell beads and a marine shell bangle, fourteen pots surrounded her, and a socketed copper-base axe rested on her left shoulder.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Charles Higham, Aggrandisers and the first copper-base metallurgy in Southeast Asia

title: Myanmar's Bronze Age Begins
text: On the edge of an old volcanic crater near the Chindwin River lies the Nyaung'gan cemetery. People here were buried with pottery, stone beads and bracelets, shell beads, spindle whorls, cattle bones and even a dog. New radiocarbon dates by a Myanmar and French team suggest the shift from stone to copper and bronze happened here in the tenth to ninth centuries BCE.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Pryce et al., A first absolute chronology for Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Myanmar: new AMS 14C dates from Nyaung'gan and Oakaie

title: A Child With Roots in India
place: Vat Komnou cemetery, Angkor Borei, Takéo, Cambodia
text: A boy aged five to seven was buried at the Vat Komnou cemetery at Angkor Borei sometime between 78 and 234 CE. When scientists read his ancient DNA, they found that about 40 to 50 percent of his ancestry came from South Asia, mainly southern India. It shows that people from South Asia were already mixing with local families in Cambodia that early.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Changmai et al., Ancient DNA from Protohistoric Period Cambodia indicates that South Asians admixed with local populations as early as 1st–3rd centuries CE

title: A Toolkit Carried to the Delta
text: Rạch Núi, a Neolithic village in the Mekong Delta, had no stone of its own. Yet archaeologists found a small, portable sandstone grinding stone there, used to polish and repair stone adzes, which probably came from a quarry more than 80 kilometres away. It hints at specialist tool makers or travelling traders, part of a trade network that moved goods over hundreds of kilometres.

source.name: Australian National University, College of Arts and Social Sciences: Archaeologists uncover ancient trading network in Vietnam

source2.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Frieman et al., Rach Nui: ground stone technology in coastal Neolithic settlements of southern Vietnam

title: Halin Falls to Nanzhao
text: The Pyu kingdom flourished in central and northern Burma from the early centuries CE until around 832, when its capital Halin was sacked by forces of the Nanzhao kingdom from southern China. Halin was one of three brick-walled, moated Pyu cities, where people built Buddhist stupas, stored the ashes of the dead in urns and managed water to farm the dry zone.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Kurt Behrendt, The Mon-Dvaravati Tradition of Early North-Central Thailand

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pyu Ancient Cities

title: Champa Strikes Back at Angkor
text: Champa, with its powerful fleet, had been conquered by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in 1145, but a new Cham king threw off Khmer rule two years later. In 1177 his successor struck back and sacked Angkor, the Khmer capital. The siege ended a troubled period for Cambodia and opened the way for the reign of Jayavarman VII.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Champa, ancient kingdom, Indochina

source2.name: Musée Guimet: Portrait of King Jayavarman VII

title: Raiders, Traders and a Chinese Fleet
text: Champa, the kingdom of the Cham people on Vietnam's central coast, had a powerful fleet used for both trade and piracy. Around 400 it was united under King Bhadravarman. In 446 the Chinese invaded in revenge for Cham raids on their coast and brought Champa under their overlordship, until a new dynasty threw off that allegiance in the 6th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Champa, ancient kingdom, Indochina

title: Đại Việt Pushes South
text: Short of farmland in the crowded north, the Lê rulers of Đại Việt looked south. In 1471, under Lê Thánh Tông, most of Champa was conquered. Soldiers of the advancing army settled in new villages from Đà Nẵng to near Nha Trang, the first great Vietnamese push to the south, which later continued into the Mekong Delta.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: William S. Turley et al., Vietnam, The Tran dynasty and The Later Le dynasty

title: Copper Smelters of the Lopburi Hills
place: Khao Wong Prachan Valley, Lopburi, Thailand
text: Just north of Lopburi, the Khao Wong Prachan Valley is one of only four known prehistoric copper-mining centres in Southeast Asia. About 100 new radiocarbon dates show that copper mining and simple smelting began there in the late second millennium BCE. Its villages of Non Pa Wai and Nil Kham Haeng grew into some of the largest copper-smelting settlements known in Eurasia.

source.name: Oxford University Research Archive: Higham et al., A prehistoric copper-production centre in central Thailand: its dating and wider implications (Antiquity)

source2.name: Penn Museum: Thailand Archaeometallurgy Project

title: One Message in Four Languages
text: At Bagan, Prince Rajakumar, son of King Kyanzittha, set up a stone pillar carved with the same text in four languages, Pyu, Mon, Burmese and Pali, one on each side. Found at the Myazedi Pagoda in 1886–1887, it is the earliest dated document in the Burmese language. Around 1911, C. O. Blagden's pioneering study of its Pyu face opened a door to the little-known Pyu language.

source.name: Google Arts & Culture (Archaeology and National Museum, Myanmar): Myazedi Stone Inscription, Pillar A

source2.name: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge): Tilman Frasch, Pyu urns, Indian calendars, and Myanmar culture

title: Rice, Millet and Jade by the Bay
place: Tràng Kênh, Thủy Nguyên, Hải Phòng, Vietnam
text: Near the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River, Tràng Kênh is the largest nephrite (jade) workshop site known in Southeast Asia. Starch grains on its grinding stones show people there used both rice and foxtail millet, the earliest evidence of growing the two together in northern Vietnam. Tools from nearby Cát Bà Island carried traces of taro, yams, palm and millet, but no rice.

source.name: Frontiers in Plant Science (via PMC): Wang et al., Rice and millet cultivated in Ha Long Bay of Northern Vietnam 4000 years ago

title: A Pilgrim Stops at Srivijaya
text: In 671 the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim I-ching (Yijing) reached Srivijaya after less than 20 days at sea from Canton, on his way to the great teaching centre of Nalanda in India. The ruler helped him on his journey. I-ching praised Palembang, with more than a thousand monks, as an excellent place to begin studying Buddhist texts.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, The Malay kingdom of Srivijaya-Palembang

title: The Hermit Prince Becomes King
text: After the eastern Javanese capital was destroyed in 1016, the half-Balinese prince Erlangga (Airlangga) lived with hermits until 1019, when he was hailed as ruler of the small principality of Pasuruan. He slowly rebuilt the kingdom, winning his final victory around 1035. Later he split it between two sons, a choice that led to fighting between Kadiri and Janggala.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, Eastern Java and the archipelago from c. 1000 to c. 1300

title: An Adventurer Seizes the Throne
text: In 1222 Kertajaya, king of Kadiri, was defeated by an adventurer named Ken Angrok. Angrok made himself king and set up a new capital at Kutaraja, later renamed Singhasari, near the harbours of east Java. A later chronicle says he saw himself as Bhatara Guru, the divine teacher linked with the god Shiva.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, Eastern Java and the archipelago from c. 1000 to c. 1300

title: Java Reaches Across to Sumatra
text: In 1275 the Javanese king Kertanagara imposed his authority on Malayu in southern Sumatra. Historians have suggested he wanted a religious alliance against the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan, though his demands were probably limited to homage and tribute. His followers revered him as a Shiva-Buddha, and the poet Prapancha admired his scholarly zeal.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, Eastern Java and the archipelago from c. 1000 to c. 1300

title: A Royal Tomb in Arabic
text: Strong evidence of Islam in Indonesia appears at the end of the 13th century in northern Sumatra, where small Muslim trading kingdoms grew up at Samudra-Pasai and Perlak. A royal tomb at Samudra-Pasai, dating to 1297, is inscribed entirely in Arabic. By the end of the 14th century Pasai had become a wealthy commercial centre, likely run with the help of Muslim traders and teachers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, The Majapahit era and Islamic influence

title: The Stone in the Riverbank
text: The Terengganu Inscribed Stone carries the oldest Jawi writing found in Malaysia. Its text names Islam as the official religion and sets out Islamic laws against wrongdoing, and it is seen as evidence that Islam had reached Terengganu by 1303. Centuries later, in 1903, it was found half-sunk in the bank of the Tersat River at Kuala Berang.

source.name: Perpustakaan Negara Malaysia (National Library of Malaysia): Batu Bersurat Terengganu

title: A Trader's Eyewitness Singapore
text: In 1349 the Chinese trader Wang Dayuan wrote Dao yi zhi lue, the only surviving eyewitness account of ancient Singapore. He described Longyamen, the Dragon's Tooth Strait, as a dangerous pirate lair and placed the meeting point of the Eastern and Western Oceans there. His Banzu is linked to today's Fort Canning Hill, where finds from 1300 to 1600 have been excavated.

source.name: National Library Board Singapore: The Yuan in the Straits of Malacca

source2.name: National Library Board Singapore, Curiocity: Bukit Larangan, Early Singapore in Maps, Texts, and Artifacts

title: A Poem Paints Majapahit
text: In 1365 the poet Prapancha finished the Nagarakertagama, a rare 14th-century view of the Majapahit kingdom under Hayam Wuruk. It follows the king on constant tours of his lands and describes a New Year ceremony where village leaders and envoys came to pay homage. The poem survives in a manuscript found on Lombok at the end of the 19th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, The Majapahit era

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, Eastern Java and the archipelago from c. 1000 to c. 1300

title: Brunei's King Sails to China
text: Friendly contact between Boni (Brunei) and China went back to the Northern Song dynasty. In 1408 Manarejiana, ruler of Boni, paid a friendly visit to China, fell ill that October and died at the age of 28. He was buried in Nanjing, and his tomb is one of only two foreign rulers' tombs in China.

source.name: ASEAN-China Centre: Visit to the Tomb of the King of Boni

title: Sulu's Eastern King Meets the Emperor
text: In 1417 Paduka Batara, the Eastern King of Sulu, travelled to China with more than 340 people. He gave Emperor Yongle a letter in golden script and pearls, and received official seals in return. Heading home after 27 days in China, he fell ill and died in Dezhou. Two sons stayed to guard his tomb, and their descendants still live there.

source.name: National Historical Commission of the Philippines, National Memory Project: Paduka Batara

title: Timor's Well-Fed First Dog
place: Matja Kuru, Lake Ira Lalaro, Lautém, Timor-Leste
text: Dogs are dated to about 3,000 years ago in Timor-Leste. At the cave of Matja Kuru 2, north of the large lake Ira Lalaro, archaeologists found a dog that had been carefully buried. Chemical and size studies show it was well nourished, suggesting it lived in a settled farming community. Pottery had reached Timor's caves at least 3,500 years ago.

source.name: Sue O'Connor, Archipel 90 (2015): Rethinking the Neolithic in Island Southeast Asia, with Particular Reference to Timor-Leste and Sulawesi

title: Red Pots on a Sulawesi River
place: Minanga Sipakko, Karama Valley, West Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Villages in Sulawesi's Karama valley, such as Minanga Sipakko and Kamassi, were lived in from about 3,500 to 2,800 years ago. Red-slipped pottery fills their earliest layers and closely resembles pots from Taiwan and the Philippines. Diggers also found schist and slate adzes like Neolithic ones from those lands, plus a few bones of domestic pigs.

source.name: Sue O'Connor, Archipel 90 (2015): Rethinking the Neolithic in Island Southeast Asia, with Particular Reference to Timor-Leste and Sulawesi

title: A Monk Blown Ashore in Java
text: Around 411 the Chinese monk Faxian sailed home from Ceylon (Sri Lanka) with Buddhist texts he had collected. A violent storm drove his ship to an island called Yepoti, probably Java, though some scholars say Sumatra. After five months there he boarded another ship, which a second storm blew off course. In all he spent more than 200 days at sea.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Faxian

source2.name: Himanshu Prabha Ray, Southeast Asian Site Reports (NUS Press): Of Bronzes and Heritage Routes across the Bay of Bengal

title: Outriggers Bound for Africa
text: People of the Indonesian archipelago may have sailed far across Asia long before written trade records begin. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder's Natural History suggests that in the 1st century CE Indonesian outriggers were trading with the east coast of Africa. Indonesian settlements may already have existed on Madagascar, an island with distinct Indonesian cultural traits.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, History (The archipelago: its prehistory and early historical records)

title: Java on Ptolemy's Map
text: In the 2nd century CE the geographer Ptolemy used reports from Indian merchants in his Guide to Geography. He wrote of Iabadiou, presumably Java, and Malaiou, which may stand for Malayu, a name once used for interior regions and kingdoms of Sumatra. Timber and spices from Java and the eastern islands were already known in faraway lands.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, History (The archipelago: its prehistory and early historical records)

title: Camphor and 'Persian' Resins
text: Regular voyages between Indonesia and China began in the 5th century CE. Chinese writings of the 5th and 6th centuries mention camphor from northern Sumatra, and they call two Indonesian resins 'Persian resins from the south ocean'. Indonesian shippers were probably taking advantage of southern China being cut off from the old overland route through Central Asia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indonesia, History (The archipelago: its prehistory and early historical records)

title: Stone Jars of the Sulawesi Highlands
place: Behoa Valley, Lore Lindu, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: In the highlands of Central Sulawesi lie at least 2,000 megaliths: giant stone burial jars called kalamba with carved lids, stone mortars and ancestor statues up to 380 cm tall. The culture that made them reached its peak in the Early Metal Period, around 2,500 to 1,500 years ago. People lived in villages of pile-built houses on stone pillars.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Megalithic Cultural Heritage of Lore Lindu Area

title: The Nutmeg Island Empties Out
place: Pulau Ay, Banda Islands, Maluku, Indonesia
text: On tiny Pulau Ay in the Banda Islands, people settled for over a thousand years and left pottery holding traces of nutmeg, the earliest known human use of the spice, at least 3,500 years old. They also raised pigs brought from afar. Then, about 2,300 years ago, the village was suddenly abandoned, and researchers still do not know why.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Archaeologists Uncover Earliest Human Use of Nutmeg

title: Bali's Water-Sharing Farmers
text: Bali's subak, a cooperative system of canals and weirs run through water temples, dates back to the 9th century. Groups of farmers share water from each source, and water flows through the temples before reaching the rice fields. The Pakerisan watershed holds Bali's oldest known irrigation system, and today the island has about 1,200 water collectives.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Cultural Landscape of Bali Province, the Subak System

title: A Bengali Sage Studies in Sumatra
text: In the 11th century Atisha, a great Buddhist scholar from Bengal, sailed for 13 months to study with the Sumatran teacher Swarnadwipa Dharmakirti. He stayed 12 years at Muarajambi, a vast Buddhist learning centre linked to Nalanda in India. Atisha later went to Tibet, where his reforms gave rise to the Kadampa school, and Dharmakirti is still honoured there.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Muarajambi Temple Compound

title: Mountains of Shells on the Cagayan
text: Along the Cagayan River, people piled up the shells of kabibe clams for thousands of years. By the Neolithic, about 4,200 to 4,000 years ago, these middens were about 100 by 50 metres and 3 metres deep. Their layers hold red-slipped pottery, clay spindle whorls, bark-cloth beaters, ornaments of Taiwan jade, domestic pig bones and grains of rice.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Prehistoric Sites of the Cagayan Valley Basin

dateLabel: About 400,000 years ago (cave used until about 200,000 years ago)
title: Fire, Flint and Shared Meat
place: Qesem Cave, near Rosh Ha'ayin, Israel
text: Qesem Cave near Rosh Ha'ayin was lived in between 400,000 and 200,000 years ago. Tel Aviv University archaeologists studied eight human teeth from the cave and found that its people made flint blades in a systematic way and used fire regularly. They hunted animals, cut up and shared the meat, and even mined flint from under the ground to make their tools.

source.name: American Friends of Tel Aviv University (EurekAlert!): Was Israel the birthplace of modern man?

title: Children's Handprints in Tibet
text: On a rocky promontory at Quesang on the Tibetan Plateau, someone pressed five handprints and five footprints into soft travertine laid down by a hot spring. Found in 2018, they date to between 169,000 and 226,000 years ago. Researchers think a child of about 7 made the footprints and one of about 12 the handprints, and argue the panel was a deliberate work of art.

source.name: Cornell University (EurekAlert!): Hand and footprint art dates to mid-Ice Age

title: A Rest Stop in the Zeravshan Valley
place: Soii Havzak rock shelter, Zeravshan Valley, Tajikistan
text: Archaeologists from Tajikistan's National Academy of Sciences and the Hebrew University dug a rock shelter in the Zeravshan Valley that people used from 150,000 to 20,000 years ago. Its layers are rich in bones, stone tools and charcoal. The team thinks Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans may all have stopped here, long before the valley became a Silk Road route.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): Major Paleolithic Site Excavated in Central Asia

title: A Human Found in a Cement Quarry
text: In the mining area of a cement plant near Ramla, archaeologist Yossi Zaidner found skull and jaw fossils of a kind of human previously unknown to science, dated to 140,000 to 120,000 years ago. The 'Nesher Ramla Homo' had no chin and very large teeth. These people made advanced stone tools and left behind bones of horses, fallow deer and aurochs.

source.name: Tel Aviv University (EurekAlert!): A new type of Homo unknown to science

title: A Denisovan Girl in Cobra Cave
place: Tam Ngu Hao 2 (Cobra Cave), Houaphanh, Laos
text: In December 2018, scientists pulled a human molar out of a block of rock in Tam Ngu Hao 2, called Cobra Cave, in the Annamite Mountains of Laos. The rock is between 164,000 and 131,000 years old. Proteins in the enamel suggest the tooth came from a young, likely female child, and its shape points to a Denisovan, the first found in Southeast Asia.

source.name: Demeter et al., Nature Communications (PMC): A Middle Pleistocene Denisovan molar from the Annamite Chain of northern Laos

source2.name: Southern Cross University: Fossil tooth unlocks mystery of Denisovans in Asia

dateLabel: At least 118,000 years ago (perhaps up to 194,000)
title: Mystery Toolmakers of Sulawesi
text: Stone tools dug up near the village of Talepu on Sulawesi are most likely between 118,000 and 194,000 years old, long before modern humans reached the region. Nobody knows who made them. Lead researcher Gerrit van den Bergh thinks Homo erectus is the likely maker, though they could be the work of still-undiscovered relatives of Flores's 'hobbits'.

source.name: National Geographic: Stone tools on Sulawesi (2016 report on the Talepu finds)

title: A Finger Bone by a Desert Lake
place: Al Wusta, Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
text: Al Wusta, in today's bone-dry Nefud Desert, was once a freshwater lake in grassland, home to hippos and tiny snails. There, researchers found a human finger bone dated to 88,000 years old, alongside plenty of stone tools. It showed that early members of our species spread across a wide area of southwest Asia, not just the Levant.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History (EurekAlert!): Early modern human migration out of Africa more geographically widespread than previously thought

dateLabel: By about 80,000 years ago, through the Toba eruption 74,000 years ago
title: Toolmakers Who Outlasted a Supervolcano
place: Dhaba, Middle Son Valley, Madhya Pradesh, India
text: At Dhaba in India's Middle Son Valley, layers of earth hold an 80,000-year record of stone tools. People were making tools there both before and after the Toba super-eruption on Sumatra about 74,000 years ago, a blast about 5,000 times bigger than Mount St Helens. Lead author Chris Clarkson says their toolkits resembled those of Homo sapiens in Africa.

source.name: Max Planck Institute (EurekAlert!): Human populations survived the Toba volcanic super-eruption 74,000 years ago

title: Rainforest Teeth from Lida Ajer
place: Lida Ajer cave, Padang Highlands, Sumatra, Indonesia
text: Dutch scientist Eugene Dubois dug in Lida Ajer cave in the 1880s. Modern researchers used his rough sketch and map to find the cave again, recognising it by a big rock column at its entrance. Human teeth from the cave date to between 73,000 and 63,000 years ago, the first evidence of modern humans living in rainforests.

source.name: The Conversation (Kira Westaway, Macquarie University): Old teeth from a rediscovered cave show humans were in Indonesia more than 63,000 years ago

title: The Oldest Picture Story
place: Leang Karampuang, Maros, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: In Leang Karampuang cave on Sulawesi, someone painted three human-like figures interacting with a wild pig at least 51,200 years ago. A team led by Indonesian rock art specialist Adhi Agus Oktaviana dated it by firing a laser at tiny crusts of calcium carbonate on top of the paint. Researchers call it the oldest known picture story.

source.name: Griffith University: Cave painting in Indonesia is the oldest known picture story

title: A Warty Pig in Red Ochre
text: In a cave in a valley closed in by steep limestone cliffs, someone painted a Sulawesi warty pig in red ochre at least 45,500 years ago. The pig seems to watch two other warty pigs. The survey that found it was led by Basran Burhan, and the age comes from 'cave popcorn' crusts that formed over the paint.

source.name: Griffith University News: Leang Tedongnge warty pig painting

title: The Woman Behind the Deep Skull
text: In 1958, Tom Harrisson's team found the 'Deep Skull' in the Hell Trench of Niah Cave in Sarawak. It was once thought to belong to a teenage boy. A fresh study showed the skull is 37,000 years old and probably came from a middle-aged woman, who most closely resembles the Indigenous people of Borneo today.

source.name: UNSW Sydney: Ancient 'Deep Skull' still holds big surprises 60 years after it was found

title: The Oldest Threads in a Georgian Cave
text: While studying tree pollen in Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia, scientists spotted flax fibres more than 34,000 years old, the oldest known fibres used by humans. Some were twisted together, one with many knots, and others were dyed black, grey, turquoise and even pink. They may have been used to sew hides into clothing and shoes, or to make ropes and baskets.

source.name: Harvard Gazette: Oldest-known fibers to be used by humans discovered

source2.name: Science News (Bruce Bower): Stone Age twining unraveled

title: A Skull Older Than Anyone Thought
text: A skullcap from the Salkhit Valley in northeast Mongolia was once linked to Homo erectus or Neanderthals. Oxford scientists radiocarbon-dated a single amino acid from its bone, getting past resin that had been used to make casts of it, and found it lived 34,950 to 33,900 years ago. Its DNA showed it was a modern human.

source.name: University of Oxford (EurekAlert!): Ancient Mongolian skull is the earliest modern human yet found in the region

title: Beads from a Pig-Deer's Tooth
place: Leang Bulu Bettue, Maros, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Ice Age people at Leang Bulu Bettue cave on Sulawesi made disc-shaped beads from a babirusa, or 'pig-deer', tooth and a pendant from the bone of a bear cuscus. They also scratched geometric patterns on stones and left ochre-stained tools. A bone tube may have been a blow-pipe for spraying hand stencils. The finds date to 30,000 to 22,000 years ago.

source.name: Griffith University (ScienceDaily): Prehistoric art and ornaments uncovered in Indonesian cave

dateLabel: About 22,000 years ago (cave used 30,000 to 14,000 years ago)
title: Finger Lines Under the Nullarbor
place: Koonalda Cave, Nullarbor Plain, South Australia
text: Inside Koonalda Cave, beneath the Nullarbor Plain, people left finger flutings and incised lines in soft limestone and mined flint during the Last Glacial Maximum, between 30,000 and 14,000 years ago. Dated to about 22,000 years ago, the markings were the first of their kind reliably dated to the Pleistocene. They proved Aboriginal people survived in this arid region during the Last Glacial Maximum.

source.name: Australian Government (Federal Register of Legislation): Inclusion of a Place in the National Heritage List, Koonalda Cave (2014)

title: New Guinea's Last Giant Kangaroos
place: Nombe rock shelter, Chimbu Province, Papua New Guinea
text: Bones from Nombe rock shelter in the Papua New Guinea Highlands suggest giant animals lingered there until about 20,000 years ago. They included two large extinct kangaroos, one of which walked on four legs, the thylacine, and a panda-like marsupial called Hulitherium. Small groups of nomadic people visited only now and then, which may explain why the megafauna lasted so long.

source.name: Flinders University News: PNG megafauna abound to 20,000 years ago

title: Australia's Oldest Known Painting
place: Unghango clan estate, Balanggarra Country, Kimberley, Western Australia
text: A two-metre-long kangaroo painted on the sloping ceiling of a rock shelter on Balanggarra Country is Australia's oldest known rock painting, most likely about 17,300 years old. Researcher Damien Finch dated it by radiocarbon-dating mud wasp nests built under and over the paint. It belongs to a style called Irregular Infill Animal, or the Naturalistic period.

source.name: University of Melbourne (EurekAlert!): Australia's oldest rock painting is a kangaroo

title: A Pet Fox for the Afterlife?
text: In a cemetery in northern Jordan about 16,500 years old, a man was buried with the skull and a foreleg bone of a red fox. Later the grave was reopened and his body moved, and the fox went with him. A Cambridge-led team suggests it was a pet, buried to keep its owner company in the afterlife, about 4,000 years before the next earliest burials with dogs.

source.name: University of Cambridge: Was the fox prehistoric man's best friend?

title: Farming Begins in the Zagros
text: At Chogha Golan in the foothills of Iran's Zagros Mountains, layers of settlement debris run from 11,700 to 9,800 years ago. The most common plants found are wild barley, goat-grass and lentil, the wild ancestors of modern crops, and domesticated emmer wheat appears about 9,800 years ago. The finds suggest farming in the Near East began in several centres, not just one.

source.name: University of Tübingen (ScienceDaily): Early roots of farming in Iran

title: Two Infants of Ancient Alaska
place: Upward Sun River site, Interior Alaska, United States
text: About 11,500 years ago, two infants who seem to have died in summer were buried together at Upward Sun River in Interior Alaska. Mourners laid antlers, a stone cutting tool and decorated dart points beside them. Found in 2013, the babies had different mothers, and their DNA belongs to two Native American lineages never before found this far north.

source.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks: Ancient Alaska infants' DNA supports human migration theory

title: The Shaman with 50 Tortoises
place: Hilazon Tachtit cave, western Galilee, Israel
text: In a cave in the western Galilee lies a 12,000-year-old Natufian woman, about 45 years old, petite and with a spinal disability. She was buried with 50 complete tortoise shells, a leopard pelvis, a golden eagle's wing tip, a cow's tail and a large human foot. Hebrew University archaeologist Leore Grosman thinks she was a shaman.

source.name: Hebrew University of Jerusalem (EurekAlert!): 12,000-year-old shaman burial

title: A Holy Child in the Ruins
text: When Miguel López de Legazpi's troops landed on Sugbu (the old name of Cebu) on 28 April 1565, sailor Juan de Camus found a wooden statue of the Santo Niño, the Holy Child, among the ruins. Its survival from fire was hailed as a miracle. Many believe it was the image Magellan's party gave Rajah Humabon's wife in 1521, and it is still honoured with the Sinulog festival.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art (Cultural Center of the Philippines): Santo Niño de Cebu

title: The Philippines' First Printed Book
text: The Doctrina Christiana, a Catholic teaching book dated to 1593, was printed in Manila by a Chinese printer working for Dominican priests. It set out its text in both Spanish and Tagalog, using Roman letters and the local Baybayin script. The only known surviving copy in the world sits in the Library of Congress in Washington.

source.name: Library of Congress blog: Doctrina Christiana, More than Four-hundred Years of Filipino-American History

title: The Dutch Arrive for Pepper
text: In 1596 the first Dutch fleet to Indonesia reached Banten in West Java, then the centre of the pepper trade, when pepper was still a luxury spice. The voyage was full of mishaps and many crew died. Its senior merchant, Cornelis de Houtman, met Banten's ruler, but his rude, undiplomatic manner got relations off to a bad start.

source.name: Wereldmuseum Amsterdam: A profitable business. But for whom?

title: A Line Drawn Through the Straits
text: Signed in London on 17 March 1824, the Anglo-Dutch Treaty split the region into British and Dutch spheres. Britain swapped Bencoolen (Bengkulu) and Billiton (Belitung) for Melaka and Singapore, and the Johor-Riau Sultanate was cut in two. Far from London, that deal still forms the basis of the borders between Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board Singapore), Peter Borschberg: On Paper, Singapore Before 1867

title: Asia's First Republic
text: Inside Barasoain Church in Malolos, the Malolos Constitution was promulgated on 21 January 1899. Two days later, on 23 January, the First Philippine Republic was inaugurated in the same church, making the Philippines the first independent republic in Asia. Since 2013, every 23 January has been marked as a day to remember it.

source.name: Official Gazette text via Lawphil: Proclamation No. 533, s. 2013 (Araw ng Republikang Filipino, 1899)

title: Taal's Deadly Base Surge
text: Taal Volcano sits on an island in Taal Lake, south of Manila. Its 1911 eruption killed 1,335 people. Philippine volcano experts say most died from a base surge, a ring-shaped cloud of gas and debris racing outward from the bottom of the eruption column, which swept the whole island and reached the lakeshore.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Hazardous base surges of Taal's 2020 eruption

source2.name: GMA News: 'Base surge' cause of death in Taal's past eruptions, PHIVOLCS

title: Filipinas Vote for the Vote
text: Filipino women won the vote by voting for it themselves. On Plebiscite Day, 30 April 1937, women across the Philippines cast 447,725 'yes' votes against 44,307 'no' votes on whether they should have the right of suffrage.
