In a special session from August to September 1937, the National Assembly ratified the result.

source.name: University of the Philippines Diliman Library, Rare Periodicals: Woman suffrage in the Philippines (Panorama, 1967)

title: Seven Shouts of Merdeka
text: At midnight the British flag came down on the Selangor Club padang. Then on 31 August 1957, before 25,000 people in the new Merdeka Stadium, Tunku Abdul Rahman read Malaya's Proclamation of Independence and shouted 'Merdeka!' (freedom) seven times. The national anthem, Negaraku, was played for the first time as the new flag rose.

source.name: Universiti Malaya Library exhibition: Hari Merdeka, The Spirit of Independent Malaysia

source2.name: Malay Mail (Bernama): A nation was born here, Stadium Merdeka keeps Malaysia's independence story alive

title: Pinatubo Wakes Up
text: After a 500-year slumber, Mount Pinatubo exploded on 15 June 1991, in the second-largest eruption of the century. Its ash cloud rose 35 kilometres, and its gas cooled global temperatures by about 0.5°C from 1991 to 1993. Forecasts by Philippine and US scientists got people out in time, saving at least 5,000 lives, but about 20,000 Aeta highlanders lost their homes.

source.name: US Geological Survey Fact Sheet 113-97: The Cataclysmic 1991 Eruption of Mount Pinatubo, Philippines

title: Trophies Taken from Manila
text: In 1762, during the Seven Years War, British and East India Company forces sailed from Madras in India and occupied Manila and Cavite until 1764. They carried off trophies: nine Spanish flags paraded into King's College chapel in Cambridge, and a carved wooden Spanish coat of arms taken from the gates of Intramuros, still kept in the Government Museum of Chennai.

source.name: Mapping Philippine Material Culture (SOAS project), Cristina Juan: The Manila-Madras Connection and the 1762 British Invasion

title: One Kingdom Becomes Two
text: After years of family feuding stirred up by the Dutch VOC, the Treaty of Giyanti was signed on 13 February 1755, splitting the Javanese kingdom of Mataram into Surakarta and Yogyakarta. Prince Mangkubumi became Sultan Hamengku Buwono I and designed his own palace, placing it between the Code and Winongo rivers, with Mount Merapi to the north and the Southern Sea beyond.

source.name: Kraton Ngayogyakarta Hadiningrat (official palace site): Sri Sultan Hamengku Buwono I

source2.name: Dinas Kebudayaan Kota Yogyakarta (Yogyakarta City Culture Office): Perjanjian Giyanti

title: A Violin Plays a Nation's Song
text: At the Second Youth Congress in a student boarding house at Kramat Raya 106, journalist W.R. Supratman played his song 'Indonesia Raya' on the violin on 28 October 1928, the day of the Youth Pledge. Delegates were moved to tears and asked to hear it again. The colonial government later seized its records, and the chorus word 'merdeka' (free) was changed to 'mulia' (noble).

source.name: Kompas: Kisah di Balik 'Indonesia Raya' yang Pertama Kali Dikumandangkan di Sumpah Pemuda 1928

source2.name: Kompas: Kisah Biola WR Supratman di Museum Sumpah Pemuda

title: Brunei Resumes Full Independence
text: Brunei had been a British protectorate since 1888, keeping its own internal rule while Britain handled foreign affairs. On 1 January 1984 Brunei Darussalam resumed full independence, and Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah also became Prime Minister, Finance Minister and Home Affairs Minister. The small, oil- and gas-rich sultanate is run under its 1959 constitution, with the Sultan as head of state.

source.name: Permanent Mission of Brunei Darussalam to the UN: Country Facts

source2.name: US Department of State: Background Notes, Brunei (October 1998)

title: East Timor Chooses
text: Despite months of militia threats, East Timorese voters turned out on 30 August 1999 for a UN-run ballot on autonomy within Indonesia. On 4 September the UN announced the result: 344,580 people, or 78.5 per cent, voted against. Pro-integration militias then unleashed violence, looting and arson across the territory, until Indonesia's assembly formally recognised the vote that October.

source.name: United Nations Peacekeeping: The United Nations and East Timor, A Chronology

title: A Map Signed 'Indio Tagalo'
text: The great 1734 map of the Philippines was charted by Jesuit Pedro Murillo Velarde, but engraved on copper plates by two Filipino artists, Nicolás de la Cruz Bagay and Francisco Suárez, who proudly signed themselves 'Indio Tagalo'. Its side panels show Manila life: cockfights, Aeta dancers, a woman with a basket of guavas, and Persian, Japanese and Indian visitors.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art (Cultural Center of the Philippines): Murillo Velarde Map of 1734

title: A Malay Scholar Tells His Story
text: In 1849 the scholar and translator Abdullah bin Abdul Kadir, known as Munsyi Abdullah, published his memoir, the Hikayat Abdullah, with the missionary Benjamin Keasberry. It records life and politics in Singapore, Melaka, Johor and Riau-Lingga. Called the 'father of Malay printing', Abdullah was the first non-European to have his works published in Malay.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board Singapore), Tan Huism: Tales of the Malay World, Manuscripts and Early Books

title: The Puputan of Badung
text: In 1906 a Dutch military expedition marched against I Gusti Gede Ngurah Den Pasar, ruler of Badung in south Bali. Hundreds of Balinese died from Dutch gunfire or took their own lives rather than surrender, in a ritual called puputan. The palace was looted, and two of its doors, each over four metres high, ended up in a Dutch museum.

source.name: Wereldmuseum Amsterdam: Bali Behind the Scenes, Tourism and colonialism

title: Dom Boaventura's Rebellion
text: Portuguese rule in Timor brought forced labour on roads and coffee plantations, and in 1908 a head tax on men aged 18 to 60. Dom Boaventura, ruler of Manufahi, united several kingdoms in the 1911–1912 rebellion, seen as the last great revolt against Portuguese rule. It was crushed in 1912 with troops brought from Mozambique; Timorese accounts say over 3,000 died.

source.name: Northern Illinois University SEAsite: East Timor, Portuguese Contact

source2.name: Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Lúcio Sousa: The Insurrect Native in Portuguese Timor, The Rebellion of Manufahi in the Australian Press

title: Batik, From Cradle to Grave
text: In 2009 UNESCO added Indonesian Batik to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. Artisans draw dots and lines of hot wax on cloth so it resists dye, then repeat for each colour. Batik follows Indonesians through life: babies ride in lucky batik slings, the dead are wrapped in funeral batik, and royal batik is even cast into a volcano.

source.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Indonesian Batik

title: The Virgin of the Sea Battles
text: In 1646 the Dutch attacked the Philippines, and five naval battles were fought near Marinduque. The outnumbered Spanish fleet won, and people credited the Virgin of the Rosary, an ivory-and-wood image carved in 1593 by a Chinese artist. Ever since, her feast, La Naval de Manila, has been held on the second Sunday of October.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art (Cultural Center of the Philippines), Rene B. Javellana and Nicanor G. Tiongson: Our Lady of La Naval

title: Snapshots of Everyday Filipinos
text: Recuerdos de Filipinas, an 1895 album by Félix Laureano of Iloilo, is believed to be the first collection of photographs made by a Filipino. Its 37 sections show weddings, funerals, bathing, washing clothes and village bands, including guests in formal dress marching barefoot. Laureano dedicated it to the painter Juan Luna, proudly calling him a fellow 'Filipino'.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art (Cultural Center of the Philippines): Recuerdos de Filipinas

title: The Longest Neck of Any Dinosaur
text: In 1987 the China–Canada Dinosaur Project found a few neck and skull bones of Mamenchisaurus sinocanadorum in rocks about 162 million years old. A 2023 study estimated its neck at about 15.1 metres, over six times longer than a giraffe's. CT scans showed the neck bones were mostly air, about 69 to 77 percent of their volume, keeping them light like a bird's.

source.name: Stony Brook University News: New Fossil Analysis Reveals Dinosaur with Record-Holding 15-Meter-Long Neck

title: The Shark-Toothed Hunter of Siam
place: Ban Saphan Hin, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: Near Ban Saphan Hin in central Thailand, a team led by Duangsuda Chokchaloemwong of Nakhon Ratchasima Rajabhat University found bones from at least four individuals of a 25-foot predator, named Siamraptor suwati in 2019. It belonged to the carcharodontosaurs, known for serrated, knife-like teeth, and is the first definite member of that group found in Southeast Asia.

source.name: National Geographic: Huge new shark-toothed dinosaur found in Thailand

source2.name: EurekAlert! (PLOS): Siamraptor suwati, a new species of giant predatory dinosaur from Thailand

title: The Tiny Deer Related to Whales
text: Whales have a surprising cousin from Kashmir. Indohyus was a deer-like animal about the size of a fox or raccoon that lived some 48 million years ago. It had dense limb bones that would have weighed it down in water, and a middle ear structure otherwise found only in whales and their relatives. Researcher Thewissen says the ancestors of both looked like a tiny deer.

source.name: Scientific American: Closest Whale Cousin—A Fox-Size Deer?

title: A Fruit-Cracking Primate from Myanmar
place: Near Ganle village, Pondaung area, Myanmar
text: Fossils first found in central Myanmar in December 2005 revealed Ganlea megacanina, a 38-million-year-old primate named after the nearby village of Ganle. Worn teeth suggest it used its big canines to pry open hard tropical fruits for their seeds. It lived in a lowland much like today's Amazon Basin, and researchers say early Asian relatives of monkeys already filled a monkey's role.

source.name: EurekAlert! (Carnegie Museum of Natural History): new Myanmar anthropoid primate

title: Before Apes and Monkeys Split
text: In 2009 a skull was found in western Saudi Arabia from a primate that lived in a black-mangrove environment 29 to 28 million years ago. Named Saadanius hijazensis and studied by Iyad Zalmout's team at the University of Michigan, it was a male weighing some 15 to 20 kilograms. It belonged to the shared group living before the ape and Old World monkey lines split apart.

source.name: Scientific American: New ape fossil challenges DNA evidence about ancient split from other primates

title: Heracles, the Giant Parrot
place: St Bathans, Central Otago, New Zealand
text: Fossils up to 19 million years old from near St Bathans in Central Otago belong to the biggest parrot known. Standing up to a metre tall and weighing about 7 kilograms, it was twice the size of the kakapo. Scientists named it Heracles inexpectatus, after the strong hero of myth and because nobody expected it. It probably feasted on fruit and seeds.

source.name: Flinders University News: Meet 'Hercules', a parrot of child-size proportions

title: The Biggest Lake Ever
place: Paratethys, from the Alps to Central Asia (Black Sea is a remnant)
text: Around 11 million years ago, a body of water called Paratethys stretched from the Alps all the way to Central Asia. At its peak it covered about 2.8 million square kilometres of brackish water and was home to Cetotherium riabinini, the smallest whale in the fossil record. In crises it lost more than two-thirds of its surface, and its water dropped by up to 250 metres.

source.name: EurekAlert! (Utrecht University): Paratethys, the largest lake the Earth has ever seen

title: Thunder Birds of Alcoota
text: About 200 kilometres north-east of Alice Springs, grassy plains hide a huge bed of tightly packed fossil bones around eight million years old, and thousands have been found. Among them is Dromornis stirtoni, known only from Alcoota and one of the largest birds that ever lived. Males weighed around 530 kilograms and females around 450.

source.name: Australian Museum: Fossils in Alcoota, NT

source2.name: Flinders University VAMP: Dromornis stirtoni

title: A Camel in the High Arctic
text: On Ellesmere Island, scientists found about 30 pieces of a camel's shinbone dated to roughly 3.5 million years ago, when the High Arctic was forested. Collagen fingerprinting, which reads a bone protein, identified the animal. Led by Natalia Rybczynski of the Canadian Museum of Nature, the study showed the camel was about 30 percent bigger than modern camels.

source.name: NBC News: Giant Camels Roamed the Arctic 3.5 Million Years Ago

title: A Horned Plant-Eater Before Dinosaurs
text: Long before Triceratops, a reptile in what is now Madhya Pradesh grew a pair of horns over its eyes. Shringasaurus, meaning "horned lizard", lived around 247 million years ago and was an unexpected plant-eater with a long neck and a thick, low-slung body. Parts of at least seven individuals were found together in a single bonebed. It was not a dinosaur.

source.name: Scientific American (Laelaps blog): Paleo Profile: The Horned Lizard

title: Predator X of the Arctic
text: Between 2004 and 2012 a University of Oslo team dug up two big pliosaurs on the Arctic island of Svalbard. The sea reptile, nicknamed Predator X, lived roughly 150 million years ago and was about 33 to 42 feet long, with a skull up to about eight feet. It was named Pliosaurus funkei after Bjorn and May-Liss Funke, the volunteers who first found the fossils.

source.name: National Geographic: Paleontologists reveal identity of Predator X

source2.name: NBC News: Ancient giant 'Predator X' sea monster finally gets a name

title: Kronosaurus Rules the Inland Sea
text: Kronosaurus queenslandicus was the largest and fiercest predator of the inland seas of Early Cretaceous Australia. About 11 metres long, it had a skull almost two metres long and cone-shaped teeth up to nearly 30 centimetres. Stomach contents show it ate turtles, smaller sea reptiles, fish and sharks. Fossils come from near Hughenden, Richmond and Boulia.

source.name: Queensland Government: Queensland's fossil emblem, Kronosaurus queenslandicus

title: Ocean Floor on a Mountaintop
text: The mountains of Oman and the UAE hold a rare treasure: a slab of ancient ocean crust and upper mantle now sitting on land. The Semail ophiolite formed about 96 million years ago in the Tethys Ocean and was then thrust onto the edge of Arabia as a sheet roughly 15 to 20 kilometres thick. It is the largest and best-studied ophiolite on Earth.

source.name: Eos (AGU): UAE-Oman Mountains Give Clues to Oceanic Crust and Mantle Rocks

title: Antarctica's Forgotten First Dinosaur Bone
place: Abernethy Flats, James Ross Island, Antarctica
text: On 9 December 1985, Michael Thomson of the British Antarctic Survey and Reinhard Förster collected a small tail bone on James Ross Island. It sat unrecognised for decades until a 2025 study identified it as a titanosaur, a long-necked plant-eater, from rocks dated to about 82.6 million years ago. That makes it the first dinosaur bone ever collected from Antarctica.

source.name: Acta Palaeontologica Polonica: Barrett et al., titanosaurian caudal vertebra from James Ross Island

title: Saudi Arabia's First Dinosaurs
place: Near Al Khuraybah, Midyan region, Saudi Arabia
text: Along the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia, rocks about 75 million years old yielded tail bones of a titanosaur, a giant long-necked plant-eater, and teeth from an abelisaurid meat-eater. Found with fish, turtles, crocodilians and sea reptiles, they are the first identifiable dinosaur fossils described from the whole Arabian Peninsula. The bones show wear from waves or currents.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Kear et al., First Dinosaurs from Saudi Arabia

title: The Swan-Necked Swimming Raptor
text: Poachers smuggled this fossil out of Mongolia, but it was later donated and prepared for its return home. Synchrotron scans in Grenoble proved it was real. Halszkaraptor, almost 80 centimetres long, had a swan-like neck, fish-catching teeth and probably flipper-like hands. It was named after the Polish palaeontologist Halszka Osmólska and lived 71 to 75 million years ago.

source.name: Vrije Universiteit Brussel: Stolen dinosaur skeleton turns out to be swimming raptor

title: The Heaviest Penguin Ever Found
place: North Otago, South Island, New Zealand
text: In 2016 and 2017 Alan Tennyson found fossils in 57-million-year-old beach boulders in North Otago. Freed from the rock, the flipper bones revealed Kumimanu fordycei, a penguin estimated at 154 kilograms. The biggest emperor penguins, the largest alive today, weigh around 45 kilograms. Scientists suggest a big body helped catch larger prey and keep warm in cold water.

source.name: University of Cambridge: Giant penguin

source2.name: Natural History Museum, London: Largest ever penguin species discovered in New Zealand

title: Vasuki, the Giant Snake of Kutch
place: Panandhro Lignite Mine, Kutch, Gujarat, India
text: In a lignite mine in Kutch, Sunil Bajpai and Debajit Datta found 27 vertebrae of an enormous snake from about 47 million years ago, when temperatures averaged around 28 °C. Named after Vasuki, the serpent around Lord Shiva's neck, it may have been 11 to 15 metres long. It was probably a slow ambush predator that squeezed its prey.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Datta and Bajpai, Largest known madtsoiid snake from warm Eocene period of India

title: The Oldest DNA Ever Read
place: Kap København Formation, Peary Land, Greenland
text: Today Peary Land in North Greenland is a polar desert, but DNA from its sediments, dated to around two million years ago, tells another story. It reveals an open forest of poplar, birch and thuja trees, with hares, mastodons, ants and even horseshoe crabs nearby. The climate was more than 10 °C warmer than now, and the DNA is considerably older than any DNA sequenced before.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): Kjær et al., A 2-million-year-old ecosystem in Greenland uncovered by environmental DNA

title: Early Humans on Java
text: North of Solo in Central Java, Sangiran's layers record about 2.4 million years of change. Homo erectus remains and stone flakes were found here from the 1930s, and the site holds archaeological occupation floors from around 1.2 million years ago. More than 100 Homo erectus individuals have been found, some at least 1.5 million years old.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sangiran Early Man Site

title: The Khan Who Wrote History
text: Abu al-Ghazi Bahadur, khan of Khiva, had spent ten years in exile at the Safavid court in Isfahan studying Persian and Arabic histories. In 1659 he finished The Genealogical Tree of the Turkmen, written in Chagatai Turkish and mixing Persian chronicles with Turkic oral traditions. A second history, left unfinished, was completed by his son and later translated into German, French, Russian, Latin and English.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Abu al-Ghazi Bahadur

title: A Fort Where the Irkut Meets the Angara
text: Russian colonists first made a winter camp where the Irkut River joins the Angara in 1652. In 1661 they built a fort there, and Irkutsk quickly became the main centre of the lands west of Lake Baikal and of the Russian trade route to China and Mongolia. It gained town status in 1686, and many old wooden houses still line its streets.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Irkutsk

title: The Monk Who Became a Warlord
text: Galdan was a younger son sent to Tibet to train as a Buddhist lama. When his brother, the Dzungar leader, was murdered in 1671, he came home for revenge, and from 1676 he ruled the Dzungar Mongols. He conquered East Turkistan and Outer Mongolia, but in 1696 the Kangxi emperor, using artillery made under Jesuit instruction, crushed him near present-day Ulaanbaatar.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dga'-ldan (Galdan)

title: A Swedish Captive Maps the Kalmuks
text: Johan Gustaf Renat, a Swedish artillery officer captured at Poltava, was travelling with a Russian expedition up the Irtysh in 1716 when Kalmuks attacked the 700-man convoy. He spent years among his captors, teaching them to smelt iron and commanding their troops against China. Returning home in 1733, he brought a map of Central Asia, which August Strindberg found in a Linköping library in 1879.

source.name: Toyo Bunko Archive, NII Digital Silk Road: Southern Tibet, vol. 1, p. 399

title: The Year Samarkand Emptied
text: In 1722 tribal chiefs rebelled against Bukhara's khan in Samarkand and crowned a rival, who called in Kazakh allies. For seven years the Kazakhs ravaged the heart of Transoxiana, wrecking fields and orchards and plundering towns. A later Bukharan historian wrote that Samarkand was entirely abandoned and only two quarters of Bukhara stayed inhabited, as refugees fled to Fergana and other outlying regions.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Yuri Bregel): Central Asia vii. In the 18th–19th Centuries

title: The End of the Dzungars
text: For years the Dzungar Mongols had troubled the Qing empire's northwest. Between 1755 and 1757 the Qing general Zhaohui led several campaigns against them; on the last, his troops were cut off and surrounded until relief arrived. He then virtually wiped out the Dzungar tribes and placed the region under a military governor, with Chinese garrisons and penal colonies.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Zhaohui

title: Bukhara's Rulers Become Amirs
text: For decades, chiefs of the Manghit tribe ran Bukhara from behind puppet khans of the old dynasty. In 1785 Shah Murad, son of the powerful Daniyal Biy, deposed the puppet Abu'l-Ghazi and took the throne himself. From then on, he and the Manghit rulers who followed him used amir, not khan, as their main title.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Yuri Bregel): Central Asia vii. In the 18th–19th Centuries

title: A 19-Ton Vase from the Altai
text: Stone-cutters at the Kolyvan lapidary works in the Altai spent almost fourteen years carving this giant bowl from a slab of greenish jasper found at the foot of Revnev Mountain. Finished in 1843 to a design by Avraam Melnikov, it weighs almost 19 tons, and its bowl measures 5.04 by 3.22 metres. It still stands in the Hermitage in St Petersburg.

source.name: State Hermitage Museum, via Google Arts & Culture: Kolyvan vase

title: An Exiled Poet Sails the Aral Sea
text: Ukrainian poet and painter Taras Shevchenko was exiled as a private soldier, and Tsar Nicholas I personally banned him from writing, drawing or painting. Yet in 1848–49 he was included in a military expedition to survey and describe the Aral Sea. He kept working in secret, and many of his drawings from exile show the life of the Kazakhs.

source.name: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Shevchenko, Taras

title: Writing Down a Kyrgyz Epic
place: Kyrgyz lands of the northern Tian Shan, Kyrgyzstan
text: Kyrgyz bards carried the great Manas epic in their memories. In 1856 the scholar Chokan Valikhanov wrote down one of its heroic poems, about the death and funeral feast of Kökötöy-khan, and began a Russian translation he never finished. Only a few couplets of the Kyrgyz original survive, and one of his Manas excerpts was lost until Soviet times.

source.name: A. T. Hatto, Bulletin of SOAS (Cambridge Core): Kukotay and Bok Murun

source2.name: Central Eurasian Studies Society 2022 (Indira Musaeva): The history of recordings of the epic Manas

title: Into the Heavenly Mountains
place: Khan Tengri massif, Tian Shan, Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan
text: In 1857 Russian geographer Pyotr Semyonov climbed the Khan Tengri group and discovered broad glaciers high in the range. He also showed that the Chu River does not flow out of Lake Issyk Kul, as geographers had believed, and he noted how high the snow line sits in Central Asia's dry mountains. His surname later gained the honour Tyan-Shansky.

source.name: Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, via Encyclopedia.com: Semyonov-Tyan-Shansky, Petr Petrovich

title: A Bukharan Thinker Asks for Reform
text: Ahmad Donish taught himself astronomy, medicine and music, and three trips to St Petersburg convinced him Bukhara needed change. Between 1875 and 1882 he wrote his major work, urging the emir to fix wages, train honest officials and add science to religious schools. Critics called him an infidel, and the displeased emir sent him off to be a judge in remote provinces.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Vincent Fourniau): Dāneš, Aḥmad Maḵdūm

title: Afghan Victory at Maiwand
text: Ayub Khan, a son of the late emir Sher Ali, marched from Herat to claim Afghanistan's throne. On 27 July 1880 a British-Indian force sent to stop him was overwhelmed at Maiwand by an army up to ten times its size. The survivors fled back to Kandahar, which Ayub Khan's victorious army soon besieged.

source.name: National Army Museum: Second Afghan War

title: The Quake That Flattened Mud-Brick Verny
text: In June 1887 a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck Verny, the town now called Almaty. It destroyed nearly all of the town's adobe buildings and killed 300 people. Seismologists who later compared it with a 1911 quake nearby found that both shook the ground about equally, but frozen winter soil made the 1911 one cause far more ground failure.

source.name: Seismological Society of America news release (EurekAlert): Earthquake impact can be affected by seasonal factors

title: A Mountain Kingdom Split by a River
text: Darvaz was a largely self-ruling Tajik principality of steep gorges and fruit trees on both banks of the Panj River, ruled by its own shahs from the mid-1600s. After Russia's conquest it was attached to Bukhara, and boundary deals in 1893 and 1895 split it. Land south of the Panj went to Afghanistan; the north is now part of Tajikistan.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Jan-Heeren Grevemeyer): Darvāz

title: Digging Into the Mounds of Anau
text: In 1904 an American expedition led by Raphael Pumpelly dug into the two mounds at Anau. They found layers reaching back to about 5000 BCE and gathered unusual amounts of plant, animal and geological evidence. The deepest ten feet held only wild animal bones, showing early people hunted; later layers revealed domestic oxen, pigs and sheep as farming took over.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (T. Cuyler Young): Anaw i. Prehistoric Period

title: Khiva's Last Great Tower
text: Between 1908 and 1910 builders in Khiva raised the Islam Khwaja madrasah and its minaret. At 45 metres, the minaret is the city's tallest structure, and Britannica counts the pair as the last major architectural achievements of Central Asia's Islamic era. It rises inside the walled Ichan-Kala, where most buildings date from 1780 to 1850.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Khiva

title: A Disguised Traveller Finds Petra
text: Calling himself Sheikh Ibrahim ibn Abdallah, a pilgrim vowing to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb, the traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt followed a Bedouin guide through a narrow, dark gorge. Before him rose a building carved from solid rock. The Bedouin had long kept Petra's location a closely guarded secret, and his suspicious guide accused him of being an infidel hunting treasure.

source.name: National Geographic: Ancient Petra, Jordan's Lost Oasis

title: Iran's First Printing Press
text: As late as 1815 a British envoy wrote that printing was unknown in Persia. Then, around 1816-17, crown prince Abbas Mirza backed a press with movable type in Tabriz, run by the printer Mirza Zayn-al-Abedin. Among its first books was an account of a Persian-Russian battle, and a British doctor's guide to vaccination against smallpox probably appeared the same year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Willem M. Floor): ČĀP (printing)

title: Peace Treaty on the Gulf Coast
text: By the late 1700s the Qasimi family of Ras al-Khaimah dominated the southern Gulf coast and grew rich from sea trade. After attacks on British and Indian ships, a British naval assault defeated them in 1819. In 1820 the main coastal sheikhs signed a general treaty of peace, the first of the agreements that turned their towns into the Trucial States.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: United Arab Emirates, History

title: The Night Aleppo Fell
text: At about 8 in the evening, a foreshock rattled northwestern Syria. Half an hour later the main earthquake struck, with an estimated moment magnitude of 7.3, wrecking Aleppo and damaging Antakya and Latakia. Researchers studying newly found historical records say at least 10,000 people were killed, and aftershocks kept shaking the region for months.

source.name: Geofísica Internacional (Darawcheh, Abdul-Wahed and Hasan): The Great 1822 Aleppo Earthquake

title: First Recorded Climb of Ararat
text: Local tradition said Noah's Ark still lay on Ararat's summit but that God had declared no one should see it, and Armenians honoured St. Jacob for trying and failing to reach the top. In September 1829 the German Johann Jacob von Parrot made the first recorded successful ascent of Great Ararat, at 5,165 metres the highest peak in today's Turkey.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mount Ararat

title: Copying the Cliff of Darius
text: High on a rock face beside the old road to Babylon, King Darius I had carved his victories in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Starting in 1835, Henry Rawlinson, an East India Company officer, became the first to reach and copy the inscriptions. His work cracked Old Persian cuneiform, and the other two versions were soon translated too.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bīsitūn

title: Tahereh Removes Her Veil
place: Badasht, near Shahrud, Semnan Province, Iran
text: In gardens near a small village east of Shahrud, followers of the Bab met to announce a break with Islamic law. Qorrat-al-Ayn, one of the Bab's earliest disciples, who received the title Tahereh here, argued for a radical break and won the debate. When she then appeared in public unveiled, many were shocked, and some left the movement.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Moojan Momen): BADAŠT

title: A Constitution for Ottoman Armenians
text: In the 1800s Armenians lived through a cultural renaissance, fed partly by contact with liberal ideas from Russia and western Europe. Inside the Ottoman Empire they shared in the Tanzimat reforms, and in 1863 the Ottoman government recognized a special Armenian constitution. Progress was slow, though, and Armenians in Anatolia still suffered many abuses.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ronald Grigor Suny et al.): Armenia, Modern Armenia

title: Georgia's Peasants Are Freed
text: After Russia freed its serfs in 1861, the peasants of Georgia, then part of the Russian Empire, began receiving their freedom too, from 1864 onward. Many found the terms burdensome. Old family-centred ways were already fading as schools and European ideas spread, and Russian, Armenian and Western entrepreneurs were opening mines, factories and plantations.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ronald Grigor Suny et al.): Georgia, National revival

title: Cholera Strikes the Pilgrimage
text: In 1865 cholera, probably brought by pilgrims from India, struck the holy cities of Islam with great violence, killing a third of the 90,000 believers gathered there. Returning pilgrims, travelling faster than ever by steamship, carried it to Mediterranean ports and onward to Europe, Russia and the Americas. In response, Europe and the Ottoman Empire built a vast quarantine system along the Red Sea.

source.name: EHNE, Sorbonne Université (Sylvia Chiffoleau): The Pilgrimage to Mecca, Epidemics, and Health Protection in Europe

title: Twelve Days Become Six Minutes
text: In 1868 Naser al-Din Shah let the Siemens brothers build a telegraph from Tehran to the Russian border at Jolfa. Its 480-mile double wire opened in 1869, and by January 1870 the line ran on through Tiflis, Odessa, Warsaw and Berlin to London. Messages between Europe and India that once took 12 days now took just over six minutes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Michael Rubin): INDO-EUROPEAN TELEGRAPH COMPANY

title: Baku's Oil Goes Commercial
text: People around Baku had known about its oil since ancient times, and by the 15th century they were scooping lamp oil from shallow surface wells. Modern commercial drilling began in 1872. At the start of the 20th century the Baku oil field was the largest in the world, and derricks still stand in the gulf facing the city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Baku

title: The First Shah to See Europe
text: Invited to the World Fair in Vienna, Naser al-Din Shah accepted and became the first shah ever to visit Europe. He left Tehran on 20 April 1873 and travelled through Russia, Germany, England, France, Switzerland and Italy. In Vienna, Emperor Franz Joseph received him with great courtesy, and the shah toured the fair and its Persian pavilion.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Helmut Slaby): AUSTRIA i. Relations with Persia

title: An Underground Ride up the Hill
text: Visiting Istanbul in 1867, Eugène-Henri Gavand saw some 40,000 people toiling up a steep, narrow street between Galata, the banking centre, and lively Beyoğlu. His answer was an underground railway, the world's second after London's. It opened on 17 January 1875 with a 2.5-minute ride, and carried 75,000 passengers in its first two weeks. Gavand skipped the opening ceremony.

source.name: Istanbul Technical University (Kayaoğlu, Kocabal et al.): Early Application of Underground Funicular 'Tunnel' in Istanbul

title: Painted Tombs of Sidon's Kings
text: In 1887 a royal burial ground at Sidon gave up a set of perfectly preserved Greek marble sarcophagi. Osman Hamdi Bey, painter and director of Istanbul's archaeological museum, secured them for his collection. The finest, nicknamed the Alexander Sarcophagus because people once thought it held Alexander the Great, still shows traces of its original paint.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Osman Hamdi Bey

title: Steam Train to Jerusalem
text: In 1892 a single-track railway opened between the port of Jaffa and Jerusalem, winding through the Hills of Judaea past spectacular views. For many years the line linked Jerusalem with the coast at Tel Aviv-Yafo and Haifa and with Beersheba inland, and before 1948 travellers could even continue by rail to Lebanon, Syria and Egypt.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jerusalem, Economy

title: A Witty Reply Called Faults of Men
text: Annoyed by an older tract on how to discipline wives, Bibi Khanom Astarabadi wrote back in 1894 with The Faults of Men. Mixing Persian poetry, Qur'an verses, street songs and jokes, she spoke directly to her 'sisters' about husbands. It wasn't printed until 1992, but copies circulated, and one written in her own hand survives in Tehran's Majles Library.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Afsaneh Najmabadi): MAʿĀYEB AL-REJĀL

title: Thousands of Bricks from Babylon
place: Babylon, near Hillah, Babil Governorate, Iraq
text: In 1899 the German Oriental Society began digging at Babylon under Robert Koldewey. Locals had long reused the ancient baked bricks, so little of Nebuchadnezzar II's glazed Ishtar Gate still stood. But the team found thousands of small glazed-brick fragments in the rubble and collected them. Agreements in 1903 and 1926 let them take the pieces to Berlin, where the gate was rebuilt.

source.name: The Ancient Near East Today, ASOR (Helen Gries): The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, One Monument, Multiple Narratives

title: Hammurabi's Laws Found in Iran
text: Digging at Susa in southwest Iran in 1901-1902, a French mission led by Jacques de Morgan unearthed a basalt pillar 225 centimetres tall. It was covered in cuneiform laws in Old Babylonian, and on top a carving shows the sun god Shamash meeting King Hammurabi of Babylon, who reigned from 1792 to 1750 BCE. Today it stands in the Louvre.

source.name: Musée du Louvre, Collections: Code de Hammurabi, roi de Babylone

title: Shamakhi Shaken Again
text: Shamakhi, a former capital of Azerbaijan, had suffered many earthquakes, and in 1902 a huge one killed about 2,000 people and destroyed 4,000 homes. A researcher named Weber mapped its shaking using reports from 120 villages. More than 120 years later, geologists still found dropped keystones in a nearby chapel and argued the quake may have reached magnitude 7.4.

source.name: Tectonics, AGU (Pierce et al. 2024): Surface Rupturing Earthquakes of the Greater Caucasus Frontal Thrusts, Azerbaijan

title: A Line Drawn Across Yemen
place: Frontier between Ottoman North Yemen and British Aden, Yemen
text: In the late 1800s the Ottomans moved back into Sanaa and Taiz, while Britain had spread out from Aden to protect its hinterland. Clashes along the unmarked border grew, so in 1904 a joint commission surveyed it, and a treaty set the frontier between Ottoman North Yemen and the British south. Yemenis on both sides later saw it as outsiders meddling in their affairs.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Robert Burrowes et al.): Yemen, The age of imperialism

title: A Painter's Academy in a Palace
text: Court painter Kamal-ol-Molk had long dreamed of his own painting school. In 1911 the education minister Hakim-al-Molk set about helping him, and Iran's new parliament approved a budget and a plot in the grounds of the old Negarestan Palace. The Academy of Fine Arts became one of the achievements of the Constitutional movement, and he even lived there with his students.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Ahmad Ashraf): KAMĀL-AL-MOLK i. Life

title: Malindi Points the Way to India
text: Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored at the Swahili port of Malindi on April 14, 1498. There a Gujarati pilot who knew the route to Calicut, on India's southwest coast, came aboard. After a 23-day run across the Indian Ocean, the crew sighted India's Ghats mountains, and the ships reached Calicut on May 20.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vasco da Gama

title: Sapi Ivories for Portuguese Patrons
text: Sapi carvers in Sierra Leone turned West African ivory, which Europeans called "white gold", into lidded saltcellars and spoons for Portuguese buyers. Patrons sometimes brought silverware to copy, yet the artists added their own flat geometric patterns. The round bowls may echo the calabash gourd, still used across Africa as a container and in musical instruments.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Afro-Portuguese Ivories

title: Brass Plaques for Benin's Palace
text: Benin traded pepper, textiles and ivory for large amounts of imported metal, and the royal brass-casters' guild turned it into art. Around 1540 to 1570 they cast plaques that hung on the wooden pillars of the oba's palace, showing the king, courtiers and foreign visitors. One shows Portuguese traders with brass manillas, linking these newcomers with wealth.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Plaque with Oba (King) or Chief

source2.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Plaque with Portuguese Traders and Manillas

title: Galawdewos Wins Back Ethiopia
place: Weyna Dega, near Lake Tana, Ethiopia
text: After years of defeats by Ahmad Gran of Adal, the young emperor Galawdewos switched to hit-and-run warfare in Ethiopia's rugged hills. Near Lake Tana he caught Ahmad in the open, and Ahmad was killed in the fighting. His army broke, and that single death ended the war, returning north-central Ethiopia to the Christian kingdom.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ethiopia, the Zagwe and Solomonic dynasties

title: Idris Alawma Rebuilds Bornu
text: Around 1571 Idris Alawma became mai, or king, of Kanem-Bornu, an old Muslim trading empire around Lake Chad that linked North Africa, the Nile valley and lands to the south. Ruling from Birni Ngazargamu, west of the lake, he extended and consolidated the state until about 1603. The earliest mention of firearms in this region appears to date from his reign.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kanem-Bornu

source2.name: Journal of African History (H.J. Fisher and V. Rowland): Firearms in the Central Sudan

title: Queen Amina Expands Zazzau
text: Zazzau was the southernmost of the Hausa states, where camel caravans from the Sahara traded salt for cloth, leather, grain and captives. In the later 1500s its ruler, Queen Amina, enlarged her realm by conquering the Nupe and Jukun kingdoms. Even the powerful Hausa cities of Kano and Katsina had to pay her tribute.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Zaria (historical kingdom)

title: The Oromo Spread North
text: The Oromo were herders from the upper Genale River basin. Their gada system grouped all males born in the same eight-year span, who moved through life's stages together. In the 1500s their warrior groups began long-distance expeditions, and by 1600 the Oromo had spread so widely that the emperor governed only Ethiopia's northern regions.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Assefa Mehretu et al.): Ethiopia, the Zagwe and Solomonic dynasties

title: Malagasy Written in Arabic Letters
text: Between 1507 and 1513, Afro-Arab newcomers known as the "Moors from Malindi" settled in the Matitana valley of southeastern Madagascar and merged with local people to form the Antemoro. By the 1630s the Antemoro had a state led by holy clans, the only one on the island with written texts: Malagasy words in the Arabic alphabet.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Maureen Ann Covell et al.): History of Madagascar

title: Muzura's Maravi Strike the Coast
place: Southern end of Lake Malawi, Malawi
text: From the southern end of Lake Malawi, the Maravi ruler Muzura built a powerful state that took tribute from the Portuguese and their allies. In the early 1630s he joined a Karanga and Manyika alliance to drive the Portuguese out of the Zambezi lands and attacked the port of Quelimane. The attack failed, and he turned to the Shire Highlands, trading ivory and, increasingly, slaves.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Shula E. Marks): Southern Africa, European and African interaction from the 15th through the 18th century

title: The Saint Who Defied the Jesuits
text: Walatta Petros, born in 1594 to noble parents, publicly rebuked Emperor Susenyos when he turned Catholic, even though he threatened her family. She resisted Jesuit efforts to re-educate her and founded seven monastic communities. After her death in 1642, nuns told her story aloud, and a monk wrote it down in 1672, the oldest known book-length biography of an African woman by an African author.

source.name: American Historical Association, Perspectives on History (Allison Miller): The Saint Who Sent the Jesuits Packing

title: The Cape's Windowless Slave Lodge
place: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa
text: In 1679 the Dutch East India Company built a new lodge beside its gardens for the people it enslaved, who came from Madagascar and parts of western and eastern Africa. The building had no windows, only barred slits, and was wet, dark and dirty. By the mid-1700s about a thousand people lived there. Today it is a museum.

source.name: Iziko Museums of South Africa: The building (Slave Lodge)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Shula E. Marks): Southern Africa, European and African interaction

title: Pate Leads the Swahili Resistance
text: The Swahili town of Pate, in the Lamu islands, became the centre of East Africa's resistance to Portuguese rule. In 1696, allied with Pate, the imam of Oman sailed in with more than 3,000 men to besiege Mombasa, which fell in 1698. Afterwards Pate, Lamu, Kilwa and Zanzibar largely kept free of both Omani and Portuguese control.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Harold G. Marcus et al.): Eastern Africa, the Portuguese invasion

title: Smallpox Strikes the Khoekhoe
place: Southwestern Cape (near Paarl), Western Cape, South Africa
text: Since the late 1500s, Khoekhoe herders at the Cape had bartered cattle with passing ships for iron, copper, beads and tobacco. As Dutch demand for livestock grew, they became wary and conflicts followed. Then, beginning in 1713, smallpox ravaged many Khoekhoe communities. By the end of the 1700s their chiefdoms were largely destroyed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Andries Nel et al.): South Africa, the Iron Age and Europeans in South Africa

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Shula E. Marks): Southern Africa, European and African interaction

title: Oyo's Horsemen Ride on Dahomey
text: Oyo, the northernmost Yoruba kingdom, used its cavalry to control trade routes to the coast. In 1726 Oyo first invaded Dahomey, easily defeating King Agaja's army and burning his capital, Abomey. Although Dahomey's soldiers carried muskets, Oyo's horsemen were consistently successful against them, and by 1730 Agaja had to pay tribute.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (T.C. McCaskie): Western Africa, the southward expansion of Oyo

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Agaja

title: A Muslim State in the Highlands
text: In the late 1720s, Fulbe and Malinke Muslims led by Karamoko Alfa and Ibrahima Sori launched a jihad in the Fouta Djallon highlands of Guinea, where great rivers like the Gambia and Senegal begin. It created a Muslim state ruled from Timbo, which went on to organise trade with the coast and dominated central and coastal Guinea.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Fouta Djallon

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (T.C. McCaskie): Western Africa, the Islamic revolution in the western Sudan

title: Lunda Explorers Found Kazembe
text: About 1740 an exploring party from the western Lunda empire created a new kingdom, Kazembe. Its greatest ruler, Kazembe II Kaniembo, conquered neighbouring states and gave citizenship to the people he conquered, binding them with a network of tribute and trade. Kazembe became the largest and most highly organised of all the Lunda kingdoms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kazembe

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lunda empire

title: Asante Kings Hire on Merit
place: Besease, near Kumasi, Ashanti Region, Ghana
text: Starting with Osei Kwadwo, who took the throne about 1764, Asante kings built a strong central state with a merit-based bureaucracy and a fine communications system. Shrines near Kumasi from this great age have walls of timber, bamboo and mud plaster, decorated with bold reliefs of spirals, animals and plants linked to Adinkra symbols.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Asante empire

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Asante Traditional Buildings

title: Black Loyalists Sail to Freetown
text: Thomas Peters was born around 1738 in what is now Nigeria and enslaved in North America. He escaped, served the British, then fought for the land Black Loyalists had been promised in Nova Scotia. In January 1792 almost 1,200 Black settlers, about a third recruited by Peters, sailed from Halifax to Africa, where they founded Freetown.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia (James W. St.G. Walker, Tabitha de Bruin): Thomas Peters

title: The Hearth Under Hedgepeth Mound
place: Hedgepeth Mounds, Lincoln Parish, Louisiana, USA
text: Hedgepeth Mounds is a pair of earthen mounds in north-central Louisiana, tested by archaeologists in 1991. Charcoal from a hearth buried beneath Mound A was radiocarbon dated to about 2888 BCE, give or take a century. Together with soil and other evidence, that places the site in the Archaic period. Today the old ground surface lies under about a metre of river-laid silt.

source.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Hedgepeth Mounds, an Archaic Mound Complex in North-Central Louisiana

title: A Killer Whale in the Grave
place: Port au Choix, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
text: In 1967 a bulldozer digging a basement at Port au Choix, Newfoundland, turned up human bones. Archaeologist James Tuck went on to excavate a Maritime Archaic cemetery, where burials began about 4,400 years ago. Bodies were sprinkled with red ochre, a symbol of life, and buried with bone harpoon heads, carvings of diving birds and a killer whale carved nearly 20 cm long.

source.name: Parks Canada, Port au Choix National Historic Site: Maritime Archaic Traditions

source2.name: Parks Canada, Port au Choix National Historic Site: Archeology history

title: The Tallest Shell Ring
place: Fig Island, near Edisto Island, South Carolina, USA
text: On a marsh island near Edisto Island, South Carolina, Fig Island holds shell rings occupied between about 4240 and 3680 calibrated years before present. Ring A of Fig Island 1 rises 5 to 6 metres above the marsh, the tallest shell ring known in the Southeast, around a plaza only 20 to 30 metres across. Probing also revealed a shell walkway now hidden beneath the marsh.

source.name: South Carolina Department of Archives and History (report by R. Saunders, ed., Louisiana State University and NPS): The Fig Island Ring Complex (38CH42)

title: No Oysters in Summer
place: St. Catherines Shell Ring, St. Catherines Island, Georgia, USA
text: On St. Catherines Island off Georgia, people heaped oyster shells into a ring 70 metres across between about 2230 and 2030 BCE. Were they there all year? Scientists measured tiny parasitic snails gathered by accident along with the oysters. Their sizes showed harvesting ran from late fall to late spring, so these Archaic people may have chosen to skip summer oysters.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Seasonal oyster harvesting recorded in a Late Archaic period shell ring

title: Whalers With Two Kinds of House
place: Cape Krusenstern National Monument, Alaska, USA
text: Around 1800 BCE, people of the Old Whaling culture hunted whales along the coast of Cape Krusenstern in northwest Alaska. They built two different house styles, one for winter and one for summer, and their house pits can still be seen. Special harpoons and butchering tools turn up at the site, yet the animal remains show whales were not their main resource.

source.name: National Park Service, Cape Krusenstern National Monument: History and Culture

source2.name: National Park Service: Cape Krusenstern Archeological District

title: Jasper Beads at Jaketown
place: Jaketown, near Belzoni, Humphreys County, Mississippi, USA
text: At Jaketown in the Mississippi Delta, Late Archaic hunter-gatherers began Mound A and at least two other mounds sometime between about 1500 and 1350 BCE. Red jasper beads and hematite plummets found there show trade networks reaching the Appalachian Mountains and the Great Lakes. Later floods buried that landscape under about 10 feet of deposits, hiding parts of as many as 13 mounds.

source.name: Mississippi Department of Archives and History, Mississippi Mound Trail: Jaketown Mounds

dateLabel: About 1000 BCE (c. 2,950 calibrated years before present)
title: The Woman in Lawyer's Cave
place: Lawyer's Cave, Blake Channel, near Wrangell, Alaska, USA
text: A small arm bone from Lawyer's Cave, in Tlingit territory in Southeast Alaska, belonged to a woman radiocarbon dated to about 2,950 calibrated years before present. Working with the Wrangell Cooperative Association, scientists named her Tatóok yík yées sháawat and read her DNA. She ate almost nothing but seafood, and her genes link her closely to today's Indigenous peoples of the northern Northwest Coast.

source.name: iScience (via Europe PMC): A paleogenome from a Holocene individual supports genetic continuity in Southeast Alaska

title: The First Pots on the Arctic Coast
place: Cape Krusenstern, Northwest Arctic, Alaska, USA
text: At Cape Krusenstern in northwest Alaska, the Choris tradition was practised between about 750 and 250 BCE. Its people left temporary camps on the coast and winter camps inland, and archaeologists think some groups began living on the coast for all or most of the year. This period saw a highly significant new technology arrive here: pottery vessels.

source.name: National Park Service: Cape Krusenstern Archeological District

title: Fishhooks Saved by River Mud
place: Hoko River, Clallam County, Washington, USA
text: Excavations at the mouth of the Hoko River in Washington yielded fishhooks and nets about 2,600 years old. A National Park Service study calls Hoko a particularly important Early Maritime site because normally perishable objects survived there, including simple chipped stone tools still set in split cedar handles. Net and weir fragments and bentwood fishhooks show how skilled these fishers were.

source.name: University of Washington Libraries, Makah Cultural and Research Center exhibit: Fishing

dateLabel: From c. 550 BCE (2,500 cal BP) onward
title: A Great Mound on the Bay Shore
place: Near Newark and Union City, Alameda County, California, USA
text: Near today's Newark and Union City, ancestral Ohlone people used a great earthen mound, 91 by 122 metres at its base and about 3 metres high, from about 2,500 to 180 calibrated years before present. It once stood on the shore of San Francisco Bay. With the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe, scientists studied bones from 154 burials and found the diet barely changed over time.

source.name: American Journal of Biological Anthropology (via Europe PMC): Late Holocene Paleodietary Patterns Among the Ancestral Ohlone

title: Basketmakers Who Lived on Maize
place: Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona, USA
text: Scientists measured carbon and nitrogen in the bones of many Basketmaker people buried at Marsh Pass and nearby parts of northeastern Arizona, and radiocarbon dated them. The results show these Basketmaker II people were heavily dependent on maize by 400 BCE, as much as later Pueblo farmers of the Four Corners. Maize farming seems to have arrived quickly, perhaps with migrants.

source.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge Core): The Stable- and Radio-Isotope Chemistry of Western Basketmaker Burials

title: 57,000 Tons of Earth at Grave Creek
place: Grave Creek Mound, Moundsville, West Virginia, USA
text: Adena people raised Grave Creek Mound in stages from about 250 to 150 BCE, placing burials at different levels inside it. The work meant moving more than 57,000 tons of sand and earth, and a ditch about 40 feet wide and five feet deep once circled the mound. When local amateurs dug into it in 1838, they found two burial vaults.

source.name: West Virginia Department of Arts, Culture and History: Grave Creek Mound

title: Ivory People of the Bering Strait
text: In the Bering Strait region of Alaska, Okvik carvers shaped walrus ivory into small human figures. One at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, titled Transformational Figure, is just 7.6 centimetres tall and dated to about 200 BCE–100 CE. A related incised figure at Princeton, labelled Okvik/Old Bering Sea I, stands 16.6 centimetres tall and is dated 100–400 CE.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Transformational figure, Okvik (collection record)

source2.name: Princeton University Art Museum: Human figure, Okvik/Old Bering Sea I

title: Indiana's Great Mound
place: Mounds State Park, Anderson, Indiana, USA
text: Near Anderson, Indiana, Adena-Hopewell people built 10 earthworks. The largest, the Great Mound, is believed to have been constructed around 160 BCE. Research suggests these mounds were gathering places for religious ceremonies, sited so that astronomical alignments could be viewed from them. Today the Great Mound is the focal point of Indiana's Mounds State Park.

source.name: Indiana Department of Natural Resources: Mounds State Park

dateLabel: c. 160–1 BCE (start of the plank house)
title: An Early Plank House in Oregon
text: At Seaside on the northern Oregon Coast, the Palmrose site holds one of the earliest rectangular plank houses known on that coast. Smithsonian and amateur archaeologists dug there in the 1960s and 1970s. New radiocarbon dates on ancient deer-family bones suggest people lived in the plank house from sometime between 160 and 1 BCE until about 170 to 320 CE.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Reevaluating the antiquity of the Palmrose site, an early plank house on the northern Oregon Coast

title: 194 Painted Figures in a Texas Canyon
place: Lower Pecos Canyonlands, Val Verde County, Texas, USA
text: In the Lower Pecos Canyonlands of Texas, foragers painted vast murals in limestone rock shelters. One, at site 41VV1230, holds about 194 figures of people, animals and puzzling shapes, dated to 1990–1925 calibrated years before present. Its painters laid down black, then red, yellow and white, the same order used in a far older mural, part of some 4,000 years of continuity.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Mapping the chronology of an ancient cosmovision, 4000 years of continuity in Pecos River style mural painting

title: A 'Fort' That Faced the Solstice
place: Old Stone Fort, Manchester, Tennessee, USA
text: Between the Big and Little Duck Rivers in Tennessee, ancient builders raised long walls, one stretch running more than 2,000 feet. Radiocarbon dates of about 30, 230 and 430 CE suggest the walls were built, repaired and changed over some 400 years. Despite the name, archaeologists rule out a fort: no one lived inside, and the entrance walls point at the summer solstice sunrise.

source.name: Tennessee Technological University, Duck River Manual: Old Stone Fort

title: Fences of Stakes on the Tide Flats
place: Tide flats of Southeast Alaska, Tongass National Forest, USA
text: Across Southeast Alaska, people drove sharpened saplings into tidal mud to build fish traps and weirs; as the tide ebbed, fish were trapped behind them. Some looked like picket fences, probably with boughs woven between the stakes. Of 369 known trap and weir sites, 108 have dated stakes, and most were built between about 2250 and 1500 calibrated years before present.

source.name: USDA Forest Service, Tongass Archaeology Notes: Ancient Fish Traps in Southeast Alaska (J. L. Smith, 2012)

title: Pharr's Eight Dome-Shaped Mounds
place: Pharr Mounds, Natchez Trace Parkway, Mississippi, USA
text: Pharr Mounds in northeast Mississippi is a group of eight dome-shaped mounds spread over about 90 acres. Excavators found burials and cremation basins under the mounds, plus a copper-covered wooden object, a greenstone pipe and a cache of flint blades, with traits suggesting a date of about 1–200 CE. Modern Chickasaw people consider the mounds sacred and return as pilgrims.

source.name: National Park Service: Pharr Mounds

title: Marksville's Mounds and Dogs
text: At Marksville in Louisiana, an earthen embankment encloses a group of mounds, and the site gave its name to the Marksville culture of about 1–400 CE. Thirty-six people and two dogs were buried in the site's only burial mound, along with a few pots, a copper artifact and two plain platform pipes. Marksville potters were the first to add temper to their clay.

source.name: 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities): Marksville Culture

title: Pond Mud Remembers the Dorset
text: On Somerset Island in Arctic Canada, scientists took sediment cores from ponds beside abandoned camps. Chemical markers such as coprostanol, extra nitrogen and algae rose whenever people lived nearby. The cores revealed Dorset people there from about 200 to 500 CE, at sites where archaeologists had found no Dorset traces, and later Thule hunters who killed many caribou around 1185–1510 CE.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (via Europe PMC): Sedimentary biomarkers and bone specimens reveal a history of prehistoric occupation on Somerset Island

title: Pithouse Villages of Chaco
place: Chaco Culture National Historical Park, New Mexico, USA
text: In Chaco Canyon, the Late Basketmaker period began about 400 or 500 CE, and some 200 sites from it are recorded in the park. Most are clusters of 1 to 20 semi-underground pithouses. In this period the bow and arrow replaced the spear-thrower and a ceramic tradition developed, and the type site, Shabik'eshchee Village, even has a great kiva.

source.name: National Park Service, Chaco Culture National Historical Park: Late Basketmaker Period

title: Angkor Joins the World Heritage List
place: Angkor Archaeological Park, Siem Reap, Cambodia
text: In 1992 UNESCO inscribed Angkor, a park of some 400 square kilometres holding the capitals of the Khmer Empire from the 9th to the 15th century. Besides famous temples like Angkor Wat and the Bayon, it has reservoirs, dykes and canals. Conservation went so well that Angkor was taken off the List of World Heritage in Danger in 2004.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Angkor

title: The Mystery Jars of Laos
text: In 2019 UNESCO listed the Plain of Jars in central Laos, named after more than 2,100 giant stone jars used for Iron Age funerals. The jars were carved in quarries and moved to burial sites between about 500 BCE and 500 CE. Little is known about the people who made them, and some jars were damaged by wartime bombing.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang - Plain of Jars

title: A Trading Port Frozen in Time
text: Hội An, a trading port active from the 15th to 19th centuries, became a World Heritage Site in 1999. Its trade declined in the later 1800s, so no one rebuilt its 1,107 timber-frame buildings in modern materials. Shops face narrow streets while their backs open onto the river, and an 18th-century Japanese bridge carries a small pagoda.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hoi An Ancient Town

title: The Twins Who Named a Word
text: Chang and Eng, born in 1811 in Meklong, Siam, were joined at the breastbone by a small piece of cartilage. They worked as merchants and raised ducks for their eggs. On April 1, 1829, they sailed with merchant Robert Hunter on a 138-day voyage to Boston, and doctors and journalists later began calling them the Siamese twins.

source.name: Arizona State University, Embryo Project Encyclopedia: Chang and Eng Bunker (1811-1874)

title: Elephants for America
text: In a letter dated February 14, 1861, King Mongkut of Siam offered the United States several pairs of elephants, to be turned loose in forests until there were large herds. He thought they could carry loads through uncleared woods. Abraham Lincoln kindly accepted the king's sword and photograph, but declined the elephants, saying the American climate did not favour them.

source.name: U.S. National Archives: Special Display of King of Siam's Letter to President Buchanan

title: The Death Railway Is Finished
text: Japan's railway through the jungle between Thailand and Burma was completed in October 1943. It was built by about 60,000 Allied prisoners of war and 200,000 Asian labourers called romusha, and perhaps 75,000 romusha died. At Hellfire Pass, starving men cut through solid rock with hammers and chisels, working by torchlight that looked like a scene from hell.

source.name: Australian War Memorial: Stolen Years - The Burma-Thailand Railway

source2.name: Hellfire Pass Interpretive Centre (Australian Government DVA): History

title: America's First Asian Treaty
text: On March 20, 1833, Siam and the United States signed a Treaty of Amity and Commerce, their first official diplomatic contact. It was negotiated by Edmund Roberts, a special agent sent on a mission to the Far East to make treaties with Siam and other powers. It became the first treaty the United States ever made with an Asian country.

source.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: Thailand - Countries

title: A Court Decides a Cliff-Top Temple
place: Preah Vihear Temple, Preah Vihear, Cambodia
text: Preah Vihear, a temple to Shiva from the early 11th century, sits on the edge of a plateau above the Cambodian plain. Cambodia and Thailand both claimed it, and on June 15, 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that it stood on Cambodian territory. Thailand had to withdraw its forces and return objects taken from the ruins since 1954.

source.name: International Court of Justice: Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Temple of Preah Vihear

title: Ayutthaya Under Water
text: In October 2011 the Chao Phraya River spilled over its floodplains, and satellites saw much of the historic city of Ayutthaya under water. Fields, roads and buildings were swamped by muddy floodwater, factories closed, and Bangkok flooded too. Such a wide flood was unusual even for the monsoon, and by mid-December the Bangkok Post reported 740 deaths nationwide.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Floods Swamp Historic City in Thailand

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Flooding in Thailand

title: Siam's Ambassador Dazzles Versailles
text: On September 1, 1686, Kosa Pan, ambassador of King Narai of Siam, was received by Louis XIV at Versailles in one of the most sumptuous events of the reign. Among countless gifts from Narai or his minister Constantine Phaulkon was a silver jug, the only known silver item. Today it is displayed at the very spot where it was handed over.

source.name: Palace of Versailles: Acquisition of the silver jug

source2.name: Musee du Louvre collections: Almanach de 1687, Audience aux ambassadeurs de Siam

title: Deer Skins and a Bamboo Fence
text: The Dutch East India Company traded near Lawec, Cambodia's capital, buying deer and manta ray skins to sell on to Japan. In 1643 a senior merchant grumbled that the lodge was rough and poor, with a light bamboo fence. That same year Company men were killed and local people, helped by the Portuguese, looted and destroyed the post.

source.name: Rijksmuseum: Two Views of Dutch East India Company Trading Posts - Lawec in Cambodia (SK-A-4475)

source2.name: Northern Illinois University SEAsite, International Conference on Lao Studies: W. Feldberg (IIAS), Gerrit Wuijsthoff's Journey to the Lao Court at Vientiane, 1641-1642

title: A Dutch Merchant Sails to Laos
text: In July 1641 Gerrit Wuijsthoff of the Dutch East India Company set out from Loveck, Cambodia's capital, up the Mekong to the Lao court of King Souligna Vongsa at Vientiane, in search of new trade. His notes made him the first European to write a detailed report on Laos, and the only long European account until the French arrived two centuries later.

source.name: Northern Illinois University SEAsite, International Conference on Lao Studies: W. Feldberg (IIAS), Gerrit Wuijsthoff's Journey to the Lao Court at Vientiane, 1641-1642

title: A Letter Made of Gold
place: Royal court of Burma, Myanmar (letter now in Hanover, Germany)
text: In 1756 the Myanmar king Alaungmintaya sent King George II of Great Britain a letter offering trade cooperation. It was engraved in the Myanmar language on a gold plaque, with a line of 12 rubies along each of two sides. Nobody in Hanover's library could read it for 250 years, and in 2015 UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World Register.

source.name: UK National Commission for UNESCO: The Golden Letter of the Burmese King

title: The 8-8-88 Uprising
text: On August 8, 1988, remembered in Burma as 8-8-88, hundreds of thousands of people, perhaps up to a million, marched in Rangoon calling for democracy, elections and economic reform. University students had sparked the protests, and Buddhist monks acted as marshals. Soldiers shot at unarmed crowds, and on September 18 the army seized back control of the cities.

source.name: Human Rights Watch: Crackdown - Repression of the 2007 Popular Protests in Burma (background on 1988)

title: A Monk's Fiery Protest
place: Near Xa Loi Pagoda, Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon), Vietnam
text: On the morning of June 11, 1963, at a Saigon street corner near Xa Loi Pagoda, the Buddhist monk Quang Duc poured gasoline on his robe and set himself alight. Hundreds of monks and nuns surrounded him, and hundreds more people watched. Buddhists used loudspeakers to link his death to five demands they had made of the South Vietnamese government.

source.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1961-1963, Vol. III, Document 163

title: A Plague Hunter's Seaside Lab
text: Having isolated the plague bacillus in 1894, Alexandre Yersin travelled to Indochina in 1895 and set up a small laboratory in Nha Trang to study cattle diseases. It became a branch of the Institut Pasteur in 1905. Yersin also explored the Lang-Bian plateau, suggesting the town that became Dalat, and brought the rubber tree to Indochina in 1899.

source.name: Institut Pasteur Archives: Alexandre Yersin chronology

title: Redcoats Land at Rangoon
text: After frontier clashes in Cachar and Arakan, Britain declared war on Burma in March 1824, and on May 10 a seaborne force landed at lightly defended Rangoon. The war dragged on until 1826. At least 15,000 British and Indian soldiers died, about three-quarters from illnesses such as malaria and dysentery, and Burma lost Arakan, Assam, Manipur and Tenasserim.

source.name: National Army Museum (UK): First Burma War

title: Rodin Chases the Royal Ballet
place: Royal Palace, Phnom Penh, Cambodia (tour to France)
text: In 1906 King Sisowath made the first trip to France by a Cambodian ruler, bringing dancers of the royal ballet. The sculptor Auguste Rodin saw them in Paris in July and found it like a revelation. He followed them to Marseille, leaving without paper or pencils, and in about a week made roughly 150 drawings, fascinated by their arms and hands.

source.name: Musee Rodin: Rodin and the Cambodian Dancers

title: A Steel Giant Over the Red River
text: Begun in September 1898 and inaugurated in February 1902, Hanoi's 1,862-metre bridge over the Red River was first named after Paul Doumer. The French firm Daydé-Pillié designed it, and many Vietnamese workers built it under French experts. It was one of the largest steel bridges in the world, renamed Long Biên after 1945, and later damaged 14 times by American bombs.

source.name: Nhân Dân: Long Bien Bridge - A priceless part of Hanoi's history

title: Siam's Envoys Meet the Telescope
place: Ayutthaya, Thailand (embassy to The Hague, Netherlands)
text: In 1608 the Dutch East India Company opened an office in Ayutthaya, and an embassy from the King of Siam reached The Hague on September 10 to meet Prince Maurits. It was the first Siamese diplomatic mission to Europe. A newsletter of the time reported both the visit and the first documented demonstration of a telescope anywhere in the world.

source.name: Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW): Zuidervaart and Zoomers, Embassies of the King of Siam sent to his excellence Prince Maurits (2008)

source2.name: Rijksmuseum: View of Ayutthaya, the Former Capital of Thailand (SK-A-4477)

title: Three Brothers Shake Vietnam
text: In 1771 three brothers from the hamlet of Tây Sơn launched an uprising that would last until 1802. Their mixed army drove out the ruling families in both halves of divided Vietnam and eventually toppled the 350-year-old Lê dynasty. The upheaval affected every region of the country and every level of society, a story historians trace through Vietnamese sources and European missionary accounts.

source.name: University of Hawai'i Press: George Dutton, The Tây Sơn Uprising - Society and Rebellion in Eighteenth-Century Vietnam

title: A Portuguese Fort on Morocco's Coast
text: In 1514 the brothers Francisco and Diogo de Arruda built the first Portuguese citadel at Mazagan, on Morocco's Atlantic coast. It was one of the first settlements Portuguese explorers created in Africa on the route to India. Between 1541 and 1548 it was enlarged into a star-shaped fortress designed for the age of firearms, and Moroccans took it over in 1769.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Portuguese City of Mazagan (El Jadida)

title: Barbarossa Takes the Island Fort
text: In 1529 the corsair Hayreddin Barbarossa bombarded the Spanish garrison on the Peñón of Algiers, a small island fortress, into surrender. His brother Oruç, whose red beard gave both men their nickname, had taken power in Algiers in 1516. Hayreddin placed the city under Ottoman sultan Süleyman, who sent him 2,000 janissaries, and from Algiers his corsairs terrorized the western Mediterranean.

source.name: National Geographic History: This 16th-century corsair was the most feared pirate of the Mediterranean

title: The Knights Lose Tripoli
text: In August 1551 an Ottoman army under Sinan Pasha and the corsair Dragut besieged Tripoli, held since 1530 by the Knights of St John of Malta. Governor Vallier had about 200 knights and 500 soldiers, but local people of Tagiura joined the attack and a renegade guard opened a gate. Tripoli fell on August 14th, and Dragut later made it one of the strongest fortresses of Africa.

source.name: University of Malta OAR@UM: Andrew P. Vella, The Order of Malta and the Defence of Tripoli 1530-1551

title: Tunis Falls to the Ottomans
text: From the middle of July 1574, a Turkish fleet of about 230 galleys carrying some 40,000 men besieged Spanish-held Tunis and La Goulette, and the soldiers camped among the ruins of Carthage. Local nomads joined the Ottomans and dug long lines of trenches. The Italian general Gabrio Serbelloni surrendered on 13 September, an outcome that decided North Africa would now be under Ottoman rule.

source.name: Royal Collection Trust: Giovanni Francesco Camocio, View of the siege of Tunis, 1574 (RCIN 721071)

title: The Battle of Three Kings
text: On August 4, 1578, beside the Loukkos River near Ksar el-Kebir, Moroccan forces backed by Ottoman janissaries crushed an invasion led by Portugal's 24-year-old King Sebastian. Three kings died that day: Sebastian, the ousted sultan Abdallah Muhammad, and Morocco's ruler Abd al-Malik, from poison, bad water or illness. His brother Ahmad was proclaimed sultan on the spot and became known as al-Mansur, 'the victorious'.

source.name: Stanford University Department of History (from Smithsonian Magazine): The Swashbuckling Tudor Mercenary Who Was Killed in a Battle That Claimed the Lives of Three 16th-Century Kings

title: Lisbon's Wave Reaches Morocco
text: On 1 November 1755 the great Lisbon Earthquake sent a tsunami across the Atlantic toward Morocco. Re-reading old reports translated for European governments, scientific societies and newspapers, a 2009 study argues the Lisbon quake was long overestimated in Morocco because accounts were mixed up with a later earthquake in the Rif. On Morocco's shore the wave may not have exceeded 2.5 metres above the tide.

source.name: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences: Blanc, Earthquakes and tsunami in November 1755 in Morocco - a different reading of contemporaneous documentary sources

title: Bonaparte at the Pyramids
text: On 21 July 1798, Napoleon Bonaparte's French army attacked twenty-three Mamluk beys entrenched at Embabeh, near Cairo, with more than sixty guns. In his own despatch, Bonaparte described the Mamluks' magnificent cavalry, decked in gold and silver, charging his infantry squares, and many fleeing riders drowning in the Nile. Murad Bey was wounded in the cheek, and French troops soon entered Cairo.

source.name: Fondation Napoléon (napoleon.org): Bonaparte's despatches from Egypt (Part I)

title: France Lands at Sidi Ferruch
place: Sidi Fredj (Sidi Ferruch), Algiers Province, Algeria
text: When a French fleet landed at Sidi Ferruch on 14 June 1830, the Regency of Algiers, though nominally Ottoman, had all the marks of a sovereign state. The official aim was to avenge the 'fly whisk incident', but King Charles X also hoped a triumph would restore his prestige. The Dey surrendered on 5 July, beginning 132 years of shared history that ended with independence in 1962.

source.name: Musée de l'Armée (Paris), Algérie 1830-1962: The end of the Ottoman Regency and the limited occupation of Algeria

title: The Red-Cloaked Leader of Kabylia
place: Kabylia mountains, Tizi Ouzou Province, Algeria
text: Born in 1830, the year France invaded Algeria, Fatima N'Soumer was a Berber holy woman of the Kabylia mountains. Clad in a red cloak, she led armed resistance to French assaults from 1854, fighting side by side with the men, and her followers believed she could cure the sick and foretell the future. The French army captured her in July 1857, and she died in prison six years later.

source.name: Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media, George Mason University - Women in World History: Imperialism in North Africa, Personal Account, Captain Carette

title: A Constitution for Tunisia
text: On April 26, 1861, Tunisia's ruler Muhammad al-Sadiq Bey adopted a full written constitution of 13 chapters and 114 articles, giving Tunisia a claim to the first written constitution in a Muslim country. It made the king answerable to a new Supreme Council, whose approval was needed for new laws and taxes. Unpopular in the provinces for its tax rises, it was suspended after a rural revolt in 1864.

source.name: American Journal of Islam and Society: Andrew March, Islamic Constitutionalism Before Sovereignty - Two Defenses of the Tunisian Constitution of 1861

title: Patched Tunics of the Mahdi's Army
text: In 1881 Mohammad Ahmad, a Sufi sheikh from Sudan, proclaimed himself the Mahdi, at a time of growing resentment against Ottoman-Egyptian rule. His followers, the ansar, wore cotton tunics covered in large appliqué patches, deliberate symbols of poverty and humility. After the fall of Khartoum, captured stores of British cloth were handed out, so later patches were often made of wool.

source.name: Textile Research Centre, Leiden (TRC Needles): Mahdi Tunics

title: Rifles and Machine Guns at Omdurman
text: On 2 September 1898, an Anglo-Egyptian army under Herbert Kitchener met the forces of the Khalifa Abdullah, successor to the Mahdi, at Omdurman. The Mahdists fought bravely but were no match for modern rifles and machine guns, and the battle effectively dismantled Mahdist power in Sudan. The Khalifa himself evaded capture until November 1899.

source.name: National Army Museum (UK): The Battle of Omdurman

title: A Princess Pays for a University
text: The secular university that became Cairo University was founded in 1908, and its great patron was Princess Fatma Ismail, daughter of Khedive Ismail. Told by her doctor about the project's money troubles, she donated six acres of land in Cairo, gave the profits of 661 acres of farmland and even sold her own jewelry. She died in 1920, before the university began admitting women in 1928.

source.name: Bibliotheca Alexandrina, SCIplanet: Egyptian Women to Whom Girls Owe Their Education

title: The First Bomb From a Plane
text: During the war between Italy and the Ottoman Empire, Lieutenant Giulio Gavotti flew a Taube monoplane over a Turkish camp at Ain Zara, near Tripoli, on November 1, 1911. Without telling his superiors, he had packed four grenades in a leather pouch, and he tossed them over the side one at a time. No one was injured, but it was the world's first aerial bomb.

source.name: NPR: 100 Years Ago, World's First Aerial Bomb Dropped Over Libya

title: Libya Becomes Independent
text: On December 24, 1951, Libya declared its independence under King Idris I, after years of British and French administration of the former Italian colony. In 1949 the United Nations had voted that Cyrenaica, Tripolitania and the Fezzan should together become an 'independent and sovereign state' by January 1, 1952, with a UN Commissioner helping Libyans draw up a constitution through a National Assembly.

source.name: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: Libya - Recognition, Diplomatic and Consular Relations
