source2.name: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1949, Vol. IV: Editorial Note on the UN General Assembly decision on Libya

title: Agadir Shaken to the Ground
text: On 29 February 1960, an earthquake struck the Atlantic port city of Agadir, killing between ten and fifteen thousand Moroccans and Europeans and damaging most of its buildings. International teams of geologists, seismologists and engineers then studied the ruins, and their idea of seismic risk shaped how Agadir was rebuilt during the first decade of Morocco's independence from France.

source.name: Technology and Culture (via Europe PMC): Williford, Seismic Politics - Risk and Reconstruction after the 1960 Earthquake in Agadir, Morocco

title: A Cairo Novelist Wins the Nobel
text: Born in Cairo in 1911, Naguib Mahfouz began writing at seventeen and worked as a civil servant until 1972. His Cairo Trilogy, published in 1957, made him famous across the Arab world for its portraits of traditional city life, and half of his novels became films. In 1988 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature for forming 'an Arabian narrative art that applies to all mankind'.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Naguib Mahfouz - Biographical

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1988

title: Four Groups Save a Democracy
text: In the summer of 2013, as Tunisia's move to democracy after the 2011 revolution risked collapsing amid political assassinations and unrest, four groups formed the National Dialogue Quartet: the General Labour Union, the industry and trade confederation, the Human Rights League and the Order of Lawyers. They steered the country onto a peaceful political path, and in 2015 the Quartet won the Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2015 - Press release

title: Sudan's Sit-In Topples a President
text: After months of protests, thousands of Sudanese camped outside military headquarters in Khartoum, and in April 2019 the army removed Omar al-Bashir, an autocrat who had seized power in a 1989 coup. The protesters refused to leave: a military council promised elections in two years, but they demanded civilian rule at once. Coup leader Awad Ibn Auf lasted a single day as president.

source.name: NPR: Bashir May Be Out, But Sudanese Protesters With 'Eye On The Prize' Won't Budge

title: The Night Derna's Dams Broke
text: On the night of 10 September 2023, Storm Daniel swept across Libya. Just after midnight, the two dams above the coastal city of Derna gave way, sending over 30 million cubic metres of water down the Wadi Derna, normally a dry riverbed, and through the sleeping city. Estimates of the dead range from 5,900 to 20,000, making it the second-deadliest dam failure in recorded history.

source.name: Norwegian Refugee Council via ReliefWeb (UN OCHA): One year on - Looking back at Derna's flood disaster

title: A Giant Museum Beside the Pyramids
text: Announced in 1992 and delayed again and again, the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Pyramids of Giza held its grand opening on 1 November 2025. It is the world's largest institution dedicated to a single civilisation. Two halls show all 5,000 artefacts from Tutankhamun's tomb together for the first time since 1922, and a six-storey staircase lined with statues leads to a view of the pyramids.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Egypt unveils Grand Egyptian Museum dedicated to its ancient civilisation

source2.name: National Geographic: The Grand Egyptian Museum is opening in full - here's what you need to know

title: A Granary Against Fire, Flood and Parrots
text: A broken stone found at Mahasthan carries one of Bengal's oldest written orders, in Brahmi letters and Prakrit language. A ruler told his official at 'Pudanagala' to help a distressed people with oil, paddy and small coins, and to keep a storehouse stocked for emergencies caused by water, fire, or parrots devastating the crops.

source.name: Banglapedia: Mahasthan Brahmi Inscription

title: A Fort-City Port on Bengal's Rivers
text: Around 2,500 years ago a fortified city stood at Wari-Bateshwar, with four mud ramparts around an enclosure 600 metres square. Beads of semi-precious stone and glass still turn up here, along with two types of silver punch-marked coins. Archaeologists see it as a wealthy trade centre and probably a river port.

source.name: Banglapedia: Wari-Bateshwar

title: The Monastery on the Throne of Origins
text: Buddhist monks founded Takht-i-Bahi, the 'Throne of Origins', on a ring of Gandharan hilltops in the early 1st century CE. Its stupa courts, meditation cells and assembly hall stayed in use until the 7th century. Perched high up, it escaped successive invasions and is now the most complete Buddhist monastery in Pakistan.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi and Neighbouring City Remains at Sahr-i-Bahlol

title: Ginger and Turmeric in a Harappan Pot
text: At the Harappan village of Farmana, occupied around 2600-2200 BCE, researchers scraped tiny starch grains from a handi, a deep narrow-mouthed cooking pot. They found traces of ginger, turmeric and eggplant. The team also studies starch trapped in tartar on human teeth, and even cattle teeth, and has identified barley, millets and mango at the site.

source.name: Antiquity Project Gallery (Kashyap and Weber, Washington State University Vancouver): Harappan plant use revealed by starch grains from Farmana, India

title: When the Monsoon Rivers Faltered
text: Harappan cities flourished for about 600 years, but from roughly 3,900 years ago settlements shrank, many were abandoned, and people shifted east. Geologists found that the region's rivers were fed by the monsoon, not Himalayan glaciers. As the monsoon weakened they dried up or became seasonal, and settlements multiplied in the moister lands of upper Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

source.name: Giosan et al., PNAS (2012): Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization

title: Banker, Merchant, Artisan and Scribe
text: Copper plates found at Damodarpur show that northern Bengal was still part of the Gupta empire under Budhagupta, in 478 CE. They also reveal how its Kotivarsa district was run: the governor worked with an advisory board of four local leaders, namely the chief banker of the town, the chief merchant, the chief artisan and the chief scribe.

source.name: Banglapedia: Gupta Rule

title: A Couple Buys Land for Jains
text: In 479 CE a Brahman couple in Bengal bought a piece of land and granted it to maintain the worship of Arhats and a resting place at a vihara at Vatagohali, run by the Jaina teacher Guhanandin. Their copper-plate charter later turned up in the ruins of the great Buddhist monastery at Paharpur, perhaps kept by monks who took over the land.

source.name: Banglapedia: Paharpur

title: South Asia's Earliest Proven Dairy
text: Kotada Bhadli was a small farming and herding settlement of the Indus Civilization, lived in from about 2300 to 1950 BCE. Chemists tested fat soaked into 59 broken cooking pots and bowls and found the earliest direct evidence of dairy processing in South Asia, mostly from cattle and possibly some water buffalo. Milk let herders build surpluses without slaughtering their animals.

source.name: Chakraborty et al., Scientific Reports (2020): Compound specific isotope analysis of lipid residues provides the earliest direct evidence of dairy product processing in South Asia

title: Hard Times in Late Harappa
text: After 1900 BCE, as the Indus Civilization came apart, skeletons from Harappa show infections and diseases such as leprosy and tuberculosis becoming more common. The risks were uneven: socially and economically marginalized groups suffered most. Outside the city wall, an ossuary held a small group of skulls, half of them showing injuries.

source.name: Robbins Schug et al., PLOS ONE (2013): Infection, disease, and biosocial processes at the end of the Indus Civilization

title: Ancient Genomes From the Himalayan Heights
text: Valleys over 3,000 metres high in the Himalayas were among the last places people settled for good, facing cold, thin air and scarce food. Genomes of eight people from Nepal's Annapurna area, spanning 3,150 to 1,250 years ago, point to a high-altitude East Asian origin. Their tools and customs changed over the centuries, yet the population itself stayed remarkably stable.

source.name: Jeong et al., PNAS (2016): Long-term genetic stability and a high-altitude East Asian origin for the peoples of the high valleys of the Himalayan arc

title: Four Ibex on a Wheel-Made Jar
text: This black-painted jar, probably from the Quetta area, was made around 2800-2500 BCE, in the world of the Indus Valley civilization. Its walls are so thin it must have been thrown on a potter's wheel. Around it march four male ibex, wild mountain goats with hugely exaggerated curving horns and three hairs drawn under each chin.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Jar with Four Ibex (2001.1)

title: A Harappan Fort Near the Arabian Sea
text: Far west of the Indus, in the Dasht River valley near today's Iran border, Harappans built Sutkagen-dor, a citadel ringed by a massive wall of semi-dressed stone. Its pottery is pure Harappan. Archaeologists from the Penn Museum argued that this fort, and a twin at Sotka-koh near Pasni, worked as way-stations for coastal sea trade with the West.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (George F. Dales, 1962): A Search for Ancient Seaports

title: The Mystery Copper Figures
text: Flat copper 'anthropomorphs', shaped roughly like a person with outstretched arms, are among the few artworks known from India in the long gap between the Indus cities and the Maurya empire. Most were discovered in the plains of the Ganges and Yamuna rivers. Their bold, abstract shape is striking, but what they meant or were used for is still a mystery.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Anthropomorph (2004.31)

title: Bones in Baskets in the Swat Valley
text: People of the Swat Valley used these graveyards from about 1400 to 800 BCE. At Udegram, some of the dead were reburied later, with the skull always placed on top of neatly packed long bones, sometimes kept in baskets. Graves held a wooden vessel, iron and copper pins, a tiny clay female figurine and a crescent-shaped gold earring.

source.name: Vidale and Micheli, Antiquity (2017): Protohistoric graveyards of the Swat Valley, Pakistan

title: A Clay Face From the Maurya Capital
text: This small terracotta head, found at Bulandibagh on the site of the Maurya capital Pataliputra, wears a large turban and earring. It may show a yaksha, a nature spirit worshipped for wealth and prosperity, and was perhaps set up in a family shrine at home. Its fleshy face and parted lips are typical of Maurya-period sculpture.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Male Head, possibly a Yaksha (1986.72)

title: Eight Fish-Tailed Women in Ivory
place: Chandraketugarh, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, India
text: Around 100 BCE, a carver in the Chandraketugarh area of Bengal made this ivory disc, possibly part of a huge earring worn in stretched earlobes that rested on the shoulders. Eight figures, half woman and half fish, hold hands in a ring around lotus flowers. Their hands and tails form a lucky trident-shaped symbol, evoking life-giving waters.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Roundel with Mermaids and Lotus (2010.295)

title: A Party Carved on Stupa Steps
text: Carved panels from the Buner area of Gandhara probably decorated the steps up to a Buddhist stupa. On them, Phrygians in trousers and pointed caps play music, dance and clap, while Greeks drink and carry wine. Such lively scenes of foreigners filled the lower parts of monuments in a region crossed by many travellers during busy trade with the Mediterranean world.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Foreigners and Non-Buddhists Drink, Dance, and Play Music, from a Buddhist Stupa Site (1930.328)

title: Mathura's Red Stone Buddha
text: Sculptors at Mathura carved this early Buddha image from mottled red sandstone around 120 CE, in the Kushan period. He sits under the Bodhi tree with a solar disc behind his head like a halo. His coiled topknot and long earlobes recall his youth as a prince wearing a turban and heavy earrings, and lions on the throne show his teaching spreading in all four directions.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Seated Shakyamuni Buddha (1970.63)

title: Heavenly Musicians of Swat
text: Set high on a Buddhist building in Swat, probably around Butkara, this carved bracket shows a pair of celestial musicians on a lotus. The bearded man plays a lute-like instrument, and the young woman, her hair in a garland-wrapped bun, holds a clapper much like the kartal still used in parts of India today. Their draped robes echo Greek clothing.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Bracket with Two Musicians (1980.15)

title: A Loving Couple on a Brick Temple
text: Gupta-period brick temples were decorated with terracotta instead of stone, and this clay roundel from Ahichchatra once adorned such a building. It shows an amorous couple, or mithuna, among the commonest images on the outside of sacred sites, because their life-affirming joy was thought to bring good fortune. Ruins of a pyramid-shaped brick Shiva temple still stand at Ahichchatra.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Amorous Couple (Mithuna) (1971.133)

dateLabel: c. 1600 BCE (start of Bengal's Copper Age)
title: Rice, Fish and Copper Fish-Hooks
place: Pandu Rajar Dhibi, Paschim Bardhaman, West Bengal, India
text: Pandu Rajar Dhibi, beside the Ajay river, was the first Copper Age site found in West Bengal, a period there dated to about 1600-750 BCE. Its villagers lived in round to square huts with mud-plastered walls and ate rice, meat, fish and fruit. Later layers held copper beads, bangles, fish-hooks and kohl-sticks, and signs of a great fire.

source.name: Banglapedia: Pandu Rajar Dhibi

title: Iron Tools on the Kopai River
text: At Mahisdal, on the Kopai river, early farmers stored rice in a pit granary; carbonized grains survive, and the earliest dates there go back to 1619-1415 BCE. That village ended in a large fire. In the next phase, dated to about 750 BCE, people used iron arrowheads, spearheads, chisels and nails alongside copper fish-hooks and bangles, until fire struck again.

source.name: Banglapedia: Mahisdal

title: The Battle That Emptied Hampi
text: Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, with temples, bazaars, stepped tanks and wide chariot streets built mostly of local granite beside the Tungabhadra River. Then came the Battle of Talikota in 1565, which destroyed the kingdom and caused massive destruction to the city. More than 1,600 remains survive today, including the Vitthala temple with its stone chariot.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Group of Monuments at Hampi

title: Saint Francis Xavier's Basilica
text: In 1605 the Basilica of Bom Jesus rose in Old Goa, capital of the Portuguese Indies, a city later nicknamed the "Rome of the Orient". It holds the tomb of Saint Francis Xavier, made in Florence with bronze work by Giovanni Battista Foggini. Goa's churches mixed European styles with local materials, creating an Indo-Portuguese style that spread to missions across Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Churches and Convents of Goa

title: A Trading Fort Becomes Madras
text: In 1639 Damarla Venkatapathy Nayak, an influential chieftain under Venkata III, granted the English a strip of waste land where the Cooum River meets the sea. There they founded Fort St. George, purely for business. The settlement that grew around it was named after Chennapatanam, and the British called the combined town Madras Patnam, today's Chennai.

source.name: Chennai District Administration (Government of Tamil Nadu): History

title: The Garden of Malabar in Print
text: In 1678 the first of 12 volumes of Hortus Malabaricus appeared in Amsterdam, compiled by the Dutch official Hendrik van Rheede. It described hundreds of plants used by Kerala's Ayurvedic physicians, with 794 plates in all. Van Rheede relied on a board of Malabar experts, whom the first volume thanked by name, a rare honour for Asian scholars in European books of the time.

source.name: Ancient Science of Life (via Europe PMC): Hortus malabaricus and the ethnoiatrical knowledge of ancient Malabar

source2.name: Berichte zur Wissenschaftsgeschichte (via Europe PMC): Kundige inlanders - Indigenous Contributions to Jacob Breyne's Work

title: Tamil Books from Tranquebar
text: In 1706 two missionaries recruited in Halle and sent by Denmark's King Frederik IV, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, arrived in Tranquebar. In 1712 their mission set up a printing press that came to play a decisive role in spreading printed Tamil literature. Its schools also gave children from the lowest castes, previously shut out of schooling, a chance to learn.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark: Schools, Missionaries and Book Printing

title: Travancore Beats the Dutch
place: Colachel, Kanyakumari District, Tamil Nadu, India
text: European powers fought one another for dominance in Kerala, and in 1663 the Dutch seized Cochin from the Portuguese. Then in 1741 the Maharaja of Travancore, Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma, defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel, a town now in Tamil Nadu. It was the biggest setback in India for the Dutch, then the greatest maritime force of the age.

source.name: Government of Kerala, Information and Public Relations Department: Kerala Calling, November 2021

title: Mysore's Iron Rockets
text: Mysore's armies fired rockets at the British during the siege of Seringapatam in 1791–1792. Each was a steel tube packed with gunpowder, lashed by a leather thong to a bamboo guide stick, and could fly up to a kilometre. They carried no explosives and were meant to frighten enemy troops. Reports of them led William Congreve to develop his improved British rockets.

source.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Model, Rocket, War, Indian, Late 18th Century

title: Midnight Revolt at Vellore Fort
text: Two hours after midnight on July 10, 1806, sepoys rose at Vellore fort, where Tipu Sultan's family were held prisoner, and hoisted the striped tiger flag of Mysore. The revolt was crushed swiftly. New army rules had banned caste marks and ordered Muslim soldiers to shave their beards; the Governor of Madras blamed the dress regulations, and they were later abolished.

source.name: Cambridge Core (Boydell & Brewer): The Vellore Mutiny and the Pamphlet War 1806–1808, in The East India Company and Religion

source2.name: National Army Museum: Sepoy of Madras Native Infantry and his wife, c1810

title: The Last Kingdom of Kandy Falls
text: Kandy, last capital of the Sinhala kings and home of the Temple of the Tooth Relic, had resisted European powers for over two hundred years. In March 1815, after political manoeuvring between Kandyan chiefs and the British, a convention handed the kingdom's sovereignty to the British Empire. In return, the British promised to protect the Buddhist Order and its customs.

source.name: Department of National Archives, Sri Lanka: 1815 Convention

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred City of Kandy

title: A Rebellion and a Sacred Tooth
place: Kandyan highlands, Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: Soon after Britain took Kandy, discontent among the chiefs grew into a rebellion that began sweeping the Kandyan regions in 1817. The Tooth Relic was at its heart: removed from the palace in May 1818, it was found with a monk hiding in the forest. The British governor implied that losing the relic ended the revolt. His 1818 order branding nineteen chiefs traitors was cancelled in 2016.

source.name: Department of National Archives, Sri Lanka: Freedom Struggle, 1818

title: A New Element in the Eclipse
text: At the total solar eclipse of August 18, 1868, visible from India, the spectroscope first revealed that the Sun's prominences are made of gas. At Masulipatam, Madras Observatory's N. R. Pogson saw strong hydrogen lines and a bright yellow line near those of sodium. That yellow line came from an unknown element, later named helium after the Sun where it was first detected.

source.name: Indian Institute of Astrophysics: A Brief History of IIA

title: The Fungus That Killed Ceylon Coffee
text: In 1869 the first major outbreak of coffee leaf rust struck Ceylon's booming, highly profitable coffee plantations. The Victorian mycologist M. J. Berkeley described the fungus, Hemileia vastatrix, from specimens sent from the island. The disease eventually drove planters to abandon coffee in favour of tea, and since then almost every coffee-growing region in the world has reported attacks.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Cryptosexuality and the genetic diversity paradox in coffee rust, Hemileia vastatrix

source2.name: Ecology and Evolution (via Europe PMC): On the hunt for the alternate host of Hemileia vastatrix

title: A Toy Train Climbs the Nilgiris
text: A railway up the Nilgiri Hills was first proposed in 1854, but the steep terrain meant work only began in 1891. Completed in 1908, the 46-kilometre metre-gauge line climbs from 326 metres to 2,203 metres above sea level, using the latest technology of its day. It still runs, and is part of the Mountain Railways of India World Heritage site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mountain Railways of India

title: Rivers of Gas in Sunspots
text: High in the hills of South India, the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory was set up by the British on April 1, 1899. There, in 1909, John Evershed discovered that gas in sunspots flows radially, now called the Evershed effect. The observatory has one of the world's longest continuous daily records of the Sun, now digitised and open to astronomers everywhere.

source.name: Press Information Bureau, Government of India: Kodaikanal Solar Observatory celebrates 125 years of studying the Sun

source2.name: Indian Institute of Astrophysics: A Brief History of IIA

title: A University That Taught in Urdu
text: On April 26, 1917, a royal farman in the princely state of Hyderabad founded Osmania University. The idea came from a civil servant, Sir Akbar Hydari, who argued it should teach in Urdu, the state's official language and understood by most of its people. Even medicine and engineering were taught in Urdu until 1947, though every student also had to learn English.

source.name: Osmania University: 104th Annual Report (Historical Background)

title: Everyone Over 21 Gets the Vote
text: Under the Donoughmore reforms of 1931, both men and women over 21 in Ceylon gained the right to vote, and voters chose 50 members for a new State Council, which first met on July 7, 1931. Evidence given to the commission by the Society for Women's Suffrage, including Agnes de Silva, helped win women the vote.

source.name: Department of National Archives, Sri Lanka: Donoughmore Commission, 1931

source2.name: Election Commission of Sri Lanka: History

title: Suriya Flowers Instead of Poppies
text: In 1933 young Sri Lankans who had studied abroad started the Suriya-Mal Movement, a welfare campaign set up as a counter to Britain's Poppy Movement. Its founding president was Doreen Wickramasinghe. Members worked to raise education levels among children from lower castes and carried medicine, food and other essentials to remote areas during the malaria epidemic, while spreading anti-imperialist ideas.

source.name: Department of National Archives, Sri Lanka: Suriyamal Movement

title: Temple Doors Open in Travancore
text: On November 12, 1936, Sri Chithira Thirunal, Maharaja of Travancore, issued the Temple Entry Proclamation, later called the "spiritual Magna Carta" of Travancore. It let Ezhavas and other communities treated as Untouchable enter temples long closed to them. Historians debate the motives: it came in the diwan Ramaswamy Aiyar's first year, under pressure from Gandhians and fears of conversion to Christianity.

source.name: Modern Asian Studies (Cambridge Core): A forgotten famine of '43? Travancore's muffled 'cry of distress'

source2.name: Kerala Legislature: Business of the Legislature

title: Rockets from a Fishing Village Church
text: On November 21, 1963, a two-stage Nike-Apache rocket lifted off from Thumba, a coastal village chosen for its closeness to the magnetic equator. It marked the start of India's space exploration. Local people gave their old St. Mary Magdalene Church to science: it became offices and laboratories, the bishop's house became the director's office, and the church is now a space museum.

source.name: Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre: Genesis

source2.name: ISRO: Diamond jubilee of first sounding rocket launch

title: The Maldives Goes It Alone
text: On July 26, 1965, the Maldives gained full independence after years as a British Protectorate. In 2009 President Nasheed paid tribute to former President Ibrahim Nasir's role in securing it. Every year on July 26 the country marks Independence Day with a flag-hoisting at Republic Square in Malé at 6 in the morning, a special prayer, and the national anthem played by the military band.

source.name: The President's Office, Maldives: Flag-hoisting ceremony to commemorate the 61st Independence Day

source2.name: The President's Office, Maldives: Concerted efforts needed to realize the requisites of freedom (2009)

title: The Wave That Struck a Train
text: On December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Sumatra sent the deadliest tsunami in recorded history across the Indian Ocean, killing more than 31,000 people in Sri Lanka. At Peraliya the waves hit a train broadside, killing everyone aboard. Sri Lanka's Geological Survey and Mines Bureau was the first scientific agency to respond, sending teams to survey the battered coasts.

source.name: USGS Pacific Coastal and Marine Science Center: The December 26, 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami: Initial Findings in Sri Lanka

source2.name: USGS Pacific Coastal and Marine Science Center: Perelyga train photo

title: A Cabinet Meeting Under the Sea
text: On October 17, 2009, the Maldives' president, vice president and eleven ministers dived 4 metres into a lagoon off Girifushi Island for the world's first underwater cabinet meeting. Using waterproof pencils on a plastic slate, they signed an "SOS from the frontline" calling for global carbon cuts before the Copenhagen climate summit. The Maldives, the president said, is a frontline state.

source.name: The President's Office, Maldives: Maldives holds world's first underwater Cabinet meeting

title: Clash on the Plain of Marj Dabiq
place: Marj Dabiq, north of Aleppo, Syria
text: On August 24, 1516, on the plain of Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo, the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeated the army of the Mamluks. His forces occupied all of Syria that year and Egypt the next. Syria then remained part of the Ottoman Empire for 400 years, with Damascus organizing the great pilgrimage to Mecca every year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Syria - Ottoman period

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Marj Dabiq

title: A Printing Press in Safed
text: In 1577 Eliezer ben Isaac Ashkenazi, a printer who moved from city to city, set up a Hebrew press in Safed, then a great centre of Jewish mysticism and learning. It printed six books, all by Safed authors. The first, a commentary on the Book of Esther by Yom Tov Zahalon, is considered the first book printed in the Land of Israel.

source.name: Jewish Virtual Library (from Judaic Treasures of the Library of Congress): First Book in the Holy Land

title: Julfa Forced Across the River
text: Old Julfa, an Armenian town on the Aras River, grew rich in the 1500s carrying raw silk to the markets of Aleppo and Bursa; an English preacher passing through in 1600 counted about 2,000 houses. In late 1604, retreating from the Ottomans, Shah Abbas I of Iran had Julfa demolished and its entire population driven across the river into Iran.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Julfa i. Safavid Period (Vazken S. Ghougassian)

title: The Messiah Who Became Mehmed Efendi
text: In 1665 crowds in Smyrna hailed Shabbetai Tzevi as the Jewish messiah, and his movement spread to Venice, Amsterdam and London. Early in 1666 he was jailed on reaching Constantinople. That September he was brought before the sultan in Adrianople and, after threats of torture, converted to Islam. The sultan renamed him Mehmed Efendi and made him his personal doorkeeper.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Shabbetai Tzevi

title: Sheki Rebuilt After the Mud Flood
text: In 1772 a mud flood wrecked the old town of Sheki, at the foot of the Greater Caucasus, and it was rebuilt on higher ground in a valley to the east. Houses got tall, steep roofs so silkworms could be raised in their airy attics, and new caravanserais, shops, baths and fountains soon sprang up to serve the trade in silk cocoons.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace

title: Tbilisi Burns, Georgia Stands Alone
text: In 1783 King Erekle II of Georgia signed the Treaty of Georgievsk with Catherine the Great, accepting Russian overlordship in return for protection. Yet when Agha Mohammad Khan, first ruler of Iran's Qajar dynasty, attacked, Georgia faced him alone. In 1795 Tbilisi was sacked and burned to the ground. In 1801 Russia's Alexander I confirmed that eastern Georgia would be absorbed into his empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Georgia - Turkish and Persian domination

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tbilisi

title: The Walls That Stopped Napoleon
text: Acre's natural harbour made it a frequent target for invaders. In the late 1700s its Ottoman governor, Ahmad Pasha al-Jazzar, strengthened the old walls and citadel, and in 1799 they withstood a siege by Napoleon. Al-Jazzar also built the city's Great Mosque in 1781, and Acre's Ottoman streets still sit on top of an almost intact Crusader town.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Acre

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Old City of Acre

title: Oil Wells at Bibiheybat
text: In January 1846 engineer Nikolay Voskoboynikov, director of the Baku Oil and Salt Mines, had two wells drilled at Bibiheybat. One blew out, and industrial oil production began. Azerbaijan's Ministry of Energy calls the 21-metre well the world's first drilled oil well. The same bay had already seen offshore wells, dug in 1803 and wrecked by a Caspian storm in 1825.

source.name: Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan: It is important to know!

source2.name: Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan: Offshore oil production for the first time in the world

title: Self-Rule for Mount Lebanon
text: In the 1800s Mount Lebanon's growing Christian population spread south and into towns, and relations between Maronites and Druze worsened. The conflict ended in massacres in 1860, and France sent troops. In 1861 the European powers imposed the Organic Regulation, giving the mountain self-rule under a Christian governor named by the Ottoman sultan, with a council representing its communities. It prospered until World War I.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lebanon - Lebanon in the Middle Ages (to 1914)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Syria - Ottoman period

title: Digging Into Homer's Troy
text: In 1870 Heinrich Schliemann began the first excavations at the mound of Hisarlık, near the southern entrance to the Dardanelles, the site of the Troy made famous by Homer's Iliad. UNESCO calls his digs a starting point of modern archaeology. Later work uncovered walls, eleven gates and a paved stone ramp, and showed the region has been inhabited for 8,000 years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Troy

title: A New Town Beside Jaffa
text: In 1909 a new town, Tel Aviv, was founded just north of the old walled port of Jaffa. It grew fast under British rule into a busy city. From the early 1930s, architects trained in Europe filled its centre with white Modern Movement buildings, following a plan by Sir Patrick Geddes and adapting their designs to the local climate.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: White City of Tel-Aviv - the Modern Movement

title: The Sharif of Mecca Crowns Himself
text: Hussein ibn Ali, emir of Mecca since 1908, won British backing in a series of letters known as the Hussein-McMahon correspondence and led the Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule during World War I. In October 1916 he proclaimed himself king of the Arab countries, though the Allies recognized him only as king of the Hejaz. His sons later became kings of Transjordan and Iraq.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hussein ibn Ali

title: Armenia's First Republic
text: On May 28, 1918, after a brief union with Georgia and Azerbaijan fell apart, Armenia declared independence. It was the first independent Armenian state since the Middle Ages, born in the shadow of the 1915 deportations and massacres of Ottoman Armenians. Squeezed by war on several sides, the young republic was proclaimed a Soviet republic in December 1920.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Armenia - Modern Armenia

title: Turkish Women Win the Vote
text: On December 5, 1934, women in Turkey gained the right to vote and run in national elections, after winning local voting rights in 1930. In February 1935 they voted nationally for the first time, and 18 women entered parliament, though the single ruling party chose every candidate. Turkish women won the vote a decade or more before women in France, Italy and Belgium.

source.name: UN Women Europe and Central Asia: Turkey's Parliament celebrates women's rights to vote and run for office

source2.name: OUPblog (Oxford University Press): Turkish women vote

title: The Spitak Earthquake
text: At 11:41 a.m. on December 7, 1988, a magnitude-6.8 earthquake shook northern Armenia, then part of the Soviet Union, and destroyed the town of Spitak. Between 25,000 and 60,000 people died, two-thirds of them under 18. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev asked the United States for aid, and rescue teams flew in with dogs trained to sniff out survivors.

source.name: EARTH Magazine (American Geosciences Institute): December 7, 1988: A Massive Earthquake Devastates Armenia

title: A Jaw Under a Saber-Tooth Cat
text: Archaeologists had been digging the crumbling ruins of a medieval citadel at Dmanisi since the 1930s. In 1991, on the last day of the field season, the crew found a fossil jaw of an early human relative beneath the skeleton of a saber-toothed cat. David Lordkipanidze and Leo Gabunia dated it to around 1.6 million years, which would make it the oldest known hominid outside Africa.

source.name: Scientific American: Stranger in a New Land (Kate Wong)

title: The Beirut Port Explosion
text: Shortly after 6 p.m. on August 4, 2020, a fire at Warehouse 12 in the Port of Beirut set off a colossal explosion. The prime minister blamed 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate stored unsafely there. The blast left a crater about 140 metres wide, killed more than 200 people, injured around 5,000 and was heard in Cyprus. Lebanon's government resigned amid public anger.

source.name: BBC News: Beirut explosion: What we know so far

title: A Rainforest Near the South Pole
place: Seabed near Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers, West Antarctica
text: A sediment core drilled into the seabed of West Antarctica held a dense network of fossil roots, plus countless grains of pollen and spores. They come from a 90-million-year-old temperate rainforest, like those of New Zealand today, growing within 900 km of the South Pole. Summers averaged about 19 degrees Celsius, and swamp and river water reached up to 20 degrees.

source.name: Imperial College London: Traces of ancient rainforest in Antarctica point to a warmer prehistoric world

title: Ice Age Hunters at the Arctic Circle
place: Mamontovaya Kurya, Usa River, Komi Republic, Russia
text: At Mamontovaya Kurya, in the European part of the Russian Arctic, people were living nearly 40,000 years ago, during the last ice age. Russian and Norwegian archaeologists dug up hundreds of animal bones, stone tools, and a mammoth tusk that appears to have been cut by those very tools. Their report appeared in the journal Nature in 2001.

source.name: Scientific American: Humans Lived North of the Arctic Circle During Last Ice Age

title: The Oldest Art of the Arctic
place: Yana RHS, Yana River, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Russia
text: The Yana site in Arctic Siberia, dated to about 28,000 years ago, holds the earliest art ever excavated in the Arctic zone. Its people made decorated beads, pendants and needles, plus shallow dishes and human-like designs carved on mammoth tusks. Archaeologists see echoes of these images in the hunting and shamanic art of the Indigenous Yukaghir people recorded in the early 1900s.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Oldest art of the Eurasian Arctic: personal ornaments and symbolic objects from Yana RHS, Arctic Siberia

title: Siberian Roots on the Kola Peninsula
place: Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov, Murmansk Region, Russia
text: About 3,500 years ago, people were buried at Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov on the Kola Peninsula, a region where Saami live today. Their DNA revealed that about half their ancestry came from Siberia, the earliest evidence of Siberian ancestry in Fennoscandia. Among Europeans today, the Saami carry the largest share of this ancient Siberian ancestry.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe

source2.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History: First ancient DNA from mainland Finland

title: A Town of Whalebone Houses
place: Ipiutak site, Tikigaq (Point Hope), North Slope, Alaska, USA
text: On the Tikigaq spit, which juts into the Chukchi Sea, over 500 house ruins line the old beach ridges, making Ipiutak one of the largest early village sites in Arctic Alaska. The houses were surrounded by big whale and walrus bones. Ipiutak communities, famous for fine carving in ivory, wood, bone and stone, reached their peak population between AD 650 and 870.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Ipiutak Site

title: The Dorset, or Tuniit, Appear
text: Around 2,800 years ago, the Dorset Palaeo-Inuit emerged in the Arctic, named by archaeologist Diamond Jenness after Kinngait, then called Cape Dorset. They built sunken-floor houses for winter and lit and heated their world with soapstone lamps, yet show little sign of dogsleds or bows. Inuit oral histories remember an earlier people, the Tuniit, whom many consider the same group.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Dorset Culture (Patrick Jolicoeur)

title: The Bone Man of Ust-Polui
place: Ust-Polui, Salekhard, Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, Russia
text: Inside today's city of Salekhard lies Ust-Polui, a sanctuary used around 100 BCE to 100 CE. Digs in the 1930s found about 7,000 objects, 1,500 of them finely made from bone. In 2009 archaeologists uncovered a 7.3 cm figure of a seated man hugging his knees, carved from deer antler with an iron knife. Permafrost even preserved decorated birch-bark objects.

source.name: SCIENCE First Hand (Siberian Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences): The Land of Ancestors. The Bone Man and Other Secrets of the Ancient Sanctuary

source2.name: Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia: Decorated Birch-Bark Artifacts from the Ust-Polui Sanctuary (100 BC to 100 AD)

title: Rome's Smog, Frozen in Greenland
text: Lead from Roman silver mining and smelting drifted all the way to Greenland and was locked in its ice. Scientists measuring about 1,300 feet of ice found lead pollution peaked in the first century CE, then dropped dramatically around the year 165, likely because of the Antonine Plague. It stayed low for more than 500 years.

source.name: Archaeology magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): Ice Core Study Tracks Roman Lead Levels

source2.name: PNAS (University of Copenhagen research portal): Lead pollution recorded in Greenland ice indicates European emissions tracked plagues, wars, and imperial expansion during antiquity

title: Polynesians in the Subantarctic
place: Sandy Bay, Enderby Island, Auckland Islands, New Zealand
text: Radiocarbon dates show that a group of Polynesians and their dogs lived on windswept Enderby Island for at least one summer in the 1200s or 1300s. Food remains reveal they ate Hooker's sea lions, fur seals, sooty shearwaters, albatrosses and penguins. Their camp at Sandy Bay is the southernmost known site of prehistoric Polynesian voyaging.

source.name: New Zealand Department of Conservation: Enderby Island Māori occupation

title: Kerguelen Thinks He Found a Continent
place: Kerguelen Islands, French Southern and Antarctic Lands
text: Sailing south from Mauritius with the ships Fortune and Gros Ventre, Breton officer Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen reached an island in the southern Indian Ocean in February 1772, and it was claimed for France. Fog split the ships, and Kerguelen returned to France claiming he had found the great southern land. In truth the island was icy and inhospitable; Cook later named it after him.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: De Kerguelen and de Saint Aloüarn 1771–1772

title: What Inuit Saw of Franklin's Men
place: Near O'Reilly Island, Adelaide Peninsula, Nunavut, Canada
text: Franklin's ships Erebus and Terror were trapped in ice in 1846, and in April 1848 the 105 surviving crew abandoned them. Inuit later said about 40 white men were seen heading south along King William Island. An Inuk named Inukpujijuk marked a wreck's location on explorer Charles Francis Hall's chart, and in 2014 searchers found HMS Erebus close to that spot.

source.name: Parks Canada: Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror National Historic Site, Inuit traditional knowledge

title: The First International Polar Year
text: Austro-Hungarian naval officer Karl Weyprecht argued that big results needed many expeditions observing at the same time. The result was the first International Polar Year, 1882–1883, with 12 camps. Near Barrow, Ray's team adapted to local ways, once travelling with local people by dog sled to the Prudhoe Bay area; all came home healthy. Far north on Ellesmere Island, Greely's party of 25 shrank to seven.

source.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Alaska Science Forum: First International Polar Year was edgy affair (Ned Rozell)

title: An Ice Shelf Shatters in a Month
place: Larsen B Ice Shelf, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: In the southern summer of 2002, almost the entire Larsen B Ice Shelf, about 3,250 square kilometres, splintered and collapsed in just over a month. A run of warm summers ended in an exceptionally warm one, and melt ponds on the surface acted like wedges. Freed from the shelf, the glaciers behind it sped up, by about 300 percent on average.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: World of Change: Collapse of the Larsen-B Ice Shelf

title: Stones Rain on L'Aigle
text: A shower of stones, with deafening explosions, fell just north of the Normandy village of L'Aigle. Villagers sold some to collectors, and the young physicist Jean-Baptiste Biot was sent to investigate. He interviewed hundreds of witnesses, studied hundreds of stones and printed the first ever map of a meteorite fall. After his report, nearly everyone accepted that such stones came from space.

source.name: Linda Hall Library: Scientist of the Day - Jean-Baptiste Biot

title: Silent Night Is Sung First
place: St. Nicholas Church, Oberndorf bei Salzburg, Austria
text: On Christmas Eve, assistant priest Joseph Mohr gave organist Franz Xaver Gruber a poem and asked for a melody with guitar accompaniment. That evening at St. Nicholas church, Mohr sang tenor and played guitar while Gruber sang bass, to a congregation of mostly boatmen and shipping workers. 'Silent Night' has since been translated into some 300 languages.

source.name: Silent Night Association (Stille Nacht Gesellschaft): History of the Song

source2.name: Austrian Commission for UNESCO: "Silent Night" - the Christmas carol

title: Wash Your Hands, Doctor
text: After a colleague died from a scalpel cut during an autopsy, with symptoms just like childbed fever, Ignaz Semmelweis decided doctors were carrying the disease to new mothers. He made all doctors and students in his ward disinfect their hands in chlorinated lime before examining pregnant women. Deaths on his ward fell from 18.27% to 1.27% in 1848.

source.name: Science History Institute: Ignaz Semmelweis

title: Champollion Cracks the Code
text: After ten years of stubborn research, Jean-François Champollion could finally read part of the hieroglyphs, signs that had been silent for nearly fifteen centuries. Using the names Ptolemy and then Cleopatra, he saw that Egyptians spelled foreign rulers' names with sound-signs, like an alphabet. He set it out in his Letter to Monsieur Dacier, and wrote his own name and the date in hieroglyphs in his notebook.

source.name: Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF Essentiels): En 1822, Champollion perce le secret des hiéroglyphes

title: Applause He Could Not Hear
text: Beethoven finished his Ninth Symphony, with its setting of Schiller's ode 'To Joy', in March 1824. It premiered in Vienna that May at a concert he planned himself, with the choir placed in front of the orchestra. The composer was by then deaf, and at the end he had to be turned around to see the tumultuous applause he could not hear.

source.name: Los Angeles Philharmonic: Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125 (program note)

source2.name: Beethoven-Haus Bonn: 200 years of Beethoven's Ninth

title: The View From Niépce's Window
text: Nicéphore Niépce coated a polished pewter plate with light-sensitive bitumen dissolved in oil of lavender, put it in a camera obscura by his upstairs window and waited several days. The plate slowly recorded the courtyard, outbuildings and trees outside. He called it 'the first uncertain step in a completely new direction', and it is the earliest surviving camera photograph.

source.name: Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin: The Niépce Heliograph

title: Pride and Prejudice Goes on Sale
text: Jane Austen first wrote this story as 'First Impressions' at age 20, but a publisher rejected it by return mail. Years later she cut and revised it, and in January 1813 it went on sale in three volumes for 18 shillings, credited only to 'the Author of Sense and Sensibility'. The first edition sold out in less than a year.

source.name: Jane Austen Society of North America (JASNA): Pride and Prejudice

title: A Planet Found by Maths
text: Urbain Le Verrier in Paris had worked out where an unknown planet should be from wobbles in the orbit of Uranus, and wrote to Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory. Using a Fraunhofer telescope and a new star chart, Galle spotted an object not on the chart on the very first night, about one degree from the predicted spot. It was the planet later named Neptune.

source.name: Linda Hall Library: Scientist of the Day - Johann Galle

title: The Pump on Broad Street
place: Broad Street (Broadwick Street), Soho, London, England, UK
text: In 1854 cholera killed upwards of five hundred people in ten days around Soho. Doctor John Snow found that nearly all the deaths were close to the Broad Street water pump, while brewery workers with their own deep well and workhouse residents with their own pump mostly escaped. After Snow met the parish Board of Guardians, the pump's handle was removed the next day.

source.name: T. H. Tulchinsky, Case Studies in Public Health (2018), via PubMed Central: John Snow, Cholera, the Broad Street Pump

title: Bones in the Neander Valley
place: Feldhofer Grotto, Neander Valley, Mettmann, Germany
text: Workers clearing a small cave in a limestone gorge near Mettmann threw out a skullcap and fifteen other bones, thinking they belonged to a cave bear. Local teacher Johann Carl Fuhlrott saw that they were human and prehistoric, a bold idea almost nobody shared then. They became the first scientifically described fossil human remains: the Neanderthal. Limestone mining later destroyed the cave itself.

source.name: Neanderthal Museum: History of the discovery of Neanderthal man

source2.name: Schmitz et al., PNAS 2002 (PubMed Central): The Neandertal type site revisited

title: A Red Cross on White
text: A Geneva committee that included Henry Dunant, author of a book calling for better care of wounded soldiers, persuaded governments to act. In August 1864 delegates from a dozen countries adopted the first Geneva Convention. It obliged armies to care for wounded soldiers whatever side they were on, and gave medical services one shared emblem: a red cross on a white background.

source.name: International Committee of the Red Cross: History of the ICRC

source2.name: ICRC Archives and Library blog (Cross-Files): ICRC History, a primer

title: Meeting Cro-Magnon
place: Cro-Magnon rock shelter, Les Eyzies-de-Tayac, Dordogne, France
text: Workers building a railway line near Les Eyzies stumbled on human remains in a rock shelter. Neanderthals were already known, but these were the first prehistoric people found who looked exactly like us. Louis Lartet led the dig and presented the find in Paris that April. Shells used to decorate the burials were later dated to between 32,000 and 31,000 years ago.

source.name: French Ministry of Culture (Archéologie de la France): The Cro-Magnon rock shelter

source2.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins: Cro-Magnon 1

title: Digging Up the Palace of Minos
text: Cretan Minos Kalokairinos had already dug trenches at Knossos in 1878, but war with the Ottomans delayed new work. Once Crete had its own government, Arthur Evans bought the land and began digging on 23 March 1900, helped by his local foreman Manolis Akoumianakis. They uncovered a grand palace with bright wall paintings and clay tablets in a script later called Linear B.

source.name: University of Oxford, Faculty of Classics (Crete course): Evans at Knossos

source2.name: Ashmolean Museum: Sir Arthur Evans, Biography

title: Doctor Hopeful's New Language
text: Eye doctor Ludwik Zamenhof had worked on a planned language since his school days in Warsaw, but no publisher would take it. After the censors approved it, he published a 40-page textbook himself, paid for with the dowry of his wife Klara Zilbernik. Worried for his reputation, he signed it 'Doktoro Esperanto', meaning 'Doctor Hopeful'. The Esperanto movement had begun.

source.name: Austrian National Library (ÖNB), Bernhard Tuider: Die Lingvo Internacia des Dr. Esperanto

title: A Woman Takes the Chair
text: Russian mathematician Sofia Kovalevskaya first had to lecture in Stockholm for a year without pay to prove herself, and one local writer called a female professor 'a monstrosity'. She won France's Prix Bordin for work on spinning bodies, and in June 1889 became the first woman since Laura Bassi and Maria Gaetana Agnesi to hold a chair at a European university.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Sofia Kovalevskaya

title: Earthquake and Wave at Messina
place: Strait of Messina, Messina, Sicily, Italy
text: An earthquake of magnitude greater than 7 struck southern Italy, and within minutes a tsunami hit the coasts of Calabria and Sicily. South of Reggio Calabria the wave reached about 13 metres, even dragging a boat inside a church, and it flooded streets as far away as Malta. About 80,000 people died from collapsed buildings and the quake, while the sea killed several hundred more, perhaps 2,000 or more.

source.name: INGV Tsunami Alert Centre (Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia): Tsu-Memo, the tsunami of Reggio Calabria and Messina

title: Swan Lake's Bumpy Start
text: Tchaikovsky threw himself into his first ballet, studying every dance step to fit the music. But at the Bolshoi premiere almost everything went wrong: critics called the choreography 'gymnastics exercises', a silly quarrel replaced the star ballerina with her understudy, and an inexperienced conductor struggled with the score. Swan Lake only found lasting fame in a new 1895 production in St Petersburg.

source.name: Mariinsky Theatre: Swan Lake (programme note by Natalia Rogudeeva)

title: Blériot Flies the Channel
place: Les Baraques, near Calais, France, to Dover, England
text: Early one morning, headlamp maker Louis Blériot took off from near Calais in his little Type XI monoplane, chasing a £1,000 newspaper prize, while his rival Hubert Latham was still fast asleep. Flying with an injured foot through rain and poor visibility, he reached Dover in 36 minutes and 30 seconds, damaging his plane on landing. It was the first aeroplane flight over a large body of water.

source.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Blériot's Cross-Channel Flight

title: A Republic From the Balcony
text: Republican ideas spread through Portugal's cities at rallies drawing thousands. Republicans and allies in the army and navy took to Lisbon's streets in the early hours of 4 October 1910, and fighting raged from the riverside square to the Rotunda. Some mishaps nearly wrecked the revolt, but royal forces failed to take advantage, and next morning the Republic was proclaimed from the balcony of Lisbon City Hall.

source.name: Museu da Presidência da República (Portugal): Implantação da República

title: Gaudí Takes Over a Church
place: Sagrada Família, Eixample, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain
text: The cornerstone of a new church in Barcelona had been laid in 1882, on the feast of Saint Joseph, on land surrounded by gardens and paths. When its first architect, Francisco de Paula del Villar, stepped down, the young Antoni Gaudí took over and proposed 'a Temple that strives to be universal'. Its crypt Chapel of Saint Joseph was consecrated in 1885.

source.name: Basílica de la Sagrada Família (official blog): 144 years of shared history

title: Venice's Bell Tower Falls
place: Piazza San Marco, Venice, Veneto, Italy
text: For almost 1,000 years St Mark's bell tower had survived lightning strikes and an earthquake, and from 1885 experts warned that its foundations were too weak. On 14 July 1902 it collapsed into a deserted square that police had closed to the public, and nobody was hurt. Venice rebuilt it 'as it was and where it was', opening it again on St Mark's Day 1912.

source.name: Procuratoria di San Marco (Basilica di San Marco): The Bell Tower

title: The Doctor Who Hung Up Meat
text: The physician al-Razi was born in Rayy in 865 and later worked in Baghdad. Asked to choose a site for a new hospital, he hung pieces of meat around the city and picked the spot where the meat rotted most slowly. His Treatise on Smallpox and Measles told the two diseases apart by their symptoms and contains the earliest known description of smallpox.

source.name: Heart Views (PMC): The Air of History (Part IV): Great Muslim Physicians Al Rhazes

title: Ibn Sina Slips Away in Disguise
text: Ibn Sina served as court physician in Hamadan and was twice made vizier, but rivals forced him into hiding and he spent time as a political prisoner. In 1022, after the death of the prince he served, he decided to leave and escaped to Isfahan disguised as a Sufi. His Canon of Medicine has been called the most famous single book in the history of medicine.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Abu Ali al-Husain ibn Abdallah ibn Sina (Avicenna)

title: A Monastery That Was Also an Academy
text: In 1106 King David IV 'the Builder' began building Gelati Monastery on a wooded hill near his capital, Kutaisi. It was more than a monastery: its Academy drew scholars such as the philosopher Johannes Petritzi, who translated Proclus. Inside the main church, finished in 1130, a 12th-century mosaic shows the Virgin and Child flanked by archangels, and the walls hold more than 40 royal and clerical portraits.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gelati Monastery

title: Anjar, the Unfinished Trade Town
text: The Umayyad caliph Walid I founded Anjar early in the 8th century where the road from Beirut to Damascus crossed the route through the Bekaa. Its walls had forty towers, and two main streets ran above the sewers, splitting the town into four quarters. Anjar was never finished: in 744 Caliph Ibrahim, Walid's son, was defeated and the damaged town was abandoned.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Anjar

title: Queen Khosrovanush Founds Haghpat
text: In 976 Queen Khosrovanush, wife of the Armenian king Ashot III the Merciful, founded the monastery of Haghpat. Its oldest building, the domed church of St Nshan, was built between 976 and 991 by the architect Trdat. Carvings on its east wall show two kings holding a model of the church. Haghpat and nearby Sanahin became important centres of learning.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Monasteries of Haghpat and Sanahin

title: Churches Dug Into a Cliff
text: At Geghard, once called Ayrivank, the 'Monastery in the Cave', builders did not stack stones so much as carve them away. A first church was dug entirely into the living rock before 1250, and a second rock-cut church followed in 1283, reached through a princely tomb chamber of the Proshyan family. Most monks lived in cells cut into the cliff face.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Monastery of Geghard and the Upper Azat Valley

title: Mosques Held Up by Wooden Forests
place: Great Mosque of Afyon, Afyonkarahisar, Turkey
text: Most mosques of the time were stone or brick, but the Great Mosque of Afyon, built in 1272–77, rests on rows of wooden columns topped with carved honeycomb capitals that hold up a flat wooden ceiling. It is one of five such Anatolian mosques. Their building is linked to the Mongol invasions of the 1240s and the Central Asian woodworkers who arrived afterwards.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Wooden Hypostyle Mosques of Medieval Anatolia

title: Zabid, Yemen's City of Scholars
text: In 820 the caliph al-Mamun sent Ibn Ziyad to Yemen's coastal plain to put down a rebellion, and the round, walled town of Zabid owes its growth to him. Canals brought it water. Zabid later served as Yemen's capital and became famous for its mosques and madrasas, which drew students from all over the world; it has some 86 mosques in all.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Town of Zabid

title: Twelve Centuries in One Mosque
text: Isfahan's Friday Mosque began in 841 and kept growing for twelve centuries, from the Abbasids to the Safavids. Under the Seljuqs it gained four great iwans (vaulted halls) around its courtyard, the first use of that plan in Islamic architecture. Its Nezam al-Molk dome was the first double-shell ribbed dome in the Islamic world, a design copied across the region.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Masjed-e Jāmé of Isfahan

title: Crusader Acre Goes Underground
text: From 1104 to 1291 the port of Acre was the Crusaders' main harbour and the capital of their Kingdom of Jerusalem, a busy centre of international trade. After the Mamluks took over at the end of the 13th century, the Crusader town was buried. Much of it still survives almost intact below today's streets, and excavations have only recently begun to reveal it.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Old City of Acre

title: Court Life on a Brass Jug
text: In 1232 Shuja ibn Mana of Mosul signed and dated a brass ewer inlaid with silver and copper. Its medallions show court life: a noblewoman gazing into a mirror, another riding in a camel litter, a hunter with a cheetah on his horse, musicians and dancers. Mosul's glittering inlaid brass was exported and given to rulers. The ewer is now in the British Museum.

source.name: Discover Islamic Art (Museum With No Frontiers), Emily Shovelton: Ewer (the Blacas Ewer)

title: Coins Without Faces
text: Early Umayyad gold coins showed the caliph Abd al-Malik standing alone holding his sword, replacing the Byzantine emperor and his sons seen on older coins. Then, in 77 AH (696 CE), he ordered that coins carry no images at all. The new dinars, believed to have been struck in Damascus, bore only words: religious phrases, the denomination and the date.

source.name: Qatar Museums, Museum of Islamic Art collection: Umayyad Dinar

source2.name: Qatar Museums, Museum of Islamic Art collection: Standing Caliph Dinar

title: A Trap at the Spring of Goliath
place: 'Ain Jalut, Jezreel Valley (Plain of Esdraelon), Israel
text: In 1260 the Mamluk sultan Qutuz marched from Egypt to meet a Mongol army led by Kitbuqa. At 'Ain Jalut, where the plain narrows below Mount Gilboa, Qutuz hid cavalry in the hills. His commander Baybars clashed with the Mongols, then pretended to retreat. As the Mongols chased him, the hidden horsemen struck their flanks, and Kitbuqa was captured and executed.

source.name: AramcoWorld, David W. Tschanz: History's Hinge: 'Ain Jalut

title: Damascus Prays Through the Plague
text: When the traveller Ibn Battuta reached Damascus in 1348, plague was killing about 2,000 people a day, by his account. The people fasted for three days and crowded the Great Mosque, then walked out barefoot carrying Qur'ans. Jews came with their book of the law and Christians with the Gospel, all praying together for God's help.

source.name: ORIAS, UC Berkeley: The Travels of Ibn Battuta: Return Home, 1346-1349

title: Anatolia's Brotherhoods of Hospitality
text: Landing at Alanya from a Genoese ship, the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta found a 'Young Brotherhood' in every Turkmen town of Anatolia. Members worked by day, pooled their earnings each afternoon to buy food, and lodged any traveller who arrived; if none came, they ate together, sang and danced. He also noted that Turkish women went unveiled and were shown great respect.

source.name: ORIAS, UC Berkeley: The Travels of Ibn Battuta: Anatolia, 1330-1331

title: Dayfa Khatun's Garden of Paradise
text: Dayfa Khatun, Saladin's niece, ruled Aleppo on her own for nearly 20 years. Her Madrasat al-Firdaws, 'Paradise' or 'Garden', dated by inscription to 1235–36, combined a tomb, mosque, school and lodging for Sufis, with eleven domes around a courtyard. Inside runs one of the longest continuous Arabic inscriptions in the world, nearly 92 metres long, describing the Sufi experience of worship.

source.name: Discover Islamic Art (Museum With No Frontiers): Madrasat al-Firdaws

title: Armenia's Perfect Domed Church
place: St Hripsime Church, Echmiatsin (Vagharshapat), Armavir, Armenia
text: St Hripsime Church, built in 618 at Echmiatsin, is the perfect example of an Armenian four-apse church, with niches and corner rooms gathered under a central dome. Central-domed churches spread across Armenia in the 7th century. Nearby St Gayane (630) was the first to join a three-aisle basilica to a central dome, a form that became widespread in Armenia and Western Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Cathedral and Churches of Echmiatsin and the Archaeological Site of Zvartnots

title: Timing the Year From Raqqa
text: Working mostly at ar-Raqqah in Syria, the astronomer al-Battani observed the sky between 877 and 918. He measured the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes and 24 seconds, catalogued 489 stars, and used trigonometry where Ptolemy had used geometry. His Kitab al-Zij, in 57 chapters, influenced Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, Kepler and Galileo.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Al-Battani

title: A Mosque Over the Emperors' Church
text: Ten years after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, Sultan Mehmed II built a new mosque under his own name in 1463: the Fatih Mosque, or Mosque of the Conqueror. Its site was chosen with care. The Church of the Holy Apostles, burial place of Byzantine emperors, was torn down to make way. An earthquake in 1766 largely destroyed the mosque, but its courtyard is still largely original.

source.name: Society of Architectural Historians blog, Patricia Blessing: Creating an Ottoman Capital: Istanbul in the Late Fifteenth Century

title: The Zanj Rise in the Marshes
text: In 869 enslaved workers, mostly of African origin, revolted in southern Iraq around Basra. Their job was reclaiming land by removing the nitrous topsoil to make it farmable. Led by the mysterious, charismatic Ali ibn Muhammad, the Zanj built a capital, al-Mukhtara, deep in the marshes and held out for about 15 years until the caliphate turned much of its army and resources against them.

source.name: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History, Adam Ali (University of Toronto): Zanj Revolt in the Abbasid Caliphate (Iraq)

title: Wild Cattle on a Borneo Wall
place: Lubang Jeriji Saléh, East Kalimantan, Indonesia
text: High in the limestone mountains of East Kalimantan, a cave called Lubang Jeriji Saléh holds three rotund, cow-like animals painted on its wall, the largest more than seven feet across. Uranium-thorium dating of mineral crusts suggests they are at least 40,000 years old. Hundreds of hand outlines in red-orange paint wave from the ceilings nearby.

source.name: National Geographic: World's oldest known figurative paintings discovered in Borneo cave

title: Bird-Headed Hunters Chase an Anoa
place: Leang Bulu' Sipong 4, Maros-Pangkep, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: In December 2017, Indonesian researchers found a cave mural in South Sulawesi showing small part-human, part-animal figures hunting wild pigs and buffalo-like anoa with what seem to be ropes or spears. One figure appears to have a bird-like head and beak. Cave popcorn grown over the paint gave uranium-series ages of up to 43,900 years.

source.name: The Conversation (Brumm, Oktaviana, Aubert, Griffith University): Indonesian cave paintings show the dawn of imaginative art and human spiritual belief

title: An Ancient Hand Stencil Dated
place: Leang Timpuseng, Maros, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Scholars had reported hand stencils and animal paintings in Sulawesi's caves since the 1950s, but nobody knew their age. In 2014, uranium in mineral layers coating the art showed a hand stencil at Leang Timpuseng was at least 39,900 years old. A painting of a babirusa, or pig-deer, in the same cave dates back at least 35,400 years.

source.name: The Conversation (Taçon, Brumm, Aubert, Griffith University): 40,000-year-old rock art found in Indonesia

source2.name: National Geographic: Cave art in Indonesia rivals Europe's oldest

title: Tiny Blades on the Narmada
place: Mehtakheri, Narmada Valley, Madhya Pradesh, India
text: Near the village of Mehtakheri, above the Narmada River, archaeologists dug up microblades, tiny stone blades. Optical dating put them at about 45,000 years old. In India this toolmaking tradition then continued all the way to the Iron Age, and the researchers argued it arrived with the earliest modern humans rather than being invented locally after 35,000 years ago.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Mishra, Chauhan & Singhvi 2013): Continuity of Microblade Technology in the Indian Subcontinent Since 45 ka

title: A Toolmakers' Workshop in Lenggong
place: Bukit Jawa, Lenggong Valley, Perak, Malaysia
text: Along the Perak River, the Lenggong Valley preserves undisturbed Stone Age workshops where stone tools were made, on the shores of an ancient lake and on old river gravel beds. One of these workshop sites, Bukit Jawa, dates from about 200,000 to 100,000 years ago. UNESCO says the valley's sites together show a sequence of human history unrivalled in the region.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Heritage of the Lenggong Valley

dateLabel: Between about 37,400 and 28,500 years ago (minimum age)
title: The Wajak Skulls Grow Older
text: Around 1890 the scientist Eugène Dubois collected human skulls, animal bones and tools at Wajak in Java. Older tests had made the bones seem fairly recent, but in 2013 laser ablation uranium-series dating gave a minimum age of between 37,400 and 28,500 years for the whole assemblage. The researchers said this means rethinking how early modern humans in Southeast Asia were related.

source.name: Journal of Human Evolution (Storm et al. 2013), via ANU Research Portal: U-series and radiocarbon analyses of human and faunal remains from Wajak, Indonesia

source2.name: Naturalis Biodiversity Center, Scripta Geologica (Storm 1995): The evolutionary significance of the Wajak skulls

title: When Ostriches Roamed India
text: Ostriches are extinct in India today, but fossil eggshells from sites in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat prove they once lived there. In 2017, scientists recovered ancient DNA from shells at least 25,000 years old, and one from Runija matched the African ostrich completely. People used the shells too: some had been made into beads or scratched with crisscross patterns.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Jain et al. 2017), PubMed Central: Ancient DNA Reveals Late Pleistocene Existence of Ostriches in Indian Sub-Continent

title: Buried with Her Fish-Hooks
place: Tron Bon Lei rockshelter, Alor Island, East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia
text: In 2014, archaeologists digging a rockshelter on Alor's south coast found the skull of probably an adult woman buried with five shell fish-hooks, a perforated shell and two cobbles coated in red ochre. Dating showed she was buried shortly after about 12,000 years ago. With few other protein sources on the island, fishing seems to have mattered to this community in life and in death.

source.name: Antiquity (O'Connor et al. 2017), Cambridge Core: Fishing in life and death: Pleistocene fish-hooks from a burial context on Alor Island, Indonesia

title: Tortoise on the Ice Age Menu
text: The lowest layers of Lang Rongrien rockshelter in southern Thailand date from about 43,000 to 27,000 years ago. Their animal bones show what Ice Age foragers ate: a few fish, snails and birds, but mostly tortoises, turtles and mammals, and no pigs at all. The shelter seems to have been used now and then by people moving between the interior and the coast.

source.name: Asian Perspectives (Mudar & Anderson 2007), Project MUSE: New Evidence for Southeast Asian Pleistocene Foraging Economies: Faunal Remains from the Early Levels of Lang Rongrien Rockshelter

title: Sudden Arrival on Timor
text: Laili rockshelter overlooks the Laleia river on Timor's north coast. Its deepest layer, laid down between 59,000 and 54,000 years ago, shows no sign of people. Then, around 44,000 years ago, intensive human living begins abruptly, with chert tools, burnt bones, ash and masses of fish bone and shellfish. The researchers suggest this was a colonisation phase.

source.name: Nature Communications (2024), PubMed Central: Abrupt onset of intensive human occupation 44,000 years ago on the threshold of Sahul

title: A Hand with a Claw
place: Liang Metanduno, Muna Island, Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: In a cave that locals call Liang Metanduno, on Muna island off southeastern Sulawesi, one painted hand stencil has a finger that looks pointy like an animal claw. Laser-ablation uranium-series dating, announced in 2026, showed it is at least 67,800 years old. That makes it the oldest rock art attributed to modern humans found so far.

source.name: National Geographic: The world's oldest rock art discovered in Indonesia

title: Ice Age Savanna in the Thai Hills
place: Tham Lod rockshelter, Pang Mapha, Mae Hong Son, Thailand
text: Hunter-gatherers used Tham Lod rockshelter, 640 metres up in Thailand's northwestern highlands, from about 34,000 to 12,000 years ago. Chemical clues in the teeth of animals found there, from tigers and elephants to rhinoceroses and wild cattle, reveal a mosaic of forest and grassland. Scientists think this savanna corridor may have helped people and animals spread across mainland Southeast Asia.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Suraprasit et al. 2021), PubMed Central: Late Pleistocene human paleoecology in the highland savanna ecosystem of mainland Southeast Asia

title: The Human Tooth That Wasn't
text: Nam Lot sits in the Laos mountains about 1,120 metres above sea level, in karst deposits dated to about 86,000 to 72,000 years ago. An incisor from the site had been reported as human. In 2021, scientists studied the ancient proteins in its enamel and found it belonged to an orangutan, leaving no human remains older than about 70,000 years known in the area.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Bacon et al. 2021), PubMed Central: A multi-proxy approach to exploring Homo sapiens' arrival, environments and adaptations in Southeast Asia

title: Hunters Among Trang An's Towers
text: Near the edge of Vietnam's Red River Delta, limestone towers up to 200 metres high rise over partly submerged valleys. Caves at different heights hold traces of people over more than 30,000 years: seasonal hunter-gatherers who had to adapt as the sea repeatedly flooded the landscape after the last ice age. Later, Hoa Lu, an early Vietnamese capital, was built here.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Trang An Landscape Complex

title: Hidden Paint at Lene Hara
place: Lene Hara cave, Tutuala, Lautém, Timor-Leste
text: Red paintings decorate Lene Hara cave in East Timor. Scientists dated the thin calcite layers that sandwich the paint and found the visible paintings are less than 6,300 years old. But an older layer of similar red pigment within the calcite gave an age of 24,000 to 29,300 years, possible evidence that people painted here much earlier.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science (Aubert et al. 2007), via ANU Research Portal: Uranium-series dating rock art in East Timor

title: Shellfish Feasts on Ilin Island
place: Bubog 1, Ilin Island, Occidental Mindoro, Philippines
text: On little Ilin Island off Mindoro, foragers left a thick, layered heap of shells: its base dates to 28,000 to 33,000 years ago and its top to about 4,000 years ago. The lowest layer is packed with valves of the clam Geloina, and two shell tools were dated to 31,000 to 28,000 years ago. Beach pebbles served as hammers to crack open larger marine shells.

source.name: Frontiers in Earth Science (Pawlik & Fuentes 2023): Prehistoric Hunter-Gatherers in the Philippines: Subsistence strategies, adaptation, and behaviour in maritime environments

title: From Deer to Pig in Ille Cave
place: Ille Cave, El Nido, Palawan, Philippines
text: Excavations at Ille Cave in northern Palawan show people living there from about 11,000 years ago, at the end of the Pleistocene. Their stone tools and food bones reveal hunter-foragers who switched from relying on deer to relying on pig. Later, around 9,500 to 9,000 years ago, a cremation burial was placed here in a container, the earliest known in the region.

source.name: Antiquity (Lewis et al. 2008), Cambridge Core: Terminal Pleistocene to mid-Holocene occupation and an early cremation burial at Ille Cave, Palawan, Philippines

title: A Rainforest Before People
text: Fossil bones from Coc Muoi, a site in Vietnam's Lang Son province, date to about 148,000 to 117,000 years ago. Chemical signals in the animals' teeth show that closed rainforest held most of the mammal life, mostly browsing animals. No human remains or tools turned up with the bones: researchers found no clear sign of people in the region before about 70,000 years ago.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Bacon et al. 2021), PubMed Central: A multi-proxy approach to exploring Homo sapiens' arrival, environments and adaptations in Southeast Asia

title: A New Star Over Chaco
place: Peñasco Blanco Trail, Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, USA
text: Painted on a cliff overhang six meters up, near the great house of Peñasco Blanco, are a crescent moon, a star shape and a life-size hand print. The painting may record the supernova first seen on July 4, 1054, which Chinese astronomers also noted. Calculations show that on July 5, 1054 the moon was a waning crescent.

source.name: High Altitude Observatory (NCAR/UCAR): Supernova Pictograph

source2.name: National Park Service, Chaco Culture: Petroglyphs & Pictographs

title: Moonrise Between Two Spires
place: Chimney Rock National Monument, Colorado, USA
text: At Chimney Rock, an outlier community on the far northeastern border of the Chacoan world, stands a great house, and tree-ring dating shows building work in 1076 and again in 1093. Both years matched a major lunar standstill, when the moon rises at its northernmost point and appears between the twin sandstone chimneys. That happens only every 18.6 years.

source.name: Notre Dame Magazine (University of Notre Dame): Moonrise Over Chimney Rock

title: The Great House Called Aztec
place: Aztec Ruins National Monument, Aztec, New Mexico, USA
text: Around 1110, Ancestral Pueblo builders began the biggest construction phase at Aztec West, raising multi-story rooms in its north and east wings. With about 400 rooms and 30 kivas, it is the largest known great house outside Chaco Canyon. Its long, straight back wall marks both the summer and winter solstices.

source.name: National Park Service, Aztec Ruins: Engineering in Aztec Ruins

title: Wupatki, Town on the Cinders
place: Wupatki National Monument, near Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
text: About a century after Sunset Crater erupted, people gathered here and slowly built a pueblo of about 100 rooms with a community room, a ballcourt and a natural blowhole. By 1182 perhaps 85 to 100 people lived at Wupatki, the largest building for at least fifty miles. Hopi clans still return, saying the place is remembered, not abandoned.

source.name: National Park Service: Wupatki Pueblo & Blowhole

title: A Bishop for Greenland
text: Greenland's Norse farmers asked King Sigurd of Norway for a bishop of their own, and he chose a Norwegian priest named Arnaldur. The diocese was set up at Garðar in 1124. The bishop consecrated priests and collected church taxes, and Garðar grew into the largest farm in Greenland, with a cathedral, a big barn and storehouses.

source.name: Trap Greenland (Gads Forlag): The Norse

title: Greenland Agrees to Pay Norway
text: In 1261, sailors came home to Norway after four winters in Greenland with news: the Greenlanders had agreed to pay taxes and levies to the Norwegian king. They probably did so willingly, hoping the king would keep ships, trade and supplies coming. The king had little presence in Greenland and mostly cared about customs duties on Greenland ships arriving in Bergen.

source.name: Trap Greenland (Gads Forlag): The Norse

title: Runes in the Far North
place: Kingittorsuaq Island, north of Upernavik, Greenland
text: Three Norsemen, Erling Sigvatsøn, Bjarne Thordarsøn and Einride Oddsøn, carved runes on a small slate stone saying they built a cairn on the Saturday before Rogation Day. Found in 1824 by the hunter Pelimut, it shows that Greenland Norse sailed far north, likely hunting walrus for ivory, and sometimes had to spend the winter there.

source.name: National Museum of Denmark, Collections Online: Slate stone with runes from Kingittorsuaq, Upernavik

source2.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Greenland Norse walrus exploitation deep into the Arctic

title: Mounds That Watch the Sun
place: Toltec Mounds (Plum Bayou Mounds), near Scott, Arkansas, USA
text: Beside an old channel of the Arkansas River, Plum Bayou people built flat-topped mounds around two plazas, with Mound S in use from about 750. From Mound A, the sun rose over Mound B on the summer solstice. Perhaps only 50 leaders lived here; farm families came several times a year for ceremonies and to renew family ties.
