source.name: Arkansas Archeological Survey (Martha Ann Rolingson): Toltec Mounds Site & State Park

title: The White House in the Cliff
place: Canyon de Chelly National Monument, Chinle, Arizona, USA
text: Built against a sheer 500-foot sandstone cliff, the White House was lived in from 1060 to 1275 by ancient Puebloan people, ancestors of today's Pueblo and Hopi Indians. It is named for the white plaster coating the long back wall of its upper dwelling. Today the canyon still sustains a living community of Navajo people.

source.name: National Park Service: Arizona: Canyon de Chelly National Monument

title: Chocolate in Chaco's Tall Jars
place: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, USA
text: Pueblo Bonito is famous for tall, narrow cylinder jars, many found in its Room 28. When UNM ceramics expert Patricia Crown had sherds from them tested by W. Jeffrey Hurst, three held traces of theobromine, a sign of cacao or chocolate. The sherds date between 1000 and 1125, and the nearest possible source of cacao was Central Mexico.

source.name: National Park Service, Chaco Culture: Pre-Columbian Chocolate Discovered at Chaco

title: The Day a Beach Rose 7 Meters
place: Restoration Point, Bainbridge Island, Washington, USA
text: Sometime around 900 to 930, a major earthquake struck the Seattle fault. Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island was lifted 7 meters (23 feet) out of Puget Sound in an instant, and tsunami deposits were left behind. Modeling of the raised shorelines suggests a magnitude of about 7.5, though the fault's exact shape is still uncertain.

source.name: U.S. Geological Survey: Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island in the greater Seattle area

source2.name: U.S. Geological Survey: Rupture models for the A.D. 900-930 Seattle fault earthquake from uplifted shorelines

title: Six Longhouses Behind a Wall
text: In the 1200s, ancestral Huron-Wendat families lived in a village of six longhouses in what is now Pickering, each 45 to 60 feet long. An irregular wooden palisade ringed the village, and the Royal Ontario Museum excavators who dug it in the 1950s found no sign of a gate. Fortified villages like this became more common as violent conflict increased.

source.name: Government of Ontario: Indigenous culture and history along the TransCanada Trail

title: Corn Grown by Wendat Women
place: Dunsmore site, Sunnidale Park, Barrie, Ontario, Canada
text: In the mid- to late 1400s, the Dunsmore site in Barrie was both a seasonal fishing camp and a farming village with sixteen houses. Women planted, tended and harvested the corn, which could make up as much as 60% of the Huron-Wendat diet. It was eaten in soup, roasted, baked into bread for long journeys, and traded for hides, fish, meat and tobacco.

source.name: Government of Ontario: Indigenous culture and history along the TransCanada Trail

title: The Seal Hunters of Phillip's Garden
place: Phillip's Garden, Port au Choix, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
text: For centuries the Dorset people, an Arctic culture, hunted harp seals at Port au Choix, leaving at least 50 house depressions, sled runners, soapstone pots and harpoon heads. They seem to have left about 1,300 years ago. A new Indigenous population or a warming climate that changed the sea ice and their access to seal herds may explain why.

source.name: Parks Canada, Port au Choix National Historic Site: Dorset Peoples

title: Calusa Fish Pens at Mound Key
place: Mound Key, Estero Bay, Florida, USA
text: The Calusa did not grow staple crops; fishing fed their society. Between 1300 and 1400, at the mouth of the Grand Canal on Mound Key, later their capital, they built two huge 'watercourts' on oyster shell, ringed by berms about 3 feet high. They likely trapped fish with the tide and held them, including leaping mullet, before cooking, smoking or drying.

source.name: Florida Museum, Randell Research Center (Bill Marquardt): Mystery of the Watercourts

title: Emerald Mound Rises in Mississippi
place: Emerald Mound, Natchez Trace Parkway, near Stanton, Mississippi, USA
text: Mississippian builders began this flat-topped ceremonial mound around 1200, and it stayed in use until 1730. It is 35 feet high, covers eight acres, and measures 770 by 435 feet at its base; two smaller mounds on top bring it to about 60 feet. Only Monks Mound at Cahokia is a bigger Mississippian ceremonial mound in the United States.

source.name: National Park Service, Natchez Trace Parkway: Emerald Mound

title: Spruce Tree House Takes Shape
place: Spruce Tree House, Mesa Verde National Park, Colorado, USA
text: Between about 1211 and 1278, ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples built Spruce Tree House in an alcove 216 feet wide and 89 feet deep. Its roughly 130 rooms and 8 kivas, or ceremonial chambers, were home to perhaps 60 to 80 people. It is the third largest cliff dwelling in the park, and about 90% of its walls, wood and plaster are original.

source.name: National Park Service, Mesa Verde: Spruce Tree House

title: The Strong Tuniit
text: Inuit legends from Arctic Canada and Greenland tell of the Tuniit, big and strong people who spoke another language, lived in square, half-buried houses and used neither bow nor kayak. Archaeologists now link them to the Late Dorset culture. Inuit arrived by the North Water around 1150, and the latest Dorset date in the area is from the early 1300s, so the two peoples may have met.

source.name: Trap Greenland (Gads Forlag): The strong Tuniit people

title: Inuit Winter Houses at Nuulliit
text: Inuit ancestors travelled over 4,000 miles in a few generations from St. Lawrence Island, hunting whales from big skin boats and travelling far by dog sled in winter. In the 1300s they built winter houses at Nuulliit, near Qaanaaq, partly dug into the ground with walls of stone, peat and sometimes whale bone. A ring of chainmail dug up there hints at meetings with the Norse.

source.name: Trap Greenland (Gads Forlag): The Inuit culture, precolonial period

title: Vah Ki, the Great House
place: Casa Grande Ruins National Monument, Coolidge, Arizona, USA
text: Around 1350, ancient Sonoran Desert people raised a four-story, 11-room building from about 3,000 tons of caliche soil. Sunlight passes through a small hole at sunset on the longest day, and twin openings catch the March and September sunrise. O'odham oral tradition calls such a place a Vah Ki, a water house, perhaps used to mark times to plant and harvest.

source.name: National Park Service, Casa Grande Ruins: The Casa Grande

source2.name: National Park Service, Casa Grande Ruins: Why Build the Casa Grande?

title: The Sinagua Leave Their Castle
place: Montezuma Castle National Monument, Camp Verde, Arizona, USA
text: First built in the early 1100s, the five-story, 20-room cliff dwelling now called Montezuma Castle was part of a larger Sinagua settlement, with irrigation canals near Montezuma Well begun before 1150. Around 1425, for reasons still unknown, the Sinagua left both places. When Europeans came in the late 1500s, Yavapai people were living around the castle and the well.

source.name: National Park Service: Arizona: Montezuma Castle National Monument

title: Bridge River's Pithouse Village
place: Bridge River village (Xwísten), near Lillooet, British Columbia, Canada
text: Near Lillooet, a village of pithouses founded about 1,800 years ago grew steadily until about 1,000 years ago, when it was temporarily abandoned. Its 80 housepits range from about 10 to nearly 20 meters across. Xwísten, the Bridge River Indian Band, studies the site with University of Montana archaeologists; the village was re-established in the last 400 years.

source.name: University of Montana, Department of Anthropology: The Bridge River Project

title: The Bauhaus Begins in Weimar
text: In 1919 the Bauhaus school began in Weimar, later moving to Dessau. Until 1933 its teachers, among them Walter Gropius, Wassily Kandinsky and László Moholy-Nagy, rethought building with the new materials of the age, reinforced concrete, glass and steel, and threw out traditional decoration. Their buildings launched the Modern Movement that shaped much of 20th-century architecture.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Bauhaus and its Sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau

title: Pigeons Over Antwerp's Olympics
text: Antwerp was given the 1920 Olympics when World War I had been over only a year, and the war-ravaged Belgians staged decidedly austere Games. The opening ceremony brought three firsts: the Olympic flag, an athlete taking the Olympic Oath, and homing pigeons released as a symbol of peace. Germany, Austria, Hungary and Bulgaria were barred from competing.

source.name: Olympedia: 1920 Summer Olympics Overview

title: The Play That Invented Robots
text: The word "robot" first appeared in Karel Čapek's play R.U.R., short for Rossum's Universal Robots, which opened at Prague's National Theatre on 25 January 1921. Amateur actors in Hradec Králové, directed by a State Railways inspector, had actually staged the world premiere on 2 January. Within a few years the play reached Warsaw, Belgrade, New York, London, Tokyo and Paris.

source.name: Embassy of the Czech Republic in Copenhagen: The Czech word ROBOT celebrates its 100th birthday

title: A House Like a Painting
text: In 1924 Truus Schröder-Schräder had architect Gerrit Rietveld build her a small family house on the edge of Utrecht. Its flexible layout, which let the rooms change over time as their uses changed, made it a manifesto of the Dutch De Stijl group of artists and architects. Its interiors and furniture are part of the design, and it became an icon of modern architecture.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rietveld Schröderhuis (Rietveld Schröder House)

title: The Day the Zuiderzee Vanished
text: At half past one on Saturday 28 May 1932, workers closed the Vlieter, the last gap in the Afsluitdijk, a 32-kilometre dike between North Holland and Friesland. The Zuiderzee was sealed off from the sea and was called the IJsselmeer from then on. Engineer Cornelis Lely had drawn up the first plans in 1891; a deadly flood in 1916 came before work finally began.

source.name: Rijkswaterstaat: Afsluitdijk

title: Splitting the Uranium Atom
place: Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, Berlin, Germany
text: In December 1938, chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin bombarded uranium with neutrons and found what looked like barium. Puzzled, Hahn wrote to his longtime colleague Lise Meitner. On a walk in the snow, Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch realised the uranium nucleus had split in two. Hahn won the 1944 Nobel Prize in chemistry; Meitner was never recognised.

source.name: APS News: December 1938, Discovery of Nuclear Fission

title: Warsaw Rebuilds Its Old Town
text: During the Warsaw Uprising in August 1944, Nazi troops destroyed more than 85 percent of Warsaw's historic centre. From 1945 to 1951 the Warsaw Reconstruction Office, backed by the determination of the city's people and the support of the whole nation, rebuilt the Old Town: its market square, townhouses, city walls and churches, using surviving buildings and pre-war conservation records.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Warsaw

title: A Bog Body Mistaken for Murder
text: On 6 May 1950, a family cutting peat for fuel near Silkeborg found a body so fresh-looking they thought it was a recent murder victim. Grethe Højgaard first noticed something strange and started digging in the mud herself. He lay 2.5 metres down in the peat with a rope around his neck, so the police soon handed the case to the museum. He became Tollund Man.

source.name: Museum Silkeborg: The discovery of Tollund Man

title: Under Four Minutes at Last
place: Iffley Road track, Oxford, England, UK
text: On 6 May 1954, in front of 3,000 people at Oxford's Iffley Road track, 25-year-old medical student Roger Bannister became the first man to run a mile in under four minutes, in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds. He had worked a morning shift at St Mary's Hospital in London first. Years earlier, a groundsman at the same track had told him he'd never be any good.

source.name: World Athletics: Roger Bannister's sub-four-minute mile, 70 years on

title: "Austria Is Free!"
text: On 15 May 1955, Austria and the victorious powers of World War II signed the State Treaty at Vienna's Belvedere Palace, making the young Second Republic sovereign again. Foreign Minister Leopold Figl ended his speech there with "Österreich ist frei!" ("Austria is free!"). The key had been neutrality: Austria promised to stay out of military alliances, and passed its neutrality law that October.

source.name: Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung: Vor 65 Jahren: Österreich unterzeichnet Staatsvertrag

title: Only Stalin's Boots Remained
text: What began as peaceful student demonstrations in Budapest on 23 October 1956 quickly became an armed uprising. Students demanded reforms and the withdrawal of Soviet troops, and protesters tore down a towering statue of Stalin, leaving behind only his boots. Soviet forces crushed the revolution in November; about 2,600 Hungarians died and some 200,000 fled to the West.

source.name: Origins (Ohio State University), Harrison King: Remembering '56, The Hungarian Revolution at Sixty

title: The Arno Drowns Florence's Art
text: After days of heavy rain, the Arno overflowed in the early hours of 4 November 1966 and swept through Florence, rising 3 metres around the cathedral. Mud and heating oil soaked the city's treasures. In Santa Croce, Cimabue's great crucifix lost 60 percent of its painted surface. Thousands of volunteers came from all over the world to help Florence climb out of the mud.

source.name: Gallerie degli Uffizi: The 1966 flood's damages to the art heritage of Florence

title: Sweden Swaps Sides of the Road
text: On 3 September 1967, a day many Swedes would remember as "Dagen H", the whole country switched from driving on the left to driving on the right. Voters had rejected the idea in a 1955 referendum, with 82.9 percent against, but parliament decided on the change anyway in 1963. Little souvenir pins stamped "3.9 1967" marked the big day.

source.name: Arkiv Gävleborg via DigitaltMuseum: Högertrafikomläggningen 1967 (pin)

title: Concorde Takes to the Sky
text: On 2 March 1969, Concorde 001, the first prototype of a supersonic airliner built under a 1962 treaty between France and Great Britain, took off from Toulouse with André Turcat at the controls. It reached twice the speed of sound in November 1970. In 1973 it flew from Las Palmas to Fort-Lamy so that astronomers could watch a solar eclipse for 74 minutes without a break.

source.name: Musée de l'Air et de l'Espace: BAC-Sud Aviation Concorde prototype 001 F-WTSS

title: A Peace Prize He Couldn't Collect
text: In 1975 Andrei Sakharov, the physicist known as the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, won the Nobel Peace Prize for his struggle for human rights. Furious Soviet leaders refused to let him travel to Oslo, so his wife, Jelena Bonner, received it for him. The couple were later kept under strict surveillance in the town of Gorky until Gorbachev came to power.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Andrei Sakharov, Facts

title: Unlooted Tomb of Philip II
text: In 1977, digging at Vergina in northern Greece uncovered unlooted royal tombs, one identified as that of Philip II, father of Alexander the Great, and the find made a worldwide sensation. Vergina sits on ancient Aigai, the first royal capital of Macedon, with a great palace and a cemetery of hundreds of burial mounds. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Site of Aigai (modern name Vergina)

title: Louise, the First IVF Baby
place: Oldham General Hospital, Greater Manchester, England, UK
text: At 11:47 pm on 25 July 1978, Louise Brown was born at Oldham General Hospital, the first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF). The technique was developed by Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards and Jean Purdy. In 1971 the Medical Research Council had refused to fund their work on ethical grounds. A government film crew raced to Oldham to record the birth.

source.name: The National Archives (UK): Louise Brown, A glimmer of hope

title: Winter Games in Sarajevo
text: In February 1984 Sarajevo hosted the first Winter Olympics held in the Eastern Bloc. A blizzard after the opening ceremony delayed the men's downhill by a week. Finland's Marja-Liisa Hämäläinen won three cross-country gold medals, and British ice dancers Torvill and Dean skated to Ravel's Bolero for 12 perfect 6.0s. Many Olympic sites were later destroyed in the 1990s war.

source.name: Olympedia: 1984 Winter Olympics Overview

title: A Cave Sealed for 20,000 Years
text: A cave in a limestone plateau above the Ardèche River in southern France had been sealed by a rock fall about 20,000 years ago, until its discovery in 1994. Inside were more than 1,000 images, among the earliest-known figurative drawings in the world: mammoths, cave lions, rhinos, bears and bison, along with human footprints and 4,000 remains of prehistoric animals.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Decorated Cave of Pont d'Arc, known as Grotte Chauvet-Pont d'Arc

title: A Nobel for the Poet of Peat
text: On 5 October 1995 the Swedish Academy gave the Nobel Prize in Literature to Seamus Heaney, "for works of lyrical beauty and ethical depth". Born on a farm in Northern Ireland, he had lived in Dublin since 1976. His down-to-earth poems often paint the grey, damp Irish landscape, peat moss has a special place in them, and some reach back to prehistoric times.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1995, Press release

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: Seamus Heaney, Facts

title: Titanium on the Riverbank
place: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, Basque Country, Spain
text: Built between October 1993 and October 1997 on a former industrial wharf on the Nervión, Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao reclaimed the riverbank for culture and leisure. His design was so mathematically complex that he used CATIA, software first made for the aerospace industry. Its skin is about 33,000 extremely thin titanium sheets that change colour with the weather and light.

source.name: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao: The construction

title: Writing Against a Dictatorship
text: Herta Müller grew up in a farming family of Romania's German-speaking minority in Nițchidorf, outside Timișoara. She lost her job as a translator after refusing to cooperate with the Securitate secret police, and her first book appeared in Romania only in a censored version. She went into exile in Germany in 1987. In 2009 her books about fear under Ceaușescu won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Herta Müller, Facts

source2.name: NobelPrize.org: The Nobel Prize in Literature 2009, Press release

title: A Minaret Lost in the Mountains
text: Far from any town, in a deep river valley about 215 km east of Herat, the Ghurid Sultan Ghiyas-od-din raised a 65-metre minaret of fired brick in 1194. Geometric relief and a Kufic inscription in turquoise tiles cover it completely. It probably marks the lost Ghurid summer capital of Firuzkuh, and its design influenced Delhi's Qutb Minar.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam

title: Timur's White Palace at Kesh
place: Ak-Sarai Palace, Shakhrisyabz, Kashkadarya Region, Uzbekistan
text: Construction of the Ak-Sarai Palace in Shakhrisyabz began in 1380, the year after Timur conquered Khorezm. Khorezm's artisans were deported to work on it and to create its rich decoration. Today only the foundations of its immense gate survive, yet UNESCO judges that none of Samarkand's many Timurid monuments can rival it.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Shakhrisyabz

title: A Market Street Built in Twenty Days
text: On September 8, 1404, Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo, envoy of King Henry III of Castile, reached Samarkand and was greeted by six elephants carrying wooden castles. He then watched Timur order a covered street of shops, with stone benches and fountains, cut straight through the city. Crews worked day and night and finished it in twenty days, though evicted homeowners had good cause to complain.

source.name: Origins (Ohio State University): A Castilian in Samarkand, 1404

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Clavijo's Embassy to Tamerlane

title: A Taoist Master Winters in Samarkand
text: Summoned by Genghis Khan, the elderly Taoist monk Changchun reached Samarkand in December 1221. His disciple's diary describes canals bringing river water to every house, but notes that only a quarter of the city's families remained after the Mongol conquest. Changchun wintered in the Sultan's palace, saw elephants from India, and compared notes on a solar eclipse with a local astronomer.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): The Travels of Ch'ang Ch'un to the West, 1220-1223

title: A Friar in a Market Town of Many Faiths
place: Kayalyk (Cailac), near Koylyk, Zhetysu Region, Kazakhstan
text: Heading for the Mongol court in 1253, the Flemish friar William of Rubruck rested twelve days at Cailac, a big market town frequented by many traders. He entered its 'idol temples', whose priests shaved their heads and wore saffron robes. Leaving town, his party found a village entirely of Nestorian Christians and sang the Salve Regina in their church, overjoyed to see one after so long.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): William of Rubruck's account of the Mongols

title: A Silk Coat Fit for a Prince
text: In the 700s a five-colour silk was woven with paired ducks inside pearl roundels, hallmarks of the precious silks of Sogdia. It was made into a child's coat lined with Chinese floral damask, presumably for a Tibetan prince. The coat looks so pristine that it may never have been worn; it might have served as a diplomatic gift or even as currency.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Child's Coat with Ducks in Pearl Medallions

title: A Pharmacy Jar with a Proverb
text: This albarello, a jar designed to hold ointments and drugs for pharmacists, was made in Samarkand in the 900s, under the Samanid dynasty. Such jars usually carried flowers or geometric patterns, but this one bears elegant Arabic writing in Eastern Kufic script: 'Modesty comes from faith, and faith comes from Paradise,' a saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Albarello Jar with an Aphorism

title: Gawharshad's Tiled Mosque in Herat
text: Gawharshad, wife of the Timurid ruler Shahrukh, was a great builder. Her mosque in Herat, raised between 1417 and 1438 beside an open-air prayer ground north of the city walls, had a courtyard 116 by 64 metres, polychrome tiles everywhere and marble-clad minarets with exquisite calligraphy. Her mausoleum of 1432, crowned by a ribbed blue-tiled dome, still stands.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: Gawharshad Complex, Herat

title: The Mosque with Tile Dragons
place: Anau, near Ashgabat, Ahal Region, Turkmenistan
text: In 1455–1456 a Timurid shrine for Shaykh Jamal al-Din rose on a hill over Anau's old city wall, near today's Ashgabat. Its mosque portal was famous for a tile mosaic of a pair of dragons, with panels fastened by lead pins, and its windows glowed with coloured glass. An earthquake destroyed it in 1948, but scholar Galina Pugachenkova had recorded the site in 1947.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: Shrine of Shaykh Jamal al-Din (1455-1456)

title: The Oldest Madrasa on the Registan
text: Built in 1417–1420, Ulugh Beg's madrasa, an Islamic religious school, is the oldest surviving monument on Samarkand's Registan Square. Its later story is dramatic: photographs from 1901 show its northern and southern facades as piles of rubble, and its whole courtyard had to be rebuilt. In 1932 an engineer from Moscow straightened a leaning minaret on the square's facade.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: The Registan Square (15th-17th century)

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Samarkand, Ulugh Beg's Observatory

title: A Mother Builds a Tomb for Her Daughter
text: In 1372 Turkan Aqa built a mausoleum at Samarkand's Shah-i Zinda shrine for her daughter Shad-i Mulk Aqa, Timur's niece, and she may be buried there too. Its deeply carved terracotta tiles resemble Chinese lacquerware, hinting at influence from objects brought from China. Unusually, the tomb's inner dome still keeps its tiles, though so many domes there collapsed within a century or so.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington), Daniel C. Waugh: Samarkand, Shah-i-Zinde

title: Giant Melons and Fist-Sized Pomegranates
text: Yelü Chucai, an official marching west with Genghis Khan's army in 1219, filled his notes with fruit. Khujand's pomegranates were as large as two fists and were squeezed into a thirst-slaking drink. In the town of Ba-p'u, he wrote, watermelons weighed fifty pounds, so a donkey could carry only two, while Samarkand's melons were as large as a horse's head.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Ye-lü Ch'u-ts'ai's account of Central Asia (Si Yu Lu)

title: A Silk Road City in the Clouds
text: Between the 6th and 11th centuries, Tugunbulak flourished 2,000 to 2,200 metres up in the mountains of southeastern Uzbekistan. Drone-mounted lidar has revealed its plazas, fortifications, roads and homes across 120 hectares, making it one of the largest highland cities of its time. Its fortress, with rammed-earth walls three metres thick, may have been a factory where smiths turned iron ore into steel.

source.name: Washington University in St. Louis, Arts & Sciences: High-res lidar exposes large, high-elevation cities along Asia's Silk Roads

source2.name: Nature (Frachetti et al. 2024): Large-scale medieval urbanism traced by UAV-lidar in highland Central Asia

title: A Coin Stamped 'Turk-Kagan'
text: A small bronze coin from the late 6th or early 7th century, found at an ancient site near Tashkent, is stamped 'Turk-Kagan' in the Sogdian language. Archaeologist Gaybulla Babayarov argues it is the oldest known reference to Turkic identity. Probably minted in the Western Gokturk Khaganate, it suggests these supposedly purely nomadic rulers had towns, a ruling elite and money.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): Bronze Coin May Contain Earliest Known Usage of the Word 'Turk'

title: A Papal Envoy Crosses Ruined Lands
place: Lower Syr Darya steppe, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: Riding to the Mongol court in 1246, the papal envoy John of Plano Carpini crossed steppe where human skulls and bones lay scattered on the ground like cattle dung. Next came the land of Turkic-speaking Muslims, with 'innumerable ruined cities' along a great river, among them Ianckint, Barchin and Ornas. Their sultan, he heard, had been killed by the Mongols with all his family.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): John of Pian de Carpine's journey

title: The Astronomer King Loses His Head
text: Ulugh Beg, Timur's scholarly grandson, governed Samarkand for decades and became supreme ruler when his father Shahrukh died in 1447. He survived only two years on his own before being overthrown and beheaded in 1449. Some scholars he had supported then left Samarkand for more stable capitals such as Istanbul, and his observatory was destroyed within a few generations. He lies at Timur's feet in the Gur-i Amir.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Samarkand, Ulugh Beg's Observatory

title: Sorghum Caught in Clay
text: Broken pots from a site called KG23 in eastern Sudan hold Africa's earliest known evidence of domesticated sorghum. Archaeologists studied plant impressions left in the pottery by people of the Butana Group, who harvested wild sorghum intensively until the plant began to change genetically into domesticated forms. Sorghum went on to become one of the world's five most important cereal crops.

source.name: Current Anthropology (University of Chicago Press) via EurekAlert: Earliest evidence for a native African cultigen discovered in Eastern Sudan

title: Boxes Labelled From Punt
place: Mersa/Wadi Gawasis, Red Sea coast, Egypt
text: In caves cut into a bluff above an ancient Red Sea port, archaeologists found stone anchors, ship timbers, cedar steering oars and about 26 coils of rigging rope. Outside lay more than 40 cargo boxes; two carry King Amenemhet IV's name and the label "the wonderful things of Punt." Ships were built at Coptos, taken apart and carried by donkey caravan across the desert to the sea.

source.name: Boston University Arts & Sciences Magazine: Kathryn Bard's excavations at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis

title: A Temple for the Lion God
place: Musawwarat es-Sufra, River Nile State, Sudan
text: Built for the Meroitic king Arnakhamani, the Lion Temple at Musawwarat es-Sufra honoured Apedemak, a powerful lion-headed god of Kush. It is the first known Meroitic one-room temple, a type made for local gods rather than Egyptian ones. A hymn on its walls calls Apedemak lord of Aborepe, the site's ancient name. The temple fell down in antiquity, but neatly enough to be stood up again.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for the History of Science, Musawwarat Graffiti Archive: The Lion Temple

title: Buried Half Egyptian, Half Nubian
text: After Egypt conquered Nubia, Tombos in northern Sudan became an important colonial hub. In one middle-class tomb, archaeologists found a woman laid in an Egyptian-style tomb but buried the Nubian way, flexed on her side on a bed, wearing amulets of the Egyptian household god Bes. Skeletons and graves here point to intermarriage, and to Nubians sharing in running the colony.

source.name: UC Santa Barbara News: Identity Unearthed (Tombos excavations, Smith and Buzon)

source2.name: Current Anthropology via EurekAlert: Ancient tomb sheds new light on Egyptian colonialism

title: Yemeni Stonework in Ethiopia
text: Early in the first millennium BCE, Sabaean groups from Yemen settled in the northern Ethiopian highlands and made Yeha their political and religious centre. Its Great Temple honoured Almaqah, the top Sabaean god. Excavators found a second temple of the same seventh century BCE, built the South Arabian way: stones laid without mortar or dowels, each with a smoothed edge and a roughened centre.

source.name: German Archaeological Institute (DAI) press release via idw: 2.700 Jahre alter Tempel im äthiopischen Hochland entdeckt

source2.name: University of Jena press release via idw: Preserving northern Ethiopia's ancient cultural heritage

title: Bananas in the Rainforest
text: At Nkang, in the forests of southern Cameroon, Belgian-led scientists found phytoliths, tiny silica bodies left by plants, which they identified as banana and dated to about 500 BC. Bananas were thought to have come to Africa from Southeast Asia much later, so the find pushed their arrival back by about a thousand years. Critics challenged it, and the team agreed that more finds were needed.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): Africa's Earliest Bananas

source2.name: Azania (2006), Mbida et al.: The initial history of bananas in Africa, a reply (Université libre de Bruxelles repository)

title: Castles of the Garamantes
text: From satellite images, archaeologists spotted more than 100 fortified farms and villages and several towns in Libya's south-western desert, most dating from AD 1 to 500. Built by the Garamantes, their mud-brick, castle-like walls still stand up to four metres high, beside wells and irrigation systems. Roman writers called these people barbaric nomads; the researchers describe oasis farmers with towns and a written language.

source.name: European Research Council: Castles in the desert, satellites reveal lost cities of Libya

dateLabel: First half of the 1st century CE
title: A Royal City in the Steppe
text: Naga, a secondary royal residence of the Kingdom of Meroe, lies in the steppe 30 km from the Nile. Its Chapel of Hathor, once called the "Roman Kiosk", blends Hellenistic-Roman and Egyptian features into a new, Meroitic design. It dates to the reigns of king and queen Natakamani and Amanitore. Today local people still water their animals at the well in the city's centre.

source.name: Naga Project (State Museum of Egyptian Art, Munich): The Site

source2.name: Naga Project (State Museum of Egyptian Art, Munich): The Excavation Project

title: A Lakeside Grave in the Sahara
text: Gobero, in Niger, holds the largest early cemetery in the Sahara, beside a long-vanished lake where people ate clams and fish and kept some cattle. Around 3315 BCE an adult woman was buried facing two children of about 8 and 5, their arms, hands and legs intertwined. Four stone points lay with her; other graves held bracelets of hippo ivory.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2008), Sereno et al.: Lakeside Cemeteries in the Sahara, 5000 Years of Holocene Population and Environmental Change

title: Honey in Nok Cooking Pots
text: The Nok people of central Nigeria were early farmers whose diet included millet. Chemists analysed 458 of their pottery vessels and found beeswax in over a third of those that kept fat residues, direct evidence of collecting and processing bee products, probably honey, around 3,500 years ago. Acidic soils have destroyed all animal bones at Nok sites, so pots are a precious window on what people ate.

source.name: Nature Communications (2021), Dunne et al.: Honey-collecting in prehistoric West Africa from 3500 years ago

title: A Reluctant Priest at Hippo
text: Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in Roman Africa, today Souk Ahras in Algeria. In 391 he was ordained a priest in the port city of Hippo Regius, apparently against his will, and about five years later he became its bishop. Preaching daily and writing in fierce religious debates, he became perhaps the greatest Christian philosopher of antiquity. He died in 430 as the Vandals besieged Hippo.

source.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Augustine of Hippo

title: The Tophet's Tiny Urns
text: Ancient Greek writers claimed Carthaginians burned infants as sacrifices, and some scholars say the practice lasted until Rome won the last Punic War in 146 BCE. Scientists who studied 348 burial urns from Carthage's Tophet, holding 540 individuals, found most were babies who died shortly before or after birth. They argue it was a cemetery for the very young, whatever killed them, though the debate goes on.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2010), Schwartz et al.: Skeletal Remains from Punic Carthage Do Not Support Systematic Sacrifice of Infants

title: Arrest Warrant From a Rubbish Dump
text: On 28 February AD 256, the head of the council of Oxyrhynchus ordered police in a country village to arrest a man described as a Christian; no reason was given. It is one of the earliest uses of the word "Christian" on papyrus. Like thousands of other texts, it survived in the town's ancient rubbish dumps, which Oxford classicists Grenfell and Hunt dug from 1896.

source.name: University of Oxford, The Oxyrhynchus Papyri Project: Daily Life

source2.name: University of Oxford, The Oxyrhynchus Papyri Project: home page

title: The Man in the Pot
place: Nuwayrat, near Beni Hasan, Minya, Egypt
text: Buried in a large pottery vessel inside a rock-cut tomb at Nuwayrat, near Beni Hasan, this man gave scientists the first whole genome of an ancient Egyptian. He lived a few centuries after Egypt's unification. Most of his ancestry was North African, but about 20% traced to the eastern Fertile Crescent, including Mesopotamia. Worn teeth and arthritis suggest years of hard labour, possibly as a potter.

source.name: Nature (2025), Morez Jacobs et al.: Whole-genome ancestry of an Old Kingdom Egyptian

title: An Embalmers' Labelled Pots
text: Just south of King Unas's pyramid at Saqqara lay an embalming workshop of Egypt's 26th Dynasty. Its pots were labelled with their contents, letting chemists match Egyptian names to real substances: juniper or cypress and cedar oils or tars, animal fat, and resins such as elemi and dammar. Some came from tropical forest regions, showing that mummification depended on long-distance trade, including imports from Asia.

source.name: Nature (2023), Rageot et al.: Biomolecular analyses enable new insights into ancient Egyptian embalming

title: The Day the Sea Struck Egypt
place: Nile Delta coast, near Alexandria, Egypt
text: On 21 July 365 a huge earthquake struck in the eastern Mediterranean. Historical accounts describe a tsunami that destroyed cities and drowned thousands of people along coasts from the Nile Delta to modern Dubrovnik. Geologists later found that western Crete was lifted out of the sea by up to 10 metres at the same moment, and estimate a quake like it on that one fault every 5,000 years or so.

source.name: Nature Geoscience (2008), Shaw et al.: Eastern Mediterranean tectonics and tsunami hazard inferred from the AD 365 earthquake

title: A Baby's Horoscope on Papyrus
text: A large papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, once probably sixteen columns wide, is a horoscope recording the zodiac positions of the Sun, Moon and five planets, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, at someone's birth. Scholars computed the moment as 4 a.m. on 7 July AD 430. The person's name is lost, and only one other comparable fragment, also from Oxyrhynchus, survives from antiquity.

source.name: University of Oxford, The Oxyrhynchus Papyri Project: Daily Life

title: Peru's Oldest Known Monument
text: In the Andes foothills of Casma, people built a circular, sunken plaza of stones and adobe. Carbon dating announced in 2008 placed it between 3500 and 3000 BCE, making it the oldest known monument in Peru. Excavation leader Peter Fuchs said the plaza was a social and ritual space where people celebrated their thoughts about the world and their place within it.

source.name: Taipei Times (AP): Scientists discover oldest Peruvian monument

title: The Earth Monster Comes Home
text: At Chalcatzingo in Morelos, the only Olmec-linked settlement founded in the Central Highlands, carvers made a one-ton relief of an "Earth monster" whose open jaws mark a passage to the underworld, with bromeliad-like plants sprouting from its mouth. Monument 9 dates from 800 to 400 BCE. Illegally removed from Mexico, it was recovered in New York and announced for return in 2023.

source.name: Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (Mexico): Chalcatzingo Monument 9 to be repatriated to Mexico

title: An Olmec-Style City in Guerrero
text: Teopantecuanitlán, south-east of Iguala, flourished from 1400 to 600 BCE and is unique in the region for its monumental Olmec-style architecture. Archaeologist Guadalupe Martínez Donjuan pioneered its study. Villagers of the Alto Balsas region call it their most sacred place, and since 2024 its site museum labels have been written first in Náhuatl, translated by local teachers.

source.name: INAH Boletín 777: Concluye rehabilitación de la Zona Arqueológica Teopantecuanitlán

source2.name: INAH Boletín 552: El INAH reconoce labor arqueológica de Guadalupe Martínez Donjuan

title: Gold Masks Under the Sugar Cane
place: Hacienda Malagana, El Bolo, Palmira, Valle del Cauca, Colombia
text: Beneath sugar-cane fields in Colombia's Cauca Valley lay the rich cemetery of a culture now named Malagana, carbon-dated to 300 BCE to 140 CE. Chiefs were buried in stone-lined tombs with several fine gold masks over their faces. Its discovery in 1992 set off a gold rush and looting, but Colombia's central bank saved about 150 gold pieces for the Museo del Oro.

source.name: Boletín Museo del Oro (Banco de la República): Los tesoros de los señores de Malagana

title: A Mystery Eruption Near Lake Titicaca
place: Khonkho Wankane, Jesús de Machaca, La Paz, Bolivia
text: Sometime between 400 and 720 CE, a huge explosive eruption showered ash across the southern Lake Titicaca Basin, even though the nearest active volcano is far away. Scientists found the layer at Khonkho Wankane and two other sites. In those same centuries many communities moved to Tiwanaku, where one of the Andes' first large complex societies was born. The source volcano is still unknown.

source.name: USGS Publications Warehouse: The Khonkho tephra (Marsh, Harpel and Damby, The Holocene, 2024)

title: Round Pyramids in Tequila Country
text: Above the town of Teuchitlán stand circular pyramids unlike any others, built by the Teuchitlán tradition, which peaked between 200 BCE and 350 CE. More than 50,000 people may have lived near the Tequila volcano, trading as far as Guatemala and Arizona. Art historian Celia García de Weigand and her husband Phil spent about 30 years studying this West Mexican civilization.

source.name: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America): Surprise Finds in Tequila Country

title: Amazon Farmers Tame Wild Rice
place: Monte Castelo shell mound, Rondônia, Brazil
text: At the Monte Castelo shell mound in south-west Amazonia, people learned to manipulate wild rice so it gave larger grains and bigger crops, beginning roughly 4,000 years ago. A Brazilian and British team studied 16 samples of microscopic rice residue there. It is the first evidence of rice domestication in the Americas, though the know-how may have been lost after European colonizers arrived.

source.name: Revista Pesquisa FAPESP: Rice domesticated in the Amazon 4,000 years ago

title: Caracol Crowns Its First King
text: In 331 CE Te K'ab Chaak took the throne at Caracol, founding the royal dynasty of what became the largest Maya site in Belize. In 2025 archaeologists Diane and Arlen Chase found what they identify as his tomb. The toothless old king lay with jadeite jewelry, a jadeite mosaic mask, Pacific spondylus shells and a vessel showing Ek Chuah, god of traders.

source.name: University of Houston: Archaeologists Discover Tomb of First King of Caracol

title: A Plateau Built by Many Hands
text: Around 950 BCE, people above Guatemala's Pasión River began a vast artificial plateau, later 600 by 340 metres, with a formal ceremonial complex at its centre. Lowland Maya were then turning to maize farming, settled village life and pottery, and neighbours who still moved home from time to time probably helped build it. Unlike a pyramid top, the open plateau probably welcomed everyone.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Artificial plateau construction during the Preclassic period at the Maya site of Ceibal, Guatemala (Inomata et al., 2019)

dateLabel: About the start of the Common Era
title: A Village Under Popocatépetl's Ash
place: Tetimpa, San Nicolás de los Ranchos, Puebla, Mexico
text: Around the beginning of the Common Era, ash from Popocatépetl buried the farming village of Tetimpa on the volcano's north-eastern flank. Villagers left so quickly that household goods stayed where they were. Each home had rooms of wattle and daub on stone platforms around a patio, with a small shrine at its centre, showing the volcano was part of family worship.

source.name: Latin American Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Preclassic Household Patterns Preserved under Volcanic Ash at Tetimpa, Puebla, Mexico (Plunket and Uruñuela)

title: A Mud Village Saved by Sand Dunes
place: Tulor, San Pedro de Atacama, Antofagasta, Chile
text: Around 380 BCE, farming pioneers from the oases near San Pedro de Atacama gave rise to the village of Tulor. Its round mud buildings were later linked by a complex system of entrances, passages and vestibules as the village grew. Oasis people farmed with the rivers' outflows and gathered chañar and algarrobo fruit. Tulor's mud walls survived because sand dunes covered them.

source.name: Estudios Atacameños (Universidad Católica del Norte): Agüero, Aproximación al asentamiento humano temprano en los oasis de San Pedro de Atacama (2005)

title: Panama's First Potters
text: On the shores of Panama's Parita Bay, some of the region's first potters made simple open bowls of crumbly, sandy clay, often greyish, sometimes coated with red slip and only rarely decorated with incised curving lines. A radiocarbon date for this Monagrillo ware at its namesake site centred on about 2610 BCE. Later finds in inland rock shelters showed these potters ranged widely.

source.name: Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Sánchez Herrera, Componentes cerámicos de Cerro Cebollal (LP-134), La Pintada, Coclé (2007)

title: A Clay Bird of Prey on a Temple
place: Huaca Partida, Nepeña Valley, Áncash, Peru
text: At the ruins of Huaca Partida in northern Peru, archaeologist Koichiro Shibata uncovered temple reliefs of a man and a bird of prey made about 3,000 years ago; one is believed to be 3 metres high. Clay reliefs rarely survive the weather, but this temple stayed well preserved because it was covered with stones when a later temple was built on top.

source.name: Andina (Peru News Agency): Reliefs of man, bird discovered in Peru

title: Izapa's Plazas Fall Silent
text: Izapa became the Soconusco region's first urban centre, and at its peak in 300 to 100 BCE a dozen plazas were lined with stelae and altars carved with complex narrative scenes. Then, some time before 100 CE, a violent disruption left central parts of the town abandoned. Later residents moved to a group of mounds to the north and reset older stelae there.

source.name: University at Albany: Izapa Regional Settlement Project, Project History

title: Terraced Fields Still Farmed Today
place: Coctaca, Quebrada de Humahuaca, Jujuy, Argentina
text: In the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a valley used as a major trade route for some 10,000 years, farmers began building the extensive stone-walled terrace fields of Coctaca around 1,500 years ago. They are still in use today. Between 400 and 900 CE, large structured farming societies lived in the valley, and the terraces are linked to a string of fortified towns called pucaras.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Quebrada de Humahuaca

title: Duck-Shaped Jugs of Central Chile
place: Central Chile, between the Aconcagua and Cachapoal rivers, Chile
text: From about 150 CE, the Llolleo people of Central Chile grew maize and quinoa, ground grain into flour and kept tame guanacos. Skilled potters, they made duck-shaped jugs and faces with "coffee bean" eyes. Many pipes found at large gathering places suggest smoking was central to their rituals, and they buried their dead beneath house floors, children in pottery urns.

source.name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino (Chile Precolombino): Llolleo Culture 150–900 CE

source2.name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino: Llolleo, Culto y Funebria

title: Southeast Asia's Oldest Sanskrit Stone
place: Võ Cạnh village, near Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa, Vietnam
text: A four-sided sandstone pillar from Võ Cạnh carries Brahmi-script lines, partly in Sanskrit verse, praising a king of the Sri Mara family, founder of Champa's first dynasty. Phrases about compassion for all beings show Buddhist influence from India. Vietnam's National Museum of History calls it the earliest evidence of Sanskrit reaching Champa, and the oldest stone in Southeast Asia to show India's influence.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Vo Canh stele

title: The Many Faces of Maitum
place: Ayub Cave, Pinol, Maitum, Sarangani, Mindanao, Philippines
text: In a Mindanao cave, people reburied selected bones in clay jars whose lids were shaped as human heads, each with its own expression: male or female, young or old, happy or sad. Soot from a pot inside one jar gave radiocarbon dates of 5 BCE to 225 CE and 70 to 370 CE. Archaeologists excavated 29 of these jars in the 1990s.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art: Maitum Jar No. 21

title: A Chieftain's Boat to the Afterlife
place: Việt Khê, Thủy Nguyên, Hải Phòng, Vietnam
text: Beside the Han River near Hải Phòng, Đông Sơn people buried someone in a hollowed tree trunk shaped like a boat, 4.76 metres long. Over 100 objects went with them: a bronze drum, vessels, axes and knives, a handbell, lacquered leather, spears and wooden paddles. It is the biggest Đông Sơn boat coffin found and became a national treasure in 2013.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Viet Khe boat tomb

dateLabel: Đông Sơn culture, c. 2,500–2,000 years ago
title: Four Couples on a Bronze Lid
place: Đào Thịnh, Trấn Yên, Yên Bái, Vietnam
text: This huge Đông Sơn bronze jar was made for storing food but was later used as a coffin, holding a smaller jar with ash and human teeth. Its lid shows a 12-rayed sun and four embracing couples, probably celebrating fertility. Around the body sail six boats carrying warriors with crossbows, spears and axes. It was discovered in 1961.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Dao Thinh jar

title: The Kneeling Lamp-Bearer of Lạch Trường
place: Lạch Trường, Hoằng Hóa, Thanh Hóa, Vietnam
text: A smiling bronze man kneels with an oil dish in his hands, while three S-shaped branches rise from his shoulders and back to hold more lamp dishes. His spiral hair, turban and earrings make many scholars see Indian influence. Found in a brick grave, the lamp mixes local, Chinese and Indian traditions from the late Đông Sơn period.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Bronze Lamp in the Shape of a Kneeling Man

title: Prohear's Golden Graves
text: At Prohear, one of Southeast Asia's richest Early Iron Age cemeteries, an old woman was buried with her head inside a bronze Đông Sơn drum, wearing gold bracelets, earrings and rings. A gold ring shows a man on horseback, the region's earliest evidence of horse riding. Archaeologists think the site was linked to the Yelang culture of southern China.

source.name: World Archaeology (Charles Higham): Why silence is golden

source2.name: Angkor Database: The First Golden Civilization of Cambodia (Reinecke et al.)

title: Rice Farmers on the An Sơn Mound
place: An Sơn, Đức Hòa, Long An, Vietnam
text: Just north of the Mekong Delta, Neolithic villagers built up a mound metres deep by spreading fresh layers of river soil as living floors. They grew japonica rice, a type that came from Neolithic China, and kept pigs and dogs. People buried there between about 1800 and 1200 BCE were laid out with finely made pots, some with wavy or serrated rims.

source.name: Asian Perspectives (Bellwood et al. 2011), via ANU Research Portal: An Son and the Neolithic of Southern Vietnam

source2.name: ANU Press, Terra Australis 42: Contextualising the Neolithic Occupation of Southern Vietnam

title: Non Nok Tha's First Bronze Axe
place: Non Nok Tha, Phu Wiang, Khon Kaen, Thailand
text: Non Nok Tha, dug in 1966 and 1968, was once claimed to show bronze in Thailand by 2000 BCE. Dating the skeletons themselves told a different story: the grave holding the site's earliest socketed copper-base axe dates to 980–900 BCE. Later Bronze Age burials there were given bronzes, crucibles and moulds, the tools of metalworkers.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Higham, Douka & Higham 2015): A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand

title: A Carnelian Lion From India
place: Ban Don Ta Phet, Phanom Thuan, Kanchanaburi, Thailand
text: This Iron Age cemetery, excavated from 1975, gave what was then the earliest clear, dated evidence of contact between Southeast Asia and India. Graves held hexagonal carnelian beads, little stone lions and tigers, and thin knobbed bowls of high-tin bronze. One carnelian lion pendant was tentatively read as a symbol of the Buddha, a possible forerunner of Buddhism's arrival.

source.name: Cambridge Core (Glover & Bellina 2011): Ban Don Ta Phet and Khao Sam Kaeo: The Earliest Indian Contacts Re-assessed

source2.name: Thammasat Review (Silapanth 2018): Knobbed Ware from Archaeological Sites in Thailand

dateLabel: Iron Age, from c. 400 BCE (possibly earlier)
title: The Copper Mines of Vilabouly
text: In central Laos, ancient miners dug for malachite and smelted it in crucibles to make pure copper, which they cast on site. These mines and smelting sites date to the Iron Age, about 400 BCE to 500 CE, and possibly the Bronze Age before that. Lead isotope studies suggest Laos was a major copper supplier for Southeast Asia for about 1,500 years.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science (Cadet et al. 2019), via James Cook University ResearchOnline

source2.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2022), via James Cook University ResearchOnline

title: The Giant-Clam Toolkit of Duyong Cave
place: Duyong Cave, Lipuun Point, Quezon, Palawan, Philippines
text: In a small Palawan cave, a muscular young man was buried face down, knees tucked under him, about 2680 BCE. Beside him lay a polished stone adze and four adzes carved from giant clam shell. He wore cone-shell ear discs, and a lime-filled ark shell by his feet probably served for betel chewing. Excavator Robert Fox called it the Philippines' first excavated Early Neolithic burial.

source.name: National Museum of the Philippines, Monograph 1 (Robert B. Fox 1970): The Tabon Caves, via University of the Philippines Diliman

title: Sumatra's Oldest Ancient Genome
place: Loyang Mendale Cave, Takengon, Central Aceh, Indonesia
text: A person buried in Loyang Mendale cave in northern Sumatra, radiocarbon-dated to 3,347 years ago, has given the earliest ancient DNA yet read from western Indonesia. They already carried a large share of Austronesian-related ancestry mixed with mainland Southeast Asian lineages. The cave's layers record Hoabinhian foragers, Austronesian arrivals and mainland influences in turn.

source.name: iScience (Xu et al. 2026), PubMed Central: Reconstructing the west-east genetic division in Indonesia using ancient genomes

dateLabel: c. 1290–1170 BCE (start of Bronze Age burials)
title: Dated by Their Shell Beads
place: Ban Lum Khao, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: At Ban Lum Khao on Thailand's Khorat Plateau, Neolithic villagers dug pits about 1400–1300 BCE, and the first Bronze Age graves followed around 1290–1170 BCE. The skeletons held no usable collagen, so scientists dated the shell beads and clam shells placed with the dead instead. The pots buried there closely match those from Ban Non Wat's second Bronze Age phase.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Higham, Douka & Higham 2015): A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand

dateLabel: Late Neolithic/Bronze Age, c. 3,200–2,700 years ago
title: Myanmar's Ancestors Arrive From the North
place: Oakaie 1 cemetery, near Nyaung'gan, Sagaing Region, Myanmar
text: DNA read from inner-ear bones at the Oakaie 1 cemetery in central Myanmar, dated about 3,200 to 2,700 years ago, told a distinct story. Unlike ancient people at Mán Bạc, Ban Chiang and Vat Komnou, these individuals lacked an Austroasiatic genetic signature. They were closer to speakers of Sino-Tibetan languages, including people in Myanmar today, pointing to a separate East Asian origin.

source.name: Science (Lipson et al. 2018), PubMed Central: Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory

title: Newcomers in Gua Harimau Cave
place: Gua Harimau, Padang Bindu, Ogan Komering Ulu, South Sumatra, Indonesia
text: Excavations since 2012 in Gua Harimau, a cave in southern Sumatra, have uncovered 84 skeletons spanning pre-Neolithic times to the Bronze and Iron Ages. Neolithic graves, the oldest dated to about 3,100 years ago, held paddle-impressed, incised and cord-marked pottery. Skull shapes and ancient DNA reveal at least two distinct populations, backing the 'Out of Taiwan' model of Austronesian dispersal.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Matsumura et al. 2018): Cranio-morphometric and aDNA corroboration of the Austronesian dispersal model, Gua Harimau

title: The Wounded Warriors of Phum Snay
text: Graves in this village cemetery in north-west Cambodia, used from about 350 BCE to 200 CE, held swords and other weapons. Bioarchaeologists found an exceptionally high number of injuries on the skeletons, especially to the head, most likely from fighting between people. They link these warriors to struggles between rising Iron Age chiefdoms, long before Angkor dominated the region.

source.name: Antiquity (Domett, O'Reilly & Buckley 2011): Bioarchaeological evidence for conflict in Iron Age north-west Cambodia

source2.name: Asian Perspectives (Domett & O'Reilly 2009), via ANU Research Portal: Health in Pre-Angkorian Cambodia

title: A Cemetery Found by Rubber Planters
place: Village 10.8, near Memot, Kampong Cham, Cambodia
text: Workers digging laterite for the Krek Rubber Plantation found this burial ground by chance, and archaeologists learned of it in 2001. In seven seasons from 2002 to 2008, the Memot Centre for Archaeology, with a German adviser, uncovered 56 burials with offerings, including 11 children buried in jars. The graves date between the 4th and 1st centuries BCE.

source.name: Angkor Database: The First Golden Civilization of Cambodia (Reinecke, Laychour & Sonetra)

title: Buddhism Takes Root Among the Pyu
place: Halin, Sagaing Region, Myanmar (one of the three Pyu cities)
text: From the 2nd century BCE, the walled, moated Pyu cities of Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra traded with Indic cultures, and Buddhism won its first lasting foothold in Southeast Asia, embraced by rulers and farm workers alike. The Pyu built brick stupas, kept cremated remains in urns inside shared funerary buildings, and dug water systems, some still in use.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pyu Ancient Cities

title: New Arrivals in Bronze Age Vietnam
text: Ancient DNA from Núi Nấp, a Bronze Age site about 2,100 to 1,900 years old, shows a big change from Vietnam's Neolithic. Earlier people at Mán Bạc were genetically close to Austroasiatic speakers, but the Núi Nấp individuals resemble present-day Vietnamese and Dai. Geneticists see substantial turnover, likely a new wave of migrants from China.

source.name: Science (Lipson et al. 2018), PubMed Central: Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory

title: Staircases of Rice in the Cordilleras
text: UNESCO describes the Ifugao rice terraces of northern Luzon as built about 2,000 years ago and still farmed. Stone or mud walls hug steep mountain contours, and channels bring water from the forests on the peaks. Families pass the know-how down through generations, following a farming calendar tied to the phases of the moon.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras

title: New Arrivals Reshape Vanuatu
text: Ancient DNA from Efate and Epi shows that people of almost entirely Papuan ancestry had reached Vanuatu by around 2,300 years ago, coming from the Bismarck Archipelago rather than the closer Solomon Islands. Yet the islanders kept speaking the Austronesian language of the first Lapita settlers, and its descendants, more than 120 languages, are still spoken in Vanuatu today.

source.name: Current Biology (Lipson et al. 2018, via PubMed Central): Population Turnover in Remote Oceania Shortly after Initial Settlement

source2.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History: Ancient DNA reveals genetic replacement despite language continuity in the South Pacific

title: Settlers on Tiny Fais Island
place: Fais Island, Yap State, Federated States of Micronesia
text: Fais is a raised coral island of just 2.8 square kilometres, with no safe anchorage, about 80 km from Ulithi atoll. Its earliest layer, radiocarbon-dated to about AD 230–410, held giant-clam shell adzes, shell bracelets and beads, and a few potsherds. Rats arrived with the first settlers, and pots kept coming over the sea from Yap throughout the island's history.

source.name: Asian Perspectives 47(1), University of Hawai'i ScholarSpace (Intoh 2008): Ongoing Archaeological Research on Fais Island, Micronesia

title: Taro Clues in Swamp Mud
place: Emaotfer Swamp, near Teouma, Efate, Vanuatu
text: A sediment core from Emaotfer swamp, 1 km from the Teouma Lapita cemetery, holds chemical traces of the first settlers. Molecules made by human gut microbes rise at the same time as a marker of taro farming, showing gardens arrived with the newcomers. The first unmistakable sign dates to about 2,800 years ago, during a spell of increasingly wet weather.

source.name: Communications Earth & Environment (2024, via PubMed Central): Sedimentary biomarkers of human presence and taro cultivation reveal early horticulture in Remote Oceania

title: Seal-Hunters' Villages of the Tarkine
place: West Point (Nongor), Tarkine coast, northwest Tasmania, Australia
text: About 1,900 years ago, Aboriginal people on Tasmania's northwest coast began a more settled way of life that lasted until the 1830s. In summer, groups gathered in villages of huts beside rich spots such as West Point, next to an elephant seal colony, then split up in leaner winters. Their shell middens hold seal and shellfish remains but strikingly few fish bones.

source.name: Australian Government, Australian Heritage Database: Western Tasmania Aboriginal Cultural Landscape

dateLabel: About 1260 BCE (earliest dates for the site)
title: The Beach That Named Lapita
place: Site 13A, Foué peninsula, Koné, North Province, New Caledonia
text: The famous Lapita culture takes its name from a misspelled Kanak name for a beach in Koné. People began living on this narrow spit of land around 1260 BCE, leaving pottery, adzes and shell armbands. In 1952 excavators found finely decorated pots here and used radiocarbon dating to prove the site was far older than expected, with pottery resembling finds from Fiji, Tonga and Watom.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Lapita (13A)

title: Remote Oceania's Earliest Village?
place: Nanggu (SE-SZ-8), Nendö, Santa Cruz Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
text: On Nendö in the Santa Cruz Islands, a Lapita village beside Tepiai Lagoon was settled roughly 3,400 to 3,100 years ago and lived in for about a century. Excavated in 1971 by Roger Green, it is described as the earliest settlement yet found in Remote Oceania. Its pottery, stone adzes, gravers and animal bones offer clues about the very first colonists.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Nanggu (SE-SZ-8)

dateLabel: About 1340 BCE (oldest dates about 3,300 years ago)
title: Early Lapita Life on Babase
place: Kamgot, Babase Island, Anir Group, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
text: Kamgot, on a raised limestone shelf of Babase Island, stretches over 400 metres and is one of the few sites from the very start of Lapita, the oldest of four Lapita sites in the Anir group. Its oldest radiocarbon dates centre around 3,300 years ago. Diggers found decorated pottery, obsidian, shell fishhooks, rings and beads, engraved bone and drilled dog teeth.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Kamgot (ERA)

dateLabel: By about 650 BCE (no later than 2,600 years ago)
title: A Painted Pot From Vao
place: Vao Island, off Malakula, Malampa Province, Vanuatu
text: On little Vao Island, off Malakula, archaeologists found Late Lapita burials dated to no later than 2,600 years ago. They also pieced together a pot from 20 sherds. Its makers stamped toothed patterns on the upper half, then covered them with white paint and added red, partly hiding the stamped designs. The site was found in 2002 during heritage training with the Vanuatu Cultural Centre.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Vao

title: Mountains of Shells at Weipa
place: Wathayn, Albatross Bay, Weipa, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia
text: Around Albatross Bay on Cape York, Aboriginal people heaped up more than 500 shell mounds, the biggest over 10 metres high with up to 10,000 tonnes of shell. Radiocarbon dates from 70 mounds at Wathayn show mounds growing 2,300 to 1,800 years ago, a time once thought quiet. Aboriginal people today say the mounds were where shellfish were opened before the meat was carried away.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2017, via PubMed Central): Temporal variability in shell mound formation at Albatross Bay, northern Australia

dateLabel: About AD 87 (oldest pottery date, 1,863 years BP)
title: Pohnpei's Drowned First Villages?
text: Pottery, a sure sign of settlers, first appears on Pohnpei about 1,863 years before 1950, and on Kosrae a little earlier. But mangrove mud shows the sea around both islands has risen about 4.3 metres over 5,700 years as the land sank. Much early evidence already comes from tidal or underwater sites, so even older villages may lie below the waves.

source.name: PNAS (2022, via PubMed Central): Implications of anomalous relative sea-level rise for the peopling of Remote Oceania

title: Palau's Long Family Line
place: Ucheliungs burial cave, Rock Islands, Koror, Palau
text: People first lived on Palau's Rock Islands and Babeldaob about 3,200 years ago. DNA from a person buried in the Ucheliungs cave about 2,800 years ago shows roughly 60 percent East Asian and 40 percent Papuan ancestry, much like Palauans today. The two groups had mixed before reaching Palau, giving the islands the longest population continuity known in Remote Oceania.

source.name: Cell (2026, via PubMed Central): Papuan admixture predated the settlement of Palau

title: Schoolchildren Find a Lapita Village
place: Tamuarawai (EQS), Emirau Island, St Matthias Group, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
text: In 2006 a teacher, Mr K. Vito, and pupils from Rongol Top Up primary school on Emirau Island found old pottery. Photos sent to archaeologist G.R. Summerhayes showed it was Lapita, and digs followed. Dated to roughly 3,360 to 3,160 years ago, the village left shell fishhooks, net sinkers, octopus lures, beads and even a slingshot stone.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Tamuarawai (EQS)

title: Lapita Settlers Reach Maré
place: Kurin (LPO023), Maré, Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia
text: On a dune beside the reef on Maré, in the Loyalty Islands, Lapita people lived from about 1050–1000 BCE to 850–800 BCE. Their oldest dates come from a stone cooking oven. The site shows the Loyalty Islands were settled at roughly the same time as New Caledonia's main island. It was found in 1997 by Christophe Sand and F. Wadra of the Yéwéné Cultural Centre.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Kurin (LPO023)

dateLabel: About 910 BCE (cumulative date for first occupation)
title: New Pots on the Isle of Pines
place: St Maurice-Vatcha (KVO003), Vao, Isle of Pines, New Caledonia
text: On a dune at the southern tip of the Isle of Pines, Lapita settlers arrived around 910 BCE, just decades after others reached New Caledonia's main island. They left pottery, shell rings, beads and adzes. In the upper layers, incised pots seen as forerunners of the later Puen style appear beside Lapita ware, showing the old tradition flowing into a new one.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Vatcha (KVO003)

title: The Man Under the Bus Stop
place: Narrabeen, northern beaches, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: Digging beneath a bus shelter at Narrabeen revealed an Aboriginal man killed on the dunes about 4,000 years ago. Small stone points called backed microliths, plus injuries to his bones, showed he died from stone-tipped spears: the first archaeological evidence of death by spearing in Australia. It also revealed how these points were used, and hints at a ritual punishment.

source.name: Antiquity 81 (McDonald et al. 2007), Australian National University research portal: The first archaeological evidence for death by spearing in Australia

source2.name: Cambridge Core, Antiquity: The first archaeological evidence for death by spearing in Australia

title: A Turtle Made of Beeswax
place: Gunbilngmurrung, western Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Some rock art in Arnhem Land was made from beeswax rather than paint. A naturalistic beeswax turtle at Gunbilngmurrung, radiocarbon-dated in 1995 and confirmed by a second test in 2002, is more than 4,000 years old: the oldest visible image of confirmed age in Arnhem Land. Drawn in the early X-ray style, it even shows a thin-line backbone.

source.name: ANU Press, The Archaeology of Rock Art in Western Arnhem Land, Australia (2017), chapter 1

title: A New Toolkit at Murujuga
place: Dampier Archipelago (Murujuga), Pilbara, Western Australia, Australia
text: Before about 3,500 years ago, campsites in the Dampier Archipelago held scrapers, horsehoof cores and retouched flakes. After that, Aboriginal toolmakers added microliths, tula adzes and slugs. These smaller tools were probably fixed to handles rather than held in the hand, and many were made from stone brought in from outside the islands. Rock engravings here show spears, boomerangs and nets.

source.name: Australian Government, Australian Heritage Database: Dampier Archipelago (including Burrup Peninsula)

title: A Dingo Buried With Care
place: Curracurrang Rockshelter, Royal National Park, New South Wales, Australia
text: In a rockshelter about 30 km south of Sydney, a nearly complete dingo skeleton was buried about 2,000 years ago. Its teeth are unusually worn, hinting it ate harder food than wild dingoes. Researchers note that Aboriginal people usually buried dingoes much as they buried community members, sometimes beside people, and that some tame dingoes lived in camps.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2023, via PubMed Central): Dingoes, companions in life and death: The significance of archaeological canid burial practices in Australia

dateLabel: By about AD 250–400 (1,700–1,550 years BP at the latest)
title: Settling Lonely Pingelap Atoll
place: Pingelap Atoll, Pohnpei State, Federated States of Micronesia
text: Pingelap is an atoll of only 1.8 square kilometres, nearly 70 km from the nearest island. Radiocarbon dates show people were living there by 1,700–1,550 years ago at the latest, only a few centuries after Kosrae and Pohnpei were settled. Early layers hold shell tools, ornaments, heaps of sea-creature remains and burnt remains of crop plants.

source.name: Radiocarbon 61(3), Cambridge Core (Levin, Seikel and Miles 2019): A Partial Chronological Sequence of Human Habitation for Pingelap Atoll

title: Smoke Rituals High in the Pamirs
text: At a cemetery more than 3,000 metres up in the eastern Pamirs, mourners laid hot stones in wooden braziers and burned cannabis during funerals. Chemists found traces of a THC breakdown product inside the braziers, some of the earliest scientifically verified evidence of ritual cannabis smoking. The tombs also held an angular harp, an instrument used in ancient funeral ceremonies.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): The origins of cannabis smoking: Chemical residue evidence from the first millennium BCE in the Pamirs

title: Silkworms Before the Silk Road
text: Three tiny cocoons found at Sapalli Tepe, a walled Bronze Age stronghold near the Amu Darya, turned out to come from the domesticated silkworm. Directly dated to about 1940 to 1765 BCE and found with plenty of mulberry charcoal, they suggest that silkworm farming had spread from East Asia to southern Central Asia long before the Silk Road.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Silkworm cultivation predating the Silk Road in southern Central Asia (2000 BCE)

title: The Tall Man in the Golden Diadem
place: Yingpan cemetery, Lop Nur region, Xinjiang, China
text: Yingpan Man was about 1.9 metres tall and around 30 when he died, probably in spring. He was buried in a poplar-wood coffin, wearing a red and yellow wool caftan embroidered with goats, bulls, pomegranate trees and nude cherubs, and a hemp mask with a gold band. Chemical tests suggest he stayed near home in his last years rather than travelling the Silk Road.

source.name: Scientific study (via PMC): Revealing lost secrets about Yingpan Man and the Silk Road

title: A Merchant's Expedition to China
text: Around 101 CE, Maes Titianus, a merchant described as Macedonian, paid for a trading expedition from Roman Syria toward China. His traders crossed Mesopotamia and the Tigris to reach Bactria, today's Balkh, which was still only halfway. Weeks more led to Tashkurgan and Kashgar. Nobody knows if they ever reached the Han capital.

source.name: National Geographic: Rome wanted silk, China had the goods. Here's how the Silk Roads got their start

title: Farmers at 2,000 Metres
place: Chap II, Kochkor Valley, Naryn Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: In the Kochkor valley of central Kyrgyzstan, at 2,000 metres, early farmers left thousands of charred grains of wheat and barley. Radiocarbon dates on the grains place them between about 2467 and 2047 BCE. Chaff and weeds show the crops were grown on the spot, and the very compact grains look like types adapted to life in the mountains.

source.name: PLoS ONE (via PMC): Southwest Asian cereal crops facilitated high-elevation agriculture in the central Tien Shan during the mid-third millennium BCE

title: A Herdswoman's Saddle
text: In the Yanghai cemetery near Turpan, a woman was buried dressed to ride, in a hide coat, woollen trousers and leather boots, with her saddle beside her. Its two hide cushions were stuffed with straw, deer hair and camel hair. Dated to between 700 and 400 BCE, it is the oldest saddle yet found, and it shows that ordinary women herded and travelled on horseback.

source.name: National Geographic: The world's oldest horse saddle

title: The Oldest Sogdian Writing
place: Kultobe, Arys River valley, Turkistan Region, Kazakhstan
text: At Kultobe, scribes cut letters into wet clay plaques with bone or wooden styluses before firing them. The texts turned out to be the oldest known writing in the Sogdian language, probably from the 2nd or early 3rd century CE. One names the lords of Samarkand, Kish, Nakhshab and Bukhara. The first fragments appeared in the 1940s, when the shifting Arys River ate into the old citadel.

source.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): Les plus anciens monuments de la langue sogdienne : les inscriptions de Kultobe au Kazakhstan

dateLabel: About 2625 BCE (radiocarbon date, give or take 300 years)
title: A Bronze Age Mound Near Kandahar
text: Mundigak's 20-metre mound began as a camp of tent posts, then grew into a mud-brick village with steatite stamp seals and clay figurines of humped bulls. A radiocarbon test dated one layer to about 2625 BCE. Later the mound became the base for one great building, its north face decorated with half-columns and stepped merlons under white plaster.

source.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): J.-M. Casal, Mundigak : un site de l'Âge du Bronze en Afghanistan (1952)

source2.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): J.-M. Casal, Fouilles de Mundigak en 1954

dateLabel: Around the turn of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE
title: The Golden Kurgan of Shilikty
place: Shilikty valley, south of Lake Zaysan, East Kazakhstan Region, Kazakhstan
text: In the Shilikty valley south of Lake Zaysan, archaeologist S. S. Chernikov opened burial mound No. 5, nicknamed the 'Golden Kurgan'. It held 524 gold objects and 13 bronze arrowheads. Most of the gold pieces are small ornaments in the Scythian or early Siberian animal style, and a quiver decorated with golden deer points to around the turn of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

source.name: Dialogues d'histoire ancienne (Persée): La transition de l'Âge du bronze à l'Âge du fer au Kazaxstan central

dateLabel: 1st century CE (its Chinese lacquers are placed about 40–50 CE)
title: Two Rooms Full of the World
text: In 1937 and 1939, two rooms at Begram, north-east of Kabul, gave up Roman glassware and bronzes, Chinese lacquer boxes and bowls, and Indian-style ivory carvings, all side by side. Once called a royal treasure, the hoard may instead have been a merchant's stock. Its Chinese lacquers have been placed around 40 to 50 CE, and its ivories closely resemble one found at Pompeii.

source.name: Topoi (Persée): S. Mehendale, The Begram Ivory and Bone Carvings: Some Observations on Provenance and Chronology

title: A Deadly Banquet at Maracanda
text: Maracanda, today's Samarkand, had been the Achaemenid capital of Sogdiana, guarding the empire's frontier north of Bactria. Alexander the Great led two expeditions there in 329 and 328 BCE. In its satrapal palace, at a tragic banquet, he killed his own companion Cleitus. Excavations on the Afrasiab plateau have since traced the city's mud-brick ramparts, with posterns and arrow-shaped slits.

source.name: Topoi (Persée): M. Isamiddinov and Cl. Rapin, Fortifications hellénistiques de Samarcande (Samarkand-Afrasiab)

dateLabel: Around 1000 BCE (turn of the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE)
title: A Temple for a Sacred Drink?
place: Togolok 21, Murghab delta (Margiana), Mary Region, Turkmenistan
text: Togolok 21, in the ancient Murghab delta, was a building around an inner courtyard, with hearths set into the walls of many rooms. In one 'white room', big vessels stood built into stepped platforms. Its excavator, Viktor Sarianidi, suggested it was a temple for preparing haoma, the sacred drink of Zoroastrian ritual. Iron fragments helped date it to around the turn of the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE.

source.name: Arts Asiatiques (Persée): V. I. Sarianidi, Le complexe cultuel de Togolok 21 en Margiane

title: An Indus Colony on the Oxus
text: Between 2400 and 2200 BCE, settlers from the distant Indus basin founded a colony at Shortughai in north-eastern Afghanistan. They worked copper, and a drop of gold on a crucible plus shavings of pure gold leaf show they were goldsmiths too, using local river gold. Nearby, lapis lazuli pebbles washed down by the Kokcha could be gathered in winter and traded far away.

source.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): H.-P. Francfort, Aux marches orientales de la Bactriane antique. Nouvelles perspectives

title: Central Asia's Oldest Canals
place: Geoksyur oasis, Tedzhen delta, Ahal Region, Turkmenistan
text: In the oases of the Tedzhen delta, found in 1956, early farmers of the Geoksyur culture dug the oldest known canal network in Central Asia, at Geoksyur-I, and a reservoir at nearby Mullali-depe. These were simple, direct channels. Estimates put about 1,000 to 1,200 people on Geoksyur's 8 hectares, enough to build and maintain such networks themselves.

source.name: Annales. Histoire, Sciences Sociales (Persée): H.-P. Francfort and O. Lecomte, Irrigation et société en Asie centrale des origines à l'époque achéménide

title: A Family Portrait of Future Kings
text: Sculptures from the palace at Khalchayan form a group portrait of the clan of Heraios at the start of the Kushan era. The ruler stands with his wife, grown children and Bactrian and Parthian nobles, while princes receive a line of prisoners and horsemen gallop beside a niche for the sacred fire. Their slim, high-cheeked faces show reshaped skulls and a non-Greek ideal of beauty.

source.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): G. Pugachenkova, L'art antique de la Bactriane (IVe s. avant - IVe s. après notre ère)

title: A Granite Tomb for a Clan Leader
text: Kurgan 3 at Aksu-Ayuly is one of central Kazakhstan's giant 'cyclopean' tombs.
