Three stone enclosures nest inside each other, the outer ring 24.5 metres across and built of granite slabs up to 1.6 metres high. Robbers broke in and the wooden roof burned soon after. Such tombs were made for notable clan members, a sign that some families were growing richer than others.

source.name: Dialogues d'histoire ancienne (Persée): La transition de l'Âge du bronze à l'Âge du fer au Kazaxstan central

title: Greek Stones in an Old Riverbed
place: Tepe Zargaran, Balkh (ancient Bactra), Balkh Province, Afghanistan
text: Bactra, today's Balkh, was the capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Bactria and stayed a regional capital after Alexander's conquest. Yet proof of its Greek phase came only after looters dug at a spot called 'The Forty Columns'. Hellenistic architectural blocks lay 8 metres down in the gravels of an old riverbed, the first archaeological evidence of Greeks in the city.

source.name: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions (Persée): Nouvelles découvertes en Bactriane 2007-2009

title: Greek Receipts on Broken Pots
place: Kampyr-Tepe, near Termez, Surkhandarya Region, Uzbekistan
text: On the citadel of Kampyr-Tepe, a small fortified town on the Amu Darya west of Termez, scratched Greek notes turned up on pieces of thin pottery. One reads '15 drachmas'; another records seven choes, a Greek liquid measure, probably of wine. They look like receipts, a kind of bookkeeping not known before in the Greco-Bactrian kingdom. Scraps of Greek papyrus were found too.

source.name: Revue numismatique (Persée): E. V. Rtveladze, Découvertes en numismatique et épigraphie gréco-bactriennes à Kampyr-Tepe

title: The Cemetery of Fire
text: On a horseshoe-shaped hill above the Bustan stream, a Bronze Age cemetery shows fire at the heart of funeral rites. Archaeologists excavated 130 graves and three brick boxes where bodies were cremated, at least twice in one of them. Some graves were empty cenotaphs; others held offerings of sacrificed animals. The excavator dates it to the late 2nd millennium BCE.

source.name: Arts Asiatiques (Persée): N. Avanessova, Bustan VI, une nécropole de l'âge du Bronze dans l'ancienne Bactriane (Ouzbékistan méridional)

title: A Flute Carved From Mammoth Ivory
place: Geißenklösterle Cave, near Ulm, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
text: In a cave in the mountains near Ulm, archaeologists rebuilt a flute from 31 fragments of mammoth ivory. It is 18.7 centimetres long with three finger holes, from layers dated 30,000 to 37,000 years old. Making it meant splitting a curved tusk, hollowing both halves and gluing them back with an airtight seam. Its excavator compared it to a Rolls-Royce beside the cave's simpler swan-bone flutes.

source.name: Nature News: Ice-age musicians fashioned ivory flute

title: A Seashell Horn Sounds Again
text: Found at the entrance of Marsoulas cave in the Pyrenean foothills in 1931, this big Atlantic seashell was labelled a 'loving cup' and then forgotten for 80 years. A fresh look revealed human changes and red finger dots like those painted on the cave walls. Magdalenian people had turned it into a horn, and in 2021 researchers revealed its deep, strong, echoing voice.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): First record of the sound produced by the oldest Upper Paleolithic seashell horn

title: Tiny Flutes That Call Like Falcons
text: Among more than 1,000 bird bones at the Natufian village of Eynan-Mallaha, researchers spotted several flutes carved from the bones of small waterfowl, about 12,000 years old. One intact flute is just two and a half inches long. A digital replica whistled like a sparrowhawk or a kestrel. Ochre traces show the flutes were painted red, and wear hints they hung on strings.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Prehistoric Bird Bone Flutes Found in Israel

title: Crane-Bone Flutes You Can Still Play
text: At Jiahu, a village occupied from 7000 to 5700 BCE, excavators found six complete flutes in radiocarbon-dated layers, plus fragments of perhaps 30 more. They were carved from the wing bones of red-crowned cranes and have five to eight holes. The best-preserved one, nearly 9,000 years old, was played and its notes analysed, making these possibly the oldest playable multinote instruments known.

source.name: Nature: Oldest playable musical instruments found at Jiahu early Neolithic site in China

title: The Bull-Headed Lyre of Ur
place: Royal Cemetery, Ur, Dhi Qar, Iraq
text: Ur's Royal Cemetery gave up eleven stringed instruments, two harps and nine lyres. Without them, not one real stringed instrument from ancient Sumer would survive. The largest is a lyre topped with a gold bull's head wearing a lapis lazuli beard. Playable replicas show its long strings sounded like a bass viol, while a smaller silver lyre sounds closer to a cello.

source.name: Penn Museum Expedition Magazine: The Musical Instruments from Ur and Ancient Mesopotamian Music

title: Cymbals Hidden Under an Omani Floor
place: Dahwa, Saham, North Al Batinah, Oman
text: On a hilltop at Dahwa in northern Oman, archaeologists found two copper-alloy cymbals laid carefully one atop the other beneath a stone floor, perhaps as an offering. Made around 2200 to 2000 BCE, each is 5.4 inches across. Lead isotopes trace the copper to mines about 100 miles away, and the pair closely resembles cymbals from Mohenjo-Daro and Mesopotamia, hinting at shared music.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Musical Melting Pot

title: The Bronze 'Dancing Girl' of the Indus
text: When excavators at Mohenjo Daro found a miniature bronze statuette of a nude woman in 1926, they celebrated, and she became known as the 'Dancing Girl.' She was cast by the lost-wax method sometime around 2300 to 1751 BCE. Her nickname is a guess, much like the city's 'Priest King' sculpture, so called even though there is no evidence he was a priest or king.

source.name: National Geographic: The lost city of Mohenjo Daro

source2.name: National Geographic: Did this ancient society thrive without elites?

title: A Tomb With Its Own Harp Quartet
text: A tomb at Saqqara from Egypt's 19th Dynasty held fragments of four cedar angular harps of different sizes, plus wooden castanets shaped like hands. That's why it's called the Tomb of the Harps. One curator thinks its owner was probably a musician. The angular harp was a big innovation: it could hold far more strings than the older arched harp, which had eight at most.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Accompanying the Afterlife

title: The Singer of Amun's Unlooted Coffin
place: Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
text: In 2012, a Swiss team excavated a small tomb, spotted the year before, in Egypt's Valley of the Kings holding a black sycamore coffin painted with yellow hieroglyphs. It belonged to Nehemes-Bastet, a 'chantress of Amun' whose father was a priest at Karnak. Her burial, from about 945 to 715 BCE, reused an older tomb. It was the valley's first unlooted burial found since Tutankhamun's in 1922.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Tomb of the Chantress

title: War Horns With Boar Heads
text: At a Celtic sanctuary at Tintignac in central France, an archaeologist in 2004 found about 50 pieces of seven carnyces, metal war horns as tall as a man. One bell was a boar's head with ears flaring 18 inches; another had a serpent's head. Buried in the late first century BCE, the horns seem to have been dismantled on purpose as offerings, never to be played again.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: War Pigs

title: A Warrior Buried Cradling His Lyre
text: In 2001, on the grounds of a former Hohner factory in Trossingen, archaeologists opened a sixth-century CE grave of a nobleman holding a maple lyre in his left arm and a sword at his right side. The lyre still has six tuning pegs and a willow bridge, and is decorated with 12 warriors flanking a lance. Its owner may have been a warlord who sang heroic songs.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Medieval Warrior Troubadours

title: Flutes That Seemed to Make Rain
place: Broken Flute Cave, Prayer Rock District, northeastern Arizona, USA
text: At Broken Flute Cave in northeastern Arizona, archaeologists found wooden flutes from the mid-600s CE, the largest nearly two and a half feet long, played by blowing at an angle into one end. A Jemez Pueblo flute maker says that as you play them, breath condenses inside until they drip, 'like you're making it rain.' Rock art of the time shows bird-headed flutists.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Southwest Symphony

title: The World's Last Five-Stringed Lute
text: Nara's Shōsōin has guarded treasures since 756, when Empress Kōmyō offered Emperor Shōmu's favourite belongings to the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji. One star is a lute of rare red sandalwood sparkling with mother-of-pearl inlay. Unlike the Shōsōin's other biwa, it has five strings and a straight neck, a type from ancient India. It is the only one left anywhere in the world.

source.name: Imperial Household Agency: Shosoin

source2.name: Tokyo National Museum: Shosoin, Essential Treasures of Ancient Japan

title: A 12-Year-Old Actor Wins a Shogun
text: The shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu watched a sarugaku show by the troupe leader Kan'ami and his son Zeami, then just 12 years old, and was so charmed that he became their generous patron. Zeami went on to study classical literature, shape Noh into graceful drama built on beautiful songs and dances, and write treatises such as Fushi Kaden, The Transmission of the Flower.

source.name: Japan Arts Council: Invitation to Nohgaku, Ascent to Greatness

title: Scroll Theatre Banned at Court
place: Mataram court, near Yogyakarta, Java, Indonesia
text: Wayang beber tells stories with long painted scrolls; beber means unfolding. It is arguably Java's oldest art form tied to narrative storytelling and probably goes back to the Majapahit kingdom of the 1400s and 1500s. In 1630 a ruler of Mataram banned it as court entertainment. Later it nearly vanished, leaving a few scroll sets and even fewer dalangs, the master narrators.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Wayang Beber

title: Painting the Mood of a Melody
text: Ragamala, 'garland of ragas,' paintings turn musical modes into scenes, with each raga and ragini acting as a male or female character in stories of love. In this one, painted at Amer around 1680, a lady plays her vina to two peacocks while a maid waves a fly-whisk and others prepare beds. The mode is Gujari ragini, and its mood is melancholy longing.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Gujari ragini

title: A Real Scandal Becomes a Puppet Hit
text: In 1684 the narrator Takemoto Gidayu opened the Takemoto-za theatre in Osaka's Dotonbori, and Chikamatsu Monzaemon wrote plays for him. In 1703 their puppet drama The Love Suicides at Sonezaki retold a real Osaka double suicide from just a month before. Starring townspeople instead of samurai, it was a huge hit; love suicides followed, and the shogunate banned such plays.

source.name: Japan Arts Council: Invitation to Bunraku, Developmental period

title: Snowstorms on the Emperor's Stage
place: Belvedere of Pleasant Sounds, Forbidden City, Beijing, China
text: The grandest Qing palace opera shows played at the Belvedere of Pleasant Sounds, a stage with three floors so actors could perform on each. It had a skylight, pulleys, trapdoors and a real well beneath the floor for water effects. Old performers recalled shredded paper falling like snow and gods floating on harnesses, while the emperor watched from the tower opposite.

source.name: Palace Museum Youth: The Festive Gathering of the Emperor and Empress Dowager

title: Sunday Drums at Congo Square
place: Congo Square, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
text: By the mid-1700s, enslaved people in New Orleans gathered socially on Sundays at a special market outside the city's rampart. The spot became known as Congo Square, famous for African dances and drumming that kept African musical traditions alive. Dancing there ended before the Civil War, but the National Park Service names this tradition as a key early influence on jazz.

source.name: National Park Service: Jazz Origins in New Orleans

title: Skull Whistles in a Victim's Hands
place: Temple of Ehecatl, Tlatelolco, Mexico City, Mexico
text: In front of the temple of the wind god Ehecatl at Tlatelolco, archaeologists found a sacrificed person holding two clay whistles decorated with skull faces. These 'death whistles' belong to a family of noise-makers that can mimic animal cries or the wind. One scholar suggests they kept bad energies away from the sacrificed, and a Mexican composer now writes them into concert works.

source.name: INAH, Arqueología: Silbato de la muerte

source2.name: Gaceta UNAM: Música y sonoridad en el México prehispánico

title: Dancers Hidden Under the Plaster
text: In 2003, Lucas Asicona was fixing his adobe house in Chajul, in Guatemala's highlands, when falling plaster revealed murals on three walls. They show musicians with a drum and a flute or chirimía, and dancers mixing Spanish trousers and heeled shoes with Ixil Maya feathered mantles and headdresses. Painted in the 1600s or 1700s, probably by Indigenous artists, they were repainted seven times.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Dancing Days of the Maya

title: The Merrie Monarch Brings Back Hula
text: With public hula outlawed under missionary influence, families kept dancing in caves and cane fields late at night. Then in 1883 King David Kalākaua held an extravagant coronation at the newly built ʻIolani Palace and filled the two-week celebration with once-forbidden hula, music and a lūʻau. The revival faded after 1893, but Hilo's Merrie Monarch Festival has honoured him since 1964.

source.name: National Geographic: The surprising history of Hawaiʻi's hula tradition

title: A Harp Shaped Like a Boat
text: This saung-gauk, possibly made in Prome, today's Pyay, has a curved boat-shaped body topped with animal skin and 13 strings tied to a long arching prow. Black-and-gold panels around it tell scenes from the Ramayana, with inscriptions explaining the action. Boat harps appear in art at Pagan from about the 11th century. Lord Curzon probably acquired this one in 1901.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Harp (saung-gauk)

title: The Record That Made Jazz a Craze
place: New York City, New York, USA
text: In 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, musicians who had left New Orleans, cut the first commercial jazz recording while playing in New York City. The Victor release was an unexpected hit, and suddenly New Orleans-style jazz was a national craze. Demand lured more musicians north: clarinetist Sidney Bechet left for Chicago that year, and by 1919 the band was playing in England.

source.name: National Park Service: Jazz Origins in New Orleans

title: Griot Songs Confirmed by the Spade
text: For generations, griots of the Kaabu kingdom sang its history to the kora, including how a king blew up his capital, Kansala, by igniting the gunpowder house. To one griot it felt like legend. Then in 2024 archaeologists mapped nearly 150 acres at Kansala and found fortresses, signs of wide trade and that gunpowder house. They asked him to turn their report into song.

source.name: NPR: For one griot, the unearthing of this ancient West African capital offers vindication

title: Ninety-Three Game Pieces From Lewis
place: Camas Uig (Uig Bay), Isle of Lewis, Scotland, UK
text: In 1831 a hoard of 93 gaming pieces from the Isle of Lewis went on show in Edinburgh. Most were carved from walrus ivory, probably from Greenland, by Norwegian craftsmen in the late 1100s or early 1200s. They came from at least four chess sets. Within months a Stornoway man, Roderick Ririe, had broken up the hoard and sold it, so the pieces now live in several museums.

source.name: National Museums Scotland: The story of the Lewis chess pieces

title: A Prince Buried With His Board Game
text: Around 1,600 years ago, a Germanic prince was laid to rest near Poprad, in the shadow of the Tatra Mountains, with a wooden game board beside him. It is the best-preserved ancient wooden board game found north of the Mediterranean. Its playing pieces were green and white glass, probably made far away in the eastern Mediterranean, perhaps in Syria.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Wooden Board Game Identified in Slovakia

title: Etruscan Fans in the Cheap Seats
place: Tomb of the Two-Horse Chariot, Monterozzi necropolis, Tarquinia, Italy
text: A painted tomb at Tarquinia shows a full program of Etruscan funeral games: chariot racing, riding, wrestling, boxing, jumping, discus and javelin, with umpires and judges watching. It is the only tomb painting showing a purpose-built stadium, with wooden stands under a canopy. Well-dressed men and women sit in the upper tier, while nude spectators lounge below without seats.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: Etruscan Athletics

title: Dice for Norway's Iron Age Elite
place: Ytre Fosse burial cairn, near Bergen, western Norway
text: On the sea route linking northern and southern Norway, a burial cairn at Ytre Fosse held 18 game pieces and an almost intact elongated die, buried around 300 CE among pottery and burnt glass. No board survived. Archaeologist Morten Ramstad thinks the set was a status object, obtained through contact with the Roman Empire and played by the local aristocracy.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Iron Age Dice and Game Pieces Unearthed in Norway

title: A Computer Beats the World Champion
place: Equitable Center, Manhattan, New York, USA
text: In May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue faced world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a rematch in New York. Kasparov won the first game, the machine the second, then came three draws. Deep Blue took the sixth game and the match, 3.5 to 2.5. Using 32 processors, it weighed 200 million positions every second. "The computer is far stronger than anybody expected," Kasparov admitted.

source.name: IBM: Deep Blue

title: Rolling Stones of Cahokia
place: Cahokia, near St. Louis, Illinois, USA
text: At Cahokia, which rose around 1050 CE, crowds of perhaps a thousand watched chunkey, a game of hurling spears at a rolling stone disc. Archaeologist Timothy Pauketat argues the game helped organize the city's social and political life, and that envoys carried chunkey stones far afield. A carved stone figure of a player about to release his disc turned up in Oklahoma in 1900.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: America's First Pastime

title: A Noblewoman's Polo Donkeys
place: Tomb of Cui Shi, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China
text: When noblewoman Cui Shi died in Xi'an in 878, she was buried with her donkeys. DNA identified the animals, and their bones showed sprinting and sharp turning, not hauling loads. They were polo mounts, the first archaeological proof of donkey polo, a gentler version of Tang China's craze. Her husband had lost an eye playing polo, yet won a generalship through his skill.

source.name: National Geographic: Archaeologists discover first evidence for polo, on donkeys

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Prized Polo...Donkeys?

title: Liubo Boards Carved in Brick
place: Han dynasty tombs, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China
text: Two Han dynasty tombs in Xi'an held game boards for liubo carved into square bricks, one plain and one with a geometric pattern. Most liubo boards were lacquered wood or stone. Nobody fully knows the rules today; each player probably moved six pieces by throwing sticks or dice. These bricks may have been symbolic boards made only for the dead to play.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 2,000-Year-Old Game Boards Identified in China

title: Tanikaze, Sumo's Star of the Street
text: Tanikaze Kajinosuke, a sumo champion from what is now Sendai, was one of the first wrestlers given the top rank of yokozuna while still alive. In a mid-1780s colour woodblock print, artist Katsukawa Shunshō shows him strolling down an avenue as admiring fans spot him. Tanikaze was still dominating the ring when influenza killed him at 44.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tanikaze Kajinosuke, by Katsukawa Shunshō

title: Go Stones in a Clam Shell
place: Lafuqueke Cemetery, Wubao Town, Hami, Xinjiang, China
text: In a Tang dynasty tomb near Hami, a clam shell beside the dead person's head held 17 white and two black Go pieces. Lab tests show the white ones are calcite and the black ones clinochlore, likely from the Qilian Mountains near Dunhuang, which supplied Go pieces to the imperial court. They are the first actual Tang Go pieces found in Xinjiang.

source.name: npj Heritage Science (Nature): Scientific analysis of Tang Dynasty Go pieces excavated from the Lafuqueke Cemetery in Xinjiang

title: Akbar's Board Game With Living Pieces
text: Chaupar, a cross-shaped race game played with three long stick dice and sixteen pieces, was a favourite gamble at Akbar's Mughal court. At Fatehpur Sikri the emperor had a huge board laid in flagstones in a palace courtyard, and he and his courtiers played using slaves as the pieces. Its humbler cousin, pachisi, is named for the top cowrie throw: twenty-five.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: The Indian Games of Pachisi, Chaupar, and Chausar

title: Greek-Style Wrestlers for the Buddha
text: A small schist bracket from Gandhara, carved in the 100s or 200s CE and only about 20 centimetres wide, shows a pair of wrestlers. The figures probably copy Greco-Roman models of nude athletes, but the sculptor likely turned them into a scene from the Buddha's boyhood, when he was said to excel at every kind of athletics. It once supported part of a building.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Architectural Bracket with Wrestlers

title: Dice and Game Boards of the Indus
text: People in the Indus cities loved games of chance. Harappan sites of about 2300 BCE have yielded both cubical and long oblong dice, and a gaming diagram scratched on a brick at Mohenjo-daro may date to the late third millennium BCE. Centuries later the Rig-Veda included a hymn that worked as a charm against a ruinous gambling habit.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: The Indian Games of Pachisi, Chaupar, and Chausar

title: A Workaday Game Board in Oman
place: Ayn Bani Saidah, Qumayrah Valley, Oman
text: In a large building in northern Oman's Qumayrah Valley, a Polish team led by Piotr Bieliński found a stone game board about 4,000 years old. Its playing fields and cup holes were hewn "slightly clumsily", and Bieliński stressed that it "is not a luxury item". The same site, on an ancient trade route, also held evidence of copper processing.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 4,000-Year-Old Game Board Discovered in Oman

title: Hounds and Jackals in a Rock Shelter
text: Among the rock art of Gobustan, researcher Walter Crist recognised pits carved into a shelter as a board for 58 Holes, also called Hounds and Jackals, about 4,000 years old. Two rows run down the middle with holes arching around them, and every fifth hole is marked. Copies of the same game turned up in Egypt, Mesopotamia and Anatolia.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 4,000-Year-Old Game Board Identified in Azerbaijan

title: A Grave Paid in Wrestler Coins
text: In the eastern cemetery of Aspendos, a Pamphylian city on Turkey's south coast, archaeologists opened a stone-lined grave about 2,400 years old. Inside were locally minted coins stamped with images of wrestlers. Turkey's culture minister, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, suggested the grave may have belonged to a wrestler, or at least to someone closely connected with the sport.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Possible Ancient Wrestler's Tomb Found in Turkey

title: A Moon-Faced Polo Player in Gold Luster
text: Luster potters who moved to Kashan made it the capital of shimmering luster ware from the 1170s until about 1220. One dish, about 35 centimetres across, shows a polo player on horseback with a round, moon-like face, the Iranian ideal of beauty. Lacking fine clay, Kashan potters mixed ground quartz, clay and glass into fritware that imitated porcelain.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Luster Dish with Polo Player

title: Shepherds' Games on a Ruined City
text: After Ptolemais was destroyed during the Arab conquest in the 600s CE, sheep and goats grazed its ruins. Someone carved about 120 game boards into the fallen city, mostly rows of round hollows like seega and mancala. Many sit on top of surviving walls with good views over the pastures, so archaeologist Zosia Kowarska suspects bored shepherds made them.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Gaming Atop Ancient Ruins

title: A Wrestling Match Fixed on Papyrus
text: A papyrus from Oxyrhynchus records a deal for a wrestling bout in 267 CE between two teenagers, Nicantinous and Demetrius. Demetrius had to "fall three times and yield" for 3,800 drachmas. If his side backed out, it owed 18,000. Historian Dominic Rathbone calls it the first known papyrus evidence of bribery in an athletic competition.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Taking a Dive

title: A Ballcourt High in Oaxaca
text: At Etlatongo, in the highlands of Oaxaca, archaeologists found two ballcourts. One dates to between 1443 and 1305 BCE, about 3,400 years ago, which makes it roughly 800 years older than any other playing field known from a highland setting. It shows that mountain communities took up the Mesoamerican ballgame almost as early as the lowland peoples.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Play Ball!

title: Scoreboards Pressed Into a Shell Mound
place: Tlacuachero shell mound, Chiapas coast, Mexico
text: On clay floors inside a shell mound in Chiapas, archaeologist Barbara Voorhies found holes punched in C-shaped arcs, the oldest about 4,800 years old. Made by Chantuto foragers, they closely resemble 19th-century Walapai dice-game scoreboards from Arizona. If she is right, they are the oldest evidence of games in Mesoamerica. The dice, probably wooden, have never been found.

source.name: National Geographic: Prehistoric Dice Boards Found, Oldest Games in Americas?

title: A Maya Game Board Set in the Floor
text: At the Maya city of Naachtun, CNRS archaeologists found part of a fifth-century game board built into the floor of a house, perhaps an elite home or small office. It was a board for patolli, a game named in later documents and codices. Complete, the board measured about 76 by 109 centimetres and needed more than 475 red and orange pottery pieces.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mosaic Game Board Found at Maya Site of Naachtun

title: The Biggest Ballcourt in the Americas
place: Great Ball Court, Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
text: Chichén Itzá, a major centre from 750 to 1200 CE, built the largest known ballcourt in the Americas: 168 metres long and 70 metres wide. Players in protective belts and knee pads tried to send a solid rubber ball through stone hoops set high on the walls, using hips rather than hands or feet. Accounts disagree over whether the winners or the losers were sacrificed.

source.name: National Geographic: Chichén Itzá, World Heritage Site

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: The Rubber Ball Game

title: Three Turkeys Against a Kingdom
text: Aztec nobles bet jewels, fine mantles and even towns on the rubber ballgame. Montezuma's father Axayacatl reportedly staked a year's tribute against the king of Xochimilco, lost, and then had his opponent killed. Montezuma himself is said to have played the king of Texcoco, wagering three turkeys against his rival's entire realm. Sending the ball through the stone ring won outright.

source.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine: The Rubber Ball Game

title: A Stone Board for Hawaiian Checkers
text: Hawaiians settled the Kalaupapa peninsula around 1300 CE, and excavations there have turned up traces of kōnane, a strategy game like checkers, and ʻulu maika, a kind of bowling. One find is a notched kōnane board of basalt. For chiefs, kōnane was more than a pastime: tradition tells of two warring chiefs who made peace by playing it.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Hawaiian Material Culture, Kalaupapa National Historical Park

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service: Lā Pāʻani, Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau

title: A Song Junk Lifted in a Steel Cage
place: Maritime Silk Road Museum, Hailing Island, Yangjiang, Guangdong, China
text: In 1987 a British firm hunting a Dutch wreck off Guangdong found a 100-foot Southern Song junk instead. For two decades the Chinese Navy kept fishermen away with tales of live wartime bombs. In 2007 a 3,000-ton steel cage scooped up the ship with its sediment, 15,600 tons in all. An ink inscription links its building to 1183, and it holds 60,000 to 80,000 objects.

source.name: National Geographic: China kept this 800-year-old shipwreck a secret for decades

title: Cargo Tagged for a Kyoto Temple
place: Off Sinan, between Jeungdo and Imjado, South Jeolla, South Korea
text: In 1975 a fisherman off Korea's southwest coast found a piece of pottery caught in his net. Divers then spent until 1984 excavating a merchant ship that left Ningbo for Japan around the sixth month of 1323. It held over 22,000 catalogued objects and about 28 tons of Chinese copper coins. Of 364 wooden shipping tags, 41 name Tofukuji, a Kyoto temple.

source.name: International Journal of Korean Art and Archaeology: Sinan Shipwreck Collection at the National Museum of Korea

title: The Fleet the Divine Wind Sank
place: Off Takashima Island, Matsuura, Nagasaki, Japan
text: In 1281 Kublai Khan sent some 4,400 ships carrying at least 140,000 Korean, Mongol and Chinese troops to invade Japan. A two-day typhoon, remembered as the kamikaze or 'divine wind', apparently wrecked about 80 percent of them. In 2011 archaeologists off Takashima found a ship believed to be from that fleet, under 25 metres of water and a metre of sand, with over 4,000 artifacts.

source.name: The Conversation: The original kamikaze: Kublai Khan's invasion shipwreck found?

title: Saved by a Lighthouse Beam
place: Kashinozaki, Kii Oshima, Kushimoto, Wakayama, Japan
text: The Ottoman frigate Ertugrul came to Japan on a goodwill visit with over 600 men. Heading home on 16 September 1890, it broke up on rocks off Kii Oshima in a typhoon, and 587 died. Sixty-nine survivors followed the Kashinozaki lighthouse beam, some climbing a 40-metre cliff, and islanders shared scarce food. In 1985 Turkey flew 215 Japanese out of Tehran, citing that old debt.

source.name: Nippon.com: The Sinking of the Ertugrul: Japan and Turkey Mark the 125th Anniversary of the Tragedy

title: A Sewn Ship Full of Tang Bowls
place: Batu Hitam reef, off Belitung Island, Indonesia
text: Around the 830s, an 18-metre ship sewn together in Persian Gulf style sank off Sumatra after loading cargo in southern China. It lay untouched until found by chance in 1998. Inside were more than 50,000 hand-painted bowls from Changsha in Hunan, fine celadons, early blue-and-white dishes, and a gold cup from Yangzhou with Central Asian musicians, the largest of its type known.

source.name: Asian Civilisations Museum: Tang Shipwreck

title: Singapore's First Ancient Shipwreck
place: Eastern entrance of the Singapore Strait, Singapore
text: No ancient wreck had ever been found in Singapore's waters until the Temasek Wreck. Lead researcher Michael Flecker thinks it was a Chinese junk that sailed from Quanzhou between 1340 and 1352, when Temasek, the port before Singapore, was a busy hub. Divers raised about 3.8 tons of ceramics, including pieces of around 300 Yuan blue-and-white bowls, more than any other documented shipwreck.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Singapore's First Ancient Shipwreck Reveals Cargo of Yuan Dynasty Porcelain

title: A Scuttled Submarine in the Strait
place: Strait of Malacca, off Malaysia and Thailand
text: During the Second World War, the US submarine Grenadier was bombed by a Japanese plane in the Strait of Malacca. All 76 crew survived, scuttled their boat and were held prisoner for more than two years; four died from harsh treatment. In 2020 divers said they believed they had found the wreck. Diver Lance Horowitz said its measurements match the submarine's naval records.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: World War II-Era Sub Spotted in Southeast Asian Waters

title: A Silk Road Wreck Off Sri Lanka
place: Off Godavaya, Hambantota District, Sri Lanka
text: Off Sri Lanka's southern coast, near the fishing village of Godavaya, lies a ship about 2,000 years old. Strong Indian Ocean currents have left only a concreted mound of timber scraps, glass ingots, corroded iron and copper ingots, grinding stones and pottery. German archaeologists had found a second-century CE port nearby, a stop on the maritime Silk Road, so its goods may have been bound for Rome.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Shipwreck May Offer Clues to Ancient East-West Trade

title: Da Gama's Uncle Ignores a Storm
place: Al Hallaniyah, Khuriya Muriya Islands, Oman
text: In 1503 Vicente Sodré, Vasco da Gama's uncle, left his post guarding India's coast to loot Arab ships. Anchored off Al Hallaniyah, his squadron ignored local warnings of a storm, and the Esmeralda went down with its crew. Divers have recovered about 2,800 artifacts, including a bell that may read 1498, believed to be the oldest ship's bell found, and a rare silver coin minted for India trade.

source.name: National Geographic: Shipwreck Discovered from Explorer Vasco da Gama's Fleet

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Is it Esmeralda?

title: A Stone Age Wall Against the Sea
text: Off Israel's Carmel coast, a drowned farming village holds what researchers call the oldest known coastal defence. Some 7,000 years ago villagers dragged boulders weighing up to a tonne into a wall over 100 metres long to hold back the waves. Hundreds of waterlogged olive pits hint they made oil. But the sea kept rising, 4 to 7 mm a year, and the village was finally swamped.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A submerged 7000-year-old village and seawall demonstrate earliest known coastal defence against sea-level rise

title: An Ancient Town Under a Reservoir
text: Hasankeyf, carved into a plateau above the Tigris, had been lived in for some 12,000 years, overlooked by caves cut by Neolithic settlers. Then came Turkey's Ilisu Dam. Residents were told to leave by 8 October 2019, and the reservoir was expected to drown about 80 percent of the town, displacing some 3,000 people. Its minaret and some artifacts were to be moved to safer ground.

source.name: National Geographic: In Turkey, a power play will leave ancient towns underwater

title: The Wreck That Taught Archaeologists to Dive
text: In summer 626 CE, during the last great war of antiquity, a 60-ton Byzantine ship carrying about 800 amphorae of wine and oil for the troops sank off a rocky islet near Bodrum. From 1961 George Bass's team dived about 120 feet down, pinning hull scraps with sharpened bicycle spokes and tagging finds with cut linoleum, proving archaeology could be done properly underwater.

source.name: National Geographic: This shipwreck off Bodrum transformed underwater archaeology

title: The Slave Ship Wrecked off Cape Town
place: Off Clifton, Cape Town, South Africa
text: In December 1794 the Portuguese ship São José sailed from Mozambique for Brazil with more than 400 enslaved people aboard. Rough seas drove it onto rocks off Cape Town. More than 200 captives died in the waves, and about 300 survivors were sold into slavery in Cape Town. Forgotten for two centuries, it became the first wreck known to have sunk with captive Africans aboard to be found.

source.name: Iziko Museums of South Africa: Unshackled History: The Wreck of the Slave Ship, São José, 1794

source2.name: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries: Connecting Ancestral Memory Through the São José Paquete de Africa and the Clotilda

title: Treasure Ship in the Diamond Desert
place: Sperrgebiet, north of the Orange River mouth, Namibia
text: In April 2008 a geologist in a Namibian diamond mine picked a copper ingot out of the sand. It came from the Bom Jesus, a Portuguese ship that left Lisbon in 1533 and vanished in a storm. Archaeologists uncovered 22 tons of copper ingots, more than 2,000 gold coins and elephant tusks. Toe bones inside a shoe were the only human remains found.

source.name: National Geographic: Shipwreck in the Forbidden Zone

title: Da Gama's Last Fleet off Kenya
text: Found in 2013 about 20 feet down and 1,600 feet from Malindi's shore, this wreck may be the São Jorge, one of some 20 ships in Vasco da Gama's final fleet, known to have sunk in 1524. Divers from the National Museum of Kenya recovered hull timbers, copper ingots and elephant tusks. A survey of 15 miles of coral reef helped researchers support the identification.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mystery Shipwreck Off Coast of Kenya Confirmed to Be Part of Vasco da Gama's Final Voyage

title: A Viceroy's Ship Taken by Pirates
text: In 1721 the Portuguese ship Nossa Senhora do Cabo left India for Portugal carrying gold, silver, gems, the outgoing viceroy and the Archbishop of Goa. Off Madagascar, pirates led by Olivier Levasseur, known as La Buse, and John Taylor captured it. Divers near Nosy Boraha, once the pirate haunt of Île Sainte-Marie, have recovered more than 3,300 artifacts, including religious objects made in Goa.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Divers Discover Portuguese Shipwreck Off Madagascar

title: Statues Rise From Drowned Canopus
place: Abu Qir Bay, near Alexandria, Egypt
text: In August 2025 cranes lifted three statues out of Egypt's Abu Qir Bay: a quartzite sphinx bearing Ramesses II's cartouche, a granite colossus from the late Ptolemaic era and a marble Roman nobleman. They came from a 2,000-year-old settlement, probably part of Canopus, that earthquakes and rising seas pushed under the Mediterranean. Divers also mapped temples, houses and a 400-foot dock.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Statues from Sunken Egyptian City Reemerge

title: The Last Slave Ship, Burned and Sunk
place: Mobile River, near Africatown, Mobile, Alabama, USA
text: On 9 July 1860 the Clotilda sailed into Mobile Bay with 110 captives from present-day Benin, the last known slave ship to reach the United States. To destroy the evidence, Timothy Meaher and Captain William Foster burned, sank and abandoned it. The survivors built a new home now called Africatown. The wreck was found in the Mobile River and confirmed in 2019.

source.name: Alabama Historical Commission: Clotilda

source2.name: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries: Connecting Ancestral Memory Through the São José Paquete de Africa and the Clotilda

title: La Salle's Last Ship in Texas Mud
text: In 1684 Louis XIV sent La Salle with four ships and about 400 people to settle near the Mississippi's mouth. He overshot, lost ships to pirates and disaster, and was killed by his own men. La Belle, the last ship, sank in a 1686 storm in Matagorda Bay. Found in 1995, it yielded over 1.8 million artifacts, including 785,000 glass beads and 600 muskets.

source.name: Bullock Texas State History Museum: La Belle

title: The Ironclad Lost on New Year's Eve
place: Off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, USA
text: The Civil War ironclad USS Monitor was under tow by the Rhode Island when a storm struck off Cape Hatteras on 31 December 1862. Leaks flooded the engine room, the crew raised a red distress lantern, and men crossing the deck to the turret were swept away. Sixteen died. Found in 1973 under about 230 feet of water, the wreck became the first US national marine sanctuary.

source.name: NOAA Monitor National Marine Sanctuary: History of USS Monitor

source2.name: NOAA Monitor National Marine Sanctuary: Discovery and Designation

title: Two and a Half Miles Down
place: North Atlantic, about 350 nautical miles off Newfoundland, Canada
text: In April 1912, five days out of Southampton, RMS Titanic struck an iceberg, broke apart and sank. More than 1,500 passengers and crew died. The wreck stayed hidden until 1 September 1985, when a joint American-French expedition found it about 12,500 feet down. In 1986 a plaque was placed on the wreck asking that it be left undisturbed in memory of those lost.

source.name: NOAA Office of General Counsel: R.M.S. Titanic, History and Significance

title: Mutiny on a Shipwreck Island
place: Morning Reef, Beacon Island, Houtman Abrolhos, Western Australia, Australia
text: On 4 June 1629 the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia struck a reef near Beacon Island in the Houtman Abrolhos. Of the 322 aboard, 40 drowned and the rest got ashore. Commander Francisco Pelsaert sailed to Batavia for help, and while he was gone Jeronimus Cornelisz led a murderous mutiny among the stranded survivors. Divers salvaged cannon, an anchor and stern timbers in 1970 to 1974.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: Batavia (Maritime Archaeology Database)

title: Australia's Oldest Known Shipwreck
place: Trial Rocks, off north-west Western Australia, Australia
text: In May 1622 the English East Indiaman Trial, bound from Plymouth to Batavia, struck rocks off north-west Australia at night. Commander John Brooke escaped in a small skiff with his son and nine others, while Thomas Bright and 35 more took the longboat; about 93 sailors were lost. Divers found the likely site in 1969, and it is Australia's oldest known shipwreck.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: Trial (Maritime Archaeology Database)

title: Stone Tools on the Drowned Shelf
place: Cape Bruguieres Channel, Murujuga (Dampier Archipelago), Western Australia, Australia
text: At the height of the last Ice Age, the sea stood about 130 metres lower and Australia was a third larger. Off Murujuga, divers found 269 stone artefacts in the Cape Bruguieres Channel, about 190 permanently underwater and at least 7,000 years old, plus a tool 14 metres down beside a drowned freshwater spring. They are Australia's first confirmed ancient underwater sites on the continental shelf.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Aboriginal artefacts on the continental shelf reveal ancient drowned cultural landscapes in northwest Australia

title: Streets Beneath the Greek Sea
text: Off southern Greece lie the streets of Pavlopetri, settled by around 3500 BCE and later a trading centre of Mycenaean Greece. Three main roads linked some 50 rectangular buildings, each with an open courtyard, and Minoan-style loom weights hint at weaving. Earthquakes, tsunamis and rising seas submerged it more than 3,000 years ago. Nicholas Flemming discovered it in 1967.

source.name: National Geographic: These ancient cities sunk to the ocean floor. Here's how they were rediscovered.

title: The Shrine Rebuilt Every Twenty Years
text: In 690, Emperor Tenmu's decree set off a custom that still runs today: every 20 years, Ise's Inner and Outer shrines, plus 14 affiliated shrines, are built anew on the plot next door. The goddess Amaterasu is then moved into her fresh home. The old shrine is taken apart piece by piece, and its wood goes to other shrines across Japan. The 62nd rebuilding took place in 2013.

source.name: Japan Tourism Agency: Ise Jingu (long version)

title: A Gate Standing in the Sea
text: Itsukushima's great torii gate rises from the sea, and the first one is said to have stood there since 1168. The warlord Taira no Kiyomori is credited with building it. The gate is not sunk into the seabed: about 60 tons of wood and stone hold it up by sheer weight. Its main pillars are camphor trees more than 500 years old.

source.name: Japan Tourism Agency: Itsukushima Shrine, Great Torii (O-torii)

title: A Buddha Relic Under Nanjing
place: Grand Bao'en Temple, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
text: Deep in a crypt under Nanjing's Grand Bao'en Temple, archaeologists found a stone chest from the reign of Song emperor Zhenzong (997–1022). Inside was a model stupa about four feet tall, and inside that, in a gold casket within a silver one, lay a piece of skull. An inscription claimed it was the Buddha's own, one of 19 shares sent to China. Monks later reburied it at another temple.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Possible Remains of the Buddha Found in China

title: Temples Along Kedah's Rivers
place: Candi Bukit Batu Pahat, Bujang Valley, Kedah, Malaysia
text: South of Mount Jerai, more than 30 temple ruins dot the river banks of Malaysia's Bujang Valley. A Buddhist temple and a bronze Buddha found there probably date to the 600s CE, when traders from Arabia, India and China called at this port. Around 1025 the Hindu Chola Empire took the valley. In one granite temple, diggers found gold foil stamped with Nandi, Shiva's bull.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Lembah Bujang, Malaysia

title: The Biggest Thing the Khmer Built
place: Preah Khan of Kompong Svay, Preah Vihear, Cambodia
text: Building began in the 1000s at Preah Khan of Kompong Svay. Inside four rings of walls stand temples of brick, laterite and sandstone, and one archaeologist calls it the largest construction the Khmer ever made, bigger even than Angkor Thom. It was probably an important Buddhist pilgrimage centre. It is also perhaps Cambodia's most looted site, stripped of reliefs in the 1970s and 1980s.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Preah Khan of Kompong Svay, Cambodia

title: King Bodawpaya's Mountain of Bricks
text: On the west bank of the Irrawaddy, King Bodawpaya had millions of cubic feet of brick fired for a pagoda at Mingun. It has a base 256 feet square and rises about 150 feet, the largest brick temple in Asia. Its bell weighs 90 tons. An 1839 earthquake cracked its walls, and the British called it an unfinished folly, a tale they used to justify taking Upper Burma.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: An "Extraordinary Folly"?

title: Gandhara's Early Roadside Temple
place: Barikot, Swat Valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
text: In the town of Barikot, Pakistani and Italian archaeologists uncovered a Buddhist temple from the middle of the 100s BCE, and an older one may lie underneath. It sat along the road to the town's main stupa, which was 65 feet wide. The temple had a platform with a stupa about ten feet tall, a smaller stupa and a room for monks. Diggers found coins, seals and inscribed statues.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Buddhist Temple Discovered in Pakistan's Swat Valley

title: Monks and Nuns Under One Roof
text: In a village in Odisha, archaeologists dug up what looks like a Buddhist monastery that thrived from about 150 BCE into the first century CE. Roughly 200 people may have lived there. It is the only monastery in Odisha with evidence of monks and nuns living together. A copper plate found by the British in the 1800s, six miles away, mentioned exactly such a monastery.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Early Buddhism in India

title: Vishnu's Female Form in Bengal
text: At Madhabgaon in northern Bangladesh, students from Jahangirnagar University uncovered a Vishnu temple from the 1000s or 1100s, called the country's first Navarath temple. Its main figure is Mohini, the only female avatar of Vishnu, well known in south and west India. This may be the first stone Mohini ever found in the eastern subcontinent. A conch and a spiked disc, Vishnu's emblems, turned up too.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 800-Year-Old Vishnu Temple Found in Bangladesh

title: A Temple Pond for a Grieving Queen
text: When their son died in the 1600s, King Pratap Malla built Rani Pokhari, the Queen's Pond, for his wife in the heart of Kathmandu. A causeway runs across the square pool to the Balgopaleshwor temple in the middle. After earthquake damage, rebuilding began in 2019 with soil, sand and brick rather than concrete, after protests from conservationists who wanted the old methods kept.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Restoration of Kathmandu's Rani Pokhari Underway

title: The Storm God on Aleppo's Hill
place: Temple of the Storm God, Aleppo Citadel, Syria
text: Under Aleppo's citadel stood a temple of the storm god Hadad, visited by Ebla's rulers around 2400 BCE. Around 900 BCE new reliefs showed the god riding a chariot pulled by bulls, and a seven-foot sphinx and lion flanked the door. French diggers in the 1920s stopped just short of the carvings. Later excavators found their old trowel there, and an empty champagne bottle.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Temple of the Storm God

title: A Church House Beneath a Mosque
text: In Samahij, Bahrain, archaeologists found an eight-room building that Christians used from the mid-300s to the mid-700s CE, with a kitchen, dining room and living rooms. Plaster crosses showed who lived there, and a bishop may have been among them. Residents ate pork, fish and shellfish and drank from small wine glasses. When locals became Muslim, a mosque was built on top.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Early Christian Building Uncovered in the Arabian Gulf

title: A Cathedral at Aksum's Seaport
place: Adulis, Northern Red Sea Region, Eritrea
text: Adulis was the Red Sea port of the Aksum kingdom, whose King Ezana became Christian in the mid-300s. Radiocarbon dates show its cathedral, which had a baptistry, went up between 400 and 535 CE. A second church, with a ring of columns that once held a Byzantine-style dome, followed between 480 and 625. Their different styles suggest Christianity did not spread by royal order alone.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: New Dates Obtained for Ethiopia's Early Christian Churches

title: Home of the Vulture Goddess
place: El Kab (ancient Nekheb), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
text: South of Luxor, the town of Nekheb was home to Nekhbet, the vulture goddess of Upper Egypt. Huge mud-brick walls enclose about 125 acres, holding houses and two New Kingdom temples, one for Nekhbet and one for Thoth, god of wisdom. In nearby tombs, a mayor named Paheri had his funeral painted, along with pigs, an animal rarely shown in Egyptian tombs.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, El Kab, Egypt

title: Holy Men of the Semien Mountains
place: Semien Menata, Semien Mountains, Amhara, Ethiopia
text: The Beta Israel, Ethiopian Jews, built round prayer houses in the Semien Mountains. Their ascetic high priests, a line traced to Abba Sabra in the 1400s, lived apart under strict purity rules. They left bread, stew and beer outside their compound so hungry people could eat without touching them. Pilgrims to a holy hilltop purified themselves by eating raw chickpeas and bathing.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Exploring a Forgotten Jewish Land

title: Norway's First Saint in a Cave
text: Legend says the Irish queen Sunniva fled a pagan suitor, drifted to Selja and died in a cave when rocks sealed it. In 996 King Olaf Tryggvason and his bishop came to the island, found bones they believed were hers and built Norway's first Christian sanctuary. Pilgrims flocked there, Benedictine monks arrived around 1100, and in 1170 her relics moved to Bergen.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Selja Island, Norway

title: Holy Circuits on a Tiny Island
text: In the 600s, Saint Leo founded a monastery on Inishark, an island barely a mile across off Ireland's west coast. A church ruin, a holy well, stone altars and a beehive-shaped hut said to be Leo's home survive. For centuries islanders walked ritual circuits between these holy spots. The island's population once reached about 300, but its last 24 people left in 1960.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Inishark Island, County Galway, Ireland

title: Frescoes in a Lake Island Cave
place: Church of St. Mary, Maligrad, Great Prespa Lake, Albania
text: On Maligrad, a tadpole-shaped islet in Great Prespa Lake, a church dedicated to Mary was built inside a cave in 1345. Its walls, inside and out, carry some of the best-preserved Late Byzantine frescoes in the region. Along the nearby shore, Christian hermits once lived in churches hollowed out of the rock, reachable today only by kayak or motorboat.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Great Prespa Lake Islands

title: A Copying Error Hid Artemis
place: Sanctuary of Artemis Amarysia, Amarynthos, Euboea, Greece
text: Eretria's holiest place, the sanctuary of Artemis at Amarynthos, got its first temple around 700 BCE. Searchers trusted the geographer Strabo's distance and looked in the wrong spot for over a century. One scholar argued that a medieval copyist had misread a Greek numeral. He was right: a tile stamped 'of Artemis' confirmed the site in 2017, under modern villas.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Hunting for the Lost Temple of Artemis

title: Climbers Step Back Each June
place: Devils Tower National Monument, Wyoming, USA
text: More than two dozen tribes, among them the Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow, Arapaho and Shoshone, hold Devils Tower sacred, with names meaning Bear Lodge, Bear's Tipi or Gray Horn Butte. Many see climbing it as disrespectful. In a compromise worked out for the 1995 Climbing Management Plan, climbers are asked to stay off the Tower each June, when many ceremonies happen. Prayer cloths hang from trees beside the trail.

source.name: National Park Service: Climbing at Devils Tower

source2.name: National Park Service: American Indians and Devils Tower

title: A Temple Carved From the Mountain
place: Cuauhcalli, Malinalco, State of Mexico, Mexico
text: After conquering Malinalco in 1476, the Aztecs carved the Cuauhcalli, or House of the Eagles, straight into a hillside about 700 feet above town. It is the only rock-cut building in the Aztec world. You enter through a doorway shaped like a serpent's open mouth. Inside, eagle and jaguar warriors held rites around animal-shaped thrones, facing a carved eagle linked to Huitzilopochtli.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Malinalco, Mexico

title: Priests Who Spoke Through Fire
place: El Paraíso, Chillón Valley, Lima, Peru
text: Inside a wing of the main pyramid at El Paraíso, near Lima, archaeologists found a temple about 5,000 years old. Its stone walls were covered in yellow clay with traces of red paint, and a narrow passage led in. At its centre was a hearth. Priests may have used the fire to speak with the gods, since, as one excavator put it, fire was the heart of their religion.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Temple Found at Peru's El Paraiso

title: A Stone Snake Coils Around a Mound
text: Near Jaén, at the edge of the Amazon, a mound at Montegrande was rebuilt at least eight times starting around 1000 BCE. Just under its summit, a spiral of stones about 40 feet across coils round the mound like a huge snake. It ends in a shallow pit full of ash, maybe from ritual fires. At some times of year, its tip lines up with the sunrise.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Letter From Peru, Connecting Two Realms

title: A Temple to End a War
place: Puʻukoholā Heiau, Kawaihae, Island of Hawaiʻi, USA
text: A Kauaʻi priest named Kapoukahi told Kamehameha that the war on Hawaiʻi Island would end if he built a temple to the war god Kū on Puʻukoholā, the Hill of the Whale. Kamehameha built it in 1790–91. In 1791 his rival and cousin Keōua was killed there. The temple is now a symbol of unity, with a Hawaiian ceremony held every August.

source.name: National Park Service: Puʻukoholā Heiau History & Culture

source2.name: National Park Service: Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site

title: Polynesia's Biggest Temple Platform
place: Piʻilanihale Heiau, Kahanu Garden, Hāna, Maui, Hawaiʻi, USA
text: On Maui's east coast rises Piʻilanihale, a stepped platform of lava rock almost 50 feet high, with a top about the size of two football fields. Built in four stages, perhaps starting in the 1100s, it is thought to be the biggest temple in Polynesia. It served the Piʻilani family who ruled Maui. Native Hawaiians still use it for rituals, so visitors stay below.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Piʻilanihale Heiau

title: Buying the Trees, Not the Land
text: A small clay tablet from Nippur in southern Iraq is a receipt for 15 date palms. A second tablet records another deal between the same buyer and seller. The land itself was probably sacred: its trees could change hands, but the ground went on belonging to the god. Writing may have been invented for exactly this kind of record-keeping.

source.name: Penn Museum Expedition: Clay Tablets to Text Messages

title: Bronze Rings That Worked Like Cash
text: Early Bronze Age people in southern Germany, Lower Austria and Czechia buried thousands of copper rings, ribs and axe blades in hoards. Researchers weighed over 5,000 of them. About 70 percent of the rings feel identical in the hand to a standard of roughly 195 grams. Such near-copies, the study argues, were an early commodity money, long before coins.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The origins of money (Kuijpers and Popa 2021)

title: Chopped Silver Before Coins
text: Hoards from Megiddo, Gezer, Shiloh and Tel el-'Ajjul hold hacksilber: silver cut into pieces of set weights, sometimes stored in pots or wrapped in cloth. A study found it was used as money over 3,600 years ago, about 500 years earlier than thought. The Levant had no silver mines; lead isotopes point to Anatolia. Coins arrived nearly a thousand years later.

source.name: The Times of Israel: Newly analyzed 3,600-year-old silver pieces are 1st currency in Levant

title: Twin Coins From One Die
text: Silver coins stamped with a rising sun on one side and a Srivatsa, an Indian religious symbol, on the other circulated across mainland Southeast Asia. Studying 245 of them, researchers found two coins, one from Bangladesh and one from Vietnam, struck from the very same die, perhaps by one mint master at the Pyu city of Halin. Overlooked coins revealed a far-reaching trade web.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 'Rising Sun' Coins Reveal Extensive Ancient Trade Networks Across Southeast Asia

title: When Silk Was Cash
text: In the Tang-era oasis towns around Turfan, silk was still a major currency, and tombs at the Astana cemetery reflect a busy commerce. Graves along the northern routes between China and Central Asia held Sasanian Iranian coins and eastern Mediterranean glass. In the 8th century, Uyghur horse breeders received huge quantities of Chinese silk in exchange for their horses.

source.name: Penn Museum Expedition: The Silk Roads in History (Daniel C. Waugh)

title: Japan's Coin That Built a Palace
text: In 708 Japan's government minted the Wadō Kaichin, a copper coin modeled on China's Tang Kaiyuan Tongbao. It paid for building the Heijō imperial palace, and because its face value exceeded its metal value, the state profited. Later coins shrank and turned to lead, one new coin was declared worth ten old ones, and trust collapsed. The last coin came in 958.

source.name: Bank of Japan Currency Museum: Historical Events and Currencies in Use

title: A Ming Coin on a Kenyan Island
text: In 2012 anthropologist Chapurukha Kusimba's team found a 600-year-old Chinese coin, a Yongle Tongbao, at Manda, an ancient trading port on Kenya's coast. It was issued under Emperor Yongle of the Ming dynasty, whose admiral Zheng He sailed beyond the South China Sea nearly 80 years before Vasco da Gama reached India. Swahili kings and merchants traded across the Indian Ocean.

source.name: The Conversation: When and why did people first start using money?

title: Brass Bracelets That Bought a Coast
text: Manillas, horseshoe-shaped brass rings, were shipped by the hundreds of thousands to West Africa as currency once Portuguese trade began. Analysis of 67 manillas from shipwrecks, including a Flemish ship lost off Getaria, Spain, in 1524, traced the earliest ones to the German Rhineland. Lead isotopes in the famous Benin Bronzes match Rhenish ores, suggesting melted manillas went into the art.

source.name: PLOS ONE: German brass for Benin Bronzes (Skowronek et al. 2023)

title: A Turkey Costs 100 Cacao Beans
text: Cacao beans were everyday small change in Aztec Mexico. A price list from Tlaxcala in 1545 sets a small rabbit at 30 beans, a turkey hen at 100 and a ripe avocado at one; a single bean bought 20 small tomatoes. Shriveled beans were worth less than plump ones. Cheats faked beans from wax or amaranth dough, and the Florentine Codex calls such sellers tricksters.

source.name: Mexicolore: Beanz meanz money! (Frances Berdan)

title: Japan's First Paper Money From a Shrine Town
text: Around 1600 a priest-merchant in the Ise Yamada area, the town that served the great Ise shrines, issued Yamada Hagaki: paper receipts that could be swapped for silver traded by weight. They solved a shortage of small change and circulated locally. Later, feudal clans printed their own notes; by the end of the Edo period nearly 80 percent had done so, fueling severe inflation.

source.name: Bank of Japan Currency Museum: Historical Events and Currencies in Use

title: A Bank Born to Pay for War
place: Mercers' Hall, Cheapside, London, United Kingdom
text: The Bank of England was founded on 27 July 1694 as a private bank to lend to the government, mainly to fund war against France. King William and Queen Mary were among its first stockholders. It opened on 1 August in borrowed rooms at Mercers' Hall in Cheapside with 17 clerks and two gatekeepers, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734.

source.name: Bank of England: Our history

title: The South Sea Bubble Bursts
place: Threadneedle Street, City of London, United Kingdom
text: In 1720 the South Sea Company offered to take over about £30 million of Britain's national debt in exchange for its shares. Prices soared from around £140 in January to nearly £1,000 that summer, then crashed back to about £200 by October, ruining thousands of investors. Inquiries exposed corruption reaching ministers and King George I; Robert Walpole organized the rescue.

source.name: Encyclopedia.com: South Sea Bubble

title: The Banker of the World
text: In 1723 the Mughal emperor granted Fateh Chand of Murshidabad the title Jagat Sheth, 'banker of the world.' His family collected Bengal's revenue, ran its treasury and controlled the Murshidabad mint, turning bullion into coin. One English historian called them the richest family in the empire. Their loans to the East India Company helped make the British victory at Plassey possible.

source.name: Banglapedia: Jagat Sheth Family

title: Futures Trading on Rice
text: Osaka's rice traders gathered at Dojima from around 1697, and in 1730, under Shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune, the market was officially licensed. Its successor calls it the world's first futures market. Traders bought and sold rice bills, even for unharvested rice, posting a margin called shikigin, with members and a clearing system. Couriers carried Dojima's prices to other cities.

source.name: Osaka Dojima Exchange: The Birthplace of Futures Trading

title: Franklin Prints Money With Leaves
text: From the early 1730s Benjamin Franklin printed millions of pounds' worth of paper money for Pennsylvania and other colonies. To beat forgers he pressed real leaves to capture their veins, since no two leaves match, and mixed blue fibers and shimmering mica into the paper. A study of nearly 600 colonial bills found his inks were also surprisingly experimental.

source.name: The Conversation: We analyzed paper money printed by Ben Franklin

title: Paying the Rent in Seashells
text: Glossy cowrie shells, mostly from the Maldives, served as coins in Bengal until the end of the 18th century. Villages far from big trading towns relied on them, and peasants could pay land revenue in shells. In frontier districts like Rangpur and Sylhet, rent was still paid mainly in cowries in the early 19th century. In Bangla, 'cowrie' can still mean money.

source.name: Banglapedia: Cowrie

title: Copper Crosses as Currency
place: Katanga copper belt, Haut-Katanga, Democratic Republic of the Congo
text: In Central Africa, copper alloy was cast into ingots and anklets that served as currency for a very long time. Ingots shaped like an H or an X are called Katanga crosses, after the copper-mining region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. One 19th-century example at Princeton, possibly made by Luba metalworkers, measures 44 centimeters across.

source.name: Princeton University Art Museum: H-shaped ingot (Katanga cross or possibly handa)

title: Four Languages in One Bazaar
text: High in the Himalayas, Leh's bazaar and caravanserais drew traders from Lhasa, Kashmir and Chinese Central Asia during the brief summers when passes opened. A 1905 memoir counted at least four languages in common use there. Yaks, ponies and dzo carried carpets, Yarkand bronzes and cotton cloth, and Ladakhi ledgers show Japanese cotton gaining ground on British goods.

source.name: Penn Museum Expedition: Trade at the Crossroads of Continents

title: The Panic That Created the Fed
place: Knickerbocker Trust, Fifth Avenue, New York City, USA
text: In October 1907, speculators failed to corner United Copper stock, setting off runs on banks tied to them. When Knickerbocker Trust suspended payments on 22 October, panic swept New York. J. P. Morgan gathered cash from banks and companies to keep the stock exchange's lending alive. The scare launched the reform movement that produced the Federal Reserve System.

source.name: Federal Reserve History: The Panic of 1907

title: Germany's Money Collapses
text: Germany's war reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks. When it defaulted in January 1923, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region and met passive resistance. Inflation spiraled into hyperinflation and the currency collapsed. The 1924 Dawes Plan cut payments, introduced the Reichsmark and floated a $200 million loan; Charles Dawes shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: Office of the Historian, U.S. State Department: The Dawes Plan, the Young Plan, German Reparations

title: A Hotel Meeting Remakes World Money
place: Mount Washington Hotel, Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA
text: In July 1944, delegates from 44 nations met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire's mountains to plan the postwar economy. Following drafts by Harry Dexter White and John Maynard Keynes, they created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, with fixed exchange rates centered on the U.S. dollar and gold. The system lasted until 1971.

source.name: Office of the Historian, U.S. State Department: Bretton Woods-GATT, 1941-1947

title: Ten Turtles for a Feather Coil
place: Santa Cruz Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
text: In the Santa Cruz Islands, specialists made tevau, long coils of red feathers used as money for canoes, pigs, turtles and root crops, and as marriage gifts. Makers caught honeyeaters and took just four tiny feathers from each, so one coil holds feathers from over 300 birds. As the red faded, value fell. In 1948 the navigator Tevake paid ten turtles for one.

source.name: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa: Tevau (red feather currency)

title: Mexico Says It Cannot Pay
text: In August 1982 Mexico's finance minister Jesús Silva Herzog told U.S. officials and the IMF that his country could no longer service about $80 billion in debt. Latin America's debts had ballooned from $29 billion in 1970 to $327 billion. Sixteen countries rescheduled, and austerity brought a 'lost decade.' Under the 1989 Brady plan, lenders forgave about a third.

source.name: Federal Reserve History: Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s

title: The Banknote Made of Plastic
place: Reserve Bank of Australia, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: In January 1988, for Australia's bicentenary, the Reserve Bank issued a commemorative $10 note printed on polymer instead of paper, a world first developed with the science agency CSIRO. Rising counterfeiting with modern copiers drove the change, and polymer also lasts longer and can be recycled. Between 1992 and 1996 Australia became the first country with a full polymer series.

source.name: Reserve Bank of Australia: History of banknotes

title: Roman Coins in an Okinawan Castle
text: Excavations at Katsuren Castle in Okinawa, occupied from the 12th to the 15th century, turned up four small Roman copper coins from around 320 to 370 CE, one apparently of Constantius II. An Ottoman coin dated 1687 to 1688 was found too. Rome had fallen long before the castle rose, so the coins probably arrived later, maybe as curiosities.

source.name: The Conversation: How did 4th-century Roman coins end up in a medieval Japanese castle?

title: Silk Hidden in 8,500-Year-Old Graves
text: Silk thread rots fast, so how do you prove people had it 8,500 years ago? Scientists scooped soil from under the pelvis of skeletons in three Neolithic graves at Jiahu and tested it for proteins. Two graves held traces of silkworm fibroin, the protein that makes silk. A bone needle lay in one of them, and rough weaving tools turned up across the site.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Biomolecular Evidence of Silk from 8,500 Years Ago

title: A 5,500-Year-Old Shoe Stuffed with Grass
text: In 2008, archaeologists in a dry Armenian cave found a leather shoe more than 5,500 years old. It was cut from a single piece of cowhide, laced with a leather thong, and stuffed with loose grass, perhaps to hold its shape. About a modern European size 37, it was worn on someone's right foot. It lay upside down in a pit, under a broken pot, beside goat horns.

source.name: PLOS ONE: First Direct Evidence of Chalcolithic Footwear from the Near Eastern Highlands

title: Sea-Snail Purple in a Copper Camp
text: At Slaves' Hill, a copper-smelting camp in the desert of southern Israel, archaeologists found scraps of wool dyed true purple. Chemical tests traced the colour to Mediterranean sea snails, so the cloth had travelled inland from the coast. Dated to around 1000 BCE, they are the oldest true purple textiles known from the southern Levant, and they were lying among the smelting waste.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Early evidence of royal purple dyed textile from Timna Valley (Israel)

title: Sagebrush Sandals Under Volcanic Ash
place: Fort Rock Cave, Lake County, Oregon, USA
text: In 1938, Luther Cressman dug nearly 100 sandals made of sagebrush bark out of Fort Rock Cave. They lay beneath ash from the eruption that created Crater Lake, and radiocarbon dating later showed they were made about 10,250 to 9,300 years ago. Sizes range from big adults to small children. Many are worn through at the heel, and one pair has tiny scorch marks.

source.name: University of Oregon: Focus on Footwear

title: The Mill Girls Walk Out
text: In February 1834, Lowell's cotton-mill owners cut wages by 12.5 percent. When they fired a worker named Julia Wilson, she gave the signal by waving her calash headdress, and about 800 young women walked out. They paraded through town calling themselves 'daughters of freemen.' They lost, but in 1836 up to 2,000 struck again, and several companies backed down.

source.name: National Park Service: Labor Reform, Early Strikes (Lowell National Historical Park)

title: Phoenix Boots Fit for the Liao Court
text: These tall boots come from the Liao, a dynasty that ruled northern China from 907 to 1125. Their outer silk is kesi, a tapestry weave, showing pairs of phoenixes chasing a flaming pearl among clouds, with two kinds of metal thread. Tailors cut the cloth so a pearl sits right at the shin, the calf and the instep. Liao emperors even sent kesi robes to the Song emperor as gifts.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Boot (Liao dynasty)

title: Birds for Scholars, Beasts for Soldiers
text: In 1391, new Ming clothing rules ordered court officials to wear decorated squares showing their rank: birds for civil officials, animals for military ones. These rank badges were sewn to the front and back of robes, and an official's wife wore badges matching her husband's. Later Qing badges showed the creature facing a sun, which stood for the emperor, as a sign of loyalty.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Rank Badge (buzi)

title: Edo Firefighters in European Wool
text: Edo was a crowded city of wooden houses, so fires broke out often. Firefighters wore protective jackets of leather or wool, and the wool came all the way from Europe. One late-1700s suit, now in Cleveland, carries a white crest of three interlocking rings inside a tortoise-shell frame, telling everyone which house its wearer served. Uniform, armour and badge, all in one outfit.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Firefighter's Suit (Kaji shozoku)

title: Crocodiles and Kings on Sumba Cloth
text: On the Indonesian island of Sumba, mantles called hinggi were worn at ceremonies and given as required gifts at births, marriages and deaths. Their patterns are dyed into the cotton threads before weaving, a method called ikat. This one shows an open shellfish and crocodiles, both signs of royal power, plus standing men in horned headdresses, a motif going back to Neolithic times.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Hinggi

title: Ship Cloths for Life's Big Crossings
text: For several hundred years, cloths called tampan pasisir played a part in nearly every ritual in southern Sumatra. This one shows a ship, woven with extra threads into a cotton base. No written myths explain these cloths, so their exact meaning is lost, but the ship may stand for safe passage from one stage of life to the next. Cloths this old rarely survive Indonesia's tropical climate.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tampan Pasisir (Ship Cloth)

title: Spirit Patterns in Abacá Thread
text: The Mandaya people of southeastern Mindanao weave a cloth called dagmay, not from cotton or silk but from abacá fibres stripped by hand. Before weaving, chosen threads are bound tightly so the dye cannot reach them, leaving patterns that appear as the cloth grows on the loom. The designs carry Mandaya ideas about protection, fertility and the umagad, or ancestral spirits.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Mandaya ikat textile (dagmay)

title: Ten Metres of Cloth, 320 Grams
text: Dhaka was famous for cotton muslin so fine it sold across India and the Middle East. From the late 1700s it also became the fabric of choice in Britain and France for white, high-waisted dresses, worn with Kashmir shawls. A length made around 1855, now in London's V&A, is about 10 metres long yet weighs only 320 grams, and is decorated with delicate chikan embroidery.

source.name: V&A: Chikan Embroidered Muslin

title: A Shawl That Maps a City
text: Kashmir's famous shawls were made of pashmina, fine goat hair. Around 1870, embroiderers in Srinagar made one that was never meant to be worn: a map of their own city, stitched so finely it looks woven. Dal Lake, the Jhelum River, a fort and the main mosque appear among many little buildings, and a haloed man in a boat may be Maharaja Ranbir Singh.

source.name: V&A: Map shawl of Srinagar

title: Bukhara's Blazing Silk Ikats
text: In 19th-century Bukhara, wealthy townspeople hung dazzling silk ikat panels in their reception rooms. Every colour meant binding the warp threads tightly and dyeing them before weaving, which gives the patterns soft, 'fuzzy' edges. This hanging, joined from five loom widths in five colours, shows amulets and palmettes. It dates from the early 1800s, among the earliest known Central Asian ikats.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Wall Hanging (pardah)

title: Gold Letters on Yemen's Flame Cloth
text: Ikat means dyeing threads in patterns before they are woven. The name is a Malay word, yet it may have begun in South Arabia, and Yemeni ikats from the 900s are among the oldest known. This cotton cloth from Sanaa has 'flame' patterns and a Kufic inscription in gold leaf naming the Zaydi imam Yusuf ibn Yahya. One phrase, 'to God,' sits upside down.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Ikat tiraz

title: Silver-Threaded Kaftans for Sultans
text: In the late 1500s, Ottoman silk weaving reached its height. Imperial kaftans covered in big medallions of flowers and leaves, including some worn by young princes, are still kept in Istanbul's Topkapı Palace. A length from one such kaftan, now in Cleveland, glitters with silver thread. It uses lampas, two weaves combined in one cloth to give two contrasting surfaces.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Brocaded silk with foliate medallions from a kaftan

title: Hands, Birds and Knives in Kente
place: Ewe weaving country, Volta Region, Ghana
text: This Ewe-style kente cloth from Ghana or Togo was woven as one long strip, then cut into twenty pieces and sewn together by hand. Extra weft threads form tiny pictures: hands, birds, insects, knives, combs and four-legged animals. An important man wore it on special occasions, wrapped around his waist and tossed over his shoulder, its colours and patterns announcing his wealth.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Prestige cloth (kete or kente)

title: A Rainbow from a Few Dye Pots
text: A woollen curtain from 6th-century Antinoë in Egypt shows a saddled horse galloping inside a ring of hearts. Its many shades came from just a few dyes, often the costliest part of making cloth: an insect red, perhaps Armenian cochineal; indigo blue; yellow and brown from fustic trees; green from fustic plus indigo; and a purple mane from madder mixed with indigo.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Curtain Fragment with Galloping Horse

title: A Silk Cap Praising the Sultan
text: In medieval Egypt, a man's outfit wasn't complete without headwear. This 14th-century silk cap was woven with stripes of prancing animals, crescent moons and Arabic words: 'Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir.' Such caps came from tightly regulated workshops in Cairo. Mamluk rulers gave lavish garments as tokens of honour, and the cap's pale pink trim may once have been bold red.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Cap with Striped Inscribed Silk

title: Madagascar's Silk Turns White
text: Across much of Madagascar, people of every age and class wore the lamba, an untailored wrap. Merina weavers made splendid ones from shining silk, decorated with floating-thread motifs called akotifahana. White had once been the colour of commoners and enslaved people, but when Christianity became the state religion in 1869, elite churchgoers chose white silk lambas. Knotted fringes copied Chinese-made 'Manila shawls.'

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Wrapper (Lamba Akotifahana)

title: The Diné Dress That Protects
text: Diné (Navajo) weaver D. Y. Begay says every Diné woman should own a biil'éé, a woven dress that holds spiritual power and gives protection. This wool example from the early 1880s is two matching tapestry-woven panels joined at the sides and shoulders, a style that grew out of one-piece dresses in the late 1700s. It could be cinched with a woven belt or a silver concha belt.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Woman's Two-Piece Dress (Biil'éé)

title: Ninety-Six Panels of Macaw Feathers
text: In the ancient Andes, cloth covered in feathers was among the most prized luxuries. This panel probably came from an offering on Peru's far south coast: over half a dozen big ceramic vessels shaped like people, buried with 96 rolled panels inside. Each was covered in blue-and-yellow macaw feathers, knotted onto strings and stitched to cotton. Ties suggest they were hung up to make a space radiant.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Feathered Panel

title: Tunics Woven by the Chosen Women
text: In the Inca Empire, finely woven tapestry tunics were a privilege of nobles. Some were made by noblewomen and professional weavers, others by the Aclla, or Chosen Women, who lived in cloistered communities, brewing beer and weaving fine cloth for the state.
