The state handed tunics out as prized gifts to loyal allies. This one carries the 'Inca Key,' one of the commonest tunic patterns.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tunic (Inca)

title: A Chief's Feather Cloak Flies Home
text: In January 1779 at Kealakekua Bay, the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu gave Captain Cook the feathered cloak he was wearing, the ʻahu ʻula, together with his feathered helmet. The cloak used feathers from about 20,000 birds. After passing through English collections, it reached New Zealand's national museum in 1912. In March 2016 it flew home to Hawaiʻi, and in 2020 it was returned for good.

source.name: Te Papa: Feather cloak and helmet gifted to Captain Cook to return permanently to Hawaiʻi

source2.name: Te Papa: Te Papa to return treasures gifted to Captain Cook to Hawaiʻi

title: The Loom That Read Punched Cards
text: Joseph Marie Jacquard of Lyon made weaving complex cloth such as damask far simpler. His loom, first shown in 1801, read thousands of punched cards laced together, each row of holes matching one row of the pattern. Charles Babbage later borrowed the idea to program his Analytical Engine. By the 1820s Scottish weavers used Jacquard looms for Paisley shawls and Dunfermline damask.

source.name: National Museums Scotland: The Jacquard loom, innovation in textiles and computing

source2.name: Science Museum Group: Joseph Marie Jacquard

title: Sanada's Fort Outside Osaka Castle
place: Sanada Maru, Osaka Castle, Osaka, Japan
text: During the winter campaign of the Siege of Osaka in 1614, the warlord Sanada Nobushige built an outwork called the Sanada Maru to help the Toyotomi clan hold off the Tokugawa armies. The shogunate answered with artillery and tunnels dug under its walls. After victory they destroyed the fort and filled in the castle moat. Traces suggest it measured about 380 by 330 yards.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Excavation Reveals Traces of 17th-C. Fortress in Japan

title: Japan Braces for a Tang Invasion
text: In 663 Japan sent an army to Korea to help the kingdom of Baekje against a rival allied with Tang China, and lost. Fearing invasion, the regional government at Dazaifu on Kyushu raised defences. On a hilltop in Chikushino, about four miles away, excavators found seventh-century castles and big earthworks. Some scholars think they formed a continuous wall, like Chinese frontier fortifications.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Seventh-Century Earthworks Discovered in Japan

title: Moss That Holds the Great Wall Together
text: Scientists led by Bo Xiao of China Agricultural University sampled eight stretches of the Great Wall built between 1368 and 1644. Most were coated with a living crust of cyanobacteria, mosses and lichens, encouraged by the clay, sand and lime in the rammed earth. These organisms secrete substances that bind the soil like natural cement, making crusted sections up to three times stronger than bare earth.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Organic Material Blend Said to Strengthen China's Great Wall

title: The Great Wall's Oldest Stretch
place: Qi Wall, near Jinan, Shandong, China
text: Long before the famous Ming ramparts, the state of Qi in eastern China built its own wall to guard its frontiers and key trade routes. New dating of the Qi Wall in Shandong places its origins in the late Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods, about 300 years earlier than thought. It began about 30 feet wide and was later widened to roughly 100 feet.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Oldest Section of China's Great Wall Uncovered

title: A Han Fort Deep in Xiongnu Land
text: At Bayanbulag in southern Mongolia, Han China built a walled fortress, known in the chronicles as Shouxiangcheng, as a base for sending soldiers deep into Xiongnu territory. Excavators found a mass grave of at least 17 executed soldiers, some forced to kneel. Isotope and DNA tests confirmed they came from northern China. A halberd laid with them may be a memorial from their comrades.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: A Chinese Frontier Fort

title: A Great Wall Built for Tax Collectors?
place: Northern Line of the Great Wall, eastern Mongolia
text: The Northern Line of the Great Wall runs about 460 miles, mostly through Mongolia, and was built of pounded earth between the 11th and 13th centuries. Many assumed it was raised against Genghis Khan. Mapping with drones and satellite images showed much of it is low and sits beside paths, so it may have been for watching or taxing moving people and herds.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Researchers Map Great Wall of China's Northern Line

title: The Persian Wall at the Caspian Gate
text: At Derbent the Caucasus Mountains come within a mile of the Caspian Sea, a natural gateway for steppe raiders. The Sasanian Persians sealed it with a limestone wall over 30 miles long and more than 20 feet tall, linking dozens of small forts. Khosrow I ordered the hilltop citadel of Narin Kala, with walls about 60 feet high. The defences stayed in use into the 19th century.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The Shah's Great Wall

title: Poison Smoke Under Dura's Walls
text: When the Sasanians besieged the Roman fortress city of Dura around 256 CE, they tunnelled under its walls and the Romans dug countermines. In one tunnel lay 20 Roman soldiers, long blamed on a collapse. Archaeologist Simon James argued the Sasanians lit braziers of pitch and sulfur, sending choking sulfur dioxide into the Roman tunnel. One Sasanian soldier also died there.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Top 10 Discoveries of 2009: Earliest Chemical Warfare

title: Urartu's Citadel Above Lake Van
text: The Urartian king Rusa II founded the citadel of Ayanis on a ridge over 750 feet above the shore of mile-high Lake Van. Its southern walls were dark basalt, its gate and towers pale andesite, and mudbrick walls on top reached up to 56 feet high. Its temple bears an 88-line inscription, the longest in Urartu. Like every late Urartian citadel, it ended in fire.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Urartu's Kingdom of Fortresses

title: Egypt's Last Stand at Jaffa
text: Jaffa was Egypt's only purely military outpost in Canaan, a walled enclave whose gate bore Ramesses' name. Legend said Thutmose III's men first took the city hidden in 200 tribute baskets. The garrison brewed its own beer and ate imported Nile perch. Two fires about ten years apart destroyed the gate; scorched seeds date the final blaze to around 1125 BCE.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Egypt's Final Redoubt in Canaan

title: Eleven Towers on the Way of Horus
text: On the Way of Horus, the military road running from Egypt along the coast to Canaan, archaeologists found a 3,500-year-old fortress with 11 towers covering about two acres. Pottery stamped with Thutmose I's name lay in its foundation deposits. A zigzag wall inside probably resisted wind and sand. Outside lay small ovens and unbaked bread dough for a garrison of about 500.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Fortress Located on Egypt's Way of Horus

title: Nubia's Fortress Before the Pharaohs Came
text: Around 2500 BCE builders at Kerma in Nubia raised a large fort, and a dense town grew around it, entered through a gate of mudbrick and wood. As rivalry with Egypt grew, the walls became ever stronger. At nearby Dukki Gel, round African buildings were guarded by walls with no known models in the Nile Valley. Thutmose III finally conquered Kerma in 1450 BCE.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: A Nubian Kingdom Rises

title: Mohenjo-daro's Walls Push Back the Clock
text: Archaeologists from Sindh's antiquities department dated samples from the mudbrick wall around Mohenjo-daro's western Stupa Mound. The results show the Indus city was occupied as early as 2700 to 2600 BCE, about two centuries earlier than thought, and that the wall was enlarged and kept up until at least 2200 BCE. The team now plans to trace the wall and hunt for its gates.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: New Dates Push Back Occupation of Mohenjo-Daro

title: Hunting the Lost Bricks of Jaffna Fort
place: Jaffna Fort, Jaffna, Northern Province, Sri Lanka
text: Dutch colonists built Jaffna's star-shaped fort in the 17th century, but war and neglect left it battered. In 2015 archaeologist Prashantha Mandawala led its restoration, which began with clearing unexploded mines and shells. Some residents had carried off its coral limestone to rebuild war-damaged homes, so about 150 workers searched houses and the moat for missing bricks, since new quarrying is banned.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Conservators Are Repairing Sri Lanka's Jaffna Fort

title: Hadrian Draws a Line Across Britain
text: Building probably began in 122 CE, the year Emperor Hadrian visited Britain. Three legions built the wall 73 miles from the Tyne to the Solway, with a guarded gate every Roman mile and two turrets between each. To speed the work, its width was cut from 10 Roman feet to 8 or less. Long after Rome left, its stones were quarried for castles, churches and farms.

source.name: English Heritage: History of Hadrian's Wall

title: Pits Full of Slingshot Pebbles
place: Maiden Castle, Dorchester, Dorset, England, UK
text: Maiden Castle in Dorset is one of Europe's largest Iron Age hillforts, bigger than 50 football pitches. Work on its defences began about 2,400 years ago and went on for some 300 years, its inner rampart alone about 2 km long. Pits by both gateways held thousands of beach pebbles, slingshot ammunition that could fly about 100 metres. Over 100 roundhouses stood inside.

source.name: English Heritage: History of Maiden Castle

title: Sulla's Missiles at Pompeii's Walls
text: Long before Vesuvius buried it, Pompeii was besieged by Roman forces under Lucius Cornelius Sulla, probably around 89 BCE. Its weak north walls still bear impact scars, and excavators found catapult balls, lead sling bullets and scorpio bolts inside the city. Archaeologist Ivo van der Graaff thinks the Romans fired into the town to wreck buildings and morale, not to topple the walls.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Weapons of the Ancient World: Siege Weapons

title: A 63-Pound Trebuchet Ball at Hay
place: Hay Castle, Hay-on-Wye, Powys, Wales, UK
text: Excavators at Hay Castle on the Welsh border found a stone ball weighing 63 pounds, hurled by a trebuchet. Documents record several attacks on the castle in the 1200s, and in July 1265 Simon de Montfort, rebel against King Henry III, took it with help from allied Welsh princes. As archaeologist Chris Caple notes, one hit rarely mattered; only repeated strikes demolished a wall.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Weapons of the Ancient World: Siege Weapons

title: 1,500 People Inside the Castillo
place: Castillo de San Marcos, St. Augustine, Florida, USA
text: In November 1702 Carolina governor James Moore laid siege to Spanish St. Augustine. Almost 1,500 townspeople crowded into the Castillo de San Marcos, built of coquina, the only local stone. English cannon barely hurt its walls, so Moore sent to Jamaica for bigger guns. Instead four Spanish warships arrived from Havana on 26 December. The English burned their own ships and the town, then retreated.

source.name: National Park Service: The Siege of 1702

title: New Englanders Take Louisbourg
place: Fortress of Louisbourg, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, Canada
text: France began fortifying Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1719 to guard its cod fishery, finishing just before the first siege. Its harbour was strong, but low hills overlooked the landward walls, perfect for siege guns. In 1745 fervent New England forces took it in 46 days, only for a treaty to hand it back to France three years later. The British retook it in 1758 and destroyed the walls.

source.name: Parks Canada: History of the Fortress of Louisbourg

title: The Cloud People's Walled Mountain
text: Kuélap, the largest fortress city of the Chachapoya, sits at 9,500 feet behind a 65-foot wall of pale yellow stone. Only three funnel-like entrances led inside, where about 420 houses and ceremonial buildings held some 3,500 people. Friezes may show the eyes of a puma, a Chachapoya deity. Built over a thousand years ago, it fell under Inca rule in the 1470s.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Realm of the Cloud People

title: A Wall Against El Niño Floods
place: Muralla La Cumbre, near Trujillo, La Libertad, Peru
text: The Muralla La Cumbre is an earthen wall six miles long and eight feet tall, built across two dry riverbeds in northern Peru. It was long seen as a Chimú defence against the Inca. But its lowest layers date to around 1100 CE, just after a huge El Niño flood, and flood mud piles against its eastern side, suggesting it shielded fields and Chan Chan from water.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: New Thoughts on Peru's Muralla La Cumbre

title: Maya Walls in the Rain Forest
place: Near Tecolote, Petén, Guatemala (Yaxchilan–Piedras Negras border)
text: About 1,300 years ago the rival Maya kingdoms of Yaxchilan and Piedras Negras fortified their border. Archaeologists Charles Golden and Andrew Scherer, helped by local guides and rangers, traced stone walls three to six feet high across four miles of forest. Built between hills, they funnelled enemies into valleys watched from hilltop towers. The war ended in 808 when Yaxchilan captured Piedras Negras's last king.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Defending a Jungle Kingdom

title: The Bat's Nest Pā
place: Ruapekapeka, near Kawakawa, Northland, New Zealand
text: Te Ruki Kawiti built Ruapekapeka, the 'bat's nest', in Northland, naming it for its roofed underground chambers with narrow entrances. Massive palisades, trenches, tunnels and bunkers let it withstand British artillery for weeks. About 1,300 British troops and 400 Māori allies advanced in December 1845. After the bombardment the defenders slipped out and ambushed their pursuers. British commander Despard admitted the builders' skill.

source.name: Auckland Museum: Ruapekapeka and Ōhaeawai Pā

title: A Flax Screen That Stopped an Army
text: At Ōhaeawai in 1845, Pene Taui and Kawiti held a pā against Colonel Despard's 615 men and five cannon with no more than 100 fighters. An outer screen of posts and flax matting soaked up musket shot and hid an inner fence of hard puriri logs. When 250 British troops charged, defenders killed 40 and wounded 70. The flax screen has been compared to barbed wire.

source.name: Auckland Museum: Ruapekapeka and Ōhaeawai Pā

title: The Desert Post House That Fed Kings
text: Out in the Gobi, Xuanquanzhi was one of more than 80 major Han post stations strung between Chang'an and Dunhuang. It had a stable, a horse doctor's clinic, a mill and a restaurant. Its wooden slips record envoys passing through, including up to 1,074 guests travelling with the King of Yutian. That delegation ate huge amounts of beef and mutton and broke over 300 cups.

source.name: China Daily: Reviving the glory of millennia-old posthouse ruins in Dunhuang

title: A Map on Silk for a General
text: In 168 BCE a Han general, probably the son of Changsha's ruler Li Cang, was buried with a lacquer box holding three silk maps. One shows the mountains, rivers and towns of the kingdom's southern half, with squares marking cities. Another plots military garrisons near a hostile frontier. Beside the Nine Beguiling Mountains, the mapmaker drew shadowy shapes that may be peaks reflected in a lake.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, Han Dynasty Map

title: A Merchant's Map of the China Seas
text: The Selden Map, probably drawn in the early 1600s, covers all of East and Southeast Asia, with China taking up less than half. Shipping routes with compass bearings fan out from Quanzhou. A London lawyer, John Selden, owned it by 1653, and it reached Oxford in 1659. Its importance went unnoticed until 2008. When old backing was removed, its main sea routes turned up on the reverse, a first draft.

source.name: Bodleian Libraries: The Selden Map of China

title: A Retired Merchant Measures Japan
text: Inō Tadataka ran a merchant business in Sawara until he retired at fifty. Then he moved to Edo to study astronomy, hoping to find the exact length of one degree of latitude. In 1800 he surveyed Ezo, now Hokkaido, almost on his own. The government then hired him to map all Japan. His Great Map was handed over in 1821, three years after his death.

source.name: Tokyo National Museum: Maps of Japan by Ino Tadataka

title: Rest Stops on the Roads of Angkor
place: Preah Khan of Kompong Svay, Preah Vihear, Cambodia
text: Jayavarman VII, who ruled Angkor from 1181 to 1218, lined his roads with rest stops every seven to nine miles. The network crossed land that is now Cambodia, southern Vietnam, Laos and Thailand. Each stop had a small stone fire shrine for the gods, plus lighter buildings where travellers could rest, pray and water their animals. One archaeologist compares them to modern highway rest areas.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The Pursuit of Wellness, Rest

title: An Inn for Sher Shah's Mail Riders
text: Close to the ruins of Harappa, archaeologists found a brick serai, an inn where postal convoys stopped on the road of Sher Shah Suri, who ruled from 1540 to 1545. Three rooms sit on each side of the main gateway, with a veranda and a pond. Finds include terracotta figurines, gaming pieces, bangles and a toy cart, so travellers had time to relax.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Sixteenth-Century Inn Uncovered in Pakistan

title: A World Map Centred on Kashgar
text: Mahmud al-Kashgari finished his three-volume book on Turkic languages in 1074 and presented it to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, who ordered copies made. It holds about 290 proverbs and a round map of the world. Arab maps of the time usually put Mecca in the middle. Kashgari put the Karakhanid cities of Kashgar, Barskan and Balasagun there instead.

source.name: e-history.kz: Diwan Lughat al-Turk, or The Compendium of the Turkic Languages

title: Fields and Canals on Clay
text: This clay map, about 13 by 11 centimetres, shows the land around Nippur. Lines mark irrigation canals, and circles mark towns and farm estates. A cuneiform label calls the central part a field of the palace. Most landholdings in Mesopotamia were described in writing, not drawn. At the top sits a field of Marduk, a sign that Babylon's god was taking land in Enlil's own city.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, Nippur Map Tablet

title: A Very Angry Letter About Copper
text: Around 1750 BCE a man named Nanni pressed a furious letter into clay for the merchant Ea-nasir. Ea-nasir had promised fine copper ingots and sent poor ones, then told Nanni's messenger to take them or leave. Nanni wrote that he would accept no more copper unless it was good, and he would pick the ingots in his own yard. It is called the first recorded customer complaint.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The World's Oldest Writing

title: A Letter Left in a Sailor's Shoe
place: Post Office Tree, Mossel Bay, Western Cape, South Africa
text: In 1500 the Portuguese captain Pedro de Ataíde, cut off from Cabral's fleet, landed at what is now Mossel Bay. He left a letter in a sailor's shoe tied to a tree. It warned of hostility at Calicut and rough waters to the east. In July 1501 the next fleet bound for India found it. A boot-shaped postbox now stands beside the tree.

source.name: Dias Museum: Post Office Tree

title: Egypt's Map of a Desert Quarry
text: About 1150 BCE Amennakhte, chief scribe of the royal tomb builders, drew a papyrus almost three metres long showing the Wadi Hammamat. It marks roads labelled in hieroglyphs, a well, a temple of Amun and blocks of prized greywacke stone. Colours show what the hills hold: dark brown for greywacke, pink for granite and gold. It is called the world's oldest known geological map.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, The Goldmine Papyrus

title: A Nubian King's Note About Sheep
text: Excavating a wealthy house in Dongola, archaeologists found a small paper letter, about 10 centimetres wide, written in Arabic in the late 1500s or 1600s. Its author was King Qashqash, a ruler many thought half legend. The letter proves he was real. Its message is very ordinary: an order to hand over livestock, including a ewe and her lambs, along with pieces of cloth.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Post-Makurian Letter (from Dongola)

title: Tamil Names in Pharaohs' Tombs
place: Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
text: About 2,000 years ago, visitors from India carved roughly 30 messages into six royal tombs in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Most are in Old Tamil. One traveller, Cikai Korran, carved his name high on the walls of five tombs. One tag reads, "Cikai Korran, having come, has seen." He copied the style of the Greek graffiti beside it, a language useful for Indian Ocean trade.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Tamil Tourists

title: The World on One Calfskin
text: Around 1300, someone drew the whole known world on a single sheet of calfskin about 1.6 metres tall. The Hereford Mappa Mundi puts Jerusalem at the centre and east at the top, where medieval Christians expected Christ to return. Europe, Asia and North Africa crowd around, and the British Isles squeeze into the bottom left. It mixes geography with history and Christian belief.

source.name: Hereford Cathedral: The Mappa Mundi

title: Rome Carved on a Marble Wall
text: Under Emperor Septimius Severus, Rome was mapped in marble at a scale of 1:240. The whole plan measured about 18 by 13 metres and covered a wall in the Temple of Peace. It showed streets and blocks, even colonnades and staircases inside buildings. Only a small part survives. Its huge size suggests it was more of a monument to Severus than a map for daily use.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, The Forma Urbis Romae

title: An Archaeologist's Note to the Future
text: In 1874 Anders Lorange dug into a Viking ship burial at Myklebust Farm but recorded little. When Bergen archaeologists reopened the mound, they found his bottle near the centre. Inside were a letter to future archaeologists and his business card. Above it lay more than 600 ship nails he had pulled out. The letter ends with his sweetheart's name, Emma Gade, written in Viking runes.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Hidden Messages

title: 1,800 Miles in Ten Days
text: In April 1860 the Pony Express began carrying letters on horseback between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, promising more than 1,800 miles in ten days. Riders were offered $50 a month. Yet the service lasted only about 18 months. On October 26, 1861, the telegraph linked San Francisco to New York, and the riders were no longer needed.

source.name: National Park Service: Pony Express National Historic Trail, History and Culture

title: Circles and Squares on a Deerskin
text: Around 1721 the new governor of South Carolina, Francis Nicholson, received a map drawn on deerskin, probably by a Catawba mapmaker. It shows 13 Native nations as circles joined by lines, with the Catawba town of Nasaw in the middle. English settlements, including Charleston and Virginia, appear as squares. One archaeologist thinks the squares marked the English as outsiders, perhaps as a quiet criticism.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, Catawba Map

title: Coastlines Carved in Wood
text: In 1885 an Inuit hunter named Kunit traded three small wooden maps to the Danish explorer Gustav Holm at Ammassalik. One shows a jagged coast of land and fjords, another a string of islands, a third a peninsula. A curved groove marks where a traveller would carry a kayak overland. They were storytelling aids, and no others like them are known.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, Wooden Inuit Maps

title: A Coded Note That Came Too Late
text: A glass bottle from the American Civil War held a coded message, and modern codebreakers finally read it. Meant for Confederate general John C. Pemberton, trapped in the Siege of Vicksburg, it begins: "You can expect no help from this side of the river." The note never reached him. It is dated July 4, 1863, the same day Pemberton surrendered to Grant.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Virginia

title: A Telegraph Wire Into the Amazon
text: In 1907 Brazil sent Cândido Rondon to run a telegraph line from Cuiabá towards the Madeira River. About 150 people surveyed and mapped the region and met Indigenous peoples such as the Paresí and Nambikwara. The line reached Santo Antônio do Madeira in January 1915. Rondon later said the wire was only the pretext, and the scientific exploration was everything.

source.name: SciELO, História, Ciências, Saúde-Manguinhos: Telegraphs and an inventory of the territory of Brazil, the scientific work of the Rondon Commission

title: A Parade That Maps Time
text: Made by the Nazca culture between 100 and 300 CE, the Paracas Textile was probably wrapped around a dead person's head. Its border holds 90 tiny figures, each in different dress, many carrying plants and animals. One geographer reads it as a map of time: a procession circling a village plaza forever, which the dead person could join on the way to the next world.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, The Paracas Textile

title: A Gin Bottle Afloat Since 1886
text: In January 2018 Tonya Illman picked up an old Dutch gin bottle in the dunes near Wedge Island, north of Perth. Inside was a note dated 12 June 1886, thrown from the German ship Paula about 950 kilometres offshore. Germany ran a 69-year experiment tracking ocean currents with thousands of such bottles. The captain's own logbook confirmed it: the oldest message in a bottle found.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: 132 year old message in a bottle found on WA beach

source2.name: National Geographic: World's Oldest Message in a Bottle Found in Australia

title: Charts Made of Sticks and Shells
text: Marshallese navigators built charts from wood and cowrie shells to model how ocean swells bend around islands. The charts were mainly teaching tools, not aids used at sea. Training could start with a blindfolded canoe ride to feel the waves. The charts teach the dilep, or backbone wave, which navigators still treat as the most important wave to follow between islands.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mapping the Past, Marshall Islands Stick Chart

title: Mail by Biscuit Tin and Swimmer
text: Niuafo'ou has no harbour, so from 1882 passing ships dropped the island's mail overboard in sealed tins. Swimmers swam about a mile out to fetch them, and at night a bonfire on shore guided them home. Cruise passengers came to watch. After a shark killed a swimmer in 1931, canoes took over. The system only ended when the island got an airport in 1983.

source.name: Vincent Graves Greene Philatelic Research Foundation: Tin Can Mail, Niuafo'ou, Tonga

title: When Dan's Springs Ran Low
text: Tel Dan was a well-watered city fed by streams from Mount Hermon, with a mudbrick gate from about 1750 BCE that is among the world's earliest surviving arches. Pollen studies show water flow dropped sharply around 1050 to 840 BCE. Settlement thinned, canals went unrepaired, and the fields slid back into a stagnant, disease-ridden marsh. Drought hurt even a place that never fully dried out.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Climate change and water management in the biblical city of Dan

title: Thin Grass Pushes the Xiongnu West
text: Tree rings from Siberian larch, Siberian pine and Qilian juniper let scientists estimate how much the steppe's plants grew each year back to 200 BCE. They found a long slump in plant growth from the 70s to the 100s CE. It matches the westward migration of the Northern Xiongnu. Later slumps in the 360s to 380s and 470s to 560s line up with more nomad movements.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Climate-driven reduction in biomass production of the Eurasian steppe coincides with nomadic migration

title: Fifteen Wet Years for Genghis Khan
text: Stunted Siberian pines growing on a bare lava flow in central Mongolia hold a 1,112-year rainfall diary. Their rings show that from 1211 to 1225 every single year was wetter than average, a streak unmatched in the record. That run matches the rise of Genghis Khan's empire. Lush grass meant more livestock and horses, after dry decades of chaos in the 1180s.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Pluvials, droughts, the Mongol Empire, and modern Mongolia

title: The Droughts That Drained Angkor
text: Angkor ran on water: canals, embankments and reservoirs like the West Baray, 16 square kilometres in size. Rings from rare Fokienia cypress trees in Vietnam's highlands reveal decades-long droughts in the mid-1300s and early 1400s, broken by violent monsoons that wrecked waterworks. The driest year in 759 years of record was 1403, right when the great Khmer capital was fading.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Climate as a contributing factor in the demise of Angkor, Cambodia

title: The God Who Walks Across the Ice
text: When Lake Suwa froze, a ridge of ice called the omiwatari pushed up across it. Shinto priests said it was the footsteps of the god Takeminakata crossing to visit the goddess Yasakatome. Since 1443 they wrote down the freeze dates, through at least 15 generations of observers. Today the lake no longer freezes every year, so the god often cannot make his trip.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Nature): Direct observations of ice seasonality reveal changes in climate over the past 320–570 years

title: Printing Your Name on the Frozen Thames
place: River Thames, City of London, England, UK
text: In the long, cold winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze so solidly that Londoners built a street of booths on it. There were puppet shows, horse races and whole oxen roasting, and shopkeepers lit fires in their tents. Diarist John Evelyn noted ladies paying to have their names printed on the ice, likely the first mention of a frost fair printing press.

source.name: London Museum: Souvenir, frost-fair keepsake (1684)

source2.name: London Museum: Frost fairs, festivities on a frozen River Thames

title: The Deadliest Atlantic Hurricane
text: In mid-October 1780 the Great Hurricane tore through the Lesser Antilles. About 22,000 people died: around 9,000 on Martinique, 4,000 to 5,000 on St. Eustatius and 4,326 on Barbados, plus thousands at sea. No Atlantic storm on record has killed more. News crawled so slowly that the first report in London's Lloyd's List only appeared on 19 December.

source.name: NOAA National Hurricane Center: The Deadliest Atlantic Tropical Cyclones, 1492–1996 (part 4)

source2.name: NOAA National Hurricane Center: The Deadliest Atlantic Tropical Cyclones, 1492–1996 (part 2)

title: The Man Who Named the Cyclone
text: Captain Harry Piddington, working in Calcutta, wrote 40 papers on tropical storms for the Asiatic Society of Bengal between 1835 and 1855. He coined the word cyclone, meaning the coil of a snake, and wrote a book on the Laws of the Storms. After a disastrous cyclone hit Calcutta in 1864 and monsoons failed, the India Meteorological Department was founded in 1875.

source.name: India Meteorological Department: History of IMD

title: Twenty-Six Metres of Rain in a Year
text: Between August 1860 and July 1861, the hill town of Cherrapunji in northeast India collected 26.47 metres of rain, the most ever measured anywhere in twelve months. That is deep enough to drown an eight-storey building. Cherrapunji still holds the world 48-hour record too: 2.49 metres in June 1995. Nearby Mawsynram has Asia's highest average yearly rainfall.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: The First Public Weather Forecast
text: Robert FitzRoy, once captain of HMS Beagle, founded Britain's Met Office in 1854. After the ship Royal Charter sank in a storm in 1859, he pushed for coastal weather reports, and a storm warning service began in early 1861. That service lives on as the shipping forecast. FitzRoy then wrote the first public weather forecast, for 31 July 1861, and coined the term synoptic forecasting.

source.name: Met Office: Our history

title: A Jesuit Forecasts the Typhoon
text: Federico Faura, a Spanish Jesuit, came to Manila in 1866 to teach physics and run a small observatory. After visiting European observatories, he studied the warning signs of typhoons and in 1879 began issuing typhoon forecasts. He later designed a barometer for detecting typhoons. In 1884 a royal decree made his observatory the official weather service for the Philippines.

source.name: Manila Observatory Archives: Federico P. Faura, S.J. (1840–1897)

source2.name: Manila Observatory: History

title: Typhoon Gun or Mail Gun?
place: Police Barracks, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, China
text: Soon after the Hong Kong Observatory opened in 1883, it fired a typhoon gun facing Victoria Harbour: once for gales, twice for hurricane winds. It first boomed on 21 August 1884. The trouble was that the same gun announced the mail arriving from London, which confused everyone. After a disastrous typhoon in 1906, louder explosives took over, fired for the last time in 1937.

source.name: Hong Kong Observatory: A Brief History of the Typhoon Gun

title: Mahina Smashes the Pearling Fleet
place: Bathurst Bay, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia
text: On 4 March 1899 Cyclone Mahina struck Bathurst Bay, home anchorage of the Great Barrier Reef pearling fleet. About 400 people died, some 300 on boats and about 100 Aboriginal people on land. Its surge was long listed as a 13-metre world record, though newer research suggests 3 to 5 metres. Its name came from Clement Wragge, who began naming cyclones after women.

source.name: NOAA AOML Hurricane Research Division: 115th anniversary of Cyclone Mahina's landfall

source2.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: Fourteen Years Without Rain
text: The port of Arica on Chile's Atacama coast went 172 months without measurable rain, from October 1903 to January 1918. That is more than 14 years, the longest dry spell on Earth's books. Even in normal times Arica averages only 0.76 millimetres of rain a year, the lowest average recorded in South America. That is less than a millimetre, thinner than a coin.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: A Tornado Across Three States
place: Southern Illinois, between Missouri and Indiana, USA
text: On 18 March 1925 a tornado tore from southeast Missouri across southern Illinois into Indiana, killing at least 695 people, the deadliest in American history. Its official path ran 352 kilometres over about three and a half hours. Back then the Weather Bureau refused to even use the word tornado in forecasts, fearing panic. The forecast simply promised rains and strong shifting winds.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Heritage: The Tri-State Tornado of 1925

source2.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: 231 Miles an Hour on a Mountaintop
place: Mount Washington Observatory, New Hampshire, USA
text: On 12 April 1934 three observers on New Hampshire's Mount Washington, in their station's second year, expected a routine 150 mph blow. Instead they recorded a gust of 231 miles per hour, a world record for over 60 years. It is still the fastest wind ever measured at a staffed weather station, and the top gust in the Northern and Western hemispheres.

source.name: Mount Washington Observatory: Remembering the Big Wind

source2.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: Almost Two Metres of Rain in a Day
text: As Tropical Cyclone Denise passed La Réunion in January 1966, a rain gauge high in the mountains at Foc-Foc caught 1.825 metres of rain in 24 hours. That is still the world record, and 1.144 metres fell in just 12 hours. The same small island also holds the world records for rainfall over three, four and ten days.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: A Hailstone Heavier Than a Bag of Sugar
text: On 14 April 1986 a storm over Gopalganj district in Bangladesh dropped the heaviest hailstone ever weighed: 1.02 kilograms, more than a standard bag of sugar. Bangladesh holds other grim weather records too. A tornado in Manikganj district in 1989 killed about 1,300 people, the deadliest on record, and the 1970 cyclone took an estimated 300,000 lives.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: The Fastest Wind Ever Measured
place: Barrow Island, Pilbara coast, Western Australia, Australia
text: At 10:55 UTC on 10 April 1996, as Tropical Cyclone Olivia swept past Barrow Island off Western Australia, a weather station logged a gust of 113.2 metres per second, about 408 km/h or 253 mph. It is the fastest wind gust ever recorded on Earth. It beat a record set on New Hampshire's Mount Washington in 1934 that had stood for over 60 years.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

source2.name: Mount Washington Observatory: Remembering the Big Wind

title: A Hurricane Where None Should Be
text: Until March 2004, only two tropical cyclones had ever been noticed in the South Atlantic, and no hurricanes. Then a storm off southern Brazil grew an eye, reached hurricane strength and came ashore in Santa Catarina state. Astronauts on the International Space Station photographed it at landfall, spinning clockwise as southern storms do. It was nicknamed Hurricane Catarina.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: "Hurricane" Catarina hits Brazil

source2.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: The Drought Before the War
text: From 2007 to 2010 the Fertile Crescent suffered its worst drought in the instrumental record. In Syria's northeast breadbasket, which grew over two-thirds of the crops, farming collapsed and livestock died. Up to 1.5 million people left the land for city outskirts. Researchers found such a drought had become more than twice as likely because of long-term drying linked to greenhouse gases.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Climate change in the Fertile Crescent and implications of the recent Syrian drought

title: Haiyan's Wall of Water
text: Super Typhoon Haiyan, called Yolanda in the Philippines, hit Samar and Leyte with sustained winds estimated at 196 mph, possibly the strongest landfall ever recorded. Its storm surge, perhaps 7.5 metres, swept through low-lying Tacloban, and even official storm shelters were washed away. About 6,300 people died. It had formed unusually close to the equator, south of Pohnpei.

source.name: NOAA Climate.gov: 2013 State of the Climate, record-breaking Super Typhoon Haiyan

title: Asia's Hottest Day in the Desert
text: On 21 July 2016 a weather station at Mitribah in Kuwait recorded 53.9°C, give or take 0.1°C. The World Meteorological Organization checked it and accepted it as the highest temperature ever measured in Asia. Less than a year later, on 28 May 2017, Turbat in Pakistan came close behind with 53.7°C. The world record is still Death Valley's 56.7°C, from 1913.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Records of Weather and Climate Extremes (table, July 2025)

title: Kyoto's Earliest Blossoms in 1,200 Years
text: Kyoto's mountain cherry trees have had their peak bloom recorded since the 9th century, with dates going back to 812 CE. On 26 March 2021 they reached full flower earlier than ever in that 1,200-year record. A 2022 study found climate change and city warming have moved blooming about 11 days earlier, and almost half of that shift comes from urban heat.

source.name: Met Office: Kyoto cherry blossom dates shifted by human influence

source2.name: New Phytologist (PMC): The onset of phenological plant response to climate warming

title: Freddy, the 36-Day Cyclone
text: Tropical Cyclone Freddy formed off northwest Australia in February 2023 and crossed the whole Indian Ocean to southern Africa. It stayed at tropical storm strength or above for 36 days, the longest-lasting tropical cyclone on record, and travelled 12,785 kilometres, nearly a third of the way around Earth. It survived several landfalls, causing heavy losses in southeast Africa.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: Tropical Cyclone Freddy is the longest tropical cyclone on record at 36 days

title: Crowded Living at Çatalhöyük
text: For about 1,150 years, families at Çatalhöyük rebuilt their houses on the same spots, sometimes four or more times, piling up a mound 21 metres deep. At its busiest, between 3,500 and 8,000 people crowded together. Floors were swept clean, yet scientists found human and animal dung in walls and floors, and most of the dead were buried right beneath them.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Bioarchaeology of Neolithic Çatalhöyük reveals fundamental transitions in health, mobility, and lifestyle in early farmers

title: Kaifeng's Million and Its Firefighters
text: The Song capital Kaifeng may have held about a million people, while London then had around 15,000. Shops, restaurants and houses lined its streets, some several stories tall, and the crowd spilled past the outer wall. To fight fires, the government kept 2,000 soldiers at 14 fire stations inside the city. The state also ran public clinics and old-age homes.

source.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: A New Kind of City Emerges

title: Marco Polo's City of Heaven
text: Marco Polo wrote that Hangzhou, the old Southern Song capital at the end of the Grand Canal, had 12,000 stone bridges and streets paved with stone or brick. He counted ten great markets, each drawing 40,000 to 50,000 people three days a week, and about 3,000 spring-fed bathhouses, some big enough for 100 bathers. He claimed pears there weighed up to ten pounds.

source.name: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Hangzhou and the Urban Elite

title: Laying Out Seoul by the Rules
text: In 1394 King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty, chose Hanyang for his new capital and planned it by geomancy and Confucian ideas. Gyeongbokgung Palace sat at the foot of Baegaksan Mountain, the royal ancestral shrine to the east and the Sajik Altar to the west. Six government ministries lined up before the palace, and licensed shops filled the main east-west street.

source.name: Seoul Museum of History: The Joseon Capital

title: A Town Built for Railcar Workers
text: Ground broke in 1880 on Pullman, a planned town for the Pullman Palace Car Company's workers south of Chicago. Its brick row houses had indoor plumbing, far above the standards of the day, and over 100 railroad cars of supplies arrived each week that first summer. By 1883 over 8,000 people lived there, but George Pullman set rents to earn a six percent return.

source.name: National Park Service, Pullman National Historical Park: The Town of Pullman

title: Rome Burns, Nero Builds
text: In July 64 CE a fire damaged or destroyed 10 of Rome's 14 regions, fed by narrow streets and wooden upper floors. Nero rushed back from Antium. Tacitus says he sheltered the homeless, paid people to rebuild fast and enforced new fire-safety rules. He then seized burned land for his Golden House, a palace with its own artificial lake and woodlands.

source.name: National Geographic: Rethinking Nero

title: Chicago Rises From the Ashes
text: On October 8, 1871, a fire starting in the O'Leary barn swept through dried-out wooden Chicago, destroying 17,500 buildings and leaving 90,000 people, one in three residents, homeless. New laws demanded brick and stone. Fireproof terra cotta spread, and in 1884 William Le Baron Jenney's steel-framed Home Insurance Building rose, considered the world's first skyscraper. The public library reopened inside a surviving water tank.

source.name: National Geographic Education: The Chicago Fire of 1871 and the 'Great Rebuilding'

title: Champagne and Land in Marvellous Melbourne
text: In the 1880s Melbourne boomed on borrowed money and was among the world's richest cities by 1888. An 1884 law authorised 66 new railway lines, and land agents gave buyers free first-class train tickets to auctions with chicken and champagne lunches. Electric light, telephones and lifts were commoner there than in London. Then an 1891 banking collapse brought decades of hardship.

source.name: State Library Victoria: Victoria through the ages, the boom years

title: Paris Buries Its Second River
text: The Bièvre, barely three metres wide, powered Paris's tanners, millers and the dyers who became the Gobelins tapestry works, and it turned into a stinking open sewer. In 1858 Baron Haussmann vowed it would no longer pour its muddy water into the Seine, and engineer Eugène Belgrand sent it into sewers. Its last open stretches in Paris were covered in 1912.

source.name: National Geographic: Parisians want to recover a legendary river now buried under the city

title: Tikal's Poisoned Drinking Water
text: Tikal depended on reservoirs to get through the dry season. Mud cores from the Palace and Temple reservoirs in the city centre show that mercury, probably washed off cinnabar-painted buildings, and blooms of toxic blue-green algae made the water unsafe to drink. These problems peaked during droughts of the 800s CE, shortly before the great Maya city was abandoned.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Lentz et al. 2020, contamination of drinking water reservoirs at Tikal

title: Lasers Find Angkor's Hidden City Grid
text: In April 2012 an aircraft fired lasers through the Cambodian forest canopy over about 370 square kilometres. Inside and around Angkor Wat's moat, the scans revealed a grid of city blocks dotted with mounds and ponds. The planned core covered at least 35 square kilometres, not the 9 inside Angkor Thom's walls, and a lost earlier capital appeared on Phnom Kulen.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar

title: Water From 265 Miles Away
text: When Constantine made Constantinople the new Roman capital, builders began a water supply that eventually stretched about 265 miles, with 90 large bridges and tunnels up to three miles long. It worked for more than 700 years. Its limescale holds only about 27 years of buildup, so crews must have kept cleaning it, perhaps switching between double channels.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Constantinople's Ancient Aqueduct Examined

title: The Great Bathhouse of Aghmat
text: In 1058 the Almoravids took Aghmat, in the High Atlas foothills, and made it their first capital before moving to Marrakech in 1062. Townspeople already enjoyed one of the largest medieval bathhouses in the western Islamic world, with cold, warm and hot rooms on a Roman plan, toilets, dressing rooms and a domed hall around an octagonal pool.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Splendor at the Edge of the Sahara

title: A Cistern in Every Swahili House
text: Songo Mnara was built quickly to a plan in the 1300s, its coral-stone houses plastered gleaming white. With a nine-month dry season and salty groundwater, every house had a cistern to catch rain, and wells stood at each of its six mosques. Chinese celadon dishes set into the bottom of the mosque cisterns may have shown whether the water was clean.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Saving for the Season

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Stone Towns of the Swahili Coast

title: Dholavira Saves Every Drop
text: In the dry land of Kachchh, the Indus city of Dholavira caught rain with dams and stored it in giant reservoirs. The biggest measured 263 by 39 feet and was 24 feet deep, and together they held more than 325,000 cubic yards of water. Wells linked to the reservoirs filled cisterns used for drinking and bathing across the 123-acre city.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Aqua Dholavira

title: Garbage Bins on Indus Street Corners
text: Archaeologists from the Archaeological Survey of India digging at Rakhigarhi, a planned Harappan city, found straight streets, brick walls, drains and multistory homes. Refuse bins stood on the street corners, a sign that someone organised the rubbish. Nearby lay a jewelry workshop about 5,000 years old, with copper and gold objects, beads and seals carved with Indus script.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Indus Valley Civilization Site Investigated in Northern India

title: Merv, the City That Moved Next Door
text: Merv kept moving over. The Achaemenid Persians first settled Erk Kala in the 400s BCE. The Seleucid king Antiochus I then built Gyaur Kala beside it, and by the 700s CE the Abbasids ran their eastern capital from Sultan Kala, one of the world's largest cities. The oldest layers now lie up to 60 feet underground.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Off the Grid, Merv, Turkmenistan

title: A Capital Built to Order
text: Rio de Janeiro was crowded, with government buildings far apart and traffic heavy, so between 1956 and 1960 Brazil built a brand-new capital in its interior. Planners, architects and political scientists designed Brasília purely as a government city, meant to pull development inland. It was planned for 500,000 people. Today about two million more live beyond the lake and park meant to stop sprawl.

source.name: National Geographic Education: Capital

source2.name: National Geographic: The City Solution

title: The Capital That Is Sinking
text: Parts of northern Jakarta sink up to 11 inches a year, mostly because residents pump groundwater when piped water reaches only about a quarter of households. Roughly 40 percent of the city of 10 million now lies below sea level. In 2019 President Joko Widodo announced that the capital would move to a new city on Borneo, on land that is now forest.

source.name: National Geographic: Indonesia's giant capital city is sinking. Can the government's plan save it?

title: Water Pipes Under a Maya Metropolis
text: Kaminaljuyú, the most populous Maya city of the southern highlands, was built mostly of adobe and timber rather than limestone. Its canals ranged from narrow culverts to navigable channels about 30 feet wide, clay pipes ran water under the streets, and a three-mile earthen aqueduct tapped a spring. Today Guatemala City covers most of it; the park preserves under 10 percent.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Maya Metropolis

title: The Samurai Town in a Narrow Valley
text: For about a century the Asakura clan ruled from Ichijōdani, a valley town of up to 10,000 people with gates at each end. Refugees from war-torn Kyoto brought artists and craftspeople, and even townspeople drank tea from fine ceramics. Oda Nobunaga's forces burned it in August 1573. Excavators have since recovered over 1.7 million artifacts, including Japan's oldest known flower bed.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Lost City of the Samurai

title: Four Channels Into Luoyang's Palace
place: Qianqiu Gate, Han-Wei city of Luoyang, Henan, China
text: Near the Qianqiu Gate of Luoyang's old imperial palace, archaeologists traced more than 260 feet of water channels: four built side by side to one plan between 220 and 420 CE. Their covers had square holes to catch rainwater. They carried water from outside the city into the palace and on to garden lakes, and the Northern Wei emperor Xiaowen likely reused them.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Water System Unearthed in Central China

title: Ten Thousand Mounds on Tongatapu
text: Aerial scanning and fieldwork led by Phillip Parton of the Australian National University mapped about 10,000 earth mounds on Tongatapu, traces of an ancient city. People were already building earth structures around 300 CE, about 700 years earlier than thought. Between the 1200s and 1800s the city's influence spread across the southwest Pacific, until diseases brought by Europeans led to collapse.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Traces of an Ancient City Discovered on a Pacific Island

title: Digging Beneath Rebuilt Beirut
text: A 15-year civil war, from 1975 to 1990, wrecked central Beirut. As builders rebuilt, archaeologists won rules making developers pay for digs, and by 2011 six big excavations were under way. They found a Phoenician seawall, a grid of 4th-century BCE houses and a Byzantine stable with seven donkeys and a camel. Some Hellenistic streets stayed in use until the 1800s.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Rebuilding Beirut

title: A Hospital in Ancient Anuradhapura
place: Near Thuparama Dagoba, Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka
text: Near the Thuparama Dagoba, a stupa said to hold the Buddha's right collarbone, archaeologists in the ancient city of Anuradhapura uncovered a hospital about 2,000 years old. It had medical rooms and a spa. Excavators found grinding stones and knives, and a latrine system carved straight out of the rock.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Hospital Unearthed in Sri Lanka

title: Mousers in a Millet Village
text: In a Yangshao farming village, rodents tunnelled straight into the grain pits. Small cats moved in too. Their bones carry the chemical stamp of millet, so they were eating grain-fed mice and maybe scraps from people. One cat seems to have been fed directly. The twist: later skull studies showed these were leopard cats, not the ancestors of today's house cats, a partnership that lasted about 3,500 years.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Earliest evidence for commensal processes of cat domestication

source2.name: PLOS ONE: Earliest 'Domestic' Cats in China Identified as Leopard Cat

title: Where the First Chickens Pecked
place: Ban Non Wat, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: The earliest bones that are clearly from domestic chickens come from this Neolithic village in Thailand. Researchers think rice and millet fields drew wild red junglefowl into settlements, and taming followed. Chickens then spread slowly, reaching the Mediterranean around 800 BCE. In early Europe they were often buried whole with no cut marks, prized as something special long before they became dinner.

source.name: PNAS (via Europe PMC): The biocultural origins and dispersal of domestic chickens

title: The Shogun Who Protected Dogs
text: Born in the Year of the Dog, shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi began issuing his Orders on Compassion for Living Things in 1687. Abusing animals could eventually bring a death sentence. Frightened owners dumped their dogs, so the government built huge kennels, with Nakano said to hold about 100,000 strays. The laws died with him in 1709, and some kennel managers spent 48 years repaying their dog-care funds.

source.name: Japan Medical Association Journal: Shoguns and Animals (Tsuruoka, 2016)

title: An Elephant Gets a Court Rank
text: Shogun Yoshimune ordered two elephants from Vietnam, and the surviving young male set off from Nagasaki in 1729, walking about 1,000 km to Edo. In Kyoto it was presented to the emperor. Only people with court rank could enter the palace, so officials hastily gave the elephant one. It later ended up as a show animal in Nakano and died in 1742, aged just 21.

source.name: Japan Medical Association Journal: Shoguns and Animals (Tsuruoka, 2016)

title: An Arabian Camel in Song China
place: Wei River floodplain, Gaoling District, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China
text: Most camels on China's Silk Road were two-humped Bactrians, so a forearm bone dug from the Wei River floodplain was a shock. DNA showed it came from a one-humped Arabian camel of the Song period, the first genetically confirmed in China. Stranger still, nearly half its ancestry was Bactrian, hinting that caravan people deliberately crossbred the two species for tougher pack animals.

source.name: Zoological Research (via Europe PMC): Domestic camel paleogenomics in Xi'an, China

title: Kungas, the First Designer Hybrids
place: Tell Umm el-Marra, near Aleppo, Syria
text: Bronze Age elites at Umm el-Marra buried 25 male equids in their own graves. DNA revealed they were kungas, bred from a domestic donkey mother and a wild Syrian ass father: the earliest known human-made hybrid animals. Cuneiform texts priced a kunga at up to six times a donkey. Big males pulled war wagons and the carts of nobles and gods, until horses arrived and took over.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): The genetic identity of the earliest human-made hybrid animals, the kungas

title: Egyptian Donkeys Under the Floor
text: Beneath ordinary house floors at early Bronze Age Gath, archaeologists found four young female donkeys, each trussed in its own pit with its head facing east. Chemical signals in their teeth showed they were born and raised in Egypt, fed on Nile Valley plants, then brought north and sacrificed as building offerings. One was beheaded and its head laid on its belly.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): An isotopic perspective on equid selection in cult at Tell es-Safi/Gath

title: Cats Raised to Become Offerings
text: In 1890 a ship brought about 200,000 animal mummies from Beni Hassan to Liverpool to be ground into fertiliser. Some cat skulls were saved, and 131 now sit in Vienna. Most were probably domestic cats, with a few jungle cats. Over 60 percent show disease, mostly bad teeth, hinting at cramped captivity, and some bear deliberate blows from people preparing them as votive offerings.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science (via Europe PMC): Keeping cats for mummification in ancient Egypt

title: The Elephant Duel That Maybe Wasn't
place: Nong Sarai, Don Chedi, Suphanburi, Thailand
text: Thai schoolbooks tell how Prince Naresuan challenged the Burmese crown prince to a duel on war elephants at Nong Sarai in 1593. Historian Barend Terwiel compared ten accounts and found they clash. Burmese annals say one of their own elephants in musth, unblindfolded, gored the prince's mount before a gunshot finished him. Naresuan's elephant later received a noble rank and a state funeral.

source.name: Journal of the Siam Society: What Happened at Nong Sarai? (Terwiel, 2013)

title: Akbar's Wild Ride on Hawa'i
place: Agra Fort, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: Outside Agra Fort in 1561, the young emperor Akbar climbed onto Hawa'i, one of the fiercest elephants in the imperial stables, and set him against the equally wild Ran Bagha. The chase thundered onto a bridge of boats across the Jumna, which lurched and gave way under the giants, sending servants diving into the river. Court painters later recorded the scene for the Akbarnama.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Akbar (Akbarnama painting, IS.2:22-1896)

title: Catching Cheetahs for the Emperor
place: Countryside near Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: Akbar first hunted cheetahs in 1560, and his chronicler Abu'l Fazl called catching them the most remarkable hunting art in Hindustan. Wild cheetahs were lured into specially dug pits so they would not be hurt, then tamed and trained for the chase. The finest joined the royal establishment, led out by keepers on jewelled collars, as Akbarnama paintings of hunts near Agra show.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Akbar assists in capturing a cheetah

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Akbar hunting with cheetahs near Agra (IS.2:24-1896)

title: A Moscow Stray Goes to Orbit
text: On 3 November 1957, less than a month after Sputnik 1, a rocket from Baikonur carried a dog named Laika into orbit. She was a part-Samoyed terrier picked up as a stray in Moscow, chosen partly for her calm temper. Sputnik 2 was rushed for propaganda, with no way home. Laika probably survived only hours, apparently after its temperature controls failed.

source.name: NASA: 60 Years Ago, The First Animal in Orbit

source2.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: What was the first animal in space?

title: A Nursed Cat on the Silk Road
place: Dzhankent, Syr Darya delta, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: In a rubbish heap inside Dzhankent, a walled Silk Road town near the Aral Sea, lay a small male cat from about 775 to 940 CE. He had a broken leg that was still healing, a damaged elbow and few front teeth, yet his bones show a rich, protein-heavy diet. Someone fed and nursed him, though the local Oghuz were herders with no known habit of keeping cats.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via Europe PMC): The earliest domestic cat on the Silk Road

title: Wolves Fed on Salmon
place: Swan Point, Tanana Valley, Alaska, USA
text: Around 12,000 years ago at Swan Point in interior Alaska, a canid lived on a diet more than half salmon, just when people there began eating salmon too. At nearby Hollembaek's Hill, canids from about 8,100 years ago got 61 to 82 percent of their food from salmon, too much for scavenging. Researchers think they were tame wolves or early dogs fed by people.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Late Pleistocene onset of mutualistic human/canid relationships in subarctic Alaska

title: The US Army's Camel Experiment
place: Camp Verde, Kerr County, Texas, USA
text: In May 1856 the ship USS Supply landed camels in Texas, the start of a US Army experiment pushed by War Secretary Jefferson Davis with $30,000 from Congress. Based at Camp Verde, the camels needed less food and water than mules and carried heavier loads, marching on through rocky country where horses and mules were exhausted. The Civil War ended it, and the camels were sold or escaped.

source.name: U.S. Army: The history of the Army Camel Corps

source2.name: National Park Service, Big Bend: Camel Expedition Story

title: Llamas Buried Beside the Diaguita
place: El Olivar, Elqui River mouth, La Serena, Chile
text: At El Olivar, a huge Diaguita burial ground at the mouth of the Elqui River, people laid 57 whole camelids in graves between about 1090 and 1440 CE, some bigger than the humans buried with them. Bone chemistry, DNA and tartar on their teeth point to llamas tended by people, even fed cooked food. Researchers call it the first solid evidence of domestic llamas here before the Inca.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Multi-proxy analysis of El Olivar camelids (1,090-1,440 cal AD)

title: Patagonia's Early Horse Keepers
place: Chorrillo Grande 1, Gallegos River, Santa Cruz, Argentina
text: Written records put the first horses in southern Patagonia around 1741, but bones at Chorrillo Grande 1 tell an earlier story. Aónikenk hunter-gatherers were raising and eating horses perhaps by the early 1600s, within about a century of horses reaching the region. DNA showed they favoured young mares, an unusual choice for herders, and one horse's teeth record a long trip north and back.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Interdisciplinary evidence for early domestic horse exploitation in southern Patagonia

title: The Dog That Howled
place: Moncks Cave, Redcliffs, Christchurch, New Zealand
text: About 700 years ago, East Polynesian voyagers brought the kurī, a small, short-legged dog with pricked ears and a curled tail, to New Zealand. Of their dog, pig and chicken, only the dog took hold. Kurī guarded, hunted and were eaten, and their skins made kahu kurī, prized chiefs' cloaks. They reportedly howled instead of barking. A tiny carving from Moncks Cave is the only known image of one.

source.name: Canterbury Museum: Man's best friend in pre-European New Zealand

source2.name: Te Papa: Kahu kurī style of cloak

title: Camels Land in South Australia
text: On New Year's Eve 1865, a crowd at Port Augusta watched 124 camels being lifted ashore with 31 cameleers, brought by Elder & Co. for Beltana station. Called Afghans, most were Pathans from today's Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Camel trains supplied the Overland Telegraph and desert expeditions, the cameleers paid for Australia's first city mosque in Adelaide in 1888, and the Ghan train carries their name.

source.name: SA History Hub (History Trust of South Australia): Afghans

title: Horses for the Last Pagans
text: Pagan Balts in today's Lithuania, Poland and Kaliningrad buried sacrificed horses in their cemeteries for over a thousand years. DNA overturned an old assumption: about a third were mares, not just stallions. Chemical traces in teeth showed three horses came from across the sea, probably Sweden or Finland. One, buried at Marvelė around 1115 CE, may have been a prestige import.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Mares and long-distance imported horses sacrificed by the last pagans in temperate Europe

title: The Pigeon Who Stopped the Guns
text: In October 1918, an American battalion was trapped in the Argonne Forest for six days, and its own artillery began shelling it. The men's hope was a pigeon, Cher Ami, carrying a note begging the gunners to stop. He arrived with a bullet wound in the chest. Of more than 500 men, 194 survived. He won France's Croix de Guerre with palm and died in 1919.

source.name: U.S. Army: Fine, Feathered Friends!

title: Horse Breeding for Oyo's Cavalry
place: Old Bara, near Oyo-Ile, Oyo State, Nigeria
text: Just outside Oyo-Ile, capital of the Oyo Empire, lay the walled royal suburb of Old Bara. Bones from its refuse show two foals born on the spot, the first evidence of local horse breeding in the empire, while other horses' teeth point to Nupe country. The horses ate sorghum or millet fodder, perhaps sent as tribute from vassal towns in the dry season.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Multiproxy stable isotope analysis at Old Bara, Oyo Empire

title: Imported Horses of Westminster
place: Elverton Street, Westminster, London, United Kingdom
text: Late medieval Westminster had a horse cemetery: more than 70 horses buried at what is now Elverton Street, mostly around 1425 to 1517. Teeth from 15 of them showed at least seven grew up outside Britain, perhaps in Scandinavia or the Alps, arriving at about five years old. They were tall for their time. Researchers wonder whether they served the royal household or Westminster jousts.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Isotopic biographies reveal horse rearing and trading networks in medieval London

title: Buried With Horses and Dogs
text: In a Cenomani cemetery in Verona from the last centuries BCE, 16 of 161 graves held animals. A middle-aged woman lay with a nearly complete horse, parts of four more horses and a dog's skull. A newborn baby was buried with an 18-month-old dog whose broken leg had healed. A near-term fetus was only spotted after excavation, mixed in among the horse bones.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via Europe PMC): Human-animal co-burials from the Late Iron Age necropolis of Seminario Vescovile in Verona

title: Jamestown Eats Its Horses
text: During the Starving Time winter of 1609 to 1610, Jamestown's colonists butchered, boiled and cracked open their horses for marrow. Bones from a well and a kitchen cellar show four mares raised in Britain, plus a foal born in the colony. One tooth came from a donkey with partly West African ancestry, probably picked up on the voyage. Afterwards, a 1613 letter preferred donkeys to horses.

source.name: Science Advances (via Europe PMC): Early transatlantic movement of horses and donkeys at Jamestown

title: A Painted Room Inside a Mound
text: On 21 March 1972, Japan saw its first full-colour tomb mural. Inside the small Takamatsuzuka mound, built around the late 600s or early 700s, a stone chamber barely 1.1 metres high was painted floor to ceiling: a star chart overhead, the sun and moon, the Azure Dragon, White Tiger and Black Tortoise guarding the directions, and painted groups of men and women on the walls.

source.name: Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan: Takamatsuzuka Tumulus and Kitora Tumulus

title: Whole Families Buried Beside Their Lord
place: Imdang-Joyeong tombs, Gyeongsan, North Gyeongsang, South Korea
text: The Silla-era cemetery at Imdang-Joyeong holds more than 1,600 graves built in about a century. Ancient DNA from 78 people revealed 13 family groups and some children of cousin marriages. Most chilling: in three cases, parents and their children had been sacrificed together and buried as companions for a tomb owner, the first genetic proof of whole-household sacrifice in Korea.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Ancient genomes reveal an extensive kinship network and endogamy in a Three-Kingdoms period society in Korea

title: A Seaside Cemetery of Newcomers
place: Doigahama site, Hohoku, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi, Japan
text: The dunes of Doigahama have given up the bones of more than 300 people from Japan's Yayoi period. One young woman, about 149 cm tall and buried around 400 to 360 BCE, had her whole genome read. Roughly 87 percent of her ancestry traced to the Korean Peninsula and only 13 percent to Japan's older Jomon people, a snapshot of migrants reshaping the islands.

source.name: Journal of Human Genetics (PMC): Genetic analysis of a Yayoi individual from the Doigahama site

title: Mummies Smoked Over the Fire
place: Con Co Ngua and other sites, Thanh Hoa, Vietnam
text: Hunter-gatherers across southern China and Southeast Asia buried their dead tightly crouched, some folded so hard no flesh could have remained. Testing bones from 11 sites in China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, researchers found most had been heated, probably by smoke-drying bodies over fires for long periods. Some of these mummies may be older than Chile's Chinchorro mummies and Egypt's.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Earliest evidence of smoke-dried mummification more than 10,000 years ago in southern China and Southeast Asia

title: A Harappan Couple Facing Each Other
text: Among 62 graves in one part of the Rakhigarhi cemetery, only one held two people: a man and a woman, both young adults, laid on their backs with the man's head turned toward her. Red pots surrounded them and a banded agate bead lay at her collarbone. Researchers think they died at about the same time and found no sign of widow sacrifice.

source.name: Anatomy & Cell Biology (PMC): A young couple's grave found in the Rakhigarhi cemetery of the Harappan Civilization

title: Buried Alongside Their Animals in Kashmir
place: Burzahom, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: Burzahom, named after the Kashmiri word for birch, was home to people from around 2900 BCE. Its Neolithic and megalithic layers held ten human burials, some rubbed with red ochre, and some skulls even show trepanation, holes cut into the living head. Unusually, animals were laid in the graves beside the people. DNA shows contacts with the Swat Valley to the west.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Ancient mitogenomes from Neolithic, megalithic and medieval burials of the Kashmir valley

title: A Young Prince in Tuva's Valley of Kings
place: Chinge-Tey I, Turan-Uyuk Basin, Tuva, Russia
text: Four metres beneath a huge stone platform in Tuva's 'Valley of the Kings' lay a man of 20 to 25 with gold ornaments, a finely decorated weapon, a long robe and a glass bowl probably made in distant Assyria. His gold work is so like that of the nearby Arzhan-2 queen that the same craftsman may have made both.

source.name: BMC Genomics (PMC): Ancient DNA analysis of an elite nomadic warrior from the Chinge-Tey I complex

title: The Near East's Oldest Funeral Pyre
place: Beisamoun, Hula Valley, Upper Galilee, Israel
text: Beside the ancient Hula Lake, Neolithic villagers dug a plastered pit that worked like a kiln, stacked it with wood and reeds, and burned a young adult seated inside. It is the earliest directly dated intentional cremation in the Near East. The dead person had once survived an attack: a flint arrow tip was still lodged in their shoulder blade.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Emergence of corpse cremation during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic of the Southern Levant

title: Graves Under the Floors at Göbeklitepe
text: For decades Göbeklitepe's giant carved pillars had no intact graves to go with them. Then two turned up beneath plaster floors near the special buildings. One held a single young adult curled on the left side facing east. The other was a family-style tomb where earlier skeletons had been pushed aside for newcomers, their skulls gathered neatly in one corner.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): First burials give insights into mortuary rites at Göbeklitepe

title: Reading DNA From Egyptian Mummies
text: Mummies from the Middle Egyptian town of Abusir el-Meleq, now kept in Tübingen and Berlin, gave up 90 complete mitochondrial genomes spanning 1,800 years. The ancient townspeople were closer to Near Eastern and Levantine peoples than modern Egyptians are, and their genes barely changed under Greek and Roman rule. Most sub-Saharan ancestry arrived in the last 2,000 years.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient Egyptian mummy genomes suggest an increase of Sub-Saharan African ancestry in post-Roman periods

title: Hearing a Mummified Priest Speak
text: Nesyamun chanted and sang the daily liturgy as a priest and scribe at Karnak under Ramesses XI. His coffin calls him 'true of voice'. In 2016 his mummy, now in Leeds, was CT-scanned, and his throat was 3D-printed. Fed by an artificial larynx, it produced a single vowel-like sound somewhere between the vowels in English 'bed' and 'bad'.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Synthesis of a Vocal Sound from the 3,000 year old Mummy, Nesyamun 'True of Voice'

title: Tattooed Toddlers of Christian Nubia
text: Naturally dried bodies from Kulubnarti's cemeteries still carry ink. Using multispectral cameras, researchers found tattoos on at least one in five people, men and women, often a diamond of four dots on the forehead. The youngest was only 18 months old. The marks may be the region's earliest Christian tattoos, or a remedy for fevers and headaches.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Revealing tattoo traditions in ancient Nubia through multispectral imaging

title: Three Graves on Beechey Island
text: Sir John Franklin's 128 men spent their first Arctic winter at Beechey Island, where three crewmen died and were buried in the frozen ground. They were the lucky ones to get graves: not one of the expedition survived. Later tests of bone, hair and tissue found high lead levels, and scientists still debate how much poisoning hastened the disaster.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Franklin expedition lead exposure: new insights from high resolution confocal x-ray fluorescence imaging

title: The Frozen Boy of El Plomo
place: Cerro El Plomo, near Santiago, Chile
text: In 1954 treasure hunters found an eight-year-old boy seated at 5,400 metres on Cerro El Plomo, hugging his knees, frozen for about five centuries. He was an Inca capacocha offering. Long thought to have died quietly of cold, he was re-examined with CT scans and skin studies, which revealed a forceful blow to his skull at the time of death.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Pilgrimage to sacrifice: the Western Andean Capacocha

source2.name: JAAD Case Reports (PMC): Dermatoscopic findings of Niño del Plomo, an Incan mummy in Chile

title: Coca Leaves on a 6,739-Metre Summit
text: Near the top of Llullaillaco, 6,739 metres up, three frozen Inca children were found in 1999. Their hair worked like a diary: the 13-year-old 'Maiden' began taking far more coca about a year before her death, and alcohol peaked in her final weeks. She still had a wad of coca between her teeth, sitting cross-legged with her headdress undisturbed.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Archaeological, radiological, and biological evidence offer insight into Inca child sacrifice

title: A Traveller Melts Out of a Glacier
text: In 1999 a young man's frozen body, still wearing a robe, emerged from a glacier in northwest British Columbia, more than 100 km inland. Named Kwäday Dän Ts'ìnchí, he lived sometime between about 1670 and 1850. His bones showed a life spent eating seafood, but hair and tissue revealed that in his final year his diet switched to inland foods.

source.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge): Radiocarbon Dating and Dietary Stable Isotope Analysis of Kwaday Dän Ts'inchí

title: The Little Angels of Palermo
text: The Capuchin Catacombs hold 163 mummified children, many from middle- and upper-class families. Bodies were dried in a draining room, washed with vinegar and dressed, sometimes injected with preservatives such as arsenic. X-rays of 43 'angioletti', or little angels, revealed hidden metal wires, wooden boards and canes used to shape and pose them for display, plus growth lines showing childhood illness or hunger.

source.name: Frontiers in Medicine (PMC): The 'angioletti' of Palermo: mummified non-adults in late modern Palermo, Sicily (1787-1880 CE)

title: Leprosy in a Bronze Age Round Tomb
place: Dahwa, near Saham, North Batinah, Oman
text: At Dahwa, a Bronze Age trading village near Oman's Batinah coast, the dead were placed in circular Umm an-Nar tombs and their bones later jumbled together in pits. Micro-CT scans of three upper jaws revealed the tell-tale bone loss of lepromatous leprosy. It is the first Bronze Age leprosy found outside South Asia, hinting the disease travelled along ancient trade routes.

source.name: Frontiers in Medicine (PMC): Lepromatous leprosy in Bronze Age Oman: micro-CT in fragmentary and commingled assemblages

title: Mummies in Painted Plaster Shrouds
text: In late Roman Egypt, wealthy families at Saqqara wrapped their dead in stucco shrouds painted with portraits, garlands and other motifs. Two such mummies joined the Dresden collection of Augustus II, King of Poland, in 1728. CT scans found a young woman's brain still in place, necklace beads, a hairpin, lead seals, nails and two coins or medallions hidden inside the wrappings.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Decorated bodies for eternal life: late Roman Period stucco-shrouded portrait mummies from Saqqara

title: The Ancient One's Genome Speaks
text: In 1996 a skeleton about 9,000 years old turned up in Washington state. Skull measurements led scientists to claim he was closer to the Ainu or Polynesians than to Native Americans, and courts blocked tribes from reburying the man they called the Ancient One. His genome, read in 2015, proved otherwise: he was closest to Native Americans, including the Colville tribe.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The ancestry and affiliations of Kennewick Man

title: Strep Throat From a Bolivian Mummy
place: National Museum of Archaeology (MUNARQ), La Paz, Bolivia
text: A naturally mummified person who lived in Bolivia around 1300 CE still had the germ that causes strep throat in one tooth. Scientists rebuilt almost the whole genome of this Streptococcus pyogenes, very like modern sore-throat strains. It shows the bacterium was already circulating among Indigenous Americans before European contact, pushing its confirmed presence in the Americas back by several centuries.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): An ancient genome of Streptococcus pyogenes from a pre-Columbian Bolivian mummy

title: Teak Coffins on Stilts in the Caves
place: Log Coffin caves, Pang Mapha, Mae Hong Son, Thailand
text: In the hills of northwest Thailand, Iron Age people carved huge coffins from single teak trees and raised them on stilts inside more than 40 caves and rock shelters, between 2,300 and 1,000 years ago. DNA from 33 of the dead shows a large, well-connected community. Relatives were often laid to rest in the same cave, so kinship shaped who joined whom.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Genomic portrait and relatedness patterns of the Iron Age Log Coffin culture in northwestern Thailand
