title: Chiefs and Commoners in Tongan Mounds
text: At 'Atele on Tongatapu, two burial mounds hold the dead of the Tongan maritime chiefdom, one probably for commoners and one likely for the chiefly class. Chemical traces in their bones show the two groups ate differently, and women ate less protein-rich food than men. Only one of 30 people tested grew up elsewhere, a sign of tight control over who reached the sacred island.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Assessing human diet and movement in the Tongan maritime chiefdom using isotopic analyses

title: Ancestors Found During Roadworks
place: Waikato region, North Island, New Zealand
text: Roadworks in New Zealand's Waikato uncovered seven Māori tūpuna, or ancestors, reburied together in an old borrow pit in the 1700s. Scientists studied chemical traces and proteins in their teeth and bones. All seven lived mostly on plant foods like kūmara and taro, and two local children had been weaned onto plants by age two or three, proof of how central gardens were.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Horticultural intensification and plant-based diets of 18th century CE Waikato Māori

title: Sealed for Eternity With Sticky Rice
text: Song and Ming Chinese families sealed coffins inside a shell of lime, yellow clay, sand and sticky rice water that set like rock. Packed clothing, moisture-absorbing charcoal and germ-killing lime did the rest. A woman buried in De'an in 1274, 152 cm tall, emerged in excellent condition, and such mummies still held the eggs of the intestinal worms that once plagued them.

source.name: BioMed Research International (PMC): Mummification in Korea and China: Mawangdui, Song, Ming and Joseon Dynasty Mummies

title: Crushing Red Ochre in the Nihewan Basin
text: At Xiamabei, people laid out two lumps of ochre and a long limestone slab, then pounded and rubbed them into powders of different colours, staining the floor red. It is the earliest known ochre processing in East Asia. Their stone blades were tiny, more than half under 2 centimetres, and seven show clear traces of hafting. The tools were used for boring, scraping hides and whittling plants.

source.name: Max Planck Society: An innovative 40,000-year-old culture in China

title: A Graphite Pendant Worn Smooth
place: Tolbor-21, Tolbor River valley, Northern Khangai, Mongolia
text: In a Mongolian river valley, archaeologists found a black graphite pendant about 4 centimetres long, grooved so it could hang on a cord. Its flat side is glossy, as if it rubbed against clothing for a long time. No graphite exists nearby; the closest big deposits lie 400 to 500 kilometres away. The researchers think it may be a simplified phallic shape, though they admit other readings remain possible.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Symbolic innovation at the onset of the Upper Paleolithic in Eurasia shown by the personal ornaments from Tolbor-21

title: Quick Tools Knapped from Bone
text: At Lingjing, early humans used the site again and again to kill and butcher wild horses and aurochs, leaving over 50,000 animal bones. Researchers found that 56 broken leg bones had been deliberately chipped into quick, throwaway tools, knapped just like stone. Others had been used as retouchers to sharpen stone tools, and one deer antler served as a soft hammer for shaping tools.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): A 115,000-year-old expedient bone technology at Lingjing, Henan, China

title: Five Denisovans Hidden in a Bone Pile
place: Bianfu Cave, Heqing County, Yunnan, China
text: Scientists sifted more than 60,000 bone fragments from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan and flagged 22 that might be human. Ancient proteins then revealed five Denisovans: two teeth from men, two pieces of skull and part of a forearm bone, the only Denisovan radius known. No site outside Siberia's Denisova Cave has yielded more Denisovan remains. They lived here roughly 167,000 to 134,000 years ago.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from Southwest China

title: Proteins Pulled from Homo Erectus Teeth
text: DNA rarely survives this long, but tooth enamel proteins can. Researchers extracted them from six Homo erectus specimens about 400,000 years old from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong. All six shared a protein variant never seen in any other human group. Another variant also appears in Denisovans, hinting that East Asian Homo erectus and Denisovans may once have met and mixed.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Enamel proteins from six Homo erectus specimens across China

title: A Neanderthal-Style Toolkit in Yunnan
text: Quina tools, thick flakes turned into heavy scrapers and resharpened again and again, were thought to belong to Europe and western Asia, where Neanderthals used them in the cold. Then a complete Quina toolkit turned up at Longtan, an open-air site 1,540 metres up in southwest China, dated to about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago. Who made it, sapiens, Denisovans or others, is still unknown.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Quina lithic technology indicates diverse Late Pleistocene human dynamics in East Asia

title: A Neanderthal Woman's Lonely Genome
text: A single finger bone found in 2011 at Chagyrskaya Cave gave scientists a full, high-quality genome of a Neanderthal woman. Surprisingly, she was more closely related to Neanderthals in Croatia than to earlier Neanderthals from Denisova Cave, just 100 kilometres away. Long stretches of matching DNA showed her ancestors lived in small, isolated groups of fewer than 60 individuals.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): A high-coverage Neandertal genome from Chagyrskaya Cave

title: Neanderthal Dentists Drill a Rotten Tooth
text: An older Neanderthal in the Altai had a decaying molar, and someone did something about it. Microscopes and CT scans show a large hollow drilled into the tooth's chewing surface while its owner was alive, using a small pointed stone tool. Researchers repeated the job on modern teeth with jasper drills. It is the earliest known treatment of tooth decay, about 59,000 years ago.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Earliest evidence for invasive mitigation of dental caries by Neanderthals

title: Arrowheads in the Tian Shan?
place: Obi-Rakhmat rock shelter, Tashkent Region, Uzbekistan
text: High in the Tian Shan foothills, 100 kilometres from Tashkent, the Obi-Rakhmat rock shelter holds 10 metres of Ice Age layers. In its oldest levels, about 80,000 years old, researchers spotted tiny triangular stone points previously overlooked as broken scraps. They argue the points are too narrow to fit anything but arrow-like shafts, and that they resemble arrowheads left in France 25,000 years later.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Arrow heads at Obi-Rakhmat (Uzbekistan) 80 ka ago?

title: Pointed Tools by an Andhra Stream
place: Retlapalle, Gundlakamma basin, Prakasam District, Andhra Pradesh, India
text: On the bank of a small stream feeding the Gundlakamma River, toolmakers left behind stone cores and points, buried in a layer dated to about 139,000 years ago. They used several Levallois methods, carefully preparing a core before striking off flakes of a planned shape. Pointed tools dominate the finds, adding to evidence that India's Middle Palaeolithic began early and lasted through great climate upheavals.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Deep-rooted Indian Middle Palaeolithic: Terminal Middle Pleistocene lithic assemblage from Retlapalle, Andhra Pradesh

title: Tiny Quartz Tools for Rainforest Hunters
place: Kitulgala Beli-lena, Sabaragamuwa Province, Sri Lanka
text: In a big gneiss rock shelter in Sri Lanka's wet lowland rainforest, 85 kilometres east of Colombo, people began making stone tools about 45,000 years ago. They split quartz with the bipolar method to make microliths under 4 centimetres, used with bone points. Remarkably, the same toolmaking habits lasted until 8,000 years ago, suited to hunting tree-dwelling monkeys and squirrels.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Homo sapiens lithic technology and microlithization in the South Asian rainforest at Kitulgala Beli-lena

title: Two Very Different Peoples in One Cave
place: Leang Bulu Bettue, Maros-Pangkep, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Digging 8 metres down at Leang Bulu Bettue, archaeologists found a stone pick and butchered animal bones from roughly 208,000 to 132,000 years ago, long before our species reached Sulawesi. Later, people made simple cobble tools and ate dwarf buffalo and now-extinct elephant relatives. Then, by about 40,000 years ago, the record changes abruptly, with the cave's first art and symbols. Modern humans may have replaced older hominins.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): A near-continuous archaeological record of Pleistocene human occupation at Leang Bulu Bettue, Sulawesi

title: A Strange Front Tooth in Borneo
place: Trader's Cave (Gua Dagang), Niah National Park, Sarawak, Malaysia
text: Just 300 metres from the famous Niah Great Cave, a smaller cave yielded one adult upper front tooth, about 52,000 to 55,000 years old. Its crown is huge for its root and strongly shovel-shaped, a combination not normally found in our species but typical of archaic humans like Homo erectus and Neanderthals. Someone other than us apparently lived in Borneo as modern humans arrived.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): A Late Pleistocene archaic human tooth from Gua Dagang (Trader's Cave), Niah National Park, Sarawak

title: Hobbits Ate the Dragons' Leftovers
text: Homo floresiensis was once pictured hunting dwarf elephant-like Stegodon with fire. To test this, researchers fed a goat carcass to a Komodo dragon at Zoo Atlanta and compared its tooth marks with the Stegodon bones from Liang Bua. The verdict: dragons probably ate first, leaving the hobbits only low-value scraps to scavenge. No signs of deliberate fire were found either.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Taphonomic analysis at Liang Bua reveals the behavioral and technological capabilities of Homo floresiensis

title: Laid to Rest with Ochre Chunks
place: Tinshemet Cave, Nahal Beit Arif, central Israel
text: Around 97,000 years ago, people at Tinshemet Cave buried adults and children curled on their sides as if asleep, heads bowed. The cave held over 7,500 bits of ochre, densest in the burial layers, and one 4 to 5 centimetre chunk lay between an adult's legs. Some ochre came from 60 to 80 kilometres away. These are among the earliest known intentional burials anywhere.

source.name: Nature Human Behaviour (PMC): Evidence from Tinshemet Cave in Israel suggests behavioural uniformity across Homo groups in the Levantine mid-Middle Palaeolithic

title: Footprints at a Lost Arabian Lake
place: Alathar paleolake, western Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
text: Today the Nefud is a sea of sand, but about 120,000 years ago a shallow freshwater lake sat here in grassland. Its drying mud recorded 376 footprints: 107 from camels, 43 from elephants, and seven from humans, probably Homo sapiens. Four prints suggest two or three people walking together. They seem to have stopped briefly to drink and forage, leaving no tools behind.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Human footprints provide snapshot of last interglacial ecology in the Arabian interior

title: AI Finds Fire No One Could See
text: Flint tools and bones dug up at Evron Quarry in the 1970s showed no visible signs of burning. Decades later, researchers shone lasers on 26 flint artefacts and let a deep learning model read the results. Many had been heated, some to high temperatures, and pieces of elephant tusk had burned too. Whether people controlled the fire, or a wildfire did it, remains unproven.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Hidden signatures of early fire at Evron Quarry (1.0 to 0.8 Mya)

title: Leopard and Tortoise on the Menu
place: Ghar-e Boof, Dasht-e Rostam, Fars Province, Iran
text: For a long time, Stone Age diets in Iran's Zagros Mountains looked like nothing but hoofed animals. A careful study of bones from Ghar-e Boof cave, used between about 81,000 and 45,000 years ago, changed that. Hunters mostly took wild goats, but they also ate slow, easy-to-catch tortoises, and cut marks on leopard bones show they skinned and butchered big cats too.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Evidence of diverse animal exploitation during the Middle Paleolithic at Ghar-e Boof (southern Zagros)

title: The Oldest Shell Beads Yet Found
text: In a cave on a Moroccan hillside, archaeologists recovered 33 small sea-snail shells, almost all of one species, Tritia gibbosula. Their holes and edges are smoothed and polished from use, and some carry traces of red pigment. At least 142,000 years old, they are the oldest shell beads yet found, carried from a coast then perhaps 30 to 50 kilometres away.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Early Middle Stone Age personal ornaments from Bizmoune Cave, Essaouira, Morocco

title: The Oldest Poisoned Arrows
place: Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
text: Scientists scraped tiny residues from ten 60,000-year-old quartz arrow tips found at Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter. Five tested positive for toxic plant alkaloids, most likely from the bulb of Boophone disticha, a plant also recorded as an arrow poison in much later times. The previous oldest direct evidence of poisoned arrows came from an Egyptian tomb only about 4,000 years old.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Direct evidence for poison use on microlithic arrowheads in Southern Africa at 60,000 years ago

title: Javelin Hunters Above Lake Tana
place: Gorgora rockshelter, Lake Tana, Amhara, Ethiopia
text: In 1942, during the Second World War, a British officer and two unnamed Ethiopian soldiers dug a rock shelter near Lake Tana's northern shore, nearly 2,000 metres up. Their finds were shipped to Kenya and barely studied. New radiocarbon dates show people lived there intensively more than 42,000 years ago, during a wet phase, using worked ochre and neat stone points sized like hunting javelins.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): MIS 3 innovative behavior and highland occupation during a stable wet episode in the Lake Tana paleoclimate record, Ethiopia

title: Mystery Toolmakers Unmasked in Thuringia
text: Finely made stone leaf points from northern Europe had long puzzled archaeologists: nobody knew who made them. At Ranis cave, scientists tested 13 tiny bone fragments, some dug up in the 1930s. Ancient DNA showed they were Homo sapiens, about 45,000 years old. These pioneers hunted reindeer on cold steppe, 7 to 15 degrees Celsius colder than today, at a time when Neanderthals had not yet vanished from the region.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Homo sapiens reached the higher latitudes of Europe by 45,000 years ago

title: A Crimean Neanderthal with Siberian Kin
text: Among 150 unidentifiable bone scraps from Starosele, protein fingerprinting picked out one 5-centimetre piece that was human, probably from a thighbone. Its DNA was Neanderthal, about 45,000 years old. Surprisingly, its closest relatives were Neanderthals from the Altai Mountains of Siberia, some 3,000 kilometres away, suggesting Neanderthals with the same stone tool style travelled across Eurasia.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): A new late Neanderthal from Crimea reveals long-distance connections across Eurasia

title: A Neanderthal Crayon, Sharpened Again
place: Zaskalnaya V rock shelter, Belogorsk region, Crimea
text: Researchers examined 16 pieces of ochre left by Neanderthals in Crimea and Ukraine. Most could have served practical jobs like treating hides. But one yellow piece from Zaskalnaya V was shaped into a pointed crayon and resharpened repeatedly, another looks like a broken crayon, and a third bears engraved lines and polish. They suggest Neanderthals used colour to make deliberate marks.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Evidence for symbolic use of ochre by Micoquian Neanderthals in Crimea

title: First Campfires in the Kimberley
place: Riwi Cave, Gooniyandi Country, Kimberley, Western Australia
text: Riwi Cave, on Gooniyandi traditional land, preserves charcoal-filled hearths in sandy floors. Researchers ran 44 radiocarbon and 37 luminescence dates and found the two methods agreed: people first lit fires here between about 46,400 and 44,600 years ago. Below the oldest hearth lies sand with no trace of people, showing the cave sat empty for centuries to millennia beforehand.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Towards an Accurate and Precise Chronology for the Colonization of Australia: The Example of Riwi, Kimberley

title: Monkey Hunters of the Rainforest
place: Fa-Hien Lena Cave, Kalutara District, Sri Lanka
text: Fa-Hien Lena cave in Sri Lanka's rainforest has yielded more than 14,000 animal bone and tooth fragments. From about 45,000 years ago, most come from monkeys and tree squirrels, over 70 percent of the identified remains, with toque macaques slightly outnumbering leaf monkeys. Catching agile animals high in the trees is hard, and bone points and tiny stone blades hint that hunters used projectiles.

source.name: Nature Communications: Specialized rainforest hunting by Homo sapiens ~45,000 years ago (Wedage et al. 2019)

title: Steel Made by the Monsoon Wind
text: At Samanalawewa, ancient iron workers built their furnaces along the western edges of hills and ridges, facing the strong monsoon winds. Archaeologist Gill Juleff excavated them and tested replicas: the wind itself pushed air into the fire, a method unlike either bellows or chimney draught. The replicas even made high-carbon steel. This wind-powered industry thrived during the first millennium CE.

source.name: Nature: An ancient wind-powered iron smelting technology in Sri Lanka (Juleff 1996)

title: Strangers at Skeleton Lake
text: Around Roopkund, a small lake 5,029 metres up in the Himalayas, lie the bones of several hundred people. DNA from 38 skeletons revealed a surprise: 23 had South Asian ancestry and died around 800 CE, while 14 had eastern Mediterranean ancestry, close to modern Greeks and Cretans, and died around 1800 CE. Local legend blames the wrath of the mountain goddess Nanda Devi.

source.name: Nature Communications: Ancient DNA from the skeletons of Roopkund Lake reveals Mediterranean migrants in India (Harney et al. 2019)

title: The Physicist From Jhang
text: Abdus Salam was born in 1926 in Jhang, a small town in a poor farming district. At 14 he cycled home from Lahore after earning the highest marks ever recorded in the Punjab University matriculation exam, and the whole town turned out to welcome him. In 1979 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, and he gave his share entirely to help physicists from developing countries.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Abdus Salam, Biographical

title: A Wooden Shrine Around a Tree
place: Maya Devi Temple, Lumbini, Rupandehi, Nepal
text: Archaeologists digging inside the Maya Devi Temple at Lumbini, long honoured as the Buddha's birthplace, worked beside meditating monks, nuns and pilgrims. Beneath a series of brick temples they found a timber structure from the sixth century BCE, with an open central space where ancient tree roots survive. Buddhist tradition says Queen Maya Devi gave birth while holding the branch of a tree.

source.name: EurekAlert (National Geographic Society): Archaeological discoveries confirm early date of Buddha's life

title: Silk and a Gold Mask in Mustang
text: In 2009 a seismic event sheared off a cliff face in Upper Mustang, exposing ten shaft tombs carved into the rock 4,000 metres up. In one, an adult's coffin lay beside a gold and silver funeral mask, pierced with pinholes so it could be sewn onto headwear. Cloth from 400 to 650 CE held silk and dyes imported from China and India, linking this remote valley to the Silk Road.

source.name: EurekAlert (University of Cambridge): Nepali textile find suggests Silk Road extended further south than previously thought

title: A Letter From Dacca to Einstein
text: In June 1924, Satyendra Nath Bose, a little-known physics reader at Dacca University, mailed a short paper to Albert Einstein with a letter beginning "Respected Sir." It derived Planck's radiation law in a new statistical way. Einstein translated it into German himself, had it published, and built on it to predict a new state of matter. Particles obeying these statistics are now called bosons.

source.name: Physics Today: The man behind Bose statistics (Kameshwar Wali)

source2.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Satyendranath Bose

title: Dolphins Trapped Between the Barrages
place: Sukkur Barrage, Indus River, Sindh, Pakistan
text: Indus river dolphins live only in the Indus River system. Between 1886 and 1971, twenty irrigation barrages, gated dams that divert water to farms, chopped their range into 17 sections. A 2014 study found the dolphins had vanished from ten of them, mainly because too little water flows below the barrages in the dry season. One radio-tagged dolphin was seen slipping through Sukkur Barrage's open gates.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Habitat Fragmentation and Species Extirpation in Freshwater Ecosystems; Causes of Range Decline of the Indus River Dolphin (Braulik et al. 2014)

title: Earrings Made for a God
text: These gold earrings from the Kathmandu Valley are larger than life, made not for a person but to hang on a deity statue in a Nepalese temple. On the front, a green four-armed Vishnu rides a coral Garuda with lapis lazuli wings, flanked by dancing celestial beings. On the back, fine gold filigree surrounds a protective monster mask with a sun and crescent moon above.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Pair of Deity Earrings with Vishnu on Garuda

title: Fifty-Two Tales From a Parrot
place: Court of Akbar, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: Around 1560, painters at the court of the young emperor Akbar illustrated the Tuti-nama, or Tales of a Parrot. In it, a clever talking parrot tells 52 stories to its mistress Khujasta to keep her from an affair. The Persian text dates to 1329–30 and recast older Sanskrit fables. Mostly Indian artists painted this copy, which marks the very beginnings of Mughal painting.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tuti-Nama (Tales of a Parrot)

source2.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Page from Tales of a Parrot (Tuti-nama): text page

title: A Sultan Keeps His Throne, at a Price
text: Abdullah Qutb Shah became sultan of Golconda at the age of twelve. When the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan invaded the Deccan in 1635, the young sultan kept his throne, but on harsh terms: paying tribute, converting to Sunni Islam and hosting a Mughal agent at court. A watercolor portrait shows him in a see-through shawl, riding a horse almost as bejewelled as he is.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Sultan Abdullah Qutb Shah (1614-74) on Horseback

title: Shiva Dances on Ignorance
text: Chola bronze casters in Tamil Nadu shaped Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of Dance, one of the most celebrated forms in Indian art. The ring of fire and the flame in his left hand stand for destruction, and the drum in his raised right hand beats out time. His lower right hand tells devotees not to fear, and each dance step lands on a dwarf who personifies ignorance.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Nataraja, Shiva as the Lord of Dance

title: A Teenage King Storms Kangra
place: Kangra Fort, Kangra, Himachal Pradesh, India
text: In 1782, 17-year-old Raja Sansar Chand fought to win back his family's kingdom of Kangra from the Mughals, who had held it since 1620. A painting on cotton cloth shows the young, beardless king on a dark brown horse in front of a camel, blending in among his army. Residents flee toward the fortress with belongings on their heads, while cannons fire from its walls.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Raja Sansar Chand attacking Kangra Fort

title: A Shrine Painting Dated by Its Yellow
text: This Sri Lankan shrine painting shows the Buddha radiating light and flame, flanked by four disciples, with the earth goddess below balancing a water pot on her head. Island guardians gather nearby, including six-headed Kataragama. Its rows of golden figures echo temple murals like those at Dambulla. A hidden clue helps date it: the yellow pigment contains chromium, not used in paints before 1818.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Blessed Lord Buddha

title: A Goddess Turning Toward Shiva
text: This gilt bronze goddess Uma, cast in Nepal in the 1000s and set with semiprecious stones, turns gracefully toward her consort Shiva, although the matching figure of him was long ago separated from her. She embodies the god's creative energy and the beauty of creation. In Nepal, Hinduism and Buddhism have flourished side by side, while in India Buddhism faded away after the 1300s.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Goddess Uma

title: Atlas Grows Wings in Gandhara
text: Gandharan sculptors borrowed Atlas, the Greek giant who held up the sky, and gave him wings to look superhuman. This schist figure also wears Hercules's lion skin, and similar figures hold a thunderbolt, linking them to Vajrapani, the Buddha's protector. Rows of these titans circled the bases of stupas, solid domes that symbolized the sky, as if holding the heavens aloft.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Winged Atlas-Hercules

title: Poison in the Safe Water
text: For decades Bangladesh urged villagers to swap germ-laden ponds and rivers for tube wells, and by the 1990s 97 percent of people had microbiologically safe drinking water. Then in 1993, engineers found arsenic in four tube wells in Chamagram village, Nawabganj district, and eight sick villagers were identified there the next year. Testers later painted wells red if unsafe and green if safe.

source.name: PMC: Arsenic contamination in groundwater in Bangladesh: implications and challenges for healthcare policy

source2.name: PMC: Bangladesh arsenic mitigation programs: lessons from the past

title: Mosques and Tombs Built of Coral
place: Koagannu Cemetery, Hulhumeedhoo, Addu Atoll, Maldives
text: Maldivian mosques are built from an unusual material: sea coral. On Hulhumeedhoo, in Addu Atoll at the country's southern tip, local tradition says the Fandiyaaru Mosque was founded in 1586, and it is believed to be the earliest coral stone building in the Maldives. Around it, Koagannu Cemetery, the nation's largest, holds 15 mausoleums and about 500 coral tombstones, some reused over centuries.

source.name: Fondation Max van Berchem: Archaeological Investigations on the Coral Stone Mosques of the Maldives (Pradines and Balestra)

title: The Sultan Who Wrote Ragas
text: Ibrahim Adil Shah II ruled the Deccan sultanate of Bijapur from 1580 to 1627, keeping Mughal power at bay. He loved music and poetry and blended Sufi ideals with Hindu and Islamic traditions. He recast ragas, musical modes from Hindu court tradition, in his own verses in the local Dakhini language. One survives written in Arabic script on marbled paper, a Deccan art prized for its random beauty.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Dohra (Song) Five: Bhairava Raga, from a Kitab-i Nauras of Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah of Bijapur

title: The Botanist Who Sweetened India's Cane
place: Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India
text: In 1934 Janaki Ammal, born into a Thiya family from Tellicherry in Kerala, began work at the Sugarcane Breeding Institute in Coimbatore. By crossbreeding, she created a high-yielding cane suited to India's climate, helping the country rely less on imports. She even tried crossing sugarcane with maize, sorghum and bamboo, something never done before. In 1946 she became the Royal Horticultural Society's first female scientist.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society: The female botanist who sweetened a nation

title: A Banker Turned Photographer in Lahore
text: Samuel Bourne was a banker in England before he moved to India to become a professional photographer. In the 1860s he photographed Lahore from the roof of the palace in its fort. His album of 50 views travels from Himalayan hill towns down to Lahore, Delhi, Agra, Benares and Calcutta, recording monuments such as the Taj Mahal before twentieth-century restorations changed them.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: View of the City of Lahore Taken from the Roof of the Palace in the Fort

title: A Dress Woven Sideways
text: The kira, the main garment of Bhutanese women, is a single large rectangle wrapped around the body over a blouse and petticoat, held by brooches at the shoulders and a sash at the waist. This one, about 1.4 by 2.8 metres, joins three loom widths of cotton and silk. Curiously, its geometric stripes are woven running vertically, yet the dress is worn with them horizontal.

source.name: Art Institute of Chicago: Kira (Wrapped Woman's Dress) with Geometric Patterning

title: An Archer on a Gupta Coin
text: The Gupta kings unified northern India under native rule for the first time since the Maurya empire, and even took their name from Chandragupta, the Maurya founder. Chandragupta II, who ruled from about 380 to 415 CE, issued coins showing a divine archer holding a bow and arrow. Turn the coin over and Shri, the goddess of good fortune, sits on a lotus.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Coin with Figure of an Archer (reverse)

title: A Souvenir From Kalighat Temple
text: Around 1890, pilgrims visiting the Hindu temple at Kalighat in Kolkata could buy a painting to remember their trip and adorn a home altar. In this one, Rama sits crowned beside Sita, home after 14 years of exile and her rescue from the island of Lanka. His green-skinned brother Lakshmana holds a royal flywhisk, while the monkey general Hanuman lies flat before the couple in humble devotion.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Rama and Sita enthroned (recto), from a Kalighat album

title: Tea Buds in an Emperor's Tomb
place: Han Yangling Mausoleum, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China
text: Pit 15 beside the tomb of Han Emperor Jing, who died in 141 BCE, held a thick layer of millet, rice and other crops for the afterlife. Mixed in was a dark brown brick of tiny leaves. Plant crystals and chemical markers showed they were tea buds, the oldest physical tea yet found. Tea in a western Tibetan grave shows the drink had crossed the plateau by about 200 CE.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Earliest tea as evidence for one branch of the Silk Road across the Tibetan Plateau

title: A Times Table on Bamboo Strips
text: Around 2008, Tsinghua University received nearly 2,500 muddy, mouldy bamboo strips, probably looted from a tomb and bought at a Hong Kong market. Twenty-one strips held only numbers. Put in order, they formed a grid for multiplying any whole or half number from 0.5 to 99.5, the oldest known decimal times table. Officials probably used this ancient calculator to work out land areas, harvests and taxes.

source.name: Nature News: Ancient times table hidden in Chinese bamboo strips

title: Stone Age Dentists With Flint Drills
text: In an early farming village's graveyard, researchers found eleven molars from nine adults with tiny holes drilled into them. Smoothed edges show the owners kept chewing afterwards, so they were alive when it happened. Some holes sat over decay. Flint drill heads turn up with the village's beads, and a reconstructed flint-tipped bow drill bored a similar hole in enamel in under a minute. The custom lasted about 1,500 years.

source.name: Nature: Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry

title: Fish Suppers in the First Pots
place: Torihama shell midden, Wakasa, Fukui, Japan
text: Some of the world's oldest pottery was made by Japanese hunter-gatherers at the end of the Ice Age, long before farming. Scientists scraped tiny 20-milligram crusts of burnt food from 101 pots at 13 sites, including Torihama. The chemistry pointed to fish and other river or sea creatures. Pots were rare and small then, perhaps kept for special cooking rather than everyday meals.

source.name: Nature: Earliest evidence for the use of pottery

title: Betel Chewing Hidden in Tooth Plaque
text: Millions of people in Asia and the Pacific still chew areca nut, the seed often called betel nut, for a mild buzz. At a Bronze Age cemetery in central Thailand, scientists tested 36 samples of hardened dental plaque from six burials. One woman's molar held arecoline and arecaidine, chemicals from the nut. Surprisingly, her teeth showed no red-black stains, the usual giveaway of a betel chewer.

source.name: Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology: Earliest direct evidence of Bronze Age betel nut use

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Dental Analysis Reveals Earliest Evidence of Chewing Psychoactive Betel Seeds

title: A 5,000-Year-Old Beer Recipe
text: Two deep pits at a Yangshao farming village held a complete brewing kit: wide-mouthed pots, funnels, pointed jars and a pottery stove for keeping the mash warm. Yellow residue inside revealed the recipe. Broomcorn millet, Job's tears, tubers and barley were fermented together. That barley is about 1,000 years older than any other found in China, hinting that beer helped bring the grain east.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Revealing a 5,000-y-old beer recipe in China

title: The World's Oldest Cheese
place: Xiaohe Cemetery, Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China
text: Desert burials at Xiaohe preserved mummies with strange white lumps smeared on their heads and necks. Ancient DNA finally identified them as kefir cheese, made about 3,600 years ago with the same kinds of bacteria and yeast found in kefir grains today. People here kept cow and goat milk in separate batches. Their bacteria resemble Tibetan strains, challenging the idea that kefir began only in the Caucasus.

source.name: EurekAlert (Cell Press): World's oldest cheese reveals origins of kefir

title: A Rich Family's Wormy Toilet
text: Toilets were rare luxuries in Jerusalem 2,700 years ago, so a stone toilet seat in the garden of a grand villa marked its owners as wealthy. Sediment from the cesspit below told a less glamorous story. It held eggs of intestinal worms that cause stomach pain, nausea and diarrhoea, possibly spread by human waste used as fertiliser or by undercooked meat. Being rich did not keep this family healthy.

source.name: Tel Aviv University: Health Revelations from Ancient Jerusalem

title: A Sumerian Pub With a Fridge
text: Just 19 inches under the surface of the Sumerian city of Lagash, archaeologists found a public eatery with an open-air dining area, benches, an oven, leftover food and a clay refrigerator. Digging layer by layer instead of straight down revealed it. The team argues that ordinary townspeople, a kind of ancient middle class, came here to eat outside their homes nearly 5,000 years ago.

source.name: Penn Museum: Penn Museum Researchers Uncover Ancient Tavern in Southern Iraq, Complete with 5,000-Year-Old Fridge

title: Stretchy Wool Pants, 3,000 Years Old
text: A herder buried at Yanghai about 3,000 years ago wore some of the oldest trousers known. Researchers found the coarse wool was woven three different ways. Stretchy twill gave the wearer room to move, tapestry weaving reinforced patterned knee panels, and a third technique made a thick waistband. Zigzag stripes ran around the calves, mixing designs that wandering herders brought together in the Tarim Basin.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Turfan Man's Innovative Trousers Analyzed

title: A 14-Sided Die for Drinking Games
text: Mud beside Wolji Pond, a royal pleasure garden of Unified Silla, gave up a wooden die with 14 faces: six rhombuses and eight hexagons. Each face carried a dare in Chinese characters, such as 'drink three glasses of liquor at once', 'sing and drink alone' or 'ask someone to sing'. Sadly the original was lost during conservation, so museum visitors now see a replica.

source.name: Gyeongju National Museum (Google Arts & Culture): Dice

title: Dumplings Packed for the Afterlife
text: Turpan's bone-dry desert preserved real meals in graves dug between the 3rd and 9th centuries. Families left cakes in five different shapes, a lump of millet porridge and dumplings, plus little bags and jars of grain. Under the microscope, the dumplings turned out to be made of wheat with foxtail millet. One tomb even held a pillow stuffed with wheat and barley straw.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Archaeobotanical Study of Ancient Food and Cereal Remains at the Astana Cemeteries, Xinjiang, China

title: Planning Lambs for Winter Milk
place: Dzhankent, Syr Darya delta, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: Dzhankent, a Silk Road town near the Aral Sea, faced freezing Siberian winds in winter and scorching dry summers. Isotopes in the teeth of 16 sheep show how townspeople coped. They fed flocks cut, dried grass in lean times, brought in animals from elsewhere and bred ewes across the year, not just in spring. That kept milk flowing for dried, salted cheese curds, much like the qurt Kazakhs eat today.

source.name: EurekAlert (University of Michigan): What sheep's teeth can tell us about life in a medieval Kazakhstan town

title: Southeast Asia's Oldest Curry
text: Cooks in the Funan kingdom ground spices on stone slabs. Scientists tested 40 grinding and pounding tools from Óc Eo and found microscopic starch from turmeric, ginger, galangal, clove, nutmeg and cinnamon on 12 of them. Some spices had crossed oceans to get there. The largest slab, 76 centimetres long, dates to around 207 to 326 CE. Vietnamese curry today still uses many of the same spices.

source.name: The Conversation: Researchers find evidence of a 2,000-year-old curry, the oldest ever found in Southeast Asia

title: The First Farmed Bananas Reach Sri Lanka
text: For tens of thousands of years, people sheltering in Fahien Cave ate wild rainforest foods: breadfruit, durians, canarium nuts, palms, bamboo and seedy wild bananas. Then, in layers about 6,000 years old, tiny silica particles from cultivated bananas appear, and wild banana traces drop sharply. Domesticated bananas first show up in New Guinea, so they probably crossed the sea to Sri Lanka within about 800 years.

source.name: The Conversation: Prehistoric people started to spread domesticated bananas across the world 6,000 years ago

title: Baby Rattles From the Pottery Market
text: Excavators at Hama found 19 small clay objects with pebbles or clay bits rattling inside. They were long filed as musical instruments, but their sound is too low and their handles too tiny for adult hands. They fit a small child's grip perfectly. The clay matches the town's professional pottery, so the rattles were likely mass-produced and sold at market beside cups and bowls 4,500 years ago.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Baby Rattles Were Mass-Produced in Bronze Age Syria

title: Grandparents on the Ground Floor
text: A two-storey house at Tel 'Eton burned during an Assyrian campaign in the 8th century BCE. Studying its rooms and objects, archaeologists concluded that three generations lived there. The senior couple apparently slept downstairs in the largest room, sparing them the ladders, with a view over the courtyard and every doorway. Burnt cedar may come from a special chair, and a footbath could have soothed aching feet.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Iron Age Dwelling in Israel Offers "Archaeology of the Elderly"

title: Wax Notebooks Thrown Down a Well
text: Most Assyrian writing was pressed into clay, but some scribes used reusable boards of wood and wax. When Nimrud was sacked in 612 BCE, a set was tossed into a well, where the airless water preserved them. British Museum scientists found walnut wood coated with beeswax mixed with a quarter orpiment, a yellow mineral that firmed the wax. It also contains arsenic, which may have kept mould away.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Study Reveals Secrets of Neo-Assyrian Beeswax Writing Tablets

title: A Mughal Storm Drain Reopened
place: Delhi Gate, Red Fort, Delhi, India
text: Shah Jahan began his red sandstone fortress in Delhi in 1639, and its rainwater had to go somewhere. The Archaeological Survey of India uncovered a covered drain paved with stones and roofed by an arch of thin fired bricks, running from the fort's Delhi Gate to the moat. In 2020 workers began clearing its silt and strengthening it, so it could carry rainwater once again.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Seventeenth-Century Drain Discovered in Delhi

title: Pepper, Grapes and a Lone Clove
text: Soil from the old port of Mantai holds the crumbs of a global kitchen. Researchers found local rice, charred black pepper from around 600 to 700 CE, plus grape seeds and wheat that cannot grow in Sri Lanka's tropical climate and probably came from the Mediterranean world. One clove, dated around 900 to 1100, had travelled over 4,000 miles from Indonesia. Spices rarely survive in the ground.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Sri Lanka's Ancient Cosmopolitan Cuisine

title: Ivory Carvers' Rubbish Heaps
text: Beside 800-year-old workshops in the port of Banbhore, archaeologists found dumps holding nearly 90 pounds of elephant ivory scraps. Islamic-era craftsmen probably carved rings and chess pieces from ivory brought in from India, for sale abroad. In return, the town imported glassware from the Near East, pottery from India, Iran and Iraq, and Chinese porcelain. Only a small part of the industrial quarter has been dug.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Islamic-Era Ivory Workshops Found in Pakistan

title: This Jug Belongs to Sagkina
text: At Khalkajar, archaeologists from the National Museum of Tajikistan found a two-handled pottery jug from the Kushan Empire. A faint painted line in the Bactrian language reads: 'This water jug belongs to the woman Sagkina.' It is a rare glimpse of an ordinary household and a woman's name. Labelling everyday belongings suggests that reading and writing were fairly common in the region.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Unique Ancient Vessel Labeled with Woman's Name Unearthed in Tajikistan

title: Black Teeth as a Beauty Mark
text: In Vietnam, glossy black teeth were long a sign of beauty. To learn how old the custom is, scientists examined stained teeth from burials at Dong Xa, a late Dong Son site. Iron and sulfur in the enamel point to iron salts heated with tannin-rich plant extracts, making a black paste applied over several weeks. It was deliberate cosmetics, not betel stains, at least 2,000 years ago.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Cosmetic Tooth Blackening Dates Back 2,000 Years in Vietnam

title: Stripping Bamboo for String
text: Plants rot, so early weaving is hard to spot. At Tabon Cave, researchers compared tiny wear marks on three stone tools, 33,000 to 39,000 years old, with marks on tools that people use today to strip bamboo and palm into fibres. They matched. That means the cave's residents could make cords for tying and weaving, enough for baskets, traps, ropes for houses and boats, and bowstrings.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Study Pushes Back Processing of Plant Fibers in Southeast Asia

title: Singapore's Community Dining Rooms
text: In 2020 UNESCO added Singapore's hawker culture to its list of the world's intangible heritage. Hawker centres grew out of street food and now act as community dining rooms, where people of every background meet over breakfast, lunch and dinner, and even play chess or busk. Hawkers blend Chinese, Malay, Indian and other traditions. Some of the oldest began in the 1960s, often perfecting a single dish for decades.

source.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Hawker culture in Singapore

title: An Orangutan Cousin by the Ayeyarwady
place: Irrawaddy Formation, south of Magway, Magway Region, Myanmar
text: Around ten million years ago, a great ape lived in a humid evergreen forest on a floodplain in what is now central Myanmar. Its lower jaw, found by a villager near Magway, was named Khoratpithecus ayeyarwadyensis. Like today's orangutans, the jaw lacks the mark of one particular chin muscle, a quirk otherwise known only in orangutans and a Thai cousin. Its canine root hints it was male.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC): First hominoid from the Late Miocene of the Irrawaddy Formation (Myanmar)

title: Brunei's Rainforest Giants Go Way Back
text: Four to five million years ago, Brunei's coast was lined with fern swamps and mangroves near lowland rainforest. Fossil leaves pressed into clay at Berakas Beach and Kampong Lugu show that dipterocarps, the giant trees that rule Borneo's forests today, were already the most common trees. Oddly, their pollen makes up under one percent of the same rocks, so only the leaves revealed their reign.

source.name: PeerJ (PMC): First fossil-leaf floras from Brunei Darussalam show dipterocarp dominance in Borneo by the Pliocene

title: The Space Rock Hidden Under Lava
text: About 789,000 years ago, a space rock slammed into what is now southern Laos. Scientists traced the likely crater to the Bolaven Plateau, where it now lies buried under younger lava flows. Around it spreads a jumbled layer of boulders and pebbles, more than nine metres thick in places, topped with glassy beads called tektites. This impact threw out the most extensive spray of debris known on Earth.

source.name: PMC: Proximal ejecta of the Bolaven extraterrestrial impact, southern Laos

title: Surgery in a Borneo Cave
place: Liang Tebo, Sangkulirang-Mangkalihat karst, East Kalimantan, Indonesia
text: About 31,000 years ago in a Borneo cave, someone performed surgery. A young person buried at Liang Tebo had lost the lower third of the left leg, cut cleanly in childhood. The bone healed, and they lived at least six to nine more years, so their community must have cared for them in steep limestone country. It is the oldest known amputation, roughly 24,000 years older than the previous record.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Surgical amputation of a limb 31,000 years ago in Borneo

title: Ice Age Foragers Hooked on Betel
place: Leang Bulu Bettue, Maros, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Long before farming, foragers in Sulawesi had a habit. A person buried at Leang Bulu Bettue, who lived sometime between 25,000 and 16,000 years ago, has odd rounded grooves worn around the teeth. Chemists found arecoline, betel nut's stimulant, on a tooth. With no staining and no lime, researchers think whole nuts were sucked for hours, perhaps for a buzz or to ease pain.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Betel nut sucking is the earliest recorded evidence for the habitual use of a neuroactive plant drug

title: A Fatal Wound in a Tràng An Cave
place: Thung Binh 1 cave, Tràng An, Ninh Bình, Vietnam
text: About 12,000 years ago, a man of around 35 died in a cave among the limestone towers of Tràng An. His near-complete skeleton, TBH1, shows a broken extra neck rib that became infected, probably from a narrow penetrating blow. A tiny quartz point lay by his neck and shoulder. He may have lived a few months more. It is the earliest hint of interpersonal violence in mainland Southeast Asia.

source.name: PMC: TBH1: 12 000-year-old human skeleton and projectile point shed light on demographics and mortality in Terminal Pleistocene Southeast Asia

title: A Toalean Teenager's Lost Lineage
place: Leang Panninge, Mallawa, Maros, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: About 7,200 years ago, a young woman of 17 or 18 was buried curled up in Leang Panninge cave, with large cobbles placed over her head, hands and hips. She belonged to the Toalean foragers, known for tiny stone points called Maros points, and two lay beside her. Her DNA revealed a previously unknown human lineage with Denisovan ancestry. No living group carries it.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Genome of a middle Holocene hunter-gatherer from Wallacea

title: Marble Bracelets on a Limestone Terrace
place: Sab Champa, near the Pa Sak River, central Thailand
text: On a limestone terrace in central Thailand, people lived at Sab Champa for well over a thousand years. During its Iron Age, roughly 500 BCE to 570 CE, they obtained glass beads and sea shells, and a workshop about two kilometres away turned out white marble disks and bracelets. Later, Dvaravati builders ringed the site, 834 by 704 metres, with a moat between two high walls.

source.name: Antiquity Project Gallery (Cambridge): Late prehistoric and early historic archaeology in the Central Highland of Thailand: excavation at the site of Sab Champa

title: Where the Pyu Actually Lived
place: Yahanda mound, Sri Ksetra (Hmawza), near Pyay, Myanmar
text: Pyu cities in Myanmar are famous for their brick monuments, but where did ordinary people live? In 2015, test pits on Yahanda mound at Sri Ksetra found hardened work floors with cooking charcoal, iron nails and food scraps, used from about the 400s to the 600s CE. Downslope lay a wooden house floor, and one of its posts stood right on top of a cremation burial.

source.name: Antiquity Project Gallery (Cambridge): Early urban archaeology in Southeast Asia: the first evidence for a Pyu habitation site at Sri Ksetra, Myanmar

title: Krishna Holds Up a Mountain
place: Phnom Da, near Angkor Borei, Takéo Province, Cambodia
text: Around 600 CE, sculptors near the city of Angkor Borei carved eight huge Hindu gods, each from a single block of stone, for a two-peaked hill rising from the Mekong floodplain. One shows Krishna lifting a whole mountain to shelter villagers and herds from storms sent by a jealous older god. Just a fragment of it weighs about 196 kilograms, and its pierced earlobes once held gold earrings.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Upper stele with hand for Krishna Lifting Mount Govardhan

title: A Planet Guards a Cham Monastery
place: Đồng Dương, Thăng Bình, Quảng Nam, Vietnam
text: In 875, according to Sanskrit inscriptions, a Mahayana Buddhist temple and monastery was founded at Đồng Dương in the Cham lands of central Vietnam. Among its guardians were the planets in human form. One survives as a seated sandstone king of the heavens, mustached and frowning, gripping a short dagger. Below him, a monster face called a kirtimukha spits out jewels and plants, promising abundance to worshippers.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Enthroned planetary deity

title: Eight Heads, Sixteen Arms, One Dance
text: Around 1200, when King Jayavarman VII made Tantric Buddhism public across the Khmer empire, a caster made this bronze Hevajra: a god with eight heads, sixteen arms and four legs, dancing on a corpse that stands for ignorance. His hands hold skull cups filled with animals and Hindu gods. Clay in its core points to northeastern Thailand. It survived inside a clay pot under water.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Hevajra

title: A Fisherman Snags a Thai Cargo
text: In March 2012, a fisherman off the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia kept snagging broken pottery in his fishing gear. He had found a 16th-century shipwreck, now called the Bidong wreck, loaded mostly with stoneware attributed to the Thai kingdoms of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. Recent tests match the pots' clay to red clays of the Sukhothai region, and copper traces hint at corroded fittings or cargo.

source.name: PMC: Reflectance spectroscopy reveals mineralogy and preservation of ceramics from the Bidong Shipwreck

title: Rice Terraces as Resistance
place: Old Kiyyangan Village, Kiangan, Ifugao, Philippines
text: For decades, books said the Ifugao rice terraces of Luzon were 2,000 years old, a figure guessed by early 20th-century anthropologists. Excavations at Kiangan tell another story: rice appears only about 675 years ago and surges roughly 500 years ago, around when the Spanish arrived. The excavators see the terraces as a way of resisting colonial rule, though the National Museum disputes the new dating.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Letter From the Philippines, One Grain at a Time

title: Charcoal Warriors in a Refuge Cave
place: Gua Sireh, Gunung Nambi, near Serian, Sarawak, Malaysia
text: Inside Gua Sireh, a cave in western Sarawak, two charcoal figures taller than 75 centimetres loom on the wall, one seemingly gripping a knife in each hand. Radiocarbon dating places them around 1670 to 1710 and 1800 to 1830, an era of raids and heavy tolls on local Bidayuh people. An 1855 account says defenders once drove off attackers by rolling stones from the cave mouth.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Rock art and frontier conflict in Southeast Asia: Insights from direct radiocarbon ages for the large human figures of Gua Sireh, Sarawak

title: Scripture Written in Black Lacquer
place: Burma (Myanmar); manuscript now in Cleveland, USA
text: In 19th-century Burma, lay Buddhists paid for dazzling manuscripts to be read aloud at monks' ordination ceremonies. This kammavaca has leaves of lacquered cloth, its Pali words written in thick black lacquer in a rounded Burmese script nicknamed tamarind seed script. Gilded winged spirits called nats fly among plants sprouting from serpent shapes that stand for rain clouds, between jewelled covers.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Kammavacha: Buddhist Ordination Text

title: A Blouse Woven From Pineapple
place: Philippines; panel now in Cleveland, USA
text: This delicate, see-through panel from the late-1800s Philippines is woven from piña, fibre from the pineapple plant, which the Spanish brought to the islands in the 1500s. Embroiderers added pairs of flower bouquets in baskets with trailing bows, plus fine needle lace around an oval neck opening. The edges were never finished: it was meant to be sewn into a baro-camisa blouse.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Blouse front

title: From Allies to Enemies in Manila
text: On 4 February 1899, fighting broke out between US troops and Filipino nationalists led by Emilio Aguinaldo, two days before the US Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris. Americans called it an 'insurrection', while Filipinos saw resistance to a new foreign invader. Over 20,000 Filipino fighters and 4,200 Americans died, and as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians perished from violence, famine and disease.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Philippine-American War, 1899-1902

title: A Neutral Laos, on Paper
place: Vientiane, Laos (declaration agreed in Geneva, Switzerland)
text: On 23 July 1962, fourteen nations, including the US, the USSR, China and both Vietnams, agreed in Geneva that Laos would be neutral and that all foreign troops would leave. It soon unravelled. North Vietnam's showcase withdrawal began with just 15 soldiers, and it kept backing the communist Pathet Lao. The US pulled out its advisers but later backed Hmong and Thai forces.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Laos Crisis, 1960-1963

title: Two Nights in the Gulf of Tonkin
place: Gulf of Tonkin, off northern Vietnam
text: On 2 August 1964, US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin reported an attack by North Vietnamese patrol boats. On 4 August they reported a second one, though doubts later grew about whether it happened at all. The ships had been supporting South Vietnamese raids on the northern coast. Within days Congress passed a resolution, with just two Senate votes against, that underpinned years of war.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Gulf of Tonkin and Escalation, 1964

title: Indonesia's Hidden Massacre
text: In late 1965, after officers of the so-called September 30th Movement kidnapped and killed six senior army generals, Indonesia's army and its allies turned on the Communist Party. From October 1965 to March 1966, up to 500,000 alleged supporters were killed and up to a million imprisoned. US embassy cables counted at least 100,000 dead by December. General Suharto went on to rule for 32 years.

source.name: National Security Archive (George Washington University): Indonesia Mass Murder 1965, U.S. Embassy Files

title: Tet: Attack at the New Year
place: US Embassy, Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City), Vietnam
text: In late January 1968, during the Tet lunar new year holiday, communist forces launched surprise attacks on targets across South Vietnam, including the cities of Saigon and Huế. In Saigon, fighters breached the outer walls of the US Embassy. The psychological shock was huge. On 31 March, President Lyndon Johnson limited bombing of the North, capped troop levels and said he would not seek another term.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Tet Offensive, 1968

title: A Green Light Over Jakarta
text: On 6 December 1975, US President Gerald Ford and Henry Kissinger met Indonesia's President Suharto in Jakarta. When Suharto raised East Timor, Ford said the US would understand and not press him. Kissinger urged that whatever Indonesia did should succeed quickly. The next day Indonesia invaded. By 1980 the occupation had caused more than 100,000 deaths from fighting, starvation and disease.

source.name: National Security Archive (George Washington University): East Timor Revisited, Ford, Kissinger and the Indonesian Invasion, 1975-76

title: Seed Pods Bound With Bomb Wire
text: In 2015, Cambodian artist Sopheap Pich and a team of artisans in Phnom Penh wove a giant pair of seed pods from hand-shaved bamboo and rattan. The smaller pod leans toward the larger one, as if for comfort. The steel wire holding them together was recycled from bombs and mines left from Cambodia's wars of the 1970s and 1980s, and the hollow forms recall hunger under the Khmer Rouge.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Sopheap Pich, Seed Pods

title: An Earthquake Uncovers a Water Palace
text: In 2025, a major earthquake split open the ground at Inwa, once called Ratnapura Ava and a royal capital from the 1300s to the 1800s. The rift exposed a whole building complex, with foundations, stairways and traces of pavilions, from the Konbaung dynasty of 1752 to 1885. Archaeologists suspect a royal water palace for ceremonies, like those painted in palm-leaf manuscripts.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Earthquake in Myanmar Exposes Ancient Royal Structure

title: A Young Canyon in Ancient Rock
place: Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
text: The Grand Canyon looks ancient, but the gorge itself is young. The Colorado River began cutting down only 5 to 6 million years ago, slicing through rocks far older than itself: the top layer is 270 million years old, and the inner gorge holds rocks about 1.8 billion years old. A steep slope, big floods and a dry climate let the river carve astonishingly fast.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Grand Canyon Geology

title: A Crater Hiding Under Chesapeake Bay
place: Lower Chesapeake Bay, near Cape Charles, Virginia, USA
text: About 35 million years ago, a space rock roughly 2 to 3 miles wide slammed into the shallow sea shelf off what is now Virginia. It blasted out a crater about 90 kilometres across, now buried under 1,000 to 1,500 feet of rubble and sea sediment beneath the lower Chesapeake Bay. USGS scientist Wylie Poag uncovered it using drill cores and seismic surveys of the seabed.

source.name: USGS: Chesapeake Bay Meteorite Impact Crater

source2.name: USGS Virginia and West Virginia Water Science Center: The Chesapeake Bay Impact Crater

title: Lava Rivers That Reached the Pacific
place: Rowena Crest, Columbia River Gorge, Oregon, USA
text: Beginning about 16.7 million years ago, long cracks in the ground of eastern Oregon, Washington and Idaho poured out more than 350 lava flows. Many single flows held over 1,000 cubic kilometres of molten rock, and some crossed the Cascades all the way to the Pacific Ocean. Piled up to 4,000 metres thick, the layers now line the Columbia River Gorge like pages in a giant book.

source.name: USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory: Columbia River Basalt Group Stretches from Oregon to Idaho

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service: Fissure Volcanoes

title: Forty Thousand Columns of Cooled Lava
place: Giant's Causeway, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, UK
text: About 60 million years ago, as the North Atlantic was beginning to open, lava flooded across what is now Northern Ireland. Thick flows cooled, shrank and cracked into some 40,000 tidy basalt columns, the stepping stones of the Giant's Causeway. New dating shows all of Northern Ireland's volcanic rocks formed in just 5.5 million years, eight million fewer than geologists once believed.

source.name: British Geological Survey: Scientists make new discovery in the history of the Giant's Causeway

title: The Continent That Sank Out of Sight
place: Zealandia, highest point Aoraki / Mount Cook, New Zealand
text: About 84 million years ago, a long ribbon of land tore away from the supercontinent Gondwana. It had been stretched thin before breaking free, so it sank: today about 94% of its 4.9 million square kilometres lies underwater. In 2017 geologists argued it is Earth's seventh continent, Zealandia, the youngest, thinnest and most submerged of all. New Zealand is among the few bits still above the waves.

source.name: GSA Today (Mortimer et al. 2017): Zealandia: Earth's Hidden Continent

title: How Old Is the Sahara?
text: When did the Sahara become a desert? Most scientists said 2 to 3 million years ago, but petrified sand dunes in Chad, dated by nearby fossils, hinted at about 7 million. In 2014 climate modellers offered a cause: the shrinking Tethys Sea, ancestor of the Mediterranean, weakened the monsoon rains reaching North Africa. Not everyone is convinced; one desert geologist called it "numerical speculation."

source.name: Science News: Shrinking ancient sea may have spawned Sahara Desert

title: The Flood That Refilled the Mediterranean
place: Malta Escarpment, Ionian Sea, off south-east Sicily, Italy
text: After the Mediterranean had partly dried out, the Atlantic came roaring back about 5.3 million years ago. Water spilling east through a gateway in south-eastern Sicily plunged into the eastern basin, whose surface may have sat up to 2,400 metres below today's sea level. Seismic surveys have found the leftover heap: up to 860 metres thick and over 1,400 cubic kilometres, perhaps Earth's largest megaflood deposit.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Micallef et al. 2018): Evidence of the Zanclean megaflood in the eastern Mediterranean Basin

title: Twin Craters That Weren't Twins
text: About 14.8 million years ago an asteroid blasted out the Nördlinger Ries, a crater about 24 kilometres wide in southern Germany. Only 40 kilometres away lies the much smaller Steinheim Basin, and for decades textbooks called them twins made by a split asteroid. But two separate earthquake-shaken layers in nearby sediments suggest Steinheim's impact came roughly half a million to 800,000 years later.

source.name: Scientific Reports (2022): Event- and biostratigraphic evidence for two independent Ries and Steinheim asteroid impacts in the Middle Miocene

title: Patagonia's Towers Were Born Underground
place: Torres del Paine National Park, Magallanes, Chile
text: The famous granite towers of Torres del Paine began as molten rock squeezed between layers 2 to 3 kilometres underground, about 12.5 million years ago. Precise dating shows the granite arrived in at least three batches, followed by dark sheets of mafic magma slipped in beneath, all within about 150,000 years, a blink in geological time. Erosion later stripped away the rock above and exposed the roof.

source.name: European Journal of Mineralogy (2020): Contact metamorphism and the assembly of the Torres del Paine intrusive complex

source2.name: University of Bristol Research: Time resolved construction of a bimodal laccolith (Torres del Paine, Patagonia)

title: Pebbles That Sat Still for Ages
place: Coastal Cordillera above Quebrada de Jazpampa, Atacama Desert, Chile
text: Quartz pebbles lying on flat ground in Chile's Atacama Desert have barely moved for tens of millions of years. By measuring neon made inside them by cosmic rays, scientists found 32 of 135 had sat at the surface since before the Miocene, one perhaps for 62 million years. They argue the desert's core turned hyperarid by the Mid to Late Eocene, as Earth cooled.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): Evidence for Eocene aridification of the Atacama Desert's hyperarid core

title: A Tibetan Valley Climbs Two Kilometres
place: Meiduo Village, Luolong County, Tibet, China
text: Today the Luolong Basin in eastern Tibet sits 3,600 to 5,200 metres high. Yet between about 54 and 46 million years ago it lay only around 600 metres up, covered in dry scrub. By roughly 44 million years ago it had risen to about 2.9 kilometres, where palms, laurels, oaks and willows grew together. Scientists collected 2,387 fossils from that forest, including leaves, insects and fish.

source.name: National Science Review (2025): The raising and westward expansion of central Tibet

title: Scandinavian Boulders Reach the Netherlands
text: About 2.4 million years ago, a great ice sheet spread out of Scandinavia and carried boulders all the way to what is now the Netherlands. Granites from Åland and Finland and sandstones from Bornholm and Öland lie in gravels near the town of Hattem. New dating of these rocks shows Europe's first big ice sheet grew more than a million years earlier than once thought.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): A continental-scale Eurasian ice sheet 2.4 million years ago

title: Arabia Starts Tearing Away from Africa
place: Tihama Asir complex, east of the Jizan coastal plain, Saudi Arabia
text: About 26 million years ago, Arabia was beginning to tear away from Africa. A mantle plume under Afar had weakened the crust, and magma flooded into it, leaving gabbros and dike swarms thousands of kilometres long beside today's Red Sea coast. A 2025 study argues this magma actually patched and thickened the stretching crust, delaying true seafloor spreading in the southern Red Sea until about 5 million years ago.

source.name: Nature Communications (2025): Magmatic underplating and crustal intrusions accommodate extension during Red Sea continental rifting

title: Cave Stones Remember a Wetter Arabia
place: As Sulb Plateau, central Saudi Arabia
text: Beneath the stony As Sulb Plateau of central Saudi Arabia, cave formations grow only when rain soaks the ground above. Dating stalagmites and flowstones from seven caves, with names like Hotel Cave and Mossy Cave, scientists found wet spells stretching back to 7.44 million years ago. Fossils of about the same age from the nearby UAE show crocodiles and hippos once lived in what is now desert.

source.name: Nature (2025): Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past 8 million years

title: The Aleutian Volcano Chain Is Born
place: Agattu Island forearc, western Aleutian Islands, Alaska, USA
text: About 56 million years ago or earlier, the Pacific seafloor began diving beneath what became the Aleutian Islands, a volcanic arc now nearly 4,000 kilometres long. Researchers dredged basalts from the seabed near Agattu Island and dated them to about 55.6 million years, far older than most earlier estimates. The change came as the whole Pacific Plate swung from heading west-northwest to heading north.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): Tectonic and climatic implications of the Aleutian Arc initiation 56 million years ago

title: A Weak Start for Earth's Mightiest Current
place: Drake Passage, between South America and Antarctica
text: When Antarctica first froze over, about 33.7 million years ago, new ocean gaps had opened at the Tasman Gateway and Drake Passage. Yet climate simulations suggest the current circling Antarctica, today Earth's strongest, was still feeble. The gaps did not line up with the westerly winds, so the flow reached only about 35% of its pre-industrial strength, and a shallow seaway even cut off the Antarctic Peninsula.

source.name: PNAS (2026): Configuration of circum-Antarctic circulation at the last green- to icehouse climate transition

title: The Sharp Turn in Hawaii's Volcano Trail
text: On the floor of the northwest Pacific, the trail of volcanoes left by the Hawaiian hotspot makes a sharp 60° turn, formed about 47 million years ago. For decades geologists argued over whether the Pacific Plate changed direction or the hotspot itself wandered. A 2025 computer study says both mattered: the hotspot drifted south and also west, and the westward drift alone adds about 20° to the bend.

source.name: PNAS (2025): Dynamics of longitudinal Hawaiian hotspot motion and the formation of the Hawaiian-Emperor Bend

title: Volcanoes That Took the Ocean's Breath
place: Mentelle Basin, off south-west Western Australia
text: About 94 million years ago, in a super-hot world with exceptionally high seas, oxygen ran short across much of the ocean. What set it off? Drill cores from the Mentelle Basin off Western Australia hold pulses of mercury, an element volcanoes release in vast amounts, just before and during the crisis. The likely culprit: huge eruptions building the Kerguelen Plateau in the southern Indian Ocean.

source.name: Nature Communications (2024): Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 triggered by Kerguelen volcanism

title: Why Turkana Dodged the Lava Floods
text: Around 31 to 29 million years ago, one to two kilometres of lava piled up on the Ethiopian Plateau, fed by a plume of hot mantle rising beneath East Africa. Just to the south, the Turkana Depression sat on thin crust left by an older failed rift, an obvious weak spot. Yet seismic surveys show it largely escaped: its old rift had become drained and stiff, not weak.

source.name: Nature (2025): The importance of past rifting in large igneous province development

title: Rivers That Stole Their Way to Canyons
text: Along the northeastern edge of the high Andean Plateau in Peru, rivers have sawn canyons 2 to 3 kilometres deep, the largest being San Gabán. Modelling suggests the trick was capture: once mountain-building slowed after about 10 million years ago, rivers ate back into closed, inward-draining basins on the plateau and grabbed their water. Captures around 7 to 5 and 3.5 to 0.5 million years ago supercharged erosion.

source.name: Science Advances (2025): Drivers of canyon incision in the Peruvian Andes

title: Monsoon Secrets in Maldives Mud
place: Maldives Inner Sea (IODP Site U1467), Maldives
text: The Maldives' double row of atolls encloses a sheltered inner sea that rivers barely reach, so mostly windblown dust settles there. Drilling 708 metres into its mud, scientists traced dust from northeastern Africa and Arabia carried by summer monsoon winds. The record suggests the South Asian summer monsoon winds have weakened in two steps since about 12 million years ago, as ice sheets grew.

source.name: Nature Communications (2023): Weakening of the South Asian summer monsoon linked to interhemispheric ice-sheet growth since 12 Ma

title: Sea Algae Measure Tibet's Rise
place: Honggou section, Qaidam Basin, Qinghai, China
text: Tiny algae usually found only in the sea once lived in an ancient lake in the Qaidam Basin, on Tibet's northern edge, perhaps arriving with a Middle Miocene seawater incursion. Their fatty molecules record water temperature. They show the lake cooled by about 6.6°C in a geologically quick burst, either around 11 or 7.7 million years ago, meaning the basin rose roughly 1.5 kilometres.

source.name: Science Advances (2025): Terrestrial temperature history reveals Late Miocene rapid uplift of the northern Tibetan Plateau

title: Where the Loess Plateau's Red Dust Came From
place: Chaona section, Loess Plateau, Gansu, China
text: On China's Loess Plateau, reddish dust layers called the Red Clay were piling up by about 8 million years ago. Scientists long read them as a sign of inner Asia drying out. But dating tiny zircon crystals from the Chaona section showed much of the dust came from the Qilian Mountains and eastern lowlands, eroded by stronger summer monsoon rains. Meanwhile dust reaching the North Pacific rose about tenfold.

source.name: Science Advances (2018): Pre-Quaternary decoupling between Asian aridification and high dust accumulation rates

title: The Deep Door Between Two Oceans Shuts
place: Deep basin of the South China Sea (IODP drilling area)
text: Until about 10 million years ago, cold deep water from around Antarctica flowed from the Indian Ocean through gaps among the Indonesian islands into the deep South China Sea, piling up current-built sediment drifts on the seafloor. Drill cores and seismic images show that flow faded when the deep Indonesian Gateway finally closed, cutting the deep link between the Pacific and Indian Oceans and reshuffling global ocean circulation.

source.name: Nature Communications (2024): South China Sea records Late Miocene reorganization of western Pacific deep circulation

title: Malta's Cliffs Record a Cooling World
text: At Ras il-Pellegrin on Malta, the cliff layers change from Globigerina Limestone to Blue Clay. That switch, during a cooling step between about 14.7 and 12.8 million years ago when Antarctica's ice expanded, is the official global marker for the start of the Serravallian age. Chemistry in tiny shells shows the sea there then freshened in pulses, as stronger monsoon rains fell over North Africa.

source.name: Science Advances (2026): Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition

title: A Tough Jaw from Borneo's Rainforest
place: West Mouth, Niah Caves, Sarawak, Malaysia
text: In 1957, excavators at Borneo's Niah Caves collected part of a human jaw that later dating placed at about 30,000 to 28,000 years old. It is unusually small yet strikingly robust, its bone thick for its height. Researchers suggest the person chewed hard foods while growing up, perhaps tough dried meat, raw palm or starchy underground roots gathered from the rainforest.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Rare Late Pleistocene-early Holocene human mandibles from the Niah Caves (Sarawak, Borneo)

title: The Americas' Oldest Mountain Hotel?
place: Chiquihuite Cave, Astillero Mountains, Zacatecas, Mexico
text: High in the mountains of northern Mexico, 2,750 metres above sea level, Chiquihuite Cave held nearly 2,000 stone tools and flakes. Dating ties them to between about 30,000 and 25,000 years ago, 15,000 years earlier than many accept for people in the Americas. No human DNA was found, so visitors probably stayed briefly. Critics doubt the tools are human-made or correctly dated.

source.name: EurekAlert (University of Cambridge): Earliest humans stayed at the Americas 'oldest hotel' in Mexican cave

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Possible Ice Age Stone Tools Found in Mexico

title: Pendants Made from Giant Sloth Bones
place: Santa Elina rock shelter, Mato Grosso, Brazil
text: In a rock shelter in central Brazil, archaeologists found thousands of bony skin plates from an extinct giant ground sloth. Three stood out: someone had drilled and polished holes through them, probably to wear as pendants. They came from a layer dated to about 27,000 to 25,000 years ago, alongside stone tools. If that holds, people reached South America far earlier than many experts accept.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Sloth Bone Study Pushes Back Human Occupation of Brazil

title: A Beach Camp Far from the Sea
place: Pathirajawela, Bundala National Park, Southern Province, Sri Lanka
text: Today Pathirajawela sits just 200 metres from Sri Lanka's southern shore. When people first camped here about 25,000 years ago, falling seas were pushing the coast away, until at the Ice Age peak it lay roughly 22 kilometres off. Their quartz tools came first; tiny backed microliths appear only from about 14,000 years ago. It is Sri Lanka's earliest well-dated open-air coastal site.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Early Sri Lankan coastal site tracks technological change and estuarine resource exploitation over the last ca. 25,000 years

title: A Cut-Marked Jaw in the Yukon
place: Bluefish Caves, Keele Range, Yukon, Canada
text: In three small caves in Canada's northern Yukon, a horse jawbone carries the fine cuts of a stone tool. Radiocarbon dating puts it at about 24,000 years old, during the coldest stretch of the Ice Age. If the marks are human work, as the researchers argue, people were butchering horses, caribou and wapiti in Beringia long before the ice let anyone travel south. Some scientists remain skeptical.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Earliest Human Presence in North America Dated to the Last Glacial Maximum (Bluefish Caves)

title: Staying Put in the Ice Age Desert
place: Karnatukul (Serpent's Glen), Carnarvon Range, Western Australia
text: When the Ice Age peaked, Australia's deserts grew colder and drier, and many experts thought people left them. A rock shelter called Karnatukul, in the Carnarvon Range of the Little Sandy Desert, says otherwise. A layer dated between about 25,000 and 18,000 years ago holds 370 stone artefacts, the first clear proof of people living in the Western Desert at that time.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Karnatukul (Serpent's Glen): A new chronology for the oldest site in Australia's Western Desert

title: DNA in the Dirt of El Mirón
place: El Mirón Cave, Ramales de la Victoria, Cantabria, Spain
text: Scientists sifted DNA straight out of the cave floor at El Mirón in northern Spain and found 28 kinds of animals, 12 of them never seen among the bones. Ice Age layers hold traces of leopards, dholes, wolves, hyenas and woolly rhinos. Human DNA from Solutrean layers, around 24,000 to 22,000 years old, matches other Iberians of that time, a population that held on through the coldest millennia.

source.name: Nature Communications (via PMC): A sedimentary ancient DNA perspective on human and carnivore persistence through the Late Pleistocene in El Mirón Cave, Spain

title: Seafood at the Height of the Ice
place: Waterfall Bluff, Mpondoland, Eastern Cape, South Africa
text: When ice sheets peaked and sea levels fell, many coastlines moved far from where people lived. Not at Waterfall Bluff on South Africa's Wild Coast: the continental shelf there is so narrow that the sea stayed within reach. People kept returning for fish and shellfish through the coldest stretch of the Ice Age, the first direct evidence of coastal foraging in Africa during a glacial maximum.

source.name: EurekAlert (Arizona State University): Ancient people relied on coastal environments to survive the Last Glacial Maximum

title: Butchering a Glyptodont near Buenos Aires
place: Reconquista River, Merlo, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: On the bank of the Reconquista River near Merlo, Argentina, lay the back half of a glyptodont, an armoured giant related to armadillos. Its pelvis, tail bones and shell plates carry 32 cut marks with the V-shaped grooves of stone tools. Dated to about 21,000 years ago, they may be among the earliest signs of people butchering megafauna in South America.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Anthropic cut marks in extinct megafauna bones from the Pampean region (Argentina) at the last glacial maximum

title: Hunters in Spain's Coldest Corner
place: Charco Verde II, Embid, Guadalajara, Spain
text: Winters near Embid in central Spain can still drop to minus 20 °C. Yet a rock shelter here, 1,050 metres up, holds a Magdalenian camp about 21,000 years old, from the peak of the Last Glacial Maximum. Hunters brought back horse and ibex and made tiny backed bladelets for their weapons. The find shows Iberia's cold interior was not abandoned when the ice was at its height.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Human occupations of upland and cold environments in inland Spain during the LGM: Charco Verde II

title: Ice Age String from Hemp
text: On China's Loess Plateau, Ice Age foragers at Shizitan left grinding slabs and flakes that still hold hundreds of microscopic fibres.
