Most are plant bast fibres, probably hemp, and wear traces show stalks being cut, soaked, pounded and scraped between about 28,000 and 18,000 years ago. Some fibres are blue or pink, which researchers think were dyed with plants. People were likely making cord, perhaps cloth.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Unveiling bast fiber production in Upper Paleolithic North China

title: Campfires Above the Ice Age Tree Line
place: Dargan Shelter, Blue Mountains, New South Wales, Australia
text: Archaeologists once assumed Australia's high country was too harsh to live in during the last Ice Age. Dargan Shelter in the Blue Mountains proves otherwise. Sitting 1,073 metres up, about 400 metres above the tree line, it holds hearths, 693 stone artefacts and a sandstone grinding slab, with people returning for some 20,000 years. It is Australia's oldest known high-altitude occupied site.

source.name: EurekAlert (University of Sydney): Australia's oldest occupied Ice Age cave found at high elevation in Blue Mountains

title: A Basque Cave's Ice Age Dog
text: A canid's upper arm bone dug out of Erralla Cave in 1985 waited decades to tell its real story. When geneticists at the University of the Basque Country read its mitochondrial DNA, it matched other dogs known from Magdalenian Europe, not wild wolves. So this 17,000-year-old animal was a domesticated dog, living alongside Ice Age hunter-gatherers thousands of years before anyone farmed.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Early Dog Identified in Spain's Basque Country

title: Senegal's Oldest Stone Age Camps
text: Beside the Falémé River in eastern Senegal, toolmakers sat down about 17,000 to 16,000 years ago and knapped chert into tiny bladelets and crescent-shaped segments. Their camp, near the village of Toumboura, is one of the two oldest Later Stone Age sites known in Senegal. Strangely, people elsewhere in the country were still making much older-style Middle Stone Age tools at the time.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Two new Later Stone Age sites from the Final Pleistocene in the Falémé Valley, eastern Senegal

title: Dart Points Hidden in Idaho Pits
place: Cooper's Ferry (Nipéhe), Salmon River, Idaho, USA
text: On the Salmon River in Idaho, at the ancient Nez Perce village of Nipéhe, people stored complete and broken stone points in pits nearly 16,000 years ago. The 13 points, half an inch to 2 inches long, are about 3,000 years older than Clovis points. Probably tipped onto darts, they closely resemble points from Hokkaido, Japan, made 16,000 to 20,000 years ago.

source.name: Oregon State University: Archaeologists uncover oldest known projectile points in the Americas

title: Fish Caught in Engraved Nets
text: Beside the Rhine at Gönnersdorf, Ice Age hunters scratched hundreds of drawings onto flat slate slabs about 15,800 years ago. Using special lighting, researchers spotted seven new fish among them. On eight slabs, a simple fish sits inside a grid of crossing lines, engraved after the fish itself. The team reads the grids as nets, the first clear evidence of Magdalenian net fishing.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Upper Palaeolithic fishing techniques: Insights from the engraved plaquettes of Gönnersdorf, Germany

title: Puppies Buried Beside People in Anatolia
text: At Pınarbaşı on Turkey's Central Anatolian Plateau, hunter-gatherers buried newborn and young dogs in the same area as their own dead. Ancient DNA shows one of these animals, about 15,800 years old, was a true dog, making it the oldest genome-confirmed dog yet. Isotopes hint that the pups' mothers ate fish, probably fed to them by people.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): Dogs were widely distributed across western Eurasia during the Palaeolithic

source2.name: EurekAlert (University of York): Ancient DNA reveals earliest known dogs lived alongside Ice Age humans

title: Shark Suppers on Peru's Ice Age Coast
place: Huaca Prieta, Chicama Valley, La Libertad, Peru
text: Long before its giant mound was built, this spot on Peru's north coast hosted campers about 15,000 years ago. The sea was then some 30 kilometres away, yet they ate sharks, sea lions, seabirds and fish, probably trapped or clubbed rather than hooked. Among more than a million stone pieces, archaeologists found no carefully shaped spear points at all, only simple flakes knocked from beach cobbles.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Simple technologies and diverse food strategies of the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene at Huaca Prieta

title: A Shared Grave Facing Timor
place: Ratu Mali 2 cave, Kisar Island, Maluku, Indonesia
text: About 15,000 years ago, two people were laid in one shallow grave in a seaside cave on Kisar, a small island north of Timor. Both lay curled on their right sides, facing south toward Timor, with large limestone rocks beside their heads. Shellfish and obsidian flakes filled the grave. Proteins in their tooth enamel revealed that one was a man and the other a woman.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Earliest known funerary rites in Wallacea after the last glacial maximum

title: A Wolf Pup's Last Meal
place: Tumat, Ust-Yansky District, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: A wolf puppy that died near Tumat in northeastern Siberia lay frozen in permafrost until scientists autopsied it. In its stomach was a scrap of meat about 14,400 years old. DNA showed it came from a woolly rhinoceros, one of the youngest ever found. The rhino's genome showed no rise in inbreeding, suggesting the species collapsed quickly, probably as the climate warmed, rather than fading slowly.

source.name: Stockholm University: Woolly rhino genome recovered from Ice Age wolf stomach

title: The Sea Swallows Australia's Northwest
place: Northwest Shelf, Timor Sea, off the Kimberley, Australia
text: At the height of the Ice Age, a vast plain joined the Kimberley to Arnhem Land, with an inland sea, a large freshwater lake and deep gorges. Models suggest it could have supported tens of thousands of people or more. Then a burst of sea-level rise, about 14,500 to 14,100 years ago, and another later, drowned about half of it, pushing people inland.

source.name: EurekAlert (Griffith University): Ancient Sahul's submerged landscapes reveal a mosaic of human habitation

title: Flint Sickles Polished by Wild Grain
text: At Jeftelik, in Syria's Homs Gap, early Natufian foragers built round stone structures about 14,000 years ago. Researchers scanned the glossy edges of 12 flint blades with a confocal microscope and compared them with experimental tools. Five had mostly harvested wild cereals, some after more than 20 hours of use. Yet sickles seem to have been an occasional strategy, not the main way grain was gathered.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Wild cereal harvesting ca. 14,000 years ago at Jeftelik (Western Syria)

title: Island Potters Settle Down
text: On Tanegashima, an island south of Kyushu, early potters were settling down around 14,000 years ago. The Onigano site alone yielded more than 14,000 potsherds, five pit-houses, 370 chipped arrowheads and nearly 400 kilograms of pebble tools. Chemical tests show most pots were made on the island itself. These Incipient Jomon people invested more labour in their camps than islanders ever had before.

source.name: PLOS ONE: More on mobility and sedentism: Upper Paleolithic to Incipient Jomon, Tanegashima Island

title: A Songbird Carved from Burnt Bone
text: Sifting old spoil from a well dug in 1958, archaeologists found a tiny standing songbird just 19 millimetres long. Someone carved it about 13,500 years ago from a piece of bone blackened by heating. Instead of legs it stands on a block-shaped pedestal, and its oversized tail keeps it from tipping forward. It is the oldest known three-dimensional artwork from East Asia.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): A Paleolithic bird figurine from the Lingjing site, Henan, China

title: Gazelle Hunters Beside the Euphrates
text: Before farming, families on Syria's Euphrates lived in pit dwellings at Abu Hureyra and hunted goitered gazelle, probably in mass seasonal culls. Burnt dung in a fireplace from about 12,500 years ago, packed thickest beside one hut, hints that a few live animals, possibly wild sheep, were kept nearby for short spells. The site now lies beneath Lake Assad, flooded after 1974.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Epipalaeolithic animal tending to Neolithic herding at Abu Hureyra, Syria (12,800-7,800 calBP)

title: A Bronze Age City of Seven Ravines
text: Steppe herders were long thought to live on the move, yet around 1600 BCE someone planned a 140-hectare settlement on a promontory above the Irtysh River. Rows of earthen mounds mark multi-room homes, with a much larger building at the centre. On the southeastern edge, crucibles and slag reveal the first firm evidence of large-scale tin-bronze making on the Eurasian steppe, probably using Altai ores.

source.name: Durham University: Archaeologists uncover ancient Bronze Age city in Central Asia

title: The Secret Nuclear Blast in the Urals
place: Mayak nuclear complex, near Ozyorsk, Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia
text: On the afternoon of 29 September 1957, a tank of radioactive waste at the secret Mayak plant overheated unnoticed and exploded, bursting its 160-ton concrete lid. Locals saw strange bluish-violet colours in the sky, which the press called polar lights. More than 11,000 people from over 20 villages were moved and their homes demolished, but the West only learned the details in 1976.

source.name: Rachel Carson Center, Environment & Society Portal: The Kyshtym Disaster (Arcadia)

title: A Fireball Brighter Than the Sun
text: On 15 February 2013, a space rock about 20 metres wide hit the atmosphere over the southern Urals at 68,400 km/h. It burst about 27 kilometres up with at least 500 kilotons of energy, glowing so bright that some witnesses got sunburned. The shock wave shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people. A 600-kilogram fragment was later hauled out of icy Lake Chebarkul.

source.name: National Geographic: Russian meteor blast was 500 kilotons

title: The Antelope Die-Off on the Steppe
text: In May 2015, more than 200,000 saiga antelopes, the odd-nosed grazers of the steppe, died within three weeks in central Kazakhstan, about 62 percent of the world's population. Animals went from first symptoms to death in a few hours. Scientists traced it to a normally harmless bacterium, Pasteurella multocida, turned deadly after unusually hot, humid days during calving season.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Saigas on the brink: Multidisciplinary analysis of the factors influencing mass mortality events

title: The Siberian Hole That Keeps Growing
place: Batagaika Crater, near Batagay, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: Satellites watched a small gash in the Yakutian hills, likely begun in the early 1980s, swell into a tadpole-shaped crater about a kilometre long, with cliffs over 85 metres tall. As permafrost thaws, the walls retreat. The exposed frozen ground may hold up to 200,000 years of history, and has given up remains of Ice Age horses, steppe bison, cave lions and wolves.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Batagaika Crater Expands

source2.name: ESA: Earth from Space: Batagaika Crater

title: The Worm That Woke After 46,000 Years
place: Duvanny Yar, Kolyma River, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: In 2002, scientists collected frozen soil from an ancient ground-squirrel burrow about 40 metres down in Siberian permafrost. Plant material in it dated to roughly 46,000 years ago. Inside were tiny roundworms in a dormant state, and once thawed they came back to life. The new species, Panagrolaimus kolymaensis, reproduces without males and has been raised in the lab for over 100 generations.

source.name: PLOS Genetics (PMC): A novel nematode species from the Siberian permafrost

title: A Sabre-Toothed Kitten in the Permafrost
place: Badyarikha River, Indigirka basin, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: In 2020, a three-week-old cub with short, thick, dark brown fur emerged from frozen ground along a Yakutian river. It was a Homotherium, a sabre-toothed cat, dated to about 36,000 years ago. Compared with a lion cub of the same age it had a far thicker neck, longer forelimbs, tiny ears and broad round paws, perhaps for snow. Nobody had seen this extinct cat's face before.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Mummy of a juvenile sabre-toothed cat Homotherium latidens from the Upper Pleistocene of Siberia

title: The Last Emir of Bukhara, in Colour
text: In 1911, the Russian photographer Sergei Prokudin-Gorskii photographed Alim Khan, the newly enthroned Emir of Bukhara, in colour. The Emir sits solemnly, an absolute monarch, though his city-state had been a vassal of the Russian Empire since the mid-1800s. Nine years later Soviet power reached Bukhara, and Alim Khan fled to Afghanistan, where he died in 1944.

source.name: Library of Congress: The Empire That Was Russia, Ethnic Diversity

title: Saka Kin Found by a Railway Line
place: Boz-Barmak, near Balykchi, Issyk-Kul Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: Building a railway near Lake Issyk-Kul in 2022 uncovered graves of Saka herders from the 4th to 2nd centuries BCE. DNA linked them to Iron Age groups in Kazakhstan. Every man shared one father line, still common among Kyrgyz today, while each person carried a different mother line, hinting that wives married in. One woman stood apart, with ancestry closer to Siberia.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Genomic insights into the Iron Age Saka of Boz-Barmak, Kyrgyzstan

title: Stone Toolmakers of the Tajik Loess
place: Khovaling Loess Plateau, Khatlon Region, Tajikistan
text: Thick layers of wind-blown dust in southern Tajikistan hold buried soils from warm periods, and in them lie the tools of the Karatau Culture. Using 286 luminescence dates plus other methods, scientists found these early humans arrived around 580,000 years ago with a fully developed toolkit, thrived through three warm spells to about 400,000 years ago, then vanished as a glacial cold set in.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Absolute chronology of the Early Palaeolithic Karatau Culture in Central Asia

title: Barley Harvesters Before the Farmers
place: Toda-1 Cave, Surkhan Darya Valley, Uzbekistan
text: In a cave in the foothills of southern Uzbekistan, people around 9,200 years ago were cutting barley with stone sickle blades and grinding it on stones, long before pottery appeared there. They were foragers, not farmers, eating grains along with nuts and fruits. The cave also gave the earliest known evidence of people gathering the wild ancestors of pistachios and apples, or a close apple relative.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): 9,000-year-old barley consumption in the foothills of central Asia

title: Eggs for Breakfast on the Silk Road
text: Chicken bones rarely survive, but eggshells can. Studying shell fragments from 12 sites in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, scientists used ancient proteins to confirm they came from chickens, first appearing in Hellenistic layers at sites like Paykend near Bukhara. Eggshells turned up in such quantities, through medieval times, that chickens were probably an everyday food, perhaps bred to lay eggs all year round.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Archaeological and molecular evidence for ancient chickens in Central Asia

title: Where the Hungarians Came From
place: Uyelgi cemetery, near Chelyabinsk, Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia
text: Hungarian is a Uralic language marooned in Central Europe, and chronicles spoke of an eastern homeland. DNA from 131 people buried around the Urals settled the question. Magyars who reached the Carpathian Basin in the late 800s were closely related to people of the Karayakupovo horizon, dated 750 to 1000 CE, buried at cemeteries such as Uyelgi on the Asian side of the southern Urals.

source.name: Cell (PMC): Long shared haplotypes identify the southern Urals as a primary source for the 10th-century Hungarians

title: Who Lies in Jochi's Tomb?
place: Mausoleum of Jochi Khan, Ulytau region, Kazakhstan
text: Kazakhs honour a domed tomb in the Ulytau hills as the grave of Jochi, Genghis Khan's eldest son, who died in 1227. Radiocarbon dating put the man inside in the 14th century instead. Still, his DNA was strongly Mongolian, and he shared a father line with men from two nearby mausoleums: the line long suspected to descend from Genghis Khan himself.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Genomes of the Golden Horde elites and their implications for the rulers of the Mongol Empire

title: Smallpox Rides In With the Fur Hunters
text: From 1632, Russia pushed into Yakutia hunting furs, bringing cereals, tobacco, vodka, Christianity and new diseases. DNA from 122 Yakut burials showed their gene pool stayed remarkably stable through the conquest. But three bodies held smallpox, and by around 1650 the strains circulating in central Yakutia were distinct from any documented in Europe.

source.name: Nature (PMC): An ancient DNA perspective on the Russian conquest of Yakutia

title: Down Into the Door to Hell
place: Darvaza gas crater, Karakum Desert, Turkmenistan
text: In November 2013, explorer George Kourounis was lowered into Darvaza, a burning gas crater in the Karakum Desert about 69 metres wide and 30 metres deep. The usual story says it opened under a Soviet drilling rig in 1971 and was lit to burn off gas, but local geologists told him it may have collapsed in the 1960s, unlit until the 1980s. At the bottom he found heat-loving bacteria.

source.name: National Geographic: Explorer descends into Turkmenistan's 'Door to Hell'

title: A Warrior Couple of the Tagar
text: About 2,500 years ago in Siberia's Khakassia region, people of the Tagar culture laid a man and a woman in one tomb, both armed with bronze daggers and axes. Tagar women's graves more often hold bows and arrows, so her close-combat weapons stand out and may mark her as a skilled fighter. The tomb also held an elderly woman, perhaps a servant, and an infant.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Russia (January/February 2021)

title: Drawing a Border on the Roof of the World
place: Little Pamir, Wakhan Corridor, Badakhshan, Afghanistan
text: On 22 July 1895, British officers who had trekked a month from India met a Russian party with mounted Cossacks beside a lake in the Pamirs, in Afghanistan's Wakhan corridor. Afghan delegates joined days later. Over about two months they marked roughly ninety miles of border. The lake became 'Lake Victoria' and a range the 'Nicholas Range'; local names were not considered important.

source.name: University of Exeter Special Collections: The Pamir Commission (EUL MS 152)

title: What Samanid Bukhara Threw Away
text: Just outside Bukhara's early inner-city wall, archaeologists found nearly forty refuse wells and cesspits filled in the 10th century, when the city was the Samanid capital. Sifting them yielded 358,883 seeds and fruit parts, the richest plant haul yet from Central Asia. Mineral-preserved remains show townspeople ate figs, grapes, melons, watermelon and rice, and seasoned food with tangy sumac.

source.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (PMC): Food globalization in southern Central Asia: archaeobotany at Bukhara between antiquity and the Middle Ages

title: Kazakhstan's Oldest Known People
place: Koken, Upper Irtysh region, Abai Region, Kazakhstan
text: At Koken, near the Altai foothills in eastern Kazakhstan, two hunter-gatherers were buried in the sixth millennium BCE. They are the oldest human remains yet found in the country. DNA showed they were second-degree relatives, perhaps uncle and nephew or half-brothers, yet their ancestry differed noticeably. Thousands of years later, Bronze Age herders used the same spot for more than 70 burials.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Ancient genomes from eastern Kazakhstan reveal dynamic genetic legacy of Inner Eurasian hunter-gatherers

title: A Campfire at Almost 4,000 Metres
place: Kurteke Rockshelter, near Murghab, Eastern Pamir, Tajikistan
text: High on the dry Eastern Pamir plateau, at 3,980 metres, a small rockshelter 40 kilometres from Murghab held a single ancient fireplace. Charred plants from it date to around 8000 BCE. Few tools or bones were left, so people probably visited only now and then, perhaps following herds, sharing stone-tool styles with groups in the Fergana foothills far below.

source.name: iScience (PMC): Archaeobotanical investigations at high-elevation sites of the Pamir Mountains and Fergana foothills

title: Tea and Tobacco in Frozen Hair
text: Hair from 47 frozen Yakut burials, dating from first Russian contact around 1620 to the late 1800s, still held traces of nicotine and caffeine. Soon after contact a few people were already heavy smokers. Tea took longer: heavy tea drinkers appear only in the 19th century, as trade grew. One grave even held an English teapot, the oldest imported teapot found in the north.

source.name: Biology (PMC): At the Origins of Tobacco-Smoking and Tea Consumption in a Virgin Population (Yakutia, 1650-1900 A.D.)

title: When the Herds Vanished, the Steppe Burned
text: After the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, state farms crumbled and livestock herds collapsed. By around 2000, at least 20 million hectares of Kazakh cropland had been abandoned, and poaching cut saiga numbers from over a million to about 30,000. With nothing grazing, grass piled up. Across northern Kazakhstan the burned area grew sevenfold and the number of fires eightfold between 1990 and 2000.

source.name: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (PMC): Collapse and recovery of livestock systems shape fire regimes on the Eurasian steppe

title: A Tiny Ivory Lion in Denisova Cave
text: Deep in Denisova Cave in the Altai, excavators found a cave lion carved from woolly mammoth tusk, only about 4 centimetres long, dated to roughly 45,000 to 40,000 years ago. It was once painted with red ochre and decorated with cut lines, and may be among the oldest animal figurines anywhere. Nobody yet knows whether modern humans or an extinct kind of human carved it.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Russia (March/April 2020)

title: Sea Dragons Older Than Dinosaurs
text: In 2014, fossil hunters on Spitsbergen collected rock nodules in Flower's Valley on the southern shore of Ice Fjord. Inside were 11 linked tail bones from an ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped 'fish-lizard'. Dated to about two million years after Earth's worst mass extinction, they are the oldest ichthyosaur fossils known. They match much bigger, later species, hinting that these sea reptiles began before the extinction.

source.name: Uppsala University: Oldest sea reptile from Age of Dinosaurs found on Arctic island

title: A Frog Pond in Antarctica's Forests
place: La Meseta Formation, Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: Around 40 million years ago, Antarctica still had ponds among southern beech forests. On Seymour Island, Argentinian and Swedish teams working from 2011 to 2013 found a hip bone and a skull fragment from a helmeted frog, the first modern amphibian ever found in Antarctica. Its closest living relatives live in Chile's damp forests today, so even the coldest month there likely stayed above about 3.75°C.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): First fossil frog from Antarctica

title: Ice That Fell Six Million Years Ago
place: Allan Hills blue ice area, Victoria Land, East Antarctica
text: The deepest continuous Antarctic ice core reaches back 800,000 years. But in the Allan Hills, a bare 'blue ice' area brings jumbled ancient ice near the surface. Shallow cores drilled to bedrock there, up to 206 metres down, held ice and trapped air that scientists dated by their argon content: up to 6 million years old. Its chemistry shows Antarctica has cooled about 12°C since then.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Miocene and Pliocene ice and air from the Allan Hills blue ice area, East Antarctica

title: When North Greenland Was 8°C Warmer
place: NEEM ice core camp, North Greenland Ice Sheet, Greenland
text: Drilling more than 2.4 kilometres to bedrock, scientists from 14 nations at the NEEM camp recovered the first complete ice record of the Eemian, a warm spell about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago. North Greenland was then about 8°C warmer than today, and summer meltwater refroze into layers in the snow. Yet the ice surface sat only a few hundred metres lower, so Antarctica must have raised seas too.

source.name: University of Washington News: Greenland ice core provides picture of prehistoric sea level rise

title: Grandfather of the Huskies
place: Zhokhov Island, New Siberian Islands, Russia
text: About 9,500 years ago, a dog lived on tiny Zhokhov Island in the Siberian Arctic. In 2020, scientists read its full genome, the oldest complete dog genome yet sequenced. Siberian Huskies, Alaskan Malamutes and Greenland sledge dogs share most of their DNA with it, pushing sledge-dog origins back thousands of years. Like polar bears and Arctic peoples, these dogs carry adaptations for a high-fat diet.

source.name: Trinity College Dublin: Scientists sequence oldest complete dog genome, 9,500-year-old Siberian sledge dog Zhokov

title: Sixty Million Nests on the Seabed
place: Southern Weddell Sea, off the Filchner Ice Shelf, Antarctica
text: In early 2021, the icebreaker Polarstern towed a camera sled over the floor of Antarctica's southern Weddell Sea and kept finding round fish nests. They covered at least 240 square kilometres: about 60 million nests, most guarded by one adult icefish with more than 1,700 eggs. Weddell seals dive to these depths, perhaps to feed on the largest fish breeding colony ever found.

source.name: EurekAlert (Cell Press): A vast icefish breeding colony discovered in the Antarctic

title: Sponges Feeding on a Vanished World
place: Langseth Ridge seamounts, Central Arctic Ocean
text: In 2016 the icebreaker Polarstern reached seamounts on the Langseth Ridge, near 87°N under year-round sea ice. Cameras revealed the densest Arctic sponge garden yet found, with adults averaging about 300 years old. With almost no food sinking from above, the sponges seem to live partly on a mat of empty tubeworm tubes, leftovers of a seep community that died out thousands of years ago.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Giant sponge grounds of Central Arctic seamounts are associated with extinct seep life

title: A Chance Meeting at Cape Flora
place: Cape Flora, Northbrook Island, Franz Josef Land, Russia
text: In March 1895, Fridtjof Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left the drifting Fram with dog sledges, aiming for the North Pole. Constantly shifting pack ice forced them back on 9 April at 86°14′N. They wintered in a crude hut on Franz Josef Land, then paddled lashed-together kayaks along the coast. On 17 June 1896, by sheer coincidence, they met British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora.

source.name: Fram Museum: The First Fram Expedition (1893-1896)

title: Three Flags Dropped on the Pole
text: On 11 May 1926 the airship Norge, about 106 metres long, lifted off from Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard with Roald Amundsen, Lincoln Ellsworth, pilot Umberto Nobile and his dog Titina aboard. Early next morning it crossed the North Pole, and the crew dropped Norwegian, American and Italian flags onto the ice. After fog coated it in ice, the Norge landed near Teller, Alaska, about 72 hours after leaving.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Norge flight (1926)

title: Stranded Seaplanes Near the Pole
text: In May 1925, Roald Amundsen and five men flew two seaplanes, N24 and N25, north from Svalbard. After eight hours they came down on leads in the drift ice at 87°43′N, and N24 was too damaged to fly again. For about three and a half weeks they lived crammed in N25, clearing runways that the shifting ice kept wrecking. On 15 June, all six squeezed aboard and took off.

source.name: Fram Museum: The N24/N25 flight towards the North Pole (1925)

title: The Islands Norway Never Kept
text: From 1898 to 1902, Otto Sverdrup took the Fram into Canada's high Arctic and stayed four winters, the last because Goose Fjord's ice refused to break up. His crew mapped about 200,000 square kilometres of unknown land, including Axel Heiberg Island. Sverdrup claimed it all for Norway's king, but Norway's government never followed up. The islands became Canadian, and in 1930 Canada paid Sverdrup for his maps.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Second Fram Expedition (1898-1902)

title: A Continent Set Aside for Peace
place: Antarctica (treaty signed in Washington, DC, USA)
text: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries whose scientists had worked in Antarctica during the International Geophysical Year signed a treaty in Washington. It declared the continent for peaceful purposes only, guaranteed freedom of scientific research and required results to be shared openly. Rival territorial claims were frozen, with no new ones allowed. The treaty took effect in 1961, and 58 countries are now parties to it.

source.name: Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty: The Antarctic Treaty

title: Three Penguin Eggs in the Dark
text: On 27 June 1911, in the total darkness of Antarctic winter, Edward Wilson, Birdie Bowers and Apsley Cherry-Garrard set off to collect emperor penguin eggs at Cape Crozier. Temperatures fell as low as minus 68°C. Wilson hoped the embryos would link birds to reptiles. Two of five eggs cracked; three survived, but proved scientifically disappointing. Today they sit in London's Natural History Museum as relics of extraordinary effort.

source.name: The Scientist: Harrowing Egg Hunt, 1911

title: Norse Ivory Hunters in the Far North
place: Pikialasorsuaq (North Water Polynya), between Greenland and Ellesmere Island
text: Medieval Norse Greenlanders shipped walrus ivory to Europe as tusks still fixed to the front of the skull. Ancient DNA from 31 ivory pieces now shows where those walruses lived. After about 1120 CE, close to half came from the North Water, a High Arctic hunting ground some 30 days' sail from Norse farms, where Tuniit and Thule Inuit hunted too, making encounters almost certain.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Greenland Norse walrus exploitation deep into the Arctic

title: Young Nelson Versus the Polar Bear
place: Pack ice north of Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
text: In 1773 the Royal Navy ships Racehorse and Carcass sailed north of Spitsbergen to test whether the open sea itself froze, hoping for a route over the pole to the East Indies. Pack ice drove them back. According to a famous tale, young midshipman Horatio Nelson stalked a polar bear across the ice. His musket misfired, he swung its butt, and a crack in the ice saved him.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Nelson and the bear

source2.name: Captain Cook Memorial Museum: Northward Ho! A Voyage towards the North Pole

title: Graves of the Scurvy-Struck Whalers
text: At Likneset, 'Corpse Point', in northwest Svalbard, 225 graves hold European whalers of the 1600s and 1700s, the largest whaling burial ground on the islands. The 20 skeletons excavated were mostly young men, buried in woollen caps, jackets and knitted stockings. Signs of scurvy appear in 18 of 19 studied, and worn spines show brutal labour. Thawing permafrost and erosion are now destroying the graves.

source.name: PLOS One (PMC): Skeletons in the permafrost, the early modern whaling burial site of Likneset, Svalbard

title: Primate Cousins in the Polar Night
place: Margaret Formation near Bay Fiord, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: About 52 million years ago, Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic held swampy forests like the cypress swamps of the southern United States, home to crocodilians and early tapir relatives. Fossil teeth reveal two new species of Ignacius, small early primate cousins, the northernmost ever found. Larger than their southern kin, with jaws built for hard foods, they endured roughly six months of winter darkness.

source.name: PLOS One (PMC): Basal Primatomorpha colonized Ellesmere Island during the early Eocene climatic optimum

title: An Ancient Polar Bear's Genetic Twist
place: Poolepynten, Prins Karls Forland, Svalbard, Norway
text: A polar bear jawbone from Poolepynten on Svalbard dates to the Eemian warm period, 130,000 to 115,000 years ago. In 2022, scientists published a detailed genome from it and compared it with living polar and brown bears from Alaska, where the species increasingly meet. The surprise: ancient genes flowed mainly from brown bears into polar bears, partly reversing the accepted idea that mixing ran the other way.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Insights into bear evolution from a Pleistocene polar bear genome

title: A Crater Hidden Under Greenland's Ice
text: Beneath Hiawatha Glacier in northwest Greenland lies a buried impact crater about 31 kilometres wide. Some scientists suspected it was young, formed after the ice sheet began. To test this, researchers dated meltwater sand and pebbles of impact-melted rock washed out from under the glacier. Shocked zircon crystals gave an age of about 58 million years, long before Greenland's ice sheet existed.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): A Late Paleocene age for Greenland's Hiawatha impact structure

title: Life in a Lake Under the Ice
place: Subglacial Lake Whillans, Whillans Ice Stream, West Antarctica
text: In January 2013, a US-led team used a filtered, UV-sterilised hot-water drill to bore through about 800 metres of West Antarctic ice into Subglacial Lake Whillans. It was the first time anyone had directly sampled water and mud from an Antarctic subglacial lake. Though the lake was only about 2.2 metres deep, its dark water held around 130,000 microbial cells in every millilitre.

source.name: Frontiers in Microbiology (PMC): Microbial Community Structure of Subglacial Lake Whillans, West Antarctica

title: 'Yowza-Yowza': A Rock From Mars
place: Far Western Icefield, Allan Hills, Antarctica
text: On 27 December 1984, during a snowmobile ride across the Far Western Icefield of the Allan Hills, meteorite hunters picked up a greenish-grey stone. The field notes added: 'Yowza-Yowza'. Weighing 1,931 grams, ALH84001 was later recognised as a rock from Mars, more than 4 billion years old. In 1996, a team led by David McKay argued that tiny features inside it might be traces of ancient life.

source.name: NASA Astromaterials Curation: Martian Meteorite Compendium, ALH84001

title: A Secret Wartime Mission South
place: Port Lockroy, Goudier Island, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: In February 1944, in the middle of World War II, Britain's secret Operation Tabarin reached Antarctica. Led by James Marr, its men turned a disused whaling station on Deception Island into a base, then, blocked by pack ice at Hope Bay, built Bransfield House at Port Lockroy instead. At Deception they even put up a 'Port Foster Post Office' sign, claiming the farthest south post office.

source.name: British Antarctic Survey: Operation Tabarin

title: Australia's Oldest Antarctic Station
place: Mawson Station, Horseshoe Harbour, Mac. Robertson Land, Antarctica
text: On 13 February 1954, Phillip Law raised the Australian flag at Horseshoe Harbour in East Antarctica and named a new station after explorer Douglas Mawson. He had chosen the rocky site from aerial photographs. Ten men wintered in cramped quarters that first year. Mawson later gained Antarctica's first aircraft hangar and a cosmic ray observatory carved into bedrock, and it is the oldest station south of the Antarctic Circle.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Mawson station history

title: A Station Swallowed by Ice
place: Wilkes Station, Clark Peninsula, Wilkes Land, Antarctica
text: In January 1957, US Navy crews built Wilkes station in East Antarctica in just 16 days, unloading 11,000 tons of material for the International Geophysical Year. Australia took it over in 1959, allowed to use the stores but not remove anything. Leaking fuel and drifting snow soon made it unsafe, and it closed in 1969. Today it lies frozen in ice, revealed only every four or five years.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Wilkes station history

title: Two Messengers Who Never Arrived
place: Winter quarters near Cape Chelyuskin, Taymyr Peninsula, Russia
text: In 1918 Roald Amundsen's new ship Maud sailed the Northeast Passage, hoping to drift across the Arctic Ocean as Nansen's Fram had. Ice trapped it beyond Cape Chelyuskin for its first winter. In September 1919, Peter Tessem and Paul Knudsen left the ship to carry scientific results home to Norway. Neither was seen alive again; remains found later suggest Tessem froze to death near Dikson.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Maud Expedition (1918-1925)

title: Swahili Families Written in DNA
text: Ancient DNA from elite Muslim graves in Swahili stone towns such as Mtwapa shows that, from about 1000 CE, African and Asian ancestors were forming families together. Most mothers' lines came from Africa, while most of the Asian DNA came from Persian men, with a share from India. It fits the Kilwa Chronicle, the coast's own oldest history, which tells of settlers from Shiraz.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): Entwined African and Asian genetic roots of medieval peoples of the Swahili coast

title: A Spine Hidden in a Miners' Road
place: Malapa, Cradle of Humankind, Gauteng, South Africa
text: In 2008 fossils of an adult female Australopithecus sediba, nicknamed MH2, turned up in Malapa cave. Years later, scientists found more of her lower back inside rock blocks that early 20th-century limestone miners had dumped to build a track. Pieced together, the near-complete spine curves like a modern woman's, showing this roughly two-million-year-old relative walked comfortably upright on two legs.

source.name: eLife (via PMC): New fossils of Australopithecus sediba reveal a nearly complete lower back

title: When Madagascar Lost Its Giants
text: Madagascar once had elephant birds, hippos, giant tortoises and giant lemurs. Around 1000 years ago their populations crashed across the island's wetter regions, and many species vanished for good. Researchers argue the main trigger was not the arrival of the first foragers, who may have reached the island thousands of years earlier, but the spread of farming and cattle herding, plus drought in the driest south.

source.name: Cambridge Prisms: Extinction (via PMC): Patterns of late Holocene and historical extinctions on Madagascar

title: Africa's First Peace Prize Laureate
place: Groutville, near KwaDukuza (Stanger), KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
text: Albert Lutuli, a chief, teacher and trade unionist, led the African National Congress and its non-violent campaign of civil disobedience against apartheid, inspired by Gandhi. After the Sharpeville massacre in 1960 the ANC was banned and Lutuli was persecuted by his own government. Even so, he received the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize a year late, in 1961, becoming Africa's first Peace laureate.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Albert Lutuli – Facts

title: A Prison Survivor Wins the Nobel
text: Wole Soyinka, born in Abeokuta in 1934, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986. During Nigeria's civil war he wrote an article calling for a ceasefire, was accused of conspiring with Biafra, and spent 22 months as a political prisoner. He turned that ordeal into books, while his plays drew on Yoruba myth, especially Ogun, god of iron and war.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Wole Soyinka – Biographical

title: The Lake That Breathed Out Death
text: Lake Nyos, a 210-metre-deep crater lake in Cameroon, sits in permanent layers that trap gas in its deep water. In 1986 the lake suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide, which flowed into nearby towns and villages and killed about 1,800 people and 3,000 livestock. Since 2001, engineers have been degassing the lake to stop a repeat, while its chemistry is constantly monitored.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Bacterial and archaeal communities in Lake Nyos (Cameroon, Central Africa)

title: The World's First Malaria Vaccine Rolls Out
text: In April 2019 Malawi became the first country to launch the world's first malaria vaccine, RTS,S, in a pilot for children up to two years old, with Ghana and Kenya following. The vaccine took about thirty years to develop. In trials it prevented roughly 4 in 10 malaria cases, important in Africa, where malaria was killing more than 250,000 children each year.

source.name: World Health Organization: Malaria vaccine pilot launched in Malawi

title: A Village Builds Its Own Cool School
text: Diébédo Francis Kéré, son of Gando's village chief, had to leave home at seven to attend school in a hot, airless classroom with over a hundred pupils. After training in Berlin, he came back. His first building, Gando Primary School, finished in 2001, was made by villagers themselves, almost entirely by hand, from local materials. In 2022 Kéré won architecture's top honour, the Pritzker Prize.

source.name: The Pritzker Architecture Prize: Diébédo Francis Kéré

title: Floating Giants Painted in the Sahara
text: On the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau, a maze of rock arches and pillars, painters left Round Head figures with blank round heads and shapeless, floating bodies. Thought to be up to 9,000 years old, some stand nearly 4 metres tall, among Africa's largest rock paintings. Sadly, early recorders harmed some images; one researcher even tested varnishes on them, leaving a dark rectangular patch.

source.name: British Museum African Rock Art Image Project: Algeria

title: Red Circles on a Granite Rock
place: Nyero rock shelters, Kumi District, Uganda
text: At Nyero, a granite outcrop in eastern Uganda, six painted shelters are covered with red geometric designs: circles, concentric rings with rays, dots and lines, applied with fingertips. They are attributed to ancestors of the Batwa, forest-dwelling hunter-gatherers of the Great Lakes, and dated to before 1250 CE. Rayed concentric circles like these are a feature unique to Ugandan rock art.

source.name: British Museum African Rock Art Image Project: Uganda

title: Life-Size Giraffes Carved in the Desert
place: Dabous, west of the Aïr Mountains, Agadez Region, Niger
text: On top of a rocky outcrop at Dabous, west of Niger's Aïr Mountains, someone carved two life-size giraffes into the stone, perhaps up to 6,000 years ago. Today this is the Sahara, but the region's engravings show wild animals, cattle, Barbary sheep and ostriches from wetter times. Niger has more than 2,400 recorded rock art images, mostly engravings around the Aïr and the Djado Plateau.

source.name: British Museum African Rock Art Image Project: Niger

title: The Louvre of the Kalahari
text: Rising from the Kalahari in north-western Botswana, the Tsodilo Hills hold more than 4,000 rock paintings, earning the nickname Louvre of the Desert. People have lived here for perhaps 100,000 years, and the paintings, of wild animals, cattle, stick-like figures and geometric shapes, are at least 2,000 years old. One painted zebra became the first logo of Botswana's National Museum.

source.name: British Museum African Rock Art Image Project: Botswana

title: The Preacher Who Wore His Hat
text: In 1914 Baptist preacher John Chilembwe opened his church in Nyasaland, now Malawi, and posed for a photograph wearing a white hat, tilted sideways, beside a white missionary friend. Africans were forbidden to wear hats before white people, so it was a quiet act of defiance. Months later, in 1915, he led the first uprising against British rule and was killed.

source.name: The Conversation: John Chilembwe, a new statue celebrates Malawi Pan-Africanist the world forgot

title: The Women's War Against Colonial Rule
text: In 1929, after petitions to colonial officials failed, hundreds of women in southeastern Nigeria took to the streets of Owerri, Calabar and Aba against harsh British policies. Many wore little more than wreaths of grass, and they mocked the soldiers as pigs. Remembered as Ogu Umunwanyi, the Aba Women's War, the protest cost about 50 women their lives, with 50 more wounded.

source.name: The Conversation: Undressing for redress, the significance of Nigerian women's naked protests

title: An Emperor's Fortress Falls and Is Looted
text: Emperor Tewodros II wrote to Queen Victoria for military help; when his letters went unanswered, he took about 30 Europeans hostage. Britain sent some 12,000 British and Indian troops from Bombay. On 13 April 1868 they stormed his mountain fortress at Maqdala, and Tewodros took his own life. Soldiers seized manuscripts and church treasures, then auctioned the loot on a nearby plain.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Ethiopian collections at the V&A

title: King Amado's Walls and Ditches
place: Ofa and Humbo districts, Wolaita Zone, Ethiopia
text: In the 18th century, Kawo (King) Amado of Wolaita in southern Ethiopia ringed sixteen districts with defences. Where the ground was stony he raised dry-stone walls averaging 3 metres high; where stone was lacking, he dug ditches about 5 metres wide and deep. Local tradition compares them to the cattle walls that kept herds safe from wild animals and robbers.

source.name: Heliyon (via PMC): The Kawo/King Amado Kella defensive wall in Wolaita, Ethiopia

title: Stone Terraces Older Than Mapungubwe
place: Mapela Hill, Shashe region, Matabeleland South, Zimbabwe
text: Mapela Hill in south-western Zimbabwe is terraced on every side with stone walls up to two and a half metres high. Dating shows the first prestige terraces were built in the 11th century CE, nearly 200 years before Mapungubwe, long seen as the cradle of the Zimbabwe culture. Elite earthen floors with glass beads show leaders lived apart on the hill.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Zimbabwe Culture before Mapungubwe, New Evidence from Mapela Hill

title: Herders of the Green Sahara
place: Takarkori rock shelter, Tadrart Acacus, Libya
text: Seven thousand years ago the Sahara was green savannah. DNA from two women buried in Takarkori rock shelter in Libya revealed a previously unknown North African lineage that split from sub-Saharan groups long ago and stayed isolated. They kept livestock, yet their ancestry shows herding spread to them as an idea, not through incoming herders. They carried little Neanderthal DNA.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): Ancient DNA from the Green Sahara reveals ancestral North African lineage

title: Early Humans on Angola's Old Beaches
text: On raised beaches now about 100 metres above the sea in Angola's Benguela Province, early humans were making stone tools more than 600,000 years ago. At Dungo IV they shaped local coastal pebbles and cobbles to suit what the shore offered. At nearby Dungo V, similar tools lie with the bones of a stranded whale, hinting these toolmakers also used the coast for food.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Evidence for Earlier Stone Age coastal use, the site of Dungo IV, Benguela Province, Angola

title: Middle Eastern Glass in the Gold Lands
place: Djoutoubaya, Falémé Valley, Tambacounda Region, Senegal
text: Djoutoubaya, a farming village on the Falémé River in eastern Senegal, sat in one of the gold-producing areas of the Ghana and Mali empires. Chemical tests on glass beads from it and from Dogon Country in Mali showed most of the glass was made from raw materials from Egypt, the Levant and the Middle East, carried across the Sahara by caravans, even to remote rural places.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Glass beads from archaeological sites in Mali and Senegal

title: Uprooting Cotton to Defy an Empire
text: In 1905 people in south-eastern German East Africa, now Tanzania, rose against cotton plantation owners and traders. Rebels typically began by pulling up the hated cotton plants before raiding farmhouses and offices, and the revolt spread inland as a peasants' war. Germany's response was catastrophic: three years of mass starvation and disease, with as many as 300,000 people killed.

source.name: The Conversation: 300,000 Tanzanians were killed by Germany during the Maji-Maji uprising

title: Sarraounia Stands Against a Rogue Column
place: Lougou, near Dogondoutchi, Dosso Region, Niger
text: In 1899 a French column under Captain Paul Voulet and Lieutenant Julien Chanoine marched across what is now Niger, looting and massacring thousands. At Lougou, the leader Sarraounia Mangou resisted, though the town was burned. When Paris sent an officer to take over, Voulet killed him and declared he was no longer French; his own soldiers mutinied and killed him.

source.name: The Conversation (French edition): Massacre de l'armée coloniale au Niger

title: Copper Smelted in Cooking Pots
place: Kingoyi, near Mindouli, Niari Basin, Republic of the Congo
text: The Niari Basin held West Central Africa's main copper deposits, between the Kingdom of Kongo, the Tio and coastal Loango. From the mid-1400s to mid-1600s, smelters there used ordinary household pots as crucibles, one clay type unique in sub-Saharan Africa. The mines may have been deliberately hidden from the Portuguese, and no European visited them until the late 19th century.

source.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (via PMC): Smelting copper in decorated pottery, Niari Basin, Republic of the Congo

title: Freetown Recycles Captured Slave Ships
place: Freetown harbour, Western Area, Sierra Leone
text: After Britain banned the slave trade, captured slaving ships were brought to Freetown for trial. Freed captives were resettled, and the condemned ships auctioned, sometimes to groups of Sierra Leoneans who pooled money to buy them for coastal trade. West Africa's largest natural harbour grew a repair district, and the 1831 census counted 2,997 newly Liberated Africans among the colony's residents.

source.name: History of Science (via PMC): Freetown's ship repair cluster in nineteenth-century Sierra Leone

title: Desert Crops in a Forest City
text: Archaeobotanists sifting soil at medieval Ile-Ife, famous for its sculptures, found cotton seeds from the late 12th and early 13th centuries and 48 grains of wheat, the largest wheat find in sub-Saharan West Africa. Both crops suit Mediterranean climates, and wheat cannot grow locally, so they likely arrived through trans-Saharan trade as prestige foods and fabrics. Cotton may have been woven there.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Early archaeological evidence of wheat and cotton from medieval Ile-Ife, Nigeria

title: A Mammal That Attacked a Dinosaur
text: In beds nicknamed the "Chinese Pompeii", a volcanic mudflow froze a fight. A 47-centimetre mammal, Repenomamus, sits on top of a plant-eating Psittacosaurus, gripping its jaw and leg, teeth clamped on its ribs. The dinosaur was about three times heavier. Scientists checked the slab for forgery and found it genuine: proof that some early mammals were not just hiding from dinosaurs, but hunting them.

source.name: Scientific Reports: An extraordinary fossil captures the struggle for existence during the Mesozoic

title: A Giant Rhino Crosses Low Tibet
place: Wangjiachuan, Dongxiang, Linxia Basin, Gansu, China
text: Giant rhinos without horns were among the largest land mammals ever. A complete skull found near Wangjiachuan village, on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau, belongs to a new species, Paraceratherium linxiaense. Its long, flexible neck and a possible short trunk helped it browse high. The find suggests Tibet then stood under about 2,000 metres, low enough for these giants to walk through to South Asia.

source.name: Communications Biology: An Oligocene giant rhino provides insights into Paraceratherium evolution

title: The Shovel-Tusker Learns to Use Its Trunk
text: Platybelodon, an elephant relative from northern China, had flat lower tusks like a shovel with a sharp cutting edge. Computer models show the jaw was best at slicing upright stems such as soft herbs. Its skull points to a strong, flexible trunk that could coil around grass and grab it. It may be the first elephant relative to graze this way, as the trunk took over from the jaw.

source.name: eLife: The trunk replaces the longer mandible as the main feeding organ in elephant evolution

title: Storm-Buried Pterosaur Eggs Near the Tian Shan
text: South of the Tian Shan mountains lies one of the world's few pterosaur bone beds. A large number of Hamipterus, a flying reptile whose males and females looked different, were buried in an ancient lake. Storms swept their bones and even three-dimensional eggs with embryos into sandy layers. The same beds later gave up the first dinosaur bones known from the region, including a long-necked sauropod.

source.name: Scientific Reports: The first dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous Hami Pterosaur Fauna, China

title: A Whale Mother Who Gave Birth on Land
text: Maiacetus was an early whale about 2.6 metres long that still had four legs. One fossil female from Balochistan holds a nearly full-term baby inside her ribs, lying head first. Living whales are born tail first, but land mammals are born head first, so these whales probably came ashore to give birth.

source.name: PLOS ONE: New Protocetid Whale from the Middle Eocene of Pakistan: Birth on Land, Precocial Development, and Sexual Dimorphism

title: The Primate Sold in Two Halves
text: In 1983 private collectors dug up a young primate at Messel and split the slab in two, selling the halves separately. One half was partly faked to look more complete. The other, bought by Oslo's Natural History Museum in 2007, was almost perfect, with its body outline and a last meal of leaves and fruit. Named Darwinius, she had once broken her wrist and healed.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Complete Primate Skeleton from the Middle Eocene of Messel in Germany

title: A Giant Pterosaur Rules an Island
text: Hațeg in Romania was an island at the end of the dinosaur age, with no big meat-eating dinosaurs. A giant flying reptile, Hatzegopteryx, may have filled the gap. One neck bone is 24 centimetres long and almost as wide, with thick walls, showing a short, sturdy neck. Researchers suggest it stalked the ground and grabbed small dinosaurs, acting as the island's top predator.

source.name: PeerJ: Neck biomechanics indicate that giant Transylvanian azhdarchid pterosaurs were short-necked arch predators

title: The Oldest Bat Skeletons on Earth
place: Fossil Lake, Green River Formation, Wyoming, USA
text: On the shore of an ancient lake in Wyoming, two tiny bats were buried about 52 million years ago. Found in 1994 and 2017 in the same quarry, they are the oldest bat skeletons known anywhere. The new species, Icaronycteris gunnelli, weighed only about 25 grams. It shows bats were already spreading quickly across several continents.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The oldest known bat skeletons and their implications for Eocene chiropteran diversification

title: Stone Redwoods and 1,800 Fossil Species
text: Volcanic eruptions buried a valley in Colorado at the end of the Eocene. Giant redwoods turned to stone; some stumps are up to 14 feet wide, from trees that may have stood over 230 feet tall and lived 500 to 750 years. One fossil is a trio of trunks growing as one plant. Scientists have described more than 1,800 species here, and over 30 kinds of animals with backbones.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument

title: A Rainforest Frozen in Iron
place: McGraths Flat, near Gulgong, New South Wales, Australia
text: Farm ploughing near Gulgong turned up blocks of iron-rich rock holding a lost rainforest. Here, around an oxbow lake, fossils are so fine that a feather still shows its colour granules and fly eyes keep their tiny lenses. Fish guts are packed with phantom midge larvae, and pollen still clings to a sawfly's head. Today the same land is dry eucalyptus and acacia country.

source.name: Science Advances: A Lagerstätte from Australia provides insight into the nature of Miocene mesic ecosystems

dateLabel: Late Miocene, about 6 million years ago
title: The Giant Otter That Out-Bit a Sea Otter
text: Siamogale melilutra, found at Shuitangba in Yunnan, weighed about 50 kilograms, bigger than any living otter. Computer tests of its jaw show it was far stronger than a sea otter's, even allowing for size. It probably crunched shellfish and other hard prey in forested wetlands shared with deer, tapirs and beavers, where large land predators were almost unknown, leaving the giant otter as top hunter.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Feeding capability in the extinct giant Siamogale melilutra and comparative mandibular biomechanics of living Lutrinae

title: The Platypus Way of Life Is Ancient
place: Slippery Rocks, Dinosaur Cove, Victoria, Australia
text: Kryoryctes, an egg-laying mammal from Australia's polar past, is known from a single upper arm bone. Its outside shape looks like an echidna's, but inside the bone is thick-walled with almost no marrow space, like a platypus that swims and digs. So platypus-style living goes back over 100 million years, and echidnas later moved back onto dry land.

source.name: PNAS: Bone microstructure supports a Mesozoic origin for a semiaquatic burrowing lifestyle in monotremes

title: A Lost Giraffe of the Siwalik Hills
text: In 1838 the fossil hunter Cautley described a striking neck bone from India's Siwalik Hills that looked just like a modern giraffe's. Named in 1843, it was the first extinct giraffe species of the genus Giraffa ever discovered. Modern estimates from the bone suggest an animal about 3.9 metres tall, weighing roughly 400 kilograms, with a neck nearly 1.5 metres long, probably the last giraffe of South Asia.

source.name: PeerJ: On reconstructing Giraffa sivalensis, an extinct giraffid from the Siwalik Hills, India

title: Egypt's Ape Shakes Up Our Family Tree
text: A single lower jaw from Wadi Moghra in Egypt's desert belongs to Masripithecus, from Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt. Announced in 2026, it is the first definite fossil ape from North Africa. It is more closely related to living apes than any East African ape of its age, hinting that the ancestor of all today's apes may have lived in North Africa or the Middle East.

source.name: EurekAlert (Mansoura University / USC): Masripithecus, a new Miocene ape from Egypt sheds light on the origins of modern apes

title: Two Apes Shared a Bavarian Forest
place: Hammerschmiede clay pit, Pforzen, Bavaria, Germany
text: From a clay pit in Bavaria came a single tooth, a tooth fragment and a kneecap. They belong to Buronius, named after Buron, the medieval name of nearby Kaufbeuren. At about 10 kilograms it is the smallest great-ape relative known. It lived beside the larger ape Danuvius but had thin enamel for soft fruit and leaves: the first case of two such apes living together in Europe.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Buronius manfredschmidi, a new small hominid from the early late Miocene of Hammerschmiede (Bavaria, Germany)

title: An Anatolian Ape and Human Origins
text: At Çorakyerler in central Türkiye, researchers studied a female ape's partial skull with a nearly complete forehead. They named the genus Anadoluvius, from Anadolu, the Turkish word for Anatolia. Like early African human relatives, it had thick enamel and small canines. The team argues that the African apes and human line may have begun around the Mediterranean, though an African origin cannot be ruled out.

source.name: Communications Biology: A new ape from Türkiye and the radiation of late Miocene hominines

title: The Snake That Kept Its Legs
place: La Buitrera, Río Negro Province, Argentina
text: In the rocks of La Buitrera in Patagonia, researchers found eight new skulls of Najash, a snake that still had hind legs and hips. Micro-CT scans of the first 3D skulls revealed a large, lizard-like cheekbone. The scientists argue that this legged body was not a brief in-between stage, but a stable, successful design in early snakes. Najash is the best-known snake of the dinosaur age.

source.name: Science Advances: New skulls and skeletons of the Cretaceous legged snake Najash, and the evolution of the modern snake body plan

dateLabel: Late Miocene, roughly 7 million years ago
title: Sloths That Swam in the Pacific
place: Norte Bahía Caldera, Atacama Region, Chile
text: North of the port town of Caldera, in Chile's Atacama Desert, rocks hold a nearly complete skeleton of Thalassocnus, a sloth that went to sea. It foraged underwater in shallow coasts, gripping with strong hands, and probably ate some seagrass. Its bones were extra dense and heavy, like a manatee's, which helped it control buoyancy. It is the most complete such sloth found in Chile.

source.name: PeerJ: Aquatic sloths (Thalassocnus) from the Miocene of Chile and the evolution of marine mammal herbivory

title: A Swamp Forest Near the North Pole
place: Strathcona Fiord, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: At almost 79 degrees north on Ellesmere Island, stone tree stumps over a metre wide stand like a cypress swamp. Winters there stayed above freezing and summers topped 20°C. Tiny enamel fragments, the first animal fossils from this forest, belonged to Coryphodon, a big hoofed plant-eater. Its unusual tooth enamel may have helped it chew tough food through months of polar night.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Using tooth enamel microstructure to identify mammalian fossils at an Eocene Arctic forest

dateLabel: Early Eocene, about 52 million years ago
title: The Oldest Termite of a Mega-Family
place: Tadkeshwar lignite mine, Surat District, Gujarat, India
text: In lignite mines of Gujarat, scientists collected amber from forests that grew near the equator as India drifted toward Asia. Inside are termites, including the minute Nanotermes isaacae. It is the oldest definite member of the Termitidae, a family that today makes up more than 75% of all termite species, and it pushes the family's record back by about 20 million years.

source.name: ZooKeys: The termites of Early Eocene Cambay amber, with the earliest record of the Termitidae (Isoptera)

title: A Thighbone From Before Apes and Monkeys
place: Quarry M, Jebel Qatrani Formation, Fayum, Egypt
text: In 2009, at Quarry M in Egypt's Fayum Depression, researchers found the first well-preserved upper thighbone of Aegyptopithecus, a primate living before apes and Old World monkeys split. 3D analysis showed its hip shape is unlike any living monkey or ape. So both groups evolved their different ways of moving from a shared starting point that Aegyptopithecus still kept.

source.name: Nature Communications: Early anthropoid femora reveal divergent adaptive trajectories in catarrhine hind-limb evolution

title: Big Beaver-Like Mammals After the Asteroid
place: Corral Bluffs, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
text: Inside stony lumps at Corral Bluffs, on the edge of Colorado Springs, scientists found skulls of Taeniolabis, the largest known multituberculate, a group of rodent-like mammals now extinct. The oldest lay in river deposits about 730,000 years after the dinosaurs' extinction, around when legumes first appeared there. Researchers estimate it was about as heavy as a beaver, or heavier, with a skull now rebuilt from these finds.

source.name: Journal of Mammalian Evolution: New Skull Material of Taeniolabis taoensis (Multituberculata, Taeniolabididae) from the Early Paleocene of the Denver Basin, Colorado

dateLabel: Late Miocene, about 7 million years ago
title: A Whale's Comb Turned to Stone
place: Cerro Ballena, near Ocucaje, Ica, Peru
text: Baleen, the comb-like plates whales use to sieve food from seawater, almost never fossilises. But on a rocky hill near Ocucaje in Peru's desert, a small extinct whale, Piscobalaena nana, lay belly up with its baleen intact. The plates were packed close with fine tubes, like those of today's rare pygmy right whale, revealing how a whole vanished family of whales filtered their food.

source.name: Journal of Anatomy: How whales used to filter: exceptionally preserved baleen in a Miocene cetotheriid

title: The Lizard King of Myanmar
place: Pondaung Formation, near Mogaung, Sagaing Region, Myanmar
text: In the Pondaung hills of Myanmar, jawbones revealed a giant plant-eating lizard about a metre long from snout to hips, weighing around 27 kilograms. Scientists named it Barbaturex morrisoni: bearded king, honouring Jim Morrison, the singer who called himself the Lizard King. It was bigger than most meat-eating mammals around it, thriving in a climate a few degrees warmer than today's.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Giant lizards occupied herbivorous mammalian ecospace during the Paleogene greenhouse in Southeast Asia

title: Vietnam's First Ancient Primate, From a Coal Mine
place: Na Duong coal mine, Lang Son Province, Vietnam
text: In the Na Duong coal mine of northern Vietnam, layers of clay and lignite formed in an old lake. There, researchers found the first Eocene primate from Vietnam. They named it Anthradapis vietnamensis, from the Greek for coal. At about 5.3 kilograms, it is the largest sivaladapid, a family of early primates, ever found, and so odd it got a new subfamily.

source.name: Scientific Reports: A new primate from the late Eocene of Vietnam illuminates unexpected strepsirrhine diversity and evolution in Southeast Asia

title: The Last Great Auks on Eldey
place: Eldey, off the Reykjanes Peninsula, Iceland
text: In June 1844 a dealer named Carl Siemsen sent fourteen men to Eldey, a rocky islet off Iceland, to hunt great auks for collectors. Three landed and found a pair of these flightless, penguin-like seabirds. The birds ran without an alarm call and were caught and killed; their egg was broken and thrown away. Their preserved organs survive in Copenhagen. No later great auk was ever reliably documented.

source.name: The Conversation: How we're using ancient DNA to solve the mystery of the missing last great auk skins

source2.name: Cincinnati Museum Center: Is this the last Great Auk?

title: Martha, the Very Last Passenger Pigeon
text: When Europeans arrived, North America held roughly 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons, and one flock seen in Ontario in 1860 stretched about 480 kilometres. Forest clearing and heavy hunting for cheap meat emptied the skies. By 1910 a single bird remained: Martha, at the Cincinnati Zoo. She died on 1 September 1914, ending her species. Her body was frozen in ice and sent by train to Washington.

source.name: National Geographic Education: Remembering Martha, the Last Passenger Pigeon

title: The Ginkgos That Outlived the Bomb
text: On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb burned the leaves off Hiroshima's ginkgo trees, stripped their branches and scorched their bark. Yet inside, many trees lived. Less than a year later, mayor Shinzo Hamai wrote that spring had pushed a green shoot through the A-bomb desert. Seeds from these hibakujumoku, or survivor trees, have since gone to 88 cities outside Japan, including Oxford.

source.name: Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum: Seeds from Hiroshima atomic bomb 'survivor trees' planted at Oxford Botanic Garden

title: The Seeds That Cured the World's Fevers
text: In the 1860s, English trader Charles Ledger and his Bolivian servant Manuel Icamanahí spent four years in the Yungas gathering seeds of the cinchona tree, source of quinine against malaria. On one trip Icamanahí was arrested, imprisoned and beaten to death. Kew Gardens rejected the seeds sent to London, but Dutch growers planted them in Java, which supplied 85 to 90 percent of the world's quinine before World War I.

source.name: Toxins (PMC): The Fever Tree: from Malaria to Neurological Diseases

title: A Sack of Seeds Leaves the Amazon
text: Rubber trees grow wild in the Amazon, and for generations their latex was simply tapped from forest trees. Then Henry Wickham collected rubber seeds at Boim, a Brazilian Amazon village, and sent them to Kew Gardens in England, beginning the tree's domestication in 1876. Genetic studies show most rubber-tree varieties grown worldwide still descend from Wickham's collection, and this one species supplies over 98 percent of natural rubber.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Genomic insight into domestication of rubber tree

title: A Fish Back From the Dinosaur Age
place: East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa
text: In 1938 Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, curator of a small museum in East London, South Africa, checked a local trawler's catch and spotted a large, peculiar fish: over a metre long, bluish, with fleshy fins like stubby legs. Its lineage was thought to have vanished about 70 million years ago. The coelacanth was named Latimeria chalumnae after her, and a second species turned up in Indonesia in 1997.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The African coelacanth genome provides insights into tetrapod evolution

title: Su-Lin Sparks Panda-monium
text: In November 1936 Ruth Harkness, a New York dressmaker and writer who had taken over her late husband's expedition, led a team of Chinese workers deep into the mountains of Sichuan and came out with a giant panda cub, Su-Lin. The press frenzy became known as panda-monium. By July 1937 more than 320,000 visitors had come to Chicago's Brookfield Zoo to see her.

source.name: PMC: Characteristics that make trophy hunting of giant pandas inconceivable

title: The Land Lobster Comes Back From Extinction
place: Ball's Pyramid, near Lord Howe Island, New South Wales, Australia
text: Lord Howe Island's giant stick insect, nicknamed the land lobster, grew over 15 centimetres long. After a ship ran aground nearby in 1918, black rats got ashore, and within about 30 years the insect was thought extinct. Then in 2001 researchers returned to Ball's Pyramid, a steep, nearly inaccessible rock 23 kilometres away, and found living adults feeding on a single tea-tree species. Melbourne Zoo now breeds them.

source.name: The Conversation: Australian endangered species: Lord Howe Island stick insect

title: Seven Ibises Save a Species
text: The crested ibis once flocked widely across East Asia, but hunting, habitat loss and farm chemicals cut it down through the 1800s and 1900s. In 1981 Japan captured its last five wild birds for breeding, and the species seemed finished in the wild. That same year searchers found two breeding pairs and three chicks in Yangxian County, Shaanxi. From those few, nearly 2,500 birds now live in three countries.

source.name: PMC: Genome Resequencing Reveals Congenital Causes of Embryo and Nestling Death in Crested Ibis (Nipponia nippon)

title: The Oryx Returns to the Desert
text: By 1972 hunters had wiped the Arabian oryx out of the wild; it survived only in zoos. In 1982 Oman released a free-ranging herd of zoo-born oryx into the Jiddat al-Harasis, a stony desert with no springs. This small white antelope copes by reflecting sunlight and eating dew-moistened sprouts. The herd grew, though in 2007 the sanctuary lost World Heritage status after being cut by 90 percent for oil prospecting.

source.name: PMC: Wild fauna in Oman: Current situation and perspectives, with particular interest to turtles and ungulates

title: Scientists Move Onto the Great Barrier Reef
place: Low Isles, Great Barrier Reef, Queensland, Australia
text: In 1928 a Royal Society expedition led by Maurice Yonge made its headquarters on Low Isles, a small reef island about 65 kilometres north of Cairns, to study how living coral reefs work. That September the Royal Australian Air Force took the first aerial photographs of the reef, and surveyors used them to map the island, a careful job of triangulation that took eight months.

source.name: PMC: Ninety years of change on a low wooded island, Great Barrier Reef

title: Babylon's Clockwork Eclipse Watchers
text: For centuries Babylonian astronomers logged eclipses on clay tablets, timing each phase with a clock, probably a water clock, counted from sunrise or sunset. Their record of a total eclipse of the Sun in 136 BCE is so clearly dated that modern scientists use it to measure Earth's spin. Comparing such ancient timings with today shows the day has lengthened by about 1.8 milliseconds per century.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society A (PMC): Measurement of the Earth's rotation: 720 BC to AD 2015

title: A Doctor's Garden of Indian Drugs
text: Portuguese physician Garcia da Orta reached Goa in 1534 and kept a house with a garden full of medicinal herbs. After decades of study he printed his Colloquies at Goa on 10 April 1563: lively dialogues with an imaginary Spanish doctor covering 57 drugs and plants, from mangoes to opium and betel. His friend, the poet Camões, contributed verses. Orta was the first European physician to write on India's drugs.

source.name: PMC: Garcia Da Orta: His Learned Work Coloquios Dos Simples E Drogas He Cousas Medicinais Da India

title: The Lost Nile Branch Behind the Pyramids
text: The Great Pyramid now stands over 7 kilometres from the Nile, but in Khufu's day a branch of the river ran along the western edge of the floodplain. Pollen from sediment cores drilled in 2019 shows this Khufu branch held fairly steady water then, letting boats reach a harbour at the plateau's foot. The yearly flood lifted them about 7 metres. Later the branch shrank to a small channel.

source.name: PMC: Nile waterscapes facilitated the construction of the Giza pyramids during the 3rd millennium BCE

title: A Fawn Shipped to a Roman Palace
place: Fishbourne Roman Palace, West Sussex, United Kingdom
text: Soon after the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 CE, a palace rose at Fishbourne, and with it came a new animal: fallow deer, the earliest known beyond the Mediterranean. Chemical signals in the teeth of one deer, from a jaw dated to about 60 CE, suggest it was born abroad and shipped from the Mediterranean when only months old. Others were born and raised on the palace grounds.

source.name: PMC: The 10,000-year biocultural history of fallow deer and its implications for conservation policy

title: Where Every Apple Came From
place: Trans-Ili Alatau, Tian Shan, near Almaty, Kazakhstan
text: In 1793 a botanist named Sievers set out across Siberia and Central Asia and made the first formal record of the wild apple forests of the Tian Shan, the mountains where the domestic apple began. The wild tree, Malus sieversii, carries his name. Later Nikolai Vavilov found the richest apple diversity near Almaty, the 'father of apples'. Since 1930 those forests have shrunk to about 7 percent of their area.

source.name: PMC: Malus sieversii: a historical, genetic, and conservational perspective of the primary progenitor species of domesticated apples

title: Orangutans Where None Live Today
place: Sayur Matinggi, South Tapanuli, North Sumatra, Indonesia
text: In 1879 an observer named Kramm watched several orangutans for hours near Sayur Matinggi, in hills south of where any survive now. Old records like his show that the Tapanuli orangutan, named a new species only in 2017, once ranged over about 40,800 square kilometres in the 1890s. Farming and hunting shrank that by around 97 percent: fewer than 800 now live in the Batang Toru forests.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): The historical range and drivers of decline of the Tapanuli orangutan

title: The Last Three Cheetahs of India
text: Mughal courts caught wild cheetahs in huge numbers to course game, and Akbar's hunting team alone peaked at 1,000 animals. Trophy hunting and colonial bounties followed. In 1947 a maharaja shot the last three confirmed Indian cheetahs. Later, DNA from old museum specimens, one shot in the early 1800s, revealed that India's cheetahs had split from African ones far earlier than scientists expected.

source.name: PMC: Ancient mtDNA from the extinct Indian cheetah supports unexpectedly deep divergence from African cheetahs

title: One Last Stalk for Emperor Nero
text: For about six centuries Cyrene's great export was silphion, a prized plant pictured on the city's coins, and its kings tried to keep the trade a monopoly. Then it vanished. The Roman writer Pliny reported that only a single stalk had been found there in his time, sent to Emperor Nero as a curiosity. Overharvesting and sheep grazing on its land likely finished it off.

source.name: PMC: Next Chapter in the Legend of Silphion

title: Arctic Cod on a Viking Dinner Table
text: Haithabu, a Viking Age trading town in northern Germany, left cod bones in its rubbish. Their DNA shows the fish were not caught nearby but came from the North East Arctic cod that spawn along northern Norway, where fish can be dried in the cold air without salt. That pushes secure evidence of long-distance dried-cod transport back from the 1100s to the Viking Age.

source.name: PMC: Ancient DNA reveals the Arctic origin of Viking Age cod from Haithabu, Germany

title: The Sun Was Eclipsed, and It Was Total
text: The Chunqiu, or Spring and Autumn Annals, an ancient Chinese chronicle, logged eclipses of the Sun with care. For 709 BCE it says simply that the Sun was eclipsed and it was total. Modern calculation confirms a total eclipse that day, 17 July in our calendar. Of 37 solar eclipse dates in the chronicle, all but four are exactly right, a gift to scientists tracking Earth's slowing spin.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society A (PMC): Measurement of the Earth's rotation: 720 BC to AD 2015

title: An Emperor's Garden of 410 Fountains
place: Shalimar Bagh, Dal Lake, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: In 1619 the Mughal emperor Jahangir enlarged an ancient garden near Dal Lake into a royal retreat for his wife Nur Jahan and named it Farah Baksh, the Delightful. A central channel, the Shah Nahar, runs down three terraces framed by chinar trees, and the middle terrace alone holds 410 fountains. In 1630 Shah Jahan's governor extended it and renamed it Faiz Baksh, the Bountiful.

source.name: District Srinagar, Government of Jammu and Kashmir: Shalimar Garden

source2.name: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism): Shalimar Bagh in Srinagar

title: The Real Hanging Garden?
text: Around 700 BCE the Assyrian king Sennacherib built his Palace Without Rival at Nineveh and planted beside it a garden he called a replica of Mount Amanus, full of fruit trees and aromatic plants. Instead of old bucket-lifts, he boasted, large copper screws above the wells raised the water. Oxford Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley argues this, not Babylon, was the famous Hanging Garden.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Secrets of the Seven Wonders: Hanging Garden

source2.name: University of Hamburg CSMC: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were at ... Nineveh!

title: The Fungus That Felled Four Billion Trees
place: New York City, New York, USA
text: In 1904 scientists described a new fungus killing American chestnut trees in New York. Native to East Asia, it had arrived with imported infected chestnuts. The American chestnut was a keystone tree of its native forests, yet within about 50 years the blight had killed an estimated 4 billion trees, one of the greatest ecological and economic devastations of the century. It later spread to Europe too.

source.name: PMC: European and American chestnuts: An overview of the main threats and control efforts

title: The Oldest Skull of Africa's Own Mammals
place: Sidi Chennane quarries, Ouled Abdoun Basin, near Khouribga, Morocco
text: Phosphate quarries in Morocco's Ouled Abdoun Basin gave up skulls of Ocepeia, an early relative of elephants, hyraxes and sea cows. They are the oldest skulls known from the afrotherians, the mammal group that arose in Africa. Ocepeia weighed about 3.5 kilograms, roughly a hyrax's size, and had big front molars. Before such finds, the group's early history came almost entirely from DNA studies.
