source.name: PLOS ONE: Ocepeia (Middle Paleocene of Morocco): The Oldest Skull of an Afrotherian Mammal

title: An Elephant Herd Walks Across Arabia
place: Mleisa, Al Dhafra region, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
text: In the inland desert of Abu Dhabi, footprints show prehistoric elephants on the move about seven million years ago. About 13 animals of different sizes walked together as a herd, and a larger elephant walked alone for more than 260 metres, one of the longest fossil mammal trails known. Researchers read it as modern elephant life: mothers and young in herds, adult males wandering solo.

source.name: YaleNews: Desert footprints reveal ancient origins of elephants' social lives

title: Fly Pupae in a Volcanic Crater Lake
place: Foulden Maar, near Middlemarch, Otago, New Zealand
text: Foulden Maar was a small lake inside a volcanic crater in Otago, where pale layers of diatoms built up for at least 130,000 years. In them, scientists found 30 tiny fly pupae and larvae, many of them midges. One is a phantom midge very close to Chaoborus, a fly found almost worldwide today except in New Zealand, showing that some insects later vanished from the islands.

source.name: PeerJ: New records of immature aquatic Diptera from the Foulden Maar Fossil-Lagerstätte, New Zealand

title: Giant Eggs on the Campfire
place: Dune fields near Spencer Gulf, South Australia, Australia
text: Between about 54,000 and 43,000 years ago, people across Australia were cooking giant eggs. Scorched shell fragments turn up at more than 200 sites, burnt in patterns left when shells were tossed into small, quick fires. Scientists argued for years over which extinct bird laid them: the 200-kilogram flightless Genyornis, or a 5-kilogram mound-builder. Ancient proteins surviving inside the shell finally settled it: Genyornis.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Human predation contributed to the extinction of the Australian megafaunal bird Genyornis newtoni

source2.name: PNAS (PMC): Ancient proteins resolve controversy over the identity of Genyornis eggshell

title: The Volcano That Shaped Eel Farms
place: Budj Bim (Mount Eccles), western Victoria, Australia
text: About 37,000 years ago, Budj Bim in western Victoria erupted, sending the Tyrendarra lava flow more than 30 kilometres south to the Southern Ocean. People were already living in the region, so the eruption may have been witnessed. Its jumbled lava later framed something remarkable: Gunditjmara channels, weirs and dams that trapped and stored short-finned eels for about 6,000 years, now listed as World Heritage.

source.name: Bulletin of Volcanology (PMC): Complex eruption processes and deposits of basaltic fissures, the ~37 ka Budj Bim volcanic complex

title: A Stone Wall Around a Fish Farm
place: Heʻeia Fishpond, Kāneʻohe Bay, Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi, USA
text: About 800 years ago, Hawaiians on Oʻahu's windward coast walled off part of Kāneʻohe Bay to raise fish. Heʻeia Fishpond's 2.5-kilometre wall of fossil coral and basalt encloses 88 acres, with sluice gates called mākāhā letting seawater and stream water flow in and out. Around 1778 the islands held roughly 488 of these loko iʻa. Only 14 still produce fish today.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Large-scale climatic effects on traditional Hawaiian fishpond aquaculture

title: Guam's Civilians Sent to Jungle Camps
text: On 10 July 1944, as American forces closed in, Japan's commander on Guam ordered roughly 18,000 people, nearly every civilian on the island, into camps in the jungle interior. Manenggon was the largest. CHamoru families had already endured two and a half years of occupation: the island renamed Omiya Jima, bowing enforced with blows, their languages banned in school. US soldiers reached Manenggon on 31 July.

source.name: National Park Service, War in the Pacific NHP: Imperial Japanese Occupation of Guam (1941-1944)

title: Taking Back a Bombed Island
text: Starting in 1976, members of the Protect Kahoʻolawe ʻOhana landed again and again on a Hawaiian island the US military had used as a bombing range since World War II, and took the Navy to federal court. Kahoʻolawe holds nearly 3,000 recorded archaeological and historical sites. The bombing was ordered to stop in 1990, and in 1994 the island was handed to the State of Hawaiʻi.

source.name: Kahoʻolawe Island Reserve Commission (State of Hawaiʻi): History

title: An Embassy Under a Beach Umbrella
place: Lawns opposite Old Parliament House, Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, Australia
text: On 26 January 1972, four Aboriginal men from Sydney, Michael Anderson, Billy Craigie, Bertie Williams and Tony Coorey, planted a beach umbrella opposite Parliament House with a sign reading 'Aboriginal Embassy'. They were answering the Prime Minister's rejection of land rights. Calling it an embassy made a point: Aboriginal people were being treated as aliens in their own land. Camping there was not illegal, so police could not move them.

source.name: Museum of Australian Democracy: A short history of the Aboriginal Tent Embassy

title: Walls That Made Samoan Chiefs
text: Under the forest of the Falefa Valley on ʻUpolu, laser scans from the air revealed a hidden web of rock walls, ditches and platforms. Excavation shows the biggest walls, some several hundred metres long, began going up roughly 900 to 600 years ago, soon after Sāmoa's population surged. They cluster on the most fertile land, suggesting that competition for good soil helped give rise to Polynesian chiefdoms.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Collective action problems led to the cultural transformation of Sāmoa 800 years ago

title: Breadfruit Crumbs on Rapa Nui Blades
text: The first settlers of Rapa Nui left microscopic clues on their obsidian tools. From 20 blades in the deepest layer at Anakena, dated to about 1000 to 1300 CE, scientists recovered 46 starch grains. They show taro and yam, but also breadfruit and ginger, never known to have been grown on the island. Sweet potato and manioc starch point to South American crops arriving with the very first colonists.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Identification of breadfruit and South American crops introduced during early settlement of Rapa Nui, as revealed through starch analysis

title: A Forest Frozen as Settlers Arrived
place: Hoʻoumi Valley, Nuku Hiva, Marquesas Islands, French Polynesia
text: In Hoʻoumi Valley on Nuku Hiva, a waterlogged deposit preserved a snapshot of the Marquesas just as Polynesians arrived, dated to the mid-1100s CE. Seeds, fruits, pollen and more than 100 kinds of insect and other arthropod remains reveal a lowland wet forest unlike anything growing there today, including apparently extinct plants. Lying among them were specks of charcoal, insects that travelled with people, and an adzed timber.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Lost bioscapes: floristic and arthropod diversity coincident with 12th century Polynesian settlement, Nuku Hiva

title: A Healer's Fire Kept for 500 Generations
place: Cloggs Cave, near Buchan, East Gippsland, Victoria, Australia
text: In the 1800s, GunaiKurnai medicine men and women called mulla-mullung used secluded caves for rituals that were written down by ethnographers. In 2020, excavations at Cloggs Cave, invited by GunaiKurnai Elders, found two tiny fireplaces, 11,000 and 12,000 years old, each with a trimmed Casuarina stick smeared with fat. They match the described rituals and are Australia's oldest known wooden artefacts.

source.name: Nature Human Behaviour (PMC): Archaeological evidence of an ethnographically documented Australian Aboriginal ritual dated to the last ice age

title: A Giant Kangaroo That Outlived the Ice
place: Taora rockshelter, west of Vanimo, Sandaun Province, Papua New Guinea
text: Most of Australia's giant marsupials were gone by about 41,000 years ago. But in a coastal rockshelter called Taora, near Papua New Guinea's border with Indonesia, archaeologists found a single finger bone from a Protemnodon, a giant forest-dwelling relative of kangaroos, in layers dated to between 6,800 and 5,300 years ago. It is the first sign that any of the region's megafauna survived the last ice age.

source.name: npj Biodiversity (PMC): Middle Holocene survival of marsupial megafauna on the north coast of New Guinea

title: Rice Carried Across 2,300 Kilometres
text: When Europeans reached the Pacific, rice grew nowhere in the islands except the Marianas. Red-slipped pots from ritual caves at Ritidian, in northern Guam, show it arrived with the first settlers: their surfaces carry abundant rice husk and leaf traces dated to 3,500 to 3,100 years ago. The rice seems to have travelled from the Philippines across 2,300 kilometres of open sea, and was kept for special ceremonies.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Earliest evidence of rice cultivation in Remote Oceania: ritual use by the first islanders in the Marianas 3500 years ago

title: Volcanic Glass in a Time of Pā
place: Maungarei (Mount Wellington), Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland, New Zealand
text: Between 1500 and 1769, as thousands of fortified pā rose across New Zealand, Māori still needed obsidian for razor-sharp flakes. Chemists traced 253 obsidian artefacts from Maungarei, a fortified volcanic cone in Auckland, and two Northland sites. Most came straight from nearby island sources such as Aotea (Great Barrier Island), but blocks of prized glass from distant Tūhua (Mayor Island) arrived through formal trade.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Strategies for obtaining obsidian in pre-European contact era New Zealand

title: The Valet Who Was a Woman
text: In April 1768, Bougainville's French expedition reached Tahiti. Aboard the storeship Étoile was 'Jean', valet and assistant to the botanist Commerson, who bound her chest with linen and claimed to be a eunuch. By Bougainville's account, Tahitians recognised her as a woman the moment she was rowed ashore. Jeanne Baret later became the first woman known to sail all the way around the world.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Jeanne Baret, the first woman to sail around the world

source2.name: The Conversation: Friday essay: who was Jeanne Barret, the first woman to circumnavigate the globe?

title: The Storm That Stopped a Naval Standoff
text: In March 1889, American and German warships crowded Apia's harbour, locked in a colonial stand-off over Samoa, with a British cruiser among them. Then a cyclone struck. Every German and American ship was wrecked or stranded. Only HMS Calliope escaped, her crew running the engines at their limit to claw out to open sea. Robert Louis Stevenson, who lived in Samoa, wrote an account of the disaster.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Storm: study for the escape of HMS 'Calliope' from the hurricane at Apia, Samoa, 1889

title: Samoan Stone on a Solomons Outlier
place: Kahula site, Taumako, Duff Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
text: Taumako, in the Solomon Islands' remote Duff group, is a Polynesian Outlier: home to Polynesian speakers far west of the Polynesian heartland. When geochemists tested its basalt adzes, every one matched Samoa's hot-spot volcanoes, especially the Tutuila quarries of American Sāmoa, including the fortified Tatagamatau quarry. Two adzes lay in layers from the first settlement of the Kahula site, dated 1296 to 1472 CE.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Artifact geochemistry demonstrates long-distance voyaging in the Polynesian Outliers

title: Lost Sharks Hidden in Old Weapons
text: In the 1800s, Gilbertese warriors fought with daggers, swords and spears edged with rows of shark teeth, each tooth drilled and lashed to wood with coconut-fibre cord often braided with human hair. Museums collected them eagerly. Studying weapons made between 1840 and 1898, Field Museum scientists identified teeth from Spot-tail and Dusky sharks, two species missing from all historical and modern records of Kiribati's waters.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Shark tooth weapons from the 19th century reflect shifting baselines in Central Pacific predator assemblies

title: Knocks at Dawn in Auckland
text: In the mid-1970s, New Zealand police hunting people who had overstayed their visas raided homes late at night or at dawn, pulling Pacific families from their beds into police vans. Some appeared in court the next day barefoot, in pyjamas. Pacific people were about a third of overstayers but 86 percent of prosecutions. In 2021 the government formally apologised at Auckland Town Hall.

source.name: RNZ: Ardern gives formal apology on behalf of government for Dawn Raids

source2.name: University of Auckland: Dawn raids' long racist shadow persists

title: A Medical School for Twelve Colonies
place: Central Medical School, Suva, Viti Levu, Fiji
text: In 1928, a medical school opened in Suva that was unlike anything else in the British Empire. The Central Medical School trained Pacific Islanders as Native Medical Practitioners, drawing students from twelve colonies. It was run by Fiji's colonial government, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, and jointly managed by Britain, Australia, New Zealand, France and the United States. An official called it a 'microcosm of the Pacific'.

source.name: Medical History (PMC): 'Microcosm of the Pacific': colonial encounters at the Central Medical School in Fiji

title: The Disease That Took the Women
place: South Fore area, Eastern Highlands, Papua New Guinea
text: In the mid-1900s, a fatal brain disease called kuru swept through the Fore people of Papua New Guinea's Eastern Highlands, causing 2,700 recorded deaths. Caused by prions, it spread through mortuary feasts at which relatives ritually consumed the dead. Women and children, who ate the most infectious tissues, suffered most, and many villages lost nearly all their adult women. Genomes from 943 people show more women moving into hard-hit areas.

source.name: American Journal of Human Genetics (PMC): Population structure and migration in the Eastern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, a region impacted by the kuru epidemic

title: Forty-Two Days Stuck at North Head
place: North Head Quarantine Station, Manly, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: In July 1872, the steamship Hero, on its routine run from Auckland to Melbourne, was stopped at Sydney's North Head quarantine station after a steerage passenger seemed to develop smallpox. Everyone aboard was confined for 42 days. Passengers put on shows, played sport, carved marks into the sandstone and wrote a weekly journal, Loganiana, named after their captain and later printed with a sulphur-yellow cover.

source.name: Australian Historical Studies (PMC): White Men in Quarantine: Disease, Race, Commerce and Mobility in the Pacific, 1872

title: Six Boys Marooned on ʻAta
text: In 1965, six teenage boys, Sione, Stephen, Kolo, David, Luke and Mano, ran away from their Tongan boarding school in a stolen fishing boat. After eight days adrift they reached ʻAta, an uninhabited island, and were marooned there for at least 15 months, cold, hungry and praying morning and evening for rescue. An Australian, Peter Warner, finally picked them up, and back home they were charged over the boat.

source.name: ABC News: Pacific Islanders say tale of Tongans shipwrecked 50 years ago is not like Lord of the Flies

title: Self-Rule, With a Friend Nearby
text: New Zealand had run the Cook Islands since 1901. In 1965 the two entered free association: the islands governed themselves, while New Zealand helped with foreign affairs, defence and disasters. Sixty years later the partnership was tested, after the Cook Islands prime minister signed agreements with China and New Zealand paused NZ$18.2 million in funding. Tiny Palmerston Island, population 28, still sent 16 people to the anniversary festival.

source.name: RNZ: Cook Islands celebrates 60 years of self-governance amid growing rift with NZ

title: A Slow Mixing on Watom Island
place: Reber–Rakival site, Watom Island, East New Britain, Papua New Guinea
text: On Watom Island, off New Britain, Lapita pottery-makers lived at the Reber–Rakival site from about 2,800 to 2,350 years ago. Ancient genomes of people buried there tell a surprising story. The oldest people in the study carried purely Papuan ancestry, and mixing with newcomers of East Asian-related ancestry on Watom dates to about 2,100 years ago, centuries after the Lapita arrival.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): The impact of human dispersals and local interactions on the genetic diversity of coastal Papua New Guinea over the past 2,500 years

title: The Collapse That Never Happened
text: Rapa Nui is often told as a warning tale: islanders overused their resources and their population crashed in the 1600s. But genomes from 15 Rapanui people dated 1670 to 1950 CE, held in a Paris museum, show no sign of such a crash. The real catastrophe came later, when Peruvian slave raiders kidnapped a third of the population in the 1860s and smallpox followed, leaving about 110 people.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ancient Rapanui genomes reveal resilience and pre-European contact with the Americas

title: The Early Dinosaur Built to Devour
place: Marchezan site, São João do Polêsine, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
text: In the red rocks of southern Brazil, scientists found an almost complete skeleton of one of the earliest meat-eating dinosaurs, about 233 million years old. They named it Gnathovorax, roughly 'inclined to devour with the jaws.' A scan of its braincase showed a well-developed part of the cerebellum linked to steadying the eyes and head, a handy tool for a hunter with blade-like claws.

source.name: PeerJ (via PMC): Gnathovorax cabreirai, a new early dinosaur and the origin and initial radiation of predatory dinosaurs

dateLabel: Early Jurassic, about 195 million years ago
title: Baby Dinosaurs That Started on All Fours
place: El Tranquilo, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina
text: Mussaurus hatchlings from Patagonia weighed about 60 grams, light as an egg, yet adults grew past a tonne. By modelling skeletons of every age, researchers found the babies walked on four legs, then rose onto two as they grew. The switch came as the tail lengthened and the head and neck shrank in proportion, shifting the body's balance point back toward the hips.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Ontogenetic changes in the body plan of Mussaurus patagonicus

title: A Pterosaur Colony by a Desert Lake
text: Outside a small town in Paraná, a patch of sandstone under 20 square metres held hundreds of pterosaur bones, from at least 47 animals. Caiuajara dobruskii lived in colonies around an oasis lake in a Cretaceous desert, and storms later washed their remains together. Most were youngsters, and their bodies barely changed as they grew, hinting that they could fly very young.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Manzig et al. 2014, Caiuajara dobruskii, a new tapejarid pterosaur from a Cretaceous desert bone bed in Brazil

title: The Caiman With a Seven-Tonne Bite
place: Alto Acre, Assis Brasil, Acre, Brazil
text: Purussaurus brasiliensis, a giant caiman of Miocene Amazonia, reached about 12.5 metres and 8.4 tonnes, judging from a skull 1.4 metres long found in Acre. Scientists estimated its bite at about 69,000 newtons, roughly seven tonnes of force. It could tackle giant turtles and big plant-eaters, but as the Andes rose and the modern Amazon formed, its swampy world disappeared.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Aureliano et al. 2015, body size, bite force and paleobiology of Purussaurus brasiliensis

title: A Car-Sized Turtle With Fighting Horns
text: Stupendemys geographicus roamed the vast Miocene wetlands of northern South America. A shell from Urumaco measured about 2.86 metres, and the animal weighed around 1,145 kilograms, twice a leatherback. Some shells carry big forward horns, probably on males that fought each other. One Venezuelan shell still has a giant caiman's tooth stuck in it, likely from an attack by Purussaurus.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): The anatomy, paleobiology, and evolutionary relationships of the largest extinct side-necked turtle

title: When the Caribbean Flooded the Amazon
text: Deep drill cores from Colombia's Llanos Basin and Brazil's western Amazon show the sea pushed into the heart of South America at least twice during the Miocene. The longer flood, from about 16 to 12 million years ago, came in from the Caribbean. Its proof is tiny: a shark tooth, a burrowing mantis shrimp and marine plankton buried in layers of mud.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Miocene flooding events of western Amazonia

title: A Sea Cow Caught by a Caiman
place: El Limón, south of Coro, Falcón, Venezuela
text: A fossil sea cow skull from northwestern Venezuela records an Early Miocene crime scene. Round punctures and drag marks on its snout suggest a caiman grabbed it there, possibly in a death roll. Later, tiger sharks of the species Galeocerdo aduncus scavenged the body, slicing its skull, ribs and spine, and one shark tooth was left behind between the neck and ribcage.

source.name: Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (via PMC): Trophic interactions of sharks and crocodylians with a sea cow from the Miocene of Venezuela

title: Big Fruits in an Early Rainforest
text: Coal mines near Bogotá hold leaves and seeds from one of the earliest known Neotropical rainforests, from the Paleocene, soon after the dinosaurs vanished. Leaves with drip tips point to rainfall above 180 centimetres a year. Among the finds are fruit stones of a vine family up to 35 millimetres long, roughly three times the size of most of their living relatives' fruits.

source.name: American Journal of Botany (via PMC): New records of extinct Icacinaceae from Paleocene rainforests of northwestern South America

title: Cut Marks on Giant Sloth Bones
place: Arroyo del Vizcaíno, Sauce, Canelones, Uruguay
text: A streambed near Sauce, Uruguay, has yielded more than 1,000 Ice Age bones, mostly from the giant ground sloth Lestodon. About 40 bones carry marks that look like stone-tool cuts, and a small scraper-like stone lay among them. At roughly 30,000 years old, the site is unexpectedly ancient for humans in the Americas, so its excavators themselves urge caution.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (via PMC): Arroyo del Vizcaíno, Uruguay: a fossil-rich 30-ka-old megafaunal locality with cut-marked bones

title: Painted Giants on Amazon Cliffs?
place: Cerro Azul, Serranía de La Lindosa, Guaviare, Colombia
text: Red paintings cover the rock walls of La Lindosa in the Colombian Amazon, where people were using ochre by about 12,600 years ago. Some researchers see Ice Age animals among them: a giant ground sloth with its young, horses with stiff manes and a trunked gomphothere. Critics say the 'sloth' may be a capybara, and the paintings themselves have not yet been directly dated.

source.name: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (via PMC): Ice Age megafauna rock art in the Colombian Amazon?

title: Garden Islands in a Flooded Savanna
place: Isla Manechi, Llanos de Moxos, Beni, Bolivia
text: Bolivia's Llanos de Moxos floods every wet season, but thousands of small forest islands stay dry. Many grew from early foragers' food waste: charcoal, shell and bone piled up from about 10,850 years ago. On these fertile mounds people were growing manioc by about 10,350 years ago and squash soon after, among the oldest crop evidence in Amazonia. Maize followed around 6,850 years ago.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia

title: Gomphothere Hunters of Central Chile
place: Laguna de Tagua Tagua, O'Higgins, Chile
text: Scientists counted animal bones from 20 early hunting camps across southern South America older than 11,600 years. In most, extinct giants made up over 80 percent of the remains. On the Pampas and in Patagonia that meant giant sloths and Ice Age horses. At two Tagua Tagua camps in central Chile, every identified bone came from extinct megafauna, chiefly elephant-like gomphotheres. Guanaco only became common later.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Extinct megafauna dominated human subsistence in southern South America before 11,600 years ago

title: A Head Framed by Its Own Hands
place: Lapa do Santo, Matozinhos, Minas Gerais, Brazil
text: In a rock shelter in Brazil's Lagoa Santa caves lies the oldest known decapitation in the Americas, about 9,200 years old. The man's severed head was buried with amputated hands placed over his face, the right hand pointing to his chin and the left to his forehead. Isotopes in his teeth show he was a local, so researchers read it as ritual, not trophy-taking.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Strauss et al. 2015, the earliest case of decapitation in the New World, Lapa do Santo

title: The Teenage Big-Game Hunter of the Andes
text: At nearly 4,000 metres in the Peruvian Andes, a 17- to 19-year-old was buried about 9,000 years ago with a hunting kit: stone spear points, scrapers, knives and lumps of red ochre. Proteins in the tooth enamel showed the hunter was female. Looking at other early burials across the Americas, the team estimated that women made up perhaps 30 to 50 percent of big-game hunters.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Female hunters of the early Americas

title: Maize Starch on Ancient Grinding Stones
place: Xihuatoxtla Shelter, Central Balsas Valley, Guerrero, Mexico
text: In a rock shelter in Guerrero's tropical forest, scientists scraped microscopic starch grains off 19 grinding stones. Nearly all came from maize, not its wild ancestor teosinte, and tiny silica bodies from cobs turned up too. Dated to about 8,700 years ago, it is among the earliest maize anywhere. Domesticated squash was there as well, in warm lowland forest rather than dry highlands.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico

title: Zuzu, Buried With Two Spear Points
place: Toca dos Coqueiros, Serra da Capivara, Piauí, Brazil
text: In a rock shelter in Brazil's Serra da Capivara, archaeologists found a tightly folded skeleton nicknamed Zuzu, buried in an oval pit with two finely flaked spear points. Dating the tooth enamel directly gave at least 9,600 years. The long, narrow skull matched early people from Lagoa Santa, far to the south, more closely than later groups from Zuzu's own northeastern region.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Morphometric affinities and direct radiocarbon dating of the Toca dos Coqueiros' skull

title: The Survivor in the Flooded Cave
place: Chan Hol cave, near Tulum, Quintana Roo, Mexico
text: Divers found her skeleton 8 metres underwater, more than a kilometre inside a flooded cave near Tulum. Cave crust on her finger bones shows she is at least 9,900 years old. About 30 when she died, she had survived three blows to the head that later healed. Her badly decayed teeth hint at a diet rich in soft, carbohydrate-rich foods.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Stinnesbeck et al. 2020, the Chan Hol 3 skeleton from Tulum, Mexico

title: Black Soil Above the Madeira Rapids
place: Teotônio, Madeira River, Porto Velho, Rondônia, Brazil
text: On a bluff beside thundering rapids in the southwest Amazon, villagers began building up rich black soil, terra preta, about 6,500 years ago. In it archaeologists found manioc and squash traces, and bean starch stuck to stone tools, among the earliest such evidence in the Amazon lowlands. Earlier people at the same spot were already gathering Brazil nuts and fruits around 9,500 years ago.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Watling et al. 2018, direct archaeological evidence for southwestern Amazonia as an early plant domestication centre

title: A Rival to Valdivia's First Pots
place: Real Alto, Chanduy, Santa Elena, Ecuador
text: Valdivia on Ecuador's coast has long been credited with some of the oldest pottery in South America. But Russian, Ecuadorian and Japanese archaeologists digging at Real Alto found sherds of a little-known style called San Pedro, dated to 4640 to 4460 BCE. Their decoration differs from Valdivia's, hinting that two separate pottery traditions grew up side by side.

source.name: EurekAlert (Far Eastern Federal University): Pottery related to unknown culture found in Ecuador

title: The World's Oldest Indigo Blue
place: Huaca Prieta, Chicama Valley, La Libertad, Peru
text: Scraps of cotton cloth from a mound on Peru's north coast hold the oldest known indigo dye, about 6,200 years old. That beats the previous record, from Egypt, by roughly 1,500 years. Chemical tests found the blue in five of eight yarn samples. The earliest piece alternated stripes of natural tan cotton with blue yarn twisted together with white vine fibre.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru

title: Ancient DNA From Titicaca's First Foragers
text: Near Lake Titicaca, mobile hunter-gatherers camped at Soro Mik'aya Patjxa between about 8,000 and 6,500 years ago. A genome from one of them, about 6,800 years old, helped researchers estimate that highland and lowland South Americans split roughly 8,750 years ago. Later highlanders show strong natural selection near a starch-digesting gene, likely as potatoes and other tubers grew central to their diet.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): The genetic prehistory of the Andean highlands 7000 years BP through European contact

title: Maize on the Menu in Caral's Age
place: Caballete, Fortaleza Valley, Lima Region, Peru
text: When Peru's first monumental towns rose in the Norte Chico region, did people live on fish or farms? At Caballete and Huaricanga, maize pollen turned up in nearly half of soil samples, and maize starch coated most grinding stones. It even filled 69 percent of fossil droppings from people and their dogs, dated to roughly 3200 to 2400 BCE. Anchovies supplied the protein.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Evidence for maize (Zea mays) in the Late Archaic (3000-1800 B.C.) in the Norte Chico region of Peru

title: A Harpoon in a Fisherman's Chest
text: Early fisher-gatherers on Chile's Atacama coast, between about 10,000 and 4,000 years ago, were not always peaceful. Among 136 Archaic burials, a quarter showed injuries from violence, most often on men's skulls. At Morro de Arica, one man had four wounds the width of a harpoon, and another still had a complete harpoon, stone point and all, lodged in his chest.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Violence in fishing, hunting, and gathering societies of the Atacama Desert coast (10,000 BP-AD 1450)

title: Olmec Plazas Aligned to the Sunrise
text: Using laser scans of 415 ancient complexes, researchers measured which way Olmec and early Maya builders pointed their plazas. San Lorenzo's main plateau, at its height around 1400 to 1100 BCE, faces sunrise on quarter days, and its 20 edge platforms hint at counting in twenties. Later sites lined up with sunrises 260 days apart, the length of Mesoamerica's sacred calendar.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Origins of Mesoamerican astronomy and calendar: Evidence from the Olmec and Maya regions

title: DNA of the Caribbean's First Islanders
text: People first reached Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico about 6,000 years ago. Ancient DNA, including from a man buried at Andrés in the Dominican Republic about 3,000 years ago, shows these first islanders came from a population closest to Central and northern South Americans, not North Americans. Later pottery-making newcomers replaced nearly all their ancestry, except in western Cuba.

source.name: Nature (via PMC): A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean

title: The Oldest Long-Necked Giant of Its Kind
place: Jethwai village, Jaisalmer District, Rajasthan, India
text: Near the desert town of Jaisalmer, researchers dug neck, back and tail bones out of a shale bed, scattered over about 25 square metres. They named the plant-eater Tharosaurus indicus, the "Thar Desert lizard". It belongs to the dicraeosaurs, a long-necked sauropod family, and its Middle Jurassic rocks make it the earliest known member of the wider diplodocoid group anywhere on Earth.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Fossils of the oldest diplodocoid dinosaur suggest India was a major centre for neosauropod radiation

dateLabel: Late Jurassic, about 152 million years ago
title: A Sea Dragon Buried Nose-First
place: Lodai, near Bhuj, Kachchh District, Gujarat, India
text: In 2016, a Delhi University and Kachchh University team uncovered India's first Jurassic ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped marine reptile about 5 metres long, near Lodai village. The animal seems to have hit the soft seabed snout-first, then settled on its side. Its teeth carry odd grooves and chipped enamel, hinting that this top predator crunched hard prey such as armoured fish or thick-shelled ammonites.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Discovery of the first ichthyosaur from the Jurassic of India

dateLabel: Late Cretaceous, about 67 million years ago
title: Ninety-Two Nests of Giant Dinosaurs
place: Bagh and Kukshi area, Dhar District, Madhya Pradesh, India
text: Around the villages of Bagh and Kukshi, scientists mapped 92 egg clutches and 256 eggs left by titanosaurs, the huge long-necked dinosaurs. The round eggs measured about 15 to 17 centimetres across, laid in sandy ground near marshy lakes. One egg had a second egg inside it, a defect seen in birds, hinting that these giants may have laid eggs one after another, as birds do.

source.name: PLOS ONE: New Late Cretaceous titanosaur sauropod dinosaur egg clutches from lower Narmada valley, India

title: A Shiny Tooth From the First Gibbons
place: Sunetar, near Ramnagar, Udhampur District, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: In 2015, researcher Christopher Gilbert was resting on a hill near Ramnagar when he spotted something shiny in a pile of dirt. It was a complete ape molar, about 13 million years old. Named Kapi ramnagarensis, from the Hindi word for ape, it is the oldest known gibbon ancestor and pushes the gibbon fossil record back by at least five million years.

source.name: ASU News: New fossil ape is discovered in India

source2.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: New Middle Miocene ape from Ramnagar, India

title: An Ape Jaw on an Ancient Seashore
place: Tapar, Bhachau Taluka, Kachchh District, Gujarat, India
text: Miocene apes in India were long known only from the Siwalik Hills in the north. Then, in 2011, fieldworkers at Tapar in Kutch collected an upper jaw of Sivapithecus, an orangutan relative, with its canine and molars still in place. It lay among fossil fish, crocodiles and turtles from a coastal lagoon, and shifted the known range of these apes about ten degrees of latitude south.

source.name: PLOS ONE: First record of the Miocene hominoid Sivapithecus from Kutch, Gujarat state, western India

title: A Feast on a Sick Giant Elephant
place: Pampore, Kashmir Valley, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: In 2000, a brownish stump in a Pampore quarry, first taken for fossil wood, turned out to be a tusk. The skull belonged to a huge straight-tusked elephant whose sinuses show a chronic infection. Nearby lay 87 tools of basalt, a rock not found locally, and smashed bone flakes. People had broken the bones for marrow: India's earliest known evidence of butchery, though nobody knows if they hunted it.

source.name: Florida Museum: Rare fossils of extinct elephant document the earliest known instance of butchery in India

source2.name: Natural History Museum: Ancient humans feasted on a giant elephant in India over 300,000 years ago

title: Quartz Crystals Carried for No Reason
place: Singi Talav, near Didwana, Rajasthan, India
text: On the edge of the Thar Desert, handaxe makers camped beside a lake at Singi Talav when monsoon rains turned the land into grassland. Their tools, dated to about 177,000 years ago, are among the youngest Acheulean handaxes in the world. With them lay six quartz crystals that were carried in but had no obvious use: the oldest dated non-practical objects in South Asia.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Constraining the chronology and ecology of Late Acheulean and Middle Palaeolithic occupations at the margins of the monsoon

title: The Caves Where India's Animals Endured
place: Billasurgam caves, Kurnool District, Andhra Pradesh, India
text: The Billasurgam caves hold more than 10 metres of dusty cave earth packed with bones. Cathedral Cave's layers reach back about 210,000 years, and a younger cave even holds ash from the Toba super-eruption. Of 21 mammals identified, from leopards and bears to langurs and porcupines, 20 still live in India today. The odd one out is a gelada-like monkey now found only in Africa.

source.name: PNAS: Continuity of mammalian fauna over the last 200,000 y in the Indian subcontinent

title: Stone Points Near the Indian Ocean
place: Sandhav, Naira Valley, Kachchh District, Gujarat, India
text: About 15 kilometres from today's Kachchh coast, Sandhav gave scientists the first directly dated proof of people living near South Asia's shores. Around 114,000 years ago, during a wet phase of strong monsoons, toolmakers left a distinctive tanged point, perhaps a spear tip or knife. Surprisingly, their kit matched inland groups, so these were land-based people, not specialised beachcombers travelling a coastal highway.

source.name: Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology: The first directly dated evidence for Palaeolithic occupation on the Indian coast at Sandhav, Kachchh

title: Six Monsoons Written in Volcanic Ash
place: Jurreru River valley, Jwalapuram, Kurnool District, Andhra Pradesh, India
text: When Sumatra's Toba volcano erupted, ash fell up to 3 metres deep in this Indian valley, burying tree trunks and leaves. A newly exposed section shows six ash layers split by thin crusts, read as six yearly monsoons. Instead of a long volcanic winter, they record about a year of mild cooling, then roughly four years of heat and drought, before grasses returned.

source.name: PNAS Nexus: Seasonally resolved stratigraphy at Jwalapuram India shows regional surface warming after the Toba eruption

title: Newcomers Who Lived Off the Rainforest
place: Batadomba-lena rock shelter, Kuruwita, Ratnapura District, Sri Lanka
text: Batadomba-lena, a rock shelter in Sri Lanka's wet-zone rainforest, holds human remains that rank among South Asia's earliest Homo sapiens, from roughly 36,000 years ago. Rainforests were long thought too poor in food and too hard to live in for early people. Yet isotopes in human teeth show that the island's first modern humans relied on forest resources from the start, including dedicated monkey hunting.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History: Earliest evidence for human rainforest resource reliance

source2.name: PNAS: Population increase and environmental deterioration correspond with microlithic innovations in South Asia ca. 35,000 years ago

title: An Eggshell Dates the Tiny-Tool Revolution
text: At Patne in Maharashtra, an ostrich eggshell buried 4 metres deep was dated to about 30,000 years ago. By then the camp's toolmakers had swapped big flakes and scrapers for tiny backed microliths: crescents, trapezes and triangles made to slot into handles. Across South Asia, sites of this microlith age outnumber older Middle Palaeolithic ones 402 to 153, hinting at growing populations.

source.name: PNAS: Population increase and environmental deterioration correspond with microlithic innovations in South Asia ca. 35,000 years ago

title: A Rock Shelter Full of Shrinking Tools
place: Jwalapuram Locality 9, Jurreru River valley, Kurnool District, Andhra Pradesh, India
text: Jwalapuram Locality 9 is a small rock shelter in southern India with more than 3 metres of deposits and over 53,000 stone artefacts in seven layers. Its oldest layers, from before 34,000 years ago, are dominated by scrapers. Then, sometime before 20,000 years ago, slim microblades and backed pieces shaped like crescents and triangles appear, a step-by-step switch to miniature tools.

source.name: PNAS: Population increase and environmental deterioration correspond with microlithic innovations in South Asia ca. 35,000 years ago

title: When Sri Lanka's Monsoon Went Quiet
place: Frogmore grassland, Maskeliya, Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: A sediment core from the Frogmore grassland high in Sri Lanka's hills, together with cores from the seabed off Colombo and Negombo, tracks 80,000 years of rain. During the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, the island was dry. Colder oceans meant fewer storms, so springtime inter-monsoon showers, not the summer monsoon, supplied most rain.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Interplay of the Indian summer monsoon and intermonsoon precipitation in Sri Lanka due to ITCZ migration during the last 80000 years

title: Monsoon Winds Recorded in Seabed Mud
place: Indus submarine canyon, northeastern Arabian Sea, off Sindh, Pakistan
text: A 20-metre core pulled from 571 metres down, beside the Indus submarine canyon off Pakistan, holds finely layered mud from the end of the last Ice Age. Scanning it in strips thinner than a millimetre, scientists found that summer monsoon winds rose and fell with climate swings near distant Greenland, while winter monsoon winds slowly weakened over millennia as the world warmed.

source.name: Nature Geoscience: Contrasting drivers of South Asian summer and winter monsoon evolution during the last deglaciation

title: Forest Foragers Who Turned to Plants
place: Balangoda Kuragala, Ratnapura District, Sri Lanka
text: Zinc isotopes in the tooth enamel of 24 people from three Sri Lankan rainforest caves, including Balangoda Kuragala, reveal where they sat in the food chain. From the late Ice Age onward, their values drift toward those of plant-eaters. Long before millet farming arrived about 3,000 years ago, forest foragers were eating ever more plants, a menu earlier digs show included breadfruit and kekuna nuts.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution: Pre-agricultural intensification of plant use in Pleistocene Sri Lankan rainforests

title: Settlers Who Came With the Rains
text: Bhirrana, beside the dry bed of the Ghaggar-Hakra river, preserves every phase of Indus history, beginning with a pre-Harappan level of pit dwellings and incised pottery. Oxygen isotopes in cattle, goat and deer teeth suggest its first settlers arrived when the monsoon was strong, which the study dates to roughly 9,500 to 8,000 years ago. Fish bones and turtle shells point to wetter land.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Oxygen isotope in archaeological bioapatites from India: Implications to climate change and decline of Bronze Age Harappan civilization

title: Blackbuck Hunters on a Sand Dune
place: Vaharvo Timbo, Runi, Patan District, Gujarat, India
text: On a sand dune in north Gujarat, hunter-gatherers camped at Vaharvo Timbo for about 600 years. Excavators found blades, tiny geometric tools of agate, carnelian and chert, and roughly 5,000 waste chips, with many finished tools apparently never used. The hunters mostly chased blackbuck antelope, gathered wild sesame and grasses, and wore beads made from Dentalium, a tusk-shaped seashell.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Microlithic variation and the Mesolithic occupations of western India

title: Mehrgarh's Farmers Arrive Late
text: Mehrgarh is famed as the Indus region's first farming village, long thought to begin around 8000 BCE and last three millennia. New radiocarbon dates on tooth enamel from 23 graves tell a different story: its pottery-free cemetery began about 5200 to 4900 BCE and lasted only two to five centuries. The team argues farming arrived with incoming farmers, not as a local invention.

source.name: Scientific Reports: New radiocarbon dates of human tooth enamel reveal a late appearance of farming life in the Indus Valley

title: Taming Rice Without Paddy Fields
text: Near the Indus city of Rakhigarhi, archaeologists sifted village soils at Masudpur for charred rice spikelet bases, the tiny scars where grains attach. In Mature Harappan layers most looked wild; in later layers domestic types took over. Indus farmers seem to have slowly domesticated local rice, without wet paddies, before East Asian japonica rice and paddy farming arrived around 2000 BCE.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science: Approaching rice domestication in South Asia: New evidence from Indus settlements in northern India

title: Cities Filled With Childhood Migrants
place: Harappa cemetery, Sahiwal District, Punjab, Pakistan
text: Tooth enamel records where a child grew up. At Harappa, and at Farmana in India, scientists compared strontium, lead and oxygen in first molars, formed by about age three, with molars formed later. Most first molars carried non-local signatures, while later teeth shifted toward local values. The cemeteries seem filled almost entirely with people who moved to the cities as young children.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Evidence for Patterns of Selective Urban Migration in the Greater Indus Valley (2600-1900 BC)

title: Dung Cakes for Indus Kitchens
place: Kanmer, Rapar Taluka, Kachchh District, Gujarat, India
text: At Kanmer, a walled Harappan town in Kachchh, burnt remains show what fed the fires. People burned thorny scrub wood, a little mangrove, and plenty of dung, whose tell-tale crystals turned up in seven of eight fireplaces. A kiln, probably for beads or pots, held only dung ash. One charred scrap came from a nutmeg-family tree growing about 500 kilometres away.

source.name: PLOS ONE: 'Not all that burns is wood'. A social perspective on fuel exploitation and use during the Indus urban period (2600-1900 BC)

title: Swapping Barley for Millet in a Drought
text: Khirsara was a fortified Harappan town in Kachchh with a warehouse, a well and workshops for shell bangles and beads. Around 4,200 years ago, as severe drought set in, its farmers changed crops. Barley had made up about 73 percent of grains; soon millets such as foxtail, pearl and finger millet reached 85 percent. The town survived, but its pottery grew coarser.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Altered cropping pattern and cultural continuation with declined prosperity following abrupt and extreme arid event at ~4,200 yrs BP: Evidence from an Indus archaeological site Khirsara

title: Skull Surgery and Deep Roots in Kashmir
place: Burzahom, Srinagar District, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: Neolithic Burzahom buried its dead with animals and red ochre, and several skulls show trepanation, holes deliberately cut into the head, with seven complete cases reported. Now scientists have read a full mitochondrial genome from one Neolithic person dated to about 2000 BCE. Its maternal line, M65, still survives among people in Kashmir today, suggesting deep local roots.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Ancient mitogenomes from Neolithic, megalithic and medieval burials suggest complex genetic history of Kashmir valley, India

title: From Dung Fires to an Axe Factory
place: Hiregudda (Kupgal Hill), near Sanganakallu, Ballari District, Karnataka, India
text: Neolithic herders on Hiregudda, or Kupgal Hill, near Ballari first piled up a mound of burnt cattle dung ash. Later the hilltop became a village, busiest from about 1700 to 1500 BCE, its slopes dotted with rock art and stone walls. Around 1400 to 1300 BCE it turned into a large stone axe workshop, as new black-and-red pottery and child urn burials appeared.

source.name: UCL Institute of Archaeology (Fuller, Boivin and Korisettar): Dating the Neolithic of South India, author manuscript

title: A Sea Cow Graveyard in the Desert
text: 1970s mining and oil surveys turned up what looked like reptile bones in southwestern Qatar, and officials later nicknamed the spot the "dugong cemetery." The bones belong to sea cows that grazed seagrass here about 21 million years ago. New species Salwasiren qatarensis weighed only about 113 kilograms and still had hind limb bones. More than 170 fossil spots make this the world's richest sea cow bonebed.

source.name: EurekAlert (Smithsonian): Arabian Gulf fossil bed reveals new sea cow species

title: A Fossil Nautilus That Kept Its Eyes
text: Lebanon's limestone hills around Hadjoula hold some of the finest fossils of the Cretaceous seas. Researchers studied two nautiluses of the species Syrionautilus libanoticus whose soft bodies survived for about 95 million years. One, found without its shell, still shows traces of its gut, central nervous system, eyes and mantle. Its arms and hood are missing, so it may be a leftover dropped by a predator that ate the rest.

source.name: Swiss Journal of Palaeontology: Preservation of nautilid soft parts from the Lebanese Cenomanian

title: A Swordfish Before Swordfish Existed
text: Long before true billfish evolved, another fish hunted Cretaceous seas with a pointed bill. Rhamphoichthys taxidiotis had a hollow snout about half as long as its skull, a slender body with around 100 vertebrae, and fin rays longer than its body was deep. One whole skeleton comes from the fossil quarries of Haqel in Lebanon, others from Germany. Its name means "traveller beak fish," for its wide-roaming open-sea life.

source.name: Royal Society Open Science: The first articulated skeletons of enigmatic Late Cretaceous billfish-like actinopterygians

title: Thailand's First Named Serpent-Necked Giant
place: Phu Noi locality, Ban Din Chi, Kham Muang, Kalasin, Thailand
text: Near the village of Ban Din Chi, the Phu Noi fossil site keeps giving up dinosaurs from the end of the Jurassic. In 2026 scientists named Uragasaurus kalasinensis, Thailand's first known mamenchisaurid, a sauropod family famous for extremely long necks. Its name comes from the Sanskrit word for serpent. CT scans of a single back vertebra, more than half a metre tall, revealed honeycomb-like air spaces inside the bone.

source.name: Scientific Reports: A new mamenchisaurid sauropod from the Lower Phu Kradung Formation of northeastern Thailand

title: Southeast Asia's Biggest Dinosaur, by a Pond
place: Ban Pha Nang Sua, Nong Bua Rawe District, Chaiyaphum, Thailand
text: Bones in a bed beside a village pond at Ban Pha Nang Sua in Chaiyaphum turned out to belong to one giant animal. Nagatitan chaiyaphumensis, named for the serpent-like naga and the titans of Greek myth, was a long-necked sauropod roughly 27 metres long and around 27 tonnes. Its thighbone alone was nearly two metres. It is the largest sauropod yet known from Southeast Asia.

source.name: Scientific Reports: The first sauropod dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Khok Kruat Formation of Thailand

title: Toolmakers Reached Sulawesi a Million Years Ago
place: Calio, near Ujung, Soppeng Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: In old river sands near Ujung village in South Sulawesi, archaeologists found seven chert flakes alongside the jaw of Celebochoerus, an extinct big pig. Dating of the pig's teeth and the rocks' ancient magnetism shows the tools are at least 1.04 million years old, far older than any earlier sign of people on the island. Sulawesi lies across the sea from Asia, so unknown early humans somehow crossed water.

source.name: Nature: Hominins on Sulawesi during the Early Pleistocene

title: A Spear Wound in Shanidar Cave
text: Digging in Shanidar Cave in 2019 and 2022 uncovered Shanidar A, a Neanderthal of about 45, laid in the same tight cluster as other bodies around 75,000 years ago. A neat 15-millimetre hole in the left shoulder blade suggests a wooden spear passed through the chest, probably killing them quickly. Years earlier, the same person had survived a blow to the face that split a front tooth.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Funerary behaviour and lethal trauma in a new Neanderthal individual from Shanidar Cave

title: A Neanderthal Child's Lost Baby Tooth
text: Over 41,000 years ago, a Neanderthal child about six years old lost a baby canine in a rockshelter in Iran's Zagros Mountains. Archaeologists found it 2.5 metres down at Bawa Yawan, among Zagros Mousterian stone tools and the bones of hoofed animals. The little tooth finally showed that Neanderthals made these tools, and hints that they lingered in the Zagros later than experts once thought.

source.name: PLOS ONE: An in situ Neanderthal remain in the Bawa Yawan Rockshelter, Kermanshah

title: Island-Hopping Dinosaurs Reach Oman
text: Near the village of Al-Khod outside Muscat, gravels washed off newly risen mountains buried dinosaur bones about 70 to 66 million years ago. Among them are broken leg bones and vertebrae of hadrosauroids, relatives of the duck-billed dinosaurs, the first known from Late Cretaceous Afro-Arabia. Northeastern Oman may then have been an island in the Tethys Sea, so these plant-eaters probably came from Asia or Europe, perhaps by island-hopping.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Hadrosauroid Dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of the Sultanate of Oman

title: A Dinosaur Herd Crosses a Yemeni Mudflat
place: Madar, Arhab, north of Sana'a, Yemen
text: A local journalist spotted the first footprints near Madar village, 47 kilometres north of Sana'a. They became Arabia's first known dinosaur tracksite, pressed into a coastal mudflat sometime between the Middle Jurassic and the earliest Cretaceous. Eleven parallel sauropod trackways show big and small long-necks walking together as a herd at about 3 kilometres an hour, while a two-legged plant-eater left 15 footprints in a row.

source.name: PLOS ONE: First Dinosaur Tracks from the Arabian Peninsula

title: A Bird Courtship Dance in Stone
place: Chehr-Abad, west of Zanjan, Zanjan Province, Iran
text: On a cliff about 90 kilometres west of Zanjan, a slab of 13- to 15-million-year-old mud preserves some 70 trackways of small four-toed birds, probably plovers. One researcher reads the tangle as a courtship dance: high stepping, stomping, hopping, sideways leaps and brief fluttering flights. Several nearly parallel trails may even record rival males dancing at once. Because the cliff is so steep, much was studied from drone photos.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Reconstructing Miocene bird mating behavior from a fossil tracksite

title: Toolmakers by a Lake in the Nefud
place: Jebel Qattar 1, Jubbah, Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
text: Today Jebel Qattar rises from the dunes of the Nefud Desert, but about 75,000 years ago it stood beside a lake in grassland dotted with trees. Middle Palaeolithic people left Levallois flakes and a retouched point in an ancient soil there, and a deeper soil holds tools about 211,000 years old. Their style recalls toolkits from the Levant and Africa, though nobody knows which kind of human made them.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Hominin dispersal into the Nefud Desert and Middle Palaeolithic settlement along the Jubbah Palaeolake

title: The Aurochs That Escaped a Spear
place: Nesher Ramla, near Ramla, central Israel
text: About 120,000 years ago, archaic humans at Nesher Ramla in central Israel hunted aurochs, huge wild cattle, picking mostly prime-aged cows, probably in the dry summer. One aurochs shinbone holds a flint chip about 6 millimetres long, with new bone grown around it: the animal survived a hunt for at least four weeks before being caught again. The bones point to many small, planned hunts, not mass kills.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Archaic humans in the Middle Palaeolithic Levant conducted planned and selective intercepts of aurochs

title: Stone Picks in Vietnam's Highlands
place: Go Da and Roc Tung, An Khe, Gia Lai Province, Vietnam
text: Near the town of An Khe in Vietnam's Central Highlands, archaeologists dug up stone tools at Go Da and Roc Tung: bifaces, heavy picks, choppers and scrapers, mostly made from river pebbles. Tektites, bits of natural glass lying with the tools, were dated to about 806,000 and 782,000 years ago. The researchers argue early humans here invented their bifaces locally, rather than inheriting Africa's handaxe tradition.

source.name: Archaeology, Ethnology & Anthropology of Eurasia: The Discovery of a Bifacial Industry in Vietnam

title: Borneo's Oldest Stone Tool Workshop
place: Mansuli Valley, near Lahad Datu, Sabah, Malaysia
text: In 2003, an archaeological team walking to a cave about 30 kilometres from Lahad Datu in eastern Sabah stumbled on stone tools lying on the ground in the Mansuli Valley. Digs by the Sabah Museum and Universiti Sains Malaysia uncovered more than 1,000 tools and a workshop where people shaped chert, a fine silica-rich stone. Luminescence dating puts it at about 235,000 years old, Borneo's oldest known Palaeolithic site.

source.name: Department of National Heritage Malaysia: Lembah Mansuli, 235,000 years

title: Stone Tools Beneath Supervolcano Ash
place: Kota Tampan, Lenggong Valley, Perak, Malaysia
text: In 1954, a dig at Kota Tampan in Perak's Lenggong Valley found stone tools sealed beneath ash from Sumatra's Toba volcano, and later dating put the tool layer at about 70,000 years old. When researchers restudied the finds in 2020, 165 of the 234 recorded artefacts could not be found. The 69 survivors, linked to early modern humans, were flaked with hand-held hammers or smashed on an anvil.

source.name: Antiquity: The Palaeolithic stone assemblage of Kota Tampan, West Malaysia

title: Seafarers Reach the Remote Talaud Islands
place: Leang Sarru, Salibabu Island, Talaud Islands, Indonesia
text: The Talaud Islands lie more than 100 kilometres from any neighbouring island, a gap that existed even in the Pleistocene. Yet people reached Leang Sarru, a rockshelter on Salibabu Island, about 35,000 years ago. They left many chert flakes and heaps of sea and land shells, especially turban snails and nerites. It is the oldest known archaeological site anywhere around the Sulawesi Sea.

source.name: ANU Press, The Archaeology of Sulawesi: Marine and terrestrial resource use in the Talaud Islands (Ono, Sriwigati and Siswanto)

title: Mosquitoes Learn to Bite Early Humans
place: Sundaland rainforests, Borneo, Indonesia and Malaysia
text: Southeast Asia's forest malaria mosquitoes started out feeding on monkeys and other primates in the treetops. Genome studies of 11 species in the Anopheles leucosphyrus group suggest a taste for human blood evolved once, in Sundaland, roughly 2.9 to 1.6 million years ago. That window overlaps the earliest proposed arrival of Homo erectus, about 1.8 million years ago, hinting early humans were already plentiful.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Early hominin arrival in Southeast Asia triggered the evolution of major human malaria vectors

title: The Crested Skull of Khorat
place: Ban Saphan Hin, Suranaree, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: In Early Cretaceous rocks at Ban Saphan Hin near Nakhon Ratchasima, scientists found several braincases, jaws and teeth of a plant-eating dinosaur. Named Sirindhorna khoratensis in 2015, it is the best-preserved iguanodontian dinosaur known from Southeast Asia, with a bony crest running along the top of its skull. It sits close to the root of the family tree that later produced the duck-billed dinosaurs.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A New Basal Hadrosauroid Dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Khok Kruat Formation, Nakhon Ratchasima

title: The Oldest Known Blade Wound
place: Qafzeh Cave, near Nazareth, Lower Galilee, Israel
text: In 1979, excavators in Qafzeh Cave near Nazareth uncovered the skeleton of a young adult, probably male, buried at least 92,000 years ago. A 2026 restudy found a 9-millimetre V-shaped cut along the left jaw that also clipped a premolar, likely from a blow with something sharp. The bone had healed, so the person lived on. Researchers call it the earliest documented case of sharp-force trauma.

source.name: Scientific Reports: A taphonomic reassessment of Qafzeh 25 and its implications for violence, health and funerary practices

title: A Jurassic Croc in a Thai Lagoon
place: Ban Nam Pun, Bang Khan District, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Thailand
text: In 2004 a Thai-French expedition at Ban Nam Pun in southern Thailand collected two limestone blocks holding a snout, back bones and armour plates. CT scans revealed a new teleosaurid, Indosinosuchus peninsularensis, a long-snouted relative of crocodiles from the Jurassic. Its cousins lived in rivers in northeastern Thailand, but this one hunted in a calm lagoon near the sea, showing these animals coped with very different homes.

source.name: PeerJ: A new teleosaurid from the Sibumasu Terrane of Southeast Asia

title: A Rhino Near the Woolly Rhino's Roots
text: Fossil hunters at Kvabebi in eastern Georgia collected two partial skulls, a jaw, many teeth and limb bones of a rhinoceros that lived about 2.7 million years ago. Filed for decades under other names, it was renamed Scythicorhinus vekuai in 2026. Its low-crowned, deeply folded teeth mark it as an early branch close to where the woolly rhino's lineage split from its relatives. The bones are kept in Tbilisi.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Scythicorhinus vekuai from the Pliocene of Georgia

title: Bone Beds Between Volcanic Blasts
place: Yamula reservoir, north of Kayseri, Türkiye
text: When the Yamula reservoir north of Kayseri filled with water, paleontologists took a closer look at its shores. They found bone beds of Late Miocene mammals, including three kinds of ancient elephant relatives, sandwiched between layers of volcanic ignimbrite. Dating crystals from the volcanic rock put one layer at about 7.7 million years old, helping turn central Anatolia's fossils into a precise clock for animal evolution.

source.name: PNAS: Building better biochronology: New fossils and 40Ar/39Ar dates from Central Anatolia

title: Malaysia's First Dinosaur Was a Fish-Eater
text: After searching since 2012, a University of Malaya team with Japanese colleagues found Malaysia's first known dinosaur remains in the rural interior of Pahang. The key fossil is a tooth about 23 millimetres long, with serrated edges, coarse ridges and fine surface ornament typical of spinosaurids, fish-eating carnivores. It comes from rock probably 145 to 75 million years old, and the team urged protection of the site from looters.

source.name: ScienceDaily (ResearchSEA release): First dinosaur fossil found in Malaysia

title: A Gibbon Hiding in an Old Collection
place: Trinil, Solo River, East Java, Indonesia
text: In Leiden, among the fossils Eugène Dubois collected from the Solo River bonebed at Trinil in Java, sat a small thighbone labelled as a langur monkey. Researchers showed it actually belonged to a gibbon, with a round hip joint and slender neck suited to hanging from branches. At about 800,000 years old, it is the oldest gibbon known from island Southeast Asia, and hints at evergreen rainforest nearby.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The oldest gibbon fossil (Hylobatidae) from insular Southeast Asia: evidence from Trinil, East Java

title: The Giant Soft Egg of Antarctica
place: López de Bertodano Formation, Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: About 68 million years ago, something laid an enormous egg near the shore of what is now Seymour Island. The fossil, about 29 by 20 cm, is collapsed and folded like a deflated football, because its shell was thin and layered like a lizard's or snake's, not hard like a dinosaur's. Scientists suspect a giant marine reptile at least 7 metres long, perhaps a mosasaur.

source.name: Nature: A large Cretaceous egg from Antarctica (Legendre et al. 2020)

title: A Diving Bird in a Warm Arctic
place: Near Expedition Fiord, western Axel Heiberg Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: About 92 million years ago, a large bird hunted the fresh waters of what is now Axel Heiberg Island. Named Tingmiatornis, from an Inuktitut word for 'those that fly', it may have dived like a cormorant. It shared its bay with turtles, gar-like fish and crocodile-like champsosaurs. The Arctic then had no seasonal ice and averaged at least 14°C, yet still had two months of winter darkness.

source.name: Scientific Reports: A Large Ornithurine Bird (Tingmiatornis arctica) from the Turonian High Arctic

title: Viking Chain Mail in an Inuit House
place: Skraeling Island, Bache Peninsula region, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: In 1978 and 1979, archaeologists digging old Thule Inuit winter houses on tiny Skraeling Island found pieces of chain mail, ship rivets, knife blades and woollen cloth, all European. Radiocarbon dates put them around the 13th century, when Norse farmers lived far south in Greenland. Some iron here came instead from the Cape York meteorites. Whether Norse explorers came here themselves, or the goods were traded north, is still debated.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Notes on Norse Finds from the East Coast of Ellesmere Island, N.W.T. (Schledermann 1980)

title: An Execution at Starvation Camp
place: Camp Clay, near Cape Sabine, Pim Island, Ellesmere Island region, Nunavut, Canada
text: The US Army's Lady Franklin Bay Expedition went north for the first International Polar Year. By 1884 its starving men were stranded in a tiny hut at Camp Clay, living on shrimp, kelp and even sealskin. When Private Charles Henry kept stealing food, Lieutenant Greely ordered him shot in writing on 6 June 1884. Sixteen days later rescuers found only seven men alive.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): An Arctic Execution: Private Charles B. Henry of the United States Lady Franklin Bay Expedition 1881–84 (Stein 2011)

title: Hunting a Phantom Land, Then Vanishing
place: Bennett Island, De Long Islands, New Siberian Islands, Russia
text: Baron Eduard von Toll, a Russian Arctic geologist, believed an unseen 'Sannikov Land' lay north of the New Siberian Islands. In 1902 he and three companions set off by sledge and kayak for remote Bennett Island. A year later a search party under A. V. Kolchak reached the island by whaleboat and found Toll's note: they had left by kayak in November 1902. No further trace was ever found.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Baron Eduard von Toll's Last Expedition: The Russian Polar Expedition, 1900–1903 (Barr 1981)

title: An Inughuit Funeral at Fort Conger
place: Fort Conger, Lady Franklin Bay, Quttinirpaaq National Park, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: In January 1901 a young Inughuit woman named Elatu died at Robert Peary's winter base at Fort Conger, and who probably lived with Matthew Henson. Peary joined her funeral and wrote the most detailed record of a pre-Christian Inughuit funeral. Mourners wrapped her in skins, walked around the grave three times following the sun, and drew lines across the path home. Bricks still outline her grave.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Elatu's Funeral: A Glimpse of Inughuit-American Relations on Robert E. Peary's 1898–1902 Expedition (LeMoine 2014)

title: Japan's Dash Across the Ross Ice Shelf
text: Lieutenant Nobu Shirase led Japan's first Antarctic expedition aboard the small Kainan-maru. After a failed first try and a tense winter camped in Sydney, where geologist Edgeworth David befriended him, Shirase returned south and met Amundsen's Fram at the Bay of Whales. On 28 January 1912 his sledge party reached 80°05'S on the Ross Ice Shelf before turning back. Shirase later gave David his treasured samurai sword.

source.name: National Institute of Polar Research (Japan): Appendix to Nankyokuki, the Report of the Japanese Antarctic Expedition, 1910–12

source2.name: Australian Museum: Our global neighbours: Nobu Shirase

title: A Volcano Evicts the Whalers' Base
place: Whalers Bay, Deception Island, South Shetland Islands, Antarctica
text: Britain's Deception Island station grew up inside the ring-shaped island, in old dormitories of a Norwegian whaling station at Whalers Bay. On 5 December 1967 volcanic eruptions forced everyone out, rescued by the Chilean ship Piloto Pardo. Scientists returned, but in February 1969 new eruptions damaged buildings and the station was abandoned for good. Mudflows even destroyed the whalers' old cemetery.

source.name: British Antarctic Survey: History of British stations and refuges (Deception Island, Station B)

title: A Bear With Cavities Near the Pole
place: Beaver Pond fossil site, Strathcona Fiord, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: About 3.5 million years ago, a forest grew on Ellesmere Island, and a small bear of about 97 kg lived there. Its fossil teeth, from two individuals, show tooth decay. Berry fossils from the same site suggest that, like today's black bears, it gorged on sugary fruit in autumn to fatten up for hibernation. This early relative of modern bears probably came over from Asia.

source.name: Scientific Reports: A basal ursine bear (Protarctos abstrusus) from the Pliocene High Arctic (Wang et al. 2017)

title: The Year the Ice Age Switched Off
place: NorthGRIP drill site, North Greenland Ice Sheet, Greenland
text: Snow piling up year after year on Greenland's ice cap keeps a diary of past climate. Reading annual layers in the NorthGRIP ice core, scientists found that the last Ice Age ended about 11,700 years ago with astonishing speed. Dust from Asia fell off first, then within a few years the source of Greenland's snow shifted. As one researcher put it, it was 'as if somebody had pushed a button'.

source.name: EurekAlert (University of Copenhagen): Ice cores map dynamics of sudden climate changes

title: Sleeping Through the Antarctic Dark
place: Fremouw Formation, Shackleton Glacier area, Transantarctic Mountains, Antarctica
text: Just after Earth's worst mass extinction, the tusked mammal forerunner Lystrosaurus lived in a milder Antarctica that still had months of polar darkness. Its tusks grew throughout life, laying down growth marks like tree rings. Antarctic tusks show long stress bands missing from South African cousins, a sign the animals slowed into a hibernation-like torpor. It is the oldest known evidence of torpor in the fossil record.

source.name: Communications Biology: Evidence of torpor in the tusks of Lystrosaurus from the Early Triassic of Antarctica (Whitney & Sidor 2020)

title: Bathhouses and Chess in the Polar Night
text: For centuries Pomor hunters from northern Russia wintered on Svalbard, chasing walrus and furs, often sent by Old Believer Orthodox monasteries. They built huts with Russian bathhouses, raised tall wooden crosses at their stations, notched days on wooden calendars and played chess through the dark months. Scurvy grass and raw meat kept them healthy: of 20 skeletons from Russekeila's cemetery, only one showed signs of scurvy.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Russian Hunters on Svalbard and the Polar Winter (Jasinski 1991)

title: A Whaling Boat at the Top of the World
place: Herlufsholm Strand, Peary Land, North Greenland
text: In May 1949 a Danish expedition found the frame of an Inuit umiak, a skin whaling boat over 35 feet long, on a gravel beach facing the Arctic Ocean in Peary Land. It was built from driftwood spruce or larch, except one small piece of oak, a European wood. That oak was later radiocarbon dated to around the 1200s, the era of Norse Greenland, though the boat itself may be far younger.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): An Outline of the Archaeology of Peary Land (Knuth 1952)

source2.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Notes on Norse Finds from the East Coast of Ellesmere Island, N.W.T. (Schledermann 1980)

title: Giant Flightless Birds Near the Pole
place: Bay Fiord fossil area, central Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: About 52 million years ago, central Ellesmere Island, now near 79°N, was a lush coastal rainforest where winters stayed above freezing. A toe bone shows that Gastornis, a huge flightless bird, lived there, matching the size of its relatives far to the south. It probably stayed through the long dark winters, while duck-like Presbyornis waterbirds may have migrated, as geese do today.

source.name: Scientific Reports: The palaeobiology of high latitude birds from the early Eocene greenhouse of Ellesmere Island, Arctic Canada (Stidham & Eberle 2016)

title: The Jeannette Crushed in the Ice
place: Arctic Ocean north of the New Siberian Islands, Russia
text: Backed by newspaper owner James Gordon Bennett, George De Long sailed the Jeannette north in 1879, hoping for an open polar sea. Trapped in ice, the ship drifted for 21 months, proving Wrangel Land was only an island. In June 1881 ice crushed her near the New Siberian Islands. Of 33 men, only 13 survived the boat journey and trek across Siberia. Her wreckage later drifted to Greenland.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Review of In the Kingdom of Ice: The Grand and Terrible Polar Voyage of the U.S.S. Jeannette

title: Antarctica's First Flight Was a Balloon
place: Ross Ice Shelf (Ross Ice Barrier), near the Bay of Whales, Antarctica
text: The first flight of any kind in Antarctica was not a plane but a tethered hydrogen balloon called Eva. On 4 February 1902, during the British Discovery expedition, Robert Falcon Scott rose about 250 metres above the Ross Ice Barrier. Photographs taken from the balloon became the first Antarctic aerial pictures, giving explorers a glimpse of what lay beyond the horizon of the ice.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Aviation history

title: The First Woman Ashore in Antarctica
place: Tryne Islands, Vestfold Hills, Ingrid Christensen Coast, East Antarctica
text: In February 1935 Norwegian captain Klarius Mikkelsen brought the ship Thorshavn into a small bay on an ice-free coast of East Antarctica. The bare hills reminded him of Vestfold back home, so he named them the Vestfold Hills. His wife Caroline came ashore too, becoming the first woman known to land on the Antarctic continent. Mikkelsens Cairn is now a protected heritage site.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: History of Davis station

title: A Climate Diary From Under the Snow
place: Camp Century, northwest Greenland Ice Sheet, Greenland
text: Camp Century was a camp of tunnels buried under the snow of northwest Greenland. In 1964 Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard, there to collect snow samples, wandered into Trench 12 and found a deep drilling project. In 1966 the US Army's cold-regions lab pulled up the first ice core ever drilled to bedrock, 1,390 metres long. Its yearly layers revealed climate going back 8,300 years, with clues to 115,000.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Willi Dansgaard (1922–2011)

title: Saving Svalbard's Last Walruses
place: Moffen Island walrus sanctuary, north coast of Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
text: Svalbard's walrus herds were once enormous. The first recorded walrus hunt there came in 1604, and three and a half centuries of commercial killing followed, until the animals were on the verge of vanishing from the islands. In 1952 they finally got total protection. By the mid-1980s walruses were again commonly seen, hauling out on places like little Moffen Island, now a sanctuary off Spitsbergen's north coast.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Past and Present Distribution of Walruses in Svalbard (Gjertz & Wiig 1994)

title: Shipwrecked, Then Snug at Flora Cottage
place: Cape Flora, Northbrook Island, Franz Josef Land, Russia
text: English explorer Benjamin Leigh Smith had his own steam ship, Eira, built for Arctic exploring. On 21 August 1881 pack ice holed her off Cape Flora in Franz Josef Land, but she sank slowly, letting the crew save food, coal and boats. They built a stone hut roofed with sails, ate 34 bears and 24 walruses over winter, then rowed and hauled four boats to Novaya Zemlya, healthy and scurvy-free.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Review of Shipwreck at Cape Flora: The Expeditions of Benjamin Leigh Smith, England's Forgotten Arctic Explorer

title: A Stubborn Captain Finds Spitsbergen
text: In 1596 two Dutch ships sailed north seeking a northern sea route to Asia. Willem Barents wanted to steer east, but the strong-minded captain Jan Cornelisz de Rijp insisted on going north. That choice led them to Bear Island and Spitsbergen, so historians credit de Rijp with the discovery. The ships then split, and Barents went on to a winter on Novaya Zemlya he would not survive.

source.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Astronomical Observations During Willem Barents's Third Voyage to the North (1596–97) (van der Werf 1998)

source2.name: Arctic (Arctic Institute of North America): Dutch Activities in the North and the Arctic during the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (Braat 1984)

title: Antarctica's First Radio Message
place: Commonwealth Bay (Cape Denison), George V Land, Antarctica
text: Walter Hannam, a Sydney-trained engineer, joined Mawson's Australasian Antarctic Expedition to try something new: radio. He set up a relay station on Macquarie Island, then the first wireless station on the Antarctic continent at Commonwealth Bay, tapping Morse code on a Telefunken set. On 25 September 1912 the first message from Antarctica reached Hobart via Macquarie Island. Hannam is also credited with playing Antarctica's first football.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Walter Hannam

title: A Claim Sealed in Coffee Jugs
place: Walkabout Rocks, northern Vestfold Hills, East Antarctica
text: Sailing with American Lincoln Ellsworth in 1939, Australian aviator Hubert Wilkins learned Ellsworth meant to map land Australia had claimed. So Wilkins flew a small seaplane to several sites, leaving Australian flags and proclamations to back Mawson's claim. On 11 January 1939, in the northern Vestfold Hills, he wrapped his handwritten note in a copy of Walkabout magazine inside two enamel coffee jugs. The spot became Walkabout Rocks.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: History of Davis station

source2.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Sir George Hubert Wilkins

title: Counting Emperor Penguins From Space
place: Halley Bay emperor penguin colony, Brunt Ice Shelf, Weddell Sea, Antarctica
text: Emperor penguins breed on sea ice in the dark Antarctic winter, so scientists now count them using satellite images. Tracking about 50 colonies from 2009 to 2018, they found the species probably shrank by roughly 10 percent. The starkest loss was at Halley Bay, which fell from about 20,000 birds to fewer than 1,000, though many seem to have moved to the nearby Dawson-Lambton colony.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Advances in remote sensing of emperor penguins: first multi-year time series documenting trends in the global population (LaRue et al. 2024)

title: The Professor Hauls Sledges to the Magnetic Pole
place: South Magnetic Pole (1909 position), Victoria Land plateau, Antarctica
text: Geologist Edgeworth David, nicknamed 'The Professor', joined Ernest Shackleton's Nimrod expedition and brought along his former student Douglas Mawson. David led the first climb to the summit of Mount Erebus, an active volcano. Then he led a party, Mawson included, on an epic four-month journey to the South Magnetic Pole, dragging laden sledges about 1,250 kilometres across Victoria Land to reach their goal.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: T.W. Edgeworth David

title: Jaws from a Carnivore's Den
place: Grotte à Hominidés, Thomas Quarry I, Casablanca, Morocco
text: In a cave inside a Casablanca quarry, scientists studied jaws, teeth and vertebrae from adults and a child. A gnawed thigh bone suggests the cave was a carnivore's den.
