A flip of Earth's magnetic field, recorded in the layers, dates them to about 773,000 years ago. Their mix of old and new features places them near the root of the lineage that led to Homo sapiens.

source.name: Max Planck Society: Early hominins from Morocco reveal an African lineage near the root of Homo sapiens

title: Toddler Footprints Beside the Hippos
place: Gombore II-2, Melka Kunture, upper Awash Valley, Ethiopia
text: On a muddy lakeshore 2,000 metres up in the Ethiopian highlands, adults and very young children left footprints about 700,000 years ago. Some tracks were probably made by toddlers around a year old. Hippos, antelopes, horses, pigs and birds walked the same mud. Sharp obsidian flakes and butchered hippo bones show the group was making tools and cutting meat right there.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Archaeology and ichnology at Gombore II-2, Melka Kunture, Ethiopia

title: A Stone Quarry Used for 100,000 Years
place: Jojosi Dongas, near Nquthu, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
text: In the eroded gullies of Jojosi, early modern humans came back again and again for one stone: hornfels, a fine-grained rock baked by ancient magma. From about 220,000 to 110,000 years ago they knapped it on the spot and carried the blanks away. Millions of their stone flakes still pave the ground today, and researchers fitted 353 pieces back together like puzzles.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Specialised and persistent raw material procurement by humans in the Middle Pleistocene

title: Toolmakers in the Rainforest
place: Bété I, Anyama, near Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire
text: Quarrying 20 km north of Abidjan exposed deep layers holding stone picks, scrapers and points. Dating puts the first human visits at about 150,000 years ago, and plant waxes, pollen and tiny silica particles show the site sat in wet tropical forest. Before this study, the oldest clear link between humans and African rainforest was only about 18,000 years old.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Humans in Africa's wet tropical forests 150 thousand years ago

title: Fur Workers of the Smugglers' Cave
place: Contrebandiers Cave, Témara, Atlantic coast, Morocco
text: In a seaside cave near Rabat, people made 62 bone tools between 120,000 and 90,000 years ago, including smoothed spatula-like pieces probably used to work leather and fur. Bones of sand foxes, golden jackals and wildcats carry cut marks from skinning. One odd find is the tip of a tooth, probably from a sperm whale, that seems to have been used as a tool.

source.name: iScience (PMC): A worked bone assemblage from 120,000-90,000 year old deposits at Contrebandiers Cave

title: Hunters Who Reshaped a Landscape with Fire
place: Chitimwe Beds, Karonga District, northern Lake Malawi, Malawi
text: Along northern Lake Malawi, dense spreads of Middle Stone Age tools appear after about 92,000 years ago. At the same moment, a sediment core from the lake records surging charcoal and a mix of plants unlike anything in the previous half-million years. Researchers argue early modern humans were setting fires out of season, changing the vegetation and loosening soils that washed down into fans.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Early human impacts and ecosystem reorganization in southern-central Africa

title: Beads Shared Across 3,000 Kilometres
text: Researchers measured 1,516 ostrich eggshell beads from 31 African sites. Between about 50,000 and 33,000 years ago, beads from eastern African shelters such as Mumba and from Border Cave in South Africa, more than 3,000 km apart, fell in the same size range, hinting at a long social network. Around 33,000 years ago that link broke, and the regions stayed apart for many thousands of years.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ostrich eggshell beads reveal 50,000-year-old social network in Africa

title: Africa's Oldest Human DNA South of the Sahara
text: Genetic material from a forager buried at Mlambalasi Rockshelter, dated to roughly 20,000 to 17,000 years ago, helped double the time depth of ancient DNA from sub-Saharan Africa. Studying six new individuals from Tanzania, Malawi and Zambia, researchers found that people were most closely related to near neighbours, a sign that groups were settling into separate regions as the Ice Age ended.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ancient DNA and deep population structure in sub-Saharan African foragers

title: Bead Makers of the Kalahari
place: Ga-Mohana Hill North Rockshelter, near Kuruman, Northern Cape, South Africa
text: In a rock shelter 12 km from Kuruman, people were making ostrich eggshell beads about 15,000 years ago. Archaeologists found finished beads, half-drilled blanks and scraps, showing nearly every step of the craft. Most pieces turned yellow, suggesting heating to around 200 °C, ten of the 19 beads carry red residue, and one bead is black, perhaps coloured on purpose.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Ostrich eggshell beads from Ga-Mohana Hill North Rockshelter, southern Kalahari

title: Africa's Highest Ice Age Campsite
place: Dimtu rock shelter, Sanetti Plateau, Bale Mountains, Ethiopia
text: As glaciers melted from Ethiopia's Bale Mountains and rains returned about 15,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers climbed to Dimtu rock shelter at 4,023 metres, the highest known layered archaeological site in Africa. They left hearths, ash, bones and obsidian tools between about 14,800 and 13,900 years ago. Chemical tests show some obsidian came from lowland sources, proof of trade networks reaching the summit plateau.

source.name: Landscape Ecology (PMC): Human occupation of the Afroalpine Bale Mountains at the onset of the African Humid Period

title: A Medicinal Plant at an Ice Age Grave
place: Grotte des Pigeons, Taforalt, Oriental Region, Morocco
text: In a burial area of Grotte des Pigeons, archaeologists found charred cone scales of Ephedra, a shrub rich in ephedrine. Radiocarbon dates show the plant and the buried people are both about 15,000 years old, the earliest Ephedra remains of this kind. The same Iberomaurusian foragers pulled teeth and drilled skulls, and the researchers suggest the plant may have served medicine as well as funerals.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Late Pleistocene exploitation of Ephedra in a funerary context in Morocco

title: Wild Cattle Carved Beside the Nile
place: Qurta, near Kom Ombo, Aswan Governorate, Egypt
text: On rock faces at Qurta in Upper Egypt, people carved images of aurochs, the huge wild cattle of the Ice Age, alongside other animals. Wind-blown sand later buried some panels. Luminescence dating of that sand shows the carvings are at least 15,000 years old, making them the first securely dated Ice Age rock art in North Africa and the oldest found there so far.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): First evidence of Pleistocene rock art in North Africa: securing the age of the Qurta petroglyphs

title: Ancient Genomes from a Southern Shore
place: Matjes River Rock Shelter, Keurbooms, Western Cape, South Africa
text: At Matjes River on South Africa's southern coast, researchers sequenced the genomes of people who lived across 8,000 years, the oldest about 10,200 years ago. These ancient southern Africans had a genetic make-up outside the range of any people living today. Their DNA also hints at special adaptations: variants linked to kidney function across all Homo sapiens, and to sun protection in southern Africa.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Homo sapiens-specific evolution unveiled by ancient southern African genomes

title: The Oldest Wooden Hand Tools
text: By an ancient lakeshore in southern Greece, early humans butchered straight-tusked elephants about 430,000 years ago. The lake mud also preserved wood. A worked alder trunk shows wear from use as a digging stick, and a tiny willow or poplar piece was shaped, perhaps for making stone tools. They are the oldest handheld wooden tools known. Another log bears claw marks from a large carnivore.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Evidence for the earliest hominin use of wooden handheld tools found at Marathousa 1 (Greece)

title: Sparks from a Suffolk Clay Pit
place: Barnham, near Thetford, Suffolk, England, United Kingdom
text: At an old clay pit in Barnham, heat-reddened flints and repeatedly burnt sediment mark campfires about 400,000 years ago. Beside them lay two small fragments of pyrite, a mineral that throws sparks when struck with flint and does not occur naturally there. Someone carried it in to light fires, pushing back proof of fire-making by about 350,000 years. The makers were probably early Neanderthals.

source.name: Natural History Museum: Earliest fire-making dating back 400,000 years unearthed in Suffolk, England

title: A Neanderthal Fat Factory
text: Beside a lake south of Halle, Neanderthals carried in parts of at least 172 large animals about 125,000 years ago. They smashed the bones into small pieces, almost certainly to boil out grease, the fat that floats to the top and can be skimmed off. Until this find, such bone-grease rendering was known only from much later Upper Palaeolithic hunters.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Large-scale processing of within-bone nutrients by Neanderthals, 125,000 years ago

title: Finger Lines in a Sealed Cave
place: La Roche-Cotard, Langeais, Loire Valley, France
text: On a cave wall above the Loire, someone drew lines, waves and dotted patterns with their fingers in soft rock. Sediment later sealed the entrance until 1846, when it was dug out for a railway embankment. Dating shows the marks are more than 57,000 years old, before modern humans reached the area, so the artists were almost certainly Neanderthals. One panel incorporates a large fossil shell.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The earliest unambiguous Neanderthal engravings on cave walls: La Roche-Cotard, Loire Valley, France

title: Neanderthal Trays, Spears and a Club
place: Abric Romaní, Capellades, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain
text: At Abric Romaní, a limestone crust called travertine encased Neanderthal wooden objects, leaving 597 imprints and charred remains between 62,000 and 40,000 years ago. They include spears, pointed sticks, bark trays, posts and a tripod-like structure. One club-shaped object from level P has no clear match anywhere else in prehistory. The site has been dug since its discovery in 1909.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Neanderthal woodworking at Abric Romaní

title: A Woman from Europe's First Wave
place: Zlatý kůň, Koněprusy Caves, Central Bohemia, Czechia
text: A skull found in a Czech cave in 1950 long seemed only 15,000 years old, but animal glue used to conserve it probably skewed the dates. Her genome tells another story. Long Neanderthal DNA segments show she lived more than 45,000 years ago, among Europe's first modern humans, in a population that left no descendants among later Europeans or Asians. Marks on the skull look like hyena bites.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): A genome sequence from a modern human skull over 45,000 years old from Zlatý kůň in Czechia

title: The Oldest Known Identical Twins
place: Krems-Wachtberg, Krems an der Donau, Lower Austria, Austria
text: On a hill above the Danube, two newborn boys were laid in red ochre about 31,000 years ago, and a mammoth shoulder blade was placed over the grave. Ancient DNA shows they were identical twins, the earliest known. One died at birth, the other lived about 50 days and wore 53 mammoth-ivory beads. A third baby nearby was a relative.

source.name: Communications Biology (PMC): Ancient DNA reveals monozygotic newborn twins from the Upper Palaeolithic

title: Soft Shoes in a Painted Cave
place: Grotte de Cussac, Le Buisson-de-Cadouin, Dordogne, France
text: Cussac Cave, discovered in 2000, holds giant engravings and human remains laid in old bear nests. Its clay floors also kept footprints 28,000 to 31,000 years old. Strangely, the toes barely show, while bear prints beside them are crisp. Experiments with soft leather footwear produced similar prints, so the Gravettian visitors most likely wore shoes as they moved through the cave.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Evidence of the use of soft footwear in the Gravettian cave of Cussac

title: DNA from the Coldest Age in Spain
place: Cueva del Malalmuerzo, Moclín, Granada, Andalusia, Spain
text: Two teeth from Cueva del Malalmuerzo, a cave known for its Ice Age paintings, were dated to about 23,000 years ago, at the height of the last glacial maximum. The DNA of this Solutrean-era person links Europe's earlier Aurignacian people with the Magdalenian groups who came after the ice. It suggests southern Iberia sheltered old western European ancestry through the cold.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): A 23,000-year-old southern Iberian individual links human groups before and after the Last Glacial Maximum

title: Cut Marks in a Polish Cave
place: Maszycka Cave, Prądnik Valley, near Kraków, Poland
text: Maszycka Cave near Kraków was first dug in 1883. Re-examining its human bones, about 18,000 years old, researchers found remains of at least ten people, six adults and four young. Skulls were cut and broken to remove brains, and even thin leg bones were smashed for marrow. They argue cannibalism was a regular practice among Magdalenian groups, though whether ritual or warfare remains unclear.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): New insights of cultural cannibalism amongst Magdalenian groups at Maszycka Cave, Poland

title: Spear Points Made from Whales
place: Santa Catalina Cave, Lekeitio, Biscay, Spain
text: Ice Age hunters around the Bay of Biscay carved projectile points from whale bone. Protein fingerprinting of objects from caves such as Santa Catalina identified fin, sperm, gray and blue whales, plus porpoise. Radiocarbon dates of 20,000 to 14,000 years ago, peaking between 17,500 and 16,000, make this the oldest known whale-bone working. Gray whales today live only in the North Pacific.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Late Paleolithic whale bone tools reveal human and whale ecology in the Bay of Biscay

title: Dating Bison Drawn in Charcoal
place: Font-de-Gaume Cave, Les Eyzies, Dordogne, France
text: Dordogne cave art was thought to use only mineral pigments, which radiocarbon cannot date. Then imaging at Font-de-Gaume found figures drawn in carbon black, likely charcoal. Tiny samples gave the first direct dates for the region's cave art: a bison about 13,300 years old and a mysterious mask with lips about 15,000 years old. One sample from the mask's eye came out far younger.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Radiocarbon dating and chemical imaging of carbon black-based Paleolithic cave art in the Dordogne region

title: The Holy Iron That Fell From the Sky
place: Near Novosyolovo, south of Krasnoyarsk, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
text: In 1749 a huge lump of iron, around 800 kilos, was found south of Krasnoyarsk. Local Tatars treated it as a holy relic dropped from the sky. In 1772 the naturalist Peter Simon Pallas saw it, found no nearby iron workings or forge, and had it carted to Saint Petersburg. Nobody then believed rocks fell from space. Today such stony-iron meteorites are called pallasites.

source.name: University of Groningen University Museum: Meteorite of Krasnojarsk

title: A Teenage Trader Caught Between Empires
text: Around 1872 a Dagestani teenager named Mahmud borrowed goods worth 200 rubles and slipped off east. He swapped them with Kazakh nomads for sheep, sold the flock in Bukhara, then traded Ferghana silk scarves. Adopted by an older merchant, he became Hajji Ahmed. In 1875 villagers near Margilan robbed him and handed him to a rebel khan as a Russian spy. Two partners were executed on the same charge.

source.name: Slavic Review (Cambridge): The Misadventures of a Dagestani Merchant

title: Naming Streets That Did Not Exist Yet
text: Orenburg, Russia's gateway to the Kazakh steppe, had to move twice before settling on the Yaik River in 1743. In July 1744 officials gave all 25 of its streets official names at once, which was very unusual in the empire. Many streets existed only on paper, and the town still looked like a big army camp. Residents mostly ignored the names, calling the main one simply Big Street.

source.name: Urban History (Cambridge): Orenburg's toponymy: staging the Russian Empire in the steppe

title: Tuberculosis Hidden in Frozen Bones
text: Between 2002 and 2012 a French-Russian team opened 134 permafrost graves across Yakutia, dated from the 1500s to the 1800s. Thirteen people had bone damage from tuberculosis, including a young woman buried in 1728. DNA from four skeletons confirmed the human TB germ, and one strain may have come from Europe. Most cases date to the 1700s, after Russian traders and settlers had arrived.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Tuberculosis Epidemiology and Selection in an Autochthonous Siberian Population from the 16th-19th Century

title: A Sakha Woman Wearing the Tsar's Rings
place: At Daban, Tuymaada valley south of Yakutsk, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: In 2016 archaeologists south of Yakutsk opened the rich grave of a Sakha woman, At Daban 6, dressed in masses of imported glass beads. Tied to one earring were two Russian signet rings. Records say the chieftain Mazary Bozekov, who died in 1703, visited the Tsar and won the titles of duke and judge. The rings were probably his, and DNA ties her to his family.

source.name: Communications Biology (PMC): The genetic legacy of legendary and historical Siberian chieftains

title: Fisherfolk of the Desert Lake
place: Lower Tarim River and Lop Nur, Xinjiang, China
text: Deep in the desert of Xinjiang, the Loptuq people lived by fishing among reeds up to 7.6 metres tall. Sven Hedin stayed with them from 1899 to 1900. They paddled canoes carved from poplar trunks along family-owned channels, lived in reed huts and wove clothes from wild Lop hemp. A bride's family might receive two canoes, a fishing net and hemp cloth.

source.name: Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine (PMC): Loptuq material culture in Eastern Turkestan around 1900

title: The Years the Mountain Pines Stopped Growing
place: Western Sayan Mountains, southern Siberia, Russia
text: Tree rings from Siberian pines high in the Western Sayan Mountains show a sudden crash in 1698–1699. In the regional record running from 1524 to 2022, the seven worst growing years come in a row, 1699 to 1705. Scientists suspect a cold spell plus brutal winters: Mongolian chronicles record killing snowstorms and frozen pastures in those very years, battering the trees' crowns.

source.name: Plants (PMC): Central Asia Cold Case: Siberian Pine Fingers New Suspects in Growth Decline CA 1700 CE

title: Vodka Made From Sour Milk
place: Olzony ulus, Verkholensk district, Irkutsk Oblast, Russia
text: Buryat herders near Lake Baikal turned sour milk into a spirit called tarasun. Fermented milk holds only about 2 percent alcohol, so it had to be distilled again and again. In 1906 the ethnographer Tsyben Zhamtsarano watched Buryats of Olzony doing just that, and early 20th-century accounts mention up to 40 distillations. An earlier Mongol law code even punished stealing the precious milk starter.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Milk spirit using traditional Buryat fermentation and distillation technologies

title: Bread-Eating Settlers, Tartar-Coated Teeth
place: Izyuk, near Omsk, Omsk Oblast, Russia
text: Russian farmers founded the village of Izyuk on the Irtysh River near Omsk in 1648. Scientists counted hardened plaque, or calculus, on 1,304 of their teeth and compared them with Tatar, Khanty and Nenets neighbours. About 61 percent of settlers had calculus, against 26 percent of the native Siberians. The likely reason: settlers ate wheat, while Siberian peoples ate mostly fish and meat.

source.name: BioMed Research International (PMC): Dental Calculi of Siberian Natives, Russian Settlers, and Korean People of Joseon Dynasty Period

title: The Last Shaman's Grave of the Sakha
text: In the late 1700s Russian law began pressing Sakha (Yakut) people to drop their own spiritual traditions for Orthodox Christianity. One woman of that time, UsSergue1, was buried in one of the richest graves ever found, wearing an ear-flap hat with a bronze sun disc, beside a saddle, stirrup, bridle and bell. DNA showed she was the great-granddaughter of a famous chieftain's wife.

source.name: Nature (PMC): An ancient DNA perspective on the Russian conquest of Yakutia

title: Wild Horses Driven Into the Bushes
place: Dzungarian Basin, north of Qitai, Xinjiang, China
text: Between 1889 and 1898, wild Przewalski's horses and khulans were killed in Dzungaria and their hides ended up in museums in Saint Petersburg and Moscow. Over a century later, scientists read the chemistry of their long tail hairs, month by month. In winter these horses ate lots of desert shrubs, unlike today's reintroduced herds, which graze grass all year. Hunting had probably pushed them into poor scrubland.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Stable isotopes reveal diet shift from pre-extinction to reintroduced Przewalski's horses

title: An Inn at Every City Gate
text: Turkestan, in southern Kazakhstan, was a busy caravan stop, and digs there uncovered inns, bathhouses and a school from the 1700s and 1800s. Caravanserais stood beside each of the city's four gates. One had niches for storing documents, storerooms, reception rooms, a prayer room and a little one-room bathhouse. The school had two halls, perhaps keeping boys and girls apart.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Traces of Nineteenth-Century Buildings Found in Turkestan

title: Cholera Sparks a Riot in Tashkent
text: In 1892 a cholera epidemic swept across Central Asia toward Russia and Europe. In Tashkent, capital of Russian Turkestan, officials imposed anti-cholera rules that clashed with local Islamic customs. That June, local people protested. Tsarist officials and Russian settlers crushed the protest ruthlessly, and poor Russians were later blamed for violence too. The city then stayed under emergency rule until 1917.

source.name: Slavic Review (Cambridge): Epidemic and Empire: the 1892 Tashkent Cholera Riot

title: Storage Bags for a Life on the Move
place: Saryk Turkmen lands, Mary Region, Turkmenistan
text: Turkmen nomads kept their belongings in woven bags that hung from the lattice walls inside their tents, then rode on pack animals during seasonal moves. Each bag was woven in one piece, with soft knotted pile on the front and plain weave behind, then folded and sewn up the sides. A 19th-century bag face in Cleveland is the oldest known weaving of the Saryk tribe.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Turkmen Bag Face

title: Silver Ram's Horns and Red Stones
text: Turkmen nomad women wore heavy silver jewellery set with red cornelians. A head ornament wrapped the forehead, dangling dozens of little pendants, and its curved tips stood for ram's horns, a powerful Turkmen symbol. In 1884–85 a British officer bought such pieces while serving with Sir Peter Lumsden on the Anglo-Russian commission fixing Afghanistan's northwest border. Many of the designs are older than Islam.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Head ornament (sinsile), Turkestan

title: Peasant Pottery Made for Collectors?
text: In the 1800s Central Asian potters made bold, colourful dishes: bright slipwares in Bukhara, Samarkand and Rishtan, and white-glazed plates painted blue and purple in Kokand. They look like age-old village pottery, but there is no evidence of an earlier local tradition. So many reached Western collections that some scholars suspect potters were cashing in on foreign buyers' taste for 'traditional' goods.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Dish, Turkestan, probably Kokand

title: A Robe From Wedding to Funeral
text: In mid-1800s Bukhara, a woman's robe could follow her through life. Silk ikat robes like one now in Chicago were part of a bride's dowry, worn at weddings and festivals, and finally draped over her bier at her funeral. Young women wore bright colours and big patterns, older women quieter shades. Most women, though, wore cheap local cotton instead.

source.name: Art Institute of Chicago: Woman's Robe, Uzbekistan

title: A Prayer Niche Stitched in Silk
text: Women in Bukhara stitched huge silk embroideries called suzani, from the Persian word for needle, as part of a bride's dowry. One 18th-century suzani in Chicago shows an arch shaped like a mihrab, the mosque niche that points toward Mecca. Big suzanis covered beds or walls, but a mihrab suzani hung near the doorway had a friendlier job: welcoming guests.

source.name: Art Institute of Chicago: Mihrab or Jai-namaz Suzani

title: A Bukhara Pen Laments the Missing Wine
text: In 1575–76 the calligrapher Mahmud ibn Ishaq al-Shahabi, admired in both Safavid Iran and Mughal India, signed and dated a page of practice script and verses by the poet Hafiz. The playful lines mourn that the 'daughter of the vine', wine, has gone missing. Before 1811 the page was mounted in a Mughal-style album by a Scottish East India Company man, Sir Charles Forbes.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Calligraphic exercises and verses of Hafiz

title: Porridge Made From Pine Trees
text: In 1737 the Russian explorer Khariton Laptev noted that the Sakha (Yakuts) usually ate tree sapwood with milk. The soft inner bark of pines was dried into a 'wood flour' for porridge or, rarely, cake, and a poor family could eat 256 kilos a year. The habit faded as farming spread: Yakutsk had about 50 bakeries in 1838 and over 800 by 1860.

source.name: Biology (PMC): Sucrose Is Not the Whole Story: Risk Factors and Oral Health at the Contact (Yakutia, Siberia, 16th–19th)

title: Tigers in the Desert Reed Beds
text: Around 1900, Caspian tigers still prowled the reed beds of the lower Tarim River. Local Loptuq fishers caught them with iron traps or poison, because Chinese traders paid high prices for tiger flesh used as medicine. One spot was even named 'Where the tiger was killed'. DNA suggests these tigers came from China along the Gansu Corridor. They vanished from Central Asia between 1920 and 1970.

source.name: Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine (PMC): Loptuq material culture in Eastern Turkestan around 1900

source2.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Mitochondrial phylogeography illuminates the origin of the extinct Caspian tiger

title: A Swedish Captive Teaches a Princess to Crochet
text: Brigitta Scherzenfeldt, a Swede, was captured twice: first at Poltava in 1709, then in 1716 when Dzungar warriors routed a Russian gold-hunting expedition and killed her husband. Taken to the Dzungar capital Ghulja, she was passed from a rich owner to the ruler's court. She won favour by teaching Princess Seson to crochet and weave, and finally reached Stockholm in 1734.

source.name: Journal of Global History (Cambridge): Enslaved in Dzungaria: what an eighteenth-century crocheting instructor can teach us

title: The Khan Who Kept the Best Falcons
text: In 1675 Moscow sent envoys through Central Asia hoping to open a road to India. At Khiva, Anusha Khan simply kept the two finest gyrfalcons meant as gifts for Bukhara. In Bukhara the ruler refused carts and an escort. One envoy, Muhammad Yusuf Kasymov, got through with gifts and reached Kabul in 1676, but Emperor Aurangzeb would not see him, and he limped home in 1678.

source.name: Itinerario (Cambridge): A Passage to India: Rhetoric and Diplomacy between Muscovy and Central Asia in the Seventeenth Century

title: Flower Power for Fashionable Men
text: In late 19th-century Shahrisabz, south of Samarkand, professional embroiderers made some of Central Asia's showiest men's clothes. One surcoat blazes with huge cross-stitched silk palmettes and rosettes on a brilliant yellow ground, lined with ikat patterned with cypress trees. The pattern was drawn on the cloth, the coat taken apart for stitching, then sewn back together, leaving tell-tale misaligned motifs.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Man's surcoat (khalat), Shahr-i Sabz

title: Cholera on the Road to Siberia
text: Prisoners marched to Siberia along the Great Exile Road, and in 1892 cholera travelled with them. It reached the prison at Perm, a stop on the route, on 4 July, and Tobolsk reported an outbreak by late July. Across Russia's prisons 1,441 cases were recorded, about 45 percent fatal. The government rushed emergency hospitals onto the road, while George Kennan's book on the exile system publicized prison death rates.

source.name: Journal of the History of Medicine (PMC): Silences and Omissions in Reporting Epidemics in Russian and Soviet Prisons, 1890-2021

title: A Sea Goddess Comes Ashore
place: Thian Hock Keng Temple, Telok Ayer Street, Singapore
text: Hokkien migrants who survived the voyage from Fujian used to give thanks at a tiny shrine on the Telok Ayer shoreline, where they first stepped ashore. Between 1839 and 1842 they replaced it with Thian Hock Keng, built with materials shipped from China. In 1840 a statue of Mazu, Goddess of the Seas, arrived in a grand procession. Tan Tock Seng gave 3,000 Spanish dollars, the biggest single gift.

source.name: Roots.sg (National Heritage Board, Singapore): Thian Hock Keng

title: A Tiny Diaspora Builds a Church
place: Armenian Church of St Gregory the Illuminator, Hill Street, Singapore
text: Armenian traders, descended from families moved from Julfa to Persia centuries earlier, reached Singapore by way of India, Java and the Malay ports. Never more than about 100 strong, they still paid $5,058.30 for a church designed by George Coleman, laid down in 1835. It is Singapore's oldest Christian church building. Later community members founded The Straits Times and bred the orchid that became Singapore's national flower.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board, Singapore): S'pore's Armenian Church Survived Close to 180 Years

title: An 800-Year-Old 'Made in China' Tag
place: Java Sea wreck site, off Indonesia
text: Fishermen found this wreck in the Java Sea in the 1980s. The wooden hull had rotted away, but its cargo remained: an estimated 100,000 ceramics, elephant tusks and blocks of fragrant resin. Two box bases were stamped 'Jianning Fu', a district name the Song government used only from 1162 until 1278. With new radiocarbon dates, that label pushed the sinking back about a century.

source.name: EurekAlert! (Field Museum): Shipwreck and 800-year-old 'made in China' label reveal lost history

title: A Gujarati Anchor on Odisha's Shore
place: Manikapatna, Chilika Lake coast, Puri District, Odisha, India
text: Diggers next to the mosque at Manikapatna, a port on Odisha's Chilika coast, turned up a broken stone anchor of the Indo-Arabian type in 2018 to 2019. Its basalt was no local rock. Chemistry traced it to a lava flow at Palitana in Gujarat, across the subcontinent, perhaps shaped at the port of Ghogha. The same site has yielded Chinese ceramics from the 1200s and 1300s.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Geochemical provenance of an Indo-Arabian stone anchor from Manikapatna

title: Asian Rice on an African Island
text: At Sima, a village site on Anjouan in the Comoros, archaeologists sifted charred seeds from the 700s to 900s. Of 528 crop remains, 481 were Asian rice, plus cotton and mung beans: a Southeast Asian menu, off the coast of Africa. On the nearby mainland, African sorghum and millets ruled. The team argues Austronesian sailors may have settled the Comoros even before Madagascar.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Ancient crops provide first archaeological signature of the westward Austronesian expansion

title: The Wave Before the 2004 Tsunami
text: Along 40 kilometres of northern Sumatra's coast, tens of thousands of medieval ceramic sherds and over 5,000 carved gravestones tell a grim story. Around 1394 a tsunami wiped out nine trading communities. Only Lamri, perched on a headland, survived. Yet later the low coast was resettled and became the heart of the Aceh Sultanate, the same shore the 2004 tsunami struck.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): A late 14th-century tsunami devastated the coast of northern Sumatra and redirected history

title: A Joseon Tax Ship Comes Up
place: Mado waters, off Taean, South Chungcheong, South Korea
text: Joseon ships hauled grain taxes and official goods up Korea's west coast to the royal capital, Hanyang, today's Seoul. One cargo ship, Mado 4, sank off Taean around 1420. After ten years of study, Korean researchers raised it in 2025 with over 120 artifacts: rice containers, celadon dishes and wooden cargo tags marked with destinations. Its two masts were built for speed.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Joseon Shipwreck Raised from South Korean Waters

title: A Smuggler's Junk Off Nan'ao Island
place: Off Nan'ao Island, Shantou, Guangdong, China
text: In 2007 fishermen off Nan'ao Island secretly hauled up Ming porcelain and hid it, hoping to sell. Border police seized it, and archaeologists found a late Ming junk about 90 feet long, lying 90 feet down. It held over 10,000 blue-and-white pieces, many still stacked, plus bronze cannons. Sailing while the Ming banned private sea trade, its crew were probably smugglers, or worse.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Pirates of the Marine Silk Road

title: Two Ming Ships, a Mile Deep
place: Northwest slope of the South China Sea, Hainan Province, China
text: Nearly 5,000 feet under the South China Sea, about 12 miles apart, lie two Ming ships, one leaving China and one coming back. The older, from the Hongzhi reign (1488 to 1505), held pottery and logs cut from persimmon trees. The younger, from the Zhengde reign (1506 to 1521), carried more than 100,000 porcelain bowls, plates and jars. Together they show the maritime Silk Road flowing both ways.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 500-Year-Old Shipwrecks Found in South China Sea

title: Persian Wine in a Desert Fort
place: Fulayj fort, near Sohar, Al Batinah, Oman
text: Soldiers at Fulayj, a Sasanian Persian fort about 30 kilometres from the Omani port of Sohar, received tall, pointed 'torpedo jars' lined inside with bitumen. Chemists traced that tar to different provinces of Iran, and residues inside revealed red wine. It is the first published proof of what scholars long suspected: these jars carried wine from Persia's heartlands into the Gulf and Indian Ocean world.

source.name: Molecules (PMC): Origin and Function of Bitumen-Coated Torpedo Jars from the Fort of Fulayj in Oman

title: Indian Cotton in an Arabian Fire
text: When a fortified building at Mleiha, an oasis town in today's UAE, burned down around 150 to 250 CE, the fire charred and preserved its stores: barley, dates, lentils, and exotic pepper and Asian rice. Cotton seeds and scraps of cloth lay there too. Strontium in the cotton did not match the Oman peninsula but did match north-western India, likely Gujarat, across the Arabian Sea.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Strontium isotope evidence for a trade network between southeastern Arabia and India

title: A Sangam Port on the Vaigai
place: Alagankulam, Ramanathapuram District, Tamil Nadu, India
text: Where the Vaigai River nears the sea, Alagankulam thrived as a Tamil port of the Sangam Age, radiocarbon dated from the 300s to the 100s BCE. Diggers found shell-bangle workshops, punch-marked silver coins, luxury black pottery from the distant Ganga plain, Mediterranean wares and Greek and Roman coins. Scientists now read rare earth elements in its soil to map firing and dumping that left no visible trace.

source.name: Heliyon (PMC): Rare earth elements sediment analysis tracing anthropogenic activities at Alagankulam

title: Baghdad's Glass on Zanzibar
text: Unguja Ukuu, an early Swahili port on Zanzibar, has yielded 3,625 fragments of glass vessels, mostly from the 600s to 800s. Laser analysis of 82 pieces showed some were made with natron, matching Egyptian and Levantine glass, others with plant ash. One group matches glass from Samarra, the Abbasid capital in Iraq. Fragile tableware was crossing thousands of kilometres of ocean as the early Islamic world grew.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Early Islamic glass (7th-10th centuries AD) in Unguja Ukuu, Zanzibar

title: The Frigate That Failed Fort Jesus
place: Mombasa harbour, below Fort Jesus, Mombasa, Kenya
text: In 1696 an Omani Arab army laid siege to Fort Jesus, Portugal's stronghold at Mombasa. Goa sent a relief squadron of two frigates and two galliots, led by the Santo António de Tanná. In 1697 the frigate was lost off the fort, and Fort Jesus fell to Oman in 1698. Local divers found the wreck; excavations from 1976 to 1980 recovered over 6,000 objects from shipboard life.

source.name: Institute of Nautical Archaeology: Santo Antonio de Tanna Shipwreck Excavation

source2.name: CHAM, NOVA University Lisbon: The Santo António de Tanná project

title: A Royal Navy Frigate Made in Bombay
text: Britain's warships were usually oak, but HMS Trincomalee was built of Malabar teak at the East India Company's dockyard in Bombay, under master shipbuilder Jamsetjee Bomanjee Wadia. Her plans were lost when HMS Java was sunk by the USS Constitution, so a second set took two years to arrive. Launched on 12 October 1817, the frigate still floats today as a museum ship in Hartlepool, England.

source.name: National Historic Ships UK: HMS Trincomalee

source2.name: University of Victoria, Colonial Despatches: HMS Trincomalee

title: Island Graves at the Ocean's Crossroads
text: Medieval islanders on Soqotra buried their dead in tafoni, small rounded caves in the rock. DNA from 39 of them, living between the 600s and 1400s, shows about 86% of their ancestry came from people like those of Yemen's Hadramawt, and about 14% from an Iranian-related source with a trace from India. Surprisingly, despite lying 250 kilometres from the Horn of Africa, they had almost no sub-Saharan African ancestry.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): Medieval DNA from Soqotra points to Eurasian origins

title: A Wedding Night Sends the Bugis Sailing
place: Tanjung Pinang, Bintan Island, Riau Islands, Indonesia
text: On 26 December 1819, Bugis guests at a chief's wedding in Riau fired celebratory shots, and the nervous Dutch garrison read it as a threat. Arrests and killings followed. In January 1820 about 400 Bugis besieged the Dutch fort for 15 days before reinforcements broke through. Almost 500 Bugis men, women and children then fled by boat to Singapore, bringing their prized trade with them.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board, Singapore): The 1820 Uprising in Riau That Brought the Bugis to Singapore

title: Bones of the English Samurai
text: William Adams reached Japan in 1600 aboard the Liefde, the last survivor of a five-ship Dutch fleet. Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu made the English pilot a samurai, Miura Anjin, and he died at the trading port of Hirado in 1620. Foreign graves there were later destroyed. Bones dug up in 2017 carried mitochondrial DNA haplogroup H, common in Europe but never seen in Japanese populations.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): A biomolecular anthropological investigation of William Adams, the first SAMURAI from England

title: Cholera Sails From Calcutta
place: Port of Calcutta, Hooghly River, Kolkata, West Bengal, India
text: Nineteenth-century Calcutta was notorious as a disease port, and British seamen feared its cholera. In February 1854 the ship Sultany left with 80 crew and 375 passengers; by the time it reached Mauritius, 30 were dead. Ship surgeons improvised cures from the spice trade itself, dosing patients with black pepper, ginger and asafoetida mixed with opium, brandy or arrack.

source.name: Medical History (PMC): Cholera, British seamen and maritime anxieties in Calcutta, c.1830s-1890s

title: Fire Ants Ride the Galleons
text: Tropical fire ants, named for their burning stings, now live around the world. Genetic markers from 192 colonies show they began in the Americas and left in the 1500s. Philippine ants carry a subset of southwestern Mexico's types, and Taiwan's a subset of the Philippines'. The likely ride: ballast soil on Spanish ships from Acapulco to Manila, dumped to make room for silk, porcelain and spices.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ant Explorers

title: Cannonballs Under Old Goa
place: Near the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa, Goa, India
text: After Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510, the Portuguese rebuilt the city as a fortified enclosure. In 2025 builders near the Basilica of Bom Jesus struck a pile of cannonballs marking the old arsenal. It was part of a complex with a gun foundry, mint, stables and naval dockyard that may have employed 700 workers at its sixteenth-century peak. It closed in 1856.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Former Portuguese Colonial Arsenal Unearthed in India

title: Cambodia's 'Dark Age' Was Trading
text: After Siam sacked Angkor in 1431, Cambodia's later centuries were often called a dark age. Excavations at the palace of Longvek, a Mekong capital with access to the sea, tell another story. An international team found earthen fortifications, a bronze workshop and porcelain from both China and Japan. As archaeologist Martin Polkinghorne put it, Cambodian history went on, tied closely to international trade.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Excavations at Cambodia's Longvek

title: Bead Workshops Made for Export
place: Vembakottai, Virudhunagar District, Tamil Nadu, India
text: At Vembakottai, a site of the Pandya country in southern Tamil Nadu, three years of digging have produced more than 12,000 artifacts from roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE. Thousands of glass beads and painted shell bangles show it was a major ornament workshop. Locals wore simple terracotta pendants, while the glass and shell pieces were reportedly made only for export, part of Sangam-era trade.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Shell and Bead Workshop Excavated in Tamil Nadu

title: An Arab-Style Dhow Under a Shrimp Farm
text: Beneath a shrimp farm in Samut Sakhon, near Bangkok, lay the timbers of an 8th- or 9th-century Arab-style dhow, its planks sewn together with rope. It had sunk where a canal or mangrove shore once lay. Inside were ceramics, coconuts, betel nuts, rice, fish and pointed jars never before found in Thailand, of a type carried across the Persian Gulf.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Arab Dhow Unearthed in Thailand

source2.name: Molecules (PMC): Bitumen-Coated Torpedo Jars from Fulayj (cites Phanom-Surin torpedo jars)

title: Card Games on a Mongol Warship
place: Off Takashima Island, Matsuura, Nagasaki, Japan
text: Off Takashima, a third wreck from the Mongol-led Yuan invasion of Japan in 1281 has turned up something unexpected: five dice and 29 small cards for koppai, a Chinese game considered a forerunner of mahjong tiles. The ship, about 100 feet long with living quarters, may have been the fleet's mother ship. The cards were likely used for recreation, a rare glimpse of daily life aboard an invasion fleet.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Playing Cards Found in Mongol Invasion Shipwreck off Japan

title: Cracked Pots by Lake Pontchartrain
place: Tchefuncte site, Fontainebleau State Park, Mandeville, Louisiana, USA
text: On the marshy north shore of Lake Pontchartrain, people of the Tchefuncte culture left two crescent-shaped heaps of clam shells and trash. Diggers in the late 1930s and 1940s recovered more than 47,000 pottery sherds from some of Louisiana's earliest widely made pots. The potters added no temper and didn't knead out air pockets, so vessels often cracked while drying or firing. They also left 67 little clay pipes.

source.name: 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities): Tchefuncte Site

title: Yellowstone Glass in Ohio Graves
place: Obsidian Cliff, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, USA
text: Hopewell people in the Ohio Valley buried their dead with gleaming black volcanic glass, and about 90 percent of it came from a single cliff in today's Yellowstone National Park, far to the west. The cliff exposes about 30 meters of obsidian and had already been quarried for thousands of years. Some Hopewell obsidian bladelets are said to be sharper than modern surgical steel.

source.name: National Park Service, Yellowstone: Obsidian Cliff

source2.name: National Park Service: Ohio's Prehistoric Past

title: Sacred Mounds Inside an Army Camp
place: Mound City Group, Hopewell Culture National Historical Park, near Chillicothe, Ohio, USA
text: Inside a low earthen wall beside the Scioto River, Hopewell people raised 25 mounds over several centuries. Each covered a ceremonial building where fires burned in clay basins and cremated remains were laid under small clay heaps; about a hundred have been found. During World War I the site became Camp Sherman, an army training ground, and soldiers rested atop the largest mound.

source.name: National Park Service, Hopewell Culture NHP: Mound City Group

title: The Comet That Probably Wasn't
text: In 2022 researchers claimed a comet exploded over the Cincinnati area sometime around 252 to 383 CE, scorching Hopewell villages and helping end their culture. Other archaeologists took the case apart: the burned layers looked like ceremonial basins and burned mound floors, samples came from different spots than reported, and the radiocarbon dates spread over a long time. The original paper was later retracted.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Refuting the sensational claim of a Hopewell-ending cosmic airburst

title: Walls Built From Chosen Soils
place: Hopeton Earthworks, near Chillicothe, Ohio, USA
text: In 1848 surveyors mapped Hopeton's huge earthen rectangle, 900 by 950 feet, joined to a circle 1,050 feet across, with twelve gateways. Digs in 2001 and 2002 showed the builders stripped off topsoil, then piled two or three layers of carefully selected soil; burned logs date one wall to about 300 CE. After the 1950s, farm tractors shrank the walls about an inch a year.

source.name: National Park Service: Archeology at Hopewell Culture National Historical Park

title: Lamps and Pots at Cape Denbigh
place: Iyatayet site, Cape Denbigh, Norton Sound, Alaska, USA
text: At Iyatayet on Alaska's Norton Sound, archaeologist J. L. Giddings dug in the early 1950s and helped define the Norton tradition, dated about 2,500 to 1,600 years ago. These sea-mammal hunters made pottery, oil lamps, ulu knives and ground slate harpoon heads. Renewed fieldwork in 2012 and 2013 found a gap of about 1,000 years between the site's Norton and later Thule occupations.

source.name: National Park Service: Iyatayet

title: Alaska's First Big Salmon Harvesters
place: Naknek River drainage, Katmai National Park, Alaska, USA
text: In what is now Katmai National Park, people of the Norton tradition, from about 2,250 to 900 years ago, were the first to harvest Alaska's salmon runs intensively. They built labor-intensive houses and returned to them each season, though not all year. They also made pottery, a craft they probably learned from neighbors across the Bering Strait in Asia.

source.name: National Park Service, Katmai: Archeology

title: A Rock Shelter Full of String
place: Windmill Way rockshelter, Quinkan Country, north of Laura, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia
text: In a dry rock shelter in Kuku Warra Country on Cape York, archaeologists found more than 500 pieces of plant-fibre string, including dillybags, fishing nets with bird feathers caught in them and tassel belts. The oldest strings date to about 1,700 years ago. Women wearing the same belts and headbands are painted on the shelter walls, and the knots barely changed for 1,700 years.

source.name: The Conversation: Perfectly preserved rock art site reveals 1,700 years of Aboriginal string craft

title: Seafood Lives Read From Bones
place: Sigatoka Sand Dunes, Viti Levu, Fiji
text: Over roughly six centuries, from about 60 to 680 CE, people buried at least 61 of their dead in Fiji's Sigatoka sand dunes, most on their backs with legs flexed and many beneath cairns of coral or basalt. Chemical traces in their bones and teeth reveal a seafood-rich diet, and women ate more marine food as they aged, hinting that men and women did different work.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Life histories in Fiji as reconstructed from first millennium CE Sigatoka Sand Dune burials using isotopes

title: Dakota Flint for Ohio Ceremonies
place: Knife River flint quarries, Dunn and Mercer counties, North Dakota, USA
text: Big blades of exotic Knife River flint, quarried in North Dakota almost 1,000 miles away, turn up in Hopewell burial mounds in Ohio's Scioto River Valley. Hardly any flaking debris was left there, so the blades were probably finished elsewhere and passed from community to community by land and river. They were not everyday tools: they lie with ceremonial objects and important people.

source.name: National Park Service: Hopewell Culture and Knife River Flint

title: Ancient Poop With Unknown Microbes
text: Two dried human droppings left in Boomerang Shelter, Utah, around the first century CE, became part of a 2021 study that rebuilt hundreds of gut-microbe genomes from 1,000- to 2,000-year-old feces. Of the best-preserved ancient gut microbes, 39 percent were species science had never described. These ancient guts looked more like those of today's non-industrial peoples and carried far fewer antibiotic-resistance genes.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Reconstruction of ancient microbial genomes from the human gut

title: Melting Cave Ice in a Drought
place: Cave 29, El Malpais National Monument, New Mexico, USA
text: High on the Colorado Plateau, Ancestral Puebloans lit fires inside a lava-tube ice cave to melt ice into drinking water. The lowest layer of charcoal trapped in the ice dates to about 167 CE, during a severe second-century drought, and four more charcoal layers line up with later droughts up to about 933. Today the ice is melting fast, threatening the record.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Late Holocene droughts and cave ice harvesting by Ancestral Puebloans

title: Two Skeletons Link Guam to Polynesia
text: DNA from two skeletons buried in Ritidian Beach Cave on Guam about 2,200 years ago traced their ancestry to the Philippines, matching the idea that the Marianas' first settlers sailed from Island Southeast Asia. Surprisingly, they were close genetic relatives of early Lapita people from Vanuatu and Tonga, hinting that the Marianas and Polynesia were settled from the same source population.

source.name: EurekAlert (Max Planck Institute): Ancient DNA sheds light on the peopling of the Mariana Islands

source2.name: PNAS (PMC): Ancient DNA from Guam and the peopling of the Pacific

title: Polynesia's Oldest Known Monument
place: Mala'e Vakapuna, near Fua'amotu, Tongatapu, Tonga
text: On a hilltop overlooking Tongatapu's lagoon, people began heaping up an earth mound by about 350 to 500 CE and finished it over several generations. Mala'e Vakapuna is about 41 meters across and up to 3 meters high, needing roughly 1,000 person-days of work. Archaeologists call it the oldest known Polynesian architecture, a sign that chiefdoms were forming long before East Polynesia was settled.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Early architecture in Tonga: implications for the development of Polynesian chiefdoms

title: Island Kids Who Snacked on Seafood
place: Uripiv Island, off northeast Malakula, Vanuatu
text: On tiny Uripiv, less than one square kilometre off Malakula, villagers in the centuries after Lapita buried 23 people in one layer. Their bones show a diet of garden crops plus reef, seagrass and mangrove foods, and their pigs ate seafood too. Children ate more marine food than adults, perhaps as snacks, and three of eleven people tested had grown up elsewhere.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Diet and human mobility from the Lapita to the early historic period on Uripiv Island, Vanuatu

title: When the Tortoises Ran Out
text: At Teouma on Efate, where Lapita settlers had feasted on giant tortoises and sea turtles, the early post-Lapita years around 2,500 years ago brought hard times. Animal bones grow sparse: the tortoises had been badly depleted, turtles were caught only now and then, and pig herds shrank while people butchered the remaining animals more intensively. Eventually the settlement was abandoned.

source.name: Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology: Vanuatu in the vanguard: new frontiers in Lapita zooarchaeology

title: A Shelter With Its Own Paint Quarry
place: Gunu Cave, near Mitchell Falls, northwest Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia
text: Near Mitchell Falls in the northwest Kimberley, Gunu Cave holds 90 painted motifs spanning every known Kimberley art period, from Gwion figures to Wanjina. Its floor deposit begins about 2,500 years ago, and most of its ochre lies near the bottom. An outcrop in the shelter is the only known Kimberley source of mulberry-coloured pigment that shows signs of being quarried.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Archaeology and art in context: Excavations at the Gunu Site Complex, Northwest Kimberley

title: A Dog Lineage That Stayed Home
place: Bogi 1, Caution Bay, Central Province, Papua New Guinea
text: A dog from Bogi 1 on Caution Bay, near today's Port Moresby, lived about 2,150 to 2,100 years ago. Its ancient DNA belongs to haplogroup B, never before found in Pacific dogs, and seems to share an ancestor with Iron Age dogs from Taiwan. Yet researchers found no evidence that this lineage was ever carried beyond New Guinea.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Complex history of dog origins and translocations in the Pacific revealed by ancient mitogenomes

title: First Sign of Polynesia's Dogs
place: Taurama, near Port Moresby, Central Province, Papua New Guinea
text: A dog from Taurama, near Port Moresby, dated somewhere between 2,000 and 1,200 years ago, carries the earliest known Oceanic example of a DNA lineage called A2b2. The same lineage later turns up in dogs from Tokelau, Hawai'i, the Cook Islands and New Zealand, suggesting Polynesia's dogs arrived after Lapita times from a different source, probably southern Island Southeast Asia.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Complex history of dog origins and translocations in the Pacific revealed by ancient mitogenomes

title: Rains Return, People Fill the Deserts
place: Puritjarra rock shelter, Cleland Hills, Northern Territory, Australia
text: As more frequent La Niña conditions returned after about 2,000 years ago, Aboriginal people moved back into marginal desert country abandoned during drier El Niño times. Modelling of radiocarbon dates from across Australia suggests that by 2,000 to 1,500 years ago people ranged over about 7.7 million square kilometres, nearly the whole continent, with dense occupation at shelters such as Puritjarra.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Holocene Demographic Changes and the Emergence of Complex Societies in Prehistoric Australia

title: Cloth Saved by Copper Rust
place: Seip Earthworks, near Bainbridge, Ohio, USA
text: At Seip in southern Ohio, more than two miles of earthen walls enclose a great circle, a smaller circle and a square. Its central mound, 30 feet high, is the third-largest the Hopewell built, covering the floors and burials of two big connected buildings. Copper breastplates buried there preserved scraps of cloth in their copper salts: milkweed fibre, dyed with circles and curves.

source.name: National Park Service, Hopewell Culture NHP: Seip Earthworks

title: A Cactus-Spine Tattoo Needle
place: Turkey Pen site, Grand Gulch, Cedar Mesa, Utah, USA
text: Sorting the last of 64 boxes from old digs at Turkey Pen in Utah, archaeologist Andrew Gillreath-Brown spotted a tool about 10 centimetres long: a sumac handle bound with yucca to prickly pear spines stained with pigment. Dated to 79 to 130 CE, it is a Basketmaker II tattoo needle, finally proving a practice archaeologists had long suspected among early Puebloans.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancestral Pueblo Tattoo Needle

title: Necklaces of Shimmering Beetle Legs
place: Boomerang Shelter and Atlatl Cave, Bears Ears National Monument, Utah, USA
text: Basketmaker II people in southeastern Utah strung jewellery from the iridescent green legs of June beetles. A fibre fragment from Boomerang Shelter holds 16 legs, and a complete necklace, probably from Atlatl Cave about 20 miles away and radiocarbon dated to the Basketmaker II period, has more than 200, threaded on fine yucca cord. Each necklace took over 100 insects.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The Beauty of Bugs

title: Postholes in Miami's Bedrock
place: North bank of the Miami River, downtown Miami, Florida, USA
text: Across the Miami River from the famous Miami Circle, archaeologist Bob Carr's team uncovered a Tequesta village about 2,000 years old. Eight large circles of postholes were cut into the limestone bedrock, linked by lines of postholes that may mark boardwalks between dwellings. Carr called it one of the earliest urban plans in eastern North America, and a Tequesta burial ground lay nearby.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The Birthplace of Miami

title: A Shell Island Gets Its Start
place: Mound Key, Estero Bay, Florida, USA
text: Mound Key, a 51-hectare island in Estero Bay built largely from shell, later became the capital of the Calusa kingdom. Intensive radiocarbon dating suggests people first settled it sometime between about 300 and 500 CE, perhaps when a slight drop in sea level exposed high ground. Over the following centuries their shell heaps grew into mounds up to 10 meters high.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): From Shell Midden to Midden-Mound: The Geoarchaeology of Mound Key

title: The Desert Predator Named for an Astronomer
place: Dzharakuduk, Kyzylkum Desert, Navoi Region, Uzbekistan
text: Long before the Kyzylkum became a desert, a big meat-eater hunted here. Ulughbegsaurus, named after the 15th-century astronomer-sultan Ulugh Beg, is known from pieces of its upper jaw, the largest about 24 centimetres long. Scientists estimate it reached 7.5 to 8 metres and over a tonne, making it the top predator, while the local tyrannosaur relative Timurlengia was only 3 to 4 metres long.

source.name: Royal Society Open Science: A new carcharodontosaurian theropod dinosaur occupies apex predator niche in the early Late Cretaceous of Uzbekistan

title: A Pocket-Sized Salamander from a Coal Pit
place: Berezovsk Quarry, Sharypovo District, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
text: A few tiny backbones from a Siberian coal quarry revealed a new Middle Jurassic salamander. Egoria malashichevi, named after the zoologist Egor Malashichev, was only about 18 to 21 centimetres long. It shared its waters with a giant cousin, Urupia, about half a metre long, and a minuscule one under 8 centimetres. It is the first small stem salamander ever found.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A new small-sized stem salamander from the Middle Jurassic of Western Siberia, Russia

title: Chewing Stegosaurs of the Far North
place: Teete locality, Suntar District, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Russia
text: Stegosaurs are famous for their back plates, but at Teete in Yakutia they are known from teeth: 63 of them, and nearly all show wear facets from precise tooth-on-tooth chewing, perhaps of tough conifer stems. This is the northernmost stegosaur record. Each tooth formed in about 95 days, and a juvenile's tooth suggests these dinosaurs lived and bred there all year round.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Wear patterns and dental functioning in an Early Cretaceous stegosaur from Yakutia, Eastern Russia

title: Dinosaur Footprints Above a Uranium Town
place: Nichkesai Formation ridge, near Mayluu-Suu, Jalal-Abad Region, Kyrgyzstan
text: In 2001 a landslide uncovered a slab of Late Cretaceous rock, now tilted at about 30 degrees, on a ridge above Mayluu-Suu. Across it run five trackways of three-toed dinosaurs, one with footprints nearly 38 centimetres long, left by at least four animals. Uranium mine tailings lie in the valley below, and track blocks keep falling, so scientists recorded them in 3D.

source.name: Royal Society Open Science: Dinosaur trackways from the Upper Cretaceous Nichkesai Formation near Mayluu Suu City, Southern Tien Shan Mountains, Kyrgyzstan

title: The Last Days of the Siberian Unicorn
text: The so-called Siberian unicorn was a rhino weighing up to 3.5 tonnes, about twice a modern rhino, with a shoulder hump and a huge skull boss that probably held a horn, though no horn has ever been found. It grazed tough, dry grasses on steppes that reached into Kazakhstan. Dating 23 fossils showed it survived until at least 39,000 years ago, alongside modern humans.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: The Siberian unicorn lived at the same time as modern humans

title: One Tail Bone, a Long Journey
place: Dzharakuduk, Kyzylkum Desert, Navoi Region, Uzbekistan
text: In 1997 an international team in Uzbekistan's Kyzylkum Desert dug up a single tail bone from a long-necked dinosaur, its spine almost 19 centimetres tall. Named Dzharatitanis kingi, it is the first rebbachisaurid sauropod known from Asia; the group was previously known only from Africa, Europe and South America. Its ancestors may have walked in from Europe over a land link across the Turgai Strait.

source.name: PLOS ONE: First rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from Asia

title: Squirrels and Grebes on Baikal's Island
place: Tagay Bay, Olkhon Island, Lake Baikal, Irkutsk Oblast, Russia
text: On Olkhon Island in Lake Baikal, clay beds at Tagay Bay preserve a Miocene world of small creatures. First found in 1958, the fossils include snails, fish teeth, frogs, turtles, lizards and an early grebe. Among the tiny rodent teeth is a new ground squirrel, Spermophilinus debruijni, named after palaeontologist Hans de Bruijn. Archaic rodent teeth date the beds to about 16 million years ago.

source.name: Palaeobiodiversity and Palaeoenvironments: Geology and lithology of the Tagay-1 section at Olkhon Island (Lake Baikal, Eastern Siberia)

title: Pond Creatures in a Mammoth's Skull
place: Oyogos Yar coast, Laptev Sea, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Russia
text: In 2010, local Yukagir people found a mummified young mammoth hanging from a melting bank on the Laptev Sea coast. Nicknamed Yuka, she was a female aged 6 to 9 who died about 39,000 years ago. Mud taken from her skull held tiny pond animals: fairy shrimp eggs, tadpole shrimp parts, water fleas and seed shrimps. Some are now rare there but live in Eurasia's dry zones.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Crustacean remains from the Yuka mammoth raise questions about non-analogue freshwater communities in the Beringian region

title: The Oldest Denisovan Was a Little Girl
text: In 1984, archaeologists digging the deepest layer of Denisova Cave's Main Gallery found a worn baby tooth. Decades later, its DNA revealed it belonged to a female Denisovan child. Her mitochondrial DNA shows she lived tens of thousands of years before the owner of the famous Denisovan finger bone, perhaps 54,000 to 99,000 years earlier. Denisovans, it seems, lived around this cave for a very long time.

source.name: Science Advances: A fourth Denisovan individual

title: A Camel Painted in the Ice Age Urals
text: Deep in Shulgan-Tash Cave in the southern Urals, Ice Age artists used red ochre to paint mammoths, woolly rhinos, horses and bison, plus more than 70 geometric signs. In 2017, removing a crust of flowstone revealed a Bactrian camel. Layers linked to the art date to about 16,000 to 20,000 years ago. Yet one charcoal 'running fox' turned out, by radiocarbon, to be drawn around 1900 CE.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Late Palaeolithic cave art and permafrost in the Southern Ural

source2.name: Data in Brief: Data on the 14C date obtained from the charcoal figure 'Black fox' in Shulgan-Tash (Kapova) cave

title: The Cave Where Bears Slept Forever
place: Prokoshev Cave, Chusovaya River basin, Middle Urals, Russia
text: In a chamber of Prokoshev Cave in the Middle Urals, the bones of at least 18 cave bears lie where they fell, partly sunk in the loam. Twelve were adults, four only about a year old. No bites, no cut marks, no trace of people: the bears seem to have died during hibernation, roughly one a year. One jaw is about 53,000 years old.

source.name: Doklady Biological Sciences: A New Mass Burial of Cave Bears (Ursus kanivetz) from the Middle Urals

title: Mammoths on the Walls Above the Sim
place: Ignatievskaya (Yamazy-Tash) Cave, Sim River, Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia
text: Ignatievskaya Cave opens in a limestone cliff 12 metres above the Sim River, and its passages run about 800 metres. Inside, painted mammoths and a rhinoceros-like animal hide among walls blackened by the torches of later visitors. Charcoal dates once suggested the art was only 6,000 to 7,400 years old, but dating of flowstone around it supports an Ice Age origin instead.

source.name: Geoarchaeology: 230Th dating of flowstone from Ignatievskaya Cave, Russia: Age constraints of rock art and paleoclimate

title: The Giant Wooden Idol from a Peat Bog
place: Shigir peat bog, Middle Urals, Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia
text: In 1890, a carved wooden figure was pulled from a peat bog in the Ural Mountains. It may once have stood over 5 metres tall, and it bears a human face and geometric motifs. Old wax and pigment treatments had skewed its radiocarbon dates. Testing only the untouched innermost wood showed the tree was felled and carved about 12,100 years ago.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Scientists Reevaluate Date of Russia's Shigir Idol

title: The Sheep That Carried Bronze Age Plague
text: Arkaim was a fortified settlement of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals, near today's Kazakhstan border. Bones of a sheep dug up there in the 1980s and 1990s held DNA of plague bacteria, the first Bronze Age plague found in an animal. This ancient strain could not spread through fleas, so herds of livestock may have helped carry it across Eurasia.

source.name: EurekAlert! (University of Arkansas): How did Bronze Age plague spread? A sheep might solve the mystery

title: Six Brothers and Their Family Mound
place: Nepluyevsky kurgan cemetery, Kartaly District, Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia
text: Genomes from 32 people buried in one Bronze Age mound near Nepluyevka in the southern Urals rebuilt a family tree across three generations, with six brothers at its centre. The eldest had eight children with two women, the most of anyone. Daughters over five are missing from the mound, while wives came from elsewhere and were buried with their husbands' families.

source.name: PNAS: Descent, marriage, and residence practices of a 3,800-year-old pastoral community in Central Eurasia

title: A Baby Girl Buried Under the Floor
text: Ulug-depe, a 13-hectare town about 175 kilometres east of Ashgabat, was one of the largest proto-urban sites of the Oxus (Bactria-Margiana) culture. Its people buried their dead inside their houses. In one room corner lay a girl about 10 months old, curled on her left side. Her genome shows ancestry from earlier local farmers, Iran and the Indus borderlands, but none from the steppe.

source.name: Frontiers in Genetics: Genetic analysis of a bronze age individual from Ulug-depe (Turkmenistan)

title: A Sword Decorated With Birds of Prey
place: Karabie burial site, Karaganda Region, Kazakhstan
text: In central Kazakhstan, archaeologists from the Karaganda Regional History Museum opened a Saka-era grave at Karabie dating to the 7th or 6th century BCE. The dead warrior still gripped a bronze akinak, a short sword about 30 centimetres long, in the right hand. Its blade is decorated with steppe birds of prey, a design not yet found elsewhere in Kazakhstan. Five arrowheads and a gold earring lay nearby.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 2,700-Year-Old Warrior's Grave Discovered in Kazakhstan

title: Cooking Pots of Recycled Copper
place: Ili River valley (Tekes and Zhaosu), Xinjiang, China
text: In the Ili valley of western Xinjiang, early Iron Age herders cooked in large cauldrons, a vessel type used by steppe peoples from western China to eastern Europe. Analysis of 44 copper-based objects, including cauldrons from Zhaosu and Tekes, found the cauldrons were often pure copper. Lead isotopes point to western Tian Shan ores such as the Nulasai mine, but also reveal metal that was mixed and recycled.

source.name: Archaeometry: New scientific analyses reveal mixing of copper sources in the early Iron Age metal production at Ili, western China

title: Graves of the Bronze Masters
place: Rostovka burial ground, near Omsk, Omsk Oblast, Russia
text: Rostovka in western Siberia is one of very few sites of the Seima-Turbino phenomenon with human remains. Most of its graves held bronze weapons and tools, casting moulds, jewellery and armour plates. Seima-Turbino was a network of tin-bronze makers spanning northern Eurasia's forests around 2200 to 1900 BCE, perhaps born in the Altai and Sayan mountains. The buried people's DNA varies widely along a Siberian genetic gradient.

source.name: Communications Biology: Bronze age Northern Eurasian genetics in the context of development of metallurgy and Siberian ancestry

title: Wheat, Not Millet, in the Trans-Urals
text: Bones remember what people ate. Isotopes from Bronze Age herders across the Eurasian steppe show many groups slowly adding millet to their meals, but the Trans-Urals went another way. At sites such as Lisakovsk, wheat appears around 1750 BCE and becomes a staple by about 1600 BCE. Wheat and barley still dominated there in the Iron Age, while millet mattered little.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Intensification in pastoralist cereal use coincides with the expansion of trans-regional networks in the Eurasian Steppe

title: Power Ran in Saka Families
place: Akbeit, Nurken and Karashoky kurgans, Kazakh steppe, Kazakhstan
text: Saka elites of the Kazakh steppe were buried under big mounds, some with gold, and some with skulls opened after death, probably to preserve the body. Ancient DNA from 85 Iron Age people shows power ran in families: a man over 55 at Akbeit, his brother at Nurken and two grandchildren at Karashoky, buried 50 to 140 kilometres apart. Some elites were children of related parents.

source.name: Science Advances: Ancient DNA reveals elite dynastic rule among Iron Age Eurasian Steppe nomads

title: Grape Earrings and a Roman Brooch
place: Burial mounds, Turkistan Region, southern Kazakhstan
text: Three burial mounds in southern Kazakhstan, about 2,000 years old, tie local nomads to a wide world. Though two were robbed long ago, they still held crescent-shaped gold earrings of the 1st century BCE decorated with grape clusters, a large bronze mirror like those of Han China, and a Roman-style brooch. Archaeologists link them to the Kangju state, which traded with Rome, China and the Kushans.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 2,000-Year-Old Burial Mounds Excavated in Kazakhstan

title: Hard Lives Hidden in a Mountain Cave
place: Alpysbaev Cave, Sairam-Ugam National Park, Turkistan Region, Kazakhstan
text: High in the western Tian Shan, about 1,700 metres up, a small cave held the scattered bones of at least four people, most from the Iron Age Kangju period. Their skeletons tell of hard work: a healed rib fracture, an arthritic neck and stress fractures in a lower back. Little is known about cave burials in this land of kurgans, so the find opens a new window.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Human occupations at the Alpysbaev Cave (western Tian Shan): Bioarchaeological insights from the Iron Age burial cluster

title: A Silk Road Town of the Dayuan
place: Ming-Tepe, Andijan Region, Ferghana Valley, Uzbekistan
text: In the Ferghana Valley, Chinese and Uzbek archaeologists working at Ming-Tepe uncovered a Silk Road settlement about 2,000 years old, complete with a tomb, a workshop and a garrison for travellers. The city is thought to have belonged to Dayuan, a Hellenistic kingdom that ancient accounts say linked the descendants of Greek colonists with Chinese civilisation.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Early Silk Road Settlement Found in Uzbekistan

title: Two Hundred Stone Tombs by the Silk Road
text: Near Turpan, close to the Silk Road, a national heritage survey identified a necropolis of more than 200 tombs spread over about 10,000 square metres. Built between the Warring States period and the Han dynasty, the round or square mounds are heaps of piled stones. Many hold several burials, suggesting shared use. Who built them is unknown, though similar sites across Central Asia belonged to nomads.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: More Than 200 Burial Mounds Found at Site Near Silk Road

title: Africa's Oldest DNA Holds a Mystery
place: Grotte des Pigeons, Taforalt, Oriental Region, Morocco
text: About 15,000 years ago, Stone Age people began burying their dead at the back of Grotte des Pigeons, a cave near Taforalt. In 2018 scientists read nuclear DNA from these burials, the oldest yet recovered in Africa at the time. About two-thirds of the ancestry matched people then living in the Near East. The other third most resembled sub-Saharan Africans, yet no known population carries quite the same mix.

source.name: Max Planck Society: Scientists analyse oldest human DNA from Africa

title: Harpoon Fishers of a Brimming Lake
place: Lothagam, west shore of Lake Turkana, Turkana County, Kenya
text: When the Sahara was green, Lake Turkana stood far higher than today, and people at Lothagam lived along its shore. Digs in 1965 and 1966 turned up hundreds of barbed bone harpoon points and one of East Africa's largest collections of early Holocene human remains. Their pottery carried wavy-line patterns shared across the Sahara. Later drying cut the lake level by about half.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): New archaeological investigations at the Lothagam harpoon site at Lake Turkana

title: Paddling Across a Monster Current
place: Yonaguni Island, Okinawa, Japan (from eastern Taiwan)
text: About 30,000 years ago, people reached Japan's southern Ryukyu Islands by crossing the Kuroshio, one of the world's strongest ocean currents. To test how, a team built a 7.5-metre dugout and in 2019 paddled from Taiwan with no map, compass or GPS, steering by sun, stars and swells. They reached Yonaguni after 225 km and 45 hours. Simulations show success needed a smart launch point.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Traversing the Kuroshio: Paleolithic migration across one of the world's strongest ocean currents

title: Bare Feet Under a Canadian Beach
text: In 2014, archaeologists digging under the sand of Calvert Island found a footprint about 60 cm down. Further digging exposed 29 prints pressed into clay about 13,000 years ago, when the sea stood 2 to 3 metres lower. Their sizes match at least three people, including a child, and toe marks show some went barefoot. Most faced up the beach, as if gathering around something.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Terminal Pleistocene epoch human footprints from the Pacific coast of Canada

title: When Zebras Grazed on Zanzibar
text: During the Ice Age, low seas joined Zanzibar to mainland Africa. Hunters camping in Kuumbi Cave around 19,000 to 17,000 years ago brought home zebra, buffalo, waterbuck and reedbuck, animals that no longer live on the island, and broke the bones while fresh. As seas rose after about 12,000 years ago, the land bridge drowned, Zanzibar became an island, and the zebras slowly vanished.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Continental Island Formation and the Archaeology of Defaunation on Zanzibar, Eastern Africa

title: A Lone Footprint Beside a Mastodon
place: Pilauco site, Osorno, Los Lagos Region, Chile
text: Under the city of Osorno in southern Chile, excavators found a single print pressed into water-soaked ground about 15,600 years ago, near the skull of a gomphothere, an elephant relative. Volunteers stamped barefoot through matching mud to test it, and experts now assign the print to a human, most likely Homo sapiens. Monte Verde, another early site, lies only 100 km away.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): A late Pleistocene human footprint from the Pilauco archaeological site, northern Patagonia, Chile

title: The Americas' Oldest Dated Carved Figure
place: Lapa do Santo, Lagoa Santa Karst, Minas Gerais, Brazil
text: In July 2009, in the last days of a dig at Lapa do Santo, a limestone shelter in Brazil, excavators reached bedrock 4 metres down and found a tiny pecked figure. Just 30 cm tall, it shows a stick-like man with three-fingered hands, a C-shaped head and an oversized phallus. Buried by sediments at least 10,500 years old, it may be the oldest reliably dated figurative petroglyph in the Americas.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Rock art at the Pleistocene/Holocene boundary in Eastern South America

title: Spear Points Older Than Clovis
place: Gault Site, Buttermilk Creek valley, central Texas, USA
text: At the Gault Site in central Texas, springs and fine chert drew people for thousands of years. Beneath a layer of famous Clovis tools, excavators found an older layer holding small stemmed and lanceolate spear points unlike anything Clovis. Luminescence dating of the sediments gave ages of about 16,000 to 20,000 years ago, suggesting Clovis spread among people who already lived across North America.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Evidence of an early projectile point technology in North America at the Gault Site, Texas, USA

title: A Cooking Pot from a Hunan Cave
place: Yuchanyan Cave, Daoxian County, Hunan, China
text: Ice Age foragers camping in Yuchanyan Cave, in southern China, left crumbly pieces of pottery among the bones of deer, boar, birds, tortoises and fish. One pot could be rebuilt: a pointed-bottomed cauldron 29 cm tall, with walls up to 2 cm thick, fired at only about 400 to 500 °C. Radiocarbon dates put the earliest sherds at roughly 18,000 years old, among the oldest pottery anywhere.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and bone collagen associated with early pottery at Yuchanyan Cave, Hunan Province, China

title: Stalking a Giant Sloth at White Sands
place: Alkali Flat, White Sands, New Mexico, USA
text: On the Alkali Flat at White Sands, a giant ground sloth's trackway twists and turns. Inside its footprints are more than ten human prints, left by someone stretching their stride to follow it while the tracks were still fresh. Where people appear, the sloth's path zigzags, and rings of claw marks show it rearing on its hind legs to defend itself. Researchers think humans were harassing or hunting it.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Footprints preserve terminal Pleistocene hunt? Human-sloth interactions in North America

title: A Clovis Baby Raised on Mammoth
place: Anzick site, near Wilsall, Montana, USA
text: Near Wilsall, Montana, a boy about 18 months old was buried with Clovis stone tools roughly 12,800 years ago. Because nursing babies carry their mother's chemical signature, scientists used isotopes in his bones to reconstruct her diet. The answer: mammoth probably made up 35 to 40 percent of what she ate, alongside deer or elk, bison or camel, and horse, with little sign of plant foods.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Mammoth featured heavily in Western Clovis diet

title: The Puzzling People of Maludong
place: Maludong (Red Deer Cave), near Mengzi, Yunnan, China
text: A thighbone dug up in 1989 at Maludong cave in Yunnan sits in layers about 14,000 years old.
