Its long neck and other features look archaic, and its owner weighed only about 50 kg, so a 2015 study suggested an archaic population had survived remarkably late. Later, ancient DNA from the cave instead pointed to an early, distinct branch of southern East Asian people.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A Hominin Femur with Archaic Affinities from the Late Pleistocene of Southwest China

source2.name: Genome Biology (via PMC): Ancient genomes give insight into 160,000 years of East Asian population dynamics

title: Volcanic Glass Carried 800 Kilometres
place: Shinbuk (Sinbuk) site, Jangheung County, South Jeolla, South Korea
text: At Shinbuk, near Korea's southern tip, Ice Age toolmakers left obsidian flakes and quartz crystals in a layer dated by charcoal to about 20,000 radiocarbon years ago. Chemical fingerprinting traced three flakes to Paektusan, the volcano on today's China–North Korea border, roughly 800 km away. Four others seem to come from Japan, making Shinbuk the only Korean Palaeolithic site known with Japanese obsidian.

source.name: Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association Bulletin 27: PIXE provenancing of obsidian artefacts from Paleolithic sites in Korea

title: Beads from a Giant Ostrich's Eggs
text: On China's Loess Plateau, Ice Age people at Shizitan wore ornaments cut from the eggshell of Struthio anderssoni, an extinct giant ostrich. Across 14,000 years, 41 pieces show fashion changing: blackened pendants came first, then beads, some rubbed with red ochre. By the Younger Dryas cold snap, beads were made on site and shrank to about 4 mm across, drilled perhaps with tiny stone microblades.

source.name: Frontiers in Earth Science: Diachronic Change in the Utilization of Ostrich Eggshell at the Late Paleolithic Shizitan Site, North China

title: Japan's Ancestors Built for the Cold
place: Japanese archipelago (Jomon genomes from Kosaku shell mound, Funabashi, Chiba)
text: Japan's Jomon hunter-gatherers descend from a lineage that split from mainland East Asians about 27,000 to 19,000 years ago, around the coldest stretch of the Ice Age. A 2026 study of 42 Jomon genomes found variants in genes such as UCP1 and FTO, which help brown fat burn energy to make heat, plus a cold-sensing gene. Researchers see a legacy of that frozen past in people today.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Jomon genomics reveal cold adaptation in Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers of eastern Eurasia

title: A Lone Skull from Kenya's Coldest Age
place: GvJm-22, Lukenya Hill, Athi-Kapiti Plain, Kenya
text: Dug up in the early 1970s on Lukenya Hill, a rocky outcrop above the plains of southern Kenya, a partial skull with a low, sloping forehead puzzled experts for decades. In 2015, 26 dates on ostrich eggshell placed it about 23,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age. Its owner shared the hill with grindstones, ochre, eggshell beads and an extinct antelope.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Late Pleistocene age and archaeological context for the hominin calvaria from GvJm-22 (Lukenya Hill, Kenya)

title: Ice Age Campers Near 4,500 Metres
place: Cuncaicha rockshelter, Pucuncho Basin, Arequipa, Peru
text: High on Peru's treeless Andean plateau, Ice Age hunters made a base camp in Cuncaicha rockshelter, 4,480 metres above sea level, where air is thin and nights bitter. They sooted its ceiling with fires of cushion plants, left rock art, and ate vicuña, guanaco and taruca deer. Its oldest layers, about 12,400 years old, made it the highest Ice Age home known when reported in 2014.

source.name: EurekAlert! (University of Maine): Archaeologists document highest-altitude Ice Age human occupation

source2.name: University of Tübingen: Ice Age life high in the Andes

title: The Corridor That Opened Too Late
place: Ice-Free Corridor, northeastern British Columbia, Canada
text: For decades, textbooks said the first Americans walked south through a gap between two vast ice sheets in western Canada. Scientists sampled boulders and bedrock along 1,200 km of that route and measured beryllium made by cosmic rays since the ice melted. The corridor fully opened only about 13,800 years ago, after people were already living farther south, so the first travellers probably followed the Pacific coast.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): The age of the opening of the Ice-Free Corridor and implications for the peopling of the Americas

title: Horse and Camel on the Menu in Alberta
text: At Wally's Beach in southern Alberta, hunters butchered seven horses and a camel, leaving 29 plain stone tools beside the bones. It is the only certain evidence that people in North America hunted these Ice Age animals. Twenty-seven radiocarbon dates on the bones show the kills all happened around 13,300 years ago, within a short span, not long before both species vanished from the continent.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Late Pleistocene horse and camel hunting at the southern margin of the ice-free corridor: reassessing the age of Wally's Beach, Canada

title: A Lake in the Karoo's Driest Corner
place: Grootvloer pan, Northern Cape, South Africa
text: Today Grootvloer in South Africa's Northern Cape is a dry, dusty pan. But freshwater mussel shells in its old shorelines date to about 21,000 years ago, at the peak of the last Ice Age, when a lake filled the basin. Along its edge lie bladelets and small cores left by Later Stone Age people, suggesting the interior was a magnet for life, not a barren waste.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Paleolakes and socioecological implications of last glacial greening of the South African interior

title: Gift Beads in the Lesotho Highlands
place: Sehonghong rock shelter, Thaba-Tseka District, Lesotho
text: Ostriches have never been known to live in highland Lesotho, yet Sehonghong shelter, 1,800 metres up, held 553 ostrich eggshell beads, some about 15,500 years old. Strontium in 27 beads showed most were made from eggs laid at least 109 km away, a few over 326 km away. Researchers see the beads as gifts swapped between distant groups, a safety net kept up for over 33,000 years.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Ostrich eggshell bead strontium isotopes reveal persistent macroscale social networking across late Quaternary southern Africa

title: Zebra Hunters of the Oujda Mountains
place: Rhafas Cave, Oujda Mountains, Oriental Region, Morocco
text: High in Morocco's Oujda Mountains, Rhafas Cave sheltered Stone Age hunters through the Ice Age. Most bones they left are from a North African zebra and wild ass, with some gazelle and hartebeest. A layer about 15,400 years old is dark with ash, a sign of busier fires and longer stays, as a warm spell spread forest across the region's highlands.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Expansion of forest cover and coeval shifts in Later Stone Age land-use at Taforalt and Rhafas Caves, Morocco

title: Clovis Hunters and Young Gomphotheres
place: El Fin del Mundo, Sonoran Desert, about 100 km northwest of Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico
text: In 2007 a rancher in Mexico's Sonoran Desert reported bones and stone tools washing out of a gully wall. Excavators found two young gomphotheres, elephant relatives, with Clovis spear points lying among their bones, about 13,400 years old. It was the first evidence of Clovis people hunting gomphotheres, and one of the oldest and southernmost Clovis sites, hinting the culture began farther south than thought.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Human (Clovis)-gomphothere (Cuvieronius sp.) association about 13,390 calibrated yBP in Sonora, Mexico

title: Painters in an Amazon Cave
place: Caverna da Pedra Pintada, Monte Alegre, Pará, Brazil
text: Near Monte Alegre on the lower Amazon, the walls of Pedra Pintada cave carry red and yellow paintings of circles, crosses, frogs, snakes, fish, a manatee and human figures. Digging beneath one painted wall in 2014, archaeologists found people living there about 12,400 years ago, and a stone flake marked with paint in layers around 12,000 years old, suggesting painting began very early.

source.name: Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi (SciELO): The chronology of the cave paintings in the Pedra Pintada Cave, Monte Alegre, Pará

title: Sabretooth Bites on Pampas Giants
place: Salto de Piedra, Tapalqué Creek, near Olavarría, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: Sabre-toothed cats were long thought too fragile-toothed to bite through bone. Fossils at Salto de Piedra on Argentina's Pampas prove otherwise. Bones of toxodons, giant sloths, a glyptodont and a gomphothere, dated between about 22,000 and 13,000 years ago, carry grooves up to 33 mm wide gouged by Smilodon canines. The cat, up to about 400 kg, specialised in giants and was still hunting when the first people arrived nearby.

source.name: BMC Ecology and Evolution (via PMC): Smilodon sabertooth bite marks, new perspectives on prey-predator models in South American Pleistocene

title: Su Song's Water-Powered Clock Tower
text: In 1088 the Song dynasty scholar Su Song built a water-powered astronomical clock tower. Inside it, a waterwheel worked as an escapement, releasing energy in small, regular steps, the same job that makes a mechanical clock tick. When scholars rediscovered his written description in the 1960s, it shook the old idea that mechanical clocks were invented only in Europe.

source.name: Science Museum Group: Scale model of Su Song's Water-Balance Escapement

title: A Village Doctor Puts Pain to Sleep
text: In October 1804 Seishu Hanaoka, a village doctor in Kishu, gave a woman an oral drug he called Mafutsu-san and, once it had put her under, cut out her breast cancer. It is widely counted as the first surgery under general anaesthesia. Hanaoka never wrote a medical book, so a modern researcher repeated animal experiments with the drug to work out how he developed it.

source.name: Journal of Japan Society for Clinical Anesthesia (J-STAGE): The Mysterious Life of Seishu Hanaoka

title: Berenice and the Kissing-Bug Parasite
text: In April 1909 the Brazilian doctor Carlos Chagas examined Berenice, a gravely ill two-year-old whose rural home was infested with blood-sucking triatomine bugs. In her blood he spotted a new trypanosome parasite, which he named after his teacher Oswaldo Cruz. Berenice became the first known case of Chagas disease, and doctors still found the parasite in her blood in 1978, when she was about 71.

source.name: PMC: Beyond the first case of Chagas disease: the Berenice strain

source2.name: PMC: A note on the discovery of Chagas' disease

title: A Farmer Digs Up Zero's Ancestor
place: Bakhshali, near Mardan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
text: In 1881 a farmer found 70 fragile leaves of birch bark buried in a field at Bakhshali, near Peshawar, all covered in mathematics. Radiocarbon dating at Oxford later showed that some pages go back to the 3rd or 4th century CE, about five centuries older than scholars had thought. Scattered through the sums are little dots used as placeholders, ancestors of the zero we write today.

source.name: University of Oxford GLAM: Carbon dating finds Bakhshali manuscript contains oldest recorded origins of the symbol 'zero'

title: An Egyptian Surgeon's 48 Injuries
text: Written in Egypt in the 17th century BCE, probably copied from an older text, this papyrus walks through 48 injuries from the skull down to the spine. Each case gives an examination, a diagnosis and a verdict, and some end bluntly: a condition that cannot be healed. Case 48 breaks off mid-sentence. The dealer Edwin Smith bought it in 1862, reportedly from a tomb at Thebes.

source.name: PMC (European Spine Journal): The Edwin Smith papyrus: a clinical reappraisal of the oldest known document on spinal injuries

title: An Aztec Healer's Book of Herbs
place: Colegio de Santa Cruz, Tlatelolco, Mexico City, Mexico
text: On 22 July 1552, at a Franciscan college for Indigenous nobles in Tlatelolco, the Nahua physician Martín de la Cruz finished a painted book of native remedies, which Juan Badiano translated into Latin. Sent as a gift for Emperor Charles V, it lists hundreds of plants, ordered from head ailments down to the feet. It resurfaced in the Vatican Library in 1929 and returned to Mexico in 1990.

source.name: PMC (Archivos de Cardiología de México): Libellus de Medicinalibus Indorum Herbis. Martín de la Cruz-Juan Badiano Codex

title: The Doctor Who Corrected Galen's Heart
place: Great Nuri Hospital (Bimaristan al-Nuri), Damascus, Syria
text: Born near Damascus in 1210 and trained at the city's Great Nuri Hospital, Ibn al-Nafis dared to contradict Galen. The wall between the heart's chambers, he wrote, is thick and has no hidden pores, so blood must pass through the lungs, mixing with air, to reach the left side. His manuscript lay forgotten until 1924, when an Egyptian doctor found it in a Berlin library.

source.name: PMC (Annals of Saudi Medicine): Ibn al-Nafis: discoverer of the pulmonary circulation

title: Angkor's Giant Rectangle of Water
place: West Baray, Angkor, Siem Reap, Cambodia
text: In the first half of the 11th century, Angkor's builders raised earthen banks around a rectangle about 8 kilometres long and 2 kilometres wide. Filled to the brim, the West Baray held about 53 million cubic metres of water, probably for flood control, irrigation and ritual, with a temple on an island at its centre. It is the only one of Angkor's four great reservoirs that still holds water.

source.name: PMC (PNAS): Paleoenvironmental history of the West Baray, Angkor (Cambodia)

title: A Caesarean Section in Bunyoro
text: In 1879 a British medical student, Robert Felkin, watched a Bunyoro surgeon deliver a first-time mother's baby by caesarean section. She was left half-drunk on banana alcohol, which the surgeon also used to wash her belly and his own hands. He stopped the bleeding with a heated iron rod and pinned the wound with iron spikes. Eleven days later, mother and baby were both doing well.

source.name: PMC (Pan African Medical Journal): Overview of surgical and anesthesia practice in sub-Saharan Africa during the 19th century

title: A Medical Treasure for Khwarazm's King
text: In 1110 the physician Ismail Jorjani, already in his late sixties, entered the service of the Khwarazmshah. He poured a lifetime of travel and study into a vast medical encyclopedia, the Treasure of the King of Khwarazm, covering everything from surgery to dentistry, and wrote it in Persian just as medicine in Iran was switching to that language. He kept teaching and treating patients until he died aged 94.

source.name: PMC (Iranian Red Crescent Medical Journal): The Life of Jorjani, one of the Persian pioneers of medical encyclopedia compiling

title: A Calcutta Cure for Kala-Azar
place: Campbell Medical School (now NRS Medical College), Kolkata, India
text: Working with limited resources at Campbell Hospital in Calcutta, Upendranath Brahmachari made a breakthrough in 1920. By combining urea with an antimony compound, he created urea stibamine, a drug against kala-azar, a deadly parasitic disease. By 1925 the death rate among treated patients had fallen to 10 percent, and by 1933 Assam alone had treated over 328,000 people with it. He was nominated for a Nobel Prize.

source.name: PMC (Cureus): Dr. Upendranath Brahmachari: The Unsung Hero of Indian Medical Research

title: Flickering Stars in a Desert Story
place: Kokatha Country, Great Victoria Desert, South Australia, Australia
text: A Kokatha story from South Australia tells of Nyeeruna, seen in Orion, whose fire-magic in his right hand (Betelgeuse) is countered by fire-magic in the left foot of Kambugudha (Aldebaran). In 2014 two astronomers realised the tale tracks real changes in the sky: Betelgeuse varies in brightness faster than Aldebaran. In Europe, John Herschel only recorded Betelgeuse's changes in the 1830s.

source.name: The Conversation (Duane Hamacher, Monash University): Stars that vary in brightness shine in the oral traditions of Aboriginal Australians

title: Tracking Jupiter With Trapezoids
text: Between about 350 and 50 BCE, Babylonian astronomers worked out how far Jupiter moved across the sky by treating its changing speed over time as the area of a trapezoid. Historian Mathieu Ossendrijver spent 13 years puzzling over four odd tablets in the British Museum before a nearly intact one cracked the code. Europeans were thought to have invented the trick in 14th-century Oxford.

source.name: National Geographic: Babylonians Tracked Jupiter With Advanced Tools: Trapezoids

title: A Bukhara Doctor Describes Sleep Paralysis
text: Before 983, the Bukhara physician Akhawayni packed 20 years of practice into his Learner's Guide to Medicine, the oldest surviving medical treatise in New Persian. One chapter covers kabus, the 'night-mare', what doctors now call sleep paralysis. He blamed vapours rising from the stomach to the brain and prescribed bloodletting. A Dutch doctor's account from 1664 is often called the earliest description.

source.name: PMC (Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment): Sleep paralysis in medieval Persia - the Hidayat of Akhawayni

title: Smallpox Scabs Blown Up the Nose
place: Taiping County (now Huangshan District), Anhui, China
text: Records show practitioners in Taiping County inoculating children against smallpox during the Ming Longqing reign (1567–1572). In the 'dry' method, scabs from a smallpox patient were ground to powder and blown into a child's nostril through a slender silver or bamboo tube while the mother held the child steady. The milder infection that followed usually gave long-lasting protection, centuries before Jenner's cowpox vaccine.

source.name: PMC (Emerging Infectious Diseases): Variolation Techniques, Medical Explanations, and Dissemination in Late Imperial China

title: The Training Ship That Beat Beriberi
place: Tokyo, Japan (home of the Naval Medical Bureau)
text: Japanese navy doctor Kanehiro Takaki suspected beriberi came from a diet too heavy in rice. In 1884 he sent the training ship Tsukuba on the same route and season as the beriberi-stricken Ryujo, changing only the food to a more Western menu. Nearly every sailor came home healthy, though some hated the bread so much they threw it overboard. By 1885 navy beriberi was near zero.

source.name: PMC (Journal of Epidemiology): Short history of epidemiology for noninfectious diseases in Japan, Part 1

title: A Cold Herbal Recipe Waits 1,600 Years
place: Jurong, Jiangsu, China (Ge Hong's home region)
text: The scholar Ge Hong (284–346 CE) wrote A Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, full of quick remedies. One was strikingly simple: soak a handful of qinghao, sweet wormwood, in two litres of water, wring out the juice and drink it all. No boiling. Centuries later that detail suggested to Chinese researchers that heat destroys the herb's active compound, a clue on the road to the malaria drug artemisinin.

source.name: PMC (Frontiers in Pharmacology): Innovating Chinese Herbal Medicine: From Traditional Health Practice to Scientific Drug Discovery

title: A Pocket Universe Made in Lahore
text: Around 1570, in the earliest workshop tradition of the Mughal court at Lahore, a brass astrolabe 16 centimetres across was engraved, probably by Ilah-Dad, first of a family of Lahore astrolabe makers. Its body carries a gazetteer of coordinates for 59 places, its lacy star map has about 19 star pointers, and five swappable plates let users work at latitudes from 21 to 54 degrees, including Samarqand.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Astrolabe (AST0560)

title: Copán's Stones That Count the Sunsets
text: Around 650, Copán's ruler K'ahk' Uti' Witz' K'awiil set up 'solar stelae' that tracked the Sun along the horizon. In the 1920s archaeologist Sylvanus Morley noticed that, seen from Stela 12, the Sun sets behind Stela 10 on two days each year. Astronomer Anthony Aveni later showed that these sunsets marked out 20-day intervals, the same span as the dates carved on the stones.

source.name: The Conversation (Gerardo Aldana, UC Santa Barbara): Solstices brought Mayan communities together using monuments shaped by science and religion

title: A Sultan's Hospital With Music Therapy
place: Sultan Bayezid II Complex, Edirne, Turkey
text: Between 1484 and 1488 the architect Hayrettin built a complex for Sultan Bayezid II at Edirne: a mosque, a hospital, a medical school, a poorhouse and a bathhouse. Alongside the usual remedies, its doctors tried music and occupational therapy on patients. Abandoned after the empire fell, the buildings were restored by Trakya University from 1984 and became a museum of medicine in 1997.

source.name: PMC (Balkan Medical Journal): A Short Note About the Reconsideration of the Image of Bayezid II Darüşşifa

title: A Surveyor's Perfect Right Angles
place: Sippar (Tell Abu Habbah), southwest of Baghdad, Iraq
text: About 3,700 years ago a Babylonian surveyor drew a clay plan of a small field bought from a man named Sîn-bêl-apli, measuring the marshy patches with special care. Unlike older plans, its corners are exact right angles, laid out using three Pythagorean triples. Dug up at Sippar in 1894, tablet Si.427 sat misunderstood for over a century and is now on display in Istanbul.

source.name: The Conversation (Daniel Mansfield, UNSW): How ancient Babylonian land surveyors developed a unique form of trigonometry

title: Star Clocks Painted Inside Coffins
text: Around 2000 BCE, some wooden coffins at Asyut had astronomical tables painted inside their lids. Each column covered ten days and each of the 12 rows named a star, modelled on Sirius, that vanished from view for about 70 days a year. Watching which star rose let people tell the hours of the night, and the Egyptians' 12-part night may be the root of our hours.

source.name: The Conversation (Robert Cockcroft and Sarah Symons, McMaster University): Ancient Egyptians measured the first hour

title: Calcutta's Pioneering Woman Doctor
text: In 1886 Kadambini Ganguly won her medical degree from Calcutta Medical College, which had until then registered only male students. She is regarded as the first woman to practise Western medicine in India. She treated members of Nepal's royal family, took further qualifications in Edinburgh, Glasgow and Dublin, and studied the lives of women working in coal mines, despite an orthodox journal calling her a whore.

source.name: PMC (Cureus): Dr. Kadambini Ganguly (1861-1923): A Pioneer in Indian Medicine

title: Cahokia's Calendar of Wooden Posts
place: Woodhenge, Cahokia Mounds, Collinsville, Illinois, USA
text: At Cahokia, people raised about five 'woodhenges', circles or arcs of evenly spaced wooden posts. Seen from the centre, certain posts mark where the Sun rose or set on the first days of the solstices and equinoxes, and the winter solstice sunrise lines up with a distant temple mound. Beside the winter solstice post, an offering pit held a small beaker painted with a cross inside a circle.

source.name: Illinois State Museum RiverWeb: Woodhenges

source2.name: The Conversation (Rosalyn LaPier, University of Montana): What winter solstice rituals tell us about Indigenous people

title: Miracle Rice From Los Baños
place: International Rice Research Institute, Los Baños, Laguna, Philippines
text: In late 1966 the International Rice Research Institute at Los Baños released IR8, soon nicknamed 'miracle rice'. Its parents were Dee-Geo-Woo-Gen, a short Taiwanese landrace, and Peta, a tall Indonesian rice prized for its taste. Breeders had aimed for short, stiff stems and big harvests when fertilised. By 1980 over three-quarters of the Philippines' rice land grew modern varieties like it.

source.name: PMC (Botanical Studies): Both semi-dwarf and photoperiod-insensitive traits in rice were important for the Green Revolution

source2.name: PMC (PLOS ONE): Farmers' Preference for Rice Traits: Insights from Farm Surveys in Central Luzon, Philippines, 1966-2012

title: Antarctic Air Bubbles and the Americas
text: After Europeans reached the Americas, epidemics and abandoned farmland may have let forests regrow and soak up carbon. Antarctic ice keeps old air in tiny bubbles, so scientists went looking. A 651-metre core drilled on Skytrain Ice Rise in 2018–2019 shows carbon dioxide sliding gently, about 8 parts per million over 157 years, not the sudden 1610 dip once proposed as the start of the Anthropocene.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Reconciling ice core CO2 and land-use change following New World-Old World contact

title: Thirteen Dry Years in a Stalagmite
place: Grutas Tzabnah, near Tecoh, Yucatán, Mexico
text: Inside Grutas Tzabnah cave, a stalagmite grew so fast that every year left a visible layer. Scientists took about 12 samples from each layer, tracking rainy seasons from 871 to 1021 CE. They found eight droughts lasting three years or more, and one brutal run of 13 straight failed rainy seasons, 929 to 942 CE. Nearby Uxmal's political system ended around 950, while Chichén Itzá held on.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Classic Maya response to multiyear seasonal droughts in Northwest Yucatán, Mexico

title: The Pestilence Hidden in Teeth
text: Between 1545 and 1550, a catastrophic die-off swept through Mexico. Nahuatl speakers called it cocoliztli, best translated as “pestilence”, setting it apart from the earlier smallpox and measles outbreaks. Centuries later, scientists screened teeth from an epidemic cemetery in Oaxaca and found DNA of Salmonella Paratyphi C, a cause of enteric fever. Forced relocations under Spanish rule may have helped it spread.

source.name: Microbial Genomics (PMC): The past, present and future of ancient bacterial DNA

source2.name: Current Biology (PMC): The Recovery, Interpretation and Use of Ancient Pathogen Genomes

title: Horses Reached the Plains Early
text: European records claimed Native peoples took up horses only after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. The bones disagree. Radiocarbon dates and ancient DNA show Spanish-descended horses at Paa-ko Pueblo in New Mexico around 1600, and as far north as Idaho soon after. At Blacks Fork in Wyoming, a locally raised horse found in a ceremonial setting had a healed fracture, a sign of care.

source.name: U.S. National Science Foundation: Horses part of Indigenous cultures longer than Western historians thought

source2.name: CNRS: The untold history of the horse in the American Plains

title: The Day an Island Rose Nine Feet
text: At ten in the morning on 20 February 1835, huge flocks of seabirds flew over Concepción, Chile. Then an earthquake ruined the city and three waves struck the coast. Visiting Santa María Island weeks later, Captain FitzRoy of HMS Beagle found the land pushed up about nine feet. Beds of dead mussels clung to rocks ten feet above high water, and rotting shellfish raised an abominable stench.

source.name: Darwin Online: FitzRoy, Narrative of the surveying voyages of HMS Adventure and Beagle, vol. 2 (1839)

source2.name: Darwin Correspondence Project: The geology of the Beagle voyage

title: The Locust Album of Wartime Jerusalem
text: From March to October 1915, locust swarms stripped nearly every plant in and around Palestine, deepening wartime hunger in Jerusalem. The Ottoman commander Djemal Pasha ordered every adult and youth to dig up half a kilo of eggs, an impossible task in hard, stony soil. He also asked American Colony photographers to record the plague, and they made an album showing one fig tree before and after.

source.name: Library of Congress: The American Colony in Jerusalem, The Locust Plague

title: A Dam of God Across the Indus
place: Allah Bund, Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, India
text: In 1819 an earthquake of magnitude 7.5 or more shook the Rann of Kutch in western India. It pushed up a ridge 80 to 90 kilometres long and 4 to 6 metres high, which people named Allah Bund, the “Dam of God”. The ridge blocked a branch of the Indus, the Nara channel, while the ground at Sindri Fort sank and the fort disappeared under water.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Discovery of fossil avian footprints from Late Holocene sediments of Allahbund uplift in Great Rann of Kachchh

source2.name: Science Advances (PMC): Coseismic river avulsion on surface rupturing faults

title: The Bug That Killed France's Vines
place: Pujaut, Gard, southern Rhône valley, France
text: In the early 1860s, vines around Pujaut and other villages of the southern Rhône began to wither and die, and nobody knew why. Only in 1868 did a commission of experts find a tiny insect on the dead roots, naming it Phylloxera vastatrix. It spread across southern and central France and destroyed about 40% of the vines, a heavy blow to a farming society.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Major outbreaks in the nineteenth century shaped grape phylloxera contemporary genetic structure in Europe

title: Sea DNA in the Jōgan Tsunami Sand
place: Coastal lake about 40 km south of Sendai, Miyagi, Japan
text: In 869 CE a great tsunami struck Japan's northeast coast. In a coastal lake about 40 kilometres south of Sendai, it left a sand layer just 2 centimetres thick, buried 67 centimetres deep in peat. In 2024 scientists pulled DNA out of that sand and found marine bivalves swept in from the sea. The same lake also holds sand from the 2011 tsunami, which struck the same coast.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Identification of deposits from modern and ancient large tsunamis by means of environmental DNA

title: Algae Cysts and the Antonine Plague
place: Gulf of Taranto, off Calabria, Italy
text: In mud 270 metres under the Gulf of Taranto lie fossil cysts of tiny algae, and their species mix tracks late-summer sea temperatures. Sampling roughly every three years of mud, scientists rebuilt Roman Italy's climate from about 200 BCE to 600 CE. The warm, stable Roman era broke with cool pulses, including one from about 160 to 180 CE, when the Antonine Plague struck.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Climate change, society, and pandemic disease in Roman Italy between 200 BCE and 600 CE

title: Gaulish Oaks Under a Roman Portico
text: Beneath a lavish portico in central Rome, archaeologists found 24 waterlogged oak planks. Their tree rings matched oaks felled between 40 and 60 CE in the Jura Mountains of north-eastern France. The heavy timber probably floated down the Saône and Rhône, crossed the Mediterranean and went up the Tiber, a journey of over 1,700 kilometres. Romans prized tough, durable oak for foundations touching the ground.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Dendrochronological evidence for long-distance timber trading in the Roman Empire

title: The Virus Released on Rabbits
text: Between March and November 1950, scientists infected wild European rabbits with myxoma virus at five sites in Australia's Murray Valley. It spread poorly and seemed to die out. Then, in December, it suddenly re-emerged and swept across much of south-eastern Australia, killing up to 99.8% of infected rabbits. Milder virus strains and tougher rabbits soon evolved, turning a pest-control plan into a famous evolution experiment.

source.name: Viruses (PMC): Myxoma Virus and the Leporipoxviruses: An Evolutionary Paradigm

title: The Fur Seals Come Back Too Hard
place: Signy Island, South Orkney Islands, Antarctica
text: Sealers hunted Antarctic fur seals to the brink of extinction in the 1700s and 1800s. Later, whalers wiped out the great whales, possibly leaving extra krill for seals. Fur seal numbers then soared. From the late 1970s, summer crowds hauling out on Signy Island trampled and over-fertilised its mosses and lichens, badly damaging or destroying over 75% of the vegetation on low, accessible ground.

source.name: Ambio (PMC): Untangling unexpected terrestrial conservation challenges arising from the historical human exploitation of marine mammals

title: Perished as the Moa Perished
text: Polynesian settlers reached New Zealand around 1280 CE and found giant flightless birds called moa. Most mainland bird extinctions there happened before 1500, within about 150 years of arrival, and moa were among the species most exposed to hunters. Māori remembered the loss in ancestral sayings. One, dated to about 1500–1650, says “Kua ngaro i te ngaro o te moa”: perished as the moa perished.

source.name: Human Ecology (PMC): Human Perceptions of Megafaunal Extinction Events Revealed by Linguistic Analysis of Indigenous Oral Traditions

title: The Mystery Volcano Behind a Green Sun
place: Zavaritskii caldera, Simushir Island, Kuril Islands, Russia
text: In 1831 a huge eruption cooled the Northern Hemisphere by about 1 °C, and in August people saw a blue, purple and green sun. Famines from crop failure soon struck eastern India and Japan. For almost two centuries nobody knew which volcano was to blame. Then glass shards in polar ice cores matched Zavaritskii, a remote caldera on Simushir Island in the Kurils.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): The 1831 CE mystery eruption identified as Zavaritskii caldera, Simushir Island (Kurils)

title: The Oldest Tree Planted by People
place: Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka
text: In 288 BCE, as Buddhism arrived in Sri Lanka through the Indian emperor Ashoka, a cutting from the sacred Maha-Bodhi fig tree was planted at Anuradhapura. Called the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, it is thought to be the oldest human-planted tree in the world. The story later came full circle: the Bodhi tree now growing at Bodh Gaya in India is itself a cutting from this Sri Lankan tree.

source.name: Heliyon (PMC): Old lessons for new science: How sacred-tree metaphors can inform studies of the public-health benefits of the natural environment

title: The Quake Right Under Tashkent
text: At 05:23 on 26 April 1966, an earthquake struck Tashkent. At magnitude 5.2 it was not especially large, but its epicentre lay only about 2 kilometres away, and a surface rupture 3 to 8 kilometres long opened beneath the central districts. More than 300,000 of the city's 1.5 million people lost their homes, and hundreds of elderly people reportedly died of heart attacks brought on by fear.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Seismic risk assessment of Tashkent's residential buildings based on the 1966 earthquake scenario

title: A Golden Horde Town on the Aral Seabed
place: Aralasar and Kerderi-2, dried Aral Sea bed, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: As the Aral Sea shrank in the 20th century, receding 120 kilometres from one shore village, it exposed a medieval town on its old bed. Aralasar covered about 6 hectares, with an irrigation canal, grain fields and 15 millstones over a metre wide. Two Golden Horde silver coins date it to the mid-1300s. Nearby, the Kerderi-2 mausoleum glowed with turquoise-glazed carved tiles.

source.name: Archaeology.kz: Aralasar, the settlement and Kerderi-2 mausoleum

title: Mayon Buries the Cagsaua Church Town
text: Earthquakes rattled Albay from 31 January 1814. At 8:30 the next morning, Mayon volcano began hurling out ash and bombs “as large as big jars”, and hot rocks swept down its southern slopes. Rain formed inside the eruption clouds, and lahars buried the villages of Cagsaua, Budiao and Bubulusan up to 12 metres deep. About 1,200 people died, and ash darkened skies as far as Manila.

source.name: JICA: The Study on Comprehensive Disaster Prevention around Mayon Volcano, Data Book II (historical eruptions)

title: When Kelud's Crater Lake Poured Out
text: On 19 May 1919, Kelud volcano in East Java erupted beneath its crater lake. The lake water mixed with volcanic debris into lahars, fast-moving mudflows that killed 5,011 people and destroyed thousands of acres of coffee plantations. The disaster launched modern volcano science in Indonesia, and in 1921 engineers began digging a tunnel to drain the crater lake and reduce the danger.

source.name: USGS: Volcano hazard mitigation program in Indonesia

source2.name: National Geographic: Mount Kelud volcano eruption, Indonesia

title: Iceland's Haze and a Low Nile
place: Roda Nilometer, Roda Island, Cairo, Egypt
text: In spring 939 CE, Eldgjá in Iceland began a great eruption that lasted at least until autumn 940. Thousands of kilometres south, the Roda Nilometer in Cairo recorded an unusually low Nile flow in 939, perhaps because volcanic haze weakened the monsoon rains that feed the river. Irish chroniclers saw a blood-red sun, and food shortages followed from Baghdad to the Maghreb.

source.name: Climatic Change (PMC): The Eldgjá eruption: timing, long-range impacts and influence on the Christianisation of Iceland

title: Roman Orchards Climb the Taurus Hills
place: Sagalassos and the Bereket Basin, Burdur Province, Turkey
text: Pollen grains trapped in marsh and lake mud around Sagalassos, in the hills of southwest Turkey, record a farming boom. In the 1st century CE, pollen from olive, walnut, chestnut and grapevine rose at highland sites such as the Bereket Basin as orchards spread uphill, helped by Roman screw presses and rotary mills. In Early Byzantine times that orchard pollen faded and many highland villages were abandoned.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Settlement, environment, and climate change in SW Anatolia: Dynamics of regional variation and the end of Antiquity

title: Rinderpest, Tsetse and a Lakeside Epidemic
place: Lake Victoria shore near Entebbe, Uganda
text: After rinderpest reached Africa through Eritrea in the late 1880s, it killed over 90% of susceptible cattle. Bush and wild game reclaimed empty pastures, and tsetse flies followed. In 1901 sleeping sickness, spread by those flies, exploded along the shores and islands of Lake Victoria in Uganda. By 1905 over 200,000 people, a third of the region's population, had died.

source.name: PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases (PMC): Sleeping Sickness Epidemics and Colonial Responses in East and Central Africa, 1900–1940

source2.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Genome-wide analysis reveals differential admixture dynamics and historical demographic contractions in African cattle

title: An Alaskan Volcano and Rome's Hungry Years
place: Okmok caldera, Umnak Island, Aleutian Islands, Alaska, USA
text: Early in 43 BCE, Okmok volcano in Alaska's Aleutian Islands produced one of the largest eruptions of the past 2,500 years, its fallout preserved in six Arctic ice cores. The next two years were among the Northern Hemisphere's coldest in millennia, and frost struck California's bristlecone pines in early September. Ancient writers report that the Nile failed to flood and famine gripped Egypt and Rome.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Extreme climate after massive eruption of Alaska's Okmok volcano in 43 BCE and effects on the late Roman Republic and Ptolemaic Kingdom

source2.name: Alaska Volcano Observatory: Okmok

title: Stalagmites Remember India's Worst Droughts
place: Mawmluh Cave, near Cherrapunji (Sohra), Meghalaya, India
text: In Mawmluh Cave, near one of the wettest places on Earth, two stalagmites recorded the Indian monsoon year by year. Their chemistry marks 1780 to 1810 as the weakest 30-year monsoon spell of the past millennium. Records list at least 11 drought famines then, six between about 1782 and 1792, including the Chalisa and Skull Famines. Failed harvests may have helped undercut India's textile industry.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Protracted Indian monsoon droughts of the past millennium and their societal impacts

title: One Olympic Opening, Four Stages
text: The Milan Cortina Winter Olympics opened on February 6, 2026, with a ceremony split across four places: San Siro stadium in Milan, Cortina d'Ampezzo, Livigno and Predazzo. For the first time there were two cauldrons, both inspired by Leonardo da Vinci's geometric studies, one in Milan and one some 400 kilometers away in Cortina. Mariah Carey sang "Volare" and Laura Pausini sang the anthem.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Photos: The Milan Cortina Olympics begin with opening ceremony

title: Goodbye Lev, Hello Euro
text: On January 1, 2026, Bulgaria became the 21st EU country to use the euro, now shared by over 357 million EU citizens. The rate was fixed for good at 1.95583 lev to one euro. Through January shoppers could still hand over lev, but their change came back only in euros, and shops had to show prices in both currencies until August 2026.

source.name: European Commission Access2Markets: Bulgaria adopts euro as of 1 January 2026

title: Bulgaria's Surprise Song Contest Win
text: At the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna's Stadthalle arena, singer Dara won with "Bangaranga", giving Bulgaria its first-ever victory. She was not among the favorites; at home she is a mentor on The Voice Bulgaria. Acts from 25 countries performed, while five longtime entrants, including Spain and Ireland, stayed away in protest over Israel's participation. Australia's Delta Goodrem came fourth.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Bulgaria wins the 70th Eurovision Song Contest with 'Bangaranga'

title: Hungary Votes Out Orbán
text: In Hungary's April 12, 2026 election, Péter Magyar's Tisza party took over 53 percent of the counted vote against about 37 percent for Viktor Orbán's Fidesz. Orbán, the EU's longest-serving leader after 16 years in power, conceded, calling the result painful. Magyar, 45, was a former Fidesz insider who broke with the party in 2024 and quickly formed Tisza. Turnout neared 80 percent, a post-Communist record.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán ousted

title: The Biggest World Cup Kicks Off
text: The 2026 World Cup, co-hosted by Mexico, Canada and the United States and with 48 teams, the most ever, opened at Mexico City's Estadio Azteca before 80,824 fans. Mexico beat South Africa 2-0, with goals from Julián Quiñones and a Raúl Jiménez header. It was a fiery start: referees showed three red cards, two to South Africa and one to Mexico.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Mexico hosts South Africa in opening match as World Cup begins

title: Costa Rica Picks a President in One Round
text: About 3.7 million Costa Ricans could vote on February 1, 2026. Laura Fernández, 39, of the Sovereign People's Party, won nearly 49 percent in early counts, clearing the 40 percent needed to avoid an April runoff. Chosen by outgoing president Rodrigo Chaves as his successor, she campaigned on tougher security policies, including finishing a maximum-security prison. Her main rival conceded.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Laura Fernandez declares victory in Costa Rica's presidential election

title: Two Big Quakes in One Minute
text: On the evening of June 24, 2026, a national holiday, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck Venezuela, and less than a minute later came a magnitude 7.5. The USGS placed the larger quake near the coast west of Caracas, and the capital suffered worst, with rescuers pulling survivors from the rubble of a 22-storey building in Altamira. The main airport closed. Officials reported at least 235 deaths.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Venezuela rocked by 7.5, 7.2 earthquakes: What happened and what we know

source2.name: USGS: M 7.5 - 20 km W of Catia La Mar, Venezuela

title: Five Kicks Win a Super Bowl
place: Levi's Stadium, Santa Clara, California, USA
text: Super Bowl LX was played at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California, on February 8, 2026. The Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 29-13 for the second title in team history, powered by their defense. Seattle kicker Jason Myers made five field goals, the most in any Super Bowl. At halftime Bad Bunny headlined the show, performing in Spanish.

source.name: ABC7 News: Super Bowl LX live updates

title: The Final Where a Team Walked Off
place: Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Rabat, Morocco
text: Before 66,526 fans in Rabat, Senegal beat hosts Morocco 1-0 after extra time to win the Africa Cup of Nations. In stoppage time a penalty was given against Senegal, and their coach ordered the players off the pitch. Sadio Mané talked them back after about 14 minutes. Brahim Díaz's chipped penalty was saved, and Pape Gueye scored the winner.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Senegal beat hosts Morocco to win AFCON 2025 after farcical walk-off

title: Uganda Votes Behind a Blackout
text: Uganda voted for president on January 15, 2026, during a nationwide internet blackout that observers said disrupted their work. Two days later the Electoral Commission declared Yoweri Museveni, 81 and in power since 1986, the winner of a seventh term with 71.65 percent. Opposition leader Bobi Wine, credited with 24.72 percent, rejected the result, and his party called it a sham.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni wins seventh term: Electoral Commission

title: 1.7 Million Pilgrims Reach Mecca
text: Saudi Arabia's statistics authority counted 1,707,301 pilgrims at the Hajj of 1447 AH, held in late May 2026, about two percent more than the year before. Of them, 1,546,655 travelled from abroad: nearly 1.49 million by air, about 54,000 overland and just under 6,500 by sea. Another 160,646 were Saudi citizens or residents.

source.name: Arab News: 1.7m pilgrims performing Hajj this year, 2.04% more than last year

title: Bangladesh Votes After the Uprising
text: On February 12, 2026, Bangladesh held its first election since the 2024 student-led uprising that ousted Sheikh Hasina. More than 127 million people could vote, and turnout was nearly 60 percent. Unofficial results gave the BNP 209 seats, led by Tarique Rahman, back from 17 years of exile. Voters also answered a referendum on reforms such as prime-ministerial term limits.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Bangladesh's BNP claims landslide win in first election since 2024 uprising

title: Nepal's New Party Sweeps the Vote
text: Nepal held snap elections for all 275 seats of its House of Representatives on March 5, 2026, the first national vote since youth-led protests in September 2025. The Rastriya Swatantra Party, with Balendra Shah as its candidate for prime minister, won a majority of 182 seats. The older Nepali Congress fell from 89 seats to 38. Observers called the vote peaceful and orderly.

source.name: International IDEA Democracy Tracker: Nepal, March 2026

title: Thailand Votes Twice in One Day
text: On February 8, 2026, Thai voters chose a new parliament and also voted on changing the constitution. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, who had called the vote after fewer than 100 days in office, saw his Bhumjaithai party on track for at least 194 of 500 seats. Nearly two-thirds of voters backed replacing the charter put in place after a 2014 military coup.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Thailand's Bhumjaithai set for coalition talks after surprise election win

title: An Earthquake on the First School Day
text: At 7:37 in the morning on June 8, 2026, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck about 32 kilometers off Maasim in Sarangani province, Mindanao. It hit just as millions of children were returning to school after the summer break. Classes were suspended at over 6,200 schools for safety checks, tsunami alerts sent coastal residents inland, and the UN reported at least 19 deaths.

source.name: UN News: Deadly quake strikes Philippines on first day of school year

title: Japan Votes Through Record Snow
text: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called a snap election about three months after taking office, and on February 8, 2026, her Liberal Democratic Party won 316 of 465 lower house seats, according to NHK. Only 233 were needed for a majority. Record snowfall in parts of Japan snarled traffic and forced some polling stations to close early, yet voters still turned out.

source.name: Al Jazeera: PM Sanae Takaichi's party wins supermajority in Japan snap elections

title: A Small Tsunami Off Iwate
place: Pacific Ocean off Miyako, Iwate, Japan
text: On the afternoon of April 20, 2026, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck the seafloor about 100 kilometers east-northeast of Miyako on Japan's Pacific coast, at a depth of around 25 kilometers, according to the USGS. It raised a small local tsunami, with waves of 80 and 40 centimeters recorded. The Associated Press reported at least one injury. Japan sits where four major tectonic plates meet.

source.name: EarthScope Consortium: M 7.4 Miyako, Japan

source2.name: USGS: M 7.4 - 102 km ENE of Miyako, Japan

title: Kazakhstan Rewrites Its Constitution
text: On March 15, 2026, Kazakhstan voted in a referendum on a new constitution, and preliminary results showed over 87 percent in favor, with turnout above 73 percent. The changes merge the two-chamber parliament into one, restore the post of vice-president, widen the president's appointment powers and create a People's Council. It was President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's second constitutional change in four years.

source.name: All India Radio News: Kazakhstan's voters approved referendum on new constitution

title: A Deep Quake Under Tonga
place: Tonga Trench region, west of Neiafu, Vava'u, Tonga
text: On March 24, 2026, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck about 158 kilometers west of Neiafu in Tonga's Vava'u islands. The USGS placed its source about 234 kilometers below the surface, so deep that its loss-estimate system gave it a green alert, its lowest level, meaning little damage was expected. The Associated Press first reported it using a preliminary magnitude of 7.6.

source.name: USGS: M 7.5 - 158 km W of Neiafu, Tonga

source2.name: WTOP (AP): USGS says a preliminary magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near Tonga

title: A Strong Quake Beneath Espiritu Santo
text: Six days after Tonga's deep quake, the Pacific shook again. On the evening of March 30, 2026, a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck about 51 kilometers east-northeast of the town of Luganville on Espiritu Santo, Vanuatu. The USGS located it roughly 120 kilometers underground. Its loss-estimate system issued a green alert, its lowest level, meaning low expected casualties and damage.

source.name: USGS: M 7.3 - 51 km ENE of Luganville, Vanuatu

title: Spain Wins the 48-Team World Cup
place: MetLife Stadium, East Rutherford, New Jersey, United States
text: The largest World Cup ever, with 48 nations, ended in New Jersey with Spain beating Argentina 1-0. Argentina played all of extra time with 10 men, and Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. Spain had outshot Argentina 20 to 3, but goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez made 12 saves, the most ever in a final. It was Spain's second title, after 2010.

source.name: CBS News: Spain beats Argentina to win 2026 World Cup

title: Darkness Falls Over Spain at Sunset
text: Millions of people in cloudless Spanish towns watched the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century. In Medinaceli, a Roman-era hilltop town, a language teacher said no photo or video comes close to the real feeling. Totality lasted about a minute near sunset, with temperatures above 35°C. Spain set up about 350 official viewing sites, and many pharmacies ran out of eclipse glasses.

source.name: OPB (AP): Millions crowd cities to see Spain's first total solar eclipse in over a century

title: A Judge From Durban Wins the Peace Prize
text: Navi Pillay, born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for promoting peace and international law. She once defended Nelson Mandela and other anti-apartheid activists. Later, as a judge at the Rwanda tribunal, she helped establish that rape could be a crime against humanity and genocide. She also served as UN human rights chief.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Peace Prize 2026 press release

title: Asia's Games Return to Japan
place: Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, Nagoya, Aichi, Japan
text: The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya, the first hosted by Japan since Hiroshima in 1994. Athletes from 45 nations would compete for 469 gold medals across 43 sports until October 4, with swimming held in Tokyo. The ceremony's theme was "Harmonic Heart Beat", and former hammer thrower Koji Murofushi lit the cauldron together with his father, Shigenobu.

source.name: The Korea Times: Competition begins with celebration of host city's hospitality

title: Lula's Comeback in Brazil's Runoff
text: After losing Brazil's first round on October 4, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, aged 80, won the runoff against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro with over 51 percent and more than 64 million ballots. It gave him a fourth, non-consecutive term. No other modern Brazilian politician had lost the first round and then won the runoff. Bolsonaro did not concede and said he would challenge the result.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election

title: A Classicist Poet Wins the Nobel
text: Toronto-born poet Anne Carson, 76, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. A professor of classics, she blends poetry and essay with ancient Greek literature; her Trojan Women retells Euripides as a graphic book. She holds Icelandic citizenship and was in Iceland when the news came. Asked by Icelandic broadcaster RUV for her reaction, she called it simply "crazy."

source.name: Al Jazeera: Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature

title: New Zealand's Knife-Edge Election
text: New Zealanders voted in an election with no clear winner. Labour and National each won just over 29 percent of the party vote, and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's conservative bloc held 67 of 131 seats, one above a majority, before nearly 400,000 special votes were counted. The Opportunity Party, led by 38-year-old Qiulae Wong, entered Parliament with seven seats. Final results were due November 27.

source.name: OPB (AP): No clear winner in New Zealand election

title: A Sweltering 250th Birthday
place: Independence Hall, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
text: The United States marked 250 years since independence in a heat wave, with Washington's heat index near 115°F. In Philadelphia, fireworks went off around midday near Independence Hall, where the Declaration was adopted. In New York, 43 tall ships paraded past the Statue of Liberty, and at Coney Island Joey Chestnut ate 66 hot dogs in 10 minutes for his 18th win.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Fireworks, heat, hot dogs and politics as America celebrates its 250th birthday

title: A Mountain Collapse Floods Nepal's Valleys
text: On August 26, a glacial collapse high on the Nepal-China border sent a tsunami-like flood down Nepal's river valleys. Nuwakot district, including Devighat on the Tadi and Trishuli rivers, was among the places hit. Nepal counted over 1,000 deaths within a week, and Al Jazeera later reported more than 1,400 killed. A month on, Nuwakot and Rasuwa were told to stay alert as new monsoon rains came.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Floods and landslides kill at least 56 people in India, 12 in Nepal

source2.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Nepal's death toll from glacier collapse and flood exceeds 1,000

title: Israel's Election Ends in Deadlock
text: Israel's parliamentary election left neither main bloc with the 61 seats needed to govern. Final official results gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats and the opposition bloc of Gadi Eisenkot 48. Arab-led parties, including the Joint List and Ra'am, held the balance. Israel's Central Elections Committee said the vote was conducted lawfully, rejecting claims of systematic interference.

source.name: ABC30 (AP): Israel final election results

title: Yurt Villages for the Nomad Games
text: More than 3,000 competitors from 110 countries came to Kyrgyzstan for the World Nomad Games, with horse riding and archery staged in the Kyrchyn Gorge. Each Kyrgyz region built a village of decorated yurts and nomad dwellings with felt-making, carpet-weaving and food cooked on the spot. Over 150,000 visitors came in the first two days. A Mongolian champion kept his title by crushing 58 animal bones in one minute.

source.name: Euronews: Kyrgyzstan's World Nomad Games continues as new village brings history to life

title: A Nobel for a Telescope Made of Ice
place: IceCube Neutrino Observatory, South Pole, Antarctica
text: Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for IceCube, a cubic kilometre of South Pole ice fitted with light sensors. He first proposed the idea in 1988. Neutrinos pass through Earth unnoticed, but when one rarely hits an atomic nucleus it makes a flash of light in the clear glacial ice. IceCube, finished in 2011, found neutrinos from far outside our solar system.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 press release

title: Solving the Mirror-Molecule Mystery
place: Tokyo University of Science, Tokyo, Japan
text: Living things use only one mirror-image form of molecules like amino acids, a puzzle over a century old. The 2026 Chemistry Nobel went to Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai, a Hiroshima-born professor emeritus at Tokyo University of Science. In 2003 Soai presented a reaction producing only one of two mirror images, something nothing except life itself had achieved before.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026 press release

title: Switching Brain Cells On With Light
place: Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Martinsried, Germany
text: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honoured optogenetics. Peter Hegemann, working at Martinsried's Max Planck institute, and Georg Nagel found channelrhodopsin in a single-celled alga that swims toward light; blue light opens a channel through it. Karl Deisseroth put its gene into rat nerve cells and fired them with light, and by 2007 in living mice. Researchers now use it to map memories and behaviour.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 press release

title: Zambia Re-Elects Hichilema
text: Five days after Zambians voted, the electoral commission declared President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of a second five-year term with about 61.4 percent of valid votes. It was his seventh run for the presidency. His rival Brian Mundubile, on his first bid, took about 38 percent and called for an investigation into result forms. EU observers called the vote largely peaceful but said freedoms were limited.

source.name: Al Jazeera: Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema wins second term

title: Eleven Nations Meet by Manila Bay
text: Leaders of the 11-nation ASEAN bloc opened their annual summit at a heavily guarded convention center by Manila Bay. Timor-Leste's prime minister, Xanana Gusmão, stood in the group photo. On the agenda: Myanmar's civil war, South China Sea tensions, energy security and the fallout of distant wars. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. was to hand the rotating chairmanship to Singapore.

source.name: Boston Globe (AP): Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit

title: A Record Storm Hugs Mexico's Coast
text: Category 4 Hurricane Simon, with 140 mph winds, crept along Mexico's Pacific coast with its eye just offshore. Puerto Vallarta closed its waterfront, and Jalisco suspended classes in 22 coastal towns. Simon pushed the eastern Pacific to a record for accumulated cyclone energy, beating 2018, in a season of 21 named storms fuelled partly by El Niño.

source.name: PBS NewsHour (AP): Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast

source2.name: Al Jazeera: Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico's coast

title: Glasgow Closes Its Commonwealth Games
text: Glasgow's Commonwealth Games ended after 11 days with a closing ceremony on August 2. Athletes from 74 nations and territories competed in 215 events across 10 sports and 6 para sports, and 1,168 medals were handed out. More than 630,000 people joined in at venues, city live sites and festival events. The Games were hailed as a "game-changer" for the event's future.

source.name: Glasgow Life: Glasgow 2026 Games ends on a high

title: Taming Booms and Busts Wins a Nobel
place: Stanford University, Stanford, California, United States
text: The 2026 economics prize went to Robert E. Hall of Stanford, born in nearby Palo Alto, and Michael Woodford of Columbia. After the 1970s oil crises, many thought governments should stop trying to smooth booms and recessions. The pair rebuilt economic models on how forward-looking households and businesses behave, and central banks and governments around the world now use such models.

source.name: NobelPrize.org: Prize in Economic Sciences 2026 press release

title: Four Astronauts Swing Around the Moon
place: Launch Pad 39B, Kennedy Space Center, Florida, USA
text: On 1 April 2026, NASA's giant SLS rocket lifted off from Pad 39B carrying Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen in an Orion capsule they named Integrity. Passing 4,067 miles above the Moon, they reached 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans before, beating Apollo 13's 1970 record. They splashed down off San Diego on 10 April.

source.name: NASA: NASA Welcomes Record-Setting Artemis II Moonfarers Back to Earth

title: Homo erectus Hid in the Rainforest
place: Baxian and Naxian caves, Chongzuo, Guangxi, China
text: In November 2026, scientists announced eight Homo erectus teeth from two karst caves in Guangxi, dated 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. That makes them the youngest securely dated Homo erectus in mainland China. Chemistry in the teeth showed these people lived in dense tropical forest, a habitat once thought open only to our own species, alongside orangutans and an extinct forest elephant.

source.name: EurekAlert (Macquarie University): Hidden in the rainforest: The surprising last chapter of Homo erectus in China

source2.name: National Geographic: Homo Erectus May Have Survived in China 200,000 Years Longer Than We Thought

title: Old Skull Pieces Turn Out Denisovan
text: A skull fragment and a jaw piece dug up at Xujiayao in the 1970s got a new identity in October 2026. Qiaomei Fu's team found 18 ancient proteins in them, including a collagen variant seen only in Denisovans. 3D reconstructions suggest these lost cousins had low, flat skulls, thick bones, heavy brows and flattened faces, and probably lived right across East Asia.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Denisovan Fossils Identified

title: A Roman Glass Cup on the Steppe
place: Duurlig Nars cemetery, Bayan-Adarga, Khentii, Mongolia
text: In November 2026, Korean and Mongolian museum and academy teams reported on a 240-foot-long Xiongnu tomb at Duurlig Nars, buried under nine layers of stones more than 45 feet deep. Inside lay a lacquered carriage, 15 jade pieces echoing Han Dynasty disks, a silver gourd-shaped harness pendant, and a clear handled glass vessel thought to come from the Roman Empire.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Monumental Mongolian Tomb Excavated

title: A Pocket Cannon With Its Maker's Name
place: Mount Geumseong, Naju, South Jeolla, South Korea
text: In 2026, researchers in Naju identified a bronze handheld gun found on Mount Geumseong as a Hwangja Hwatong, which fired arrows or pellets. About nine inches long, it is engraved with its name, weight, supervisor, craftsman and a partial date pointing to 1377 or 1437. Firearms from the late Goryeo and early Joseon years are extremely rare finds.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Early South Korean Gunpowder Weapon Identified

title: Two Baby Girls in One Nazca Jar
text: In November 2026, Peruvian researchers described two infant girls buried together in one pot in a Nazca cemetery between 325 and 440 CE. One had cyclopia, a rare condition: a single eye socket in the middle of her forehead and no nose bones. DNA revealed an extra copy of chromosome 13, a likely cause, and showed the girls had different mothers.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Remains of Two Infant Girls Found in Peruvian Nazca Cemetery

title: Red Glyphs Read Like Writing
text: In October 2026, Christophe Helmke's team published new images of three red glyphs in a cliff cave at Chalcatzingo, left by settlers from Teotihuacan. One shows a mountain with speech scrolls, perhaps a place called Singing Mountain. Another lists a warrior's necklace, cloak and dart, like a title. Helmke argues Teotihuacan signs were a true writing system.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Cave Paintings May Have Been Part of Mesoamerican Writing System

title: A 3,000-Year-Old Andean Face Returns
text: In 2026, forensic artist Christopher Rynn rebuilt the face of Punín-2, a man who died around age 50 about 3,000 years ago in Ecuador's Chimborazo region. His skull had lain in a ravine until the 1970s. Rynn asked local people, likely his descendants, how to style the hair and place the eyes, since a wrong hairstyle looks like a different tribe.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Face of Ancient Andean Man Reconstructed

title: Rare Stencilled People on a Cliff
place: La Rochelle rock shelter, near Carolina, Mpumalanga, South Africa
text: In October 2026, David Pearce of Wits University reported two humanlike figures stencilled onto the La Rochelle rock shelter, beside painted hartebeest and eland. Southern Africa's rock art is usually brushed or finger-painted, so stencils are rare. Pearce thinks paint was blown over a template, perhaps of beeswax, clay or wood, and the trick may once have decorated bodies and clothing too.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Stenciled Rock Art Found in South Africa

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine (archaeologymag.com): First stencilled rock art in southern Africa

title: A Church Built Around a King
text: In September 2026, University of Warsaw archaeologists suggested that a life-sized rock carving at Miseeda, near the Nile's Third Cataract, may show an ancient Kushite ruler. In the 7th century CE, Christians built a church right around it. The hill also bears a lion, an elephant, ships and crosses, and it may once have marked a border.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Carving May Represent Nubian King

source2.name: University of Warsaw, Faculty of Archaeology: Miseeda – church and surroundings, Mahas region, Sudan

title: A Swimming Mouse Lost for a Century
place: Yayu Coffee Forest Biosphere Reserve, southwestern Ethiopia
text: In November 2026, ecologist Mengistu Wale announced that a peanut-butter trap by a stream where villagers wash clothes had caught what appears to be an Ethiopian water mouse, unseen since its discovery in 1927; genetic tests are still confirming it. White spots behind its ears helped identify it. Its silky fur may keep it afloat, and its big hind feet may work like paddles.

source.name: National Geographic: Ethiopian water mouse rediscovered after nearly a century

title: Six Million Antelope Win World Heritage
place: Boma and Badingilo National Parks, South Sudan
text: In July 2026, UNESCO listed South Sudan's Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape under its emergency procedure. Covering about 11 million hectares where the Sudd wetlands meet savanna, it may host the largest remaining land mammal migration on Earth: an estimated six million white-eared kob, tiang and Mongalla gazelle each year. It went straight onto the endangered list too.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Decision 48 COM 8B.2, Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: New Inscribed Properties (48COM)

title: Hippo Hunters of Green Arabia
place: 'Uruq Aljelibah, Mundafan basin, Rub' al-Khali, Saudi Arabia
text: In November 2026, a Saudi and Australian team described a 125,000-year-old lakeshore in the Empty Quarter, now one of Earth's driest places. Among over 5,000 stone tools lay hippo, buffalo, camel and oryx bones. Some spear points were hafted with resin and fibre, and several carried traces of the arrow-poison tree, hinting that hunters may have used poison.

source.name: EurekAlert (Griffith University): 125,000-year-old Arabian lakeshore reveals poisoned hunting weapons

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Did Paleolithic Arabians Poison Their Weapons?

title: Beer on Credit Near Baghdad
text: In November 2026, Nicola Laneri's team reported a possible 3,800-year-old tavern at Tell Muhammad near the Tigris: a room with a curved mudbrick counter facing the street and a basin perhaps for brewing or baking. There, a cuneiform tablet records a loan of barley and beer, signed before two witnesses. The city also had a 16-foot-thick wall and reed-and-clay water pipes.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Possible Ancient Tavern Investigated Near Baghdad

title: The Northernmost Tropical Reef Is Honoured
place: Aqaba Marine Reserve, Gulf of Aqaba, Jordan
text: In July 2026, UNESCO added Jordan's Aqaba Marine Reserve to the World Heritage List. At the tip of the Red Sea, it is the world's northernmost tropical coral reef system, with heat-tolerant corals. It holds over 150 hard coral species, more than 500 kinds of fish and over 1,000 molluscs, many found only in the Red Sea.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Decision 48 COM 8B.5, Aqaba Marine Reserve

title: A Pigeon With a Bleeding Heart Returns
place: Puerto Galera rainforest, Mindoro Island, Philippines
text: In August 2026, a camera trap in the Puerto Galera rainforest on Mindoro photographed a Mindoro bleeding-heart, a critically endangered ground pigeon unconfirmed for about 20 years. The project was run by Philippine conservationists with Indigenous Iraya Mangyan communities. Once common in Mindoro's lowland forests, the bird faded as most were cleared last century; its last sure photos came from near Sablayan Prison in 2005.

source.name: Search for Lost Birds: Critically Endangered Mindoro Bleeding-heart Rediscovered After More Than 20 Years

source2.name: Mongabay: A lost Philippine pigeon reappears after 20 years, but its forest is disappearing

title: Lost Songs on Guadalcanal's Highest Ridge
text: In August 2026, after a landslide forced one retreat, birder Julien Mazenauer's group climbed back up a ridge on Mount Popomanaseu, the Solomon Islands' tallest peak. They heard and saw a pair of Guadalcanal honeyeaters, greyish birds with yellow neck patches, undocumented since 2015. On the same climb they photographed a rare moustached kingfisher at dawn, its first photo there since 2015.

source.name: Search for Lost Birds: Guadalcanal Honeyeater Rediscovered and Moustached Kingfisher Photographed

title: India's Longest Ancient Iron Spear
place: Thirumalapuram, near Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, India
text: In January 2026, Tamil Nadu archaeologists reported an eight-foot iron spear from a burial at Thirumalapuram, said to be the longest Iron Age iron implement yet found in India. A second, 6.5-foot spear lay crossed over it in an X beside an urn holding gold objects. The burial has reportedly been dated to about 5,300 years ago, and the spear may have been a battle weapon or a mark of high status.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Iron Age Spear Excavated in Southern India

title: The Buddha's First Sermon Site Listed
place: Sarnath, near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: In July 2026, UNESCO inscribed the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, where the Buddha is believed to have given his first sermon and met his first disciples. Its two parts, the Chaukhandi Stupa and Sarnath's ruins, hold stupas, temples and monasteries built over centuries. The site declined in the 12th century, was rediscovered in the 18th, and pilgrims returned in the 20th.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Decision 48 COM 8B.17, Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath

title: Underground Mosques by the Caspian
place: Shakpak-Ata and other sacred sites, Mangystau Peninsula, Kazakhstan
text: In July 2026, UNESCO listed five sacred complexes on Kazakhstan's dry Mangystau Peninsula, including Shopan-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Bekete-Ata. Carved into cliffs and caves in the 12th to 14th centuries, these underground mosques honour Sufi masters, blending Islam with older Turkic ancestor veneration. Pilgrims still come, and grave guardians called shirakshi still tend the tombs and welcome them.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Decision 48 COM 8B.20, Rock Mosques and Associated Sacred Sites of Mangystau

title: The Giant Bird That Wasn't
place: Akkurgan hill, northeastern Aral Sea region, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: A study published in 2011 named a pair of toothless jaws from Akkurgan, a lone hill north of the Aral Sea, as Samrukia, after the mythical Kazakh phoenix. It was hailed as a giant Cretaceous bird, albatross-sized if it flew and ostrich-sized if not. Other experts disagreed. A 2015 review concluded the jaw came from a pterosaur, a toothless azhdarchid living on a coastal floodplain beside the Turgai Sea.

source.name: ZooKeys (PMC): The paleoenvironments of azhdarchid pterosaurs localities in the Late Cretaceous of Kazakhstan

source2.name: Biology Letters (PMC): A gigantic bird from the Upper Cretaceous of Central Asia

title: An Ostrich-Footed Runner in Siberia
place: Shestakovo, Kiya River, Kemerovo Oblast, Russia
text: A long-legged predator about 2.5 metres long ran along the Kiya River in Western Siberia during the Early Cretaceous. Named Kiyacursor longipes in 2024, it is the first Early Cretaceous ceratosaur known from Asia, stretching that group's Asian record by about 40 million years. Its foot was built like an ostrich's. It shared its world with parrot-beaked Psittacosaurus and survivors of older Jurassic lineages.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC): The last ceratosaur of Asia, a new noasaurid from the Early Cretaceous Great Siberian Refugium

title: A Jurassic Lake Full of Insects
place: Galkino, Karatau Range, Turkistan Region, Kazakhstan
text: In 1921 a mining engineer named A.A. Aniskovich found fossil insects near the village of Galkino in southern Kazakhstan. The find caused a sensation, and researchers flocked to the Karatau hills. The rocks preserve a Late Jurassic lake so rich that more than 800 insect species have been described from it, including 22 kinds of woodwasp. Only China's Daohugou beds rival it for described Jurassic insects.

source.name: Insects (PMC): Anaxyelidae of Karatau, 100 Years After

title: The Oldest Salamander's Lakeside Home
text: A small salamander-like animal lived around a Triassic lake in what is now southwestern Kyrgyzstan. Its first fossil puzzled scientists for decades. In 2020 a second specimen from the same Madygen rock beds showed that Triassurus sixtelae was a stem-salamander, the oldest known. It pushed the rock record of salamanders back by at least 60 to 74 million years, yet kept features of far older amphibians.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): A Triassic stem-salamander from Kyrgyzstan and the origin of salamanders

title: Wildfires in an Arctic Forest
place: Lena River Delta, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: Cave formations from the Lena River Delta, high in Arctic Siberia, grew about 8.7 million years ago. Scientists studied pollen, carbon and chemical traces of burnt plants locked inside them. Today the delta is treeless tundra, but then a mixed forest grew here, able to keep wildfires going. Global temperatures were about 4.5°C warmer than now, with carbon dioxide levels similar to today's.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Late Miocene speleothems show significant warming, temperate vegetation, and wildfires in Arctic Siberia

title: Tiny Mammals Near the Cretaceous Arctic
place: Teete locality, Suntar District, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: Three kinds of small mammals lived in what is now western Yakutia in the Early Cretaceous. Their teeth and jaw fragments, from the Teete site, were described in 2018, including the newly named Khorotherium and Sangarotherium. The site then lay around 63 to 70 degrees north. Oddly, the mammals look Jurassic, which suggests that stable conditions let life in northern Asia change only slowly.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): A high-latitude fauna of mid-Mesozoic mammals from Yakutia, Russia

title: A Landslide Buries the First Geyser
place: Valley of the Geysers, Kronotsky Reserve, Kamchatka, Russia
text: On 3 June 2007 a landslide of mud, melting snow, trees and boulders roared through Kamchatka's Valley of the Geysers, one of the world's rare geyser fields. It left a scar about 1.5 kilometres long and dammed the Geyser River into a new warm lake. Among the geysers buried under up to 60 metres of debris was Pervenets, 'Firstborn', the first one found here in 1941.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Landslide Buries Valley of the Geysers

title: The Smelter City That Rivals Volcanoes
text: Norilsk, an Arctic city of about 175,000 people, sits on one of Earth's largest nickel, copper, platinum and palladium deposits. Its smelters make it the biggest human source of sulfur dioxide seen by satellites, almost double the next. Between 2005 and 2017 only one volcano, Ambrym in Vanuatu, released more of the gas by passive degassing. Forests around the city are browning and dying.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: A Manmade Volcano over Norilsk

title: Blue Clay Full of Red Garnets
place: Zarnitsa pipe, Daldyn River, Sakha Republic, Russia
text: In 1954 geologist Larisa Popugaeva and her assistant Fedor Belikov followed tiny red pyrope garnets up the Daldyn River in Yakutia, sampling streams until the grains vanished. On a rainy day, sitting on a stone warmed by their campfire, she suddenly jumped up with her lens: blue clay full of pyropes. It was Zarnitsa, the first kimberlite pipe found in Russia, opening Siberia's diamond fields.

source.name: Science First Hand: The Discovery of Zarnitsa, the Dawn of Siberian Diamonds

title: A Gold Pit You Can See From Space
place: Muruntau gold mine, Navoiy Region, Uzbekistan
text: In the Kyzylkum desert of central Uzbekistan, a giant round pit stands out in satellite images. The Muruntau gold deposit, among the largest on Earth, was found in 1958, and mining began in 1967. The pit is now 3.5 kilometres wide and 600 metres deep. Hundreds of trucks haul ore, and in 2021 the mine produced as much as 85,000 kilograms of gold.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Muruntau Gold Mine

title: A River Pulled Across the Desert
text: People dreamed of watering Turkmenistan's Garagum Desert from the Amu Darya as early as the 18th century. Under Soviet rule, building began in 1954 and lasted until 1988. The canal carries river water about 1,375 kilometres through the sands, one of the largest canals in the world, and opened a million hectares to cotton, wheat and melons. It still feeds the fields around Mary.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Hanhowuz Reservoir, Turkmenistan

source2.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Agriculture Fans Out in Turkmenistan

title: A Dam That Brought a Sea Back
place: Kok-Aral Dam, North Aral Sea, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: By 2000 the Aral Sea had shrunk to a quarter of its old size. In 2005 Kazakhstan finished the Kok-Aral Dam, an $85.8 million project backed by a World Bank loan, which cut the northern part off from the saltier south. The North Aral rose far faster than expected, mostly within a year, and by spring 2006 the stranded port of Aralsk was close to water again.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: North Aral Sea Recovery

title: The Day the Test Site Closed
place: Semipalatinsk Test Site, Abai Region, Kazakhstan
text: On 29 August 1991 the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site in Kazakhstan was closed. In 2009, at Kazakhstan's initiative, the UN General Assembly made that date the International Day against Nuclear Tests. The damage lingered: a recent study found that nearby villagers who received a median radiation dose of 864 millisieverts died of cancer about six times as often as a low-dose group in the late 1960s.

source.name: United Nations: International Day against Nuclear Tests

source2.name: IJERPH (PMC): Radiation Exposure and Cancer Mortality in Populations Living Around the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site

title: A River of Soil Swallows a Village
place: Kurbu-Tash, near Uzgen, Osh Region, Kyrgyzstan
