text: In April 2017 a hillside soaked by snowmelt and rain gave way near the village of Kurbu-Tash in southern Kyrgyzstan. Over the following weeks a slow river of fine soil crept down the valley and engulfed dozens of homes, moving 2.8 million cubic metres of earth. The Tien Shan foothills are full of loess, which turns unstable when wet, so landslides destroy homes here every year.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Landslide in Southern Kyrgyzstan

title: The Bear Glacier Lunges Forward
place: Medvezhiy Glacier, Vanch valley, Pamir Mountains, Tajikistan
text: Medvezhiy, the 'Bear' glacier in Tajikistan's Pamirs, normally creeps 200 to 400 metres a year. In early summer 2011 it slid 800 to 1,000 metres in weeks, its farthest jump in at least 22 years. Its icy snout blocked the Abdukagor River behind a wall up to 200 metres high. In 1963 and 1973 similar ice dams burst, releasing over 20 million cubic metres of water.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Medvezhiy Glacier Advances

title: Spy Satellites Find Lost Bactria
place: Pashkhurt Basin, near Sherabad, Surxondaryo Region, Uzbekistan
text: Southern Uzbekistan's Surkhandarya province was once the heart of Bactria, a kingdom that flourished along the Amu River from 600 BCE to 600 CE. Since 2008 a Charles University team led by Ladislav Stančo has hunted for its sites from above, mostly using declassified Corona spy satellite photos. They spotted dozens of new sites, some near oasis villages beneath the Kugitangtau Range.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Archaeology from Afar in Uzbekistan

title: A Turnip Left Cooking in Siberia
text: Tara, a garrison town founded in 1594, was one of the first Russian settlements in Siberia. Archaeologists led by Maria Chernaya of Tomsk State University have dug up its wooden walls and burned log houses. Toys, chess pieces, leather shoes and knitted stockings show frontier life was not so grim. The oddest find was a clay pot holding a charred turnip, probably about to be cooked.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Squeezing History from a Turnip

title: Gold Rush in the Ancient Graves
place: Upper Ob steppes around Tomsk, Tomsk Oblast, Russia
text: As Russians settled Siberia, rumours spread of gold in ancient nomad burial mounds. Commanders in Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk sent out bands of 'mound-diggers', 200 to 300 strong, who dug graves from spring to autumn and sold the loot in town markets. A dispatch to Tsar Alexei in 1670 reported Russians digging gold and silver from 'Tatar graves' in the Tobolsk district, and Moscow took notice.

source.name: Science First Hand: Nomads' Gold in the Siberian Collection of Peter I

title: Digging a Burial Mound in Midwinter
place: Left bank of the Yenisei near Abakan, Khakassia, Russia
text: On 5 and 6 January 1722, in the depths of the Siberian winter, the scholar D. G. Messerschmidt, on a 1719 to 1727 Siberian expedition, began excavating a burial mound on the left bank of the Yenisei near Abakan. He described the site in detail and sketched the grave's construction. This frozen dig is counted as the first scientific excavation in Siberia, the start of the region's archaeology.

source.name: Science First Hand: The First Researchers of the Altai Caves

title: Three Waves Strike Kamchatka
place: Pacific coast of southern Kamchatka, Russia
text: At about 3 a.m. on 17 October 1737 a great earthquake shook Kamchatka for about a quarter of an hour. The sea rose in waves; the third reached about 21 metres and swept away many native dwellings, and the water surged in and out for two days. Stepan Krasheninnikov of the Second Kamchatka Expedition reached Kamchatka two weeks later and wrote a report on the disaster.

source.name: Science First Hand: Megaquakes Pose Main Threat to Coastal Safety

title: Skulls in an Altai Cave
place: Inya River near Tigirek, Altai Krai, Russia
text: In July 1771 Academician P. S. Pallas explored every reachable karst cave along the middle Inya River in the Altai. The richest lay three kilometres below the mouth of the Tigirek. Inside, his party gathered bones of large mammals, six human skulls and wooden and bone tools. Published in 1786, it was the first scientific record of the Altai caves.

source.name: Science First Hand: The First Researchers of the Altai Caves

title: Tobolsk Silver in Forest Shrines
text: Petr Bryukhanov was a silversmith of the Tobolsk guild. His earliest known piece, a small plate stamped in 1793, shows a galloping deer beside a tree; others show bears, hunters and dogs. Several turned up not in palaces but in the home sanctuaries of Khanty and Mansi families, found by researchers between 1983 and 2013. Eighteen silver pieces from his workshop are known.

source.name: Science First Hand: Petr Bryukhanov of the Tobolsk Guild of Craftsmen

title: A Fur Coat Cut From the Ice
place: Katanda Kurgan, Katanda Valley, Ust-Koksa District, Altai Republic, Russia
text: In 1865 Academician V. V. Radlov dug into a large Pazyryk burial mound in the Katanda Valley, the first frozen Scythian-period grave studied in the Altai Mountains. His team lit fires to thaw the ground. Two skeletons crumbled to dust at a touch, but a block of ice cut from the log chamber held a sable-fur 'tailcoat' covered with silk and trimmed with small gold pieces.

source.name: Science First Hand: The Fellowship of the Ring, Burial Mounds of the Katanda Valley

title: Two Golden Teenagers of the Saka
text: About 2,700 years ago, two Saka teenagers were buried under a kurgan in a valley of eastern Kazakhstan's remote Tarbagatai Mountains. The young woman, about 16, had been robbed, but the young man, no older than 19, lay untouched. He wore a golden torc and held a gold and bronze dagger, with a gold-plated quiver of bronze-tipped arrows. Tiny gold deer heads with huge antlers decorated their clothes.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Iron Age Teenagers

title: Mapping the Unknown Khatanga Basin
place: Khatanga River basin, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
text: In 1905 the Russian Geographical Society sent geologist Innokentiy Tolmachev to one of Siberia's blank spaces, the Khatanga River basin by the Taimyr Peninsula. With topographer M. Ya. Kozhevnikov he drew the first map of this huge area and worked out its river system. The expedition's greatest prize was the discovery and description of the Anabar Plateau. Its success won him the 1909 Chukotka expedition.

source.name: Science First Hand: The Chukotka Expedition of I. P. Tolmachev

title: A Painted Room Kept Cool in Damascus
text: Between 1785 and 1788, craftsmen in Damascus painted and lacquered the wooden walls of a reception room with flower bouquets bursting from vases and gilded sprays. Damascus houses had flat roofs, and main halls rose through both floors, keeping rooms airy and cool in summer. The varnish probably came from a scented cypress resin. In 1883 a London museum bought the whole room for 500 pounds.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: The Damascus Room, doors, Syria, 1785-88

title: A Priest's Robe Woven Like a Carpet
text: Armenian Christians in Safavid Isfahan wove this priest's vestment as a carpet with a superfine silk pile. Worn at Mass, it showed the Crucifixion on the priest's back, while Mary and the Archangel Gabriel faced each other across his chest. The Crucifixion copied a Western picture, perhaps from a printed Armenian Bible. Centuries later, an owner began cutting it up to sell as carpet samples.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Armenian church vestment (The Isfahan Cope)

title: The Shah Who Painted Himself Young
text: Fath 'Ali Shah, second ruler of Iran's Qajar dynasty, revived oil painting with a purpose. His uncle, the dynasty's founder, had been castrated as a child by enemies, so the new shah had himself painted slim-waisted, youthful and with a magnificent beard. These life-size portraits went abroad as diplomatic gifts or were built into palace walls, flanked by paintings of sons, courtiers and acrobatic dancers.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Portrait of Fath 'Ali Shah

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Female Tumbler

title: Iznik Potters Find a Brilliant Red
text: When the Süleymaniye mosque rose in Istanbul between 1550 and 1557, the Ottoman court turned again to the potters of Iznik. They made their first tiles for it and added a dazzling new colour: a bright red under the glaze, made from a slip of special clay. Soon dishes and bottles bloomed with big tulips, roses and carnations in red, green and blue.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Bottle, Iznik, 1575-1580

title: An Archangel on an Armenian Dish
text: In 1718, Armenian potters in Ottoman Kütahya painted a dish of the Archangel Michael holding a sword and a dead man's soul. Michael's blouse folds into a hidden face with ears and a moustache. The patron, a cleric named Abraham, later became head of the whole Armenian church. Three years earlier, a French merchant had shipped home a dozen Kütahya coffee cups.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Dish with the Archangel Michael, Kütahya, 1718

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Coffee pot, Kütahya, about 1725

title: Honduran Foragers Grow Bigger Avocados
place: El Gigante rockshelter, Estanzuela River, western Honduras
text: High on a volcanic plateau in western Honduras, a huge dry rockshelter 42 metres wide kept avocado leftovers for 11,000 years, including more than 1,600 bits of rind. Measuring them, researchers found people were already favouring bigger fruit with thicker skins by about 7,400 years ago. Selection continued for millennia, and the seeds resemble today's Guatemalan avocado variety, a highland fruit shaped by human hands.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Early evidence of avocado domestication from El Gigante Rockshelter, Honduras

title: A Lost Family Line in the Andes
text: Around 6,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers buried their dead at Checua on Colombia's high Bogotá plateau. Ancient DNA from seven of them revealed a surprise: a previously unknown branch of the very first peoples to spread across South America. Yet these foragers left no genetic trace in later South Americans. By 2,000 years ago, newcomers with Central American ancestry had replaced them on the plateau.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): A 6000-year-long genomic transect from the Bogotá Altiplano

title: A Giant Wave Empties the Desert Coast
place: Zapatero shell midden, near Taltal, Antofagasta, Chile
text: About 3,800 years ago, a fault roughly 1,000 kilometres long ruptured off northern Chile, probably a magnitude 9.5 quake. Its tsunami tore into fishing camps on the Atacama coast. At Zapatero, waves toppled stone houses on a shell midden, and sand still fills the wreckage. Afterwards, sites in the Taltal area dropped by about 65 percent, and a cemetery of sea-fishing people soon appeared at an oasis 40 kilometres inland.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Did a 3800-year-old Mw ~9.5 earthquake trigger major social disruption in the Atacama Desert?

title: Patagonia's Oldest Dated Paintings
text: In a desert cave in northern Patagonia, people began painting about 8,200 years ago and kept adding images for over 3,000 years, roughly 130 generations. Most are red hematite dots, lines, grids and crosses, with a few humans, guanacos and rheas. Dating the pigments made them South America's oldest directly dated paintings. They began during a harsh dry spell, perhaps as a way to share knowledge.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Earliest directly dated rock art from Patagonia

title: Snuff Tubes in Chavín's Secret Tunnel
place: Gallery 3, Chavín de Huántar, Áncash, Peru
text: Deep inside Chavín de Huántar, Peru's great temple, archaeologists opened a sealed underground gallery about seven metres long. It held bone tubes like those used for sniffing plants elsewhere in the Andes. Chemical tests on six found DMT, bufotenine and nicotine, traces of vilca seeds and wild tobacco. It is the first direct proof that rituals in Chavín's hidden rooms involved mind-altering plants.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Pre-Hispanic ritual use of psychoactive plants at Chavín de Huántar, Peru

title: Zigzag Fish Traps in a Belize Swamp
place: Crooked Tree Wildlife Sanctuary, Belize District, Belize
text: Drones flying over Belize's largest inland wetland in the dry season spotted 167 zigzag channels, about 108 kilometres in total, many paired with ponds. Dug by hunter-gatherer-fishers and later used by their Maya descendants, they steered fish during yearly floods. Most radiocarbon dates fall before 1200 BCE, making this the earliest large fish-trapping system known in Mesoamerica. Today the channels are only 20 centimetres deep.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Late Archaic large-scale fisheries in the wetlands of the pre-Columbian Maya Lowlands

title: Puerto Rico's Oldest Graves
place: Ortiz site, Cabo Rojo, Puerto Rico
text: Fewer than twenty burials survive from Puerto Rico's first islanders, so five skeletons from the Ortiz site in Cabo Rojo matter a lot. Radiocarbon dating made them the island's oldest known graves, spread over more than 1,000 years. Each person was buried with a pendant, plus shell, stone tools, coral and ochre. Their teeth were worn almost to the roots, from tough food or using teeth as tools.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Reconsidering the lives of the earliest Puerto Ricans: the Ortiz site

title: A Ring of Standing Stones in Peru
text: Around 2750 BCE, people in Peru's northern highlands raised a circular plaza 18 metres across, walled with huge stones set upright and free-standing. Charcoal under the walls gave the date. It is one of the earliest megalithic ceremonial monuments in the Americas, dating between Stonehenge (about 2900 BCE) and Giza's pyramids (about 2650 BCE). No other Andean circular plaza is known to be built this way.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): A monumental stone plaza at 4750 B.P. in the Cajamarca Valley of Peru

title: Painters Stranded by War in Muscat
text: In June 1793, the painter Thomas Daniell and his nephew William sailed from Bombay to Muscat, planning to head home to England. In Muscat they learned that Britain and France were at war, so they turned back to India. They sketched the harbour, guarded by two 16th-century Portuguese forts. Few European artists ever reached Muscat, and William exhibited his view nearly forty years later.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: East View of The Forts Jellali & Merani, Muscat, by William Daniell

title: The Shah's Doctor and the Fever Tick
text: Joseph Tholozan, a French doctor born in the Indian Ocean, came to Tehran in 1858 as Naser al-Din Shah's personal physician and stayed 38 years. Puzzled by a fever that kept returning in waves, he picked ticks off his patients and mailed them to colleagues in France. In 1882 entomologists named the culprit after him: Ornithodoros tholozani, still the main carrier of the disease in Iran.

source.name: Archives of Iranian Medicine (PMC): Discovery of Ornithodoros tholozani, the main vector of Iranian tick-borne relapsing fever

title: A Head Count That Noted Beards
text: In 1839, Ottoman officials listed every male in the silk city of Bursa, boys included, to plan army recruitment and taxes. For each they wrote name, age and job, plus height (short, medium or tall), facial hair, and any disability. Women were left out until the empire's first modern census in 1881. Historians have now typed the whole register into a database, household by household.

source.name: Scientific Data (PMC): A nineteenth-century urban Ottoman population micro dataset from the 1840s Bursa registers

title: Gertrude Bell Photographs Hatra
text: In 1911, on her third great journey across the Middle East, 43-year-old Gertrude Bell reached the desert ruins of Hatra in Ottoman Iraq. An amateur archaeologist, she took a set of 42 photographs there. In one, a moustached Turkish soldier with field glasses leans against a ruined Parthian temple. Years later, Bell would advise British officials, including Winston Churchill, on creating modern Iraq.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Photograph by Gertrude Bell of a ruined temple at Hatra, Iraq, 1911

title: Mother-of-Pearl Souvenirs for Pilgrims
text: Christian pilgrims to Jerusalem went home with glittering souvenirs. Craftsmen, probably in Jerusalem, made little wooden shrines inlaid with mother-of-pearl, some shaped as sections of model churches copying the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, with cross-shaped spaces inside for relics. Later, carvers, probably including Franciscan friars, cut Nativity scenes into shells to make baptismal spoons. One of the largest models, the Pearson Model, is now in Paris.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Miniature shrine, possibly Jerusalem, 17th century

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Baptismal spoon, The Nativity, Jerusalem, early 19th century

title: Yemen's Jewish Silversmiths
text: In 19th-century Yemen, Jewish goldsmiths made most of the country's silver jewellery, famed for delicate filigree. Muslim and Jewish women alike wore their necklaces, such as the many-stranded lazem with a tiny amulet case. Its knobbly beads, built from little pyramids of silver granules soldered together, are found nowhere else. The craft continued until the smiths left for Israel in the 1950s.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Multi-strand necklace (lazem), Yemen, 1850-1900

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Necklace (douggeh) of silver filigree beads, Yemen, 1850-1900

title: Two Englishmen Measure Palmyra's Ruins
text: In 1751 two English antiquaries, Robert Wood and James Dawkins, reached the ruined Roman-era city of Palmyra in the Syrian desert. Their 1753 book, The Ruins of Palmyra, was packed with careful plans and architectural details. A later painting showed them arriving in Roman togas. In 1859 the painter Carl Haag swore he would walk there in Bedouin sandals if he had to, and did reach it.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Dawkins and Wood discovering Palmyra, engraving, 1773

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: The Triumphal Arch, Palmyra, by Carl Haag, 1859

title: The First Camera at the Hajj
text: Muhammad Sadiq Bey, an Egyptian army engineer and treasurer of Egypt's Hajj caravan, carried a glass-plate camera to the holy cities. In 1880 and 1881 he photographed the Great Mosque of Mecca, Medina, and pilgrims camped at Mina. His album of 12 views, including four panoramas, won a gold medal at a geography congress in Venice in 1881. A single unmounted print sold for 40 francs.

source.name: Khalili Collections: Panorama of the Meccan Sanctuary and its environs, Muhammad Sadiq Bey

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Encampment of pilgrims at Mina, by Sadic Bey, 1880

title: A Brass Star Map from Isfahan
text: In 1667 an Isfahan craftsman named Khalil Muhammad made this brass astrolabe, and an artist from Yazd decorated it. Its lace-like top disc is a rotating star map with pointers marking the stars. Owners could find the five daily prayer times or the direction of Mecca, or cast horoscopes. Many survive from this era, when astrolabe-making revived and astrology was popular at court.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Astrolabe, Isfahan, dated 1667

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Astrolabe, Isfahan, 1715

title: An Envoy Sails Home to Persia
text: On 1 March 1811, a British mission to the Shah dropped anchor at Bushehr, Persia's Gulf port, almost eight months after leaving England. With them came Mirza Abul Hassan Khan, Persia's ambassador, returning from London. While the party waited in port until 25 March before setting out for Tehran, Colonel Joseph D'Arcy sketched how water was raised from a well to irrigate the fields.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Method of Raising Water for Irrigation, al-Bushire, by Joseph D'Arcy, 1811

title: The Only Maya City Built on a Grid
place: Nixtun-Ch'ich', Lake Petén Itzá, Petén, Guatemala
text: On a peninsula jutting into Lake Petén Itzá, the largest lake in the Maya lowlands, early Maya laid out a city on a grid before 500 BCE. Streets running east to west cross avenues at near-right angles, a plan known nowhere else in the Maya world. Archaeologist Prudence Rice thinks the blocks may echo the scales of a mythical crocodile from a creation story.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The City at the Beginning of the World

title: Pots from an Amazon Shell Heap
place: Taperinha shell midden, near Santarém, Pará, Brazil
text: Near Santarém on the Amazon, generations of people left a heap of shells more than six metres deep at Taperinha. Its deepest layers held pottery about 7,000 years old, among the earliest in the Americas, made by people who lived largely on fish and shellfish. Archaeologist Anna Roosevelt first estimated the mound's age from old shells in museum drawers before she dug it.

source.name: Pesquisa FAPESP: Anna Curtenius Roosevelt, the rainforest archaeologist

title: The First Thing Ever Cast From Wax
text: A copper charm no wider than a coin, shaped like a six-spoked wheel, turned up at Mehrgarh in 1985. Its spokes cross in ways no open mould could make, so its maker first modelled it from wax rods, packed clay around it, melted the wax out and poured in copper. About 6,000 years old, it is the oldest known lost-wax casting, made of unusually pure, probably native, copper.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): High spatial dynamics-photoluminescence imaging reveals the metallurgy of the earliest lost-wax cast object

title: Pigs That Rode Across the Indus
text: Indus streets bear cart ruts, and clay toy carts are common, but did animals travel far? Scientists read strontium in the tooth enamel of cattle, buffalo, sheep and pigs from thirteen sites. Most beasts grew up near where they died. The surprise was pigs: several at Harappa, and one at Rakhigarhi, came from distant regions, probably shipped alive as cargo rather than walking.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Animal movement on the hoof and on the cart and its implications for understanding exchange within the Indus Civilisation

title: Dining Safely on a Poisonous Fish
place: Bubog and Bilat sites, Ilin Island and Mindoro, Occidental Mindoro, Philippines
text: Porcupinefish puff up into spiky balls, and parts of them carry a deadly toxin. Yet foragers on Ilin Island and Mindoro kept catching them from about 13,000 years ago. Charred spines and jaws show the fish were carried whole back to cave and rock-shelter camps, not cleaned at the shore. Eating them again and again means people knew how to separate the poison from the edible flesh.

source.name: Animals (PMC): The Exploitation of Toxic Fish from the Terminal Pleistocene in Maritime Southeast Asia: A Case Study from the Mindoro Archaeological Sites, Philippines

title: Missing Teeth in a Laotian Rock Shelter
place: Tam Hang rock shelter, Pa Hang mountain, Houaphanh Province, Laos
text: In 1934 geologist Jacques Fromaget dug at Tam Hang, high in the hills of northern Laos, and found seventeen human skulls. Decades later a rib was radiocarbon dated to about 15,700 years ago. Six of the people had teeth deliberately removed, a custom called tooth ablation, making them among the oldest known examples anywhere in eastern Asia. Fromaget's tools, sadly, have been lost.

source.name: Comptes Rendus Palevol (MNHN): The place of Tam Hang in Southeast Asian human evolution

title: An African Grain on the Indus
place: Bhando Qubo, near Rato Dero, Larkana, Sindh, Pakistan
text: Pearl millet was first tamed in West Africa's Sahel. Yet charred grains dug up in 2019 at Bhando Qubo, a Harappan town in Sindh, were radiocarbon dated to about 2578 to 2356 BCE. They are as old as the earliest domesticated pearl millet known in Africa itself, and the oldest directly dated grains anywhere, showing the crop crossed to South Asia five centuries earlier than thought.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): New evidence reveals dispersal of pearl millet from West Africa to South Asia by 2500 BCE

title: Malaria's Mark on Vietnam's Foragers
place: Con Co Ngua, Thanh Hoa Province, Vietnam
text: Thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder that also guards against malaria, and today it is very common in Southeast Asia. Scientists long assumed farming drove the rise of malaria there. But skeletons from Con Co Ngua, a hunter-gatherer cemetery in northern Vietnam used about 6,800 to 6,200 years ago, show signs of thalassemia, so it took hold before farming even arrived.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Forager and farmer evolutionary adaptations to malaria evidenced by 7000 years of thalassemia in Southeast Asia

source2.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Skeletal trauma in northern Vietnam during the hunter-gatherer Da But period

title: Toolstones Carried Through the Karst
place: Hang Trong cave, Tràng An, Ninh Bình Province, Vietnam
text: Most stone tools in the caves of Tràng An were knapped from local limestone. Yet about one in five at Hang Trong, in layers dated between roughly 38,000 and 18,000 years ago, are igneous rock, much of it andesite. None occurs among Tràng An's limestone towers: the nearest known source lies about 35 kilometres away, so Ice Age foragers carried their toolstone a long way.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Geochemical fingerprinting of Pleistocene stone tools from the Tràng An Landscape Complex, Ninh Bình Province, Vietnam

title: First Footprints on the Batanes Islands
place: Torongan Cave, east coast of Itbayat, Batanes, Philippines
text: The Batanes Islands sit in the strait between Taiwan and Luzon. Their oldest known archaeological finds come from Torongan Cave on Itbayat, whose mouth opens right at sea level, perhaps an early landing place. Inside, excavators counted nearly 300 red-slipped pottery sherds, left by settlers who lived there between about 4,000 and 3,000 years ago.

source.name: ANU Press, Bellwood, Dizon and Mijares: Archaeological Excavations on Itbayat and Siayan Islands

title: A Burial From Sundaland's Ice Age
place: Moh Khiew Cave, Krabi Province, Thailand
text: Human skeletons from Ice Age Southeast Asia are rare, so a well-preserved burial in Moh Khiew Cave in southern Thailand was a prize. Charcoal from the grave gave a radiocarbon age of about 25,800 years, when the region was part of the low-sea-level landmass called Sundaland. Skull and tooth measurements most resemble Ice Age Australians from Coobool Creek.

source.name: Homo (Europe PMC abstract): A morphometric analysis of the Late Pleistocene human skeleton from the Moh Khiew Cave in Thailand

title: Snail Shell Heaps in a Glacial Cave
place: Diêm Cave, Cúc Phương National Park, Ninh Bình, Vietnam
text: During the coldest part of the last Ice Age, foragers in the limestone hills around the Hanoi Basin piled up heaps of land-snail shells inside Diêm Cave. The oldest layer is about 23,000 years old. The middens held some 2,200 stone tools, a bone awl and a decorated ochre object, and one layer held a woman buried in a crouched position.

source.name: Philosophical Transactions B (PMC): Late Pleistocene shell midden microstratigraphy in the uplands of North Vietnam

title: Island Foragers Turn Toward the Forest
place: Asitau Kuru and Matja Kuru caves, Lautém, Timor-Leste
text: The first people on Timor and nearby Alor leaned heavily on the sea; one individual from about 42,000 to 39,000 years ago ate plenty of coastal food. Carbon and oxygen in tooth enamel show a change from about 20,000 years ago, as forests spread across island Southeast Asia: people relied more on inland resources, though some still feasted on seafood.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Isotopic evidence for initial coastal colonization and subsequent diversification in the human occupation of Wallacea

title: A Stalagmite Records Vietnam's Rains Returning
place: Hoa Huong cave, Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park, Quảng Bình, Vietnam
text: A broken stalagmite 3.7 metres long, from Hoa Huong cave, holds 41,000 years of central Vietnam's weather. It shows a long dry spell through the Ice Age's peak, when low seas exposed land in the Gulf of Tonkin and starved the autumn monsoon of moisture. About 14,000 years ago, as rising water flooded that land, the region abruptly turned wet.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Glacial changes in sea level modulated millennial-scale variability of Southeast Asian autumn monsoon rainfall

title: Myanmar's Caves Get Older
place: Badahlin (Padah-lin) Cave, Ywangan, Shan State, Myanmar
text: Old Stone Age tools had been dug from Badahlin and Gu Myaung caves in Myanmar, but how old were they? In 2019 a team produced the country's first luminescence dates, measuring the light trapped in single feldspar grains from the sediment. People were living at Badahlin by about 30,000 years ago and at Gu Myaung by about 25,000, far older than Gu Myaung's radiocarbon dates suggested.

source.name: University of Washington Anthropology: pIRIR and IR-RF dating of archaeological deposits at Badahlin and Gu Myaung Caves (Quaternary Geochronology)

title: When Kathmandu Lay Under a Lake
text: Nepal's capital stands on the bed of a vanished lake. Muddy lake sediments buried under the slopes at the edge of the Kathmandu basin date to about 30,000 years ago, when the water rose to some 1,400 to 1,440 metres and covered almost the whole valley. Soon afterwards the Bagmati River began draining it, the only outlet researchers could find.

source.name: Himalayan Journal of Sciences (NepJOL): Expansion of an ancient lake in the Kathmandu basin of Nepal during the Late Pleistocene

title: Ice Age Rain Hidden Under the Sundarbans
place: Pusur River, Khulna to the Sundarbans, Bangladesh
text: Coastal Bangladesh is short of fresh water, yet electrical soundings along the Pusur River found huge fresh aquifers reaching 800 metres deep. They probably filled during the last Ice Age, when sea level was up to 120 metres lower and the Bengal shoreline lay 150 to 200 kilometres offshore. Rising seas later sealed them under a stiff ancient clay soil.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Buried deep freshwater reserves beneath salinity-stressed coastal Bangladesh

title: A Crowded Valley at the Ice Age's End
place: Belan Valley, Prayagraj District, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: As the last Ice Age ended, hunters, fishers and foragers were well established on India's low plains. Surveys have counted perhaps more than 100 sites of this age in the Belan Valley and about 100 in the Son Valley, and 204 Mesolithic sites in the middle Ganges region, 177 of them in Pratapgarh district alone, though older dating methods call for caution.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Early to Mid-Holocene land use transitions in South Asia: A new archaeological synthesis

title: Back to the Cave After 20,000 Years
place: Fa-Hien Lena Cave, Yatagampitiya, Kalutara District, Sri Lanka
text: Fa-Hien Lena's layers jump a 20,000-year gap. When people returned to this big rainforest cave about 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, they left its densest pile of debris: charcoal, burned bone and snail shell, and about 2,700 stone artefacts. Their quartz-knapping methods matched those of the cave's first users, and one core was even smeared with red ochre.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Microliths in the South Asian rainforest ~45-4 ka: New insights from Fa-Hien Lena Cave, Sri Lanka

title: X-Raying a Bean's Path to the Farm
text: Wild horsegram, a hardy Indian bean, has a thick, hard seed coat that keeps most seeds from sprouting. Scientists scanned charred seeds from Southern Neolithic villages with a synchrotron, without cutting them. Seeds from Piklihal, about 1900 to 1600 BCE, still had thick or intermediate coats, and the coats thinned between 2000 and 1200 BCE as cultivation went on.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Seed coat thinning during horsegram domestication documented through synchrotron tomography of archaeological seeds

title: Wild or Tame? Lahuradewa's Early Rice
place: Lahuradewa, Sant Kabir Nagar District, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: People were living at Lahuradewa on the Ganges plain, at least seasonally, by the 7th millennium BCE, and rice turns up in their earliest layers. Excavators argued some grains were already domesticated. Critics counter that the grains look closer to wild or unripe rice, that early dates came from bulk charcoal, and that every animal bone there is wild. Was this farming or gathering?

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Early to Mid-Holocene land use transitions in South Asia: A new archaeological synthesis

title: Hunters Who Stayed Put on the Ganges
place: Damdama, Pratapgarh District, Uttar Pradesh, India
text: Foragers are usually pictured on the move, but on the Ganges plain they settled down beside lakes and streams at sites such as Damdama, Mahadaha and Sarai Nahar Rai. They built huts with plastered floors, used heavy grinding stones, hunted in more than one season and buried their dead again and again. Worn teeth show a coarse, wild diet.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Early to Mid-Holocene land use transitions in South Asia: A new archaeological synthesis

title: When Inamgaon's Farms Turned Salty
place: Inamgaon, Shirur, Pune District, Maharashtra, India
text: Inamgaon, a Chalcolithic village on the Deccan, mixed farming with herding, hunting, fishing and foraging from about 1600 BCE. Over time, unsustainable farming and salty soils wore the land down, and eventually people shifted away from agriculture. Their skeletons show the cost of that change, which fell hardest on babies.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Climate change, human health, and resilience in the Holocene

source2.name: Data in Brief (PMC): Human tooth enamel stable isotope dataset from chalcolithic Inamgaon (India)

title: Village Potters of the Indus Age
place: Dabli-vas Chugta, Hanumangarh District, Rajasthan, India
text: Most Indus people probably lived in villages, not cities. At small sites like Dabli-vas Chugta, near Kalibangan, potters made city-style dish-on-stands and perforated jars from local clays. Many coiled pots by hand and only finished the rims on the wheel, a skill needing long training, and here they painted floral designs rarely seen on Indus pottery of that time.

source.name: World Archaeology (PMC): 'We are inheritors of a rural civilisation': rural complexity and the ceramic economy in the Indus Civilisation

title: Whose Ancestors Lived at Ban Chiang?
place: Ban Chiang, Udon Thani Province, Thailand
text: Ancient DNA from people buried at Ban Chiang, between about 3,500 and 2,400 years ago, was compared with genomes from across Asia. They share the most ancestry with today's Austroasiatic speakers, such as the Mlabri and Htin of Thailand, as do Neolithic villagers at Mán Bạc in Vietnam, suggesting farmers related to these groups spread widely across mainland Southeast Asia.

source.name: Science (PMC): Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory

title: The Great Cemetery in Niah's West Mouth
place: West Mouth, Niah Great Cave, Sarawak, Malaysia
text: For more than a thousand years, from about 1500 to 200 BCE, the mouth of Niah's Great Cave in Borneo served as a burial ground, the largest Neolithic cemetery in Southeast Asia, with 170 burials. Around 1000 BCE, mourners switched from burying whole bodies to reburying bones, a custom that later grew into cremation, perhaps as wealth allowed grander funerals.

source.name: Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society (Cambridge Core): The West Mouth Neolithic Cemetery, Niah Cave, Sarawak

title: Did Pottery Sail South From Taiwan?
text: The classic story says pottery-making farmers sailed from Taiwan to Luzon, then spread south. A statistical study of radiocarbon dates from 20 sites put Luzon's first pottery, including red-slipped, stamped and dentate wares at the Nagsabaran shell midden, between about 5,430 and 4,290 years ago. That is about the same time as western Borneo, hinting at movements from several directions.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Radiocarbon chronologies for initial pottery in Island Southeast Asia support multi-directional Neolithic dispersal

title: A Handful of Flakes, 930,000 Years Old
place: Kuldara, Khovaling district, Khatlon Region, Tajikistan
text: Near the bottom of a towering stack of wind-blown dust at Kuldara, about 1,300 metres up in southern Tajikistan, lie a few simple stone flakes. Two ancient soils holding them date to roughly 915,000 and 970,000 years ago, giving a modelled age near 930,000 years. That makes them the earliest dated sign of human relatives anywhere in Central Asia, a possible corridor between the Near East and East Asia.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Absolute chronology of the Early Palaeolithic Karatau Culture in Central Asia

title: A Stalagmite Logs Forty-Year Droughts
place: Amir Timur Cave, Zaravshan Mountains, south of Samarkand, Uzbekistan
text: A stalagmite from Amir Timur Cave in Uzbekistan's Zaravshan mountains grew layer by layer around 391,000 years ago. By counting its yearly bands across about 780 years and reading their chemistry, scientists found three dry spells, each lasting about 40 years, separated by wetter times. In that era, moisture carried inland by westerly winds may have made today's arid Central Asian plains intermittently livable for early humans.

source.name: PMC: Paleolithic occupation of arid Central Asia in the Middle Pleistocene

title: Hyenas and Hunters Took Turns
place: Bukhtarma Cave, southern Altai foothills, East Kazakhstan, Kazakhstan
text: In a limestone cave above Kazakhstan's Bukhtarma River, a cut mark on a large animal bone shows people were there about 47,000 years ago. For thousands of years, carnivores such as cave hyenas and humans used the cave in turns. Hunters butchered horses, bison, red deer and brown bears, and the bones include camel, rhino and mammoth. A reservoir flooded the cave in 1958, so no one can dig again.

source.name: PMC: A Newly Dated Late Pleistocene and Holocene Archaeological Assemblage from Bukhtarma Cave in the Southern Altai Piedmont, East Kazakhstan

title: A Camp at Asia's Crossroads
place: Ushbulak, Shilikty Valley, East Kazakhstan, Kazakhstan
text: Found in 2016 by a Russian-Kazakh team, Ushbulak sits in the Shilikty Valley, where routes from southwestern Central Asia, southern Siberia and northern China meet. One of its deepest layers gave radiocarbon ages of about 41,000 and 36,000 years and holds retouched blades, endscrapers, beveled points and stemmed tools. They closely match toolkits from the Altai's Kara-Bom and Denisova Cave and from Mongolia and northern China, hinting ideas travelled widely.

source.name: Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia: Ushbulak, a new stratified Upper Paleolithic site in northeastern Kazakhstan

title: Spruce Forests Welcome Newcomers to Baikal
place: Posolskoe Bank, southern Lake Baikal, Buryatia, Russia
text: Pollen drilled from the bed of southern Lake Baikal shows sudden bursts of forest in a mostly treeless, wormwood-covered land. The strongest came around 45,000 years ago, when spruce spread and summers were only about 3°C cooler than today. That is just when modern humans with new blade tools appear at sites like Kamenka and Makarovo-4, perhaps drawn by the mix of forest and steppe.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Climate amelioration, abrupt vegetation recovery, and the dispersal of Homo sapiens in Baikal Siberia

title: Ivory Children in Hooded Fur Suits
place: Mal'ta, Belaya River, Irkutsk Oblast, Russia
text: Mammoth hunters at Mal'ta, near Lake Baikal, carved dozens of little human figures from ivory as the Ice Age's coldest phase began. Eight from Mal'ta and nearby Buret' show young children and teenagers, just 2 to 5 centimetres tall, and the smallest wear fur coveralls. A hooded teenage girl still bears traces of red ochre. Flat-based animals and hanging birds may have been toys or cradle charms.

source.name: PMC: The Siberian Paleolithic site of Mal'ta: a unique source for the study of childhood archaeology

title: Beetles Return After an Altai Megaflood
place: Kebezen, Turachak stream near the Biya River, Altai Republic, Russia
text: Mud near the Altai village of Kebezen piled up astonishingly fast, about a centimetre a year, around 20,000 years ago, probably after a megaflood. Inside it, scientists found 105 kinds of beetles. Spruce bark beetles, alpine-meadow and waterside species reveal a cold, humid world of spruce forest. Some of those species now live far to the east, in Transbaikalia or the Russian Far East.

source.name: PMC: Subfossil Insects of the Kebezen Site (Altai Mountains): New Data on the Last Deglaciation Environment

title: Tiny Blades for a Colder Mongolia
text: On a low pass above a river that feeds Lake Baikal, the Mongolian site of Tolbor-17 holds two toolkits. The older, about 33,000 to 34,000 years old, has blades and bladelets. Above it, in loess that nearby sites date to after about 29,000 years ago, come microblades: tiny, standard blades struck from small, easily carried cores. They suited hunters who had to roam farther as the Ice Age cold deepened.

source.name: PMC: Analyzing blank cutting edge efficiency associated with the adoption of microblade technology: A case study from Tolbor-17, Mongolia

title: Japan's 'Tigers' Were Cave Lions
text: For decades, big cat bones from Ice Age Japan were labelled tigers. A 2026 study pulled ancient DNA and proteins from them and found cave lions instead. The best-preserved specimen, from Mine in Yamaguchi, is about 35,000 years old, and its protein carries a lion-type amino acid where tigers differ. Lions likely walked in over a northern land bridge and reached far southwest Honshu.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): The Japanese Archipelago sheltered cave lions, not tigers, during the Late Pleistocene

title: The Oldest Planned Sea Voyage?
text: About 38,000 years ago, people carried shiny volcanic glass from Kozushima, a small island roughly 38 kilometres off Honshu even when sea levels were low, back to Honshu. Researchers call this obsidian the world's oldest secure evidence of a planned sea voyage. Around the same time, people also crossed from Korea to Kyushu, and by 30,000 years ago they had settled most of the Ryukyu chain.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Palaeolithic seafaring in East Asia: testing the bamboo raft hypothesis

source2.name: Current Anthropology (Hokkaido University repository): On the Pleistocene Population History in the Japanese Archipelago (Nakazawa 2017)

title: A Soldier's Find Upends a Theory
place: Jeongok-ri, Hantan River, Yeoncheon, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea
text: In 1978 Greg Bowen, an American soldier, picked up stone tools near Korea's Hantan River and passed them to Seoul National University. They turned out to be Acheulean-style hand axes, two-sided tools that Harvard's Hallam Movius had argued were never made east of India. Excavated more than 17 times since, the Jeongok-ri site is at least 350,000 years old, resting on basalt dated near 500,000.

source.name: Jeongok Prehistory Museum (Google Arts & Culture): Jeongok-ri Paleolithic site

title: A Riverside Workshop for Spear Tips
place: Hajin-ri (Suyanggae Locality VI), Danyang, North Chungcheong, South Korea
text: Excavators at Hajin-ri in central Korea collected more than 40,000 stone artefacts, mostly of fine siliceous shale. The two deepest levels, dated to about 43,000 to 40,000 years ago, hold nearly 3,000 slim blades and many tanged points, blades shaped with a narrow stem at the base. The lowest level alone yielded 61 points, two-thirds unbroken, marking Korea's early switch to new blade-making ways.

source.name: Radiocarbon (Cambridge): The Early Upper Paleolithic of Korea: A chronological review

title: A Denisovan Jaw in a Fishing Net
place: Penghu Channel, between Penghu and Taiwan
text: Fishermen trawling the Penghu Channel off Taiwan, 60 to 120 metres down, hauled up a human jaw with big teeth, along with bones of buffalo, tigers and straight-tusked elephants. In 2025 proteins from its teeth and bone showed he was a male Denisovan. He probably lived when ice-age seas fell and dry land joined Taiwan to the mainland, either 10,000 to 70,000 or 130,000 to 190,000 years ago.

source.name: Natural History Museum, London: Denisovan jawbone helps reveal appearance of ancient human species

source2.name: EurekAlert: A male Denisovan mandible from Pleistocene Taiwan

title: Stone Tips Fixed to Handles
text: At Xigou, beside the Laoguanhe River in central China, excavators recovered 2,601 stone artefacts from layers dated between about 160,000 and 72,000 years ago. Twenty-two tools have tangs, shoulders or blunted backs. Wear on two borers shows they were set into handles, one used to drill reed or wood. The team argues these are East Asia's earliest known composite tools, though their makers remain unknown.

source.name: PMC: Technological innovations and hafted technology in central China ~160,000-72,000 years ago

title: The First Beads Made of Fired Clay
text: In a sealed gully at Nanzhuangtou in northern China lay two small tubes of fired clay about 10,000 years old. Each was moulded around a plant stem, which left marks inside one, then baked at about 500 to 600°C. One end is shorter than the other, which may have helped the bead hang straight. They are among the oldest known ornaments made from a human-made material.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): The earliest known ceramic beads as adornment from Nanzhuangtou site in North China 10,000 years ago

title: Water Fleas Remember Ice Age Floods
place: Lake Yunlong Tianchi, Yunlong County, western Yunnan, China
text: Mud from a small mountain lake in western Yunnan records seven mega-floods over 30,000 years. Scientists spotted them through sudden jumps in tiny open-water crustaceans called water fleas, along with surges of sediment washed in from the hills. The first struck about 20,400 years ago, near the depths of the last Ice Age, when wild monsoon downpours fell on thinly covered slopes.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Mega-floods over the past 30,000 years in western Yunnan, southwest China

title: The World's Biggest Kangaroo by the Creek
place: South Walker Creek, near Nebo, Queensland, Australia
text: Barada Barna Traditional Owners found fossil bones at South Walker Creek in tropical Queensland, leading to digs that revealed a lost world. Beside leaves, seeds and insects lay several kinds of crocodile, the giant lizard Varanus priscus, Diprotodon, a marsupial lion and the world's largest kangaroo. They survived until at least 40,000 years ago. Researchers link their loss to a drying climate, not a sudden human-caused wipeout.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Extinction of eastern Sahul megafauna coincides with sustained environmental deterioration

title: Rainforest Kangaroos That Stayed Close to Home
place: Mount Etna, near Rockhampton, Queensland, Australia
text: Around 300,000 years ago, Queensland's Mount Etna was rainforest roamed by Protemnodon, extinct kangaroos weighing roughly 50 to 170 kilograms. Animals that big usually need wide ranges, but strontium in most of their fossil teeth matched the local limestone, so they fed close to home. Scientists suggest these homebodies were poorly prepared when the climate dried and rainforest gave way after about 280,000 years ago.

source.name: PLOS One (PMC): Megafauna mobility: Assessing the foraging range of an extinct macropodid from central eastern Queensland, Australia

title: Ice Age Campers on a Giant Sand Island
place: Wallen Wallen Creek and Middle Canalpin Creek, Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island), Queensland, Australia
text: Community-led digs on Minjerribah, the world's second-largest sand island, pushed back human history on Australia's east coast. Charcoal and heavily retouched tools made from imported stone show people camped there from roughly 40,000 years ago, long before rising seas cut it off from the mainland. By about 30,000 years ago they were heat-treating silcrete to improve it, among the oldest such tools in Australia.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Early human occupation of Australia's eastern seaboard

title: Wallabies Far from Today's Homes
place: Boodie Cave, Barrow Island, Western Australia, Australia
text: Boodie Cave, now on an island 60 kilometres off the Pilbara coast, sheltered people from about 51,000 to 7,000 years ago. Measuring tiny foot bones from their meals, researchers identified a banded hare-wallaby from 13,000 to 10,000 years ago and a northern nail-tail wallaby from about 10,000 years ago. Today one survives only on Shark Bay islands and the other in wetter tropical woodland, far from Barrow Island.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Morphometric classification of kangaroo bones reveals paleoecological change in northwest Australia during the terminal Pleistocene

title: Manus Islanders Who Lived Off the Forest
place: Pamwak rockshelter, Manus Island, Papua New Guinea
text: People were sheltering at Pamwak on remote Manus Island by about 25,000 years ago, and a further metre of undated layers below hints at an earlier arrival. Human teeth from the site, the oldest about 11,800 years old, are the oldest human fossils yet found beyond mainland New Guinea and Aru. Chemical signals in their enamel show these seafarers' descendants relied mainly on the island's inland forests, not the reef.

source.name: Philosophical Transactions B (PMC): Fossils, fish and tropical forests: prehistoric human adaptations on the island frontiers of Oceania

title: Volcanic Glass Travels 350 Kilometres
place: Matenbek cave, southern New Ireland, Papua New Guinea
text: About 20,000 years ago, people in Matenbek, a cave in southern New Ireland, were flaking obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass. Chemical sourcing traced it to outcrops in West New Britain, 350 kilometres away in a straight line, across sea. It is the region's earliest evidence of obsidian on the move, and for the next 16,500 years the glass kept travelling to sites across New Britain and New Ireland.

source.name: Records of the Australian Museum: The nature of prehistoric obsidian importation to Anir (Summerhayes 2004)

source2.name: Records of the Australian Museum: From Misisil Cave to Eliva Hamlet (Pavlides 2004)

title: Deer Hunters Who Shared Palawan with Tigers
text: Re-excavating Pilanduk Cave on Palawan, a University of the Philippines-led team confirmed with new radiocarbon dates that people lived there 20,000 to 25,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age. They specialised in hunting deer and ate freshwater molluscs. Among nine kinds of vertebrates in the deposits are fossils of the tiger.

source.name: University of the Philippines OVPAA: New research confirms the Philippines' Last Glacial Maximum antiquity at 20,000 to 25,000 years ago

source2.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Tropical island adaptations in Southeast Asia during the Last Glacial Maximum: evidence from Palawan

title: No Savanna Highway After All
place: Sunda Shelf (now under the South China and Java seas), Southeast Asia
text: When Ice Age seas dropped about 120 metres, a vast lowland joined Java, Sumatra and Borneo to Asia. Many scholars pictured a grassy savanna corridor running through it. A 2023 review of 59 pollen and plant-chemistry records disagrees, proposing that montane forest spread downhill while seasonally dry forest replaced lowland rainforest. Early humans crossing the region found a varied, wooded mosaic rather than open plains.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Forest mosaics, not savanna corridors, dominated in Southeast Asia during the Last Glacial Maximum

title: Homo Erectus on the Seafloor
place: Madura Strait, between Java and Madura, East Java, Indonesia
text: Sand dredged from Indonesia's Madura Strait to build an artificial island held a drowned world. Working alone on his hands and knees from 2015 to 2018, geologist Harold Berghuis picked out 6,372 fossils, including two skull pieces of Homo erectus. They lived 131,000 to 146,000 years ago in a Solo River valley on dry land, cutting up turtles and cracking the bones of buffalo and other mammals for marrow.

source.name: Science News: A drowned landscape held clues to the lives of ancient human relatives

source2.name: Quaternary Environments and Humans: A late Middle Pleistocene lowstand valley of the Solo River on the Madura Strait seabed (Berghuis et al. 2025)

title: A Child's Grave Under Labrador Stones
place: L'Anse Amour, southern Labrador, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
text: About 7,700 years ago, Maritime Archaic people in southern Labrador laid a young person in a stone burial box, covered the body in red ochre and lit fires on either side. Then they heaped a careful mound of rocks over it. Inside lay spearheads, a walrus tusk, a bone whistle and the earliest known toggling harpoon in the world. It is North America's oldest known First Nations funerary monument.

source.name: Parks Canada: L'Anse Amour National Historic Site of Canada

title: Caribou Hunters Beneath Lake Huron
place: Alpena-Amberley Ridge, Lake Huron, southeast of Alpena, Michigan, USA
text: Nine thousand years ago, a dry ridge crossed what is now Lake Huron, linking Michigan to Ontario. Caribou walked it, and hunters waited. Today their stone drive lanes and hunting blinds lie deep underwater, first spotted when a line of rocks appeared on sonar in 2008. Researchers think small family groups hunted here in autumn, while larger groups worked together to steer herds through the lanes in spring.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Where the Ice Age Caribou Ranged

title: A Burial Pond Under the Gulf
place: Manasota Key Offshore site, near Venice, Florida, USA
text: About 7,000 years ago, people on Florida's Gulf Coast buried their dead in a marsh pond, probably wrapping the bodies in woven fiber and ringing them with sharpened wooden stakes. Rising seas later swallowed it. It now lies 21 feet underwater off Manasota Key, found after a diver picked up a human jaw in 2016. The Seminole Tribe of Florida is helping plan for the ancestors to rest undisturbed.

source.name: National Geographic: 7,000-Year-Old Native American Burial Site Found Underwater

title: Skin Boats Across Shelikof Strait
place: Amalik Bay, Shelikof Strait coast, Katmai National Park, Alaska, USA
text: More than 7,500 years ago, people of the Ocean Bay tradition paddled small skin boats across Alaska's stormy Shelikof Strait, the first known to reach Kodiak Island. They hunted seals, sea lions and sea otters, ground slate into bayonets, fished deep water with bone hooks on kelp lines, and burned blubber in stone lamps through the winter darkness. They were ancestors of today's Alutiiq people.

source.name: National Park Service, Katmai: The Ocean Bay Tradition

title: The Mountain That Fell on Llao
place: Crater Lake (Mount Mazama), Crater Lake National Park, Oregon, USA
text: About 7,700 years ago, Mount Mazama in Oregon erupted and collapsed, leaving the hole that became Crater Lake, today 1,943 feet deep. People saw it happen: archaeologists have found sandals buried under its ash. The Klamath Tribes, descendants of the Makalak people, tell of Llao, chief of the Below World, battling Skell, chief of the Above World, until the mountain fell in on Llao.

source.name: National Park Service, Crater Lake: History (park brochure)

source2.name: National Park Service: Traditional Knowledge of Prehistoric Eruptions

title: Copper Mines on a Lake Superior Island
place: Minong Ridge, Isle Royale National Park, Michigan, USA
text: By about 2500 BCE, Indigenous miners were crossing to Isle Royale in Lake Superior for something rare: nearly pure copper sitting in the bedrock. They pounded it loose with rounded beach cobbles, then cold-hammered it into knives, points and ornaments. More than 1,000 ancient pits survive, many along Minong Ridge, yet archaeologists have found almost no trace of where the miners themselves lived.

source.name: National Park Service: Archaeological History and Ancient Copper Mining on Isle Royale

title: A Salmon Village 7,000 Years Old
place: Namu, central coast, Heiltsuk Nation territory, British Columbia, Canada
text: At Namu, on British Columbia's central coast, people were living year-round by about 5000 BCE, in what is now the territory of the Heiltsuk Nation. Ancient DNA from fish bones shows they caught several kinds of salmon but relied most on pink salmon, storing it to last the year. Later, after 2000 BCE, failures in the pink salmon runs seem to have brought hard times.

source.name: American Antiquity (Cannon and Yang 2006): Early Storage and Sedentism on the Pacific Northwest Coast

title: What Ancient Toilets Say About Dinner
place: Hinds Cave, lower Pecos River canyonlands, Val Verde County, Texas, USA
text: In a dry rock shelter above the lower Pecos River, people camped on and off for more than 9,000 years, sleeping on grass-lined beds. They also used the back wall as a latrine. Hundreds of dried human feces survived there, some over 6,000 years old, and Texas A&M researchers studied them in the 1970s. The verdict on the diet: high fiber, low fat, and almost any animal they could catch.

source.name: Texas Beyond History (University of Texas at Austin): Hinds Cave

title: Carvings Made From Boats
place: Petroglyph Point, Lava Beds National Monument, Modoc County, California, USA
text: Petroglyph Point in northern California was once an island in Tule Lake, reachable only by boat. Its soft volcanic cliff, in the homeland of the Modoc people, holds over 5,000 carvings, mostly geometric patterns. Researchers think people carved them from boats whenever dry spells lowered the lake, including one between 4,500 and 2,600 years ago. Similar patterns appear on household items up to 5,000 years old from nearby Nightfire Island.

source.name: National Park Service, Lava Beds: Images in Stone

title: Moccasins With Dew Claws for Grip
place: Fremont River valley, Capitol Reef National Park, Utah, USA
text: By about 300 CE, people archaeologists call the Fremont were living in the canyons of what is now Capitol Reef, Utah. They farmed corn, beans and squash, gathered pinyon nuts and wove tight rod-and-bundle baskets. Their moccasins, cut from the leg hide of deer or bighorn sheep, kept the dew claws on the soles, possibly for grip. Oral traditions link them to the Hopi, Zuni and Paiute.

source.name: National Park Service, Capitol Reef: Fremont Culture

title: Where Two Rivers Met the Trade Routes
place: The Forks, junction of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada
text: Two old campfires on the Assiniboine River show people stopping where it meets the Red River by 4000 BCE. By 1000 BCE, groups were camping at this spot in today's Winnipeg for long stretches, fishing the rich waters and hunting deer, elk and bison. Archaeologists have found objects here that came from as far away as the Lake Superior region and northern Texas, signs of a vast trade network.

source.name: Parks Canada, The Forks National Historic Site: Land Use

title: It Is Pictured, It Is Written
place: Áísínai'pi (Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park), Milk River, Alberta, Canada
text: Along Alberta's Milk River, sandstone cliffs and hoodoos carry one of the largest concentrations of rock art on the Great Plains, in more than 200 panels. The Niitsítapi, or Blackfoot, call the place Áísínai'pi, "it is pictured, it is written." Its carvings and paintings record vision quests and life events from about 4000 BCE into the 20th century, messages tied to Spirit Beings who dwell in the hoodoos.

source.name: Parks Canada: Áísínai'pi National Historic Site of Canada

title: Racing the Storms at Coast Guard Beach
place: Carns site, Coast Guard Beach, Cape Cod National Seashore, Eastham, Massachusetts, USA
text: In November 1990, erosion at Coast Guard Beach on Cape Cod exposed an old buried ground surface. Archaeologists spent 16 months digging more than 300 square meters while severe storms kept scouring the site away. The finds dated mostly to between 2,100 and 1,100 years ago, a poorly understood stretch of Cape Cod's Woodland past. Over 200 boxes of soil samples were still waiting to be processed a decade later.

source.name: National Park Service, Cape Cod: The Carns Site

title: A Sacred Mound on the Miramichi
place: Augustine Mound, Metepenagiag (Red Bank), Miramichi River, New Brunswick, Canada
text: About 2,500 years ago, Mi'kmaw ancestors at Metepenagiag, on New Brunswick's Miramichi River, raised a low, circular burial mound. It follows the Adena burial tradition of the faraway Ohio Valley, and held textiles, basketry, ornaments of Lake Superior copper and Ohio clay pipes. Just 700 meters away lies Oxbow, a riverbank site used for 3,000 years. The mound remains a sacred place for the Metepenagiag Mi'kmaq Nation.

source.name: Parks Canada, Directory of Federal Heritage Designations: Augustine Mound National Historic Site of Canada

source2.name: Canada's Historic Places: Oxbow National Historic Site of Canada

title: Giant Pithouses Above the Fraser
place: Keatley Creek site, near Lillooet, British Columbia, Canada
text: On a terrace above the Fraser River near Lillooet stood one of the largest ancient villages in western Canada. About 115 house pits survive, and some semi-underground homes reached 25 meters across. Many big houses were lived in through the Plateau period, roughly 2,400 to 1,200 years ago, fed by salmon dried for winter. One large house held eight dog skulls in its storage pits, perhaps a sign of wealth.

source.name: BC Studies (Hayden and Spafford 1993): The Keatley Creek Site and Corporate Group Archaeology

title: Burial Mounds Inside a Modern City
place: Indian Mounds Park, Dayton's Bluff, St. Paul, Minnesota, USA
text: On a bluff above the Mississippi in St. Paul, six burial mounds survive, built between about 200 BCE and 400 CE. They are the only ancient Native American burial mounds still standing inside a major US city. Diggers in the 1800s found wood and stone burial chambers, copper, shell beads and about fifty people, including a small child's skull bearing a clay mask. Most finds were later burned or stolen.

source.name: MNopedia, Minnesota Historical Society: Indian Mounds Park, St. Paul

title: Copper and Galena for the Honored Dead
place: Oakville Indian Mounds, near Moulton, Lawrence County, Alabama, USA
text: In Alabama's Tennessee Valley, Middle Woodland people of about 1 to 500 CE buried some of their dead in caves and burial mounds, like those at Oakville near Moulton. Archaeologists call the tradition Copena, from COPper and galENA, a shiny lead ore found again and again in the graves. Copper earspools, ocean-shell cups and long stone points, some traded from far away, hint that certain people held special status.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama: Woodland Period

title: The Bow Reaches the Alberta Plains
text: About 2,000 years ago, a new weapon reached the plains of what is now Alberta: the bow and arrow, which seems to have developed first in the Arctic before spreading south. For thousands of years before, hunters there had used the atlatl, a weighted spear-thrower that hurled darts with deadly force. Yet the bow did not simply replace it. People kept using both, choosing whichever suited the local landscape.

source.name: Alberta's Energy Heritage (Government of Alberta): The Atlatl

title: A Cliff Quarried for Lamps and Pots
place: Fleur de Lys Soapstone Quarry, Baie Verte Peninsula, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
text: About 1,600 years ago, Dorset Paleo-Inuit people began quarrying a soapstone cliff at Fleur de Lys in northern Newfoundland, and kept at it for roughly 500 years. Soapstone is soft to carve and holds heat, ideal for oil lamps and cooking pots. Around a thousand scars remain where vessel blanks were cut out, matching the size of finished Dorset bowls. Waterlogged clay below even preserved wooden poles.

source.name: Canada's Historic Places: Fleur de Lys Soapstone Quarry

source2.name: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador: Field Report for the 1997 Fleur de Lys Archaeology Project

title: A Stone Stamp for Printing Falcons
place: Montgomery County, Bluegrass region, Kentucky, USA
text: Adena people of Kentucky's Bluegrass, living from about 500 BCE to 200 CE, carved palm-sized stone tablets. One engraved fragment, found at the base of a Montgomery County mound, shows a stylized falcon or hawk. Traces of pigment, red on one tablet, survive in some grooves, so archaeologists think they were printing blocks, perhaps inked with red ochre to stamp rows of birds onto leather or deerskin capes.

source.name: Kentucky Heritage Council and Kentucky Archaeological Survey: Adena, Woodland Period Moundbuilders of the Bluegrass

title: A Rock Face Carved for 1,500 Years
place: Newspaper Rock, Indian Creek, San Juan County, Utah, USA
text: On a sandstone face beside Indian Creek in southeastern Utah, people began pecking images through the dark desert varnish about 1,500 years ago, and kept adding more into the early 20th century, sometimes right over older ones. The oldest carvings are attributed to Basketmaker and Ancestral Puebloan people, while riders on horseback are thought to be Ute work. Look closely for bighorn sheep, bison and feet with six toes.

source.name: Bureau of Land Management: Newspaper Rock

source2.name: Bureau of Land Management: Newspaper Rock brochure

title: Salmon Nets and Labrets on Kodiak
text: About 4,000 years ago, people on Alaska's Kodiak Island began fishing more intensely than ever, launching what archaeologists call the Kachemak tradition. They developed nets for salmon, and slate knives called ulus and smokehouses to process big catches of cod and salmon for storage. As the population grew, labrets, decorative plugs worn in the face, came into fashion, perhaps showing who belonged to which group.

source.name: Alutiiq Museum: Our Stories

title: When People Joined the Bison on the Rock
place: Jeffers Petroglyphs, Red Rock Ridge, Cottonwood County, Minnesota, USA
text: On smooth quartzite outcrops in southwestern Minnesota, people pecked an estimated 8,000 images over about 11,000 years: bison, elk, turtles, atlatls and arrowheads. For thousands of years animals dominated, but around 3000 BCE human figures performing ceremonies began to appear beside them. The site lies in Dakota homeland and is sacred to the Cheyenne, Arapaho, Iowa and Ojibwe, whose elders say people came here to fast and seek guidance.

source.name: MNopedia, Minnesota Historical Society: Jeffers Petroglyphs

title: The Bison Jump That Set Itself Alight
place: Bonfire Shelter, near Langtry, Val Verde County, Texas, USA
text: About 2,600 years ago, a brief wet spell spread grassland into the dry canyons of the lower Pecos, and bison herds followed. Hunters stampeded them over a cliff near today's Langtry, Texas, and butchered them in the rock shelter below, where remains of an estimated 800 animals piled up. The leftover bones, meat and fat apparently caught fire on their own, giving Bonfire Shelter its name.

source.name: Handbook of Texas (Texas State Historical Association): Bonfire Shelter

title: The Stopping Place Between Two Coasts
place: Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site, Nova Scotia, Canada
text: By 3,000 to 4,000 years ago, Late Archaic people were camping around the lakes of Kejimkujik in the heart of Nova Scotia, and finds on the Mersey River suggest earlier visitors 6,000 years ago. Rich in caribou, moose and fish, the area became a regular stop on canoe routes linking the south and north coasts. Over 60 sites survive, and over millennia these peoples developed the culture of today's Mi'kmaq.

source.name: Parks Canada, Kejimkujik: Mi'kmaw History

title: A Mammoth Speared Near the Kara Sea
place: Sopochnaya Karga, Taymyr Peninsula, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
text: Marks on a mammoth skeleton from Siberia's far north suggest it was stabbed and butchered about 45,000 years ago. The tip of one tusk was damaged in a way that hints people chipped off ivory to make tools. It is by far the northernmost sign of humans in Eurasia from that time, though one sceptical archaeologist called the hunting evidence pretty marginal.

source.name: Phys.org: Bones of hunted mammoth show early human presence in Arctic

source2.name: Science: Early human presence in the Arctic, evidence from 45,000-year-old mammoth remains (Pitulko et al. 2016)

title: Whale DNA in a Saqqaq Rubbish Heap
place: Qajaa, Ilulissat Icefjord, Disko Bay, Greenland
text: Early Greenlanders of the Saqqaq culture left frozen rubbish heaps full of bones. When scientists read the ancient DNA in the soil, a giant appeared: bowhead whale, barely visible among the bones themselves. Did Saqqaq hunters kill these huge whales with lances and small harpoons, or scavenge stranded carcasses? Either way, whales mattered far more to them 4,000 years ago than anyone had guessed.

source.name: Nature Communications: DNA evidence of bowhead whale exploitation by Greenlandic Paleo-Inuit 4,000 years ago

title: Penguins Wiped Out by a Neighbouring Volcano
place: Ardley Lake, Ardley Island, South Shetland Islands, Antarctica
text: Penguin droppings pile up in Ardley Island's lake, so its mud records the colony since its founding about 6,700 years ago. At least three times the record suddenly goes quiet, right where ash from Deception Island's volcano, about 120 km away, lands in the layers. One of those eruptions struck around 4,300 years ago. Each time penguins needed roughly 400 to 800 years to fully come back.

source.name: Nature Communications: Past penguin colony responses to explosive volcanism on the Antarctic Peninsula

title: Moss That Woke After 1,500 Years
place: Signy Island, South Orkney Islands, Antarctica
text: Deep in an Antarctic moss bank, stems that last grew around 300 to 450 CE lay frozen in permafrost. In 2003 scientists drilled a 1.4-metre core, sliced it up and gave the pieces light and warmth in the lab. Within three to six weeks, green shoots sprouted even from the oldest layers. Before this, moss was only known to revive after about 400 years under a glacier.

source.name: National Geographic: Ancient Moss Brought Back to Life After 1,500 Years

title: Wintering on a Mountain to Catch the Aurora
place: Haldde (Halde) observatory, near Alta, Finnmark, Norway
text: To measure how high the northern lights shine, Kristian Birkeland built what the Alta Museum calls the world's first northern lights observatory on Mount Haldde in 1899. He spent the winter on the summit with two assistants. Gales struck every other day, stove smoke filled the hut, and instruments broke. One assistant died in an avalanche. The aurora, it turned out, never came anywhere near the summit.

source.name: Alta Museum: The Northern Lights, from mythology to science in Alta

source2.name: University of Oslo, Apollon: The king of northern lights

title: A Hunters' Lookout Above the Arctic Circle
place: Mesa site, north flank of the Brooks Range, North Slope, Alaska, USA
text: From the top of a rocky mesa in northern Alaska, about 200 feet above the tundra, Ice Age hunters had a 360-degree view for spotting bison and perhaps mammoths. They left stone spear points there. Archaeologists found the site in 1978 while surveying ahead of oil exploration. First dated to 7,600 years old, better radiocarbon methods later showed some artifacts were nearly 12,000 years old.

source.name: Bureau of Land Management: Mesa Site

title: Fossil Bird Spit Far Inland
place: Greenall Glacier, southern Prince Charles Mountains, East Antarctica
text: Snow petrels defend their nests by spitting stomach oil at intruders. In Antarctica's cold, dry air the oil turns waxy and builds up in layers called mumijo. At Greenall Glacier, 450 km inland, the oldest layer is about 3,680 years old, so the birds have nested there at least that long. These are the furthest-inland snow petrels known, and they arrived thousands of years after the ice retreated.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Program: Fossilised spit reveals 3600 years of snow petrel colonisation

title: A Farthest North That Stood 236 Years
place: Entrance to Smith Sound, northern Baffin Bay, between Greenland and Ellesmere Island
text: In 1616 the little ship Discovery, with Robert Bylot in command and William Baffin as pilot, sailed past every earlier record into the bay now named for Baffin. They reached 77°45′N, a farthest north for that sea that stood for 236 years, and named Smith, Jones and Lancaster sounds. Later mapmakers doubted them and erased the bay, until John Ross confirmed it in 1818.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Baffin, William

title: Hauling Away the Great Iron
place: Meteorite Island, near Savissivik, Cape York district, Northwest Greenland
text: For about a thousand years, Inuit of northwest Greenland chipped knives from three iron meteorites they called a woman, her dog and her tent, thrown from the sky. Robert Peary wanted them to sell to a museum. The biggest, 34 tons, defeated him in 1896. In 1897 he winched it onto the whaler Hope and took it to New York, naming it Ahnighito after his daughter.

source.name: National Geographic: Meteorite Hunters, Peary and the Cape York meteorite

title: The Glacier That Bleeds Salt Water
place: Blood Falls, Taylor Glacier, Taylor Valley, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
text: Griffith Taylor first saw Blood Falls in 1911: red water seeping from a white Antarctic glacier. In 2017, radar mapping showed the source is a salty brine, maybe trapped under Taylor Glacier for over a million years, flowing about 300 feet to the falls. Its iron turns red when it meets air. Salt keeps the water liquid, making Taylor the coldest known glacier with persistently flowing water.

source.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks: Researchers solve the century-old mystery of Blood Falls

title: A Tunnel Into an Ice Age Coast
place: Arne Qvamgrotta, Storsteinhola cave system, Kjøpsvik, Nordland, Norway
text: In 1991, tunnel builders in northern Norway broke into a cave holding 13 metres of sediment and bones. Recent work dated the main bone layer to roughly 85,000 to 71,000 years ago and identified 46 kinds of animals, from polar bear, walrus and bowhead whale to blue whale and reindeer. It also held the collared lemming, never before found in Scandinavia and now extinct there.

source.name: PNAS: A 75,000-y-old Scandinavian Arctic cave deposit reveals past faunal diversity and paleoenvironment

title: A Warm-Water Fish North of the Arctic Circle
place: Nygrotta, Storsteinhola cave system, Kjøpsvik, Nordland, Norway
text: A small cave above the Arctic Circle in Norway trapped bones over thousands of years. In a layer about 5,800 years old, when the region was warmer than today, ancient DNA picked up amberjack, a temperate fish genus, alongside forest birds like capercaillie and hazel grouse. Cold-water fish such as lumpfish had vanished from the record. Scientists compare it with amberjacks moving north into the English Channel today.

source.name: Science Advances: A unique Early Holocene cave deposit reveals postglacial faunal expansion into the Scandinavian Arctic

title: Elephant Seals on Antarctica's Cold Coast
place: Cape Hallett, Victoria Land, Ross Sea, Antarctica
text: Southern elephant seals breed on sub-Antarctic islands today, yet their remains turn up along the Ross Sea coast, far to the south. Scientists think a warm spell, roughly 2,300 to 1,100 radiocarbon years ago, thinned the sea ice and let colonies form there. At Cape Hallett, elephant seal DNA lies beneath what is now an Adélie penguin colony. Penguins expanded after this seal optimum ended.

source.name: PNAS: Holocene elephant seal distribution implies warmer-than-present climate in the Ross Sea

source2.name: Nature Communications: Sedimentary DNA insights into Holocene Adélie penguin populations and ecology in the Ross Sea

title: Glaciers Grew While Vikings Settled Greenland
place: Naqsaq valley, eastern Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: The 'Medieval Warm Period' was not warm everywhere. Boulders on moraines in Baffin Island's Naqsaq valley, dated by beryllium-10 that builds up in rock exposed to the sky, show glaciers pushing forward around 1040, 1070 and 1220 CE, near their Little Ice Age maximum. So while Norse farmers settled Greenland from about 985 CE, the lands around Baffin Bay stayed relatively cool.

source.name: Science Advances: Glacier maxima in Baffin Bay during the Medieval Warm Period coeval with Norse settlement

title: Seven Centuries of Beluga Hunting
place: Kitigaaryuit, East Channel, Mackenzie River Delta, Northwest Territories, Canada
text: Inuvialuit families settled the Mackenzie Delta around 1200 CE, and beluga whales fed them. At the Kuukpak site, belugas supplied about two-thirds of all meat and fat. In 1893, one hunt at Kitigaaryuit took about 155 belugas, nearly one for each of its 159 people. Yet ancient DNA shows 700 years of hunting barely dented the belugas' genetic diversity.

source.name: PNAS: Elucidating the sustainability of 700 y of Inuvialuit beluga whale hunting in the Mackenzie River Delta

title: Plants Unseen for 40,000 Years
place: Ice cap margins, eastern Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: As small ice caps on Baffin Island melt back, they uncover tundra plants still rooted where they grew. Scientists collected 48 of them at the edges of 30 ice caps and radiocarbon dated them: nearly all came out 40,000 to over 50,000 years old. Those spots had likely been buried continuously ever since. The team concluded that the past century's summers were likely the warmest in about 115,000 years.

source.name: Nature Communications: Rapidly receding Arctic Canada glaciers revealing landscapes continuously ice-covered for more than 40,000 years

title: The Fugitive Who Brought Back the Kayak
place: Inglefield Land, Avanersuaq (Thule region), Northwest Greenland
text: When John Ross met the Inughuit in 1818, they had no kayaks; the knowledge had died with its last makers. In the 1840s an Inuk named Qillarsuaq fled Baffin Island after a killing and led a group north, reaching Inglefield Land in the early 1860s. His people reintroduced the kayak, the umiak, bows and fishing leisters, rescuing a community feared to be dying out.

source.name: Ambio: Living in an oasis, rapid transformations in the North Water Area societies and ecosystems

title: The Inuit Brought Their Own Dogs
place: Chukchi Sea coasts, between Chukotka (Russia) and Alaska (USA)
text: When the ancestors of today's Inuit crossed from Siberia into North America about 2,000 years ago, they brought a specialised breed of sled dog. A study of 922 Arctic dog and wolf remains spanning 4,500 years found these Inuit dogs were genetically distinct from, and larger than, the earlier Palaeo-Inuit dogs. Their genetic legacy survives in modern Arctic sledge dogs, which probably helped the Inuit spread east.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Specialized sledge dogs accompanied Inuit dispersal across the North American Arctic

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Arctic (March/April 2020)

title: Fewer Whales, More Little Auks
place: Waters off western Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
text: Before industrial whaling began in 1610, perhaps 50,000 bowhead whales ranged from northern Iceland to Novaya Zemlya. Three centuries of hunting left perhaps a few dozen by 1910. That left more tiny zooplankton for the little auk, a 160-gram seabird that feeds on similar prey.
