A 2024 study's model estimated the auks increased by about 70 percent, from 2.8 to 4.8 million breeding pairs.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Food chain without giants, bowhead whaling and little auk populations

title: Parkas Sewn From Walrus Gut and Whale Sinew
text: In the 1300s, families in far northwest Greenland made some of the oldest gut-skin parkas found in the Arctic. Protein analysis of these 600-year-old garments shows threads of whale and walrus sinew, waterproof gut skins from seal and walrus, and furs from dog, Arctic fox and polar bear. In the pieces studied, sewers seem never to have mixed sea-animal and land-animal materials in one garment.

source.name: Scientific Reports: Paleoproteomic identification of the species used in fourteenth century gut-skin garments from Nuulliit

title: Where Caribou Cross the Kobuk River
place: Paatitaaq (Onion Portage), Kobuk Valley National Park, Alaska, USA
text: For more than 8,000 years, people have met at this bend of Alaska's Kobuk River to hunt caribou migrating through each fall. Iñupiat call it Paatitaaq, meaning 'onion', after the wild alliums growing along the river. Digging down through its layers, archaeologists found microblades, scrapers, tent remains and large oval buildings, probably men's ceremonial houses, scattered with tools of obsidian, chert, bone and antler.

source.name: National Park Service: Over 8,000 Years of Arctic History (Kobuk Valley)

source2.name: National Park Service: Paatitaaq-Onion Portage

title: The Winter 61,000 Reindeer Starved
place: Yamal Peninsula, Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, Russia
text: In the winter of 2013–14, about 61,000 reindeer starved to death on Russia's Yamal Peninsula, a disaster for the Yamal Nenets, who herd them for food. Unusual warm spells made snow melt and refreeze, or rain freeze on the ground, sealing the lichen reindeer eat under a sheet of ice. The animals can smell the plants beneath but cannot dig through, and wander until they starve.

source.name: The Conversation: Mass starvation of reindeer linked to climate change and habitat loss

title: Four Hydrogen Bombs on the Sea Ice
place: Wolstenholme Fjord, near Thule Air Base (Pituffik), Northwest Greenland
text: On 21 January 1968, someone aboard a US B-52 bomber stuffed seat cushions in front of a heating vent, and they caught fire. Six of the seven crew parachuted out before the plane hit the frozen Wolstenholme Fjord near Thule Air Base, carrying four hydrogen bombs. None exploded, but they broke open and contaminated the fjord, revealing nuclear flights over Greenland that Denmark's policy forbade.

source.name: The Conversation: 50 years ago, a US military jet crashed in Greenland with 4 nuclear bombs on board

title: What Medieval Polar Bears Were Eating
text: Polar bear bones from Dorset and Thule sites around Lancaster Sound, roughly 1,500 to 500 years old, hold a record of the Arctic food web. Their carbon isotopes show the same mix of sea-ice algae and open-water plankton at its base through the Medieval Warm Period and early Little Ice Age. Only bears hunted in 1998–2007 show a big shift away from sea-ice-based food.

source.name: The Conversation: How analyzing ancient and modern polar bear samples reveals the full scope of global warming

title: Four Rivers and a Magnetic Mountain
place: Central Arctic Ocean, as imagined on Mercator's map
text: Early European maps did not leave the Arctic blank. Martin Behaim's globe of 1492 showed four rivers flowing symmetrically from the North Pole, and Gerard Mercator repeated them on his world map of 1569 and his Arctic map of 1595. Some maps also put a vast magnetic mountain at the top of the world, possibly linked to compasses behaving strangely in the far north.

source.name: The Conversation (British Library curator): Magic mountains and sea serpents, the secrets of early Arctic maps

title: The Flood Behind Yu the Great?
text: Around 1920 BCE an earthquake shook the upper Yellow River. It wrecked the cave homes of Lajia, and a landslide dammed the river near Jishi Gorge. A lake filled for months, then the dam burst, releasing about nine months of river water in hours, rising 40 metres above the banks at Lajia. Some geologists link this flood to China's legend of Yu the Great, but the idea remains debated.

source.name: National Geographic: Evidence Found for China's Ancient Great Flood

source2.name: Eos: Evidence Found for China's Ancient Origin Story

title: A Pharaoh's Report of a Terrible Storm
text: At Thebes, archaeologists found a broken calcite block about 1.8 metres tall, carved for Pharaoh Ahmose around 1550 BCE. Its 40 lines describe rain, darkness and a sky "in storm without cessation", with bodies floating down the Nile like papyrus skiffs. Two University of Chicago scholars argue it records the far-off eruption of Thera, but this is debated: other researchers read it as a metaphor for invasion.

source.name: University of Chicago News: World's oldest weather report could revise Bronze Age chronology

source2.name: EurekAlert: Tempest Stela news release

title: Revolt and a Darkened Sun in Ashur
text: Assyrians named each year after an official. For the year of Bur-Sagalê, governor of Guzana, their eponym chronicle notes a rebellion in the inner city of Ashur and that "in the month of Simanu an eclipse of the sun took place." NASA's list of historic eclipses matches it to the total solar eclipse of 15 June 763 BCE. That date now anchors ancient Near Eastern chronology.

source.name: NASA Goddard: Eclipses in History

source2.name: Oracc (University of Pennsylvania): Assyrian Eponym Chronicle, State Archives of Assyria Studies 2

title: The Lava Flood Behind a Viking Poem
text: Around spring 939, the Eldgjá fissure split open in southern Iceland, only decades after settlers began arriving around 874. For at least a year and a half it poured out some 20 cubic kilometres of lava, enough to cover England ankle-deep, and sulphurous haze drifted over Europe. Researchers think the poem Völuspá, with its darkened skies and fire, remembers the eruption and helped nudge Iceland toward Christianity.

source.name: University of Cambridge: Volcanic eruption influenced Iceland's conversion to Christianity

title: The Rhino Dürer Never Saw
place: Royal court of Manuel I, Lisbon, Portugal
text: In 1515 an Indian rhinoceros named Genda reached Lisbon, a gift from Sultan Muzafar II of Gujarat to King Manuel I, the first rhino seen in Europe since Roman times. Manuel planned a fight with an elephant, but the elephant panicked and fled. Albrecht Dürer never saw Genda, yet his woodcut, with an extra horn and armour plates, stayed Europe's favourite rhino picture until the late 1700s.

source.name: Natural History Museum: The legacy of Dürer's rhinoceros

title: Burning the Harvest to Beat a Tsunami
text: When a tsunami from a magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck the Kii Peninsula on 5 November 1854, village leader Hamaguchi Goryō set fire to sheaves of freshly harvested rice in his field. Using the blaze as a landmark, he guided villagers to safety, and many lives were saved. He then built a breakwater 600 metres long and 5 metres high. Today 5 November is World Tsunami Awareness Day.

source.name: UN News: Feudal-era Japanese village leader stands as beacon for tsunami education

source2.name: Inamura-no-Hi no Yakata (Hirogawa Town): Hamaguchi Goryo

title: Moctezuma's Zoo, Revealed by Bones
place: Sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan, Mexico City, Mexico
text: Spanish accounts describe a royal animal house in Tenochtitlan, often called Moctezuma's zoo. A city map published in 1524 places it behind the sacred precinct, but no trace of it has been excavated under Mexico City. Instead, bones of 28 animals from eight Templo Mayor offerings, including golden and harpy eagles, jaguars, wolves and roseate spoonbills, show healed injuries and diseases they could not have survived in the wild.

source.name: INAH: Novedad editorial indaga sobre el cautiverio de animales en Tenochtitlan

title: Oracle Bones Fretting Over Heavy Rain
text: People of the late Shang dynasty kept asking their oracles about the weather, carving questions into bones and shells. Researchers counted rain questions in about 55,000 of these pieces. In one phase, worry about coming heavy rain jumped far above any other, matching storm layers left by stronger typhoons in Japan and Korea. One Shang character for disaster even looks like waves of water.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Typhoon-induced disasters in inland China around 3000 yr B.P.

title: A Dam Against Drought and Flash Floods
place: Siloam Pool, City of David, Jerusalem
text: Around 800 BCE, Jerusalem faced dry winters broken by sudden flash floods. Its rulers, probably King Jehoash or his successor Amaziah, answered with a huge dam across the end of the Tyropoeon Valley, at least 19 metres long and 11 metres high, creating the Siloam Pool to catch rain and spring water. Straw and twigs in the dam's mortar dated it to about 805 to 795 BCE.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Radiocarbon dating of Jerusalem's Siloam Dam links climate data and major waterworks

title: Red Skies Over Babylon, Again and Again
text: In autumn 145 BCE, Babylonian scribes noted that "a little redness was found repeatedly in the east and in the west", and the next summer they wrote almost the same words. Scientists searching Babylon's astronomical diaries judged these likely auroras, oddly filed among political news, perhaps as omens. An earlier red glow in the western sky, from 567 BCE, had been called the world's oldest aurora record.

source.name: Earth, Planets and Space (PMC): Earliest datable records of aurora-like phenomena in the astronomical diaries from Babylonia

title: Tomb Timbers Remember Han Rains
place: Huangwan tomb, Jingyuan County, Gansu, China
text: In Jingyuan County, Gansu, old pine timbers from a Han dynasty tomb lie weathering in the open, and some have even been used as a country road. Scientists sliced their growth rings year by year and matched them with living pines from the nearby Hasi Mountains. The rings show northern China stayed steadily humid from 270 to 77 BCE, with yearly rainfall 18 to 34 percent above today's.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Persistent humid climate favored the Qin and Western Han Dynasties in China around 2,200 y ago

title: Sand From a Forgotten Tsunami
place: Kachchh coast near Mandvi, Gujarat, India
text: Old reports describe an earthquake and sea wave in the Arabian Sea in 1008 CE, but where it struck stayed a puzzle that scientists called an enigma. In 2018 geologists found a likely trace in Gujarat: a sand sheet more than 250 kilometres long, reaching over 250 metres inland along the Kachchh coast. Its sand came from offshore, torn up and thrown ashore by a powerful wave.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Geological evidence for AD 1008 tsunami along the Kachchh coast, Western India

title: When Volcanoes Starved the Nile
place: Abu Qir, near ancient Canopus, Beheira, Egypt
text: In 245 BCE Ptolemy III had marched as far as Babylon when, a Roman historian wrote, troubles at home called him back. A papyrus names an Egyptian revolt. Researchers link such revolts to distant volcanic eruptions that weakened the monsoon rains feeding the Nile flood. In 238 BCE, priests in the Canopus Decree praised the king for importing grain at great expense after the river failed.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Volcanic suppression of Nile summer flooding triggers revolt and constrains interstate conflict in ancient Egypt

title: The Silk Road Kingdom That Drank Its Lake
place: Loulan ruins, Lop Nur region, Xinjiang, China
text: Loulan thrived on the Silk Road while Han soldier-farmers irrigated the Tarim Basin, and Lop Nur was a lake of 17,000 to 50,000 square kilometres. Lake mud shows it shrank while nearby lakes rose, so researchers blame water taken upstream for fields, an early Aral Sea-style disaster. Loulan even punished tree-felling in the 3rd century CE. By 645, the monk Xuanzang found its cities abandoned.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): The world's earliest Aral-Sea type disaster: the decline of the Loulan Kingdom

title: The Thousand-Year Flood of Saint Magdalene
text: Around Saint Mary Magdalene's day in late July 1342, the Main and the Rhine rose to levels expected perhaps once in 100 to 1,000 years, sweeping away bridges, mills and villages and killing thousands. A 2026 study found it was one of 16 major floods across Europe from 1341 to 1343. Towns responded with stone bridges, flood-proof walls and dykes, a turning point in European flood defence.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Cascading continental-scale floods across Europe in 1342-1343

title: The Teenager Who Hand-Pollinated Vanilla
text: Vanilla cuttings reached Réunion in the 1820s. Around 1841, Edmond Albius, an enslaved teenager born in 1829 and raised on Féréol Bellier-Beaumont's estate at Sainte-Suzanne, found a practical way to pollinate the flowers by hand, turning vanilla into a major crop across the region. A 2024 study argues the method itself may trace back to the Belgian naturalist Charles Morren, sparking fresh debate over credit.

source.name: Plants (PMC): A Historical Review of the Artificial Pollination of Vanilla planifolia

title: Cannons to Shake Rain From the Sky
place: Town of Singapore, Straits Settlements, Singapore
text: In 1877 an El Niño drought, a cause nobody then understood, hit Singapore, Penang and Malacca. Shallow wells gave little water, most of it bad, and one newspaper reported Malays "dying off like flies". Some even proposed firing the guns at Fort Canning to trigger rain. Singapore's Toa Payoh reservoir, finished in 1867 but too low to push water to town, finally began supplying water around late October.

source.name: Water History (PMC): Managing urban water scarcity in the late nineteenth-century Straits Settlements

title: Shakespeare's Birds Take Over America
place: Central Park, Manhattan, New York, USA
text: In 1890 the American Acclimatization Society released about 60 European starlings in New York's Central Park, part of a plan to fill the park with birds from Shakespeare's plays. Another 40 followed in 1891. From those roughly 100 birds, starlings spread across all of North America. Today more than 200 million live there, over a third of all the starlings in the world.

source.name: Ecology and Evolution (PMC): Contrasting mitochondrial diversity of European starlings across three invasive distributions

title: A Lake Records the Long Dry Spell
text: Horseshoe Lake lies within Greater Cahokia, the largest Mississippian settlement, whose main city held perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people around 1100 to 1200 CE. Chemical layers in the lakebed mud show that from 1200 to 1400 CE the region stayed persistently dry, with evaporation outpacing rain. This long drought set in during the lead-up to the great city's abandonment, supporting the idea that climate played a part.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Severe Little Ice Age drought in the midcontinental United States during the Mississippian abandonment of Cahokia

title: The Horse Tooth Mistaken for a Cow's
place: Puerto Real, near Limonade, Nord, Haiti
text: Horses vanished from the Americas at the end of the last Ice Age. They returned in 1493, when Andalusian horsemen sailed on Columbus's second voyage. At Puerto Real, a Spanish town in northern Haiti founded in 1503, a tooth first labelled as cow turned out to be a horse's molar. It gave the earliest complete mitochondrial genome of a post-Columbian horse, confirming Iberian roots.

source.name: PLoS One (PMC): Analysis of the earliest complete mtDNA genome of a Caribbean colonial horse from 16th-century Haiti

title: African Giants Growing in India
text: Baobabs are African trees, yet giants grow across India, some perhaps more than a thousand years old. Comparing their DNA with African trees, botanists found that Indian baobabs are closest to those of the Mombasa to Dar es Salaam coast, pointing to many arrivals over a long period. Chennai's baobabs instead resemble West African ones, probably planted through 18th and 19th century European colonial networks.

source.name: Royal Society Open Science (PMC): The history of introduction of the African baobab in the Indian subcontinent

title: The Blast That Caught Keōua's Army
place: Kaʻū Desert, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, Hawaii, USA
text: In 1790, warriors of the chief Keōua were marching around Kīlauea toward Kaʻū to fight Kamehameha when the summit exploded. Ash columns rose about 9 kilometres, and a hurricane-like blast of hot gas probably killed about a third of them. Footprints in the Kaʻū Desert ash were long credited to Keōua's warriors, but USGS scientists found that at least some prints are older than 1790.

source.name: USGS Volcano Watch: Not all eruptions as passive as this

source2.name: USGS Volcano Watch: At least some footprints in the Ka'u Desert are older than 1790

title: Dry Grasslands Open the Way West
place: East European Plain, near Kyiv, Ukraine
text: Tree rings show that from 1230 to 1238 the East European Plain suffered one of its driest spells in more than a thousand years. Failing harvests brought famine and war, thinning people, horses and livestock in lands such as Kyivan Rus. Then from 1237 to 1241 Batu Khan's Mongol armies swept in, and researchers argue the arid grasslands helped their cavalry move fast.

source.name: Fundamental Research (PMC): Drought facilitated the westward expansion of the Mongol Empire in the 1230s

title: Drought, Sheep and an Anatolian Revolt
text: After cold, dry spells in the 1580s, a major drought gripped Anatolia and the southern Balkans from 1591 to 1596, bringing failed harvests and famine. Rural flocks dwindled, yet the Ottoman state kept demanding sheep, and the countryside rose in the Celâlî Rebellion of 1596 to 1610. Climate models also show the eastern Mediterranean turning cooler and drier as the century closed, an Ottoman Little Ice Age crisis.

source.name: Human Ecology (PMC): Modelling Climate and Societal Resilience in the Eastern Mediterranean in the Last Millennium

title: Poppy Oil in the Mustard Jar
place: Suburbs of Calcutta (Kolkata), West Bengal, India
text: In 1877, possibly the strongest El Niño of the last 250 years brought drought and famine to southern India, and colonial responses helped double staple prices in Calcutta. That year Calcutta suffered the first recorded epidemic of dropsy, which later reached Mauritius. Its cause, confirmed only in the 1940s, was cooking oil mixed with oil from the weedy Mexican poppy, likely a way to stretch costly mustard oil.

source.name: Medical History (PMC): The first recorded outbreak of epidemic dropsy, 1877-80: Climate, empire, and colonial medical science

title: Thirty Floors Laid One on Another
place: Loc Giang, Duc Hoa, Long An, Vietnam
text: Beside the Vam Co Dong River, Neolithic villagers kept laying new floors of lime mortar, probably made by burning shells. Excavators counted more than 30 surfaces stacked on top of each other, probably kept clean by sweeping or mats, with worn patches replaced and spots of burning where hearths stood. They tempered the mortar with rice husk and sometimes broken pots. Quarrying has since almost destroyed the site.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Early settlement construction in Southeast Asia: lime mortar floor sequences at Loc Giang

title: A Village Wrapped in a Moat
place: Lovea, Puok District, Siem Reap, Cambodia
text: Long before Angkor's temples, villagers at Lovea lived on a mound wrapped in a circular bank and moat. Laser scans from an aircraft revealed ox-cart tracks fanning out from the village like spokes, and a bank kept at almost the same height even where the ground slopes. That suggests it was built to hold water. Graves inside date to roughly 130 to 345 CE.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Airborne LiDAR prospection at Lovea, an Iron Age moated settlement in central Cambodia

title: Indian Dishes on Bali's North Shore
text: Buried under about three metres of river sediment, the coastal villages of Pacung and Sembiran hold over 600 fine sherds of pottery made in India. Radiocarbon dates on the burials place this contact as early as the last centuries BCE. One sherd even carries Kharoshthi, a script of the far northwest of the Indian subcontinent, and a mung bean from India turned up just above the graves.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Sembiran and Pacung on the north coast of Bali

title: A Stone Mould for Bronze Drums
text: Bronze drums of the Dong Son culture of northern Vietnam were imported into Indonesia, and Balinese smiths soon cast their own. At Sembiran, archaeologists found a mould carved from volcanic tuff with patterns for a Pejeng-type drum, Bali's local style. A second mould, for a socketed axe, lay in the same layer. Lead isotopes from a bronze point suggest imported metal was melted down and recast locally.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Sembiran and Pacung on the north coast of Bali

title: Roman Glass in a Balinese Coffin
place: Pangkung Paruk, Seririt district, Buleleng, Bali, Indonesia
text: A stone sarcophagus at Pangkung Paruk, west of Sembiran on Bali's north coast, held about 40 beads with gold foil sealed in glass. Tests on two showed soda natron glass, the same kind as a red striped bead from Sembiran identified as Roman. Researchers call these finds the first evidence of Roman materials in a prehistoric context anywhere in Island Southeast Asia.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Sembiran and Pacung on the north coast of Bali

title: Humped Cattle Arrive From India
place: Khao Khuram, west coast of peninsular Thailand
text: Earlier DNA studies found only humpless taurine cattle in ancient Thailand. Then DNA from three cow bones at Khao Khuram, an early historic site on Thailand's west coast, turned out to be zebu, the humped cattle of India, about 1,700 to 1,500 years old. The same site has carnelian beads, a classic Indian trade good. Researchers think zebu came with traders, overland through Myanmar or by sea.

source.name: Animals (MDPI), via PMC: The First Ancient DNA Evidence of Zebu Husbandry in Thailand

title: A Gold Ring Signed in Brahmi
place: Don Yai Thong, Phetchaburi Province, Thailand
text: A burial at Don Yai Thong held a rare gold ring engraved in Brahmi, an Indian script, reading 'pusarakhitasa', meaning 'the one protected by Pushya', a sign in Indian astrology. Its owner may have been a merchant. The cemetery, about 1,500 to 2,000 years old, also gave up six bronze drums and skeletons with bronze vessels laid over their heads and chins.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Thailand (Sept/Oct 2026)

source2.name: Archaeology Magazine: Skeletons Uncovered at Thailand's Don Yai Thong Burial Site

title: A Pocket-Sized Sun on Wetar
place: Huknaur rock shelter, Wetar Island, Maluku, Indonesia
text: Ancient seafarers painted red suns and circles on cave walls across the western Pacific. At Huknaur rock shelter on Wetar Island, excavators found the same sun-ray design on something you could carry: a small stone plaque in a layer about 4,000 years old, some 500 years before the first Austronesian pottery there. It may have been a voyager's charm or badge of belonging.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Around the World, Indonesia (Nov/Dec 2026)

source2.name: The Conversation (ANU authors): 4,000-year-old rock painting in Indonesia offers clues to one of humanity's greatest migrations

title: A Fijian Family Tree in the Bones
text: Ancient DNA from 72 people in Vanuatu, Fiji and Tonga shows waves of newcomers arriving and mixing over the last 3,000 years. In one Fijian community about 1,500 years old, geneticists traced a family tree across five generations. One kin group stood out with its own ancestry, and the researchers think its customs may have helped keep wealth or status inside the family.

source.name: Phys.org (University of Tübingen): Early settlement dynamics in the Pacific revealed through ancient DNA

title: Knives Made From Tiger Shark Teeth
place: Leang Bulu' Sipong 1, Pangkep, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
text: Toalean foragers in southwest Sulawesi drilled holes through the roots of two-metre tiger sharks' teeth and bound them to handles with plant thread and a glue of mineral, plant and animal ingredients. Found at Leang Bulu' Sipong 1 and Leang Panninge, the 7,000-year-old teeth show wear from cutting flesh and bone. Tests showed they gash deeply but blunt fast, so perhaps they were ritual or fighting weapons.

source.name: The Conversation (Griffith University authors): 7,000-year-old shark-tooth knives discovered in Indonesia

title: Eighty Thousand Beads From the Rivers
place: Ban Non Wat, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: Bronze Age graves at Ban Non Wat held tiny shell discs by the tens of thousands: over 83,000 in one phase alone, many still stuck to skulls, perhaps from a shroud or head covering. Isotope tests show almost all came from freshwater shells, not the sea. With no bead workshop found at the village, they were probably imported, perhaps from several makers around the Khorat Plateau's wetlands.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Isotopic and provenance analysis of shell disc beads from Ban Non Wat

title: Burials in a Volcanic Cave
place: Krông Nô volcanic cave system, Đắk Nông, Vietnam
text: Vietnam's Central Highlands hold a system of volcanic caves. In one at Krông Nô, archaeologists found two adults and a child of about four, buried some 7,000 years ago and surrounded by the bones of ten more people. The red basalt soil rarely preserves bones, but the cave dwellers ate snails and mussels, whose calcium-rich shells changed the chemistry inside the cave.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Neolithic Human Remains Discovered in Central Vietnam

title: Hedgehog and Oysters in Puong Cave
place: Puong Cave, Ba Bể, Bắc Kạn, Vietnam
text: In the mountains of northern Vietnam, Puong Cave kept the leftovers of people of the Hoa Binh culture. They made tools from stones taken from streams and rivers, and ate pigs, monkeys, deer and even hedgehogs, along with oysters, snails and nuts. Trinh Nang Chung of the Vietnam Archaeology Institute estimated in 2019 that the site is about 9,000 years old.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Neolithic Artifacts Discovered in Northern Vietnam

title: Lying Down Instead of Curled Up
place: Nenggiri Valley, Gua Musang, Kelantan, Malaysia
text: In 13 limestone caves of Malaysia's Nenggiri Valley, archaeologists recovered 16 people. Fifteen were buried curled up, the oldest 14,000 to 16,000 years ago. One stood apart: a Neolithic person laid out flat about 6,000 years ago, with a stone bracelet, polished stone tools and pottery. A hydroelectric dam is expected to flood the caves in 2027.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Prehistoric Burials Unearthed in Malaysia

title: Necklaces Tapped Open the Old Way
place: Lene Hara and Jerimalai caves, Tutuala, Lautém, Timor-Leste
text: At the eastern tip of Timor, people strung tiny shiny Oliva shells into necklaces for roughly 38,000 years. Experiments showed they opened each shell by tapping its tip against a hard surface, a job of under a minute, and the same method appears on the oldest bead. Over half carry red ochre, and bead numbers jumped about 5,000 to 6,000 years ago.

source.name: PLOS ONE: An Enduring Shell Artefact Tradition from Timor-Leste (Langley and O'Connor 2016)

title: Crouching Stone Ancestors of Srobu
text: On New Guinea's north coast, graves cut into limestone at Mount Srobu and capped with shell mounds held ornately carved stone statues about 90 centimetres tall. The figures crouch, a pose like statues known from Polynesia. Lead researcher Erlin Novita links them to honoured ancestors, and to the crouched smoked mummies of Papuan chiefs still venerated today. The cemetery may be over 3,000 years old.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Honoring the Ancestors (Mar/Apr 2019)

title: Stone Mounds in Borneo's Highlands
text: Deep in Borneo's interior, the Kelabit Highlands hide stone mounds called perupun, up to about 30 metres wide and 3 metres high, linked to roughly 2,000 years ago. The Cultured Rainforest Project also found open-air Early Metal Age villages with stone walls and iron tools, 1,000 to 2,300 years old, plus rice and sago plots up to 2,300 years old.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: The Landscape of Memory (Letter From Borneo)

title: Fancy Pots on a Volcanic Plug
place: Navatu 17A, near Rakiraki, Viti Levu, Fiji
text: Around the middle of the first millennium CE, Fijians began building in places that were easier to defend. Navatu 17A sat on the flanks of a steep volcanic plug, while hilltop forts rose in the Sigatoka Valley. Navatu's lowest layers hold ornate double-spouted pots alongside turtle bone and cannibalised human remains, foods that archaeologists suspect were reserved for people of high status.

source.name: ANU Press (Terra Australis 31): Clark and Anderson, Colonisation and culture change in the early prehistory of Fiji

title: Climbing to the Hilltops of Lau
text: A few centuries after the first Lapita settlers, life in Fiji's Lau islands changed. Sites from about 2,500 to 2,100 years ago turn up in every part of the landscape, even the highest hilltops, and archaeologist Best read hilltops plus cannibalism as signs of stress and strife. On Lakeba, mud from Waitabu Swamp records burning and erosion that grew massively between about 1,900 and 1,750 years ago.

source.name: ANU Press (Terra Australis 31): Clark and Anderson, Colonisation and culture change in the early prehistory of Fiji

title: A Plateau Splits Fiji's Speech
place: Nadrau Plateau, central Viti Levu, Fiji
text: As people moved into the rugged interior of Viti Levu, roughly 1,500 to 2,000 years ago, the high Nadrau Plateau came between eastern and western communities. Their speech drifted apart. Today Fiji's Eastern dialect group covers most of the islands, including Vanua Levu and Lau, while the Western group is limited to western Viti Levu, the Yasawas and Vatulele.

source.name: ANU Press (Terra Australis 31): Clark and Anderson, Colonisation and culture change in the early prehistory of Fiji

dateLabel: Post-Lapita era, roughly first millennium CE
title: Big Clay Pans for Sea Salt?
text: After decorated Lapita pottery faded, Fijian potters on Viti Levu and the Yasawa Islands made something new: large clay pans with flat bases. Archaeologists think they may have been used to evaporate seawater into salt. In later centuries, salt was an important trade good passing from coastal villages to inland groups, and that exchange may have begun this early.

source.name: ANU Press (Terra Australis 31): Clark and Anderson, Colonisation and culture change in the early prehistory of Fiji

title: Dugong and Dolphin on Velanai
text: Northern Sri Lanka was long thought empty until herders arrived from India in the 5th century BCE. Then a shell midden on Velanai Island turned out to be about 6,000 years old. Hunter-gatherers there ate shellfish, sea bream, deer, wild boar, dugongs and dolphins, and used quartz and chert carried more than 48 kilometres from the mainland, about 5 kilometres of it across water.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Prehistoric Midden Excavated in Northern Sri Lanka

title: A Rhino Among the Cattle Herders
place: Molapalayam, Noyyal River valley, near Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India
text: At Molapalayam, a Neolithic site in Tamil Nadu, animal bones show a herding village raising cattle, sheep and goats, hunting deer and antelope, and eating small millets and pulses. Among bones of 28 kinds of animals were four from an Indian rhinoceros, about 3,600 years old. Today the species survives only in Assam and northeastern India, far from the south.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Rhino Bones Discovered at Tamil Nadu Neolithic Site

source2.name: ThePrint: Rhinos roamed Tamil Nadu 3,600 years ago

title: Graves Facing East in Kutch
text: A University of Kerala team dug more than 20 graves in Gujarat's Kutch region, used between about 3300 and 2600 BCE, early in the Indus story. Some were rectangular pits aligned east to west with the head at the eastern end. Mourners left pots, conch-shell bangles, terracotta and stone beads, grinding stones and animal remains. Some bones may have been moved from an older site.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Harappan Cemetery Excavated in India

source2.name: Dawn (via BBC): Discovery of massive Indus Valley burial site in Gujarat puzzles scientists

title: Cracking Ice Age Horse Bones
place: Arroyo Seco 2, near Tres Arroyos, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: About 14,000 years ago, people camped on a low knoll between a lake and a creek near today's Tres Arroyos, on Argentina's Pampas. They left quartzite tools carried from hills 110 km away, along with bones of giant ground sloths, toxodons and extinct horses. One horse leg bone shows two hammerstone blows from cracking it while fresh. Oddly, no spear points turn up in these early layers.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The Arroyo Seco 2 Site and Its Significance for the Peopling of the Americas

title: A Lord Buried With Whale-Tooth Earrings
place: El Caño Archaeological Park, Coclé, Panama
text: Around 1,200 years ago, a Coclé lord of about 30 was laid face down on top of a woman's body in a tomb at El Caño, Panama. As many as 31 other people may have been sacrificed to go with him. His grave goods included crocodile-shaped earrings, gold-covered sperm whale teeth, bone flutes, two bells and skirts made of dog teeth.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 1,200-Year-Old Lord's Tomb Unearthed in Panama

title: Four Children Rewrite Cameroon's Past
place: Shum Laka rock shelter, Grassfields, Northwest Region, Cameroon
text: About 8,000 years ago, two boys were buried together in Shum Laka rock shelter in Cameroon's Grassfields, the younger lying across the older one's legs. Two more children were buried there about 3,000 years ago. Each pair were close relatives, and DNA shows all four were most like West-Central African hunter-gatherers, not today's local people. The older boy carried an extremely rare, deep Y-chromosome line called A00.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ancient West African foragers in the context of African population history

title: Drowned Salt Kitchens of the Maya
place: Paynes Creek salt works, Punta Ycacos Lagoon, Toledo District, Belize
text: Between about 600 and 900 CE, Maya workers in Belize's Punta Ycacos Lagoon boiled brine in clay pots inside pole-and-thatch kitchens, making salt for inland cities. Rising seas later drowned more than 100 of these salt works, and mangrove peat preserved their wooden posts. Wear on their stone knives shows most were used to cut fish or meat, hinting that salted fish travelled inland too.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Salt and marine products in the Classic Maya economy from use-wear study of stone tools

title: Africa's Oldest Funeral Pyre
place: Hora 1 rock shelter, Mount Hora, Mzimba District, Malawi
text: About 9,500 years ago, hunter-gatherers at Hora 1 rock shelter in northern Malawi gathered at least 30 kg of deadwood and grass and cremated a small adult, probably a woman. It is Africa's earliest known intentional cremation. Cut marks show her body was first taken apart, and her skull is missing, perhaps kept for later rituals. Stone points lay among the burnt bones.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Earliest evidence for intentional cremation of human remains in Africa

title: Deer and Guinea Pig Above Bogotá
place: Tequendama rock shelter, Sabana de Bogotá, Cundinamarca, Colombia
text: About 13,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers began using Tequendama rock shelter, 2,570 m up on the Sabana de Bogotá in Colombia's Andes. Bones from its oldest layers come from white-tailed deer and guinea pigs. People kept returning for over 10,000 years. Chemical signatures in later skeletons show a diet built on C3 plants and animals, while at nearby Aguazuque maize shows up in bones around 4,400 years ago.

source.name: iScience (PMC): Human dietary diversity in the Colombian Andes at the terminal Pleistocene-late Holocene sites Tequendama and Aguazuque

title: Ancient Smelting Smoke Frozen in Andean Ice
place: Nevado Illimani, Cordillera Real, La Paz Department, Bolivia
text: Around 700 BCE, copper pollution starts showing up in the ice of Nevado Illimani, a 6,300-metre Bolivian peak. Scientists who drilled a 138.7 m ice core there linked it to early metalworkers such as the Chiripa culture around Lake Titicaca. Surprisingly, Inca and colonial-era copper levels were lower than these early peaks, and Andean copper smelting began about 1,200 years before widespread silver working.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Ice-core evidence of earliest extensive copper metallurgy in the Andes 2700 years ago

title: The Caribbean's Oldest Campsite
place: Banwari Trace, near Penal, Oropuche Lagoon, Trinidad and Tobago
text: About 7,900 years ago, people from the South American mainland were already camping at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, long counted as the oldest known archaeological site in the West Indies. Their shell midden holds bone points used as arrow tips and fish spears, fishhooks made from bevelled peccary teeth, and double-pointed bone hooks for fishing lines. A crouched skeleton found here in 1969 became known as Banwari Man.

source.name: University of the West Indies: Banwari Trace

source2.name: Latin American Antiquity: Geochronology and Paleoenvironmental Framework for the Oldest Archaeological Site (7800-7900 cal BP) in the West Indies, Banwari Trace, Trinidad

title: Snail-Shell Pendants From 1,500 km Away
place: Baño Nuevo 1 cave, Ñirehuao River valley, Aysén, Chile
text: Around 2,900 years ago, hunter-gatherers using Baño Nuevo cave in Chile's Aysén region wore pendants cut from the shell of a big land snail, Megalobulimus. The nearest place that snail lives is at least 1,500 km to the northeast. Wear marks suggest the pendants were tied or sewn onto something, not hung as necklaces. The cave, 100 km from the sea, also held beads made from keyhole limpet shells.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Long-distance transport of exotic shell personal adornments in Central West Patagonia: Baño Nuevo 1

title: A Spider Monkey Sent as a Gift?
place: Plaza of the Columns, Teotihuacan, State of Mexico, Mexico
text: Around 250 to 300 CE, a young female spider monkey was buried alive in the Plaza of the Columns at Teotihuacan, beside a golden eagle and rattlesnakes. Born somewhere humid, she spent at least two years captive in the dry central highlands, eating maize and chili. It is the earliest known captive primate in the Americas, and archaeologists think she was a diplomatic gift linked to Maya lords.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Earliest evidence of primate captivity and translocation supports gift diplomacy between Teotihuacan and the Maya

title: Axe-God Pendants and Fake Jade
place: Greater Nicoya region, Guanacaste, Costa Rica
text: By about 500 BCE, people in Costa Rica were carving 'axe-god' pendants from green stone, and by around 300 BCE jadeitite appears, probably brought from Guatemala's Motagua Valley. A study of 926 greenstone objects found jadeitite in about a quarter of Greater Nicoya's pieces, but many supposed jades are really green quartz, which looks almost identical. A raw jadeitite block from Las Huacas shows some was carved locally.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Greenstone artifacts in pre-Columbian Costa Rica: from raw material to local and interregional exchanges

title: Amazon Macaws Carried Over the Andes
place: Uhle Cemetery, Pachacamac, Lurín Valley, Lima, Peru
text: Sometime between about 1000 and 1400 CE, the Ychsma people buried feather-decorated bundles in a tomb at Pachacamac, on Peru's dry central coast. DNA shows the feathers came from Amazonian scarlet, red-and-green and blue-and-yellow macaws and mealy parrots. The birds' high genetic diversity suggests they were caught wild, carried alive across the Andes, then probably fed maize on the coast for a while.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient DNA and spatial modeling reveal a pre-Inca trans-Andean parrot trade

title: A Painting of the Fever Year
text: In 1871, yellow fever killed about 14,000 people in Buenos Aires, a city of roughly 180,000. That same year Uruguayan painter Juan Manuel Blanes captured the tragedy on a canvas over two metres tall: a dead mother on a stone floor, her orphaned child beside her. In the background stand lawyer José Roque Pérez and Dr Manuel Argerich, volunteers who later died from helping the sick.

source.name: Emerging Infectious Diseases (PMC): Yellow Fever in Buenos Aires

title: The Student Who Infected Himself
place: Dos de Mayo Hospital, Lima, Peru
text: On 27 August 1885, in a Lima hospital, Peruvian medical student Daniel Carrión cut his arm and rubbed in blood from a verruga, the wart-like skin lesion of a mysterious Andean disease. He wanted to record its early symptoms. When he grew too weak to keep his diary, classmates carried on. He died on 5 October, having shown that verruga and Oroya fever were one disease, now named after him.

source.name: Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC), June 2010: Photo Quiz on Daniel Carrión

source2.name: Revista Peruana de Medicina Experimental y Salud Pública (PMC): Chilean physicians and the study of Peruvian wart, a critical review

title: Stone Toolmakers on a Mozambique Hilltop
place: Chessungalane, near the Save River, Inhambane Province, Mozambique
text: About 23,000 years ago, Stone Age people began working stone on a flat-topped hill 12 km north of the Save River in Mozambique. They returned on and off until about 7,000 years ago, flaking quartz from the hill's gravels into simple tools and, in the last phase, using scarcer chert to make tiny bladelets. Found in 2023, Chessungalane is the first Stone Age site in Mozambique studied in such detail.

source.name: African Archaeological Review (PMC): Lithic Techno-economics and OSL Chronology of the Later Stone Age at Chessungalane, Save River Valley, Mozambique

title: Nine Thousand Years, Same Ancestors
place: Oakhurst rock shelter, near George, Western Cape, South Africa
text: About 10,000 years ago, a person buried in Oakhurst rock shelter near George, South Africa, left the oldest human DNA yet recovered from the country. Genomes from people buried there over the next 9,000 years show the same local hunter-gatherer ancestry, even as stone-tool styles changed. Across southern Africa, herder and farmer ancestry from farther north only reshaped the gene pool after about 1,300 years ago.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): 9,000 years of genetic continuity in southernmost Africa demonstrated at Oakhurst rockshelter

title: Stone Toolmakers Deep in a Gabon Cave
place: Pahon Cave, near Lastoursville, Ogooué-Lolo, Gabon
text: Between about 7,500 and 2,500 years ago, people repeatedly came 50 m inside Pahon Cave, in the dense rainforest of central Gabon. They knapped chert and quartz into small tools and left remains of giant African snails, freshwater crabs, porcupines, bushpigs and duikers. Bats, including fruit bats, make up most of the identified bones. A broken polished axe or adze turned up too.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Pahon Cave, Gabon: New insights into the Later Stone Age in the African rainforest

title: Cowpeas, Cattle and a Painted Wall
place: Kakapel rock shelter, Chelelemuk Hills, Busia County, Kenya
text: About 2,300 years ago, Early Iron Age people at Kakapel rock shelter, at the foot of Mount Elgon in western Kenya, left behind cowpeas, along with a cattle bone of about the same age. Hunter-gatherers making Kansyore pottery had used the shelter for thousands of years before. Its rock-art panel, painted in red and white over different periods, shows people, antelopes, buffalo, an elephant hunt and spirals.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Cultural, economic, and settlement shifts over the last 9,000 years at Kakapel Rockshelter, Western Kenya

title: A Cemetery Where the Rich Lay Apart
place: Jebel Moya, near Sennar, southern Gezira, Sudan
text: Between about the 1st century BCE and 500 CE, herding people on the southern edge of the Meroitic world buried most of the more than 3,000 people later dug up at Jebel Moya in Sudan. The only animals placed in their graves were cattle and dogs. The 27 richest burials cluster together, with fewer poor graves than expected within about 20 m, hinting at a rule that kept them apart.

source.name: Journal of World Prehistory (PMC): Interactions and Pastoralism Along the Southern and Southeastern Frontiers of the Meroitic State, Sudan

title: Phoenician Towns With Few Phoenicians
text: Ancient DNA from Punic-era people buried at Carthage and nearby Kerkouane, in today's Tunisia, holds a surprise. None showed significant ancestry from the Phoenician homeland in the Levant. Most descended mainly from people like those of Sicily and the Aegean, many with some North African ancestry too. One Kerkouane person was a second or third cousin of someone buried at Birgi, across the sea in Sicily.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The genetic diversity of Punic people

title: The World's Largest Earthen Enclosure
place: Sungbo's Eredo, around Ijebu-Ode, Ogun State, Nigeria
text: Around the old Ijebu kingdom of southwest Nigeria, which arose in the late 1300s, runs Sungbo's Eredo: an estimated 170 km of ditches and earth banks, considered the largest earthen enclosure in the world. No one knows exactly when it was dug. Tradition says a wealthy woman named Sungbo paid for the work. Airborne laser scans of 1,000 square kilometres show it is even bigger than earlier surveys predicted.

source.name: William & Mary News: LiDAR project maps world's largest earthen enclosure

title: Indian Beads at a Nubian Shrine
place: Banganarti, near Old Dongola, Northern State, Sudan
text: Between the 800s and 1300s, Christian pilgrims came to Banganarti, a shrine of Nubia's Makuria kingdom in today's Sudan. Carnelian beads found there reveal long trade routes: chemical tests match about half to Indian sources, and others to places such as Yemen and Egypt. All were bored with diamond-tipped drills, a technique that began in ancient India. Later beads from nearby Old Dongola show the same pattern.

source.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (PMC): Carnelian ornaments from medieval upper Nubia

title: Three Steamers Struck Down by Fever
place: Confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers, Lokoja, Kogi State, Nigeria
text: In August 1841, three British steamers, the Albert, Wilberforce and Soudan, entered the Niger. Within weeks fever broke out, and as it spread they set up a model farm on Stirling Hill, where the Niger meets the Tchadda (Benue). Of 145 white crew, nearly 130 fell ill and 40 died, while only 11 of 158 Black crew got sick and none died. The Albert's surgeon ended up working the ship.

source.name: Medico-Chirurgical Review, 1843 (PMC): Medical History of the Expedition to the Niger, during the Years 1841-2

title: When Ostrich Plumes Were Gold
text: From around 1880, Jewish traders, mainly from Lithuania, settled in Oudtshoorn, South Africa, and helped build world markets for ostrich feathers. Max Rose, the 'ostrich feather king', arrived in 1890. In 1913 South Africa's industry peaked, with more than 775,000 birds producing a million pounds in weight of plumes for export. Then fashionable feathered hats fell out of favour, and the market crashed around World War I.

title: A Swahili Fever Name Crosses Oceans
text: In 1870, a disabling fever with painful joints swept Zanzibar, where people called it 'kidinga pepo', pronounced something like 'denga'. James Christie, a Scottish-trained doctor serving the Sultan, argued that an 1823 East African outbreak had spread to India and the West Indies, and that both the disease and its name reached the Caribbean from Africa. Researchers today think his 1871 outbreak was chikungunya.
